title: Definition:Angle of Contingence
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be two points on a plane curve. 400px The angle of contingence $A$ and $B$ is defined as the angle between the positive directions of the tangents to the curve at $A$ and $B$.

title: Definition:Angle of Depression
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be points in space such that $A$ is lower than $B$. The angle of depression of $A$ from $B$ is the angle between the line $AB$ and the horizontal.

title: Definition:Angle of Depression/Also known as
snippet: == Angle of Depression: Also known as == An angle of depression is also known as a declination. However, as that term has a more specialised meaning in the context of spherical astronomy, its use in this context is deprecated.

title: Definition:Angle of Elevation
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be points in space such that $A$ is higher than $B$. The angle of elevation of $A$ from $B$ is the angle between the line $AB$ and the horizontal.

title: Definition:Angle of Elevation/Also known as
snippet: == Angle of Elevation: Also known as == The angle of elevation of a point can also be seen referred to as its elevation. However, the term elevation is ambiguous, so it not endorsed in this context on .

title: Definition:Angle of Friction
snippet: Let $B$ be a body at rest on a plane surface $S$ on which friction acts. Let $\mu_s$ denote the coefficient of static friction between $B$ and $S$. The angle of friction is the angle $\lambda$ defined as: $\tan \lambda = \mu_s$

title: Definition:Angle of Intersection of Circles
snippet: Let $\CC$ and $\CC'$ be circles whose centers are at $C$ and $C'$ respectively. Let $\CC$ and $\CC'$ intersect at $A$ and $B$. The angle of intersection of $\CC$ and $\CC'$ is the angle between the tangents at the point of intersection. 540px Of the two angles formed by the tangents, the angle taken is between: the half-line of one tangent that passes completely outside both circles and: the half-line of the other tangent that passes through the interior of one circle.

title: Definition:Angle of Sector/Also known as
snippet: == Angle of Sector: Also known as == The angle of a sector of a circle is also seen referred to as a central angle.

title: Definition:Angstrom/Also denoted as
snippet: == Angstrom: Also denoted as == Some sources use a bodface $\mathbf A$ to denote the angstrom. This possibly arises from the difficulty of rendering $\mathring {\mathrm A}$.

title: Definition:Angstrom/Also known as
snippet: == Angstrom: Also known as == The angstrom is often seen in older sources presented as angstrom unit.

title: Definition:Angstrom/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Angstrom: Conversion Factors == {{eqn | r = 10^{-1} | c = nanometres }} {{eqn | r = 10^{-4} | c = micrometres }} {{eqn | r = 10^{-7} | c = millimetres }} {{eqn | r = 10^{-8} | c = centimetres }} {{eqn | r = 10^{-10} | c = metres }}

title: Definition:Angstrom/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Angstrom Unit == The angstrom was formally used for measurements of wavelengths and intramolecular distances, but has been superseded by the nanometre ($10^{-9} \, \mathrm m$)

title: Definition:Angstrom/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Angstrom == The word angstrom is derived from a Swedish name, and properly has diacritics: ångström. However, this "correct" presentation is tedious to implement and a nuisance to maintain, so prefers the simple version angstrom. Its symbol, however, does need the small circle above the A in order to be accurate and unambiguous. This, unfortunately, is not straightforward to render in $\LaTeX$ without including further expansion sets. Hence the $\LaTeX$ form as $\mathring {\mathrm A}$ (not a strictly accurate rendition) is how it is presented on .

title: Definition:Angstrom/Symbol
snippet: == Angstrom: Symbol == The symbol for the angstrom is $\mathring {\mathrm A}$.

title: Definition:Angular Acceleration
snippet: Angular acceleration is the rate of increase of angular velocity with time.

title: Definition:Angular Coordinate/Also known as
snippet: == Angular Coordinate: Also known as == The angular coordinate in a system of polar coordinates is also known as the polar angle, or azimuth. Other words that can be seen to mean the same thing are: amplitude anomaly argument vectorial angle inclination. Beware the term azimuth, as it is used in astronomy in a similar but significantly different way, to mean the angle measured from the principal vertical circle.

title: Definition:Angular Distance
snippet: The angular distance between two points $A$ and $B$ a reference point $P$ is the angle between the straight lines $AP$ and $BP$, that is: $\angle APB$

title: Definition:Angular Frequency
snippet: Let $f$ be a physical process that can be modelled by a periodic function whose nature is that of a sinusoid. The angular frequency of $f$ is a measure of the rate of oscillation of $f$ equal to $2 \pi \nu$, where $\nu$ is the frequency of $f$.

title: Definition:Angular Frequency/Also known as
snippet: == Angular Frequency: Also known as == Angular frequency is also known as pulsatance.

title: Definition:Angular Frequency/Dimension
snippet: Angular frequency has dimension $\mathsf T^{-1}$. Category:Definitions/Angular Frequency Category:Definitions/Dimensions of Measurement

title: Definition:Angular Frequency/Symbol
snippet: == Angular Frequency: Symbol == The usual symbol used to denote angular frequency is $\omega$.

title: Definition:Angular Frequency/Unit
snippet: The unit of measurement of angular frequency is the radian per second.

title: Definition:Angular Measure
snippet: The usual units of measurement for angle are as follows:

title: Definition:Angular Measure/Degree
snippet: The degree (of angle) is a measurement of plane angles, symbolized by $\degrees$. {{eqn | r = \dfrac 1 {360} | c = full angle (by definition) }}

title: Definition:Angular Measure/Minute
snippet: The minute (of angle) is a measurement of plane angles. {{eqn | r = \dfrac 1 {60} | c = degree of angle (by definition) }}

title: Definition:Angular Measure/Radian
snippet: The radian is the SI unit of plane angle. It can be symbolized either by the word $\radians$ or without any unit. Radians are pure numbers, as they are ratios of lengths. The addition of $\radians$ is merely for clarification. $1 \radians$ is the angle subtended at the center of a circle by an arc whose length is equal to the radius: 360px

title: Definition:Angular Measure/Second
snippet: The second (of angle) is a measurement of plane angles. {{eqn | r = \dfrac 1 {60} | c = minute of angle (by definition) }} {{eqn | r = \dfrac 1 {60 \times 60} = \dfrac 1 {3600} | c = degree of angle }}

title: Definition:Angular Momentum/Aggregation of Particles
snippet: Let $\PP = \set {P_i: i \in I}$ be an aggregation of particles, indexed by $I$, all in motion relative to a point $O$. For all $i \in I$, let: the mass of particle $P_i$ be $m_i$ the velocity of particle $P_i$ relative to $O$ be $\mathbf v_i$. The angular momentum of $\PP$ relative to (or about) $O$ is defined as the sum of the angular momenta of each of the particles in $\PP$: $\ds \mathbf L = \sum_{i \mathop \in I} \mathbf r_i \times \mathbf p_i = m \paren {\mathbf r_i \times \mathbf v_i}$ where: $\mathbf p_i$ denotes the (linear) momentum of particle $P_i$ for $i \in I$ $\mathbf r_i$…

title: Definition:Angular Momentum/Also known as
snippet: == Angular Momentum: Also known as == Angular momentum is also (rarely) known as moment of momentum or rotational momentum.

title: Definition:Angular Momentum/Dimension
snippet: The dimension of measurement of angular momentum is $\mathsf {M L}^2 \mathsf T^{-1}$. Category:Definitions/Dimensions of Measurement Category:Definitions/Angular Momentum

title: Definition:Angular Momentum/Particle
snippet: Let $P$ be a particle of mass $m$ moving with velocity $\mathbf v$ relative to a point $O$. The angular momentum of $P$ relative to (or about) $O$ is defined as: $\mathbf L = \mathbf r \times \mathbf p = m \paren {\mathbf r \times \mathbf v}$ where: $\mathbf p$ denotes the (linear) momentum of $P$ $\mathbf r$ denotes the position vector of $P$ $O$ $\times$ denotes the vector cross product.

title: Definition:Angular Momentum/Rigid Body
snippet: The angular momentum of a rigid body about a point $O$ is the vector cross product of its moment of inertia $\mathbf I$ about $O$ by its angular velocity $\omega$ about $O$: $\mathbf L = \mathbf I \times \omega$

title: Definition:Angular Momentum/Symbol
snippet: == Angular Momentum: Symbol == The usual symbol used to denote the angular momentum of a body is $\mathbf L$.

title: Definition:Angular Momentum of Particle/Also presented as
snippet: Some sources present the definition of the angular momentum of a particle $P$ relative to a point $A$ as: $\mathbf L = \paren {\mathbf r - \mathbf r_A} \times m \mathbf v$ where: $m$ denotes the mass of $P$ $\mathbf v$ velocity of $P$ relative to the frame of reference in which the motion of $P$ is defined $\mathbf r$ denotes the position vector of $P$ $\mathbf r_A$ denotes the position vector of $A$ $\times$ denotes the vector cross product.

title: Definition:Angular Speed
snippet: Angular speed is defined as the magnitude of angular velocity.

title: Definition:Angular Velocity
snippet: Let $P$ be a particle moving in the plane. Let $O$ be a distinguished point in the plane. Let $\map {\mathbf r} t$ be the position vector of $P$ $O$ as a function of time. Let $\map {\mathbf v} t$ be the velocity of $P$ $O$ as a function of time. 600px The vector $\bsomega = \dfrac {\mathbf r \times \mathbf v} {\size {\mathbf r}^2}$ is known as the angular velocity of $P$ $O$.

title: Definition:Angular Velocity/Dimension
snippet: Angular velocity has dimension $\mathsf T^{-1}$. Category:Definitions/Angular Velocity Category:Definitions/Dimensions of Measurement

title: Definition:Angular Velocity/Symbol
snippet: == Angular Velocity: Symbol == The usual symbol used to denote angular velocity is $\bsomega$.

title: Definition:Angular Velocity/Unit
snippet: The unit of measurement of angular velocity is the radian per second. Category:Definitions/Angular Velocity Category:Definitions/Units of Measurement

title: Definition:Anharmonic
snippet: The behaviour of a real function is defined as anharmonic if it is periodic but not harmonic.

title: Definition:Annihilator
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring. Let $M$ and $N$ be modules over $R$. Let $B : M \times N \to R$ be a bilinear mapping. The annihilator of $D \subseteq M$ is the set defined and denoted as: $\map {\operatorname {Ann}_N} D := \set {n \in N : \forall d \in D: \map B {d, n} = 0}$

title: Definition:Annihilator/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Annihilator == The word annihilator calls to mind a force of destruction which removes something from existence. In fact, the word is a compound construct based on the Latin nihil, which means nothing. Thus annihilator can be seen to mean, literally, an entity which causes (something) to become nothing. The pronunciation of annihilator is something like an-nile-a-tor. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Annihilator/Special Cases
snippet: == Special Cases of Annihilators == Various special cases of annihilators can be found in the literature, including:

title: Definition:Annihilator of Ideal of Ring
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $I \subseteq A$ be an ideal.

title: Definition:Annihilator of Ideal of Ring/Definition 1
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $I \subseteq A$ be an ideal. The annihilator of $I$ is the ideal consisting of the elements $a \in A$ such that: $\forall x \in I: a \cdot x = 0$ where $0 \in A$ is its zero.

title: Definition:Annihilator of Ideal of Ring/Definition 2
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $I \subseteq A$ be an ideal. The annihilator of $I$ is the ideal quotient: $\ideal {0 : I}$ where $0$ is the zero ideal.

title: Definition:Annihilator of Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \times}$ be a ring or, more usually, a field. Let $B: R \times \Z$ be a bilinear mapping defined as: $B: R \times \Z: \tuple {r, n} \mapsto n \cdot r$ where $n \cdot r$ defined as an integral multiple of $r$: $n \cdot r = r + r + \cdots \paren n \cdots r$ Note the change of order of $r$ and $n$: $\map B {r, n} = n \cdot r$ Let $D \subseteq R$ be a subring of $R$.

title: Definition:Annihilator of Subspace of Banach Space
snippet: Let $X$ be a Banach space. Let $M$ be a vector subspace of $X$. Let $X^\ast$ be the normed dual space of $X$. The annihilator is defined and denoted: $M^\bot = \set {g \in X^\ast : \map g x = 0 \text { for all } x \in M}$

title: Definition:Annihilator of Subspace of Normed Dual Space
snippet: Let $X$ be a Banach space. Let $X^\ast$ be the normed dual space of $X$. Let $N$ be a vector subspace of $X^\ast$. The annihilator of $N$ is defined and denoted: ${}^\bot N = \set {x \in X : \map g x = 0 \text { for all } g \in N}$

title: Definition:Annihilator on Algebraic Dual
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $G$ be a module over $R$. Let $G^*$ be the algebraic dual of $G$. Let $M$ be a submodule of $G$. The annihilator of $M$ is denoted and defined as: $M^\circ := \set {t \in G^*: \forall x \in M: \map t x = 0}$

title: Definition:Annualized Percentage Rate
snippet: The annualized percentage rate is the true cost of borrowing money from a lender.

title: Definition:Annualized Percentage Rate/Also known as
snippet: == Annualized Percentage Rate: Also known as == Annualized percentage rate is also known by its abbreviation APR.

title: Definition:Annualized Percentage Rate/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Annualized Percentage Rate == The annualized percentage rate was introduced as a concept in $1977$ in the UK in order to provide customers of financial services a reliable basis for comparison of the products of the various lenders. Before its introduction, it was commonplace for lenders to present their products in ways which made them look misleadingly good.

title: Definition:Annuity Amount/Also known as
snippet: == Annuity Amount: Also known as == An annuity amount is also known as an accumulated value.

title: Definition:Annuity Amount/Symbol
snippet: == Annuity Amount: Symbol == The symbol for an annuity amount accumulated over $n$ conversion periods is $S_n$.

title: Definition:Annulus
snippet: Geometry: Annulus: the region between two concentric circles Topology: Annulus: a topological space which is homeomorphic with an annulus in the context of geometry Abstract Algebra: Annulus: another word for a ring

title: Definition:Annulus/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Annulus == The word annulus (pronounced an-nu-lus) is Latin for little ring. Its plural form is annuli (pronounced an-nu-lee). Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Annulus (Geometry)
snippet: An annulus is a plane figure whose boundary consists of $2$ concentric circles: 400px In the above diagram, the annulus is the colored area.

title: Definition:Annulus (Geometry)/Also known as
snippet: == Annulus: Also known as == The more contemporary word ring can sometimes be seen for annulus. However, as the term ring is ubiquitous in the field of abstract algebra to refer to an algebraic structure of a particular type, it is the policy of to use the term annulus instead, so as to reduce the possibility of confusion.

title: Definition:Annulus (Geometry)/Center
snippet: 400px The center of an annulus is the common center of the $2$ concentric circles that form its boundary. In the above diagram, the center is the point $O$. Category:Definitions/Annuli

title: Definition:Annulus (Geometry)/Inner Radius
snippet: 400px The inner radius of an annulus is the radius of the smaller of the $2$ concentric circles that form its boundary. In the above diagram, the inner radius is denoted $r$.

title: Definition:Annulus (Geometry)/Outer Radius
snippet: 400px The outer radius of an annulus is the radius of the larger of the $2$ concentric circles that form its boundary. In the above diagram, the outer radius is denoted $R$.

title: Definition:Annulus (Geometry)/Width
snippet: 400px The width of an annulus is the difference between its outer radius and the inner radius In the above diagram, the width of the annulus is $R - r$.

title: Definition:Annulus (Topology)
snippet: An annulus in the context of topology is a topological space which is homeomorphic with an annulus in the context of geometry. 400px

title: Definition:Anomalistic Year
snippet: The anomalistic year is the mean time interval between two consecutive passages of the Earth through perihelion.

title: Definition:Anomalous Cancellation
snippet: Let $r = \dfrac a b$ be a fraction where $a$ and $b$ are integers expressed in conventional decimal notation. Anomalous cancellation is a phenomenon whereby deleting (that is, cancelling) common digits from the numerator $a$ and the denominator $b$ of $r$, the value of $r$ the fraction does not change.

title: Definition:Anomalous Cancellation/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Anomalous Cancellation == The phenomenon of anomalous cancellation appears frequently in volumes and articles on recreational mathematics. A popular technique is to introduce it as an amusingly incorrect piece of classroom work by a particularly shiftless pupil with an entertainingly alliterative cognomen, for example "Irving the idiot", or "Dennis the dunce" as used by in his $1986$ work .

title: Definition:Anomaly
snippet: Polar Coordinates: Anomaly: another name for angular coordinate.

title: Definition:Anonymity of Survey Data
snippet: When gathering data by the technique of asking people to answer personal questions, it is important to make sure that the subjects of the questions understand that their replies are anonymous. Otherwise the truth value of their answers may be compromised.

title: Definition:Ansari-Bradley Test
snippet: The Ansari-Bradley test is a non-parametric test for homogeneity of variance.

title: Definition:Ansari-Bradley Test/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Ansari-Bradley Test == The Ansari-Bradley test was designed by and in $1960$.

title: Definition:Ansatz
snippet: An Ansatz is a guessed solution, or general form of a solution, to a mathematical problem. A mathematician making the Ansatz will then attempt to prove that the Ansatz is indeed a solution to the original problem. If he or she succeeds, the Ansatz is justified retroactively.

title: Definition:Ansatz/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Ansatz == The word Ansatz is German, and means approach, or attempt, or beginning. In all cases, the implication is that this is a first tentative step towards finding a solution. Also note that, when used in this context, the word always starts with an uppercase A. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Ante Meridiem
snippet: Ante meridiem specifies a time of day according to the $12$-hour clock after midnight and before noon.

title: Definition:Ante Meridiem/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Ante Meridiem == The phrase ante meridiem is Latin for before noon. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Antecedent/Also defined as
snippet: == Antecedent: Also defined as == Let $P = a \circ b$ be an expression. The term $a$ is known as the antecedent of $P$. The term is usually applied when the expression in question is a ratio. For example, in $5 : 7$, the number $5$ is the antecedent.

title: Definition:Antecedent/Also known as
snippet: == Antecedent: Also known as == The terms: premise assumption hypothesis can often be found in the literature as a word for antecedent, but on we reserve the use of premise, assumption and hypothesis for elements of the structure of logical arguments. The term antecedent clause can sometimes be seen, particularly when the conditional it is part of consists of a statement in natural language. The archaic terms implicans and protasis can sometimes be found.

title: Definition:Antecedent/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Antecedent == The word antecedent is usually found in classical mathematical literature, notably . The word comes from the Greek, and literally means leading term, or the thing that comes first. It is pronounced an-tee-see-dent. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Anti-
snippet: The prefix anti- is used in the following contexts:

title: Definition:Anti-/Contrast
snippet: The prefix anti- can be used to denote an opposite, or a contrast, to a given concept.

title: Definition:Anti-/Inverse
snippet: The prefix anti- is often used to denote the inverse of a given function.

title: Definition:Anti-Hermitian Matrix
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a square matrix over $\C$. $\mathbf A$ is anti-Hermitian : $\mathbf A = -\mathbf A^\dagger$ where $\mathbf A^\dagger$ is the Hermitian conjugate of $\mathbf A$.

title: Definition:Anti-Hermitian Matrix/Also known as
snippet: An anti-Hermitian matrix is also called a skew-Hermitian matrix

title: Definition:Anti-Realism
snippet: Anti-realism is a philosophical position that rejects the realist position that mathematical concepts have an existence independent of human knowledge.

title: Definition:Anti-Self-Dual 2-Form
snippet: Let $M$ be a $4$-dimensional oriented Riemannian manifold. Let $\omega$ be a $2$-form on $M$. Let $*$ be the Hodge star operator. Suppose: $* \omega = -\omega$ Then $\omega$ is known as the anti-self-dual $2$-form.

title: Definition:Antiassociative Operation
snippet: Let $\circ$ be a binary operation on the set $S$. $\circ$ is an antiassociative operation on $S$ : $\forall x, y, z \in S: \paren {x \circ y} \circ z \ne x \circ \paren {y \circ z}$

title: Definition:Antiassociative Structure
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic strcuture. Then $\struct {S, \circ}$ is an antiassociative structure $\circ$ is an antiassociative operation. That is, : $\forall x, y, z \in S: \paren {x \circ y} \circ z \ne x \circ \paren {y \circ z}$

title: Definition:Antichain
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set. An antichain in $S$ is a subset $A \subseteq S$ such that no two distinct elements in $A$ are comparable. That is: $\forall x, y \in A: x \ne y \implies \lnot \paren {x \preccurlyeq y} \land \lnot \paren {y \preccurlyeq x}$

title: Definition:Anticlastic Surface
snippet: Let $S$ be a surface in space. Let $P$ be a point at which the Gaussian curvature of $S$ at $P$ is negative. Then $S$ is described as being anticlastic at $P$.

title: Definition:Anticlockwise
snippet: Anticlockwise is this direction: 400px

title: Definition:Anticlockwise/Also known as
snippet: == Anticlockwise: Also known as == Instead of anticlockwise, some authors use counterclockwise. The terms are completely synonymous. Category:Definitions/Anticlockwise

title: Definition:Anticommutative/Structure with One Operation
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure Then $\circ$ is anticommutative on $S$ : $\forall x, y \in S: x \circ y = y \circ x \iff x = y$ Equivalently, it can be defined as: $\forall x, y \in S: x \ne y \iff x \circ y \ne y \circ x$ The word can also be applied to the structure itself: $\struct {S, \circ}$ is referred to as an anticommutative structure, or described as being anticommutative.

title: Definition:Anticommutative/Structure with Two Operations
snippet: Let $\struct {S, +, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. Let every element $x$ in $\struct {S, +}$ have an inverse element $-x$. Then $\circ$ is anticommutative on $S$ with respect to $+$ : $\forall x, y \in S: x \circ y = -\paren {y \circ x}$

title: Definition:Anticompact Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is anticompact every compact subset of $T$ is finite.

title: Definition:Anticompact Space/Also known as
snippet: == Anticompact Space: Also known as == An anticompact space is also known as a compact subsets are finite space.

title: Definition:Antihomomorphism
snippet: Let $\phi: \struct {S, \circ} \to \struct {T, *}$ be a mapping from one algebraic structure $\struct {S, \circ}$ to another $\struct {T, *}$. Then $\phi$ is an antihomomorphism : $\forall x, y \in S: \map \phi {x \circ y} = \map \phi y * \map \phi x$ For structures with more than one operation, $\phi$ may be antihomomorphic for a subset of those operations.

title: Definition:Antihomomorphism/Field Antihomomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ and $\struct {S, \oplus, *}$ be fields. Then a ring antihomomorphism $\phi: \struct {R, +, \circ} \to \struct {S, \oplus, *}$ is called a field antihomomorphism. Category:Definitions/Field Theory Category:Definitions/Antihomomorphisms

title: Definition:Antihomomorphism/Group Antihomomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ and $\struct {T, *}$ be groups. Then $\phi: S \to T$ is a group antihomomorphism : $\forall x, y \in S:\map \phi {x \circ y} = \map \phi y * \map \phi x$ Category:Definitions/Group Theory Category:Definitions/Antihomomorphisms

title: Definition:Antihomomorphism/Ring Antihomomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ and $\struct {S, \oplus, *}$ be rings. Then $\phi: R \to S$ is a ring antihomomorphism : {{eqn | q = \forall a, b \in R | l = \map \phi {a + b} | r = \map \phi a \oplus \map \phi b }} {{eqn | q = \forall a, b \in R | l = \map \phi {a \circ b} | r = \map \phi b * \map \phi a }} Category:Definitions/Antihomomorphisms Category:Definitions/Ring Homomorphisms

title: Definition:Antilexicographic Order
snippet: Let $\struct {S_1, \preccurlyeq_1}$ and $\struct {S_2, \preccurlyeq_2}$ be ordered sets. The antilexicographic order $\struct {S_1, \preccurlyeq_1} \otimes^a \struct {S_2, \preccurlyeq_2}$ on $\struct {S_1, \preccurlyeq_1}$ and $\struct {S_2, \preccurlyeq_2}$ is the ordered set $\struct {T, \preccurlyeq_a}$ where: $T := S_1 \times S_2$, that is, the Cartesian product of $S_1$ and $S_2$ $\preccurlyeq_a$ is the relation defined on $T$ as: $\tuple {x_1, x_2} \preccurlyeq_a \tuple {y_1, y_2} \iff \tuple {x_2 \prec_2 y_2} \lor \paren {x_2 = y_2 \land x_1 \preccurlyeq_1 y_1}$

title: Definition:Antilexicographic Order/Also known as
snippet: == Antilexicographic Order: Also known as == Antilexicographic order can also be referred to as colexicographic order. Some sources classify the antilexicographic order as a variety of order product. Hence the term antilexicographic product can occasionally be seen. Some sources which focus more directly on real analysis refer to this merely as the ordered product, or order product. This is because the other types of order product as documented on are not of such importance in that context.

title: Definition:Antilexicographic Order/Family
snippet: Let $\struct {I, \preceq}$ be an ordered set such that its dual $\struct {I, \succeq}$ is well-ordered. For each $i \in I$, let $\struct {S_i, \preccurlyeq_i}$ be an ordered set. Let $\ds D = \prod_{i \mathop \in I} S_i$ be the Cartesian product of the family $\family {\struct {S_i, \preccurlyeq_i} }_{i \mathop \in I}$ indexed by $I$.

title: Definition:Antilexicographic Order/General Definition
snippet: Let $S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_n$ all be ordered sets. Then we define $T_n$ as the antilexicographic order on $S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_n$ as: $\forall n \in \N_{>0}: T_n = \begin {cases} S_1 & : n = 1 \\ T_{n - 1} \otimes^a S_n & : n > 1 \end {cases}$

title: Definition:Antilogarithm
snippet: Let $x \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number. Let $b \in \R_{>1}$ be a real number which is greater than $1$. Let $y = \log_b x$ be the logarithm of $x$ base $b$. Then $x$ is the antilogarithm of $y$ base $b$.

title: Definition:Antilogarithm/Also denoted as
snippet: == Antilogarithm: Also denoted as == Some authors use $\operatorname {antilog}_b$ to denote the antilogarithm to base $b$.

title: Definition:Antilogarithm/Also known as
snippet: == Antilogarithm: Also known as == The shortened form antilog is frequently seen for antilogarithm.

title: Definition:Antilogarithm/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Antilogarithm == Since the use of log tables has mostly been superseded by use of handheld electronic calculators, the concept of the antilogarithm is barely used nowadays.

title: Definition:Antilogarithm/Symbol
snippet: == Antilogarithm: Symbol == The symbol used to denote the antilogarithm of $y$ to base $b$ is $\map {\operatorname {alog}_b} y$.

title: Definition:Antilogarithm/Symbol/Base 10
snippet: == Antilogarithm Base $10$: Symbol == The symbol used to denote the antilogarithm of $y$ to base $10$ is $\map {\operatorname {alog} } y$. That is, $\operatorname {alog} y$ generally means the same as $\operatorname {alog}_{10} y$. However, in the context of antilogarithms to base $10$, some sources prefer the notation $10^y$ over $\operatorname {alog} y$.

title: Definition:Antinomy
snippet: An antinomy is a self-contradictory statement which arises as the result of a valid argument from a set of premises which contains an inherent ambiguity or contradiction. Such apparent paradoxes can also often be classified as fallacies.

title: Definition:Antinomy/Also defined as
snippet: == Antinomy: Also defined as == Some sources define an antinomy as synonymous with paradox. To be more precise, such sources restrict the scope of the term paradox merely to that of antinomy.

title: Definition:Antiparallel Vectors
snippet: Let $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ be vector quantities in space such that: the lines of action of $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ are the same or parallel their directions are opposite. Then $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ are antiparallel.

title: Definition:Antiperiodic Function/Antiperiod
snippet: Let $f: X \to X$ be an antiperiodic function, where $X$ is either $\R$ or $\C$. The antiperiod of $f$ is the smallest value $\cmod L \in \R_{\ne 0}$ such that: $\forall x \in X: - \map f x = \map f {x + L}$ where $\cmod L$ is the modulus of $L$.

title: Definition:Antiperiodic Function/Antiperiodic Element
snippet: Let $f: X \to X$ be a function, where $X$ is either $\R$ or $\C$. Let $L \in X_{\ne 0}$. Then $L$ is an anti-periodic element of $f$ : $\forall x \in X: - \map f x = \map f {x + L}$ Category:Definitions/Antiperiodic Functions

title: Definition:Antiperiodic Function/Complex
snippet: Let $f: \C \to \C$ be a complex function. Then $f$ is anti-periodic : $\exists L \in \C_{\ne 0}: \forall x \in \C: -f \left({x}\right) = f \left({x + L}\right)$

title: Definition:Antiperiodic Function/Real
snippet: Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a real function. Then $f$ is anti-periodic : $\exists L \in \R_{\ne 0}: \forall x \in \R: -f \left({x}\right) = f \left({x + L}\right)$

title: Definition:Antipodal Points
snippet: Two points at opposite ends of a diameter of an ellipsoid are referred to as antipodal.

title: Definition:Antipodal Points/Also defined as
snippet: == Antipodal Points: Also defined as == Some sources define antipodal points just a sphere, rather than addressing the more general case of the ellipsoid.

title: Definition:Antiprism
snippet: An antiprism is a prismatoid which has $2$ congruent polygonal bases: One such base is rotated to the other one so the lateral faces are triangles.

title: Definition:Antiprism/Also defined as
snippet: == Antiprism: Also defined as == Some sources define an antiprism as having: regular polygons for bases. isosceles triangles for lateral faces. That is, as defines a right-regular antiprism.

title: Definition:Antiprism/Base
snippet: The bases of an antiprism are the two congruent faces embedded in the parallel planes which define the nature of the antiprism.

title: Definition:Antiprism/Lateral Edge
snippet: The lateral edges of an antiprism are the edges which connect the vertices of one base to the other base.

title: Definition:Antiprism/Lateral Face
snippet: The lateral faces of an antiprism are the faces bounded by the lateral edges.

title: Definition:Antireflexive Relation
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation in $S$. $\RR$ is antireflexive : $\forall x \in S: \tuple {x, x} \notin \RR$

title: Definition:Antireflexive Relation/Also known as
snippet: == Antireflexive Relation: Also known as == Some sources use the term irreflexive for antireflexive. However, as irreflexive is also found in other sources to mean non-reflexive, it is better to use the clumsier, but less ambiguous, antireflexive. The term aliorelative can sometimes be found, but this is rare.

title: Definition:Antisymmetric Matrix
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $\mathbf A$ be a square matrix over $R$. $\mathbf A$ is antisymmetric : $\mathbf A = -\mathbf A^\intercal$ where $\mathbf A^\intercal$ is the transpose of $\mathbf A$.

title: Definition:Antisymmetric Matrix/Also known as
snippet: == Antisymmetric Matrix: Also known as == An antisymmetric matrix is also known as a skew-symmetric matrix. Some sources hyphenate: anti-symmetric.

title: Definition:Antisymmetric Quotient
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \RR}$ be a preordered set. Let $\sim_\RR$ be the equivalence relation on $S$ induced by $\RR$. Let $S / {\sim_\RR}$ be the quotient set of $S$ by $\sim_\RR$. Let $\preccurlyeq$ be the ordering on $S / {\sim_\RR}$ induced by $\RR$: $\forall P, Q \in S / {\sim_\RR}: \exists p \in P, q \in Q: p \mathrel \RR q$ Then $\struct {S / {\sim_\RR}, \preccurlyeq}$ is the antisymmetric quotient of $\struct {S, \RR}$.

title: Definition:Antisymmetric Relation
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation in $S$.

title: Definition:Antisymmetric Relation/Also known as
snippet: == Antisymmetric Relation: Also known as == Some sources render antisymmetric relation as anti-symmetric relation.

title: Definition:Antisymmetric Relation/Class Theory
snippet: Let $V$ be a basic universe. Let $\RR \subseteq V \times V$ be a relation in $V$.

title: Definition:Antisymmetric Relation/Class Theory/Definition 1
snippet: Let $V$ be a basic universe. Let $\RR \subseteq V \times V$ be a relation in $V$. $\RR$ is antisymmetric : $\tuple {x, y} \in \RR \land \tuple {y, x} \in \RR \implies x = y$ that is: $\set {\tuple {x, y}, \tuple {y, x} } \subseteq \RR \implies x = y$

title: Definition:Antisymmetric Relation/Class Theory/Definition 2
snippet: Let $V$ be a basic universe. Let $\RR \subseteq V \times V$ be a relation in $V$. $\RR$ is antisymmetric : $\tuple {x, y} \in \RR \land x \ne y \implies \tuple {y, x} \notin \RR$

title: Definition:Antisymmetric Relation/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation in $S$. $\RR$ is antisymmetric : $\tuple {x, y} \in \RR \land \tuple {y, x} \in \RR \implies x = y$ that is: $\set {\tuple {x, y}, \tuple {y, x} } \subseteq \RR \implies x = y$

title: Definition:Antisymmetric Relation/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation in $S$. $\RR$ is antisymmetric : $\tuple {x, y} \in \RR \land x \ne y \implies \tuple {y, x} \notin \RR$

title: Definition:Antitransitive Relation
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation in $S$. $\RR$ is an antitransitive relation : $\tuple {x, y} \in \RR \land \tuple {y, z} \in \RR \implies \tuple {x, z} \notin \RR$ that is: $\set {\tuple {x, y}, \tuple {y, z} } \subseteq \RR \implies \tuple {x, z} \notin \RR$

title: Definition:Antitransitive Relation/Also known as
snippet: == Antitransitive Relation: Also known as == Some sources use the term intransitive relation to mean antitransitive relation. However, as intransitive is also found in other sources to mean non-transitive, it is better to use the clumsier, but less ambiguous, antitransitive.

title: Definition:Ap-
snippet: Let $A$ be a body in elliptical orbit $O$ around another body $B$. Ap- and apo- are prefixes which indicates the more distant of the two apsides of $O$ from the center of mass of $B$.

title: Definition:Aperiodic
snippet: An object (of arbitrary type) is described as being aperiodic it is not periodic.

title: Definition:Aperiodic Logical Matrix
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a logical matrix. $\mathbf A$ is aperiodic the period of $\mathbf A$ is $1$.

title: Definition:Aperiodic State
snippet: Let $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \ge 0}$ be a Markov chain. Let $\mathbf M$ be the transition matrix for $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \ge 0}$. Let $d$ be the period of the $i$th state of $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \ge 0}$: $d = \gcd \set {n: \sqbrk {\mathbf M}_{ii} > 0}$ Then the $i$th state of $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \ge 0}$ is aperiodic $d = 1$.

title: Definition:Aperiodic Tiling
snippet: An aperiodic tiling is a set of tiles which can tile the plane, but can never form a periodic tiling.

title: Definition:Aperiodic Tiling/Also known as
snippet: == Aperiodic Tiling: Also known as == An aperiodic tiling is also known as a nonperiodic tiling or non-periodic tiling.

title: Definition:Apex
snippet: The apex of a geometric figure is the point which is distinguished from the others by dint of it being furthest away from its base. Not all figures have a discernible apex. For example, parallelograms, prisms and parallelepipeds do not.

title: Definition:Apex/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Apex: Linguistic Note == The plural of apex is apices, which is pronounced ay-pi-seez. The form apexes can often be seen, but this is technically incorrect. Compare vertex, whose plural is vertices. Hence the colloquial phrase base over apex as the description of a particularly flamboyant physical tumble.

title: Definition:Apex of Cone/Also known as
snippet: == Apex of Cone: Also known as == The apex of a cone is also known as its vertex.

title: Definition:Apex of Isosceles Triangle/Also known as
snippet: == Apex of Isosceles Triangle: Also known as == The apex of an isosceles triangle is also called variously: head angle vertex Neither of these terms is endorsed on . Category:Definitions/Isosceles Triangles Category:Definitions/Apices

title: Definition:Apex of Pyramid/Also known as
snippet: == Apex of Pyramid: Also known as == The apex of a pyramid is seen in some sources as vertex.

title: Definition:Apex of Tetrahedron/Also known as
snippet: == Apex of Tetrahedron: Also known as == The apex of a tetrahedron is seen in some sources (for example ) as vertex. However, the term vertex can be used to define any of the corners of a polyhedron, so its use in this context is limited. Category:Definitions/Apices Category:Definitions/Tetrahedra

title: Definition:Aphelion
snippet: Let $P$ be a body in orbit around the sun. The aphelion of $P$ is the more distant of the two apsides of $P$'s orbit.

title: Definition:Apodosis/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Apodosis == The word Apodosis is from the Ancient Greek ἀπόδοσις (apódosis), from ἀπό (apó), meaning back again, and δόσις (dósis), meaning gift. The word has been adopted by the theatre world as a word meaning the last part of a play, usually the third act of a traditional $3$-act play. Really would not expect this word to come up in a serious mathematical exposition, but, you know, some people may come across it at some point. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Apogee
snippet: Let $P$ be a body in orbit around Earth. The apogee of $P$ is the more distant of the two apsides of $P$'s orbit.

title: Definition:Apothecaries' Weights and Measures
snippet: The apothecaries' (system of) weights and measures is a system of mass and volume units, derived from the Roman system. They were used by physicians and apothecaries for medical recipes, and also sometimes by scientists. Although in some cases bearing the same names as their imperial counterparts, the actual units themselves were subtly different in size.

title: Definition:Apothecaries' Weights and Measures/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Apothecaries' Weights and Measures == An apothecary is a medical professional who specialises in formulating and dispensing materia medica to physicians, surgeons and patients. The modern counterpart is pharmacist (also referred to as a (dispensing) chemist in British English). However, in some languages and regions the word apothecary can still be found referring to a retail pharmacy or a pharmacist who owns one.

title: Definition:Apothecaries' Weights and Measures/Mass
snippet: The apothecaries' system is one of the three imperial systems of measurement of mass. Its units are defined as follows:

title: Definition:Apothecaries' Weights and Measures/Mass/Drachm
snippet: The drachm is an apothecaries' unit of mass.

title: Definition:Apothecaries' Weights and Measures/Mass/Ounce
snippet: The apothecaries' ounce is an apothecaries' unit of mass.

title: Definition:Apothecaries' Weights and Measures/Mass/Ounce/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Apothecaries' Ounce == The apothecaries' ounce derived from the uncia (Roman ounce). It is seen that an apothecaries' ounce is the same size as a troy ounce, while weighing approximately $1 \cdotp 1$ ounces avoirdupois. Some sources do not recognise the existence of the apothecaries' ounce separately from the troy ounce, and when tabulating the various conversion factors refer merely to the fact that $8$ drachms make $1$ troy ounce.

title: Definition:Apothecaries' Weights and Measures/Mass/Pound
snippet: The apothecaries' pound is an apothecaries' unit of mass.

title: Definition:Apothecaries' Weights and Measures/Mass/Pound/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Apothecaries' Pound == The apothecaries' pound derived from the libra (Roman pound). It is seen that an apothecaries' pound and a troy pound have the same mass. Some sources do not recognise the existence of the apothecaries' ounce separately from the troy ounce, and when tabulating the various conversion factors refer merely to troy ounces and troy pounds.

title: Definition:Apothecaries' Weights and Measures/Mass/Scruple
snippet: The scruple is an apothecaries' unit of mass.

title: Definition:Apothecaries' Weights and Measures/Mass/Scruple/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Scruple == The scruple was defined to be the $\dfrac 1 {24}$ part of the Roman uncia, better known in modern times as the ounce. It survives in the modern age as a unit of the apothecaries' scale whose ounce is approximately $1.1$ ounce avoirdupois. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Apothecaries' Weights and Measures/Mass/Scruple/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Scruple == The word scruple is derived from the Latin scrupulus, which means small sharp stone. A scruple in contemporary language means pang of conscience, probably deriving from the irritation given by a small stone in one's footwear. Hence ones scruples are loosely understood as things that one does not do, as a result of one's sense of personal decency. The phrase he would not scruple to ... is interpreted to mean his conscience would not prevent him from ..., usually in the context of performing some act generally considered socially unacceptable.

title: Definition:Apothecaries' Weights and Measures/Volume
snippet: The apothecaries' system is an imperial systems of measurement of volume. Its units are defined as follows:

title: Definition:Apothecaries' Weights and Measures/Volume/Fluid Drachm
snippet: The fluid drachm is an apothecaries' unit of volume.

title: Definition:Apothecaries' Weights and Measures/Volume/Minim
snippet: The minim is an apothecaries' unit of volume.

title: Definition:Apothem/Also known as
snippet: == Apothem: Also known as == The apothem of a regular polygon is also known as its short radius.

title: Definition:Apothem/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Apothem == The word apothem is pronounced ap-o-th'm (the last syllable with as little stress as the second). It comes from Ancient Greek ἀπόθεμα (apóthema), meaning deposit, from: ἀπό (apó), meaning off or away θέμα (théma), meaning that which is laid down. Compare the similar but unrelated word or . Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Apotome
snippet: Let $a, b \in \set {x \in \R_{>0} : x^2 \in \Q}$ be two rationally expressible numbers such that $a > b$. Then $a - b$ is an apotome : $(1): \quad \dfrac a b \notin \Q$ $(2): \quad \paren {\dfrac a b}^2 \in \Q$ where $\Q$ denotes the set of rational numbers.

title: Definition:Apotome/Annex
snippet: Let $a, b \in \set {x \in \R_{>0} : x^2 \in \Q}$ be two rationally expressible numbers such that $a > b$. Let $a - b$ be an apotome. The real number $b$ is called the annex of the apotome. Category:Definitions/Apotome

title: Definition:Apotome/Fifth Apotome
snippet: Let $a, b \in \set {x \in \R_{>0} : x^2 \in \Q}$ be two rationally expressible numbers such that $a - b$ is an apotome. Then $a - b$ is a fifth apotome : $(1): \quad b \in \Q$ $(2): \quad \dfrac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2}} a \notin \Q$ where $\Q$ denotes the set of rational numbers. '

title: Definition:Apotome/First Apotome
snippet: Let $a, b \in \set {x \in \R_{>0} : x^2 \in \Q}$ be two rationally expressible numbers such that $a - b$ is an apotome. Then $a - b$ is a first apotome : $(1): \quad a \in \Q$ $(2): \quad \dfrac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2}} a \in \Q$ where $\Q$ denotes the set of rational numbers. '

title: Definition:Apotome/Fourth Apotome
snippet: Let $a, b \in \set {x \in \R_{>0} : x^2 \in \Q}$ be two rationally expressible numbers such that $a - b$ is an apotome. Then $a - b$ is a fourth apotome : $(1): \quad a \in \Q$ $(2): \quad \dfrac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2}} a \notin \Q$ where $\Q$ denotes the set of rational numbers. '

title: Definition:Apotome/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Apotome == The term apotome is archaic, and is rarely used nowadays. It is pronounced a-POT-o-mee, just as "epitome" is pronounced e-PIT-o-mee. It is transliterated directly from the Ancient Greek word ἀποτομή, which is the noun form of ἀποτέμνω, from ἀπο- (away) and τέμνω (to cut), meaning roughly to cut away. Therefore, ἀποτομή means roughly (the portion) cut off. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Apotome/Order
snippet: Let $a, b \in \set {x \in \R_{>0} : x^2 \in \Q}$ be two rationally expressible numbers such that $a > b$. Let $a - b$ be an apotome. The order of $a - b$ is the name of its classification into one of the six categories: first, second, third, fourth, fifth or sixth. Category:Definitions/Apotome

title: Definition:Apotome/Second Apotome
snippet: Let $a, b \in \set {x \in \R_{>0} : x^2 \in \Q}$ be two rationally expressible numbers such that $a - b$ is an apotome. Then $a - b$ is a second apotome : $(1): \quad b \in \Q$ $(2): \quad \dfrac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2}} a \in \Q$ where $\Q$ denotes the set of rational numbers. '

title: Definition:Apotome/Terms
snippet: Let $a, b \in \set {x \in \R_{>0} : x^2 \in \Q}$ be two rationally expressible numbers such that $a > b$. Let $a - b$ be an apotome. The terms of $a - b$ are the elements $a$ and $b$.

title: Definition:Apotome/Third Apotome
snippet: Let $a, b \in \set {x \in \R_{>0} : x^2 \in \Q}$ be two rationally expressible numbers such that $a - b$ is an apotome. Then $a - b$ is a third apotome : $(1): \quad a \notin \Q$ $(2): \quad b \notin \Q$ $(3): \quad \dfrac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2}} a \in \Q$ where $\Q$ denotes the set of rational numbers. '

title: Definition:Apotome/Warning
snippet: It is a mistake to suggest that $a$ and $b$ may be any real numbers such that $\dfrac a b \notin \Q$ and $\paren {\dfrac a b}^2 \in \Q$. For example, let $a = \pi \sqrt 2$ and $b = \pi$. Then we see that: $(1): \quad \dfrac a b = \sqrt 2 \notin \Q$ $(2): \quad \paren {\dfrac a b}^2 = 2 \in \Q$ But $a - b = \pi \paren {\sqrt 2 - 1}$ is not an apotome.

title: Definition:Apotome/Whole
snippet: Let $a, b \in \set {x \in \R_{>0} : x^2 \in \Q}$ be two rationally expressible numbers such that $a > b$. Let $a - b$ be an apotome. The real number $a$ is called the whole of the apotome. Category:Definitions/Apotome

title: Definition:Apotome of Medial/Annex
snippet: LLet $a, b \in \set {x \in \R_{>0} : x^2 \in \Q}$ be two rationally expressible numbers such that $a > b$. Let $a - b$ be an apotome of a medial. The real number $b$ is called the annex of the apotome of a medial. Category:Definitions/Apotome

title: Definition:Apotome of Medial/First Apotome
snippet: Let $a, b \in \set {x \in \R_{>0} : x^2 \in \Q}$ be two rationally expressible numbers such that $a > b$ be in the forms: $a = k^{1/4} \rho$ $b = k^{3/4} \rho$ where: $\rho$ is a rational number $k$ is a rational number whose square root is irrational. Then $a - b$ is a first apotome of a medial.

title: Definition:Apotome of Medial/Order
snippet: Let $a, b \in \set {x \in \R_{>0} : x^2 \in \Q}$ be two rationally expressible numbers such that $a - b$ is an apotome of a medial. The order of $a - b$ is the name of its classification into one of the two categories: first or second. Category:Definitions/Apotome

title: Definition:Apotome of Medial/Second Apotome
snippet: Let $a, b \in \set {x \in \R_{>0} : x^2 \in \Q}$ be two rationally expressible numbers such that $a > b$ be in the forms: $a = k^{1/4} \rho$ $b = \dfrac {\lambda^{1/2} \rho} {k^{1/4} }$ where: $\rho$ is a rational number $k$ is a rational number whose square root is irrational. $\lambda$ is a rational number whose square root is irrational. Then $a - b$ is a second apotome of a medial.

title: Definition:Apotome of Medial/Terms
snippet: Let $a, b \in \set {x \in \R_{>0} : x^2 \in \Q}$ be two rationally expressible numbers such that $a > b$. Let $a - b$ be an apotome of a medial. The terms of $a - b$ are the elements $a$ and $b$.

title: Definition:Apotome of Medial/Whole
snippet: Let $a, b \in \set {x \in \R_{>0} : x^2 \in \Q}$ be two rationally expressible numbers such that $a > b$. Let $a - b$ be an apotome of a medial. The real number $a$ is called the whole of the apotome of a medial. Category:Definitions/Apotome

title: Definition:Appert Space
snippet: Let $\Z_{>0}$ denote the (strictly) positive integers. For a given subset $H$ of $\Z_{>0}$ and element $n$ of $\Z_{>0}$, let $\map N {n, H}$ denote the number of integers in $E$ which are less than or equal to $n$: $\forall n \in \Z_{>0}, H \subseteq \Z_{>0}: \map N {n, H} = \card {\set {x \in H: x \le n} }$ Let $\tau$ be the topology defined as: $1 \notin H \implies H \in \tau$ $1 \in H$ and $\ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \dfrac {\map N {n, H} } n = 1 \implies H \in \tau$ for $H \subseteq \Z_{>0}$. $\tau$ is referred to as the Appert topology.

title: Definition:Applied Mathematics
snippet: Applied mathematics is the branch of mathematics which concerns the solution of real world applications by the construction of mathematical models.

title: Definition:Approximate Eigenvalue/Densely-Defined Linear Operator
snippet: Let $\struct {\HH, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be a Hilbert space over $\C$. Let $\struct {\map D T, T}$ be a densely-defined linear operator. Let $\lambda \in \C$. We say that $\lambda$ is an approximate eigenvalue : there exists a sequence $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ in $\map D T$ with $\norm {x_n} = 1$ for each $n \in \N$ such that: $\paren {T - \lambda I} x_n \to 0$

title: Definition:Approximate Fermat Equation
snippet: An approximate Fermat equation is a Diophantine equation of the form: $x^n = y^n + z^n \pm c$ such that $\dfrac {x^n} {y^n + z^n} \approx 1$. That is, the numbers $x, y, z, n$ almost, but not quite, form a solution to: $x^n = y^n + z^n$ and thus almost form a counterexample to Fermat's Last Theorem.

title: Definition:Approximate Identity of C*-Algebra
snippet: Let $\struct {A, \ast, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a $\text C^\ast$-algebra. Let $\struct {\Lambda, \preceq}$ be a directed set. Let $\le_A$ be the canonical preordering of $A$. Let $\family {e_\lambda}_{\lambda \mathop \in \Lambda}$ be a net in $A$ such that for each $\lambda, \mu \in \Lambda$: $\map {\sigma_A} {e_\lambda} \subseteq \closedint 0 1$ and: $\lambda \preceq \mu$ implies $e_\lambda \le_A e_\mu$ We say that $\family {e_\lambda}_{\lambda \mathop \in \Lambda}$ is an approximate identity for $A$ : for each $x \in A$, the net $\family {x e_\lambda}_{\lambda \mathop \in \Lambda}$…

title: Definition:Approximating Relation
snippet: Let $L = \struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $\RR$ be a relation on $S$. Then $\RR$ is an approximating relation on $S$ $\forall x \in S: x = \map \sup {x^\RR}$ where $x^\RR$ denotes the $\RR$-segment of $x$.

title: Definition:Approximation
snippet: An approximation is an estimate of a quantity. It is usually the case that there exists some knowledge about the accuracy of the estimate. The notation: $a \approx b$ indicates that $b$ is an approximation to $a$.

title: Definition:Approximation/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Approximation == The form of approximation is approximate, whose meaning is: to find a value or expression for a quantity within a specified degree of accuracy and whose pronunciation is something like ap-prox-i-mayt. The form of approximation is also approximate, and means: within a specified degree of accuracy but its pronunciation is more like ap-prox-i-mut. Note the difference in the final syllable.

title: Definition:Approximation Error
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function defined over an interval $\openint a b$. Let $A$ be an approximation to $f$ over $\openint a b$. For $x \in \openint a b$, the approximation error of $\map A x$ $\map f x$ is defined as: $\map f x - \map A x$

title: Definition:Approximation Theory
snippet: Approximation theory is a branch of numerical analysis and applied mathematics concerned with the approximation of a function over an interval by a simpler function (usually polynomial).

title: Definition:Approximation Theory/Motivation
snippet: == Approximation Theory: Motivation == The broad aim of approximation theory is for approximation errors to be as small as possible over the interval $\openint a b$ of interest.

title: Definition:Apsis
snippet: Let $A$ be a body in orbit $O$ around another body $B$. Let $\mathbf r$ be the radius of $O$. An apsis is a point on $O$ at which: the rate of change of the length of $\mathbf r$ is zero and: the velocity of $A$ is perpendicular to $\mathbf r$.

title: Definition:Apsis/Also known as
snippet: == Apsis: Also known as == An apsis is also known as an apse. Some sources use the term apsidal point.

title: Definition:Apsis/Apsidal Distance
snippet: The length of the radius of the orbit of an apsis is known as the apsidal distance.

title: Definition:Apsis/Line of Apsides
snippet: The direction of the radius of the orbit of an apsis is known as the line of apsides.

title: Definition:Apsis/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Apsis: Linguistic Note == The word apsis comes from the ancient Greek ἁψίς (hapsís), which means arch or vault. The plural of apsis (and apse) is apsides, pronounced ap-si-dees. Some sources use apses for the plural form.

title: Definition:Apéry's Constant
snippet: Apéry's constant is the value of the infinite sum: $\map \zeta 3 = \ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \frac 1 {n^3}$ where $\zeta$ denotes the Riemann zeta function. Its approximate value is given by: $\map \zeta 3 \approx 1 \cdotp 20205 \, 69031 \, 59594 \, 28539 \, 97381 \, 61511 \, 44999 \, 07649 \, 86292 \ldots$

title: Definition:Apéry's Constant/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Apéry's Constant == Apéry's constant was first investigated by , who tried but failed to calculate its value. Its precise value is still unknown. However, in $1979$ published a proof that it is irrational. The statement of this fact is now known as Apéry's Theorem, and the constant itself is known as Apéry's constant.

title: Definition:Arabian Nights Factorial
snippet: A fanciful name for $450!$ (factorial).

title: Definition:Arabic Numerals
snippet: The Arabic numerals are a decimal system of numerals as follows: They are used in conjunction with the positional decimal system of numeric representation.

title: Definition:Arabic Numerals/Also known as
snippet: == Arabic Numerals: Also known as == The Arabic numerals are also known as the Hindu-Arabic numerals, or Hindu numerals. An archaic name for the Arabic numerals is ciphers or cyphers.

title: Definition:Arabic Numerals/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Arabic Numerals == The Arabic numerals were supposedly invented in the sphere of influence of the Arab culture in mediaeval times, but were in fact defined by Hindu mathematicians in approximately the $5$th or $6$th century CE. Hence they are also referred to as Hindu-Arabic numerals or Hindu numerals. They first arrived in Europe by way of the translation by of by . However, the Arabic numeral system was slow to catch on, because of the general philosophical difficulty at the time with accepting the existence of the concept of zero.

title: Definition:Arbitrarily Large
snippet: Let $P$ be a property of real numbers. We say that: $\map P x$ holds for arbitrarily large $x$ or: there exist arbitrarily large $x$ such that $\map P x$ holds $\forall a \in \R: \exists x \in \R: x \ge a: \map P x$ That is: For any real number $a$, there exists a (real) number not less than $a$ such that the property $P$ holds. or, more informally and intuitively: However large a number you can think of, there will be an even larger one for which $P$ still holds. or: $\set {x: \map P x}$ is not bounded above.

title: Definition:Arbitrarily Small
snippet: Let $P$ be a property of real numbers. We say that: $\map P x$ holds for arbitrarily small $\epsilon$ or: there exist arbitrarily small $x$ such that $\map P x$ holds $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{> 0}: \exists x \in \R: \size x \le \epsilon: \map P x$ That is: For any real number $a$, there exists a (real) number not more than $a$ such that the property $P$ holds. or, more informally and intuitively: However small a number you can think of, there will be an even smaller one for which $P$ still holds.

title: Definition:Arbitrary
snippet: An object which is introduced into an argument with the descriptor arbitrary means that the object is unconstrained beyond whatever specified constraints are applied.

title: Definition:Arbitrary Constant
snippet: An arbitrary constant is a symbol used to represent an object which is neither a specific number nor a variable. It is used to represent a general object (usually a number, but not necessarily) whose value can be assigned when the expression is instantiated.

title: Definition:Arbitrary Join Preserving Mapping
snippet: Let $L_1 = \struct{S_1, \preceq_1}$ and $L_2 = \struct{S_2, \preceq_2}$ be complete lattices. Let $\phi: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping between the underlying sets of $L_1$ and $L_2$. Then: $\phi$ is arbitrary join preserving: $\forall A \subseteq S_1 : \map \phi {\sup A} = \sup \set{\map \phi a : a \in A}$

title: Definition:Arbitrary Meet Preserving Mapping
snippet: Let $L_1 = \struct{S_1, \preceq_1}$ and $L_2 = \struct{S_2, \preceq_2}$ be complete lattices. Let $\phi: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping between the underlying sets of $L_1$ and $L_2$. Then: $\phi$ is arbitrary meet preserving: $\forall A \subseteq S_1 : \map \phi {\inf A} = \inf \set{\map \phi a : a \in A}$

title: Definition:Arborescence
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, A}$ be a digraph. Let $r \in V$.

title: Definition:Arborescence/Also defined as
snippet: Variants of the definitions can be found, as follows: defines an arborescence of root $r$ so as to reverse the orientation of $G$, so that the arcs are all directed toward the root rather than away from it. specifies that the successors of each vertex to be ordered "from the left", without specifying exactly what that means.

title: Definition:Arborescence/Also known as
snippet: An arborescence of root $r$ can be referred to as an an $r$-arborescence, or just an arborescence. Various sources use different terms, for example: calls an arborescence an oriented tree calls an arborescence an ordered, directed tree.

title: Definition:Arborescence/Definition 1
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, A}$ be a digraph. Let $r \in V$. $G$ is an arborescence of root $r$ : For each $v \in V$ there is exactly one directed walk from $r$ to $v$.

title: Definition:Arborescence/Definition 2
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, A}$ be a digraph. Let $r \in V$. $G$ is an arborescence of root $r$ : $(1): \quad$ $G$ is an orientation of a tree $(2): \quad$ For each $v \in V$, $v$ is reachable from $r$.

title: Definition:Arborescence/Definition 3
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, A}$ be a digraph. Let $r \in V$. $G$ is an arborescence of root $r$ : $(1): \quad$ Each vertex $v \ne r$ is the final vertex of exactly one arc $(2): \quad$ $r$ is not the final vertex of any arc $(3): \quad$ For each $v \in V$ such that $v \ne r$ there is a directed walk from $r$ to $v$.

title: Definition:Arborescence/Definition 4
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, A}$ be a digraph. Let $r \in V$. $G$ is an arborescence of root $r$ : $(1): \quad$ Each vertex $v \ne r$ has exactly one predecessor $(2): \quad$ $r$ has no predecessors $(3): \quad$ For each $v \in V$ such that $v \ne r$ there is a path from $r$ to $v$.

title: Definition:Arborescence/Root
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, A}$ be a digraph. Let $r \in V$. Let $G$ be an arborescence of $r$. The distinguished vertex $r$ of $G$ is known as the root of (the arborescence) $G$.

title: Definition:Arc
snippet: Graph theory: An arc of a directed graph is a line, with a directional arrow, that joins one vertex to another. Geometry: An arc is a specific part of a general curve. Particular usages: Arc of Circle: any part of its circumference; Arc of Cycloid: one of the parts of a cycloid between two cusps. Topology: An arc from $a$ to $b$ in a topological space is a continuous injection $f: I \to T$ such that $\map f 0 = a$ and $\map f 1 = b$.

title: Definition:Arc-Connected
snippet: Arc-connectedness is a property of a topological space $T$ which relates to the existence of certain homeomorphic embeddings from a closed real interval (in practice, usually just the closed unit interval) into $T$.

title: Definition:Arc-Connected/Also defined as
snippet: == Arc-Connected: Also defined as == Some sources define arc-connected as defines injectively path-connected, but this is usually reserved for a weaker concept.

title: Definition:Arc-Connected/Also known as
snippet: == Arc-Connected: Also known as == The term arc-connected can also be seen unhyphenated: arc connected. Some sources also refer to this condition as: but the extra syllable does not appear to add to the understanding. Some sources use the term injectively path-connected, but this is usually reserved for a weaker concept.

title: Definition:Arc-Connected/Points
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $a, b \in S$ be such that there exists an arc from $a$ to $b$. That is, there exists a homeomorphic embedding $f: \closedint 0 1 \to S$ such that $\map f 0 = a$ and $\map f 1 = b$. Then $a$ and $b$ are arc-connected. It is also declared that any point $a$ is arc-connected to itself.

title: Definition:Arc-Connected/Subset
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $U \subseteq S$ be a subset of $T$. Let $T' = \struct {U, \tau_U}$ be the subspace of $T$ induced by $U$. Then $U$ is arc-connected in $T$ every two points in $U$ are arc-connected in $T'$. That is, $U$ is arc-connected : for every $x, y \in U$, there exists a homeomorphic embedding $f: \closedint 0 1 \to S$ such that $\map f 0 = x$ and $\map f 1 = y$.

title: Definition:Arc-Connected/Topological Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is arc-connected every two points in $T$ are arc-connected in $T$. That is, $T$ is arc-connected : $\forall x, y \in S: \exists$ a homeomorphic embedding $f: \closedint 0 1 \to S$ such that $\map f 0 = x$ and $\map f 1 = y$.

title: Definition:Arc (Topology)
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\mathbb I \subset \R$ be the closed unit interval $\closedint 0 1$. Let $a, b \in S$. An arc from $a$ to $b$ is a homeomorphic embedding $f: \closedint 0 1 \to S$ such that: The mapping $f$ can be described as an arc (in $T$) joining $a$ and $b$.

title: Definition:Arc (Topology)/Also known as
snippet: == Arc in context of Topology: Also known as == An arc is also known as an open curve.

title: Definition:Arc Component
snippet: Let $T$ be a topological space. Let us define the relation $\sim$ on $T$ as follows: $x \sim y \iff x$ and $y$ are arc-connected. We have that $\sim $ is an equivalence relation, so from the Fundamental Theorem on Equivalence Relations, the points in $T$ can be partitioned into equivalence classes. These equivalence classes are called the arc components of $T$. If $x \in T$, then the arc component of $T$ containing $x$ (that is, the set of points $y \in T$ with $x \sim y$) can be denoted by $\map {\operatorname {AC}_x} T$.

title: Definition:Arc Distance
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be points on a curve $\CC$. The arc distance from $A$ to $B$ is defined as the length of the arc of $\CC$ connecting $A$ and $B$.

title: Definition:Arc Distance/Also known as
snippet: == Arc Distance: Also known as == Arc distance is also known as distance along a curve. Category:Definitions/Arc Distance

title: Definition:Arc Length
snippet: Let $y = \map f x$ be a real function which is: continuous on the closed interval $\closedint a b$ and: continuously differentiable on the open interval $\openint a b$.

title: Definition:Arc Length/Also known as
snippet: == Arc Length: Also known as == An arc length can also be referred to as the length of a curve. Category:Definitions/Arc Length

title: Definition:Arc Length/Definition 1
snippet: Let $y = \map f x$ be a real function which is: continuous on the closed interval $\closedint a b$ and: continuously differentiable on the open interval $\openint a b$. The arc length $s$ of $f$ between $a$ and $b$ is defined as: $\ds s := \int_a^b \sqrt {1 + \paren {\frac {\d y} {\d x} }^2} \rd x$

title: Definition:Arc Length/Definition 2
snippet: The length of the arc of a curve is defined as the limit of the length of a polygonal line inscribed within the curve as the maximum length of the chords which form that polygonal line tends to zero.

title: Definition:Arc Length/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Arc Length == The formula for the arc length of a curve was first obtained by around $1680$.

title: Definition:Arc Length/Intuition
snippet: The arc length of a curve $C$ can be thought of as how long the graph of the function of $C$ would be if cut at the points $\tuple {a, \map f a}$ and $\tuple {b, \map f b}$ and then straightened out.

title: Definition:Arc Length of Regular Curve/3-Dimensional Real Vector Space
snippet: Let $\alpha : I \to \R^3$ be a regular curve. Let $t_0 \in I$. Then the arc length of $\alpha$ from $t_0$ is defined as: $\ds \map s t := \int_{t_0}^t \norm {\map {\alpha '} t} \rd t$ where: $\alpha '$ denotes the derivative of $\alpha$ $\norm \cdot$ denotes the Euclidean norm on $\R^3$

title: Definition:Arc of Cycloid/Also known as
snippet: == Arc of Cycloid: Also known as == Some sources refer to the arc of a cycloid as an arch, while others call it a hump.

title: Definition:Arc of Digraph/Also known as
snippet: == Arc of Digraph: Also known as == An arc of a digraph is also known as: an arrow a directed edge.

title: Definition:Arc of Digraph/Endvertex
snippet: Let $D = \struct {V, E}$ be a digraph. Let $e = u v$ be an arc of $D$, that is, $e \in E$. The endvertices of $e$ are the vertices $u$ and $v$.

title: Definition:Arc of Digraph/Endvertex/Final Vertex
snippet: Let $D = \struct {V, E}$ be a digraph. Let $e = u v$ be an arc of $D$, that is, $e \in E$. The final vertex of $e$ is the endvertex $v$ which $e$ is incident to.

title: Definition:Arc of Digraph/Endvertex/Initial Vertex
snippet: Let $D = \struct {V, E}$ be a digraph. Let $e = u v$ be an arc of $D$, that is, $e \in E$. The initial vertex of $e$ is the endvertex $u$ which $e$ is incident from.

title: Definition:Archimedean Polyhedron
snippet: An Archimedean polyhedron is a convex polyhedron with the following properties: $(1): \quad$ Each of its faces is a regular polygon $(2): \quad$ It is isogonal $(3): \quad$ The faces are not all congruent. $(4): \quad$ It is not a uniform prism or a uniform antiprism.

title: Definition:Archimedean Preordered Vector Space
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \succeq}$ be a preordered vector space over $\GF$. Let $X^+$ be the positive cone of $X$. Let ${\mathbf 0}_X$ be the zero vector of $X$. We say that $\struct {X, \succeq}$ is Archimedean : for all $y \in X$ such that: there exists $x \in X$ such that $x \succeq \alpha y$ for each $\alpha \ge 0$ we have ${\mathbf 0}_X \succeq y$.

title: Definition:Archimedean Spiral/Archimedes' Definition
snippet: ' definition of his Archimedean spiral is as follows: If a straight line of which one extremity remains fixed be made to revolve at a uniform rate in a plane until it returns to the position from which it started, and if, at the same time as the straight line revolves, a point moves at a uniform rate along the straight line, starting from the fixed extremity, the point will describe a spiral in the plane.

title: Definition:Area
snippet: Area is the measure of the extent of a surface. It has $2$ dimensions and is specified in units of length squared. Hence the term square as a general vague term for a quantity in $2$ dimensions.

title: Definition:Area Element
snippet: An area element $\delta \mathbf S$ is a (usually) infinitesimal vector area,(usually) containing a particular point $P$. In the cartesian $3$-space such an area element is modelled as a rectangle whose edges are parallel to two of the coordinate axes, and assigned lengths $\delta x$, $\delta y$ or $\delta z$ respectively.

title: Definition:Area Element/Outward Normal
snippet: Let $\delta \mathbf S$ be an area element embedded in a coordinate frame with position vector $\mathbf r$. The outward normal of $\delta \mathbf S$ is defined to be the normal vector $\mathbf n$ to $\delta \mathbf S$ such that: $\mathbf r \cdot \mathbf n > 0$ where $\cdot$ denotes the dot product. In the event that $\mathbf r \cdot \mathbf n = 0$, the outward normal may be chosen arbitrarily.

title: Definition:Area Sampling
snippet: Area sampling is a method of sampling where a geographical region is divided into smaller sub-regions by a grid, usually of squares or rectangles. Such sub-regions are chosen at random, and all units within those sub-regions are included in the sample.

title: Definition:Arens-Fort Space
snippet: Let $S$ be the set $\Z_{\ge 0} \times \Z_{\ge 0}$ be the Cartesian product of the set of positive integers $\Z_{\ge 0}$: $S = \set {0, 1, 2, \ldots} \times \set {0, 1, 2, \ldots}$ Let $\tau \subseteq \powerset S$ be a subset of the power set of $S$ such that: $(1): \quad \forall H \subseteq S: \tuple {0, 0} \notin H \implies H \in \tau$ $(2): \quad H \subseteq S: \tuple {0, 0} \in H$ and, for all but a finite number of $m \in \Z_{\ge 0}$, the sets $S_m$ defined as: $S_m = \set {n: \tuple {m, n} \notin H}$ are finite.

title: Definition:Arens Square
snippet: Let $A$ be the subset of the unit square defined as: $A := \set {\tuple {i, j}: 0 < i < 1, 0 < j < 1, i, j \in \Q} \setminus \set {\tuple {i, j}: i = \dfrac 1 2}$ That is: $A := \openint 0 1^2 \cap \Q \times \Q \setminus \set {\tuple {\dfrac 1 2}, j: j \in \Q}$ That is, the set of rational points in the interior of the unit square from which are excluded the points whose $x$ coordinates are equal to $\dfrac 1 2$.

title: Definition:Argand Diagram
snippet: An Argand diagram is a graphical representation of a set of complex numbers on the complex plane: 400px A complex number can be represented on an Argand diagram as a vector from the origin $O = \tuple {0, 0}$ to the point $P = \tuple {x, y}$ whose coordinates are the complex number $x + i y$.

title: Definition:Argument
snippet: Complex Numbers: The argument of a complex number. Logic: A logical argument. Mapping Theory: The argument of a mapping. Argument: The same thing as an independent variable. Polar Coordinates: Argument: the angular coordinate of a point.

title: Definition:Argument Form
snippet: An argument form is a collation of symbols which contains statement variables such that: when statements are used to replace statement variables (the same statement replacing the same statement variable throughout), the result is a logical argument.

title: Definition:Argument Form/Also known as
snippet: == Argument Form: Also known as == An argument form is also known as a logical form by some writers, but the latter term is imprecise and is also found to mean statement form. Some sources use the term symbolic argument.

title: Definition:Argument Form/Specific Form
snippet: The specific form of a given logical argument is that argument form from which the logical argument results from replacing each distinct statement variable by a different simple statement.

title: Definition:Argument of Complex Number
snippet: Let $z = x + i y$ be a complex number. An argument of $z$, or $\arg z$, is formally defined as a solution to the pair of equations: $(1): \quad \dfrac x {\cmod z} = \map \cos {\arg z}$ $(2): \quad \dfrac y {\cmod z} = \map \sin {\arg z}$ where $\cmod z$ is the modulus of $z$. From Sine and Cosine are Periodic on Reals, it follows that if $\theta$ is an argument of $z$, then so is $\theta + 2 k \pi$ where $k \in \Z$ is any integer. Thus, the argument of a complex number $z$ is a continuous multifunction.

title: Definition:Argument of Complex Number/Also known as
snippet: == Argument of Complex Number: Also known as == The argument of a complex number is also seen as: its amplitude, denoted $\am z$ its phase, denoted $\ph z$

title: Definition:Argument of Complex Number/Flawed Definition
snippet: == Warning: Argument of Complex Number: Flawed Definition == It appears at first glance that it would be simpler to define the argument of a complex number $z = x + i y$ as: $\theta = \arg z := \map \arctan {\dfrac y x}$ This arises from the definition of the tangent as sine divided by cosine. This, however, does not determine $\theta$ uniquely. The image set of $\arctan$ is usually defined as: $\openint {-\dfrac \pi 2} {\dfrac \pi 2}$ and in any case, is a open interval of length $\pi$.

title: Definition:Argument of Complex Number/Principal Argument
snippet: Let $R$ be the principal range of the complex numbers $\C$. The unique value of $\theta$ in $R$ is known as the principal argument, of $z$. This is denoted $\Arg z$. Note the capital $A$. The standard practice is for $R$ to be $\hointl {-\pi} \pi$. This ensures that the principal argument is continuous on the real axis for positive numbers. Thus, if $z$ is represented in the complex plane, the principal argument $\Arg z$ is intuitively defined as the angle which $z$ yields with the real ($y = 0$) axis.

title: Definition:Argument of Complex Number/Principal Range
snippet: It is understood that the argument of a complex number $z$ is unique only up to multiples of $2 k \pi$. With this understanding, we can limit the choice of what $\theta$ can be for any given $z$ by requiring that $\theta$ lie in some half open interval of length $2 \pi$. The most usual of these are: $\hointr 0 {2 \pi}$ $\hointl {-\pi} \pi$ but in theory any such interval may be used. This interval is known as the principal range.

title: Definition:Argumentum ad Baculum
snippet: An argumentum ad baculum is a logical argument that, rather than prove or present evidence for a claim, threatens any who dare argue with the person or group making the claim. The presence of such a threat is often a good reason to avoid stating an opposing view, but manifestly does not support the truth or falsity of the claim under consideration.

title: Definition:Argumentum ad Hominem
snippet: An argumentum ad hominem is a logical argument that concludes the falsehood of a statement because it is made by a particular person or group of people. It can be argued that it is reasonable to be suspicious of an argument if: most of the assertions made by said person or group regarding the topic under discussion are false the person may have a vested interest in people believing an assertion made by that person. However, such reasoning is still fallacious.

title: Definition:Argumentum ad Hominem/Also known as
snippet: == Argumentum ad Hominem: Also known as == An argumentum ad hominem is also called an argument against the person.

title: Definition:Argumentum ad Passiones
snippet: An argumentum ad passiones is a logical argument that, rather than prove or present evidence for a claim, attempts to generate support for an idea by instilling either: an emotional attachment to the argument being presented a feeling of embarrassment at holding a position which is subject to ridicule or a feeling of distaste for the argument being refuted. Such arguments are commonly seen along with argumentum ad hominem.

title: Definition:Argumentum ad Verecundiam
snippet: Argumentum ad verecundiam, or argument from authority, is a logical argument that infers something is true on the basis that a knowledgeable and well-reputed person has said it. An argument from authority may be valid or invalid, depending on the circumstances. If the trustworthy person is also an expert in the field, and is free to speak their mind about the matter, then the argument has some validity. Otherwise, it generally does not. That said, argumentum ad verecundiam can never serve as a (mathematical) proof, since no authority could ever be infallible.

title: Definition:Argumentum ad Verecundiam/Also known as
snippet: == Argumentum ad Verecundiam: Also known as == Argumentum ad Verecundiam is also known as argument from authority. Category:Definitions/Argumentum ad Verecundiam

title: Definition:Arithmetic
snippet: Arithmetic is the branch of mathematics which concerns the manipulation of numbers, using the operations addition, subtraction, multiplication and division, and the taking of powers.

title: Definition:Arithmetic-Geometric Mean
snippet: The arithmetic-geometric mean of two numbers $a$ and $b$ is the limit of the sequences obtained by the arithmetic-geometric mean iteration. This is denoted $\map M {a, b}$.

title: Definition:Arithmetic-Geometric Sequence
snippet: An arithmetic-geometric sequence is a sequence $\sequence {a_k}$ in $\R$ defined as: $a_k = \paren {a_0 + k d} r^k$ for $k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$ Thus its general form is: $a_0, \paren {a_0 + d} r, \paren {a_0 + 2 d} r^2, \paren {a_0 + 3 d} r^3, \ldots$
