title: Definition:Arithmetic/Linguistic Note
snippet: The word arithmetic, when used as a noun, is pronounced with the stress on the second syllable: a-rith-me-tic. Its adjectival form, on the other hand, places the stress on the first and third syllables: a-rith-met-ic. To avoid confusion between the noun and adjective, the adjectival form arithmetical is often used, being pronounced a-rith-met-ic-al.

title: Definition:Arithmetic Function
snippet: An arithmetic function is a real-valued or complex-valued function defined on the strictly positive integers. That is, a mapping: $f: \Z_{>0} \to \R$ or: $f: \Z_{>0} \to \C$

title: Definition:Arithmetic Function/Also known as
snippet: == Arithmetic Function: Also known as == An arithmetic function is also known as an arithmetical function. The term number-theoretic function can sometimes be seen.

title: Definition:Arithmetic Function/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Arithmetic Function == In the context of an arithmetic function, the word arithmetic is pronounced with the stress on the first and third syllables: a-rith-me-tic, rather than on the second syllable: a-rith-me-tic. This is because the word is being used in its adjectival form.

title: Definition:Arithmetic Geometry
snippet: Arithmetic geometry is the application of techniques from algebraic geometry to problems in number theory.

title: Definition:Arithmetic Mean
snippet: Let $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n \in \R$ be real numbers. The arithmetic mean of $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is defined as: {{eqn | l = A_n | o = := | r = \dfrac 1 n \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n x_k | c = }} {{eqn | r = \dfrac {x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n} n | c = }} That is, to find out the arithmetic mean of a set of numbers, add them all up and divide by how many there are.

title: Definition:Arithmetic Mean/Also known as
snippet: == Arithmetic Mean: Also known as == The arithmetic mean is the quantity that is usually referred to in natural language as the "average" of a set of numbers. It is also known as: the common average the common mean the mean value just the mean. In the context of probability theory, the arithmetic mean of a random variable is often used as a synonym for its expectation.

title: Definition:Arithmetic Mean/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Arithmetic Mean == In the context of an arithmetic mean, the word arithmetic is pronounced with the stress on the first and third syllables: a-rith-me-tic, rather than on the second syllable: a-rith-me-tic. This is because the word is being used in its adjectival form. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Arithmetic Ordered Set
snippet: Let $L = \struct {S, \vee, \preceq}$ be a bounded below join semilattice. $L$ is arithmetic $L$ is algebraic $\map K L$ is meet closed where $\map K L$ denotes the compact subset of $L$.

title: Definition:Arithmetic Progression
snippet: The term arithmetic progression is used to mean one of the following:

title: Definition:Arithmetic Sequence
snippet: An arithmetic sequence is a finite sequence $\sequence {a_k}$ in $\R$ or $\C$ defined as: $a_k = a_0 + k d$ for $k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots, n - 1$ Thus its general form is: $a_0, a_0 + d, a_0 + 2 d, a_0 + 3 d, \ldots, a_0 + \paren {n - 1} d$

title: Definition:Arithmetic Sequence/Also known as
snippet: == Arithmetic Sequence: Also known as == An arithmetic sequence is also known as a linear sequence. The term arithmetic progression is usual. Arithmetical progression is also sometimes seen. Hence the abbreviation A.P. is well-understood. However, use of the term progression, although ubiquitous in the literature, is deprecated on on account of the fact that the term is used both for arithmetic sequence and arithmetic series, and this can be a source of confusion.

title: Definition:Arithmetic Sequence/Common Difference
snippet: Let $\sequence {a_k}$ be the arithmetic sequence: $a_k = a_0 + k d$ for $k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots, n - 1$ The term $d$ is the common difference of $\sequence {a_k}$.

title: Definition:Arithmetic Sequence/Initial Term
snippet: Let $\sequence {a_k}$ be the arithmetic sequence: $a_k = a_0 + k d$ for $k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots, n - 1$ The term $a_0$ is the initial term of $\sequence {a_k}$. Category:Definitions/Arithmetic Sequences

title: Definition:Arithmetic Sequence/Last Term
snippet: Let $\sequence {a_k}$ be the arithmetic sequence: $a_k = a_0 + k d$ for $k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots, n - 1$ The term $a_{n-1} = a_0 + \paren {n - 1} d$ is the last term of $\sequence {a_k}$. Category:Definitions/Arithmetic Sequences

title: Definition:Arithmetic Sequence/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Arithmetic Sequence == In the context of an arithmetic sequence or arithmetic-geometric sequence, the word arithmetic is pronounced with the stress on the first and third syllables: a-rith-me-tic, rather than on the second syllable: a-rith-me-tic. This is because the word is being used in its adjectival form. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Arithmetic Series
snippet: An arithmetic series is a series whose underlying sequence is an arithmetic sequence: {{eqn | l = S_n | r = \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} a + k d | c = }} {{eqn | r = a + \paren {a + d} + \paren {a + 2 d} + \cdots + \paren {a + \paren {n - 1} d} | c = }}

title: Definition:Arithmetical Hierarchy
snippet: For every $i \in \N$, $\Sigma_i$ and $\Pi_i$ are sets of well-formed formulae in the language of arithmetic. They are defined recursively as follows: Let $\phi$ be logically equivalent to a well-formed formula in the language of arithmetic containing no quantifiers. Then $\phi \in \Sigma_0$ and $\phi \in \Pi_0$ Let $\phi$ be logically equivalent to $Q_1 Q_2 \dotsm Q_k \psi$ where: $\psi \in \Pi_n$ $Q_j$ is either $\exists x$ or $\forall x < y$, for some variable $x$ and term $y$ Then $\phi \in \Sigma_{n \mathop + 1}$.

title: Definition:Arity/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Arity == The term arity is a [http://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/neologism neologism] generated from the -ary suffix of the specific terms unary, binary and so on. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Arm of Angle/Also known as
snippet: == Arm of Angle: Also known as == The arms of an angle are also known as its sides.

title: Definition:Array
snippet: An array is an arrangement (usually rectangular) of objects of the same type (usually numbers) such that the relations between the entries borne by their relative positions in that arrangement have a particular significance.

title: Definition:Array/Also known as
snippet: == Array: Also known as == In the world of computer science, an array is often referred to as a subscripted variable.

title: Definition:Array/Column
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be an array. The columns of $\mathbf A$ are the lines of elements reading down the page.

title: Definition:Array/Diagonal
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ be an array. The diagonals are the lines of elements of $\mathbf A$ running from: $(1): \quad$ the element in the first row and first column running downwards and to the right $(2): \quad$ the element in the first row and last column running downwards and to the left $(3): \quad$ the element in the last row and first column running upwards and to the right $(4): \quad$ the element in the last row and last column running upwards and to the left If $m = n$, that is, if $\mathbf A$ is a square array, then $(1)$ and $(4)$ coincide, and $(2)$ and $(3)$ also…

title: Definition:Array/Dimensions
snippet: Let $\sqbrk a_{m n}$ be an $m \times n$ array. Then the parameters $m$ and $n$ are known as the dimensions of the array. The array is not limited to $1$ or $2$ dimensions, but may conceptually have as many dimensions as may be needed. It will, however, be noted that the visualizaton and depiction of an array of more than $2$ dimensions can offer challenges.

title: Definition:Array/Element
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be an array. The individual $n \times n$ symbols that go to form $\mathbf L$ are known as the elements of $\mathbf L$. The element at row $i$ and column $j$ is called element $\tuple {i, j}$ of $\mathbf A$, and can be written $a_{i j}$, or $a_{i, j}$ if $i$ and $j$ are of more than one character. If the indices are still more complicated coefficients and further clarity is required, then the form $\map a {i, j}$ can be used. Note that the first subscript determines the row, and the second the column, of the array where the element is positioned.

title: Definition:Array/Element/Absolute Address
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be an array. When referring to a specific element of $\mathbf A$ directly by its indices $\tuple {i, j}$, those indices can be referred to as the absolute address of that element. This terminology is most often seen in the context of computer spreadsheet programs.

title: Definition:Array/Element/Index
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be an $m \times n$ array. Let $a_{i j}$ be an element of $\mathbf A$. Then the subscripts $i$ and $j$ are referred to as the indices (singular: index) of $a_{i j}$.

title: Definition:Array/Row
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be an array. The rows of $\mathbf A$ are the lines of elements reading across the page.

title: Definition:Array/Square
snippet: An array whose dimensions are equal is called a square array. That is, a square array is an array which has the same number of rows as it has columns. A square array $\sqbrk a_{n n}$ is usually denoted $\sqbrk a_n$.

title: Definition:Array/Square/Order
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be an $n \times n$ square array. That is, let $\mathbf A$ have $n$ rows (and by definition $n$ columns). Then the order of $\mathbf A$ is defined as being $n$. Category:Definitions/Arrays

title: Definition:Array (Statistics)
snippet: In the context of statistics, an array is a display of a set of data, often arranged into whatever order may be appropriate.

title: Definition:Arrow
snippet: Category Theory: Arrow: another word for morphism Arrow Functor Arrow Category Graph Theory: Edge of Graph Arc of Digraph Topology: Arrow Topology Logic: Quine Arrow: The symbol used to denote the logical NOR operation Linear Algebra and Physics: Another name for a vector quantity, particularly when rendered $\vec x$

title: Definition:Artificial Intelligence
snippet: Artificial intelligence is a branch of computer science which studies intelligent behavior, and attempts to model it via computing techniques.

snippet: {{eqn | l = C_{\text {Artin} } | r = \prod_{\text {$p$ prime} } \paren {1 - \dfrac 1 {p^2 - p} } | c = }}

snippet: == Artin Stack: Also known as == An Artin stack is also known as an algebraic stack. Category:Definitions/Stacks

snippet: Definition:Artinian Ring Definition:Artinian Module Definition:Artinian Scheme Definition:Artinian Topological Space

title: Definition:Artinian Module
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $M$ be an $A$-module.

title: Definition:Artinian Module/Definition 1
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $M$ be an $A$-module. $M$ is a Artinian module : $M$ satisfies the descending chain condition.

title: Definition:Artinian Module/Definition 2
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $M$ be an $A$-module $M$ is a Artinian module : $M$ satisfies the minimal condition.

title: Definition:Artinian Ring
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Then $A$ is Artinian it is Artinian as an $A$-module.

title: Definition:Asankhyeya
snippet: Asankhyeya is a Jaina word for a koti to the power of $20$: that is: $10 \, 000 \, 000^{20} = 10^{140}$

title: Definition:Ascending Chain Condition
snippet: Let $\struct {P, \le}$ be an ordered set. Then $S$ is said to have the ascending chain condition every increasing sequence $x_1 \le x_2 \le x_3 \le \cdots$ with $x_i \in P$ eventually terminates: there is $n \in \N$ such that $x_n = x_{n + 1} = \cdots$.

title: Definition:Ascending Chain Condition/Ideals
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring. Then $R$ is said to have the ascending chain condition on ideals every increasing sequence of ideals stabilizes.

title: Definition:Ascending Chain Condition/Module
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $M$ be an $R$-module. Let $\struct {D, \subseteq}$ be a set of submodules of $M$ ordered by inclusion. Then $M$ is said to have the ascending chain condition on submodules every increasing sequence $N_1 \subseteq N_2 \subseteq N_3 \subseteq \cdots$ with $N_i \in D$ eventually stabilizes: $\exists k \in \N: \forall n \in \N, n \ge k: N_n = N_{n + 1}$

title: Definition:Assignment Problem
snippet: An assignment problem is a problem in operations research in which objects of one type are to be matched with the same number of objects of another type in such a way as to optimize a given criterion.

title: Definition:Assignment for Structure
snippet: Let $\LL_1$ be the language of predicate logic. Let $\mathrm{VAR}$ be the collection of variables of $\LL_1$. Let $\AA$ be an $\LL_1$-structure on a set $A$. An assignment for $\AA$ is a mapping $\sigma$ such that: the codomain of $\sigma$ is $A$ the domain of $\sigma$ is a subset of $\mathrm{VAR}$ That is, the domain of $\sigma$ contains only variables, and maps them to elements of $A$.

title: Definition:Assignment for Structure/Formula
snippet: Let $\LL_1$ be the language of predicate logic. Let $\mathrm{VAR}$ be the collection of variables of $\LL_1$. Let $\AA$ be an $\LL_1$-structure on a set $A$. Let $\mathbf A$ be a well-formed formula of $\LL_1$. Denote with $\map V {\mathbf A}$ the variables which occur freely in $\mathbf A$. An assignment for $\mathbf A$ in $\AA$ is a mapping $\sigma$ with codomain $A$, whose domain is subject to the following condition: $\map V {\mathbf A} \subseteq \Dom \sigma \subseteq \mathrm{VAR}$ That is, the domain of $\sigma$ contains only variables, and at least those with a free occurrence in…

title: Definition:Assignment for Structure/Term
snippet: Let $\LL_1$ be language of predicate logic. Let $\mathrm{VAR}$ be the collection of variables of $\LL_1$. Let $\AA$ be an $\LL_1$-structure on a set $A$. Let $\tau$ be a term of $\LL_1$. Denote with $\map V \tau$ the variables which occur in $\tau$. An assignment for $\tau$ in $\AA$ is a mapping $\sigma$ with codomain $A$, whose domain is subject to the following condition: $\map V \tau \subseteq \Dom \sigma \subseteq \mathrm{VAR}$ That is, the domain of $\sigma$ contains only variables, and at least those which occur in $\tau$.

title: Definition:Associate/Commutative and Unitary Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $x, y \in R$. Then $x$ and $y$ are associates (in $R$) there exists a unit $u$ of $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ such that $u \circ x = y$.

title: Definition:Associate/Integers
snippet: Let $x, y \in \Z$. Then $x$ is an associate of $y$ they are both divisors of each other. That is, $x$ and $y$ are associates $x \divides y$ and $y \divides x$.

title: Definition:Associate/Integral Domain
snippet: Let $\struct {D, +, \circ}$ be an integral domain. Let $x, y \in D$.

title: Definition:Associate/Integral Domain/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {D, +, \circ}$ be an integral domain. Let $x, y \in D$. $x$ is an associate of $y$ (in $D$) they are both divisors of each other. That is, $x$ and $y$ are associates (in $D$) $x \divides y$ and $y \divides x$.

title: Definition:Associate/Integral Domain/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {D, +, \circ}$ be an integral domain. Let $x, y \in D$. $x$ and $y$ are associates (in $D$) : $\ideal x = \ideal y$ where $\ideal x$ and $\ideal y$ denote the ideals generated by $x$ and $y$ respectively.

title: Definition:Associate/Integral Domain/Definition 3
snippet: Let $\struct {D, +, \circ}$ be an integral domain. Let $x, y \in D$. $x$ and $y$ are associates (in $D$) there exists a unit $u$ of $\struct {D, +, \circ}$ such that: $y = u \circ x$ and consequently: $x = u^{-1} \circ y$ That is, $x$ and $y$ are unit multiples of each other.

title: Definition:Associated Bilinear Form
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be a field of characteristic $\Char {\mathbb K} \ne 2$. Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb K$. Let $q : V \to \mathbb K$ be a quadratic form. The bilinear form associated to $q$ is the bilinear form: $b : V \times V \to \mathbb K : \tuple {v, w} \mapsto \dfrac 1 2 \paren {\map q {v + w} - \map q v - \map q w}$

title: Definition:Associated Legendre Function
snippet: The associated Legendre functions are the solutions to Legendre's associated differential equation.

title: Definition:Associated Legendre Function of the First Kind
snippet: Let $m, n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be non-negative integers. The associated Legendre functions of the first kind are the real functions defined and denoted as: $\map { {P_n}^m} x = \paren {1 - x^2}^{m / 2} \dfrac {\d^m} {\d x^m} \map {P_n} x$ where $\map {P_n} x$ is the Legendre polynomial of order $n$.

title: Definition:Associated Legendre Function of the First Kind/Also known as
snippet: == Associated Legendre Function of the First Kind: Also known as == Sources which do not delve deeply into this area often call the associated Legendre functions of the first kind as just the associated Legendre functions. However, the definition of the associated Legendre function is considerably more general than this.

title: Definition:Associated Prime of Module
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $M$ be a module over $A$. Let $\mathfrak p$ be a prime ideal in $A$.

title: Definition:Associated Prime of Module/Definition 1
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $M$ be a module over $A$. Let $\mathfrak p$ be a prime ideal in $A$. $\mathfrak p$ is an associated prime of $M$ : $\exists x \in M : \map {\operatorname {Ann}_A} x = \mathfrak p$ where $\map {\operatorname {Ann}_A} x$ is the annihilator of $x$. That is: $\exists x \in M : \set {a \in A : a x = 0} = \mathfrak p$

title: Definition:Associated Prime of Module/Definition 2
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $M$ be a module over $A$. Let $\mathfrak p$ be a prime ideal in $A$. $\mathfrak p$ is an associated prime of $M$ : $M$ contains a submodule which is isomorphic to the quotient ring $A / \mathfrak p$.

title: Definition:Associated Quadratic Form
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be a field. Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb K$. Let $b : V\times V \to \mathbb K$ be a bilinear form. The quadratic form associated to $b$ is the quadratic form: $q : V \to \mathbb K : x \mapsto \map b {x, x}$

title: Definition:Associated Section of Étalé Space
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\FF$ be a presheaf of sets. Let $\map {\operatorname {\acute Et} } \FF$ be its étalé space. Let $U \subseteq S$ be open in $T$. Let $s \in \map \FF U$ be a section. The associated section of $\map {\operatorname {\acute Et} } \FF$ is the mapping: $\overline s : U \to \map {\operatorname {\acute Et} } \FF: x \mapsto \tuple {x, s_x}$ where $s_x$ is the image in the stalk at $x$.

title: Definition:Associative/Historical Note
snippet: == Associative: Historical Note == The term associative was coined by in about $1844$ while thinking about octonions, which aren't.

title: Definition:Associative Algebra
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring. Let $\struct {A_R, *}$ be an algebra over $R$. Then $\struct {A_R, *}$ is an associative algebra $*$ is an associative operation. That is: $\forall a, b, c \in A_R: \paren {a * b} * c = a * \paren {b * c}$

title: Definition:Associative Operation
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\circ : S \times S \to S$ be a binary operation. Then $\circ$ is associative : $\forall x, y, z \in S: \paren {x \circ y} \circ z = x \circ \paren {y \circ z}$

title: Definition:Associator
snippet: Let $\struct {A_R, \oplus}$ be an algebra over a ring. Consider the trilinear mapping $\sqbrk {\cdot, \cdot, \cdot}: A_R^3 \to A_R$ defined as: $\forall a, b, c \in A_R: \sqbrk {a, b, c} := \paren {a \oplus b} \oplus c - a \oplus \paren {b \oplus c}$ Then $\sqbrk {\cdot, \cdot, \cdot}$ is known as the associator of $\struct {A_R, \oplus}$. It can be considered a measure of how much associativity of $\oplus$ fails in $\struct {A_R, \oplus}$.

title: Definition:Assumption
snippet: An assumption is a statement which is introduced into an argument, whose truth value is (temporarily) accepted as true. In mathematical expositions, the keyword let is often the indicator here that an assumption is going to be introduced.

title: Definition:Assumption/Also defined as
snippet: == Assumption: Also defined as == Some authors use the term assumption to mean the antecedent of a conditional statement.

title: Definition:Astroid
snippet: An astroid is a hypocycloid with $4$ cusps. 400px

title: Definition:Astroid/Also known as
snippet: == Astroid: Also known as == Some sources do not recognise the name astroid, but instead just refer to it as what it is, that is: a hypocycloid with $4$ cusps. Some sources refer to the astroid as a star curve.

title: Definition:Astrolabe
snippet: An astrolabe is a device for measuring the celestial altitude of a celestial body. It consists of a series of disks on which are shown the positions of prominent stars. These are aligned with their positions on what can be seen of the celestial sphere, and hence obtain a reading of their altitudes.

title: Definition:Astrolabe/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Astrolabe == The astrolabe dates to the time of , although some sources credit it invention to . wrote a detailed treatise on the astrolabe. It is supposed that may have used an astrolabe to provide the data for his . Some authors attribute the invention of the astrolabe to , based on a misinterpretation of a letter written by one of her students, but it is well established that it had been invented some $500$ years earlier. Use of the astrolabe was adopted by the medieval Arab world, where its design was made considerably more sophisticated and intricate.

title: Definition:Astrolabe/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Astrolabe == The word astrolabe derives ultimately from the Greek word astrolabos from astron (star) and lambanein (to take). Hence it literally means star-taker. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Astronomical Coordinate System
snippet: An astronomical coordinate system is a coordinate system used for locating the position of bodies in the celestial sphere. In such systems, there is no indication of the distance of such bodies from Earth.

title: Definition:Astronomical Distance Units
snippet: This page gathers together various units of measurement used in astronomy.

title: Definition:Astronomical Distance Units/Astronomical Unit
snippet: The astronomical unit is a derived unit of length. It is defined as being $149 \, 597 \, 870 \, 700$ metres. The astronomical unit is the standard unit of measurement used by astronomers when discussing distances within the solar system. It is derived as the approximate mean distance from the center of Earth to the center of the Sun.

title: Definition:Astronomical Distance Units/Light Year
snippet: The light year is a derived unit of length. It is derived as the distance travelled by light in a vacuum over the course of $1$ Julian year ($365.25$ days). It is defined as being exactly $9 \, 460 \, 730 \, 472 \, 580 \, 800$ metres. The light year is a standard unit of measurement used by astronomers when discussing distances between stars and galaxies, particularly in popular and non-scientific literature. Serious astronomers use the term parsec instead.

title: Definition:Astronomical Distance Units/Parsec
snippet: The parsec is a derived unit of length. It is derived as the distance at which $1$ astronomical unit subtends an angle of $1$ second of angle. It is therefore exactly $\dfrac {648 \, 000} \pi$ astronomical units. The parsec is the standard unit of measurement used by astronomers when discussing distances.

title: Definition:Astronomical Triangle
snippet: Let $P$ be a point on the celestial sphere $\CC$. Consider the following $3$ great circles on $\CC$: the great circle between $P$ and the zenith the great circle between $P$ and the north celestial pole the great circle between the zenith and the north celestial pole. The spherical triangle formed by these $3$ great circles is called the astronomical triangle $P$.

title: Definition:Astronomical Unit/Approximate Values
snippet: The astronomical unit is approximately $150 \, 000 \, 000 \, \mathrm {k m}$, or $93$ million (international) miles.

title: Definition:Astronomical Unit/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Astronomical Unit: Conversion Factors == {{eqn | o = \approx | r = 1 \cdotp 58125 \, 07409 \, 8 \times 10^{-5} | c = light years }} {{eqn | o = \approx | r = 4 \cdotp 84813 \, 68111 \times 10^{-6} | c = parsec }}

title: Definition:Astronomy
snippet: Astronomy is the branch of physics which studies the features which can be seen in the sky that are outside the atmosphere of Earth. Certain of its mathematical aspects can be considered a subfield of solid geometry.

title: Definition:Astronomy/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Astronomy == The word astronomy derives from the Greek for naming of stars. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Astrophysics
snippet: Astrophysics is the branch of physics which studies the internal nature of celestial bodies as opposed to their positions and movements.

title: Definition:Asymmetric Figure
snippet: A geometric figure is asymmetric it has no symmetries apart from the identity mapping.

title: Definition:Asymmetric Figure/Plane
snippet: A plane figure is asymmetric it has neither: (plane) bilateral symmetry nor: rotational symmetry.

title: Definition:Asymmetric Relation
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation in $S$.

title: Definition:Asymmetric Relation/Also defined as
snippet: == Asymmetric Relation: Also defined as == Some sources (possibly erroneously or carelessly) gloss over the differences between this and the definition for an antisymmetric relation, and end up using a definition for antisymmetric which comes too close to one for asymmetric. An example is : [After having discussed antireflexivity] ... antisymmetry expresses the additional fact that at most one of the possibilities $a \mathrel \RR b$ or $b \mathrel \RR a$ can take place. Some sources specifically define a relation as anti-symmetric what has been defined on as asymmetric.

title: Definition:Asymmetric Relation/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation in $S$. $\RR$ is asymmetric : $\tuple {x, y} \in \RR \implies \tuple {y, x} \notin \RR$ That is: $x \mathop \RR y \implies \neg \paren {y \mathop \RR x}$

title: Definition:Asymmetric Relation/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation in $S$. $\RR$ is asymmetric it and its inverse are disjoint: $\RR \cap \RR^{-1} = \O$

title: Definition:Asymmetry
snippet: An object or an operation which is not symmetric is defined as asymmetric.

title: Definition:Asymptote
snippet: $y$-axis, and the line $x = y$ (red)]] Let $C$ be a curve in the plane. Let $L$ be a line (usually straight) such that the distance between $C$ and $L$ approaches zero as they tend to infinity. Then $L$ is an asymptote to (or of) $C$.

title: Definition:Asymptote/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Asymptote == The word asymptote is derived from the Greek ἀσύμπτωτος (asumptōtos) which means not falling together. It was coined by during his analysis of conic sections. The adjectival form of asymptote is asymptotic.

title: Definition:Asymptotic Distribution
snippet: For all $n \in \N$, Let $Z_n$ be a random variable. The asymptotic distribution of $Z_n$ is the limiting probability distribution as $n \to \infty$.

title: Definition:Asymptotic Equality/Also known as
snippet: == Asymptotic Equality: Also known as == If $f \sim g$, then $f$ and $g$ are also said to be asymptotically equivalent. Such $f$ and $g$ are also (together) referred to as asymptotic functions.

title: Definition:Asymptotic Equality/General Definition/Point
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $V$ be a normed vector space over $\R$ or $\C$ with norm $\norm {\, \cdot \,}$. Let $f, g: S \to V$ be mappings. Let $x_0 \in X$. Then: $f$ is asymptotically equal to $g$ as $x \to x_0$ $f - g = \map \oo g$ as $x \to x_0$ where $\oo$ denotes little-$\oo$ notation.

title: Definition:Asymptotic Equality/Notation
snippet: == Asymptotic Equality: Notation == The notation $a_n \sim b_n$ and $f \sim g$ is frequently seen to denote asymptotic equality.

title: Definition:Asymptotic Equality/Real Functions/Infinity
snippet: Let $f$ and $g$ real functions defined on $\R$. Then: $f$ is asymptotically equal to $g$ $\dfrac {\map f x} {\map g x} \to 1$ as $x \to +\infty$. That is, the larger the $x$, the closer $f$ gets (relatively) to $g$.

title: Definition:Asymptotic Equality/Real Functions/Point
snippet: Let $f$ and $g$ real functions defined on a punctured neighborhood of $x_0$. Then: $f$ is asymptotically equal to $g$ at $x_0$ $\dfrac {\map f x} {\map g x} \to 1$ as $x \to x_0$. That is, the closer $x$ gets to $x_0$, the closer $f$ gets (relatively) to $g$.

title: Definition:Asymptotic Equality/Sequences
snippet: Let $\sequence {a_n}$ and $\sequence {b_n}$ be sequences in $\R$.

title: Definition:Asymptotic Equality/Sequences/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\sequence {a_n}$ and $\sequence {b_n}$ be sequences in $\R$. Let $b_n \ne 0$ for all $n$. $\sequence {a_n}$ is asymptotically equal to $\sequence {b_n}$ : $\ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \dfrac {a_n} {b_n} = 1$

title: Definition:Asymptotic Equality/Sequences/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\sequence {a_n}$ and $\sequence {b_n}$ be sequences in $\R$. $\sequence {a_n}$ is asymptotically equal to $\sequence {b_n}$ : $a_n - b_n = \map \oo {b_n}$ where $\oo$ denotes little-$\oo$ notation.

title: Definition:Asymptotic Equality/Sequences/Definition 3
snippet: Let $\sequence {a_n}$ and $\sequence {b_n}$ be sequences in $\R$. $\sequence {a_n}$ is asymptotically equal to $\sequence {b_n}$ : $a_n - b_n = \map \oo {a_n}$ where $\oo$ denotes little-$\oo$ notation.

title: Definition:Asymptotic Relative Efficiency
snippet: Let $T_1$ and $T_2$ be estimators of a parameter $\theta$. The asymptotic relative efficiency of $T_1$ $T_2$ is the limit of the relative efficiency of $T_1$ $T_2$ as $n \to \infty$.

title: Definition:Asymptotic Series
snippet: An asymptotic series is a divergent series of the form: $a_0 + \dfrac {a_1} x + \dfrac {a_1} {x_2} + \cdots + \dfrac {a_n} {x_n} + \cdots$ where $a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots$ are constants. This is an asymptotic representation of a function $\map f x$ if: $\forall n \in \N: \ds \lim_{\size x \mathop \to \infty} x^n \paren {\map f x - \map {s_n} x} = 0$ where $s_n$ is the sum of the first $n$ terms.

title: Definition:Asymptotic Stability
snippet: Let $S$ be a dynamical system. Let $d$ be a metric on the phase space of $S$. Let $E$ be an equilibrium of $S$ which is Lyapunov stable. Then $E$ is in a state of asymptotic stability, or is asymptotically stable, : $\forall \delta \in \R_{>0}: \map d {\map x 0, E} < \delta \implies \map x t \to E$ as $t \to \infty$ where $\map x t$ denotes the evolution of $S$ following the perturbation. That is, $E$ is asymptotically stable $S$ converges to the original solution.

title: Definition:Asymptotically Non-Negative
snippet: Let $f$ be a real-valued functions. Let $f$ be such that: $\exists n_0 \in \Dom f: \forall n \ge n_0: \map f n \ge 0$ That is, $f$ is non-negative when $n$ is sufficiently large. Then $\map f n$ is an asymptotically non-negative.

title: Definition:Asymptotically Tight Bound
snippet: Let $f$ and $g$ be real-valued functions. Let $f$ and $g$ be such that: $f \in \map \Theta g$ where $\Theta$ denotes $\Theta$ notation. That is: $\exists c_1, c_2 \in \R: \exists n_0 \in \Dom f: \forall n \ge n_0: c_1 \map g n \le \map f n \le c_2 \map g n$ That is, $f$ is equal to $g$ within a constant factor when $n$ is sufficiently large. Then $\map g n$ is an asymptotically tight bound for $\map f n$.

title: Definition:Asymptotics
snippet: Suppose the task to evaluate a certain number is sufficiently unwieldy that it becomes impractical to calculate it directly. In such cases it is frequently useful to have a completely different method to calculate an approximation to that number. Let the accuracy of this approximation improve as the number of operations involved in its calculation increases. The field of mathematics concerned with studying such techniques is called asymptotics.

title: Definition:Atlas
snippet: Let $M$ be a topological space. An atlas of class $C^k$ and dimension $d$ on $M$ is a set of $d$-dimensional charts $\mathscr F = \family {\struct {U_\alpha, \phi_\alpha}: \alpha \in A}$ indexed by some set $A$ such that: $(1): \quad \ds \bigcup_{\alpha \mathop \in A} U_\alpha = M$ $(2): \quad$ Every two charts $\struct {U, \phi}$ and $\struct {V, \psi}$ are $C^k$-compatible.

title: Definition:Atlas/Also known as
snippet: == Atlas: Also known as == Some sources refer to an atlas as a pre-differentiable structure. Some sources call an atlas a pre-atlas, and refer to a maximal atlas simply as an atlas.

title: Definition:Atlas/Maximal Atlas
snippet: Let $M$ be a topological space. Let $A$ be a $d$-dimensional atlas of class $C^k$ of $M$.

title: Definition:Atlas/Maximal Atlas/Definition 1
snippet: Let $M$ be a topological space. Let $A$ be a $d$-dimensional atlas of class $C^k$ of $M$. $A$ is a maximal $C^k$-atlas of dimension $d$ $A$ is not strictly contained in another $C^k$-atlas.

title: Definition:Atlas/Maximal Atlas/Definition 2
snippet: Let $M$ be a topological space. Let $A$ be a $d$-dimensional atlas of class $C^k$ of $M$. $A$ is a maximal $C^k$-atlas $A$ contains all charts of $M$ that are $C^k$-compatible with $A$.

title: Definition:Atlas/Maximal Atlas/Definition 3
snippet: Let $M$ be a topological space. Let $A$ be a $d$-dimensional atlas of class $C^k$ of $M$. $A$ is a maximal $C^k$-atlas $A$ is a maximal element of some differentiable structure, partially ordered by inclusion. That is, a maximal element of some equivalence class of the set of atlases of class $\CC^k$ on $M$ under the equivalence relation of compatibility.

title: Definition:Atlas/Maximal Smooth Atlas
snippet: Let $M$ be a topological manifold. Let $A$ be a $d$-dimensional atlas of $M$. $A$ is a $d$-dimensional maximal smooth atlas of $M$ $A$ is both maximal and smooth.

title: Definition:Atlas/Smooth Atlas
snippet: Let $M$ be a topological space. A smooth atlas on $M$ is a $C^\infty$-atlas on $M$.

title: Definition:Atmospheric Pressure
snippet: Atmospheric pressure is the physical property defined as the pressure at a point in the atmosphere (of Earth, usually) caused by the gravitational force on the air.

title: Definition:Atom
snippet: Logic: Atom: a concept at an irreducible level of simplicity, for example: a simple statement in propositional logic Measure theory: Atom of a measure Abstract algebra: Atom of a $\sigma$-algebra Irreducible element of an integral domain Lattice Theory: Atom of a lattice Physics: Atom: the smallest piece of matter that can exist of a particular type of substance Whatever this is: Definition:Atomic Formula

title: Definition:Atom/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Atom == The word atom comes from the Greek ἄτομον, meaning unbreakable or indecomposable. It is pronounced with a short a, as at-tom, as opposed to ay-tom. Category:Definitions/Logic

title: Definition:Atom (Logic)
snippet: In a particular branch of logic, certain concepts are at such a basic level of simplicity they can not be broken down into anything simpler. Those concepts are called atoms or described as atomic. Different branches of logic admit different atoms.

title: Definition:Atom (Logic)/Propositional Logic
snippet: In propositional logic, the atoms are simple statements.

title: Definition:Atom (Physics)
snippet: An atom (in the context of physics and chemistry) is the smallest piece of matter that can exist of a particular type of substance. Atoms can be subdivided into smaller particles, but then it ceases to be that substance.

title: Definition:Atom (Physics)/Classical
snippet: The classical model of the atom is as a hard spherical body which is electrically neutral. In this model, atoms exert no forces on one another until they are brought into contact, at which point they cannot be brought any closer together, no matter how hard they are pushed to do so.

title: Definition:Atom (Physics)/Diameter
snippet: The diameter of an atom (considered approximately spherical) is between about $1$ and $5$ angstroms.

title: Definition:Atom (Physics)/Nucleus
snippet: The nucleus of an atom is the relatively dense core at its center. It consists (to a first degree of approximation) of a number of protons and a similar number of neutrons. The number of protons determines the nature of the chemical element which consists of aggregations of instances of the atom. The number of neutrons determines the isotope of the element.

title: Definition:Atom of Countably Generated Sigma-Algebra
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\Sigma$ be a countably generated $\sigma$-algebra of $X$. Let $x \in X$. Then: $ \ds \sqbrk x_\Sigma = \bigcap \set {A \mathop \in \Sigma : x \in A }$ is called the atom of $\Sigma$ containing $x$.

title: Definition:Atom of Lattice
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \preceq}$ be a lattice. An atom of $\struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \preceq}$ is an element $A \in S$ such that: $\forall B \in S: B \preceq A, B \ne A \implies B = \bot$ $A \ne \bot$ where $\bot$ denotes the bottom of $\struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \preceq}$.

title: Definition:Atom of Lattice/Also defined as
snippet: == Atom of Lattice: Also defined as == Some sources omit the stipulation that an atom of a lattice is not the bottom of that lattice. By definition of bottom, there exist no $B$ such that $B \prec \bot$. Hence $B = \bot$ is vacuously true. Hence: $\forall B \in S: B \prec \bot \implies B = \bot$ is true. That is, without explicitly stating that an atom is not the bottom, $\bot$ would be classified as an atom vacuously.

title: Definition:Atom of Lattice/Mistake
snippet: == Source Work == atom

title: Definition:Atom of Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space.

title: Definition:Atom of Measure/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. An element $x \in X$ is an atom (of $\mu$) : $(1): \quad \set x \in \Sigma$ $(2): \quad \map \mu {\set x} > 0$

title: Definition:Atom of Measure/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. An element $x \in X$ is an atom (of $\mu$) : $(1): \quad$ for every $y \subseteq x$, either $\map \mu {\set y} = 0$ or $\map \mu {\set y} = \map \mu {\set x}$ $(2): \quad \map \mu {\set x} > 0$

title: Definition:Atom of Propositional Logic/Also defined as
snippet: == Atom of Propositional Logic: Also defined as == Some sources define an atom of propositional logic to mean what is defined in as a literal: a statement variable or the negation of a statement variable. Category:Definitions/Atoms of Propositional Logic

title: Definition:Atom of Propositional Logic/Also known as
snippet: == Atom of Propositional Logic: Also known as == An atom of propositional logic is also known by some sources in the longer form atomic sentence. Some sources use the term indecomposable sentence.

title: Definition:Atom of Sigma-Algebra
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $E \in \Sigma$ be non-empty. $E$ is said to be an atom (of $\Sigma$) it satisfies: $\forall F \in \Sigma: F \subsetneq E \implies F = \O$ Thus, atoms are the minimal non-empty sets in $\Sigma$ with respect to the subset ordering.

title: Definition:Atomic Charge Density
snippet: Let $B$ be a body of matter. The atomic charge density $\rho_{\text {atomic} }$ of $B$ is the electric charge density within $B$ associated with the atoms that make up $B$. Hence: inside the nucleus $\rho_{\text {atomic} }$ is high and positive in the electron cloud $\rho_{\text {atomic} }$ is negative.

title: Definition:Atomic Electric Field
snippet: Let $B$ be a body of matter. Let $P$ be a point inside $B$. The atomic electric field $\mathbf E_{\text {atomic} }$ at $B$ is the electric field at $P$ caused by the atomic charge density due to the electric charges within the atoms that make up $B$.

title: Definition:Atomic Physics
snippet: Atomic physics is the branch of physics concerned with the structure and behaviour of the atom.

title: Definition:Atomic WFF of Predicate Logic
snippet: An atomic WFF of predicate logic is a WFF not containing any connectives or quantifiers. In the formal grammar of predicate logic, the atomic WFFs are precisely those WFFs which can be formed by only applying the rule $\mathbf W ~ \PP_n$.

title: Definition:Attainable Set
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, A}$ be a digraph. Let $u \in V$. The attainable set of $u$ is the set of all vertices of $G$ which are reachable from $u$.

title: Definition:Attracting Fixed Point
snippet: Let $x_{n + 1} = \map \phi {x_n}$ be a direct iteration for the purpose of finding a solution to the equation: $x = \map \phi x$ for some real function $\phi: \R \to \R$. Let $\alpha$ be such that $\alpha = \map \phi \alpha$. Let $\sequence {\map \phi {x_n} }$ converge to $\alpha$ for $\size {x_0 - \alpha}$ sufficiently small. Then $\alpha$ is known as an attracting fixed point.

title: Definition:Attractor
snippet: Let $S$ be a dynamical system in a space $X$. Let $T$ be an iterated mapping in $S$: $x_{n + 1} = \map T {x_n}$ An attractor is an invariant set $A$ in $X$ towards which nearby points $x$ converge, that is: $T \sqbrk A = A$ $x_n = \map {T^n} x$ approaches $A$ as $n$ increases for points close to $A$.

title: Definition:Augmented Matrix
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a matrix of order $n \times m$. Let $\mathbf B$ be a matrix of order $n \times k$. The augmented matrix of $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ is the block matrix $\begin {pmatrix} \mathbf A & \mathbf B \end {pmatrix}$ of order $n \times \paren {m + k}$.

title: Definition:Aurifeuillian Factorization
snippet: An Aurifeuillian factorization is an operation to find the prime factors of integers of various forms based upon the identity: $a^2 + b^2 = \paren {a - \sqrt {2 a b} + b} \paren {a + \sqrt {2 a b} + b}$ $a^3 + b^3 = \paren {a + b} \paren {a - \sqrt {3 a b} + b} \paren {a + \sqrt {3 a b} + b}$

title: Definition:Aurifeuillian Factorization/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Aurifeuillian Factorizations ==

title: Definition:Autocorrelation
snippet: Let $S$ be a stochastic process giving rise to a time series $T$. The autocorrelation of $S$ at lag $k$ is defined as: $\rho_k := \dfrac {\expect {\paren {z_t - \mu} \paren {z_{t + k} - \mu} } } {\sqrt {\expect {\paren {z_t - \mu}^2} \expect {\paren {z_{t + k} - \mu}^2} } }$ where: $z_t$ is the observation at time $t$ $\mu$ is the mean of $S$ $\expect \cdot$ is the expectation.

title: Definition:Autocorrelation/Also known as
snippet: == Autocorrelation: Also known as == Autocorrelation is also known as serial correlation.

title: Definition:Autocorrelation/Coefficient
snippet: Let $S$ be a stochastic process giving rise to a time series $T$. Let $\rho_k$ denote the autocorrelation of $S$ at lag $k$. $\rho_k$ is known as the autocorrelation coefficient of $S$ at $k$.

title: Definition:Autocorrelation Function
snippet: Let $S$ be a stochastic process giving rise to a time series $T$. Let $\rho_k$ denote the autocorrelation coefficient of $S$ at $k$. The function that maps $k$ to its corresponding $\rho_k$ is referred to as the autocorrelation function.

title: Definition:Autocorrelation Matrix
snippet: Let $S$ be a strictly stationary stochastic process giving rise to a time series $T$. Let $\sequence {s_n}$ be a sequence of $n$ successive values of $T$: $\sequence {s_n} = \tuple {z_1, z_2, \dotsb, z_n}$ The autocorrelation matrix associated with $S$ for $\sequence {s_n}$ is: $\mathbf P_n = \begin {pmatrix} 1 & \rho_1 & \rho_2 & \cdots & \rho_{n - 1} \\ \rho_1 & 1 & \rho_1 & \cdots & \rho_{n - 2} \\ \rho_2 & \rho_1 & 1 & \cdots & \rho_{n - 3} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \rho_{n - 1} & \rho_{n - 2} & \rho_{n - 3} & \cdots & 1 \end {pmatrix}$ where $\rho_k$ is the…

title: Definition:Autocovariance
snippet: Let $S$ be a stochastic process giving rise to a time series $T$. The autocovariance of $S$ at lag $k$ is defined as: $\gamma_k := \cov {z_t, z_{t + k} } = \expect {\paren {z_t - \mu} \paren {z_{t + k} - \mu} }$ where: $z_t$ is the observation at time $t$ $\mu$ is the mean of $S$ $\expect \cdot$ is the expectation.

title: Definition:Autocovariance/Coefficient
snippet: Let $S$ be a stochastic process giving rise to a time series $T$. Let $\gamma_k := \cov {z_t, z_{t + k} }$ denote the autocovariance of $S$ at lag $k$. $\gamma_k$ is known as the autovariance coefficient of $S$ at $k$.

title: Definition:Autocovariance Function
snippet: Let $S$ be a stochastic process giving rise to a time series $T$. Let $\gamma_k$ denote the autocovariance coefficient of $S$ at $k$. The function that maps $k$ to its corresponding $\gamma_k$ is referred to as the autocovariance function.

title: Definition:Autocovariance Matrix
snippet: Let $S$ be a strictly stationary stochastic process giving rise to a time series $T$. Let $\sequence {s_n}$ be a sequence of $n$ successive values of $T$: $\sequence {s_n} = \tuple {z_1, z_2, \dotsb, z_n}$ The autocovariance matrix associated with $S$ for $\sequence {s_n}$ is: $\boldsymbol \Gamma_n = \begin {pmatrix} \gamma_0 & \gamma_1 & \gamma_2 & \cdots & \gamma_{n - 1} \\ \gamma_1 & \gamma_0 & \gamma_1 & \cdots & \gamma_{n - 2} \\ \gamma_2 & \gamma_1 & \gamma_0 & \cdots & \gamma_{n - 3} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \gamma_{n - 1} & \gamma_{n - 2} & \gamma_{n - 3} &…

title: Definition:Automatic Repeat Request
snippet: An automatic repeat request is an error control method for data transmission that uses acknowledgements by the receiver within a defined time period. If the sender has not received an acknowledgement within that time period, the sender automatically repeats the transmission.

title: Definition:Automorphic Function/Complex Analysis
snippet: Let $f$ be a complex function Let $S$ be a group of transformations. Then $f$ is automorphic $S$ : $(1): \quad f$ is analytic except for poles in a region of $\C$ $(2): \quad$ For every $T \in S$, if $z \in D$ then $\map T z \in D$ and: $\map f {\map T z} = \map T {\map f z}$

title: Definition:Automorphic Function (Group Theory)
snippet: Let $G$ be a group with identity $e$. Let $X$ be a set. Let $\phi: G \times X \to X$ be a group action: $\forall \tuple {g, x} \in G \times X: g * x := \map \phi {g, x} \in X$ Let $f: X \to X$ be a mapping. Then $F$ is an automorphic function : $\forall \tuple {g, x} \in G \times X: \map f {g * x} = \map f x$

title: Definition:Automorphic Number
snippet: An automorphic number is a positive integer all of whose powers end in that number.

title: Definition:Automorphism
snippet: Automorphism (Abstract Algebra) Automorphism (Model Theory)

title: Definition:Automorphism/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Automorphism == The word automorphism derives from the Greek morphe (μορφή) meaning form or structure, with the prefix auto- meaning self. Thus automorphism means self structure.

title: Definition:Automorphism (Abstract Algebra)
snippet: An automorphism is an isomorphism from an algebraic structure to itself. This applies to the term isomorphism as used both in the sense of bijective homomorphism as well as that of an order isomorphism. Hence an automorphism is a permutation which is either a homomorphism or an order isomorphism, depending on context.

title: Definition:Automorphism (Abstract Algebra)/Also defined as
snippet: == Automorphism: Also defined as == An automorphism is defined by some sources as: a bijection mapping the elements of a set onto itself, so the domain and codomain are the same that is, as defines a permutation. However, this makes no mention of the structure imposed on that set, which is essential for this definition to be of any use.

title: Definition:Automorphism Group/Group
snippet: Let $\struct {S, *}$ be an algebraic structure. Let $\mathbb S$ be the set of automorphisms of $S$. Then the algebraic structure $\struct {\mathbb S, \circ}$, where $\circ$ denotes composition of mappings, is called the automorphism group of $S$. The structure $\struct {S, *}$ is usually a group. However, this is not necessary for this definition to be valid.

title: Definition:Automorphism Group/Symbol
snippet: == Automorphism Group: Symbol == The automorphism group of an algebraic structure $S$ is denoted on as $\Aut S$.

title: Definition:Automorphism Group/Symbol/Also denoted as
snippet: == Automorphism Group: Symbol == Some sources denote the automorphism group of an algebraic structure $S$ by $\map {\mathscr A} S$.

title: Definition:Autumnal Equinox/Also known as
snippet: == Autumnal Equinox: Also known as == The autumnal equinox is also known as the September equinox or the fall equinox. The term southward equinox can also be seen in contexts requiring hemisphere neutrality. Category:Definitions/Equinoxes

title: Definition:Autumnal Equinox/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Autumnal Equinox == The term autumnal equinox derives from word autumn, which is British English for (the season of) fall, and aequinoctium, from aequus meaning equal and nox meaning night. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Auxiliary
snippet: Differential equations: Auxiliary equation Order theory: Auxiliary relation Geometry: Auxiliary circle Trigonometry: Auxiliary angle

title: Definition:Auxiliary Angle
snippet: Consider the expression: $(1): \quad p \sin x + q \cos x$ where $x \in \R$. Let $(1)$ be expressed in the form: $(2): \quad R \map \cos {x + \alpha}$ or: $(3): \quad R \map \sin {x + \alpha}$ The angle $\alpha$ is known as the auxiliary angle of either $(2)$ or $(3)$ as appropriate.

title: Definition:Auxiliary Circle
snippet: Let $\KK$ be a central conic, that is, an ellipse or a hyperbola. The auxiliary circle of $\KK$ is the eccentric circle whose diameter coincides with the major axis of $\KK$.

title: Definition:Auxiliary Circle/Ellipse
snippet: Let $E$ be an ellipse. The auxiliary circle of $E$ is the eccentric circle whose diameter coincides with the major axis of $E$: 400px In the above diagram, the auxiliary circle of $E$ is the circle $C$.

title: Definition:Auxiliary Circle/Hyperbola
snippet: Let $H$ be a hyperbola. The auxiliary circle of $H$ is the eccentric circle whose diameter coincides with the major axis of $H$: 400px In the above diagram, the auxiliary circle of $H$ is the circle $C$.

title: Definition:Auxiliary Equation
snippet: Let: $(1): \quad y' ' + p y' + q y = 0$ be a constant coefficient homogeneous linear second order ODE. The auxiliary equation of $(1)$ is the quadratic equation: $m^2 + p m + q = 0$

title: Definition:Auxiliary Equation/Also known as
snippet: == Auxiliary Equation: Also known as == Some sources refer to the auxiliary equation as the characteristic equation of $(1)$.

title: Definition:Auxiliary Relation
