title: Definition:Average Acceleration
snippet: Let $B$ be a body in motion. Let $\Bbb I = \closedint {t_1} {t_2}$ be a time interval. Let $\mathbf v_1$ and $\mathbf v_2$ be the velocity of $B$ at $t_1$ and $t_2$ respectively. The average acceleration of $B$ during $\Bbb I$ is defined as the change of velocity during $\Bbb I$ divided by the length of $\Bbb I$: $\overline {\mathbf a} := \dfrac {\mathbf v_2 - \mathbf v_1} {t_2 - t_2}$

title: Definition:Average Speed
snippet: Let $B$ be a body in motion. Let $t$ be the time it takes to travel a distance $d$. The average speed of $B$ is defined as the distance travelled by $B$ divided by the time taken: $s := \dfrac d t$

title: Definition:Average Velocity
snippet: Let $B$ be a body in motion. Let $\Bbb I = \closedint {t_1} {t_2}$ be a time interval. Let $\mathbf s_1$ and $\mathbf s_2$ be the displacement of $B$ at $t_1$ and $t_2$ respectively. The average velocity of $B$ during $\Bbb I$ is defined as the change of displacement during $\Bbb I$ divided by the length of $\Bbb I$: $\overline {\mathbf v} := \dfrac {\mathbf s_2 - \mathbf s_1} {t_2 - t_2}$

title: Definition:Avogadro's Constant
snippet: Avogadro's constant is defined as the number of particles in a mole, expressed in a form where its unit of measurement is the reciprocal mole. Hence its value is defined as: $6 \cdotp 02214 076 \times 10^{23} \, \mathrm {mol^{-1} }$

title: Definition:Avogadro's Constant/Also known as
snippet: == Avogadro's Constant: Also known as == Avogadro's constant can also be seen referred to as the Avogadro constant.

title: Definition:Avogadro's Number
snippet: Avogadro's number is defined as the number of particles in a mole. Its value is defined as: $6 \cdotp 02214 076 \times 10^{23}$ Thus it is the constant of proportion for converting the mass of one mole of a substance to the (arithmetic) mean mass of one molecule of that substance.

title: Definition:Avogadro's Number/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Avogadro's Number == The name Avogadro's number was coined in $1909$ by , who defined it as the number of molecules in exactly $16$ grams of oxygen. In $1971$, Avogadro's number was redefined as the number of atoms in $0.012$ kilograms of carbon-$12$. It was further redefined in $2019$ to have the fixed number $6.02214076 \times 10^{23}$, and to base the mole on that. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Avogadro's Number/Mistake
snippet: == Source Work == $3.$ Physical Constants This mistake can be seen in the $1969$ edition as published by Pergamon International.

title: Definition:Avoirdupois
snippet: The avoirdupois system is one of the three imperial systems of measurement of mass. Its units are defined as follows:

title: Definition:Avoirdupois/Dram
snippet: The dram is an avoirdupois unit of mass.

title: Definition:Avoirdupois/Dram/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Dram == The word dram evolved as a shorter version of the word drachm, which is still in existence as part of the apothecaries' system of weights. The term dram is also used for a measure of liquid. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Avoirdupois/Hundredweight
snippet: The hundredweight is an avoirdupois unit of mass.

title: Definition:Avoirdupois/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Avoirdupois == The word avoirdupois derives from the Norman French word whose literal translation is goods (that is property, or things owned) of weight. The avoir part also means to have in modern French, and derives from the Latin habere. It is pronounced something like av-wah-doo-pwah, although Francophones will be aware that there are further subtleties to this. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Avoirdupois/Ounce
snippet: The ounce is an avoirdupois unit of mass. The gram / kilogram equivalent is defined to be exact.

title: Definition:Avoirdupois/Pound
snippet: The pound is an avoirdupois unit of mass. It is defined as being exactly $453 \cdotp 59237$ grams.

title: Definition:Avoirdupois/Quarter
snippet: The quarter is an avoirdupois unit of mass.

title: Definition:Avoirdupois/Quarter/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Quarter (Avoirdupois) == The word quarter was in common use (and probably still is) in the domestic context, in societies using imperial measurements of mass, to mean a quarter of a pound, that is, $4$ ounces. This particularly applies to old-fashioned retailers of confectionery to children. In the US, the term quarter is used for a quarter of a (short) ton, that is $500$ pounds avoirdupois. It should be clear from the context whether a quarter of a pound, a quarter of a hundredweight or a quarter of a (short) ton is under discussion. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Avoirdupois/Quarter/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Quarter (Avoirdupois) == The word quarter in the context of the imperial systems of measurement of mass derives directly from its definition as $\dfrac 1 4$ (a quarter) of a hundredweight. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Avoirdupois/Quarter/Symbol
snippet: The symbol for the quarter is $\text{qtr}$. Category:Definitions/Mass Category:Definitions/Avoirdupois System

title: Definition:Avoirdupois/Short
snippet: The following unit of mass are variants of the avoirdupois versions:

title: Definition:Avoirdupois/Short/Hundredweight
snippet: The short hundredweight is an avoirdupois unit of mass.

title: Definition:Avoirdupois/Short/Quarter
snippet: The quarter is an avoirdupois unit of mass used mainly in the USA.

title: Definition:Avoirdupois/Short/Ton
snippet: The short ton is an avoirdupois unit of mass.

title: Definition:Avoirdupois/Short/Ton/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Short Ton == The short ton is mainly used in America, where both that and the long ton can be found. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Avoirdupois/Stone
snippet: The stone is an avoirdupois unit of mass. The gram equivalent is exact.

title: Definition:Avoirdupois/Stone/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Stone == The stone was originally used to weigh agricultural commodities. Before standardisation, not only did the stone vary according to commodity, it also varied according to location. While it is commonplace in Britain to report one's weight in stone, in America the weight is not used, and pounds (avoirdupois) are used instead. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Avoirdupois/Stone/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Stone == The plural of stone, in the context of weight avoirdupois, is not stones but stone. When reporting a weight in stone and pounds, it is also customary not actually to say pound. Hence prime.mover would (if asked) report his weight as "$16$ stone $6$" instead of saying "$16$ stones and $6$ pounds" in full. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Avoirdupois/Ton
snippet: The ton is an avoirdupois unit of mass.

title: Definition:Avoirdupois/Ton/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Ton == The word ton derives from the same source as the word tun or tunne, a cask holding $216$ gallons of wine. The word ton is pronounced tun. In colloquial language, the word ton is in common use as a rhetorical flourish for a weight too heavy to be easily managed, for example: This suitcase weighs a ton! It is also motoring slang, at least in Britain, for $100$ miles per hour: Took the beamer up to a ton going up the M6 last night, good job there weren't no fuzz around. The usage is commonly seen as doing the ton, meaning driving at $100$ miles per hour.

title: Definition:Axial Vector/Also known as
snippet: == Axial Vector: Also known as == An axial vector is also known as a pseudovector.

title: Definition:Axial Vector/Definition 1
snippet: An axial vector is a vector quantity $\mathbf V$ used to specify action which takes place around an axis of rotation. In this case, the $\mathbf V$ is considered as acting parallel to the axis about which $\mathbf V$ acts. As for a polar vector, the length of $\mathbf V$ indicates the magnitude of $\mathbf V$. The direction of $\mathbf V$ is determined by convention to be according to the right-hand rule.

title: Definition:Axial Vector/Definition 2
snippet: An axial vector is a vector quantity $\mathbf V$ which is not transformed to its negative when you reverse the axes of the coordinate system in which $\mathbf V$ is embedded.

title: Definition:Axiom
snippet: In all contexts, the definition of the term axiom is by and large the same. That is, an axiom is a statement which is accepted as being true. A statement that is considered an axiom can be described as being axiomatic.

title: Definition:Axiom/Also known as
snippet: An axiom is also known as a postulate. Among ancient Greek philosophers, the term axiom was used for a general truth that was common to everybody (see Euclid's "common notions"), while postulate had a specific application to the subject under discussion. For most authors, the distinction is no longer used, and the terms are generally used interchangeably. This is the position of . However, some believe there is a difference significant enough to matter: ...

title: Definition:Axiom/Formal Systems
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a formal language. Part of defining a proof system $\mathscr P$ for $\LL$ is to specify its axioms. An axiom of $\mathscr P$ is a well-formed formula of $\LL$ that $\mathscr P$ approves of by definition.

title: Definition:Axiom/Formal Systems/Axiom Schema
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a formal language. Part of defining a proof system $\mathscr P$ for $\LL$ is to specify its axiom schemata. An axiom schema is a well-formed formula $\phi$ of $\LL$, except for it containing one or more variables which are outside $\LL$ itself. This formula can then be used to represent an infinite number of individual axioms in one statement. Namely, each of these variables is allowed to take a specified range of values, most commonly WFFs. Each WFF $\psi$ that results from $\phi$ by a valid choice of values for all the variables is then an axiom of $\mathscr P$.

title: Definition:Axiom/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Axiom == The usual plural form of axiom is axioms. However, the form axiomata can also sometimes be found, although it is sometimes considered archaic. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Axiom/Logical
snippet: A logical axiom is an axiom which does not stand in the context of a wider subject matter. That is, it is a statement which is considered as self-evident. Note, however, that there has been disagreement for as long as there have been logicians and philosophers as to whether particular statements are true or not. For example, the Law of Excluded Middle is accepted as axiomatic by philosophers and logicians of the Aristotelian school but is denied by the intuitionist school.

title: Definition:Axiom/Nonlogical
snippet: An axiom which deals with some specific subject matter is known as a nonlogical axiom. Hence it is a statement which is accepted as true for a particular branch of mathematics. Different fields of mathematics usually have different sets of statements which are considered as being axiomatic. So statements which are taken as axioms in one branch of mathematics may be theorems, or irrelevant, in others.

title: Definition:Axiom (Formal Systems)/Also known as
snippet: == Axiom (Formal Systems): Also known as == When $\LL$ is a logical language, then one also speaks of logical axioms instead of (formal system) axioms.

title: Definition:Axiom Schema/Also known as
snippet: == Axiom Schema: Also known as == An axiom schema is also known as just a schema.

title: Definition:Axiom Schema/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Axiom Schema == The plural of axiom schema is correctly axiom schemata, but it is commonplace to see the word schemas used for schemata.

title: Definition:Axiomatic Set Theory
snippet: Axiomatic set theory is a system of set theory which differs from so-called naive set theory in that the sets which are allowed to be generated are strictly constrained by the axioms. The best known systems of axiomatic set theory are: ZF (Zermelo-Fraenkel) ZFC (Zermelo-Fraenkel with the Axiom of Choice). Lesser known examples include: Von Neumann-Bernays-Gödel Set Theory

title: Definition:Axiomatization
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a logical language. Let $\mathscr M$ be a formal semantics for $\LL$. Let $\FF$ be an $\LL$-theory. An axiomatization of $\FF$ is a subset $\AA \subseteq \FF$ such that: $\FF = \set {\phi \in \LL: \AA \models_{\mathscr M} \phi}$ That is, all of $\FF$ is a semantic consequence of $\AA$.

title: Definition:Axiomatization/Axiom
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a logical language. Let $\mathscr M$ be a formal semantics for $\LL$. Let $\FF$ be an $\LL$-theory. Let $\AA$ be an axiomatization of $\FF$. Then a formula $\phi \in \AA$ is called an axiom.

title: Definition:Axis
snippet: An axis is the name used for a general infinite straight line which is particularly significant in some particular way in the study of linear transformations of a real vector space.

title: Definition:Axis/Coordinate Axes
snippet: Consider a coordinate system. One of the reference lines of such a system is called a coordinate axis.

title: Definition:Axis/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Axis == The plural of axis is axes, which is pronounced ax-eez not ax-iz. Compare basis.

title: Definition:Axis/Negative Direction
snippet: Consider a coordinate system whose axes are each aligned with an instance of the real number line $\R$. The direction along an axis in which the corresponding elements of $\R$ are decreasing is called the negative direction. Category:Definitions/Coordinate Axes

title: Definition:Axis/Positive Direction
snippet: Consider a coordinate system whose axes are each aligned with an instance of the real number line $\R$. The direction along an axis in which the corresponding elements of $\R$ are increasing is called the positive direction. Category:Definitions/Coordinate Axes

title: Definition:Axis/X-Axis
snippet: In a cartesian coordinate system, the $x$-axis is the one usually depicted and visualised as going from left to right. It consists of all the points in the real vector space in question (usually either $\R^2$ or $\R^3$) at which all the elements of its coordinates but $x$ are zero.

title: Definition:Axis/Y-Axis
snippet: In a cartesian coordinate system, the $y$-axis is the one usually depicted and visualised as going from "bottom" to "top" of the paper (or screen). It consists of all the points in the real vector space in question (usually either $\R^2$ or $\R^3$) at which all the elements of its coordinates but $y$ are zero.

title: Definition:Axis/Z-Axis
snippet: In a cartesian coordinate system, the $z$-axis is the axis passing through $x = 0, y = 0$ which is perpendicular to both the $x$-axis and the $y$-axis. It consists of all the points in the real vector space in question (usually $\R^3$) at which all the elements of its coordinates but $z$ are zero. As the visual field is effectively two-dimensional, it is not possible to depict a three-dimensional space on a visual presentation (paper, screen and so on) directly. Therefore the representation of the third axis of such a cartesian coordinate system is necessarily a compromise.

title: Definition:Axis/Z-Axis/Right-Hand Rule
snippet: The usual convention for the orientation of the $z$-axis is that of the right-hand rule: Let the coordinate axes be oriented as follows: Let the $x$-axis increase from West to East. Let the $y$-axis increase from South to North. Then the $z$-axis increases from below to above. If the $x$-axis and $y$-axis are aligned with a piece of paper or a screen aligned perpendicular to the line of sight, this translates into the following orientation: Let the $x$-axis increase from left to right. Let the $y$-axis increase from bottom to top.

title: Definition:Axis of Bilateral Symmetry/Also known as
snippet: == Axis of Bilateral Symmetry: Also known as == An axis of bilateral symmetry is also known as just an axis of symmetry, if it is clear that the symmetry under discussion is indeed bilateral.

title: Definition:Axis of Pencil of Planes
snippet: The line of intersection of a pencil of planes $P$ is called the axis of $P$.

title: Definition:Axis of Perspective/Also known as
snippet: == Axis of Perspective/Also known as == The axis of perspective of two figures is also known as the axis of perspectivity.

title: Definition:Axis of Reflection/Also known as
snippet: == Axis of Reflection: Also known as == An axis of reflection is also known as a mirror line.

title: Definition:Axis of Revolution
snippet: Consider a surface of revolution or a solid of revolution generated by $F$ around a straight line $L$. The straight line around which the rotation is being performed is known as the axis of revolution.

title: Definition:Axis of Revolution/Also known as
snippet: == Axis of Revolution: Also known as == An axis of revolution is also known as an axis of rotation. However, that latter term is also used for a general geometrical rotation, not just one used in the generation of a surface of revolution or a solid of revolution.

title: Definition:Axis of Rotation/Also known as
snippet: == Axis of Rotation: Also known as == An axis of rotation of a rotation in the plane is usually called a center of rotation. In British English, this is spelt centre of rotation

title: Definition:Axis of Rotational Symmetry/Also known as
snippet: == Axis of Rotational Symmetry: Also known as == An axis of rotational symmetry is also known as just an axis of symmetry, if it is clear that the symmetry under discussion is indeed rotational.

title: Definition:Axis of Rotational Symmetry/Order
snippet: Let $F$ be a geometric figure. Let $\map R F$ be a rotational symmetry around the axis of symmetry $AB$. Let the order of $R$ be $n$. Then $AB$ is likewise defined as being an axis of order $n$.

title: Definition:Axis of Tractrix/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Axis of Tractrix == Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Axis of Wrench/Also known as
snippet: == Axis of Wrench: Also known as == The axis of a wrench is also known as the Poinsot central axis for .

title: Definition:Azimuth (Astronomy)
snippet: Let $X$ be a point on the celestial sphere. The spherical angle between the principal vertical circle and the vertical circle on which $X$ lies is the azimuth of $X$. The azimuth is usually measured in degrees, $0 \degrees$ to $180 \degrees$ either west or east, depending on whether $X$ lies on the eastern or western hemisphere of the celestial sphere.

title: Definition:Azimuth (Astronomy)/Also defined as
snippet: == Azimuth (in the context of astronomy): Also defined as == Some sources define the azimuth as from $0 \degrees$ to $360 \degrees$ measured east of the principal vertical circle, that is, clockwise.

title: Definition:Azimuth (Astronomy)/Symbol
snippet: == Azimuth (Astronomy): Symbol == The symbol for azimuth (in the context of astronomy) is $A$.

title: Definition:B-Algebra
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. $\struct {X, \circ}$ is a $B$-algebra $\struct {X, \circ}$ satisfies the $B$-algebra axioms:

title: Definition:B-Algebra/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on $B$-Algebra == A literature search has failed to reveal the origin or derivation of the term $B$-algebra. Hence the reason for why it is called that is still under investigation. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:BIDMAS
snippet: BIDMAS is a mnemonic for determining the binding priority of the operations of arithmetic: $(1): \quad$ Brackets $(2): \quad$ Indices $(3)$ and $(4): \quad$ Division and Multiplication $(5)$ and $(6): \quad$ Addition and Subtraction

title: Definition:BIDMAS/Also presented as
snippet: == BIDMAS: Also presented as == The mnemonic BIDMAS can also presented as: BODMAS, where O in this case stands for order BEDMAS, where E in this case stands for exponent. Sometimes BOMDAS is encountered.

title: Definition:Babbage's Analytical Engine
snippet: Babbage's analytical engine was a proposed mechanical general-purpose computer designed by English mathematician and computer pioneer .

title: Definition:Babbage's Analytical Engine/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Babbage's Analytical Engine == Babbage's analytical engine contained in its design a number of essential features that are used in modern electronic computers. Unfortunately, partly through lack of funds, was unable to complete his analytical engine.

title: Definition:Babbage's Analytical Engine/Mistake
snippet: == Source Work == analytical engine or difference engine

title: Definition:Babbage's Difference Engine
snippet: Babbage's difference engine was an automatic mechanical calculator designed to tabulate polynomial functions.

title: Definition:Babbage's Difference Engine/Also known as
snippet: == Babbage's Difference Engine: Also known as == Babbage's difference engine is also seen referred to as Babbage's engine. However, this can be taken to mean either this or Babbage's analytical engine, which is a different machine. Some sources conflate the two machines.

title: Definition:Babbage's Difference Engine/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Babbage's Difference Engine == Because of many factors, personal and financial among others, was unable to develop his machine as he originally intended.

title: Definition:Babylonian Clay Tablets
snippet: The Babylonian clay tablets are the written remains of the .

title: Definition:Babylonian Clay Tablets/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Babylonian Clay Tablets == There are about a million Babylonian clay tablets that have been dug up from the ground in . Of these, a few hundred are concerned with mathematics and astronomy. They indicate that the had a sophisticated knowledge of astronomy, and a number system which could express numbers to high precision. They also indicate that they had the knowledge of how to solve quadratic equations.

title: Definition:Babylonian Mathematics
snippet: Babylonian mathematics is the name given to the mathematics of the . Its content was arithmetical and algebraical, and considerably in advance of the mathematics of the approximately contemporaneous .

title: Definition:Babylonian Number System
snippet: The number system as used in the was a positional number system where the number base was a combination of decimal (base $10$) and sexagesimal (base $60$). The characters were written in by a combination of: a thin vertical wedge shape, to indicate the digit $1$ a fat horizontal wedge shape, to indicate the digit $10$ arranged in groups to indicate the digits $2$ to $9$ and $20$ to $50$. 600px At $59$ the pattern stops, and the number $60$ is represented by the digit $1$ once again.

title: Definition:Babylonian Number System/Also denoted as
snippet: == Babylonian Number System: Also denoted as == When representing numbers using the Babylonian number system, it is laborious to represent the actual symbols themselves. Hence it is commonplace to use their decimal counterparts, separated by commas, so that the number represented, for example, in as: 30px 30px 30px would be represented as: $7, 7, 7$ In such a system, the radix point is represented by a semicolon.

title: Definition:Bach or Stravinsky?
snippet: Bach or Stravinsky? is an instance of a class of games whose mechanics are as follows: There are two players: $\text A$lexis and $\text B$everley. They wish to go out together to a musical concert, but $\text A$ prefers Bach and $\text B$ prefers Stravinsky. The key points are: $\text A$lexis and $\text B$everley wish to coordinate their behaviour but: they have conflicting interests.

title: Definition:Bach or Stravinsky?/Payoff Table
snippet: == Payoff Table for Bach or Stravinsky? == The following payoff table specifies the game Bach or Stravinsky?: {{PayoffTable|table = $\begin {array} {r c } & \text {Bach} & \text{Stravinsky} \\ \hline \text {Bach} & 2, 1 & 0, 0 \\ \hline \text {Stravinsky} & 0, 0 & 1, 2 \\ \hline \end {array}$}}

title: Definition:Back-Substitution
snippet: Let $S$ be a system of simultaneous linear equations: $\ds \forall i \in \closedint 1 m: \sum _{j \mathop = 1}^n {\alpha_{i j} x_j} = \beta_i$ where all of $\alpha_1, \ldots, a_n, x_1, \ldots x_n, \beta_i, \ldots, \beta_m$ are elements of a field $K$. Let $S$ be expressed in matrix representation: $\sqbrk \alpha_{m n} \sqbrk x_{n 1} = \sqbrk \beta_{m 1}$ where $\sqbrk a_{m n}$ is an $m \times n$ matrix in echelon form.

title: Definition:Back-Substitution/Also known as
snippet: == Back-Substitution: Also known as == Back-substitution is also sometimes seen referred to as backward substitution. However, reserves the term backward substitution for a specific operation in the solution of simultaneous equations using LU factorization. Category:Definitions/Back-Substitution

title: Definition:Backus-Naur Form
snippet: Backus-Naur form (abbrevated BNF) is a (formal) metalanguage for defining the syntax of a formal language $\LL$. As such, it is a formal grammar for $\LL$. BNF is only applicable to formal languages that use the collation system of words and concatenation.

title: Definition:Backus-Naur Form/Alphabet
snippet: The alphabet of Backus-Naur form has the following components: The signs: The primitive symbol ::= which means consists of The primitive symbol | which means or The letters: A collection of metasymbols, typically rendered as $\meta {metasymbol}$ Words in the object language. Category:Definitions/Backus-Naur Form

title: Definition:Backus-Naur Form/Also known as
snippet: == Backus-Naur Form: Also known as == Backus-Naur form was originally called Backus normal form. However, after had worked on refining the work initially done by , his name was added. Although would prefer it kept its old name, the current name is prevalent. Category:Definitions/Backus-Naur Form

title: Definition:Backus-Naur Form/Non-Terminal
snippet: Symbols that appear on the of a specification in Backus-Naur form are called non-terminals.

title: Definition:Backus-Naur Form/Rules of Formation
snippet: Let $\meta {word}$ be a metasymbol of an object language. Let $\meta {word1}, \meta {word2}, \ldots, \meta {wordn}$ be letters of Backus-Naur form. That is, $\meta {word1}, \ldots, \meta {wordn}$ may be either metasymbols of, or words in, the object language. The rules of formation of Backus-Naur form specify two kinds of well-formed formulae: $\meta {word} \ ::= \ \meta {word1} \meta {word2} \cdots \meta {wordn}$ This means that $\meta {word}$ on the may be replaced by the specified sequence of $n$ words on the .

title: Definition:Backus-Naur Form/Specification
snippet: A definition of an object language $\LL$ in Backus-Naur form is called a specification of $\LL$. Category:Definitions/Backus-Naur Form

title: Definition:Backus-Naur Form/Terminal
snippet: Symbols that never appear on the of a specification in Backus-Naur form are called terminals.

title: Definition:Backward Path (Class Theory)
snippet: Let $A$ be a class under a total ordering $\preccurlyeq$. Let $S = \sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $A$ (either finite or infinite) such that: $\forall i \in \N: x_i \in S \implies x_{i + 1} \prec x_i$ Then $S$ is referred to as a backward path of $\preccurlyeq$ (in $A$).

title: Definition:Backward Reparametrization of Curve
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $I, I' \subseteq \R$ be real intervals. Let $\gamma : I \to M$ be a smooth curve. Let $\phi : I' \to I$ be a diffeomorphism. Let $\tilde \gamma$ be a curve defined by: $\tilde \gamma := \gamma \circ \phi : I' \to M$ where $\circ$ denotes the composition of mappings $\gamma$ and $\phi$. Suppose $\phi$ is decreasing. Then $\tilde \gamma$ is called the backward reparametrization of $\gamma$.

title: Definition:Backward Shift Operator
snippet: Let $T = \sequence {z_t}$ be a discrete time series. The backward shift operator $B$ is defined as: $\forall t: \map B {z_t} = z_{t - 1}$

title: Definition:Baire Category
snippet: The Baire category of a topological space $T$ is a way of specifying how dense $T$ is:

title: Definition:Baire Category/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Baire Category == The concept of categorizing topological spaces into meager and non-meager was introduced by , during his work to define what is now known as a Baire space. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Baire Function
snippet: Let $X \subseteq \R$. For each $n$, let $f_n : X \to \R$ be a continuous function. Suppose that the sequence $\sequence {f_n}$ converges pointwise to a function $f : X \to \R$. We call $f$ a Baire function.

title: Definition:Baire Product Metric
snippet: Let $X := \R^\omega$ be the set defined as: $\ds \R^\omega = \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^\infty \R_i$ where each $\R_i$ is a copy of the real number line under the Euclidean metric. We define the Baire product metric on $X$ as: $\map d {\family {x_i}, \family {y_i} } = \dfrac 1 j$ where $j \in \N$ is the smallest such that $x_j \ne y_j$.

title: Definition:Baire Product Metric/Also known as
snippet: == Baire Product Metric: Also known as == The Baire product metric is also known as just the Baire metric.

title: Definition:Baire Property
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. Then $H$ has the Baire property there exists an open set $U \in \tau$ such that the symmetric difference $U \symdif H$ is meager.

title: Definition:Baire Space
snippet: A Baire Space (Topology): A topological space such that the intersection of each countable collection of open subsets which are everywhere dense is also everywhere dense. The Baire Space (Set Theory): The set of all infinite sequences of natural numbers.

title: Definition:Baire Space (Set Theory)
snippet: The Baire space $\mathbf B$ is defined as the set of all infinite sequences of natural numbers. It can also be defined as the Cartesian product of a countably infinite number of copies of the set of natural numbers.

title: Definition:Baire Space (Topology)/Definition 1
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a Baire space the union of any countable set of closed sets of $T$ whose interiors are empty also has an empty interior.

title: Definition:Baire Space (Topology)/Definition 2
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a Baire space the intersection of any countable set of open sets of $T$ which are everywhere dense is everywhere dense.

title: Definition:Baire Space (Topology)/Definition 3
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a Baire space the interior of the union of any countable set of closed sets of $T$ which are nowhere dense is empty.

title: Definition:Baire Space (Topology)/Definition 4
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a Baire space , whenever the union of any countable set of closed sets of $T$ has an interior point, then one of those closed sets must have an interior point.

title: Definition:Baker's Dozen
snippet: A baker's dozen is another name for a set whose cardinality is $13$.

title: Definition:Baker's Dozen/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Baker's Dozen == The term baker's dozen arises from the medieval tradition in which a would occasionally slip an extra loaf of bread into a consignment of a dozen so as to make sure the batch was not underweight. Hence it is used in general to mean $12$ plus an extra one. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Balance
snippet: A balance is a tool for measuring the mass of a body by comparing its weight against that of a set of weights whose mass is known. 600px

title: Definition:Balance/Arm
snippet: The balance consists of two arms. These are the two halves of a rigid rod placed on the fulcrum such that the arms are of the same length. In the above diagram, both arms are of length $d$. Category:Definitions/Balances

title: Definition:Balance/Fulcrum
snippet: The fulcrum of the balance is a fixed point upon which the arms rest, and upon which they are free to pivot. Category:Definitions/Balances

title: Definition:Balance/Pan
snippet: At the end of each of the two arms of the balance is a pan. Into one of these pans the body is placed which is being weighed. Into the other pan, the user is to place exactly the weights which will cause the arms to be horizontal. Category:Definitions/Balances

title: Definition:Balanced Block Design
snippet: A balanced block design is a randomized block design in which: each randomized block is the same size each treatment is applied the same number of times.

title: Definition:Balanced Hull
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a vector space over $\GF$. Let $A \subseteq X$ be a non-empty set. We define the balanced hull of $A$ as the $\subseteq$-smallest balanced set containing $A$. We denote this by: $\map {\operatorname {bal} } A$

title: Definition:Balanced Incomplete Block Design
snippet: A balanced incomplete block design with parameters $v, b, r, k, \lambda$ is a block design such that: $v$ is the number of treatments $b$ is the number of blocks $k$ is the size of each block $r$ is the number of blocks any treatment can be in $\lambda$ is the number of times any two treatments can occur in the same block and has the following properties: Each block is of size $k$ All of the $\dbinom v 2$ pairs occur together in exactly $\lambda$ blocks.

title: Definition:Balanced Incomplete Block Design/Also known as
snippet: == Balanced Incomplete Block Design: Also known as == A balanced incomplete block design is also known by its abbreviation BIBD. Category:Definitions/Balanced Incomplete Block Designs

title: Definition:Balanced Incomplete Block Design/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Balanced Incomplete Block Design == The incomplete descriptor of a balanced incomplete block design arises from the fact that there are not enough units to receive all treatments: $k < v$.

title: Definition:Balanced Prime/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\left({p_{n - 1}, p_n, p_{n + 1} }\right)$ be a triplet of consecutive prime numbers. $p_n$ is a balanced prime : $p_n = \dfrac {p_{n - 1} + p_{n + 1} } 2$ $p$ is a balanced prime it is the arithmetic mean of the prime numbers on either side of it.

title: Definition:Balanced Prime/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\paren {p_{n - 1}, p_n, p_{n + 1} }$ be a triplet of consecutive prime numbers. $p_n$ is a balanced prime : {{eqn | l = p_{n - 1} + d | r = p_n | c = }} {{eqn | l = p_{n - 1} + 2 d | r = p_{n + 1} | c = }} for some $d \in \Z$. That is, $p_n$ is the middle term of a $3$-term arithmetic sequence in which the $1$st and last terms are the previous and following primes.

title: Definition:Balanced Prime/Definition 3
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. $p$ is a balanced prime the prime gaps either side of it are equal.

title: Definition:Balanced Prime/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Balanced Primes == Category:Definitions/Balanced Primes

title: Definition:Balanced Set
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a vector space over $\GF$. Let $A \subseteq X$. We say that $A$ is balanced : $s A \subseteq A$ for all $s \in \GF$ with $\cmod s \le 1$ where $s A$ is the dilation of $A$ by $s$.

title: Definition:Balanced Set/Also defined as
snippet: == Balanced Set: Also defined as == A subset $A$ of a vector space $V$ over a field $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$ is also by some sources defined as a balanced set : $\forall x \in A: \forall s \in \GF: \cmod s < 1 \implies s x \in A$

title: Definition:Balanced Signed Graph
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a signed graph. Then $G$ is balanced it is possible to partition $V$ into two subsets $A, B$ such that: the positive edges have both ends in $A$ or both ends in $B$; the negative edges have one end in $A$ and the other end $B$. It is a frequent practice to apply a different colour to the vertices in each set to enhance clarity.

title: Definition:Balanced String
snippet: Let $S$ be a string in an alphabet containing brackets.

title: Definition:Balanced String/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ be a string in an alphabet containing brackets. $S$ is said to be balanced : $(1): \quad S$ contains equally many left and right brackets. $(2): \quad$ Every prefix of $S$ contains at least as many left brackets as it does right brackets.

title: Definition:Balanced String/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ be a string in an alphabet containing brackets. $S$ is said to be balanced it satisfies the following: $(1): \quad$ The null string $\epsilon$ is a balanced string. $(2): \quad$ If $x$ is a symbol that is specifically not a bracket, then the string consisting just of $x$ is a balanced string. $(3): \quad$ If $S$ is a balanced string, then $\paren S$ is a balanced string. $(4): \quad$ If $S$ and $T$ are balanced strings, then $S T$ is a balanced string. $(5): \quad$ Nothing is a balanced string unless it has been created by one of the rules $(1)$ to $(4)$.

title: Definition:Balanced Ternary Representation
snippet: Let $n \in \Z$ be an integer. Balanced ternary representation is the unique representation of $n$ in the form: $\sqbrk {r_m r_{m - 1} \ldots r_2 r_1 r_0}$ such that: $\ds n = \sum_{j \mathop = 0}^m r_j 3^j$ where: $m \in \Z_{>0}$ is a strictly positive integer such that $3^m \le \size n < 3^{m + 1}$ all the $r_j$ are such that $r_j \in \set {\underline 1, 0, 1}$, where $\underline 1 := -1$.

title: Definition:Ball/Also known as
snippet: == Ball: Also known as == Instead of ball, some sources use the term disk (or disc in British English), and prefer to use $\Bbb D$ for $B$. Some sources use disk (or disc) specifically to mean closed ball, and use open disk (or open disc) for open ball. prefers to reserve the term disk, if at all, for a disk in the complex plane, as there is an intuitive $2$-dimensional nuance to the word disk, while ball guides intuition down the path of $3$ dimensions.

title: Definition:Ballistics
snippet: Ballistics is the branch of applied mathematics involved in the study of the motion of projectiles.

Let $R$ be either the real numbers $\R$ or the complex numbers $\C$.. Let $\struct {A, \circ}$ be an algebra over $R$ which is also a Banach space. Then $\struct {A, \circ}$ is a Banach algebra : $ orall a, b \in R:

title: Definition:Banach Algebra/Also known as
snippet: == Banach Algebra: Also known as == Some sources refer to a Banach algebra as a normed ring, but on this term is used to mean a ring with a norm on it.

title: Definition:Banach Algebra of Continuous Functions on Compact Hausdorff Space
snippet: Let $X$ be a compact $T_2$ (Hausdorff) space. Let $\map \CC X = \map \CC {X, \C}$ be the vector space of continuous functions on $X$. Let $\ast$ be pointwise multiplication on $\C^X$. Let $\norm {\, \cdot \,}$ be the supremum norm on $\map \CC X$. We call $\struct {\map \CC X, \ast, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ the Banach algebra of continuous functions on $X$.

title: Definition:Banach Limit
snippet:
Let $\struct {\map {\ell^\infty} \R, 
orm \cdot_\infty}$ be the normed vector space of bounded sequences on $\R$. Let $\struct {\paren {\map {\ell^\infty} \R}^\ast, 
orm \cdot_{\paren {\ell^\infty}^\ast} }$ be the normed dual space of $\struct {\map {\ell^\infty} \R, 
orm \cdot_\infty}$. Let $S: \map {\ell^\infty} \R 	o \map {\ell^\infty} \R$ be the left shift operator on $\map {\ell^\infty} \R$. Let $\mathbf 1$ be the sequence with ${\mathbf 1}_n = 1$ for each $n \in \N$.

title: Definition:Banach Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\mu: \Sigma \to \overline \R$ be a mapping, where $\overline \R$ denotes the set of extended real numbers. {{axiom | n = 2 | q = \forall n \in \N: \forall \tuple {S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_n} \subseteq \Sigma: \forall i, j \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n}: S_i \cap S_j = \O | ml= \map \mu {\bigcup_{k \mathop = 1}^n S_k} | mo= = | mr= \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n \map \mu {S_k} | rc= that is, $\mu$ is a finitely additive function }}

title: Definition:Banach Space
snippet: A Banach space is a complete normed vector space. That is, a Banach space is a normed vector space where every Cauchy sequence is convergent.

title: Definition:Banach Space/Also defined as
snippet: == Banach Space: Also defined as == Some sources additionally specify that the normed vector space over which a Banach space is defined also has to be over the real or complex numbers. This distinction is of limited importance, as it is vanishingly rare for a Banach space to be used in a different context.

title: Definition:Band Matrix
snippet: A band matrix is a matrix whose elements outside a band of diagonals around the leading diagonal are all zero.

title: Definition:Band Matrix/Also known as
snippet: == Band Matrix: Also known as == A band matrix is also known as a banded matrix.

title: Definition:Bandwidth of Transmission System
snippet: The bandwidth of a transmission system is the rate of data transmission that can be supported by an interface or a network connection, usually measured in bits per second.

title: Definition:Bar
snippet: Statistics Bar of a bar chart: one of the vertical or horizontal lines or rectangles to indicate a statistic. Physics: Bar: a unit of measurement of atmospheric pressure. Mechanics: Bar: a straight rigid body whose length in one dimension is substantially greater than its width in the other two dimensions.

title: Definition:Bar/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Bar: Conversion Factors ==

title: Definition:Bar (Mechanics)
snippet: A bar is a straight rigid body whose length in one dimension is such that its width in the other two dimensions is negligible.

title: Definition:Bar (Unit)
snippet: The bar is a CGS unit of pressure. It is defined as being: The amount of pressure equal to exactly $100 \, 000$ pascals.

title: Definition:Bar Chart
snippet: A bar chart is a form of graph which consists of a finite set of (usually) vertical bars whose length determines the statistic being communicated. 500px

title: Definition:Bar Chart/Also known as
snippet: == Bar Chart: Also known as == A bar chart is often seen referred to as a bar graph. Some sources use bar diagram, but that is rarer. Some sources use the term histogram, but that is usually used to apply to a specialised graph of this type.

title: Definition:Bar Coding
snippet: Bar coding is a technique for stock control and retail transaction where each item of merchandise carries a Universal Product Code which is shown as a series of black bars, whose width and spacing encode the appropriate information. This is scanned by an optical reader.

title: Definition:Bar Coding/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Bar Coding == Bar coding was introduced in $1973$ to provide a means of automating stock control. The technique was exploited further by using it to provide an itemized receipt showing the full details of their transactions.

title: Definition:Barrel (Vector Space)
snippet: Let $V$ be a normed vector space or a topological vector space. Let $W \subseteq V$ be a subset of $V$. Then $W$ is a barrel : $W$ is closed $W$ is convex $W$ is absorbing $W$ is balanced.

title: Definition:Barrelled Space
snippet: Let $V$ be a topological vector space. Then $V$ is a barrelled space : Every barrel of $V$ contains a neighborhood of the zero vector.

title: Definition:Barrier
snippet: A complex function $\varphi \in \map \C {\overline \Omega}$ is a barrier for $\Omega$ at $z \in \partial \Omega$ : $\varphi$ is subharmonic $\map \varphi z = 0$ $\varphi < 0$ on $\partial \Omega \setminus \set z$ {{explain|Define $\map \C {\overline \Omega}$}}

title: Definition:Bartlett's Test
snippet: Bartlett's test is a technique for testing for homogeneity of variance, given a sample set from a number of populations.

title: Definition:Bartlett's Test/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Bartlett's Test == Bartlett's test was devised by in $1934$.

title: Definition:Barycenter
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an affine space over a field $k$. Let $p_1, \ldots, p_n \in \EE$ be points. Let $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n \in k$ such that $\ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \lambda_i = 1$. The barycenter of $p_1, \ldots, p_n$ with weights $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n$ is the unique point $q$ of $\EE$ such that for every point $r \in \EE$ $\ds q = r + \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \lambda_i \vec {r p_i}$

title: Definition:Barycenter/Also known as
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Barycenter == In UK English, the word barycenter is presented as barycentre.

title: Definition:Barycenter/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Barycenter == The adjectival form of barycenter is barycentric. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Barycenter/Notation
snippet: == Barycenter: Notation == It is conventional to use the following notation for a barycenter: $q = \lambda_1 p_1 + \cdots + \lambda_n p_n$ despite the fact that linear combinations are not defined in affine spaces. Category:Definitions/Barycenters

title: Definition:Barycenter (Locally Convex Space)
snippet: Let $X$ be a locally convex vector space over $\R$. Let $K \subseteq X$ be a convex subset. Let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $K$. Then $x \in K$ is the barycenter of $\mu$ : $\ds \forall \ell \in X^\ast : \map \ell x = \int_K \map \ell u \rd \map \mu u$ where: $X^\ast$ is the dual space of $X$ It is also said that $\mu$ represents $x$ in the weak sense.

title: Definition:Barycentric Body
snippet: Let $B$ be a body. Let the matter in $B$ be distributed with spherical symmetry. Then $B$ is described as being barycentric.

title: Definition:Barycentric Body/Also known as
snippet: == Barycentric Body: Also known as == A body which is barycentric can also be referred to as centrobaric.

title: Definition:Barycentric Coordinate Interpolation
snippet: Let $\tuple {x_0, x_1, ..., x_k}$ be a set of $k+1$ affinely independent points in $\mathbb R^k$. Let $f : \mathbb R^k \to \mathbb R$ be a real-valued function. Let $\tuple {y_0, y_1, ..., y_k}$ be a set of $k+1$ known values of $f$ at $x_0, x_1, ..., x_k$, respectively. Let $x'$ be a point in $\mathbb R^k$. Let the barycentric coordinates of $x'$ $\tuple {x_0, x_1, ..., x_k}$ be $\tuple {\lambda_0, \lambda_1, ..., \lambda_k}$. Then, the barycentric coordinate interpolation of $f$ at $x'$ is given by $\ds y' = \sum_{i \mathop = 0}^k \lambda_i y_i$

title: Definition:Barycentric Coordinates
snippet: Barycentric coordinates are a set of numbers representing the position of a point in a Euclidean space a set of fixed points. In $n$ dimensional space a total of $n + 1$ points must be used.

title: Definition:Barycentric Coordinates/2 Dimensions
snippet: In the plane, barycentric coordinates are a set of $3$ numbers representing the position of a point as follows: Let $\mathbf a$, $\mathbf b$ and $\mathbf c$ be the position vectors of the $3$ vertices of a triangle in the plane. Then the position vector of an arbitrary point $p$ can be expressed uniquely in the form: $\mathbf p = \alpha \mathbf a + \beta \mathbf b + \gamma \mathbf c$ such that: $\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 1$ The set $\set {\alpha, \beta, \gamma}$ consists of the barycentric coordinates of $p$.

title: Definition:Barycentric Coordinates/3 Dimensions
snippet: In $3$ dimensional space, barycentric coordinates are a set of $4$ numbers representing the position of a point as follows: Let $p_0, p_1, p_2, p_3$ be fixed non-coplanar points, such that $p_i = \tuple {x_i, y_1, z_i}$. Then an arbitrary point $p$ can be expressed in the form: $p = \lambda_0 p_0 + \lambda_1 p_1 + \lambda_2 p_2 + \lambda_3 p_3$ such that: $\lambda_0 + \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \lambda_3 = 1$ The set $\set {\lambda_0, \lambda_1, \lambda_2, \lambda_3}$ consists of the barycentric coordinates of $p$.

title: Definition:Barycentric Refinement
snippet: Let $\CC \subseteq \powerset S$ be a cover for a set $S$.

title: Definition:Barycentric Refinement/Also known as
snippet: == Barycentric Refinement: Also known as == A barycentric refinement of $\CC$ over a set $S$ is also known as a star refinement by some authors. However, a star refinement is generally defined a general subset of $S$, rather than a single element.

title: Definition:Barycentric Refinement/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\CC \subseteq \powerset S$ be a cover for a set $S$. $\VV$ is a barycentric refinement of $\CC$ $\VV$ is a cover for $S$ such that: $\forall x \in S: \exists U \in \CC: \Star x \VV \subseteq U$ where $\Star x \VV$ is the star of $x$ with respect to $\VV$.

title: Definition:Barycentric Refinement/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\CC \subseteq \powerset S$ be a cover for a set $S$. $\VV$ is a barycentric refinement of $\CC$ $\VV$ is a refinement of $\CC$ such that: $\VV = \set {\Star x \VV: x \in S}$ where $\Star x \VV$ is the star of $x$ with respect to $\VV$.

title: Definition:Barye
snippet: The barye is the CGS unit of pressure. It is defined as being: The amount of pressure required to apply a force of $1$ dyne over an area of $1$ square centimetre.

title: Definition:Barye/Also known as
snippet: == Barye: Also known as == The term barye can be seen in various forms: barad barrie bary baryd baryed barie The term barye in the context of a unit of pressure is in fact relatively new. Hence older works will generally use the term dyne per square centimetre.

title: Definition:Barye/Base Units
snippet: == Barye: Base Units == The CGS base units of the barye are: $\mathrm {Ba} := \mathrm {g \, cm^{-1} \, s^{-2} }$ where: $\mathrm g$ denotes grams $\mathrm {cm}$ denotes centimetres $\mathrm s$ denotes seconds (of time). Category:Definitions/Barye

title: Definition:Barye/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Barye: Conversion Factors == {{eqn | r = 10^{-1} | c = pascal }} {{eqn | r = 10^{-3} | c = millibars }} {{eqn | o = \approx | r = 1 \cdotp 450377 \times 10^{-5} | c = pounds per square inch }} Category:Definitions/Barye

title: Definition:Barye/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Barye == The word barye originates from the $19$th century French, and ultimately derives from Greek barus, meaning heavy. It is pronounced bar-ry, that is, rhyming completely with the word carry. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Base
snippet: Geometry: The base of a geometric figure, for example: Base of a triangle (Plane geometry) Base of an isosceles triangle (Plane geometry) Base of a parallelogram (Plane geometry) Base of a segment of a circle (Plane geometry) Base of a cone (Solid geometry) Base of a right circular cone (Solid geometry) Base of a pyramid (Solid geometry) Base of a hemisphere (Solid geometry) Base angles of an isosceles triangle (Plane geometry) Number theory: Number Base (Number theory and arithmetic) Analysis: Base of Logarithm Matroid Theory: Base of Matroid

title: Definition:Base-Orderable Matroid
snippet: Let $M = \struct {S, \mathscr I}$ be a matroid. Let $\mathscr B$ denote the bases of $M$. Then: $M$ is said to be a base-orderable matroid $\mathscr B$ satisfies the base-orderable axiom:

title: Definition:Base Field (Linear Algebra)
snippet: Let $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_K$ be a vector space, where: $\struct {K, +_K, \times_K}$ is a field $\struct {G, +_G}$ is an abelian group $\struct {G, +_G}$ $\ast: K \times G \to G$ is a binary operation. Then the field $\struct {K, +_K, \times_K}$ is called the base field of $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_K$. If the base field is understood, then $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_K$ can be rendered $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}$.

title: Definition:Base Field (Linear Algebra)/Also known as
snippet: == Base Field in context of Linear Algebra: Also known as == A base field, as used in this context, is also known as as scalar field, or just field of scalars. The term ground field can also be found.

title: Definition:Base Period
snippet: A base period is a time period used as a reference point for comparing variables such as an index number The index number for that base period is usually assigned a round number, for example $100$ of $1000$.

title: Definition:Base of Antiprism/Also known as
snippet: == Base of Antiprism: Also known as == A base of an antiprism is also known as an end face.

title: Definition:Base of Geometric Figure
snippet: The base of a geometric figure is a specific part of that figure which is distinguished from the remainder of that figure and placed (actually or figuratively) at the bottom of a depiction or visualisation. In some cases the base is truly qualitiatively different from the rest of the figure. In other cases the base is selected arbitrarily as one of several parts of the figure which may equally well be so chosen.

title: Definition:Base of Logarithm/Also known as
snippet: == Base of Logarithm: Also known as == The base of a logarithm is also known as its radix.

title: Definition:Base of Matroid
snippet: Let $M = \struct{S, \mathscr I}$ be a matroid. A base of $M$ is a maximal independent subset of $S$.

title: Definition:Base of Number System
snippet: The fundamental grouping unit of a number system is referred to as its base.

title: Definition:Base of Prism/Also known as
snippet: == Base of Prism: Also known as == The bases of a prism can be referred to as their end faces or endfaces. The term base can suggest that the prism be specifically situated so that one of the end faces is coincident with a plane of reference, which may be misleading. Category:Definitions/Bases of Prisms

title: Definition:Base of Root System
snippet: Let $\struct {E, \Phi}$ be a root system. $\Delta \subset \Phi$ is called a base of $\Phi$ : {{axiom | n = 2 | t = $\forall \beta \in \Phi: \beta = \ds \sum_{\alpha \mathop \in \Delta} k_\alpha \alpha$ such that all $k_\alpha$s are either non-negative integers or all non-positive integers.}} The roots in $\Delta$ are called simple.

title: Definition:Base of Solid Figure
snippet: The base of a solid figure is one of its faces which has been distinguished from the others in some way. The solid figure is usually oriented so that the base is situated at the bottom.

title: Definition:Baseline Risk
snippet: Baseline risk is defined as the risk at the beginning of a time period or under specific conditions.

title: Definition:Basic Null Sequence
snippet: The sequences defined as: $\sequence {\dfrac 1 {n^r} }_{n \mathop \in \N}$ for $r \in \R: r > 0$ $\sequence {\alpha^n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ for $\alpha \in \C: \cmod {\alpha} < 1$ are known as the basic null sequences.

title: Definition:Basic Open Set
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\BB \subseteq \tau$ be a basis for $T$. Let $U \in \BB$. Then $U$ is a basic open set of $T$. That is, a basic open set of a topology is an open set of that topology which is an element of a basis for that topology. The basis itself needs to be specified for this definition to make sense. Category:Definitions/Topology Category:Definitions/Topological Bases

title: Definition:Basic Primitive Recursive Function
snippet: The basic primitive recursive functions are:

title: Definition:Basic Primitive Recursive Function/Identity Function
snippet: The identity function $I_\N: \N \to \N$ is a basic primitive recursive function, defined as: $\forall n \in \N: \map {I_\N} n = n$ Note that this is an implementation of the projection function: $\pr_1^1: \N \to \N: \map {\pr_1^1} {n_1} = n_1$ It is URM computable by a single-instruction URM program. Category:Definitions/Primitive Recursive Functions

title: Definition:Basic Primitive Recursive Function/Projection Function
snippet: The projection functions $\pr_j^k: \N^k \to \N$ are basic primitive recursive functions, defined as: $\forall \tuple {n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_k} \in \N^k: \map {\pr_j^k} {n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_k} = n_j$The usual notation for the projection function omits the superscript that defines the arity of the particular instance of the projection in question at the time, for example: $\pr_j$. However, in the context of computability theory, it is a very good idea to be completely certain of exactly which projection function is under discussion. where $j \in \closedint 1 k$.

title: Definition:Basic Primitive Recursive Function/Successor Function
snippet: The successor function $\Succ: \N \to \N$ is a basic primitive recursive function, defined as: $\forall n \in \N: \map \Succ n = n + 1$ It is URM computable by a single-instruction URM program. Category:Definitions/Primitive Recursive Functions

title: Definition:Basic Primitive Recursive Function/URM Computability
snippet: The basic primitive recursive functions: Zero Function Successor Function Projection Function Identity Function are each URM computable by a single-instruction URM program. Category:Definitions/Primitive Recursive Functions

title: Definition:Basic Primitive Recursive Function/Zero Function
snippet: The zero function $\Zero: \N \to \N$ is a basic primitive recursive function, defined as: $\forall n \in \N: \map \Zero n = 0$ It is URM computable by a single-instruction URM program. Category:Definitions/Primitive Recursive Functions

title: Definition:Basic Proposition
snippet: Let $f: \mathbb B^k \to \mathbb B$ be a boolean function, where: $\mathbb B = \set {0, 1}$ is a boolean domain $k$ is a natural number. A basic proposition is one of the projection functions $\pr_j: \mathbb B^k \to \mathbb B$, defined as follows: Let $X = \tuple {p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_k} \in \mathbb B^k$. Then: $\map {\pr_j} X = p_j$ That is, a basic proposition is one of the elements of the $k$-tuple $\tuple {p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_k}$.

title: Definition:Basic Sequence
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be an normed vector space over $\GF$. Let $\sequence {e_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $X$. Let $\sqbrk {e_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be the closed linear span of $\sequence {e_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$. We say that $\sequence {e_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is a basic sequence if it is a Schauder basis for $\sqbrk {e_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$.

title: Definition:Basic URM Instruction/Also known as
snippet: == Basic URM Instruction: Also known as == Basic URM instructions are also (and more commonly) known as commands, because the word is shorter and quicker to say. During the course of the exposition, the term instruction will also be found, which again means the same thing.

title: Definition:Basic WFF of Predicate Logic
snippet: Let $\LL$ be the language of predicate logic. A WFF $\mathbf A$ of $\LL$ is called basic it does not start with a logical connective. Basic WFFs are useful to consider as atoms when analysing propositional logic within the larger context of predicate logic. Expressed more formally, we can take the basic WFFs as the vocabulary of the language of propositional logic. Do note that e.g. $\forall x: x = x \land x = x$ is considered basic even though it contains the logical connective $\land$. This is because $\land$ is not the main connective.

title: Definition:Basis (Hilbert Space)
snippet: Let $H$ be a Hilbert space. A basis for $H$ is a maximal orthonormal subset of $H$. Thus, $B$ is a basis for $H$ for all orthonormal subsets $B'$ of $H$: $B \subseteq B' \implies B = B'$

snippet: == Basis in context of Linear Algebra: Also known as == The phrase basis for $G$ can also be seen instead of basis of $G$.

title: Definition:Basis Constant
snippet:
Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $\sequence {e_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a Schauder basis for $X$. Let $\sequence {S_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be the projections associated with $\sequence {e_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$. Let $\map \BB X$ be the space of bounded linear transformations on $X$. Let $
orm {\, \cdot \,}_{\map \BB X}$ be the norm on $\map \BB X$. We define the basis constant for $\sequence {e_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$, $K_b$, by: $\ds K_b = \sup_{n \mathop \in \N}

title: Definition:Basis Element
snippet: Let $S^n$ be a cartesian space. An element $s \in S$ is known as a basis element of $S^n$. Alternatively, let the ordered tuple $X = \left({x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}\right)$ be any element of $S^n$. Let $x_j \in \left({x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}\right)$. Then $x_j$ is a basis element of $S^n$. Category:Definitions/Set Theory

title: Definition:Basis Expansion/Negative Real Numbers
snippet: Let $x \in \R: x < 0$. We take the absolute value $y$ of $x$, that is: $y = \size x$ Then we take the expansion of $y$ in base $b$: $\size {s . d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots}_b$ where $s = \floor y$. Finally, the expansion of $x$ in base $b$ is defined as: $-\sqbrk {s . d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots}_b$

title: Definition:Basis Expansion/Positive Real Numbers
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number such that $x \ge 0$. Let $b \in \N: b \ge 2$. Let us define the recursive sequence: $\forall n \in \N: n \ge 1: \sequence {f_n} = \begin {cases} b \paren {x - \floor x} & : n = 1 \\ b \paren {f_{n - 1} - \floor {f_{n - 1} } } & : n > 1 \end{cases}$ Then we define: $\forall n \in \N: n \ge 1: \sequence {d_n} = \floor {f_n}$ It follows from the method of construction and the definition of the floor function that: $\forall n: 0 \le f_n < b$ and hence $\forall n: 0 \le d_n \le b - 1$ $\forall n: f_n = 0 \implies f_{n + 1} = 0$ and hence $d_{n + 1} = 0$.

title: Definition:Basis Expansion/Recurrence
snippet: Let $b \in \N: b \ge 2$. Let $x$ be a real number. Let the basis expansion of $x$ in base $b$ be: $\sqbrk {s \cdotp d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots}_b$ Let there be a finite sequence of $p$ digits of $x$: $\tuple {d_{r + 1} d_{r + 1} \ldots d_{r + p} }$ such that for all $k \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ and for all $j \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, p}$: $d_{r + j + k p} = d_{r + j}$ where $p$ is the smallest $p$ to have this property.

title: Definition:Basis Expansion/Recurrence/Non-Recurring Part
snippet: Let $b \in \N: b \ge 2$. Let $x$ be a real number. Let the basis expansion of $x$ in base $b$ be recurring: $\sqbrk {s \cdotp d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots d_r d_{r + 1} d_{r + 2} \ldots d_{r + p} d_{r + 1} d_{r + 2} \ldots d_{r + p } d_{r + 1} d_{r + 2} \ldots d_{r + p} d_{r + 1} \ldots}_b$ The non-recurring part of $x$ is: $\sqbrk {s \cdotp d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots d_r}$

title: Definition:Basis Expansion/Recurrence/Notation
snippet: Let $b \in \N: b \ge 2$. Let $x$ be a real number. Let the basis expansion of $x$ in base $b$ be: $\sqbrk {s \cdotp d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots}_b$ such that $x$ is recurring. Let the non-recurring part of $x$ be: $\sqbrk {s \cdotp d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots d_r}_b$ Let the recurring part of $x$ be: $\sqbrk {\ldots d_{r + 1} d_{r + 2} \ldots d_{r + p} \ldots}_b$ Then $x$ is denoted: $x = s.d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots d_r \dot d_{r + 1} d_{r + 2} \ldots \dot d_{r + p}$ That is, a dot is placed over the first and last digit of the first instance of the recurring part. This notation is referred to as recurrence notation

title: Definition:Basis Expansion/Recurrence/Period
snippet: Let $b \in \N: b \ge 2$. Let $x$ be a rational number. Let the basis expansion of $x$ in base $b$ be: $\sqbrk {s \cdotp d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots}_b$ From Basis Expansion of Rational Number, $x$ either terminates or recurs. The period of recurrence is the number of digits in the recurring part after which it repeats itself. Category:Definitions/Basis Expansions

title: Definition:Basis Expansion/Recurrence/Recurring Part
snippet: Let $b \in \N: b \ge 2$. Let $x$ be a real number. Let the basis expansion of $x$ in base $b$ be recurring: $\sqbrk {s \cdotp d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots d_r d_{r + 1} d_{r + 2} \ldots d_{r + p} d_{r + 1} d_{r + 2} \ldots d_{r + p } d_{r + 1} d_{r + 2} \ldots d_{r + p} d_{r + 1} \ldots}_b$ The recurring part of $x$ is: $\sqbrk {d_{r + 1} d_{r + 2} \ldots d_{r + p}}$

title: Definition:Basis Expansion/Termination
snippet: Let $b \in \N: b \ge 2$. Let the basis expansion of $x$ in base $b$ be: $\sqbrk {s \cdotp d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots}_b$ Let it be the case that: $\exists m \in \N: \forall k \ge m: d_k = 0$ That is, every digit of $x$ in base $b$ after a certain point is zero. Then $x$ is said to terminate.

title: Definition:Basis Representation
snippet: Let $b \in \Z$ be an integer such that $b > 1$. Let $n \in \Z$ be an integer such that $n \ne 0$. The (basis) representation of $n$ to the base $b$ is the unique string of digits: $\pm \sqbrk {r_m r_{m - 1} \ldots r_2 r_1 r_0}_b$ where $\pm$ is: the negative sign $-$ $n 0$ If $n = 0$, then $n$ is represented simply as $0$.

title: Definition:Basis Representation/Also known as
snippet: == Basis Representation: Also known as == A (basis) representation of $n$ to the base $b$ is also known as a (basis) development of $n$ to the base $b$. Informally, we can say: $n$ is (written or expressed) in base $b$ $n$ is (written or expressed) to base $b$.

title: Definition:Basis Vector
snippet: Let $K$ be a division ring. Let $\struct {G, +_G, \circ}_K$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $\BB$ be a basis of $\struct {G, +_G, \circ}_K$. Let $\mathbf v$ be an element of $\BB$. Then $\mathbf v$ is known as a basis vector of $\struct {G, +_G, \circ}_K$ ( $\BB$).

title: Definition:Basis for Neighborhood System
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. Let $a \in A$ be a point in $M$. Let $\BB_a$ be a set of neighborhoods of $a$ in $M$. Then $\BB_a$ is a basis for the neighborhood system at $a$ : $\forall N_a \subseteq M: \exists B \in \BB_a: B \subseteq N_a$ where $N_a$ denotes a neighborhood of $a$ in $M$. That is, $\BB_a$ is a basis for the neighborhood system at $a$ every neighborhood of $a$ contains an element of $\BB_a$ as a subset.

title: Definition:Basis for Open Sets (Metric Space)
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. Let $\BB$ be a set of open sets of $M$. Then $\BB$ is a basis for the open sets of $M$ : for each open set $U$ of $M$, $U$ is the union of sets of $\BB$.

title: Definition:Baudot Code/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Baudot Code == The Baudot code was invented by in the $1870$s. It was widely used in telegraphy. It superseded Morse code but has now been mostly replaced by ASCII.

title: Definition:Bayes' Factor
snippet: Let $D$ be a set of data which may be assumed to have arisen from one of only $2$ possible models: $M_1$ or $M_2$. Let the prior probabilities of $M_1$ and $M_2$ be denoted $\map \Pr {M_1}$ and $\map \Pr {M_2}$ such that $\map \Pr {M_2} = 1 - \map \Pr {M_1}$. Let the posterior probabilities be denoted $\condprob {M_1} D$ and $\condprob {M_2} D$ such that $\condprob {M_2} D = 1 - \condprob {M_1} D$.

title: Definition:Bayes' Factor/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Bayes' Factor == The concept of the Bayes' factor was introduced in $1935$ by .

title: Definition:Bayesian Confidence Interval
snippet: A Bayesian confidence interval is conceptually different from a confidence interval, but in many cases is numerically equivalent.

title: Definition:Bayesian Decision Theory
snippet: Bayesian decision theory is a branch of decision theory which is informed by Bayesian probability. It is a statistical system that tries to quantify the tradeoff between various decisions, making use of probabilities and costs.

title: Definition:Bayesian Inference
snippet: Bayesian inference is a method of statistical inference based on Bayes' Theorem. The unknowns to be estimated are assumed to have a prior probability distribution. Using Bayes' Theorem, this is combined with the information from observed data expressed in terms of the likelihood of forming a posterior probability distribution for the unknowns. As and when further data become available, the posterior distribution may be used as a prior distribution for further analysis.

title: Definition:Bayesian Inference/Belief-Based
snippet: Belief-based Bayesian inference is a method of Bayesian inference in which the prior distribution is based on a personal belief about how it is likely to be. The precise nature of this prior probability distribution influences the posterior distribution.

title: Definition:Bayesian Inference/Noncommittal Approach
snippet: Noncommittal Bayesian inference is a method of Bayesian inference in which there is a noncommittal attitude towards what the prior distribution is likely to be. Under such an approach, the prior distribution is typically taken to be a uniform distribution over a plausible range of values.

title: Definition:Bayesian Probability Model
snippet: The Bayesian probability model is a mathematical model that defines the probability of an event occurring as a degree of belief. That is, that probability is defined as the degree of which it is rational to believe certain statements based on intuition, experience, judgment, or opinion.

title: Definition:Bayesian Statistics
snippet: Bayesian statistics is a type of statistics in which the parameters of the probability distributions themselves are considered as having probability distributions.

title: Definition:Bead
snippet: A bead is a particle whose motion is constrained by a wire, along which it can slide with zero friction. Category:Definitions/Ideals in Physics

title: Definition:Bearing
snippet: Let $A$ be a point on the surface of Earth such that $P$ is neither the North Pole nor the South Pole. Let $B$ be another point on the surface of Earth. The bearing of $B$ $A$ is defined as the angle measured clockwise between $AB$ and $AN$, where $N$ is the North Pole. 300px

title: Definition:Bearing/Symbol
snippet: == Bearing: Symbol == The angle of a bearing is measured in degrees, and its presentation padded out to $3$ digits. Hence, for example, a bearing of $45$ degrees is expressed as $045 \degrees$.

title: Definition:Bearing/Warning
snippet: == Bearing: Warning == For the concept of a bearing to make proper sense, it is important to note that $B$ must be sufficiently close to $A$ so as to allow the surface of Earth to be approximated to a plane. Category:Definitions/Bearing

title: Definition:Beats
snippet: When two harmonic waves of slightly different frequency are superimposed, the resulting fluctuations of amplitude are known as beats. 620px

title: Definition:Beats/Frequency
snippet: Let $W_1$ and $W_2$ be harmonic waves whose superimposition exhibits beats. The beat frequency is defined as the frequency at which the amplitude fluctuates. 620px

title: Definition:Beatty Sequence
snippet: Let $x$ be an irrational number. The Beatty sequence on $x$ is the integer sequence $\BB_x$ defined as: $\BB_x := \sequence{\floor{n x} }_{n \mathop \in \Z_{\ge 0} }$ That is, the terms are the floors of the successive integer multiples of $x$.

title: Definition:Beatty Sequence/Complementary
snippet: Let $x$ be an irrational number. Let $\BB_x$ be the Beatty sequence on $x$. The complementary Beatty sequence on $x$ is the integer sequence formed by the integers which are missing from $\BB_x$.

title: Definition:Because
snippet: If statement $p$ logically implies statement $q$, then we may say: $q$, because $p$. The symbol $\dashv$ is interpreted to mean because. Thus: $r \dashv p, q$ means: Given as premises $p$ and $q$, we may validly conclude $r$ or $r$, because $p$ and $q$.

title: Definition:Becquerel
snippet: The becquerel is the SI unit of radioactivity. One becquerel is defined as the radioactivity of a given quantity of radioactive substance in which one nucleus decays per second.

title: Definition:Becquerel/Base Units
snippet: The SI base units of the Becquerel are: $\mathrm {Bq} := \mathrm s^{-1}$ where $\mathrm s$ denotes seconds (of time). Category:Definitions/Becquerel

title: Definition:Becquerel/Symbol
snippet: == Becquerel: Symbol == The symbol for the becquerel is $\mathrm {Bq}$.

title: Definition:Behrens-Fisher Test
snippet: The Behrens-Fisher test involves $2$ independent samples. It is an extension of the $t$-test in which the requirement of equal population variances is relaxed. It is still a subject of controversy, and its validity may not be universally accepted.

title: Definition:Behrens-Fisher Test/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Behrens-Fisher Test == The Behrens-Fisher test was invented by in $1929$, and subsequently expanded upon by in $1937$.

title: Definition:Bei Function
snippet: Let $J_n$ denote the Bessel function of the first kind. The Bei function is defined as: $\map {\Bei_n} x = \map \Im {\map {J_n} {x \map \exp {\dfrac {3 \pi i} 4} } }$ where: $\exp$ denotes the exponential function $x$ is real $\map \Im z$ denotes the imaginary part of $z$.

title: Definition:Bei Function/Also known as
snippet: == Bei Function: Also known as == The Bei function, along with: its real counterpart the Ber function the Ker function and Kei function are known collectively as the Kelvin functions, for . Some sources report and denote the Bei function uncapitalised: bei function.

title: Definition:Bel
snippet: The bel is a unit for comparing levels of power. The number of bels is equal to the (common) logarithm of the ratio of the two levels of power.

title: Definition:Bel/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Bel: Conversion Factors == Category:Definitions/Bel

title: Definition:Bel/Symbol
snippet: == Bel: Symbol == The symbol for the bel is $\mathrm B$.

title: Definition:Belief-Based Bayesian Inference/Motivation
snippet: == Belief-Based Bayesian Inference: Motivation == Many regard the use of a belief-based Bayesian inference as controversial. The use of belief-based Bayesian inference is motivated on the grounds that the influence of any prior distribution becomes diluted in the posterior distribution by the impact of the data.

title: Definition:Bell Number
snippet: The Bell Numbers $B_n$ are a sequence of natural numbers defined as the number of ways a set with $n$ elements can be partitioned.

title: Definition:Bell Number/Sequence
snippet: The sequence of Bell numbers begins: $(1), 1, 2, 5, 15, 52, 203, 877, 4140, 21 \, 147, \ldots$ where the first $(1)$ is the zeroth Bell number $B_0$. Category:Definitions/Bell Numbers

title: Definition:Below
snippet: Numbers: Number $a$ is below number $b$ $a$ is less than $b$. Solid Geometry: Point $a$ is below point $b$ the height of $a$ a given frame of reference $R$ is less than the height of $b$ $R$. Plane Geometry: Point $a$ is below Point $b$ the $y$ coordinate of $a$ is less than the $y$ coordinate of $b$.

title: Definition:Below (Number)
snippet: In the context of numbers, below means less than. Note that this applies to: the natural numbers $\N$ the integers $\Z$ the rational numbers $\Q$ the real numbers $\R$ but specifically not the complex numbers $\C$ because the complex numbers do not have a usual ordering.

title: Definition:Below (Plane Geometry)
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be points in the cartesian plane $\R^2$. Then: $a$ is below $b$ the $y$ coordinate of $a$ is less than the $y$ coordinate of $b$.

title: Definition:Below (Solid Geometry)
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be points in $3$-dimensional Euclidean space $\R^3$. Let $P$ be an arbitrary plane embedded in $S$ be distinguished and defined as horizontal. Then: $a$ is below $b$ the height of $a$ $P$ is less than the height of $b$ $P$.

title: Definition:Bending Moment
snippet: The bending moment is the sum of the moments of the forces acting on one side of a cross-section of a beam.

title: Definition:Ber Function
snippet: Let $J_n$ denote the Bessel function of the first kind. The Ber function is defined as: $\map {\Ber_n} x = \map \Re {\map {J_n} {x \map \exp {\dfrac {3 \pi i} 4} } }$ where: $\exp$ denotes the exponential function $x$ is real $\map \Re z$ denotes the real part of $z$.

title: Definition:Ber Function/Also known as

title: Definition:Bernoulli's Equation
snippet: Bernoulli's equation is a first order ordinary differential equation which can be put into the form: $\dfrac {\d y} {\d x} + \map P x y = \map Q x y^n$ where $n \ne 0$ and $n \ne 1$.

title: Definition:Bernoulli's Equation/Also known as
snippet: == Bernoulli's Equation: Also known as == Some sources report Bernoulli's equation as a Bernoulli equation.

title: Definition:Bernoulli's Equation/Historical Note
snippet: == Bernoulli's Equation: Historical Note == Bernoulli's equation was first solved by and , and also .

title: Definition:Bernoulli's Equation (Fluid Mechanics)
snippet: Bernoulli's equation is a statement of conservation of energy in the context of fluid mechanics: $\ds \int \dfrac {\d p} \rho + \dfrac 1 2 v^2 + V = C$ where: $p$ is the pressure of the fluid $\rho$ is the density of the fluid $V$ is the gravitational potential $C$ is constant for a given stream line.

title: Definition:Bernoulli's Equation (Fluid Mechanics)/Bernoulli's Constant
snippet: Consider Bernoulli's equation: $\ds \int \dfrac {\d p} \rho + \dfrac 1 2 v^2 + V = C$ The constant $C$ is known as Bernoulli's constant.

title: Definition:Bernoulli's Equation (Fluid Mechanics)/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Bernoulli's Equation == Bernoulli's equation was first formulated by in $1738$.

title: Definition:Bernoulli Distribution
snippet: Let $X$ be a discrete random variable on a probability space. Then $X$ has the Bernoulli distribution with parameter $p$ : $(1): \quad X$ has exactly two possible values, for example $\Img X = \set {a, b}$ $(2): \quad \map \Pr {X = a} = p$ $(3): \quad \map \Pr {X = b} = 1 - p$ where $0 \le p \le 1$. That is, the probability mass function is given by: $\map {p_X} x = \begin {cases} p & : x = a \\ 1 - p & : x = b \\ 0 & : x \notin \set {a, b} \\ \end {cases}$ If we allow: $\Img X = \set {0, 1}$ then we can write: $\map {p_X} x = p^x \paren {1 - p}^{1 - x}$

title: Definition:Bernoulli Distribution/Also defined as
snippet: == Bernoulli Distribution: Also defined as == In the definition of a Bernoulli distribution, some sources insist that $0 < p < 1$. However, it can be useful in certain circumstances to include the condition when the outcome is certainty. Category:Definitions/Bernoulli Distribution

title: Definition:Bernoulli Distribution/Notation
snippet: == Bernoulli Distribution: Notation == The Bernoulli distribution can be written: $X \sim \Bernoulli p$ but as, from Binomial Experiment has Binomial Distribution, the Bernoulli distribution is the same as the binomial distribution where $n = 1$, the notation: $X \sim \Binomial 1 p$ is often preferred, for notational economy. Frequently $q$ is used for $1 - p$ in which case the probability mass function is given by: $\map {p_X} x = \begin {cases} p & : x = a \\ q & : x = b \\ 0 & : x \notin \set {a, b} \\ \end {cases}$ where $p + q = 1$.
