title: Definition:Bernoulli Numbers/Generating Function
snippet: The Bernoulli numbers $B_n$ are a sequence of rational numbers defined by the exponential generating function: $\ds \frac x {e^x - 1} = \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \frac {B_n x^n} {n!}$

title: Definition:Bernoulli Numbers/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Bernoulli Numbers == The Bernoulli numbers were introduced by in his investigations into the power series expansion of the tangent function.

title: Definition:Bernoulli Numbers/Recurrence Relation
snippet: The Bernoulli numbers $B_n$ are a sequence of rational numbers defined by the recurrence relation: $B_n = \begin {cases} 1 & : n = 0 \\ \ds - \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \binom n k \frac {B_k} {n + 1 - k} & : n > 0 \end {cases}$ or equivalently: $B_n = \begin {cases} 1 & : n = 0 \\ \ds - \frac 1 {n + 1} \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \binom {n + 1} k B_k & : n > 0 \end {cases}$

title: Definition:Bernoulli Numbers/Sequence
snippet: The sequence of Bernoulli numbers begins: {{eqn | l = B_4 | ro= - | r = \dfrac 1 {30} | c = }} {{eqn | l = B_6 | r = \dfrac 1 {42} | c = }} {{eqn | l = B_8 | ro= - | r = \dfrac 1 {30} | c = }} {{eqn | l = B_{10} | r = \dfrac 5 {66} | c = }} {{eqn | l = B_{12} | ro= - | r = \dfrac {691} {2730} | c = }} The odd index Bernoulli numbers, apart from $B_1$, are all equal to $0$.

title: Definition:Bernoulli Polynomial
snippet: The Bernoulli polynomials $\map {B_n} x$ are the terms of the sequence of polynomials defined as: $\ds \map {B_n} x = \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^n \binom n k B_{n - k} x^k$ where $B_k$ are the Bernoulli numbers.

title: Definition:Bernoulli Trial
snippet: A Bernoulli trial is an experiment whose sample space has two elements, which can be variously described, for example, as: Success and failure True and False $1$ and $0$ the classic heads and tails. Formally, a Bernoulli trial is modelled by a probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ such that: $\Omega = \set {a, b}$ $\Sigma = \powerset \Omega$ $\map \Pr a = p, \map \Pr b = 1 - p$ where: $\powerset \Omega$ denotes the power set of $\Omega$ $0 \le p \le 1$ That is, $\Pr$ obeys a Bernoulli distribution.

title: Definition:Bernoulli Trial/Also defined as
snippet: == Bernoulli Trial: Also defined as == Some sources insist that the valid codomain of a Bernoulli trial is $0 < p < 1$, but it can be useful in certain circumstances to include the condition when the outcome is certainty. Category:Definitions/Bernoulli Trials

title: Definition:Bernoulli Trial/Bernoulli Variable
snippet: Let $\EE = \struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a Bernoulli trial. Let $X$ be a discrete random variable whose sample space is $\Omega$ in such a Bernoulli trial. Then $X$ is known as a Bernoulli variable.

title: Definition:Bernoulli Trial/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Bernoulli Trial == The concept of a Bernoulli trial was first raised by in $1713$.

title: Definition:Bessel's Equation
snippet: == Equation == Bessel's equation is a second order ODE of the form: $x^2 \dfrac {\d^2 y} {\d x^2} + x \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} + \paren {x^2 - n^2} y = 0$ The parameter $n$ may be any arbitrary real or complex number.

title: Definition:Bessel's Equation/Also known as
snippet: == Bessel's Equation: Also known as == Bessel's equation is also referred to as Bessel's differential equation. The parameter $n$ is variously presented. Some sources use $p$.

title: Definition:Bessel's Equation/Also presented as
snippet: == Equation == Some sources give Bessel's equation as: $x^2 \dfrac {\d^2 y} {\d x^2} + x \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} + \paren {\lambda^2 x^2 - n^2} y = 0$

title: Definition:Bessel's Equation/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Bessel's Equation == Bessel's equation occurs in a number of applications in the fields of physics and engineering. In particular, it arises in the analysis of the harmonics of the vibration of a circular drum.

title: Definition:Bessel's Modified Equation
snippet: == Equation == Bessel's modified equation is a second order ODE of the form: $x^2 \dfrac {\d^2 y} {\d x^2} + x \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} - \paren {x^2 + n^2} y = 0$ The parameter $n$ may be any arbitrary real or complex number.

title: Definition:Bessel's Modified Equation/Also known as
snippet: == Bessel's Modified Equation: Also known as == Bessel's modified equation is also referred to as Bessel's modified differential equation. Some sources present it as the modified Bessel equation. The parameter $n$ is variously presented. Some sources use $p$.

title: Definition:Bessel Function
snippet: The Bessel functions are solutions to Bessel's equation: $x^2 \dfrac {\d^2 y} {\d x^2} + x \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} + \paren {x^2 - n^2} y = 0$ These solutions have two main classes: the Bessel functions of the first kind $J_n$ and: the Bessel functions of the second kind $Y_n$.

title: Definition:Bessel Function/First Kind
snippet: A Bessel function of the first kind of order $n$ is a Bessel function which is non-singular at the origin. It is usually denoted $\map {J_n} x$, where $x$ is the dependent variable of the instance of Bessel's equation to which $\map {J_n} x$ forms a solution.

title: Definition:Bessel Function/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Bessel Functions == Bessel functions were introduced by in $1824$. They arise in many problems of physics and engineering. However, despite bearing the name of , they were first studied by . He encountered them during his study of the vibrations of a stretched circular membrane.

title: Definition:Bessel Function/Order
snippet: Consider Bessel's equation: $x^2 \dfrac {\d^2 y} {\d x^2} + x \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} + \paren {x^2 - n^2} y = 0$ Let: $\map {J_n} x$ denote the Bessel function of the first kind $\map {Y_n} x$ denote the Bessel function of the second kind be the solutions of Bessel's equation as defined. The parameter $n$ is known as the order of the Bessel function.

title: Definition:Bessel Function/Second Kind
snippet: A Bessel function of the second kind of order $n$ is a Bessel function which is singular at the origin. It is usually denoted $\map {Y_n} x$, where $x$ is the dependent variable of the instance of Bessel's equation to which $\map {Y_n} x$ forms a solution.

title: Definition:Bessel Function of the First Kind/Also known as
snippet: == Bessel Function of the First Kind: Also known as == Some sources (for whatever reason) do not address Bessel functions of the second kind, and as a consequence refer to Bessel functions of the first kind simply as Bessel functions.

title: Definition:Bessel Function of the First Kind/Mistake
snippet: == Source Work == Bessel function

title: Definition:Bessel Function of the Second Kind/Also known as
snippet: == Bessel Function of the Second Kind: Also known as == Bessel functions of the second kind are also known as Neumann functions. These are named for .

title: Definition:Best-Response Function
snippet: Let a strategic game $G$ be modelled by: $G = \stratgame N {A_i} {\succsim_i}$ Let $a^*$ be a Nash equilibrium of $G$: $\forall i \in N: \forall a_i \in A_i: \tuple {a^*_{-i}, a^*_i} \succsim_i \tuple {a^*_{-i}, a_i}$ For any $a_{-1} \in A_{-i}$, let $\map {B_i} {a_{-i} }$ be the set of player $i$'s best moves, defined as: $\map {B_i} {a_{-i} } = \set {a_i \in A_i: \forall a'_i \in A_i: \tuple {a_{-i}, a_i} \precsim_i \tuple {a_{-i}, a'_i} }$ Then $B_{-i}$ is known as the best-response function of player $i$.

title: Definition:Best Approximation
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. Let $B \subsetneq A$ be a proper subset of $A$. Let $x \in A \setminus B$ be an element of $A$ which is outside $B$. The best approximation to $x$ $B$ is the element $y$ of $B$ such that the distance between $x$ and $y$ is smallest. That is, it is the element of $B$ which lies closest to $x$.

title: Definition:Best Rational Approximation
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be an (irrational) real number. The rational number $a = \dfrac p q$ is a best rational approximation to $x$ : $(1): \quad a$ is in canonical form, that is $p$ is coprime to $q$: $p \perp q$ $(2): \quad \left\vert{x - \dfrac p q}\right\vert = \min \left\{ {\left\vert{x - \dfrac {p'} {q'} }\right\vert: q' \le q}\right\}$ That is: $\left\vert{x - \dfrac p q}\right\vert$ is smaller than for any $\dfrac {p'} {q'}$ where $q' \le q$ where $\left\vert{x}\right\vert$ denotes the absolute value of $x$.

title: Definition:Best Unbiased Estimator
snippet: Let $\theta$ be a population parameter of some statistical model. Let $\delta$ be an unbiased estimator of $\theta$. $\delta$ is the best unbiased estimator it has the smallest variance of all unbiased estimators of $\theta$.

title: Definition:Beta-Formula
snippet: Let $\mathbf B$ be a WFF of propositional logic that is not a literal. Then $\mathbf B$ is a $\beta$-formula : $\mathbf B$ is semantically equivalent to a disjunction $\mathbf B_1 \lor \mathbf B_2$ for some WFFs $\mathbf B_1, \mathbf B_2$.

title: Definition:Beta Distribution
snippet: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable on a probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $\Img X = \closedint 0 1$. $X$ is said to have a beta distribution it has probability density function: $\map {f_X} X = \dfrac {x^{\alpha - 1} \paren {1 - x}^{\beta - 1} } {\map \Beta {\alpha, \beta} }$ for $\alpha, \beta > 0$, where $\Beta$ denotes the beta function. This is written: $X \sim \BetaDist \alpha \beta$

title: Definition:Beta Distribution/Technical Note
snippet: == Technical Note for Beta Distribution == {{LatexFor|for = \BetaDist {\alpha} {\beta} }} When the arguments are single characters, it is usual to omit the braces: \BetaDist \alpha \beta This command is specific to . Category:Technical Notes

title: Definition:Beta Function
snippet: The beta function $\Beta: \C \times \C \to \C$ is defined for $\map \Re x, \map \Re y > 0$ as:

title: Definition:Beta Function/Also defined as
snippet: == Beta Function: Also known as == The beta function can also be defined as: $\map \Beta {m, n} := \dfrac {\paren {n - 1}! \paren {m - 1}!} {\paren {m + n - 1}!}$ when $m$ and $n$ are (strictly) positive integers.

title: Definition:Beta Function/Also known as
snippet: == Beta Function: Also known as == The beta function can also be referred to as the Eulerian integral of the first kind.

title: Definition:Beta Function/Definition 1
snippet: The beta function $\Beta: \C \times \C \to \C$ is defined for $\map \Re x, \map \Re y > 0$ as: $\ds \map \Beta {x, y} := \int_{\mathop \to 0}^{\mathop \to 1} t^{x - 1} \paren {1 - t}^{y - 1} \rd t$

title: Definition:Beta Function/Definition 1/Also rendered as
snippet: == Beta Function: Definition $1$: Also rendered as == In a frequently-seen abuse of notation, the improper nature of the integral defining the beta function is often ignored, and the expression is rendered: $\ds \map \Beta {x, y} := \int_0^1 t^{x - 1} \paren {1 - t}^{y - 1} \rd t$

title: Definition:Beta Function/Definition 2
snippet: The beta function $\Beta: \C \times \C \to \C$ is defined for $\map \Re x, \map \Re y > 0$ as: $\ds \map \Beta {x, y} := 2 \int_0^{\pi / 2} \paren {\sin \theta}^{2 x - 1} \paren {\cos \theta}^{2 y - 1} \rd \theta$

title: Definition:Beta Function/Definition 3
snippet: The beta function $\Beta: \C \times \C \to \C$ is defined for $\map \Re x, \map \Re y > 0$ as: $\map \Beta {x, y} := \dfrac {\map \Gamma x \map \Gamma y} {\map \Gamma {x + y} }$ where $\Gamma$ is the gamma function.

title: Definition:Beta Function/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on the Beta Function == The beta function $\map \Beta {x, y}$ was discovered by .

title: Definition:Between
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $a, b, c \in S$ such that $a \preceq b$ and $b \preceq c$. Then $b$ is between $a$ and $c$.

title: Definition:Between-Groups Design
snippet: A between-groups design is an experimental design whose purpose is to measure the value of a (dependent) variable for distinct groups, under each of the experimental conditions.

title: Definition:Between-Groups Design/Also known as
snippet: == Between-Groups Design: Also known as == A between-groups design is also known as a between-subjects design.

title: Definition:Between-Treatments Sum of Squares
snippet: Between-treatments sum of squares is a technique in analysis of variance. It is defined as: what the sum of squares of deviations from the mean would have been if the response for each experimental unit had been equal to the mean response for all units receiving that treatment. It is obtained by dividing the sum of squares by the number of degrees of freedom.

title: Definition:Between (Geometry)
snippet: Betweenness is one of the undefined terms in Tarski's Geometry. Intuitively, a point $b$ is between two others $a$ and $c$ it lies on the line segment $a c$. However as line segment has not yet been defined, we are not allowed to call upon it at this stage. We offer an ostensive definition: File:Betweenness.png In the picture, point $b$ is between the two points $a, c$, and we write: $\mathsf{B}abc$ However, point $d$ is not between the two points $a$ and $c$, and we write: $\map \neg {\mathsf B a d c}$

title: Definition:Between (Geometry)/N-dimensional Euclidean space Intuition
snippet: The intuition behind this definition comes from the fact that when we think that $B$ is between $A$ and $C$, we think of three things. The first thing is that $A$, $B$ and $C$ are collinear. So: $\size {\map \cos {\angle {BAC} } } = 1$ Hence, from Cosine Formula for Dot Product, we should have: $\size {\vec{AB} \cdot \vec{AC} } = \norm {\vec {AB} } * \norm {\vec {AC} }$ Secondly, the vectors $\vec {AB}$ and $\vec {AC}$ have the same direction. Therefore, their dot product should be positive.

title: Definition:Bi-/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Use of Bi- == The prefix bi- can be found in the following contexts: biannual: something which happens twice a year bidual: normed dual of the dual of a normed space binary: an adjective indicating $2$-ness binomial: an expression with two terms binormal: the vector in $3$-space which is perpendicular to both the normal and tangent to a curve

title: Definition:Bi-/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Bi- == The prefix bi- derives from the Latin bis, meaning twice, or Latin bīnus, meaning double. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Bi-Invariant Riemannian Metric
snippet: Let $G$ be a Lie group. Let $\struct {G, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Suppose $g$ is both left-invariant and right-invariant. Then $g$ is said to be bi-invariant.

title: Definition:Bi-Orthogonal Sequences
snippet: Let $\HH$ be a Hilbert space. Let $\sequence {a_n}$ and $\sequence {b_n}$ be sequences in $\HH$. $\sequence {a_n}$ and $\sequence {b_n}$ are described as bi-orthogonal : $\forall m, n \in \N: \innerprod {a_m} {b_n} = \begin {cases} 1 & : m = n \\0 & : m \ne n \end {cases}$ where $\innerprod {a_m} {b_n}$ denotes inner product of $a_m$ and $b_n$.

title: Definition:Biadditive Mapping
snippet: Let $M, N, P$ be abelian groups. Let $M \times N$ be the cartesian product. A biadditive mapping $f : M \times N \to P$ is a mapping such that: $\forall m_1, m_2 \in M : \forall n \in N: \map f {m_1 + m_2, n} = \map f {m_1, n} + \map f {m_2, n}$ $\forall m \in M: \forall n_1, n_2 \in N: \map f {m, n_1 + n_2} = \map f {m, n_1} + \map f {m, n_2}$

title: Definition:Biannual
snippet: == Examples of Use of Bi- == A biannual event is one which occurs twice a year.

title: Definition:Bias
snippet: Bias is defined as a prejudice or a lack of objectivity or randomness causing an imbalance which makes it likely that the outcome will tend to be distorted. This can happen in statistics when a process contains some systematic imbalance, resulting in the outcome not being equal to the true value being sought.

title: Definition:Bias/Estimator
snippet: Let $\theta$ be a population parameter of some statistical model. Let $\mathbf X$ be a random sample from this population. Let $\delta$ be an estimator of $\theta$. The bias in $\delta$ is defined as: $\map {\operatorname {bias} } \delta = \expect {\map \delta {\mathbf X} } - \theta$

title: Definition:Biased Estimator
snippet: Let $\delta$ be an estimator of a population parameter $\theta$ of some statistical model. $\delta$ is a biased estimator it is not an unbiased estimator. That is, its bias is not equal to $0$ for some true value of $\theta$.

title: Definition:Biased Sample
snippet: A biased sample is a sample whose composition is not only dependent upon the population from which it was drawn, but also by some property of the method of taking that sample which tends to cause over-representation of some parts of that population. It is a property of the method of sampling rather than the sample itself.

title: Definition:Bicentral Tree
snippet: A tree $T$ is bicentral it has a bicenter.

title: Definition:Biconditional
snippet: The biconditional is a binary connective: $p \iff q$ defined as: $\paren {p \implies q} \land \paren {q \implies p}$ That is: $p \iff q$ can be voiced: $p$ $q$.

title: Definition:Biconditional/Also known as
snippet: == Biconditional: Also known as == Other names for the biconditional include: bi-implication equivalence material equivalence logical equivalence logical equality. It can sometimes be seen hyphenated: bi-conditional.

title: Definition:Biconditional/Boolean Interpretation
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ be propositional formulas. Let $\mathbf A \iff \mathbf B$ denote the biconditional operator. The truth value of $\mathbf A \iff \mathbf B$ under a boolean interpretation $v$ is given by: $\map v {\mathbf A \iff \mathbf B} = \begin{cases} \T & \text{if } \map v {\mathbf A} = \map v {\mathbf B} \\ \F & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$

title: Definition:Biconditional/Constituent
snippet: Let $p \iff q$ be a compound statement whose main connective is the biconditional: If $p$ is true, then $q$ is true, and if $q$ is true, then $p$ is true. The substatements $p$ and $q$ are known as the constituents.

title: Definition:Biconditional/Notational Variants
snippet: Various symbols are encountered that denote the concept of biconditionality: {| border="1" cellpadding="4" cellspacing="0" style="font-weight:bold; text-align:center; |- ! Symbol ! Origin |- | $p \iff q$ | |- | $p\ \mathsf{EQ} \ q$ | |- | $p \equiv q$ | |- | $p = q$ | |- | $p \leftrightarrow q$ | |- | $\operatorname E p q$ | Łukasiewicz's Polish notation |} It is usual in mathematics to use $\iff$, as there are other uses for the other symbols.

title: Definition:Biconditional/Semantics of Biconditional
snippet: The concept of the biconditional has been defined such that $p \iff q$ means both: $p \iff q$ can be considered as a shorthand to replace the use of the longer and more unwieldy expression involving two conditionals and a conjunction. If we refer to ways of expressing the conditional, we see that: Thus we arrive at the usual way of reading $p \iff q$ which is: $p$ is true ' $q$ is true. This can also be said as:

title: Definition:Biconditional/Semantics of Biconditional/Necessary and Sufficient
snippet: Let: $p \iff q$ where $\iff$ denotes the biconditional operator. Then it can be said that $p$ is necessary and sufficient for $q$. This is a consequence of the definitions of necessary and sufficient conditions.

title: Definition:Biconditional/Truth Function
snippet: The biconditional connective defines the truth function $f^\leftrightarrow$ as follows: {{eqn | l = \map {f^\leftrightarrow} {\F, \F} | r = \T }} {{eqn | l = \map {f^\leftrightarrow} {\F, \T} | r = \F }} {{eqn | l = \map {f^\leftrightarrow} {\T, \F} | r = \F }} {{eqn | l = \map {f^\leftrightarrow} {\T, \T} | r = \T }}

title: Definition:Biconditional/Truth Table
snippet: The characteristic truth table of the biconditional operator $p \iff q$ is as follows: $\begin{array}{|cc||c|} \hline p & q & p \iff q \\ \hline \F & \F & \T \\ \F & \T & \F \\ \T & \F & \F \\ \T & \T & \T \\ \hline \end{array}$

title: Definition:Biconditional/Truth Table/Matrix Form
snippet: The characteristic truth table of the biconditional operator $p \iff q$ can be presented in matrix form as follows: $\begin{array}{c|cc} \iff & \T & \F \\ \hline \T & \T & \F \\ \F & \F & \T \\ \end{array}$

title: Definition:Biconditional/Truth Table/Number
snippet: The truth table number of the biconditional operator $p \iff q$ is as follows: Ascending and descending order: $1001$ or $\T \F \F \T$

title: Definition:Biconnected Set
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a connected set in $T$. Then $H$ is biconnected it is not the union of two disjoint non-degenerate connected sets.

title: Definition:Bid
snippet: Let $A$ be an auction. A bid is a move by a player in $A$ which consists of the submission of a non-negative number. Such a bid is associated with a payment which is to be made by the winning player in exchange for the prize. Category:Definitions/Game Theory

title: Definition:Bidiagonal Matrix
snippet: A bidiagonal matrix is a square matrix in which the elements outside the leading diagonal and either the subdiagonal or the superdiagonal are all zero.

title: Definition:Bidiagonal Matrix/Lower
snippet: A lower bidiagonal matrix is a square matrix in which the elements outside the leading diagonal and subdiagonal are all zero. $\begin {pmatrix} a & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\ b & c & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & d & e & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & x & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & y & z \end {pmatrix}$ That is, a square matrix such that $a_{i j} = 0$ when $i j + 1$.

title: Definition:Bidiagonal Matrix/Upper
snippet: An upper bidiagonal matrix is a square matrix in which the elements outside the leading diagonal and superdiagonal are all zero. $\begin {pmatrix} a & b & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & c & d & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & e & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & x & y \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & z \end {pmatrix}$ That is, a square matrix such that $a_{i j} = 0$ when $i > j$ or $j > i + 1$.

title: Definition:Bifunctor
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$, $\mathbf D$, $\mathbf E$ be categories. Then: a bifunctor is a functor $F:\mathbf C \times \mathbf D \to \mathbf E$, from a product $\mathbf {C \times D}$ to a category $E$. A bifunctor is often viewed as a functor of two variables.

title: Definition:Bifunctor/Substitution of First Variable
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$, $\mathbf D$, $\mathbf E$ be categories. Let $F:\mathbf C \times \mathbf D \to \mathbf E$ be a bifunctor. Let $C$ be an object of $\mathbf C$. Then: $\map F {C, -}$ denotes the functor from $\mathbf D$ to $\mathbf E$ defined as: {{DefineFunctor |ob = for each object $D \in \mathbf D : \map {\map F {C, -} } D := \map F {C, D}$ |mor = for each morphism $g \in \mathbf D : \map {\map F {C, -} } g := \map F {\operatorname{id}_C, g}$ }}

title: Definition:Bifunctor/Substitution of Second Variable
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$, $\mathbf D$, $\mathbf E$ be categories. Let $F:\mathbf C \times \mathbf D \to \mathbf E$ be a bifunctor. Let $D$ be an object of $\mathbf D$. Then: $\map F {-, D}$ denotes the functor from $\mathbf C$ to $\mathbf E$ defined as: {{DefineFunctor |ob = for each object $C \in \mathbf C : \map {\map F {-, D} } C := \map F {C, D}$ |mor = for each morphism $f \in \mathbf C : \map {\map F {-, D} } f := \map F {f, \operatorname{id}_D}$ }}

title: Definition:Bifurcation
snippet: A bifurcation is a sudden change in the nature of an attractor or repellor as the defining mapping or flow undergoes a change changes in the defining equations.

title: Definition:Bifurcation/Flip
snippet: A flip bifurcation is a bifurcation in which a family of mappings $T_\lambda$, indexed by a real bifurcation parameter $\lambda$, has an repelling fixed point replaced by a pair of periodic points of period $2$, forming an attractor.

title: Definition:Bifurcation/Hopf
snippet: A Hopf bifurcation is a bifurcation in which a family of flows $\map {x_\lambda} t$, indexed by a real bifurcation parameter $\lambda$, has an attractor consisting of: a fixed point replaced by a circle a repelling fixed point for a small change in the index.

title: Definition:Bifurcation Theory
snippet: Bifurcation theory is the mathematical study of changes in the qualitative or topological structure of a given family, such as the integral curves of a family of vector fields, and the solutions of a family of differential equations.

title: Definition:Big-O Notation/Also defined as
snippet: == Also defined as == Some authors require that the inequality be valid on the entire domain of definition. On , this is known as a uniform big-$\OO$ estimate. The statement $f = \map \OO g$ is sometimes seen to be defined as: $\ds \exists \alpha \in \R_{\ge 0}: \lim_{x \mathop \to \infty} \frac {\map f x} {\map g x} = \alpha$ However, requiring that the limit exists is generally viewed to be too restrictive. title: Definition:Big-O Notation/Also denoted as
snippet: == Also denoted as == In analytic number theory, sometimes Vinogradov's notations $f \ll g$ or $g \gg f$ are used for big-$\OO$ notation, to mean $f = \map \OO g$. This can often be clearer for estimates leading to typographically complex error terms. Some sources use an ordinary $O$: $f = \map O g$

title: Definition:Big-O Notation/Also known as
snippet: == Also known as == Some sources refer to big-$\OO$ notation unhyphenated: big $\OO$ notation. The big-$\OO$ notation, along with little-$\oo$ notation, are also referred to as Landau's symbols or the Landau symbols, for .

title: Definition:Big-O Notation/Complex/Infinity
snippet: Let $f$ and $g$ be complex functions defined for all complex numbers whose modulus is sufficiently large. The statement: $\map f z = \map \OO {\map g z}$ as $\cmod z \to \infty$ is equivalent to: $\exists c \in \R_{\ge 0}: \exists r_0 \in \R: \forall z \in \C: \paren {\cmod z \ge r_0 \implies \cmod {\map f z} \le c \cdot \cmod {\map g z} }$ That is: $\cmod {\map f z} \le c \cdot \cmod {\map g z}$ for all $z$ in a neighborhood of infinity in $\C$. Category:Definitions/Complex Analysis Category:Definitions/Big-O Notation

title: Definition:Big-O Notation/Complex/Point
snippet: Let $z_0 \in \C$. Let $f$ and $g$ be complex functions defined on a punctured neighborhood of $z_0$. The statement: $\map f z = \map \OO {\map g z}$ as $z \to z_0$ is equivalent to: $\exists c \in \R_{\ge 0}: \exists \delta \in \R_{>0}: \forall z \in \C : \paren {0 < \cmod {z - z_0} < \delta \implies \cmod {\map f z} \le c \cdot \cmod {\map g z} }$ That is: $\cmod {\map f z} \le c \cdot \cmod {\map g z}$ for all $z$ in a punctured neighborhood of $z_0$. Category:Definitions/Big-O Notation Category:Definitions/Complex Analysis

title: Definition:Big-O Notation/Implied Constant
snippet: Let $f$ and $g$ be real functions such that $f$ is big-$\OO$ of $g$. From the definition of the limit of a function, it can be seen that this is also equivalent to: $\exists c \in \R: c > 0, k \ge 0: \forall n > k: \map f n \le c \map g n$ For some fixed $k$ (appropriate to the function under consideration) the infimum of such $c$ is called the implied constant.

title: Definition:Big-O Notation/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Big-$\OO$ Notation == The expression $\map f n \in \map \OO {\map g n}$ is read as: $\map f n$ is big-O of $\map g n$ While it is correct and accurate to write: $\map f n \in \map \OO {\map g n}$ it is a common abuse of notation to write: $\map f n = \map \OO {\map g n}$ This notation offers some advantages. Category:Definitions/Big-O Notation

title: Definition:Big-O Notation/Real/Infinity
snippet: Let $f$ and $g$ be real functions defined on a neighborhood of $+ \infty$ in $\R$. The statement: $\map f x = \map \OO {\map g x}$ as $x \to \infty$ is equivalent to: $\exists c \in \R_{\ge 0}: \exists x_0 \in \R: \forall x \in \R: \paren {x \ge x_0 \implies \size {\map f x} \le c \cdot \size {\map g x} }$ That is: $\size {\map f x} \le c \cdot \size {\map g x}$ for $x$ sufficiently large. This statement is voiced $f$ is big-$\OO$ of $g$ or simply $f$ is big-$\OO$ $g$.

title: Definition:Big-O Notation/Real/Point
snippet: Let $x_0 \in \R$. Let $f$ and $g$ be real-valued or complex-valued functions defined on a punctured neighborhood of $x_0$. The statement: $\map f x = \map \OO {\map g x}$ as $x \to x_0$ is equivalent to: $\exists c \in \R_{\ge 0}: \exists \delta \in \R_{>0}: \forall x \in \R : \paren {0 < \size {x - x_0} < \delta \implies \size {\map f x} \le c \cdot \size {\map g x} }$ That is: $\size {\map f x} \le c \cdot \size {\map g x}$ for all $x$ in a punctured neighborhood of $x_0$. This statement is voiced $f$ is big-$\OO$ of $g$ at $x_0$ or simply $f$ is big-$\OO$ $g$ at $x_0$.

title: Definition:Big-O Notation/Sequence/Also defined as
snippet: == Big-$\OO$ Notation: Also defined as == Some authors require that $b_n$ be nonzero for $n$ sufficiently large. Some authors require that the functions appearing in the $\OO$-estimate be positive or strictly positive. Category:Definitions/Big-O Notation

title: Definition:Big-O Notation/Sequence/Definition 1
snippet: Let $g: \N \to \R$ be a real sequence, expressed here as a real-valued function on the set of natural numbers $\N$. Then $\map \OO g$ is defined as: $\map \OO g = \set {f: \N \to \R: \exists c \in \R_{>0}: \exists n_0 \in \N: \forall n > n_0: 0 \le \size {\map f n} \le c \cdot \size {\map g n} }$

title: Definition:Big-O Notation/Sequence/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\sequence {a_n}$ and $\sequence {b_n}$ be sequences of real or complex numbers. $a_n$ is big-$\OO$ of $b_n$ : $\exists c \in \R_{\ge 0}: \exists n_0 \in \N: \forall n \in \N: \paren {n \ge n_0 \implies \size {a_n} \le c \cdot \size {b_n} }$ That is: $\size {a_n} \le c \cdot \size {b_n}$ for all sufficiently large $n$. This is denoted: $a_n \in \map \OO {b_n}$

title: Definition:Big-O Notation/Uniform
snippet:
Let $X$ be a set. Let $V$ be a normed vector space over $\R$ or $\C$ with norm $
orm {\, \cdot \,}$. Let $f, g : X 	o V$ be mappings. Then $f$ is big-$\OO$ of $g$ uniformly : $\exists c > 0 :  orall x \in X : 
orm {\map f x} \le c \cdot 
orm {\map g x}$ This is denoted: $f = \map \OO g$ Category:Definitions/Big-O Notation

title: Definition:Big-Omega Notation/Also known as
snippet: == $\Omega$ Notation: Also known as == Note that in the Greek alphabet, $\Omega$ is the capital letter counterpart of the minuscule $\omega$. Hence the former is called big-omega and the latter little-omega. Some sources, therefore, write $\Omega$ notation as big-$\Omega$ notation, despite the fact that $\Omega$'s "big"-ness is intrinsic. may sometimes adopt this convention if clarity is improved. Category:Definitions/Big-Omega Notation

title: Definition:Big-Omega Notation/Definition 1
snippet: Let $g: \N \to \R$ be a real sequence, expressed here as a real-valued function on the set of natural numbers $\N$. Then $\map \Omega g$ is defined as: $\map \Omega g = \set {f: \N \to \R: \exists c \in \R_{>0}: \exists n_0 \in \N: \forall n > n_0: 0 \le c \cdot \size {\map g n} \le \size {\map f n} }$

title: Definition:Big-Omega Notation/Definition 2
snippet: Let $f: \N \to \R, g: \N \to \R$ be two real sequences, expressed here as real-valued functions on the set of natural numbers $\N$. Let there exist $c \in \R_{>0}$ such that: $\ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} {\frac {\map f n} {\map g n} } = c > 0$ Then: $\map f n \in \map \Omega {\map g n}$

title: Definition:Big-Omega Notation/Motivation
snippet: == Motivation for $\Omega$ Notation == $\Omega$ notation is a type of order notation for typically comparing run-times or growth rates between two growth functions. Category:Definitions/Big-Omega Notation

title: Definition:Big-Omega Notation/Notation
snippet: == Notation for $\Omega$ Notation == The expression $\map f n \in \map \Omega {\map g n}$ is read as: $\map f n$ is big-omega of $\map g n$ While it is correct and accurate to write: $\map f n \in \map \Omega {\map g n}$ it is a common abuse of notation to write: $\map f n = \map \Omega {\map g n}$ This notation offers some advantages. Category:Definitions/Big-Omega Notation

title: Definition:Big Data
snippet: Big data is a generic term for extremely large sets of data in the context of data science.

title: Definition:Big Model
snippet: Let $\MM$ be an $\LL$-structure with universe $M$. Let $\kappa$ be a cardinal. $\MM$ is $\kappa$-big if for every subset $A \subset M$ with cardinality $\card A < \kappa$, the following holds: if $\LL_A$ is the language obtained from $\LL$ by adding new constant symbols for each $a \in A$, then for every language $\LL_A^*$ obtained by adding a new relation symbol $R$ to $\LL_A$, and for every $\LL_A^*$-structure $\NN$ such that $\MM$ and $\NN$ are elementary equivalent as $\LL_A$-structures, there is a relation $R^\MM$ on $M$ such that $\struct {\MM, R^\MM}$ is elementary equivalent to $\NN$…

title: Definition:Big Monoid Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {M, \cdot}$ be a divisor-finite monoid. Let $\struct {R, +, \times}$ be an additive semiring. The big monoid ring of $R$ over $M$ is the ringoid $\struct {R^M, +, *}$ where: $R^M$ be the set of all mappings $M \to R$ $+$ is the pointwise operation induced by $+$ $*$ denotes convolution of mappings

Definition:Biholomorphic Function
snippet: Let $U$ and $V$ be open sets of the complex plane $\C$. Let $f: U \to V$ be a complex bijection from $U$ to $V$. Then $f$ is a biholomorphic function $f$ is a holomorphic function and: its inverse $f^{-1}: V \to U$ is also a holomorphic function.

title: Definition:Biholomorphic Function/Also known as
snippet: == Biholomorphic Function: Also known as == A biholomorphic function is also known as: a biholomorphism a conformal equivalence.

title: Definition:Bijection/Also known as
snippet: The terms biunique correspondence bijective correspondence bijective mapping are sometimes seen for bijection. Authors who prefer to limit the jargon of mathematics tend to use the term one-one and onto mapping for bijection. If a bijection exists between two sets $S$ and $T$, then $S$ and $T$ are said to be in one-to-one correspondence. Some sources refer to exact correspondence to mean exactly this. Some sources refer to it just as a correspondence.

title: Definition:Bijection/Class Theory
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be classes. Let $f: A \to B$ be a class mapping from $A$ to $B$. Then $f$ is said to be a bijection : $f$ is both a class injection and a class surjection.

title: Definition:Bijection/Definition 1
snippet: A mapping $f: S \to T$ is a bijection both: $(1): \quad f$ is an injection and: $(2): \quad f$ is a surjection. That is, $f$ is a relation which is: $(1): \quad$ left-total $(2): \quad$ right-total $(3): \quad$ functional (many-to-one) $(4): \quad$ injective (one-to-many).

title: Definition:Bijection/Definition 2
snippet: A mapping $f: S \to T$ is a bijection : $f$ has both a left inverse and a right inverse.

title: Definition:Bijection/Definition 3
snippet: A mapping $f: S \to T$ is a bijection : the inverse $f^{-1}$ of $f$ is a mapping from $T$ to $S$. That is, $f$ admits an inverse.

title: Definition:Bijection/Definition 4
snippet: A mapping $f \subseteq S \times T$ is a bijection : for each $y \in T$ there exists one and only one $x \in S$ such that $\tuple {x, y} \in f$.

title: Definition:Bijection/Definition 5
snippet: A relation $f \subseteq S \times T$ is a bijection : $(1): \quad$ for each $x \in S$ there exists one and only one $y \in T$ such that $\tuple {x, y} \in f$ $(2): \quad$ for each $y \in T$ there exists one and only one $x \in S$ such that $\tuple {x, y} \in f$.

title: Definition:Bijective Restriction
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping which is not bijective. A bijective restriction of $f$ is a restriction $f {\restriction_{S' \times T'} }: S' \to T'$ of $f$ such that $f {\restriction_{S' \times T'} }$ is a bijection.

title: Definition:Bilateral Shift
snippet: Let $T$ be a linear operator acting on a sequence. Let $T$ be such that if $\sequence v = \map T {\sequence u}$, then $v_k = u_{k - 1}$ for all $k$. Then $T$ is a bilateral shift.

title: Definition:Bilateral Symmetry
snippet: Let $F$ be a geometric figure.

title: Definition:Bilateral Symmetry/Axis
snippet: Let $F$ be a plane geometric figure. Let $\map R F$ be a bilateral symmetry in an axis of reflection $AB$. Then $AB$ is referred to as an axis of bilateral symmetry of $F$.

title: Definition:Bilateral Symmetry/Linguistic Note
snippet: The word bilateral derives from the Latin bis (meaning ‎twice) and laterālis (meaning pertaining to the side). It literally translates as two-sided. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Bilateral Symmetry/Plane
snippet: Let $F$ be a solid geometric figure. Let $\map R F$ be a bilateral symmetry in a plane of reflection $P$. Then $P$ is referred to as an plane of bilateral symmetry of $F$.

title: Definition:Bilateral Symmetry/Plane Figure
snippet: Let $F$ be a plane geometric figure. Let there exist a reflection $R$ in an axis of reflection $AB$ such that $\map R F$ is a (reflectional) symmetry. Then $F$ has (plane) bilateral symmetry about $AB$.

title: Definition:Bilateral Symmetry/Solid Figure
snippet: Let $F$ be a solid geometric figure. Let there exist a reflection $R$ in an plane of reflection $P$ such that $\map R F$ is a (reflectional) symmetry. Then $F$ has (solid) bilateral symmetry about $AB$.

title: Definition:Bilinear
snippet: A mathematical expression is bilinear $2$ variables it is linear each of those $2$ variables separately.

title: Definition:Bilinear Equation
snippet: A bilinear equation is an equation of $2$ variables which is linear each of those variables individually.

title: Definition:Bilinear Form (Functional Analysis)
snippet: Let $B$ be a bilinear functional. Let $B$ be defined on a finite-dimensional space. Then $B$ is a bilinear form.

title: Definition:Bilinear Form (Linear Algebra)
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $R_R$ denote the $R$-module $R$. Let $M_R$ be an $R$-module. A bilinear form on $M_R$ is a bilinear mapping $B : M_R \times M_R \to R_R$.

title: Definition:Bilinear Form (Linear Algebra)/Also known as
snippet: == Bilinear Form: Also known as == It is usual to gloss over the modular nature of $R_R$ and consider $B$ merely as a mapping from the $R$-module $M$ directly to the ring $R$: Hence in this manner, a bilinear form on $M$ is defined as a bilinear mapping $B : M \times M \to R$.

title: Definition:Bilinear Form (Polynomial Theory)
snippet: A bilinear form is a linear form of order $2$.

title: Definition:Bilinear Form (Polynomial Theory)/Also known as
snippet: == Bilinear Form in context of Polynomial Theory: Also known as == A bilinear form in the context of polynomial theory is also known as a bilinear function. However, that term is also used as a synonym for a Möbius transformation, so to avoid ambiguitty and misunderstanding it is recommended it not be used.

snippet: Let $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ be a commutative ring. Let $\struct {A_1, +_1, \circ_1}_R, \struct {A_2, +_2, \circ_2}_R, \struct {A_3, +_3, \circ_3}_R$ be $R$-modules. title: Definition:Bilinear Space
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be a field. A bilinear space over $\mathbb K$ is a pair $\struct {V, f}$ where: $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb K$ of finite dimension $n > 0$ $f$ is a bilinear form on $V$.

title: Definition:Billiard
snippet: Billiard is an archaic name for $10^{15}$.

title: Definition:Billion/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Billion == The word billion derives from the prefix bi-, meaning twofold, and million, originating as the number $1 \, 000 \, 000$ to the power of $2$.

title: Definition:Billion/Long Scale
snippet: Billion is a name for $10^{12}$ in the long scale system: One billion $= 10^{6 \times 2}$

title: Definition:Billion/Short Scale
snippet: Billion is a name for $10^9$ in the short scale system: One billion $= 10^{3 \times 2 + 3}$

title: Definition:Billion (Long Scale)/Also defined as
snippet: == Billion: Also known as == In the short scale system: One billion $= 10^{3 \times 2 + 3} = 10^9$

title: Definition:Billion (Short Scale)/Also defined as
snippet: == Billion: Also known as == In the long scale system: One billion $= 10^{6 \times 2} = 10^{12}$

title: Definition:Billion (Short Scale)/Also known as
snippet: == Billion: Also known as == Archaic and rare terms for $10^9$ are: Milliard Gillion

title: Definition:Bimedial/First Bimedial
snippet: Let $a, b \in \R_{>0}$ be in the forms: $a = k^{1/4} \rho$ $b = k^{3/4} \rho$ where: $\rho$ is a rational number $k$ is a rational number whose square root is irrational. Then $a + b$ is a first bimedial.

title: Definition:Bimedial/Order
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be two positive real numbers such that $a + b$ is a bimedial. The order of $a + b$ is the name of its classification into one of the two categories: first or second. Category:Definitions/Euclidean Number Theory

title: Definition:Bimedial/Second Bimedial
snippet: Let $a, b \in \R_{>0}$ be in the forms: $a = k^{1/4} \rho$ $b = \dfrac {\lambda^{1/2} \rho} {k^{1/4} }$ where: $\rho$ is a rational number $k$ is a rational number whose square root is irrational. $\lambda$ is a rational number whose square root is irrational. Then $a + b$ is a second bimedial.

title: Definition:Bimodal Distribution
snippet: A bimodal distribution is a probability distribution whose probability density function has $2$ distinct maxima. The maxima do not need to be equal.

title: Definition:Bimodal Distribution/Major Mode
snippet: The larger of the two maxima of a bimodal distribution whose maxima are not exactly equal is called the major mode.

title: Definition:Bimodal Distribution/Minor Mode
snippet: The smaller of the two maxima of a bimodal distribution whose maxima are not exactly equal is called the minor mode.

title: Definition:Bimodule
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ and $\struct {S, +_S, \times_S}$ be rings. Let $\struct {G, +_G}$ be an abelian group. Let $\circ_R : R \times G \to G$ and $\circ_S : G \times S \to G$ be binary operations such that: {{item|(1):|$\struct {G, +_G, \circ_R}$ is a left module}} {{item|(2):|$\struct {G, +_G, \circ_S}$ is a right module}} {{item|(3):|$\forall \lambda \in R: \forall \mu \in S: \forall x \in G: \paren {\lambda \circ_R x} \circ_S \mu \lambda \circ_R \paren {x \circ_S \mu}$}} Then $\struct {G, +_G, \circ_R, \circ_S}$ is a bimodule over $\tuple {R, S}$.

title: Definition:Bimodule/Also known as
snippet: == Bimodule: Also known as == A bimodule over $\tuple {R, S}$ can also be referred to as an $\tuple {R, S}$-bimodule.

title: Definition:Bin/Width
snippet: The length of the subintervals of a set of grouped data that form the bins of that grouped data is known as the bin width.

title: Definition:Bin Packing Problem
snippet: The bin packing problem is a type of scheduling problem of how to pack a number of boxes into a number of bins. The boxes with the same cross-section as the bins, but of various heights. The aim is to use as few bins as possible.

title: Definition:Binary Biproduct

title: Definition:Binary Code
snippet: A binary code is a character encoding consisting of a set of codewords each of which is a sequence of instances of $0$ and $1$. It is usual in a given binary code for each of the codewords to be the same length.

title: Definition:Binary Logical Connective/Also defined as
snippet: == Binary Logical Connective: Also defined as == Some sources use the term logical connective to mean binary logical connective exclusively, on the grounds that a unary logical connective does not actually "connect" anything. However, this is a trivial distinction which can serve only to confuse.

title: Definition:Binary Logical Connective/Also known as
snippet: == Binary Logical Connective: Also known as == A binary logical connective is also known as: a two-place connective. a dyadic connective. Some sources just call it a binary connective.

title: Definition:Binary Mess
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $I$ be the set of all finite subsets of $S$. Let $\Bbb B$ be a Boolean domain. Let $M$ be a set defined as: $\ds M \subseteq \bigcup_{P \mathop \in I} \Bbb B^P$ where $\Bbb B^P$ denotes the set of all mappings from $P$ to $\Bbb B$. That is, such that $M$ is a set of mappings from finite subsets of $S$ to $\Bbb B$. Suppose that $M$ satisfies the binary mess axioms: Then $M$ is a binary mess on $S$.

title: Definition:Binary Mess/Consistent Mapping
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $M$ be a binary mess on $S$. Let $f : S \to \Bbb B$ be a mapping from $S$ to a Boolean domain. Then, $f$ is consistent with $M$ , for every finite subset $P \subseteq S$: $f {\restriction_P} \in M$ where $f {\restriction_P}$ denotes the restriction of $f$ to $P$.

title: Definition:Binary Notation
snippet: Binary notation is the positional number system whose base is $2$. That is, every number $x \in \R$ is expressed in the form: $\ds x = \sum_{j \mathop \in \Z} r_j 2^j$ where $\forall j \in \Z: r_j \in \set {0, 1}$.

title: Definition:Binary Notation/Also known as
snippet: == Binary Notation: Also known as == Binary notation is also known as binary representation.

title: Definition:Binary Notation/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Binary Notation == The earliest known reference to binary notation appears to be in a Chinese book dating from approximately $3000$ B.C.E. In Europe, binary notation was invented by . He associated God with $1$ and nothingness with $0$, and believed that it was mystically significant that all numbers could be built from $1$-ness and $0$-ness.

title: Definition:Binary Notation/Motivation
snippet: Binary notation, like hexadecimal notation, has particular relevance in the field of computer science. This is because the two binary digits, $0$ and $1$, can be represented by two well-defined states of a component.

title: Definition:Binary Number
snippet: A binary number is a number expressed in binary notation.

title: Definition:Binary Operation/Also defined as
snippet: == Binary Operation: Also defined as == Some authors specify that a binary operation $\circ$ is defined such that the codomain of $\circ$ is the same underlying set as that which forms the domain. That is: $\circ: S \times S \to S$ and thus gloss over the fact that a binary operation defined in such a way is closed. Such a treatment can obscure the detail of the development of the theory of algebraic substructures; closedness is a fundamental concept in this context.

title: Definition:Binary Operation/Also known as
snippet: == Binary Operation: Also known as == Some authors use the term (binary) composition or law of composition for (binary) operation. Some sources refer to a binary operation just as an operation. Most authors use $\circ$ for composition of relations (which, if you think about it, is itself an operation) as well as for a general operation. To avoid confusion, some authors use $\bullet$ for composition of relations to avoid ambiguity.

title: Definition:Binary Product UMP (Category Theory)
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $A$ and $B$ be objects of $\mathbf C$. An object $P$ and morphisms $p_1: P \to A$, $p_2: P \to B$: $\begin{xy}\xymatrix@+1em@L+3px{ A & P \ar[l]_*+{p_1} \ar[r]^*+{p_2} & B }\end{xy}$ satisfy the (binary product) universal mapping property (or UMP) :

title: Definition:Binary Product UMP (Category Theory)/Property
snippet: == Property for Binary Product UMP == For any object $X$ and morphisms $x_1:X \to A, x_2: X \to B$ like so: $\begin{xy}\xymatrix@+1em@L+3px{ A & X \ar[l]_*+{x_1} \ar[r]^*+{x_2} & B }\end{xy}$ there is a unique morphism $u: X \to P$ such that: $x_1 = p_1 \circ u$ and $x_2 = p_2 \circ u$ That is: $\begin{xy}\xymatrix@+1em@L+3px{ & X \ar[ld]_*+{x_1} \ar@{-->}[d]^*+{u} \ar[rd]^*+{x_2} \\ A & P \ar[l]^*+{p_1} \ar[r]_*+{p_2} & B }\end{xy}$ is a commutative diagram

title: Definition:Binary Search Algorithm
snippet: Let $\SS$ be a finite sequence of length $n$ from an ordered set $\struct {\EE, \preccurlyeq}$. Let $\SS$ be sorted into order by $\preccurlyeq$. Let $x$ be an element of $\EE$ which may or may not be present in $\SS$. The binary search algorithm $\AA$ is an algorithm whose purpose is to see whether $\SS$ contains $x$: $(1): \quad x$ is compared $\preccurlyeq$ with the element $m$ of $\SS$ closest to the middle. $(2): \quad$ If $x = m$ then we have found $x$ in $\SS$. $(3): \quad$ If $x \ne m$ then either $x \prec m$ or $m \prec x$.

title: Definition:Binary String
snippet: A binary string is a string whose alphabet of symbols consists of $2$ elements. It is usual that its alphabet is $\set {0, 1}$.

title: Definition:Binary String/Also known as
snippet: == Binary String: Also known as == A binary string is also known as a binary word.

title: Definition:Binary String/Motivation
snippet: == Binary String: Motivation == Conversion of information into binary strings makes it easier to transmit.

title: Definition:Binary System
snippet: A binary system is a number system in which the base is $2$.

title: Definition:Binary Tree
snippet: A binary tree is a rooted tree which has at most two branches at any node. That is, every node in a binary tree has (apart from the root) degree of either $1$ (for the leaf nodes) or $3$ (one for the parent, two for the children).

title: Definition:Binary Tree/Applications
snippet: == Binary Tree: Applications == Binary trees are frequently used in computer science to store data in an efficiently searchable fashion. Category:Definitions/Binary Trees

title: Definition:Binary Tree/Branches
snippet: The branches at any particular node of a binary tree are frequently called the left-hand branch and the right-hand branch, and a distinction is made between them. Category:Definitions/Rooted Trees

title: Definition:Binary Tuple
snippet: A binary tuple is an ordered tuple whose domain is the set $\set {0, 1}$. That is, it is an ordered $n$-tuple $\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ such that each $x_i$ is either $0$ or $1$. The set of all binary $n$-tuples can often be seen denoted $V_n$: $V_n := \set {\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}: \forall i \in \set {1, 2, \ldots n}: x_i \in \set {0, 1} }$

title: Definition:Binary Variable
snippet: A binary variable is a random variable which can take one of only $2$ values. It is conventional for the purposes of data analysis to encode such binary variables by use of a random variable which takes the values $0$ and $1$.

title: Definition:Binding Constraint
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a weak inequality on some set $S$. Let $a \mathrel \RR b$ be a constraint given by a weak inequality $\RR$. Let $P \in S$ such that $P \mathrel \RR b$ is an equality. Then $a \mathrel \RR b$ is binding at $P$.

title: Definition:Binding Constraint/Also known as
snippet: == Binding Constraint: Also known as == A binding constraint is also known as an active constraint.

title: Definition:Binding Priority
snippet: The binding priority is the convention defining the order of binding strength of the individual connectives in a logical formula. Binding priorities can be overridden by using parenthesis in appropriate places. Parenthesis always takes priority over conventional binding priority.

title: Definition:Binding Priority/Also known as
snippet: == Binding Priority: Also known as == Binding priority is also known as: Precedence: a higher precedence is the same thing as a tighter binding priority. Rank: a higher rank is the same thing as a tighter binding priority.

title: Definition:Binding Priority/Arithmetic
snippet: The binding priority convention used for arithmetic and algebra is: $(1): \quad$ the exponential and power operators take highest binding priority $(2): \quad \times$ and $\div$ bind more tightly than $+$ and $-$ $(3): \quad$ In all other cases, expressions are evaluated from left to right.

title: Definition:Binding Priority/Propositional Logic
snippet: The binding priority convention which is almost universally used for the connectives of propositional logic is: Note that there is no overall convention defining which of $\land$ and $\lor$ bears a higher binding priority, and therefore we consider them to have equal priority. Because of this fact, unless specifically defined, expressions such as $p \land q \lor r$ can not be interpreted unambiguously, and parenthesis must be used to determine the exact priorities which are to be used to interpret particular statements which may otherwise be ambiguous.

title: Definition:Binding Priority (Propositional Logic)/Also defined as
snippet: == Binding Priority for Propositional Logic: Also defined as == When defining binding priority for propositional logic, some sources do impose a priority of $\land$ over $\lor$. Similarly, some sources also impose a priority of $\implies$ over $\iff$. However, these are not a universal convention, and such a binding priority is artificial. Some sources express the binding priority rules by saying that $\iff$ and $\implies$ dominate $\land$ and $\lor$.

title: Definition:Binomial
snippet: Euclidean number theory: A binomial is a term in the form $a + b$ where $\dfrac a b$ and $a + b$ are irrational, but $\paren {\dfrac a b}^2$ is rational. The concept is considered archaic. Algebra: A binomial is an expression with two terms, that is, of the form $a + b$, where $a$ and $b$ are such that $a + b$ cannot be simplified. Definition:Binomial Coefficient Probability theory: Definition:Binomial Distribution

title: Definition:Binomial (Algebra)
snippet: A binomial is an expression which has $2$ terms.

title: Definition:Binomial (Euclidean)
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be two (strictly) positive real numbers such that: $(1): \quad \dfrac a b \notin \Q$ $(2): \quad \left({\dfrac a b}\right)^2 \in \Q$ where $\Q$ denotes the set of rational numbers. Then $a + b$ is a binomial.

title: Definition:Binomial (Euclidean)/Fifth Binomial
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be two (strictly) positive real numbers such that $a + b$ is a binomial. Then $a + b$ is a fifth binomial : $(1): \quad b \in \Q$ $(2): \quad \dfrac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2}} a \notin \Q$ where $\Q$ denotes the set of rational numbers. '

title: Definition:Binomial (Euclidean)/Fifth Binomial/Example
snippet: == Example == Let $a$ and $b$ be two (strictly) positive real numbers such that $a + b$ is a binomial. By definition, $a + b$ is a fifth binomial : $(1): \quad b \in \Q$ $(2): \quad \dfrac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2}} a \notin \Q$ where $\Q$ denotes the set of rational numbers. Let $a = \sqrt {13}$ and $b = 3$. Then: {{eqn | l = \frac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2} } a | r = \frac {\sqrt {13 - 9} } {\sqrt {13} } }} {{eqn | r = \sqrt {\frac 4 {13} } | rr= \notin \Q }} Therefore $\sqrt {13} + 3$ is a fifth binomial. Category:Definitions/Euclidean Number Theory

title: Definition:Binomial (Euclidean)/First Binomial
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be two (strictly) positive real numbers such that $a + b$ is a binomial. Then $a + b$ is a first binomial : $(1): \quad a \in \Q$ $(2): \quad \dfrac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2} } a \in \Q$ where $\Q$ denotes the set of rational numbers. '

title: Definition:Binomial (Euclidean)/First Binomial/Example
snippet: == Example == Let $a$ and $b$ be two (strictly) positive real numbers such that $a + b$ is a binomial. By definition, $a + b$ is a first binomial : $(1): \quad a \in \Q$ $(2): \quad \dfrac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2} } a \in \Q$ where $\Q$ denotes the set of rational numbers. Let $a = 9$ and $b = \sqrt {17}$. Then: {{eqn | l = \frac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2} } a | r = \frac {\sqrt {81 - 17} } 9 }} {{eqn | r = \frac {\sqrt {64} } 9 }} Therefore $9 + \sqrt {17}$ is a first binomial. Category:Definitions/Euclidean Number Theory

title: Definition:Binomial (Euclidean)/Fourth Binomial
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be two (strictly) positive real numbers such that $a + b$ is a binomial. Then $a + b$ is a fourth binomial : $(1): \quad a \in \Q$ $(2): \quad \dfrac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2}} a \notin \Q$ where $\Q$ denotes the set of rational numbers. '

title: Definition:Binomial (Euclidean)/Fourth Binomial/Example
snippet: == Example == Let $a$ and $b$ be two (strictly) positive real numbers such that $a + b$ is a binomial. By definition, $a + b$ is a fourth binomial : $(1): \quad a \in \Q$ $(2): \quad \dfrac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2}} a \notin \Q$ where $\Q$ denotes the set of rational numbers. Let $a = 3$ and $b = \sqrt 2$. Then: {{eqn | l = \frac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2} } a | r = \frac {\sqrt {9 - 2} } 3 }} {{eqn | r = \frac {\sqrt 7} 3 | rr= \notin \Q }} Therefore $3 + \sqrt 2$ is a fourth binomial. Category:Definitions/Euclidean Number Theory

title: Definition:Binomial (Euclidean)/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Binomial == The term binomial arises from a word meaning two numbers. This sense of the term is rarely used (if at all) outside of nowadays. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Binomial (Euclidean)/Order
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be two positive real numbers. Let $a + b$ be a binomial. The order of $a + b$ is the name of its classification into one of the six categories: first, second, third, fourth, fifth or sixth. Category:Definitions/Euclidean Number Theory

title: Definition:Binomial (Euclidean)/Second Binomial
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be two (strictly) positive real numbers such that $a + b$ is a binomial. Then $a + b$ is a second binomial : $(1): \quad b \in \Q$ $(2): \quad \dfrac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2}} a \in \Q$ where $\Q$ denotes the set of rational numbers. '

title: Definition:Binomial (Euclidean)/Second Binomial/Example
snippet: == Example == Let $a$ and $b$ be two (strictly) positive real numbers such that $a + b$ is a binomial. By definition, $a + b$ is a second binomial : $(1): \quad b \in \Q$ $(2): \quad \dfrac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2}} a \in \Q$ where $\Q$ denotes the set of rational numbers. Let $a = 2 \sqrt 3$ and $b = 3$. Then: {{eqn | l = \frac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2} } a | r = \frac {\sqrt {12 - 9} } {2 \sqrt 3} }} {{eqn | r = \frac {\sqrt 3} {2 \sqrt 3} }} Therefore $2 \sqrt 3 + 3$ is a second binomial. Category:Definitions/Euclidean Number Theory

title: Definition:Binomial (Euclidean)/Term
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be two positive real numbers. Let $a + b$ be a binomial. The terms of $a + b$ are the elements $a$ and $b$. Category:Definitions/Euclidean Number Theory

title: Definition:Binomial (Euclidean)/Third Binomial
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be two (strictly) positive real numbers such that $a + b$ is a binomial. Then $a + b$ is a third binomial : $(1): \quad a \notin \Q$ $(2): \quad b \notin \Q$ $(3): \quad \dfrac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2}} a \in \Q$ where $\Q$ denotes the set of rational numbers. '

title: Definition:Binomial (Euclidean)/Third Binomial/Example
snippet: == Example == Let $a$ and $b$ be two (strictly) positive real numbers such that $a + b$ is a binomial. By definition, $a + b$ is a third binomial : $(1): \quad a \notin \Q$ $(2): \quad b \notin \Q$ $(3): \quad \dfrac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2}} a \in \Q$ where $\Q$ denotes the set of rational numbers. Let $a = \sqrt {11}$ and $b = \sqrt {\dfrac {143} {49} }$.

title: Definition:Binomial Coefficient/Complex Numbers
snippet: Let $z, w \in \C$. Then $\dbinom z w$ is defined as: $\dbinom z w := \ds \lim_{\zeta \mathop \to z} \lim_{\omega \mathop \to w} \dfrac {\map \Gamma {\zeta + 1} } {\map \Gamma {\omega + 1} \map \Gamma {\zeta - \omega + 1} }$ where $\Gamma$ denotes the Gamma function. When $z$ is a negative integer and $w$ is not an integer, $\dbinom z w$ is infinite.

title: Definition:Binomial Coefficient/Historical Note
snippet: The binomial coefficients have been known about since at least the ancient Greeks and Romans, who were familiar with them for small values of $k$. See the historical note to Pascal's Triangle for further history.

title: Definition:Binomial Coefficient/Integers/Definition 1
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ and $k \in \Z$. Then the binomial coefficient $\dbinom n k$ is defined as: $\dbinom n k = \begin {cases} \dfrac {n!} {k! \paren {n - k}!} & : 0 \le k \le n \\ & \\ 0 & : \text { otherwise } \end{cases}$ where $n!$ denotes the factorial of $n$.

title: Definition:Binomial Coefficient/Integers/Definition 2
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ and $k \in \Z$. The number of different ways $k$ objects can be chosen (irrespective of order) from a set of $n$ objects is denoted: $\dbinom n k$ This number $\dbinom n k$ is known as a binomial coefficient.

title: Definition:Binomial Coefficient/Integers/Definition 3
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ and $k \in \Z$. Then the binomial coefficient $\dbinom n k$ is defined as the coefficient of the term $a^k b^{n - k}$ in the expansion of $\paren {a + b}^n$.

title: Definition:Binomial Coefficient/Multiindices
snippet: Let $k = \sequence {k_j}_{j \mathop \in J}$ and $\ell = \sequence {\ell_j}_{j \mathop \in J}$ be multiindices. Let $\ell \le k$. Then $\dbinom k \ell$ is defined as: $\ds \binom k \ell = \prod_{j \mathop \in J} \binom {k_j} {\ell_j}$ Note that since by definition only finitely many of the $k_j$ are non-zero, the product in the definition of $\dbinom k \ell$ is convergent. Category:Definitions/Binomial Coefficients Category:Definitions/Polynomial Theory

title: Definition:Binomial Coefficient/Notation
snippet: The notation $\dbinom n k$ for the binomial coefficient was introduced by in his $1826$ work . It appears to have become the de facto standard in recent years. As a result, $\dbinom n k$ is frequently voiced the binomial coefficient $n$ over $k$. Other notations include: $\map C {n, k}$ ${}^n C_k$ ${}_n C_k$ $C^n_k$ ${C_n}^k$ all of which can cause a certain degree of confusion.

title: Definition:Binomial Coefficient/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $r \in \R, k \in \Z$. Then $\dbinom r k$ is defined as: $\dbinom r k = \begin {cases} \dfrac {r^{\underline k} } {k!} & : k \ge 0 \\ & \\ 0 & : k < 0 \end {cases}$ where $r^{\underline k}$ denotes the falling factorial. That is, when $k \ge 0$: $\ds \dbinom r k = \dfrac {r \paren {r - 1} \cdots \paren {r - k + 1} } {k \paren {k - 1} \cdots 1} = \prod_{j \mathop = 1}^k \dfrac {r + 1 - j} j$ It can be seen that this agrees with the definition for integers when $r$ is an integer. For most applications the integer form is sufficient.

title: Definition:Binomial Coefficient/Technical Note
snippet: The $\LaTeX$ code to render the binomial coefficient $\dbinom n k$ can be written in the following ways: \dbinom n k or: \ds {n \choose k} The \dbinom form is preferred on because it is simpler. It is in fact an abbreviated form of \ds \binom n k, which is the preferred construction when \ds is required for another entity in the expression. While the form \binom n k is valid $\LaTeX$ syntax, it renders the entity in the reduced size inline style: $\binom n k$ which does not endorse.

title: Definition:Binomial Distribution
snippet: Let $\sequence {X_i}$ be a finite binomial experiment of length $n$ such that each of the $X_i$ in the sequence is a Bernoulli trial with parameter $p$ such that $0 \le p \le 1$. Let $X$ be the discrete probability distribution that models the number of successes in $\sequence {X_i}$ . Then $X$ is a binomial distribution with parameters $n$ and $p$.

title: Definition:Binomial Distribution/Also defined as
snippet: == Binomial Distribution: Also defined as == Some sources insist, in the definition of the binomial distribution, that $0 < p < 1$, but it can be useful in certain circumstances to include the condition when the outcome is certainty.

title: Definition:Binomial Distribution/Notation
snippet: == Binomial Distribution: Notation == The binomial distribution with parameters $n$ and $p$ is denoted: $X \sim \Binomial n p$ Some sources use $\map {\mathrm {Bi} } {n, p}$.

title: Definition:Binomial Distribution/Technical Note
snippet: == Technical Note for Binomial Distribution == {{LatexFor|for = \Binomial {n} {p} }} When the arguments are single characters, it is usual to omit the braces: \Binomial n p This command is specific to . Category:Technical Notes

title: Definition:Binomial Expansion
snippet: Consider the binomial theorem, which in one of its various forms is given here: $\paren {1 + x}^\alpha = 1 + \dbinom \alpha 1 x + \dbinom \alpha 2 x^2 + \dbinom \alpha 3 x^3 + \cdots$ The above algebraic expansion is known as the binomial expansion.

title: Definition:Binomial Experiment
snippet: A binomial experiment is a sequence (either finite or infinite) of Bernoulli trials, each of which has the same parameter $p$. That is, a binomial experiment (with parameter $p$) is a sequence $\sequence {X_i}$ (either finite or infinite) such that: $(1): \quad$ the value of each $X_i$ is one of two values (for example: $a$ or $b$). $(2): \quad$ the probability that $X_i = a$ is the same for all $i$ (for example: $p$). $(3): \quad$ the outcomes of all the Bernoulli trials are independent. That is, it is a sequence of experiments, all of which can be modelled by the same Bernoulli distribution.

title: Definition:Binomial Experiment/Also known as
snippet: == Binomial Experiment: Also known as == A binomial experiment is also known as a Bernoulli process, for . Category:Definitions/Binomial Experiments

title: Definition:Binomial Series
snippet: Consider the Binomial Theorem, which in one of its various forms is given here: $\paren {1 + x}^\alpha = 1 + \dbinom \alpha 1 x + \dbinom \alpha 2 x^2 + \dbinom \alpha 3 x^3 + \cdots$ for arbitrary real $\alpha$. The above infinite series is known as the binomial series.

title: Definition:Binormal Vector
snippet: Let $\alpha : I \to \R^3$ be a (smooth) curve parameterized by arc length. Let $s \in I$ be such that the curvature $\map \kappa s \ne 0$. The binormal vector of $\alpha$ at $s$ is defined as: $\map b s := \map t s \times \map n s$ where: $\map t s$ is the unit tangent vector $\map n s$ is the normal vector $\times$ denotes the vector cross product

title: Definition:Binormal Vector/Also known as
snippet: == Binormal Vector: Also known as == A binormal vector is also known just as a binormal.

title: Definition:Biology
snippet: Biology is the branch of science concerned with the processes of life.

title: Definition:Biometrics
snippet: Biometrics are individual human characteristics which are studied with a view towards using them as a means of identifying a particular human being.

title: Definition:Biometrics/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Biometrics == Fingerprints, signatures and DNA have been in widespread use for some considerable time. More recent biometrics include such techniques as retinal scanning, and facial and voice recognition. Developments are in progress to use smell as a biometric technique. Digital signatures are also showing themselves to be useful, as they have advantages over signatures in that they can record and measure such things as applied pressure of the stylus and the speed of writing.

title: Definition:Biometry
snippet: Biometry is the branch of statistics concerned with the development and application of statistical methods to biologial problems. This includes the design of experiments and the analysis and interpretation of the results.

title: Definition:Biometry/Also known as
snippet: == Biometry: Also known as == Biometry is also known as biostatistics.

title: Definition:Bipartite Graph
snippet: A bipartite graph is a graph $G = \struct {V, E}$ where: $V$ is partitioned into two sets $A$ and $B$ such that: each edge is incident to a vertex in $A$ and a vertex in $B$. That is: no two vertices in $A$ are adjacent and no two vertices in $B$ are adjacent. It is a common practice when illustrating such a graph to draw the vertices of $A$ in one colour, and those of $B$ in another. $G$ can be denoted $G = \struct {A \mid B, E}$ to emphasise that $A$ and $B$ partition $V$.

title: Definition:Bipartite Graph/Partite Set
snippet: Let $G = \struct {A \mid B, E}$ be a bipartite graph. Then $A$ and $B$ are called the partite sets of $G$.

title: Definition:Bipolar Set
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\innerprod E F$ be a dual system over $\GF$. Let $A \subseteq E$ be non-empty. Let $A^\circ \subseteq F$ be the absolute polar of $A$. Let $\paren {A^\circ}_\circ \subseteq E$ be the absolute prepolar of $A^\circ$. We say that $\paren {A^\circ}_\circ$ is the bipolar (set) of $A$.

title: Definition:Bipyramid
snippet: A bipyramid is a polyhedron formed by taking two pyramids with congruent bases and placing those bases together: 400px

title: Definition:Bipyramid/Also known as
snippet: == Bipyramid: Also known as == The term dipyramid can be found at least as frequently as bipyramid. Some sources use the term double pyramid.

title: Definition:Biquadrate
snippet: A biquadrate number (or just biquadrate) is a number which can be expressed as the fourth power of an integer. The sequence of positive biquadrates begins: $1, 16, 81, 256, 625, 1297, 2401, 4096, 6561, 10000, \ldots$

title: Definition:Biquadrate/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Biquadrate == The term biquadrate is archaic, deriving from the concept of a square of a square. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Biquadratic Residue
snippet: Let $p$ be an odd prime. Let $a \in \Z$ be an integer such that $a \not \equiv 0 \pmod p$. Then $a$ is a biquadratic residue of $p$ $x^4 \equiv a \pmod p$ has a solution. That is, : $\exists x \in \Z: x^4 \equiv a \pmod p$

title: Definition:Biquadratic Residue/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Biquadratic Residue == The concept of a biquadratic residue was investigated by in his papers of $1828$ and $1832$.

title: Definition:Birectangular Spherical Triangle
snippet: A spherical triangle is described as birectangular it has $2$ right angles.

title: Definition:Birectangular Spherical Triangle/Also known as
snippet: == Birectangular Spherical Triangle: Also known as == A birectangular spherical triangle is also known as just a birectangular triangle. Category:Definitions/Spherical Triangles

title: Definition:Birkhoff-James Orthogonality
snippet:
Let $\struct {V, 
orm {\,\cdot\,} }$ be a normed linear space. Let $x, y \in V$. Then $x$ and $y$ are Birkhoff-James orthogonal $
orm {x + \lambda y} \ge 
orm y$ for all scalars $\lambda$. This is denoted: $x \perp_B y$

title: Definition:Birth-Death Process
snippet: A birth-death process is a Markov process which models changes in population caused by births and deaths.

title: Definition:Birth-Death Process/Also defined as
snippet: == Birth-Death Process: Also defined as == A birth-death process can also be defined more generally so as to include the effects of immigration and emigration.

title: Definition:Bisection
snippet: To bisect a finite geometrical object is to cut it in half, that is, into two equal parts. The act of cutting in half is known as bisection.

title: Definition:Bisection/Bisector
snippet: A bisector is an object which bisects another object.

title: Definition:Bisection Method
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function such that: $f$ is continuous over a closed interval $\closedint a b$ $\map f a$ and $\map f b$ are of opposite sign. The bisection method is an iterative technique for finding an approximation to at least one solution to the equation $\map f x = 0$ to any desired accuracy. First, let $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ be our chosen level of accuracy. So, we assume that $\map f a \map f b < 0$ and that $a < b$. We evaluate $c = \dfrac {a + b} 2$, thereby bisecting $\closedint a b$. We evaluate $\map f c$. If $\map f c = 0$, then we have a solution to $\map f x = 0$.

title: Definition:Biserial Correlation Coefficient
snippet: A biserial correlation coefficient is a measure of dependence between: a continuous random variable $X$ a discrete random variable $Y$ which can take one of only $2$ values: $y_1$ and $y_2$.

title: Definition:Bit
snippet: A bit is a binary digit.

title: Definition:Bit/Also known as
snippet: == Bit: Also known as == Sources which are not focused on computer science may not use the term bit, but instead just use the full form binary digit.

title: Definition:Bit/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Bit == The word bit derives directly from the term Binary digIT.

title: Definition:Bitangent
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a curve in the plane. A bitangent is a straight line which is tangent to $\CC$ at two distinct points.

title: Definition:Bitangent/Also known as
snippet: == Bitangent: Also known as == A bitangent is also known as a double tangent, but that term is also used for a different concept. Hence on we keep the concepts separate.

title: Definition:Bivariate
snippet: An expression is bivariate it involves two variables. The term is usually encountered when the variables concerned are random.

title: Definition:Bivariate Data
snippet: Bivariate data consists of pairs of observations of two variables for each of a number of units.

title: Definition:Bivariate Distribution
snippet: A bivariate distribution is the joint distribution of two random variables $X$ and $Y$.

title: Definition:Black-Scholes Equation
snippet: The Black-Scholes equation is a second-order partial differential equation whose purpose is to model a financial market in order to provide estimates for stock options. It is of the form: $\dfrac {\partial V} {\partial t} + \dfrac 1 2 \sigma^2 S^2 \dfrac {\partial^2 V} {\partial S^2} + r S \dfrac {\partial V} {\partial S} - r V = 0$ where: $V$ is the price of the stock option $S$ is the price of the stock $r$ is the interest rate $\sigma$ represents the volatility of the stock price $t$ represents time.

title: Definition:Blancmange Function
snippet: The blancmange function is the real function $b: \closedint 0 1 \to \R$ defined as: $\forall x \in \closedint 0 1: \map b x = \ds \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \dfrac {\map a {2^n x} } {2^n}$ where $a: \R \to \Z$ denotes the distance to nearest integer function.

title: Definition:Blancmange Function/Mistake

title: Definition:Blinding
snippet: Blinding is a technique in experimental design whereby the subjects of the experiment are not aware what treatment they are receiving, or even whether they are receiving treatment at all.

title: Definition:Blinding/Double-Blind
snippet: In a double-blind experiment, neither the recipients of the treatment nor those responsible for directly administering that treatment know which treatments have been assigned to whom.

title: Definition:Blinding/Double-Dummy
snippet: In a double-dummy experiment, the subjects appear to be given both of two treatments. However, one of those treatments is secretly a placebo, while a control group are given a placebo for both treatments. This technique can be used when it is not possible to hide the actual nature of the treatment from the subject.

title: Definition:Blinding/Motivation
snippet: When evaluating whether a particular medical intervention is effective or not, there exists the possibility that beneficial effects occur because the patient expects an improvement. This interferes with identifying whether the treatment is actually effective. Hence the subjects of the experiment are not told whether the treatments being administered are the actual thing being tested, or just a placebo.

title: Definition:Blinding/Single-Blind
snippet: In a single-blind experiment, the recipients of the treatment do not know which of a number of treatments they have been assigned.

title: Definition:Bloch's Constant
snippet: Recall Bloch's Theorem: The lower bound of $B$ is known as Bloch's constant.
