title: Definition:Block
snippet: Design Theory: Block Matrix Theory: Block: another term for a submatrix

title: Definition:Block Basic Sequence
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a normed vector space over $\GF$. Let $\sequence {e_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a Schauder basis for $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$. Let $\sequence {p_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a strictly increasing sequence and let $p_0 = 0$. Let $\sequence {\alpha_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $\GF$. Define: $\ds u_n = \sum_{j \mathop = p_{n - 1} + 1}^{p_n} \alpha_j e_j$ for each $n \in \N$. We say that $\sequence {u_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is a block basic sequence of $\sequence {e_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$.

title: Definition:Block Code
snippet: A block code is a code in which all the codewords are of the same length.

title: Definition:Block Design
snippet: Let $S$ be a set with $n$ elements. A block design is a collection of subsets $B_r$ of a set $S$ such that: each $B_r$ contains the same number $k$ of elements for every subset $T$ of $S$ with exactly $t$ elements, $T$ is a subset of exactly $\lambda$ of the $B_r$. The numbers $k$, $t$, $\lambda$ and $n$ are characteristic of the particular block design.

title: Definition:Block Design/Also defined as
snippet: == Block Design: Also defined as == Some sources use the term block design to mean a randomized block design. That is, as a specific application of the technique of consigning experimental units to randomized blocks, where the latter are set up as elements of a block design as defined here.

title: Definition:Block Diagonal Matrix
snippet: A block diagonal matrix $\mathbf A$ is a square block matrix with submatrices $A_{i j}$ such that $A_{i j}$ is a zero matrix for $i \ne j$. Hence the only non-zero submatrices appear on the principal diagonal of $\mathbf A$.

title: Definition:Block Incidence Matrix of BIBD
snippet: The block incidence matrix of a $\tuple {v, b, r, k, \lambda}$-BIBD is a $v \times b$ incidence matrix $A = \sqbrk {a_{ij} }$ such that: $a_{ij} = \begin {cases} 1 & : \text {if the $i$th point is in the $j$th block} \\ 0 & : \text {otherwise} \end {cases}$

title: Definition:Block Matrix
snippet: A block matrix is a representation of a matrix as an array of submatrices. This may be defined as follows: Let $S$ be a set. Let $m, n \ge 1$ be positive integers. Let $A = \sqbrk {A_{i j} }$ be an $m \times n$ matrix of matrices over $S$. Let for every $i \in \set {1, \ldots, m}$, the elements of the $i$th row of $A$ have equal height $m_i$. Let for every $j \in \set {1,\ldots, n}$ the elements of the $j$th column of $A$ have equal width $n_i$. Define $M = \ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^m m_i$ and $N = \ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n n_i$ as indexed summations.

title: Definition:Block Multiplication
snippet: Block multiplication is (conventional) matrix multiplication in which the matrices involved are block matrices. That is, the entries are submatrices rather than single elements. The submatrices still multiply together as though they were single elements.

title: Definition:Block Triangular Matrix
snippet: A block triangular matrix $\mathbf A$ is a square block matrix with submatrices $A_{i j}$ such that either: $A_{i j}$ is a zero matrix for $i > j$ or: $A_{i j}$ is a zero matrix for $i < j$.

title: Definition:Block Triangular Matrix/Lower
snippet: A block lower triangular matrix $\mathbf A$ is a block triangular matrix with submatrices $A_{i j}$ such that $A_{i j}$ is a zero matrix for $i < j$.

title: Definition:Block Triangular Matrix/Upper
snippet: A block upper triangular matrix $\mathbf A$ is a block triangular matrix with submatrices $A_{i j}$ such that $A_{i j}$ is a zero matrix for $i > j$.

title: Definition:Blotto
snippet: Blotto is a class of game of which an example has the mechanics as follows: There are two players: General $A$ and Colonel $B$(lotto). $A$ commands $4$ companies. $B$ commands $5$ companies. $A$ can reach a town on either of two different roads. It is the aim of $A$ to reach a town, which can be achieved by travelling down either of two different roads. He can send each of his $4$ companies on whatever road he chooses. $B$ can order any of his $5$ companies to defend either of the two roads. $A$ wins if, on either road, he has (strictly) more companies than $B$.

title: Definition:Bob
snippet: Bob is the name used by convention for the receiver of an encrypted message.

title: Definition:Bochner Integrable Function
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $I$ be a real interval. Let $\lambda$ be the Lebesgue measure on $I$. Let $f : I \to X$ be a Bochner measurable function. We say that $f$ is Bochner integrable there exists simple functions $s_n : I \to X$ such that: $\map {s_n} t \to \map f t$ for each $t \in I$ and: $\ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \int_I \norm {\map f t - \map {s_n} t}_X \rd \map \lambda t = 0$

title: Definition:Bochner Integral
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $I$ be a real interval. Let $\lambda$ be the Lebesgue measure on $I$. Let $f : I \to X$ be a Bochner integrable function. Let $\sequence {s_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence of simple functions such that: $\map {s_n} t \to \map f t$ for each $t \in I \setminus \Omega_0$ and: $\ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \int_I \norm {\map f t - \map {s_n} t}_X \rd \map \lambda t = 0$ where $\Omega_0$ is a Lebesgue measurable set with $\map \lambda {\Omega_0} = 0$.

title: Definition:Bochner Integral of Simple Function
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $I$ be a real interval. Let $\lambda$ be the Lebesgue measure on $I$. Let $f : I \to X$ be a simple function. Take: Lebesgue measurable subsets $\Omega_1, \ldots, \Omega_n$ of $I$ with finite Lebesgue measure $x_1, \ldots, x_n \in X$ such that: $\ds f = \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n x_j \chi_{\Omega_j}$ We define the Bochner integral of $f$ over $I$ by: $\ds \int_I f \rd \lambda = \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n x_j \map \lambda {\Omega_j}$

title: Definition:Bochner Measurable Function
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $I$ be a real interval. Let $X$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $f : I \to X$ be a function. We say that $f$ is Bochner measurable there exists a sequence of simple functions $\sequence {s_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ such that: $\ds \map f t = \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \map {s_n} t$ for almost all $t \in I$.

title: Definition:Body
snippet: In the context of physics and applied mathematics, a body is an object (possibly idealized) which is imagined to have a material existence in the physical universe. A body can be considered as an aggregate of particles to which it is possible to apply a force.

title: Definition:Body-Centered Cubic Lattice
snippet: 300px A body-centered cubic lattice is a set of points in Cartesian $3$-space whose coordinates are of the form: $\tuple {\dfrac 1 2 a x, \dfrac 1 2 a y, \dfrac 1 2 a z}$ such that: $a$ is a positive real constant $x$, $y$ and $z$ are all either even integers or odd integers.

title: Definition:Body-Centered Cubic Lattice/Also known as
snippet: == Body-Centered Cubic Lattice: Also known as == A body-centered cubic lattice can also be presented as body-centred cubic lattice, using the British English centre rather than center.

title: Definition:Body/Deformable
snippet: A deformable body is a body $B$ which is not rigid. That is, when under the influence of a force, the distance between any two points of $B$ may not remain constant.

title: Definition:Body/Rigid
snippet: A rigid body is a body $B$ with the property that the distance between any two points of $B$ remains constant regardless of any external forces.

title: Definition:Boltzmann's Constant
snippet: Boltzmann's constant is the constant of proportion that relates the average relative thermal energy of particles in a gas with the thermodynamic temperature of the gas.

title: Definition:Boltzmann's Constant/Also known as
snippet: == Boltzmann's Constant: Also known as == Boltzmann's constant is also known as the Boltzmann constant.

title: Definition:Boltzmann's Constant/Dimension
snippet: Boltzmann's constant has the dimension $\mathsf {M L^2 T^{-2} \Theta^{-1} }$. This arises from its definition as energy per unit temperature: $\dfrac {\mathsf {M L^2 T^{-2} } } {\Theta}$ Category:Definitions/Dimensions of Measurement Category:Definitions/Boltzmann's Constant

title: Definition:Boltzmann's Constant/Units
snippet: The SI unit for Boltzmann's constant is given as joules per kelvin: $\mathrm {J \, K^{-1} }$ The CGS unit for Boltzmann's constant is given as ergs per kelvin: $\mathrm {erg \, K^{-1} }$ Category:Definitions/Units of Measurement Category:Definitions/Boltzmann's Constant

It is a common approach to define (the) Boolean algebra to be an algebraic structure consisting of: a boolean domain (that is, a set with two elements, typically $\set {0, 1}$) together with: the two operations addition $+$ and multiplication $\times$ defined as follows: $\begin{array}{c|cc} + & 0 & 1 \\ \hline 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ \end{array} \qquad \begin{array}{c|cc} \times & 0 & 1 \\ \hline 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ \end{array}$ Hence expositions discussing such a…

title: Definition:Boolean Algebra/Also known as

Other common notations for the elements of a Boolean algebra include: $0$ and $1$ for $\bot$ and $\top$, respectively $a'$ for $\neg a$. When this convention is used, $0$ is called zero, and $1$ is called one or unit.

snippet: Consider the Boolean algebra $\struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \neg}$ The operation $\vee$ is called join.

title: Definition:Boolean Algebra/Meet
snippet: Consider the Boolean algebra $\struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \neg}$ The operation $\wedge$ is called meet.

snippet: Consider the Boolean algebra $\struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \neg}$ The identity element $\top$ for join ($\vee$) is called top.

title: Definition:Boolean Domain
snippet: A Boolean domain is a $2$-element set of (Aristotelian) truth values, usually defined and denoted as: $\Bbb B = \set {\T, \F}$

title: Definition:Boolean Domain/Also defined as
snippet: == Boolean Domain: Also defined as == The symbology for true and false in a Boolean domain is often one of the rows of the following table: {| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center;" ! True !! False |- | $\T$ || $\F$ |- | $1$ || $0$ |- | $\top$ || $\bot$ |- | $\mathbf{true}$ || $\mathbf{false}$ |} or a typographical variant thereof. Category:Definitions/Boolean Domains

title: Definition:Boolean Domain/Also known as
snippet: == Boolean Domain: Also known as == Some sources refer to a Boolean domain as the set of truth values of propositional logic. Category:Definitions/Boolean Domains

title: Definition:Boolean Fiber
snippet: Let $\Bbb B = \set {\T, \F}$ be a boolean domain. Let $f : X \to \Bbb B$ be a boolean-valued function. Then $f$ has two fibers: $(1): \quad$ The fiber of $\F$ under $f$, defined as $\map {f^{-1} } \F = \set {x \in X: \map f x = \F}$ $(2): \quad$ The fiber of $\T$ under $f$, defined as $\map {f^{-1} } \T = \set {x \in X: \map f x = \T}$. These fibers are called boolean fibers.

title: Definition:Boolean Group
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group. Then $\struct {G, \circ}$ is a Boolean group all its elements, other than the identity, have order $2$.

title: Definition:Boolean Interpretation
snippet: Let $\LL_0$ be the language of propositional logic, with vocabulary $\PP_0$. A boolean interpretation for $\LL_0$ is a propositional function: $v: \PP_0 \to \set {\T, \F}$ When dealing with explicit situations, it is often convenient to let $v$ be a partial mapping, only defining it on the part of the vocabulary one is currently dealing with. In such cases $v$ may be called a partial boolean interpretation; note that this term is taken to include bona fide boolean interpretations as well.

title: Definition:Boolean Interpretation/Formal Semantics
snippet: Let $\LL_0$ be the language of propositional logic. The boolean interpretations for $\LL_0$ can be interpreted as a formal semantics for $\LL_0$, which we denote by $\mathrm{BI}$. The structures of $\mathrm{BI}$ are the boolean interpretations. A WFF $\phi$ is declared ($\mathrm{BI}$-)valid in a boolean interpretation $v$ : $\map v \phi = \T$ Symbolically, this can be expressed as: $v \models_{\mathrm{BI}} \phi$

title: Definition:Boolean Interpretation/Formal Semantics/Invalid
snippet: Let $\phi$ be a WFF of propositional logic. $\phi$ is declared ($\mathrm{BI}$-)invalid in a boolean interpretation $v$ : $\map v \phi = \F$ Symbolically, this can be expressed as: $v \not\models_{\mathrm{BI}} \phi$ Category:Definitions/Boolean Interpretations

title: Definition:Boolean Interpretation/Formula
snippet: Let $\LL_0$ be the language of propositional logic. Let $v: \LL_0 \to \set {\T, \F}$ be a (partial) boolean interpretation. Let $\phi$ be a WFF of propositional logic. Then $v$ is called a boolean interpretation for $\phi$ $v$ is defined at $\phi$. Otherwise, $v$ is called a partial (boolean) interpretation for $\phi$.

title: Definition:Boolean Interpretation/Set of Formulas
snippet: Let $\LL_0$ be the language of propositional logic. Let $v: \LL_0 \to \set {\T, \F}$ be a (partial) boolean interpretation. Let $\FF$ be a set of WFFs of $\LL_0$. Then $v$ is called a boolean interpretation for $\FF$ $v$ is defined on $\FF$. Otherwise, $v$ is called a partial (boolean) interpretation for $\FF$.

title: Definition:Boolean Interpretation/Truth Value
snippet: Let $\LL_0$ be the language of propositional logic. Let $\PP_0$ be the vocabulary of $\LL_0$. Let $\phi$ be a WFF of propositional logic. Let $v: \LL_0 \to \set {\T, \F}$ be a boolean interpretation of $\phi$. The truth value of $\phi$ under $v$ is $\map v \phi$.

title: Definition:Boolean Lattice/Also known as
snippet: == Boolean Lattice: Also known as == Some sources refer to a Boolean lattice as a Boolean algebra. However, the latter has a different meaning on . Category:Definitions/Boolean Lattices

title: Definition:Boolean Lattice/Definition 1
snippet: A Boolean lattice is a complemented distributive lattice.

title: Definition:Boolean Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Then $R$ is called a Boolean ring $R$ is an idempotent ring with unity.

title: Definition:Boolean Ring/Also defined as
snippet: == Boolean Ring: Also defined as == Some sources use the (deprecated) name Boolean ring to mean what is better known as a Boolean algebra. Others define it simply to mean what we have called an idempotent ring, not imposing that it have a unity. Category:Definitions/Boolean Rings

title: Definition:Boolean Satisfiability Problem
snippet: Let $X$ be a set of propositional variables. Let $L$ be a set of one or more propositional formulas constructed using only: elements of $X$ the $4$ unary logical connectives $\operatorname{True}$, $\operatorname{False}$, identity, and $\neg$ the $16$ binary logical connectives. The problem is to find truth values for all $x \in X$ such that all the formulas in $L$ are true. Such a problem is known as a boolean satisfiability problem.

title: Definition:Boolean Satisfiability Problem/Also known as
snippet: == Boolean Satisfiability Problem: Also known as == A boolean satisfiability problem is also known as a SAT problem. Category:Definitions/Boolean Satisfiability Problems

title: Definition:Boolean Variable
snippet: A Boolean variable is a variable whose value is one of the elements of a Boolean domain.

title: Definition:Boolean Variable/Also known as
snippet: == Boolean Variable: Also known as == Some sources use lowercase: boolean variable. Category:Definitions/Boolean Variables

title: Definition:Bootstrapping
snippet: Bootstrapping is a method for obtaining information about the distribution of a population by taking a random sample of $n$ observations, then from this random sample forming further random samples from this.

title: Definition:Bootstrapping/Bootstrap Sample
snippet: In a process of bootstrapping, let $n$ observations be taken. Then let the secondary random samples be taken from that original random sample. These secondary random samples are called bootstrap samples. They will also typically be of $n$ observations. They are obtained by sampling with replacement.

title: Definition:Bootstrapping/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Bootstrapping == The concept of bootstrapping was pioneered by .

title: Definition:Bootstrapping/Motivation
snippet: Bootstrapping is useful when either: there is insufficient information to specify the distribution of the population or: there is little analytic theory about properties or estimators. Refinements are available to improve the estimates exemplified here. In practice, a statistical software package is generally used, with a reliable random number generator. This process is heavily dependent upon computer power .

title: Definition:Bordered Matrix
snippet: A bordered matrix is a matrix to which one or more extra rows or columns have been added at the edges.

title: Definition:Bordering
snippet: Bordering is the technique of adding a row and a column to an array, so as to increase its order. The array in question is usually a determinant or square matrix. It is frequently the case that: the common element of that row and column is set to $1$ all the other elements of that row and column are set to $0$. In that case, the order is increased, but the value of the determinant of that array is unchanged.

title: Definition:Bordering/Also defined as
snippet: == Bordering: Also defined as == Some sources specifically insist that: the bordering row is added at the bottom the bordering column is added at the right of the determinant or matrix so treated. However, while this is usually convenient, it is not a necessary restriction.

title: Definition:Bordering/Motivation
snippet: Bordering can improve computational efficiency when determining properties of a matrix.

title: Definition:Borel Algebra
snippet: A Borel algebra is sometimes used as another name for a $\sigma$-algebra or $\delta$-algebra. Can be confused with Borel $\sigma$-Algebra, which is a specific kind of $\sigma$-algebra.

title: Definition:Borel Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\map \BB {X, \tau}$ be the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on $\struct {X, \tau}$. Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\map \BB {X, \tau}$ such that: $\map \mu K < \infty$ for all compact $K \subseteq X$. We say that $\mu$ is a Borel measure.

title: Definition:Borel Probability Space
snippet: A probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ is a Borel probability space : $\Omega$ is a dense subset of a compact metric space $M$ and: $\Sigma$ is the trace $\sigma$-algebra of $\Omega$ in the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $M$.

title: Definition:Borel Sigma-Algebra/Also defined as
snippet: == Borel Sigma-Algebra: Also defined as == Some sources reserve the name Borel $\sigma$-algebra for $\map \BB {\R^n, \tau}$, where $\tau$ is the usual (Euclidean) topology. Category:Definitions/Borel Sigma-Algebras

title: Definition:Borel Sigma-Algebra/Also known as
snippet: The Borel $\sigma$-algebra is also found with the name topological $\sigma$-algebra, or even just $\sigma$-algebra. When the set $S$ or the topology $\tau$ are clear from the context, one may encounter $\map \BB \tau$, $\map \BB S$ or even just $\BB$. Some authors write $\BB^n$ for $\map \BB {\R^n, \tau}$. Category:Definitions/Borel Sigma-Algebras

title: Definition:Borel Sigma-Algebra/Borel Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\map \BB {S, \tau}$ be the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\struct {S, \tau}$. The elements of $\map \BB {S, \tau}$ are called the Borel (measurable) sets of $\struct {S, \tau}$.

title: Definition:Borel Sigma-Algebra/Metric Space
snippet: Let $\struct {S, d}$ be a metric space. The Borel sigma-algebra (or $\sigma$-algebra) on $\struct {S, d}$ is the $\sigma$-algebra generated by the open sets in $\powerset S$. By the definition of a topology induced by a metric, this definition is a particular instance of the definition of a Borel $\sigma$-algebra on a topological space.

title: Definition:Borel Sigma-Algebra/Topological Space
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space The Borel sigma-algebra $\map \BB {S, \tau}$ of $\struct {S, \tau}$ is the $\sigma$-algebra generated by $\tau$. That is, it is the $\sigma$-algebra generated by the set of open sets in $S$.

title: Definition:Borromean Rings
snippet: The Borromean rings is an arrangement of $3$ interlinked rings such that no $2$ of the rings are themselves linked. That is, if one of them is removed, then the other $2$ are unlinked. 600px

title: Definition:Borromean Rings/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Borromean Rings == The Borromean rings were named after the , a wealthy merchant family who were important politically in the in the late middle ages. They incorporated a design based on these rings on their coat of arms in the $15$th century.

title: Definition:Bottleneck Problem
snippet: A bottleneck problem is a member of a class of problems in optimization theory concerning restrictions on network flows.

title: Definition:Bottom
snippet: Definition:Bottom of Lattice Definition:Bottom (Logic) Definition:Denominator: the bottom of a fraction $\dfrac a b$ or a rational function $\dfrac {\map P x} {\map Q x}$, and so on.

title: Definition:Bottom-Up Form of Top-Down Grammar
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a formal language. Let $\LL$ be given by a top-down formal grammar $\TT$. The bottom-up form of $\TT$ is the formal grammar $\BB$ defined by declaring that: Each letter of $\LL$ is a $\BB$-WFF and, for each rule of formation $\mathbf R$ of $\TT$ of the form: A metasymbol may be replaced by the collation $\phi$ with metasymbols $\phi_1, \ldots, \phi_n$ declaring that $\BB$ has the rule of formation $\mathbf R_\BB$: If $\phi_1, \ldots, \phi_n$ are $\BB$-WFFs, so is $\phi$.

title: Definition:Bottom-Up Specification of Propositional Logic/Also defined as
snippet: == Bottom-Up Specification of Propositional Logic: Also known as == Some sources muddy the water by attempting exhaustively to define the class of statements, for example as follows: {{item|(3):|If $\phi$ and $\psi$ are statements, then: {{item||$\paren {\phi \implies \psi}$}} {{item||$\paren {\phi \land \psi}$}} {{item||$\paren {\phi \lor \psi}$}} {{item||$\paren {\phi \iff\psi}$}} are statements.}}

title: Definition:Bottom (Logic)
snippet: Bottom is a constant of propositional logic interpreted to mean the canonical, undoubted contradiction whose falsehood nobody could possibly ever question. The symbol used is $\bot$.

title: Definition:Bottom (Logic)/Boolean Interpretation
snippet: Let $\bot$ denote the bottom constant in the language of propositional logic. There is only one boolean interpretation for $\bot$: $\map v \bot = \F$ where $\F$ symbolises false.

title: Definition:Bottom (Logic)/Truth Table
snippet: The characteristic truth table of the bottom constant $\bot$ of propositional logic is as follows: $\begin{array}{|c|} \hline \bot \\ \hline \F \\ \hline \end{array}$

title: Definition:Bottom of Lattice
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \preceq}$ be a lattice.

title: Definition:Bottom of Lattice/Also known as
snippet: == Bottom of Lattice: Also known as == The bottom of a lattice is also known as a null. Some sources denote this bottom or null by $0$.

title: Definition:Bottom of Lattice/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \preceq}$ be a lattice. Let $S$ admit a smallest element $\bot$. Then $\bot$ is called the bottom of $S$.

title: Definition:Bottom of Lattice/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \preceq}$ be a lattice. Let $\vee$ have an identity element $\bot$. Then $\bot$ is called the bottom of $S$.

title: Definition:Boubaker Polynomials
snippet: The Boubaker polynomials are the components of the following sequence of polynomials: {{eqn | l = \map {B_0} x | r = 1 }} {{eqn | l = \map {B_1} x | r = x }} {{eqn | l = \map {B_2} x | r = x^2 + 2 }} {{eqn | l = \map {B_3} x | r = x^3 + x }} {{eqn | l = \map {B_4} x | r = x^4 - 2 }} {{eqn | l = \map {B_5} x | r = x^5 - x^3 - 3 x }} {{eqn | l = \map {B_6} x | r = x^6 - 2 x^4 - 3 x^2 + 2 }} {{eqn | l = \map {B_7} x | r = x^7 - 3 x^5 - 2 x^3 + 5 x }} {{eqn | l = \map {B_8} x | r = x^8 - 4 x^6 + 8 x^2 - 2 }} {{eqn | l = \map {B_9} x | r = x^9 - 5 x^7 + 3 x^5 + 10 x^3 - 7 x }}

title: Definition:Bound
snippet: Bound of Subset of Real Numbers Bound of Real-Valued Function Bound of Real Sequence

title: Definition:Bound Occurrence
snippet: Let $\LL_1$ be the language of predicate logic. Let $\mathbf A$ be a WFF of $\LL_1$. Let $Q x$ be an occurrence of a quantifier in $\mathbf A$. Any occurrence of the variable $x$ in the scope of $Q$ is called a bound occurrence.

title: Definition:Bound Variable
snippet: A bound variable is a variable which, when it occurs in an expression, can be replaced with another variable without changing the meaning of the statement.

title: Definition:Bound Variable/Also known as
snippet: == Bound Variable: Also known as == A bound variable is also popularly seen with the name dummy variable, but that term has a different definition on . Sometimes dummy letter can be seen. In treatments of pure logic, this is sometimes known as an individual variable. Some sources call it an apparent variable, reflecting the fact that it only "appears" to be a variable. Some authors gloss over the difference between: a bound variable: a variable which exists in a WFF only as bound occurrences and: a bound occurrence of a variable which may otherwise exist as a free occurrence.

title: Definition:Bound Variable/Predicate Logic
snippet: In predicate logic, a bound variable is a variable which exists in a WFF only as bound occurrences.

title: Definition:Bound of Real-Valued Function
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real-valued function. Let $f$ be bounded. Then $B$ is a bound for $f$ : $\forall x \in S: B \ge \size {\map f x}$

title: Definition:Bound of Subset of Real Numbers
snippet: Let $S \subseteq \R$ be a subset of the real numbers $\R$. Let $S$ be bounded. Then $K$ is a bound for $S$ : $\forall x \in S: \size x \le K$

title: Definition:Boundary
snippet: Geometry: Boundary: The line that goes around a geometric figure. Topology: Boundary: The elements in the closure of a set which are not in the interior of that set. Graph Theory: Boundary: The set of all the vertices of a simple graph that are adjacent to a given vertex.

title: Definition:Boundary (Geometry)
snippet: For example, the endpoints of a line segment are its boundaries.

title: Definition:Boundary (Geometry)/Containment
snippet: A geometric figure is said to be contained by its boundary or boundaries.

title: Definition:Boundary (Graph Theory)/Simple Graph
snippet: Let $G = \tuple {V, E}$ be a simple graph. Let $v \in V$ be a vertex of $G$. Then the boundary of $v$ is the set of all vertices of $G$ which are adjacent to $v$: $\map B v = \set {u \in V: \set {u, v} \in E}$

title: Definition:Boundary (Topology)
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$.

title: Definition:Boundary (Topology)/Also defined as
snippet: == Boundary in the context of Topology: Also defined as == Some sources define the boundary of a subset of a topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ as: the set of elements of $S$ which can be approached from within $S$ and from outside $S$. However, this definition is of little use without rigorous definitions of approach, inside and outside. Consequently, such imprecise definitions are not used on .

title: Definition:Boundary (Topology)/Also known as
snippet: == Boundary in the context of Topology: Also known as == The boundary of a subset $H$ of a topological space $T$ is also seen referred to as the frontier of $H$.

title: Definition:Boundary (Topology)/Definition 1
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. The boundary of $H$ consists of all the points in the closure of $H$ which are not in the interior of $H$. Thus, the boundary of $H$ is defined as: $\partial H := H^- \setminus H^\circ$ where $H^-$ denotes the closure and $H^\circ$ the interior of $H$.

title: Definition:Boundary (Topology)/Definition 2
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. The boundary of $H$ is the set of all the boundary points of $H$.

title: Definition:Boundary (Topology)/Definition 3
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. The boundary of $H$ is the intersection of the closure of $H$ with the closure of the complement of $H$ in $T$: $\partial H = H^- \cap \paren {\overline H}^-$

title: Definition:Boundary (Topology)/Definition 4
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. The boundary of $H$ consists of all the points in $H$ which are not in either the interior or exterior of $H$. Thus, the boundary of $H$ is defined as: $\partial H := H \setminus \paren {H^\circ \cup H^e}$ where: $H^\circ$ denotes the interior of $H$ $H^e$ denotes the exterior of $H$.

title: Definition:Boundary (Topology)/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Boundary == The boundary of $H$ is variously denoted (with or without the brackets): $\partial H$ $\map {\mathrm b} H$ $\map {\mathrm {Bd} } H$ $\map {\mathrm {fr} } H$ or $\map {\mathrm {Fr} } H$ (where $\mathrm {fr}$ stands for frontier) $H^b$ The notations of choice on are $\partial H$ and $H^b$.

title: Definition:Boundary Condition
snippet: Let $\Phi$ be a differential equation to which a particular solution is to be found. A boundary condition is an equation relating particular values of the dependent and independent variables which the particular solution to $\Phi$ must satisfy. It is usual for such boundary condition to correspond to the physical extremities of bodies, aspects of whose internal nature is being modelled by means of $\Phi$.

title: Definition:Boundary Layer
snippet: A boundary layer is a thin layer of a body of fluid close to the surface where effects of viscosity are important. At the boundary layer, the Navier-Stokes equations can then be separately

title: Definition:Boundary Layer/Motivation
snippet: By separately identifying a boundary layer distinct from the main body of the fluid, the Navier-Stokes equations can be separately applied to: the boundary layer itself, which is sufficiently thin as to be negligible analysis of the main body in the body of the fluid beyond the boundary layer, where effects of viscosity are similarly negligible.

title: Definition:Boundary Point
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$.

title: Definition:Boundary Point/Definition 1
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. $x \in S$ is a boundary point of $H$ every neighborhood $N$ of $x$ satisfies: $H \cap N \ne \O$ and $\overline H \cap N \ne \O$ where $\overline H$ is the complement of $H$ in $S$.

title: Definition:Boundary Point/Definition 2
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. $x \in S$ is a boundary point of $H$ $x$ is an element of the boundary of $H$ in $S$.

title: Definition:Boundary Point (Complex Analysis)
snippet: Let $S \subseteq \C$ be a subset of the complex plane. Let $z_0 \in \C$. $z_0$ is a boundary point of $S$ every $\epsilon$-neighborhood $\map {N_\epsilon} {z_0}$ of $z_0$ contains points of $\C$ in $S$ and also points of $\C$ which are not in $S$.

title: Definition:Boundary Value Problem
snippet: A boundary value problem is a differential equation for which a particular solution is to be found, such that the particular solution must satisfy certain boundary conditions.

title: Definition:Boundary Value Problem/Also known as
snippet: == Boundary Value Problem: Also known as == The term boundary value problem can be hyphenated as boundary-value problem.

title: Definition:Bounded Above
snippet: Bounded Above Set Bounded Above Subset of Real Numbers Bounded Above Mapping Bounded Above Real-Valued Function Bounded Above Sequence Bounded Above Real Sequence

title: Definition:Bounded Above Mapping
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping whose codomain is an ordered set $\struct {T, \preceq}$. Then $f$ is bounded above on $S$ by the upper bound $H$ : $\forall x \in S: \map f x \preceq H$ That is, $f \sqbrk S = \set {\map f x: x \in S}$ is bounded above by $H$.

title: Definition:Bounded Above Mapping/Real-Valued
snippet: Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real-valued function. $f$ is bounded above on $S$ by the upper bound $H$ : $\forall x \in S: \map f x \le H$ That is, the set $\set {\map f x: x \in S}$ is bounded above in $\R$ by $H$.

title: Definition:Bounded Above Mapping/Real-Valued/Unbounded
snippet: Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real-valued function. Then $f$ is unbounded above on $S$ it is not bounded above on $S$: $\neg \exists H \in \R: \forall x \in S: \map f x \le H$

title: Definition:Bounded Above Mapping/Unbounded
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping whose codomain is an ordered set $\struct {T, \preceq}$. Then $f$ is unbounded above on $S$ it is not bounded above on $S$: $\neg \exists H \in T: \forall x \in S: \map f x \preceq H$

title: Definition:Bounded Above Sequence
snippet: Let $\struct {T, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $T$. Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is bounded above : $\exists M \in T: \forall i \in \N: x_i \preceq M$

title: Definition:Bounded Above Sequence/Real
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a real sequence. Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is bounded above : $\exists M \in \R: \forall i \in \N: x_i \le M$

title: Definition:Bounded Above Sequence/Real/Unbounded
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a real sequence. $\sequence {x_n}$ is unbounded above there exists no $M$ in $\R$ such that: $\forall i \in \N: x_i \le M$ Category:Definitions/Unbounded Above Sequences Category:Definitions/Real Sequences

title: Definition:Bounded Above Sequence/Unbounded
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $T$. $\sequence {x_n}$ is unbounded above there exists no $M$ in $T$ such that: $\forall i \in \N: x_i \preceq M$ Category:Definitions/Unbounded Above Sequences Category:Definitions/Sequences

title: Definition:Bounded Above Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. A subset $T \subseteq S$ is bounded above (in $S$) $T$ admits an upper bound (in $S$).

title: Definition:Bounded Above Set/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $\R$ be the set of real numbers. A subset $T \subseteq \R$ is bounded above (in $\R$) $T$ admits an upper bound (in $\R$).

title: Definition:Bounded Above Set/Real Numbers/Unbounded
snippet: Let $\R$ be the set of real numbers. Let $T \subseteq \R$ be a subset of $\R$ . $T \subseteq \R$ is unbounded above (in $\R$) it is not bounded above.

title: Definition:Bounded Above Set/Unbounded
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. A subset $T \subseteq S$ is unbounded above (in $S$) it is not bounded above.

title: Definition:Bounded Below
snippet: Bounded Below Set Bounded Below Subset of Real Numbers Bounded Below Mapping Bounded Below Real-Valued Function Bounded Below Sequence Bounded Below Real Sequence

title: Definition:Bounded Below Mapping
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping whose codomain is an ordered set $\struct {T, \preceq}$. Then $f$ is said to be bounded below (in $T$) by the lower bound $L$ : $\forall x \in S: L \preceq \map f x$ That is, iff $f \sqbrk S = \set {\map f x: x \in S}$ is bounded below by $L$.

title: Definition:Bounded Below Mapping/Real-Valued
snippet: Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real-valued function. Then $f$ is bounded below on $S$ by the lower bound $L$ : $\forall x \in S: L \le \map f x$ That is, the set $\set {\map f x: x \in S}$ is bounded below in $\R$ by $L$.

title: Definition:Bounded Below Mapping/Real-Valued/Unbounded
snippet: Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real-valued function. Then $f$ is unbounded below on $S$ it is not bounded below on $S$: $\neg \exists L \in \R: \forall x \in S: L \le \map f x$

title: Definition:Bounded Below Mapping/Unbounded
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping whose codomain is an ordered set $\struct {T, \preceq}$. Then $f$ is unbounded below (in $T \ $) there exists no $L \in S$ such that: $\forall x \in S: L \preceq \map f x$

title: Definition:Bounded Below Sequence
snippet: Let $\struct {T, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $T$. Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is bounded below : $\exists m \in T: \forall i \in \N: m \preceq x_i$

title: Definition:Bounded Below Sequence/Real
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a real sequence. Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is bounded below : $\exists m \in \R: \forall i \in \N: m \le x_i$

title: Definition:Bounded Below Sequence/Real/Unbounded
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a real sequence. $\sequence {x_n}$ is unbounded below there exists no $m$ in $\R$ such that: $\forall i \in \N: m \le x_i$ Category:Definitions/Unbounded Below Sequences Category:Definitions/Real Sequences

title: Definition:Bounded Below Sequence/Unbounded
snippet: Let $\struct {T, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $T$. $\sequence {x_n}$ is unbounded below there exists no $m$ in $T$ such that: $\forall i \in \N: m \preceq x_i$ Category:Definitions/Unbounded Below Sequences Category:Definitions/Sequences

title: Definition:Bounded Below Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. A subset $T \subseteq S$ is bounded below (in $S$) $T$ admits a lower bound (in $S$).

title: Definition:Bounded Below Set/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $\R$ be the set of real numbers. A subset $T \subseteq \R$ is bounded below (in $\R$) $T$ admits a lower bound (in $\R$).

title: Definition:Bounded Below Set/Real Numbers/Unbounded
snippet: Let $\R$ be the set of real numbers. Let $T \subseteq \R$ be a subset of $\R$ . $T \subseteq \R$ is unbounded below (in $\R$) it is not bounded below.

title: Definition:Bounded Below Set/Unbounded
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. A subset $T \subseteq S$ is unbounded below (in $S$) it is not bounded below.

title: Definition:Bounded Class
snippet: == Definition == Let $B$ be a class.

title: Definition:Bounded Class/Bounded Subset of Class
snippet: Let $B$ be a class. Let $B$ be a subclass of a class $A$. Then $B$ is a bounded subset of $A$ : there exists a set $x \in A$ such that $B$ is bounded by $x$ That is, every element of $B$ is a subset of $x$.

title: Definition:Bounded Class/Bounded by Set
snippet: Let $B$ be a class. Let $x$ be a set. $B$ is bounded by $x$ : every element of $B$ is a subset of $x$.

title: Definition:Bounded Euclidean Space/Unbounded
snippet: Let $A \subseteq \R^n$ be a subset of a Euclidean space under the usual metric. $A$ is unbounded (in $\R^n$) $A$ is not bounded (in $\R^n$).

title: Definition:Bounded Lattice/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $S$ admit all finite suprema and finite infima. Let $\vee$ and $\wedge$ be the join and meet operations on $S$, respectively. Then the ordered structure $\struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \preceq}$ is a bounded lattice.

title: Definition:Bounded Lattice/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \preceq}$ be a lattice. Let $\vee$ and $\wedge$ have identity elements $\bot$ and $\top$ respectively. Then $\struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \preceq}$ is a bounded lattice. Thus $\struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \preceq}$ is a bounded lattice the bounded lattice axioms are satisfied:

title: Definition:Bounded Lattice/Definition 3
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \wedge, \vee, \preceq}$ be a lattice. Let $S$ be bounded in $\struct {S, \preceq}$. Then $\struct {S, \wedge, \vee, \preceq}$ is a bounded lattice.

title: Definition:Bounded Lattice/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Greatest and Smallest Elements == The greatest element and smallest element of a bounded lattice are denoted on by $\top$ and $\bot$ respectively. Some sources use $1$ for the greatest element and $0$ for the smallest element.

title: Definition:Bounded Lattice Homomorphism
snippet: Let $L_1 = \struct{S_1, \vee_1, \wedge_1, \preceq_1}$ be a bounded lattice with greatest element $\top_1$ and smallest element $\bot_1$ Let $L_2 = \struct{S_2, \vee_2, \wedge_2, \preceq_2}$ be a bounded lattice with greatest element $\top_2$ and smallest element $\bot_2$ Let $f: \struct{S_1, \vee_1, \wedge_1, \preceq_1} \to \struct{S_2, \vee_2, \wedge_2, \preceq_2}$ be a lattice homomorphism.

title: Definition:Bounded Linear Functional
snippet: Let $\mathbb F$ be a subfield of $\C$. Let $\struct {X, \norm \cdot}$ be a normed vector space over $\mathbb F$. Let $f : X \to \mathbb F$ be a linear functional. We say that $f$ is a bounded linear functional : there exists $C > 0$ such that $\cmod {\map f x} \le C \norm x$ for each $x \in X$.

orm {x_0}_X = 1$ such that: $\ds \map f {x_0} =

title: Definition:Bounded Linear Operator/Inner Product Space
snippet:
Let $\struct {V, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be an inner product space. Let $
orm \cdot$ be the inner product norm for $V$. Let $A : V 	o V$ be a linear operator. We say that $A$ is a bounded linear operator : there exists $c > 0$ such that $
orm {A v} \le c 
orm v$ for each $v \in V$. That is, a bounded linear operator on an inner product space is a bounded linear transformation from the space to itself.

title: Definition:Bounded Linear Operator/Normed Vector Space
snippet:
Let $\struct {V, 
orm {\cdot}_V}$ be a normed vector space. Let $A : V 	o V$ be a linear operator. $A$ is a bounded linear operator : $\exists c \in \R_{>0} :  orall v \in V: 
orm {A v}_V \le c 
orm v_V$ That is, a bounded linear operator on a normed vector space is a bounded linear transformation from the space to itself.

title: Definition:Bounded Linear Transformation/Inner Product Space
snippet:
Let $\struct {V, \innerprod \cdot \cdot_V}$ and $\struct {U, \innerprod \cdot \cdot_U}$ be inner product spaces. Let $
orm \cdot_V$ and $
orm \cdot_U$ be the inner product norms of $V$ and $U$ respectively. Let $A : V 	o U$ be a linear transformation. We say that $A$ is a bounded linear transformation : there exists $c > 0$ such that $
orm {A v}_U \le c 
orm v_V$ for each $v \in V$.

title: Definition:Bounded Linear Transformation/Normed Vector Space
snippet:
Let $\struct {V, 
orm \cdot_V}$ and $\struct {U, 
orm \cdot_U}$ be normed vector spaces. Let $A : V 	o U$ be a linear transformation. We say that $A$ is a bounded linear transformation : $ orall v \in V: \exists c > 0: 
orm {A v}_U \le c 
orm v_V$.

title: Definition:Bounded Linear Transformation/Topological Vector Space
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be topological vector spaces over $\GF$. Let $T : X \to Y$ be a linear transformation. We say that $T$ is a bounded linear transformation : for each von Neumann-bounded subset $E$ of $X$, $T \sqbrk E$ is von Neumann-bounded.

title: Definition:Bounded Mapping
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\struct {T, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. Let the image of $f$ be bounded. Then $f$ is bounded. That is, $f$ is bounded it is both bounded above and bounded below.

title: Definition:Bounded Mapping/Complex-Valued
snippet: Let $f: S \to \C$ be a complex-valued function. Then $f$ is bounded the real-valued function $\cmod f: S \to \R$ is bounded, where $\cmod f$ is the modulus of $f$. That is, $f$ is bounded if there is a constant $K \ge 0$ such that $\cmod {\map f z} \le K$ for all $z \in S$.

title: Definition:Bounded Mapping/Complex-Valued/Unbounded
snippet: Let $f: S \to \C$ be a complex-valued function. Then $f$ is unbounded $f$ is not bounded. That is, $f$ is unbounded if there does not exist a constant $K \ge 0$ such that $\cmod {f \paren z} \le K$ for all $z \in S$.

title: Definition:Bounded Mapping/Metric Space
snippet: Let $M$ be a metric space. Let $f: X \to M$ be a mapping from any set $X$ into $M$. Then $f$ is a bounded mapping $f \sqbrk X$ is bounded in $M$.

title: Definition:Bounded Mapping/Metric Space/Warning
snippet: == Warning concerning Bounded Mapping to Metric Space == From Real Number Line is Metric Space, we can in theory consider defining boundedness on a real-valued function in terms of boundedness of a mapping into a metric space. However, as a metric space is itself defined in terms of a real-valued function in the first place, this concept can be criticised as being a circular definition. Category:Definitions/Metric Spaces

title: Definition:Bounded Mapping/Normed Division Ring
snippet:
Let $\struct {R, 
orm {\,\cdot\,}}$ be a normed division ring. Let $f: S 	o R$ be a mapping from $S$ into $R$. Then $f$ is bounded the real-valued function $
orm {\,\cdot\,} \circ f: S 	o \R$ is bounded, where $
orm {\,\cdot\,} \circ f$ is the composite of $
orm {\,\cdot\,}$ and $f$. That is, $f$ is bounded if there is a constant $K \in \R_{\ge 0}$ such that $
orm{f \paren {s}} \le K$ for all $s \in S$.

title: Definition:Bounded Mapping/Normed Vector Space
snippet:
Let $\struct {R, 
orm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a normed division ring. Let $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a normed vector space over $R$. Let $S$ be a set. Let $f : S 	o X$ be a mapping. We say that $f$ is bounded there exists a real number $M > 0$ such that: $
orm {\map f x} \le M$ for each $x \in S$.

title: Definition:Bounded Mapping/Real-Valued
snippet: Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real-valued function.

title: Definition:Bounded Mapping/Real-Valued/Attaining its Bounds
snippet: Let $f: S \to \R$ be a bounded real-valued function. Let $T$ be a subset of $S$. Suppose that: $\exists a, b \in T: \forall x \in S: \map f a \le \map f x \le \map f b$ Then $f$ attains its bounds on $T$.

title: Definition:Bounded Mapping/Real-Valued/Definition 1
snippet: Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real-valued function. $f$ is bounded on $S$ : $f$ is bounded above on $S$ and also: $f$ is bounded below on $S$.

title: Definition:Bounded Mapping/Real-Valued/Definition 2
snippet: Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real-valued function. $f$ is bounded on $S$ : $\exists K \in \R_{\ge 0}: \forall x \in S: \size {\map f x} \le K$ where $\size {\map f x}$ denotes the absolute value of $\map f x$.

title: Definition:Bounded Mapping/Real-Valued/Definition 3
snippet: Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real-valued function. $f$ is bounded on $S$ : $\exists a, b \in \R_{\ge 0}: \forall x \in S: \map f x \in \closedint a b$ where $\closedint a b$ denotes the (closed) real interval from $a$ to $b$.

title: Definition:Bounded Mapping/Real-Valued/Unbounded
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real-valued function.

title: Definition:Bounded Mapping/Unbounded
snippet: Let $\struct {T, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. $f$ is unbounded $f$ is not bounded. That is, $f$ is either unbounded above or unbounded below, or both.

title: Definition:Bounded Metric Space/Also defined as
snippet: == Bounded Metric Space: Also defined as == Some sources place no emphasis on the fact that the subset $B$ of the underlying set $A$ of $M$ is in fact itself a subspace of $M'$, and merely refer to a bounded set. This, however, glosses over the facts that: {{item|\text{(a)}:|from Subspace of Metric Space is Metric Space, any such subset is also a metric space by dint of the induced metric $d_B$}} {{item|\text{(b)}:| without reference to such a metric, boundedness is not defined.}} Hence strives to ensure that boundedness is consistently defined in the context of a metric space, and not just a…

title: Definition:Bounded Metric Space/Also known as
snippet: == Bounded Metric Space: Also known as == If the context is clear, it is acceptable to use the term bounded space for bounded metric space.

title: Definition:Bounded Metric Space/Complex
snippet: Let $D$ be a subset of the complex plane $\C$. Then $D$ is bounded (in $\C$) there exists $M \in \R$ such that: $\forall z \in D: \cmod z \le M$

title: Definition:Bounded Metric Space/Complex/Unbounded
snippet: Let $D$ be a subset of the complex plane $\C$. Then $D$ is unbounded (in $\C$) : $\nexists M \in \R: \forall z \in D: \cmod z \le M$ That is, if $D$ is not bounded in $\C$.

title: Definition:Bounded Metric Space/Definition 1
snippet: A subspace $M' = \struct {B, d_B}$ of a metric space $M = \struct {A, d}$ is bounded (in $M$) : $\exists a \in A, K \in \R: \forall x \in B: \map {d} {x, a} \le K$ That is, there exists an element of $A$ within a finite distance of all elements of $B$.

title: Definition:Bounded Metric Space/Definition 2
snippet: A subspace $M' = \struct {B, d_B}$ of a metric space $M = \struct {A, d}$ is bounded (in $M$) : $\exists K \in \R: \forall x, y \in M': \map {d_B} {x, y} \le K$ That is, there exists a finite distance such that all pairs of elements of $B$ are within that distance.

title: Definition:Bounded Metric Space/Definition 3
snippet: A subspace $M' = \struct {B, d_B}$ of a metric space $M = \struct {A, d}$ is bounded (in $M$) : $\exists x \in A, \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: B \subseteq \map {B_\epsilon} {x; d}$ where $\map {B_\epsilon} {x; d}$ is the open $\epsilon$-ball of $x$ the metric of $M$. That is, $M'$ can be fitted inside an open ball in $M$.

title: Definition:Bounded Metric Space/Definition 4
snippet: A subspace $M' = \struct {B, d_B}$ of a metric space $M = \struct {A, d}$ is bounded (in $M$) : $\exists K \in \R: \forall x \in B: \map d {x, a} \le K$ for some $a \in A$.

title: Definition:Bounded Metric Space/Definition 5
snippet: A subspace $M' = \struct {B, d_B}$ of a metric space $M = \struct {A, d}$ is bounded (in $M$) : $\exists x \in B, \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: B = \map {B_\epsilon} {x; d_B}$ where $\map {B_\epsilon} {x; d_B}$ is the open $\epsilon$-ball of $x$ the metric of $M'$. That is, $M'$ is equal to an open ball of itself.

title: Definition:Bounded Metric Space/Euclidean
snippet: Let $A \subseteq \R^n$ be a subset of a Euclidean space under the usual metric. $A$ is bounded (in $\R^n$) : $\exists N \in \R: \forall x \in A: \size x \le N$ That is, every element of $A$ is within a finite distance of any point we may choose for the origin.

title: Definition:Bounded Metric Space/Unbounded
snippet: Let $M = \struct {X, d}$ be a metric space. Let $M' = \struct {Y, d_Y}$ be a subspace of $M$. Then $M'$ is unbounded (in $M$) $M'$ is not bounded in $M$.

title: Definition:Bounded Region of Plane
snippet: Let $D \subseteq \R^2$ be a subset of the plane. $D$ is bounded there exists a circle in the plane which completely encloses $D$.

title: Definition:Bounded Sequence
snippet: A special case of a bounded mapping is a bounded sequence, where the domain of the mapping is $\N$. Let $\struct {T, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $T$. Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is bounded $\exists m, M \in T$ such that $\forall i \in \N$: $(1): \quad m \preceq x_i$ $(2): \quad x_i \preceq M$ That is, it is bounded above and bounded below.

title: Definition:Bounded Sequence/Complex
snippet: Let $\sequence {z_n}$ be a complex sequence. Then $\sequence {z_n}$ is bounded : $\exists M \in \R$ such that $\forall i \in \N: \cmod {z_i} \le M$ where $\cmod {z_i}$ denotes the complex modulus of $z_i$.

title: Definition:Bounded Sequence/Complex/Unbounded
snippet: Let $\sequence {z_n}$ be a complex sequence. $\sequence {z_n}$ is unbounded it is not bounded.

title: Definition:Bounded Sequence/Metric Space
snippet: Let $M$ be a metric space. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $M$. Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is a bounded sequence $\sequence {x_n}$ is bounded in $M$. That is: $\exists K \in \R: \forall n, m \in \N: \map d {x_n, x_m} \le K$

title: Definition:Bounded Sequence/Metric Space/Unbounded
snippet: Let $M$ be a metric space. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $M$. $\sequence {x_n}$ is unbounded it is not bounded.

title: Definition:Bounded Sequence/Normed Division Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a normed division ring. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $R$. Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is bounded : $\exists K \in \R$ such that $\forall n \in \N: \norm {x_n} \le K$

title: Definition:Bounded Sequence/Normed Division Ring/Unbounded
snippet: Let $\struct {R, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a normed division ring. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $R$. $\sequence {x_n}$ is unbounded it is not bounded.

title: Definition:Bounded Sequence/Normed Vector Space
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a normed vector space. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $X$. Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is bounded : $\exists K \in \R$ such that $\forall n \in \N: \norm {x_n} \le K$

title: Definition:Bounded Sequence/Normed Vector Space/Unbounded
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a normed vector space. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $R$. $\sequence {x_n}$ is unbounded it is not bounded.

title: Definition:Bounded Sequence/Real
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a real sequence. Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is bounded $\exists m, M \in \R$ such that $\forall i \in \N$: $m \le x_i$ $x_i \le M$ That is, it is bounded above and bounded below.

title: Definition:Bounded Sequence/Real/Unbounded
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a real sequence. $\sequence {x_n}$ is unbounded it is not bounded.

title: Definition:Bounded Sequence/Unbounded
snippet: A sequence which is not bounded is unbounded. Category:Definitions/Boundedness

title: Definition:Bounded Sesquilinear Form
snippet: Let $\HH, \KK$ be Hilbert spaces over $\Bbb F \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $u: \HH \times \KK \to \Bbb F$ be a sesquilinear form. Then $u$ is a bounded sesquilinear form, or to be bounded, : $\exists M \in \R: \forall h \in \HH, k \in \KK: \size {\map u {h, k} } \le M \norm h_\HH \norm k_\KK$ A constant $M$ satisfying the above is called a bound for $u$.

title: Definition:Bounded Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $T \subseteq S$ be both bounded below and bounded above in $S$. Then $T$ is bounded in $S$.

title: Definition:Bounded Set/Also known as
snippet: == Bounded Set/Also known as == A bounded set can also be referred to as a bounded ordered set. However, it is unnecessary to refer specifically to the ordered nature of such a set, as boundedness cannot be applied to a set which has no ordering. The term bounded poset can also be found. Some sources use the term order-bounded set. Category:Definitions/Bounded Sets

title: Definition:Bounded Set/Real Numbers/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\R$ be the set of real numbers. Let $T \subseteq \R$ be both bounded below and bounded above in $\R$. Then $T$ is bounded in $\R$.

title: Definition:Bounded Set/Real Numbers/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\R$ be the set of real numbers. Let $T \subseteq \R$ be a subset of $\R$ such that: $\exists K \in \R: \forall x \in T: \size x \le K$ where $\size x$ denotes the absolute value of $x$. Then $T$ is bounded in $\R$.

title: Definition:Bounded Set/Real Numbers/Unbounded
snippet: Let $\R$ be the set of real numbers. Let $T \subseteq \R$ be a subset of $\R$ . $T \subseteq \R$ is unbounded (in $\R$) it is not bounded.

title: Definition:Bounded Set/Unbounded
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. A subset $T \subseteq S$ is unbounded (in $S$) it is not bounded.

title: Definition:Bounded Subset of Connected Riemannian Manifold
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a connected Riemannian manifold. Let $A \subseteq M$ be a subset. Let $p,q \in M$ be points. Let $d_g$ be the Riemannian distance. Let $C \in \R$ be a constant. Suppose: $\exists C \in \R : \forall p, q \in A : \map {d_g} {p, q} \le C$ Then $A$ is said to be bounded.

title: Definition:Bounded Subset of Normed Vector Space
snippet: Let $M = \struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}}$ be a normed vector space. Let $M' \subseteq X$.

title: Definition:Bounded Subset of Normed Vector Space/Definition 1
snippet:
Let $M = \struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}}$ be a normed vector space. Let $M' = \struct {Y, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_Y}$ be a subspace of $M$. $M'$ is bounded (in $M$) : $\exists x \in X, C \in \R_{> 0}:  orall y \in Y: 
orm {x - y} \le C$

title: Definition:Bounded Subset of Normed Vector Space/Definition 2
snippet: Let $M = \struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}}$ be a normed vector space. Let $M' = \struct {Y, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_Y}$ be a subspace of $M$. $M'$ is bounded (in $M$) : $\exists \epsilon \in \R_{>0} : \exists x \in X : Y \subseteq \map {B_\epsilon^-} x$ where $\map {B_\epsilon^-} x$ is a closed ball in $M$.

title: Definition:Bounded Subset of Topological Vector Space
snippet: Let $\mathbb F \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {V, \tau}$ be a topological vector space over $\mathbb F$. A subset $B \subseteq V$ is bounded : for each $U \in \tau$ such that $\mathbf 0_V \in U$ there is an $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ such that: $\epsilon B \subseteq U$ where: $\bf 0_V$ denotes the zero vector of $V$ $\epsilon B$ denotes the dilation of $B$ by $\epsilon$

title: Definition:Bounded Variation/Also known as
snippet: == Bounded Variation: Also known as == Some sources say that $f$ is of finite variation rather than of bounded variation. It is also acceptable to say that such an $f$ has bounded variation.

title: Definition:Bounded Variation/Closed Bounded Interval
snippet: Let $a, b$ be real numbers with $a < b$. Let $f : \closedint a b \to \R$ be a real function.

title: Definition:Bounded Variation/Closed Bounded Interval/Definition 1
snippet: Let $a, b$ be real numbers with $a < b$. Let $f : \closedint a b \to \R$ be a real function. For each finite subdivision $P$ of $\closedint a b$, write: $P = \set {x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_n}$ with: $a = x_0 < x_1 < x_2 < \cdots < x_{n - 1} < x_n = b$ Also write: $\ds \map {V_f} {P ; \closedint a b} = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \size {\map f {x_i} - \map f {x_{i - 1} } }$ We say $f$ is of bounded variation there exists an $M \ge 0$ such that: $\map {V_f} {P ; \closedint a b} \le M$ for all finite subdivisions $P$.

title: Definition:Bounded Variation/Closed Bounded Interval/Definition 2
snippet: Let $a, b$ be real numbers with $a < b$. Let $f : \closedint a b \to \R$ be a real function. For each finite non-empty subset $\SS$ of $\closedint a b$, write: $\SS = \set {x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_n}$ with: $a \le x_0 < x_1 < x_2 < \cdots < x_{n - 1} < x_n \le b$ Also write: $\ds \map {V_f^\ast} {\SS; \closedint a b} = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \size {\map f {x_i} - \map f {x_{i - 1} } }$ We say $f$ is of bounded variation there exists an $M \ge 0$ such that: $\map {V_f^\ast} {\SS; \closedint a b} \le M$ for all finite non-empty subsets $\mathcal S$ of $\closedint a b$.

title: Definition:Bounded Variation/Closed Unbounded Interval
snippet: Let $I$ be an unbounded closed interval or $\R$. Let $f : I \to \R$ be a real function. For each finite non-empty subset $\SS$ of $I$, write: $\SS = \set {x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_n}$ with: $x_0 < x_1 < x_2 < \cdots < x_{n - 1} < x_n$ Also write: $\ds \map {V_f^\ast} {\SS; I} = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \size {\map f {x_i} - \map f {x_{i - 1} } }$ for $n \ge 1$, and $\map {V_f^\ast} {\SS ; I} = 0$ otherwise. We say $f$ is of bounded variation there exists an $M \ge 0$ such that: $\map {V_f^\ast} {\SS; I} \le M$ for all finite non-empty subsets $\SS$ of $I$.

title: Definition:Bourbaki Assembly
snippet: The notion of assembly is an example of a collation used in . An assembly is a succession of signs written one after another. Certain signs which are not variables are allowed to be joined in pairs by links, as follows: $\overbrace {\tau A \Box}^{} A'$

title: Definition:Bourbaki Assembly/Link
snippet: In an assembly, certain signs which are not variables can be joined in (ordered) pairs by links, as follows: $\overbrace {\tau A \Box}^{} A'$ where the $\overbrace {}{}$ depicts a link between $\tau$ and $\Box$.

title: Definition:Bowley Skewness
snippet: Let $X$ be a random variable with quartiles $Q_1$, $Q_2$ and $Q_3$, denoting the lower quartile, median and upper quartile respectively. Then the Bowley skewness of $X$ is defined as: $\dfrac {Q_3 - 2 Q_2 + Q_1} {Q_3 - Q_1}$

title: Definition:Bowley Skewness/Also known as
snippet: == Bowley Skewness: Also known as == Bowley skewness is also known as the quartile skewness coefficient.

title: Definition:Bowley Skewness/Also presented as
snippet: == Bowley Skewness: Also known as == The Bowley skewness is also presented in the following forms: $\dfrac {\paren {Q_3 - Q_2} - \paren {Q_2 - Q_1} } {Q_3 - Q_1}$ $\dfrac {Q_3 - 2 M + Q_1} {Q_3 - Q_1}$ where $M$ denotes the median.

title: Definition:Box-Jenkins Model
snippet: The Box-Jenkins model is a very general mathematical model for time series analysis in forecasting and prediction.

title: Definition:Box-Jenkins Model/ARIMA
snippet: Let $S$ be a stochastic process based on an equispaced time series. Let the values of $S$ at timestamps $t, t - 1, t - 2, \dotsc$ be $z_t, z_{t - 1}, z_{t - 2}, \dotsc$ Let $a_t, a_{t - 1}, a_{t - 2}, \dotsc$ be a sequence of independent shocks at timestamps $t, t - 1, t - 2, \dotsc$ Let: $w_t = \nabla^d z_t$ where $\nabla^d$ denotes the $d$th iteration of the backward difference operator.

title: Definition:Box-Jenkins Model/ARMA
snippet: Let $S$ be a stochastic process based on an equispaced time series. Let the values of $S$ at timestamps $t, t - 1, t - 2, \dotsc$ be $z_t, z_{t - 1}, z_{t - 2}, \dotsc$ Let $\tilde z_t, \tilde z_{t - 1}, \tilde z_{t - 2}, \dotsc$ be deviations from a constant mean level $\mu$: $\tilde z_t = z_t - \mu$ Let $a_t, a_{t - 1}, a_{t - 2}, \dotsc$ be a sequence of independent shocks at timestamps $t, t - 1, t - 2, \dotsc$ Let $M$ be a model where the current value of $\tilde z_t$ is expressed as a combination of a finite linear aggregate of the past values along with a finite linear aggregate of the…

title: Definition:Box-Jenkins Model/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Box-Jenkins Model == The Box-Jenkins model was first proposed by and in $1967$.

title: Definition:Box-and-Whisker Diagram
snippet: A box-and-whisker diagram is a graphical representation of the information contained in a five-number summary. By presenting more than one such plot next to each other in the same diagram, it is then possible to see major differences between their characteristics.

title: Definition:Box-and-Whisker Diagram/Also known as
snippet: == Box-and-Whisker Diagram: Also known as == A box-and-whisker diagram is also known as a boxplot or box plot.

title: Definition:Box-and-Whisker Diagram/Box
snippet: Context: box-and-whisker diagram. The box is a rectangle whose length is an indication of the interquartile range, divided in two by the median. The breadth of this box is arbitrary.

title: Definition:Box-and-Whisker Diagram/Whiskers
snippet: Context: box-and-whisker diagram. The whiskers are lines extending from the box which indicate the range.

title: Definition:Box Topology
snippet: Let $\family {\struct {X_i, \tau_i}}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an $I$-indexed family of topological spaces. Let $X$ be the cartesian product of $\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$, that is: $\ds X := \prod_{i \mathop \in I} X_i$ Define: $\ds \BB := \set {\prod_{i \mathop \in I} U_i: \forall i \in I: U_i \in \tau_i}$ Then $\BB$ is a synthetic basis on $X$, as shown on Basis for Box Topology. The box topology on $X$ is defined as the topology $\tau$ generated by the synthetic basis $\BB$.

title: Definition:Bozo Bit
snippet: The concept of bozo bit was adopted by the computer industry in the following manner. The typical stereotype of a worker in the computer software industry is that he (usually male) is limited in his ability to interact skilfully with his colleagues. In a team of people, there are bound to be clashes of personality. During the course of interactions with one of your colleagues, one of them sticks in your mind for making unhelpful suggestions, or crafting inept designs, or otherwise demonstrating a modicum of stupidity that is likely to become a hindrance to the task in progress.

title: Definition:Brachistochrone
snippet: Let a point $A$ be joined by a wire to a lower point $B$. Let the wire be allowed to be bent into whatever shape is required. Let a bead be released at $A$ to slide down without friction to $B$. The shape of the wire so that the bead takes least time to descend from $A$ to $B$ is called the brachistochrone.

title: Definition:Brachistochrone/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Brachistochrone == The brachistochrone was investigated by , using the techniques of calculus.

title: Definition:Brachistochrone/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Brachistochrone == The word brachistochrone comes from the Greek βράχιστος χρόνος (brakhistos khrónos), which means shortest time.

title: Definition:Braid
snippet: A braid is a number of cords plaited together.

title: Definition:Braid Group
snippet: The braid group on $n$ strands is generated by $\sigma_1, \sigma_2, \ldots, \sigma_{n-1}$ and the following relations: $\sigma_i \sigma_j = \sigma_j\sigma_i, \forall i, j: |i-j| \ge 2$ $\sigma_i \sigma_{i+1} \sigma_i = \sigma_{i+1} \sigma_i \sigma_{i+1}, \forall i \in \{ 1, 2, \ldots, n-2 \}$

title: Definition:Braid Theory
snippet: Braid theory studies the number of different ways a number of cords can be braided.

title: Definition:Braid Theory/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Braid Theory == related the study of braids to group theory in the $1930$s. In the $1960$s, pointed out the relevance of braid theory the theory of mappings. Thus, if $n$ points are moved continuously in the plane back to their original positions, the motion can be interpreted as a braid. Hence showed how the roots of a polynomial vary according to how the polynomial coefficients are varied. Also in the $1930$s, established the close relationship between braid theory and knot theory. This was then exploited in the $1980$s by .

snippet: Graph Theory: Branch of a rooted tree: A path from the root node of a rooted tree to one of its leaf nodes Set Theory: Branch of a set-theoretical tree: A maximal chain in a set-theoretical tree Mapping Theory: Branch of a multifunction Branch point of complex multifunction Complex Analysis: Holomorphic Branch Analytic Geometry: Branch of a curve Branch point of a curve Branch of a hyperbola

title: Definition:Branch Point of Complex Multifunction
snippet: Let $U \subseteq \C$ be an open set. Let $f: U \to \C$ be a complex multifunction.

title: Definition:Branch Point of Complex Multifunction/Definition 1
snippet: Let $U \subseteq \C$ be an open set. Let $f: U \to \C$ be a complex multifunction. A branch point of $f$ is a point $a$ in $U$ such that: $f$ has more than one value at one or more points in every neighborhood of $a$ $f$ has exactly one value at $a$ itself.

title: Definition:Branch Point of Complex Multifunction/Definition 2
snippet: Let $U \subseteq \C$ be an open set. Let $f: U \to \C$ be a complex multifunction. Let $a$ be a point of $f$ such that there does not exist a holomorphic branch of $f$ on some punctured $\epsilon$-disk $\set {z \in \C: 0 < \cmod {z - a} < \epsilon}$ around $a$. Then $a$ is a branch point of $f$.

title: Definition:Branch and Bound Method
snippet: The branch and bound method is an algorithmic procedure for solving the knapsack problem which works as follows: It constructs a branching method that terminates each branch once the constraint limit has been reached It allows items to be added in a predetermined order. This reduces the number of combinations that need to be tried. The algorithm works as follows. Let $\KK$ be a knapsack with maximum weight capacity of $C$ (arbitrary) units. Let $S = \set {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ be a finite set of $n$ items, with a weight $w: S \to \R$ and a value $v: S \to \R$.

title: Definition:Branch of Curve
snippet: A branch of a curve $\CC$ is a part of $\CC$ which is separated from another part of $\CC$ by a discontinuity or a singular point.

title: Definition:Branch of Curve/Branch Point
snippet: A branch point of a curve $\CC$ is a point on $\CC$ at which two or more branches of $\CC$ meet.

title: Definition:Branching Process
snippet: A branching process is a stochastic process where individuals give rise to offspring. The distribution of descendants is on a par with branches of a family tree.

title: Definition:Bravais Lattice
snippet: A Bravais lattice is a model of the way the structure of a crystal is replicated throughout space.

title: Definition:Break-Even Point
snippet: The break-even point is the sales volume at which total revenue equals total cost. When sales volume is smaller, the total cost tends to exceed total revenue, while when sales volume is smaller, the total revenue tends to exceed total cost.

title: Definition:Breaking Stress
snippet: Let a body $\BB$ be deformed under stress. Consider the following stress-strain diagram. 500px The breaking stress is the stress at which $\BB$ eventually fractures. This breaking stress is indicated on the stress-strain diagram as point $E$. Note that the breaking stress in this case is actually less than the stress needed to take $\BB$ to the end of the plastic region. At this point $\BB$ has already started to break down internally, and it is no longer able to sustain that level of stress placed upon it.

title: Definition:Bridge (Game)
snippet: Bridge is a game for $4$ players whose mechanism depends on the fact that each of the $4$ players are dealt a hand of $13$ cards from the standard deck of $52$ cards. For the purposes of at its current stage of evolution, details of the play of Bridge are not immediately relevant. As and when a deeper analysis of Bridge becomes appropriate, further details can be incorporated.

title: Definition:Bridge (Game)/Linguistic Note

title: Definition:Bridge (Graph Theory)
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a connected graph. Let $e \in E$ be an edge of $G$ such that the edge deletion $G - e$ is disconnected. Then $e$ is known as a bridge of $G$.

title: Definition:Brill-Noether Theory
snippet: Brill-Noether Theory is the branch of algebraic geometry which studies special divisors.

title: Definition:British Thermal Unit
snippet: The British thermal unit is an imperial unit of heat energy. It was originally defined as being: the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of $1$ pound (avoirdupois) of water by $1$ degree Fahrenheit.

snippet: == British Thermal Unit: Also known as == The British thermal unit is presented by some sources with all words capitalised: British Thermal Unit

title: Definition:British Thermal Unit per Hour-Foot-Fahrenheit
snippet: The British thermal unit per hour-foot-fahrenheit is an imperial unit of thermal conductivity.

The units are identical because the degree Rankine is the same as the degree Fahrenheit but for its reference points. Category:Definitions/British Thermal Unit per Hour-Foot-Fahrenheit

title: Definition:British Units of Length
snippet: The British units of length consists of a system of length based on the yard. As such, they form a subset of the imperial system.

title: Definition:Brocard Angle
snippet: 700px Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle such that $A \to B \to C \to A$ travels anticlockwise around $\triangle ABC$. Let $P$ and $Q$ be the first and second Brocard points of $\triangle ABC$ respectively. Let: From Brocard Angle is Unique: $\omega = \omega'$ This angle $\omega = \omega'$ is the Brocard angle of $\triangle ABC$.

title: Definition:Brocard Points
snippet: 700px Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle such that $A \to B \to C \to A$ travels anticlockwise around $\triangle ABC$.

title: Definition:Brocard Points/First
snippet: 700px Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle such that $A \to B \to C \to A$ travels anticlockwise around $\triangle ABC$. Let the point $P$ be constructed such that: $\angle PAB = \angle PBC = \angle PCA$ Then $P$ is the first Brocard point of $\triangle ABC$.

title: Definition:Brocard Points/Second
snippet: 700px Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle such that $A \to B \to C \to A$ travels anticlockwise around $\triangle ABC$. Let the point $Q$ be constructed such that: $\angle QAC = \angle QCB = \angle QBA$ Then $Q$ is the second Brocard point of $\triangle ABC$.

title: Definition:Broken Line
snippet: A broken line is a line which is formed from a number of discrete straight line segments joined together. Hence a curve may be approximated by a broken line, like how a circle can be approximated by a regular polygon.

title: Definition:Broken Line/Also known as
snippet: == Broken Line: Also known as == A broken line is also known as a polygonal line. Category:Definitions/Broken Lines

title: Definition:Brouwerian Lattice
snippet: Let $\struct {L, \wedge, \vee, \preceq}$ be a lattice. Then $\struct {L, \wedge, \vee, \preceq}$ is a Brouwerian lattice : for each $x, y \in L$: $x$ has a relative pseudocomplement with respect to $y$. This pseudocomplement is denoted $x \to y$.

title: Definition:Brouwerian Lattice/Also known as
snippet: == Brouwerian Lattice: Also known as == A Brouwerian lattice is also known as a relatively pseudocomplemented lattice .

title: Definition:Brown Numbers
snippet: Brown numbers are pairs of integers $\left({m, n}\right)$ such that: $n! + 1 = m^2$ There are only $3$ known such pairs: $\left({5, 4}\right)$ $\left({11, 5}\right)$ $\left({71, 7}\right)$

title: Definition:Brown Numbers/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Brown Numbers == The origin of the term Brown numbers is currently unclear. It is supposed that they may be named after a mathematician, but research will be needed to establish which one. It is understood that there is no association with the urban industrial street definition for the term [http://www.urbandictionary.com/define.php?term=Brown%20Numbers brown numbers]: numbers which are made up as you go along, in order to support a deliberately fallacious argument or false statement: literally brown, because you've just pulled them out of your arse.

title: Definition:Brownian Motion
snippet: Brownian motion is the physical phenomenon of random jittery motion of microscopic particles suspended in a fluid, such as pollen grains in water. This is caused by the random motion of the molecules of the fluid impacting on the particles. It may be modelled as a stochastic process.

title: Definition:Brownian Motion/Historical Note
snippet: == Brownian Motion: Historical Note == Brownian motion was first noticed by in $1827$. He observed under a microscope that pollen grains moved erratically and seemingly randomly in a sort of zigzag path. He confirmed that it was not a phenomenon of life, as he repeated the experiment with inorganic dust. The term Brownian motion is now also used for the stochastic model that is used to describe such random movements.

title: Definition:Brun's Constant
snippet: Brun's constant is the sum of the series consisting of the reciprocals of the twin primes: $B_2 := \paren {\dfrac 1 3 + \dfrac 1 5} + \paren {\dfrac 1 5 + \dfrac 1 7} + \paren {\dfrac 1 {11} + \dfrac 1 {13} } + \paren {\dfrac 1 {17} + \dfrac 1 {19} } + \paren {\dfrac 1 {29} + \dfrac 1 {31} } + \cdots$ Its approxmiate decimal expansion is: $B_2 \approx 1 \cdotp 90216 \, 05831 \, 04 \ldots$ Estimates of its value are occasionally refined as further work is done to establish its nature.

title: Definition:Bubble Sort/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Bubble Sort == The bubble sort is so called because the out-of-order elements supposedly rise to their correct position like bubbles rising through a medium.

title: Definition:Bulk Modulus
snippet: Let $B$ be an elastic body. The bulk modulus of $B$ is a physical property of $B$ which measures its resistance to change in volume without change of shape. It is defined as the ratio of compressive stress per surface area of $B$ to its change of volume per unit volume associated with this stress, assuming uniform pressure over the surface of $B$.

title: Definition:Buoyancy
snippet: Let $B$ be immersed (either fully or partly) in a fluid $F$. The buoyancy of $B$ is defined as the upward force on $B$ exerted by $F$.

title: Definition:Buoyancy/Center
snippet: Let $B$ be immersed (either fully or partly) in a fluid $F$. The center of buoyancy of $B$ is defined as the center of gravity of the displaced volume of $F$.

title: Definition:Burnout Height
snippet: Let $R$ be a rocket which is propelled by backwards expulsion of the exhaust products of the burning of its internal fuel supply. Let $R$ be fired straight up from the surface of a planet. The burnout height of $R$ is the height attained by $R$ at the instant when its fuel has become exhausted.

title: Definition:Burnout Velocity
snippet: Let $R$ be a rocket which is propelled by backwards expulsion of the exhaust products of the burning of its internal fuel supply. Let $R$ be fired straight up from the surface of a planet. The burnout velocity of $R$ is the velocity attained by $R$ at the instant when its fuel has become exhausted.

title: Definition:Butterfly Effect/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Butterfly Effect == The butterfly effect is so called as a result of the notion in popular culture that: a flapping its wings in can cause a in . Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:By Hypothesis
snippet: When demonstrating a proof, it is frequently necessary to refer to the specification of the result which is to be proved. This result often contains wording along the lines Suppose that ... or Let ... It is convenient to refer back to these specifications during the course of the proof. To do that, the term by hypothesis is often used.

title: Definition:Byte
snippet: The byte is a unit of digital information that most commonly consists of $8$ bits. It is usually encountered in its context as the code for a single typographical character.

title: Definition:Byte/Also defined as
snippet: == Byte: Also defined as == While it is standard now to refer to a byte as a string of exactly $8$ bits, this is not completely universal. In the early days of computer science in particular, the nature of a byte was dependent upon the machine on which it was implemented. Hence a byte could be $8$ bits, $2$ bits or $32$ bits, and so on. It is still occasionally possible to encounter this usage in contemporary accounts, but except for historical treatises, this is more rare than it used to be.

title: Definition:Bézout Domain/Definition 1
snippet: A Bézout domain is an integral domain in which the sum of two principal ideals is again principal.

title: Definition:Bézout Domain/Definition 2
snippet: A Bézout domain is an integral domain in which every finitely generated ideal is principal.

title: Definition:Bézout Domain/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Bézout Domain == The definition of an integral domain, and even that of a ring, was not formulated until over a century after the death of . However, a Bézout domain bears his name because in such an algebraic structure, each pair of elements satisfies an algebraic formulation of Bézout's Identity. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Bézout Numbers
snippet: Let $a, b \in \Z$ such that $a \ne 0$ or $b \ne 0$. Let $d$ be the greatest common divisor of $a$ and $b$. By Bézout's Identity: $\exists x, y \in \Z: a x + b y = d$ The numbers $x$ and $y$ are known as Bézout numbers of $a$ and $b$.
