title: Definition:Categorical Syllogism/Conclusion
snippet: The conclusion of a categorical syllogism is stated last, conventionally prefaced with the word Therefore. It is a categorical statement which expresses the logical relationship between the primary term and the secondary term of the syllogism. Furthermore, this categorical statement is specifically of the form in which the secondary term occurs first and the primary term occurs second.

title: Definition:Categorical Syllogism/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Categorical Syllogism == The predicate calculus was undiscovered $100$ years ago... For well over $2,000$ years before that, some of the same logical material was handled by the theory of the syllogism, which we owe to ; virtually nothing was added to it in that period. There can today be no doubt that predicate calculus has replaced the syllogism as an instrument for serious logical work; predicate calculus is to syllogism what a precision tool is to a blunt knife...

title: Definition:Categorical Syllogism/Middle Term
snippet: The middle term of a categorical syllogism is the term that does not appear in the conclusion of the syllogism. It appears once in each of the premises of the syllogism. It is usually denoted by $M$.

title: Definition:Categorical Syllogism/Premises
snippet: There are two premises in a categorical syllogism:

title: Definition:Categorical Syllogism/Premises/Major Premise
snippet: The major premise of a categorical syllogism is conventionally stated first. It is a categorical statement which expresses the logical relationship between the primary term and the middle term of the syllogism.

title: Definition:Categorical Syllogism/Premises/Minor Premise
snippet: The minor premise of a categorical syllogism is conventionally stated second. It is a categorical statement which expresses the logical relationship between the secondary term and the middle term of the syllogism.

title: Definition:Categorical Syllogism/Primary Term
snippet: The primary term of a categorical syllogism is the term that appears as the second predicate of the conclusion of the syllogism. It also appears once in one of the premises of the syllogism, traditionally the major premise. It is usually denoted by $P$.

title: Definition:Categorical Syllogism/Secondary Term
snippet: The secondary term of a categorical syllogism is the term that appears as the first predicate of the conclusion of the syllogism. It also appears once in one of the premises of the syllogism, traditionally the minor premise. It is usually denoted by $S$.

title: Definition:Categorical Syllogism/Shorthand
snippet: In order to specify the pattern of a categorical syllogism completely, it is necessary and sufficient to specify: $(1) \quad$ The figure ($\text I$ to $\text {IV}$) of the syllogism and $(2) \quad$ The mood of the syllogism. Hence, for example, the following categorical syllogism, which is of the first figure: $\begin {array} {r|rl} \text I & & \\ \hline \text {Major Premise}: & \mathbf E & \tuple {M, P} \\ \text {Minor Premise}: & \mathbf I & \tuple {S, M} \\ \hline \text{Conclusion}: & \mathbf O & \tuple {S, P} \\ \end {array}$ is specified completely by: $\text I: EIO$

title: Definition:Category
snippet: A category is an interpretation of the metacategory axioms within set theory. It consists of objects and morphisms. Because a metacategory is a metagraph, this means that a category is a graph. Let $\mathfrak U$ be a class of sets. A metacategory $\mathbf C$ is a category : $(1): \quad$ The objects form a subset $\mathbf C_0$ or $\operatorname {ob} \ \mathbf C \subseteq \mathfrak U$ $(2): \quad$ The morphisms form a subset $\mathbf C_1$ or $\operatorname{mor} \ \mathbf C$ or $\operatorname{Hom} \ \mathbf C \subseteq \mathfrak U$

title: Definition:Category (Descriptive Statistics)
snippet: Let $Q$ be a qualitative variable. Let $D$ be a finite set of $n$ observations of $Q$. Let $D$ be partitioned into a finite set of subsets of $D$. Each of the components of $D$ is known as a category.

title: Definition:Catenary

snippet: == Linguistic Note on Catenary == The word catenary comes from the Latin word catena meaning chain.

title: Definition:Catenoid
snippet: The catenoid is the surface of revolution obtained by revolving a catenary defined as $y = a \cosh \dfrac x a$ about the $x$-axis.

title: Definition:Cauchy's Criterion for Products
snippet: Let $\struct {\mathbb K, \norm {\,\cdot\,}}$ be a valued field. Let $\sequence {a_n}$ be a sequence of elements of $\mathbb K$. The infinite product $\ds \prod_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n$ satisfies Cauchy's criterion : $\ds \forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists N \in \N: \forall m, n \in \N: m\geq n \ge N: \norm {\prod_{k \mathop = n}^m a_n - 1} < \epsilon$

title: Definition:Cauchy-Crofton Formula
snippet: The Cauchy-Crofton formula calculates the length of a curve by counting the number of times the curve crosses lines in the plane.

title: Definition:Cauchy-Crofton Formula/Also known as
snippet: == Cauchy-Crofton Formula: Also known as == The Cauchy-Crofton formula is also known as Crofton's formula.

title: Definition:Cauchy-Crofton Formula/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Cauchy-Crofton Formula == The Cauchy-Crofton formula was discovered in the $19$th century.

title: Definition:Cauchy-Crofton Formula/Mistake
snippet: == Source Work == Cauchy-Crompton formula

title: Definition:Cauchy-Euler Equation
snippet: The linear second order ordinary differential equation: $x^2 \dfrac {\d^2 y} {\d x^2} + p x \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} + q y = 0$ is the Cauchy-Euler equation.

title: Definition:Cauchy-Euler Equation/General Form
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a strictly positive integer. The linear ordinary differential equation: $a_n x^n \, \map {y^{\paren n} } x + \dotsb + a_1 x \, \map {y'} x + a_0 \, \map y x = 0$ is the $n$th order Cauchy-Euler equation. Category:Definitions/Ordinary Differential Equations

title: Definition:Cauchy-Riemann Equations
snippet: Let $D \subseteq \C$ be an open subset of the set of complex numbers $\C$. Let $f: D \to \C$ be a complex function on $D$. Let $u, v: \set {\tuple {x, y} \in \R^2: x + i y = z \in D} \to \R$ be the two real-valued functions defined as: {{eqn | l = \map u {x, y} | r = \map \Re {\map f z} }} {{eqn | l = \map v {x, y} | r = \map \Im {\map f z} }} where: $\map \Re {\map f z}$ denotes the real part of $\map f z$ $\map \Im {\map f z}$ denotes the imaginary part of $\map f z$.

title: Definition:Cauchy-Riemann Equations/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Cauchy-Riemann Equations == The Cauchy-Riemann Equations were used by as the basis for his theory of the concept of the analytic function.

title: Definition:Cauchy Criterion
snippet: The Cauchy criterion is the necessary and sufficient condition for an infinite sequence in a complete metric space to converge that the absolute difference between successive terms with sufficiently large indices tends to zero. It can be applied in a number of contexts:

title: Definition:Cauchy Criterion/Also known as
snippet: == Cauchy Criterion: Also known as == Some sources refer to the Cauchy criterion as the Cauchy condition, but the same term is used for the Cauchy boundary condition. Hence in order to reduce possible confusion, prefers the use of Cauchy criterion Category:Definitions/Cauchy Criterion

title: Definition:Cauchy Determinant
snippet: A Cauchy determinant of order $n$ is the determinant of a square Cauchy matrix of order $n$: $\map \det {C_n} = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac 1 {x_1 + y_1} & \dfrac 1 {x_1 + y_2} & \cdots & \dfrac 1 {x_1 + y_n} \\ \dfrac 1 {x_2 + y_1} & \dfrac 1 {x_2 + y_2} & \cdots & \dfrac 1 {x_2 + y_n} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \dfrac 1 {x_n + y_1} & \dfrac 1 {x_n + y_2} & \cdots & \dfrac 1 {x_n + y_n} \\ \end{vmatrix}$ or: $\map \det {C_n} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac 1 {x_1 - y_1} & \dfrac 1 {x_1 - y_2} & \cdots & \dfrac 1 {x_1 - y_n} \\ \dfrac 1 {x_2 - y_1} & \dfrac 1 {x_2 - y_2} & \cdots & \dfrac 1…

title: Definition:Cauchy Distribution
snippet: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable on a probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $\Img X = \R$. $X$ is said to have a Cauchy distribution it has probability density function: $\map {f_X} x = \dfrac 1 {\pi \lambda \paren {1 + \paren {\frac {x - \gamma} \lambda}^2} }$ for: $\lambda \in \R_{>0}$ $\gamma \in \R$ This is written: $X \sim \Cauchy \gamma \lambda$

title: Definition:Cauchy Distribution/Also defined as
snippet: == Cauchy Distribution: Also defined as == Let $X$ be a continuous random variable on a probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $\Img X = \R$. Some sources define the Cauchy distribution of $X$ as the standard Cauchy distribution: $\map {f_X} x = \dfrac 1 {\pi \paren {1 + x^2} }$ which is obtained from the full form by setting: $\lambda = 1$ $\gamma = 0$ Some sources give it as: $\map {f_X} x = \dfrac 1 {\pi \paren {1 + \paren {x - \gamma}^2} }$ which is obtained from the full form by setting $\lambda = 1$.

title: Definition:Cauchy Distribution/Also presented as
snippet: == Cauchy Distribution: Also presented as == Let $X$ be a continuous random variable on a probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $\Img X = \R$. The Cauchy distribution of $X$ can be found expressed in the form: $\map {f_X} x = \dfrac \lambda {\pi \paren {\lambda^2 + \paren {x - \gamma}^2} }$ for: $\lambda \in \R_{>0}$ $\gamma \in \R$ This is written: $X \sim \Cauchy \gamma \lambda$

title: Definition:Cauchy Distribution/Notation
snippet: == Cauchy Distribution: Notation == The notation used to denote a Cauchy distribution is generally consistent, except for the parameter labels. Some sources use $\theta$ for $\gamma$. [https://mathworld.wolfram.com/CauchyDistribution.html MathWorld] uses $m$ and $b$ for $\lambda$ and $\gamma$. All notation is perfectly good, as long as it is clear what the parameters are.

title: Definition:Cauchy Distribution/Scale Parameter
snippet: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with a Cauchy distribution: $\map {f_X} x = \dfrac 1 {\pi \lambda \paren {1 + \paren {\frac {x - \gamma} \lambda}^2} }$ for: $\lambda \in \R_{>0}$ $\gamma \in \R$ The parameter $\lambda$ is referred to as the scale parameter of $X$.

title: Definition:Cauchy Distribution/Standard
snippet: The standard Cauchy distribution is the Cauchy distribution with $\lambda = 1$ and $\gamma = 0$: $\map {f_X} x = \dfrac 1 {\pi \paren {1 + x^2} }$

title: Definition:Cauchy Distribution/Technical Note
snippet: == Technical Note for Cauchy Distribution == {{LatexFor|for = \Cauchy {\gamma} {\lambda} }} When either of the arguments is a single character, it is usual to omit the braces: \Cauchy \gamma \lambda This command is specific to . Category:Technical Notes Category:Definitions/Cauchy Distribution

title: Definition:Cauchy Equivalent Metrics
snippet: Let $X$ be a set upon which there are two metrics $d_1$ and $d_2$. That is, $\struct {X, d_1}$ and $\struct {X, d_2}$ are two different metric spaces on the same underlying set $X$. Then $d_1$ and $d_2$ are said to be Cauchy equivalent for every sequence $\sequence {x_n}$ of points in $X$: $\sequence {x_n}$ is a Cauchy sequence in $\struct {X, d_1} \iff \sequence {x_n}$ is a is a Cauchy sequence in $\struct {X, d_2}$

title: Definition:Cauchy Functional Equation
snippet: Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a real function. Then the Cauchy functional equation is: $\forall x, y \in \R: \map f {x + y} = \map f x + \map f y$

title: Definition:Cauchy Integral
snippet: Let $f$ be a continuous real function. Let $\closedint a b$ be a closed real interval such that $a < b$. Let $P = \set {a, x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{n - 1}, b}$ be a normal subdivision of $\closedint a b$ such that $x_k - x_{k - 1} = \delta x$. The Cauchy integral of $f$ from $a$ to $b$ is defined as: $\ds A = \lim_{\delta x \mathop \to 0} \sum \map f x \rdelta x$

title: Definition:Cauchy Integral/Historical Note
snippet: == Cauchy Integral: Historical Note == The method of forming a definite integral known as a Cauchy integral was first put forward by .

title: Definition:Cauchy Matrix
snippet: The Cauchy matrix, commonly denoted $C_n$, can be found defined in two forms. The Cauchy matrix is an $m \times n$ matrix whose elements are in the form: either $a_{ij} = \dfrac 1 {x_i + y_j}$ or $a_{ij} = \dfrac 1 {x_i - y_j}$. where $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_m$ and $y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n$ are elements of a field $F$. They are of course equivalent, by taking $y'_j = -y_j$. Note that $x_i + y_j$ (or $x_i - y_j$, depending on how the matrix is defined) must not be zero, or the element will be undefined.

title: Definition:Cauchy Principal Value
snippet: The Cauchy principal value is an extension of the concept of an improper integral when the latter might not exist. {{expand|Needs to be include the situation where there is an undefined point at some $b \in \R$ where $\map f b$ is undefined, for example $\ds \int_{-\infty}^x \dfrac {e^u} u \rd u$ at $u 0$}}

title: Definition:Cauchy Principal Value/Also denoted as
snippet: == Cauchy Principal Value: Also denoted as == Variants of the notation $\PV$ for the Cauchy principal value can often be seen, most of which use the letters $\text{PV}$, such as: $\operatorname {PV} \ds \int$ $\operatorname {P.V.} \ds \int$ $\operatorname {p.v.} \ds \int$ $PV \ds \int$ and so on. Category:Definitions/Cauchy Principal Value

title: Definition:Cauchy Principal Value/Complex Integral
snippet: Let $f: \R \to \C$ be a bounded complex function. Then the Cauchy principal value of $\ds \int f$ is defined as: $\PV_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \map f t \rd t := \lim_{R \mathop \to +\infty} \int_{-R}^R \map f t \rd t$ where $\ds \int_{-R}^R \map f t \rd t$ is a complex Riemann integral.

title: Definition:Cauchy Principal Value/Contour Integral
snippet: Let $C$ be a contour defined by a directed smooth curve. Let $C$ be parameterized by the smooth path $\phi: \closedint {-R} R \to \C$, where $R > 0$. Let $f: \Img C \to \C$ be a continuous complex function, where $\Img C$ denotes the image of $C$. Then the Cauchy principal value of $\ds \int f$ is defined as: $\PV_C \map f z \rd z = \PV_{\map \phi {-\infty} }^{\map \phi {+\infty} } \map f z \rd z := \lim_{R \mathop \to +\infty} \int_{-R}^R \map f {\map \phi t} \map {\phi'} t \rd t$ where $\ds \int_{-R}^R \map f {\map \phi t} \map {\phi'} t \rd t$ is a complex Riemann integral defining a…

title: Definition:Cauchy Principal Value/Real Integral
snippet: Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a real function which is piecewise continuous everywhere. Then the Cauchy principal value of $\ds \int f$ is defined as: $\PV_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \map f t \rd t := \lim_{R \mathop \to +\infty} \int_{-R}^R \map f t \rd t$ where $\ds \int_{-R}^R \map f t \rd t$ is a Riemann integral.

title: Definition:Cauchy Principal Value/Technical Note
snippet: == Technical Note for Cauchy Principal Value == This command is specific to . Category:Technical Notes Category:Definitions/Cauchy Principal Value

title: Definition:Cauchy Product
snippet: Let $A := \ds \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty a_n$ and $B := \ds \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty b_n$ be two series. The Cauchy product $C$ of $A$ and $B$ is defined as: $\ds C := \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty c_n = \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty a_n \cdot \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty b_n$ where: $\ds \forall n \in \N: c_n = \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^n a_k b_{n - k} = \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^n a_{n - k} b_k$

title: Definition:Cauchy Sequence/Also known as
snippet: == Cauchy Sequence: Also known as == A Cauchy sequence is also known as: a fundamental sequence a regular sequence.

title: Definition:Cauchy Sequence/Cauchy Criterion
snippet: The Cauchy criterion is the condition: For any (strictly) positive real number $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$, for a sufficiently large natural number $N \in \N$, the difference between the $m$th and $n$th terms of a Cauchy sequence, where $m, n \ge N$, will be less than $\epsilon$. Informally: For any number you care to pick (however small), if you go out far enough into the sequence, past a certain point, the difference between any two terms in the sequence is less than the number you picked. Or to put it another way, the terms get arbitrarily close together the farther out you go.

title: Definition:Cauchy Sequence/Complex Numbers
snippet: Let $\sequence {z_n}$ be a sequence in $\C$. Then $\sequence {z_n}$ is a Cauchy sequence : $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists N \in \N: \forall m, n \in \N: m, n \ge N: \size {z_n - z_m} < \epsilon$ where $\size {z_n - z_m}$ denotes the complex modulus of $z_n - z_m$. Considering the complex plane as a metric space, it is clear that this is a special case of the definition for a metric space.

title: Definition:Cauchy Sequence/Metric Space
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $A$. Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is a Cauchy sequence : $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists N \in \N: \forall m, n \in \N: m, n \ge N: \map d {x_n, x_m} < \epsilon$

title: Definition:Cauchy Sequence/Normed Division Ring
snippet:
Let $\struct {R, 
orm {\,\cdot\,} } $ be a normed division ring Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $R$. Then $\sequence {x_n} $ is a Cauchy sequence in the norm $
orm {\, \cdot \,}$ : $\sequence {x_n}$ is a cauchy sequence in the metric induced by the norm $
orm {\, \cdot \,}$ That is: $ orall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists N \in \N:  orall m, n \in \N: m, n \ge N: 
orm {x_n - x_m} < \epsilon$

title: Definition:Cauchy Sequence/Normed Vector Space
snippet: Let $\struct {V, \norm {\,\cdot\,} }$ be a normed vector space. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $V$. Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is a Cauchy sequence : $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists N \in \N: \forall m, n \in \N: m, n \ge N: \norm {x_n - x_m} < \epsilon$

title: Definition:Cauchy Sequence/Rational Numbers
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a rational sequence. Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is a Cauchy sequence : $\forall \epsilon \in \Q_{>0}: \exists N \in \N: \forall m, n \in \N: m, n \ge N: \size {x_n - x_m} 0}$ denotes the set of all strictly positive rational numbers. Considering the set of rational numbers as a metric space, it is clear that this is a special case of the definition for a metric space. Category:Definitions/Cauchy Sequences Category:Definitions/Analysis

title: Definition:Cauchy Sequence/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $\R$. Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is a Cauchy sequence : $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists N \in \N: \forall m, n \in \N: m, n \ge N: \size {x_n - x_m} < \epsilon$

title: Definition:Cauchy Sequence/Topological Vector Space
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological vector space. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $X$. We say that $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is Cauchy : for each open neighborhood $V$ of ${\mathbf 0}_X$ there exists $N \in \N$ such that: $x_n - x_m \in V$ for each $n, m \ge N$.

title: Definition:Cauchy Sequence in Topological Group
snippet: Let $G$ be a topological group with identity element $e$. Let $\sequence {a_n}$ be a sequence in $G$. Then $\sequence {a_n}$ is a Cauchy sequence for every neighborhood $U$ of $e$ there exists $N \in \N$ such that for all $m, n \ge N : a_n a_m^{-1} \in U$.

title: Definition:Cauchy in Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $\sequence {f_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence of real-valued $\Sigma$-measurable functions. We say that $\sequence {f_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is Cauchy in measure : for each $\epsilon > 0$, there exists $N \in \N$ such that for all $n, m \ge N$ we have: $\map \mu {\set {x \in X : \size {\map {f_n} x - \map {f_m} x} > \epsilon} } < \epsilon$

title: Definition:Causation
snippet: Causation is the phenomenon of producing an effect.

title: Definition:Causation/Warning
snippet: It is often assumed that the existence of correlation between two random variables indicates causation. However, this is often not the case. Both variables may be related to a third confounding variable.

title: Definition:Cause Variable/Also known as
snippet: == Cause Variable: Also known as == The cause variable of a regression is also known as: the explanatory variable the fixed variable the predicated variable the predictor variable the regressor. It is also known as the independent variable. However, this name is used in a wider context than regressions, and so is not endorsed on .

title: Definition:Caustic
snippet: A caustic is a curve formed by reflected or refracted light. It is formed as the envelope of the reflected or refracted rays.

title: Definition:Cayley-Dickson Construction
snippet: Let $A = \struct {A_F, \oplus}$ be a $*$-algebra. The Cayley-Dickson Construction on $A$ is the procedure which generates a new algebra $A'$ from $A$ as follows. Let: $A' = \struct {A'_F, \oplus'} = \struct {A, \oplus}^2$ where $\struct {A, \oplus}^2$ denotes the Cartesian product of $\struct {A, \oplus}$ with itself.

title: Definition:Cayley-Menger Determinant
snippet: The Cayley-Menger determinant is a determinant that gives the volume of a simplex in $j$ dimensions.

title: Definition:Cayley-Menger Determinant/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Cayley-Menger Determinant == The Cayley-Menger determinant was given this name by in $1953$. His justification was that it had been proposed initially in $1841$ by , and subsequently by in $1923$.

title: Definition:Cayley Algebra
snippet: The Cayley algebra is the non-associative division algebra formed by the octonions under octonion multiplication.

title: Definition:Cayley Algebra/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Cayley Algebra == The octonions were first discovered by in $1843$. However, in $1845$ was the first to discuss the Cayley algebra in print.

title: Definition:Cayley Table
snippet: A Cayley table is a technique for describing an algebraic structure (usually a finite group) by putting all the products in a square array: $\qquad \begin {array} {c|cccc} \circ & a & b & c & d \\ \hline a & a & a & b & a \\ b & b & c & a & d \\ c & d & e & f & a \\ d & c & d & a & b \\ \end {array}$ The column down the denotes the first (leading) operand of the operation. The row across the top denotes the second (following) operand of the operation.

title: Definition:Cayley Table/Also known as
snippet: == Cayley Table: Also known as == Some sources refer to a Cayley table as an operation table, but there exists the view that this sounds too much like a piece of hospital apparatus. Another popular name for this is a multiplication table, but this holdover from grade school terminology may be considered irrelevant to a table where the operation has nothing to do with multiplication as such. In the field of logic, a truth table in this format is often referred to as matrix form, but note that this terminology clashes with the definition of a matrix in mathematics.

title: Definition:Cayley Table/Entry
snippet: The occurrences in a Cayley table of the elements of the algebraic structure it defines are called the entries of the Cayley table. Category:Definitions/Cayley Tables

title: Definition:Cayley Table/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Cayley Table == The concept of the Cayley table was proposed in $1854$ by .

title: Definition:Ceiling Function
snippet: Let $x$ be a real number. Informally, the ceiling function of $x$ is the smallest integer greater than or equal to $x$.

title: Definition:Ceiling Function/Also denoted as
snippet: == Ceiling Function: Also denoted as == Some sources use $\set x$ to denote the ceiling function, but this has too many other interpretations for it to be acceptable on . Category:Definitions/Ceiling Function

title: Definition:Ceiling Function/Also known as
snippet: == Ceiling Function: Also known as == The ceiling function is also known as the least integer function or lowest integer function.

title: Definition:Ceiling Function/Definition 1
snippet: Let $x$ be a real number. The ceiling function of $x$ is defined as the infimum of the set of integers no smaller than $x$: $\ceiling x := \inf \set {m \in \Z: x \le m}$ where $\le$ is the usual ordering on the real numbers.

title: Definition:Ceiling Function/Definition 2
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number. The ceiling function of $x$, denoted $\ceiling x$, is defined as the smallest element of the set of integers: $\set {m \in \Z: x \le m}$ where $\le$ is the usual ordering on the real numbers.

title: Definition:Ceiling Function/Definition 3
snippet: Let $x$ be a real number. The ceiling function of $x$ is the unique integer $\ceiling x$ such that: $\ceiling x - 1 < x \le \ceiling x$

title: Definition:Ceiling Function/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Ceiling Function == The notation $\ceiling x$ for the ceiling function was introduced in the $1960$s by and made popular by .

title: Definition:Ceiling Function/Notation
snippet: The notation $\ceiling x$ for the ceiling function is a relatively recent development. Compare the notation $\floor x$ for the corresponding floor function.

title: Definition:Ceiling Function/Technical Note
snippet: == Technical Note for Ceiling Function == {{LatexFor|for = \ceiling {x} }} When the argument is a single character, it is usual to omit the braces: \ceiling x This command is specific to . Category:Definitions/Ceiling Function Category:Technical Notes

title: Definition:Celestial
snippet: In the context of astronomy, the word celestial is an adjective whose meaning is loosely of the sky. It is used to define bodies and phenomena vaguely defined as being outside Earth's atmosphere, hence does not apply to meteorological phenomena. It is often used as an antithesis for the word terrestrial, which means of Earth.

title: Definition:Celestial/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Celestial == The adjective celestial, in the context of astronomy, is derived from the Latin caelestis, from caelum (meaning sky or heaven). The term has religious connotations, dating from the time where the prevailing belief was that supernatural beings lived somewhere out there in the sky, taking an interest in what happens on Earth. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Celestial Altitude
snippet: Let $X$ be a point on the celestial sphere. The (celestial) altitude of $X$ is defined as the angle subtended by the the arc of the vertical circle through $X$ between the celestial horizon and $X$ itself.

title: Definition:Celestial Altitude/Symbol
snippet: == Celestial Altitude: Symbol == The symbol for celestial altitude is $a$.

title: Definition:Celestial Altitude/Symbol/Variant
snippet: == Celestial Altitude: Symbol == A variant symbol for celestial altitude is $h$.

title: Definition:Celestial Axis
snippet: Consider the celestial sphere with observer $O$. The celestial axis is the line which joins the north celestial pole and the south celestial pole. 480px In the above diagram, the celestial axis is the line $PQ$.

title: Definition:Celestial Body
snippet: A celestial body is a more-or-less internally coherent body of matter that exists outside the Earth's atmosphere.

title: Definition:Celestial Equator
snippet: Consider the celestial sphere with observer $O$. Let $P$ be the north celestial pole. The great circle whose plane is perpendicular to $OP$ is known as the celestial equator. 480px

title: Definition:Celestial Horizon
snippet: The celestial horizon is the great circle on the celestial sphere whose plane is perpendicular to the line from the zenith to the observer. Thus the celestial horizon is the edge of the visible part of the celestial sphere. The rest of it is hidden by Earth itself. 480px

title: Definition:Celestial Horizon/Also known as
snippet: == Celestial Horizon: Also known as == The celestial horizon is also known just as the horizon, and as such is used in common parlance to mean as far as can be seen, figuratively as well as literally. However, the word horizon has multiple uses, so on the full name is preferred.

title: Definition:Celestial Horizon/Pole
snippet: The poles of the celestial horizon are known as the zenith and the nadir.

title: Definition:Celestial Latitude/Also known as
snippet: == Celestial Latitude: Also known as == The term celestial latitude is also seen as ecliptic latitude.

title: Definition:Celestial Longitude/Also known as
snippet: == Celestial Longitude: Also known as == The term celestial longitude is also seen as ecliptic longitude.

title: Definition:Celestial Mechanics
snippet: Celestial mechanics is the branch of astronomy which studies the motion of celestial bodies such as planets, stars and comets.

title: Definition:Celestial Pole
snippet: Consider the celestial sphere $C$. The celestial poles of $C$ are the north celestial pole and the south celestial pole:

title: Definition:Celestial Sphere
snippet: The celestial sphere is an imaginary sphere, an indeterminate distance from Earth, which intersects the straight lines from the celestial bodies to the observer. 480px It is then convenient to identify the directions of the celestial bodies with their position on the celestial sphere.

title: Definition:Celestial Sphere/Observer
snippet: In the context of astronomy, in particular spherical astronomy, the (celestial) observer is considered to be a reference point located at the center of the celestial sphere. In practice, of course, an actual observer is physically located on the surface of Earth. However, the celestial sphere is so much larger than the radius of Earth that the observer is considered to be at the center of Earth. 480px In the above diagram, the position of the observer is indicated by $O$.

title: Definition:Cell (Statistics)
snippet: When data are grouped together into categories, the subcategories are referred to as cells.

title: Definition:Cell (Statistics)/Frequency
snippet: Cell frequency is the frequency with which observations fall into cells.

title: Definition:Cell (Topology)
snippet: An $n$-cell, in the context of topology, is a topological space which is homeomorphic to a closed Euclidean ball of $n$ dimensions.

title: Definition:Cellular Automaton Theory
snippet: Cellular automaton theory is that branch of mathematics concerned with cellular automata.

title: Definition:Celsius
snippet: Celsius is a temperature scale. Its two reference points are: $0 \cels$, which is set at the melting point of water. $100 \cels$, which is set at the boiling point of water, as defined at sea level and standard atmospheric pressure. A temperature measured in Celsius is often referred to as so many degrees Celsius.

title: Definition:Celsius/Also known as
snippet: == Celsius: Also known as == The Celsius scale is also known as the centigrade scale, but this usage has been obsolete since $1948$.

title: Definition:Celsius/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Celsius: Conversion Factors ==

title: Definition:Celsius/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Celsius == The Celsius scale is based on that proposed in $1742$ by the astronomer . He defined the upper and lower reference points from the melting and boiling points of water. These were initially the other way round from their current definitions: $0 \cels$ was for the boiling point and $100 \cels$ was for the melting point. originally called it the centigrade scale, but for various reasons the name was a source of confusion, and so in $1948$ the name Celsius was adopted. This is the system of measurement of temperature that is generally taught in schools.

title: Definition:Celsius/Symbol
snippet: The symbol for the degree Celsius is $\cels$.

title: Definition:Celsius/Symbol/Mistake
snippet: == Source Work == Celsius (centigrade)

title: Definition:Censored Observation
snippet: Censored observations are observations which cannot be made because they are unavailable, usually because of timing constraints.

title: Definition:Censored Observation/Left
snippet: Consider a statistical study of a disease. There exists a difficulty if the time of onset is unknown. This is because it may not be known if the disease is detected only when the patient is examined medically at the point where symptoms of the disease are apparent. In these circumstances, such data are said to be left censored.

title: Definition:Censored Observation/Right
snippet: Consider a statistical study which involves times to failure. Such data may be incomplete, in the sense that some experimental units: may not have failed by the end of the study or: may have been withdrawn or lost before failure. Such data are said to be right censored.

title: Definition:Census
snippet: A census is a survey of a complete population, as distinct from a sample survey.

title: Definition:Center
snippet: Analysis: Center of a power series Abstract Algebra: Center of a semigroup Center of a group Center of a ring Geometry: Center of a circle Center of a sphere Center of a conic section Center of curvature of a curve at a point Graph Theory: Center of a tree Topology and metric spaces: Center of an open ball Vector spaces: Star center of a star convex set

title: Definition:Center/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Center == The British English spelling of center is centre. The convention on is to use the American English spelling center, but it is appreciated that there may be lapses.

title: Definition:Center (Abstract Algebra)/Group
snippet: The center of a group $G$, denoted $\map Z G$, is the subset of elements in $G$ that commute with every element in $G$. Symbolically: $\map Z G = \map {C_G} G = \set {g \in G: g x = x g, \forall x \in G}$ That is, the center of $G$ is the centralizer of $G$ in $G$ itself.

title: Definition:Center (Abstract Algebra)/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Center in the context of Abstract Algebra == The notation $\map Z S$, conventionally used for the center of a structure $\struct {S, \circ}$, derives from the German Zentrum, meaning center. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Center (Abstract Algebra)/Ring
snippet: The center of a ring $\struct {R, +, \circ}$, denoted $\map Z R$, is the subset of elements in $R$ that commute under $\circ$ with every element in $R$. Symbolically: $\map Z R = \map {C_R} R = \set {x \in R: \forall s \in R: s \circ x = x \circ s}$ That is, the center of $R$ is the centralizer of $R$ in $R$ itself. It is clear that the center of a ring $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ can be defined as the center of the semigroup $\struct {R, \circ}$.

title: Definition:Center (Abstract Algebra)/Semigroup
snippet: The center of a semigroup $\struct {S, \circ}$, denoted $\map Z S$, is the subset of elements in $S$ that commute with every element in $G$. Symbolically: $\map Z S = \set {s \in S: \forall x \in S: s \circ x = x \circ s}$

title: Definition:Center of Complex Disk
snippet: Let $\map B {a, R}$ be the open (complex) disk $\set {z \in \C: \cmod {z - a} < R}$. Let $\map {\overline B} {a, R}$ be the closed (complex) disk $\set {z \in \C: \cmod {z - a} \le R}$. In either case, the parameter $a$ is referred to as the center of $\map B {a, R}$ or $\map {\overline B} {a, R}$.

title: Definition:Center of Curvature
snippet: Let $C$ be a curve embedded in the plane. Let $N$ be the normal to $C$ at a point $P$. Let $\rho$ be the radius of curvature of $C$ at $P$. Let $Q$ be the point on $N$ which is at a distance $\rho$ from $P$ on the concave side of $C$. $Q$ is known as the center of curvature of $C$ at $P$.

title: Definition:Center of Ellipsoid
snippet: The center of an ellipsoid $\EE$ is defined as the midpoint of the major axis of $\EE$.

title: Definition:Center of Gravity
snippet: Let $B$ be a body. The center of gravity of $B$ is that point through which the resultant of the system of parallel forces formed by the weights of all the particles constituting $B$ passes for all positions of $B$.

title: Definition:Center of Gravity/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note for Center of Gravity == The concept of the center of gravity of a body originated with . He subsequently found the centers of gravity of a number of geometric figures, both plane and solid.

title: Definition:Center of Mass
snippet: Let $B$ be a body of mass $M$.

title: Definition:Center of Mass/Also known as
snippet: == Center of Mass: Also known as == The center of mass of a body is also known as its mass center. Also note that in UK English, center is spelt centre. Some sources use the term barycenter, but that term has wider applications than applied mathematics, and is used for a more general concept in affine geometry.

title: Definition:Center of Mass/Continuous
snippet: Let $B$ be a body of mass $M$. Let $B$ be of density $\map \rho {\mathbf r}$ at the point with position vector $\mathbf r$. The center of mass of $B$ is the point whose position vector $\bar {\mathbf r}$ is given by: $\ds M \bar {\mathbf r} = \int_V \map \rho {\mathbf r} \mathbf r \rd V$ where: $V$ is the volume of space occupied by $B$ $\d V$ is an infinitesimal volume element $\mathbf r$ is the position vector of $\d V$.

title: Definition:Center of Mass/Discrete
snippet: Let $B$ be a body of mass $M$. Let $B$ be made up of $n$ discrete particles each with: mass $m_i$ position vector $\mathbf r_i$ where $i \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n}$ The center of mass of $B$ is the point whose position vector $\bar {\mathbf r}$ is given by: $\ds M \bar {\mathbf r} = \sum_{i = \mathop 1}^n m_i \mathbf r_i$

title: Definition:Center of Perspective/Also known as
snippet: == Center of Perspective/Also known as == The center of perspective of two figures is also known as the center of perspectivity. Note that the UK English spelling of center is centre.

title: Definition:Center of Pressure
snippet: Let $P$ be a plane surface immersed in liquid. The center of pressure is the point on $P$ at which the resultant pressure on $P$ is considered to act.

title: Definition:Center of Symmetry
snippet: Let $\FF$ be a geometric figure. A center of symmetry $C$ of $\FF$ is a point such that: every point $P$ of $\FF$ has a corresponding point $P'$ which is also in $\FF$ such that $C$ is the midpoint of the straight line segment $PP'$.

title: Definition:Center of Symmetry/Also known as
snippet: == Center of Symmetry: Also known as == Center of symmetry is rendered in non-US English as centre of symmetry.

title: Definition:Center of Tree
snippet: Take a tree, and remove all the nodes whose degree is $1$, along with all their incident edges. Repeat the process until either: One node is left or: Two nodes are left, joined by a single edge. If one node is left, it is called the center of the tree. If two nodes are left, joined by a single edge, this is called the bicenter of the tree.

title: Definition:Centered Hexagonal Number
snippet: A centered hexagonal number is a figurate number which is represented by: a point in the center all other points surrounding the center at the points of a triangular lattice.

title: Definition:Centered Hexagonal Number/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Centered Hexagonal Number == The first few centered hexagonal numbers are as follows: 800px

title: Definition:Centered Hexagonal Number/Linguistic Note
snippet: A centered hexagonal number is rendered in British English as centred hexagonal number, on account of the British spelling of centre. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Centered Hexagonal Number/Sequence
snippet: The sequence of centered hexagonal numbers, for $n \in \Z_{> 0}$, begins: $1, 7, 19, 37, 61, 91, 127, 169, 217, 271, 331, 397, 469, 547, 631, 721, 817, 919, \ldots$ Category:Definitions/Centered Hexagonal Numbers

title: Definition:Centesimal
snippet: Centesimal is a word used to denote $100$-ness. It is usually used to mean the division of a unit of measurement into $100$ parts.

title: Definition:Centi-/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Centi- == The prefix centi- derives from the Latin centum, which means hundred.

title: Definition:Centillion/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Centillion == The word centillion is created from the Latin-derived prefix centi-, meaning hundredfold, together with -illion, a back-formation from the word million.

title: Definition:Centillion/Long Scale
snippet: Centillion is a name for $10^{600}$ in the long scale system: One centillion $= 10^{6 \times 100}$

title: Definition:Centillion/Short Scale
snippet: Centillion is a name for $10^{303}$ in the short scale system: One centillion $= 10^{3 \times 100 + 3}$

title: Definition:Centimetre/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Centimetre: Conversion Factors == {{eqn | r = 10^{-2} | rr= = 0 \cdotp 01 | c = metre }}

title: Definition:Centimetre/Cubic Centimetre
snippet: == Cubic Centimetre== The cubic centimetre is the CGS unit of volume. It is defined as the volume contained by a cube whose edges are $1$ centimetre long.

title: Definition:Centimetre/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Centimetre == The centimetre was initially defined as: $10^{-9}$ the distance from the Earth's equator to the North Pole at sea level that is: $\frac 1 {100}$ the length of a metre. Its importance as one of the base units of the CGS system has waned, as the MKS system has supplanted it in importance. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Centimetre/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Centimetre == The spelling centimetre is the one adopted by the International Bureau of Weights and Measures. Centimeter is the variant used in standard American English. See the linguistic note on metre. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Centimetre/Square Centimetre
snippet: The square centimetre is the CGS unit of area. It is the area of a square whose sides are $1$ centimetre in length.

title: Definition:Centimetre of Mercury
snippet: The centimetre of mercury is an metric unit of pressure. It is defined as being: The amount of pressure generated by a column of mercury of density $13 \, 595 \cdotp 1 \, \mathrm {kg \, m}^{-3}$ one centimetre high under standard gravity.

title: Definition:Centimetre of Mercury/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Centimetre of Mercury: Conversion Factors == Category:Definitions/Centimetre of Mercury

title: Definition:Centimetre per Second/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Centimetre per Second: Conversion Factors == {{eqn | o = | r = 1 | rr= \mathrm {cm \, s^{-1} } | c = centimetre per second | cc= CGS unit }} {{eqn | r = 10^{-2} | rr= \mathrm {m \, s^{-1} } | c = metre per second | cc= SI unit }} {{eqn | o = \approx | r = 3 \cdotp 2808 \times 10^{-2} | rr= \mathrm {ft \, s^{-1} } | c = foot per second | cc= FPS unit }} Category:Definitions/Centimetre per Second

title: Definition:Central Binomial Coefficient
snippet: Let $n \in \N$ be a natural number. The binomial coefficient: $\dbinom {2 n} n$ is known as a central binomial coefficient.

title: Definition:Central Conic
snippet: A central conic is a non-degenerate conic section which has a center of symmetry. Hence a central conic is a conic section which is a circle, an ellipse or a hyperbola.

title: Definition:Central Conic/Also defined as
snippet: == Central Conic: Also defined as == Many sources define a central conic as a conic section which is either an ellipse or a hyperbola. However, this coincides with the definition as given here, given Circle is Ellipse with Equal Major and Minor Axes.

title: Definition:Central Difference Approximation
snippet: Let $f$ be a differentiable real function. The central difference approximation is an approximation to the derivative of $f$ at some $x \in \R: x = x_0$. It is defined as: $\map {f'} {x_0} \approx \dfrac {\map f {x_0 + h} - \map f {x_0 - h} } {2 h}$ where $h$ is arbitrarily small. Hence the central difference approximation is the slope of the chord of the graph of $f$ passing through the two points $\map f {x_0 \pm h}$.

title: Definition:Central Difference Operator/Mistake
snippet: == Source Work == central difference

title: Definition:Central Dilatation Mapping/Also known as
snippet: == Central Dilatation Mapping: Also known as == A central dilatation mapping may also be called the multiplication operator. It can also be referred to as a dilation mapping, but that can be interpreted ambiguously, as it can also refer to a general dilatation mapping, which includes the possibility of such being a translation. Some sources use the term enlargement or magnification, but that can be misleading as the word is also used when the effect is to shrink the domain. The terms homothety and similitude can also be seen on occasion.

title: Definition:Central Dilatation Mapping/Center of Enlargement
snippet: Let $f$ be a central dilatation mapping with fixed point $C$. $C$ is known as the center of enlargement of $f$.

title: Definition:Central Dilatation Mapping/Definition 1
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $X$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $\lambda \in K$. The central dilatation mapping $c_\lambda : X \to X$ is defined as: $\forall x \in X: \map {c_\lambda} x = \lambda x$ where $\lambda x$ denotes the scalar product of $\lambda$ with $x$.

title: Definition:Central Dilatation Mapping/Definition 2
snippet: A central dilatation mapping is a linear transformation involving a fixed point $C$ such that the image $P'$ of a point $P$ is the point on the directed line segment $CP$ such that $CP' = k CP$ where $k$ is a real non-zero constant.

title: Definition:Central Dilatation Mapping/Scale Factor
snippet: Let $f$ be a central dilatation mapping with fixed point $C$ such that the image of the directed line segment $CP$ is $k CP$. The real non-zero constant $k$ is known as the scale factor of $f$.

title: Definition:Central Field
snippet: Let $R$ be a simply connected region in $\paren {n + 1}$-dimensional space. Let $\tuple {x, \mathbf y}$ be a point in $R$. Let $c = \tuple {\sequence {c_i}_{0 \mathop \le i \mathop \le n} }$ be a point lying outside of $R$. Let $J$ be a functional such that: $\ds J \sqbrk {\mathbf y} = \int_a^b \map F {x, \mathbf y, \mathbf y'} \rd x$ whose extremals $\mathbf y$ are curves in $\paren{n+1}$-dimensional space.

title: Definition:Central Force
snippet: Consider a particle $p$ of mass $m$ moving in the plane under the influence of a force $\mathbf F$. Let the position of $p$ at time $t$ be given in polar coordinates as $\left\langle{r, \theta}\right\rangle$. Let $\mathbf F$ be expressed as: $\mathbf F = F_r \mathbf u_r + F_\theta \mathbf u_\theta$ where: $\mathbf u_r$ is the unit vector in the direction of the radial coordinate of $p$ $\mathbf u_\theta$ is the unit vector in the direction of the angular coordinate of $p$ $F_r$ and $F_\theta$ are the magnitudes of the components of $\mathbf F$ in the directions of $\mathbf u_r$ and $\mathbf…

title: Definition:Central Moment
snippet: Let $X$ be a random variable on some probability space with mean $\mu$. Then the $n$th central moment of $X$, usually denoted $\mu_n$, is defined as: $\mu_n = \expect {\paren {X - \mu}^n}$ where $\expect X$ denotes the expectation of $X$. That is, the $n$th central moment of $X$ is its $n$th moment about $\mu$.

title: Definition:Central Moment/Also known as
snippet: == Central Moment: Also known as == Some sources refer to the $n$th central moment of a random variable as its $n$th moment about the mean.

title: Definition:Central Moment/First
snippet: Let $X$ be a random variable on some probability space with mean $\mu$. The $1$st central moment of $X$, usually denoted $\mu_1$, is defined as: $\mu_1 = \expect {X - \mu}$ which, by definition, equals $0$.

title: Definition:Central Moment/Second
snippet: Let $X$ be a random variable on some probability space with mean $\mu$. The $2$nd central moment of $X$, usually denoted $\mu_2$, is defined as: $\mu_2 = \expect {\paren {X - \mu}^2}$ which, by definition, equals the variance of $X$.

title: Definition:Central Polyhedral Angle
snippet: A central polyhedral angle is a polyhedral angle formed at the center of a sphere. That is, the polyhedral angle at the apex of a spherical pyramid.

title: Definition:Central Processing Unit
snippet: A central processing unit is the item of computer hardware which performs the actual calculations.

title: Definition:Central Processing Unit/Also known as
snippet: == Central Processing Unit: Also known as == A central processing unit is often referred to by its abbreviation CPU or cpu.

title: Definition:Central Product
snippet: Let $G$ and $H$ be groups. Let $Z$ and $W$ be central subgroups of $G$ and $H$ respectively. Let: $Z \cong W$ where $\cong$ denotes isomorphism. Let such a group isomorphism be $\theta: Z \to W$. Let $X$ be the set defined as: $X = \set {\tuple {x, \map \theta x^{-1} }: x \in Z}$ Then the quotient group $\struct {G \times H} / X$ is denoted $\struct {G \times_\theta H}$ and is called the central product of $G$ and $H$ via $\theta$.

title: Definition:Central Projection
snippet: Central Projection of $\set {A, B}$ onto $\PP_2$ from $C$ Let $\PP_1$ and $\PP_2$ be planes. Let $C$ be a fixed point which lies on neither $\PP_1$ nor $\PP_2$. Let $S$ be a set of points on $\PP_1$. For each point $x \in S$, let a straight line be constructed through $C$ and $x$ to intersect $\PP_2$ at $y$. The set of all $y$ is called the central projection of $S$ onto $\PP_2$.

title: Definition:Central Projection/Also known as
snippet: == Central Projection: Also known as == A central projection is also known as a projective transformation. Category:Definitions/Central Projections

title: Definition:Central Projection/Center of Projection
snippet: Central Projection of $\set {A, B}$ onto $\PP_2$ from $C$ Let $\PP_1$ and $\PP_2$ be planes. Let $C$ be a fixed point which lies on neither $\PP_1$ nor $\PP_2$. Let $S$ be a set of points on $\PP_1$. Let $f$ be a central projection of $S$ onto $\PP_2$. The fixed point $C$ is called the center of projection of $f$.

title: Definition:Central Quadric
snippet: A central quadric is a quadric surface with a center of symmetry. That is, an ellipsoid or a hyperboloid of one sheet or two sheets.

title: Definition:Central Subgroup
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$ which is a subset of the center of $G$. Then $H$ is a central subgroup of $G$.

title: Definition:Central Tree
snippet: A tree $T$ is central it has a center.

title: Definition:Central Vertex
snippet: Let $G$ be a simple graph. Let $v \in \map V G$ be a vertex of $G$. $v$ is a central vertex of $G$ the eccentricity of $v$ equals the radius of $G$.

title: Definition:Centralizer/Group Element
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group. Let $a \in \struct {G, \circ}$. The centralizer of $a$ (in $G$) is defined as: $\map {C_G} a = \set {x \in G: x \circ a = a \circ x}$ That is, the centralizer of $a$ is the set of elements of $G$ which commute with $a$.

title: Definition:Centralizer/Group Subset
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group. Let $S \subseteq G$. The centralizer of $S$ (in $G$) is the set of elements of $G$ which commute with all $s \in S$: $\map {C_G} S = \set {x \in G: \forall s \in S: x \circ s = s \circ x}$

title: Definition:Centralizer/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Centralizer == The UK English spelling of centralizer is centraliser. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Centralizer/Ring Subset
snippet: Let $S$ be a subset of a ring $\struct {R, +, \circ}$. The centralizer of $S$ in $R$ is defined as: $\map {C_R} S = \set {x \in R: \forall s \in S: s \circ x = x \circ s}$ That is, the centralizer of $S$ is the set of elements of $R$ which commute with all elements of $S$.

title: Definition:Centralizer/Subgroup
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group. Let $H \le \struct {G, \circ}$. The centralizer of $H$ (in $G$) is the set of elements of $G$ which commute with all $h \in H$: $\map {C_G} H = \set {g \in G: \forall h \in H: g \circ h = h \circ g}$

title: Definition:Centralizer of Group Element/Also denoted as
snippet: == Centralizer of Group Element: Also denoted as == Some sources confusingly use $\map {C_a} G$ for the centralizer of $a$ (in $G$) instead of $\map {C_G} a$. The style of $C$ varies: some sources use $\mathbf C$.

title: Definition:Centralizer of Group Element/Also known as
snippet: == Centralizer of Group Element: Also known as == Some sources call the centralizer of $a$ in $G$ the normalizer of $a$ in $G$, but that term generally has another meaning.

title: Definition:Centralizer of Group Subset/Also denoted as
snippet: == Centralizer of Group Subset: Also denoted as == The notation $\map C {S; G}$ is sometimes seen for the centralizer of $S$ in $G$. Some sources confusingly use $\map {C_S} G$ instead of $\map {C_G} S$.

title: Definition:Centrifugal Force
snippet: Centrifugal force is the inertial force which is the reaction to a centripetal force.

title: Definition:Centripetal Component of Acceleration
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$ be an acceleration of a particle $P$ in space. Let $\mathbf a$ be expressed in intrinsic coordinates as: $\mathbf a = \dfrac {\d \map v t} {\d t} \mathbf s + \dfrac {\paren {\map v t}^2} \rho \bspsi$ where: $\mathbf s$ denotes the unit vector along the tangential direction of $P$ $\bspsi$ denotes the unit vector toward the center of curvature of the motion of $P$ $\map v t$ is the speed of $P$ at the time $t$ $\rho$ is the radius of curvature of the motion of $P$ at time $t$ as demonstrated in Acceleration of Point in Plane in Intrinsic Coordinates.

title: Definition:Centripetal Component of Acceleration/Also known as
snippet: == Centripetal Component of Acceleration: Also known as == The centripetal component of acceleration is also known as the normal component.

title: Definition:Centripetal Force
snippet: A centripetal force is a force $\mathbf F$ that causes a body $B$ moving in a straight line to deviate that it moves in a curved path, or constrains it to move in a curved path. $\mathbf F$ is directed towards the center of curvature of the curved path. Its magnitude is equal to the mass of $B$ multiplied by the centripetal component of the acceleration of $B$.

title: Definition:Centroid/Also known as
snippet: == Centroid: Also known as == A centroid is also referred to as a center of mean position. Some sources refer to it as a mean point. Approaches to this subject from the direction of physics and mechanics can be seen referring to it as a center of mass or center of gravity. However, it needs to be noted that these latter terms are merely special cases of a centroid. Beware that some sources use the term center of mass or center of gravity even when approaching the topic from a pure mathematical perspective, which can cause confusion.

title: Definition:Centroid/Set of Points
snippet: Let $S = \set {A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n}$ be a set of $n$ points in Euclidean space.

title: Definition:Centroid/Solid Figure
snippet: Let $F$ be a solid figure. Let $F$ be divided into a large number $n$ of small elements. Consider one point of each of these elements. Let a weight function be associated with this set of points. Let $G$ be the centroid of each of these weighted points. Let $n$ increase indefinitely, such that each element of $F$ converges to a point. Then the limiting position of $G$ is the centroid of $F$.

title: Definition:Centroid/Surface
snippet: Let $S$ be a surface. Let $S$ be divided into a large number $n$ of small elements. Consider one point of each of these elements. Let a weight function be associated with this set of points. Let $G$ be the centroid of each of these weighted points. Let $n$ increase indefinitely, such that each element of $S$ converges to a point. Then the limiting position of $G$ is the centroid of $S$.

title: Definition:Centroid/Triangle
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle. The centroid of $\triangle ABC$ is the point $G$ where its three medians $AL$, $MB$ and $CN$ meet. 520px

title: Definition:Centroid/Weighted Set of Points
snippet: Let $S = \set {A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n}$ be a set of $n$ points in Euclidean space whose position vectors are given by $\mathbf a_1, \mathbf a_2, \dotsc, \mathbf a_n$ repectively. Let $W: S \to \R$ be a weight function on $S$. Let $G$ be the point whose position vector is given by: $\vec {OG} = \dfrac {w_1 \mathbf a_1 + w_2 \mathbf a_2 + \dotsb + w_n \mathbf a_n} {w_1 + w_2 + \dotsb + w_n}$ where $w_i = \map W {A_i}$ for each $i$. Then $G$ is known as the centroid of $S$ with weights $w_i, w_2, \dotsc, w_n$.

title: Definition:Centroid of Set of Points/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S = \set {A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n}$ be a set of $n$ points in Euclidean space. Let the position vectors of the elements of $S$ be given by $\mathbf a_1, \mathbf a_2, \dotsc, \mathbf a_n$ respectively. Let $G$ be the point whose position vector is given by: $\vec {OG} = \dfrac 1 n \paren {\mathbf a_1 + \mathbf a_2 + \dotsb + \mathbf a_n}$ Then $G$ is known as the centroid of $S$.

title: Definition:Centroid of Set of Points/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S = \set {A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n}$ be a set of $n$ points in Euclidean space. Let the Cartesian coordinates of the elements of $S$ be $\tuple {x_j, y_j, z_j}$ for each $j \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n}$. Let $G$ be the point whose Cartesian coordinates are given by: $G = \tuple {\dfrac 1 n \ds \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n x_j, \dfrac 1 n \ds \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n y_j, \dfrac 1 n \ds \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n z_j}$ That is, the arithmetic mean of the Cartesian coordinates of the elements of $S$ Then $G$ is known as the centroid of $S$.

title: Definition:Certain Event/Also known as
snippet: == Certain Event: Also known as == A certain event is also known as a sure event.

title: Definition:Cesàro Equation/Formulation 1
snippet: A Cesàro equation is an intrinsic equation for a curve $C$ such that $C$ is expressed in terms of its intrinsic properties: Arc length $s$ Curvature $\kappa$

title: Definition:Cesàro Equation/Formulation 2
snippet: A Cesàro equation is an intrinsic equation for a curve $C$ such that $C$ is expressed in terms of its intrinsic properties: Arc length $s$ Radius of curvature $\rho$

title: Definition:Cesàro Summation
snippet: Let $\ds \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^\infty a_k$ be a series. Define $s_n := \ds \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n a_k$ The Cesàro summation of the series is $S$ if: $S = \ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \dfrac 1 n \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n s_k$

title: Definition:Cesàro Summation/Also known as
snippet: == Cesàro Summation: Also known as == The end result of a Cesàro summation operation is also known as a Cesàro sum.

title: Definition:Cesàro Summation Operator
snippet: Let $\ell^\infty$ be the space of bounded sequences. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N} \in \ell^\infty$ be a sequence. Let $A : \ell^\infty \to \ell^\infty$ be an operator such that: $\ds \map A {x_1, x_2, x_3, \ldots} = \tuple {x_1, \frac {x_1 + x_2} 2, \frac {x_1 + x_2 + x_3} 3, \ldots}$ Then $A$ is called the Cesàro summation operator.

title: Definition:Cesàro Summation Operator/Also known as
snippet: == Cesàro Summation Operator: Also known as == The Cesàro summation operator is also known as the averaging operator. Category:Definitions/Cesàro Summation Operator

title: Definition:Ceteris Paribus
snippet: Ceteris paribus is a Latin phrase meaning all other things being equal. It is also translated as in the absence of any other change (in the conditions of a theorem, for example). It is often used in logical arguments in natural language when expressing a general comparison between two effects, and is a plea to the hearer to suspend counterarguments based on differences in the general situations.

title: Definition:Cevian
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle. 400px A cevian is a line segment from a vertex of the triangle to the opposite side. In the above diagram, $CD$ is a cevian.

title: Definition:Chain
snippet: Order Theory: Chain: a totally ordered subset $\struct {T, \preceq}$ of an ordered set $\struct {S, \preceq}$. Chain of Sets: a chain whose ordering is the subset relation, that is, a nest which is also a set. Physics: A chain is an idealized inelastic thread whose stiffness and width (but not mass) are approximated to zero. Chain (Linear Measure): imperial unit of length: $1$ chain $= 22$ yards. Number Theory: A sociable chain is a sequence of positive integers such that the $n + 1$th term is the aliquot sum of the $n$th.

title: Definition:Chain (Linear Measure)/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Chain == The chain was invented by for the purpose of land surveying. The original Gunter's chain was a physical chain, $66$ feet in length, of $100$ links. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Chain (Order Theory)
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. A chain in $S$ is a totally ordered subset of $S$. Thus a totally ordered set is itself a chain in its own right.

title: Definition:Chain (Order Theory)/Also defined as
snippet: == Chain (Order Theory): Also defined as == Some sources use the term chain to mean the same thing as totally ordered set. While this is perfectly valid, as there is no source of confusion here, such usage is surprisingly uncommon.

title: Definition:Chain (Order Theory)/Subset Relation
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\powerset S$ be its power set. Let $N \subseteq \powerset S$ be a subset of $\powerset S$. Then $N$ is a chain (of sets) : $\forall X, Y \in N: X \subseteq Y$ or $Y \subseteq X$

title: Definition:Chain (Physics)
snippet: A chain is an inelastic thread whose stiffness and width are approximated to zero. The mass of a chain is usually defined in terms of linear mass density. Category:Definitions/Ideals in Physics

title: Definition:Chain Complex
snippet: Let $\AA$ be an abelian category. A chain complex in $\AA$ is a family of objects: $\family {C_i}_{i \mathop \in \Z}$ of $\AA$ and a family of morphisms: $\family {d_i : C_i \to C_{i - 1} }_{i \mathop \in \Z}$ such that for all $i \in \Z$, the composition $d_{i - 1} \circ d_i$ is the zero morphism $0 : C_i \to C_{i - 2}$.

title: Definition:Chain Complex/Visualization
snippet: == Chain Complex: Visualization== A chain complex can be visualized as a diagram: $\cdots \longrightarrow C_{i + 1} \stackrel {d_{i + 1} } \longrightarrow C_i \stackrel {d_i} \longrightarrow C_{i - 1} \stackrel {d_{i - 1} } \longrightarrow C_{i - 2} \longrightarrow \cdots$

title: Definition:Chain of Sets/Also known as
snippet: == Chain of Sets: Also known as == A chain (of sets) is also known as a nest, particularly in the wider context of class theory. Some sources use the term tower (of sets).

title: Definition:Champernowne Constant
snippet: The Champernowne constant is the real number whose decimal expansion is formed by concatenating the positive integers in ascending order: $C_{10} = 0 \cdotp 12345 \, 67891 \, 01112 \, 13141 \, 51617 \, 18192 \, 02122 \ldots$

title: Definition:Champernowne Constant/Also known as
snippet: == Champernowne Constant: Also known as == The Champernowne constant is also known as Mahler's number for , who proved it transcendental in $1937$. Some sources report it as Champernowne's number.

title: Definition:Champernowne Constant/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Champernowne Constant == The Champernowne constant was invented by as an example of a real number which can be demonstrated to be normal base $10$. He achieved this in $1933$ while still an undergraduate.

title: Definition:Change of Basis
snippet: Definition:Change of Basis Matrix

title: Definition:Change of Basis Matrix
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $G$ be a finite-dimensional free $R$-module. Let $A = \sequence {a_n}$ and $B = \sequence {b_n}$ be ordered bases of $G$.

title: Definition:Change of Basis Matrix/Definition 1
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $G$ be an $n$-dimensional free $R$-module. Let $A = \sequence {a_n}$ and $B = \sequence {b_n}$ be ordered bases of $G$. The matrix of change of basis from $A$ to $B$ is the matrix whose columns are the coordinate vectors of the elements of the new basis $\sequence {b_n}$ relative to the original basis $\sequence {a_n}$.

title: Definition:Change of Basis Matrix/Definition 2
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $G$ be an $n$-dimensional free $R$-module. Let $A = \sequence {a_n}$ and $B = \sequence {b_n}$ be ordered bases of $G$. Let $I_G$ be the identity linear operator on $G$. Let $\sqbrk {I_G; \sequence {a_n}, \sequence {b_n} }$ be the matrix of $I_G$ relative to $\sequence {b_n}$ and $\sequence {a_n}$. Then $\sqbrk {I_G; \sequence {a_n}, \sequence {b_n} }$ is called the matrix corresponding to the change of basis from $\sequence {a_n}$ to $\sequence {b_n}$.

title: Definition:Change of Basis Matrix/Warning
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $G$ be a finite-dimensional free $R$-module. Let $A = \sequence {a_n}$ and $B = \sequence {b_n}$ be ordered bases of $G$. Let $I_G$ be the identity linear operator on $G$. Let $\sqbrk {I_G; \sequence {a_n}, \sequence {b_n} }$ be the matrix corresponding to the change of basis from $\sequence {a_n}$ to $\sequence {b_n}$. Note the order of the above, which gives rise to the intuitive cancellation law in Product of Change of Basis Matrices.

title: Definition:Change of Observer
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be observers in $2$ different positions, possibly moving relative to each other. The same event will be observed differently by $A$ and $B$. Knowing one observation and the relative position of $A$ and $B$ allows the calculation of what the other observer would see. This is called a change of observer.

title: Definition:Change of Observer/Also known as
snippet: == Change of Observer: Also known as == A change of observer is also known as a change of reference.

title: Definition:Channel
snippet: A channel is a means of sending messages from one place to another.

title: Definition:Channel/Also known as
snippet: == Channel: Also known as == A channel is also known as a transmission line. Category:Definitions/Channels

title: Definition:Chaos
snippet: Chaos is a phenomenon of nonlinear dynamics. It is a type of behaviour found in certain deterministic dynamical systems whose evolution appears to be random or otherwise unpredictable. Typically, such a system exhibits sensitive dependence on initial conditions.

title: Definition:Chaos/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Chaos == The term chaos was introduced in $1975$ by and in their work on periodic points for transformations of the real number line.

title: Definition:Chaos Theory
snippet: Chaos theory is the branch of nonlinear systems that studies the behavior and condition of dynamical systems that are highly sensitive to initial conditions.

title: Definition:Character
snippet: Number theory: Character Dirichlet Character Quadratic Character Representation theory Character (Representation Theory) Topology: Character of Topological Space Character of Point in Topological Space Analysis Character (Banach Algebra)

title: Definition:Character (Banach Algebra)
snippet: Let $\struct {A, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a Banach algebra over $\C$. Let $\phi : A \to \C$ be a non-zero algebra homomorphism on $A$. We say that $\phi$ is a character on $A$.

title: Definition:Character (Number Theory)
snippet: Let $\struct {G, +}$ be a finite abelian group. Let $\struct {\C_{\ne 0}, \times}$ be the multiplicative group of complex numbers. A character of $G$ is a group homomorphism: $\chi: G \to \C_{\ne 0}$

title: Definition:Character (Representation Theory)
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \cdot}$ be a finite group. Let $V$ be a finite dimensional vector space over a field $F$. Consider a linear representation: $\rho: G \to \GL V$ of $G$ where $\GL V$ denotes the general linear group over $V$. For $g \in G$, let $\map \tr {\map \rho g}$ denote the trace of $\map \rho g$. The character associated with $\rho$ is defined as: $\chi_\rho: G \to F$ where $\map {\chi_\rho} g = \map \tr {\map \rho g}$.

title: Definition:Character (Representation Theory)/Degree
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \cdot}$ be a finite group. Let $V$ be a finite dimensional vector space over a field $F$. Consider a linear representation: $\rho: G \to \GL V$ of $G$ where $\GL V$ denotes the general linear group over $V$. For $g \in G$, let $\map \tr {\map \rho g}$ denote the trace of $\map \rho g$. Let $\chi_\rho: G \to F$ denote the character associated with $\rho$. The degree of $\chi_\rho$ is defined as the dimension of $V$.

title: Definition:Character Table
snippet: A character table is a tabulation of the irreducible characters of a finite group $G$. This provides a concise summary of a lot of useful information about $G$ and its normal subgroups. Because Character is Constant on Conjugacy Class, only one representation needs to be shown per conjugacy class. The character in the first row is the trivial character. The first column contains the degrees of the characters.

title: Definition:Character of Point in Topological Space
snippet: Let $T$ be a topological space. Let $x$ be a point of $T$. Let $\map {\mathbb B} x$ be the set of all local bases at $x$. The character of (the point) $x$ in $T$ is the smallest cardinality of the elements of $\map {\mathbb B} x$: $\map \chi {x, T} := \min \set {\card \BB: \BB \in \map {\mathbb B} x}$

title: Definition:Character of Topological Space
snippet: Let $T$ be a topological space. The character of (the topological space) $T$ is the supremum of the set of characters of the points of $T$: $\chi \left({T}\right) := \sup \left\{ {\chi \left({x, T}\right): x \in T}\right\}$

title: Definition:Characteristic
snippet: Abstract Algebra: Characteristic of Ring Characteristic of Field Characteristic Subgroup Characteristic Matrix Characteristic Polynomial Characteristic Equation of Matrix Differential Equations: Characteristic Equation of Differential Equation Set Theory: Characteristic Function, also known as Characteristic Mapping and Indicator Function Arithmetic Characteristic of Common Logarithm

title: Definition:Characteristic Equation
snippet: A characteristic equation is a member of the class of equations which in some way allows one to sum up a number of characteristics of a particular mathematical object.

title: Definition:Characteristic Equation of Matrix
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $\mathbf A$ be a square matrix over $R$ of order $n > 0$. Let $\mathbf I_n$ be the $n \times n$ identity matrix. Let $R \sqbrk x$ be the polynomial ring in one variable over $R$. The characteristic equation of $\mathbf A$ is the equation defined as the determinant of the characteristic matrix of $\mathbf A$ over $R \sqbrk x$: $\map \det {\mathbf I_n x - \mathbf A} = 0$ where $\map \det {\mathbf I_n x - \mathbf A}$ is the characteristic polynomial of the characteristic matrix of $\mathbf A$ over $R \sqbrk x$.

title: Definition:Characteristic Function
snippet: A characteristic function is a member of the class of functions which in some way allows one to sum up a number of characteristics of a particular mathematical object.

title: Definition:Characteristic Function (Set Theory)/Also known as
snippet: == Characteristic Function (Set Theory): Also known as == The characteristic function is also known as the indicator function, and $\map {\chi_E} x$ denoted $\map {\mathbf 1_E} x$. However, that name is also used for the Euler $\phi$ function, and so is not endorsed on . Some sources, in an attempt to apply consistency to the terminology, refer to this concept as a characteristic mapping, but this term appears to be rare. Some sources use the symbol $\phi$ to denote a characteristic function.

title: Definition:Characteristic Function (Set Theory)/Relation
snippet: The concept of a characteristic function of a subset carries over directly to relations. Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation. The characteristic function of $\RR$ is the mapping $\chi_\RR: S \times T \to \set {0, 1}$ defined as: $\map {\chi_\RR} {x, y} = \begin {cases} 1 & : \tuple {x, y} \in \RR \\ 0 & : \tuple {x, y} \notin \RR \end{cases}$ It can be expressed in Iverson bracket notation as: $\map {\chi_\RR} {x, y} = \sqbrk {\tuple {x, y} \in \RR}$ More generally, let $\ds \mathbb S = \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n S_i = S_1 \times S_2 \times \ldots \times S_n$ be the cartesian product of…

title: Definition:Characteristic Function (Set Theory)/Set
snippet: Let $E \subseteq S$. The characteristic function of $E$ is the function $\chi_E: S \to \set {0, 1}$ defined as: $\map {\chi_E} x = \begin {cases} 1 & : x \in E \\ 0 & : x \notin E \end {cases}$ That is: $\map {\chi_E} x = \begin {cases} 1 & : x \in E \\ 0 & : x \in \relcomp S E \end {cases}$ where $\relcomp S E$ denotes the complement of $E$ relative to $S$.

title: Definition:Characteristic Function (Set Theory)/Set/Support
snippet: Let $S$ be a set Let $E \subseteq S$ be a subset. Let $\chi_E: S \to \set {0, 1}$ be the characteristic function of $E$. The support of $\chi_E$, denoted $\map \supp {\chi_E}$, is the set $E$. That is: $\map \supp {\chi_E} = \set {x \in S: \map {\chi_E} x = 1}$

title: Definition:Characteristic Function of Random Variable
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $X$ be a real-valued random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. The characteristic function of $X$ is the mapping $\phi: \R \to \C$ defined by: $\map \phi t = \expect {e^{i t X} }$ where: $i$ is the imaginary unit $\expect \cdot$ denotes expectation.

title: Definition:Characteristic Function of Set/Also denoted as
snippet: == Characteristic Function of Set: Also denoted as == The characteristic function of a set $E$ can be expressed in Iverson bracket notation as: $\map {\chi_E} x = \sqbrk {x \in E}$ Category:Definitions/Characteristic Functions of Sets

title: Definition:Characteristic Matrix
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $\mathbf A$ be a square matrix over $R$ of order $n > 0$. Let $\mathbf I_n$ be the $n \times n$ identity matrix. Let $R \sqbrk x$ be the polynomial ring in one variable over $R$. The characteristic matrix of $\mathbf A$ over $R \sqbrk x$ is the square matrix: $\mathbf I_n x - \mathbf A$

title: Definition:Characteristic Matrix/Also defined as
snippet: == Characteristic Matrix: Also defined as == Some sources define the characteristic matrix of $\mathbf A$ over $R \sqbrk x$ as: $\mathbf A - x \mathbf I_n$ where: $R$ is a commutative ring with unity. $\mathbf A$ is a square matrix over $R$ of order $n > 0$. $\mathbf I_n$ is the $n \times n$ identity matrix. $R \sqbrk x$ is the polynomial ring in one variable over $R$.

title: Definition:Characteristic Polynomial
snippet: A characteristic polynomial is a member of the class of polynomials which in some way allows one to sum up a number of characteristics of a particular mathematical object.

title: Definition:Characteristic Polynomial of Element of Algebra
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $B$ be an algebra over $A$ such that $B$ is a finite-dimensional free module over $A$. Let $b \in B$. The characteristic polynomial of $b$ is the characteristic polynomial of the regular representation $\lambda_b : B \to B$ over $A$.

title: Definition:Characteristic Polynomial of Field Extension
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $L / K$ be a finite field extension of $K$. Then by Vector Space on Field Extension is Vector Space, $L$ is naturally a vector space over $K$. Let $\alpha \in L$, and $\theta_\alpha$ be the linear operator: $\theta_\alpha: L \to L : \beta \mapsto \alpha \beta$ The characteristic polynomial of $\alpha$ with respect to the extension $L / K$ is: $\det \sqbrk {X I_L - \theta_\alpha}$ where: $\det$ denotes the determinant of a linear operator $X$ is an indeterminate $I_L$ is the identity mapping on $L$.

title: Definition:Characteristic Polynomial of Linear Operator
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $M$ be a free module over $A$ of finite rank $n > 0$. Let $\phi : M \to M$ be a linear operator.

title: Definition:Characteristic Polynomial of Linear Operator/Definition 1
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $M$ be a free module over $A$ of finite rank $n > 0$. Let $\phi : M \to M$ be a linear operator. The characteristic polynomial of $\phi$ is the characteristic polynomial of the relative matrix of $\phi$ with respect to a basis of $M$.

title: Definition:Characteristic Polynomial of Linear Operator/Definition 2
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $M$ be a free module over $A$of finite rank $n > 0$. Let $\phi : M \to M$ be a linear operator. Let $A \sqbrk x$ be the polynomial ring in one variable over $A$. Let $I_M$ denote the identity mapping on $M$. Let $M \otimes_A A \sqbrk x$ be the extension of scalars of $M$ to $A \sqbrk x$. The characteristic polynomial of $\phi$ is the determinant of the linear operator $x I_M - \phi$ on $M \otimes_A A \sqbrk x$.

title: Definition:Characteristic Polynomial of Matrix
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $\mathbf A$ be a square matrix over $R$ of order $n > 0$. Let $\mathbf I_n$ be the $n \times n$ identity matrix. Let $R \sqbrk x$ be the polynomial ring in one variable over $R$. The characteristic polynomial of $\mathbf A$ is the determinant of the characteristic matrix of $\mathbf A$ over $R \sqbrk x$: $\map {p_{\mathbf A} } x = \map \det {\mathbf I_n x - \mathbf A}$

title: Definition:Characteristic Polynomial of Matrix/Also defined as
snippet: Some sources define the characteristic polynomial of $\mathbf A$ as: $\map {p_{\mathbf A} } x = \map \det {\mathbf A - x \mathbf I_n}$ where: $R$ is a commutative ring with unity. $\mathbf A$ is a square matrix over $R$ of order $n > 0$. $\mathbf I_n$ is the $n \times n$ identity matrix. $R \sqbrk x$ is the polynomial ring in one variable over $R$. This characteristic polynomial differs from the standard one by a factor of $-1$ when $n$ is odd.

title: Definition:Characteristic Property of Set
snippet: Let $S$ be a set which is specified by means of such a propositional function: $S = \set {a: \map P a}$ The open statement $\map P x$ is known as a characteristic property of $S$.

title: Definition:Characteristic Subgroup
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a subgroup such that: $\forall \phi \in \Aut G: \phi \sqbrk H = H$ where $\Aut G$ is the automorphism group of $G$. Then $H$ is characteristic (in $G$), or a characteristic subgroup of $G$.

title: Definition:Characteristic Subset
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $S \subseteq G$ be a subset of $G$ such that: $\forall \phi \in \Aut G: \map \phi S = S$ where $\Aut G$ is the automorphism group of $G$. Then $S$ is characteristic (in $G$), or a characteristic subset of $G$.

title: Definition:Characteristic of Field
snippet: As a field is a ring, the definition of characteristic carries over directly from that of the characteristic of a ring :

title: Definition:Characteristic of Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring with unity whose zero is $0_R$ and whose unity is $1_R$.

title: Definition:Characteristic of Ring/Also defined as
snippet: == Characteristic of Ring: Also defined as == Some authors insist that the characteristic is defined on integral domains only. Some others define the concept only on fields. Some sources use $\infty$ rather than $0$ for rings which have no characteristic defined.

title: Definition:Characteristic of Ring/Also denoted as
snippet: == Characteristic of Ring: Also denoted as == Some sources use $\map {\operatorname {char} } R$ to denote the characteristic of a ring $R$. Category:Definitions/Characteristics of Rings

title: Definition:Characteristic of Ring/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring with unity whose zero is $0_R$ and whose unity is $1_R$.
