title: Definition:Complex Number/Also known as
snippet: == Complex Number: Also known as == Some sources refer to a complex number as an imaginary number, but it is too easy to confuse this with a wholly imaginary number. Hence this usage is not endorsed by .

title: Definition:Complex Number/Complex Plane
snippet: Because a complex number can be expressed as an ordered pair, we can plot the number $x + i y$ on the real number plane $\R^2$: 400px This representation is known as the complex plane.

title: Definition:Complex Number/Complex Plane/Imaginary Axis
snippet: Let the set $\C$ of complex number be expressed as an ordered pairs on the complex plane. Complex numbers of the form $\tuple {0, y}$, being wholly imaginary, appear as points on the points on the $y$-axis. Hence the $y$-axis of the complex plane is known as the imaginary axis.

title: Definition:Complex Number/Complex Plane/Real Axis
snippet: Let the set $\C$ of complex number be expressed as an ordered pairs on the complex plane. Complex numbers of the form $\tuple {x, 0}$, being wholly real, appear as points on the $x$-axis. Hence the $x$-axis of the complex plane is known as the real axis.

title: Definition:Complex Number/Construction from Cayley-Dickson Construction
snippet: The complex numbers can be defined by the Cayley-Dickson construction from the set of real numbers $\R$. From Real Numbers form Algebra, $\R$ forms a nicely normed $*$-algebra. Let $a, b \in \R$. Then $\tuple {a, b} \in \C$, where: $\tuple {a, b} \tuple {c, d} = \tuple {a c - d \overline b, \overline a d + c b}$ $\overline {\tuple {a, b} } = \tuple {\overline a, -b}$ where: $\overline a$ is the conjugate of $a$ and $\overline {\tuple {a, b} }$ is the conjugation operation on $\C$.

title: Definition:Complex Number/Definition 1
snippet: A complex number is a number in the form $a + b i$ or $a + i b$ where: $a$ and $b$ are real numbers $i$ is a square root of $-1$, that is, $i = \sqrt {-1}$.

title: Definition:Complex Number/Definition 2
snippet: A complex number is an ordered pair $\tuple {x, y}$ where $x, y \in \R$ are real numbers, on which the operations of addition and multiplication are defined as follows:

title: Definition:Complex Number/Definition 2/Addition
snippet: Let $\tuple {x_1, y_1}$ and $\tuple {x_2, y_2}$ be complex numbers. Then $+$ is a binary operation defined as: $\tuple {x_1, y_1} + \tuple {x_2, y_2}:= \tuple {x_1 + x_2, y_1 + y_2}$

title: Definition:Complex Number/Definition 2/Multiplication
snippet: Let $\tuple {x_1, y_1}$ and $\tuple {x_2, y_2}$ be complex numbers. Then $\tuple {x_1, y_1} \tuple {x_2, y_2}$ is defined as: $\tuple {x_1, y_1} \tuple {x_2, y_2} := \tuple {x_1 x_2 - y_1 y_2, x_1 y_2 + y_1 x_2}$

title: Definition:Complex Number/Definition 2/Scalar Product
snippet: Let $\tuple {x, y}$ be a complex number. Let $m \in \R$ be a real number. Then $m \tuple {x, y}$ is defined as: $m \tuple {x, y} := \tuple {m x, m y}$

title: Definition:Complex Number/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Complex Number == The concept of a complex number originated in the $16$th century as during the course of developing the solution to the general cubic equation. In his of $1545$, considered the simultaneous equations: $\begin {cases} x + y & = 10 \\ x y & = 40 \end {cases}$ and obtained the solution: $\begin {cases} x & = 5 + \sqrt {-15} \\y & = 5 - \sqrt {-15} \end {cases}$ He made no attempt to interpret the meaning of the square root of a negative number, dismissing it with the comment: So progresses arithmetic subtlely, the end result of which ...

title: Definition:Complex Number/Imaginary Part
snippet: Let $z = a + i b$ be a complex number. The imaginary part of $z$ is the coefficient $b$ (note: not $i b$). The imaginary part of a complex number $z$ is usually denoted on by $\map \Im z$ or $\Im z$.

title: Definition:Complex Number/Imaginary Unit
snippet: Let $\C = \set {a + b i: a, b \in \R}$ be the set of complex numbers. The entity $i := 0 + 1 i$ is known as the imaginary unit.

title: Definition:Complex Number/Irrational
snippet: A complex number is classified as irrational its imaginary part is non-zero.

title: Definition:Complex Number/Notation
snippet: == Complex Number: Also denoted as == The set of complex numbers is usually denoted $\C$. Variants on $\C$ are often seen, for example $\mathbf C$, $\CC$ and $\mathfrak C$, or even just $C$. When $a$ and $b$ are symbols representing variables or constants, the form $a + i b$ is usually (but not universally) seen. Similarly, when $a$ and $b$ are actual numbers, for example $3$ and $4$, it is usually (but not universally) written $3 + 4 i$. In the field of electronics, the letter $j$ is usually used instead of $i$, as $i$ is generally used as the symbol denoting electric current.

title: Definition:Complex Number/Polar Form/Exponential Form
snippet: Let $z := \polar {r, \theta}$ be a complex number in polar form. From Euler's Formula: $e^{i \theta} = \cos \theta + i \sin \theta$ so $z$ can also be written in the form: $z = r e^{i \theta}$ This form of presentation of a complex number is known as exponential form.

title: Definition:Complex Number/Real Part
snippet: Let $z = a + i b$ be a complex number. The real part of $z$ is the coefficient $a$. The real part of a complex number $z$ is usually denoted on by $\map \Re z$ or $\mathop \Re z$.

title: Definition:Complex Number/Wholly Imaginary
snippet: A complex number $z = a + i b$ is wholly imaginary $a = 0$.

title: Definition:Complex Number/Wholly Real
snippet: A complex number $z = a + i b$ is wholly real $b = 0$.

title: Definition:Complex Number as Vector
snippet: Let $z = x + i y$ be a complex number. Then $z$ can be considered as a vector $OP$ in the complex plane such that: its initial point is the origin its terminal point $P$ is the point $\tuple {x, y}$. Two vectors which have the same magnitude and direction, but different initial points, are considered equal.

title: Definition:Complex Plane/Also known as
snippet: == Complex Plane: Also known as == Some sources refer to the complex plane as an Argand plane, for . It is also sometimes known as a Gauss plane, or Gaussian plane, for . As it is now recognised that neither nor had precedence over the concept of plotting complex numbers on the cartesian plane, the more neutral term complex plane is usually preferred nowadays. The term Argand diagram is also in common use, but this strictly speaking should refer to an actual instance of a graphical representation of a particular configuration of complex numbers on such a complex plane.

title: Definition:Complex Plane/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Complex Plane == It is reported by and , in their of $1983$, that represented a complex number using this technique in his , but for some reason was ignored. This has not been corroborated by , and there may be some doubt as to its truth, considering the given publication date of ($1673$) does not match that given by all other sources found ($1685$). It is widely reported that the concept of the complex plane was an invention of , independently of and .

title: Definition:Complex Point at Infinity
snippet: The zero in the set of complex numbers $\C$ has no inverse for multiplication. That is, the expression: $\dfrac 1 0$ has no meaning. The (complex) point at infinity is the element added to $\C$ in order to allow $\C$ to be closed under division: $\forall x, y \in \C: \dfrac x y \in \C$ The set $\C$ with that point added is known as the extended complex plane. Conceptually, it can be imagined as a point which is at infinity in all directions. It can also be considered as the $N$ point on the Riemann sphere which does not map to the complex plane. This point can be denoted $\infty$.

title: Definition:Complex Potential
snippet: Let $\map u z$ be a flow in the complex plane. Let $\map u z$ be inviscid, incompressible and irrotational. Let the velocity potential of $\map u z$ be $\varphi$. Let the stream function of $\map u z$ be $\psi$. Then the complex potential of $\map u z$ is defined and denoted: $w := \varphi + i \psi$

title: Definition:Complex Root
snippet: Let $z \in \C$ be a complex number such that $z \ne 0$. Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. Let $w \in \C$ such that: $w^n = z$ Then $w$ is a (complex) $n$th root of $z$, and we can write: $w = z^{1 / n}$

title: Definition:Complex Sequence
snippet: A complex sequence is a sequence (usually infinite) whose codomain is the set of complex numbers $\C$.

title: Definition:Complex Subfield
snippet: Let $\C$ be the field of complex numbers. A field $\GF$ is a complex subfield $\GF$ is a subfield of $\C$. Category:Definitions/Subfields Category:Definitions/Complex Numbers

title: Definition:Complex System
snippet: A complex system is a system with many interacting constituent parts. Complex systems are often modeled using a network, using nodes for subsystems and edges as the interactions between them.

title: Definition:Complex Transformation
snippet: A complex transformation is a mapping on the complex plane $f: \C \to \C$ which is specifically not a multifunction. Let $z = x + i y$ be a complex variable. Let $w = u + i v = \map f z$. Then $w$ can be expressed as: $u + i v = \map f {x + i y}$ such that: $u = \map u {x, y}$ and: $v = \map v {x, y}$ are real functions of two variables. Thus a point $P = \tuple {x, y}$ in the complex plane is transformed to a point $P' = \tuple {\map u {x, y}, \map v {x, y} }$ by $f$. Thus $P'$ is the image of $P$ under $f$.

title: Definition:Complex Vector Inner Product/Also defined as
snippet: == Complex Vector Inner Product: Also defined as == The definition of complex vector inner product as given here is common in most areas of mathematics. Other fields, especially quantum mechanics, define the complex vector inner product as: $\ds \innerprod {\mathbf a} {\mathbf b} = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \overline a_i b_i$ or, if $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ are represented as column vectors: $\innerprod {\mathbf a} {\mathbf b} = \mathbf a^\dagger \mathbf b$ This definition uses a slightly different definition of complex inner product in that it is linear in the second argument, rather than…

title: Definition:Complex Vector Inner Product/Also denoted as
snippet: == Complex Vector Inner Product: Also denoted as == In the field of quantum mechanics, the complex vector inner product is usually written using Dirac notation: $\braket {\mathbf a} {\mathbf b}$.

title: Definition:Complex Vector Inner Product/Also known as
snippet: == Complex Vector Inner Product: Also known as == A complex vector inner product is also referred to by some sources as a complex vector dot product, and classified with other implementations of the dot product. However, it is the view of that such nomenclature is non-intuitive and misleading. Category:Definitions/Complex Vector Inner Product

title: Definition:Complex Vector Space
snippet: Let $\C$ be the set of complex numbers. Then the $\C$-module $\C^n$ is called the complex ($n$-dimensional) vector space.

title: Definition:Complex Vector Space/Also known as
snippet: == Complex Vector Space: Also known as == A complex vector space is also known as a complex linear space. Category:Definitions/Complex Vector Spaces

title: Definition:Complexity Theory
snippet: Complexity theory is a branch of mathematics used for the modelling and analysis of complex systems.

title: Definition:Component (Topology)
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let the relation $\sim $ be defined on $T$ as follows: $x \sim y$ $x$ and $y$ are connected in $T$. That is, there exists a connected set of $T$ that contains both $x$ and $y$.

title: Definition:Component (Topology)/Definition 1
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let the relation $\sim $ be defined on $T$ as follows: $x \sim y$ $x$ and $y$ are connected in $T$. That is, there exists a connected set of $T$ that contains both $x$ and $y$. From Connectedness of Points is Equivalence Relation, $\sim$ is an equivalence relation. From the Fundamental Theorem on Equivalence Relations, the points in $T$ can be partitioned into equivalence classes. These equivalence classes are called the (connected) components of $T$.

title: Definition:Component (Topology)/Definition 2
snippet: Let $T = \struct{S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let the relation $\sim $ be defined on $T$ as follows: $x \sim y$ $x$ and $y$ are connected in $T$. That is, there exists a connected set of $T$ that contains both $x$ and $y$. The component of $T$ containing $x$ is defined as: $\ds \map {\operatorname{Comp}_x} T = \bigcup \leftset {A \subseteq S: x \in A \land A}$ is connected $\rightset{}$

title: Definition:Component (Topology)/Definition 3
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let the relation $\sim $ be defined on $T$ as follows: $x \sim y$ $x$ and $y$ are connected in $T$. That is, there exists a connected set of $T$ that contains both $x$ and $y$. The component of $T$ containing $x$ is defined as: the maximal connected set of $T$ that contains $x$.

title: Definition:Component of Graph
snippet: Let $G$ be a graph. Let $H$ be a subgraph of $G$ such that: $H$ is connected $H$ is not contained in any connected subgraph of $G$ which has more vertices or edges than $H$ has. Then $H$ is a component of $G$.

title: Definition:Component of Tensor
snippet: The elements $A^1, A^2, \ldots, A^n$ of a tensor $A^i$ are referred to as its components.

title: Definition:Component of Vector/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Component of Vector == The idea of resolving a vector into $3$ components was originally due to .

title: Definition:Componentwise
snippet: Le $A$ and $B$ both be compound objects of some nature, but both of the same nature. It is appreciated that there may be perceived some vagueness of terminology here. Let $\map \phi {A, B}$ be an operation acting on $A$ and $B$. Then: $\phi$ acts componentwise on $A \times B$ $\phi$ is defined as suboperations consisting of operations acting on corresponding components of $A$ and $B$.

title: Definition:Composable Morphisms
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $f, g \in \mathbf C_1$ be morphisms of $\mathbf C$. Then $f$ is said to be composable with $g$ : $\Cdm f = \Dom g$ that is, the codomain of $f$ is the domain of $g$. When the order of composition is to be made more explicit, one says that $\tuple {g, f}$ is a composable pair. The collection of all such composable pairs in $\mathbf C$ is denoted $\mathbf C_2$.

title: Definition:Composant
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a continuum in $T$. Let $C \subseteq H$ be a subset of $H$.

title: Definition:Composant/Continuum
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a continuum in $T$. Let $C \subseteq H$ be a subset of $H$. $C$ is a composant of $H$ : there exists some $p \in H$ such that $C$ contains all points $x \in S$ such that $x$ and $p$ are both contained in some proper subcontinua of $H$.

title: Definition:Composant/Point
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a continuum in $T$. Let $C \subseteq H$ be a subset of $H$. Let $p \in H$. Then $C$ is the composant of $p$ : $C$ is the union of all proper subcontinua of $H$ that contain $p$.

title: Definition:Composite
snippet: Composite (Abstract Algebra): the value at $\tuple {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n}$ of the $n$-ary operation defined by $\circ$. Composite number: A number greater than $1$ which is not a prime.

Then the composite of the ordered $n$-tuple defined by the sequence $\sequence {a_{\map \sigma k} }_{k \mathop \in A}$ is defined as: {{eqn | l = \bigoplus_{k \mathop \in A} a_{\map \sigma k} | r = \begin {cases} a_{\map \sigma 1} & : n = 1 \\ \map \oplus {a_{\map \sigma 1}, a_{\map \sigma 2}, \ldots, a_{\map \sigma m} } \oplus a_{\map \sigma {n + 1} } & : n = m + 1 \end{cases} | c = }} {{eqn | r = a_{\map \sigma 1} \oplus…

title: Definition:Composite Gaussian Integer
snippet: Let $x \in \Z \sqbrk i$ be a Gaussian integer. $x$ is defined as being composite it is the product of two Gaussian integers, neither of which is a unit (that is, $\pm 1$ or $\pm i$).

title: Definition:Composite Hypothesis
snippet: Let $\theta$ be a population parameter of some population. Let the parameter space of $\theta$ be $\Omega$. Let $\Omega_0$ and $\Omega_1$ be disjoint subsets of $\Omega$ such that $\Omega_0 \cup \Omega_1 = \Omega$. Consider the hypotheses: $H_0: \theta \in \Omega_0$ $H_1: \theta \in \Omega_1$ We call $H_i$, for $i \in \set {0, 1}$, a composite hypothesis if $\Omega_i$ contains more than a single element.

title: Definition:Composite Hypothesis Test
snippet: Let $\delta$ be a hypothesis test. Then $\delta$ is a composite hypothesis test the probability distribution of the population random variable is not completely specified.

title: Definition:Composite Number
snippet: A composite number $c$ is a positive integer that has strictly more than two positive divisors. That is, an integer greater than $1$ which is not prime is defined as composite. '

title: Definition:Composite Number/Also known as
snippet: == Composite Number: Also known as == Some sources refer to a composite number as a factorable or factorizable number. For many reasons, one being that composite is of fewer syllables and therefore more economical to say, composite is the preferred form on .

title: Definition:Composite Number/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Composite Number == The concept of classifying numbers as prime or composite appears to have originated with the Pythagoreans.

title: Definition:Composite Number/Negative Composite
snippet: A negative integer $n$ is composite $\size n$ is composite. Category:Definitions/Composite Numbers

title: Definition:Composition
snippet: Set Theory: Composition of Mappings Composition of Relations: $\RR_2 \circ \RR_1 = \set {\tuple {x, z}: x \in S_1, z \in S_3: \exists y \in S_2: \tuple {x, y} \in \RR_1 \land \tuple {y, z} \in \RR_2}$ Order theory: Definition:Composition of Galois Connections Abstract Algebra: Another word for an operation, usually binary.

title: Definition:Composition (Combinatorics)
snippet: A $k$-composition of a (strictly) positive integer $n \in \Z_{> 0}$ is an ordered $k$-tuple: $c = \tuple {c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_k}$ such that: $(1): \quad c_1 + c_2 + \cdots + c_k = n$ $(2): \quad \forall i \in \closedint 1 k: c_i \in \Z_{>0}$, that is, all the $c_i$ are strictly positive integers. Category:Definitions/Combinatorics

title: Definition:Composition Functor
snippet: Composition Functor on Slice Categories Composition Functor on Categories of Subobjects

title: Definition:Composition Functor on Categories of Subobjects
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $C$ and $D$ be objects of $\mathbf C$. Let $\map {\mathbf{Sub}_{\mathbf C} } C$ and $\map {\mathbf{Sub}_{\mathbf C} } D$ be the associated categories of subobjects. Let $g: C \to D$ be a monomorphism of $\mathbf C$. Then $g$ defines a composition functor $g_* : \map {\mathbf{Sub}_{\mathbf C} } C \to \map {\mathbf{Sub}_{\mathbf C} } D$: That it is in fact a functor is shown on Composition Functor on Categories of Subobjects is Functor.

title: Definition:Composition Functor on Slice Categories
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $C$ and $D$ be objects of $\mathbf C$. Let $\mathbf C / C$ and $\mathbf C / D$ be the associated slice categories. Let $g: C \to D$ be a morphism of $\mathbf C$. Then $g$ defines a composition functor $g_* : \mathbf C / C \to \mathbf C / D$: That it is in fact a functor is shown on Composition Functor on Slice Categories is Functor.

title: Definition:Composition Series
snippet: Let $G$ be a finite group.

title: Definition:Composition Series/Composition Factor
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $\set e = G_0 \lhd G_1 \lhd \cdots \lhd G_{n - 1} \lhd G_n = G$ be a composition series for $G$. Each of the quotient groups: $G_1 / G_0, G_2 / G_1, \ldots, G_n / G_{n - 1}$ are the composition factors of $G$.

title: Definition:Composition Series/Composition Length
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $\HH$ be a composition series for $G$. The composition length of $G$ is the length of $\HH$.

title: Definition:Composition Series/Definition 1
snippet: Let $G$ be a finite group. A composition series for $G$ is a normal series for $G$ which has no proper refinement.

title: Definition:Composition Series/Definition 2
snippet: Let $G$ be a finite group. A composition series for $G$ is a sequence of normal subgroups of $G$: $\set e = G_0 \lhd G_1 \lhd \cdots \lhd G_n = G$ where: $G_{i - 1} \lhd G_i$ denotes that $G_{i - 1}$ is a proper normal subgroup of $G_i$ such that: for all $i \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n}$, $G_{i - 1}$ is a proper maximal normal subgroup of $G_i$.

title: Definition:Composition of Densely-Defined Linear Operators
snippet: Let $\HH$ be a Hilbert space. Let $\struct {\map D S, S}$ and $\struct {\map D T, T}$ be densely-defined linear operators. Let: $\map D {S T} = \set {x \in \map D T : T x \in \map D S}$ Define $S T : \map D {S T} \to \HH$ by: $\map {\paren {S T} } x = \map {\paren {S \circ T} } x$ for each $x \in \map D {S T}$. We say that $\struct {\map D {S T}, S T}$ is the composition of $\struct {\map D S, S}$ and $\struct {\map D T, T}$.

title: Definition:Composition of Functors
snippet: Let $\mathbf C, \mathbf D$ and $\mathbf E$ be metacategories. Let $F: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ and $G: \mathbf D \to \mathbf E$ be (covariant) functors. The composition of $G$ with $F$ is the functor $GF: \mathbf C \to \mathbf E$ defined by: {{DefineFunctor |ob = $\map {GF} C := \map G {FC}$ for all objects $C$ of $\mathbf C$ |mor = $\map {GF} f := \map G {Ff}$ for all morphisms $f: C_1 \to C_2$ of $\mathbf C$ }} $GF$ is said to be a composite functor.

title: Definition:Composition of Integer
snippet: Let $n$ be a (positive) integer. A composition of $n$ is an ordered tuple $\tuple {n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_k}$ of positive integers such that: $n = \ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^k n_i$

title: Definition:Composition of Mappings
snippet: Let $f_1: S_1 \to S_2$ and $f_2: S_2 \to S_3$ be mappings such that the domain of $f_2$ is the same set as the codomain of $f_1$.

title: Definition:Composition of Mappings/Also known as
snippet: == Composition of Mappings: Also known as == Let $f_1: S_1 \to S_2$ and $f_2: S_2 \to S_3$ be mappings such that the domain of $f_2$ is the same set as the codomain of $f_1$. Let $f_2 \circ f_1$ denote the composition of $f_1$ with $f_2$. In the context of analysis, this is often found referred to as a function of a function, which (according to some sources) makes set theorists wince, as it is technically defined as a function on the codomain of a function. Such a composition is also known as a composite mapping or composite function.

title: Definition:Composition of Mappings/Binary Operation
snippet: Let $\sqbrk {S \to S}$ be the set of all mappings from a set $S$ to itself. Then the concept of composite mapping defines a binary operation on $\sqbrk {S \to S}$: $\forall f, g \in \sqbrk {S \to S}: g \circ f = \set {\tuple {s, t}: s \in S, \tuple {f \paren s, t} \in g} \in \sqbrk {S \to S}$ Thus, for every pair $\tuple {f, g}$ of mappings in $\sqbrk {S \to S}$, the composition $g \circ f$ is another element of $\sqbrk {S \to S}$.

title: Definition:Composition of Mappings/Commutative Diagram
snippet: Let $S_1$, $S_2$ and $S_3$ be sets. Let $f_1: S_1 \to S_2$ and $f_2: S_2 \to S_3$ be mappings such that the domain of $f_2$ is the same set as the codomain of $f_1$. The concept of composition of mappings can be illustrated by means of a commutative diagram. This diagram illustrates the specific example of $f_2 \circ f_1$: $\begin{xy}\xymatrix@+1em{ S_1 \ar[r]^*+{f_1} \ar@{-->}[rd]_*[l]+{f_2 \mathop \circ f_1} & S_2 \ar[d]^*+{f_2} \\ & S_3 }\end{xy}$

title: Definition:Composition of Mappings/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S_1$, $S_2$ and $S_3$ be sets. Let $f_1: S_1 \to S_2$ and $f_2: S_2 \to S_3$ be mappings such that the domain of $f_2$ is the same set as the codomain of $f_1$. The composite mapping $f_2 \circ f_1$ is defined as: $\forall x \in S_1: \map {\paren {f_2 \circ f_1} } x := \map {f_2} {\map {f_1} x}$ 850px

title: Definition:Composition of Mappings/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S_1$, $S_2$ and $S_3$ be sets. Let $f_1: S_1 \to S_2$ and $f_2: S_2 \to S_3$ be mappings such that the domain of $f_2$ is the same set as the codomain of $f_1$. The composite of $f_1$ and $f_2$ is defined and denoted as: $f_2 \circ f_1 := \set {\tuple {x, z} \in S_1 \times S_3: \tuple {\map {f_1} x, z} \in f_2}$ 850px

title: Definition:Composition of Mappings/Definition 3
snippet: Let $S_1$, $S_2$ and $S_3$ be sets. Let $f_1: S_1 \to S_2$ and $f_2: S_2 \to S_3$ be mappings such that the domain of $f_2$ is the same set as the codomain of $f_1$. The composite of $f_1$ and $f_2$ is defined and denoted as: $f_2 \circ f_1 := \set {\tuple {x, z} \in S_1 \times S_3: \exists y \in S_2: \map {f_1} x = y \land \map {f_2} y = z}$ That is: $f_2 \circ f_1 := \set {\tuple {x, z} \in S_1 \times S_3: \exists y \in S_2: \tuple {x, y} \in f_1 \land \tuple {y, z} \in f_2}$ 850px

title: Definition:Composition of Mappings/General Definition
snippet: Let $f_1: S_1 \to S_2, f_2: S_2 \to S_3, \ldots, f_n: S_n \to S_{n + 1}$ be mappings such that the domain of $f_k$ is the same set as the codomain of $f_{k - 1}$. Then the composite of $f_1, f_2, \ldots, f_n$ is defined and denoted as: {{eqn | q = \forall x \in S_1 | l = \map {\paren {f_n \circ \cdots \circ f_2 \circ f_1} } x | o = := | r = \begin {cases} \map {f_1} x & : n = 1 \\ \map {f_n} {\map {\paren {f_{n - 1} \circ \cdots \circ f_2 \circ f_1} } x} : & n > 1 \end {cases} | c = }} {{eqn | r = \map {f_n} {\dotsm \map {f_2} {\map {f_1} x} \dotsm} | c = }}

title: Definition:Composition of Mappings/Warning
snippet: Let $f_1: S_1 \to S_2$ and $f_2: S_2 \to S_3$ be mappings such that: $\Dom {f_2} \ne \Cdm {f_1}$ where $\Dom {f_2}$ and $\Cdm {f_1}$ denote domain and codomain respectively. Then the composite mapping $f_2 \circ f_1$ is not defined. Compare with the definition of composition of relations in the context of the fact that a mapping is a special kind of relation.

title: Definition:Composition of Morphisms
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $\tuple {g, f}$ be a pair of composable morphisms. Then the composition of $f$ and $g$ is a morphism $g \circ f$ of $\mathbf C$ subject to: $\map {\operatorname{dom} } {g \circ f} = \operatorname{dom} f$ $\map {\operatorname{cod} } {g \circ f} = \operatorname{cod} g$ This composition of morphisms can be thought of as an abstraction of both composition of mappings and transitive relations.

title: Definition:Composition of Morphisms of Ringed Spaces
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \OO_X}$, $\struct {Y, \OO_Y}$ and $\struct {Z, \OO_Z}$ be ringed spaces. Let $\struct {f, f^\sharp: \OO_Y \to f_* \OO_X} : \struct {X, \OO_X} \to \struct {Y, \OO_Y}$ $\struct {g, g^\sharp: \OO_Z \to g_* \OO_Y} : \struct {Y, \OO_Y} \to \struct {Z, \OO_Z}$ be morphisms of ringed spaces. Let $g_* f^\sharp: g_* \OO_Y \to g_* f_* \OO_X$ denote the pushforward of $f^\sharp$ along $g$.

title: Definition:Composition of Ratio
snippet: Let $R = a : b$ be a ratio. Then the composition of $R$ is the ratio $a + b : b$. Category:Definitions/Euclidean Algebra

title: Definition:Composition of Reduced Group Words
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $v$ and $w$ be reduced group words on $X$. The composition of $v$ and $w$ is the reduced form of their concatenation: $v \cdot w = \operatorname{red}(vw)$

title: Definition:Composition of Relations
snippet: Let $\RR_1 \subseteq S_1 \times T_1$ and $\RR_2 \subseteq S_2 \times T_2$ be relations. Then the composite of $\RR_1$ and $\RR_2$ is defined and denoted as: $\RR_2 \circ \RR_1 := \set {\tuple {x, z} \in S_1 \times T_2: \exists y \in S_2 \cap T_1: \tuple {x, y} \in \RR_1 \land \tuple {y, z} \in \RR_2}$ {{Mistake|I think this should be $\RR_2 \circ \RR_1 \sqbrk {S_1} \equal \RR_2 \sqbrk {\RR_1 \sqbrk {S_1} \cap S_2}$, in which case this doesn't define a relation, otherwise the notation needs to be defined}} It is clear that the composite relation $\RR_2 \circ \RR_1$ can also be defined as:…

title: Definition:Composition of Subsets of Topological Group
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \odot, \tau}$ be a topological group. Let $A, B \subseteq G$. We define the composition $A \odot B$ by: $A \odot B = \set {a \odot b : a \in A, \, b \in B}$

title: Definition:Compound Distribution
snippet: Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_N$ be pairwise independent random variables such that: the $X_i$ may or may not have the same probability distribution $N$ itself may also be a (discrete) random variable. Let: $S_N : X_1 + X_2 + \cdots + X_N$ Then the probability distribution of $S_N$ is known as a compound distribution.

title: Definition:Compound Fraction/Also known as
snippet: == Compound Fractions: Also known as == A compound fraction is also known as a complex fraction. However, the latter is not endorsed by as it could be construed to mean something involving complex numbers.

title: Definition:Compound Interest Table
snippet: A compound interest table is a reference table which is used to aid calculations involving compound interest. It typically contains calculated values for the following items:

title: Definition:Compound Interest Table/Accumulation Factor
snippet: Let $P$ be a principal invested under compound interest with an interest rate $r$ over a number of conversion periods $n$. The accumulation factor of $P$ is defined as: $\paren {1 + r}^n$ This is the amount to which $1$ unit of $P$ will increase to after $n$ conversion periods at interest rate $r$

title: Definition:Compound Interest Table/Also known as
snippet: == Compound Interest Table: Also known as == A compound interest table is also known as a table of compound interest.

title: Definition:Compound Interest Table/Annuity Amount
snippet: Let a principal $P$ be invested every conversion period, and accumulated under compound interest with an interest rate $r$ over a number of conversion periods $n$. The annuity amount of $P$ is defined as: $P \dfrac {\paren {1 + r}^n - 1} r$

title: Definition:Compound Interest Table/Annuity Present Value
snippet: Let a principal $P$ be invested every conversion period, and accumulated under compound interest with an interest rate $r$ over a number of conversion periods $n$. The present value of $P$ is defined as: $\dfrac {1 - \paren {1 + r}^{-n} } r$ That is, it is the amount necessary to provide $1$ unit payment at the end of $n$ conversion periods.

title: Definition:Compound Interest Table/Discount Factor
snippet: Let $P$ be a principal invested under compound interest with an interest rate $r$ over a number of conversion periods $n$. The discount factor of $P$ is defined as: $\paren {1 + r}^{-n}$ This is the amount of principal which will increase to $1$ unit after $n$ conversion periods at interest rate $r$.

title: Definition:Compound Number
snippet: A compound number is a specification of a physical quantity using a mixture of units of measurement.

title: Definition:Compound Pendulum/Period
snippet: The period of a compound pendulum $\PP$ is the time period through which $\PP$ takes to travel from one end of its path to the other, and back again.

title: Definition:Compound Ratio
snippet: Let $R_1 = a : b$ and $R_2 = c : d$ be ratios. The compound ratio of $R_1$ and $R_2$ is defined as: $R_1 R_2 = a c : b d$ That is, it is the product of the two ratios.

title: Definition:Compound Statement
snippet: A compound statement is a statement which results from the application of one or more logical connectives to a collection of simple statements.

title: Definition:Compound Statement/Also defined as
snippet: == Compound Statement: Also defined as == Some sources define a compound statement, in the context of symbolic logic, as a statement form other than: logical not conjunction disjunction conditional biconditional. Such is the approach of , who separately categorises the truth tables of those five statement forms as fundamental. Hence any statement form which is not one of those fundamental five is (implicitly) defined as being compound.

title: Definition:Compound Statement/Also known as
snippet: == Compound Statement: Also known as == A compound statement can also be referred to as: a compound sentential function a compound sentence a molecular sentence.

title: Definition:Compound Statement/Ill-Formed
snippet: The substatements in a compound statement, which are joined by a connective, may be compound statements themselves. It is clearly necessary that the interpretation of such a compound statement is unambiguous. A compound statement is said to be ill-formed if it is ambiguous as to how its substatements are grouped by the action of the connectives. For example, in natural language: I would like some juice or water with ice. can mean either: I would like some juice, or water with ice. or: I would like some juice with ice, or water with ice.

title: Definition:Compound Statement/Substatement
snippet: A substatement of a compound statement is one of the statements that comprise it.

title: Definition:Compression
snippet: Compression is a force on a body whose action tends to make that body smaller. The word is also used to denote the change in shape of that body as a result of the force applied. 600px In the above diagram: the solid line indicates the original shape of the body the dotted line indicates the shape of the body under compression.

title: Definition:Compression/Stress
snippet: Compressive stress is a measure of the internal forces on a body in reaction to a force of compression. 600px In the above diagram: the solid line indicates the original shape of the body the dotted line indicates the shape of the body under compression.

title: Definition:Compton Wavelength
snippet: Let $P$ be a particle. The Compton wavelength of $P$ is defined as the wavelength of the photon which has the same rest energy as $P$. It is defined as: $\lambda = \dfrac h {m c}$ where: $\lambda$ denotes the Compton wavelength of $P$ $m$ denotes the mass of $P$ $h$ denotes Planck's constant $c$ denotes the speed of light.

title: Definition:Compton Wavelength/Dimension
snippet: The Compton wavelength has the dimension $\mathsf L$. This arises from its definition as energy per unit frequency divided by mass times speed: $\dfrac {\mathsf {M L^2 T^{-2} } } {\mathsf {T^{-1} } \times \mathsf {L T^{-1} } \times \mathsf M}$ Category:Definitions/Compton Wavelength Category:Definitions/Dimensions of Measurement

title: Definition:Computability Theory
snippet: Computability theory is a branch of mathematical logic which concerns itself with the algorithmic implementation of mathematical proofs. It focuses on: the theoretical limits of computers and algorithms whether certain problems are decidable.

title: Definition:Computability Theory/Also defined as
snippet: == Computability Theory: Also known as == Some sources bracket computability theory and recursion theory into the same category.

title: Definition:Computable
snippet: An object is said to be computable it can be calculated by means of an algorithm.

title: Definition:Computable/Number
snippet: A number is said to be computable it can be determined by means of an algorithm to an arbitrary given level of accuracy.

title: Definition:Computable Complex Number
snippet: Let: $z = a + b i$ be a complex number. Suppose that both $a$ and $b$ are computable real numbers. Then $z$ is a computable complex number.

title: Definition:Computable Rational Sequence
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \in \N}$ be a infinite sequence of rational numbers. Then, $\sequence {x_n}$ is a computable rational sequence there exist total recursive functions $f, g : \N \to \N$ such that, for all $n \in \N$: $x_n = \dfrac {k_n} {\map g n + 1}$ where $\map f n$ codes the integer $k_n$.

title: Definition:Computable Real-Valued Function
snippet: Let $D \subseteq \R^n$ be a subset of real cartesian $n$-space. Let $f : D \to \R$ be a real-valued function on $D$. Suppose that $f$ is both sequentially computable and computably uniformly continuous. Then, $f$ is computable.

title: Definition:Computable Real Function
snippet: Let $f : \R \to \R$ be a real function. Suppose that $f$ is both sequentially computable and computably uniformly continuous. Then $f$ is a computable real function.

title: Definition:Computable Real Number
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number. Suppose there exists a total recursive function $f : \N \to \N$ such that: For every $n \in \N$, $\map f n$ codes an integer $k$ such that: $\dfrac {k - 1} {n + 1} < x < \dfrac {k + 1} {n + 1}$ Then $x$ is a computable real number.

title: Definition:Computable Real Sequence
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a real sequence. Suppose that there exists a total recursive function $f : \N^2 \to \N$ such that: For every $m, n \in \N$, $\map f {m, n}$ codes an integer $k$ such that: $\dfrac {k - 1} {n + 1} < x_m < \dfrac {k + 1} {n + 1}$ Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is a computable real sequence.

title: Definition:Computably Uniformly Continuous Real-Valued Function
snippet: Let $D \subseteq \R^n$ be a subset of real cartesian $n$-space. Let $f : D \to \R$ be a real-valued function on $D$. Suppose there exists a total recursive function $d : \N \to \N$ such that: For every $n \in \N$ and $\bsx, \bsy \in D$ such that: $\norm {\bsx - \bsy} < \dfrac 1 {\map d n + 1}$ where $\norm \cdot$ is the Euclidean norm, it holds that: $\size {\map f \bsx - \map f \bsy} < \dfrac 1 {n + 1}$ Then $f$ is computably uniformly continuous.

title: Definition:Computably Uniformly Continuous Real Function
snippet: Let $f : \R \to \R$ be a real function. Suppose there exists a total recursive function $d : \N \to \N$ such that: For every $n \in \N$ and $x, y \in \R$ such that: $\size {x - y} < \dfrac 1 {\map d n + 1}$ it holds that: $\size {\map f x - \map f y} < \dfrac 1 {n + 1}$ Then $f$ is computably uniformly continuous.

title: Definition:Computational Group Theory
snippet: Computational group theory is the study of groups by means of computers. It is concerned with designing and analysing algorithms and data structures to compute information about groups.

title: Definition:Computational Method
snippet: A computational method is an ordered quadruple $\left({Q, I, \Omega, f}\right)$ in which: $Q$ is a set representing the states of the computation $I$ is a set representing the input to the computation $\Omega$ is a set representing the output from the computation $f: Q \to Q$ is a mapping representing the computational rule subject to the following constraints: $I \subseteq Q$ and $\Omega \subseteq Q$ $\forall x \in \Omega: f \left({x}\right) = x$

title: Definition:Computational Method/Computational Sequence
snippet: Consider the computational method $\left({Q, I, \Omega, f}\right)$ in which: $Q$ represents the set of states of the computation $I$ represents the input to the computation $\Omega$ represents the output from the computation $f: Q \to Q$ represents the computational rule Each $x \in I$ defines a computational sequence $x_0, x_1, x_2, \ldots$ as follows: $x_0 = x$ $\forall k \ge 0: x_{k+1} = f \left({x_k}\right)$

title: Definition:Computational Method/Computational Sequence/Termination
snippet: A computational sequence $x_0, x_1, x_2, \ldots$ is said to terminate in $k$ steps if $k$ is the smallest integer for which $x_k \in \Omega$. In this case, it produces the output $x_k$ from $x$. Some computational sequences may never terminate.

title: Definition:Concatenation
snippet: Topology: Concatenation: the joining together of two maps on the unit order-$n$ cube Concatenation of Paths: an instance of such topological concatenation Vector Analysis: Concatenation of Contours: the joining together of two contours to form a longer contour. Formal Systems: Concatenation (Formal Systems): the placing of symbols next to each other to form a string. Set Theory, Abstract Algebra and so on: Concatenation of Ordered Tuples: putting together two ordered tuples to form a new one. Mathematical Logic: Concatenation of URM Programs

title: Definition:Concatenation/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Concatenation == The word concatenation derives from the Latin com- for with/together and the Latin word catena for chain. However, the end result of such an operation is not to be confused with a (set theoretical) chain. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Concatenation (Formal Systems)
snippet: Let $\AA$ be an alphabet of symbols. Concatenation is the process of placing elements of $\AA$ and words in $\AA$ next to each other to form a longer word.

title: Definition:Concatenation (Topology)
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $c_1, c_2: \closedint 0 1^n \to S$ be maps. Let $c_1$ and $c_2$ both satisfy the concatenation criterion: $\map c {\partial \closedint 0 1^n} = x_0$. Then the concatenation $c_1 * c_2$ is defined as: $\map {\paren {c_1 * c_2} } {t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_n} = \begin {cases} \map {c_1} {2 t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_n} & : t_1 \in \closedint 0 {1/2} \\ \map {c_2} {2 t_1 - 1, t_2, \ldots, t_n} & : t_1 \in \closedint {1/2} 1 \end{cases}$ where $\tuple {t_1, \ldots, t_n}$ are coordinates in the $n$-cube.

title: Definition:Concatenation of Contours
snippet: Let $\R^n$ be a real cartesian space of $n$ dimensions. Let $C$ and $D$ be contours in $\R^n$. Thus: $C$ is a (finite) sequence of directed smooth curves $\sequence {C_1, \ldots, C_n}$ $D$ is a (finite) sequence of directed smooth curves $\sequence {D_1, \ldots, D_m}$. Let $C_i$ be parameterized by the smooth path: $\gamma_i: \closedint {a_i} {b_i} \to \R^n$ for all $i \in \set {1, \ldots, n}$ Let $D_i$ be parameterized by the smooth path: $\sigma_i: \closedint {c_i} {d_i} \to \R^n$ for all $i \in \set {1, \ldots, m}$ Let $\map {\gamma_n} {b_n} = \map {\sigma_1} {c_1}$.

title: Definition:Concatenation of Contours/Complex Plane
snippet: Let $C$ and $D$ be contours in the complex plane $\C$. Thus: $C$ is a (finite) sequence of directed smooth curves $\sequence {C_1, \ldots, C_n}$ $D$ is a (finite) sequence of directed smooth curves $\sequence {D_1, \ldots, D_m}$. Let $C_i$ be parameterized by the smooth path: $\gamma_i: \closedint {a_i} {b_i} \to \C$ for all $i \in \set {1, \ldots, n}$ Let $D_i$ be parameterized by the smooth path: $\sigma_i: \closedint {c_i} {d_i} \to \C$ for all $i \in \set {1, \ldots, m}$ Let $\map {\gamma_n} {b_n} = \map {\sigma_1} {c_1}$.

title: Definition:Concatenation of Ordered Tuples
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $w, w'$ be ordered tuples in $S$ of lengths $n$ and $n'$, respectively. Then the concatenation of $w$ and $w'$, denoted $w * w'$ or simply $w w'$, is the ordered tuple of $n + n'$ terms defined by: $\quad \map {w * w'} i := \begin{cases} \map w i & : \text {if } 1 \le i \le n \\ \map {w'} {i - n} & : \text {if } n < i \le n + n' \end{cases}$

title: Definition:Concatenation of Paths
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space. Let $f, g: \closedint 0 1 \to X$ be paths. Let $\map f 1 = \map g 0$. The concatenation of $f$ and $g$ is the mapping $f * g: \closedint 0 1 \to X$ defined by: $\ds \map {\paren {f * g} } s = \begin {cases} \map f {2 s} & : 0 \le s \le \dfrac 1 2 \\ \map g {2 s - 1} & : \dfrac 1 2 \le s \le 1 \end {cases}$

title: Definition:Concatenation of URM Programs
snippet: Let $P$ and $Q$ be URM programs. The concatenation of $P$ and $Q$ is denoted $P * Q$. It consists of program $P$ followed immediately by program $Q$. If $P$ and $Q$ compute particular functions, then it is usually necessary to make modifications to either $P$ or $Q$, or both, to make sure that the concatenated program continues to compute a function. The simplest concatenation is illustrated in Composition of One-Variable URM Computable Functions.

snippet: Geometry: Concave Geometric Figure Concave Polygon Concave Polyhedron Real Analysis Concave Real Function

snippet: == Historical Note on Concave Circumference == The concept of the concave circumference arises in as a way of rigorously specifying the relationship between a point and the circumference of the circle under investigation. As such it is not specifically defined in , but is tacitly understood. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Concave Envelope
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological vector space over $\R$. Let $C \subseteq X$ be a non-empty closed convex set. Let $f : C \to \R$ be a function. Define an extended real-valued function $\hat f : C \to \overline \R$ by: $\map {\hat f} x = \inf \set {\map g x : g \ge f \text { and } g \text { is affine and continuous} }$ where we take $\inf \O = \infty$. We say that $\hat f$ is the concave envelope of $f$.

title: Definition:Concave Polygon
snippet: Let $P$ be a polygon. $P$ is a concave polygon : at least one internal angle of $P$ is greater than $180 \degrees$.

title: Definition:Concave Polyhedron
snippet: Let $P$ be a polyhedron.

title: Definition:Concave Polyhedron/Definition 1
snippet: Let $P$ be a polyhedron. $P$ is a concave polyhedron : at least one face of $P$ lies in a plane which intersects at least one other face.

title: Definition:Concave Polyhedron/Definition 2
snippet: Let $P$ be a polyhedron. $P$ is a concave polyhedron : at least one face of $P$ lies in a plane such that $P$ does not lie completely on one side of that plane.

title: Definition:Concave Real Function
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function which is defined on a real interval $I$.

title: Definition:Concave Real Function/Also known as
snippet: == Concave Real Function: Also known as == A concave function can also be referred to as: a concave down function a convex up function.

title: Definition:Concave Real Function/Definition 1
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function which is defined on a real interval $I$. $f$ is concave on $I$ : $\forall x, y \in I: \forall \alpha, \beta \in \R_{>0}, \alpha + \beta = 1: \map f {\alpha x + \beta y} \ge \alpha \map f x + \beta \map f y$ 700px

title: Definition:Concave Real Function/Definition 1/Strictly
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function which is defined on a real interval $I$. $f$ is strictly concave on $I$ : $\forall x, y \in I, x \ne y: \forall \alpha, \beta \in \R_{>0}, \alpha + \beta = 1: \map f {\alpha x + \beta y} > \alpha \map f x + \beta \map f y$ 700px The geometric interpretation is that any point on the chord drawn on the graph of any strictly concave function always lies below the graph.

title: Definition:Concave Real Function/Definition 2
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function which is defined on a real interval $I$. $f$ is concave on $I$ : $\ds \forall x_1, x_2, x_3 \in I: x_1 < x_2< x_3: \frac {\map f {x_2} - \map f {x_1} } {x_2 - x_1} \ge \frac {\map f {x_3} - \map f {x_2} } {x_3 - x_2}$ Hence a geometrical interpretation: the slope of $P_1 P_2$ is greater than that of $P_2 P_3$: 500px

title: Definition:Concave Real Function/Definition 2/Strictly
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function which is defined on a real interval $I$. $f$ is strictly concave on $I$ : $\forall x_1, x_2, x_3 \in I: x_1 \dfrac {\map f {x_3} - \map f {x_2} } {x_3 - x_2}$ Hence a geometrical interpretation: the slope of $P_1 P_2$ is greater than that of $P_2 P_3$: 500px

title: Definition:Concave Real Function/Definition 3
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function which is defined on a real interval $I$. $f$ is concave on $I$ : $\forall x_1, x_2, x_3 \in I: x_1 < x_2< x_3: \dfrac {\map f {x_2} - \map f {x_1} } {x_2 - x_1} \ge \dfrac {\map f {x_3} - \map f {x_1} } {x_3 - x_1}$ Hence a geometrical interpretation: the slope of $P_1 P_2$ is greater than that of $P_1 P_3$: 500px

title: Definition:Concave Real Function/Definition 3/Strictly
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function which is defined on a real interval $I$. $f$ is strictly concave on $I$ : $\forall x_1, x_2, x_3 \in I: x_1 \dfrac {\map f {x_3} - \map f {x_1} } {x_3 - x_1}$ Hence a geometrical interpretation: the slope of $P_1 P_2$ is greater than that of $P_1 P_3$: 500px

title: Definition:Concave Real Function/Geometric Interpretation
snippet: == Geometric Interpretation of Concave Real Function == Let $f$ be a concave real function. Then: for every pair of points $A$ and $B$ on the graph of $f$, the chord $AB$ lies entirely below the graph.

title: Definition:Concave Real Function/Point
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function which is defined on a real interval $I$. Let $a \in I$ be a point in the domain of $f$. Then: $f$ is concave at $a$ there exists a neighborhood of $a$ on which $f$ is concave.

title: Definition:Concave Real Function/Vector Space
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a vector space over $\GF$. Let $C \subseteq X$ be a convex set. Let $f: C \to \overline \R$ be an extended real-valued function. We say that $f$ is concave : $\map f {t x + \paren {1 - t} y} \ge t \map f x + \paren {1 - t} \map f y$ for each $t \in \openint 0 1$ and $x, y \in C$.

title: Definition:Concentration on Measurable Set
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space.

title: Definition:Concentration on Measurable Set/Complex Measure/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\mu$ be a complex measure on $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. Let $\size \mu$ be the variation of $\mu$. Let $E \in \Sigma$. We say that $\mu$ is concentrated on $E$ : $\map {\size \mu} {E^c} = 0$

title: Definition:Concentration on Measurable Set/Complex Measure/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\mu$ be a complex measure on $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. Let $E \in \Sigma$. We say that $\mu$ is concentrated on $E$ : for every $\Sigma$-measurable set $A \subseteq E^c$, we have $\map \mu A = 0$.

title: Definition:Concentration on Measurable Set/Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. Let $E \in \Sigma$. We say that $\mu$ is concentrated on $E$ : $\map \mu {E^c} = 0$

title: Definition:Concentration on Measurable Set/Signed Measure/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\mu$ be a signed measure on $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. Let $\size \mu$ be the variation of $\mu$. Let $E \in \Sigma$. We say that $\mu$ is concentrated on $E$ : $\map {\size \mu} {E^c} = 0$

title: Definition:Concentration on Measurable Set/Signed Measure/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\mu$ be a signed measure on $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. Let $E \in \Sigma$. We say that $\mu$ is concentrated on $E$ : for every $\Sigma$-measurable set $A \subseteq E^c$, we have $\map \mu A = 0$.

title: Definition:Concentric
snippet: Two or more geometric figures are described as being concentric they share the same center of symmetry.

title: Definition:Concentric/Circles
snippet: Circles are said to be concentric if they both have the same point as the center. 320px

title: Definition:Concentric Circle Topology
snippet: Open Set of $T$ Let $C_1$ and $C_2$ be concentric circles in the Cartesian plane $\R^2$ such that $C_1$ is inside $C_2$. Let $S = C_1 \cup C_2$. Let $\BB$ be the set of sets consisting of: all singleton sets of $C_2$ all open intervals on $C_1$ each together with its projection from the center of the circles onto $C_2$ except for the midpoint. $\BB$ is then taken to be the sub-basis for a topology $\tau$ on $S$. Thus $\tau$ is referred to as the concentric circle topology. The topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is referred to as the concentric circle space.

title: Definition:Concentric Spheres
snippet: Spheres are said to be concentric if they both have the same point as the center.

title: Definition:Conchoid
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a curve. Let $P$ be a fixed point which may or may not lie on $\CC$ itself. A conchoid is the locus of points $p$ such that: each $p$ is on a straight line $\LL$ that passes through $P$ and intersects $\CC$ the distance from $p$ to the point of intersection with $\CC$ is a specified constant. As there are in general $2$ such points $p$ which satisfy the criteria, a conchoid has in most cases two branches.

title: Definition:Conchoid/Branch
snippet: Let $\KK$ be a conchoid. The two parts of $\KK$ corresponding to the loci of the points at either endpoint of the generating line segment are referred to as the branches of $\KK$.

title: Definition:Conchoid/Directrix
snippet: Let $\KK$ be a conchoid. Let $\CC$ be the curve which the conchoid is constructed. $\CC$ is known as the directrix of $\KK$.

title: Definition:Conchoid/Focus Point
snippet: Let $\KK$ be a conchoid. Let $P$ be the fixed point on which the moving straight line $\LL$ is constrained to lie. $P$ is known as the focus point of $\KK$.

title: Definition:Conchoid/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Conchoid == The word conchoid derives from the Latin concha, which means . Ultimately the word derives from the Ancient Greek κόγχη (kónkhē) plus -oid, or directly from Ancient Greek κογχοειδής (konkhoeidḗs), which refers to anything with the general shape of a shell. It is properly pronounced kon-khoid, where the kh sound is the one found in the Scots loch or German ich. However, it is commonplace to use the pronunciation kon-koid. Note that the pronunciations kon-tshoid and kon-shoid are technically incorrect. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Conchoid of Nicomedes
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a straight line. Let $P$ be a fixed point not on $\CC$ but a perpendicular distance $a$ from $\CC$. The conchoid of Nicomedes is the conchoid defined as the locus of points $Q$ such that a straight line segment between $Q$ and $\CC$ passing through $P$ has a constant length $b$. 520px

title: Definition:Conchoid of Nicomedes/Also known as
snippet: == Conchoid of Nicomedes: Also known as == Some sources suggest that the conchoid of Nicomedes can also be referred to as a cochloid. However, this usage can be confused easily with the cochleoid which some dictionaries give cochloid as an alternative for. Others refer to it as merely a conchoid, but that term is best used to refer to the more general object of which the conchoid of Nicomedes is an example.

title: Definition:Conchoid of Nicomedes/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Conchoid of Nicomedes == designed the curve now known as the conchoid of Nicomedes specifically for solving the problem of Doubling the Cube. It can also be used for Trisecting the Angle.

title: Definition:Conclusion
snippet: A conclusion is a statement that is obtained as the result of the process of an argument.

title: Definition:Conclusion/Statistics
snippet: In the context of statistics, a conclusion is a decision as to accept or reject a statistical hypothesis on the basis of the available evidence.

title: Definition:Concomitant Variable
snippet: A concomitant variable is a variable which is not influenced by treatments.

snippet: A concrete category $\mathbf C$ is a category such that:

title: Definition:Concrete Category/Definition 2

title: Definition:Concrete Number
snippet: A concrete number is a number which is used to enumerate a specific set of physical objects.

title: Definition:Concrete Number/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Concrete Number == The concrete number is the first stage of the appreciation of a number as an abstract concept.

title: Definition:Concurrent
snippet: Concurrent means having a common point.

title: Definition:Concurrent Lines
snippet: A set of $3$ or more (straight) lines through a single point are concurrent. Such lines are said to concur.

title: Definition:Concyclic Points
snippet: A set of $4$ or more points $S = \set {P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_n}$ is concyclic if they all lie on the circumference of a circle. 320px In the above diagram, points $A, B, C, D$ are concyclic, as they all lie on the circumference of the circle centered at $O$.

title: Definition:Condensation Point
snippet: Let $T = \struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $A \subseteq X$. A condensation point of $A$ is a limit point $x$ of $A$ such that every open set containing $x$ also contains an uncountable number of points of $A$.

title: Definition:Condensed Series
snippet: Let $\sequence {a_n}: n \mapsto \map a n$ be a decreasing sequence of strictly positive terms in $\R$ which converges with a limit of zero. That is, for every $n$ in the domain of $\sequence {a_n}$: $a_n > 0, a_{n + 1} \le a_n$, and $a_n \to 0$ as $n \to +\infty$. The series: $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty 2^n \map a {2^n}$ is called the condensed form of the series: $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n$

title: Definition:Condition Number
snippet: A condition number is a coefficient which measures the degree of ill-conditioning of a mathematical problem.

title: Definition:Conditional
snippet: The conditional is a binary connective: $p \implies q$ defined as: If $p$ is true, then $q$ is true. This is known as a conditional statement. $p \implies q$ is voiced: if $p$ then $q$ or: $p$ implies $q$ We are at liberty to write this the other way round. $q \impliedby p$ means the same as $p \implies q$. $q \impliedby p$ is sometimes known as a reverse implication. The rest of this article interprets the conditional in its usual mathematical sense. That is, $p \implies q$ is considered to be true whenever: $p$ is false or: $q$ is true.

title: Definition:Conditional/Also known as
snippet: == Conditional: Also known as == A conditional is also known as: a conditional statement a conditional sentence a conditional proposition a hypothetical an implication an implicative statement a logical implication a material implication.

title: Definition:Conditional/Antecedent
snippet: In a conditional $p \implies q$, the statement $p$ is the antecedent.

title: Definition:Conditional/Boolean Interpretation
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ be propositional formulas. Let $\implies$ denote the conditional operator. The truth value of $\mathbf A \implies \mathbf B$ under a boolean interpretation $v$ is given by: $\map v {\mathbf A \implies \mathbf B} = \begin{cases} \T & : \map v {\mathbf A} = \F \text{ or } \map v {\mathbf B} = \T \\ \F & : \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$ and the truth value of $\mathbf A \impliedby \mathbf B$ under a boolean interpretation $v$ is given by: $\map v {\mathbf A \impliedby \mathbf B} = \begin{cases} \T & : \map v {\mathbf A} = \T \text{ or } \map v {\mathbf B} = \F \\…

title: Definition:Conditional/Consequent
snippet: In a conditional $p \implies q$, the statement $q$ is the consequent. That is, the consequent expresses the necessary outcome of the antecedent.

title: Definition:Conditional/Formal Implication
snippet: Formal implication is a usage of an implication in which it is necessary for there to be a formal connection between the antecedent and the consequent in order for the implication to have any semantic meaning.

title: Definition:Conditional/Language of Conditional
snippet: The conditional has been discussed at great length throughout the ages, and a whole language has evolved around it. For now, here are a few definitions:

title: Definition:Conditional/Language of Conditional/Strong
snippet: In a conditional $p \implies q$, the statement $p$ is stronger than $q$.

title: Definition:Conditional/Language of Conditional/Weak

title: Definition:Conditional/Necessary Condition
snippet: Let $p \implies q$ be a conditional statement. Then $q$ is a necessary condition for $p$. That is, if $p \implies q$, then it is necessary that $q$ be true for $p$ to be true. This is because unless $q$ is true, $p$ cannot be true.

title: Definition:Conditional/Notational Variants/Sign of Illation
snippet: The sign of illation $-\!\!\!<$ is a notation invented by to denote the conditional operator. derives $-\!\!\!<$ as a variant of the sign $\le$ for less than or equal to, so as to denote that: $A \mathop {-\!\!\!<} B$ represents the situation such that whenever a particular statement $A$ is true, then so is statement $B$. It is rarely (if ever) seen nowadays except as a historical curiosity.

title: Definition:Conditional/Notational Variants/Sign of Illation/Linguistic Note

title: Definition:Conditional/Subimplicant
snippet: In a conditional $p \implies q$, the statement $q$ is subimplicant to $p$.

title: Definition:Conditional/Sufficient Condition
snippet: Let $p \implies q$ be a conditional statement. Then $p$ is a sufficient condition for $q$. That is, if $p \implies q$, then for $q$ to be true, it is sufficient to know that $p$ is true. This is because of the fact that if you know that $p$ is true, you know enough to know also that $q$ is true.

title: Definition:Conditional/Superimplicant
snippet: In a conditional $p \implies q$, the statement $p$ is superimplicant to $q$.

title: Definition:Conditional/Truth Table
snippet: The characteristic truth table of the conditional (implication) operator $p \implies q$ is as follows: $\begin {array} {|cc||c|} \hline p & q & p \implies q \\ \hline \F & \F & \T \\ \F & \T & \T \\ \T & \F & \F \\ \T & \T & \T \\ \hline \end {array}$ As $\implies$ is not commutative, it is also instructive to give a characteristic truth tables for $p \impliedby q$ (which of course is the same as $q \implies p$).

title: Definition:Conditional/Truth Table/Matrix Form
snippet: The characteristic truth table of the conditional (implication) operator $p \implies q$ can be presented in matrix form as follows: $\begin{array}{c|cc} \implies & \T & \F \\ \hline \T & \T & \F \\ \F & \T & \T \\ \end{array}$ As $\implies$ is not commutative, it is also instructive to give a truth table for $p \impliedby q$ (which of course is the same as $q \implies p$).

title: Definition:Conditional/Truth Table/Number
snippet: The truth table number of the conjunction operator $p \land q$ is as follows: Ascending order: $1101$ or $\T \T \F \T$ Descending order: $1011$ or $\T \F \T \T$ As $\implies$ is not commutative, it is also instructive to give a truth table number for $p \impliedby q$ (which of course is the same as $q \implies p$).
