title: Definition:Connection on Manifold
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold with or without boundary. Let $\map {\mathfrak X} M$ be the space of smooth vector fields on $M$. Let $\map {C^\infty} M$ be the space of smooth real functions on $M$. Let $\nabla : \map {\mathfrak X} M \times \map {\mathfrak X} M \to \map {\mathfrak X} M$ be the map be written $\tuple {X, Y} \mapsto \nabla_X Y$ where $X, Y \in \map {\mathfrak X} M$, and $\times$ denotes the cartesian product.

title: Definition:Connectivity
snippet: Let $G$ be a graph. Then the connectivity of $G$, denoted $\map \kappa G$, is the smallest $k \in \Z_{>0}$ such that $G$ is $k$-connected. If $G$ is disconnected, or if $G$ has fewer than $2$ vertices, then $\map \kappa G = 0$.

title: Definition:Conover Squared Rank Test
snippet: The Conover squared rank test is a nonparametric test for homogeneity of variance.

title: Definition:Conover Squared Rank Test/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Conover Squared Rank Test == The Conover squared rank test was designed by in $1980$.

title: Definition:Consecutive Strategic Games
snippet: The interpretation of a strategic game $G$ can be that a particular play of $G$ is one of a sequence of such plays. In such a case, it is assumed that a player can form an expectation of the behaviour of other players through experience of previous plays.

title: Definition:Consequence
snippet: Logic: In particular, the term logical consequence may refer to: Logical Implication Provable Consequence Semantic Consequence Game Theory: Consequence (Game Theory) Consequence Function

title: Definition:Consequence (Game Theory)
snippet: A consequence is a state in a game which results from a move made by a player in that game made according to the rules.

title: Definition:Consequence Function
snippet: Let $G$ be a game. Let $P$ be a player of $G$. Let $A$ be the set of moves available to $P$. Let $C$ be the set of consequences of those moves. A consequence function for $P$ is a mapping from the set $A$ to the set $C$: $g: A \to C$

title: Definition:Consequence Function with Probability
snippet: Let $G$ be a game. Let $P$ be a player of $G$. Let $A$ be the set of moves available to $P$. Let $C$ be the set of consequences of those moves. Let the consequences of those moves be affected by a random variable on a probability space $\Omega$ whose realization is not known to the players before they make their moves. A consequence function for $P$ is a mapping from $A \times \Omega$ to $C$: $g: A \times \Omega \to C$ interpreted as that $\map g a$ is the consequence when the move is $a \in A$ and the realization $\omega$ of the random variable is $\omega \in \Omega$.

title: Definition:Consequent/Also defined as
snippet: Let $P = a \circ b$ be an expression. The term $b$ is known as the consequent of $P$. The term is usually applied when the expression in question is a ratio. For example, in $5 : 7$, the number $7$ is the consequent.

title: Definition:Consequent/Also known as
snippet: Some authors use the term conclusion for consequent, but on we reserve the use of conclusion for an element of the structure of a logical argument. The term consequent clause can sometimes be seen, particularly when the conditional it is part of consists of a statement in natural language. The archaic terms implicate and apodosis can sometimes be found.

title: Definition:Consequent/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Consequent == The word consequent is usually found in classical mathematical literature, notably . The word comes from the Greek, and literally means following term. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Conservation Condition
snippet: A network satisfies the conservation condition , at every node which is neither a source nor a sink, the weights going in match the weights going out.

title: Definition:Conservative Force/Definition 1
snippet: A conservative force is a force which gives rise to a conservative vector field. That is, a vector field which acts on a particle $p$ in such a way that the work done on moving $p$ depends only on where it started and where it ended up, and not on the path taken to get there.

title: Definition:Conservative Force/Definition 2
snippet: A conservative force is a force such that the work evaluated around every simple closed contour is zero.

title: Definition:Conservative Strategy
snippet: There are two conservative strategies:

title: Definition:Conservative Strategy/Maximin Strategy
snippet: Let $G$ be a two-person game between players $A$ and $B$. A maximin strategy for $A$ is one in which: $(1): \quad A$ assumes that $B$ will make that move which makes $A$'s payoff (or average payoff, in the case of a random element) as small as possible. $(2): \quad A$ then makes the move which makes this smallest gain the largest possible. Hence it is the strategy that will maximise $A$'s minimum payoff. The reasoning is: I fear that my opponent will make the move which makes my payoff the smallest possible. Hence I make my move so as to make this smallest payoff as large as possible.

title: Definition:Conservative Strategy/Minimax Strategy
snippet: Let $G$ be a two-person game between players $A$ and $B$. A minimax strategy for $B$ is one in which: $(1): \quad B$ assumes that $A$ will make that move which makes $A$'s payoff (or average payoff, in the case of a random element) as large as possible. $(2): \quad B$ then makes the move which makes this largest gain the smallest possible. Hence it is the strategy that will minimise $A$'s maximum payoff. The reasoning is: I expect that my opponent will make the move which makes his payoff the largest possible. Hence I make my move so as to make this largest payoff as small as possible.

title: Definition:Conservative Vector Field
snippet: Let $R$ be a simply connected region of space. Let $\mathbf V$ be a vector field with continuous first partial derivatives acting over $R$.

title: Definition:Conservative Vector Field/Also known as
snippet: == Conservative Vector Field: Also known as == A conservative vector field is also known in the literature as: a conservative field a scalar potential field (from its property that it is the gradient of some scalar field) a non-curl field an irrotational field a lamellar field. A vector in such a conservative vector field is sometimes known as: an irrotational vector a lamellar vector.

title: Definition:Conservative Vector Field/Definition 1
snippet: Let $R$ be a simply connected region of space. Let $\mathbf V$ be a vector field with continuous first partial derivatives acting over $R$. $\mathbf V$ is a conservative vector field its curl is everywhere zero: $\curl \mathbf V = \bszero$

title: Definition:Conservative Vector Field/Definition 2
snippet: Let $R$ be a simply connected region of space. Let $\mathbf V$ be a vector field with continuous first partial derivatives acting over $R$. $\mathbf V$ is a conservative vector field the contour integral over $\mathbf V$ around every simple closed contour within $R$ is zero: $\ds \oint \mathbf V \cdot \d \mathbf l = 0$

title: Definition:Conservative Vector Field/Definition 3
snippet: Let $R$ be a simply connected region of space. Let $\mathbf V$ be a vector field with continuous first partial derivatives acting over $R$. Let $A$ and $B$ be two points within $R$. $\mathbf V$ is a conservative vector field the contour integral from $A$ to $B$: $\ds \int_A^B \mathbf V \cdot \rd \mathbf l$ is independent of the path of integration, which has to lie entirely within $R$.

title: Definition:Conservative Vector Field/Definition 4
snippet: Let $R$ be a simply connected region of space. Let $\mathbf V$ be a vector field with continuous first partial derivatives acting over $R$. $\mathbf V$ is a conservative vector field $\mathbf V \cdot \d \mathbf l$ is an exact differential.

title: Definition:Conservative Vector Field/Definition 5
snippet: Let $R$ be a simply connected region of space. Let $\mathbf V$ be a vector field with continuous first partial derivatives acting over $R$. $\mathbf V$ is a conservative vector field there exists some real-valued function $W$ on $R$ such that $\mathbf V = \grad W$.

title: Definition:Consistent
snippet: Logic: Consistent (Logic): a proof system is consistent it does not contain a contradiction. Simultaneous equations: Consistent Simultaneous Equations: a system of simultaneous equations is referred to as consistent it has at least one solution. Statistics: Consistent Estimator: an estimator such that its limit gets arbitrarily close to the population parameter it is estimating.

title: Definition:Consistent (Logic)
snippet: Informally, a proof system is consistent it does not contain a contradiction. Let $\LL$ be a logical language. Let $\mathscr P$ be a proof system for $\LL$.

title: Definition:Consistent (Logic)/Also defined as
snippet: == Consistent in context of Logic: Also defined as == Common confusion arises in the precise interpretation of consistency in logic. On , consistency is placed in the realm of proof systems. It is also common to place it in the realm of formal semantics. That is, to define consistent as what is satisfiable on . Because of the variation, any use of these terms in a source work should be treated with the utmost care and precision to determine the exact meaning. Category:Definitions/Logical Consistency

title: Definition:Consistent (Logic)/Proof System
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a logical language. Let $\mathscr P$ be a proof system for $\LL$. Then $\mathscr P$ is consistent : There exists a logical formula $\phi$ such that $\not \vdash_{\mathscr P} \phi$ That is, some logical formula $\phi$ is not a theorem of $\mathscr P$.

title: Definition:Consistent (Logic)/Proof System/Propositional Logic
snippet: Let $\LL_0$ be the language of propositional logic. Let $\mathscr P$ be a proof system for $\LL_0$.

title: Definition:Consistent (Logic)/Proof System/Propositional Logic/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\LL_0$ be the language of propositional logic. Let $\mathscr P$ be a proof system for $\LL_0$. Then $\mathscr P$ is consistent : There exists a logical formula $\phi$ such that $\not \vdash_{\mathscr P} \phi$ That is, some logical formula $\phi$ is not a theorem of $\mathscr P$. Category:Definitions/Proof Systems Category:Definitions/Propositional Logic

title: Definition:Consistent (Logic)/Proof System/Propositional Logic/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\LL$ be the language of propositional logic. Let $\mathscr P$ be a proof system for $\LL_0$. Suppose that in $\mathscr P$, the Rule of Explosion (Variant 3) holds. Then $\mathscr P$ is consistent : For every logical formula $\phi$, not both of $\phi$ and $\neg \phi$ are theorems of $\mathscr P$

title: Definition:Consistent (Logic)/Set of Formulas
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a logical language. Let $\mathscr P$ be a proof system for $\LL$. Let $\FF$ be a collection of logical formulas. Then $\FF$ is consistent for $\mathscr P$ : There exists a logical formula $\phi$ such that $\FF \nvdash_{\mathscr P} \phi$. That is, some logical formula $\phi$ is not a provable consequence of $\FF$.

title: Definition:Consistent (Logic)/Set of Formulas/Propositional Logic
snippet: Let $\LL_0$ be the language of propositional logic. Let $\mathscr P$ be a proof system for $\LL_0$. Let $\FF$ be a collection of logical formulas.

title: Definition:Consistent (Logic)/Set of Formulas/Propositional Logic/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\LL_0$ be the language of propositional logic. Let $\mathscr P$ be a proof system for $\LL_0$. Let $\FF$ be a collection of logical formulas. Then $\FF$ is consistent for $\mathscr P$ : There exists a logical formula $\phi$ such that $\FF \not \vdash_{\mathscr P} \phi$ That is, some logical formula $\phi$ is not a $\mathscr P$-provable consequence of $\FF$. Category:Definitions/Proof Systems Category:Definitions/Propositional Logic

title: Definition:Consistent (Logic)/Set of Formulas/Propositional Logic/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\LL$ be the language of propositional logic. Let $\mathscr P$ be a proof system for $\LL_0$. Let $\FF$ be a collection of logical formulas. Suppose that in $\mathscr P$, the Rule of Explosion (Variant 3) holds. Then $\FF$ is consistent for $\mathscr P$ : For every logical formula $\phi$, not both of $\phi$ and $\neg \phi$ are $\mathscr P$-provable consequences of $\FF$

title: Definition:Consistent Estimator
snippet: Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ be random variables. Let the joint distribution of $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ be indexed by a population parameter $\theta$. Let $\hat \theta$ be an estimator of $\theta$. Then $\hat \theta$ is consistent : $\ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \map \Pr {\size {\hat \theta - \theta} \ge \epsilon} = 0$ for all $\epsilon > 0$.

title: Definition:Consistent Proof System/Also defined as
snippet: == Consistent Proof System: Also defined as == Consistency is obviously necessary for soundness in the context of a given semantics. Therefore it is not surprising that some authors obfuscate the boundaries between a consistent proof system (in itself) and a sound proof system (in reference to the semantics under discussion).

title: Definition:Consistent Simultaneous Equations
snippet: A system of simultaneous equations is referred to as consistent it has at least one solution. That is, there exists a set of values for its variables such that all the equations are satisfied.

title: Definition:Consistent Simultaneous Equations/Inconsistent
snippet: A set of equations is described as inconsistent they are not consistent That is, there exists no set of values for its variables such that all the equations are satisfied.

title: Definition:Constant
snippet: A constant is a name for an object (usually a number, but the concept has wider applications) which does not change during the context of a logical or mathematical argument. A constant can be considered as an operator which takes no operands. A constant can also be considered as a variable whose domain is a singleton.

title: Definition:Constant-Speed Curve
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $I$ be a closed real interval. Let $\gamma : \R \to M$ be smooth curve. Suppose the speed of $\gamma$ is constant. Then $\gamma$ is a constant-speed curve.

title: Definition:Constant/Also known as
snippet: == Constant: Also known as == A constant in an expression in algebra is also seen referred to as an absolute term. In the same context, the term literal (constant) can sometimes be seen in order to differentiate it from a numerical constant.

title: Definition:Constant/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Constant == The term constant, as opposed to a variable, was introduced by .

title: Definition:Constant/Linguistic Note
snippet: The word constant can be used either as a : Let $c$ be a constant between $0$ and $1$ or as an : Let $c$ be a constant real number between $0$ and $1$ Which is intended can usually be deduced from the context. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Constant (Category Theory)
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory, and let $1$ be a terminal object of $\mathbf C$. A constant of $\mathbf C$ is a morphism $f: 1 \to C$ of $\mathbf C$ which has $1$ as its domain.

title: Definition:Constant (Physics)
snippet: A physical quantity is defined as being constant it does not change with the passage of time.

title: Definition:Constant Distribution
snippet: Let $\map \DD {\R^n}$ be the test function space. Let $T : \map \DD {\R^n} \to \C$ be a Schwartz distribution. Let $c \in \C$ be a complex number. Suppose, $T$ is generated by $c$: $T = T_c$ Then $T$ is called the constant distribution. Category:Definitions/Examples of Schwartz Distributions Category:Definitions/Functional Analysis

title: Definition:Constant Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf C, \mathbf D$ be a categories. Let $D \in \mathbf D$ be an object of $\mathbf D$. Then the $D$-valued constant functor is the covariant functor $F: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ defined by: {{DefineFunctor |ob = for each object $C \in \mathbf C: F C = D$ |mor = for each morphism $f: C \to B \in \mathbf C:F f = \operatorname{id}_D$ }}

title: Definition:Constant Mapping
snippet: == Definitions == A constant mapping is a mapping $f_c: S \to T$ defined as: $c \in T: f_c: S \to T: \forall x \in S: \map {f_c} x = c$ That is, every element of $S$ is mapped to the same element $c$ in $T$. In a certain sense, a constant mapping can be considered as a mapping which takes no arguments.

title: Definition:Constant Mapping/Also known as
snippet: == Constant Mapping: Also known as == A constant mapping is also known as: a constant function a constant transformation.

title: Definition:Constant Matrix
snippet: A constant matrix is a matrix whose entries are all constants.

title: Definition:Constant Mean Level
snippet: Let $S$ be a stochastic process giving rise to a time series $T$. $T$ has a constant mean level the mean of $S$ does not change as time progresses.

title: Definition:Constant Natural Transformation
snippet: Let $\mathbf C, \mathbf D$ be a categories. Let $f : D_1 \to D_2 \in \mathbf D$ be a morphism. Let $F_{D_1}: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D, F_{D_2}: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ denote the $D_1$, $D_2$-valued constant functors respectively. Then the $f$-valued constant natural transformation is the natural transformation $\eta: F_{D_1} \to F_{D_2}$ defined by: for each object $C \in \mathbf C: \eta_C = f$

title: Definition:Constant Operation
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. For a given $c \in S$, a constant operation on $S$ is defined as: $\forall x, y \in S: x \sqbrk c y = c$

title: Definition:Constant Polynomial
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $P \in R \sqbrk x$ be a polynomial in one variable over $R$.

title: Definition:Constant Polynomial/Definition 1
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $P \in R \sqbrk x$ be a polynomial in one variable over $R$. The polynomial $P$ is a constant polynomial its coefficients of $x^k$ are zero for $k \ge 1$.

title: Definition:Constant Polynomial/Definition 2
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $P \in R \sqbrk x$ be a polynomial in one variable over $R$. The polynomial $P$ is a constant polynomial $P$ is either the zero polynomial or has degree $0$.

title: Definition:Constant Polynomial/Definition 3
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $P \in R \sqbrk x$ be a polynomial in one variable over $R$. The polynomial $P$ is a constant polynomial it is in the image of the canonical embedding $R \to R \sqbrk x$.

title: Definition:Constant Polynomial/Nonconstant
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $P \in R \sqbrk x$ be a polynomial in one variable over $R$. The polynomial $P$ is a nonconstant polynomial $P$ is not a constant polynomial. Category:Definitions/Polynomial Theory

title: Definition:Constant Presheaf
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space. Let $S$ be a set. The constant presheaf with value $S$ on $X$ is the set-valued presheaf $\ds F : \map {\mathbf{Ouv} }{X}^{\mathrm{op} } \to \mathbf{Set}$ from the category of open sets $\map {\mathbf{Ouv} }{X}$ of $X$ to the category of sets $\mathbf{Set}$, defined as follows: For each open subset $U \subset X$, let $\map F U := S$ For each inclusion map $i : U \to V$, let $\map F i := \operatorname{id}_S$.

title: Definition:Constant Sheaf
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space. Let $S$ be a set. The constant sheaf with value $S$ on $X$ is the set-valued presheaf $\ds F : \map {\mathbf{Ouv} } X^{\mathrm {op} } \to \mathbf {Set}$ from the category of open sets $\map {\mathbf{Ouv}} X$ of $X$ to the category of sets $\mathbf {Set}$, defined as follows: For each open subset $U \subset X$, let $\map F U$ be the set of continuous maps $U \to S$ for the discrete topology on $S$. For each inclusion map $i : U \to V$, let $\map F i : \map F V \to \map F U$ denote restriction of mapping.

title: Definition:Constant Speed
snippet: A body $B$ is moving at constant speed the magnitude of the velocity of $B$ is constant.

title: Definition:Constant Symbol
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a formal language (for example, the language of predicate logic $\LL_1$). A constant symbol is a letter of $\LL$ used to describe a constant. The name constant symbol is a gesture to the reader to make clear what such a symbol should (intuitively) represent in the formal language $\LL$.

title: Definition:Constant Tempered Distribution
snippet: Let $\map \DD {\R^n}$ be the Schwartz space. Let $T : \map \DD {\R^n} \to \C$ be a tempered distribution. Let $c \in \C$ be a complex number. Suppose, $T$ is generated by $c$: $T = T_c$ Then $T$ is called the constant tempered distribution. Category:Definitions/Functional Analysis Category:Definitions/Tempered Distributions

title: Definition:Constant Term of Polynomial
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $P \in R \sqbrk X$ be a nonzero polynomial over $R$: $\ds f = \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^n a_k \circ x^k$ where $n$ is the degree of $P$. The constant term of $P$ is the coefficient $a_0$ of $x^0$.

title: Definition:Constant of Integration/Also known as
snippet: == Constant of Integration: Also known as == The term constant of integration is often referred to inprecisely as an arbitrary constant. It can also be found being referred to as a disposable constant -- that is, it may be "disposed as desired", not "disposed of".

title: Definition:Constant of Proportion/Also known as
snippet: == Constant of Proportion: Also known as == The constant of proportion is also known nowadays by the less elegant and more cumbersome constant of proportionality. Some sources use proportionality constant.

title: Definition:Constrained Optimization
snippet: A constrained optimization problem is a problem of optimization theory in which certain variables have restrictions or constraints on the values they are allowed to take.

title: Definition:Constrained Optimization/Feasible
snippet: A constrained optimization problem is described as feasible all the constraints can be satisfied simultaneously.

title: Definition:Constraint
snippet: A constraint is a condition which causes a restriction.

title: Definition:Constructed Semantics
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a formal language. A constructed semantics for $\LL$ is a formal semantics which is invented solely for proving a property about $\LL$ or other entities related to $\LL$.

title: Definition:Constructed Semantics/Instance 1
snippet: Let $\LL_0$ be the language of propositional logic. The constructed semantics $\mathscr C_1$ for $\LL_0$ is used for the following results: Hilbert Proof System Instance 2 is Consistent

title: Definition:Constructed Semantics/Instance 1/Factor Principle
snippet: The Factor Principle: $\left({p \implies q}\right) \implies \left({\left({r \lor p}\right) \implies \left ({r \lor q}\right)}\right)$ is a tautology in Instance 1 of constructed semantics.

title: Definition:Constructed Semantics/Instance 1/Rule of Addition
snippet: The Rule of Addition: $q \implies (q \lor p)$ is a tautology in Instance 1 of constructed semantics.

title: Definition:Constructed Semantics/Instance 1/Rule of Commutation
snippet: The Rule of Commutation: $\left({p \lor q}\right) \implies \left({q \lor p}\right)$ is a tautology in Instance 1 of constructed semantics.

title: Definition:Constructed Semantics/Instance 1/Rule of Idempotence
snippet: The Rule of Idempotence: $(p \lor p) \implies p$ is a tautology in Instance 1 of constructed semantics.

title: Definition:Constructible Number
snippet: Let $a \in \R$ be a real number. Then $a$ is a constructible number the point $\tuple {a, 0}$ is a constructible point from the points $\tuple {0, 0}$ and $\tuple {1, 0}$.

title: Definition:Constructible Point in Plane
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a Cartesian coordinate plane. Let $S$ be a set of points in $\CC$. Let $P$ be a point in $\CC$. Let there exist a compass and straightedge construction for $P$ from a line segment $AB$, where $A, B \in S$. Then $P$ is defined as constructible from $S$.

title: Definition:Construction
snippet: Construction is the process of creating a particular mathematical object according to an appropriate system of axioms. To construct means to build.

title: Definition:Construction/Geometric Construction
snippet: Geometric construction is the process of creating a particular geometric figure, according to an appropriate system of axioms. The unspoken understanding is that those axioms are at base Euclid's postulates and common notions.

title: Definition:Constructive Definition
snippet: A constructive definition is a definition in which there exists an effective procedure for the construction of every object in it.

title: Definition:Constructive Proof
snippet: A constructive proof is a proof in which there exists an effective procedure for the construction of every object in it.

title: Definition:Constructivism
snippet: == Philosophical Position == It is the position of certain cognitive psychologists that humans learn most effectively in an environment where new information can be assimilated by expanding directly upon previously gained knowledge. Hence constructivism is the philosophical position that a mathematical objects actually needs to be determined or constructed in order for is existence to be demonstrated.

title: Definition:Consumer's Risk
snippet: Consumer's risk is the probability that a consumer accepts a batch with a number of defectives which is unacceptable to that consumer. The consumer's risk can be denoted by the symbol $\beta$ (beta).

title: Definition:Contact
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be bodies. Then $A$ and $B$ are in contact the distance between $A$ and $B$ is zero for at least one point in $A$ and at least one point in $B$.

title: Definition:Contact Force
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be bodies in contact. The contact force is the force exerted by $A$ on $B$, and likewise the force exerted by $B$ on $A$, which is the sum of: the frictional force, which is tangential to the surfaces at the point of contact the normal reaction, which is normal to the surfaces at the point of contact.

title: Definition:Containment
snippet: Geometry Containment of an angle: The two lines that form an angle are said to contain that angle. Containment of a geometric figure: a figure is intuitively described as being contained by its boundary. Containment of a solid geometric figure: a solid figure is intuitively described as beingcontained by the surfaces that form its boundary. Containment of a rectangle: In , two adjacent sides of a rectangle are said to contain it. In set theory, the concept of containment can be used in either of two senses: A set is said to contain its elements: $S$ contains $a$ means $a \in S$.

title: Definition:Containment of Cuboid
snippet: A cuboid is said to be contained by the lengths of $3$ pairwise perpendicular edges.

title: Definition:Containment of Cuboid/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Containment of Cuboid == The concept of a cuboid being contained by its edges can be found as an undefined concept in . There is little relevance in this to modern mathematics. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Containment of Solid Figure
snippet: A solid geometric figure is said to be contained by the surfaces that form its boundary. Category:Definitions/Solid Geometry

title: Definition:Contemplative School
snippet: == Philosophical Position == The Contemplative School is a philosophical position whose attitude is that it is important to analyse and organise the developments of the activist school.

title: Definition:Content
snippet: Definition:Content of Polynomial Definition:Content of Integer Polynomial Definition:Content of Rational Polynomial Definition:Content (Measure Theory)

title: Definition:Content of Polynomial/Also denoted as
snippet: == Content of Polynomial: Also denoted as == The content of a polynomial $f$ can be seen in the literature variously denoted as: $\cont f$ (currently used on ) $c_f$ $\left\langle \! \left\langle {f} \right\rangle \! \right\rangle$ Category:Definitions/Content of Polynomial

title: Definition:Content of Polynomial/Commutative and Unitary Ring
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $f \in R \sqbrk X$ be a polynomial. The content of $f$ is the ideal generated by its coefficients.

title: Definition:Content of Polynomial/GCD Domain
snippet: Let $D$ be a GCD domain. Let $K$ be the field of quotients of $D$. Let $f \in K \sqbrk X$ be a polynomial. Let $a \in D$ be such that $a f \in D \sqbrk X$. Let $d$ be the greatest common divisor of the coefficients of $a f$. Then we define the content of $f$ to be: $\cont f := \dfrac d a$

title: Definition:Content of Polynomial/Integer
snippet: Let $f \in \Z \sqbrk X$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients. Then the content of $f$, denoted $\cont f$, is the greatest common divisor of the coefficients of $f$.

title: Definition:Content of Polynomial/Rational
snippet: Let $f \in \Q \sqbrk X$ be a polynomial with rational coefficients. The content of $f$ is defined as: $\cont f := \dfrac {\cont {n f} } n$ where $n \in \N$ is such that $n f \in \Z \sqbrk X$.

title: Definition:Content of Rectangle
snippet: Let $\ds R = \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n \closedint {a_i} {b_i}$ be a closed $n$-rectangle. Then, the content of $R$ is defined and denoted as: $\ds \map V R = \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n \paren {b_i - a_i}$ Category:Definitions/Jordan Content

title: Definition:Contingency Table
snippet: A contingency table is an array of $r$ rows and $c$ columns in which: each row and each column is associated with a specific attribute the number $n_{i j}$ in row $i$ and column $j$ is a count of the number of units having that combination of attributes. It is then commonplace to perform a chi-squared test to investigate how the data may differ between categories. Row and column categories may be either nominal or ordinal. If a sample is categorised into more than $2$ categories, multiple contingency tables need to be created to compare each of those categories with each other.

title: Definition:Contingency Table/Cell
snippet: The element in row $i$ and column $j$ of a contingency table is referred to as cell $\tuple {i, j}$ of that contingency table.

title: Definition:Contingency Table/Marginal Total
snippet: The marginal totals of a contingency table are the totals of each of the rows and columns of that contingency table.

title: Definition:Contingent Statement
snippet: A contingent statement is a statement form which is neither a tautology nor unsatisfiable, but whose truth value depends upon the truth value of its component substatements. <!--

title: Definition:Continuation
snippet: Analytic Continuation Continuation of Woset Both concepts are equivalent to an extension.

title: Definition:Continuation of Woset
snippet: Let $\left({S, \preccurlyeq}\right)$ be a woset. Let $\left({T, \preccurlyeq}\right)$ be a set with an ordering such that: $(1): \quad T$ is an initial segment of $S$ $(2): \quad$ The ordering of the elements of $T$ is the same as their ordering in $S$. Then $S$ is a continuation of $T$.

title: Definition:Continued Fraction
snippet: Let $F$ be a field, such as the field of real numbers $\R$.

title: Definition:Continued Fraction/Also defined as
snippet: == Continued Fraction: Also defined as == When one is primarily concerned with simple continued fractions of real numbers, it is common to require a continued fraction to have strictly positive partial denominators, except perhaps the first.

title: Definition:Continued Fraction/Also known as
snippet: == Continued Fraction: Also known as == A continued fraction is also known as a: continued fraction in canonical form regular continued fraction simple continued fraction in order to distinguish such a continued fraction from a generalized continued fraction. Category:Definitions/Continued Fractions

title: Definition:Continued Fraction/Finite
snippet: Let $F$ be a field, such as the field of real numbers $\R$. Let $n \ge 0$ be a natural number. Informally, a finite continued fraction of length $n$ in $F$ is an expression of the form: $a_0 + \cfrac 1 {a_1 + \cfrac 1 {a_2 + \cfrac 1 {\ddots \cfrac {} {a_{n - 1} + \cfrac 1 {a_n} } } } }$ where $a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n \in F$. Formally, a finite continued fraction of length $n$ in $F$ is a finite sequence, called sequence of partial denominators, whose domain is the integer interval $\closedint 0 n$. A finite continued fraction should not be confused with its value, when it exists.

title: Definition:Continued Fraction/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Continued Fraction == The concept of the continued fraction has been around a long time, since at least, and a great deal of research has been done and terminology developed. Much of its modern theory was established by .

title: Definition:Continued Fraction/Infinite
snippet: Let $F$ be a field, such as the field of real numbers $\R$. Informally, an infinite continued fraction in $F$ is an expression of the form: $a_0 + \cfrac 1 {a_1 + \cfrac 1 {a_2 + \cfrac 1 {\ddots \cfrac {} {a_{n-1} + \cfrac 1 {a_n + \cfrac 1 {\ddots}}} }}}$ where $a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n, \ldots \in F$. Formally, an infinite continued fraction in $F$ is a sequence, called a sequence of partial denominators, whose domain is $\N_{\ge 0}$. An infinite continued fraction should not be confused with its value, when it exists.

title: Definition:Continued Fraction/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Continued Fraction == A continued fraction can be denoted using ellipsis: $a_0 + \cfrac 1 {a_1 + \cfrac 1 {a_2 + \cfrac 1 {\ddots \cfrac {} {} } } }$ Another notation that can sometimes be seen is: $a_0 + \dfrac 1 {a_1 +} \dfrac 1 {a_2 +} \dfrac 1 {a_3 + \cdots}$ By definition, a continued fraction is its sequence of partial denominators and can thus be denoted: $\sequence {a_n}_{n \mathop \ge 0}$ $\sqbrk {a_0; a_1, a_2, \ldots}$ $\sqbrk {a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots}$ where the last two notations are usually reserved for its value.

title: Definition:Continued Fraction Expansion of Laurent Series
snippet: Let $k$ be a field. Let $\map k {\paren {t^{-1} } }$ be the field of formal Laurent series in the variable $t^{-1}$.

title: Definition:Continued Product
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \times}$ be an algebraic structure where the operation $\times$ is an operation derived from, or arising from, the multiplication operation on the natural numbers. Let $\tuple {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n} \in S^n$ be an ordered $n$-tuple in $S$.

title: Definition:Continued Product/Also known as
snippet: == Continued Product: Also known as == A continued product can also be seen as product notation, but such a term is not only imprecise but also ambiguous.

title: Definition:Continued Product/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Continued Product == The originally investigation into the theory of infinite products was carried out by .

title: Definition:Continued Product/Index
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \times}$ be an algebraic structure where the operation $\times$ is an operation derived from, or arising from, the multiplication operation on the natural numbers. Let $\tuple {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n} \in S^n$ be an ordered $n$-tuple in $S$. The composite is called the continued product of $\tuple {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n}$, and is written: $\ds \prod_{j \mathop = 1}^n a_j = \paren {a_1 \times a_2 \times \cdots \times a_n}$

title: Definition:Continued Product/Index Variable
snippet: Consider the continued product, in either of the three forms: $\ds \prod_{j \mathop = 1}^n a_j \qquad \prod_{1 \mathop \le j \mathop \le n} a_j \qquad \prod_{\map R j} a_j$ The variable $j$, an example of a bound variable, is known as the index variable of the continued product.

title: Definition:Continued Product/Inequality
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \times}$ be an algebraic structure where the operation $\times$ is an operation derived from, or arising from, the multiplication operation on the natural numbers. Let $\tuple {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n} \in S^n$ be an ordered $n$-tuple in $S$. The continued product of $\tuple {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n}$ can be written: $\ds \prod_{1 \mathop \le j \mathop \le n} a_j = \paren {a_1 \times a_2 \times \cdots \times a_n}$

title: Definition:Continued Product/Multiplicand
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \times}$ be an algebraic structure where $\times$ is an operation derived from, or arising from, the multiplication operation on the natural numbers. Let $\set {a_1, a_2, \ldots} \subseteq S$ be a set of elements of $S$. Let: $\ds \prod_{\map R j} a_j$ be a continued product on $\set {a_1, a_2, \ldots}$. The set of elements $\set {a_j \in S}$ is called the multiplicand.

title: Definition:Continued Product/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Continued Product == The sign $\ds \prod$ is called the product sign and is derived from the capital Greek letter $\Pi$, which is $\mathrm P$, the first letter of product. Category:Definitions/Continued Products

title: Definition:Continued Product/Propositional Function
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \times}$ be an algebraic structure where the operation $\times$ is an operation derived from, or arising from, the multiplication operation on the natural numbers. Let $\tuple {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n} \in S^n$ be an ordered $n$-tuple in $S$. Let $\map R j$ be a propositional function of $j$. Then we can write: $\ds \prod_{\map R j} a_j = \text { the product of all $a_j$ such that $\map R j$ holds}$. If more than one propositional function is written under the product sign, they must all hold. Such an operation on an ordered tuple is known as a continued product.

title: Definition:Continued Product/Propositional Function/Iverson's Convention
snippet: Let $\ds \prod_{\map R j} a_j$ be the continued product over all $a_j$ such that $j$ satisfies $R$. This can also be expressed: $\ds \prod_{j \mathop \in \Z} a_j^{\sqbrk {\map R j} }$ where $\sqbrk {\map R j}$ is Iverson's convention.

title: Definition:Continued Product/Vacuous Product
snippet: Take the composite expressed as a continued product: $\ds \prod_{\map R j} a_j$ where $\map R j$ is a propositional function of $j$. Suppose that there are no values of $j$ for which $\map R j$ is true. Then $\ds \prod_{\map R j} a_j$ is defined to be $1$. Beware: not zero. This composite is called a vacuous product. This is because: $\forall a: a \times 1 = a$ where $a$ is a number. Hence for all $j$ for which $\map R j$ is false, the value of the product is unaffected. This is most frequently seen in the form: $\ds \prod_{j \mathop = m}^n a_j = 1$ where $m > n$.

title: Definition:Continued Proportion/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Continued Proportion == The term continued proportion is rarely seen outside . Indeed, while used the term continued proportion throughout Book $\text{VIII}$ of , he never formally defined it. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Continued Square Root
snippet: A continued square root is an expression of the form: $a_0 + \sqrt {a_1 + \sqrt {a_2 + \sqrt {a_3 + \sqrt {\cdots} } } }$ where $\left\langle{a_n}\right\rangle$ is an arbitrary sequence of numbers.

title: Definition:Continuity/Functional
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of mappings. Let $y \in S$ be a mapping. Let $J \sqbrk y: S \to \R$ be a functional. Suppose: $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists \delta \in \R_{>0}: \size {y - y_0} < \delta \implies \size {J \sqbrk y - J \sqbrk {y_0} } < \epsilon$ Then $J \sqbrk y$ is said to be a continuous functional and is continuous at the point $y_0 \in S$.

title: Definition:Continuity Correction
snippet: Let $X$ be a discrete random variable which takes integer values. A continuity correction for $X$ is the addition or subtraction of $0 \cdotp 5$ in order to obtain closer agreement to a continuous approximation.

title: Definition:Continuity Equation
snippet: A continuity equation is an equation in physics which is applied to continuous flow of a conserved quantity.

title: Definition:Continuity Equation/Also known as
snippet: == Continuity Equation: Also known as == A continuity equation is also known as an equation of continuity.

title: Definition:Continuous
snippet: Continuous Mapping Continuous Geometry Continuous Lattice Subframe Continuous Data Analysis: Continuous Real Function One-Sided Continuity Left-Continuous at Point Right-Continuous at Point Continuous Real-Valued Vector Function Continuous Complex Function Calculus of Variations: Continuous Functional Metric Spaces: Continuous Mapping (Metric Spaces) Topology: Continuous Extension Continuous Mapping (Topology) Category Theory: Continuous Functor

title: Definition:Continuous Complex Function
snippet: As the complex plane is a metric space, the same definition of continuity applies to complex functions as to metric spaces. Let $A_1, A_2 \subseteq \C$ be subsets of the complex plane. Let $f: A_1 \to A_2$ be a complex function from $A_1$ to $A_2$. Let $a \in A_1$.

title: Definition:Continuous Complex Function/Epsilon-Delta
snippet: Let $A_1, A_2 \subseteq \C$ be subsets of the complex plane. Let $f: A_1 \to A_2$ be a complex function from $A_1$ to $A_2$. Let $a \in A_1$. $f$ is continuous at (the point) $a$ : $\forall \epsilon > 0: \exists \delta > 0: \forall z \in A_1: \cmod {z - a} < \delta \implies \cmod {\map f z - \map f a} < \epsilon$

title: Definition:Continuous Complex Function/Epsilon-Neighborhood
snippet: Let $A_1, A_2 \subseteq \C$ be subsets of the complex plane. Let $f: A_1 \to A_2$ be a complex function from $A_1$ to $A_2$. Let $a \in A_1$. Let $A_1$ be open in $\C$. $f$ is continuous at (the point) $a$ : $\forall \map {\NN_\epsilon} {\map f a}: \exists \map {\NN_\delta} a: f \sqbrk {\map {\NN_\delta} a} \subseteq \map {\NN_\epsilon} {\map f a}$ where $\map {\NN_\epsilon} a$ is the $\epsilon$-neighborhood of $a$ in $A_1$.

title: Definition:Continuous Complex Function/Open Sets
snippet: Let $A_1, A_2 \subseteq \C$ be subsets of the complex plane. Let $f: A_1 \to A_2$ be a complex function from $A_1$ to $A_2$. Let $A_1$ be open in $\C$. $f$ is continuous : for every set $U \subseteq \C$ which is open in $\C$, $f^{-1} \sqbrk U$ is open in $\C$.

title: Definition:Continuous Complex Function/Using Limit
snippet: Let $A_1, A_2 \subseteq \C$ be subsets of the complex plane. Let $f: A_1 \to A_2$ be a complex function from $A_1$ to $A_2$. Let $a \in A_1$. $f$ is continuous at (the point) $a$ : The limit of $\map f z$ as $z \to a$ exists, and $\ds \lim_{z \mathop \to a} \map f z = \map f a$

title: Definition:Continuous Extension
snippet: Let $T_1 = \left({S_1, \tau_1}\right)$ and $T_2 = \left({S_2, \tau_2}\right)$ be topological spaces. Let $A, B \subseteq S_1$ be subsets of $S_1$ such that $A \subseteq B$. Let $f: A \to S_2$ and $g: B \to S_2$ be continuous mappings. Then $g$ is a continuous extension of $f$ : $\forall s \in A: f \left({s}\right) = g \left({s}\right)$ That is, a continuous extension of $f$ is a continuous mapping on a superset which agrees with $f$ on the domain of $f$. Simply, it is a continuous mapping which is an extension.

title: Definition:Continuous Extension/Real Function
snippet: Let $A$, $B \subseteq \R$ be subsets of the real numbers such that $A \subseteq B$. Let $f: A \to \R$ and $g: B \to \R$ be continuous real functions. Then $g$ is a continuous extension of $f$ : $\forall x \in A : \map f x = \map g x$ Category:Definitions/Continuous Real Functions

title: Definition:Continuous Functional Calculus
snippet: Let $\struct {A, \ast, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a unital $\text C^\ast$-algebra. Let $x \in A$ be normal. Let $\map {\sigma_A} x$ denote the spectrum of $x$ in $A$. Let $\iota : \map {\sigma_A} x \to \C$ be the inclusion mapping. Let $\Theta_x : \map \CC {\map {\sigma_A} x} \to A$ be a unital $\ast$-algebra homomorphism such that: $\map {\Theta_x} \iota = x$ where $\map \CC {\map {\sigma_A} x}$ is the space of continuous functions on $\map {\sigma_A} x$. We call $\Theta_x$ the continuous functional calculus of $x$.

title: Definition:Continuous Functional Calculus/Non-Unital Algebra
snippet:
Let $\struct {A, \ast, 
orm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a $	ext C^\ast$-algebra that is not necessarily unital. Let $\struct {A_+, \ast, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_\ast}$ be the unitization of $\struct {A, \ast, 
orm {\, \cdot \,} }$. Let: $A_0 = \set {	uple {a, 0} : a \in A}$ Let $x \in A$ be normal. Let $\map {\sigma_A} x$ denote the spectrum of $x$ in $A$. Let $\map {\sigma_{A_+} } {	uple {x, 0} }$ denote the spectrum of $	uple {x, 0}$ in $A_+$. Let $f : \map {\sigma_{A_+} } {	uple {x, 0} } 	o \C$ be continuous with $\map f 0 = 0$.

title: Definition:Continuous Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$, $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. Let $F: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be a functor. Then $F$ is continuous for all diagrams $D: \mathbf J \to \mathbf C$ with limit ${\varprojlim \,}_j \, D_j$: $\map F {{\varprojlim \,}_j \, D_j} \cong {\varprojlim \,}_j \, F D_j$ where $F D: \mathbf J \to \mathbf D$ is the diagram obtained by composition of $F$ with $D$, and $\mathbf J$ is an arbitrary metacategory.

title: Definition:Continuous Geometry
snippet: Continuous geometry is a branch of the projective geometry which investigates spaces whose dimension can range over the continuous interval $\closedint 0 1$.

title: Definition:Continuous Group Action
snippet: Let $G$ be a topological group. Let $X$ be a topological space. A group action $\phi: G \times X \to X$ is defined as continuous $\phi$ is continuous.

title: Definition:Continuous Invariant
snippet: Let $P$ be a property whose domain is the set of all topological spaces. Suppose that whenever $\map P T$ holds, then so does $\map P {T'}$, where: $T$ and $T'$ are topological spaces $\phi: T \to T'$ is a continuous mapping from $T$ to $T'$ $\phi \sqbrk T = T'$, where $\phi \sqbrk T$ denotes the image of $\phi$. Then $P$ is a continuous invariant. Loosely, a continuous invariant is a property which is preserved under a continuous mapping.

title: Definition:Continuous Lattice Subframe
snippet: Let $L = \left({X, \preceq}\right)$ be an ordered set. Let $S = \left({Y, \preceq'}\right)$ be an ordered subset of $L$. Then $S$ is continuous lattice subframe of $L$ $S$ inherits infima and directed suprema.

title: Definition:Continuous Linear Functional Supporting Subset of Topological Vector Space at Point
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological vector space over $\R$. Let $A \subseteq X$ be non-empty. Let $f : X \to \R$ be a continuous linear functional. Let $x \in X$. We say that $f$ supports $A$ at $x$ : $\ds \map f x = \sup_{y \mathop \in A} \map f y$ or: $\ds \map f x = \inf_{y \mathop \in A} \map f y$

title: Definition:Continuous Linear Transformation Space
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $X, Y$ be normed vector spaces over $K$. Let $\map \LL {X, Y}$ be the set of all linear transformations. Let $\map C {X, Y}$ be the continuous mapping space. Then $\map {CL} {X, Y}$ is the continuous linear transformation space defined as: $\map {CL} {X, Y} := \map C {X, Y} \cap \map \LL {X, Y}$

title: Definition:Continuous Map (Locale)
snippet: Let $\mathbf{Loc}$ denote the category of locales. A morphism of $\mathbf{Loc}$ is called a continuous map. That is, for locales $L_1 = \struct{S_1, \preceq_1}$ and $L_2 = \struct{S_2, \preceq_2}$: $f: L_1 \to L_2$ is a continuous map: there exists a frame homomorphism $\phi: L_2 \to L_1$ such that $f = \phi^{\operatorname{op}}$ The frame homomorphism corresponding to a continuous map $f: L_1 \to L_2$ is denoted by $\loweradjoint f: L_2 \to L_1$. Hence $f = \paren{\loweradjoint f}^{\operatorname{op}}$.

title: Definition:Continuous Map (Locale)/Also defined as
snippet: == Continuous Map: Also defined as == From Frame Homomorphism is Lower Adjoint of Galois Connection, every frame homomorphism is the lower adjoint of a unique Galois connection. From All Infima Preserving Mapping is Upper Adjoint of Galois Connection, every continuous map is uniqely determined by the localic mapping that is the upper adjoint of the frame homomorphism that corresponds to the continuous map.

title: Definition:Continuous Map (Locale)/Localic Mapping
snippet: Let $L_1 = \struct{S_1, \preceq_1}, L_2 = \struct{S_2, \preceq_2}$ be locales. Let $f : L_1 \to L_2$ be a continuous map. That is, $f$ is the dual morphism of a frame homomorphism $\loweradjoint f : L_2 \to L_1$. The frame homomorphism $\loweradjoint f : L_2 \to L_1$ corresponding to $f$ is a lower adjoint of a Galois connection $\struct{\upperadjoint f, \loweradjoint f}$. The upper adjoint $\upperadjoint f : L_1 \to L_2$ of $\struct{\upperadjoint f, \loweradjoint f}$ is called a localic mapping.

title: Definition:Continuous Map Induced by Continuous Mapping
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct{S_1, \tau_1}$ and $T_2 = \struct{S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $f: T_1 \to \T_2$ be a continuous maping. Let $\map \Omega {T_1}, \map \Omega {T_2}$ be the locales of $T_1$ and $T_2$ respectively. Let $\map \Omega f : \map \Omega {T_2} \to \map \Omega {T_1}$ be the frame homomorphism of $f$ (where $\map \Omega {T_1}, \map \Omega {T_2}$ are considered to be frames). Then the continuous map $\paren{\map \Omega f}^{\operatorname{op}} : \map \Omega {T_1} \to \map \Omega {T_2}$ is called the continuous map induced by $f$.

title: Definition:Continuous Mapping
snippet: The concept of continuity makes precise the intuitive notion that a function has no "jumps" at a given point. Loosely speaking, in the case of a real function, continuity at a point is defined as the property that the graph of the function does not have a "break" at the point. Thus, a small change in the independent variable causes a similar small change in the dependent variable This concept appears throughout mathematics and correspondingly has many variations and generalizations.

title: Definition:Continuous Mapping/Also known as
snippet: == Continuous Mapping: Also known as == A continuous mapping is often referred to as a continuous function, particularly in the context of analysis, both real and complex. Some sources use the terminology continuous map.

title: Definition:Continuous Mapping/Metric Subspace
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct {A_1, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct {A_2, d_2}$ be metric spaces. Let $f: A_1 \to A_2$ be a mapping from $A_1$ to $A_2$. Let $Y \subseteq A_1$. By definition, $\struct {Y, d_Y}$ is a metric subspace of $M_1$. Let $a \in Y$ be a point in $Y$. Then $f$ is $\tuple {d_Y, d_2}$-continuous at $a$ : $\forall \epsilon > 0: \exists \delta > 0: \map {d_Y} {x, a} < \delta \implies \map {d_2} {\map f x, \map f a} < \epsilon$ Similarly, $f$ is $\tuple {d_Y, d_2}$-continuous : $\forall a \in Y: f$ is $\tuple {d_Y, d_2}$-continuous at $a$

title: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Metric Space)
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct {A_1, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct {A_2, d_2}$ be metric spaces. Let $f: A_1 \to A_2$ be a mapping from $A_1$ to $A_2$. Let $a \in A_1$ be a point in $A_1$.

title: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Metric Space)/Also known as
snippet: == Continuous Mapping (Metric Space): Also known as == A mapping which is continuous from $\struct {A_1, d_1}$ to $\struct {A_2, d_2}$ can also be referred to as $\tuple {d_1, d_2}$-continuous. Category:Definitions/Continuous Mappings on Metric Spaces

title: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Metric Space)/Point
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct {A_1, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct {A_2, d_2}$ be metric spaces. Let $f: A_1 \to A_2$ be a mapping from $A_1$ to $A_2$. Let $a \in A_1$ be a point in $A_1$.

title: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Metric Space)/Point/Definition 1
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct {A_1, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct {A_2, d_2}$ be metric spaces. Let $f: A_1 \to A_2$ be a mapping from $A_1$ to $A_2$. Let $a \in A_1$ be a point in $A_1$. $f$ is continuous at (the point) $a$ ( the metrics $d_1$ and $d_2$) : $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists \delta \in \R_{>0}: \forall x \in A_1: \map {d_1} {x, a} 0}$ denotes the set of all strictly positive real numbers.

title: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Metric Space)/Point/Definition 2
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct {A_1, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct {A_2, d_2}$ be metric spaces. Let $f: A_1 \to A_2$ be a mapping from $A_1$ to $A_2$. Let $a \in A_1$ be a point in $A_1$. $f$ is continuous at (the point) $a$ ( the metrics $d_1$ and $d_2$) : $(1): \quad$ The limit of $\map f x$ as $x \to a$ exists $(2): \quad \ds \lim_{x \mathop \to a} \map f x = \map f a$.

title: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Metric Space)/Point/Definition 3
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct {A_1, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct {A_2, d_2}$ be metric spaces. Let $f: A_1 \to A_2$ be a mapping from $A_1$ to $A_2$. Let $a \in A_1$ be a point in $A_1$. $f$ is continuous at (the point) $a$ ( the metrics $d_1$ and $d_2$) : $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists \delta \in \R_{>0}: f \sqbrk {\map {B_\delta} {a; d_1} } \subseteq \map {B_\epsilon} {\map f a; d_2}$ where $\map {B_\epsilon} {\map f a; d_2}$ denotes the open $\epsilon$-ball of $\map f a$ with respect to the metric $d_2$, and similarly for $\map {B_\delta} {a; d_1}$.

title: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Metric Space)/Point/Definition 4
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct {A_1, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct {A_2, d_2}$ be metric spaces. Let $f: A_1 \to A_2$ be a mapping from $A_1$ to $A_2$. Let $a \in A_1$ be a point in $A_1$. $f$ is continuous at (the point) $a$ ( the metrics $d_1$ and $d_2$) : for each neighborhood $N'$ of $\map f a$ in $M_2$ there exists a corresponding neighborhood $N$ of $a$ in $M_1$ such that $f \sqbrk N \subseteq N'$.

title: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Metric Space)/Space
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct {A_1, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct {A_2, d_2}$ be metric spaces. Let $f: A_1 \to A_2$ be a mapping from $A_1$ to $A_2$.

title: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Metric Space)/Space/Definition 1
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct {A_1, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct {A_2, d_2}$ be metric spaces. Let $f: A_1 \to A_2$ be a mapping from $A_1$ to $A_2$. $f$ is continuous from $\struct {A_1, d_1}$ to $\struct {A_2, d_2}$ it is continuous at every point $x \in A_1$.

title: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Metric Space)/Space/Definition 2
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct {A_1, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct {A_2, d_2}$ be metric spaces. Let $f: A_1 \to A_2$ be a mapping from $A_1$ to $A_2$. $f$ is continuous from $\struct {A_1, d_1}$ to $\struct {A_2, d_2}$ : for every $U \subseteq A_2$ which is open in $M_2$, $f^{-1} \sqbrk U$ is open in $M_1$. By definition, this is equivalent to the continuity of $f$ with respect to the induced topologies on $A_1$ and $A_2$.

title: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Normed Vector Space)
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct{X_1, \norm {\,\cdot\,}_{X_1} }$ and $M_2 = \struct{X_2, \norm {\,\cdot\,}_{X_2} }$ be normed vector spaces. Let $f: X_1 \to X_2$ be a mapping from $X_1$ to $X_2$.

title: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Normed Vector Space)/Point
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct{X_1, \norm {\,\cdot\,}_{X_1} }$ and $M_2 = \struct{X_2, \norm {\,\cdot\,}_{X_2} }$ be normed vector spaces. Let $f: X_1 \to X_2$ be a mapping from $X_1$ to $X_2$. Let $a \in X_1$ be a point in $X_1$.

title: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Normed Vector Space)/Point/Definition 1
snippet:
Let $M_1 = \struct{X_1, 
orm {\,\cdot\,}_{X_1} }$ and $M_2 = \struct{X_2, 
orm {\,\cdot\,}_{X_2} }$ be normed vector spaces. Let $f: X_1 	o X_2$ be a mapping from $X_1$ to $X_2$. Let $a \in X_1$ be a point in $X_1$. $f$ is continuous at $a$ (with respect to the norms $
orm {\,\cdot\,}_{X_1}$ and $
orm {\,\cdot\,}_{X_2}$) : $ orall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists \delta \in \R_{>0}:  orall x \in X_1: 
orm {x - a}_{X_1} 0}$ denotes the set of all strictly positive real numbers.

title: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Normed Vector Space)/Space
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct{X_1, \norm {\,\cdot\,}_{X_1} }$ and $M_2 = \struct{X_2, \norm {\,\cdot\,}_{X_2} }$ be normed vector spaces. Let $f: X_1 \to X_2$ be a mapping from $X_1$ to $X_2$.

title: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Normed Vector Space)/Space/Definition 1
snippet:
Let $M_1 = \struct{X_1, 
orm {\,\cdot\,}_{X_1}}$ and $M_2 = \struct{X_2, 
orm {\,\cdot\,}_{X_2}}$ be normed vector spaces. Let $f: X_1 	o X_2$ be a mapping from $X_1$ to $X_2$. $f$ is continuous from $\struct{X_1, 
orm {\,\cdot\,}_{X_1} }$ to $\struct{X_2, 
orm {\,\cdot\,}_{X_2} }$ it is continuous at every point $x \in X_1$.

title: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Topology)
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping from $S_1$ to $S_2$.

title: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Topology)/Also known as
snippet: If it is necessary to distinguish between multiple topologies on the same set, then the terminology $\tuple {\tau_1, \tau_2}$-continuous can be used to define a continuous mapping.

title: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Topology)/Everywhere
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping from $S_1$ to $S_2$.

title: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Topology)/Everywhere/Open Sets
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping from $S_1$ to $S_2$. The mapping $f$ is continuous on $S_1$ : $U \in \tau_2 \implies f^{-1} \sqbrk U \in \tau_1$ where $f^{-1} \sqbrk U$ denotes the preimage of $U$ under $f$.

title: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Topology)/Everywhere/Pointwise
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping from $S_1$ to $S_2$. The mapping $f$ is continuous everywhere (or simply continuous) $f$ is continuous at every point $x \in S_1$.

title: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Topology)/Point
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping from $S_1$ to $S_2$. Let $x \in S_1$.

title: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Topology)/Point/Filters
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping from $S_1$ to $S_2$. Let $x \in S_1$. The mapping $f$ is continuous at (the point) $x$ : for any filter $\FF$ on $T_1$ that converges to $x$, the corresponding image filter $f \sqbrk \FF$ converges to $\map f x$.

title: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Topology)/Point/Neighborhood Inverse
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping from $S_1$ to $S_2$. Let $x \in S_1$. The mapping $f$ is continuous at (the point) $x$ ( the topologies $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$) : For every neighborhood $N$ of $\map f x$ in $T_2$, $f^{-1} \sqbrk N$ is a neighborhood of $x$.

title: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Topology)/Point/Neighborhoods
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping from $S_1$ to $S_2$. Let $x \in S_1$. The mapping $f$ is continuous at (the point) $x$ ( the topologies $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$) : For every neighborhood $N$ of $\map f x$ in $T_2$, there exists a neighborhood $M$ of $x$ in $T_1$ such that $f \sqbrk M \subseteq N$.

title: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Topology)/Point/Open Sets
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping from $S_1$ to $S_2$. Let $x \in S_1$. The mapping $f$ is continuous at (the point) $x$ ( the topologies $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$) : For every open set $U_2$ of $T_2$ such that $\map f x \in U_2$, there exists an open set $U_1$ of $T_1$ such that $x \in U_1$ and $f \sqbrk {U_1} \subseteq U_2$.

title: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Topology)/Set
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping from $S_1$ to $S_2$. Let $S$ be a subset of $S_1$. The mapping $f$ is continuous on $S$ $f$ is continuous at every point $x \in S$.

title: Definition:Continuous Mapping Induced by Continuous Map
snippet: Let $L_1 = \struct{S_1, \preceq_1}$ and $L_2 = \struct{S_2, \preceq_2}$ be locales. Let $f : L_1 \to L_2$ be a continuous map. Let $\map {\operatorname{Sp}} {L_1}$ and $\map {\operatorname{Sp}} {L_2}$ denote the spectra as completely prime filters of $L_1$ and $L_2$ respectively. Let $\map {\operatorname{pt}} {L_1}$ and $\map {\operatorname{pt}} {L_2}$ denote the points as completely prime filters of $L_1$ and $L_2$ respectively.

title: Definition:Continuous Mapping Induced by Frame Homomorphism
snippet: Let $L_1 = \struct{S_1, \preceq_1}$ and $L_2 = \struct{S_2, \preceq_2}$ be frames. Let $f : L_1 \to L_2$ be a frame homomorphism. Considered as locales, let $\map {\operatorname{Sp}} {L_1}$ and $\map {\operatorname{Sp}} {L_2}$ denote the spectra as completely prime filters of $L_1$ and $L_2$ respectively. Let $\map {\operatorname{pt}} {L_1}$ and $\map {\operatorname{pt}} {L_2}$ denote the points as completely prime filters of $L_1$ and $L_2$ respectively.

title: Definition:Continuous Mapping Induced by Localic Mapping
snippet: Let $L_1 = \struct{S_1, \preceq_1}$ and $L_2 = \struct{S_2, \preceq_2}$ be locales. Let $f : L_1 \to L_2$ be a localic mapping. Let $\map {\operatorname{Sp}} {L_1}$ and $\map {\operatorname{Sp}} {L_2}$ denote the spectra as completely prime filters of $L_1$ and $L_2$ respectively. Let $\map {\operatorname{pt}} {L_1}$ and $\map {\operatorname{pt}} {L_2}$ denote the points as completely prime filters of $L_1$ and $L_2$ respectively. Let $\loweradjoint f : L_2 \to L_1$ denote the lower adjoint such that $\tuple{f, \loweradjoint f}$ is a Galois connection.

title: Definition:Continuous Mapping Space
snippet: Let $X, Y$ be topological spaces. Let $f : X \to Y$ be a continuous mapping. Then the set of all such mappings $f$ is known as continuous mapping space and is denoted by $C \paren {X,Y}$: $C \paren {X, Y} = \set {f : X \to Y}$

title: Definition:Continuous Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space such that: $\set x \in \Sigma$ for all $x \in X$. Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. We say that $\mu$ is continuous : $\map \mu {\set x} = 0$ for each $x \in X$.

title: Definition:Continuous Measure/At Point
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space such that: $\set x \in \Sigma$ for all $x \in X$. Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. Let $y \in X$. We say that $\mu$ is continuous at $y$ : $\map \mu {\set y} = 0$ Category:Definitions/Diffuse Measures

title: Definition:Continuous Ordered Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Then $\struct {S, \preceq}$ is continuous (for all elements $x$ of $S$: the way below closure $x^\ll$ of $x$ is directed) and: $\struct {S, \preceq}$ is up-complete and satisfies the .

title: Definition:Continuous Probability Distribution
snippet: A continuous probability distribution is a probability distribution of a continuous random variable.

title: Definition:Continuous Probability Distribution/Also known as
snippet: == Discrete Probability Distribution: Also known as == Some sources use the term continuous distribution for continuous probability distribution.

title: Definition:Continuous Real-Valued Function Space
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space. Let $f : X \to \R$ be a continuous real valued mapping. Then the set of all such mappings $f$ is known as the continuous real-valued function space on $X$ and is denoted by $\map C X$: $\map C X := \map C {X, \R} = \set {f : X \to \R}$

title: Definition:Continuous Real-Valued Vector Function
snippet: Let $\R^n$ be the cartesian $n$-space. Let $f: \R^n \to \R$ be a real-valued function on $\R^n$. Then $f$ is continuous on $\R^n$ : $\forall a \in \R^n: \forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists \delta \in \R_{>0}: \forall x \in \R^n: \map d {x, a} < \delta \implies \size {\map f x - \map f a} < \epsilon$ where $\map d {x, a}$ is the distance function on $\R^n$: $\ds d: \R^n \to \R: \map d {x, y} := \sqrt {\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \paren {x_i - y_i}^2}$ where $x = \tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}, y = \tuple {y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n}$ are general elements of $\R^n$.

title: Definition:Continuous Real Function/Class
snippet: The class of continuous real functions is often denoted $C$. Hence: $\map f x \in C$ at $a$ $\ds \lim_{x \mathop \to a} \map f x = \map f a$

title: Definition:Continuous Real Function/Closed Interval
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function defined on a closed interval $\closedint a b$. $f$ is continuous on $\closedint a b$ it is: $(1): \quad$ continuous at every point of the open interval $\openint a b$ $(2): \quad$ continuous on the right at $a$ $(3): \quad$ continuous on the left at $b$. That is, if $f$ is to be continuous over the whole of a closed interval, it needs to be continuous at the end points. Because we only have "access" to the function on one side of each end point, all we can do is insist on continuity on the side of the end points on which the function is defined.

title: Definition:Continuous Real Function/Everywhere
snippet: Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a real function. Then $f$ is everywhere continuous $f$ is continuous at every point in $\R$.

title: Definition:Continuous Real Function/Half Open Interval
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function defined on a half open interval $\hointl a b$. Then $f$ is continuous on $\hointl a b$ it is: $(1): \quad$ continuous at every point of $\openint a b$ $(2): \quad$ continuous on the left at $b$. Let $f$ be a real function defined on a half open interval $\hointr a b$. Then $f$ is continuous on $\hointr a b$ it is: $(1): \quad$ continuous at every point of $\openint a b$ $(2): \quad$ continuous on the right at $a$.

title: Definition:Continuous Real Function/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Continuous Real Function == The concept of a continuous real function was pioneered by the work of , and .

title: Definition:Continuous Real Function/Informal Definition
snippet: The concept of continuity makes precise the intuitive notion that a function has no "jumps" or "holes" at a given point. Loosely speaking, a real function $f$ is continuous at a point $p$ the graph of $f$ does not have a "break" at $p$.

title: Definition:Continuous Real Function/Left-Continuous
snippet: Let $A \subseteq \R$ be an open subset of the real numbers $\R$. Let $f: A \to \R$ be a real function. Let $x_0 \in A$. Then $f$ is said to be left-continuous at $x_0$ the limit from the left of $\map f x$ as $x \to x_0$ exists and: $\ds \lim_{\substack {x \mathop \to x_0^- \\ x_0 \mathop \in A} } \map f x = \map f {x_0}$ where $\ds \lim_{x \mathop \to x_0^-}$ is a limit from the left. Furthermore, $f$ is said to be left-continuous : $\forall x_0 \in A$, $f$ is left-continuous at $x_0$

title: Definition:Continuous Real Function/One Side
snippet: Let $A \subseteq \R$ be an open subset of the real numbers $\R$. Let $f: A \to \R$ be a real function.

title: Definition:Continuous Real Function/Open Interval
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function defined on an open interval $\openint a b$. Then $f$ is continuous on $\openint a b$ it is continuous at every point of $\openint a b$.

title: Definition:Continuous Real Function/Point
snippet: Let $A \subseteq \R$ be any subset of the real numbers. Let $f: A \to \R$ be a real function. Let $x \in A$ be a point of $A$.

title: Definition:Continuous Real Function/Right-Continuous
snippet: Let $S \subseteq \R$ be an open subset of the real numbers $\R$. Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real function. Let $x_0 \in S$. Then $f$ is said to be right-continuous at $x_0$ the limit from the right of $\map f x$ as $x \to x_0$ exists and: $\ds \lim_{\substack {x \mathop \to x_0^+ \\ x_0 \mathop \in A}} \map f x = \map f {x_0}$ where $\ds \lim_{x \mathop \to x_0^+}$ is a limit from the right. Furthermore, $f$ is said to be right-continuous : $\forall x_0 \in S$, $f$ is right-continuous at $x_0$

title: Definition:Continuous Real Function/Subset
snippet: Let $A \subseteq \R$ be any subset of the real numbers. Let $f: A \to \R$ be a real function. Then $f$ is continuous on $A$ $f$ is continuous at every point of $A$.

title: Definition:Continuous Real Function at Point/Also defined as
snippet: == Continuous Real Function at Point: Also defined as == Often continuity is defined only for limit points of the domain. Category:Definitions/Continuous Real Functions

title: Definition:Continuous Real Function at Point/Also presented as
snippet: == Continuous Real Function at Point: Also presented as == While continuity at a point is compactly defined as a direct consequence of the nature of limit at that point, it is commonplace in the literature to include whatever definitions for limit in the actual continuity definition, for example: $f$ is continuous at $a$ : $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists \delta \in \R_{>0}: \size {x - a} < \delta \implies \size {\map f x - \map f a} < \epsilon$ $f$ is continuous at $a$ : $\ds \lim_{x \mathop \to a^-} \map f a$ and $\ds \lim_{x \mathop \to a^+} \map f a$ both exist and both are equal to…

title: Definition:Continuous Real Function at Point/Definition 1
snippet: Let $A \subseteq \R$ be a subset of the real numbers. Let $f: A \to \R$ be a real function. Let $x \in A$ be a point of $A$. $f$ is continuous at $x$ the limit $\ds \lim_{y \mathop \to x} \map f y$ exists and: $\ds \lim_{y \mathop \to x} \map f y = \map f x$

title: Definition:Continuous Real Function at Point/Definition 2
snippet: Let $A \subseteq \R$ be any subset of the real numbers. Let $f: A \to \R$ be a real function. Let $x \in A$ be a point of $A$. $f$ is continuous at $x$ the limit $\ds \lim_{y \mathop \to x} \map f y$ exists and: $\ds \lim_{y \mathop \to x} \map f y = \map f {\lim_{y \mathop \to x} y}$

title: Definition:Continuous Spectrum of Densely-Defined Linear Operator
snippet: Let $\struct {\HH, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be a Hilbert space over $\C$. Let $\struct {\map D T, T}$ be a densely-defined linear operator. We define the continuous spectrum $\map {\sigma_s} T$ as the set of $\lambda \in \C$ such that: $T - \lambda I$ is injective, $\map {\paren {T - \lambda I} } {\map D T}$ is everywhere dense in $\HH$ but $\paren {T - \lambda I}^{-1}$ is not bounded.

title: Definition:Continuous Total Preordering
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\precsim$ be a total preordering on $S$. Let $\precsim$ be such that: $a \precsim b$ whenever there exist sequences $\sequence {a^k}_k$ and $\sequence {b^k}_k$ that converge to $a$ and $b$ respectively for which $a^k \precsim b^k$ for all $k$. Then $\precsim$ is continuous.

title: Definition:Continuous Uniform Distribution/Also known as
snippet: == Continuous Uniform Distribution: Also known as == The continuous uniform distribution is also known as the rectangular distribution.

title: Definition:Continuous Uniform Distribution/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Rectangular Distribution == The name rectangular distribution for the continuous uniform distribution arises from the shape of its graph: it has the shape of a rectangle of height $\dfrac 1 {b - a}$.

title: Definition:Continuous Uniform Distribution/Technical Note
snippet: == Technical Note for Continuous Uniform Distribution == {{LatexFor|for = \ContinuousUniform {a} {b} }} When the arguments are single characters, it is usual to omit the braces: \ContinuousUniform a b This command is specific to . Category:Technical Notes

title: Definition:Continuous at Point of Metric Space/Also known as
snippet: == Continuous at Point of Metric Space: Also known as == A mapping which is continuous at $a$ with respect to $d_1$ and $d_2$ can also be referred to as $\tuple {d_1, d_2}$-continuous at $a$. Category:Definitions/Continuous Mappings on Metric Spaces

title: Definition:Continuously Differentiable
snippet: A differentiable function $f$ is continuously differentiable $f$ is of differentiability class $C^1$. That is, if the first order derivative of $f$ (and possibly higher) is continuous.

title: Definition:Continuously Differentiable/Real-Valued Function/Open Set
snippet: Let $U$ be an open subset of $\R^n$. Let $f: U \to \R$ be a real-valued function. Then $f$ is continuously differentiable in the open set $U$ : $(1): \quad f$ is differentiable in $U$. $(2): \quad$ the partial derivatives of $f$ are continuous in $U$. This can be denoted: $f \in \map {\CC^1} {\mathbb X, \R}$

title: Definition:Continuously Differentiable/Real Function/Open Interval
snippet: Let $I\subset\R$ be an open interval. Then $f$ is continuously differentiable on $I$ $f$ is differentiable on $I$ and its derivative is continuous on $I$.

title: Definition:Continuously Differentiable/Real Function/Open Set
snippet: Let $I \subset \R$ be an open set. Then $f$ is continuously differentiable on $I$ $f$ is differentiable on $I$ and its derivative is continuous on $I$. Category:Definitions/Differentiable Real Functions

title: Definition:Continuously Differentiable/Vector-Valued Function/Open Set
snippet: Let $U \subset \R^n$ be an open set. Let $f: U \to \R^m$ be a vector-valued function. Then $f$ is continuously differentiable in $U$ $f$ is differentiable in $U$ and its partial derivatives are continuous in $U$. Category:Definitions/Differentiable Vector-Valued Functions

title: Definition:Continuously Embedded
snippet: Let $\operatorname{id} : V \to W$ be an embedding of normed vector spaces. Then $V$ is continuously embedded in $W$ and $\operatorname{id}$ is a continuous embedding if the identity $\operatorname{id}$ is a continuous mapping. Category:Definitions/Functional Analysis

title: Definition:Continuum
snippet: A continuum is an object which is continuous.

title: Definition:Continuum/Also defined as
snippet: == Continuum: Also defined as == Some sources define a continuum specifically as either: the set of real numbers an arbitrary real interval, whether open, closed or half-open. However, this usage is considered archaic.

title: Definition:Continuum/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Continuum == The plural of continuum is continua, although the technically-erroneous form continuums can occasionally be found.

title: Definition:Continuum/Topology
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be both compact and connected in $T$. Then $H$ is a continuum.

title: Definition:Continuum (Topology)/Also defined as
snippet: == Continuum in context of Topology: Also known as == Some sources insist that a topological space need to be a $T_2$ space, as well as both compact and connected, in order to be considered to be a continuum.

title: Definition:Continuum Mechanics
snippet: Continuum mechanics is the branch of applied mathematics concerned with the mechanical behavior of materials considered as a continuous mass rather than as discrete particles.

title: Definition:Contour
snippet: Let $\R^n$ be a real cartesian space of $n$ dimensions. Let $C_1, \ldots, C_n$ be directed smooth curves in $\R^n$. For each $i \in \set {1, \ldots, n}$, let $C_i$ be parameterized by the smooth path $\rho_i: \closedint {a_i} {b_i} \to \R^n$. For each $i \in \set {1, \ldots, n - 1}$, let the end point of $\rho_i$ equal the start point of $\rho_{i + 1}$: $\map {\rho_i} {b_i} = \map {\rho_{i + 1} } {a_{i + 1} }$ Then the finite sequence $\sequence {C_1, \ldots, C_n}$ is called a contour (in $\R^n$).

title: Definition:Contour/Closed
snippet: Let $\R^n$ be a real cartesian space of $n$ dimensions. Let $C$ be the contour in $\R^n$ defined by the (finite) sequence $\sequence {C_1, \ldots, C_n}$ of directed smooth curves in $\R^n$. Let $C_i$ be parameterized by the smooth path $\rho_i: \closedint {a_i} {b_i} \to \R^n$ for all $i \in \set {1, \ldots, n}$. $C$ is a closed contour the start point of $C$ is equal to the end point of $C$: $\map {\rho_1} {a_1} = \map {\rho_n} {b_n}$

title: Definition:Contour/Closed/Complex Plane
snippet: Let $C$ be a contour in $\C$ defined by the (finite) sequence $\sequence {C_1, \ldots, C_n}$ of directed smooth curves in $\C$. Let $C_k$ be parameterized by the smooth path $\gamma_k: \closedint {a_k} {b_k} \to \C$ for all $k \in \set {1, \ldots, n}$. $C$ is a closed contour the start point of $C$ is equal to the end point of $C$: $\map {\gamma_1} {a_1} = \map {\gamma_n} {b_n}$

title: Definition:Contour/Complex Plane
snippet: Let $C_1, \ldots, C_n$ be directed smooth curves in the complex plane $\C$. For each $k \in \set{ 1, \ldots, n}$, let $C_k$ be parameterized by the smooth path $\gamma_k: \closedint {a_k}{b_k} \to \C$. For each $k \in \set{ 1, \ldots, n-1}$, let the endpoint of $\gamma_k$ equal the start point of $\gamma_{k + 1}$: $\map {\gamma_k}{b_k} = \map {\gamma_{k + 1} }{a_{k + 1} }$ Then the finite sequence $\sequence{C_1, \ldots, C_n}$ is a contour.

title: Definition:Contour/Endpoints
snippet: Let $\R^n$ be a real cartesian space of $n$ dimensions. Let $C_1, \ldots, C_n$ be directed smooth curves in $\R^n$. Let $C_i$ be parameterized by the smooth path $\rho_i: \left[{a_i \,.\,.\, b_i}\right] \to \R^n$ for all $i \in \left\{ {1, \ldots, n}\right\}$. Let $C$ be the contour defined by the finite sequence $C_1, \ldots, C_n$. The start point of $C$ is $\rho_1 \left({a_1}\right)$. The end point of $C$ is $\rho_n \left({b_n}\right)$. Collectively, $\rho_1 \left({a_1}\right)$ and $\rho_n \left({b_n}\right)$ are referred to as the endpoints of $C$.

title: Definition:Contour/Endpoints/Complex Plane
snippet: Let $C_1, \ldots, C_n$ be directed smooth curves in $\C$. Let $C_k$ be parameterized by the smooth path $\gamma_k: \closedint {a_k}{b_k} \to \C$ for all $k \in \set{ 1, \ldots, n}$. Let $C$ be the contour defined by the finite sequence $\sequence {C_1, \ldots, C_n}$. The start point of $C$ is $\map {\gamma_1}{a_1}$. The end point of $C$ is $\map {\gamma_n}{b_n}$. Collectively, $\map {\gamma_1}{a_1}$ and $\map {\gamma_n}{b_n}$ are referred to as the endpoints of $C$.

title: Definition:Contour/Image
snippet: Let $\R^n$ be a real cartesian space of $n$ dimensions. Let $C$ be a contour in $\R^n$ defined by the (finite) sequence $\sequence {C_1, \ldots, C_n}$ of directed smooth curves in $\R^n$. Let $C_i$ be parameterized by the smooth path $\rho_i: \closedint {a_i} {b_i} \to \R^n$ for all $i \in \set {1, \ldots, n}$. The image of $C$ is defined as: $\ds \Img C := \bigcup_{i \mathop = 1}^n \Img {\rho_i}$ where $\Img {\rho_i}$ denotes the image of $\rho_i$.

title: Definition:Contour/Image/Complex Plane
snippet: Let $C$ be a contour in $\C$ defined by the (finite) sequence $\sequence {C_1, \ldots, C_n}$ of directed smooth curves in $\C$. Let $C_k$ be parameterized by the smooth path $\gamma_k: \closedint {a_k} {b_k} \to \C$ for all $k \in \set {1, \ldots, n}$. The image of $C$ is defined as: $\ds \Img C := \bigcup_{k \mathop = 1}^n \Img {\gamma_k}$ where $\Img {\gamma_k}$ denotes the image of $\gamma_k$. If $\Img C \subseteq D$, where $D$ is a subset of $\C$, we say that $C$ is a contour in $D$.

title: Definition:Contour/Length
snippet: Let $\R^n$ be a real cartesian space of $n$ dimensions. Let $C$ be a contour in $\R^n$ defined by the (finite) sequence $\sequence {C_1, \ldots, C_n}$ of directed smooth curves in $\R^n$. Let $C_i$ be parameterized by the smooth path $\rho_i: \closedint {a_i} {b_i} \to \R^n$ for all $i \in \set {1, \ldots, n}$. The length of $C$ is defined as: $\ds \map L C := \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \int_{a_i}^{b_i} \size {\map {\rho_i'} t} \rd t$

title: Definition:Contour/Length/Complex Plane
snippet: Let $C$ be a contour in $\C$ defined by the (finite) sequence $\sequence {C_1, \ldots, C_n}$ of directed smooth curves in $\C$. Let $C_k$ be parameterized by the smooth path $\gamma_k: \closedint {a_k} {b_k} \to \C$ for all $k \in \set {1, \ldots, n}$.
