The length of $C$ is defined as: $\ds \map L C := \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n \int_{a_k}^{b_k} \size {\map {\gamma_k'} t} \rd t$ It follows from Length of Contour is Well-Defined that $\map L C$ is defined and independent of the parameterizations of $C_1, \ldots, C_n$.

title: Definition:Contour/Parameterization
snippet: Let $\R^n$ be a real cartesian space of $n$ dimensions. Let $C_1, \ldots, C_n$ be directed smooth curves in $\R^n$. Let $C_i$ be parameterized by the smooth path $\rho_i: \closedint {a_i} {b_i} \to \R^n$ for all $i \in \set {1, \ldots, n}$. Let $C$ be the contour defined by the finite sequence $C_1, \ldots, C_n$.

title: Definition:Contour/Parameterization/Complex Plane
snippet: Let $C_1, \ldots, C_n$ be directed smooth curves in the complex plane $\C$. Let $C_k$ be parameterized by the smooth path $\gamma_k: \closedint {a_k} {b_k} \to \C$ for all $k \in \set {1, \ldots, n}$. Let $C$ be the contour defined by the finite sequence $C_1, \ldots, C_n$. The parameterization of $C$ is defined as the function $\gamma: \closedint {a_1} {c_n} \to \C$ with: $\map {\gamma \restriction_{\closedint {c_k} {c_{k + 1} } } } t = \map {\gamma_k} t$ where $\ds c_k = a_1 + \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^k b_j - \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^k a_j$ for $k \in \set {0, \ldots, n}$.

title: Definition:Contour/Simple
snippet: Let $\R^n$ be a real cartesian space of $n$ dimensions. Let $C_1, \ldots, C_n$ be directed smooth curves in $\R^n$. Let $C_i$ be parameterized by the smooth path $\rho_i: \closedint {a_i} {b_i} \to \R^n$ for all $i \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n}$. Let $C$ be the contour in $\R^n$ defined by the finite sequence $C_1, \ldots, C_n$.

title: Definition:Contour/Simple/Complex Plane
snippet: Let $C_1, \ldots, C_n$ be directed smooth curves in the complex plane $\C$. Let $C_k$ be parameterized by the smooth path $\gamma_k: \closedint {a_k} {b_k} \to \C$ for all $k \in \set {1, \ldots, n}$. Let $C$ be the contour defined by the finite sequence $C_1, \ldots, C_n$. $C$ is a simple contour : $(1): \quad$ For all $j, k \in \set {1, \ldots, n}, t_1 \in \hointr {a_j} {b_j}, t_2 \in \hointr {a_k} {b_k}$ with $t_1 \ne t_2$, we have $\map {\gamma_j} {t_1} \ne \map {\gamma_j} {t_2}$.

title: Definition:Contour Integral
snippet: Let $OA$ be a curve in a vector field $\mathbf F$. Let $P$ be a point on $OA$. Let $\d \mathbf l$ be a small element of length of $OA$ at $P$. Let $\mathbf v$ be the vector induced by $\mathbf F$ on $P$. Let $\mathbf v$ make an angle $\theta$ with the tangent to $OA$ at $P$. 350px Hence: $\mathbf v \cdot \d \mathbf l = v \cos \theta \rd l$ where: $\cdot$ denotes dot product $v$ and $\d l$ denote the magnitude of $\mathbf v$ and $\d \mathbf l$ respectively.

title: Definition:Contour Integral/Also known as
snippet: == Contour Integral: Also known as == A contour integral is called a line integral or a curve integral in many texts. Category:Definitions/Contour Integrals

title: Definition:Contour Integral/Complex
snippet: Let $C$ be a contour defined by a finite sequence $C_1, \ldots, C_n$ of directed smooth curves in the complex plane $\C$. Let $C_k$ be parameterized by the smooth path: $\gamma_k: \closedint {a_k} {b_k} \to \C$ for all $k \in \set {1, \ldots, n}$. Let $f: \Img C \to \C$ be a continuous complex function, where $\Img C$ denotes the image of $C$. The contour integral of $f$ along $C$ is defined by: $\ds \int_C \map f z \rd z = \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n \int_{a_k}^{b_k} \map f {\map {\gamma_k} t} \map {\gamma_k'} t \rd t$

title: Definition:Contour Integral/Complex/Closed
snippet: Let $C$ be a closed contour in $\C$. Then the symbol $\ds \oint$ is used for the contour integral on $C$. The definition remains the same: $\ds \oint_C \map f z \rd z := \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n \int_{a_k}^{b_k} \map f {\map {\gamma_k} t} \map {\gamma_k'} t \rd t$

title: Definition:Contour Plot
snippet: Let $f: \R^2 \to \R$ be a real function of $2$ variables. A contour plot is a diagram in the Cartesian plane $\CC$ in which points in $\CC$ with the same values of $f$ are joined by curves for a selection of some specific values

title: Definition:Contour Plot/Contour Line
snippet: Consider a contour plot of a real function $f$ of $2$ variables. Each of the curves joining points with the same values under $f$ are known as contour lines.

title: Definition:Contractible Space
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space.

title: Definition:Contractible Space/Definition 1
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space. $X$ is called a contractible space the identity map $\operatorname {id}_X$ is homotopic to a constant map $X \to X$.

title: Definition:Contractible Space/Definition 2
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space. $X$ is called a contractible space it is homotopy equivalent to a point.

title: Definition:Contraction
snippet: Let $G$ be a vector space over a field $K$. Let $\beta \in K$. Let $s_\beta: G \to G$ be a similarity mapping on $G$: $\forall \mathbf x \in G: \map {s_\beta} {\mathbf x} = \beta \mathbf x$ Let the scale factor $\beta$ be such that $0 < \beta \le 1$. Then $s_\beta$ is called a contraction.

title: Definition:Contraction Mapping
snippet: Metric Spaces: Contraction Mapping (Metric Space) Linear Algebra: Contraction

title: Definition:Contraction Mapping (Metric Space)
snippet: Let $\struct {X, d_1}$ and $\struct {Y, d_2}$ be metric spaces. Let $f: X \to Y$ be a mapping. Then $f$ is a contraction (mapping) there exists $\kappa \in \R: 0 \le \kappa < 1$ such that: $\forall x, y \in X: \map {d_2} {\map f x, \map f y} \le \kappa \map {d_1} {x, y}$ That is, $f$ is Lipschitz continuous for a Lipschitz constant less than $1$.

title: Definition:Contraction of Ideal
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be commutative ring with unity. Let $f : A \to B$ be a ring homomorphism. Let $\mathfrak b$ be an ideal of $B$. The contraction of $\mathfrak b$ by $f$ is its preimage under $f$: $\mathfrak b^c = f^{-1} \sqbrk {\mathfrak b}$

title: Definition:Contradiction
snippet: A contradiction is a statement which is always false, independently of any relevant circumstances that could theoretically influence its truth value. This has the form: $p \land \neg p$ or, equivalently: $\neg p \land p$ that is: $p$ is true and, at the same time, $p$ is not true. An example of a "relevant circumstance" here is the truth value of $p$. The archetypal contradiction can be symbolised by $\bot$, and referred to as bottom.

title: Definition:Contradiction/Also known as
snippet: A contradiction is also known as: a logical falsehood or logical falsity a contravalid proposition an absurdity or absurdism, as the idea of a statement being both false and true at once is absurd. Also seen: an inconsistency an unsatisfiable formula. However, on , these terms are reserved for the analogous concepts for proof systems and formal semantics respectively.

title: Definition:Contradictory/Branch
snippet: Let $T$ be a labeled tree for propositional logic. Let $\Gamma$ be a branch of $T$. Then $\Gamma$ is a contradictory branch , for some WFF of propositional logic $\mathbf A$, both $\mathbf A$ and $\neg \mathbf A$ occur along $\Gamma$.

title: Definition:Contradictory/Propositional Formulas
snippet: Let $\Delta$ be a set of propositional formulas. Then $\Delta$ is contradictory there exists some propositional formula $P$ such that $P \in \Delta$ and $\neg P \in \Delta$.

title: Definition:Contradictory/Statements
snippet: Two statements $p$ and $q$ are said to be contradictory both:

title: Definition:Contranormal Subgroup
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$. Then $H$ is a contranormal subgroup the normal closure of $H$ is the whole of $G$.

title: Definition:Contrapositive Statement
snippet: The contrapositive of the conditional: $p \implies q$ is the statement: $\neg q \implies \neg p$

title: Definition:Contrary Statements
snippet: Two statements are said to be contrary if they can both be false, but they cannot both be true.

title: Definition:Contrary Statements/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Contrary Statements == In the context of contrary statements, the word contrary is pronounced with the stress on the first syllable: con-tra-ry. There is a different usage of contrary which means, of a person, perversely inclined to disagree or to do the opposite of what is expected or desired. In this context, the stress is on the second syllable: con-tra-ry, making it rhyme, conveniently, with Mary, hence the children's nursery rhyme: Mary, Mary, quite contrary How does your garden grow? With silver bells and cockle shells And pretty maids all in a row.

title: Definition:Contravariant Functor/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. A contravariant functor $F : \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ consists of: An object functor $F_0$ that assigns to each object $X$ of $\mathbf C$ an object $FX$ of $\mathbf D$. An arrow functor $F_1$ that assigns to each arrow $f : X \to Y$ of $\mathbf C$ an arrow $Ff : FY \to FX$ of $\mathbf D$.

title: Definition:Contravariant Functor/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. A contravariant functor $F : \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ is a covariant functor: $F: \mathbf C^{\text{op}} \to \mathbf D$ where $\mathbf C^{\text{op}}$ is the dual category of $\mathbf C$.

title: Definition:Contravariant Hom Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf{Set}$ be the category of sets. Let $\mathbf C$ be a locally small category. Let $C \in \mathbf C_0$ be an object of $\mathbf C$. The contravariant hom functor based at $C$: $\map {\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C} } {\cdot, C}: \mathbf C \to \mathbf {Set}$ is the contravariant functor defined by: {{DefineFunctor |ob = $\map {\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C} } {B, C} = \map {\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C} } {B, C}$ |mor = $\map {\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C} } {f, C}: \map {\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C} } {B, C} \to \map {\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C} } {A, C}, g \mapsto g \circ f$…

title: Definition:Contravariant Power Set Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf{Set}$ be the category of sets. The contravariant power set functor $\overline \PP: \mathbf{Set} \to \mathbf{Set}$ is the contravariant functor which sends: {{DefineFunctor |ob = An object $x$ to its power set $\powerset x$. |mor = A morphism $f : x \to y$ to the inverse image mapping $\map {\overline \PP} f : \powerset y \to \powerset x$ }}

title: Definition:Contravariant Tensor
snippet: Let $F$ be a tensor of type $\tuple {0, l}$: $\ds F : \underbrace { {V^*} \times \ldots \times {V^*} }_{\text {$l$ times} } \to \R$ Then $F$ is called a contravariant $l$-tensor (on $V$).

title: Definition:Control
snippet: A control is an implementation of a technique to rule out the effects of a random variable other than the factors that a particular experiment is designed to investigate. This may be done either by: directly controlling one or more of the possible factors which may influence the outcome or matching pairs of experimental units, and applying a treatment to one but not the other. Randomization can then be employed to ensure that any residual confounding variables do not introduce any systemic bias.

title: Definition:Control Chart
snippet: A control chart is a graph used in quality control to indicate whether or not a property of a mass-produced item falls within acceptable limits. Hence it can indicate whether there is some defect in the manufacturing process. A sample is taken at regular intervals from the production line and the property in question is measured. This is then plotted on the control chart and checked against the target line and control lines. If the plot is outside the control lines, there is a need to check that the process is working correctly.

title: Definition:Control Chart/Control Line
snippet: A control line in a control chart is one of a number of straight lines a predetermined distance away from the target line, between which the measurements of the property being measured are expected to lie. Typically there are $2$ types of control line , as follows:

title: Definition:Control Chart/Target Line
snippet: The target line in a control chart is a straight line indicating the ideal value of the property being measured.

title: Definition:Control Group
snippet: A control group is a set of experimental units in an experimental design which are specifically not given the treatment under investigation. It provides a baseline to assess what would happen to a typical experimental unit to compare those which are subject to that treatment. The control group and the experimental groups should be allocated either randomly, or, if possible, balanced.

title: Definition:Control Group/Control Condition
snippet: Consider an experimental design $\EE$ with a control group $\CC$. The control condition is the condition of $\CC$ during the course of $\EE$

title: Definition:Control Line/Action Limit
snippet: An action limit is one of the outer pair of control lines in a control chart. If the observed value falls outside the action limits, then action will be taken, in which the machine is often reset.

title: Definition:Control Line/Also known as
snippet: == Control Line: Also known as == The control lines of a control chart are also known as action limits.

title: Definition:Control Line/Warning Limit
snippet: A warning limit is one of the inner pair of control lines in a control chart. If the observed value falls outside the warning limits, but inside the action limits, then this is a signal that the process may be off target. Another sample is to be taken immediately. If that second sample is observed to also be outside the warning limits, then action will be taken. However, if that sample is observed to be within the warning limits, it is assumed that production is on target.

title: Definition:Control Scheme
snippet: A control scheme is a system whereby potential deviations of future values from a desired target may be compensated for, by adjustment of input values.

title: Definition:Control Theory
snippet: Control theory deals with the control of dynamical systems in engineered processes and machines. Category:Definitions/Control Theory Category:Definitions/Engineering

title: Definition:Convenience Sample
snippet: Let $P$ be a population in the physical universe. Let $S \subsetneq P$ be a sample. Suppose that data about some individuals in $P$ are more easily accessible than data about others. Then $S$ is a convenience sample the primary criterion for the construction of $S$ is the higher accessibility of data of certain individuals in $P$ over others. That is, the objects in $S$ are the ones conveniently at hand.

title: Definition:Convenience Sampling
snippet: Convenience sampling is the technique of gathering a sample from the most conveniently available set of possible subjects. Data collected in this way cannot be expected to be representative of a more comprehensive population.

title: Definition:Convergence
snippet: Convergence is the property of being convergent, which is defined variously according to the scope of the object in question. As follows:

title: Definition:Convergence Almost Everywhere
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $D \in \Sigma$. Let $f: D \to \R$ be a $\Sigma$-measurable function. Let $\sequence {f_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence of $\Sigma$-measurable functions $f_n: D \to \R$. Then $\sequence {f_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is said to converge almost everywhere (or converge a.e.) on $D$ to $f$ : $\map \mu {\set {x \in D : \sequence {\map {f_n} x}_{n \mathop \in \N} \text { does not converge to } \map f x} } = 0$ and we write $f_n \stackrel{a.e.} \to f$. In other words, the sequence of functions converges pointwise outside of a $\mu$-null set.

title: Definition:Convergence in Distribution
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence of real-valued random variables on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $X$ be a real-valued random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. For each $n \in \N$, let $F_n$ be the cumulative distribution function of $X_n$. Let $F$ be the cumulative distribution function of $X$. We say that $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ converges in distribution to $X$ : $\ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \map {F_n} x = \map F x$ for all $x$ for which $F$ is continuous.

title: Definition:Convergence in Distribution/Also known as
snippet: == Convergence in Distribution: Also known as == Convergence in distribution is also known as weak convergence.

title: Definition:Convergence in Mean
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $f : X \to \R$ be a $\mu$-integrable function. For each $n \in \N$, let $f_n : X \to \R$ be a $\mu$-integrable function. We say that the sequence $\sequence {f_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ converges in mean to $f$ : $\ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \int \size {f_n - f} \rd \mu = 0$

title: Definition:Convergence in Mean Square
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence of real-valued random variables on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $X$ be a real-valued random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. We say that $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is convergent in mean square to $X$ : $\ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \expect {\size {X_n - X}^2} = 0$ where $\expect X$ denotes the expectation of $X$. This is written: $X_n \xrightarrow {\text {L2} } X$

title: Definition:Convergence in Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $\sequence {f_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}, f_n: X \to \R$ be a sequence of $\Sigma$-measurable functions. Then $f_n$ is said to converge in measure to a measurable function $f: X \to \R$ : $\ds \forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \map \mu {\set {x \in D : \size {\map {f_n} x - \map f x} \ge \epsilon} } = 0$ for all $D \in \Sigma$ with $\map \mu D < + \infty$.

title: Definition:Convergence in Probability
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence of real-valued random variables on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $X$ be a real-valued random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. We say that $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ converges in probability to $X$ : $\ds \forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \map \Pr {\size {X_n - X} < \epsilon} = 1$ This is written: $X_n \xrightarrow p X$ or: $X_n \xrightarrow P X$

title: Definition:Convergent Complex Sequence/Geometrical Interpretation
snippet: == Geometrical Interpretation of Convergent Complex Sequence == The following illustration is a geometrical interpretation of the concept of a Convergent Complex Sequence. As $n$ increases, the distance from $z_n$ to $c$ gets smaller, until after $n$ is greater than $N$, $\cmod {z_n - c}$ is always less than $\epsilon$: 600px

title: Definition:Convergent Continued Fraction
snippet: Let $\struct {F, \norm {\,\cdot\,} }$ be a valued field. Let $C = \sequence {a_n}_{n \mathop \ge 0}$ be a infinite continued fraction in $F$. Then $C$ converges to its value $x \in F$ the following hold: $(1): \quad$ For all natural numbers $n \in \N_{\ge 0}$, the $n$th denominator is nonzero $(2): \quad$ The sequence of convergents $\sequence {C_n}_{n \mathop \ge 0}$ converges to $x$.

title: Definition:Convergent Continued Fraction/Also known as
snippet: == Convergent Continued Fraction: Also known as == A convergent continued fraction can also be referred to as a convergent fraction.

title: Definition:Convergent Filter
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\FF$ be a filter on $S$. Then $\FF$ converges to a point $x \in S$ : $\forall N_x \subseteq S: N_x \in \FF$ where $N_x$ is a neighborhood of $x$. That is, a filter converges to a point $x$ every neighborhood of $x$ is an element of that filter. If there is a point $x \in S$ such that $\FF$ converges to $x$, then $\FF$ is convergent.

title: Definition:Convergent Filter Basis
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\BB$ be a filter basis of a filter $\FF$ on $S$. Then $\BB$ converges to a point $x \in S$ : $\forall N_x \subseteq S: \exists B \in \BB: B \subseteq N_x$ where $N_x$ is a neighborhood of $x$. That is, a filter basis is convergent to a point $x$ if every neighborhood of $x$ contains some set of that filter basis.

title: Definition:Convergent Integral
snippet: A convergent integral is an improper integral whose limits converge to a definite value.

title: Definition:Convergent Iteration
snippet: A convergent iteration is an iteration which generates a convergent sequence.

title: Definition:Convergent Mapping/Complex Function
snippet: Let $f: \C \to \C$ be a complex function defined everywhere on $\C$ except possibly at $c$. Let $\map f z$ tend to the limit $L$ as $z$ tends to $c$. Then $f$ converges to the limit $L$ as $z$ tends to $c$.

title: Definition:Convergent Mapping/Metric Space
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct {A_1, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct {A_2, d_2}$ be metric spaces. Let $c$ be a limit point of $M_1$. Let $f: A_1 \to A_2$ be a mapping from $A_1$ to $A_2$ defined everywhere on $A_1$ except possibly at $c$. Let $\map f x$ tend to the limit $L$ as $x$ tends to $c$. Then $f$ converges to the limit $L$ as $x$ tends to $c$.

title: Definition:Convergent Mapping/Real Function
snippet: Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a real function defined everywhere on $A_1$ except possibly at $c$. Let $\map f x$ tend to the limit $L$ as $x$ tends to $c$. Then $f$ converges to the limit $L$ as $x$ tends to $c$.

title: Definition:Convergent Net
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\struct {\Lambda, \preceq}$ be a directed set. Let $\family {x_\lambda}_{\lambda \mathop \in \Lambda}$ be a net. We say that $\family {x_\lambda}_{\lambda \in \Lambda}$ converges to $x \in X$ in $\struct {X, \tau}$, denoted $\ds x_\lambda \to x$ or $\lim x_\lambda = x$, : $\forall U \in \tau: x \in U \implies \exists \lambda_0 \in \Lambda: \forall \lambda \succeq \lambda_0: x_\lambda \in U$ That is, for every open $U$ with $x \in U$, there exists an $\lambda_0 \in \Lambda$ such that forall $\lambda \succeq \lambda_0$, $x_\lambda \in U$.

title: Definition:Convergent Net/Cluster Point
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\struct {\Lambda, \preceq}$ be a directed set. Let $\family {x_\lambda}_{\lambda \mathop \in \Lambda}$ be a net. Let $x \in X$. We say that $\family {x_\lambda}_{\lambda \mathop \in \Lambda}$ clusters at $x \in X$, denoted $x_\lambda \mathop {\longrightarrow_{\text{cl} } } x$, : $\forall U \in \tau, \lambda_0 \in \Lambda: x \in U \implies \exists \lambda \succeq \lambda_0: x_\lambda \in U$ That is, for every open $U$ with $x \in U$, and for every $\lambda_0 \in \Lambda$, there is an $\lambda \ge \lambda_0$ such that $\lambda \in U$.

title: Definition:Convergent Product/Arbitrary Field
snippet: Let $\struct {\mathbb K, \norm {\,\cdot\,} }$ be a valued field.

title: Definition:Convergent Product/Arbitrary Field/Arbitrary Sequence
snippet: Let $\struct {\mathbb K, \norm {\,\cdot\,} }$ be a valued field. Let $\sequence {a_n}$ be a sequence of elements of $\mathbb K$. The infinite product $\ds \prod_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n$ is convergent : there exists $n_0 \in \N$ such that the sequence of partial products of $\ds \prod_{n \mathop = n_0}^\infty a_n$ converges to some $b \in \mathbb K \setminus \set 0$. The sequence of partial products of $\ds \prod_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n$ is then convergent to some $a \in \mathbb K$. Category:Definitions/Convergent Products

title: Definition:Convergent Product/Arbitrary Field/Nonzero Sequence
snippet: Let $\struct {\mathbb K, \norm {\,\cdot\,} }$ be a valued field. Let $\sequence {a_n}$ be a sequence of nonzero elements of $\mathbb K$. The infinite product $\ds \prod_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n$ is convergent its sequence of partial products converges to a nonzero limit $a \in \mathbb K \setminus \set 0$. Category:Definitions/Convergent Products

title: Definition:Convergent Product/Informal Definition
snippet: A convergent product is an infinite (continued) product whose sequence of partial products converges. Hence the phrase: $\ds \prod_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n$ diverges to $0$ then becomes: $\ds \prod_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n$ converges to $0$.

title: Definition:Convergent Product/Normed Algebra
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be a division ring with norm $\norm {\,\cdot\,}_{\mathbb K}$. Let $\struct {A, \norm {\,\cdot\,} }$ be an associative normed unital algebra over $\mathbb K$. Let $\sequence {a_n}$ be a sequence in $A$.

title: Definition:Convergent Product/Number Field
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be one of the standard number fields $\Q, \R, \C$.

title: Definition:Convergent Product/Number Field/Arbitrary Sequence
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be one of the standard number fields $\Q, \R, \C$. Let $\sequence {a_n}$ be a sequence of elements of $\mathbb K$. The infinite product $\ds \prod_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n$ is convergent : there exists $n_0 \in \N$ such that the sequence of partial products of $\ds \prod_{n \mathop = n_0}^\infty a_n$ converges to some $b \in \mathbb K \setminus \set 0$. The sequence of partial products of $\ds \prod_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n$ is then convergent to some $a \in \mathbb K$. Category:Definitions/Convergent Products

title: Definition:Convergent Product/Number Field/Nonzero Sequence
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be one of the standard number fields $\Q, \R, \C$. Let $\sequence {a_n}$ be a sequence of nonzero elements of $\mathbb K$. Then: The infinite product $\ds \prod_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n$ is convergent its sequence of partial products converges to a nonzero limit $a \in \mathbb K \setminus \set 0$. Category:Definitions/Convergent Products

title: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Also known as
snippet: == Convergent Sequence: Also known as== A convergent sequence is also known by its variant converging sequence. In the interests of consistency, the latter term is avoided on . Category:Definitions/Convergent Sequences

title: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Complex Numbers/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\sequence {z_k}$ be a sequence in $\C$. $\sequence {z_k}$ converges to the limit $c \in \C$ : $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists N \in \R: n > N \implies \cmod {z_n - c} < \epsilon$ where $\cmod z$ denotes the modulus of $z$.

title: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Complex Numbers/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\sequence {z_k} = \sequence {x_k + i y_k}$ be a sequence in $\C$. $\sequence {z_k}$ converges to the limit $c = a + i b$ both: $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists N \in \R: n > N \implies \size {x_n - a} < \epsilon \text { and } \size {y_n - b} < \epsilon$ where $\size {x_n - a}$ denotes the absolute value of $x_n - a$.

title: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Metric Space
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space or a pseudometric space. Let $\sequence {x_k}$ be a sequence in $A$.

title: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Metric Space/Definition 1
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space or a pseudometric space. Let $\sequence {x_k}$ be a sequence in $A$. $\sequence {x_k}$ converges to the limit $l \in A$ : $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists N \in \R_{>0}: \forall n \in \N: n > N \implies \map d {x_n, l} < \epsilon$

title: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Metric Space/Definition 2
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space or a pseudometric space. Let $\sequence {x_k}$ be a sequence in $A$. $\sequence {x_k}$ converges to the limit $l \in A$ : $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists N \in \R_{>0}: \forall n \in \N: n > N \implies x_n \in \map {B_\epsilon} l$ where $\map {B_\epsilon} l$ is the open $\epsilon$-ball of $l$.

title: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Metric Space/Definition 3
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space or a pseudometric space. Let $\sequence {x_k}$ be a sequence in $A$. $\sequence {x_k}$ converges to the limit $l \in A$ : $\ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \map d {x_n, l} = 0$

title: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Metric Space/Definition 4
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space or a pseudometric space. Let $\sequence {x_k}$ be a sequence in $A$. $\sequence {x_k}$ converges to the limit $l \in A$ : for every $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$, the open $\epsilon$-ball about $l$ contains all but finitely many of the $x_k$.

title: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Normed Division Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a normed division ring. Let $\sequence {x_n} $ be a sequence in $R$.

snippet:

title: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Normed Vector Space
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \norm {\,\cdot \,} }$ be a normed vector space. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $X$. Let $L \in X$. The sequence $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ converges to the limit $L \in X$ : $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists N \in \R_{>0}: \forall n \in \N: n > N \implies \norm {x_n - L} < \epsilon$

title: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Notation
snippet: == Notation == When $\sequence {x_k}$ converges to the limit $l \in A$ we can write: $x_n \to l$ as $n \mathop \to \infty$ or: $\ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} x_n \to l$ This is voiced: As $n$ tends to infinity, $x_n$ tends to (the limit) $l$. Some use the notation $\ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} x_n = l$ This is voiced: The limit as $n$ tends to infinity of $x_n$ is $l$. Note, however, that one must take care to use this alternative notation only in contexts in which the sequence is known to have a limit. Category:Definitions/Convergent Sequences

title: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Note on Domain of N
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_k}$ be a sequence. $\ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} x_n \to l$ be the limit of $\sequence {x_k}$. That is: $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists N \in \R_{>0}: n > N \implies \map d {x_n, l} < \epsilon$ Some sources insist that $N \in \N$ but this is not strictly necessary and can make proofs more cumbersome.

title: Definition:Convergent Sequence/P-adic Numbers
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. Let $\struct {\Q_p, \norm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$ be the $p$-adic numbers. Let $\sequence {x_n} $ be a sequence in $\Q_p$.

title: Definition:Convergent Sequence/P-adic Numbers/Definition 1
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. Let $\struct {\Q_p, \norm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$ be the $p$-adic numbers. Let $\sequence {x_n} $ be a sequence in $\Q_p$. The sequence $\sequence {x_n}$ converges to the limit $x \in \Q_p$ : $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists N \in \R_{>0}: \forall n \in \N: n > N \implies \norm {x_n - x}_p < \epsilon$

title: Definition:Convergent Sequence/P-adic Numbers/Definition 2
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. Let $\struct {\Q_p, \norm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$ be the $p$-adic numbers. Let $\sequence {x_n} $ be a sequence in $\Q_p$. The sequence $\sequence {x_n}$ converges to the limit $x \in \Q_p$ : $\sequence {x_n}$ converges to $x$ in the $p$-adic norm

title: Definition:Convergent Sequence/P-adic Numbers/Definition 3
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. Let $\struct {\Q_p, \norm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$ be the $p$-adic numbers. Let $\sequence {x_n} $ be a sequence in $\Q_p$. The sequence $\sequence {x_n}$ converges to the limit $x \in \Q_p$ : $\sequence {x_n}$ converges to $x$ in the $p$-adic metric

title: Definition:Convergent Sequence/P-adic Numbers/Definition 4
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. Let $\struct {\Q_p, \norm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$ be the $p$-adic numbers. Let $\sequence {x_n} $ be a sequence in $\Q_p$. The sequence $\sequence {x_n}$ converges to the limit $x \in \Q_p$ : the real sequence $\sequence {\norm {x_n - x}_p }$ converges to $0$ in the reals $\R$

title: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Rational Numbers
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_k}$ be a sequence in $\Q$. $\sequence {x_k}$ converges to the limit $l \in \R$ : $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists N \in \R_{>0}: n > N \implies \size {x_n - l} < \epsilon$ where $\size x$ is the absolute value of $x$.

title: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_k}$ be a sequence in $\R$. The sequence $\sequence {x_k}$ converges to the limit $l \in \R$ : $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists N \in \R_{>0}: n > N \implies \size {x_n - l} < \epsilon$ where $\size x$ denotes the absolute value of $x$.

title: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Real Numbers/Graphical Illustration
snippet: The following diagram illustrates the first few terms of a convergent real sequence. 510px For the value of $\epsilon$ given, a suitable value of $N$ such that: $n > N \implies \size {x_n - l} < \epsilon$ is $6$.

title: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Test Function Space
snippet: Let $\map \DD {\R^d}$ be the test function space with the compact support $K \subseteq \R^d$. Let $\sequence {\phi_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $\map \DD {\R^d}$. Let $\phi \in \map \DD {\R^d}$ be a test function. Let $D^k := \dfrac {\partial^{k_1 + k_2 + \ldots + k_d}} {\partial x_1^{k_1} \partial x_2^{k_2} \ldots \partial x_d^{k_d} }$ be a partial differential operator with the multiindex $k = \tuple {k_1, k_2, \ldots, k_d}$.

title: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Topology
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $A \subseteq S$. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be an infinite sequence in $A$.

title: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Topology/Definition 1
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $A \subseteq S$. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be an infinite sequence in $A$. $\sequence {x_n}$ converges to the limit $\alpha \in S$ : $\forall U \in \tau: \alpha \in U \implies \paren {\exists N \in \R_{>0}: \forall n \in \N: n > N \implies x_n \in U}$

title: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Topology/Definition 2
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $A \subseteq S$. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be an infinite sequence in $A$. $\sequence {x_n}$ converges to the limit $\alpha \in S$ : $\forall U \in \tau: \alpha \in U \implies \set {n \in \N: x_n \notin U}$ is finite.

snippet:

Let $\struct {X,

title: Definition:Convergent Sequence in Weak Operator Topology
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ and $\struct {Y, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_Y}$ be normed vector spaces. Let $\mathbb K = \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\map {CL} {X, Y}$ be a continuous linear transformation space. Let $\tau$ be the weak operator topology on $\map {CL} {X, Y}$. Suppose $\sequence {T_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is a sequence in $\map {CL} {X, Y}$. Suppose $T \in \map {CL} {X, Y}$.

title: Definition:Convergent Series
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ, \tau}$ be a topological semigroup. Let $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n$ be a series in $S$. This series is said to be convergent its sequence of partial sums $\sequence {s_N}$ converges in the topological space $\struct {S, \tau}$. If $s_N \to s$ as $N \to \infty$, the series converges to the sum $s$, and one writes $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n = s$.

title: Definition:Convergent Series/Also known as
snippet: == Convergent Series: Also known as == A convergent series is also known as a summable series. Category:Definitions/Convergent Series

title: Definition:Convergent Series/Normed Vector Space/Definition 1
snippet: Let $V$ be a normed vector space. Let $d$ be the induced metric on $V$. Let $\ds S := \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n$ be a series in $V$. $S$ is convergent its sequence $\sequence {s_N}$ of partial sums converges in the metric space $\struct {V, d}$.

title: Definition:Convergent Series/Normed Vector Space/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {V, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a normed vector space. Let $\ds S := \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n$ be a series in $V$. $S$ is convergent its sequence $\sequence {s_N}$ of partial sums converges in the normed vector space $\struct {V, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$.

title: Definition:Convergent Series/Number Field
snippet: Let $S$ be one of the standard number fields $\Q, \R, \C$. Let $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n$ be a series in $S$. Let $\sequence {s_N}$ be the sequence of partial sums of $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n$. It follows that $\sequence {s_N}$ can be treated as a sequence in the metric space $S$. If $s_N \to s$ as $N \to \infty$, the series converges to the sum $s$, and one writes $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n = s$. A series is said to be convergent it converges to some $s$.

title: Definition:Convergent Series/Number Field/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Convergent Series == Many of the basic tests for convergence of series have 's name associated with them.

title: Definition:Convergent of Continued Fraction
snippet: Let $F$ be a field, such as the field of real numbers. Let $n \in \N \cup \set \infty$ be an extended natural number. Let $C = \sqbrk {a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots}$ be a continued fraction in $F$ of length $n$. Let $k \le n$ be a natural number.

title: Definition:Convergent of Continued Fraction/Definition 1
snippet: The $k$th convergent $C_k$ of $C$ is the value of the finite continued fraction: $C_k = \sqbrk {a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_k}$

title: Definition:Convergent of Continued Fraction/Definition 2
snippet: The $k$th convergent $C_k$ of $C$ is the quotient of the $k$th numerator $p_k$ by the $k$th denominator $q_k$: $C_k = \dfrac {p_k} {q_k}$

title: Definition:Convergent of Continued Fraction/Even
snippet: Let $F$ be a field. Let $n \in \N \cup \set \infty$ be an extended natural number. Let $C = \sqbrk {a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots}$ be a continued fraction in $F$ of length $n$. The even convergents of $\sqbrk {a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots}$ are the convergents $C_0, C_2, C_4, \ldots$, that is, those with an even subscript.

title: Definition:Convergent of Continued Fraction/Odd
snippet: Let $F$ be a field. Let $n \in \N \cup \set \infty$ be an extended natural number. Let $C = \sqbrk {a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots}$ be a continued fraction in $F$ of length $n$. The odd convergents of $\sqbrk {a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots}$ are the convergents $C_1, C_3, C_5, \ldots$, that is, those with an odd subscript.

title: Definition:Converse
snippet: Definition:Converse Statement Definition:Inverse Mapping, also known as converse mapping

title: Definition:Converse Statement
snippet: The converse of the conditional: $p \implies q$ is the statement: $q \implies p$

title: Definition:Converse Statement/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Converse Statement == The word converse, in the context of the term converse statement, is pronounced with the stress on the first syllable: con-verse. When pronounced con-verse, with the stress on the second syllable, it means to communicate (usually verbally) with others. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Conversion Factor
snippet: A conversion factor is a (usually real) constant which is used to multiply the value of a physical quantity in a given unit of measurement in order to express it in a different unit of measurement.

title: Definition:Conversion Period
snippet: A conversion period is a period of time between when compound interest is calculated on a principal and any accrued interest on that principal.

title: Definition:Conversion of Ratio
snippet: Let $R = a : b$ be a ratio. Then the conversion of $R$ is the ratio $a : a - b$. Category:Definitions/Euclidean Algebra

title: Definition:Converting Form of Categorical Statement
snippet: Let $S$ and $P$ be predicates. Let $\map {\mathbf \Phi} {S, P}$ be a categorical statement connecting $S$ and $P$. Then: $\map {\mathbf \Phi} {S, P}$ is converting there exists a law of conversion which changes $\map {\mathbf \Phi} {S, P}$ into another categorical statement. Such a categorical statement is said to convert.

title: Definition:Convex
snippet: Geometry: Convex Geometric Figure Convex Polygon Convex Polyhedron Order Theory: Order-Convex Set Vector Spaces: Convex Set (Vector Space) Real Analysis Convex Real Function

title: Definition:Convex Angle
snippet: A convex angle is an angle that is larger than a zero angle and smaller than a straight angle. That is, the measurement of a convex angle is larger than $0 \degrees$ and smaller than $180 \degrees$. In radians, the measurement of a convex angle is larger than $0$ and smaller than $\pi$.

title: Definition:Convex Angle/Also known as
snippet: == Convex Angle: Also known as == Some texts targeted towards the high school level refer to a convex angle as an ordinary angle. Category:Definitions/Convex Angles

title: Definition:Convex Balanced Hull
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a vector space over $\GF$. Let $A \subseteq X$ be a non-empty set. We define the convex balanced hull of $A$ as the $\subseteq$-smallest convex balanced set including $A$. We denote the convex balanced hull by $\map {\operatorname {cobal} } A$.

title: Definition:Convex Circumference of Circle/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Convex Circumference == The concept of the convex circumference arises in as a way of rigorously specifying the relationship between a point and the circumference of the circle under investigation. As such it is not specifically defined in , but is tacitly understood. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Convex Combination
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $V$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $\family {\mathbf v_\alpha}_{\alpha \mathop \in I} \subseteq V$ be a family of elements of $V$ indexed by an indexing set $I$. Let $\ds \sum_{\alpha \mathop \in I} \lambda_\alpha \mathbf v_\alpha$ be a linear combination of $\family {\mathbf v_\alpha}$. Then $\ds \sum_{\alpha \mathop \in I} \lambda_\alpha \mathbf v_\alpha$ is a convex combination of $\family {\mathbf v_\alpha}$ : $(1): \quad \forall \alpha \in I: \lambda_\alpha > 0$ $(2): \quad \ds \sum_{\alpha \mathop \in I} \lambda_\alpha = 1$

title: Definition:Convex Component
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be a totally ordered set. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. The maximally order-convex sets into which $H$ is partitioned are the convex components of $H$.

title: Definition:Convex Cone
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a vector space over $\GF$. Let $P \subseteq X$ be a cone in $X$. We say that $P$ is a convex cone : for each $v, v' \in P$, we have $v + v' \in P$.

title: Definition:Convex Envelope
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological vector space over $\R$. Let $C \subseteq X$ be a non-empty closed convex set. Let $f : C \to \R$ be a function. Define an extended real-valued function $\check f : C \to \overline \R$ by: $\map {\check f} x = \sup \set {\map g x : g \le f \text { and } g \text { is affine and continuous} }$ where we take $\sup \O = -\infty$. We say that $\check f$ is the convex envelope of $f$.

title: Definition:Convex Geometric Figure
snippet: A geometric figure is convex a line segment joining two points on its boundary lies entirely inside it.

title: Definition:Convex Hull
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space over $\R$. Let $U \subseteq V$.

title: Definition:Convex Hull/Definition 1
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space over $\R$. Let $U \subseteq V$. The convex hull of $U$ is defined and denoted: $\ds \map {\operatorname {conv} } U = \set {\sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n \lambda_j u_j : n \in \N, \, u_j \in U \text { and } \lambda_j \in \R_{> 0} \text { for each } j, \, \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n \lambda_j = 1}$ That is, it is the set of all convex combinations of elements of $U$.

title: Definition:Convex Hull/Definition 2
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space over $\R$. Let $U \subseteq V$. The convex hull of $U$ is defined and denoted: $\map {\operatorname {conv} } U = $ the intersection of all convex sets $C \subseteq V$ of $V$ such that $U \subseteq C$. That is, it is the intersection of all convex sets containing $U$.

title: Definition:Convex Hull/Definition 3
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space over $\R$. Let $U \subseteq V$. The convex hull of $U$ is defined and denoted: $\map {\operatorname {conv} } U = $ the smallest convex set $C$ such that $U \subseteq C$.

title: Definition:Convex Polygon/Definition 1
snippet: Let $P$ be a polygon. $P$ is a convex polygon : For all points $A$ and $B$ located inside $P$, the line $AB$ is also inside $P$.

title: Definition:Convex Polygon/Definition 2
snippet: Let $P$ be a polygon. $P$ is a convex polygon : every internal angle of $P$ is not greater than $180 \degrees$.

title: Definition:Convex Polygon/Definition 3
snippet: Let $P$ be a polygon. $P$ is a convex polygon : the region enclosed by $P$ lies entirely on the same side of each side of $P$

title: Definition:Convex Polygon/Definition 4
snippet: Let $P$ be a polygon. $P$ is a convex polygon : the region enclosed by $P$ is the intersection of a finite number of half-planes. Note that an intersection of a finite number of half-planes is not necessarily a polygon.

title: Definition:Convex Polygon/Definition 5
snippet: Let $P$ be a polygon. $P$ is a convex polygon : the region enclosed by $P$ is the intersection of all half-planes that contain $P$ and that are created by all the lines that are tangent to $P$. By tangent we mean any line $l$ that contain one or more point of $P$ and has $P$ entirely in one of the half-planes created by $l$. In this sense any line, that is spanned by a side of $P$, is tangent to $P$.

title: Definition:Convex Polyhedron
snippet: Let $P$ be a polyhedron.

title: Definition:Convex Polyhedron/Definition 1
snippet: Let $P$ be a polyhedron. $P$ is a convex polyhedron : For all points $A$ and $B$ located inside $P$, the line $AB$ is also inside $P$.

title: Definition:Convex Polyhedron/Definition 2
snippet: Let $P$ be a polyhedron. $P$ is a convex polyhedron : For every face of $P$, the plane in which it is embedded does not intersect the interior of $P$.

title: Definition:Convex Polyhedron/Definition 3
snippet: Let $P$ be a polyhedron. $P$ is a convex polyhedron : For each face of $P$, the whole of $P$ lies on one side of the plane of that face.

title: Definition:Convex Polyhedron/Definition 4
snippet: Let $P$ be a polyhedron. $P$ is a convex polyhedron : For each face of $P$, the plane containing that face does not intersect any other face of $P$.

title: Definition:Convex Real-Valued Function/Real Vector Space
snippet: Let $\R^n$ be an $n$-dimensional real vector space. Let $S \subseteq \R^n$ be a subset. Let $f: S \to \overline \R$ be an extended real-valued function. $f$ is convex its epigraph is a convex subset of $\R^{n+1}$.

title: Definition:Convex Real Function
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function which is defined on a real interval $I$.

title: Definition:Convex Real Function/Also known as
snippet: == Convex Real Function: Also known as == A convex function can also be referred to as: a concave up function a convex down function.

title: Definition:Convex Real Function/Definition 1
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function which is defined on a real interval $I$. $f$ is convex on $I$ : $\forall x, y \in I: \forall \alpha, \beta \in \R_{>0}, \alpha + \beta = 1: \map f {\alpha x + \beta y} \le \alpha \map f x + \beta \map f y$ 700px The geometric interpretation is that any point on the chord drawn on the graph of any convex function always lies on or above the graph.

title: Definition:Convex Real Function/Definition 1/Also presented as
snippet: == Convex Real Function: Definition 1: Also presented as == By setting $\alpha = \lambda$ and $\beta = 1 - \lambda$, this can also be written as: $\forall x, y \in I, x \ne y: \forall \lambda \in \openint 0 1: \map f {\lambda x + \paren {1 - \lambda} y} \le t \lambda \map f x + \paren {1 - \lambda} \map f y$

title: Definition:Convex Real Function/Definition 1/Strictly
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function which is defined on a real interval $I$. $f$ is strictly convex on $I$ : $\forall x, y \in I, x \ne y: \forall \alpha, \beta \in \R_{>0}, \alpha + \beta = 1: \map f {\alpha x + \beta y} < \alpha \map f x + \beta \map f y$ 700px The geometric interpretation is that any point on the chord drawn on the graph of any convex function always lies above the graph.

title: Definition:Convex Real Function/Definition 2
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function which is defined on a real interval $I$. $f$ is convex on $I$ : $\forall x_1, x_2, x_3 \in I: x_1 < x_2 < x_3: \dfrac {\map f {x_2} - \map f {x_1} } {x_2 - x_1} \le \dfrac {\map f {x_3} - \map f {x_2} } {x_3 - x_2}$ Hence a geometrical interpretation: the slope of $P_1 P_2$ is less than or equal to that of $P_2 P_3$: 500px

title: Definition:Convex Real Function/Definition 2/Strictly
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function which is defined on a real interval $I$. $f$ is strictly convex on $I$ : $\forall x_1, x_2, x_3 \in I: x_1 < x_2 < x_3: \dfrac {\map f {x_2} - \map f {x_1} } {x_2 - x_1} < \dfrac {\map f {x_3} - \map f {x_2} } {x_3 - x_2}$ Hence a geometrical interpretation: the slope of $P_1 P_2$ is less than that of $P_2 P_3$: 500px

title: Definition:Convex Real Function/Definition 3
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function which is defined on a real interval $I$. $f$ is convex on $I$ : $\forall x_1, x_2, x_3 \in I: x_1 < x_2 < x_3: \dfrac {\map f {x_2} - \map f {x_1} } {x_2 - x_1} \le \dfrac {\map f {x_3} - \map f {x_1} } {x_3 - x_1}$ Hence a geometrical interpretation: the slope of $P_1 P_2$ is less than or equal to that of $P_1 P_3$: 500px

title: Definition:Convex Real Function/Definition 3/Strictly
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function which is defined on a real interval $I$. $f$ is strictly convex on $I$ : $\forall x_1, x_2, x_3 \in I: x_1 < x_2 < x_3: \dfrac {\map f {x_2} - \map f {x_1} } {x_2 - x_1} < \dfrac {\map f {x_3} - \map f {x_1} } {x_3 - x_1}$ Hence a geometrical interpretation: the slope of $P_1 P_2$ is less than that of $P_1 P_3$: 500px

title: Definition:Convex Real Function/Geometric Interpretation
snippet: == Geometric Interpretation of Convex Real Function == Let $f$ be a convex real function. Then: for every pair of points $A$ and $B$ on the graph of $f$, the chord $AB$ lies entirely above the graph.

title: Definition:Convex Real Function/Point
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function which is defined on a real interval $I$. Let $a \in I$ be a point in the domain of $f$. Then: $f$ is convex at $a$ there exists a neighborhood of $a$ on which $f$ is convex.

title: Definition:Convex Real Function/Vector Space
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a vector space over $\GF$. Let $C \subseteq X$ be a convex set. Let $f: C \to \overline \R$ be an extended real-valued function. We say that $f$ is convex : $\map f {t x + \paren {1 - t} y} \le t \map f x + \paren {1 - t} \map f y$ for each $t \in \openint 0 1$ and $x, y \in C$ whenever $\set {\map f x, \map f y} \ne \set {-\infty, \infty}$.

title: Definition:Convex Set
snippet: Convex Set (Geometry) Order-Convex Set Convex Set (Vector Space)

title: Definition:Convex Set (Geometry)
snippet: Let $S$ be a subset of an $n$-dimensional real Euclidean space $\R^n$. Let $S$ be such that for every pair of points in $S$, the straight line segment $AB$ lies entirely inside $S$. Then $S$ is a convex set of $S$.

title: Definition:Convex Set (Vector Space)
snippet: Let $\Bbb F \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $V$ be a vector space over $\Bbb F$. Let $C \subseteq V$.

title: Definition:Convex Set (Vector Space)/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\Bbb F \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $V$ be a vector space over $\Bbb F$. Let $C \subseteq V$. We say that $C$ is convex : $t x + \paren {1 - t} y \in C$ for each $x, y \in C$ and $t \in \closedint 0 1$.

title: Definition:Convex Set (Vector Space)/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\Bbb F \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $V$ be a vector space over $\Bbb F$. Let $C \subseteq V$. We say that $C$ is convex : $t C + \paren {1 - t} C \subseteq C$ for each $t \in \closedint 0 1$, where $t C + \paren {1 - t} C$ denotes a linear combination of $C$.

title: Definition:Convex Set (Vector Space)/Line Segment
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space over $\R$ or $\C$. Let $x, y \in V$. The set: $\set {t x + \paren {1 - t} y: t \in \closedint 0 1}$ is called the (straight) line segment joining $x$ and $y$. A convex set can thus be described as a set containing all straight line segments between its elements.

title: Definition:Convolution (Measure Theory)
snippet: Let $\BB^n$ be the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on $\R^n$, and let $\lambda^n$ be Lebesgue measure on $\R^n$.

title: Definition:Convolution Integral
snippet: Let $f$ and $g$ be real functions which are integrable. The convolution integral of $f$ and $g$ is defined as: $\ds \map f t * \map g t := \int_{-\infty}^\infty \map f u \map g {t - u} \rd u$

title: Definition:Convolution Integral/Also known as
snippet: A convolution integral is also generally known just as a convolution. However, it has to be borne in mind that the term convolution in general has a wider definition.

title: Definition:Convolution Integral/Cross-Correlation
snippet: Let $f$ and $g$ be real functions which are integrable. The cross-correlation of $f$ and $g$ is defined as: $\ds \map f t \star \map g t := \int_{-\infty}^\infty \map f u \map g {t + u} \rd u$

title: Definition:Convolution Integral/Positive Real Domain
snippet: Let $f$ and $g$ be functions which are integrable. Let $f$ and $g$ be supported on the positive real numbers $\R_{\ge 0}$ only. The convolution integral of $f$ and $g$ may be defined as: $\ds \map f t * \map g t := \int_0^t \map f u \map g {t - u} \rd u$

title: Definition:Convolution of Mappings on Divisor-Finite Monoid
snippet: Let $\struct {M, \cdot}$ be a divisor-finite monoid. Let $\struct {R, +, \times}$ be a non-associative ring. Let $f, g : M \to R$ be mappings. The convolution of $f$ and $g$ is the mapping $f * g: M \to R$ defined as: $\forall m \in M: \map {\paren {f * g} } m := \ds \sum_{x y \mathop = m} \map f x \times \map g y$ where the summation is over the finite set $\set {\tuple {x, y} \in M^2: x y = m}$.

title: Definition:Convolution of Measurable Function and Measure
snippet: Let $\mu$ be a measure on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra $\BB^n$ on $\R^n$. Let $f: \R^n \to \R$ be a $\BB^n$-measurable function such that for all $x \in \R^n$: $\ds \int_{\R^n} \map f {x - y} \rd \map \mu y$ is finite. The convolution of $f$ and $\mu$ is the mapping $f * \mu: \R^n \to \R$ defined as: $\ds \forall x \in \R^n: \map {f * \mu} x := \int_{\R^n} \map f {x - y} \rd \map \mu y$

title: Definition:Convolution of Measurable Functions
snippet: Let $\BB^n$ be the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on $\R^n$, and let $\lambda^n$ be Lebesgue measure on $\R^n$. Let $f, g: \R^n \to \R$ be $\BB^n$-measurable functions such that for all $x \in \R^n$: $\ds \int_{\R^n} \map f {x - y} \map g y \rd \map {\lambda^n} y$ is finite. The convolution of $f$ and $g$, denoted $f * g$, is the mapping defined by: $\ds f * g: \R^n \to \R, \map {f * g} x := \int_{\R^n} \map f {x - y} \map g y \rd \map {\lambda^n} y$

snippet:

title: Definition:Convolution of Probability Distributions
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be independent random variables. Let $Z = X + Y$. The probability distribution of $Z$ is called the convolution of the probability distributions of $X$ and $Y$.

title: Definition:Conway Circle
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle. Let: $AB$ be produced: from $A$ by length $BC$ from $B$ by length $AC$ $BC$ be produced: from $B$ by length $AC$ from $C$ by length $AB$ $AC$ be produced: from $A$ by length $BC$ from $C$ by length $AB$ The Conway circle is the circle on whose circumference lie these $6$ new points so generated: 500px

title: Definition:Conway Life
snippet: A cellular evolution deriving from a stencil shaped as: $(1): \quad X := \Z^2$ $(2): \quad S_X := 2 := \set {0, 1}$ $(3): \quad \map S 0 \in \paren {\Z^2 \to 2}$ $(4): \quad \Delta := \tuple {\tuple {0, 0}, \tuple {0, 1}, \tuple {1, 1}, \tuple {1, 0}, \tuple {1, -1}, \tuple {0, -1}, \tuple {-1, -1}, \tuple {-1, 0}, \tuple {-1, 1} }$ $(5): \quad \map \delta {m, n_1, n_2, n_3, n_4, n_5, n_6, n_7, n_8} := \tuple {m, \ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^8 n_i} \in \set {\tuple {0, 3}, \tuple {1, 2}, \tuple {1, 3} } \mathrel ? 1 : 0$ is called a Conway life.

title: Definition:Conway Life/Also known as
snippet: == Conway Life: Also known as == A Conway life is also known as the Game of Life, but there now exist several variants which have been developed since devised the original. Hence, while you will generally be understood when you talk about the Game of Life, it is prudent on to be specific.

title: Definition:Cooked Puzzle
snippet: A cooked puzzle is a puzzle designed by its creator to have a unique solution, but for which it is later discovered there is more than one such solution. Category:Definitions/Recreational Mathematics

title: Definition:Cooperative Game
snippet: A cooperative game is a multi-person game in which the players may form coalitions outside the game.

title: Definition:Coordinate
snippet: Definition:Coordinate of Vector Definition:Coordinate of Ordered Tuple

title: Definition:Coordinate/Also denoted as
snippet: == Coordinates: Also denoted as == It is usual to use the subscript technique to denote the coordinates where $n$ is large or unspecified: $\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ However, note that some texts (often in the fields of physics and mechanics) prefer to use superscripts: $\tuple {x^1, x^2, \ldots, x^n}$ While this notation is documented here, its use is not endorsed by because: there exists the all too likely subsequent confusion with notation for powers one of the philosophical tenets of is to present a system of notation that is as completely consistent as possible.

title: Definition:Coordinate/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Coordinate == The words coordinate and coordinates entered the mathematical mainstream via the works of , who may well have coined them.

title: Definition:Coordinate/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Coordinate == It's an awkward word coordinate. It really needs a hyphen in it to emphasise its pronunciation (loosely and commonly: coe-wordinate), and indeed, some authors spell it co-ordinate. However, this makes it look unwieldy. An older spelling puts a on the second "o": coördinate. But this is considered archaic nowadays and few sources still use it. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Coordinate Axis/Also known as
snippet: == Coordinate Axis: Also known as == A coordinate axis is also known as a reference axis. If the context is clear, it is often referred to as just an axis.

title: Definition:Coordinate Ball
snippet: Let $M$ be a topological manifold of dimension $d$. Let $\struct {U, \phi}$ be a chart of $M$. Suppose $\map \phi U$ is an open ball in $\R^d$. Then $U$ is known as the coordinate ball.

title: Definition:Coordinate Cube
snippet: Let $M$ be a topological manifold of dimension $d$. Let $\struct {U, \phi}$ be a chart of $M$. Suppose $\map \phi U$ is an open cube in $\R^d$. Then $U$ is known as the coordinate cube.

title: Definition:Coordinate Domain
snippet: Let $M$ be a topological manifold. Let $\struct {U, \phi}$ be a chart of $M$. Then $U$ is known as the coordinate domain of each of its points.

title: Definition:Coordinate Domain/Also known as
snippet: == Coordinate Domain: Also known as == A coordinate domain is also known as a coordinate neighborhood. However, the term coordinate neighborhood can also be seen to mean chart, so to guard against ambiguity, it is recommended it not be used on . Category:Definitions/Coordinate Domains

title: Definition:Coordinate Function
snippet: Let $M$ be a locally Euclidean space of dimension $n$. Let $\struct {U, \kappa}$ be a coordinate chart. Let $\pr_i: \R^n \to \R$ be the $i$th projection. Then the mapping $\kappa_i$, defined as: $\kappa_i = \pr_i \circ \kappa: U \to \map {\paren {\pr_i \circ \kappa} } U \subseteq \R$ is called the $i$th coordinate function on $U$.

title: Definition:Coordinate Functionals Associated with Schauder Basis
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a normed vector space over $\GF$. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a Schauder basis for $X$. We define the coordinate functionals $\sequence {x_n^\ast}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ such that: $(1) \quad \map {x_n^\ast} {x_k} = \delta_{n k}$ for each $n, k \in \N$ $(2) \quad x = \ds \sum_{n = 1}^\infty \map {x_n^\ast} x x_n$ for each $x \in X$ where $\delta$ denotes the Kronecker $\delta$.

title: Definition:Coordinate Plane/Also known as
snippet: == Coordinate Plane: Also known as == A coordinate plane is also known as an axial plane.

title: Definition:Coordinate System
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $\sequence {a_k}_{1 \mathop \le k \mathop \le n}$ be an ordered basis of a free unitary $R$-module $G$. Then $\sequence {a_k}_{1 \mathop \le k \mathop \le n}$ can be referred to as a coordinate system.

title: Definition:Coordinate System/3-Space
snippet: In physics and applied mathematics, it is usual for the coordinate system under discussion to be considered as superimposed on ordinary space of $3$ dimensions.

title: Definition:Coordinate System/3-Space/Curvilinear
snippet: Recall that we can define Cartesian $3$-space by means of perpendicular planes. Let us superimpose onto this coordinate system $3$ other one-parameter families of surfaces. In each of these families, the surfaces need not be parallel and they need not be planes. These families are such that every point in (ordinary) $3$-dimensional space can then be uniquely identified as the intersection of $3$ such surfaces: one surface from each family. Hence every point is identified as the ordered triple $\tuple {q_1, q_2, q_3}$, where $q_1$, $q_2$ and $q_3$ are the parameters of each of the families.

title: Definition:Coordinate System/Coordinate
snippet: Let $\sequence {a_n}$ be a coordinate system of a unitary $R$-module $G$. Let $\ds x \in G: x = \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n \lambda_k a_k$. The scalars $\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \ldots, \lambda_n$ can be referred to as the coordinates of $x$ relative to $\sequence {a_n}$.

title: Definition:Coordinate System/Coordinate/Element of Ordered Pair
snippet: Let $\tuple {a, b}$ be an ordered pair. The following terminology is used: $a$ is called the first coordinate $b$ is called the second coordinate. This definition is compatible with the equivalent definition in the context of Cartesian coordinate systems.

title: Definition:Coordinate System/Coordinate Function
snippet: Let $\sequence {a_n}$ be a coordinate system of a unitary $R$-module $G$. For each $x \in G$ let $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ be the coordinates of $x$ relative to $\sequence {a_n}$. Then for $i = 1, \ldots, n$ the mapping $f_i : G \to R$ defined by $\map {f_i} x = x_i$ is called the $i$-th coordinate function on $G$ relative to $\sequence {a_n}$.

title: Definition:Coordinate System/Coordinates on Affine Space
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an affine space of dimension $n$ over a field $k$. Let $\RR = \tuple {p_0, e_1, \ldots, e_n}$ be an affine frame in $\EE$. Let $p \in \EE$ be a point. Since Affine Coordinates are Well-Defined, there exists a unique ordered tuple $\tuple {\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n} \in k^n$ such that: $\ds p = p_0 + \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \lambda_i e_i$ The numbers $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n$ are the coordinates of $p$ in the frame $\RR$. Category:Definitions/Affine Geometry

title: Definition:Coordinate System/Origin
snippet: The origin of a coordinate system is the zero vector. In the $x y$-plane, it is the point: $O = \tuple {0, 0}$ and in general, in the Euclidean space $\R^n$: $O = \underbrace {\tuple {0, 0, \ldots, 0} }_{\text{$n$ coordinates} }$ Thus it is the point where the axes cross over each other.

title: Definition:Coordinate Transformation
snippet: Let $\CC_\alpha$ and $\CC_\beta$ be coordinate systems over a space $\EE$ of $n$ dimensions. Let $P$ be a point in $\EE$ such that: $P$ is expressed as $\tuple {\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n}$ in $\CC_\alpha$ $P$ is expressed as $\tuple {\beta_1, \beta_2, \ldots, \beta_n}$ in $\CC_\beta$ A coordinate transformation is a mapping $\phi: \EE \to \EE$ such that: $\map \phi {\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n} = \tuple {\beta_1, \beta_2, \ldots, \beta_n}$ for all such points in $\EE$.

title: Definition:Coordinate Vector
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $M$ be a unitary $R$-module of dimension $n$. Let $B = \sequence {b_k}_{1 \mathop \le k \mathop \le n}$ be an ordered basis of $M$. Let $x \in M$. Let $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n\in R$ be such that $\ds x = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \lambda_i b_i$. Then $\tuple {\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n} \in R^n$ is the coordinate vector of $x$ $B$. This can be denoted: $\sqbrk x_B$

title: Definition:Coordinate of Vector/Also known as
snippet: == Coordinate: Also known as == Coordinates of $x$ relative to $\sequence {a_n}$ are also known as coordinates of $x$ $\sequence {a_n}$.

title: Definition:Coordination Game
snippet: The coordination game is an instance of a class of games whose mechanics are as follows: There are two players: $\text A$lexis and $\text B$everley. They wish to go out together to a musical concert to experience either the music of Mozart or Mahler. Unaccountably, both $\text A$ and $\text B$ prefer Mozart. (It takes all sorts to make a world.) The key points are: $\text A$lexis and $\text B$everley wish to coordinate their behaviour but: they have common interests.

snippet: == Payoff Table for the Coordination Game == The following payoff table specifies the coordination game: {{PayoffTable|table = $\begin {array} {r c } & \text {Mozart} & \text {Mahler} \\ \hline \text {Mozart} & 2, 2 & 0, 0 \\ \hline \text {Mahler} & 0, 0 & 1, 1 \\ \hline \end {array}$}}

title: Definition:Copeland-Erdős Constant
snippet: The Copeland-Erdős constant is the real number whose decimal expansion is formed by concatenating the prime numbers in ascending order: $C_{10} = 0 \cdotp 23571 \, 11317 \, 19232 \, 93137 \, 4143 \ldots$

title: Definition:Copeland-Erdős Constant/Also known as
snippet: == Copeland-Erdős Constant: Also known as == The Copeland-Erdős constant is also known as the Copeland-Erdős number.

title: Definition:Copenhagen Interpretation
snippet: == Philosophical Position == The Copenhagen interpretation is the philosophical position that the quantum state of a particle is represented by Schrödinger's equation. This provides a probabilistic description of the particle's quantum state, which is undetermined until measured. The act of measurement collapses the wave function.

title: Definition:Coplanar
snippet: Coplanar means in the same plane.

title: Definition:Coplanar/Lines
snippet: Two (or more) lines are coplanar there exists a plane $P$ such that all the lines lie in $P$. In this context, these lines may be understood as encompassing straight lines and plane curves.

title: Definition:Coplanar/Points
snippet: Four or more points which belong to the same plane are coplanar.

title: Definition:Coplanar Vectors
snippet: Three or more vectors are coplanar they can be embedded in the same plane. Formally:

title: Definition:Coplanar Vectors/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\overline {OA}$ and $\overline {OB}$ be directed line segments representing non-zero vectors $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ in space respectively. Let $\mathbf p$ be another non-zero vector in space. Then $\mathbf p$ is coplanar with $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ $\mathbf p$ can be represented by a directed line segment $\overline {OP}$ where $O$, $A$, $B$ and $P$ are coplanar points.

title: Definition:Coplanar Vectors/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ be vectors in space. Let $\mathbf p$ be another non-zero vector in space. Then $\mathbf p$ is coplanar with $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ there exist scalars $\lambda$ and $\mu$ such that: $\mathbf p = \lambda \mathbf a + \mu \mathbf b$

title: Definition:Coplanar Vectors/Non-Coplanar
snippet: Three or more vectors are non-coplanar if they are not coplanar. That is if they cannot be embedded in the same plane.

title: Definition:Copper/63
snippet: == Isotope of Copper == Copper-$63$ is the isotope of copper which has $34$ neutrons in addition to its $29$ protons. Cu-$63$ is one of the two stable isotopes of copper, forming $69.17 \%$ of the naturally occurring copper atoms.

title: Definition:Copper/65
snippet: == Isotope of Copper == Copper-$65$ is the isotope of copper which has $36$ neutrons in addition to its $29$ protons. Cu-$65$ is one of the two stable isotopes of copper, forming $30.83 \%$ of the naturally occurring copper atoms.

title: Definition:Copper/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Copper == The symbol Cu used for copper derives from the Latin cuprum. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Coprime/Also denoted as
snippet: == Coprime: Also denoted as == The notation $\perp$ is not universal. Other notations to indicate the concept of coprimality include: $\gcd \set {a, b} = 1$ $\map \gcd {a, b} = 1$ $\tuple {a, b} = 1$ However, the first two are unwieldy and the third notation $\tuple {a, b}$ is overused. Hence the decision by to use $\perp$. Category:Definitions/Coprimality

title: Definition:Coprime/Also known as
snippet: == Coprime: Also known as == The statement $a$ and $b$ are coprime can also be expressed as: $a$ and $b$ are relatively prime $a$ and $b$ are mutually prime $a$ is prime to $b$, and at the same time that $b$ is prime to $a$.

title: Definition:Coprime/Euclidean Domain
snippet: Let $\struct {D, +, \times}$ be a Euclidean domain. Let $U \subseteq D$ be the group of units of $D$. Let $a, b \in D$ such that $a \ne 0_D$ and $b \ne 0_D$ Let $d = \gcd \set {a, b}$ be the greatest common divisor of $a$ and $b$. Then $a$ and $b$ are coprime $d \in U$. That is, two elements of a Euclidean domain are coprime their greatest common divisor is a unit of $D$.

title: Definition:Coprime/GCD Domain
snippet: Let $\struct {D, +, \times}$ be a GCD domain. Let $U \subseteq D$ be the group of units of $D$. Let $a, b \in D$ such that $a \ne 0_D$ and $b \ne 0_D$ Let $d = \gcd \set {a, b}$ be the greatest common divisor of $a$ and $b$. Then $a$ and $b$ are coprime $d \in U$. That is, two elements of a GCD domain are coprime their greatest common divisor is a unit of $D$.

title: Definition:Coprime/Integers
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be integers. Let $\gcd \set {a, b}$ denote the greatest common divisor of $a$ and $b$. Then $a$ and $b$ are coprime : $\gcd \set {a, b}$ exists and: $\gcd \set {a, b} = 1$. '

title: Definition:Coprime/Integers/Relatively Composite
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be integers such that $b \ne 0$ and $a \ne 0$ (i.e. they are both non-zero). Let $\gcd \set {a, b}$ be the greatest common divisor of $a$ and $b$. If $\gcd \set {a, b} > 1$, then $a$ and $b$ are relatively composite. That is, two integers are relatively composite if they are not coprime. ' Category:Definitions/Number Theory Category:Definitions/Coprime Integers

title: Definition:Coprime/Notation
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be objects which in some context are coprime, that is, such that $\gcd \set {a, b} = 1$. Then the notation $a \perp b$ is preferred on . If $\gcd \set {a, b} \ne 1$, the notation $a \not \!\! \mathop \perp b$ can be used. As stated in , section $4.5$: This concept is so important in practice, we ought to have a special notation for it; but, alas, number theorists haven't agreed on a very good one yet.

title: Definition:Coprime Ideals
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $I, J \subseteq A$ be ideals. Then $I$ and $J$ are coprime their sum is the unit ideal: $I + J = A$

title: Definition:Coprime Residue Class
snippet: Let $m \in \Z: m \ge 1$. Let $a \in \Z$ such that: $a \perp m$ where $\perp$ denotes that $a$ is prime to $m$. Let $\eqclass a m$ be the residue class of $a$ (modulo $m$): $\set {x \in \Z: \exists k \in \Z: x = a + k m}$ Then $\eqclass a m$ is referred to as a coprime residue class.

title: Definition:Coproduct/Also Known As
snippet: == Coproduct: Also known as == If $\CC = \family {C_j}_{j \mathop \in J}$ is a set, indexed by some indexing set $J$, the notations $\ds \coprod_{j \mathop \in J} C_j$ and $\ds \coprod_j C_j$ are often seen. In this situation, one writes $i_j$ for $i_{C_j}$ and calls it the $j$th injection. Category:Definitions/Coproducts

title: Definition:Coproduct/Binary Coproduct
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $A$ and $B$ be objects of $\mathbf C$. A coproduct diagram for $A$ and $B$ comprises an object $P$ and morphisms $i_1: A \to P$, $i_2: B \to P$: $\begin{xy} +{A} = "A", +{P} = "P", +{B} = "B", "A";"P" **@{-} ?>*@{>} ?*!/^.8em/{i_1}, "B";"P" **@{-} ?>*@{>} ?*!/_.8em/{i_2}, \end{xy}$ subjected to the following universal mapping property: In this situation, $P$ is called a coproduct of $A$ and $B$ and may be denoted $A + B$. We generally write $\sqbrk {x_1, x_2}$ for the unique morphism $u$ determined by above diagram.

title: Definition:Coproduct/Binary Coproduct Injection
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $A$ and $B$ be objects of $\mathbf C$. Let object $P$ and morphisms $i_1: A \to P$, $i_2: B \to P$ denote a binary coproduct of $A$ and $B$. The morphisms $i_1: A \to P$, $i_2: B \to P$ are called (binary coproduct) injections; if necessary, $i_1$ can be called the first injection and $i_2$ the second injection. The injections $i_1$ and $i_2$ are often taken to be implicit.

title: Definition:Coproduct/Finite Coproduct
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $\ds \coprod \CC$ be a coproduct for a finite set $\CC$ of objects of $\mathbf C$. Then $\ds \coprod \CC$ is called a finite coproduct.

title: Definition:Coproduct/General Definition
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $\CC$ be any collection of objects of $\mathbf C$. Let $\map {\mathbf {Dis} } \CC$ be the discrete category on $\CC$, considered as a subcategory of $\mathbf C$. A coproduct for $\CC$, denoted $\ds \coprod \CC$, is a colimit for the inclusion functor $D: \map {\mathbf {Dis} } \CC \to \mathbf C$, considered as a diagram.

title: Definition:Coproduct/Injection
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $\CC$ be any collection of objects of $\mathbf C$. Let $\map {\mathbf {Dis} } \CC$ be the discrete category on $\CC$, considered as a subcategory of $\mathbf C$. Let the object $\ds \coprod \CC$ and morphisms $i_C: C \to \ds \coprod \CC$ for each object $C \in \CC$ denote the coproduct of $\CC$. For an object $C$ in $\CC$, the associated morphism $i_C: \ds C \to \coprod \CC$ is called the injection on $C$.

title: Definition:Coproduct/Sets
snippet: Let $S_1$ and $S_2$ be sets. A coproduct $\struct {C, i_1, i_2}$ of $S_1$ and $S_2$ comprises a set $C$ together with mappings $i_1: S_1 \to C$, $i_2: S_2 \to C$ such that: for all sets $X$ and mappings $f_1: S_1 \to X$ and $f_2: S_2 \to X$: there exists a unique mapping $h: C \to X$ such that: $h \circ i_1 = f_1$ $h \circ i_2 = f_2$ Hence: $\begin{xy} \xymatrix@L+2mu@+1em{ & C \ar@{-->}[dd]_*{h} & \\ S_1 \ar[ru]^*{i_1} \ar[rd]_*{f_1} & & S_2 \ar[lu]_*{i_2} \ar[ld]^*{f_2} \\ & X & }\end{xy}$ is a commutative diagram.

title: Definition:Coproduct Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory with binary coproducts. Let $\mathbf C \times \mathbf C$ be the product category of $\mathbf C$ with itself. The coproduct functor on $\mathbf C$ is the functor $\sqcup: \mathbf C \times \mathbf C \to \mathbf C$ defined by: {{DefineFunctor |ob = $\map \sqcup {C, D} := C \sqcup D$ |mor = $\map \sqcup {f, f'} := f \sqcup f'$ }} where $C \sqcup D$ is a binary coproduct of $C$ and $D$, and $f \sqcup f'$ is the coproduct of $f$ and $f'$. That it is in fact a functor is shown on Coproduct Functor is Functor.

title: Definition:Coproduct UMP
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $\CC$ be any collection of objects of $\mathbf C$. Let $\map {\mathbf {Dis} } \CC$ be the discrete category on $\CC$, considered as a subcategory of $\mathbf C$. An object $\ds \coprod \CC$ and morphisms $i_C: C \to \ds \coprod \CC$ for each object $C \in \CC$: $\begin{xy} +{\ds \coprod \CC} = "CC", +{\map {\mathbf {Dis} } \CC} = "BLL", +{C} = "BL", +{\ldots} = "BC", +{C'} = "BR", "BL";"CC" **@{-} ?>*@{>} ?<>(.5)*!/_1em/{i_C}, "BR";"CC" **@{-} ?>*@{>} ?<>(.5)*!/^1em/{i_{C'} }, \end{xy}$ satisfy the (coproduct) universal mapping property or (UMP) :

title: Definition:Coproduct UMP/Property

snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory.
