title: Definition:Copunctal
snippet: Copunctal means having a common point.

title: Definition:Copunctal/Lines
snippet: Three (or more) lines are copunctal there exists a point $P$ that lies on all the lines. In this context, these lines may be understood as encompassing straight lines and plane curves.

title: Definition:Copunctal/Planes
snippet: Three (or more) planes are copunctal there exists a point $P$ that lies on all the planes.

title: Definition:Cord (Physics)
snippet: A cord is an inelastic thread whose mass, stiffness and width are approximated to zero. That is, it is a chain whose mass is zero.

title: Definition:Coreflexive Relation
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation in $S$.

title: Definition:Coreflexive Relation/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation in $S$. $\RR$ is coreflexive : $\forall x, y \in S: \tuple {x, y} \in \RR \implies x = y$

title: Definition:Coreflexive Relation/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation in $S$. $\RR$ is coreflexive : $\RR \subseteq \Delta_S$ where $\Delta_S$ is the diagonal relation.

title: Definition:Coreflexive Relation/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Coreflexive Relation == Coreflexive is pronounced co-reflexive, not core-flexive. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Coriolis Acceleration
snippet: Let $B$ be a body in a rotating frame of reference $\FF$. The Coriolis acceleration $\mathbf a$ is the acceleration imparted to $B$ caused by the Coriolis force $\mathbf F$ on $B$. The direction of $\mathbf a$ is that of the line of action of $\mathbf F$

title: Definition:Coriolis Force
snippet: A Coriolis force is an inertial force that arises when a body $B$ moves in a rotating frame of reference $\FF$. The Coriolis force acts on $B$ at right angles to both the axis of rotation and the direction of motion of $B$ in $\FF$.

title: Definition:Cornu Spiral
snippet: The Cornu spiral is the locus $C$ of the equation expressed in Cesàro form as: $s = a^2 \kappa$ where: $s$ denotes the length of arc at a point of $C$ from the origin $\kappa$ denotes the curvature of $C$ at that point. 600px

title: Definition:Cornu Spiral/Also known as
snippet: == Cornu Spiral: Also known as == Other names for the Cornu spiral include: Euler spiral (for ) klothoid or clothoid

title: Definition:Cornu Spiral/Also presented as
snippet: == Cornu Spiral: Also presented as == The Cornu spiral can be presented in Whewell form as: $s = a^2 \dfrac {\d \psi} {\d s}$ where $\psi$ is the turning angle of $C$ at the point where the length of arc from the origin is $s$. Category:Definitions/Cornu Spiral

title: Definition:Cornu Spiral/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Cornu Spiral == The Cornu spiral is used primarily for: analysis of intensities of diffraction patterns designing curves on railway lines and roller coasters so as to provide a smooth curvature transition.

title: Definition:Corollary
snippet: A corollary is a proof which is a direct result, or a direct application, of another proof. It can be considered as being a proof for free on the back of a proof which has been paid for with blood, sweat and tears.

title: Definition:Corollary/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Corollary == The word corollary is ultimately derived from the Latin corolla, meaning small garland, or the money paid for it. Hence it also has the sense of something extra, lagniappe, freebie, a cherry on the top. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Correction (Statistics)
snippet: A correction is an alteration which is made to an observation or calculation in order to improve its accuracy

title: Definition:Correlation
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables. The correlation between $X$ and $Y$ is a measure of how much the value of one is dependent upon the other. That is, it is a measure of the extent to which a change in $X$ tends to correspond to a change in $Y$, and vice versa.

title: Definition:Correlation/Also known as
snippet: == Correlation: Also known as == Correlation is also known as association.

title: Definition:Correlation/High
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables presented as data pairs. Such data pairs are highly correlated, or show a high correlation, if the values show a close relationship.

title: Definition:Correlation/Negative
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables. $X$ and $Y$ show a negative correlation a change in $X$ corresponds to a change in $Y$ in the opposite direction, and vice versa.

title: Definition:Correlation/Positive
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables. $X$ and $Y$ show a positive correlation a change in $X$ corresponds to a change in $Y$ in the same direction, and vice versa.

title: Definition:Correlation Coefficient
snippet: A correlation coefficient is a statistical coefficient which provides a measure of a particular aspect of correlation amongst a set of data.

title: Definition:Correlation Coefficient/Also known as
snippet: == Correlation Coefficient: Also known as == A correlation coefficient is also known as a cofficient of correlation.

title: Definition:Correlation Matrix
snippet: Let $\sequence a_n$ and $\sequence b_n$ be sequences of $n$ observations. A correlation matrix $\mathbf C$ is a square matrix of order $n$ defined as: $\sqbrk c_{i j} = r_{i j}$ where $r_{i j}$ denotes the sample correlation coefficient between $a_i$ and $b_j$.

title: Definition:Correspondence
snippet: A relation $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ is a correspondence $\RR$ is both left-total and right-total.

title: Definition:Correspondence/Also defined as
snippet: == Correspondence: Also defined as == Some sources define a correspondence as a relation with no restrictions upon it. That is, a correspondence from $S$ to $T$ is an arbitrary subset of the Cartesian product $S \times T$. In order to reduce confusion, it is recommended that this usage of correspondence is not used.

title: Definition:Corresponding Angles of Transversal/Also known as
snippet: == Corresponding Angles of Transversal: Also known as == The corresponding angle to an exterior angle is also known as the interior and opposite angle on the same side. The corresponding angle to an interior angle is also known as the exterior and opposite angle on the same side. Category:Definitions/Transversals (Geometry)

title: Definition:Corresponding Conditional
snippet: Let $p_1, p_2, p_3, \ldots, p_n \vdash q$ be a sequent of propositional logic. It can be expressed as a theorem as follows: $\vdash p_1 \implies \paren {p_2 \implies \paren {p_3 \implies \paren {\ldots \implies \paren {p_n \implies q} \ldots } } }$ This is known as the sequent's corresponding conditional.

title: Definition:Corresponding Magnitudes
snippet: Let $R_1 = a : b$ and $R_2 = c : d$ be ratios. Then the corresponding magnitudes of $a$ and $b$ in $R_2$ are $c$ and $d$ respectively. Category:Definitions/Euclidean Algebra

title: Definition:Corresponding Sides
snippet: Let $\PP$ and $\QQ$ be similar $n$-sided polygons. The corresponding sides of $\PP$ and $\QQ$ are the $n$ pairs of sides for which the ratio of the side of $\PP$ to the side of $\QQ$ is the same in each case. This also covers the case where $\PP$ and $\QQ$ are congruent, where the ratio in this case is $1 : 1$.

title: Definition:Cosecant/Also denoted as
snippet: == Cosecant: Also denoted as == The cosecant function: $\csc$ can often be seen written as: $\cosec$ Category:Definitions/Cosecant Function

title: Definition:Cosecant/Complex Function
snippet: Let $z \in \C$ be a complex number. The complex function $\csc z$ is defined as: $\csc z = \dfrac 1 {\sin z}$ where $\sin z$ is the sine of $z$. The definition is valid for all $z \in \C$ such that $\sin z \ne 0$.

title: Definition:Cosecant/Definition from Circle/First Quadrant
snippet: Consider a unit circle $C$ whose center is at the origin of a cartesian plane. 500px Let $P$ be the point on $C$ in the first quadrant such that $\theta$ is the angle made by $OP$ with the $x$-axis. Let a tangent line be drawn to touch $C$ at $A = \tuple {0, 1}$. Let $OP$ be produced to meet this tangent line at $B$. Then the cosecant of $\theta$ is defined as the length of $OB$. Hence in the first quadrant, the cosecant is positive.

title: Definition:Cosecant/Definition from Circle/Fourth Quadrant
snippet: Consider a unit circle $C$ whose center is at the origin of a cartesian plane. 500px Let $P$ be the point on $C$ in the fourth quadrant such that $\theta$ is the angle made by $OP$ with the $x$-axis. Let a tangent line be drawn to touch $C$ at $A = \tuple {0, 1}$. Let $OP$ be produced to meet this tangent line at $B$. Then the cosecant of $\theta$ is defined as the length of $OB$. Hence in the fourth quadrant, the cotangent is negative.

title: Definition:Cosecant/Definition from Circle/Second Quadrant
snippet: Consider a unit circle $C$ whose center is at the origin of a cartesian plane. 500px Let $P$ be the point on $C$ in the second quadrant such that $\theta$ is the angle made by $OP$ with the $x$-axis. Let a tangent line be drawn to touch $C$ at $A = \tuple {0, 1}$. Let $OP$ be produced to meet this tangent line at $B$. Then the cosecant of $\theta$ is defined as the length of $OB$. Hence in the second quadrant, the cosecant is positive.

title: Definition:Cosecant/Definition from Circle/Third Quadrant
snippet: Consider a unit circle $C$ whose center is at the origin of a cartesian plane. 500px Let $P$ be the point on $C$ in the third quadrant such that $\theta$ is the angle made by $OP$ with the $x$-axis. Let a tangent line be drawn to touch $C$ at $A = \tuple {0, 1}$. Let $OP$ be produced to meet this tangent line at $B$. Then the cosecant of $\theta$ is defined as the length of $OB$. As $OP$ needs to be produced in the opposite direction to $P$, the cosecant is therefore a negative function in the third quadrant.

title: Definition:Cosecant/Definition from Triangle
snippet: 400px In the above right triangle, we are concerned about the angle $\theta$. The cosecant of $\angle \theta$ is defined as being $\dfrac {\text {Hypotenuse}} {\text {Opposite}}$.

title: Definition:Cosecant/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Cosecant == Like secant, the word cosecant comes from the Latin secantus: that which is cutting, the present participle of secare: to cut. The co- prefix, as with similar trigonometric functions, is a reference to complementary angle: see Cosecant of Complement equals Secant. It is pronounced with an equal emphasis on both the first and second syllables: co-see-kant. Category:Definitions/Cosecant Function Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Cosecant/Real Function
snippet: Let $x \in \C$ be a real number. The real function $\csc x$ is defined as: $\csc x = \dfrac 1 {\sin x}$ where $\sin x$ is the sine of $x$. The definition is valid for all $x \in \R$ such that $\sin x \ne 0$.

title: Definition:Coset
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. Let $\struct {H, \circ}$ be a subgroup of $\struct {S, \circ}$.

title: Definition:Coset/Also defined as
snippet: == Coset: Also defined as == When defining a coset, it is usual for the algebraic structure $S$ in which it is embedded to be a group. However, this does not prevent the more general definition to be applied when necessary.

title: Definition:Coset/Left Coset
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. Let $\struct {H, \circ}$ be a subgroup of $\struct {S, \circ}$. The left coset of $x$ modulo $H$, or left coset of $H$ by $x$, is: $x \circ H = \set {y \in S: \exists h \in H: y = x \circ h}$ That is, it is the subset product with singleton: $x \circ H = \set x \circ H$

title: Definition:Coset/Right Coset
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. Let $\struct {H, \circ}$ be a subgroup of $\struct {S, \circ}$. The right coset of $y$ modulo $H$, or right coset of $H$ by $y$, is: $H \circ y = \set {x \in S: \exists h \in H: x = h \circ y}$ That is, it is the subset product with singleton: $H \circ y = H \circ \set y$

title: Definition:Coset Decoding Table
snippet: A coset decoding table is a technique for decoding a linear $\tuple {n, k}$ code. Let $C$ be a linear $\tuple {n, k}$ code whose master code is $\map V {n, p}$. Let $T$ be an array constructed as follows: The first row consists of the codewords of $C$, starting with the zero codeword first. Each subsequent row is a left coset of $C$. The entries of the first column of $T$ are the coset representatives, now called coset leaders. The $r$th coset leader is allocated by choosing any element of $\map V {n, p}$ of minimum weight which is not already included in the first $r - 1$ rows.

title: Definition:Coset Product
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group. Let $N$ be a normal subgroup of $G$. Let $a, b \in G$. The coset product of $a \circ N$ and $b \circ N$ is defined as the binary operation on the left coset space $G / N$ defined as: $\paren {a \circ N} \circ \paren {b \circ N} = \paren {a \circ b} \circ N$ where $a \circ N$ and $b \circ N$ are the left cosets of $a$ and $b$ by $N$.

title: Definition:Coset Space
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$.

title: Definition:Coset Space/Also known as
snippet: == Coset Space: Also known as == Some sources refer to the left coset space and right coset space as the left quotient set and right quotient set respectively. Category:Definitions/Coset Spaces

title: Definition:Coset Space/Left Coset Space
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$. The left coset space (of $G$ modulo $H$) is the quotient set of $G$ by left congruence modulo $H$, denoted $G / H^l$. It is the set of all the left cosets of $H$ in $G$.

title: Definition:Coset Space/Notation
snippet: == Coset Space: Notation == If we are (as is usual) concerned at a particular time with only the right or the left coset space, then the superscript is usually dropped. Thus the notation $G / H$ is used for both the right and left coset space. If, in addition, $H$ is a normal subgroup of $G$, then $G / H^l = G / H^r$ and the notation $G / H$ is then unambiguous anyway. Some sources use $G \divides H$ for the left coset space, reserving $G / H$ for the right coset space. Some sources even use $H \divides G$ for the left coset space.

title: Definition:Coset Space/Right Coset Space
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$. The right coset space (of $G$ modulo $H$) is the quotient set of $G$ by right congruence modulo $H$, denoted $G / H^r$. It is the set of all the right cosets of $H$ in $G$.

title: Definition:Coset Space of Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $S$ be a subring of $R$. For $a \in R$, let $\paren {a + S}$ denote the coset of $S$ by $a$. The coset space of $R$ $S$ is defined as the set of all cosets of $S$ in $R$: $\set {\paren {a + S}: a \in R}$

title: Definition:Coset of Subring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $S$ be a subring of $R$. Let $a \in R$ be given. The coset of $S$ by $a$ is defined as: $\paren {a + S} := \set {x \in R: \exists y \in S: x = a + y}$

title: Definition:Coset of Subring/Also defined as
snippet: == Coset of Subring: Also known as == The coset of a subring $S$ of a ring $R$ by $a$ can also be defined as: $\paren {S + a} := \set {x \in R: \exists y \in S: x = y + a}$ but as ring addition is commutative, the resulting object is identical with $\paren {a + S}$ as defined. Some sources define the coset of a subring only for the case where the subring in question is an ideal.

title: Definition:Cosine/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Cosine == The the symbol $\cos$ for cosine appears to have been invented by in his $1657$ work Trigonometrie, although some authors attribute it to .

title: Definition:Cosine/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Cosine == As with sine, the word cosine derives (erroneously, via a mistranslation) from the Latin sinus which (among other things) means fold, curve, winding or bay. The co- prefix, as with similar trigonometric functions, is a reference to complementary angle: see Cosine of Complement equals Sine. It is pronounced with the emphasis on the first syllable: co-sign. $\cos x$ is voiced cosine (of) $x$, or (as written) cos $x$ (pronounced either coss or coz depending on preference). title: Definition:Cotangent/Real Function
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number. The real function $\cot x$ is defined as: $\cot x = \dfrac {\cos x} {\sin x} = \dfrac 1 {\tan x}$ where: $\sin x$ is the sine of $x$ $\cos x$ is the cosine of $x$ $\tan x$ is the tangent of $x$ The definition is valid for all $x \in \R$ such that $\sin x \ne 0$. Category:Definitions/Cotangent Function

title: Definition:Cotangent Space
snippet: Let $M$ be an smooth manifold. Let $p \in M$ be a point in $M$. Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space at $p$. The cotangent space at $p$ is the (algebraic) dual space to $T_p M$, defined and denoted as: $T_p^*M = \paren {T_p M}^*$

title: Definition:Coterminal
snippet: Geometry: Coterminal angles Coterminal sides of a polygon Coterminal edges of a polyhedron Graph Theory Coterminal edges of graph

title: Definition:Coterminal Angles
snippet: Coterminal angles are angles which are rotations between the same $2$ lines. That is, they are angles with the same arms.

title: Definition:Cototient
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. The cototient of $n$ is defined as: $n - \map \phi n$ where $\map \phi n$ denotes the Euler $\phi$ function.

title: Definition:Cototient/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Cototient == The word cototient derives from: the prefix co- denoting complement the word totient, which is a variant term for the Euler $\phi$ function. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Coulomb
snippet: The coulomb is the SI unit of electric charge. It is defined as being: The amount of electric charge carried in one second by a constant current of one ampere.

title: Definition:Coulomb/Base Units
snippet: The SI base units of the coulomb are: $\mathrm C := \mathrm A \, \mathrm s$ where: $\mathrm A$ denotes amperes $\mathrm s$ denotes seconds (of time).

Let $\beta$ be the inverse of the natural isomorphism $\alpha$. title: Definition:Count
snippet: To count a set $S$ is to establish a bijection between $S$ and an initial segment $\N_n$ of the natural numbers $\N$. If $S \sim \N_n$ (where $\sim$ denotes set equivalence) then we have counted $S$ and found it has $n$ elements. If $S \sim \N$ then $S$ is infinite but countable.

title: Definition:Count/Also known as
snippet: == Count: Also known as == The process of counting is also known as enumeration, although that has a more specialized meaning on .

title: Definition:Countability Axioms
snippet: == Definitions == Countability axioms is the common name used to refer to a set of properties of a topological space which have to do with the existence of countable sets, or countable families of open sets, satisfying certain conditions. They are not axioms in the strict sense of the word, but they are usually named as such because one may think of them as additional basic properties that one can ask from a topological space.

title: Definition:Countable/Also defined as
snippet: Some sources define countable to be what is defined on as countably infinite. That is, they use countable to describe a collection which has exactly the same cardinality as $\N$. Thus under this criterion $X$ is said to be countable there exists a bijection from $X$ to $\N$, that is, $X$ is equivalent to $\N$. However, as the very concept of the term countable implies that a collection can be counted, which, plainly, a finite can be, it is suggested that this interpretation may be counter-intuitive.

title: Definition:Countable Basis
snippet: A countable (analytic) basis for a topology $\tau$ is an analytic basis for $\tau$ which is a countable set.

title: Definition:Countable Chain Condition
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. $T$ satisfies the countable chain condition every disjoint set of open sets of $T$ is countable.

title: Definition:Countable Chain Condition/Also known as
snippet: == Countable Chain Condition: Also known as == The countable chain condition is also known as the Suslin property, for . This can also be rendered as the Souslin property, based on alternative transliterations of the eponym. Some sources introduce the abbreviation CCC.

title: Definition:Countable Complement Extension Topology
snippet: Let $\R$ denote the real number line. Let $\tau_d$ be the Euclidean topology on $\R$. Let $\tau_c$ be the countable complement topology $\R$. Let $\tau$ be the smallest topology generated by $\tau_c \cup \tau_d$. $\tau$ is known as the countable complement extension topology on $\R$.

title: Definition:Countable Complement Topology
snippet: Let $S$ be an infinite set whose cardinality is usually taken to be uncountable. Let $\tau$ be the set of subsets of $S$ defined as: $H \in \tau \iff \relcomp S H$ is countable, or $H = \O$ where $\relcomp S H$ denotes the complement of $H$ relative to $S$. In this definition, countable is used in its meaning that includes finite. Then $\tau$ is the countable complement topology on $S$, and the topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a countable complement space.

title: Definition:Countable Complement Topology/Also known as
snippet: == Countable Complement Topology: Also known as == A countable complement topology is also known as a co-countable topology, and similarly we have the term co-countable space. Sometimes the hyphen is omitted, to give the word cocountable.

title: Definition:Countable Complement Topology/Countable
snippet: It is possible to define the countable complement topology on a countable set set $S$, but as every subset of a countable set has a countable complement, it is clear that this is trivially equal to the discrete space. This is why the countable complement topology is usually understood to apply to uncountable sets only. Category:Definitions/Countable Complement Topologies

title: Definition:Countable Finite Intersection Axiom
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $T$ be such that: Every countable set $V_\alpha$ of closed sets of $T$ such that $\ds \bigcap V_\alpha = \O$ contains a finite subset $V_\beta \subseteq V_\alpha$ such that $\ds \bigcap V_\beta = \O$. Then $T$ satisfies the countable finite intersection axiom.

title: Definition:Countable Ordinal
snippet: Let $\alpha$ be an ordinal. Then $\alpha$ is said to be countable it is a countable set.

title: Definition:Countable Set
snippet: == Definition == Let $S$ be a set.

title: Definition:Countable Set/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. $S$ is countable there exists an injection: $f: S \to \N$

title: Definition:Countable Set/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. $S$ is countable it is finite or countably infinite.

title: Definition:Countable Set/Definition 3
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. $S$ is countable there exists a bijection between $S$ and a subset of $\N$. That is, if it can be shown that it is possible to exhaustively count its elements.

title: Definition:Countable Tightness
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\cl$ be closure in $\struct {X, \tau}$. We say that $\struct {X, \tau}$ has countable tightness for each $A \subseteq X$ and $x \in \map \cl A$, there exists a countable set $S \subseteq A$ such that $x \in \map \cl S$.

title: Definition:Countable Topological Space
snippet: A countable topological space is a topological space whose underlying set is countable, whether finite or countably infinite.

title: Definition:Countable Topological Space/Also known as
snippet: == Countable Topological Space: Also known as == A countable topological space is also known as:

title: Definition:Countably Additive Function
snippet: Let $\Sigma$ be a $\sigma$-algebra. Let $f: \Sigma \to \overline \R$ be a function, where $\overline \R$ denotes the set of extended real numbers. Then $f$ is defined as countably additive : $\ds \map f {\bigcup_{n \mathop \in \N} E_n} = \sum_{n \mathop \in \N} \map f {E_n}$ where $\sequence {E_n}$ is any sequence of pairwise disjoint elements of $\Sigma$. That is, for any countably infinite set of pairwise disjoint elements of $\Sigma$, $f$ of their union equals the sum of $f$ of the individual elements.

title: Definition:Countably Compact Space/Definition 1
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a countably compact space : every countable open cover of $S$ has a finite subcover.

title: Definition:Countably Compact Space/Definition 2
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a countably compact space : every countable set of closed sets of $T$ whose intersection is empty has a finite subset whose intersection is empty. That is, $T$ satisfies the countable finite intersection axiom.

title: Definition:Countably Compact Space/Definition 3
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a countably compact space : every infinite sequence in $S$ has an accumulation point in $S$.

title: Definition:Countably Compact Space/Definition 4
snippet: A topological space $T = \left({S, \tau}\right)$ is a countably compact space : every countably infinite subset of $S$ has an $\omega$-accumulation point in $S$.

title: Definition:Countably Compact Space/Definition 5
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a countably compact space : every infinite subset of $S$ has an $\omega$-accumulation point in $S$.

title: Definition:Countably Generated Sigma-Algebra
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\Sigma$ be a $\sigma$-algebra of $X$. $\Sigma$ is countably generated : $\Sigma$ is generated by a countable collection $\GG \subseteq \Sigma$.

title: Definition:Countably Infinite/Also known as
snippet: When the terms denumerable and enumerable are encountered, they generally mean the same as countably infinite. Sometimes the term enumerably infinite can be seen. Some modern pedagogues (for example and ) use the term listable, but this has yet to catch on.

title: Definition:Countably Infinite/Cardinality
snippet: The cardinality of a countably infinite set is denoted by the symbol $\aleph_0$ (aleph-null).

title: Definition:Countably Infinite/Class
snippet: Let $A$ be a class. $A$ is countably infinite there exists a bijection: $f: S \to \N$ where $\N$ is the set of natural numbers.

title: Definition:Countably Infinite/Set
snippet: == Definition == Let $S$ be a set.

title: Definition:Countably Infinite Enumeration/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Countably Infinite Enumeration == An infinite enumeration would usually be denoted either as: Let $X = \set {x_1, x_2, \ldots}$ or: Let $x_1, x_2, \ldots$ be an enumeration of $X$. Category:Definitions/Enumerations

title: Definition:Countably Infinite Set/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. $S$ is countably infinite there exists a bijection: $f: S \to \N$ where $\N$ is the set of natural numbers. That is, it is an infinite set of the form: $\set {s_0, s_1, \ldots, s_n, \ldots}$ where $n$ runs over all the natural numbers. An infinite set is countably infinite if it is countable, and is uncountable otherwise.

title: Definition:Countably Infinite Set/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. $S$ is countably infinite there exists a bijection: $f: S \to \Z$ where $\Z$ is the set of integers. An infinite set is countably infinite if it is countable, and is uncountable otherwise.

title: Definition:Countably Infinite Topological Space
snippet: A countably infinite topological space is a (countable) topological space whose underlying set is countably infinite.

title: Definition:Countably Infinite Topological Space/Also known as
snippet: == Countably Infinite Topological Space: Also known as == A countably infinite topological space is also known as. Some sources use the term countable topological space, but 's usage of countable specifically includes the finite case.

title: Definition:Countably Metacompact Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a countably metacompact space : every countable open cover of $T$ has an open refinement which is point finite.

title: Definition:Countably Paracompact Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a countably paracompact space : every countable open cover of $T$ has an open refinement which is locally finite.

title: Definition:Countably Subadditive Function
snippet: Let $\Sigma$ be a $\sigma$-algebra over a set $X$. Let $f: \Sigma \to \overline \R$ be a function, where $\overline \R$ denotes the set of extended real numbers. Then $f$ is defined as countably subadditive for any sequence $\sequence {E_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ of elements of $\Sigma$: $\ds \map f {\bigcup_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty E_n} \le \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \map f {E_n}$

title: Definition:Counterexample
snippet: Let $X$ be the universal statement: $\forall x \in S: \map P x$ That is: For all the elements $x$ of a given set $S$, the property $P$ holds. Such a statement may or may not be true. Let $Y$ be the existential statement: $\exists y \in S: \neg \map P y$ That is: There exists at least one element $y$ of the set $S$ such that the property $P$ does not hold. It follows immediately by De Morgan's laws that if $Y$ is true, then $X$ must be false. Such a statement $Y$ is referred to as a counterexample to $X$.

title: Definition:Counting Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. The counting measure (on $X$), denoted $\size {\, \cdot \,}$, is the measure defined by: $\size {\, \cdot \,}: \Sigma \to \overline \R, \ \size E := \begin {cases} \map \# E & : \text {$E$ is finite} \\ +\infty & : \text {$E$ is infinite} \end{cases}$ where $\overline \R$ denotes the extended real numbers, and $\#$ denotes cardinality. That $\size {\, \cdot \,}$ is actually a measure is shown on Counting Measure is Measure.

title: Definition:Counts
snippet: Counts are a statistic which simply records the count of instances of various events. These can then be used as the basis of more sophisticated statistical investigation, for example the analysis of contingency tables.

title: Definition:Couple
snippet: Mechanics: Couple: a system of $2$ forces that are equal in magnitude and exactly opposite in direction, but with different lines of action. Plane Geometry: Tusi Couple: a hypocycloid with $2$ cusps Algebra: Another word for ordered pair

title: Definition:Couple (Mechanics)
snippet: A couple, in the context of mechanics, is a system of $2$ forces that are: equal in magnitude exactly opposite in direction with different lines of action.

title: Definition:Coupled Equations
snippet: Coupled equations are a pair of simultaneous equations, usually differential equations.

title: Definition:Covariance
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables. Let $\mu_X = \expect X$ and $\mu_Y = \expect Y$, the expectations of $X$ and $Y$ respectively, exist and be finite. Then the covariance of $X$ and $Y$ is defined by: $\cov {X, Y} = \expect {\paren {X - \mu_X} \paren {Y - \mu_Y} }$ where this expectation exists.

title: Definition:Covariance Matrix
snippet: Let $\sequence a_n$ and $\sequence b_n$ be sequences of $n$ observations. A covariance matrix $\mathbf C$ is a square matrix of order $n$ defined as: $\sqbrk c_{i j} = \cov {x_i, y_i}$ where $\cov {x_i, y_i}$ denotes the covariance of $x_i$ and $y_j$.

title: Definition:Covariant Derivative
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold with or without boundary. Let $E$ be a smooth manifold. Let $\pi : E \to M$ be a smooth vector bundle. Let $\map \Gamma E$ be the space of smooth sections of $E$. Let $\map {\mathfrak X} M$ be the space of smooth vector fields on $M$. Let $\map {C^\infty} M$ be the space of smooth real functions on $M$. Let $\nabla : \map {\mathfrak X} M \times \map \Gamma E \to \map \Gamma E$ be the Koszul connection, written: $\tuple {X, Y} \mapsto \nabla_X Y$ where: $X \in \map {\mathfrak X} M$ $Y \in \map \Gamma E$ $\times$ denotes the cartesian product.

snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold with or without boundary. Let $TM$ be the tangent bundle of $M$. Let $\nabla$ be a connection in $TM$. Let $I \subseteq \R$ be a real interval. Let $\gamma : I \to M$ be a smooth curve. Let $\map {\mathfrak{X}} \gamma$ be the space of smooth vector fields along $\gamma$. Let $\map {C^\infty} I$ be the space of smooth real functions on $I$.

snippet: Let $V^*$ be the algebraic dual of $V$. An element of $V^*$ is called a covector.

title: Definition:Cover of Set/Countable
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. A cover $\CC$ for $S$ is a countable cover $\CC$ is a countable set.

title: Definition:Cover of Set/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. A cover of (or for) $S$ is a set of sets $\CC$ such that: $\ds S \subseteq \bigcup \CC$ where $\bigcup \CC$ denotes the union of $\CC$.

title: Definition:Cover of Set/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. A cover of (or for) $S$ is a set of sets $\CC$ such that: $\forall s \in S : \exists C \in \CC : s \in C$

title: Definition:Cover of Set/Delta-Cover
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\struct {S, d}$ be a metric space. Let $\delta \in \R_{>0}$. A cover $\CC$ for $S$ is a $\delta$-cover $\CC$ is a countable cover such that: $\forall U \in \CC :0 < \size U \le \delta$ where $\size U$ denotes the diameter of $U$.

title: Definition:Cover of Set/Finite
snippet: A cover $\CC$ for a set $S$ is a finite cover : $\CC$ is a finite set.

title: Definition:Crackpot
snippet: In all fields of scientific endeavour, you will encounter enthusiastic amateurs: those with a fascination for the subject but for whom a rigorous (and rigidified) course of academic study does not (for whatever reason) intersect their world line. To them, the beauty of the world of nature fills them with a passion to participate in the glorious search for truth. For many of these, their lack of facility with the scientific method is no barrier. It is not a hindrance to their work that the only place they are searching for that truth is inside their heads.

title: Definition:Critical Activity
snippet: A critical activity is an activity on the critical path of a given CPA network.

title: Definition:Critical Activity/Also known as
snippet: == Critical Activity: Also known as == A critical activity is also known as a critical event.

title: Definition:Critical Path Algorithm
snippet: The critical path algorithm is an algorithm which finds the critical path in a CPA network. A forward scan determines the earliest possible time of each node. A backward scan then determines the latest possible time of each node. The critical path is the path on which the latest time equals the earliest time for each node.

title: Definition:Critical Path Analysis
snippet: Critical path analysis is a subfield of network analysis used for determining the optimum scheduling for accomplishing a task with interdependent subtasks. Its characteristics are: $(1): \quad$ There is an order of precedence for certain activities $(2): \quad$ Some activities may be able to be performed simultaneously $(3): \quad$ The duration of each activity is known.

title: Definition:Critical Path Analysis/Activity
snippet: An activity is a task which needs a certain amount of time to perform.

title: Definition:Critical Path Analysis/Critical Path
snippet: The earliest possible end time of an activity is the earliest possible start time of an activity which cannot be started until that previous activity has been completed. For some activities, the completion time of the entire project is not affected if those activities are not started at the earliest possible time. However, there is always a latest time for starting an activity without delaying the completion of the project. The edges of the CPA network for which the earliest and latest possible start time and end time are equal form the critical path.

title: Definition:Critical Path Analysis/Dummy Activity
snippet: A dummy activity is a task which needs no action or time to perform, and is included in a network to assist the solution of a CPA exercise.

title: Definition:Critical Path Analysis/Network
snippet: A CPA network is a diagram in the form of a network used in critical path analysis. Its construction requires a precedence table. There are two main types of CPA network, as follows:

title: Definition:Critical Path Analysis/Precedence Table
snippet: A precedence table is a table used in an exercise of critical path analysis to present a list of: the duration of each activity the precedence of each activity.

title: Definition:Critical Point
snippet: Topology: Critical Point Smooth Manifold: Critical Point Riemannian Manifold: Critical Point of Riemannian Length Real Analysis and Calculus: Critical Point: where the limit of the derivative tends to infinity Another (mainly US) term for Stationary Point: where the derivative is zero

title: Definition:Critical Point/Smooth Manifold
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $f \in \map {\CC^\infty} M : M \to \R$ be a smooth real-valued function. Let $p \in M$ be a base point in $M$. Let $\d f_p$ be the differential of $f$ at $p$. Suppose $\d f_p = 0$. Then $p$ is called a critical point of $f$.

title: Definition:Critical Point (Analysis)
snippet: A critical point is a point on a graph where the curve has a vertical tangent. That is, where limit of the derivative tends to infinity.

title: Definition:Critical Point (Topology)
snippet: Let $f: X \to Y$ be a smooth map of manifolds. A point $x \in X$ is called a critical point of $f$ $\d f_x: T_x \sqbrk X \to T_y \sqbrk Y$ is not surjective at $x$. Category:Definitions/Topology

title: Definition:Critical Point of Riemannian Length
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $I = \closedint a b$ be a closed real interval. Let $J \subseteq \R$ be an open real interval. Let $\gamma : I \to M$ be an admissible curve. Let $L_g$ be the Riemannian length of some admissible curve. Let $\Gamma : J \times I \to M$ be the proper variation of $\gamma$ such that: $\forall s \in J, \forall t \in I : \tuple {s, t} \stackrel {\Gamma}{\mapsto} \map {\Gamma_s} t$ Suppose: $\forall \Gamma : \ds \dfrac d {d s} \map {L_g} {\Gamma_s} = 0$ Then $\gamma$ is called the critical point of $L_g$.

title: Definition:Critical Region
snippet: Let $\theta$ be a population parameter of some population $P$. Let $\Omega$ be the parameter space of $\theta$. Let $\mathbf X$ be a random sample from $P$. Let $T = \map f {\mathbf X}$ be a sample statistic. Let $\delta$ be a hypothesis test of the form: reject $H_0$ if $T \in C$ for some null hypothesis $H_0$ and some $C \subset \Omega$. We refer to $C$ as the critical region of $\delta$. This critical region is specifically chosen so as to make it so that the $p$-value is greater than the required significance level for the given test $\delta$.

title: Definition:Critical Region/Also known as
snippet: == Critical Region: Also known as == The critical region is also referred to as the rejection region

title: Definition:Critical Value
snippet: Let $\delta$ be a hypothesis test. Let $H_0$ and $H_1$ be the null hypothesis and alternative hypothesis of $\delta$ respectively. Let $T$ be the test statistic which is being used to determine whether $H_0$ or $H_1$ holds. The critical value of $\delta$ is the value of $T$ that marks the boundary between the acceptance region and critical region of $\delta$.

title: Definition:Critically Damped
snippet: Consider a physical system $S$ whose behaviour can be described with the second order ODE in the form: $(1): \quad \dfrac {\d^2 x} {\d t^2} + 2 b \dfrac {\d x} {\d t} + a^2 x = 0$ for $a, b \in \R_{>0}$. Let $b = a$, so that the solution of $(1)$ is in the form: $x = C_1 e^{-a t} + C_2 t e^{-a t}$ Then $S$ is described as being critically damped. 500px

title: Definition:Cross-Cap
snippet: A cross-cap is a homeomorphic copy of a Möbius strip, whose boundary circle is identified with the boundary circle of a disk removed from $\Bbb S^2$.

title: Definition:Cross-Correlation
snippet: Let $T_1 := \sequence {x_n}$ and $T_2 := \sequence {y_n}$ be two time series in which, for all $k$, $x_k$ and $y_k$ happen at the same time. Then the cross-correlation between $T_1$ and $T_2$ is the correlation between $T_1$ and $T_2$ by pairing each of $x_k$ and $y_k$.

title: Definition:Cross-Correlation Integral/Also known as
snippet: == Cross-Correlation Integral: Also known as == The cross-correlation operator $\map f t \star \map g t$ is sometimes referred to as pentagram notation.

title: Definition:Cross-Covariance Matrix
snippet: Let $\mathbf X = \tuple {X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n}^T$ and $\mathbf Y = \tuple {Y_1, Y_2, \ldots, Y_m}^T$ be random vectors. Then the cross-covariance matrix of $\mathbf X$ and $\mathbf Y$ is defined by: $\cov {\mathbf X, \mathbf Y} = \expect {\paren {\mathbf X - \expect {\mathbf X} } \paren {\mathbf Y - \expect {\mathbf Y} }^T}$ where this expectation exists. title: Definition:Cross-Multiplication
snippet: Consider the equation in the form: $(1): \dfrac a b = \dfrac c d$ Cross-multiplication is the procedure whereby both sides of $(1)$ are multiplied by the product of the denominators of the fractions $\dfrac a b$ and $\dfrac c d$, thus rendering $(1)$ in the form: $a d = b c$ with a view to making it easier to find a solution.

title: Definition:Cross-Ratio/Also defined as
snippet: == Cross-Ratio: Also defined as == In their definition of cross-ratio, some sources do not restrict the points under consideration to being collinear, but merely insist on coplanarity.

title: Definition:Cross-Ratio/Also known as

title: Definition:Cross-Ratio/Complex Analysis
snippet: Let $z_1, z_2, z_3, z_4$ be distinct complex numbers. The cross-ratio of $z_1, z_2, z_3, z_4$ is defined and denoted: $\paren {z_1, z_3; z_2, z_4} = \dfrac {\paren {z_1 - z_2} \paren {z_3 - z_4} } {\paren {z_1 - z_4} \paren {z_3 - z_2} }$

title: Definition:Cross-Ratio/Lines through Origin
snippet: Let $\LL_1$, $\LL_2$, $\LL_3$ and $\LL_4$ be lines through the origin $O$ whose equations embedded in the Cartesian plane are as follows: The cross-ratio of $\LL_1$, $\LL_2$, $\LL_3$ and $\LL_4$, in that specific order, is defined and denoted: $\tuple {\lambda \mu, \lambda', \mu'} := \dfrac {\paren {\lambda - \lambda'} \paren {\mu - \mu'} } {\paren {\lambda - \mu'} \paren {\mu - \lambda'} }$

title: Definition:Cross-Ratio/Points on Line
snippet: Let $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ be points on a straight line. The cross-ratio of $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$, in that specific order, is defined as: $\dfrac {AC / CB} {AD / DB}$ or equivalently: $\dfrac {AC \cdot DB} {AD \cdot CB}$ It can be denoted: $\set {A, B; C, D}$

title: Definition:Cross-Ratio of Lines through Origin/Also presented as
snippet: == Cross-Ratio of Lines through Origin: Also presented as == Some sources present the cross-ratio of lines through the origin as: $\tuple {\lambda \mu, \lambda', \mu'} := \dfrac {\lambda - \lambda'} {\lambda - \mu'} / \dfrac {\mu - \lambda'} {\mu - \mu'}$

title: Definition:Cross-Relation
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a commutative semigroup. Let $\struct {S_1, \circ_{\restriction_1} }, \struct {S_2, \circ_{\restriction_2} }$ be subsemigroups of $S$, where $\circ_{\restriction_1}$ and $\circ_{\restriction_2}$ are the restrictions of $\circ$ to $S_1$ and $S_2$ respectively. Let $\struct {S_1 \times S_2, \oplus}$ be the (external) direct product of $\struct {S_1, \circ_{\restriction_1} }$ and $\struct {S_2, \circ_{\restriction_2} }$, where $\oplus$ is the operation on $S_1 \times S_2$ induced by $\circ_{\restriction_1}$ on $S_1$ and $\circ_{\restriction_2}$ on $S_2$.

title: Definition:Cross-Relation on Natural Numbers
snippet: Consider the commutative semigroup $\left({\N, +}\right)$ composed of the natural numbers $\N$ and addition $+$. Let $\left({\N \times \N, \oplus}\right)$ be the (external) direct product of $\left({\N, +}\right)$ with itself, where $\oplus$ is the operation on $\N \times \N$ induced by $+$ on $\N$. Let $\boxtimes$ be the relation on $\N \times \N$ defined as: $\left({x_1, y_1}\right) \boxtimes \left({x_2, y_2}\right) \iff x_1 + y_2 = x_2 + y_1$ This relation $\boxtimes$ is referred to as the cross-relation on $\left({\N \times \N, \oplus}\right)$.

title: Definition:Cross-Section
snippet: A cross-section of a 3-dimensional figure $F$ is a plane section of $F$ with a plane which is perpendicular to an axis of $F$.

title: Definition:Cross-Validation
snippet: Cross-validation is a technique in statistics in which: $(1): \quad$ data are randomly partitioned into $2$ or more subsets $(2): \quad$ A model, for example a regression model, is fitted to all but one of these subsets $(3): \quad$ A prediction error of the fitted model when applied to the omitted set is calculated. Each subset is omitted in turn, and a combined estimated prediction error is obtained. This method is useful for testing the overall goodness of fit of a model and for detecting outliers.

title: Definition:Cross-Validation/Leave-One-Out
snippet: The leave-one-out technique of cross-validation is the extreme situation in which the subsets into which the data is partitioned are singletons. That is, each of the $n$ observations is omitted in turn, and a model is fitted to the remaining $n - 1$ data.

title: Definition:Cross Cancellation Property
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. Then $\circ$ is said to have the cross cancellation property : $\forall a, b, c \in S: a \circ b = c \circ a \implies b = c$ Category:Definitions/Abstract Algebra Category:Definitions/Cancellability

title: Definition:Crossing (Jordan Curve)
snippet: Let $P$ be a polygon embedded in $\R^2$. Let $q \in \R^2 \setminus \partial P$. Let $\mathbf v \in R^2 \setminus \set {\mathbf 0}$ be a non-zero vector. Let $\LL = \set {q + s \mathbf v: s \in \R_{\ge 0} }$ be a ray with start point $q$. Then $\LL \cap \partial P$ consists of a finite number of line segments, where $\partial P$ denotes the boundary of $P$. As two adjacent sides in $P$ do not form a straight angle by the definition of polygon, each line segment is either a single point or an entire side of $P$.

title: Definition:Crossing (Jordan Curve)/Parity
snippet: Let $P$ be a polygon embedded in $\R^2$. Let $q \in \R^2 \setminus \partial P$. Let $\mathbf v \in R^2 \setminus \set {\mathbf 0}$ be a non-zero vector. Let $\LL = \set {q + s \mathbf v: s \in \R_{\ge 0} }$ be a ray with start point $q$. Let $\map N q$ be the number of crossings between $\LL$ and the boundary $\partial P$ of $P$. Then the parity of $q$ is defined as: $\map {\operatorname{par} } q := \map N q \bmod 2$.

title: Definition:Crossing Number
snippet: Let $\KK$ be a knot embedded in ordinary $3$-space. Let $\KK$ be conceptually laid flat. The crossing number of $\KK$ is the smallest number of points at which $\KK$ crosses over itself.

title: Definition:Crowd

snippet: The cruciform curve is the plane quartic curve which is the locus of the equation expressed in Cartesian coordinates as: $x^2 y^2 = a^2 \paren {x^2 + y^2}$ 520px

title: Definition:Crunode
snippet: A crunode is a double point $P$ of the locus of an equation describing a curve which intersects itself in such a way that there are $2$ distinct tangents at $P$.

title: Definition:Cryptanalysis
snippet: Cryptanalysis is the branch of mathematics which concerns the analysis of ciphertext in an attempt to work out the plaintext. This would typically happen when a party obtains an encrypted message but does not have the decryption key.

title: Definition:Cryptarithm
snippet: A cryptarithm is a puzzle in which the digits in an arithmetical calculation have been replaced by letters. The object of the exercise is to work out what letter stands for what digit. In many cryptarithms, the letters form meaningful words or even phrases in natural language, but this is not an essential feature.

title: Definition:Cryptographic Hash Function
snippet: A cryptographic hash function is an algorithm which maps sets of data to a hash value which is used either as a safeguard against either accidental corruption or as a means of providing security.

title: Definition:Cryptography
snippet: Cryptography is the branch of mathematics which concerns the encoding of information for secrecy and security.

title: Definition:Cryptography/Also known as
snippet: == Cryptography: Also known as == Cryptography is also known as cryptology.

title: Definition:Crystal
snippet: Crystals are physical solids characterized at molecular level by the repetition of a $3$-dimensional pattern. Real crystals are, of course, finite and contain imperfections regarding the content and the repetition of their pattern. For mathematical purposes, especially to study their symmetry group, crystals are idealized as perfect infinite 3-dimensional periodic crystal patterns. This periodicity means that among the symmetries of the crystal are translations spanning the whole $3$-dimensional space.

title: Definition:Crystallography
snippet: Crystallography is the branch of physics which studies the structure of crystals.

snippet: A cube number (or just cube) is a number which can be expressed as the third power of an integer. '

title: Definition:Cube Root/Real
snippet: Let $x \in \R_{\ge 0}$ be a positive real number. The cube roots of $x$ is the real number defined as: $x^{\paren {1 / 3} } := \set {y \in \R: y^3 = x}$ where $x^{\paren {1 / 3} }$ is the $3$rd root of $x$. The notation: $y = \sqrt [3] x$ is usually encountered.

title: Definition:Cubic
snippet: Cubic is a word describing a mathematical expression relating to the $3$rd degree.

title: Definition:Cubic Curve
snippet: A cubic curve is an algebraic curve which has degree $3$. That is, a cubic curve is an algebraic curve which is the locus of an equation of the $3$rd degree.

title: Definition:Cubic Equation
snippet: A cubic equation is a polynomial equation of the form: $a x^3 + b x^2 + c x + d = 0$

title: Definition:Cubic Equation/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Cubic Equation == The ancient Greeks solved quadratics by geometric constructions, using the points of intersection of conic sections. The general algebraic formulation of its solution remained unknown until as late as the end of the $15$th century, at which time wrote in his of $1494$ that the solution of the equations $x^3 + m x = n$ and $x^3 + n = m x$ were as impossible as Squaring the Circle. However, this soon changed, as it was revealed shortly after that was able to solve both of these, as well as the type $x^3 = m x + n$.

title: Definition:Cubic Equation/Resolvent
snippet: Let $P$ be the cubic equation: $a x^3 + b x^2 + c x + d = 0$ with $a \ne 0$ Let: $y = x + \dfrac b {3 a}$ $Q = \dfrac {3 a c - b^2} {9 a^2}$ $R = \dfrac {9 a b c - 27 a^2 d - 2 b^3} {54 a^3}$ Let $y = u + v$ where $u v = -Q$. The resolvent equation of the cubic is given by: $u^6 - 2 R u^3 - Q^3$

snippet: A cubic lattice is a set of points in Cartesian $3$-space whose coordinates are of the form: $\tuple {a x, a y, a z}$ such that: $a$ is a positive real constant $x$, $y$ and $z$ are integers.

snippet: A cuboctahedron is formed by truncating a cube so that the vertices lie at the midpoints of the edges of the cube. 300px

title: Definition:Culmination
snippet: Consider the celestial sphere $C$ whose observer is $O$. Let $B$ be a celestial body on $C$. Let $P_\delta$ be the parallel of declination along which $B$ travels. The two points of culmination of $B$ are the points at which it crosses the principal vertical circle. 500px

title: Definition:Cumulant
snippet: Let $\map M t$ be the moment generating function of a random variable. Let $\kappa_r$ be the coefficient of $\dfrac {t^r} {r!}$ in the power series expansion of $\ln \map M t$. $\kappa_r$ is known as the $r$th cumulant of $\map M t$.

title: Definition:Cumulative Distribution Function
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $X$ be a real-valued random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. The cumulative distribution function of $X$ is denoted $F_X$, and defined as: $\forall x \in \R: \map {F_X} x := \map \Pr {X \le x}$

title: Definition:Cumulative Distribution Function/Also known as
snippet: == Cumulative Distribution Function: Also known as == Other terms used for cumulative distribution function: Probability distribution Cumulative frequency function Distribution function, but this can then become confused with the concept of a distribution function in physics. The abbreviation c.d.f. or cdf are often used. Some sources use the notation $\Phi_X$, $\map \Phi X$ or $\map F X$ for $F_X$.

title: Definition:Cumulative Frequency
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $X$ be a discrete random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$.

title: Definition:Cumulative Frequency/Absolute
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $X$ be a discrete random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. The absolute cumulative frequency of $X$ is defined as: $\forall x \in \Dom X: \map {\text {acf} } x = \ds \sum_{y \mathop \le x} \map \Omega y$

title: Definition:Cumulative Frequency/Relative
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $X$ be a discrete random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. The relative cumulative frequency of $X$ is defined as: $\forall x \in \Dom X: \map {\text {acf} } x = \dfrac {\ds \sum_{y \mathop \le x} \map \Omega y} {\size {\Dom X} }$

title: Definition:Cumulative Frequency Distribution
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of discrete sample data. The cumulative frequency distribution for $S$ is the information consisting of: the possible values the corresponding cumulative frequencies of the data in $S$.

title: Definition:Cumulative Rounding Error
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of continuous data which is to be rounded to the nearest $n$th power of $10$. The cumulative rounding error of $S$ is defined as: $R = \ds \sum_{x \mathop \in S} \paren {x - \overline x}$ where $\overline x$ denotes the rounded value of a given $x$.

title: Definition:Curl Operator/Physical Interpretation
snippet: Let $\mathbf V$ be a vector field acting over a region of space $R$. Let a small vector area $\mathbf a$ of any shape be placed at an arbitrary point $P$ in $R$. Let the contour integral $L$ be computed around the boundary edge of $A$. Then there will be an angle of direction of $\mathbf a$ to the direction of $\mathbf V$ for which $L$ is a maximum. The curl of $\mathbf V$ at $P$ is defined as the vector: whose magnitude is the amount of this maximum $L$ per unit area whose direction is the direction of $\mathbf a$ at this maximum.

title: Definition:Curvature
snippet: Let $C$ be a curve defined by a real function which is twice differentiable. The curvature of $C$ is the rate of change of turning angle the arc length of $C$. The curvature of $C$ is often denoted $\kappa$ (Greek kappa).

The curvature $\kappa$ of $C$ at a point $P = \tuple {x, y}$ is given by: $\kappa = \dfrac {y' '} {\paren {1 + y'^2}^{3/2} }$ where: {{eqn | l = y' | r = \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} | c = is the derivative of $y$ $x$ at $P$ }} {{eqn | l = y' ' | r = \dfrac {\d^2 y} {\d x^2} | c = is the second derivative of $y$ $x$ at $P$. }}
