title: Definition:Diameter/Linguistic Note/Diametral
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Diameter == Diametral means: located on or forming a diameter. For example, a diametral plane is a plane which contains the diameter of a circle.

title: Definition:Diameter/Linguistic Note/Diametrical
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Diameter == Diametrical means: relating to or along a diameter.

title: Definition:Diameter of Bounded Subset of Connected Riemannian Manifold
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a connected Riemannian manifold. Let $p,q \in M$ be points. Let $d_g$ be the Riemannian distance. Let $A \subseteq M$ be a bounded subset of $M$. Then the diameter of $A$, denoted by $\map \diam A$ is defined as: $\map \diam A := \map \sup {\map {d_g} {p, q} : p, q \in A}$ where $\sup$ denotes the supremum.

title: Definition:Diameter of Central Conic
snippet: Let $\KK$ be a central conic. A diameter of $\KK$ is the locus of the midpoints of a system of parallel chords of $\KK$.

title: Definition:Diameter of Central Conic/Also defined as
snippet: Some sources define the diameter of a central conic $\KK$ as a chord of $\KK$ which passes through the center of $\KK$. This is a perfectly adequate definition of a diameter of an ellipse. Indeed, in the context of a circle, this is how a diameter is routinely defined. However, it falls short of providing a full definition of the diameter of a hyperbola. Hence, for the general central conic, and one that is not specifically a circle, this definition is not used on .

title: Definition:Diameter of Conic Section
snippet: Let $\KK$ be a conic section. A diameter of $\KK$ is the locus of the midpoints of a system of parallel chords of $\KK$.

title: Definition:Diameter of Conic Section/Also defined as
snippet: Some sources define the diameter of a conic section $\KK$ as a chord of $\KK$ which passes through the center of $\KK$. This is a perfectly adequate definition of a diameter of an ellipse. Indeed, in the context of a circle, this is how a diameter is routinely defined. However, the definition does not work so well in the context of: a hyperbola, as it does not encompass diameters which are not chords a parabola, which does not have a center. Hence, for the general conic section, and one that is not specifically a circle, this definition is not used on .

title: Definition:Diameter of Ellipse
snippet: Let $\KK$ be an ellipse. A diameter of $\KK$ is the locus of the midpoints of a system of parallel chords of $\KK$. 400px

title: Definition:Diameter of Ellipse/Also defined as
snippet: Some sources define the diameter of an ellipse $\KK$ as a chord of $\KK$ which passes through the center of $\KK$. This is a perfectly adequate definition of a diameter of an ellipse. However, the definition does not work so well in the context of: a hyperbola, as it does not encompass diameters which are not chords a parabola, which does not have a center.

title: Definition:Diameter of Graph
snippet: Let $G$ be a graph. The diameter of $G$ is the maximum eccentricity of all the vertices of $G$. That is, it is the largest distance between two vertices of $G$

title: Definition:Diameter of Hyperbola
snippet: Let $\KK$ be a hyperbola. A diameter of $\KK$ is the locus of the midpoints of a system of parallel chords of $\KK$. 400px

title: Definition:Diameter of Hyperbola/Also defined as
snippet: Some sources define the diameter of a hyperbola $\KK$ as a chord of $\KK$ which passes through the center of $\KK$. However, while it is true that such a chord is indeed a diameter of $\KK$, not all diameters of $\KK$ are chords of $\KK$. For example: 240px where it can be seen that the diameter (red) of the hyperbola (blue) defined by the parallel chords is not actually itself a chord of $\KK$.

title: Definition:Diameter of Parabola
snippet: Let $\KK$ be a parabola. A diameter of $\KK$ is the locus of the midpoints of a system of parallel chords of $\KK$. 180px

title: Definition:Diameter of Parallelogram
snippet: Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram: 400px The diameters of $ABCD$ are the lines $AC$ and $BD$ joining their opposite vertices.

title: Definition:Diameter of Quadric Surface
snippet: Let $\SS$ be a quadric surface. A diameter of $S$ is a straight line passing through the center of $\SS$.

title: Definition:Diameter of Quadrilateral
snippet: Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral: 380px The diameters of $ABCD$ are the lines $AC$ and $BD$ joining their opposite vertices.

title: Definition:Diameter of Subset of Metric Space
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. Let $S \subseteq A$ be subset of $A$. Then the diameter of $S$ is the extended real number defined by: $\map \diam S := \begin {cases} \sup \set {\map d {x, y}: x, y \in S} & : \text {if this quantity is finite} \\ \\ + \infty & : \text {otherwise} \end {cases}$ Thus, by the definition of the supremum, the diameter is the smallest real number $D$ such that any two points of $S$ are at most a distance $D$ apart. If $d: S^2 \to \R$ does not admit a supremum, then $\map \diam S$ is infinite.

title: Definition:Diastema/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Diastema == The word diastema is the Greek word διάστημα, meaning distance. It is pronounced di-a-stee-ma. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Dichotomous Data
snippet: Dichotomous data is nominal data such that a unit falls into exactly one of $2$ categories.

title: Definition:Dichotomous Variable
snippet: A dichotomous variable is a categorical variable which can take on exactly one of $2$ possible values.

title: Definition:Dichotomy
snippet: A dichotomy is a partition of a population into two distinct subsets. This is based on either: measurable variables (for example: age under $18$, age $18$ and over) attributes (for example: male and female).

title: Definition:Dicyclic Group
snippet: For even $n$, the dicyclic group $\Dic n$ of order $4 n$ is the group having the presentation: $\Dic n = \gen {a, b: a^{2 n} = e, b^2 = a^n, b^{-1} a b = a^{-1} }$

title: Definition:Dicyclic Group/Also denoted as
snippet: == Dicyclic Group: Also denoted as == Some sources denote the dicyclic group $\Dic n$ as $Q_{2 n}$, referring to it as the generalized quaternion group: $Q_{2 n} = \gen {a, b: a^{2 n} = e, b^2 = a^n, b^{-1} a b = a^{-1} }$ Using this notation, it can be seen that the quaternion group is represented by: $Q_4 = \gen {a, b: a^4 = e, b^2 = a^2, b^{-1} a b = a^{-1} }$ Others have a different notation again: $Q_{4 n} = \gen {a, b: a^{2 n} = e, b^2 = a^n, b^{-1} a b = a^{-1} }$ Using this notation, it can be seen that the quaternion group is represented by: $Q_8 = \gen {a, b: a^4 = e, b^2 = a^2,…

title: Definition:Dicyclic Group/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Dicyclic Group == The word dicyclic in the term dicyclic group is parsed di-cyclic, that is, having two cycles. Hence it is pronounced di-cy-clic. Please do not say dicky-click. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Dicyclic Group/Quaternion Group
snippet: The dicyclic group $\Dic 2$ is known as the quaternion group. The elements of $\Dic 2$ are: $\Dic 2 = \set {e, a, a^2, a^3, b, a b, a^2 b, a^3 b}$

title: Definition:Die
snippet: Two six-sided dice A die (plural: dice) is a device for generating random numbers, traditionally between $1$ and $6$. A die usually consists of a cube on which each face denotes a different number, usually (again) from $1$ to $6$. Traditionally, opposite faces add to $7$, so: $1$ is opposite $6$ $2$ is opposite $5$ $3$ is opposite $4$. The idea is that when you roll it, or throw it, or otherwise cause it to land upon a flattish surface, one of the sides will be face-up, and (with a good design of die) which side that is can not be precisely predicted.

title: Definition:Die/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Die == Dice have been around for thousands of years, and have formed the basis of humanity's love-affair with gambling throughout history. Even the clothing of Jesus Christ was reportedly gambled for at his crucifixion in a dice game. An early reference to the design of a die can be found in 's $1918$ translation of : The numbers on a die run so: six one, five two, three four.

title: Definition:Die/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Die == Note that the plural of die is dice. Beware the tendency to use the word dice as a singular noun: I threw a dice and it came up six as this (while colloquial) is technically incorrect.

title: Definition:Diffeomorphism/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Diffeomorphism == The form of diffeomorphism is diffeomorphic.

title: Definition:Diffeomorphism on Image
snippet: == Open Set in $\R^n$ == Let $n$ and $k$ be natural numbers. Let $U \subset \R^n$ be an open set. Let $f : U \to \R^n$ be a mapping. Then $f$ is a $C^k$-diffeomorphism on its image $\map f U$ is open and $f : U \to f \sqbrk U$ is a $C^k$-diffeomorphism.

title: Definition:Difference
snippet: Set Difference Subtraction Absolute Difference

title: Definition:Difference (Subtraction)/Warning
snippet: == Difference in context of Subtraction: Warning == It is commomplace to refer to the difference between two real numbers $a$ and $b$ without explicitly specifying whether $a - b$ or $b - a$ is meant. Usually, the difference between $a$ and $b$ is taken specifically to mean the smaller number subtracted from the greater, in which case it is better to use absolute difference instead. Sometimes the difference between $a$ and $b$ is used to mean $a - b$, particularly in common parlance. Be aware that clarity may suffer if the specific meaning of what you want to say is compromised.

title: Definition:Difference Equation
snippet: A difference equation is a type of recurrence relation involving finite differences.

title: Definition:Difference Equation/Also known as
snippet: == Difference Equation: Also known as == A difference equation is often referred to as a recurrence relation, and vice versa. However, a difference equation is in fact a particular type of recurrence relation, and the two are not strictly synonymous.

title: Definition:Difference Sequence
snippet: Let $\sequence {u_n}$ be a sequence of numbers. The difference sequence of $\sequence {u_n}$ is defined as: $\sequence {u_{n + 1} - u_n}$

title: Definition:Differentiability Class
snippet: Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a real function. Let $k \in \N$. Then $\map f x$ is of differentiability class $C^k$ : $\dfrac {\d^k} {\d x^k} \map f x \in C$ where $C$ denotes the class of continuous real functions. That is, $f$ is in differentiability class $k$ there exists a $k$th derivative of $f$ which is continuous. If $\dfrac {\d^k} {\d x^k} \map f x$ is continuous for all $k \in \N$, then $\map f x$ is of differentiability class $C^\infty$.

title: Definition:Differentiability Class/Class Zero
snippet: Differentiability class $C^0$ consists of the class of continuous real functions $C$ whether they be differentiable or not.

title: Definition:Differentiability Class/Domain Restriction
snippet: Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a real function. Let $S \subseteq \R$ be a subset of $\R$ on which the $n$th derivative of $f$ is continuous on $S$. Then $\map f x$ is of differentiability class $C^n$ on $S$.

title: Definition:Differentiable Mapping/Complex Function/Point
snippet: Let $U \subset \C$ be an open set. Let $f : U \to \C$ be a complex function. Let $z_0 \in U$ be a point in $U$. Then $f$ is complex-differentiable at $z_0$ the limit: $\ds \lim_{h \mathop \to 0} \frac {\map f {z_0+h} - \map f {z_0}} h$ exists as a finite number. This limit, if it exists, is called the derivative of $f$ at $z_0$.

title: Definition:Differentiable Mapping/Function With Values in Normed Space
snippet: Let $U \subset \R$ be an open set. Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ be a normed vector space. A function $f : U \to X$ is (strongly) differentiable at $x \in U$ there exists $\map {f'} x \in X$ such that: $\ds \lim_{h \mathop \to 0} \norm {\frac {\map f {x + h} - \map f x} h - \map {f'} x}_X = 0$ Moreover, $f$ is called (strongly) differentiable if it is differentiable at every point of $U$.

title: Definition:Differentiable Mapping/Real-Valued Function/Open Set
snippet: Let $\mathbb X$ be an open subset of $\R^n$. Let $f: \mathbb X \to \R$ be a real-valued function. Then $f$ is differentiable in the open set $\mathbb X$ $f$ is differentiable at each point of $\mathbb X$.

title: Definition:Differentiable Mapping/Real-Valued Function/Point
snippet: Let $U$ be an open subset of $\R^n$. Let $\norm \cdot $ denote the Euclidean norm on $\R^n$. Let $f: U \to \R$ be a real-valued function. Let $x \in U$.

title: Definition:Differentiable Mapping/Real-Valued Function/Point/Definition 1
snippet: Let $U$ be an open subset of $\R^n$. Let $\norm \cdot $ denote the Euclidean norm on $\R^n$. Let $f: U \to \R$ be a real-valued function. Let $x \in U$. $f$ is differentiable at $x$ there exist $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n \in \R$ and a real-valued function $r: U \setminus \set x \to \R$ such that: $(1):\quad \map f {x + h} = \map f x + \alpha_1 h_1 + \cdots + \alpha_n h_n + \map r h \norm h$ $(2):\quad \ds \lim_{h \mathop \to 0} \map r h = 0$ Category:Definitions/Differentiable Real-Valued Functions

title: Definition:Differentiable Mapping/Real-Valued Function/Point/Definition 2
snippet: Let $U$ be an open subset of $\R^n$. Let $f: U \to \R$ be a real-valued function. Let $\norm \cdot $ denote the Euclidean norm on $\R^n$. Let $x \in U$. $f$ is differentiable at $x$ there exists a linear transformation $T: \R^n \to \R$ and a real-valued function $r: U \setminus \set x \to \R$ such that: $(1): \quad \map f {x + h} = \map f x + \map T h + \map r h \norm h$ $(2): \quad \ds \lim_{h \mathop \to 0} \map r h = 0$

title: Definition:Differentiable Mapping/Real-Valued Function/Point/Definition 3
snippet: Let $U$ be an open subset of $\R^n$. Let $\norm \cdot $ denote the Euclidean norm on $\R^n$. Let $f: U \to \R$ be a real-valued function. Let $x \in U$. $f$ is differentiable at $x$ all its partial derivatives are defined at $x$.

title: Definition:Differentiable Mapping/Real Function/Interval
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function defined on an open interval $\openint a b$. Then $f$ is differentiable on $\openint a b$ $f$ is differentiable at each point of $\openint a b$.

title: Definition:Differentiable Mapping/Real Function/Interval/Closed Interval
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function defined on a closed interval $\closedint a b$. Let $f$ be differentiable on the open interval $\openint a b$. If the following limit from the right exists: $\ds \lim_{x \mathop \to a^+} \frac {\map f x - \map f a} {x - a}$ as well as this limit from the left: $\ds \lim_{x \mathop \to b^-} \frac {\map f x - \map f b} {x - b}$ then $f$ is differentiable on the closed interval $\closedint a b$.

title: Definition:Differentiable Mapping/Real Function/Point
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function defined on an open interval $\openint a b$. Let $\xi$ be a point in $\openint a b$.

title: Definition:Differentiable Mapping/Real Function/Point/Definition 1
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function defined on an open interval $\openint a b$. Let $\xi$ be a point in $\openint a b$. $f$ is differentiable at the point $\xi$ the limit: $\ds \lim_{x \mathop \to \xi} \frac {\map f x - \map f \xi} {x - \xi}$ exists.

title: Definition:Differentiable Mapping/Real Function/Point/Definition 2
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function defined on an open interval $\openint a b$. Let $\xi$ be a point in $\openint a b$. $f$ is differentiable at the point $\xi$ the limit: $\ds \lim_{h \mathop \to 0} \frac {\map f {\xi + h} - \map f \xi} h$ exists.

title: Definition:Differentiable Mapping/Real Function/Real Number Line
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function defined on $\R$. By definition, $\R$ is an (unbounded) open interval. Let $f$ be differentiable on the open interval $\R$. That is, let $f$ be differentiable at every point of $\R$. Then $f$ is differentiable everywhere (on $\R$). Category:Definitions/Differentiable Real Functions

title: Definition:Differentiable Mapping/Vector-Valued Function
snippet: Let $m, n \ge 1$ be natural numbers.

title: Definition:Differentiable Mapping/Vector-Valued Function/Point
snippet: Let $\mathbb X$ be an open subset of $\R^n$. Let $f = \tuple {f_1, f_2, \ldots, f_m}^\intercal: \mathbb X \to \R^m$ be a vector valued function.

title: Definition:Differentiable Mapping/Vector-Valued Function/Point/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\mathbb X$ be an open subset of $\R^n$. Let $f = \tuple {f_1, f_2, \ldots, f_m}^\intercal: \mathbb X \to \R^m$ be a vector valued function. $f$ is differentiable at $x \in \R^n$ there exists a linear transformation $T: \R^n \to \R^m$ and a mapping $r : U \to \R^m$ such that: $(1): \quad \map f {x + h} = \map f x + \map T h + \map r h \cdot \norm h$ $(2): \quad \ds \lim_{h \mathop \to 0} \map r h = 0$

title: Definition:Differentiable Mapping/Vector-Valued Function/Point/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\mathbb X$ be an open subset of $\R^n$. Let $f : \mathbb X \to \R^m$ be a vector valued function. $f$ is differentiable at $x \in \mathbb X$ there exists a linear transformation $T: \R^n \to \R^m$ such that: $\ds \lim_{h \mathop \to \bszero} \frac {\norm {\map f {x + h} - \map f x - \map T h}} {\norm h} = 0$

title: Definition:Differentiable Mapping/Vector-Valued Function/Point/Definition 3
snippet: Let $\mathbb X$ be an open subset of $\R^n$. Let $f = \tuple {f_1, f_2, \ldots, f_m}^\intercal: \mathbb X \to \R^m$ be a vector valued function. $f$ is differentiable at $x \in \R^n$ for each real-valued function $f_j: j = 1, 2, \ldots, m$: $f_j: \mathbb X \to \R$ is differentiable at $x$.

title: Definition:Differentiable Mapping/Vector-Valued Function/Region
snippet: Let $\mathbb X$ be an open subset of $\R^n$. Let $f = \tuple {f_1, f_2, \ldots, f_m}^\intercal: \mathbb X \to \R^m$ be a vector valued function. Let $S \subseteq \mathbb X$. Then $f$ is differentiable in the open set $S$ $f$ is differentiable at each $x$ in $S$. This can be denoted $f \in \map {\CC^1} {S, \R^m}$.

title: Definition:Differentiable Mapping between Manifolds
snippet: Let $M$ and $N$ be differentiable manifolds. Let $f : M \to N$ be continuous.

title: Definition:Differentiable Mapping between Manifolds/Point
snippet: Let $M$ and $N$ be differentiable manifolds. Let $f: M \to N$ be continuous. Let $p \in M$.

title: Definition:Differentiable Mapping between Manifolds/Point/Definition 1
snippet: $f$ is differentiable at $p$ for every pair of charts $\struct {U, \phi}$ and $\struct {V, \psi}$ of $M$ and $N$ with $p \in U$ and $\map f p \in V$: $\psi \circ f \circ \phi^{-1}: \map \phi {U \cap \map {f^{-1} } V} \to \map \psi V$ is differentiable at $\map \phi p$. Category:Definitions/Differentiable Manifolds

title: Definition:Differentiable Mapping between Manifolds/Point/Definition 2
snippet: $f$ is differentiable at $p$ there exists a pair of charts $\struct {U, \phi}$ and $\struct {V, \psi}$ of $M$ and $N$ with $p \in U$ and $\map f p \in V$ such that: $\psi \circ f \circ \phi^{-1}: \map \phi {U \cap \map {f^{-1} } V} \to \map \psi V$ is differentiable at $\map \phi p$. Category:Definitions/Differentiable Manifolds

title: Definition:Differentiable Real Function at Point/Informal Definition
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function defined on an open interval $\openint a b$. Let $\xi$ be a point in $\openint a b$. $f$ is differentiable at the point $\xi$ the slope of the graph $f$ at $y = \map f \xi$ can be defined. That is, the graph $f$ has a tangent at $\xi$.

title: Definition:Differentiable Structure
snippet: Let $M$ be a topological space. Let $d$ be a natural number. Let $k \ge 1$ be a natural number. A $d$-dimensional differentiable structure of class $\CC^k$ on $M$ is a non-empty equivalence class of the set of $d$-dimensional $\CC^k$-atlases on $M$ under the equivalence relation of compatibility.

title: Definition:Differential Calculus/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Differential Calculus == The technique used by to find the Tangent to Archimedean Spiral at Point is often suggested as anticipating the differential calculus. had the basic idea of differential calculus in its modern form in about $1628$ or $1629$, but he did not publish these ideas until a decade or so later. Much of the early work developing differential calculus was done by . His initial work on this was done during the years $1665$ to $1667$ when he was at home in Woolsthorpe. He suggested that include his ideas in his of $1670$.

title: Definition:Differential Calculus/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Differential Calculus == The term differential calculus is the Anglified version of the neo-Latin phrase calculus differentialis, coined by .

title: Definition:Differential Complex
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $\ds M = \bigoplus_{n \mathop \in \Z} M^n$ be a $\Z$-graded $R$-module that is also a differential module with differential $\d$. Then $M$ is a differential complex $\d$ satisfies: $\map \d {M^n} \subseteq M^{n + 1}$ for all $n \in \Z$. The notation $\d_n := \d \restriction_{M_n}$ is often seen.

title: Definition:Differential Entropy
snippet: Differential entropy extends the concept of entropy to continuous random variables. Let $X$ be a continuous random variable. Let $X$ have probability density function $f_X$. Then the differential entropy of $X$, $\map h X$ measured in nats, is given by: $\ds \map h X = -\int_{-\infty}^\infty \map {f_X} x \ln \map {f_X} x \rd x$ Where $\map {f_X} x = 0$, we take $\map {f_X} x \ln \map {f_X} x = 0$ by convention.

title: Definition:Differential Equation
snippet: A differential equation is a mathematical equation for an unknown function of one or several variables relating: $(1): \quad$ The values of the function itself $(2): \quad$ Its derivatives of various orders.

title: Definition:Differential Equation/Autonomous
snippet: A differential equation is autonomous if none of the derivatives depend on the independent variable. The $n$th order autonomous differential equation takes the form: $y^{\paren n} = \map f {y, y', y' ', \dots, y^{\paren {n - 1} } }$

title: Definition:Differential Equation/Degree
snippet: Let $f$ be a differential equation which can be expressed as a polynomial in all the derivatives involved. The degree of $f$ is defined as being the power to which the derivative of the highest order is raised. By default, if not specifically mentioned, the degree of a differential equation is assumed to be $1$.

title: Definition:Differential Equation/Degree/First
snippet: A quasilinear differential equation is a differential equation of the first degree.

title: Definition:Differential Equation/Distributional
snippet: A differential equation is classified as distributional if, in addition to ordinary and partial derivatives and functions, they also involve at least one of the following notions: Distributional ordinary derivative Distributional partial derivative Schwartz distribution and/or its derivatives Note that every standard differential equation can be written as a distributional one, but not the other way around.

title: Definition:Differential Equation/Explicit
snippet: A differential equation is called explicit it can be written in the form: $y^{\paren n} = \map f {x, y, y', y' ', \dots, y^{\paren {n - 1} } }$

title: Definition:Differential Equation/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Differential Equations == Differential equations, both ordinary and partial, are of great importance in the definition of mathematical models describing real-world phenomema. According to , the first person to solve a differential equation was , which he did in $1676$ by use of an infinite series, $11$ years after he had invented the differential calculus in $1665$. These results were not published till $1693$, the same year in which a differential equation occurred in the work of , whose own work on differential calculus was published in $1684$.

title: Definition:Differential Equation/Implicit
snippet: A differential equation that is not explicit is referred to as implicit. Category:Definitions/Differential Equations

title: Definition:Differential Equation/Linear
snippet: A linear differential equation is a differential equation where all dependent variables and their derivatives appear to the first power. Neither are products of dependent variables allowed. Hence a linear differential equation is of the form: $\map {P_0} x y + \map {P_1} x \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} + \map {P_2} x \dfrac {\d^2 y} {\d x^2} + \cdots + \map {P_n} x \dfrac {\d^n y} {\d x^n} = \map Q x$ where $P_0, P_1, \ldots, P_n, Q$ are functions of $x$.

title: Definition:Differential Equation/Mixed
snippet: A mixed differential equation is a partial differential equation in which both ordinary derivatives and partial derivatives occur. Category:Definitions/Differential Equations

title: Definition:Differential Equation/Nonlinear
snippet: A nonlinear differential equation is a differential equation which is not linear.

title: Definition:Differential Equation/Order
snippet: The order of a differential equation is defined as being the order of the highest order derivative that is present in the equation.

title: Definition:Differential Equation/Ordinary
snippet: An ordinary differential equation is a differential equation which has exactly one independent variable. All the derivatives occurring in it are therefore ordinary. The general ordinary differential equation of order $n$ is: $\map f {x, y, \dfrac {\d x} {\d y}, \dfrac {\d^2 x} {\d y^2}, \ldots, \dfrac {\d^n x} {\d y^n} } = 0$ or, using the prime notation: $\map f {x, y, y', y' ', \ldots, y^{\paren n} } = 0$

title: Definition:Differential Equation/Partial
snippet: A partial differential equation is a differential equation which has: one dependent variable more than one independent variable. The derivatives occurring in it are therefore partial.

title: Definition:Differential Equation/Solution
snippet: Let $\Phi$ be a differential equation defined on a domain $D$. Let $\phi$ be a function which satisfies $\Phi$ on the whole of $D$. Then $\phi$ is known as a solution of $\Phi$. Note that, in general, there may be more than one solution to a given differential equation. On the other hand, there may be none at all.

title: Definition:Differential Equation/Solution/Also known as
snippet: == Solution to Differential Equation: Also known as == Some sources refer to a solution $\phi$ of a differential equation $\Phi$ as an explicit solution of $\Phi$. The word integral can sometimes be seen to mean a solution to a differential equation.

title: Definition:Differential Equation/Solution/General Solution
snippet: Let $\Phi$ be a differential equation. The general solution to $\Phi$ is the set of all functions $\phi$ that satisfy $\Phi$.

title: Definition:Differential Equation/Solution/General Solution/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on General Solution to Differential Equation == The general solution to a differential equation was formerly known as the complete integral, or complete integral equation. The Latin term used by was æquatio integralis completa. However, the term integral equation is now used to mean something completely different, and should not be used in this context.

title: Definition:Differential Equation/Solution/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Solution to Differential Equation == The original name for a solution to a differential equation that used in $1689$ was integral. used the term particular integral in his of $1768$, but the latter term has more recently taken on a more precise definition. The term solution was first used by in $1774$. This terminology became established under the influence of .

title: Definition:Differential Equation/Solution/Particular Solution
snippet: Let $\Phi$ be a differential equation. Let $S$ denote the solution set of $\Phi$. A particular solution of $\Phi$ is the element of $S$, or subset of $S$, which satisfies a particular boundary condition of $\Phi$.

title: Definition:Differential Equation/Solution/Weak Solution
snippet: A weak solution is a solution to a non-standard formulation of a differential equation.

title: Definition:Differential Equation/System
snippet: A system of differential equations is a set of simultaneous differential equations. The solutions for each of the differential equations are in general expected to be consistent.

title: Definition:Differential Equation/System/Autonomous
snippet: A system of differential equations is autonomous if all of the differential equations which it comprises are themselves autonomous. Category:Definitions/Differential Equations

title: Definition:Differential Equation/Total
snippet: A total differential equation is a differential equation which contains: more than one dependent variable one independent variable which may or may not appear explicitly in that differential equation.

title: Definition:Differential Field
snippet: A differential field is a differential ring which is a field.

title: Definition:Differential Form
snippet: Let $M$ be an $n$-dimensional $C^1$ differentiable manifold. Let $p \in M$ be a point in $M$. Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space at $p$. Let $T_p^*M$ be the cotangent space at $p$. Let $\ds \Lambda^k T^* M = \bigcup_{p \mathop \in M} \set p \times \map {\Lambda^k} {T_p^* M}$, endowed with its natural structure as a $C^0$ manifold.

title: Definition:Differential Form/Degree
snippet: Let $M$ be an $n$-dimensional $C^1$ differentiable manifold. Let $\omega : M \to \Lambda^k T^* M$ be a differential $k$-form on $M$. The degree of $\omega$ is the number $k$.

title: Definition:Differential Geometry
snippet: Differential geometry is a branch of mathematics which uses techniques from calculus and linear algebra to study problems in geometry. It is concerned with the intrinsic properties of curves and surfaces as found using differential calculus.

title: Definition:Differential Geometry/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Differential Geometry == The subject of differential geometry was originated by who in $1827$ defined what is now called the Gaussian curvature of a surface at a point. He provided formulas for this in terms of the partial derivatives using a number of different coordinate systems. This was extended by to a general type of space with arbitrary dimensions.

title: Definition:Differential Increment of Position Vector
snippet: Let $\map {\R^3} {x, y, z}$ denote the Cartesian $3$-space. Let $\tuple {\mathbf i, \mathbf j, \mathbf k}$ be the standard ordered basis on $\R^3$. Let $\mathbf r$ be the position vector of a point $P$ in $\R^3$: $\mathbf r = x \mathbf i + y \mathbf j + z \mathbf k$ The differential increment of $\mathbf r$ is denoted and defined as: $\d \mathbf r := \d x \mathbf i + \d y \mathbf j + \d z \mathbf k$

title: Definition:Differential Module
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $M$ be an $R$-module. A differential on $M$ is a homomorphism $d: M \to M$ such that: $d^2 := d \circ d = 0$ The pair $\struct {M, d}$ is called a differential module.

title: Definition:Differential Operator
snippet: A differential operator is a symbol indicating that differentiation needs to be performed. It can be written as $D$ or $\dfrac \d {\d x}$, and so on.

title: Definition:Differential Operator/Also defined as
snippet: == Differential Operator: Also defined as == Some sources, particularly those dealing with specific physical phenomena such as electromagnetism and quantum mechanics, use the term differential operators to mean: the divergence operator $\operatorname {div}$ the gradient operator $\grad$ the curl operator $\curl$.

title: Definition:Differential Ring
snippet: A differential ring is a pair $\struct {R, D}$ where: $R$ is a ring $D$ is a derivation on $R$.

title: Definition:Differential Topology
snippet: Differential topology is the branch of topology whose concern is spaces and mappings which are smooth.

title: Definition:Differential of Mapping/Functional
snippet: Let $J \sqbrk y$ be a differentiable functional. Let $h$ be an increment of the independent variable $y$. Then the term linear $h$ is called the differential of the functional $J$, and is denoted by $\delta J \sqbrk {y; h}$.

title: Definition:Differential of Mapping/Manifolds
snippet: Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds with or without boundary. Let $F : M \to N$ be a smooth mapping. Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space at $p \in M$. Then the differential of $F$ at $p$ is defined and denoted as the smooth mapping $\d F_p : T_p M \to T_{\map F p} N$ such that: $\forall f \in \map {C^\infty} N : \forall p \in M : \forall v \in T_p M : \map {\map {\d F_p} v} f = \map v {f \circ F}$

title: Definition:Differential of Mapping/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Differential == There are various notations for the differential of a function $f$ at $x$: $\map {\d f} x$ $\d f_x$ $\d_x f$ $\map {D f} x$ $D_x f$ Substituting $\d y$ for $\map {\d f} {x; h}$ and $\d x$ for $h$, the following notation emerges: $\d y = \map {f'} x \rd x$ hence: $\d y = \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} \rd x$

title: Definition:Differential of Mapping/Real-Valued Function/Point
snippet: Let $U \subset \R^n$ be an open set. Let $f: U \to \R$ be a real-valued function. Let $f$ be differentiable at a point $x \in U$. {{eqn | l = \map {\d f} {x; h} | r = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \frac {\map {\partial f} x} {\partial x_i} h_i | c = }} {{eqn | r = \frac {\map {\partial f} x} {\partial x_1} h_1 + \frac {\map {\partial f} x} {\partial x_2} h_2 + \cdots + \frac {\map {\partial f} x} {\partial x_n} h_n | c = }} where: $h = \tuple {h_1, h_2, \ldots, h_n} \in \R^n$ $\dfrac {\partial f} {\partial x_i}$ is the partial derivative of $f$ $x_i$.

title: Definition:Differential of Mapping/Real Function/Open Set
snippet: Let $U \subset \R$ be an open set. Let $f : U \to \R$ be a real function. Let $f$ be differentiable in $U$. The differential $\d f$ is the mapping $\d f : U \to \map {\operatorname {Hom} } {\R, \R}$ defined as: $\map {\paren {\d f} } x = \map {\d f} x$ where: $\map {\d f} x$ is the differential of $f$ at $x$ $\map {\operatorname {Hom} } {\R, \R}$ is the set of all linear transformations from $\R$ to $\R$. The differential $\d f$ can be regarded as a (real) function of two variables, defined as: $\map {\d f} {x; h} = \map {f'} x h$ where $\map {f'} x$ is the derivative of $f$ at $x$.

title: Definition:Differential of Mapping/Real Function/Point
snippet: Let $U \subset \R$ be an open set. Let $f: U \to \R$ be a real function. Let $f$ be differentiable at a point $x \in U$. The differential of $f$ at $x$ is the linear transformation $\map {\d f} x : \R \to \R$ defined as: $\map {\map {\d f} x} h = \map {f'} x \cdot h$ where $\map {f'} x$ is the derivative of $f$ at $x$. Category:Definitions/Differentials

title: Definition:Differential of Mapping/Vector-Valued Function/Point
snippet: Let $U \subset \R^n$ be an open set. Let $f: U \to \R^m$ be a vector-valued function. Let $f$ be differentiable at a point $x \in U$. The differential of $f$ at $x$ is the linear transformation $\d \map f x: \R^n \to \R^m$ defined as: $\map {\d \map f x} h = \map {J_f} x \cdot h$ where: $\map {J_f} x$ is the Jacobian matrix of $f$ at $x$. Category:Definitions/Differentials

title: Definition:Differential of Mapping/Warning
snippet: == Warning == It is generally considered to be incorrect to consider $\d y$ as: a small change in $y$ caused by a small change $\d x$ in $x$. This is nearly true for small values of $\d x$, but will only ever be exactly true when $f$ has a graph which is a straight line. If it is necessary to talk about small changes then the notation $\delta x$ and $\delta y$ are to be used instead.

title: Definition:Differential of Real-Valued Function/Also known as
snippet: == Differential of Real-Valued Function: Also known as == The differential of a real-valued function $f$ as defined here is also known as the total differential of $f$.

title: Definition:Differentiation
snippet: The process of obtaining the derivative of a differentiable function $f$ $x$ is known as: differentiation (of $f$) $x$ or differentiation $x$

title: Definition:Differentiation/Also known as
snippet: == Differentiation: Also known as == The technique of differentiation was called the method of fluxions by . The word fluxion evokes the concept of quantities flowing towards zero. Hence the implicit dependence upon continuity.

title: Definition:Diffie-Hellman-Merkle Key Exchange
snippet: The Diffie-Hellman-Merkle key exchange is a safe method of exchanging a key. Suppose Alice and Bob with to communicate securely. They decide to use the order $p - 1$ cyclic group $G$ of multiplication modulo $p$ consisting of the non-zero elements of a finite field of order $p$ They choose a generator $g$ of $G$. Alice chooses an integer $a$ and calculates $A = g^a$ modulo $p$. Alice sends $A$ to Bob. Bob chooses an integer $b$ and calculates $B = g^b$ modulo $p$. Bob sends $B$ to Bob.

title: Definition:Diffie-Hellman-Merkle Key Exchange/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Diffie-Hellman-Merkle Key Exchange == The Diffie-Hellman-Merkle key exchange was invented by , and in $1976$.

title: Definition:Diffuse Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. The measure $\mu$ is said to be diffuse there are no $\mu$-atoms.

title: Definition:Diffuse Measure/Also known as
snippet: == Diffuse Measure: Also known as == A diffuse measure is also known as: a continuous measure a non-atomic measure.

title: Definition:Digamma Function
snippet: The digamma function, $\psi$, is defined, for $z \in \C \setminus \Z_{\le 0}$, by the logarithmic derivative of the gamma function: $\map \psi z = \dfrac {\map {\Gamma'} z} {\map \Gamma z}$ where $\Gamma$ is the gamma function, and $\Gamma'$ denotes its derivative.

title: Definition:Digamma Function/Also known as
snippet: == Digamma Function: Also known as == The digamma function is also known as the psi function.

title: Definition:Digit
snippet: Let $n$ be a number expressed in a particular number base, $b$ for example. Then $n$ can be expressed as: $\sqbrk {r_m r_{m - 1} \ldots r_2 r_1 r_0 . r_{-1} r_{-2} \ldots}_b$ where: $m$ is such that $b^m \le n < b^{m + 1}$; all the $r_i$ are such that $0 \le r_i < b$. Each of the $r_i$ are known as the digits of $n$ (base $b$).

title: Definition:Digit/Also known as
snippet: A digit can also be known as a figure, especially in natural language. Hence the phrase to figure (something) out, which has the overtone of calculation by arithmetic. An outdated term for a digit is cipher, also spelt cypher.

title: Definition:Digit Sum
snippet: Let $n \in \Z: n \ge 0$. The digit sum of $n$ to base $b$ is the sum of all the digits of $n$ when expressed in base $b$. That is, if: $\ds n = \sum_{k \mathop \ge 0} r_k b^k$ where $0 \le r_k < b$, then: $\ds \map {s_b} n = \sum_{k \mathop \ge 0} r_k$

title: Definition:Digital
snippet: The word digital means in numerical form.

title: Definition:Digital Computer
snippet: A digital computer is a computer whose operation is based on the binary system.

title: Definition:Digital Data
snippet: Digital data are data that are stored and represented in digital form, usually binary. Hence continuous data which has been produced from an analog source will typically be converted to digital data for transmission and processing by means of a (digital) computer.

title: Definition:Digital Device
snippet: A digital device is a device which uses numbers to present information.

title: Definition:Digital Root
snippet: Let $n \in \Z: n \ge 0$. Let $n$ be expressed in base $b$ notation. Let $n_1 = \map {s_b} n$ be the digit sum of $n$ to base $b$. Then let $n_2 = \map {s_b} {n_1}$ be the digit sum of $n_1$ to base $b$. Repeat the process, until $n_m$ has only one digit, that is, that $1 \le n_m < b$. Then $n_m$ is the digital root of $n$ to the base $b$.

title: Definition:Digital Watch
snippet: A digital watch is a small digital clock designed to be strapped to one's wrist, or kept in the pocket.

title: Definition:Digraph
snippet: A digraph is a graph each of whose edges has a direction: 310px In the above digraph, the vertices are $v_1, v_2, v_3$ and $v_4$.

title: Definition:Digraph/Also known as
snippet: == Digraph: Also known as == A digraph is also known as a directed graph. Some sources refer to a digraph as a network, but has a different definition for that.

title: Definition:Digraph/Arc
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a digraph. The arcs are the elements of $E$. Informally, an arc is a line that joins one vertex to another. If $e \in E$ is an arc joining the vertex $u$ to the vertex $v$, it is denoted by the ordered pair $\tuple {u, v}$, or just $u v$.

title: Definition:Digraph/Category-Theoretic Definition
snippet: Let $\mathbf {Set}$ be the category of sets. A digraph is an arrangement of the following form in $\mathbf {Set}$: $\begin{xy} {E} = "E", {V} = "V", "E"+/^.3em/+/r1em/;"V"+/^.3em/+/l1em/ **@{-} ?>*@{>} ?*!/_.6em/{s}, "E"+/_.3em/+/r1em/;"V"+/_.3em/+/l1em/ **@{-} ?>*@{>} ?*!/^.6em/{t}, \end{xy}$

title: Definition:Digraph/Formal Definition
snippet: 310px A directed graph or digraph $D$ is a non-empty set $V$ together with an antireflexive relation $E$ on $V$. The elements of $E$ are the arcs. Thus the above digraph can be defined as: $D = \struct {V, E}:$ $V = \set {v_1, v_2, v_3, v_4}$ $E = \set {\tuple {v_1, v_2}, \tuple {v_2, v_4}, \tuple {v_4, v_3}, \tuple {v_4, v_1}, \tuple {v_1, v_4} }$ {{mistake|$E$ is not necessarily an antireflexive relation as can be seen that $\tuple {v_4, v_1}$ and $\tuple {v_1, v_4}$ are both elements}}

title: Definition:Digraph/Simple Digraph
snippet: Let $D = \struct {V, E}$ be a digraph. If the relation $E$ in $D$ is also specifically asymmetric, then $D$ is called a simple digraph. That is, in a simple digraph there are no pairs of arcs (like there are between $v_1$ and $v_4$ in the diagram above) which go in both directions between two vertices.

title: Definition:Digraph/Symmetric Digraph
snippet: Let $D = \struct {V, E}$ be a digraph such that the relation $E$ in $D$ is symmetric. Then $D$ is called a symmetric digraph. It follows from the definition of a (simple) graph that a symmetric digraph is in fact the same thing as an undirected graph.

title: Definition:Dihedral
snippet: Geometry: Dihedral: two half-planes meeting at a common straight line. Dihedral angle: the angle contained by the straight lines drawn perpendicular to the common section at the same point, one in each of the half-planes. Group theory Dihedral group: the group of symmetries of a regular polygon.

title: Definition:Dihedral/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Dihedral == The word dihedral derives from the Ancient Greek for two sided.

title: Definition:Dihedral/Mistake
snippet: == Source Work == dihedral

title: Definition:Dihedral (Geometry)
snippet: A dihedral is a configuration in solid geometry formed by two half-planes meeting at a common straight line.

title: Definition:Dihedral (Geometry)/Angle
snippet: A dihedral angle is the angle contained by two straight lines drawn perpendicular to the common section at the same point, one in each of the two half-planes forming a dihedral.

title: Definition:Dihedral Group
snippet: The dihedral group $D_n$ of order $2 n$ is the group of symmetries of the regular $n$-gon.

title: Definition:Dihedral Group/Also denoted as
snippet: == Dihedral Group: Also known as == The dihedral group of order $2 n$ can also be found denoted as $D_{2 n}$, rather than $D_n$, so as to make the notation match the order. Beware, because this can be the source of considerable confusion.

title: Definition:Dihedral Group D3
snippet: == Example of Dihedral Group == The dihedral group $D_3$ is the symmetry group of the equilateral triangle:

title: Definition:Dihedral Group D4
snippet: == Example of Dihedral Group == The dihedral group $D_4$ is the symmetry group of the square:

title: Definition:Dihedral Group D5
snippet: == Example of Dihedral Group == The dihedral group $D_5$ is the symmetry group of the regular pentagon:

title: Definition:Dihedral Group D6
snippet: == Example of Dihedral Group == The dihedral group $D_6$ is the symmetry group of the regular hexagon:

title: Definition:Dijkstra's Algorithm
snippet: Dijkstra's algorithm is an algorithm for determining the optimum path that passes through all nodes of a network.

title: Definition:Dijkstra's Algorithm/Also known as
snippet: == Dijkstra's Algorithm: Also known as == Dijkstra's algorithm is also known as Dijkstra's method. Some sources refer to it as the shortest path algorithm.

title: Definition:Dijkstra's Algorithm/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Dijkstra's Algorithm == Dijkstra's algorithm was designed by in $1959$.

title: Definition:Dilatation
snippet: A dilatation is a mapping $T: \R^n \to \R^n$ that maps straight lines onto parallel lines. Hence a dilatation is either a translation or a central dilatation.

title: Definition:Dilatation/Also known as
snippet: == Dilatation: Also known as == A dilatation is also known as a dilation mapping, but this term is also used for a central dilatation mapping.

title: Definition:Dilation (Physics)
snippet: Dilation of a body $B$ is the increase in volume of $B$ per unit volume.

title: Definition:Dimension
snippet: Geometry: Dimension of Space Linear Algebra: Dimension (Linear Algebra) Dimensions of a Matrix, preferably referred to as its order Dimension of Hilbert Space Affine Dimension Topology: Dimension (Topology) Dimension of Locally Euclidean Space Dimension of Topological Manifold Dimension of a Riemannian Manifold Dimension of a Pseudo-Riemannian Manifold Hausdorff-Besicovitch Dimension (also known as Hausdorff Dimension} Similarity Dimension Lebesgue Covering Dimension Inductive Dimension: Small Inductive Dimension Large Inductive Dimension Representation Theory: Dimension of a Representation…

title: Definition:Dimension (Geometry)
snippet: The dimension of a (geometrical) space is the minimum number of coordinates needed to specify a point in it.

title: Definition:Dimension (Hilbert Space)
snippet: Let $H$ be a Hilbert space, and let $E$ be a basis of $H$. Then the dimension $\dim H$ of $H$ is defined as $\card E$, the cardinality of $E$.

title: Definition:Dimension (Measurement)
snippet: Every physical quantity has a dimension associated with it. No attempt is made here to provide an abstract definition of this term. Instead, it will be defined by example.

title: Definition:Dimension (Measurement)/Fundamental Dimensions
snippet: The SI-recommended fundamental dimensions are:

title: Definition:Dimension (Measurement)/Units
snippet: Compare with units of measurement. This concept of dimension is more abstract than that of units, which are standard quantities of the particular dimension in question.

title: Definition:Dimension (Representation Theory)
snippet: Let $\struct {k, +, \circ}$ be a field. Let $V$ be a vector space over $k$ of finite dimension. Let $\GL V$ be the general linear group of $V$. Let $\struct {G, \cdot}$ be a finite group. Let $\rho: G \to \GL V$ be a linear representation of $G$ on $V$. The dimension of $\rho$, written $\map \deg \rho$, is the dimension of the vector space $V$.

title: Definition:Dimension (Topology)/Also known as
snippet: == Dimension in context of Topology: Also known as == The dimension of an object, when used in this context, can also be seen described explicitly as its topological dimension. Category:Definitions/Dimension (Topology)

title: Definition:Dimension (Topology)/Locally Euclidean Space
snippet: Let $M$ be a locally Euclidean space of dimension $n$. Then the dimension of $M$ is the natural number $n$.

title: Definition:Dimension (Topology)/Topological Manifold
snippet: Let $M$ be a topological manifold of dimension $d$. Then the dimension of $M$ is the natural number $d$.

title: Definition:Dimension Theory
snippet: Dimension theory is a branch of topology which studies dimensional invariants of topological spaces.

title: Definition:Dimension of Affine Subspace of Vector Space
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $X$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $U \subseteq X$ be a vector subspace of $X$. Let $x \in X$. We define the dimension of the affine subspace $x + U$ by: $\map \dim {x + U} = \dim U$

title: Definition:Dimension of Linear Representation/Also known as
snippet: == Dimension of Linear Representation: Also known as == The dimension of a linear representation also known as its degree.

title: Definition:Dimension of Module
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $G$ be a unitary $R$-module which has a basis of $n$ elements. Then $G$ is said to have a dimension of $n$ or to be $n$-dimensional.

title: Definition:Dimension of Module/Finite
snippet: Let $G$ be a unitary module which is $n$-dimensional for some $n \in \N_{>0}$. Then $G$ is finite dimensional.

title: Definition:Dimension of Module/Symbol
snippet: == Dimension of Module: Symbol == The dimension of a unitary module $M$ is denoted on as $\map \dim M$.

title: Definition:Dimension of Simplicial Complex
snippet: Let $K$ be a simplicial complex. The dimension of $K$ is the dimension of the simplex in $K$ of the highest dimension.

title: Definition:Dimension of Vector Space
snippet: Let $K$ be a division ring. Let $V$ be a vector space over $K$.

title: Definition:Dimension of Vector Space/Definition 1
snippet: Let $K$ be a division ring. Let $V$ be a vector space over $K$. The dimension of $V$ is the cardinality of an arbitrary basis for $V$.

title: Definition:Dimension of Vector Space/Definition 2
snippet: Let $K$ be a division ring. Let $V$ be a vector space over $K$. The dimension of $V$ is the maximum cardinality of a linearly independent subset of $V$.

title: Definition:Dimension of Vector Space/Finite
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space which is $n$-dimensional for some $n \in \N_{\ge 0}$. Then $V$ is finite dimensional.

title: Definition:Dimension of Vector Space/Vector
snippet: Informally, an element of an $n$-dimensional vector space is often referred to as an $n$-dimensional vector. It must be understood that this is no more than a convenient shorthand. It is not the vector which possesses the dimensionality, but the space in which it is embedded. Category:Definitions/Dimension of Vector Space Category:Definitions/Vectors

title: Definition:Dimensional Analysis
snippet: Dimensional analysis is the branch of applied mathematics which studies the relationships between physical quantities by identifying their fundamental dimensions and units of measurement. As such it can also be considered to be a branch of number theory.

title: Definition:Dimensional Formula
snippet: Let $P$ be a physical quantity. Let $P$ be expressed as the product of powers of one or more fundamental dimensions without any numerical values attached. This expression is known as the dimensional formula of $P$. In an equation involving physical quantities, the dimensional formula must be such that the two sides have the same dimensions.

title: Definition:Dimensions of Array/Also known as
snippet: == Dimensions of Array: Also known as == The dimensions of an array, particularly when $m = n$, are often referred to as its order. Category:Definitions/Arrays

title: Definition:Diophantine Analysis
snippet: Diophantine analysis is the branch of number theory which is concerned with the solution of Diophantine equations.

title: Definition:Diophantine Approximation
snippet: Diophantine approximation is the branch of approximation theory concerned with the approximation of real numbers by rational numbers.

title: Definition:Diophantine Equation
snippet: A Diophantine equation is an indeterminate polynomial equation that allows the variables to take integer values only. It defines an algebraic curve, algebraic surface, or more general object, and asks about the lattice points on it.

title: Definition:Diophantine Equation/Linear Diophantine Equation
snippet: A linear Diophantine equation is a Diophantine equation in which all the arguments appear to no higher than the first degree. For example: $ax + by + c = 0$ $a_1 x_1 + a_2 x_2 + \cdots + a_n x_n = b$

title: Definition:Diophantine Problem
snippet: A Diophantine problem is a system of Diophantine equations which has more unknowns than it has equations.

title: Definition:Diophantine m-Tuple
snippet: A Diophantine $m$-tuple set of $m$ positive integers such that the product of any $2$ of them plus $1$ is a square number.

title: Definition:Diophantine m-Tuple/Quadruple
snippet: A Diophantine quadruple is a Diophantine $m$-tuple where $m = 4$. That is, a Diophantine quadruple is a set of $4$ positive integers such that the product of any $2$ of them plus $1$ is a square number.

title: Definition:Diophantine m-Tuple/Quintuple
snippet: A Diophantine quintuple is a Diophantine $m$-tuple where $m = 5$. That is, a Diophantine quintuple is a set of $5$ positive integers such that the product of any $2$ of them plus $1$ is a square number.

title: Definition:Diophantine m-Tuple/Triple
snippet: A Diophantine triple is a Diophantine $m$-tuple where $m = 3$. That is, a Diophantine triple is a set of $3$ positive integers such that the product of any $2$ of them plus $1$ is a square number.

title: Definition:Dipole
snippet: Let $\phi \in \map \DD \R$ be a test function. Let $\delta \in \map {\DD'} \R$ be the Dirac delta distribution. Then for any $\phi$ the distributional derivative of $\delta$ is known as the dipole and is given by: $\ds \map {\delta'} \phi = -\map {\phi'} 0$

title: Definition:Dipper Operation
snippet: Let $m \in \N$ be a natural number. Let $n \in \N_{>0}$ be a non-zero natural number. Let $\N_{< \paren {m \mathop + n} }$ denote the initial segment of the natural numbers: $\N_{< \paren {m \mathop + n} } := \set {0, 1, \ldots, m + n - 1}$ The dipper operation $+_{m, n}$ is the binary operation on $\N_{< \paren {m \mathop + n} }$ defined as: $\forall a, b \in \N_{< \paren {m \mathop + n} }: a +_{m, n} b = \begin{cases} a + b & : a + b < m \\ a + b - k n & : a + b \ge m \end{cases}$ where $k$ is the largest integer satisfying: $m + k n \le a + b$

title: Definition:Dipper Operation/Illustration
snippet: == Illustration of Dipper Operation == 600px When the stars of the are numbered as shown, the sequence: $1, 1 +_{3, 4} 1, 1 +_{3, 4} 1 +_{3, 4} 1, \ldots$ traces out those stars in the order: first the handle: $\text{Alkaid}, \text{Mizar}, \text{Alioth}$ then: round the pan indefinitely: $\text{Megrez}, \text{Dubhe}, \text{Merak}, \text{Phecda}, \text{Megrez}, \ldots$ Hence $a +_{m, n} b$ can be interpreted as: Start at $\text{Alkaid}$ and count $a$ stars along the handle and then clockwise round the pan. Then count $b$ stars more from there.

title: Definition:Dipper Relation
snippet: Let $m \in \N$ be a natural number. Let $n \in \N_{>0}$ be a non-zero natural number. The dipper relation $\RR_{m, n}$ is the relation on $\N$ defined as: $\forall x, y \in \N: x \mathrel {\RR_{m, n} } y \iff \begin {cases} x = y \\ m \le x < y \text { and } n \divides \paren {y - x} \\ m \le y < x \text { and } n \divides \paren {x - y} \end {cases}$

title: Definition:Dipper Semigroup/Definition 2
snippet: Let $m \in \N$ be a natural number. Let $n \in \N_{>0}$ be a non-zero natural number. Let $\RR_{m, n}$ be the dipper relation on $\N$: $\forall x, y \in \N: x \mathrel {\RR_{m, n} } y \iff \begin {cases} x = y \\ m \le x < y \text { and } n \divides \paren {y - x} \\ m \le y < x \text { and } n \divides \paren {x - y} \end {cases}$ Let $\map D {m, n} := \N / \RR_{m, n}$ be the quotient set of $\N$ induced by $\RR_{m, n}$. title: Definition:Dirac Delta Distribution
snippet: Let $a \in \R^d$ be a real vector. Let $\phi \in \map \DD {\R^d}$ be a test function. Let $\delta_a \in \map {\DD'} {\R^d}$ be a Schwartz distribution. Suppose $\delta_a$ is such that: $\forall \phi \in \map \DD {\R^d} : \map {\delta_a} \phi = \map \phi a$ Then $\delta_a$ is known as the Dirac delta distribution.

title: Definition:Dirac Delta Distribution/Also denoted as
snippet: == Dirac Delta Distribution: Also denoted as == The Dirac delta distribution $\delta_a$ is also written as $\map \delta a$.

title: Definition:Dirac Delta Function/2 Dimensional
snippet: Let $\delta: \R \to \R$ denote the Dirac delta function. The $2$-dimensional form of $\delta$ is defined and denoted: $\forall x, y \in \R: \map { {}^2 \delta} {x, y} := \map \delta x \map \delta y$

title: Definition:Dirac Delta Function/Also denoted as
snippet: == Dirac Delta Function: Also denoted as == Let $c$ be a constant real number. The notation $\map {\delta_c} t$ for the Dirac delta function is often used to denote: $\map {\delta_c} t := \map \delta {t - c}$

title: Definition:Dirac Delta Function/Also known as
snippet: == Dirac Delta Function: Also known as == The Dirac delta function is less commonly rendered as Dirac's delta function. Some sources refer to it just as the delta function. It is also called the unit pulse function or unit impulse function. Some sources refer to $\map \delta x$ just as the impulse function. Some, acknowledging the fact that it is not actually a function as such, refer to it as the unit impulse.

title: Definition:Dirac Delta Function/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive real number. Consider the real function $F_\epsilon: \R \to \R$ defined as: $\map {F_\epsilon} x := \begin{cases} 0 & : x \epsilon \end{cases}$ The Dirac delta function is defined as: $\map \delta x := \ds \lim_{\epsilon \mathop \to 0} \map {F_\epsilon} x$

title: Definition:Dirac Delta Function/Warning
snippet: == Warning about Dirac Delta Function == Note that while the Dirac delta function $\map \delta x$ is usually so referred to as a function and treated as a function, it is generally considered not actually to be a function at all. Thus it is commonplace to see the following definition or derivation for the Dirac delta function: $\map \delta x := \begin {cases} \infty & : x = 0 \\ 0 & : x \ne 0 \end {cases}$ While this can be considered as acceptable in the context of certain branches of engineering or physics, its use is not endorsed on because of its lack of rigor.

title: Definition:Dirac Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $x \in X$ be any point in $X$. Then the Dirac measure at $x$, denoted $\delta_x$ is the measure defined by: $\delta_x: \Sigma \to \overline \R, \ \map {\delta_x} E := \begin{cases}0 & \text{if } x \notin E \\ 1 & \text{if } x \in E \end{cases}$ where $\overline \R$ denotes the extended set of real numbers. That $\delta_x$ actually is a measure is shown on Dirac Measure is Measure. In fact, Dirac measure is a probability measure.

title: Definition:Dirac Notation
snippet: Dirac notation is used to highlight the difference between a wave function being thought of as a vector or a functional.

title: Definition:Dirac Notation/Also known as
snippet: == Dirac Notation: Also known as == Dirac notation is also known as bra and ket notation.

title: Definition:Dirac Notation/Bra
snippet: Bra is a functional: $\map {\mathrm {bra} } \phi = \bra \phi$ in the dual space, acting on states $\psi$ by: $\bra \phi : \psi \to \braket \phi \psi$ where $\braket \phi \psi$ denotes the inner product. A ket can be converted to a bra with the adjoint transformation: $\bra \phi = {\ket \phi}^*$ Or, if the ket is a column vector, then the corresponding bra is created with the Hermitian conjugate: $\bra \phi = {\ket \phi}^\dagger$

title: Definition:Dirac Notation/Inner Product
snippet: The inner product of two kets $\ket a$ and $\ket b$ is written as: $\braket a b$ where the bra $\bra a$ is the dual of $\ket a$. In contrast with the standard inner product, it is linear in the second argument, the ket $\ket b$.

title: Definition:Dirac Notation/Ket
snippet: A Ket is a vector in a normed vector space and represents a quantum state. It is written as: $\ket \psi$ where $\psi$ denotes a wave function.

title: Definition:Dirac Notation/Ket/Abuse of Notation
snippet: == Ket: Abuse of Notation == The following notation shortcuts are in common use by physicists.

title: Definition:Dirac Notation/Outer Product
snippet: The outer product of two kets $\ket \psi$ and $\ket \phi$ is written as: $\ket \psi \bra \phi$ This differs from the standard outer product by using the Hermitian conjugate instead of the transpose in the second argument.

title: Definition:Dirac Notation/Tensor Product
snippet: The tensor product of two kets (possibly from different normed vector spaces) $\ket \alpha$ and $\ket \beta$ represents the quantum state of a 2-part composite system. It is written as: $\ket \alpha \ket \beta$

title: Definition:Direct Congruence/Also known as
snippet: == Direct Congruence: Also known as == Two $3$-dimensional figures which are directly congruent are also said to be identical.

title: Definition:Direct Image Mapping
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $\powerset S$ and $\powerset T$ be their power sets.

title: Definition:Direct Image Mapping/Mapping
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $\powerset S$ and $\powerset T$ be their power sets. Let $f \subseteq S \times T$ be a mapping from $S$ to $T$. The direct image mapping of $f$ is the mapping $f^\to: \powerset S \to \powerset T$ that sends a subset $X \subseteq S$ to its image under $f$: $\forall X \in \powerset S: \map {f^\to} X = \begin {cases} \set {t \in T: \exists s \in X: \map f s = t} & : X \ne \O \\ \O & : X = \O \end {cases}$

title: Definition:Direct Image Mapping/Relation
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $\powerset S$ and $\powerset T$ be their power sets. Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation on $S \times T$. The direct image mapping of $\RR$ is the mapping $\RR^\to: \powerset S \to \powerset T$ that sends a subset $X \subseteq S$ to its image under $\RR$: $\forall X \in \powerset S: \map {\RR^\to} X = \begin {cases} \set {t \in T: \exists s \in X: \tuple {s, t} \in \RR} & : X \ne \O \\ \O & : X = \O \end {cases}$

title: Definition:Direct Image of Presheaf
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a category. Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $f : T_1 \to T_2$ be continuous. Let $\FF$ be a $\mathbf C$-valued presheaf on $T_1$.

title: Definition:Direct Image of Presheaf/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a category. Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $f: T_1 \to T_2$ be continuous. Let $\FF$ be a $\mathbf C$-valued presheaf on $T_1$. The direct image of $\FF$ via $f$ is the $\mathbf C$-valued presheaf $f_* \FF$ on $T_2$ with: $\map {f_* \FF} V = \map \FF {f^{-1} \sqbrk V}$ for all open set $V$ of $T_2$ Restrictions $\operatorname{res}^U_V = \operatorname{res}^{f^{-1} \sqbrk U}_{f^{-1} \sqbrk V}$

title: Definition:Direct Image of Presheaf/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a category. Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $f : T_1 \to T_2$ be continuous. Let $\FF$ be a $\mathbf C$-valued presheaf on $T_1$. The direct image of $\FF$ via $f$ is the $\mathbf C$-valued presheaf $f_*\FF$ that is the composition $\FF \circ \map {\operatorname{Open} } f$, where $\operatorname{Open}$ is the open subsets functor.

title: Definition:Direct Image of Sheaf
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space. Let $\mathbf C$ be a category. Let $\FF$ be a $\mathbf C$-valued sheaf on $X$. The direct image of $\FF$ is the direct image of the presheaf $\FF$.

title: Definition:Direct Iteration
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an equation of the form: $x = \map \phi x$ where $x$ ranges over the real numbers. Direct iteration is a process whose aim is to find a root of $\EE$. It consists of a sequence $\sequence {x_n}$ created by an iteration of the form: $x_{n + 1} = \map \phi {x_n}$ for $n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$, where $x_0$ is chosen as a first approximation to the desired root.

title: Definition:Direct Iteration/Also known as
snippet: == Direct Iteration: Also known as == Direct iteration is also known as fixed-point iteration.

title: Definition:Direct Limit
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a category. Let $I$ be a directed ordered set. Let $\mathbf I$ be the order category of $I$. Let $D : \mathbf I \to \mathbf C$ be a diagram. The direct limit of $D$ is the colimit of the diagram $D$.

title: Definition:Direct Limit of Sequence of Groups/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\N$ be the order category on the natural numbers. Let $\mathbf{Grp}$ be the category of groups. Let $G: \N \to \mathbf{Grp}$ be an $\N$-diagram in $\mathbf{Grp}$. A direct limit for $G$ is a colimit ${\varinjlim \,}_n \, G_n$, and is denoted $G_\infty$.

title: Definition:Direct Product of Group Homomorphisms
snippet: Let $G, H_1$ and $H_2$ be groups. Let $f_1: G \to H_1$ and $f_2: G \to H_2$ be group homomorphisms. Then $f_1 \times f_2: G \to H_1 \times H_2$, defined as: $\forall g \in G: \map{\paren {f_1 \times f_2} } g = \tuple {\map {f_1} g, \map {f_2} g}$ is called the direct product of $f_1$ and $f_2$.

title: Definition:Direct Product of Vector Spaces
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $V, W$ be $K$-vector spaces. The direct product of $V$ and $W$ is their module direct product.

title: Definition:Direct Product of Vector Spaces/Finite Case
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $V_1, V_2, \ldots, V_n$ be $K$-vector spaces. Let: $\ds V = \prod_{k \mathop = 1}^n V_k$ be their cartesian product. Let: $+$ be the operation induced on $V$ by the operations $+_1, +_2, \ldots, +_n$ on $V_1, V_2, \ldots, V_n$ $\circ$ be defined as $\lambda \circ \tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} := \tuple {\lambda \circ x_1, \lambda \circ x_2, \ldots, \lambda \circ x_n}$ $\struct {V, +, \circ}_K$ is called the direct product of $V_1, \ldots, V_n$.

title: Definition:Direct Product of Vector Spaces/General Case
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $\family {V_i, +_i, \circ_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a family of $K$-vector spaces. The (external) direct product of $\family {V_i, +_i, \circ_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ is their module direct product. Category:Definitions/Examples of Vector Spaces Category:Definitions/Direct Products

title: Definition:Direct Proof
snippet: A direct proof is an argument form which establishes the truth of a conclusion by assuming that the premises are true and demonstrating that the conclusion is necessarily true as a consequence.

title: Definition:Direct Sum of Bounded Linear Operators on Hilbert Space
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\sequence {\family {\HH_i, \innerprod \cdot \cdot_i} }_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a $I$-indexed family of Hilbert spaces over $\GF$. For each $i \in I$, let $T_i : \HH_i \to \HH_i$ be a bounded linear operator. Suppose that: $\ds \sup_{i \mathop \in I} \norm {T_i}_{\map B {\HH_i} } < \infty$ where $\norm {\, \cdot \,}_{\map B {\HH_i} }$ is the norm of a bounded linear operator on $\HH_i$.

title: Definition:Direct Sum of Densely-Defined Linear Operators

Let $\tuple {\HH, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be the Hilbert space direct sum of $\family {\tuple {\HH_n, \innerprod \cdot \cdot_n} }_{n \mathop \in \N}$. For each $n \in \N$, let $\tuple {\map D {T_n}, T_n}$ be a densely-defined linear operator.

title: Definition:Direct Sum of Groups
snippet: Let $I$ be a indexing set. Let $\family {G_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a family of groups. The direct sum of $\family {G_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ is the subgroup of their direct product consisting of mappings of finite support.

title: Definition:Direct Sum of Module Homomorphisms
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $M, N, P, Q$ be $R$-modules. Let $M\oplus N$ and $P\oplus Q$ be their direct sum. Let $f: M \to P$ and $g : N \to Q$ be module homomorphisms. The direct sum of $f$ and $g$ is the module homomorphism $f \oplus g : M \oplus N \to P \oplus Q$ defined as: $\map {\paren {f \oplus g} } {m, n} = \tuple {\map f m, \map g n}$

title: Definition:Directed Angle
snippet: Let $\LL_1$ and $\LL_2$ be two lines which intersect at a point $\PP$. The directed angle from $\LL_1$ to $\LL_2$ is defined as the amount of rotation about $\PP$ required to bring $\LL_1$ into correspondence with $\LL_2$. If the rotation about $\PP$ is anticlockwise, then the directed angle is positive in sign. If the rotation about $\PP$ is clockwise, then the directed angle is negative in sign.
