snippet: Given a digraph $G$ with $n$ vertices, to determine whether $G$ has a Hamilton cycle.

title: Definition:Directed Hamilton Cycle Problem/Function Version
snippet: Given a digraph $G$ with $n$ vertices, to find a Hamilton cycle in $G$.

title: Definition:Directed Line
snippet: A directed line is a line along which one direction is specified as being positive, while the opposite direction is specified as being negative.

title: Definition:Directed Line Segment
snippet: A directed line segment is a line segment endowed with the additional property of direction. It is often used in the context of applied mathematics to represent a vector quantity.

title: Definition:Directed Line Segment/Also known as
snippet: == Directed Line Segment: Also known as == A directed line segment can also be seen referred to as an oriented line segment. Some sources use the term directed segment.

title: Definition:Directed Number
snippet: A directed number is a number which has a positive sign or a negative sign. This is often used to indicate direction on a given directed line.

title: Definition:Directed Number/Also known as
snippet: == Directed Number: Also known as == A directed number is also known as a signed number.

title: Definition:Directed Ordering
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set. Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be such that: $\forall x, y \in S: \exists z \in S: x \preccurlyeq z$ and $y \preccurlyeq z$ That is, such that every pair of elements of $S$ has an upper bound in $S$. Then $\preccurlyeq$ is a directed ordering.

title: Definition:Directed Preordering
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \precsim}$ be a preordered set. Then $\struct {S, \precsim}$ is a directed preordering every pair of elements of $S$ has an upper bound in $S$: $\forall x, y \in S: \exists z \in S: x \precsim z$ and $y \precsim z$

title: Definition:Directed Ratio
snippet: A directed ratio is a ratio of directed numbers.

title: Definition:Directed Smooth Curve
snippet: Let $\R^n$ be a real cartesian space of $n$ dimensions. Let $\rho: \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right] \to \R^n$ be a smooth path in $\R^n$. The directed smooth curve with parameterization $\rho$ is defined as an equivalence class of smooth paths as follows: A smooth path $\sigma: \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right] \to \R^n$ belongs to the equivalence class of $\rho$ : there exists a bijective differentiable strictly increasing real function: $\phi: \left[{c \,.\,.\, d}\right] \to \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right]$ such that $\sigma = \rho \circ \phi$.

title: Definition:Directed Smooth Curve/Complex Plane
snippet: Let $\gamma : \closedint a b \to \C$ be a smooth path in $\C$. The directed smooth curve with parameterization $\gamma$ is defined as an equivalence class of smooth paths as follows: A smooth path $\sigma: \closedint c d \to \C$ belongs to the equivalence class of $\gamma$ : there exists a bijective differentiable strictly increasing real function: $\phi: \closedint c d \to \closedint a b$ such that $\sigma = \gamma \circ \phi$. It follows from Directed Smooth Curve Relation is Equivalence and Fundamental Theorem on Equivalence Relations that this does in fact define an equivalence class.

title: Definition:Directed Smooth Curve/Endpoints
snippet: Let $\R^n$ be a real cartesian space of $n$ dimensions. Let $C$ be a directed smooth curve in $\R^n$. Let $C$ be parameterized by a smooth path $\rho: \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right] \to \C$. Then: $\rho \left({a}\right)$ is the start point of $C$ $\rho \left({b}\right)$ is the end point of $C$. Collectively, $\rho \left({a}\right)$ and $\rho \left({b}\right)$ are known as the endpoints of $\rho$.

title: Definition:Directed Smooth Curve/Endpoints/Complex Plane
snippet: Let $C$ be a directed smooth curve in the complex plane $\C$. Let $C$ be parameterized by a smooth path $\gamma: \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right] \to \C$. Then: $\gamma \left({a}\right)$ is the start point of $C$ $\gamma \left({b}\right)$ is the end point of $C$. Collectively, $\gamma \left({a}\right)$ and $\gamma \left({b}\right)$ are known as the endpoints of $\rho$.

title: Definition:Directed Smooth Curve/Parameterization
snippet: Let $\R^n$ be a real cartesian space of $n$ dimensions. Let $C$ be a directed smooth curve in $\R^n$. Let $\rho: \closedint a b \to \C$ be a smooth path in $\R^n$. Then $\rho$ is a parameterization of $C$ $\rho$ is an element of the equivalence class that constitutes $C$.

title: Definition:Directed Smooth Curve/Parameterization/Complex Plane
snippet: Let $C$ be a directed smooth curve in the complex plane $\C$. Let $\gamma: \closedint a b \to \C$ be a smooth path in $\C$. Then $\gamma$ is a parameterization of $C$ $\gamma$ is a representative of the equivalence class that constitutes $C$.

title: Definition:Directed Smooth Curve/Parameterization/Complex Plane/Reparameterization
snippet: Let $\gamma : \closedint a b \to \C$ be a smooth path in $\C$. Let $C$ be a directed smooth curve in the complex plane $\C$ parameterized by $\gamma$. Let $\phi: \closedint c d \to \closedint a b$ be a bijective differentiable strictly increasing real function. Let $\sigma : \closedint c d \to \C$ be defined by: $\sigma = \gamma \circ \phi$ Then $\sigma$ is called a reparameterization of $C$.

title: Definition:Directed Subset
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \precsim}$ be a preordered set. Let $H$ be a non-empty subset of $S$. Then $H$ is a directed subset of $S$ : $\forall x, y \in H: \exists z \in H: x \precsim z$ and $y \precsim z$

title: Definition:Directed Suprema Inheriting
snippet: Let $L = \struct {X, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $S = \struct {Y, \precsim}$ be an ordered subset of $L$. Then $S$ inherits directed suprema for all directed subsets $A$ of $Y$: if $A$ admits a supremum in $L$, then $\sup_L A \in Y$

title: Definition:Directed Walk
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, A}$ be a digraph. A directed walk in $G$ is a finite or infinite sequence $\sequence {x_k}$ such that: $\forall k \in \N: k + 1 \in \Dom {\sequence {x_k} }: \tuple {x_k, x_{k + 1} } \in A$

title: Definition:Direction
snippet: The direction of a vector quantity or directed line segment is a measure of which way it is pointing, relative to a particular frame of reference.

title: Definition:Direction/Also known as
snippet: == Direction: Also known as == The direction of a vector quantity is also known as its orientation. However, this can be confused with its topological or graph-theoretical meanings.

title: Definition:Direction Angles
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a line embedded in a Cartesian $3$-space. The direction angles of $\LL$ are the three positive angles that $\LL$ makes with the coordinate axes. They are usually denoted $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$ for the angles made with the $x$-axis, $y$-axis and $z$-axis respectively.

title: Definition:Direction Cosines
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$ be a vector quantity embedded in a Cartesian $3$-space. Let the direction angles which $\mathbf a$ makes with the $x$-axis, $y$-axis and $z$-axis be $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$ respectively. Then the direction cosines of $\mathbf a$ are $\cos \alpha$, $\cos \beta$ and $\cos \gamma$, defined individually such that: $\cos \alpha$ is the direction cosine of $\mathbf a$ the $x$-axis $\cos \beta$ is the direction cosine of $\mathbf a$ the $y$-axis $\cos \gamma$ is the direction cosine of $\mathbf a$ the $z$-axis. 480px

title: Definition:Direction Cosines/Also presented as
snippet: == Direction Cosines: Also presented as == Some sources do not dwell on the actual angles themselves, but instead denote the direction cosines directly as $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$. While this technique results in more streamlined notation, it can result in confusion.

title: Definition:Direction Field/Mistake
snippet: == Source Work == direction fields

title: Definition:Direction Ratios
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a line embedded in a Cartesian $3$-space. Let $l$, $m$ and $n$ be the direction cosines of $\LL$ the $x$-axis, $y$-axis and $z$-axis respectively. Direction ratios of $\LL$ are the three numbers in the ratio $l : m : n$, where: {{eqn | l = \cos \alpha | r = \dfrac {\pm l} {\sqrt {l^2 + m^2 + n^2} } }} {{eqn | l = \cos \beta | r = \dfrac {\pm m} {\sqrt {l^2 + m^2 + n^2} } }} {{eqn | l = \cos \gamma | r = \dfrac {\pm n} {\sqrt {l^2 + m^2 + n^2} } }} where either $+$ or $-$ is taken throughout.

title: Definition:Direction Ratios/Also known as
snippet: == Direction Ratios: Also known as == Direction ratios are also known as direction numbers.

title: Definition:Directional Data
snippet: Directional data is data which consists of angular coordinates from a given point. It also includes data which has a periodic pattern, such as: time of day dates throughout the year and so on.

title: Definition:Directional Data/Also known as
snippet: == Directional Data: Also known as == Directional data is also known as: directional statistics angular data circular data cyclic data.

title: Definition:Directional Derivative/Definition 1
snippet: Let: $f: \R^n \to \R, \mathbf x \mapsto \map f {\mathbf x}$ be a real-valued function such that the gradient $\nabla \map f {\mathbf x}$ exists. Let $\mathbf u$ be a unit vector in $\R^n$. The directional derivative of $f$ in the direction of $\mathbf u$ is defined as: $\dfrac \partial {\partial \mathbf u} \map f {\mathbf x} = \nabla \map f {\mathbf x} \cdot \mathbf u$ where $\cdot$ denotes the dot product.

title: Definition:Directional Derivative/Definition 2
snippet: Let: $f: \mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R, \mathbf x \mapsto \map f {\mathbf x}$ be a differentiable real-valued function. Let $\mathbf u$ be a unit vector in $\mathbb R^n$. Let $s \in \mathbb R$ be a distance in the direction of $\mathbf u$. The directional derivative of $f$ in the direction of $\mathbf u$ is defined as: $\dfrac \partial {\partial \mathbf u} \map f {\mathbf x} = \dfrac \d {\d s} \map f {\mathbf x + \mathbf u s}$

title: Definition:Director Circle
snippet: Let $\KK$ be a central conic. The director circle of $\KK$ is the locus of the point of intersection of pairs of perpendicular tangents to $\KK$.

title: Definition:Directrix/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Directrix == The plural of directrix is directrices.

title: Definition:Directrix of Conchoid/Also known as
snippet: == Directrix of Conchoid: Also known as == The directrix of a conchoid is also known as its reference curve. Category:Definitions/Conchoids

title: Definition:Directrix of Ruled Surface
snippet: A directrix is a curve which defines the generators of a ruled surface.

title: Definition:Dirichlet Beta Function
snippet: The Dirichlet beta function $\beta$ is the complex function defined on the half-plane $\map \Re s > 0$ by the series: $\ds \map \beta s = \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \frac {\paren {-1}^n} {\paren {2 n + 1}^s}$

title: Definition:Dirichlet Character
snippet: Let $q \in \Z_{>1}$. Let $\paren {\Z / q \Z}$ denote the ring of integers modulo $q$. Let $G = \paren {\Z / q \Z}^\times$ be the group of units of $\paren {\Z / q \Z}$. Let $\C^\times$ be the group of units of $\C$. A Dirichlet character modulo $q$ is a group homomorphism: $\chi: G \to \C^\times$ By Reduced Residue System under Multiplication forms Abelian Group, $a + q \Z \in G$ $\map \gcd {a, q} = 1$. It is standard practice to extend $\chi$ to a function on $\Z$ by setting: $\map \chi a = \begin{cases} \map \chi {a + q \Z} & : \map \gcd {a, q} = 1 \\ 0 & : \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$

title: Definition:Dirichlet Character/Primitive Character
snippet: Let $q \in \Z_{>1}$. Let $\paren {\Z / q \Z}$ denote the ring of integers modulo $q$. Let $G = \paren {\Z / q \Z}^\times$ be the group of units of $\paren {\Z / q \Z}$. Let $\C^\times$ be the group of units of $\C$. Let $\chi_0$ be the trivial (Dirichlet) character modulo $q$. Let $q^*$ be the least divisor of $q$ such that: $\chi = \chi_0 \chi^*$ where $\chi^*$ is some character modulo $q^*$. If $q = q^*$ then $\chi$ is called primitive, otherwise $\chi$ is imprimitive. Category:Definitions/Dirichlet Characters

title: Definition:Dirichlet Conditions
snippet: Let $\alpha, \beta \in \R$ be a real numbers such that $\alpha < \beta$. Let $\map f x$ be a real function which is defined and bounded on the interval $\openint \alpha \beta$. The Dirichlet conditions on $f$ are sufficient conditions that $f$ must satisfy on $\openint \alpha \beta$ in order for: the Fourier series of $f$ at every $x$ in $\openint \alpha \beta$ to equal $\map f x$ the behaviour of a Fourier series to be determined at finite discontinuities of $f$ in $\openint \alpha \beta$: They are as follows:

title: Definition:Dirichlet Conditions/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Dirichlet Conditions ==

title: Definition:Dirichlet Convolution
snippet: Let $f, g$ be arithmetic functions.

title: Definition:Dirichlet Convolution/Definition 1
snippet: Let $f, g$ be arithmetic functions. The Dirichlet convolution of $f$ and $g$ is the arithmetic function: $\ds \map {\paren {f * g} } n = \sum_{d \mathop \divides n} \map f d \map g {\frac n d}$ where the summation runs over the set of positive divisors $d$ of $n$.

title: Definition:Dirichlet Convolution/Definition 2
snippet: Let $f, g$ be arithmetic functions. The Dirichlet convolution of $f$ and $g$ is the arithmetic function: $\ds \map {\paren {f * g} } n = \sum_{a b \mathop = n} \map f a \map g b$ where the summation runs over all pairs of positive integers $\tuple {a, b}$ with $a b = n$.

title: Definition:Dirichlet Density
snippet: Let $\PP$ be a set of prime numbers. For $s \in \C$, let $\ds \map f s = \sum_{p \mathop \in \PP}: p^{-s}$. $S$ has Dirichlet density $\alpha$ : $\ds \lim_{s \mathop \to 1^+} \set {\frac {\map f s} {\map \ln {s - 1} } } = -\alpha$ where $1^+$ indicates a limit from above along the real line.

title: Definition:Dirichlet Eigenvalue
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a compact connected Riemannian manifold with non-empty boundary $\partial M$. Let $u \in \map {C^\infty} M : M \to \R$ be a smooth mapping on $M$ not identically equal to zero. Let $\nabla^2$ be the Laplace-Beltrami operator. Let $\lambda \in \R$ be a real number. Suppose: $\ds \nabla^2 u + \lambda u = 0$ $\valueat u {\partial M} = 0$ Then $\lambda$ is called a Dirichlet eigenvalue of $M$.

title: Definition:Dirichlet Eta Function
snippet: The Dirichlet $\eta$ (eta) function is the complex function defined on the half-plane $\map \Re s > 0$ as the series: $\ds \map \eta s = \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \paren {-1}^{n - 1} n^{-s}$

title: Definition:Dirichlet Eta Function/Also known as
snippet: == Dirichlet $\eta$ Function: Also known as == The Dirichlet $\eta$ Function is also known as the alternating $\zeta$ (zeta) function, and denoted $\map {\zeta^*} s$.

title: Definition:Dirichlet Function
snippet: Let $I$ be a real interval. A Dirichlet function $D: I \to \R$ is a real function defined as: $\forall x \in I: \map D x = \begin {cases} c & : x \in \Q \\ d & : x \notin \Q \end {cases}$ for $c, d \in \R$ such that $c \ne d$. The canonical example of this has: $c = 1$ and $d = 0$ $I = \R$.

title: Definition:Dirichlet Inverse of Arithmetic Function
snippet: Let $f : \N \to \C$ be an arithmetic function. Let $\varepsilon$ be the identity arithmetic function. A Dirichlet inverse of $f$ is an arithmetic function $g$ such that $g*f = \varepsilon$, where $*$ denotes Dirichlet convolution. That is, an inverse of $f$ in the ring of arithmetic functions.

title: Definition:Dirichlet L-function
snippet: Let $q \in \Z_{>1}$ be a strictly positive integer. Let $\chi : \Z \to \C$ be a Dirichlet character modulo $q$. A Dirichlet $L$-function (associated to $\chi$) is a Dirichlet series: $\ds \map L {s, \chi} = \sum_{n \mathop \ge 1} \map \chi n n^{-s}$ for all $s \in \C$ such that the sum converges.

title: Definition:Dirichlet Problem
snippet: A Dirichlet problem is a problem involving the solution to a partial differential equation inside a region which meets specified values on the boundary.

title: Definition:Dirichlet Problem/Boundary Condition
snippet: The boundary conditions on the boundary of a region subject to a Dirichlet problem are specifically referred to as Dirichlet boundary conditions.

title: Definition:Dirichlet Problem/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Dirichlet Problem == The Dirichlet problem was originally defined as a problem concerning solutions to the Laplace equation. It is only in more recent times it has come to be applied to partial differential equations in general.

title: Definition:Dirichlet Series
snippet: Let $a_n: \N \to \C$ be an arithmetic function. Its Dirichlet series is a complex function $f: \C \to \C$ defined by a series: $\ds \map f s = \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n n^{-s}$ which is defined at the points where it converges.

title: Definition:Dirichlet Series/Also known as
snippet: == Dirichlet Series: Also known as == A Dirichlet series is also known as an ordinary Dirichlet series to distinguish it from a general Dirichlet series. Some sources use the term Dirichlet $L$-series. Some treatments of this subject use the possessive style: Dirichlet's series.

title: Definition:Dirichlet Series/Notation
snippet: == Dirichlet Series: Notation == In the treatment of Dirichlet series (both ordinary and general), it is a historical convention that the variable $s$ is written $s = \sigma + i t$ with $\sigma, t \in \R$. This, however, is not universal. Category:Definitions/Dirichlet Series

title: Definition:Discharged Assumption
snippet: The context of this definition is in the process of deducing the validity of sequents using logical inference in the framework of natural deduction. Assumptions that are made during the course of using certain proof rules remain in force only so long as the use of those rules requires them. Once the appropriate rules have been completed, these are known as discharged assumptions, and are not included in the pool of assumptions on which the conclusion of the rule depends.

title: Definition:Discharged Assumption/Undischarged
snippet: The context of this definition is in the process of deducing the validity of sequents using logical inference in the framework of natural deduction. An undischarged assumption is an assumption made during the course of a tableau proof of natural deduction which has not been discharged.

snippet: Topology: Disconnected (Topology) Graph Theory: Disconnected Graph

title: Definition:Disconnected (Topology)/Points
snippet: Let $T = \left({S, \tau}\right)$ be a topological space. Let $a, b \in S$. Then $a$ and $b$ are disconnected (in $T$) they are not connected (in $T$). Category:Definitions/Disconnected Spaces

title: Definition:Disconnected (Topology)/Set
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a non-empty subset of $S$.

title: Definition:Disconnected Set/Definition 1
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a non-empty subset of $S$. $H$ is a disconnected set of $T$ it is not a connected set of $T$.

title: Definition:Disconnected Set/Definition 2
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a non-empty subset of $S$. $H$ is a disconnected set of $T$ there exist open sets $U$ and $V$ of $T$ such that all of the following hold: $H \subseteq U \cup V$ $H \cap U \cap V = \O$ $U \cap H \ne \O$ $V \cap H \ne \O$

title: Definition:Disconnected Set/Definition 3
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a non-empty subset of $S$. $H$ is a disconnected set of $T$ there exist non-empty subsets $U$ and $V$ of $H$ such that all of the following hold: $H = U \cup V$ no limit point of $U$ is an element of $V$ no limit point of $V$ is an element of $U$.

title: Definition:Disconnected Space/Definition 1
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is disconnected $T$ is not connected.

title: Definition:Disconnected Space/Definition 2
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is disconnected there exist non-empty open sets $U, V \in \tau$ such that: That is, if there exists a partition of $S$ into open sets of $T$.

title: Definition:Discontinuity
snippet: Let $T_1$ and $T_2$ be topological spaces. Let $f: T_1 \to T_2$ be a mapping from $T_1$ to $T_2$. Let $D \in T_1$ be an element of $T_1$ such that $f$ is discontinuous at $D$. Then $D$ is called a discontinuity (on $f$).

title: Definition:Discontinuity/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Discontinuity == The word discontinuity, as well as meaning an element of the domain at which a mapping is discontinuous, can also be used in the abstract sense as meaning the property of being discontinuous.

title: Definition:Discontinuity (Real Analysis)
snippet: A discontinuity is an element $D$ in the domain of a real function $f$ at which $f$ is discontinuous.

title: Definition:Discontinuity (Real Analysis)/Finite
snippet: Let $X \subseteq \R$ be a subset of the real numbers. Let $f: X \to \R$ be a real function. Let $f$ be discontinuous at $c \in X$. $f$ is a finite discontinuity on $f$ $\map f c$ is finite.

title: Definition:Discontinuity (Real Analysis)/First Kind
snippet: Let $X$ be an open subset of $\R$. Let $f: X \to Y$ be a real function. Let $f$ be discontinuous at some point $c \in X$.

title: Definition:Discontinuity (Real Analysis)/Infinite
snippet: Let $X \subseteq \R$ be a subset of the real numbers. Let $f: X \to \R$ be a real function. Let $f$ be discontinuous at $c \in X$. $f$ is an infinite discontinuity on $f$ $\size {\map f x}$ becomes arbitrarily large as $\size {x - c}$ becomes arbitrarily small.

title: Definition:Discontinuity (Real Analysis)/Jump
snippet: Let $X$ be an open subset of $\R$. Let $f: X \to Y$ be a real function. Let $f$ be discontinuous at some point $c \in X$. Then $c$ is called a jump discontinuity of $f$ : $\ds \lim_{x \mathop \to c^-} \map f x$ and $\ds \lim_{x \mathop \to c^+} \map f x$ exist and are not equal where $\ds \lim_{x \mathop \to c^-} \map f x$ and $\ds \lim_{x \mathop \to c^+} \map f x$ denote the limit from the left and limit from the right at $c$ respectively. Note that $\map f c$ may equal either of these limits, or neither, or may not even be defined.

title: Definition:Discontinuity (Real Analysis)/Jump/Jump
snippet: Let $X$ be an open subset of $\R$. Let $f: X \to Y$ be a real function. Let $f$ be discontinuous at some point $c \in X$ such that $c$ is a jump discontinuity of $f$. The jump at $c$ is defined as: $\ds \lim_{x \mathop \to c^+} \map f x - \lim_{x \mathop \to c^-} \map f x$

title: Definition:Discontinuity (Real Analysis)/Non-Removable
snippet: Let $A \subseteq \R$ be a subset of the real numbers. Let $f: A \to \R$ be a real function. Let $f$ be discontinuous at $a\in A$. The point $a$ is a non-removable discontinuity of $f$ it is not a removable discontinuity.

title: Definition:Discontinuity (Real Analysis)/Removable
snippet: Let $X \subseteq \R$ be a subset of the real numbers. Let $f: X \to \R$ be a real function. Let $f$ be discontinuous at $c \in X$.

title: Definition:Discontinuity (Real Analysis)/Removable/Definition 1
snippet: Let $X \subseteq \R$ be a subset of the real numbers. Let $f: X \to \R$ be a real function. Let $f$ be discontinuous at $c \in X$. The point $c$ is a removable discontinuity of $f$ the limit $\ds \lim_{x \mathop \to c} \map f x$ exists.

title: Definition:Discontinuity (Real Analysis)/Removable/Definition 2
snippet: Let $X \subseteq \R$ be a subset of the real numbers. Let $f: X \to \R$ be a real function. Let $f$ be discontinuous at $c \in X$. The point $c$ is a removable discontinuity of $f$ there exists $b \in \R$ such that the function $f_b$ defined by: $\map {f_b} x = \begin {cases} \map f x &: x \ne c \\ b &: x = c \end {cases}$ is continuous at $c$.

title: Definition:Discontinuity of the First Kind/Also known as
snippet: == Discontinuity of the First Kind: Also known as == A discontinuity of the first kind is also known as a simple discontinuity. Some authors define a discontinuity of the first kind and a jump discontinuity to be the same thing. Some other authors allow removable discontinuities to be a subset of jump discontinuities.

title: Definition:Discontinuity of the First Kind/Definition 1
snippet: Let $X$ be an open subset of $\R$. Let $f: X \to Y$ be a real function. Let $f$ be discontinuous at some point $c \in X$. $c$ is known as a discontinuity of the first kind of $f$ : $\ds \lim_{x \mathop \to c^-} \map f x$ and $\ds \lim_{x \mathop \to c^+} \map f x$ exist where $\ds \lim_{x \mathop \to c^-} \map f x$ and $\ds \lim_{x \mathop \to c^+} \map f x$ denote the limit from the left and limit from the right at $c$ respectively.

title: Definition:Discontinuity of the First Kind/Definition 2
snippet: Let $X$ be an open subset of $\R$. Let $f: X \to Y$ be a real function. Let $f$ be discontinuous at some point $c \in X$. $c$ is known as a discontinuity of the first kind of $f$ either: $c$ is a jump discontinuity or: $c$ is a removable discontinuity.

title: Definition:Discontinuous
snippet: Analysis and topology: Definition:Discontinuous Mapping Definition:Discontinuous Real Function Definition:Discontinuous Real Function at Point Definition:Discontinuous at Point of Topological Space Group Theory: Definition:Properly Discontinuous Group Action

title: Definition:Discontinuous Mapping/Real Function
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function. Then $f$ is discontinuous there exists at least one $a \in \R$ at which $f$ is discontinuous.

title: Definition:Discontinuous Mapping/Real Function/Point
snippet: Let $A \subseteq \R$ be a subset of the real numbers. Let $f : A \to \R$ be a real function. Let $a\in A$. Then $f$ is discontinuous at $a$ $f$ is not continuous at $a$.

title: Definition:Discontinuous Mapping/Topological Space/Point
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct {A_1, \tau_1}$ and $T_2 = \struct {A_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $f: A_1 \to A_2$ $x \in T_1$ be a mapping from $A_1$ to $A_2$. Then by definition $f$ is continuous at $x$ if for every neighborhood $N$ of $\map f x$ there exists a neighborhood $M$ of $x$ such that $f \sqbrk M \subseteq N$. Therefore, $f$ is discontinuous at $x$ if for some neighborhood $N$ of $\map f x$ and every neighborhood $M$ of $x$: $f \sqbrk M \nsubseteq N$ The point $x$ is called a discontinuity of $f$.

title: Definition:Discount Factor/Symbol
snippet: == Discount Factor: Symbol == The symbol for a discount factor accumulated over $n$ conversion periods is $\gamma^n$.

title: Definition:Discrete/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Discrete == Be careful with the word discrete. A common homophone horror is to use the word discreet instead. However, discreet means cautious or tactful, and describes somebody who is able to keep silent for political or delicate social reasons. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Discrete (Word)
snippet: Discrete is a word used to define an object which is not continuous. That is, it takes only finite or countably infinite values.

title: Definition:Discrete Category
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a metacategory. Then $\CC$ is said to be discrete it comprises only identity morphisms. If the collection $\CC$ constitutes the objects of $\mathbf C$, then $\mathbf C$ may also be denoted $\map {\mathbf {Dis} } \CC$.

title: Definition:Discrete Category on Set
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. The discrete category on $S$ is the discrete category $\mathbf{Dis} \left({S}\right)$ with:

title: Definition:Discrete Extension of Reals
snippet: Let $\struct {\R, \tau_d}$ be the real number line with the usual (Euclidean) topology. Let $D$ be an everywhere dense subset of $\struct {\R, \tau_d}$ with an everywhere dense complement in $\R$. Let $\BB$ be the set of sets defined as: $\BB = \tau_d \cup \set {\set x: x \in D}$ Let $\tau*$ be the topology generated from $\BB$. $\tau^*$ is referred to as a discrete extension of $\R$. It is usual to focus attention on the two specific cases where $D$ is either the set of rational numbers or the set of irrational numbers:

title: Definition:Discrete Extension of Reals/Irrational
snippet: Let $\struct {\R, \tau_d}$ be the real number line with the usual (Euclidean) topology. Let $\Bbb I := \R \setminus \Q$ denote the set of irrational numbers. Let $\BB$ be the set of sets defined as: $\BB = \tau_d \cup \set {\set x: x \in \Bbb I}$ Let $\tau*$ be the topology generated from $\BB$. $\tau^*$ is referred to as the discrete irrational extension of $\R$.

title: Definition:Discrete Extension of Reals/Rational
snippet: Let $\struct {\R, \tau_d}$ be the real number line with the usual (Euclidean) topology. Let $\Q$ denote the set of rational numbers. Let $\BB$ be the set of sets defined as: $\BB = \tau_d \cup \set {\set x: x \in \Q}$ Let $\tau*$ be the topology generated from $\BB$. $\tau^*$ is referred to as the discrete rational extension of $\R$.

title: Definition:Discrete Fourier Transform
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_k}_{1 \mathop \le k \mathop \le n}$ be a finite sequence of complex numbers for some $n \in \N_{>0}$. The discrete Fourier transform of $\sequence {x_k}_{1 \mathop \le k \mathop \le n}$ is the sequence $\sequence {\hat x_k}_{1 \mathop \le k \mathop \le n}$ where: $\hat x_k = \ds \sum_{r \mathop = 1}^n x_r \map \exp {\dfrac {-2 \pi i k r} n}$

title: Definition:Discrete Fourier Transform/Also known as
snippet: == Discrete Fourier Transform: Also known as == A discrete Fourier transform is also known as a finite Fourier transform.

title: Definition:Discrete Fourier Transform/Inverse
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_k}_{1 \mathop \le k \mathop \le n}$ be a finite sequence of complex numbers for some $n \in \N_{>0}$. Let $\sequence {\hat x_k}_{1 \mathop \le k \mathop \le n}$ be the discrete Fourier transform of $\sequence {x_k}_{1 \mathop \le k \mathop \le n}$. The inverse discrete Fourier transform of $\sequence {\hat x_k}_{1 \mathop \le k \mathop \le n}$ is: $x_k = \ds \dfrac 1 n \sum_{r \mathop = 1}^n \hat x_r \map \exp {\dfrac {2 \pi i k r} n}$

title: Definition:Discrete Geometry
snippet: Discrete geometry is a branch of geometry that studies constructive methods of discrete geometric objects.

title: Definition:Discrete Group
snippet: A discrete group is a topological group whose topology is discrete.

title: Definition:Discrete Logarithm
snippet: Let $g$ be a generator of a cyclic group $G$. Let $y \in G$ such that: $y = g^x$ The integer $x$ is known as the discrete logarithm of $y$ to base $g$. It is usual for $G$ to be the multiplicative group of a finite field. In particular, the multiplicative group $\Z'_p$ for prime $p$ is often used as the canonical example.

title: Definition:Discrete Logarithm/Also known as
snippet: == Discrete Logarithm: Also known as == The discrete logarithm of an element of a group is also known as its index.

title: Definition:Discrete Logarithm/Symbol
snippet: The symbol to indicate that $x$ is the discrete logarithm of $y$ to base $g$ is: $x = \ind_g y$

title: Definition:Discrete Logarithm Problem
snippet: Let $g$ be a generator of a cyclic group $G$. The discrete logarithm problem is to find the discrete logarithm of a given $y \in G$ to base $g$.

title: Definition:Discrete Logarithm Problem/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Discrete Logarithm Problem == The discrete logarithm problem is known to be a "very difficult" problem to solve for a large cyclic group. Hence its usefulness in the field of cryptography, where, for example, the Diffie-Hellman-Merkle key exchange technique utilises this very difficulty.

title: Definition:Discrete Logarithm Problem/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Discrete Logarithm Problem == The discrete logarithm problem is so called because its solution is equivalent to the problem of solving $y = e^x$ where $x$ and $y$ are real numbers and whose solution is $x = \ln y$.

title: Definition:Discrete Mathematics
snippet: Discrete mathematics is the branch of mathematics which studies mathematical structures that are discrete rather than continuous. Is is usually applied to areas of mathematics such as combinatorics and graph theory. Computer science has applications of discrete mathematics on account of the discrete nature of computer states.

title: Definition:Discrete Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Then $\mu$ is said to be a discrete measure it is a series of Dirac measures. That is, there exist: a sequence $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ in $X$ and: a sequence $\sequence {\lambda_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ in $\R$ such that: $(1):\quad \forall E \in \Sigma: \map \mu E = \ds \sum_{n \mathop \in \N} \lambda_n \, \map {\delta_{x_n} } E$ where $\delta_{x_n}$ denotes the Dirac measure at $x_n$. By Series of Measures is Measure, defining $\mu$ by $(1)$ yields a measure.

title: Definition:Discrete Probability Distribution
snippet: A discrete probability distribution is a probability distribution of a discrete random variable.

title: Definition:Discrete Probability Distribution/Also known as
snippet: == Discrete Probability Distribution: Also known as == Some sources use the term discrete distribution for discrete probability distribution.

title: Definition:Discrete Probability Measure
snippet: Let $\Omega$ be a countable set. Let $\powerset \Omega$ be its power set, regarded as a $\sigma$-algebra. Let $\paren {p_\omega}_{\omega \mathop \in \Omega} \subseteq \closedint 0 1$ be a subset of the closed unit interval in $\R$, indexed by $\Omega$. Suppose that $\ds \sum_{\omega \mathop \in \Omega} p_\omega = 1$.

title: Definition:Discrete Random Variable/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\struct {S, \Sigma'}$ be a measurable space. A discrete random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ taking values in $\struct {S, \Sigma'}$ is a mapping $X: \Omega \to S$ such that: $(1): \quad$ The image of $X$ is a countable subset of $S$ $(2): \quad$ $\forall x \in S: \set {\omega \in \Omega: \map X \omega = x} \in \Sigma$ Alternatively, the second condition can be written as: $(2): \quad$ $\forall x \in S: X^{-1} \sqbrk {\set x} \in \Sigma$ where $X^{-1} \sqbrk {\set x}$ denotes the preimage of $\set x$.

title: Definition:Discrete Random Variable/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\struct {S, \Sigma'}$ be a measurable space. Let $X$ be a random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ taking values in $\struct {S, \Sigma'}$. Then we say that $X$ is a discrete random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ taking values in $\struct {S, \Sigma'}$ : the image of $X$ is a countable subset of $\Omega'$.

title: Definition:Discrete Set
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. Then $H$ is a discrete set every point of $H$ is an isolated point of $H$.

title: Definition:Discrete Set of Subsets
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\FF$ be a set of subsets of $S$. Then $\FF$ is discrete each element of $S$ has a neighborhood which intersects at most one of the sets in $\FF$.

title: Definition:Discrete Subgroup
snippet: Let $G$ be a topological group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$. Then $H$ is called a discrete subgroup it is a discrete group for the induced topology.

title: Definition:Discrete Subgroup/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $G$ be a subgroup of the additive group of real numbers. Then $G$ is discrete : $\forall g \in G: \exists \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \openint {g - \epsilon} {g + \epsilon} \cap G = \set g$ That is, there exists a neighborhood of $g$ which contains no other elements of $G$. Category:Definitions/Subgroups Category:Definitions/Topological Groups Category:Definitions/Real Numbers

title: Definition:Discrete Time Series/Accumulation
snippet: A discrete time series can be obtained by collecting a varying quantity over a period of time. The observations are the measurements of the quantities at the end of each period.

title: Definition:Discrete Time Series/Sampling
snippet: A discrete time series can be obtained by taking observations at predetermined instants from a comtinuous time series of measurements of the process in question.

title: Definition:Discrete Topology
snippet: Let $S \ne \O$ be a set. Let $\tau = \powerset S$ be the power set of $S$. That is, let $\tau$ be the set of all subsets of $S$: $\tau := \set {H: H \subseteq S}$ Then $\tau$ is called the discrete topology on $S$. The topological space $\struct {S, \tau} = \struct {S, \powerset S}$ is called the discrete space on $S$, or just a discrete space.

title: Definition:Discrete Topology/Countable
snippet: Let $S$ be an infinite set. Let $\tau = \powerset S$ be the power set of $S$. That is, let $\tau$ be the set of all subsets of $S$: $\tau := \set {H: H \subseteq S}$ Let $S$ be a countably infinite set. Then $\tau = \powerset S$ is a countable discrete topology, and $\struct {S, \tau} = \struct {S, \powerset S}$ is a countable discrete space.

title: Definition:Discrete Topology/Finite
snippet: Let $S \ne \O$ be a set. Let $\tau = \powerset S$ be the power set of $S$. That is, let $\tau$ be the set of all subsets of $S$: $\tau := \set {H: H \subseteq S}$ Let $S$ be a finite set. Then $\tau = \powerset S$ is a finite discrete topology, and $\struct {S, \tau} = \struct {S, \powerset S}$ is a finite discrete space.

title: Definition:Discrete Topology/Infinite
snippet: Let $S \ne \O$ be a set. Let $\tau = \powerset S$ be the power set of $S$. That is, let $\tau$ be the set of all subsets of $S$: $\tau := \set {H: H \subseteq S}$ Let $S$ be an infinite set. Then $\tau = \powerset S$ is an infinite discrete topology, and $\struct {S, \tau} = \struct {S, \powerset S}$ is an infinite discrete space.

title: Definition:Discrete Topology/Uncountable
snippet: Let $S \ne \O$ be a set. Let $\tau = \powerset S$ be the power set of $S$. That is, let $\tau$ be the set of all subsets of $S$: $\tau := \set {H: H \subseteq S}$ Let $S$ be an uncountably infinite set. Then $\tau = \powerset S$ is an uncountable discrete topology, and $\struct {S, \tau} = \struct {S, \powerset S}$ is an uncountable discrete space.

title: Definition:Discrete Topology on Two-Point Set
snippet: == Example of Finite Discrete Space == Let $S = \set {0, 1} = 2$ be an instance of an arbitrary doubleton. Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be the topological space on $S$ where $\tau = \powerset S$ is the power set of $S$. Then $\tau$ is the discrete topology on a two-point space. The topological space $T$ itself is hence referred to as the discrete two-point space.

title: Definition:Discrete Topology on Two-Point Set/Also known as
snippet: == Discrete Topology on Two-Point Set: Also known as == The discrete topology on a two-point space is also known as: {{item||the discrete topology on $\set {0, 1}$}}. The discrete two-point space itself can also be referred to as: {{item||the discrete space on $\set {0, 1}$}}.

title: Definition:Discrete Uniform Distribution/Also defined as
snippet: == Discrete Uniform Distribution: Also defined as == The discrete uniform distribution can also be defined as: A discrete random variable $X$ has a discrete uniform distribution with parameter $n + 1$ : $\Img X = \set {0, 1, \ldots, n}$ $\map \Pr {X = k} = \dfrac 1 {n + 1}$

title: Definition:Discrete Uniform Distribution/Also known as
snippet: == Discrete Uniform Distribution: Also known as == A discrete uniform distribution is referred to in some sources as just a uniform distribution. Such sources may also refer to a continuous uniform distribution as a rectangular distribution, and so meaning is not compromised.

title: Definition:Discrete Uniform Distribution/Technical Note
snippet: == Technical Note for Discrete Uniform Distribution == {{LatexFor|for = \DiscreteUniform {n} }} When the argument is a single character, it is usual to omit the braces: \DiscreteUniform n This command is specific to . Category:Technical Notes

title: Definition:Discrete Uniformity
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. The discrete uniformity on $S$ is the uniformity $\UU$ defined as: $\UU := \set {u \subseteq S \times S: \Delta_S \subseteq u}$ that is, all subsets of the cartesian product on $S$ which contain the diagonal relation on $S$. Hence from Relation Contains Diagonal Relation iff Reflexive it can be considered as the set of all reflexive relations on $S$.

title: Definition:Discretization
snippet: Discretization is the process of approximating a continuous function by a discrete alternative.

title: Definition:Discretization/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Discretization == Discretization generally takes huge computational power to use effectively. Hence it is only in recent years, with that power now available, that such methods become practical. An example of their use is in the study of air turbulence in air flow, which cannot be treated analytically.

title: Definition:Discriminant
snippet: Polynomial Theory: Discriminant of Polynomial Abstract Algebra: Discriminant of Number Field Discriminant of Bilinear Form Discriminant of Quadratic Form Linear Algebra: Discriminant of Matrix Analytic Geometry: Discriminant of Conic Section Statistics: Discriminant Function

title: Definition:Discriminant Function
snippet: A discriminant function is a function which assigns a given individual to one of a number of populations according to the data appertaining to that individual. It is based on measurements on individuals for whom the population to which each one belongs is known. It is chosen to minimize the probabilities or costs of misclassification.

title: Definition:Discriminant of Bilinear Form
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be a field. Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb K$ of finite dimension $n>0$. Let $b : V\times V \to \mathbb K$ be a bilinear form on $V$. Let $A$ be the matrix of $b$ relative to an ordered basis of $V$. If $b$ is nondegenerate, its discriminant is the equivalence class of the determinant $\det A$ in the quotient group $\dfrac {\mathbb K^\times} {\paren {\mathbb K^\times}^2}$. If $b$ is degenerate, its discriminant is $0$.

title: Definition:Discriminant of Conic Section
snippet: Let $K$ be a conic section embedded in a Cartesian plane with the general equation: $a x^2 + 2 h x y + b y^2 + 2 g x + 2 f y + c = 0$ where $a, b, c, f, g, h \in \R$. The discriminant of $K$ is defined as the determinant calculated as: $\Delta = \begin {vmatrix} a & h & g \\ h & b & f \\ g & f & c \end {vmatrix}$

title: Definition:Discriminant of Cubic Equation/Reduced Form
snippet: Let $P$ be a cubic equation expressed in the form: $x^3 + p x^2 + q x + r = 0$ The discriminant of $P$ is given by: $D = 4 q^3 + 4 p^3 r + 27 r^3 - p^2 q^2 - 18 p q r$

title: Definition:Discriminant of Cubic Equation/Reduced Form/Also presented as
snippet: == Discriminant of Cubic Equation: Reduced Form: Also presented as == Let $P$ be a cubic equation expressed in the form: $x^3 + p x^2 + q x + r = 0$ Some sources present the discriminant of $P$ in the form: $D = p^2 q^2 + 18 p q r - 4 q^3 - 4 p^3 r - 27 r^3$ under which regime the sign of $D$ is interpreted inversely.

title: Definition:Discriminant of Polynomial/Cubic Equation
snippet: Let $P$ be the cubic equation: $a x^3 + b x^2 + c x + d = 0$ with $a \ne 0$ Let: {{eqn | l = Q | r = \dfrac {3 a c - b^2} {9 a^2} }} {{eqn | l = R | r = \dfrac {9 a b c - 27 a^2 d - 2 b^3} {54 a^3} }} The discriminant of the cubic equation is given by: $D := Q^3 + R^2$

title: Definition:Discriminant of Polynomial/Mistake
snippet: == Source Work == discriminant (of a polynomial equation)

title: Definition:Discriminant of Polynomial/Quadratic Equation
snippet: Consider the quadratic equation: $a x^2 + b x + c = 0$ The expression $b^2 - 4 a c$ is called the discriminant of the equation.

title: Definition:Discriminant of Quadratic Equation in Two Variables
snippet: Consider the quadratic equation in $2$ variables: $(1): \quad a x^2 + b y^2 + 2 h x y + 2 g x + 2 f y + c = 0$ where $x$ and $y$ are independent variables. The discriminant of $(1)$ is the expression: $a b c + 2 f g h - a f^2 - b g^2 - c h^2$

title: Definition:Discriminatory Test
snippet: In the context of statistics, a discriminatory test is a statistical test whose power is greater than some previously specified level.

title: Definition:Disjoint
snippet: A pair of properties is described as disjoint each one can't happen if the other holds.

title: Definition:Disjoint/Also known as
snippet: == Disjoint: Also known as == Objects that are disjoint are also referred to as being mutually exclusive.

title: Definition:Disjoint Events
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be events in a probability space. Then $A$ and $B$ are disjoint : $A \cap B = \O$ It follows by definition of probability measure that $A$ and $B$ are disjoint : $\map \Pr {A \cap B} = 0$ That is, two events are disjoint the probability of them both occurring in the same experiment is zero. That is, $A$ and $B$ can't happen together.

title: Definition:Disjoint Events/Also known as
snippet: == Disjoint Events: Also known as == Two disjoint events are also referred to as mutually exclusive.

title: Definition:Disjoint Permutations
snippet: Let $S_n$ denote the symmetric group on $n$ letters. Let $\pi, \rho \in S_n$ both be permutations on $S_n$. Then $\pi$ and $\rho$ are disjoint : $(1): \quad i \notin \Fix \pi \implies i \in \Fix \rho$ $(2): \quad i \notin \Fix \rho \implies i \in \Fix \pi$ That is, each element moved by $\pi$ is fixed by $\rho$ and (equivalently) each element moved by $\rho$ is fixed by $\pi$. That is, their supports are disjoint sets. We may say that: $\pi$ is disjoint from $\rho$ $\rho$ is disjoint from $\pi$ $\pi$ and $\rho$ are (mutually) disjoint.

title: Definition:Disjoint Sets
snippet: Two sets $S$ and $T$ are disjoint : $S \cap T = \O$ That is, disjoint sets are sets such that their intersection is the empty set -- they have no elements in common.

title: Definition:Disjoint Sets/Also known as
snippet: == Disjoint Sets: Also known as == Some early sources refer to disjoint sets as non-overlapping or non-intersecting. The term mutually exclusive sets can also be seen.

title: Definition:Disjoint Sets/Family
snippet: Let $I$ be an indexing set. Let $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a family of sets indexed by $I$. Then $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ is disjoint their intersection is empty: $\ds \bigcap_{i \mathop \in I} S_i = \O$

title: Definition:Disjoint Union (Probability Theory)
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a collection of pairwise disjoint sets. That is, for all sets $A, B \in \CC: A \ne B \implies A \cap B = \O$. Then the union of all sets in $\CC$ is called their disjoint union: $\ds \bigsqcup_{A \mathop \in \CC} A \equiv \bigcup_{A \mathop \in \CC} A$ That is, in this context the term disjoint union means union of sets which are pairwise disjoint.

title: Definition:Disjoint Union (Set Theory)
snippet: Let $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an $I$-indexed family of sets. The disjoint union of $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ is defined as the set: $\ds \bigsqcup_{i \mathop \in I} S_i = \bigcup_{i \mathop \in I} \set {\tuple {x, i}: x \in S_i}$ where $\bigcup$ denotes union. Each of the sets $S_i$ is canonically embedded in the disjoint union as the set: ${S_i}^* = \set {\tuple {x, i}: x \in S_i} = S_i \times \set i$ that is, the cartesian product of $S_i$ and $\set i$. For distinct $i, j \in I$, the sets ${S_i}^*$ and ${S_j}^*$ are disjoint even if $S_i$ and $S_j$ are not.

snippet: Let $I$ be a doubleton, say $I := \set {0, 1}$. Let $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an $I$-indexed family of sets. Then the disjoint union of $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ is defined as the set: {{eqn | l = \bigsqcup_{i \mathop \in I} S_i | r = \bigcup_{i \mathop \in I} \set {\tuple {x, 0}, \tuple {y, 1} : x \in S_0, y \in S_1} | c = }} {{eqn | r = \bigcup \set {S_0 \times \set 0, S_1 \times \set 1} | c = }} {{eqn | r = \paren {S_0 \times \set 0} \cup \paren {S_1 \times \set 1} | c = }}

title: Definition:Disjoint Union (Set Theory)/Also known as
snippet: == Disjoint Union: Also known as == A disjoint union in the context of set theory is also called a discriminated union. In 's original words: We denote the uniting of many aggregates $M, N, P, \ldots$, which have no common elements, into a single aggregate by $\tuple {M, N, P, \ldots}$. The elements in this aggregate are, therefore, the elements of $M$, of $N$, of $P$, $\ldots$, taken together.

title: Definition:Disjoint Union (Set Theory)/Disjoint Sets
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be disjoint sets, that is: $A \cap B = \O$ Then the disjoint union of $A$ and $B$ can be defined as: $A \sqcup B := A \cup B$ where $A \cup B$ is the (usual) set union of $A$ and $B$.

title: Definition:Disjoint Union (Set Theory)/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Disjoint Union (Set Theory) == The notations: $\ds \sum_{i \mathop \in I} S_i$ and $\ds \coprod_{i \mathop \in I} S_i$ can also be seen for the disjoint union of a family of sets. When two sets are under consideration, the notation: $A \sqcup B$ or: $A \coprod B$ are usually used. Some sources use: $A \vee B$ The notations: $A + B$ or $A \oplus B$ are also encountered sometimes. This notation reflects the fact that, from the , the cardinality of the disjoint union is the sum of the cardinalities of the terms in the family.

title: Definition:Disjunct/Also known as
snippet: == Disjunct: Also known as == A disjunct can also been seen referred to as: an alternant or alternative, particularly where a disjunction is referred to as a (logical) alternation a summand, particularly where a disjunction is referred to as a (logical) sum. Some sources refer to the members of the disjunction.

title: Definition:Disjunction
snippet: Disjunction is a binary connective written symbolically as $p \lor q$ whose behaviour is as follows: $p \lor q$ is defined as: Either $p$ is true or $q$ is true or both $p$ and $q$ are true. This is called the disjunction of $p$ and $q$. $p \lor q$ is voiced: $p$ or $q$

title: Definition:Disjunction/Also known as
snippet: == Disjunction: Also known as == The disjunction is also known as the logical sum. The symbol $\lor$ comes from the first letter of the Classical Latin vel, whose meaning is or. This usage of or, that allows the case where both disjuncts are true, is called inclusive or, or the inclusive disjunction. In natural language the term and/or is often seen, especially in the case of legal documents. Some sources refer to this as the weak or, where the strong or is used in the sense of the exclusive or. $p \lor q$ is also called the logical alternation, or just alternation, of $p$ and $q$.

title: Definition:Disjunction/Boolean Interpretation
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ be propositional formulas. Let $\lor$ denote the disjunction operator. The truth value of $\mathbf A \lor \mathbf B$ under a boolean interpretation $v$ is given by: $\map v {\mathbf A \lor \mathbf B} = \begin{cases} \F & \text{if } \map v {\mathbf A} = \map v {\mathbf B} = \F \\ \T & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$

title: Definition:Disjunction/Disjunct
snippet: Let $p \lor q$ be a compound statement whose main connective is the disjunction: $p \lor q$ $p$ is true or $q$ is true or both are true. The substatements $p$ and $q$ are known as the disjuncts.

title: Definition:Disjunction/General Definition
snippet: Let $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n$ be statements. The disjunction of $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n$ is defined as: $\ds \bigvee_{i \mathop = 1}^n \ p_i = \begin{cases} p_1 & : n = 1 \\ & \\ \ds \paren {\bigvee_{i \mathop = 1}^{n - 1} \ p_i} \lor p_n & : n > 1 \end{cases}$ That is: $\ds \bigvee_{i \mathop = 1}^n \ p_i = p_1 \lor p_2 \lor \cdots \lor p_{n - 1} \lor p_n$ In terms of the set $P = \set {p_1, \ldots, p_n}$ this can also be rendered: $\ds \bigvee P$ and is referred to as the disjunction of $P$.

title: Definition:Disjunction/Truth Table
snippet: The characteristic truth table of the logical disjunction operator $p \lor q$ is as follows: $\begin{array}{|cc||c|} \hline p & q & p \lor q \\ \hline \F & \F & \F \\ \F & \T & \T \\ \T & \F & \T \\ \T & \T & \T \\ \hline \end{array}$

title: Definition:Disjunction/Truth Table/Matrix Form
snippet: The characteristic truth table of the logical disjunction operator $p \lor q$ can be presented in matrix form as follows: $\begin{array}{c|cc} \lor & \T & \F \\ \hline \T & \T & \T \\ \F & \T & \F \\ \end{array}$

title: Definition:Disjunction/Truth Table/Number
snippet: The truth table number of the conjunction operator $p \lor q$ is as follows: Ascending order: $0111$ or $\F \T \T \T$ Descending order: $1110$ or $\T \T \T \F$

title: Definition:Disjunctive Normal Form
snippet: A propositional formula $P$ is in disjunctive normal form it consists of a disjunction of: $(1): \quad$ conjunctions of literals and/or: $(2): \quad$ literals.

title: Definition:Disjunctive Normal Form/Also defined as
Definition:Disjunctive Normal Form/Also known as
snippet: == Disjunctive Normal Form: Also known as == Disjunctive normal form is often found referred to in its abbreviated form DNF or dnf.

title: Definition:Disk
snippet: A disk in the pure geometrical context is a circular region of the plane, which may or may not include its boundary.

title: Definition:Disk/Also defined as
snippet: == Disk: Also defined as == Many sources define a disk in the context of a general metric space as the set of points within a given distance of a given point. That is, with the definition that uses for ball. It needs to be appreciated that when the metric space in question is a Euclidean plane, the two definitions coincide. In fact, when the metric space in question is the complex plane, the term complex disk is used to mean the ball with the given radius and center.

title: Definition:Disk/Also known as
snippet: == Disk: Also known as == The spelling of the word disk in British English is disc.

title: Definition:Disk/Center
snippet: The center of a disk is the center of the circle that forms its boundary.

title: Definition:Disk/Closed
snippet: A closed disk is a disk which includes its boundary.

title: Definition:Disk/Open
snippet: An open disk is a disk which does not include its boundary.

title: Definition:Disk/Radius
snippet: The radius of a disk is the radius of the circle that forms its boundary.

title: Definition:Dismal Addition
snippet: Dismal addition is an operation defined on the natural numbers as follows. Let $a, b \in \N$ be expressed in decimal notation: $\ds a = \sum_{i \mathop = 0}^n a_i 10^i = \sqbrk {a_n a_{n - 1} \ldots a_2 a_1 a_0}_{10}$ $\ds b = \sum_{j \mathop = 0}^m b_j 10^j = \sqbrk {b_m b_{m - 1} \ldots b_2 b_1 b_0}_{10}$ The dismal sum of $a$ and $b$ is defined as: $\ds a + b = \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^{\max \set {m, n} } \max \set {a_k, b_k} 10^k$ That is, for each pair of corresponding digits, the maximum is taken.

title: Definition:Dismal Arithmetic
snippet: Dismal arithmetic is just like the arithmetic you learned in school, only simpler: there are no carries, when you add digits you just take the largest, and when you multiply digits you take the smallest.

title: Definition:Dispersion
snippet: Statistics: Dispersion Topology: Dispersion point

title: Definition:Dispersion (Statistics)
snippet: Let $S$ be a sample of a population in the context of statistics. The dispersion of $S$ is a general term meaning how much the data describing the sample are spread out. The word can also be applied to a random variable. Measures of dispersion include the following:

title: Definition:Dispersion (Statistics)/Also known as
snippet: == Dispersion (Statistics): Also known as == Dispersion is also known as spread.

title: Definition:Dispersion Point
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a connected set in $T$ and let $p \in H$. Let $p \in H$ such that $H \setminus \set p$ is totally disconnected, where $\setminus$ denotes set difference. Then $p$ is a dispersion point of $H$.

title: Definition:Displacement
snippet: The (physical) displacement of a body is a measure of its position relative to a given point of reference in a particular frame of reference. Displacement is a vector quantity, so it specifies a magnitude and direction from the point of reference. In Cartesian coordinates, the direction is implicit, as it occurs as a result of the combined distances from the various axes of the frame of reference.

title: Definition:Displacement/Dimension
snippet: The dimension of displacement is length $\mathsf L$. Category:Definitions/Dimensions of Measurement Category:Definitions/Displacement

title: Definition:Displacement/Unit
snippet: The SI unit of displacement is the metre. The CGS unit of displacement is the centimetre. The FPS unit of displacement is the foot.

title: Definition:Displacement/Unit/Centimetre
snippet: == CGS unit of Displacement == The CGS unit of displacement is the centimetre $\mathrm {cm}$.

title: Definition:Displacement/Unit/Foot
snippet: == FPS unit of Displacement == The FPS unit of displacement is the foot.

title: Definition:Displacement/Unit/Metre
snippet: == SI unit of Displacement == The SI unit of displacement is the metre.

title: Definition:Dissection
snippet: A dissection is a partition of a geometric figure into two or more components.

title: Definition:Dissection/Also known as
snippet: == Dissection: Also known as == Some sources use the term divide to mean dissect, but this has the obvious confusion with the term division, which contains within it the unspoken assumption that the parts are equal.

title: Definition:Dissection/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Dissection == The word dissection is commonly misparsed and consequently mispronounced. It is surprisingly common to conflate it with bisection, which (in certain contexts) means dissection into two equal parts. Consequently it can be seen pronounced di-section, where the first syllable is sounded as the English word die. In extreme cases, it can often also be seen spelt disection, which is always incorrect.

title: Definition:Dissection Proof
snippet: A dissection proof is a proof in geometry that involves dissection of a geometric figure into multiple parts which can then be reassembled into a different geometric figure.

title: Definition:Dissipative Force
snippet: A dissipative force is a force that causes a loss of energy.

title: Definition:Distance
snippet: Complex Analysis: Distance between Complex Numbers Metric spaces: A distance function in a measure defining a metric space. The distance between sets is the minimum distance between elements in two subsets of a metric space. Metrical Geometry: The distance between two points $A$ and $B$ is the length of a line segment joining $A$ and $B$. The distance between two lines $L_1$ and $L_2$ in ordinary space is the length of the shortest line segment joining $L_1$ and $L_2$.

title: Definition:Distance-Preserving Mapping
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct {A_1, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct {A_2, d_2}$ be metric spaces, pseudometric spaces, or quasimetric spaces. Let $\phi: M_1 \to M_2$ be a mapping such that: $\forall a, b \in M_1: \map {d_1} {a, b} = \map {d_2} {\map \phi a, \map \phi b}$ Then $\phi$ is called a distance-preserving mapping.

title: Definition:Distance-Time Graph
snippet: A distance-time graph is a graph which shows: displacement on the $y$-axis plotted against: time on the $x$-axis for a particle moving in a straight line.

title: Definition:Distance/Points/Complex Numbers
snippet: Let $x, y \in \C$ be complex numbers. Let $\cmod {x - y}$ be the complex modulus of $x - y$. Then the function $d: \C^2 \to \R$: $\map d {x, y} = \cmod {x - y}$ is called the distance between $x$ and $y$.

title: Definition:Distance/Points/Normed Vector Space
snippet:
Let $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}}$ be a normed vector space. Let $x, y \in X$ . Then the function $
orm {\, \cdot \,} : X 	imes X 	o \R$: $\map d {x, y} = 
orm {x - y}$ is called the distance between $x$ and $y$.

title: Definition:Distance/Points/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $x, y \in \R$ be real numbers. Let $\size {x - y}$ be the absolute value of $x - y$. Then the function $d: \R^2 \to \R$: $\map d {x, y} = \size {x - y}$ is called the distance between $x$ and $y$.

title: Definition:Distance/Sets/Metric Spaces
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. Let $x \in A$. Let $S, T$ be subsets of $A$. The distance between $x$ and $S$ is defined and annotated $\ds \map d {x, S} = \inf_{y \mathop \in S} \paren {\map d {x, y} }$. The distance between $S$ and $T$ is defined and annotated $\ds \map d {S, T} = \inf_{\substack {x \mathop \in S \\ y \mathop \in T} } \paren {\map d {x, y} }$.

title: Definition:Distance/Sets/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $S, T$ be a subsets of the set of real numbers $\R$. Let $x \in \R$ be a real number. The distance between $x$ and $S$ is defined and annotated $\ds \map d {x, S} = \map {\inf_{y \mathop \in S} } {\map d {x, y} }$, where $\map d {x, y}$ is the distance between $x$ and $y$. The distance between $S$ and $T$ is defined and annotated $\ds \map d {S, T} = \map {\inf_{\substack {x \mathop \in S \\ y \mathop \in T} } } {\map d {x, y} }$.

title: Definition:Distance (Geometry)
snippet: Distance, in the context of geometry, is a measure of the length of a line segment between a pair of objects.

title: Definition:Distance (Graph Theory)/Directed Graph
snippet: Let $G = \tuple {V, E}$ be a digraph. Let $u, v \in V$ be vertices of $V$. The distance from $u$ to $v$ is the length of the shortest path from $u$ to $v$.

title: Definition:Distance (Graph Theory)/Undirected Graph
snippet: Let $G = \tuple {V, E}$ be an undirected graph. Let $u, v \in V$ be vertices of $V$. The distance between $u$ and $v$ is the length of the shortest path from $u$ to $v$.

title: Definition:Distance Function/Also defined as
snippet: == Distance Function: Also defined as == The term distance function is usually encountered at elementary level in the context solely of the metric space. However, as such abstract spaces proliferate with respect to the nature of its structure, it is convenient to reserve a term for the overall category into which this sort of mapping occurs. Hence the decision at to implement the term distance function for a mapping which is one of: .

title: Definition:Distance Functional
snippet:
Let $\struct {X, 
orm \cdot_X}$ be a normed vector space. Let $\struct {X^\ast, 
orm \cdot_{X^\ast} }$ be the normed dual space of $X$. Let $Y$ be a proper closed linear subspace of $X$. Let $x \in X \setminus Y$. Let: $d = \map {\operatorname {dist} } {x, Y}$ where $\map {\operatorname {dist} } {x, Y}$ denotes the distance between $x$ and $Y$. We say that $f \in X^\ast$ is a distance functional for $x$ : $(1): \quad$ $
orm f_{X^\ast} = 1$ $(2): \quad$ $\map f y = 0$ for each $y \in Y$ $(3): \quad$ $\map f x = d$.

title: Definition:Distance across Surface
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be points on a surface $\SS$. The distance from $A$ to $B$ across $S$ is defined as the length of the geodesic of $\SS$ between $A$ and $B$.

title: Definition:Distance between Lines
snippet: Let $L_1$ and $L_2$ be straight lines in space. The distance between $L_1$ and $L_2$ is defined as the length of the shortest line segment joining $L_1$ and $L_2$.

title: Definition:Distance between Parallel Lines
snippet: Let $L_1$ and $L_2$ be parallel lines. The distance between $L_1$ and $L_2$ is defined as the length of a line segment joining $L_1$ and $L_2$ that is perpendicular to both.

title: Definition:Distance between Parallel Planes
snippet: Let $P_1$ and $P_2$ be parallel planes. The distance between $P_1$ and $P_2$ is defined as the length of a line segment joining $P_1$ and $P_2$ that is perpendicular to both.

title: Definition:Distance between Point and Curve
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a curve, which may be either straight or curved. Let $P$ be a point not on $\CC$. The distance between $P$ and $\CC$ is the length of the shortest straight line segment that can be constructed between $\CC$ and $P$.

title: Definition:Distance between Point and Surface
snippet: Let $\SS$ be a surface, which may or may not be a plane. Let $P$ be a point not on $\SS$. The distance between $P$ and $\SS$ is the length of the shortest straight line segment that can be constructed between $\SS$ and $P$.

title: Definition:Distance between Points
snippet: The distance between two points $A$ and $B$ in space is defined as the length of a straight line segment that would be drawn from $A$ to $B$.

title: Definition:Distance to Nearest Integer Function
snippet: The distance to nearest integer function $\norm \cdot: \R \to \closedint 0 {\dfrac 1 2}$ is defined in the following ways:

title: Definition:Distance to Nearest Integer Function/Definition 1
snippet: The nearest integer function $\norm \cdot: \R \to \closedint 0 {\dfrac 1 2}$ is defined as: $\norm \alpha:= \min \set {\size {n - \alpha}: n \in \Z}$

title: Definition:Distance to Nearest Integer Function/Definition 2
snippet: The nearest integer function $\norm \cdot: \R \to \closedint 0 {\dfrac 1 2}$ is defined as: $\norm \alpha:= \min \set {\set \alpha, 1 - \set \alpha}$ where $\set \alpha$ is the fractional part of $\alpha$.

title: Definition:Distinct/Indistinguishable
snippet: Two objects are indistinguishable if they can not (in a particular context) be told apart from each other. So, two objects may be distinct but (at a given level) indistinguishable, like identical twins.

title: Definition:Distinct/Plural
snippet: Two objects $x$ and $y$ are distinct $x \ne y$. If $x$ and $y$ are distinct, then that means they can be distinguished, or identified as being different from each other.

title: Definition:Distinct/Plural/Pairwise Distinct
snippet: A set $S$ of objects is pairwise distinct : for each pair $\set {x, y} \subseteq S$ of elements of $S$, $x$ and $y$ are distinct. Category:Definitions/Set Theory Category:Definitions/Distinct

title: Definition:Distinct/Singular
snippet: Let $x \in S$ be an element of a set of objects $S$. Then: $x$ is distinguished from the other elements of $S$ $x$ is endowed with a property that the other elements of $S$ are specifically deemed not to possess. Such an element is identified as being distinct from the others.

title: Definition:Distinct Elements/Also defined as
snippet: == Distinct Elements: Also defined as == Some sources restrict the scope of the definition of distinct elements to mean not numerically equal.

title: Definition:Distinct Elements/Also known as
snippet: == Distinct Elements: Also known as == Distinct means the same thing as different. If $x$ and $y$ are distinct then: a distinction can be made between $x$ and $y$ Hence: $x$ is distinct from $y$ $y$ is distinct from $x$ $x$ and $y$ are distinct from each other. Category:Definitions/Distinct

title: Definition:Distinguished Element
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. A distinguished element of $S$ is an element which is distinguished in some manner, by the imposition of some property or properties on $S$, from the other elements of $S$.

title: Definition:Distributand/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Distributand == The word distributand means that which is to be distributed. The -and derives from the of Latin verbs, expressing future necessity: that which needs to be done. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Distributed Parameter
snippet: A distributed parameter is a representation of the characteristics of an electrical component which takes its physical dimensions into account.

title: Definition:Distributed Term of Categorical Syllogism
snippet: A term in a syllogism is distributed the categorical statement in which it occurs refers to the whole of the class designated by the term.

title: Definition:Distributed Term of Categorical Syllogism/Predicate
snippet: Let $\map {\mathbf \Phi} {S, P}$ be a categorical statement, expressed in abbreviated form. Let $\mathbf \Phi$ be a negative categorical statement. Then $P$ is described as being distributed.

title: Definition:Distributed Term of Categorical Syllogism/Subject
snippet: Let $\map {\mathbf \Phi} {S, P}$ be a categorical statement, expressed in abbreviated form. Let $\mathbf \Phi$ be a universal categorical statement. Then $S$ is described as being distributed.

title: Definition:Distribution-Free Method
snippet: A distribution-free method is a method of setting up a hypothesis test or confidence intervals which includes many non-parametric methods. Such a method for making inferences from a sample does not depend on the form of the underlying population probability distribution. There may be requirements such as continuity or symmetry, but no assumption is made about the specific type of distribution from which the sample is taken.

title: Definition:Distribution-Free Method/Limitations
snippet: == Distribution-Free Method: Limitations == Many distribution-free methods have analogues where the assumption is that the samples are from a given family of probability distributions. When that assumption is valid, the distribution-free tests are generally less efficient. However, a distribution-free test is often more efficient than a parametric test when those assumptions break down. A distribution-free method requires considerable computational power, which at one time was a serious problem. However, in the days of modern computer developments, this is not such a problem that it was.

title: Definition:Distribution-Free Method/Motivation
snippet: == Distribution-Free Method: Motivation == It is often the case that a distribution-free method depends only on the rankings of observations. Therefore they can be particularly useful when only the ordering of the sample data is known, but not the precise values.

title: Definition:Distribution Function of Finite Borel Measure
snippet: Let $\mu$ be a finite Borel measure on $\R$. We define the distribution function of $\mu$, $F_\mu : \R \to \R$ by: $\map {F_\mu} x = \map \mu {\hointl {-\infty} x}$ for each $x \in \R$.

title: Definition:Distribution Function of Finite Signed Borel Measure
snippet: Let $\mu$ be a finite signed Borel measure on $\R$. We define the distribution function of $\mu$, $F_\mu : \R \to \R$ by: $\map {F_\mu} x = \map \mu {\hointl {-\infty} x}$ for each $x \in \R$.

title: Definition:Distribution Space
snippet: Let $\map \DD {\R^d}$ be the test function space. Let $T: \map \DD {\R^d} \to \C$ be a Schwartz distribution. Then the set of all $T$ is called the distribution space and is denoted by $\map {\DD'} {\R^d}$.

title: Definition:Distributional Derivative
snippet: Let $\phi \in \map \DD \R$ be a test function. Let $T \in \map {\DD'} \R$ be a Schwartz distribution. The distributional derivative $\dfrac {\d T} {\d x} \in \map {\DD'} \R$ is defined by: $\map {\dfrac {\d T} {\d x} } \phi := - \map T {\dfrac {\d \phi} {\d x}}$

title: Definition:Distributional Derivative/Higher Derivatives
snippet: The $n$th distributional derivative of a Schwartz distribution $T \in \map \DD \R$ is defined as: $T^{\paren n} := \begin {cases} \paren {T^{\paren {n - 1} } }' & : n > 0 \\ T & : n = 0 \end {cases}$

title: Definition:Distributional Partial Derivative
snippet: Let $d \in \N$. Let $\phi \in \map \DD {\R^d}$ be a test function. Let $T \in \map {\DD'} {\R^d}$ be a Schwartz distribution. Let $i \in \N : 1 \le i \le d$. The distributional partial derivative $\ds \dfrac {\partial T} {\partial x_i} \in \map {\DD'} {\R^d}$ is defined by: $\map {\dfrac {\partial T} {\partial x_i}} \phi := - \map T {\dfrac {\partial \phi} {\partial x_i}}$

title: Definition:Distributive Operation
snippet: Let $S$ be a set on which is defined two binary operations, defined on all the elements of $S \times S$, which we will denote as $\circ$ and $*$. The operation $\circ$ is distributive over $*$, or distributes over $*$, : $\circ$ is right distributive over $*$ and: $\circ$ is left distributive over $*$.

title: Definition:Distributive Operation/Distributand
snippet: Let $S$ be a set on which is defined two binary operations, defined on all the elements of $S \times S$, which we will denote as $\circ$ and $*$. Let $\circ$ be distributive over $*$. Then $*$ is a distributand of $\circ$.

title: Definition:Distributive Operation/Distributor
snippet: Let $S$ be a set on which is defined two binary operations, defined on all the elements of $S \times S$, which we will denote as $\circ$ and $*$. Let $\circ$ be distributive over $*$. Then $\circ$ is a distributor of $*$. Category:Definitions/Distributive Operations

title: Definition:Distributive Operation/Left
snippet: Let $S$ be a set on which is defined two binary operations, defined on all the elements of $S \times S$, denoted here as $\circ$ and $*$. The operation $\circ$ is left distributive over the operation $*$ : $\forall a, b, c \in S: a \circ \paren {b * c} = \paren {a \circ b} * \paren {a \circ c}$

title: Definition:Distributive Operation/Right
snippet: Let $S$ be a set on which is defined two binary operations, defined on all the elements of $S \times S$, denoted here as $\circ$ and $*$. The operation $\circ$ is right distributive over the operation $*$ : $\forall a, b, c \in S: \paren {a * b} \circ c = \paren {a \circ c} * \paren {b \circ c}$

The divergence of $\mathbf V$ at a point $A$ in $R$ is defined as: {{eqn | l = \operatorname {div} \mathbf V | o = := | r = \nabla \cdot \mathbf V | c = }} {{eqn | r = \dfrac {\partial V_x} {\partial x} + \dfrac {\partial V_y} {\partial y} + \dfrac {\partial V_z} {\partial z} | c = }} where: $\nabla$ denotes the Del operator $\cdot$ denotes the dot product $V_x$, $V_y$ and $V_z$ denote the magnitudes of the components of $\mathbf V$ at $A$ in the directions of the…

Symbol ! Used by |- | align="center" | $\nabla \cdot$ or $\operatorname {div}$ | and |- | align="center" | $\operatorname {div}$ | and |}

title: Definition:Divergence Operator/Integral Form
snippet: Let $R$ be a region of space embedded in a Cartesian coordinate frame. Let $\mathbf V$ be a vector field acting over $R$. The divergence of $\mathbf V$ at a point $A$ in $R$ is defined as: $\ds \operatorname {div} \mathbf V := \lim_{\delta \tau \mathop \to 0} \dfrac {\int_S \mathbf V \cdot \d S} {\delta \tau}$ where: $S$ is the surface of a volume element $\delta \tau$ containing $A$ $\cdot$ denotes the dot product $\ds \int_S$ denotes the surface integral over $S$.

title: Definition:Divergence Operator/Physical Interpretation
snippet: Let $\mathbf V$ be a vector field acting over a region of space $R$. The divergence of $\mathbf V$ at a point $P$ is the total flux away from $P$ per unit volume. It is a scalar field.

title: Definition:Divergence Operator/Real Cartesian Space
snippet: Let $\map {\R^n} {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ denote the real Cartesian space of $n$ dimensions. Let $\tuple {\mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_2, \ldots, \mathbf e_n}$ be the standard ordered basis on $\R^n$. Let $\mathbf f = \tuple {\map {f_1} {\mathbf x}, \map {f_2} {\mathbf x}, \ldots, \map {f_n} {\mathbf x} }: \R^n \to \R^n$ be a vector-valued function on $\R^n$. Let the partial derivative of $\mathbf f$ with respect to $x_k$ exist for all $f_k$.

title: Definition:Divergence Operator/Riemannian Manifold/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold equipped with a metric $g$. Let $\mathbf X : \map {\CC^\infty} M \to \map {\CC^\infty} M$ be a smooth vector field. The divergence of $\mathbf X$ is defined as: {{eqn | l = \operatorname {div} \mathbf X | o = := | r = \nabla \cdot \mathbf X }} {{eqn | r = \star^{−1}_g \d_{\d R} \star_g \map g {\mathbf X} }} where: $\star_g$ is the Hodge star operator of $\struct {M, g}$ $\d_{\d R}$ is de Rham differential.

title: Definition:Divergence Operator/Riemannian Manifold/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be an oriented Riemannian manifold. Let $\rd V_g$ be the volume form of $\struct {M, g}$. Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$. Then the divergence of $X$, denoted by $\operatorname {div} X$, is defined by: $\paren {\operatorname {div} X} \rd V_g := \map d {X \mathop \lrcorner \rd V_g}$ where: $\lrcorner$ denotes interior multiplication $\map \rd {X \mathop \lrcorner \rd V_g}$ denotes the exterior derivative of $X \mathop \lrcorner \rd V_g$.

title: Definition:Divergent Function
snippet: A function which is not convergent is divergent.
