snippet: An improper integral of a real function $f$ is said to diverge if any of the following hold: $(1): \quad f$ is continuous on $\hointr a \to$ and the limit $\ds \lim_{b \mathop \to +\infty} \int_a^b \map f x \rd x$ does not exist $(2): \quad f$ is continuous on $\hointl \gets b$ and the limit $\ds \lim_{a \mathop \to -\infty} \int_a^b \map f x \rd x$ does not exist $(3): \quad f$ is continuous on $\hointr a b$, has an infinite discontinuity at $b$, and the limit $\ds \lim_{c \mathop \to b^-} \int_a^c \map f x \rd x$ does not exist $(4): \quad f$ is continuous on $\hointl a b$, has an infinite…

title: Definition:Divergent Improper Integral/Also known as
snippet: == Divergent Improper Integral: Also known as == A divergent improper integral is also known just as a divergent integral.

title: Definition:Divergent Product
snippet: An infinite product which is not convergent is divergent.

title: Definition:Divergent Product/Divergence to Zero
snippet: Let $\struct {\mathbb K, \norm {\,\cdot\,} }$ be a valued field. Let $\sequence {a_n}$ be a sequence of elements of $\mathbb K$. If either: there exist infinitely many $n \in \N$ with $a_n = 0$ there exists $n_0 \in \N$ with $a_n \ne 0$ for all $n > n_0$ and the sequence of partial products of $\ds \prod_{n \mathop = n_0 + 1}^\infty a_n$ converges to $0$ the product diverges to $0$, and we assign the value: $\ds \prod_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n = 0$ Category:Definitions/Divergent Products Category:Definitions/Infinite Products

title: Definition:Divergent Real Sequence
snippet: A real sequence which is not convergent is divergent.

title: Definition:Divergent Sequence
snippet: A sequence which is not convergent is divergent.

title: Definition:Divergent Series
snippet: A series which is not convergent is divergent.

title: Definition:Divide (Model Theory)
snippet: Let $T$ be a complete $\LL$-theory. Let $\mathfrak C$ be a monster model for $T$. Let $A$ be a subset of the universe of $\mathfrak C$. Let $\map \phi {\bar x, \bar b}$ be an $\LL$-formula with free variables $\bar x$ and parameters $\bar b$ from the universe of $\mathfrak C$. Let $\map {\operatorname{tp} } {\bar b / A}$ denote the type of $\bar b$ over $A$.

title: Definition:Dividend/Also known as
snippet: == Dividend: Also known as == The dividend of an expression $a / b$ is also known as the numerator of $a / b$. Category:Definitions/Dividends

title: Definition:Dividend/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Dividend == The word dividend is a Latinesque word meaning that which is to be divided. The idea is that $a$ is divided by $b$, that is, divided into $b$ parts. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Divisibility/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Divisibility == The concept of divisibility has been studied for over $3000$ years. From before the time of , the ancient Greeks were considering questions about: odd and even numbers perfect numbers amicable numbers prime numbers as well as many others. Even today, some of those questions remain unanswered.

title: Definition:Divisible Abelian Group
snippet: Let $\struct{A, +}$ be an abelian group. Let $\struct{A, +, \circ}$ be the $\Z$-module associated with $A$. Then $\struct{A, +}$ is a divisible abelian group $\struct{A, +, \circ}$ is a divisible $\Z$-module. Category:Definitions/Group Theory Category:Definitions/Abelian Groups

title: Definition:Divisible Module
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $M$ be a left $R$-module. Let $M$ be such that: for all $m \in M$ for all non zero divisors $r \in R$ there exists some $m' \in M$ such that $r m' = m$. Then $M$ is a divisible module.

title: Definition:Division
snippet: The concept of division can be defined in the following ways, according to context:

title: Definition:Division/Dividend
snippet: Let $c = a / b$ denote the division operation on two elements $a$ and $b$ of a field or a Euclidean domain. The element $a$ is the dividend of $b$.

title: Definition:Division/Divisor
snippet: Let $c = a / b$ denote the division operation on two elements $a$ and $b$ of a field or a Euclidean domain. The element $b$ is the divisor of $a$.

title: Definition:Division/Field
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +, \times}$ be a field. Let the zero of $F$ be $0_F$. The operation of division is defined as: $\forall a, b \in F \setminus \set {0_F}: a / b := a \times b^{-1}$ where $b^{-1}$ is the multiplicative inverse of $b$.

title: Definition:Division/Field/Complex Numbers
snippet: Let $\struct {\C, +, \times}$ be the field of complex numbers. The operation of division is defined on $\C$ as: $\forall a, b \in \C \setminus \set 0: \dfrac a b := a \times b^{-1}$ where $b^{-1}$ is the multiplicative inverse of $b$ in $\C$.

title: Definition:Division/Field/Rational Numbers
snippet: Let $\struct {\Q, +, \times}$ be the field of rational numbers. The operation of division is defined on $\Q$ as: $\forall a, b \in \Q \setminus \set 0: a / b := a \times b^{-1}$ where $b^{-1}$ is the multiplicative inverse of $b$ in $\Q$.

title: Definition:Division/Field/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $\struct {\R, +, \times}$ be the field of real numbers. The operation of division is defined on $\R$ as: $\forall a, b \in \R \setminus \set 0: a / b := a \times b^{-1}$ where $b^{-1}$ is the multiplicative inverse of $b$ in $\R$.

title: Definition:Division/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Division == The symbol for division that was introduced by was in fact a colon $:$ This can still be seen in the context of ratios and proportions.

title: Definition:Division/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Division == The verb form of the word division is divide. Thus to divide is to perform an act of division.

title: Definition:Division/Notation
snippet: The operation of division can be denoted as: $a / b$, which is probably the most common in the general informal context $\dfrac a b$, which is the preferred style on for division in a number field ($\Q$, $\R$, $\C$) $a : b$, which is usually used when discussing ratios $a \div b$, the obelus, familiar from grade school. adopts it as the preferred symbol for integer division.

title: Definition:Division/Standard Number Field
snippet: The concept of division over a field is usually seen in the context of the standard number fields:

title: Definition:Division Algebra
snippet: Let $\struct {A_F, \oplus}$ be an algebra over field $F$ such that $A_F$ does not consist solely of the zero vector $\mathbf 0_A$ of $A_F$.

title: Definition:Division Algebra/Also defined as
snippet: == Division Algebra: Also defined as == Some sources define division algebra as defines a unitary division algebra. That is, a division algebra is required to have an identity element.

title: Definition:Division Algebra/Also known as
snippet: == Division Algebra: Also known as == A division algebra is also known as a associative division algebra.

title: Definition:Division Algebra/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {A_F, \oplus}$ be an algebra over field $F$ such that $A_F$ does not consist solely of the zero vector $\mathbf 0_A$ of $A_F$. $\struct {A_F, \oplus}$ is a division algebra : $\forall a, b \in A_F, b \ne \mathbf 0_A: \exists_1 x \in A_F, y \in A_F: a = b \oplus x, a = y \oplus b$ That is, for every pair of elements $a, b$ of $A_F$ where $b$ is non-zero, there exists: a unique element $x$ such that $a = b \oplus x$ a unique element $y$ such that $a = y \oplus b$

title: Definition:Division Algebra/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {A_F, \oplus}$ be an algebra over field $F$ such that $A_F$ does not consist solely of the zero vector $\mathbf 0_A$ of $A_F$. $\struct {A_F, \oplus}$ is a division algebra it has no zero divisors: $\forall a, b \in A_F: a \oplus b = \mathbf 0_A \implies a = \mathbf 0_A \lor b = \mathbf 0_A$

title: Definition:Division Product
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $\struct {U_R, \circ}$ be the group of units of $\struct {R, +, \circ}$. Then we define the following notation: $\forall x \in U_R, y \in R$, we have: $\dfrac y x := y \circ \paren {x^{-1} } = \paren {x^{-1} } \circ y$ $\dfrac y x$ is a division product, and $\dfrac y x$ is voiced $y$ divided by $x$. We also write (out of space considerations) $y / x$ for $\dfrac y x$. This notation is usually used when $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ is a field.

title: Definition:Division Ring/Also known as
snippet: == Division Ring: Also known as == Some sources use division ring as the definition of a field. However, this is non-standard: it is usually specified that a field product has to be commutative. Some sources refer to a division ring as a skew field, but the latter is usually applied to a division ring whose ring product is specifically non-commutative.

title: Definition:Division Ring/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ is a division ring it fulfils the conditions of the division ring axioms, as follows:

title: Definition:Division Ring/Definition 2
snippet: A division ring is a ring with unity $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ such that: $\forall x \in R^*: \exists! x^{-1} \in R^*: x^{-1} \circ x = x \circ x^{-1} = 1_R$ where $R^*$ denotes the set of elements of $R$ without the ring zero $0_R$, that is: $R^* = R \setminus \set {0_R}$ That is, every non-zero element of $R$ has a (unique) non-zero product inverse.

title: Definition:Division Ring/Definition 3
snippet: A division ring is a ring with unity $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ such that: Every non-zero element of $R$ is a unit.

title: Definition:Division Ring/Definition 4
snippet: A division ring is a ring with unity $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ such that: $R$ has no proper elements.

title: Definition:Division Subring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. A division subring of $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ is a subset $S$ of $R$ such that $\struct {S, +_S, \circ_S}$ is a division ring.

title: Definition:Division in Ratio
snippet: Let a quantity $X$ be partitioned into parts which are in a given ratio to one another. Then $X$ is divided in (the given) ratio.

title: Definition:Division in Ratio/Straight Line
snippet: Let $A$, $B$ and $P$ be collinear points. Then: $P$ divides $AB$ in the ratio $m : n$ $AP : PB = m : n$ where $AP$ and $PB$ are directed line segments.

title: Definition:Division in Ratio/Straight Line/External
snippet: Let $A$, $B$ and $P$ be collinear points. Let $P$ not lie between $A$ and $B$. Then $P$ divides $AB$ externally in the ratio $\size m : \size n$ $AP : PB = m : n$ and the ratio $m : n$ is negative.

title: Definition:Division in Ratio/Straight Line/Internal
snippet: Let $A$, $B$ and $P$ be collinear points. Let $P$ lie between $A$ and $B$. Then $P$ divides $AB$ internally in the ratio $m : n$ $AP : PB = m : n$ and the ratio $m : n$ is positive.

title: Definition:Division of Line Segment
snippet: Let $AB$ be a line segment. A division is the construction of a point $E$ on the straight line containing $AB$ such that $AE : EB$ is a specified ratio. There are two types of division of a line segment:

title: Definition:Division over Field/Quotient
snippet: Let $c = a / b$ denote the division operation on two elements $a$ and $b$ of a field. The element $c$ is the quotient of $a$ (divided) by $b$.

title: Definition:Divisor-Finite Monoid
snippet: Let $\struct {M, *}$ be a monoid. Then $M$ is divisor-finite for all $m \in M$ the set: $\set {\tuple {x, y} \in M^2 : x*y = m}$ is finite.

title: Definition:Divisor/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Divisor == The word divisor, in the context of a division operation $a / b$, means that which divides. The idea is that $a$ is divided by $b$, that is, divided into $b$ parts. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Divisor (Algebra)/Also known as
snippet: A divisor can also be referred to as a factor. Some sources refer to a divisor of an integer as an exact divisor.

title: Definition:Divisor (Algebra)/Factorization
snippet: Let $x, y \in D$ where $\struct {D, +, \times}$ is an integral domain. Let $x$ be a divisor of $y$. Then by definition it is possible to find some $t \in D$ such that $y = t \times x$. The act of breaking down such a $y$ into the product $t \circ x$ is called factorization.

title: Definition:Divisor (Algebra)/Gaussian Integer
snippet: Let $\struct {\Z \sqbrk i, +, \times}$ be the ring of Gaussian integers. Let $x, y \in \Z \sqbrk i$. Then $x$ divides $y$ is defined as: $x \divides y \iff \exists t \in \Z \sqbrk i: y = t \times x$

title: Definition:Divisor (Algebra)/Integer
snippet: Let $\struct {\Z, +, \times}$ be the ring of integers. Let $x, y \in \Z$. Then $x$ is a divisor of $y$ is defined as: $x \divides y \iff \exists t \in \Z: y = t \times x$

title: Definition:Divisor (Algebra)/Integer/Aliquant Part
snippet: An aliquant part of an integer $n$ is a positive integer which is less than $n$ but is not a divisor of $n$.

title: Definition:Divisor (Algebra)/Integer/Aliquot Part
snippet: An aliquot part of an integer $n$ is a divisor of $n$ which is strictly not equal to $n$.

title: Definition:Divisor (Algebra)/Natural Numbers
snippet: Let $\N$ be the natural numbers. Let $n \in \N$ and $m \in \N_{>0}$. Then $m$ divides $n$ is defined as: $m \divides n \iff \exists p \in \N: m \times p = n$

title: Definition:Divisor (Algebra)/Notation
snippet: The conventional notation for $x$ is a divisor of $y$ is "$x \mid y$", but there is a growing trend to follow the notation "$x \divides y$", as espoused by etc. From : The notation '$m \mid n$' is actually much more common than '$m \divides n$' in current mathematics literature. But vertical lines are overused -- for absolute values, set delimiters, conditional probabilities, etc. -- and backward slashes are underused. Moreover, '$m \divides n$' gives an impression that $m$ is the denominator of an implied ratio. So we shall boldly let our divisibility symbol lean leftward.

title: Definition:Divisor (Algebra)/Real Number
snippet: Let $\R$ be the set of real numbers. Let $x, y \in \R$. Then $x$ divides $y$ is defined as: $x \divides y \iff \exists t \in \Z: y = t \times x$ where $\Z$ is the set of integers. That is, that $y$ is an integer multiple of $x$.

title: Definition:Divisor (Algebra)/Real Number/Part
snippet: A more old-fashioned term for divisor is part: ' The alert student will notice the circular definition: a part is defined in terms of measuring another quantity, and measurement is defined in terms of a divisor, that is, a part. Category:Definitions/Euclidean Number Theory

title: Definition:Divisor (Algebra)/Ring with Unity
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be an ring with unity whose zero is $0_R$ and whose unity is $1_R$. Let $x, y \in D$. We define the term $x$ divides $y$ in $R$ as follows: $x \mathrel {\divides_R} y \iff \exists t \in R: y = t \circ x$ When no ambiguity results, the subscript is usually dropped, and $x$ divides $y$ in $R$ is just written $x \divides y$.

title: Definition:Divisor (Algebra)/Terminology
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \times}$ be a ring. Let $x, y \in R$. Let $x \divides y$ denote that $x$ is a divisor of $y$. Then the following terminology can be used: $x$ divides $y$ $y$ is a multiple of $x$ $y$ is divisible by $x$. In the field of Euclidean geometry, in particular: $x$ measures $y$. To indicate that $x$ does not divide $y$, we write $x \nmid y$.

title: Definition:Divisor Count Function
snippet: Let $n$ be an integer such that $n \ge 1$. The divisor count function is defined on $n$ as being the total number of positive integer divisors of $n$. It is denoted on as $\sigma_0$ (the Greek letter sigma). That is: $\ds \map {\sigma_0} n = \sum_{d \mathop \divides n} 1$ where $\ds \sum_{d \mathop \divides n}$ is the sum over all divisors of $n$.

title: Definition:Divisor Count Function/Also known as
snippet: == Divisor Count Function: Also known as == Some sources refer to this as the divisor function and denote it $\map d n$. However, as this function is an instance of a more general definition of the divisor function, on the more precise name divisor count function is preferred. It is also often referred to as the $\tau$ (tau) function, but there are a number of functions with such a name. Some sources use $\nu$, but again, that also has multiple uses. Hence the unwieldy, but practical, divisor count function, which is non-standard.

title: Definition:Divisor Function
snippet: Let $\alpha \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be a non-negative integer. A divisor function is an arithmetic function of the form: $\ds \map {\sigma_\alpha} n = \sum_{m \mathop \divides n} m^\alpha$ where the summation is taken over all $m \le n$ such that $m$ divides $n$). There exist the following special cases:

title: Definition:Divisor Function/Also known as
snippet: == Divisor Function: Also known as == A divisor function is often seen referred to as a sigma ($\sigma$) function.

title: Definition:Divisor Modulo Integer/Also known as
snippet: == Divisor Modulo Integer: Also known as == A divisor modulo $m$ is also known as a factor modulo $m$.

title: Definition:Divisor Sum Function
snippet: Let $n$ be an integer such that $n \ge 1$. The divisor sum function $\map {\sigma_1} n$ is defined on $n$ as being the sum of all the positive integer divisors of $n$. That is: $\ds \map {\sigma_1} n = \sum_{d \mathop \divides n} d$ where $\ds \sum_{d \mathop \divides n}$ is the sum over all divisors of $n$.

title: Definition:Divisor Sum Function/Also defined as
snippet: == Divisor Sum Function: Also defined as == Some sources define the divisor sum function of $n$ as the aliquot sum of $n$, that is, sum of the proper divisors of $n$.

title: Definition:Divisor Sum Function/Also known as
snippet: == Divisor Sum Function: Also known as == The divisor sum function is usually referred to as the sigma function, and denoted $\map \sigma n$. However, there is more than one function which bears that name, so on we use the more explicit name divisor sum function. Some sources refer to it as just the sum function, but that lacks precision.

title: Definition:Divisor Topology
snippet: Let $S = \set {x \in \Z: x \ge 2}$ denote the set of integers greater than $1$. Let $\BB$ be the set of all sets $U_n$ defined for all $n \ge 2$ as: $U_n = \set {x \in \Z_{>0}: x \divides n}$ where $\divides$ denotes the divisor relation. Then $\BB$ is the basis for a topology $\tau$ on $S$. Then $\tau$ is referred to as the divisor topology. The topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is referred to as the divisor space.

title: Definition:Divisor of Division Operation/Also known as
snippet: == Divisor: Also known as == The divisor of an expression $a / b$ is also known as the denominator of $a / b$. Category:Definitions/Division

title: Definition:Divisor of Polynomial
snippet: Let $D$ be an integral domain. Let $D \sqbrk x$ be the polynomial ring in one variable over $D$. Let $f, g \in D \sqbrk x$ be polynomials. Then: $f$ divides $g$ $f$ is a divisor of $g$ $g$ is divisible by $f$ $\exists h \in D \sqbrk x : g = f h$ This is denoted: $f \divides g$

title: Definition:Dodeca-/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Use of Dodeca- == The prefix dodeca- can be found in the following contexts: dodecagon: a polygon with $12$ sides and hence $12$ vertices dodecahedron: a polyhedron with $12$ faces Category:Definitions/Number Prefixes

title: Definition:Dodeca-/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on dodeca- == The prefix dodeca- is from the Ancient Greek δώδεκα (dṓdeka), meaning twelve. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Dodecagon
snippet: A dodecagon is a polygon with exactly $12$ sides. 300px

title: Definition:Dodecagon/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Dodecagon == The word dodecagon derives from the Greek dodeka, meaning twelve, and gon, deriving from the Greek for corner. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Dodecagon/Regular
snippet: A regular dodecagon is a dodecagon which is both equilateral and equiangular. That is, a regular polygon with $12$ sides. That is, a dodecagon in which all the sides are the same length, and all the vertices have the same angle: 300px

title: Definition:Dodecahedron
snippet: A dodecahedron is a polyhedron which has $12$ faces.

title: Definition:Dodecahedron/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Dodecahedron == The word dodecahedron derives from the Classical Greek δωδεκάεδρόν: dodeca (δωδεκά), meaning twelve hedron (a form of ἕδρα), meaning base or seat. The technically correct plural of dodecahedron is dodecahedra, but the word dodecahedrons can often be found.

title: Definition:Dodecahedron/Regular
snippet: A regular dodecahedron is a dodecahedron whose $12$ faces are all congruent regular pentagons. It has: $12$ faces $30$ edges $20$ vertices.

title: Definition:Domain
snippet: Set theory: The concept of domain in the contexts of mapping theory, relation theory and abstract algebra. The domain of a variable. Category theory The concept of domain. Abstract algebra: The concept of integral domain in ring theory. Analysis: Domain: another term for an open region.

title: Definition:Domain/Technical Note
snippet: == Technical Note for Domain == {{LatexFor|for = \Dom {X} }} When the argument is a single character, it is usual to omit the braces: \Dom X This command is specific to . Category:Technical Notes

title: Definition:Domain (Category Theory)
snippet: Let $f: X \to Y$ be a morphism. Then the domain of $f$ is defined to be the object $X$. This is usually denoted $X = \Dom f$ or $X = \map D f$.

title: Definition:Domain (Set Theory)/Binary Operation
snippet: Let $\circ: S \times S \to T$ be a binary operation. The domain of $\circ$ is the set $S$ and can be denoted $\Dom \circ$. This definition can be considered as the same as that for the domain of a mapping, where the domain would be defined as $S \times S$. Category:Definitions/Abstract Algebra

title: Definition:Domain (Set Theory)/Mapping
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. The domain of $f$ is $S$, and can be denoted $\Dom f$.

title: Definition:Domain (Set Theory)/Relation
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation. The domain of $\RR$ is defined and denoted as: $\Dom \RR := \set {s \in S: \exists t \in T: \tuple {s, t} \in \RR}$ That is, it is the same as what is defined here as the preimage of $\RR$.

title: Definition:Domain (Set Theory)/Relation/Class Theory
snippet: Let $V$ be a basic universe. Let $\RR \subseteq V \times V$ be a relation in $V$. The domain of $\RR$ is defined and denoted as: $\Dom \RR := \set {x \in V: \exists y \in V: \tuple {x, y} \in \RR}$ That is, it is the class of all $x$ such that $\tuple {x, y} \in \RR$ for at least one $y$.

title: Definition:Domain (Set Theory)/Relation/General Definition
snippet: Let $\ds \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n S_i$ be the cartesian product of sets $S_1$ to $S_n$. Let $\ds \RR \subseteq \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n S_i$ be an $n$-ary relation on $\ds \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n S_i$. The domain of $\RR$ is the set defined as: $\ds \Dom \RR := \set {\tuple {s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_{n - 1} } \in \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^{n - 1} S_i: \exists s_n \in S_n: \tuple {s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n} \in \RR}$ The concept is usually encountered when $\RR$ is an endorelation on $S$: $\ds \Dom \RR := \set {\tuple {s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_{n - 1} } \in S^{n - 1}: \exists s_n \in S_n: \tuple {s_1, s_2,…

title: Definition:Domain Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $\mathbf C^\to$ be its morphism category. The domain functor is the functor $\operatorname{\mathbf{dom}}: \mathbf C^\to \to \mathbf C$ defined by: {{DefineFunctor |ob = $\operatorname{\mathbf{dom} } f := \operatorname{dom} f$ |mor = $\operatorname{\mathbf{dom} } \tuple {g_1, g_2} := g_1$ }} That it is in fact a functor is shown on Domain Functor is Functor.

title: Definition:Domain of Exponential Map
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g, \nabla}$ be a Riemannian or pseudo-Riemannian manifold without boundary endowed with the Levi-Civita connection. Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space of $M$ at $p \in M$. Let $v \in T_p M$. Let $I \subseteq \R$ be an open real interval. Let $\gamma_v : I \to M$ be the unique maximal geodesic such that: $\map {\gamma '} 0 = v$ where $\gamma'$ is the velocity of $\gamma$. Let $TM$ be the tangent bundle of $M$.

title: Definition:Domain of Mapping/Also known as
snippet: The domain of (usually) a mapping is sometimes called the departure set. Some sources refer to $\Dom f$ as the domain of definition of $f$. Others refer to it on occasion as the source, but this is not recommended as there are other uses for that term. , for example, possibly forgetting themselves, in Appendix $\text{A}.7$: Here are some common functions and their inverses. Note how carefully the source and codomain are specified. Some sources denote the domain of $f$ by $\map {\mathrm D} f$. Some sources use $D_f$. Category:Definitions/Domains of Mappings

title: Definition:Domain of Relation/Also defined as
snippet: It is usual, as here, to define the domain of $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ as the subset of $S$ that bears some element of $S$ to $T$. However, it appears to make sense to define it to be the whole of the set $S$. Using this definition, $s \in \Dom \RR$ whether or not $\exists t \in T: \tuple {s, t} \in \RR$. It would then be possible to refer to $\set {s \in S: \exists t \in T: \tuple {s, t} \in \RR}$ as the preimage of $\RR$. This appears never to be done in the literature that has so far been studied as source work for .

title: Definition:Domain of Relation/Also known as
snippet: Some sources refer to the domain of $\RR$ as the domain of definition of $\RR$. Some sources use a distinctive typeface, for example, $\map {\mathsf {Dom} } \RR$. Category:Definitions/Relations

title: Definition:Domain of Variable/Also known as
snippet: == Domain of Variable: Also known as== The domain of a variable is sometimes referred to imprecisely as the values of the variable, or its range (of values). In the context of real functions, the domain is sometimes seen as the interval of definition.

title: Definition:Dominate
snippet: Set Theory Dominate (Set Theory) Analysis Dominate (Analysis)

title: Definition:Dominate (Analysis)
snippet: Let $\sequence {a_n}$ be a sequence in $\R$. Let $\sequence {z_n}$ be a sequence in $\C$. Then $\sequence {a_n}$ dominates $\sequence {z_n}$ : $\forall n \in \N: \cmod {z_n} \le a_n$ Category:Definitions/Analysis Category:Definitions/Complex Analysis

title: Definition:Dominate (Set Theory)
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets.

title: Definition:Dominate (Set Theory)/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Then $S$ is dominated by $T$ there exists an injection from $S$ to $T$. The notation $S \preccurlyeq T$ is used to indicate that $S$ dominates $T$.

title: Definition:Dominate (Set Theory)/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Then $S$ is dominated by $T$ $S$ is equivalent to some subset of $T$. That is, there exists a bijection $f: S \to T'$ for some $T' \subseteq T$. The notation $S \preccurlyeq T$ is used to indicate that $S$ dominates $T$.

title: Definition:Dominate (Set Theory)/Strictly Dominate
snippet: Let $S, T$ be sets. $S$ is strictly dominated by set $T$ $S \preccurlyeq T$ but $\neg T \preccurlyeq S$. This can be written $S \prec T$ or $S < T$. Category:Definitions/Set Theory

title: Definition:Dominating Strategy
snippet: Let $G$ be a game. Let player $P$ have pure strategies $A_1$ and $A_2$ in $G$. Then $A_1$ dominates $A_2$ : for any strategy of an opposing player, $A_1$ is at least as good as $A_2$ for at least one strategy of an opposing player, $A_1$ is strictly better than $A_2$.

title: Definition:Dominating Strategy/Also known as
snippet: == Dominating Strategy: Also known as == The specific language used for a dominating strategy can vary according to usage: $A_1$ is a dominating strategy over $A_2$ $A_1$ is dominant over $A_2$ $A_2$ is dominated by $A_1$ and so on.

title: Definition:Domino
snippet: A domino is a $2$-omino: 200px That is, it is a polyomino consisting of exactly $2$ unit squares.

title: Definition:Domino/Also known as
snippet: == Domino: Also known as == A domino is also known as a dimer.

title: Definition:Domino/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Domino == The plural of domino is generally considered to be dominoes, but the form dominos can also be seen. An older meaning of the word domino is a carnival costume featuring a black robe and a mask, often white, that covers the eyes. It is supposed that the name of the game dominoes may have derived from the carnival costume meaning. From there evolved the usage in the context of polyominoes. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Dominoes
snippet: Dominoes are a set of (usually) wooden tiles: in the shape of an oblong $2$ units by $1$ unit (of the order of an inch) with two numbers, usually in the form of dots, usually between $0$ and $6$, one at each end, divided by a line between them, on one side only such that each of the numbers appears paired with every number (including itself) exactly once such that the opposite sides of the dominoes are unmarked so as to make them indistinguishable when upside down (although of course they may have a pretty design on them).

title: Definition:Dominoes/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Domino == The singular of dominoes is domino. Note that in the field of recreational mathematics, the term domino may in fact be used just for the $2$-by-$1$ oblong shape, in its context of being two squares joined together by an edge. An older meaning of the word domino is a carnival costume featuring a black robe and a mask, often white, that covers the eyes. It is supposed that the name of the game dominoes may have derived from the carnival costume meaning. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Dominoes/Pips
snippet: The dots on the faces of a set of dominoes are usually referred to as pips.

title: Definition:Donkey and Mule Problem
snippet: A Donkey and Mule problem is of the form: $2$ participants are comparing their quantity of goods they own relative to the other. Participant $1$ suggests transferring some of the goods of one of them to the other, and remarks on their relative quantities after that exchange. Participant $2$ then suggests the same (or a similar) thing, but transferring the goods in the other direction, and again remarks on their relative quantities after that exchange. From these remarks, $2$ simultaneous linear equations can be set up and (assuming the question is well-crafted) solved.

title: Definition:Donkey and Mule Problem/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Donkey and Mule Problem == The earliest known occurrence of a Donkey and Mule problem is in a piece of Greek verse attributed to . Since then it has appeared in many places, and crops up regularly in puzzle anthologies. The general form: Let $\tuple {a, b, c, d}$ denote the general problem: If I had $a$ from you I'd have $b$ times as many as you. If I had $c$ from you I'd have $d$ times as much as you. appears never to have been completely explored. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Dorroh Extension
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. We define two operations on the cartesian product $R \times \Z$ as: $\tuple {r, n} + \tuple {s ,m} = \tuple {r + s, n + m}$ $\tuple {r, n} \cdot \tuple {s, m} = \tuple {r s + n s + m r, n m}$ The Dorroh extension of $R$ is the ring $\struct {R \times \Z, +, \cdot}$.

title: Definition:Dot Product
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ be vectors in a vector space $\mathbf V$ of $n$ dimensions: {{eqn | l = \mathbf a | r = \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n a_k \mathbf e_k }} {{eqn | l = \mathbf b | r = \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n b_k \mathbf e_k }} where $\tuple {\mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_2, \ldots, \mathbf e_n}$ is the standard ordered basis of $\mathbf V$.

title: Definition:Dot Product/Also known as
snippet: == Dot Product: Also known as == The dot product is also known as: The scalar product (but this can be confused with multiplication by a scalar so is less recommended) The standard inner product. Some sources refer to it as just the inner product, but this is a more general term of which the dot product is merely an example. The symbol used for the dot is variously presented; another version is $\mathbf a \bullet \mathbf b$, which can be preferred if there is ambiguity between the dot product and standard multiplication.

title: Definition:Dot Product/Complex
snippet: Let $z_1 := x_1 + i y_1$ and $z_2 := x_2 + i y_2$ be complex numbers.

title: Definition:Dot Product/Complex/Definition 1
snippet: Let $z_1 := x_1 + i y_1$ and $z_2 := x_2 + i y_2$ be complex numbers. The dot product of $z_1$ and $z_2$ is defined as: $z_1 \circ z_2 = x_1 x_2 + y_1 y_2$

title: Definition:Dot Product/Complex/Definition 2
snippet: Let $z_1 := x_1 + i y_1$ and $z_2 := x_2 + i y_2$ be complex numbers in vector form. The dot product of $z_1$ and $z_2$ is defined as: $z_1 \circ z_2 = \cmod {z_1} \, \cmod{z_2} \cos \theta$ where: $\cmod {z_1}$ denotes the complex modulus of $z_1$ $\theta$ denotes the angle between $z_1$ and $z_2$.

title: Definition:Dot Product/Complex/Definition 3
snippet: Let $z_1$ and $z_2$ be complex numbers. The dot product of $z_1$ and $z_2$ is defined as: $z_1 \circ z_2 := \map \Re {\overline {z_1} z_2}$ where: $\map \Re z$ denotes the real part of a complex number $z$ $\overline {z_1}$ denotes the complex conjugate of $z_1$ $\overline {z_1} z_2$ denotes complex multiplication.

title: Definition:Dot Product/Complex/Definition 4
snippet: Let $z_1$ and $z_2$ be complex numbers. The dot product of $z_1$ and $z_2$ is defined as: $z_1 \circ z_2 := \dfrac {\overline {z_1} z_2 + z_1 \overline {z_2} } 2$ where: $\overline {z_1}$ denotes the complex conjugate of $z_1$ $\overline {z_1} z_2$ denotes complex multiplication.

title: Definition:Dot Product/Einstein Summation Convention
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ be vector quantities. The dot product of $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ can be expressed using the Einstein summation convention as: {{eqn | l = \mathbf a \cdot \mathbf b | o = := | r = a_i b_j \delta_{i j} | c = }} where $\delta_{i j}$ is the Kronecker delta.

title: Definition:Dot Product/General Context
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ be vectors in a vector space $\mathbf V$ of $n$ dimensions: {{eqn | l = \mathbf a | r = \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n a_k \mathbf e_k }} {{eqn | l = \mathbf b | r = \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n b_k \mathbf e_k }} where $\tuple {\mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_2, \ldots, \mathbf e_n}$ is the standard ordered basis of $\mathbf V$.

title: Definition:Dot Product/Real Euclidean Space
snippet:
Let $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ be vectors in real Euclidean space $\R^n$. The dot product of $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ is defined as: $\mathbf a \cdot \mathbf b = 
orm {\mathbf a} \, 
orm {\mathbf b} \cos \angle \mathbf a, \mathbf b$ where: $
orm {\mathbf a}$ denotes the length of $\mathbf a$ $\angle \mathbf a, \mathbf b$ is the angle between $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$, taken to be between $0$ and $\pi$.

title: Definition:Dottie Number
snippet: The Dottie number $\d$ is defined as the unique fixed point of the cosine function: $\cos \rd = \d$ Its approximate value is given by: $\d \approx 0 \cdotp 73908 \, 51332 \, 15160 \, 64165 \, 53120 \, 87673 \ldots$

title: Definition:Double-Dummy/Also known as
snippet: == Double-Dummy: Also known as == A double-dummy experiment is also seen rendered without the hyphen, as double dummy.

title: Definition:Double-Headed Coin
snippet: A double-headed coin is an extreme example of a biased coin such that instead of a head and a tail, both sides are heads. Hence: the probability of landing heads is $1$ the probability of landing tails is $0$.

title: Definition:Double Centralizer Generated by Element of C*-Algebra
snippet: Let $\struct {A, \ast, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a $\text C^\ast$-algebra. Let $c \in A$. Define $L_c : A \to A$ and $R_c : A \to A$ by: $\map {L_c} a = c a$ and: $\map {R_c} a = a c$ for each $a \in A$. We say that $\tuple {L_c, R_c}$ is the double centralizer generated by $c$.

title: Definition:Double Centralizer of C*-Algebra
snippet: Let $\struct {A, \ast, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a $\text C^\ast$-algebra. Let $L, R : A \to A$ be bounded linear transformations such that: $\map L {a b} = \map L a b$ $\map R {a b} = a \map R b$ $\map R a b = a \map L b$ for each $a, b \in A$. We call $\tuple {L, R}$ a double centralizer for $A$.

title: Definition:Double Cusp
snippet: A double cusp is a cusp in which $2$ or more parts of the curve are both continuous through the point. That is, the curve is tangential to itself.

title: Definition:Double Cusp/Also known as
snippet: == Double Cusp: Also known as == A double cusp is also known as: a tacnode a point of osculation just an osculation. Some sources reserve the term point of osculation specifically to the double cusp of the first kind.

title: Definition:Double Cusp/First Kind
snippet: A double cusp of the first kind is a double cusp in which both parts of the curve lie on opposite sides of the coincident tangents defining that double cusp. 300px

title: Definition:Double Cusp/Point of Osculinflection
snippet: A point of osculinflection is a double cusp in which one or both parts of the curve has a point of inflection at the point of contact with the tangents defining that double cusp. 300px

title: Definition:Double Cusp/Second Kind
snippet: A double cusp of the second kind is a double cusp in which both parts of the curve lie on the same side of the coincident tangents defining that double cusp. 300px

title: Definition:Double Cusp of the First Kind/Also known as
snippet: == Double Cusp of the First Kind: Also known as == A double cusp of the first kind is also known as a point of osculation.

title: Definition:Double Factorial
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be a positive integer.

title: Definition:Double Factorial/Definition 1
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be a positive integer. The double factorial of $n$ is defined inductively as: $n!! = \begin {cases} 1 & : n \in \set {0, 1} \\ n \paren {n - 2}!! & : n > 1 \end {cases}$

title: Definition:Double Factorial/Definition 2
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be a positive integer. The double factorial of $n$ is defined as: $n!! = \begin {cases} 2^k k! & : \text {for $n = 2 k$} \\ \\ \dfrac {\paren {2 k}!} {2^k k!} & : \text {for $n = 2 k - 1$} \end {cases}$

title: Definition:Double Factorial/Definition 3
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be a positive integer. The double factorial of $n$ is defined as: {{eqn | l = n!! | r = \prod_{k \mathop = 1}^{\tfrac n 2} 2 k | c = for $n$ even }} {{eqn | r = n \times \paren {n - 2} \times \paren {n - 4} \times \cdots \times 4 \times 2 | c = }} {{eqn | l = n!! | r = \prod_{k \mathop = 1}^{\tfrac {\paren {n + 1} } 2} 2 k - 1 | c = for $n$ odd }} {{eqn | r = n \times \paren {n - 2} \times \paren {n - 4} \times \cdots \times 3 \times 1 | c = }}

title: Definition:Double Line
snippet: A double line is a line that occurs with multiplicity two in an algebraic equation. For example, the equation y^2 = 0 represents the line y = 0 with multiplicity two. In this case the line y = 0 is called a double line.

title: Definition:Double Napped Cone/Also known as
snippet: == Double Napped Cone: Also known as == A double napped cone is also known as a double cone. Some sources hyphenate: double-napped cone.

title: Definition:Double Origin Topology
snippet: 300px Let $\struct {\R^2, \tau_d}$ be the real number plane with the usual (Euclidean) topology. Let $0^*$ be an additional point. For all $z \in \R^2$, let a neighborhood basis $\BB$ be constructed as follows. For $z \in \R^2: z \notin \set {\tuple {0, 0}, 0^*}$, the neighborhoods of $z$ are the usual open sets of $R^2 \setminus \set {\tuple {0, 0} }$.

title: Definition:Double Point
snippet: Let $C$ be a locus. A singular point $P \in C$ is called a double point $C$ intersects itself at $P$ such that there are $2$ tangents to $C$ at $P$.

title: Definition:Double Pointed Countable Complement Topology on Real Numbers
snippet: == Example of Double Pointed Topology == A particular example of a double pointed topology is the topological space $T \times D$ where: {{item||$T \struct {\R, \tau}$ is the countable complement space on the real numbers $\R$}} {{item||$D \struct {\set {0, 1}, \set {\O, \set {0, 1} } }$ is the indiscrete space on $\set {0, 1}$.}}

title: Definition:Double Pointed Real Number Line
snippet: Let $T_\R = \struct {\R, \tau_d}$ be the real number line with the usual (Euclidean) topology. Let $T_D = \struct {D, \tau_D}$ be the indiscrete topology on the doubleton $D = \set {a, b}$. Let $T = T_\R \times T_D$ be the product space of $T_\R$ and $T_D$. $T$ is known as the double pointed real number line.

title: Definition:Double Pointed Topology
snippet: Let $T_S = \struct {S, \tau_S}$ be a topological space. Let $A = \set {a, b}$ be a doubleton. Let $D = \struct {A, \set {\O, A} }$ be the indiscrete space on $A$. Let $\struct {T_S \times D, \tau}$ be the product space of $T_S$ and $D$. Then: $\tau$ is known as the double pointed topology on $T_S$ $\struct {T_S \times D, \tau}$ is known as the double pointed space on $T_S$. It is seen that $T_S \times D$ is conceptually equivalent to taking the space $T_S$ and replacing each point with a pair of topologically indistinguishable points.

title: Definition:Double Position/Also presented as
snippet: == Method of Double Position: Also presented as == The formula for estimating the next values in the method of double position can also be presented as: $a_{n + 1} = \dfrac {a_n \map f {b_n} - b_n \map f {a_n} } {\map f {b_n} - \map f {a_n} }$ One follows from the other with simple algebra.

title: Definition:Double Precision
snippet: A number is held in a digital computer to double precision it uses $2$ blocks to hold it.

title: Definition:Double Root
snippet: A double root is a multiple root with multiplicity of $2$.

title: Definition:Double Root/Also known as
snippet: == Double Root: Also known as == A double root is also known as a repeated root. However, the term repeated root is also used for a general multiple root of general multiplicity. Hence, to avoid ambiguity, it is deprecated by .

title: Definition:Double Tangent
snippet: A double tangent is a pair of tangent lines to the same locus which are coincident. This happens at a cusp.

title: Definition:Double Tangent/Also defined as/Bitangent
snippet: == Double Tangent: Also defined as == The term double tangent is also used for the concept of the bitangent, but we keep the concepts separate.

snippet: == Double Tangent: Also defined as == Some sources define a double tangent as a pair of distinct tangent lines to the same locus whose points of tangency coincide. This happens at a double point which is specifically not a cusp.

snippet: == Double Tangent: Also known as == A double tangent is also known as a bitangent, but that term is also used for a different concept. Hence on we keep the concepts separate.

title: Definition:Doubleton
snippet: A doubleton is a set that contains exactly two elements. The doubleton containing the distinct elements $a$ and $b$ can be written $\set {a, b}$. The set $\set {a, b}$ is known as the doubleton of $a$ and $b$.

title: Definition:Doubleton/Also known as
snippet: == Doubleton: Also known as == A doubleton is also known as: an unordered pair a pair set a pair if no ambiguity results.

title: Definition:Doubleton/Class Theory
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be sets. The class $\set {a, b}$ is a doubleton (class). It is defined as the class of all $x$ such that $x = a$ or $x = b$: $\set {a, b} = \set {x: x = a \lor x = b: a \ne b}$

title: Definition:Doubly Periodic Function/Also known as
snippet: == Doubly Periodic Function: Also known as == Some sources hyphenate: doubly-periodic function.

title: Definition:Doubly Periodic Function/Definition 1
snippet: Let $f: \C \to \C$ be a complex function. Then $f$ is a doubly periodic function there exist $\omega_1, \omega_2 \in \C$ such that: $(1): \quad \omega_1, \omega_2 \ne 0$ $(2): \quad \dfrac {\omega_1} {\omega_2} \notin \R$ $(3): \quad \forall z \in \C: \map f z = \map f {z + \omega_1} = \map f {z + \omega_2}$

title: Definition:Doubly Periodic Function/Definition 2
snippet: Let $f: \C \to \C$ be a complex function. Then $f$ is a doubly periodic function there exist $\omega_1, \omega_2 \in \C$ such that: $(1): \quad \omega_1, \omega_2 \ne 0$ $(2): \quad \dfrac {\omega_1} {\omega_2} \notin \R$ $(3): \quad \forall z \in \C: \forall m, n \in \Z: \map f z = \map f {z + m \omega_1 + n \omega_2}$

title: Definition:Doubly Subscripted Sequence/Also known as
snippet: == Doubly Subscripted Sequence: Also known as == A doubly subscripted sequence is also known as a double sequence.

title: Definition:Doubly Subscripted Sequence/Notation
snippet: == Doubly Subscripted Sequence: Notation == A doubly subscripted sequence with indices $m$ and $n$ can be denoted variously: $\sequence {a_{m n} }_{\tuple {m, \, n} \mathop \in \N^2}$ $\sequence {a_{m, n} }_{m, \, n \mathop \ge 0}$ in various combinations, according to preference.

title: Definition:Doubly Subscripted Series
snippet: A doubly subscripted series is a series with two indices.

title: Definition:Doubly Subscripted Series/Also known as
snippet: == Doubly Subscripted Series: Also known as == A doubly subscripted series is also known as a double series.

title: Definition:Down Run
snippet: A down run is a run such that the sequence is decreasing.

title: Definition:Dozen
snippet: A dozen is another name for a set whose cardinality is $12$.

title: Definition:Dozen/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Dozen == The word dozen derives from the French douzaine, which derives from the word douze, the French for $12$. The word is falling into disuse, but lives on in the rhetorical flourish where dozens is used to mean an unspecified large number.

snippet: == Drachm: Also known as == A drachm is also known as a dram, especially in US English.

title: Definition:Drag
snippet: Drag is defined as the resistance to motion of a body $B$ through a fluid $F$. The amount of drag depends on: the velocity of $B$ the size and shape of $B$ the density and viscosity of $F$. There is no adequate formula for drag which can be applied in every situation.

title: Definition:Drag/Aerodynamic
snippet: Aerodynamic drag is the drag on a body $B$ in motion specifically through air. Aerodynamic drag is tangential to the trajectory of $B$ and in the opposite direction.

title: Definition:Dram (Avoirdupois)/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Dram: Conversion Factors == {{eqn | r = \dfrac 1 {16} | c = ounce avoirdupois }} Category:Definitions/Dram (Avoirdupois)

title: Definition:Drift Velocity of Electrons
snippet: In an electrical conductor, some of the electrons are more or less free to move between atoms. In a state of electric neutrality, such electrons move randomly. Under the influence of a potential difference, the electrons are influenced to move in a direction towards positive charge and away from negative charge. So, while the electrons are still moving in all directions at random, there is a tendency for the motion to drift towards the positive. The drift velocity is defined as the mean velocity of all the electrons within a given volume.

title: Definition:Du Bois-Reymond Constants
snippet: The du Bois-Reymond constants are the constants $C_n$ where: $C_n = \ds \int_0^\infty \size {\map {\dfrac \d {\d t} } {\dfrac {\sin t} t}^n} \rd t - 1$

snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Its dual category, denoted $\mathbf C^{\text{op} }$, is defined as follows: {{DefineCategory |ob = $X^{\text{op} }$, for all $X \in \operatorname{ob}\mathbf C$ |mor = $f^{\text{op} }: D^{\text{op} } \to C^{\text{op} }$ for all $f: C \to D$ in $\mathbf C_1$ |comp = $\left({f^{\text{op} } \circ g^{\text{op} } }\right) := \left({g \circ f}\right)^{\text{op} }$, whenever this is defined |id = $\operatorname{id}_{X^{\text{op} } } := \operatorname{id}_X^{\text{op} }$ }} It can be seen that this comes down to the metacategory obtained by reversing the direction of…

title: Definition:Dual Code
snippet: Let $C$ be a binary linear code of length $n$. The dual code to $C$ is the set of all binary strings $b_1 b_2 \cdots b_n$ such that: $a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2 + \cdots + a_n b_n = 0 \pmod 2$ for all codewords $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n$ in $C$.

title: Definition:Dual Elements
snippet: In the context of geometry, dual elements are types of object such that one type of object has a specific connection with the other type of object.

title: Definition:Dual Elements/Plane Geometry
snippet: In the context of plane geometry, dual elements are: straight lines, which can be defined by two points points, which can be defined by the intersection of two straight lines.

title: Definition:Dual Elements/Solid Geometry
snippet: In the context of solid geometry, dual elements are: planes, which can be defined by two straight lines points, which can be defined by the intersection of two straight lines.

title: Definition:Dual Graph
snippet: Let $G$ be a planar graph. The dual graph to $G$ is a planar graph $G^*$ created from $G$ as follows: $(1): \quad$ Inside every face of $G$, place a vertex of $G^*$. $(2): \quad$ For every edge of $G$ separating two faces of $G$, construct an edge of $G^*$ incident with the vertices of $G^*$ corresponding to those two faces. Then $G^*$ is the dual graph to $G$.

title: Definition:Dual Isomorphism (Order Theory)
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq_S}$ and $\struct {T, \preceq_T}$ be ordered sets. Let $\phi: S \to T$ be a bijection. Then $\phi$ is a dual isomorphism between $\struct {S, \preceq_S}$ and $\struct {T, \preceq_T}$ $\phi$ and $\phi^{-1}$ are decreasing mappings. If there is a dual isomorphism between $\struct {S, \preceq_S}$ and $\struct {T, \preceq_T}$, then $\struct {S, \preceq_S}$ is dual to $\struct {T, \preceq_T}$. Equivalently, $\struct {S, \preceq_S}$ is dual to $\struct {T, \preceq_T}$ $S$ with the dual ordering is isomorphic to $T$.

title: Definition:Dual Mapping
snippet: Let $V$ and $W$ be vector spaces. Let $V^*$ and $W^*$ denote the algebraic dual of $V$ and $W$ respectively. Let $T: V \to W$ be a linear transformation from $V$ to $W$. Let $T^*: V^* \to W^*$ be the mapping from $V^*$ to $W^*$ defined as: $\forall \phi \in W^*: \forall v \in V: \map {\paren {T^* \phi} } v = \map \phi {T v}$ Then $T^*$ is known as the dual (mapping) of $T$.

title: Definition:Dual Mapping/Also known as
snippet: == Dual Mapping: Also known as == A dual mapping is also known as a dual map.

title: Definition:Dual Matroid
snippet: Let $M = \struct {S, \mathscr I}$ be a matroid. Let $\mathscr B$ be the set of bases of the matroid $M$. The dual of $M$, denoted $M^* = \struct{S, \mathscr I^*}$, is the matroid whose bases is the set: $\mathscr B^* = \set{S \setminus B : B \in \mathscr B}$

title: Definition:Dual Operations
snippet: In the context of geometry, dual operations are types of operation such that one type of operation has a specific connection with the other type of operation.

title: Definition:Dual Operations/Plane Geometry
snippet: In the context of plane geometry, dual operations are: the connection of two points to define a straight line the intersection of two straight lines to define a point.

title: Definition:Dual Operator
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed vector spaces. Let $T : X \to Y$ be a bounded linear transformation. Let $X^\ast$ and $Y^\ast$ be the normed duals of $X$ and $Y$ respectively. We define the dual operator $T^\ast : Y^\ast \to X^\ast$ by: $T^\ast f = f \circ T$ for each $f \in Y^\ast$.

title: Definition:Dual Order Embedding
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq_1}$ and $\struct {T, \preceq_2}$ be ordered sets. A dual order embedding is a mapping $\phi: S \to T$ such that: $\forall x, y \in S: x \preceq_1 y \iff \map \phi y \preceq_2 \map \phi x$ That is: if $\phi$ is an order embedding of $\struct {S, \preceq_1}$ into $\struct {T, \succeq_2}$ where $\succeq_2$ is the dual of $\preceq_2$. Category:Definitions/Order Embeddings

title: Definition:Dual Ordering
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $\succeq$ be the inverse relation to $\preceq$. That is, for all $a, b \in S$: $a \succeq b$ $b \preceq a$ Then $\succeq$ is called the dual ordering of $\preceq$.

title: Definition:Dual Ordering/Dual Ordered Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $\succeq$ be the dual ordering of $\preceq$. The ordered set $\struct {S, \succeq}$ is called the dual ordered set (or just dual) of $\struct {S, \preceq}$. That it indeed is an ordered set is a consequence of Dual Ordering is Ordering.

title: Definition:Dual Ordering/Notation
snippet: To denote the dual of an ordering, the conventional technique is to reverse the symbol. Thus: $\succeq$ denotes $\preceq^{-1}$ $\succcurlyeq$ denotes $\preccurlyeq^{-1}$ $\curlyeqsucc$ denotes $\curlyeqprec^{-1}$ and so: $a \preceq b \iff b \succeq a$ $a \preccurlyeq b \iff b \succcurlyeq a$ $a \curlyeqprec b \iff b \curlyeqsucc a$ Similarly for the standard symbols used to denote an ordering on numbers: $\ge$ denotes $\le^{-1}$ $\geqslant$ denotes $\leqslant^{-1}$ $\eqslantgtr$ denotes $\eqslantless^{-1}$ and so on.

title: Definition:Dual Ordering/Strict/Notation
snippet: To denote the dual of an strict ordering, the conventional technique is to reverse the symbol. Thus: $\succ$ denotes $\prec^{-1}$ and so: $a \prec b \iff b \succ a$ Similarly for the standard symbol used to denote a strict ordering on numbers: $>$ denotes $<^{-1}$ and so on.

title: Definition:Dual Polyhedron
snippet: Let $P$ be a polyhedron. The dual polyhedron $D$ of $P$ is the polyhedron which can be constructed as follows: $(1): \quad$ The vertices of $D$ are the centroids of the faces of $P$. $(2): \quad$ For each edge of $P$ which is adjacent to two faces $F_1$ and $F_2$ of $P$, an edge of $D$ is constructed which is adjacent to the vertices of $D$ forming the centroids of $F_1$ and $F_2$.

title: Definition:Dual Relation/Complement of Inverse
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a binary relation. Then the dual of $\RR$ is denoted $\RR^d$ and is defined as: $\RR^d := \overline {\paren {\RR^{-1} } }$ where: $\RR^{-1}$ denotes the inverse of $\RR$ $\overline {\paren {\RR^{-1} } }$ denotes the complement of the inverse of $\RR$.

title: Definition:Dual Relation/Inverse of Complement
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a binary relation. Then the dual of $\RR$ is denoted $\RR^d$ and is defined as: $\RR^d := \paren {\overline \RR}^{-1}$ where: $\overline \RR$ denotes the complement of $\RR$ $\paren {\overline \RR}^{-1}$ denotes the inverse of the complement of $\RR$.

title: Definition:Dual Root System
snippet: Let $\struct {E, \Phi}$ be a root system. The dual root system is defined as: $\Phi^\vee := \set {\alpha^\vee := \dfrac {2 \alpha} {\innerprod \alpha \alpha}: \alpha \in \Phi}$ Elements of $\Phi^\vee$ are called coroots.

title: Definition:Dual Statement (Order Theory)
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $\succeq$ be the dual ordering to $\preceq$. Let $\Sigma$ be any statement pertaining to $\struct {S, \preceq}$ (be it in natural language or a formal language). The dual statement of $\Sigma$, denoted $\Sigma^*$, is the statement obtained from replacing every reference to $\preceq$ in $\Sigma$ with a reference to its dual $\succeq$. This dual statement may then be turned into a statement about $\preceq$ again by applying the equivalences on Dual Pairs (Order Theory).

title: Definition:Dual Statements
snippet: In the context of geometry, dual statements are statements in which: the name of each object is replaced by its dual element each operation is replaced by its dual operation.

title: Definition:Dual Statements/Also known as
snippet: == Dual Statements: Also known as == Dual statements are also known as dual theorems.

title: Definition:Dual System
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $E$ and $F$ be vector spaces over $K$. Let $\innerprod \cdot \cdot : E \times F \to K$ be a bilinear mapping. We say that the tuple $\tuple {E, F, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ is a dual system over $K$ : {{item||$\innerprod {x_0} y {\mathbf 0}_K$ for all $y \in F$ implies that $x_0 {\mathbf 0}_E$}} {{item||$\innerprod x {y_0} {\mathbf 0}_K$ for all $x \in E$ implies that $y_0 {\mathbf 0}_F$}} The dual system $\tuple {E, F, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ is frequently denoted as $\innerprod E F$.

title: Definition:Dual System/Also known as
snippet: == Dual System: Also known as == A dual system may be known as a dual pair or duality, although that latter term also has other meanings.

title: Definition:Dual of Order Type
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set. Let $\varrho = \map \ot {S, \preccurlyeq}$ denote the order type of $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$. The dual of $\varrho$ is defined and denoted as: $\varrho^* = \map \ot {S, \succcurlyeq}$ where $\struct {S, \succcurlyeq}$ is the dual of $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$.

title: Definition:Duality (Geometry)
snippet: Duality in the context of geometry is a property that conceptually connects types of object with other types of object.

title: Definition:Duality (Geometry)/Plane Geometry
snippet: In the context of plane geometry, the straight line and the point are dual elements: a straight line can be defined by two points a point can be defined by the intersection of two straight lines.

title: Definition:Duality (Geometry)/Solid Geometry
snippet: In the context of solid geometry, the plane and the point are dual elements: a plane can be defined by two straight lines a point can be defined by the intersection of two straight lines.

title: Definition:Dudeney Number
snippet: A Dudeney number is a natural number which is equal to the sum of the digits of its cube when expressed in decimal notation.

title: Definition:Dudeney Number/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Dudeney Number == The natural numbers now referred to as Dudeney numbers were identified by in $1879$, although exactly where this was published is still to be identified. picked up on it, and subsequently published it as $69$ - Root Extraction in his of $1926$. The first appearance of the term Dudeney number has not been established, but it appears to be a recent coining. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Dummy Variable
snippet: A dummy variable is a quantity written in a mathematical expression in the form of a variable, even though it does in fact represent a constant. It is usual for a dummy variable to take on the value either $0$ or $1$.

title: Definition:Dummy Variable/Also defined as
snippet: == Dummy Variable: Also defined as == It is often the case that the term dummy variable is used to apply to what on is called a bound variable. This usage, while common, is deprecated on to reduce the chance of ambiguity. Category:Definitions/Dummy Variables

title: Definition:Dunce Hat
snippet: The dunce hat is the surface obtained by taking an equilateral triangle $ABC$ and identifying the sides $AB$, $AC$ and $BC$ all together.

title: Definition:Duodecimal Notation/Symbols
snippet: In order to be able to represent numbers in a duodecimal system conveniently and readably, it is necessary to render the digits $10$ and $11$ using single characters. The following techniques accomplish this: $\mathrm T$ and $\mathrm E$ that is, the initial letters of ten and eleven. $\mathrm A$ and $\mathrm B$ Hence this is consistent with the common form for hexadecimal notation. $\mathrm X$ and $\mathrm E$ This was the suggestion from the Duodecimal Society in $1944$.

title: Definition:Duodecimal System
snippet: A duodecimal system is a number system in which the base is $12$.

title: Definition:Duodecimal System/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on the Duodecimal System == A $12$-based system is easier than a $10$-based system to divide into thirds, quarters and sixths. This partly offsets the clear advantage of a $10$-based system that it makes it easy to use the fingers for counting. Hence the duodecimal system has been suggested several times during the course of history to replace the decimal system as the basis of a universal counting system. , in describing his ideal state, determined that the system of coinage and weights and measures should be based on a duodecimal system.

title: Definition:Duodecimal System/Notation
snippet: Duodecimal notation is the positional number system whose base is $12$. That is, every number $x \in \R$ is expressed in the form: $\ds x = \sum_{j \mathop \in \Z} r_j 12^j$ where: $\forall j \in \Z: r_j \in \set {0, 1, \ldots, 10, 11}$

title: Definition:Duplicate Ratio
snippet: Let $a, b, c$ be magnitudes such that: $a : b = b : c$ Then $a$ has the duplicate ratio to $c$ of the ratio it has to $b$. That is: $a : c$ is the duplicate ratio of $a : b$. From definition of ratio: {{eqn | ll= \leadsto | l = \dfrac a c | r = \paren {\dfrac a b}^2 | c = }} That is: $a : c = \paren {a : b}^2$ Category:Definitions/Euclidean Algebra

title: Definition:Duration of Activity/Also known as
snippet: == Duration of Activity: Also known as == The duration of an activity can also be referred to informally as its length. Category:Definitions/Activities

title: Definition:Durbin-Watson Statistic
snippet: The Durbin-Watson statistic is a statistic used in time series analysis to test whether there is a correlation between successive errors.

title: Definition:Durbin-Watson Statistic/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Durbin-Watson Statistic == The Durbin-Watson statistic was developed by and in $1950$.

title: Definition:Dwarf Planet
snippet: A dwarf planet is a celestial body which orbits a star (or the remains of a star) that:

title: Definition:Dyad
snippet: A dyad is an instance of the number $2$.

title: Definition:Dyadic Rational
snippet: A dyadic rational is a rational number whose denominator, when expressed in canonical form, is an integral power of $2$. That is, $a \in \Q$ is dyadic : $\exists p \in \Z, q \in \Z_{>0}: a = \dfrac p {2^q}$

title: Definition:Dynamic Equilibrium
snippet: A body $B$ is in dynamic equilibrium : $B$ is moving with constant (non-zero) velocity the vector sum of all the forces acting upon $B$ is zero.

title: Definition:Dynamic Programming
snippet: Dynamic programming is a method of solving problems of optimization in operations research where a step-wise approach to decision making is appropriate.

title: Definition:Dynamic Viscosity
snippet: The dynamic viscosity of a fluid is the coefficient $\eta$ appearing in the equation governing viscosity: $F = \eta A \dfrac u y$

title: Definition:Dynamic Viscosity/Dimension
snippet: The dimension of measurement of dynamic viscosity is $\mathsf {M L^{-1} T^{-1} }$. Category:Definitions/Dimensions of Measurement Category:Definitions/Dynamic Viscosity

title: Definition:Dynamic Viscosity/Unit
snippet: The SI unit of measurement of dynamic viscosity is the pascal second. The CGS unit of measurement of dynamic viscosity is the poise.

title: Definition:Dynamical System
snippet: A dynamical system is a nonlinear system in which a function describes the time dependence of a point in a geometrical space $X$. It is an iterative procedure consisting of: a mapping $T$ of a $X$ onto itself and: an iteration $x_{n + 1} = \map T {x_n}$. Hence positions of points in $X$ evolve iteratively under $T$.

title: Definition:Dynamical System/Flow
snippet: In a dynamical system, a set of time-dependent equations is known as flow.

title: Definition:Dynamical System/Orbit
snippet: Let $S$ be a dynamical system consisting of a mapping $T$ and iteration $x_{n + 1} = \map T {x_n}$. The orbit of $x_0$ is the set of points $\set {x_0, x_1, x_2, \ldots}$ When $T$ is invertible, the orbit usually includes the points $x_{-1} = \inv T x, x_{-2} = \inv T {x_{-1} }, \ldots$ For a flow, the orbit of a point $x$ is the union of all the points $\map x t$ for all $t$.

title: Definition:Dynamical Systems
snippet: Dynamical systems is a branch of mathematics which studies the long-term behavior of a state space that evolves in time according to a prescribed rule. A dynamical system can be viewed as a tuple $(T, X, f)$ where $T$ is a semigroup that represents time, $X$ is the underlying state space, and $f:T\times X\to X$ is a semigroup action that describes the rule. Typically, $T$ is commutative, $X$ is a topological space, and $f$ is a continuous map.

title: Definition:Dynamical Systems Theory
snippet: Dynamical systems theory is the branch of mathematics which studies dynamical systems.

title: Definition:Dynamics
snippet: Dynamics is the branch of mechanics describing the motion of bodies under the influence of forces. It can be further subdivided into the branches of: kinetics, in which the relationships between force and motion are considered kinematics, in which motion is analysed without considering the forces involved. In general, the concerns of dynamics are with solid bodies rather than fluids.

title: Definition:Dynamics/Also defined as
snippet: == Dynamics: Also defined as == Some sources treat kinematics as a separate branch of classical mechanics, while handling dynamics and kinetics as the same thing.

title: Definition:Dyne-Centimetre
snippet: The dyne-centimetre is the CGS unit of torque. It is defined as being the torque resulting from a force of $1$ dyne applied perpendicularly to the end of a moment arm that is $1$ centimetre long.

title: Definition:Dyne/Base Units
snippet: The CGS base units of the dyne are: $\mathrm {dyn} := \mathrm g \, \mathrm {cm} \, \mathrm s^{-2}$ where: $\mathrm g$ denotes grams $\mathrm {cm}$ denotes centimetres $\mathrm s$ denotes seconds (of time).

title: Definition:Dyne/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Dyne: Conversion Factors == {{eqn | r = 10^{-5} | c = newtons }}

title: Definition:Dynkin System
snippet: Let $X$ be a set, and let $\DD \subseteq \powerset X$ be a collection of subsets of $X$. Then $\DD$ is called a Dynkin system (on $X$) it satisfies the following conditions: {{item|(3):|For all pairwise disjoint sequences $\sequence {D_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ in $\DD$, $\ds \bigcup_{n \mathop \in \N} D_n \in \DD$}}

title: Definition:Dynkin System Generated by Collection of Subsets
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\GG \subseteq \powerset X$ be a collection of subsets of $X$. Then the Dynkin system generated by $\GG$, denoted $\map \delta \GG$, is the smallest Dynkin system on $X$ that contains $\GG$. That is, $\map \delta \GG$ is subject to: $(1):\quad \GG \subseteq \map \delta \GG$ $(2):\quad \GG \subseteq \DD \implies \map \delta \GG \subseteq \DD$ for any Dynkin system $\DD$ on $X$ In fact, $\map \delta \GG$ always exists, and is unique, as proved on Existence and Uniqueness of Dynkin System Generated by Collection of Subsets.

title: Definition:E-Science
snippet: The name e-science is used to denote science that uses large computer networks to achieve computationally intensive calculations in order to achieve its results.

title: Definition:EMV Algorithm
snippet: The emv algorithm proceeds as follows. Let a decision tree be complete with all payoffs and probabilities of probabilistic outcomes known. Determine the expected monetary value for each of the chance nodes, starting with the payoffs. At each decision node, the player takes the decision which maximizes the expected monetary value.

title: Definition:EPORN
snippet: An EPORN is a natural number which can be expressed as the product of a number and its reversal in two different ways.

title: Definition:EPORN/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on EPORN == EPORNs appear to have been first investigated by , who first published on the subject in $1987$. This work has been reported on in a few outlets since.

title: Definition:EPORN/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on EPORN == The word EPORN is an acronym formed from Equal Product Of Reversible Number. The term appears to have been coined by , who has investigated them in some detail.

title: Definition:Ear
snippet: Let $P$ be a polygon. Let $A, B, C$ be vertices of $P$ such that $\angle BAC$ is an internal angle of the vertex $A$. Let $BC$ be a chord of $P$. Then the triangle $\triangle ABC$ is an ear of $P$.

title: Definition:Earth
snippet: Earth is the planet on which we live. It is the third planet of the solar system from the sun. Its orbit lies between those of Venus and Mars.

title: Definition:Earth's Axis
snippet: Let it be assumed to be established that planet Earth rotates in space about a more-or-less fixed diameter $D$. Then $D$ is known as Earth's axis. 500px

title: Definition:Earth's Poles
snippet: Let it be assumed to be established that planet Earth rotates in space about its axis. The poles of Earth are the endpoints of Earth's axis, where it intersects the surface of Earth. That is, the poles of Earth are the poles of Earth's equator. 500px

title: Definition:Earth's Poles/North
snippet: Let an observer $A$ be situated on Earth's equator. Let $A$ be facing the direction of Earth's rotation in space about its axis. Then the North Pole is the particular one of Earth's poles which is on the left of $A$. 500px

title: Definition:Earth's Poles/South
snippet: Let an observer $A$ be situated on Earth's equator. Let $A$ be facing the direction of Earth's rotation in space about its axis. Then the South Pole is the particular one of Earth's poles which is on the right of $A$. 500px

title: Definition:Earth/Also known as
snippet: == Earth: Also known as == It is a common usage to refer to Earth as the Earth. Earth can sometimes be seen referred to as the globe (sometimes with a capital: the Globe), which is of course just a synonym for sphere. This nickname is of no more significance than referring to one's own home as (for example) the house, but it gives rise to the adjective global, which is new-age speak for worldwide. In the field of the name Terra is more frequently seen than anywhere else, often used to refer affectionately as the original homeworld of the human race.

title: Definition:Earth/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Earth == Earth is a proper name: that of the planet on which (at time of writing) all humans live. As such, its correct styling is for it to start with a . This is the convention to be used on . However, in much literature it can be seen referred to as the earth, which is a bit like, for example, referring to as the albert. In recent literature, particularly popular, new-age and poetic, there is a trend to referring to the place as Planet Earth. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Earth/Shape/First Approximation
snippet: To a first approximation, the shape of Earth can be considered to be spherical, with a radius of approximately $6400 \, \mathrm {km}$. A more accurate accepted value is $6371 \, \mathrm {km}$.

title: Definition:Earth/Shape/Second Approximation
snippet: To a second approximation, Earth is an oblate spheroid, such that: its radius at its equator is $6378 \, \mathrm {km}$ its radius at its poles is $6357 \, \mathrm {km}$.

title: Definition:Earthworm Sequence
snippet: The earthworm sequence is the integer sequence $\sequence {h_n}$ defined as follows. Let $h: \Z \to \Z$ be the mapping defined as: $\forall a \in \Z: \map h a = 2 a \pmod {100}$ Then: $h_n = \begin {cases} x: x \in \set {10, 11, \dotsc, 99} & : n = 0 \\ \map h {n - 1} & : n > 0 \end {cases}$ That is: $h_0$ is an arbitrary integer between $10$ and $99$ $h_n$ is the result of multiplying the previous term in the sequence by $2$ and keeping only the last two digits.

title: Definition:Earthworm Sequence/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Earthworm Sequence == The earthworm sequence was invented by , and appears in his $1991$ work . His interest is specifically in whether each of the integers selected for $h_1$ ever returns to its starting point. He fails to document the details of what happens for $h_0 = 50$. The only reason this sequence appears here is because prime.mover found a piece of paper with his analysis on it in a big pile of material which is in the process of being recycled.

title: Definition:East (Celestial)
snippet: East is the direction along the celestial sphere in the direction of the east point of the horizon.

title: Definition:East (Terrestrial)
snippet: East is the direction on (or near) Earth's surface along the small circle in the direction of Earth's rotation in space about its axis. 600px

title: Definition:East Point of Horizon
snippet: Let an observer $O$ be facing the north point of the horizon $N$, facing directly away from the south point of the horizon $S$. Let the celestial equator meet the celestial horizon at the points $E$ and $W$. Let $E$ be the point on the right of $O$. This is called the east point of the horizon. 480px In the above diagram, the east point of the horizon is indicated by $E$.

title: Definition:East Point of Horizon/Also known as
snippet: == East Point of Horizon: Also known as == The east point of the horizon is also known as the east point.

title: Definition:Eastern Celestial Hemisphere
snippet: Consider the celestial sphere $C$ with observer $O$. Let $E$ be the east point of the horizon. The eastern celestial hemisphere is the hemisphere of $C$ defined by the principal vertical circle which contains $E$. 480px

title: Definition:Eastern Hemisphere
snippet: The eastern hemisphere of Earth is the hemisphere immediately to the east of the prime meridian. Points in the eastern hemisphere have longitude between $0 \degrees \, \mathrm E$ (the prime meridian itself) and $180 \degrees \, \mathrm E$.

title: Definition:Eccentric
snippet: Two plane figures which each have centres of symmetry are said to be eccentric their centers do not coincide.

title: Definition:Eccentric/Circles
snippet: Circles are said to be eccentric if their centers are at different points. 320px Circles $K_1$ and $K_2$, whose centers are $C_1$ and $C_2$, are eccentric.

title: Definition:Eccentric/Ellipses
snippet: Ellipses are said to be eccentric if their centers are at different points. 320px Ellipses $E_1$ and $E_2$, whose centers are $C_1$ and $C_2$, are eccentric.

title: Definition:Eccentric Angle
snippet: Let $\KK$ be a central conic. Let $P$ be a point on $\KK$. Let $\CC$ be the auxiliary circle of $\KK$. The eccentric angle of $P$ $\KK$ is defined as follows:

title: Definition:Eccentric Angle/Ellipse
snippet: Let $\KK$ be an ellipse with foci at $F_1$ and $F_2$. Let $P$ be a point on $\KK$. Let $\CC$ be the auxiliary circle of $\KK$ with center $O$. Let $PQ$ be dropped perpendicular to the major axis $F_1 F_2$ of $\KK$ such that $Q$ lies on $F_1 F_2$. Let $QP$ be produced so as to meet $\CC$ at $P'$. The angle $QOP'$ is the eccentric angle of $P$ $\KK$. 480px In the above diagram, $\alpha$ is the eccentric angle of $P$ $\KK$.

title: Definition:Eccentric Angle/Hyperbola
snippet: Let $\KK$ be a hyperbola with foci at $F_1$ and $F_2$. Let $P$ be a point on $\KK$. Let $\CC$ be the auxiliary circle of $\KK$ with center $O$. Let $PQ$ be dropped perpendicular to the major axis $F_1 F_2$ of $\KK$ such that $Q$ lies on $F_1 F_2$. Let $QP'$ be drawn tangent to $\CC$ such that $P'$ is the point of tangency with $\CC$. The angle $QOP'$ is the eccentric angle of $P$ $\KK$. 480px In the above diagram, $\alpha$ is the eccentric angle of $P$ $\KK$.

title: Definition:Eccentric Angle/Mistake
snippet: == Source Work == eccentric angle

title: Definition:Eccentric Circle of Central Conic
snippet: Let $\KK$ be a central conic whose center is at $O$. The eccentric circles of $\KK$ are the two circles whose center is at $O$ and whose diameter coincides with either the major axis of $\KK$ or the minor axis of $\KK$.

title: Definition:Eccentric Circle of Central Conic/Ellipse
snippet: Let $\KK$ be an ellipse whose center is at $O$. The eccentric circles of $\KK$ are the two circles whose center is at $O$ and whose diameter coincides with either the major axis of $\KK$ or the minor axis of $\KK$. 480px

title: Definition:Eccentric Circle of Central Conic/Hyperbola
snippet: Let $\KK$ be a hyperbola whose center is at $O$. The eccentric circles of $\KK$ are the two circles whose center is at $O$ and whose diameter coincides with either the major axis of $\KK$ or the minor axis of $\KK$. 480px

title: Definition:Eccentricity of Conic Section/Also denoted as
snippet: == Eccentricity: Also denoted as == Some sources use $\epsilon$ for the eccentricity of a conic section. Category:Definitions/Conic Sections

title: Definition:Eccentricity of Ellipse/Shape
snippet: The eccentricity of an ellipse determines its shape: 610px In the above: the semiminor axis $b$ is kept constant and arbitrarily allocated a length of $1$ the linear eccentricity $c$ is varied from $1$ to $4$ the eccentricity is calculated using Eccentricity of Ellipse in terms of Semiminor Axis and Linear Eccentricity as: $e = \dfrac c {\sqrt {b^2 + c^2} }$ As can be seen, the greater $e$ is, the longer the ellipse its width.

title: Definition:Eccentricity of Vertex
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a graph. Let $v \in V$ be a vertex of $G$. The eccentricity of $v$ is the maximum distance from $v$ to another vertex of $G$. That is: $\map E v = \ds \max_{u \mathop \in V} \map D {v, u}$ where $\map D {v, u}$ denotes the distance from $v$ to $u$.

title: Definition:Echelon Matrix

title: Definition:Echelon Matrix/Also defined as
snippet: == Echelon Matrix: Also defined as == Some sources do not require that, for a matrix to be in echelon form, the leading coefficient in each non-zero row must be $1$. Such a matrix is detailed in Non-Unity Variant of Echelon Matrix. Category:Definitions/Echelon Matrices

title: Definition:Echelon Matrix/Also known as
snippet: == Echelon Matrix: Also known as == An echelon matrix and a matrix in echelon form are the same thing. A matrix in echelon form is also sometimes seen as being in row echelon form. The definition of column echelon form is directly analogous.
