title: Definition:Echelon Matrix/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Echelon Matrix == An echelon is: a formation of troops, ships, aircraft, or vehicles in parallel rows with the end of each row projecting further than the one in front. It derives from the French word échelon, which means a rung of a ladder, which describes the shape that this formation has when viewed from above or below. It is pronounced e-shell-on or something like ay-shell-on, where the first ay is properly the French é. Avoid the pronunciation et-chell-on, which is technically incorrect. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Echelon Matrix/Reduced Echelon Form
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ be a matrix in echelon form whose order is $m \times n$. The matrix $\mathbf A$ is in reduced echelon form , in addition to being in echelon form, the leading $1$ in any non-zero row is the only non-zero element in the column in which that $1$ occurs. Such a matrix is called a reduced echelon matrix.

title: Definition:Ecliptic
snippet: The ecliptic is the great circle that is the intersection of the plane that holds Earth's orbit with the celestial sphere.

title: Definition:Ecliptic/Axis
snippet: The ecliptic axis is the axis of the great circle that is the ecliptic.

title: Definition:Ecliptic/Pole
snippet: The poles of the ecliptic are the two poles of the great circle that is the ecliptic.

title: Definition:Ecliptic/Pole/North
snippet: The north ecliptic pole is the pole of the ecliptic that is situated in the northern celestial hemisphere.

title: Definition:Ecliptic/Pole/South
snippet: The south ecliptic pole is the pole of the ecliptic that is situated in the southern celestial hemisphere.

title: Definition:Ecliptic Coordinate System
snippet: The ecliptic coordinate system is an astronomical coordinate system in which measurements are based on the ecliptic. Hence a point on the celestial sphere is located by means of $2$ angular measurements: the celestial longitude $\lambda$ is the angular distance measured eastwards along the ecliptic from the vernal equinox the celestial latitude $\beta$ is the angular distance measured north or south of the ecliptic.

title: Definition:Economics
snippet: Economics is the branch of applied mathematics which studies the movement of money.

title: Definition:Edge
snippet: Graph theory: the edge of a graph Solid geometry: the edge of a polyhedron the edge of a polyhedral angle Analytic geometry, analysis, number theory, etc.: the edge of a half-plane Category Theory: Edge: another word for morphism

title: Definition:Edge-Disjoint Trails
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be an undirected graph. Let $T_1$ and $T_2$ be trails in $G$. Then $T_1$ and $T_2$ are edge-disjoint they have no edges in common. Category:Definitions/Trails

title: Definition:Edge Contraction
snippet: Let $G$ be an undirected graph. Let $e \in \map E G$ be an edge of $G$. Then the graph obtained by contracting $e$ in $G$, denoted by $G / e$, is the graph $H$ defined by: $\map V H = \paren {\map V G \setminus e} \cup \set v$ $\map E H = \set {f \in \map E G: f \cap e = \O} \cup \set {u v: \exists f \in \map E G: u \in f \setminus e, f \cap e \ne \O}$ where $v \notin \map V G$ is a fresh object. Informally, it is the graph obtained from $G$ by replacing the vertices incident to $e$ with a single vertex adjacent to all their neighbors.

title: Definition:Edge Cut
snippet: Let $G$ be a graph. An edge cut of $G$ is a set of edges $W \subseteq \map E G$ such that the edge deletion $G \setminus W$ is disconnected.

title: Definition:Edge Deletion
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be an (undirected) graph. Let $F \subseteq E$ be a set of edges of $G$. Then the graph obtained by deleting $F$ from $G$, denoted by $G \setminus F$, is the subgraph of $G$ containing the same vertices as $G$ but with all the elements of $F$ removed. That is: $G \setminus F = \struct {V, E \setminus F}$ Informally, $G \setminus F$ is the graph obtained from $G$ by removing all edges in $F$.

title: Definition:Edge Set
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a graph. The set $E$ of edges in $G$ is called the edge set. It consists of (unordered) pairs of elements of the vertex set $V$. It is often convenient to refer to the edge set for a given graph $G$ as $\map E G$, especially if there is at any one time more than one graph under consideration.

title: Definition:Edge Set/Also known as
snippet: == Edge Set: Also known as == The term edge set can also be seen hyphenated: edge-set.

title: Definition:Edge of Graph/Notation
snippet: == Edge of Graph: Notation == If $e \in E$ is an edge joining the vertex $u$ to the vertex $v$, it is denoted $u v$. If $G$ is an undirected graph, an edge $u v$ can equivalently be denoted $v u$.

title: Definition:Edge of Polyhedron/Also known as
snippet: == Edge of Polyhedron: Also known as == The edges of a polyhedron are also seen as its sides, but this term is ambiguous as it could also be used for its faces. Category:Definitions/Edges of Polyhedra

title: Definition:Edgeless Graph
snippet: An edgeless graph is a graph with no edges. That is, an edgeless graph is a graph of size zero. Equivalently, an edgeless graph is a graph whose vertices are all isolated. The edgeless graph of order $n$ is denoted $N_n$ and can be referred to as the $n$-edgeless graph.

title: Definition:Edgeless Graph/Also known as
snippet: == Edgeless Graph: Also known as == An edgeless graph is sometimes called an empty graph. Thus the term $n$-empty graph can often be seen for $N_n$. The symbol $\overline K_n$ is frequently used to denote the $n$-edgeless graph, which follows from Complement of Complete Graph is Edgeless Graph. Some sources use the term size zero graph. The term null graph can also be found, but this can be confused with the graph with no vertices.

title: Definition:Education Theory
snippet: Education theory is the branch of mathematics concerned with effective techniques for teaching the subject. It is concerned with the study of the teaching and learning of mathematics at all levels from basic numeracy upwards.

title: Definition:Effective Domain/Convex Real-Valued Function/Real Vector Space
snippet: Let $\R^n$ be an $n$-dimensional real vector space. Let $S \subseteq \R^n$ be a subset. Let $f: S \to \overline \R$ be a convex function. The effective domain of $f$ is: $\Dom f := \set {x \in S : \map f x < + \infty }$

title: Definition:Effective Domain of Convex Real Function
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a vector space over $\GF$. Let $f: X \to \overline \R$ be an extended real-valued function. We define the effective domain of $f$ by: $\Dom f = \set {x \in X : \map f x < \infty}$

title: Definition:Effective Force
snippet: Let $M$ be a machine. The force which $M$ produces at a different point from the effort is called the effective force. This effective force is then applied to the load on $M$.

title: Definition:Effective Procedure
snippet: An effective procedure is an algorithm for determining whether or not a given object has a given property.

title: Definition:Effective Rate of Interest
snippet: Let $I$ be an interest rate calculated over time period of less than a year. The effective rate is the yearly interest rate that would give the same interest as the compound interest calculated at the nominal rate over the specified conversion periods.

title: Definition:Effective Transformation Group
snippet: Let $G$ be a group whose identity is $e$. Let $X$ be a set. Let $\phi: G \times X \to X$ be a group action. Then $G$ is an effective transformation group for $\phi$ $\phi$ is faithful.

title: Definition:Effectively Computable Function
snippet: Let $f$ be a function. $f$ is an effectively computable function , given the arguments of $f$, there exists an algorithm that determines its value.

title: Definition:Effectively Computable Function/Also known as
snippet: == Effectively Computable Function: Also known as == An effectively computable function is also known just as a computable function.

title: Definition:Efficiency
snippet: Statistics: Efficiency: a comparison of the variances of two statistics used as estimators. Experimental design: Efficiency: Physics: Efficiency: Computer science: Efficiency:

title: Definition:Efficiency (Computer Science)
snippet: In the context of computer science, efficiency is used to define the properties of an algorithm relating to the resources used by the coding.

title: Definition:Efficiency (Computer Science)/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Efficiency in context of Computer Science == The recent huge increase in the computational power of computers is not only because of improvements in hardware. A lot of the increase is because of software becoming more efficient.

title: Definition:Efficiency (Experimental Design)
snippet: One design is more efficient than another : the same precision can be achieved with less resources or greater precision can be achieved with the same resources.

title: Definition:Efficiency (Physics)
snippet: Let $S$ be a system.

title: Definition:Efficiency (Physics)/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ be a system. The efficiency of $S$ is defined as: $\EE = \dfrac {E_O} {E_I} \times 100 \%$ where: $E_I$ denotes the energy input to $S$ over a particular time interval $T$ $E_O$ denotes the energy output from $S$ over that same time interval $T$.

title: Definition:Efficiency (Physics)/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ be a system. The efficiency of $S$ is defined as: $\EE = \dfrac {W_L} {W_E} \times 100 \%$ where: $W_L$ denotes the work done by the load of $S$ $W_E$ denotes the work done by the effort of $S$.

title: Definition:Efficiency (Statistics)
snippet: Let $T_0$ and $T_1$ both be statistics used as estimators. Efficiency is a comparison of the variances of $T_0$ and $T_1$. Thus $T_0$ is of higher efficiency than $T_1$ $T_0$ has a smaller variance than $T_1$.

title: Definition:Efficiency (Statistics)/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Efficiency in context of Statistics == The concept of efficiency in the context of statistics was pioneered by in $1921$.

title: Definition:Effort
snippet: Let $M$ be a machine. The force applied to a particular part of $M$ is called the effort applied to $M$.

title: Definition:Efron Dice
snippet: The Efron dice are a set of intransitive dice whose faces are as follows: 800px Hence: die $\text A$ beats die $\text B$ die $\text B$ beats die $\text C$ die $\text C$ beats die $\text D$ die $\text D$ beats die $\text A$

title: Definition:Efron Dice/Also known as
snippet: == Efron Dice: Also known as == The Efron dice can also be seen styled as Efron's dice. Category:Definitions/Efron Dice

title: Definition:Egyptian Fraction
snippet: An Egyptian fraction is a fraction either: whose numerator is $1$ or which is $\dfrac 2 3$ All other fractional quantities are expressed as sums of different Egyptian fractions.

title: Definition:Egyptian Fraction/Also defined as
snippet: == Egyptian Fraction: Also defined as == Some sources define an Egyptian fraction as the sum of a set of distinct unit fractions, and do not include the anomalous $\dfrac 2 3$ as one of those addends.

title: Definition:Egyptian Fraction/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Egyptian Fraction == Egyptian fractions are so called because they were the only means of representations of fractional values in the mathematics of ancient Egypt. , in his $1986$ book , refers to $2 / 3$ as "uniquely unrepresentative".

title: Definition:Egyptian Numerals
snippet: The Ancient Egyptian system of counting consisted of grouping a number of symbols of powers of $10$. The Egyptian numerals are: To express other numbers than these, symbols are repeated.

title: Definition:Egyptian Numerals/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Egyptian Numerals == The Egyptian numerals arose around .

title: Definition:Eigenbasis/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Eigenbasis == The plural form of eigenbasis is eigenbases. The word eigenbasis derives from the German eigen, meaning characteristic, or (literally) own. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Eigenbasis/Real Square Matrix
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a square matrix of order $n$ over $\R$. An eigenbasis for $\mathbf A$ is a basis for $V$ which consists of eigenvectors.

title: Definition:Eigenbasis/Square Matrix
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $\mathbf A$ be a square matrix over $R$ of order $n > 0$. An eigenbasis for $\mathbf A$ is a basis for $V$ which consists of eigenvectors.

title: Definition:Eigenbasis/Vector Space
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space. An eigenbasis for $V$ is a basis for $V$ which consists of eigenvectors.

title: Definition:Eigenfunction
snippet: An eigenfunction is a non-trivial solution to a differential equation subject to boundary conditions involving a parameter, for certain values of that parameter.

title: Definition:Eigenfunction/Eigenvalue
snippet: Let $F$ be an eigenfunction to a differential equation. The parameter which so defines $F$ is referred to as an eigenvalue of $F$.

title: Definition:Eigenspace/Linear Operator
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $V$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $A : V \to V$ be a linear operator. Let $I : V \to V$ be the identity mapping on $V$. Let $\lambda \in K$ be an eigenvalue of $A$. Let $\map \ker {A - \lambda I}$ be the kernel of $A - \lambda I$. We say that $\map \ker {A - \lambda I}$ is the eigenspace corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda$.

title: Definition:Eigenspace/Square Matrix
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $\mathbf A$ be a square matrix over $R$ of order $n > 0$. Let $\mathbf A$ have an eigenvalue $\lambda$. Let $\mathbf I_n$ denote the $n \times n$ identity matrix. The eigenspace of $\lambda$ is the kernel of $\mathbf A - \lambda \mathbf I_n$.

title: Definition:Eigenvalue
snippet: An eigenvalue is a characteristic value of an expression in a given context.

title: Definition:Eigenvalue/Also known as
snippet: == Eigenvalue: Also known as == An eigenvalue can also be referred to as: a characteristic root a characteristic value a latent root, particularly in older texts.

title: Definition:Eigenvalue/Linear Operator
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $V$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $A : V \to V$ be a linear operator. $\lambda \in K$ is an eigenvalue of $A$ : $\map \ker {A - \lambda I} \ne \set {0_V}$ where: $0_V$ is the zero vector of $V$ $I : V \to V$ is the identity mapping on $V$ $\map \ker {A - \lambda I}$ denotes the kernel of $A - \lambda I$. That is, $\lambda \in K$ is an eigenvalue of $A$ the kernel of $A - \lambda I$ is non-trivial.

title: Definition:Eigenvalue/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Eigenvalue == The word eigenvalue derives from the German eigen, meaning characteristic, or (literally) own.

title: Definition:Eigenvalue/Real Square Matrix
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a square matrix of order $n$ over $\R$. Let $\lambda \in \R$. $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $A$ there exists a non-zero vector $\mathbf v \in \R^n$ such that: $\mathbf A \mathbf v = \lambda \mathbf v$

title: Definition:Eigenvalue/Square Matrix
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $\mathbf A$ be a square matrix over $R$ of order $n > 0$. Let $\mathbf I_n$ be the $n \times n$ identity matrix. Let $R \sqbrk x$ be the polynomial ring in one variable over $R$. The eigenvalues of $\mathbf A$ are the solutions to the characteristic equation of $\mathbf A$: $\map \det {\mathbf I_n x - \mathbf A} = 0$ where $\map \det {\mathbf I_n x - \mathbf A}$ is the characteristic polynomial of the characteristic matrix of $\mathbf A$ over $R \sqbrk x$.

title: Definition:Eigenvalue of Compact Riemannian Manifold without Boundary
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a compact Riemannian manifold without boundary. Let $u \in \map {C^\infty} M : M \to \R$ be a smooth mapping on $M$. Let $\nabla^2$ denote the Laplace-Beltrami operator. Let $\lambda \in \R$ be a real number. Suppose: $\ds \nabla^2 u + \lambda u = 0$ Then $\lambda$ is called an eigenvalue of $M$.

title: Definition:Eigenvector/Also known as
snippet: == Eigenvector: Also known as == An eigenvector is also known as a characteristic vector.

title: Definition:Eigenvector/Linear Operator
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $V$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $A : V \to V$ be a linear operator. Let $\lambda \in K$ be an eigenvalue of $A$. A non-zero vector $v \in V$ is an eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda$ : $v \in \map \ker {A - \lambda I}$ where: $I : V \to V$ is the identity mapping on $V$ $\map \ker {A - \lambda I}$ denotes the kernel of $A - \lambda I$. That is, : $A v = \lambda v$

title: Definition:Eigenvector/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Eigenvector == The word eigenvector derives from the German eigen, meaning characteristic, or (literally) own. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Eigenvector/Real Square Matrix
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a square matrix of order $n$ over $\R$. Let $\lambda \in \R$ be an eigenvalue of $\mathbf A$. A non-zero vector $\mathbf v \in \R^n$ is an eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda$ : $\mathbf A \mathbf v = \lambda \mathbf v$

title: Definition:Eigenvector/Square Matrix
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $\mathbf A$ be a square matrix over $R$ of order $n > 0$. Let $\lambda \in \R$ be an eigenvalue of $\mathbf A$. A non-zero vector $\mathbf v \in R^n$ is an eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda$ : $\mathbf A \mathbf v = \lambda \mathbf v$

title: Definition:Eigenvector of Linear Operator/Also known as
snippet: == Eigenvector of Linear Operator: Also known as == An eigenvector of a linear operator is also known as an eigenfunction. In the field of quantum mechanics, such an eigenvector is also known as an eigenstate.

title: Definition:Eighth Power
snippet: A eighth power is an integer which can be expressed as the $8$th power of an integer. The sequence of eighth powers begins: $1, 256, 6561, 65 \, 536, 390 \, 625, 1 \, 679 \, 616, 5 \, 764 \, 801, \ldots$

title: Definition:Einstein's Notation/Mistake
snippet: == Source Work == Einstein's notation (Einstein's summation convention)

title: Definition:Einstein Summation Convention
snippet: The Einstein summation convention is a notational device used in the manipulation of matrices and vectors, in particular square matrices in the context of physics and applied mathematics. If the same index occurs twice in a given expression involving matrices, then summation over that index is automatically assumed. Thus the summation sign can be omitted, and expressions can be written more compactly.

title: Definition:Einstein Summation Convention/Also known as
snippet: == Einstein Summation Convention: Also known as == Some sources do not credit with the Einstein summation convention, merely referring to it as the summation convention. It can also be seen styled as Einstein's summation convention. Some sources refer to it as Einstein's notation.

title: Definition:Einstein Summation Convention/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Einstein Summation Convention == When was working with summations in the context of vectors and tensors, he noticed that the subscript or superscript to denote the index appeared twice. So he had the idea of omitting the summation signs and instead using, for example, $x_i y_i$ to mean summation over the repeated subscripts over the entire applicable range. himself jocularly referred to this as: ... a great discovery in mathematics ...

title: Definition:Eisenstein Integer
snippet: An Eisenstein integer is a complex number of the form $a + b \omega$ where $a$ and $b$ are both integers and: $\omega = e^{2 \pi i / 3} = \dfrac 1 2 \paren {i \sqrt 3 - 1}$ that is, the (complex) cube roots of unity. The set of all Eisenstein integers can be denoted $\Z \sqbrk \omega$: $\Z \sqbrk \omega = \set {a + b \omega: a, b \in \Z}$

title: Definition:Eisenstein Integer/Also known as
snippet: == Eisenstein Integer: Also known as == The Eisenstein integers are also known as: the Eisenstein-Jacobi integers, after the Eulerian integers, after .

title: Definition:Eisenstein Prime
snippet: Let $\Z \sqbrk \omega$ be the ring of Eisenstein integers. Let $\alpha \in \Z \sqbrk \omega$ be an Eisenstein integer. Then $\alpha$ is an Eisenstein prime $\alpha$ is prime in $\Z \sqbrk \omega$. Category:Definitions/Number Theory Category:Definitions/Eisenstein Integers Category:Definitions/Prime Elements of Rings

title: Definition:Either-Or Topology
snippet: Let $S = \closedint {-1} 1$ be the closed interval on the real number line from $-1$ to $1$. Let $\tau = \set {U \in \powerset S: \paren {\set 0 \nsubseteq U} \lor \paren {\openint {-1} 1 \subseteq U} }$ where: $\powerset S$ is the power set of $S$ $\lor$ is the inclusive-or logical connective. Then $\tau$ is the either-or topology, and $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is the either-or space. That is, a set is open in $\tau$ it does not contain $\set 0$ or it does contain $\openint {-1} 1$.

title: Definition:Elastic
snippet: Let a body $\BB$ change its shape under the influence of a force or forces applied to it. Let $\BB$ be such that it regains its original shape after the force or forces cease to act on it. Then $\BB$ is described as being elastic.

title: Definition:Elastic Collision
snippet: An elastic collision is a collision in which the total kinetic energy of the interacting bodies is the same after the collision as it was before.

title: Definition:Elastic Collision/Also known as
snippet: == Elastic Collision: Also known as == An elastic collision is also known as a perfectly elastic collision.

title: Definition:Elastic Constant
snippet: An elastic constant is one of a number of constants that describe the properties of a homogeneous body under the action of a deforming force.

title: Definition:Elastic Modulus
snippet: An elastic modulus is a ratio of stress to strain for a body or a substance which obeys Hooke's Law. Hence an elastic modulus is the slope of the linear region of a stress-strain diagram. The type of elastic modulus is dependent on the type of strain under discussion.

title: Definition:Elastic Modulus/Also known as
snippet: == Elastic Modulus: Also known as == An elastic modulus is also known as a modulus of elasticity.

title: Definition:Elastic Region
snippet: Let a body $\BB$ be deformed under stress. Consider the following stress-strain diagram. 500px The elastic region is the line $OB$, in which when the stress is removed, $\BB$ returns to its original shape.

title: Definition:Elastic String
snippet: An elastic string is an elastic thread whose mass, stiffness and width are approximated to zero. Hence when extended it exhibits elasticity like a spring, but offers no intrinsic restorative force in compression.

title: Definition:Elastic Wave
snippet: An elastic wave is a wave whose mechanism is that a particle of the medium is displaced such that it transfers its momentum to another particle and then returns to its original position. The second particle then causes a further particle to be displaced in the same manner, and so on.

title: Definition:Elasticity
snippet: Elasticity is the property of a (usually) solid body which determines whether and how much it can return to its original shape and size after a deforming force has been removed. The relationship between a deforming force and the resulting change of shape or size can be described using the elastic constants for the body. The deforming force and the resulting deformation are considered in terms of stress and strain.

title: Definition:Eleatic School
snippet: The Eleatic School was a pre-Socratic school of Greek philosophy. Its guiding tenet was the concept of Oneness. God was the eternal Unity, who permeated the universe and guided it with his thought.

title: Definition:Electric Charge
snippet: Electric charge is a physical quantity of matter which causes it to experience a force when near other electrically charged matter. It is a scalar quantity. It has been discovered by experiment that the corresponding force depends on the magnitudes of those electric charges, their displacements from each other, and their velocities.

title: Definition:Electric Charge/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Electric Charge: Conversion Factors == Some conversion factors between the various units of electric charge are as follows: {{eqn | l = \text {corresponds to} | o = | r = 10^{-1} | c = abcoulomb (or e.m.u. of electric charge) }} {{eqn | l = \text {corresponds to (approximately)} | o = | r = 3 \times 10^9 | c = statcoulomb (or e.s.u., or franklin) }}

title: Definition:Electric Charge/Dimension
snippet: The dimension of measurement of electric charge is $\mathsf {I T}$. This derives from its definition as the total electric current flowing over a period of time: $\mathrm Q = \ds \int I \rd t$

title: Definition:Electric Charge/Neutral
snippet: A body which has no electric charge on it is described as (electrically) neutral.

title: Definition:Electric Charge/Polarity
snippet: The polarity of an electric charge can be one of $2$ types:

title: Definition:Electric Charge/Polarity/Convention
snippet: It appears at first glance that the definition of the polarity of an electric charge is both arbitrary and circular. That is: a positive electric charge is the type of electric charge that can be found on a proton while: a proton is defined as carrying a positive electric charge. Early in the development of the theory of electrostatics, it was noticed that there were two types of electric charge. What they were called was indeed arbitrary at that point in time; one type was called positive, and the other type was called negative.

title: Definition:Electric Charge/Polarity/Like
snippet: If $2$ electric charges are of the same polarity, they are referred to as being like (electric) charges. The usage is archaic; the word one would expect is alike.

title: Definition:Electric Charge/Polarity/Negative
snippet: A negative electric charge is an electric charge which is of the same polarity as the electric charge on an electron. When it is necessary to assign a value to a negative electric charge, a $-$ (minus) sign is used, and the value assigned is a negative number.

title: Definition:Electric Charge/Polarity/Positive
snippet: A positive electric charge is an electric charge which is of the same polarity as the electric charge on a proton. When it is necessary to assign a value to a positive electric charge, a $+$ (plus) sign is used, and the value assigned is a positive number.

title: Definition:Electric Charge/Polarity/Unlike
snippet: If $2$ electric charges are of different polarity, they are referred to as being unlike (electric) charges. The usage is archaic; the word one would expect is unalike or non-alike.

title: Definition:Electric Charge/Quantum
snippet: Electric charge has been demonstrated to be quantized. The quantum of electric charge is the elementary charge $\E$: {{eqn | l = \E | r = 1 \cdotp 60217 \, 6634 \times 10^{−19} | c = coulombs exactly (by definition) | cc = }} {{eqn | r = 1 \cdotp 60217 \, 6634 \times 10^{−20} | c = abcoulombs | cc = }} {{eqn | r = 4 \cdotp 80320 \, 425(10) \times 10^{-10} | c = statcoulombs }} This is so small that to all practical purposes in everyday measurement of electricity, it can be treated as though it were continuous.

title: Definition:Electric Charge/Symbol
snippet: The usual symbol used to denote the electric charge on a body is $q$.

title: Definition:Electric Charge/Units
snippet: The SI unit of electric charge is the coulomb $\mathrm C$. In the CGS unrationalised electromagnetic system, the base unit of electric charge is the abcoulomb $\mathrm {abC}$. In the CGS unrationalised electrostatic system, the base unit of electric charge is the statcoulomb $\mathrm {statC}$.

title: Definition:Electric Charge Density
snippet: Let $A$ be a point in space in which an electric field acts. Let $\delta V$ be a volume element containing $A$. The (electric) charge density $\map \rho {\mathbf r}$ at $A$ is defined as: {{eqn | l = \map \rho {\mathbf r} | r = \lim_{\delta V \mathop \to 0} \dfrac Q {\delta V} | c = }} {{eqn | r = \dfrac {\d Q} {\d V} | c = }} where: $Q$ denotes the electric charge within $\delta V$ $\mathbf r$ denotes the position vector of $A$. Thus the electric charge density is the quantity of electric charge per unit volume, at any given point in that volume:

title: Definition:Electric Charge Density/Also known as
snippet: == Electric Charge Density: Also known as == Electric charge density can also be referred to as charge density if it is understood that electric charge is the quantity under discussion.

title: Definition:Electric Charge Density/Dimension
snippet: The dimension of electric charge density is $\mathsf {I T L}^{-3}$: electric charge per unit volume.

title: Definition:Electric Charge Density/Symbol
snippet: == Electric Charge Density: Symbol == The usual symbol used to denote electric charge density is $\rho$ (Greek letter rho).

title: Definition:Electric Charge Density/Units
snippet: The SI units of electric charge density are $\mathrm C \, \mathrm m^{-3}$ (coulombs per cubic metre). Category:Definitions/Electric Charge Density Category:Definitions/Units of Measurement

title: Definition:Electric Current
snippet: Electric current is the physical process caused by the flow of electrically charged particles, usually electrons. Thus it is defined as the rate of flow of electric charge: $I = \dfrac {\d Q} {\d t}$ It is often treated as a scalar quantity, but more properly it is a vector quantity whose direction is that in which the electrically charged particles are traveling.

title: Definition:Electric Current/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Electric Current: Conversion Factors == Some conversion factors between the various units of electric current are as follows: {{eqn | l = \text {corresponds to} | o = | r = 10^{-1} | c = abampere (or e.m.u., or biot) }} {{eqn | l = \text {corresponds to (approximately)} | o = | r = 3 \times 10^9 | c = statampere (or e.s.u. of electric current) }}

title: Definition:Electric Current/Dimension
snippet: Electric current is one of the fundamental dimensions of physics. In dimensional analysis it is assigned the symbol $\mathsf I$.

title: Definition:Electric Current/Mistake
snippet: == Source Work == Introduction Electromagnetic Theory

title: Definition:Electric Current/Symbol
snippet: == Electric Current: Symbol == The usual symbol used to denote an electric current is $I$ or $i$.

title: Definition:Electric Current/Units
snippet: The SI base unit of electric current is the ampere $\mathrm A$. In the CGS unrationalised electromagnetic system, the base unit of electric current is the abampere $\mathrm {abA}$. In the CGS unrationalised electrostatic system, the base unit of electric current is the statampere $\mathrm {statA}$. Category:Definitions/Units of Measurement Category:Definitions/Electric Current

title: Definition:Electric Current Density
snippet: Electric current density is a vector quantity that measures the amount of electric charge that moves through a surface with unit area that is perpendicular to the motion of the charges. It is defined as $\mathbf J \cdot \mathbf n \rd S = \d I$ where $\mathbf J$ is the electric current density $\d S$ is the infinitesimal surface area that the charges are passing through $\mathbf n$ is the normal vector to $\d S$ $\d I$ is the infinitesimal electric current passing through $\d S$.

title: Definition:Electric Current Density/Symbol
snippet: == Electric Current Density: Symbol == The symbol used to denote electric current density is $\mathbf J$.

title: Definition:Electric Current Density/Units
snippet: == Electric Current Density: Units == The SI base unit of electric current density is ampere per square meter: $\mathrm A / \mathrm m^2$ or $\mathrm A \, \mathrm m^{-2}$.

title: Definition:Electric Dipole
snippet: An electric dipole is a pair of point charges of equal but opposite charges $+q$ and $-q$, separated by a constant distance apart.

title: Definition:Electric Displacement Field
snippet: The electric displacement field is a vector quantity defined as the electric field strength multiplied by the permittivity of the medium through which it passes: $\mathbf D = \varepsilon \mathbf E$ where: $\varepsilon$ is the permittivity of the medium $\mathbf E$ is the electric field strength

title: Definition:Electric Displacement Field/Also known as
snippet: == Electric Displacement Field: Also known as == An electric displacement field is also known as electric induction. Category:Definitions/Electric Displacement Field

title: Definition:Electric Displacement Field/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Electric Displacement Field: Conversion Factors == Some conversion factors between the various units of electric displacement field are as follows: {{eqn | r = 10^{-5} | c = e.m.u. of electric displacement }}

title: Definition:Electric Displacement Field/Dimension
snippet: Electric displacement field has the dimension $\mathsf {I T L}^{-2}$.

title: Definition:Electric Displacement Field/Symbol
snippet: == Electric Displacement Field: Symbol == The usual symbol used to denote an electric displacement field is $\mathbf D$.

title: Definition:Electric Displacement Field/Units
snippet: The SI units of electric displacement field are coulombs per square metre: $\mathrm C \, \mathrm m^{-2}$ In the CGS unrationalised electromagnetic system, the unit of electric displacement field is the electromagnetic unit of electric displacement $\mathrm {e.m.u.}$ In the CGS unrationalised electrostatic system, the unit of electric displacement field is the electrostatic unit of electric displacement $\mathrm {e.s.u.}$ Category:Definitions/Electric Displacement Field Category:Definitions/Units of Measurement

title: Definition:Electric Field
snippet: An electric field is a vector field that associates to each point in space the (electrostatic or Coulomb) force per unit of charge exerted on an infinitesimal positive test charge at rest at that point.

title: Definition:Electric Field/Also known as
snippet: == Electric Field: Also known as == An electric field is also known as an electrostatic field. However, that term contains within it the stationary nature of the electric charges giving rise to such a field, whereas in general the charges may well be in motion. Category:Definitions/Electric Fields

title: Definition:Electric Field Strength
snippet: Electric field strength is the measure of the intensity of an electric field. It is defined as: $\mathbf E = \dfrac {\mathbf F} q$ where: $\mathbf E$ denotes the electric field strength at a given point $\mathbf F$ denotes the force exerted on a test charge $q$ by $\mathbf E$ at that point. Electric field strength is a vector quantity.

title: Definition:Electric Field Strength/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Electric Field Strength: Conversion Factors == Some conversion factors between the various units of electric field strength are as follows:

title: Definition:Electric Field Strength/Dimension
snippet: Electric field strength has the dimension $\mathsf {M L T^{-3} I^{-1} }$. This arises from its definition as: force, with dimension $\mathsf {M L T}^{-2}$ per unit electric charge, with dimension $\mathsf {I T}$.

title: Definition:Electric Field Strength/Units
snippet: The SI unit for electric field strength can be given either as: volt per metre: $\mathrm V / \mathrm m$ newton per coulomb: $\mathrm N / \mathrm C$ The CGS unit of electric field strength is the electrostatic unit $\mathrm {e.s.u.}$.

title: Definition:Electric Flux
snippet: Let $\delta \mathbf S$ be an element of a vector area in an electric field whose strength is $\mathbf E$. The electric flux through $\delta \mathbf S$ is defined as the dot product of $\mathbf E$ with $\delta \mathbf S$: $\mathbf E \cdot \delta \mathbf S$ That is, by definition of dot product: the magnitude $E$ of $\mathbf E$ multiplied by: the projection of $\delta \mathbf S$ onto $\mathbf E$ That is: $E \rdelta S \cos \psi$ where $\psi$ is the angle made by $\delta \mathbf S$ with $\mathbf E$.

title: Definition:Electric Flux Density
snippet: Electric flux density is the measure of the intensity of an electric field inside a substance $S$. It is defined as: $\mathbf D = \varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r \mathbf E$ where: $\mathbf E$ denotes the electric field strength at a given point within $S$ $\varepsilon_0$ denotes the vacuum permittivity $\varepsilon_r$ denotes the relative permittivity of $S$ Electric flux density is a vector quantity.

title: Definition:Electric Flux Density/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Electric Flux Density: Conversion Factors == Some conversion factors between the various units of electric flux density are as follows: {{eqn | r = \dfrac 1 {12 \pi} \times 10^{-5} | c = coulombs per square metre }}

title: Definition:Electric Flux Density/Dimension
snippet: Electric flux density has the dimension $\mathsf {I T L^{-2} }$.

title: Definition:Electric Flux Density/Units
snippet: The SI unit for electric flux density is the coulomb per square metre: $\mathrm {C / m^2}$ The CGS unit of electric flux density is the electrostatic unit $\mathrm {e.s.u.}$.

title: Definition:Electric Polarization
snippet: Electric polarization is the slight relative shift of positive and negative electric charge in opposite directions within an insulator, induced by an external electric field.

title: Definition:Electric Polarization/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Electric Polarization: Conversion Factors == Some conversion factors between the various units of electric polarization are as follows:

title: Definition:Electric Polarization/Dimension
snippet: Electric polarization has the dimension $\mathsf {I T L^{-2} }$.

title: Definition:Electric Polarization/Units
snippet: The SI unit of electric polarization is the coulomb per square metre: $\mathrm {C / m^2}$. In the CGS unrationalised electromagnetic system, the unit of electric polarization is the electromagnetic unit of electric displacement $\mathrm {e.m.u.}$ In the CGS unrationalised electrostatic system, the unit of electric polarization is the electrostatic unit of electric displacement $\mathrm {e.s.u.}$ Category:Definitions/Units of Measurement Category:Definitions/Electric Polarization

title: Definition:Electric Potential/Also known as
snippet: == Electric Potential Also known as == An electric potential is also known as: electric field potential potential drop or potential difference electrostatic potential. In common parlance, an electric potential is referred to as voltage, from the fact that it is usually specified in volts. Some sources also use this term, but this is deprecated on .

title: Definition:Electric Potential/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Electric Potential: Conversion Factors == Some conversion factors between the various units of electric potential are as follows: {{eqn | l = \text {corresponds to} | o = | r = 10^8 | c = abvolt (or e.m.u. of electric potential) }} {{eqn | l = \text {corresponds to (approximately)} | o = | r = \dfrac 1 3 \times 10^{-2} | c = statvolt (or e.s.u. of electric potential) }}

title: Definition:Electric Potential/Dimension
snippet: The dimension of measurement of electric potential is $\mathsf M \mathsf L^2 \mathsf T^{−3} \mathsf I^{−1}$.

title: Definition:Electric Potential/Symbol
snippet: The usual symbol used to denote the electric potential on a body is $v$.

title: Definition:Electric Potential/Units
snippet: The SI unit of electric potential is the volt $\mathrm V$. In the CGS unrationalised electromagnetic system, the base unit of electric potential is the abvolt $\mathrm {abV}$. In the CGS unrationalised electrostatic system, the base unit of electric potential is the statvolt $\mathrm {statV}$. Category:Definitions/Units of Measurement Category:Definitions/Electric Potential

title: Definition:Electrical Component
snippet: An electrical component is a device whose purpose is to control electricity in a specific manner.

title: Definition:Electrical Conductor
snippet: An electrical conductor is a type of substance which allows a flow of electric charge to pass through it. This is because a certain proportion of the electrons are not attached to any atom in particular, and can be induced to move through the substance under the influence of an electric field.

title: Definition:Electrical Conductor/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Electrical Conductor == Category:Definitions/Electrical Conductors

title: Definition:Electrical Conductor/Examples/Electrolyte
snippet: == Example of an Electrical Conductor ==

title: Definition:Electrical Conductor/Examples/Metal
snippet: == Example of an Electrical Conductor ==

title: Definition:Electrical Insulator
snippet: An electrical insulator is a substance which allows practically no electric current to flow through it. This effect is caused by the fact that in such substances all the electrons are firmly attached to the positively charged nuclei of the atoms to which they belong. Hence they cannot be induced to move under the influence of an electric field, unless the latter is overwhelmingly large.

title: Definition:Electrical Insulator/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Electrical Insulators ==

title: Definition:Electrical Insulator/Examples/Amber
snippet: == Example of Electrical Insulator == is a good electrical insulator.

title: Definition:Electrical Insulator/Examples/Glass
snippet: == Example of Electrical Insulator == is a good electrical insulator.

title: Definition:Electrical Insulator/Examples/Porcelain
snippet: == Example of Electrical Insulator == is a good electrical insulator. In order to overcome the forces which bind its electrons to its atoms, an electric field of the order of $10^9 \ \mathrm V \, \mathrm m^{-1}$ is needed.

title: Definition:Electrical Insulator/Examples/Shellac
snippet: == Example of Electrical Insulator == is a good electrical insulator.

title: Definition:Electricity
snippet: Electricity is a phenomenon of physics associated with the behavior of matter that has a property of electric charge.

title: Definition:Electrolyte
snippet: An electrolyte is a liquid which is characterised by the fact that its molecules are easily ionized into positively charged and negatively charged ions. These are free to move independently of each other, and hence move through the liquid under the influence of a potential difference. This gives rise to an electric current.

title: Definition:Electrolyte/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Electrolytes ==

title: Definition:Electrolyte/Examples/Dilute Sulphuric Acid
snippet: == Example of Electrolyte == Dilute sulphuric acid is an electrolyte. The molecules of sulphuric acid separate into: positive ions containing a hydrogen nucleus negative sulphate ions. Under the influence of a potential difference, a current flows that consists of: the positive ions moving towards the negative charge together with: the negative sulphate ions moving towards the positive charge.

title: Definition:Electromagnetic Field
snippet: An electromagnetic field is a physical field which describes the interaction between magnetic fields and electric fields, which affect the behaviour of charged bodies.

title: Definition:Electromagnetic Field Tensor
snippet: The electromagnetic field tensor is the tensor which defines the electromagnetic field of a physical system.

title: Definition:Electromagnetic Field Tensor/Motivation
snippet: == Electromagnetic Field Tensor: Motivation == Use of the electromagnetic field tensor allows for a very concise and compact form for Maxwell's equations.

title: Definition:Electromagnetic Force
snippet: The electromagnetic force is one of the four fundamental forces of nature. It is the dominant force in the interactions of atoms and molecules.

title: Definition:Electromagnetic Induction
snippet: Electromagnetic induction is the phenomenon whereby an electromotive force is generated across an electrical conductor in a changing magnetic field.

title: Definition:Electromagnetic Potential
snippet: The electromagnetic potentials are quantities which simplify Maxwell's Equations:

title: Definition:Electromagnetic Potential/Electric Scalar Potential
snippet: The electric scalar potential is the quantity $\phi$ defined as: $\mathbf E = -\nabla \phi - \dfrac 1 c \dfrac {\partial \mathbf A} {\partial t}$ where: $\mathbf E$ is the electric field strength $c$ is the speed of light $\nabla$ is the gradient operator $\mathbf A$ is the magnetic vector potential.

title: Definition:Electromagnetic Potential/Extra Condition
snippet: As defined, the electromagnetic potentials are not uniquely determined. Hence they are normally chosen to satisfy the extra condition: $\nabla \cdot \mathbf A + \dfrac 1 c \dfrac {\partial \phi} {\partial t} = 0$ where: $\nabla \cdot$ is the divergence operator $\phi$ is the electric scalar potential $c$ is the speed of light $\mathbf A$ is the magnetic vector potential.

title: Definition:Electromagnetic Potential/Magnetic Vector Potential
snippet: The magnetic vector potential is the quantity $\mathbf A$ defined as: $\mathbf B = \nabla \times \mathbf A$ where: $\mathbf B$ is the magnetic flux density $\nabla \times$ is the curl operator.

title: Definition:Electromagnetic Radiation
snippet: Electromagnetic radiation is a physical process whereby a changing electric field brings about a changing magnetic field, which in turn brings about a changing electric field. These effects propagate through space in the form of waves. The components of the vectors comprising the electric field and magnetic field oscillate in planes perpendicular both to each other and the direction of travel of the wave.

title: Definition:Electromagnetic Theory
snippet: Electromagnetic theory is the branch of physics concerned with the study of the combined phenomena of electricity and magnetism, and their interconnected nature. This phenomenon is usually referred to as electromagnetism.

title: Definition:Electromagnetic Theory/Also known as
snippet: == Electromagnetic Theory: Also known as == Some sources refer to the subject of electromagnetic theory as electromagnetism. However, takes the position that electromagnetism is the word for the physical phenomenon in question, rather than the study of it. Category:Definitions/Electromagnetic Theory

title: Definition:Electromagnetic Unit
snippet: The electromagnetic unit is the CGS unit of electric current.

title: Definition:Electromagnetic Wave
snippet: An electromagnetic wave is caused by an oscillating electric field which causes and is caused by an oscillating magnetic field, both perpendicular to the direction of propagation of the wave. Neither of these fields causes or is caused by displacement of the particles of the medium in which the wave propagates. Hence an electromagnetic wave can propagate through a vacuum.

title: Definition:Electromagnetism
snippet: Electromagnetism is a phenomenon of physics associated with the interactions of electricity and magnetism.

title: Definition:Electromagnetism/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Electromagnetism == Many advances in communications and medical technology are based on electromagnetism.

title: Definition:Electromotive Force
snippet: Electromotive force is a quantity that measures the source of potential energy in an electronic circuit. It is defined as the amount of work per unit electric charge. It can be denoted $\EE$.

title: Definition:Electromotive Force/Also known as
snippet: == Electromotive Force: Also known as == Electromotive force can be abbreviated EMF, emf or e.m.f, and so on. In common parlance, an electromotive force is referred to as voltage, from the fact that it is usually specified in volts. Some sources also use this term, but this is deprecated on . Category:Definitions/Electromotive Force

title: Definition:Electromotive Force/Dimension
snippet: The dimension of measurement of electromotive force is $\mathsf {M L}^2 \mathsf T^{-3} \mathsf I^{-1}$. This derives from its definition as: $\dfrac {\text{Work} } {\text {Charge} }$

title: Definition:Electromotive Force/Symbol
snippet: == Electromotive Force: Symbol == The usual symbol used to denote electromotive force is $\EE$. Category:Definitions/Electromotive Force

title: Definition:Electromotive Force/Unit
snippet: The SI unit of electromotive force is the volt $\mathrm V$: $1 \ \mathrm V = 1 \ \mathrm J \ \mathrm C^{-1}$ that is, $1$ joule per coulomb. In the CGS unrationalised electromagnetic system, the base unit of electromotive force is the abvolt $\mathrm {abV}$. In the CGS unrationalised electrostatic system, the base unit of electromotive force is the statvolt $\mathrm {statV}$. Category:Definitions/Units of Measurement Category:Definitions/Electromotive Force

title: Definition:Electron
snippet: == Electron == An electron is an elementary particle which contains a single unit of negative elementary electric charge.

title: Definition:Electron/Charge
snippet: == Electric Charge on Electron == The electric charge on the electron is $-1.60217 \, 6634 \times 10^{−19}$ coulombs. That is, a negative charge whose magnitude is the value of the elementary charge.

title: Definition:Electron/Charge/Also known as
snippet: == Charge on Electron: Also known as == The electric charge on the electron is also known as the electronic charge.

title: Definition:Electron/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Electron == The electron was discovered by , who measured the Electron Charge to Mass Ratio in $1897$. This happened as a result of several decades of work by many scientists.

title: Definition:Electron/Historical Note/Mistake
snippet: == Source Work == Chapter $\text {I}$: Preliminary Survey $\S 1$. Electrostatics

title: Definition:Electron/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Electron == The form of the word electron is electronic. Hence the word electronics as a collective term for devices exploiting the behaviour of electrons Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Electron/Mass
snippet: == Mass of Electron == The mass of the electron is given as: {{eqn | l = m_\E | o = \approx | r = 9 \cdotp 10938 \, 37015 \, (28) \times 10^{-31} | c = kilograms | cc= }} {{eqn | o = \approx | r = 9 \cdotp 10938 \, 37015 \, (28) \times 10^{-28} | c = grams | cc= }} {{eqn | o = \approx | r = 5 \cdotp 48579 \, 90906 \, 5(16) \times 10^{-4} | c = daltons | cc= }}

title: Definition:Electron/Mass/Also known as
snippet: == Mass of Electron: Also known as == The mass of the electron is also known as: the electronic rest mass the electron rest mass.

title: Definition:Electron/Radius
snippet: == Radius of Electron == The actual size of the electron is still unknown. The current best estimate is that its radius has an upper limit of the order of $10^{-22}$ metres.

title: Definition:Electron Cloud
snippet: == Physical Law == Within an atom, an electron is not a stationary point charge. According to quantum mechanics, it is not possible to determine the actual position of an electron at any specific instant of time. Instead, it is more realistic to consider an electron as "smeared out" in an electron cloud around the nucleus.

title: Definition:Electron Volt/Also known as
snippet: == Electron Volt: Also known as == The term electron volt can also be seen presented without a space: electronvolt.

title: Definition:Electron Volt/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Electron Volt: Conversion Factors == {{eqn | r = 1.60217 \, 6634 \times 10^{−19} | c = joule | cc= (exact) }}

title: Definition:Electronic Circuit
snippet: An electronic circuit is a configuration of electrical components whose collective properties can be modelled by means of a network each of whose edges corresponds to a specific component. Its purpose is to guide and direct energy within a device.

title: Definition:Electronic Circuit/Also known as
snippet: == Electronic Circuit: Also known as == An electronic circuit can also be referred to as: an electric circuit an electrical circuit. Some sources refer merely to a circuit, but without extra context this concept is ambiguous.

title: Definition:Electronics
snippet: Electronics is the branch of electromagnetism which studies how to control electricity.

title: Definition:Electrostatic Force
snippet: An electrostatic force is the force exerted on an electric charge caused by an electric field due to stationary electric charges. Electrostatic force is a vector quantity. The magnitude and direction of an electrostatic force depends upon the positions and magnitudes of those electric charges.

title: Definition:Electrostatic Force/Also known as
snippet: == Electrostatic Force: Also known as == An electrostatic force is also known as a Coulomb force for . Some sources refer to it as electric force.

title: Definition:Electrostatic Unit
snippet: The electrostatic unit is the CGS unit of electric charge.

title: Definition:Electrostatics
snippet: Electrostatics is the branch of physics concerned with the study of stationary electrically charged bodies, and the forces and fields they give rise to.

title: Definition:Electrostatics/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Electrostatics == The phenomenon of static electricity was known about as early as $2500$ years ago, when remarked on the fact that a piece of amber, when rubbed, can attract small particles of matter. From this demonstration has evolved the entire field of electrostatics.

title: Definition:Element
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. An element of $S$ is a member of $S$.

title: Definition:Element/Also known as
snippet: The term member is sometimes used as a synonym for element (probably more for the sake of linguistic variation than anything else). In the contexts of geometry and topology, elements of a set are often called points, in particular when they are (geometric) points. $x \in S$ can also be read as: $x$ is in $S$ $x$ belongs to $S$ $S$ includes $x$ $x$ is included in $S$ $S$ contains $x$ However, beware of this latter usage: $S$ contains $x$ can also be interpreted as $x$ is a subset of $S$.

title: Definition:Element/Class
snippet: Let $S$ be a class. An element of $S$ is a member of $S$.

title: Definition:Element/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Element == The symbol for is an element of originated as $\varepsilon$, first used by in his of $1889$. It comes from the first letter of the Greek word meaning is. The stylized version $\in$ was first used by in in $1903$. See [http://jeff560.tripod.com/set.html Earliest Uses of Symbols of Set Theory and Logic] in Jeff Miller's website [http://jeff560.tripod.com/mathsym.html Earliest Uses of Various Mathematical Symbols]. $x \mathop \varepsilon S$ could still be seen in works as late as and .

title: Definition:Element/Notation
snippet:
The symbol universally used in modern mainstream mathematics to mean $x$ is an element of $S$ is: $x \in S$ Similarly, $x 
otin S$ means $x$ is not an element of $S$. The symbol can be reversed: $S 
i x$ means $S$ has $x$ as an element, that is, $x$ is an element of $S$ but this is rarely seen. Some texts (usually older ones) use $x \mathop {\overline \in} S$ or $x \mathop {\in'} S$ instead of $x 
otin S$.

title: Definition:Element is Way Below
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $x, y \in S$. Then $x$ is way below $y$, denoted $x \ll y$, : for every directed subset $D$ of $S$: if $D$ admits a supremum and $y \preceq \sup D$ then there exists $d \in D$ such that $x \preceq d$

title: Definition:Element of Array/Also denoted as
snippet: == Element of Array: Also denoted as == Some sources prefer to use the uppercase form of the letter for the element: $ A_{i j}$ Category:Definitions/Arrays

title: Definition:Element of Array/Also known as
snippet: == Element of Array: Also known as == The elements of an array are sometimes seen as entries of an array. Category:Definitions/Arrays

title: Definition:Element of Contact
snippet: Let $\SS$ be a surface embedded in a Cartesian $3$-space. Let $\TT$ be a tangent plane to $\SS$. The set of points at which $\TT$ intersects $\SS$ is called the element of contact between $\SS$ and $\TT$.

title: Definition:Element of Integration
snippet: Consider the indefinite integral: $\ds \int \map f x \rd x$ or the definite integral: $\ds \int_a^b \map f x \rd x$ The part of the expression after the integral sign: $\map f x \rd x$ is known as the element of the integration operation.

title: Definition:Element of Matrix/Also known as
snippet: == Element of Matrix: Also known as == An element of a matrix is sometimes seen as entry of a matrix, or just (matrix) entry. Earlier sources may be seen to use the words constituent or even coordinate, but these names have now been superseded.

title: Definition:Elementary Abelian P-Group
snippet: Let $G$ be an abelian group. Then $G$ is an elementary abelian $p$-group all its non-trivial elements are of order $p$.

title: Definition:Elementary Charge/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Elementary Charge == Until the $2019$ definition of the elementary charge as exactly $\E = 1.60217 \, 6634 \times 10^{−19} \, \mathrm C$, it was the subject of measurement. This measurement has been accomplished to greater and greater accuracy over time. By $1964$, it was established as: $\E = 1 \cdotp 60219 \, 17 \pm 0 \cdotp 00000 \, 70 \times 10^{−19} \, \mathrm C$ Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Elementary Charge/Symbol
snippet: The symbol used to denote the elementary charge is usually $\E$ or $e$. The preferred symbol on is $\E$.

title: Definition:Elementary Charge/Technical Note
snippet: == Technical Note for Elementary Charge == This command is specific to . Category:Technical Notes

title: Definition:Elementary Column Operation/Also known as
snippet: == Elementary Column Operation: Also known as == Some sources refer to an elementary column operation as just a column operation. The abbreviation ECO is commonly used.

title: Definition:Elementary Embedding
snippet: Let $\MM$ and $\NN$ be $\LL$-structures with universes $M$ and $N$ respectively. An $\LL$-embedding $j:\MM \to \NN$ is an elementary embedding it preserves truth; that is: $\MM \models \map \phi {a_1, \ldots, a_n} \iff \NN \models \map \phi {\map j {a_1}, \ldots, \map j {a_n} }$ holds for all $n \in \N$, all $\LL$-formulas $\phi$ with $n$ free variables, and for all $a_1, \ldots, a_n \in M$.

title: Definition:Elementary Embedding/Partial Elementary Embedding
snippet: Let $\MM$ and $\NN$ be $\LL$-structures with universes $M$ and $N$ respectively. Let $A \subseteq M$ be a subsets of $M$. $j: A \to \NN$ is a partial elementary embedding it is a partial $\LL$-embedding which preserves truth for elements of $A$; that is: $\MM \models \map \phi {a_1, \ldots, a_n} \iff \NN \models \map \phi {\map j {a_1}, \ldots, \map j {a_n} }$ holds for all $n \in \N$, all $\LL$-formulas $\phi$ with $n$ free variables, and for all $a_1, \ldots, a_n \in A$.

title: Definition:Elementary Equivalence
snippet: Let $\MM, \NN$ be $\LL$-structures. We say that $\MM$ and $\NN$ are elementarily equivalent if for all $\LL$-sentences $\phi$, we have $\MM \models \phi$ $\NN \models \phi$. Category:Definitions/Model Theory for Predicate Logic

title: Definition:Elementary Event
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an experiment. An elementary event of $\EE$, often denoted $\omega$ (Greek lowercase omega) is one of the elements of the sample space $\Omega$ (Greek capital omega) of $\EE$.

title: Definition:Elementary Event/Also known as
snippet: == Elementary Event: Also known as == An elementary event is one of the possible outcomes of $\EE$. Thus outcome means the same thing as elementary event. Some sources refer to an elementary event as a sample point.

title: Definition:Elementary Function
snippet: An elementary function is one of the following: The constant function: $\map {f_c} x = c$ where $c \in \R$ Powers of $x$: $\map f x = x^y$, where $y \in \R$ Exponentials: $\map f x = e^x$ Natural logarithms: $\map f x = \ln x$ Trigonometric functions: $\map f x = \sin x$, $\map f x = \cos x$ Inverse trigonometric functions: $\map f x = \arcsin x$, $\map f x = \arccos x$ All functions that are compositions of the above, for example $\map f x = \ln \sin x$, $\map f x = e^{\cos x}$ All functions obtained by adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing any of the above types any finite number of…

title: Definition:Elementary Matrix/Also known as
snippet: == Elementary Matrix: Also known as == In treatments of linear algebra and matrix theory, it is usual to focus attention on elementary row operations and their associated elementary row matrices. Hence it is usual to use the term elementary matrix to mean exclusively an elementary row matrix. When handling elementary column operations, the full term is then used: elementary column matrix. On , where both treatments are discussed, it will be usual to use the full description for both types of elementary matrix.

title: Definition:Elementary Matrix/Column Operation
snippet: Let $\mathbf E$ be a unit matrix on which exactly one elementary column operation $e$ has been performed. Then $\mathbf E$ is called the elementary column matrix for the elementary column operation $e$.

title: Definition:Elementary Matrix/Row Operation
snippet: Let $\mathbf E$ be a unit matrix on which exactly one elementary row operation $e$ has been performed. Then $\mathbf E$ is called the elementary row matrix for the elementary row operation $e$.

title: Definition:Elementary Matrix Operation/Also presented as
snippet: == Elementary Matrix Operation: Also presented as == The order of presentation of the elementary matrix operations, either row or column, may vary according to the source. Some sources use the Greek letter $\rho$ to enumerate the rows, and $\kappa$ to enumerate the columns, and jocularly remind us that the name rho of the letter $\rho$ is pronounced row. Category:Definitions/Elementary Matrix Operations

title: Definition:Elementary Operation
snippet: The elementary operations are: addition subtraction multiplication division finding integer roots.

title: Definition:Elementary Operation/Column
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ be an $m \times n$ matrix over a field $K$. The elementary column operations on $\mathbf A$ are operations which act upon the columns of $\mathbf A$ as follows. For some $i, j \in \closedint 1 n: i \ne j$: {{axiom | n = \text {ECO} 1 | t = For some $\lambda \in K_{\ne 0}$, multiply column $i$ by $\lambda$ | m = \kappa_i \to \lambda \kappa_i }} {{axiom | n = \text {ECO} 2 | t = For some $\lambda \in K$, add $\lambda$ times column $j$ to column $i$ | m = \kappa_i \to \kappa_i + \lambda \kappa_j }} {{axiom | n = \text {ECO} 3 | t = Interchange columns $i$ and $j$…

title: Definition:Elementary Operation/Row
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ be an $m \times n$ matrix over a field $K$. The elementary row operations on $\mathbf A$ are operations which act upon the rows of $\mathbf A$ as follows. For some $i, j \in \closedint 1 m: i \ne j$: {{axiom | n = \text {ERO} 1 | t = For some $\lambda \in K_{\ne 0}$, multiply row $i$ by $\lambda$ | m = r_i \to \lambda r_i }} {{axiom | n = \text {ERO} 2 | t = For some $\lambda \in K$, add $\lambda$ times row $j$ to row $i$ | m = r_i \to r_i + \lambda r_j }} {{axiom | n = \text {ERO} 3 | t = Exchange rows $i$ and $j$ | m = r_i \leftrightarrow r_j }}

title: Definition:Elementary Particle
snippet: An elementary particle is one of the basic building blocks of matter. To a first degree of approximation, those building blocks can be considered to be protons, neutrons and electrons. Modern research in particle physics suggests the existence of smaller constituents of protons and neutrons, but at time of writing, electrons are believe to be truly, fundamentally indivisible.

title: Definition:Elementary Reduction of Group Word on Set
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $v$ and $w$ be group words on $X$. Let $n$ be the length of $v$. Then $w$ is an elementary reduction of $v$ : $w$ has length $n - 2$ There exists $k \in \set {1, \ldots, n - 1}$ such that: $v_k = {v_{k + 1} }^{-1}$ $w_i = \begin {cases} v_i & : i k + 1 \end {cases}$ This is denoted $v \overset 1 \longrightarrow w$.

title: Definition:Elementary Row Operation/Also known as
snippet: == Elementary Row Operation: Also known as == Some sources refer to an elementary row operation as just a row operation. The abbreviation ERO is commonly used.

title: Definition:Elementary Symmetric Function/Also known as
snippet: == Elementary Symmetric Function: Also known as == An elementary symmetric function is also known as an elementary symmetric polynomial. Category:Definitions/Elementary Symmetric Functions

title: Definition:Elementary Symmetric Function/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Elementary Symmetric Function == Let $U$ be established such that $\size U = n$. It is commonplace for $U$ to be presented in the form $\set {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$. Consequently, the elementary symmetric function of degree $m$ is often presented $\map {e_m} {\set {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} }$, which is unwieldy.

title: Definition:Elementary Symmetric Polynomial
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $K \sqbrk {X_1, \ldots, X_n}$ be the ring of polynomial forms over $K$. The elementary symmetric polynomials in $n$ variables are: $\ds \map {f_r} {X_1, \ldots, X_n} = \sum_{1 \mathop \le i_1 \mathop < \cdots \mathop < i_r \mathop \le n} x_{i_1} \cdots x_{i_r}$ for $r = 1, \ldots, n$.

title: Definition:Elementary Unit
snippet: Every substance is composed of indivisible particles of that substance. These particles are referred to as the elementary units of that substance.

title: Definition:Elementary Unit/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Elementary Units == Elementary units may be: atoms (of a specified element) molecules (of a specified substance) ions (of a specified type) electrons photons and so on.

title: Definition:Elementary Valid Argument
snippet: An elementary valid argument is a logical argument which is a substitution instance of an elementary valid argument form. The argument forms which are considered to be elementary valid argument forms will depend on the specific approach to propositional logic which is under discussion.

title: Definition:Elevated/Line
snippet: Let $P$ be a plane. An elevated line (relative to $P$) is a line in space which does not lie entirely in $P$. Category:Definitions/Solid Geometry

title: Definition:Elevated/Point
snippet: Let $P$ be a plane. An elevated point (relative to $P$) is a point in space which does not lie on $P$. Category:Definitions/Solid Geometry

title: Definition:Elevation of Point
snippet: The elevation of a point $P$ is the height of $P$ above some reference horizontal baseline or plane.

title: Definition:Eliminant
snippet: Let $S$ be a system of simultaneous linear equations. The eliminant of $S$ is the determinant formed by removing the variables between the equations.

title: Definition:Eliminant/Also known as
snippet: == Eliminant: Also known as == An eliminant is also known as a resultant.

title: Definition:Elimination
snippet: Elimination is the process of solving a system of simultaneous equations by removing variables by algebra.

title: Definition:Elimination Method
snippet: The elimination method is a technique of finding the solution to a system of simultaneous linear equations. The technique reduces the number of independent variables by taking appropriate linear combinations of the equations.

title: Definition:Ellipse/Axis
snippet: Let $K$ be an ellipse whose foci are at $F_1$ and $F_2$.

title: Definition:Ellipse/Covertex
snippet: 500px Consider an ellipse $K$. A covertex of $K$ is either one of the endpoints of the minor axis of $K$. In the above diagram, $C_1$ and $C_2$ are the covertices of $K$.

title: Definition:Ellipse/Directrix
snippet: Let $K$ be the ellipse specified as the locus of points $P$ to a straight line $D$ and a point $F$ such that $PD$ and $PF$ are related by the condition: $\size {PF} = e \size {PD}$ where $0 < e < 1$. The line $D$ is known as the directrix of the ellipse.

title: Definition:Ellipse/Eccentricity
snippet: Let $K$ be the ellipse specified as the locus of points $P$ to a straight line $D$ and a point $F$ such that $PD$ and $PF$ are related by the condition: $\size {PF} = e \size {PD}$ where $0 < e < 1$. The constant $e$ is known as the eccentricity of the ellipse.

title: Definition:Ellipse/Equidistance
snippet: 400px Let $F_1$ and $F_2$ be two points in the plane. Let $d$ be a length greater than the distance between $F_1$ and $F_2$. Let $K$ be the locus of points $P$ which are subject to the condition: $d_1 + d_2 = d$ where: $d_1$ is the distance from $P$ to $F_1$ $d_2$ is the distance from $P$ to $F_2$. Then $K$ is an ellipse. This property is known as the equidistance property. The points $F_1$ and $F_2$ are the foci of $K$.

title: Definition:Ellipse/Focus
snippet: Let $K$ be an ellipse specified in terms of: a given straight line $D$ a given point $F$ a given constant $\epsilon$ such that $0 < \epsilon < 1$ where $K$ is the locus of points $P$ such that the distance $p$ from $P$ to $D$ and the distance $q$ from $P$ to $F$ are related by the condition: $q = \epsilon \, p$ The point $F$ is known as the focus of the ellipse.

title: Definition:Ellipse/Focus-Directrix
snippet: 400px Let $D$ be a straight line. Let $F$ be a point. Let $e \in \R: 0 < e < 1$. Let $K$ be the locus of points $P$ such that the distance $p$ from $P$ to $D$ and the distance $q$ from $P$ to $F$ are related by the condition: $e p = q$ Then $K$ is an ellipse.

title: Definition:Ellipse/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Ellipse == The word ellipse was provided by , who did considerable work on establishing its properties.

title: Definition:Ellipse/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Ellipse == The word ellipse is pronounced with the stress on the second syllable: el-lipse. The adjectival form of ellipse is elliptical, that is: denoting or concerning an ellipse.

title: Definition:Ellipse/Major Axis
snippet: 500px Consider an ellipse $K$ whose foci are $F_1$ and $F_2$.

title: Definition:Ellipse/Major Axis/Semimajor Axis
snippet: 500px Consider an ellipse $K$. A semimajor axis of $K$ is either half of the major axis of $K$ from its midpoint to its endpoint. In the above diagram, $O V_1$ and $O V_2$ are the semimajor axes of $K$.

title: Definition:Ellipse/Minor Axis
snippet: 500px Consider an ellipse $K$ whose foci are $F_1$ and $F_2$.

title: Definition:Ellipse/Minor Axis/Semiminor Axis
snippet: 500px Consider an ellipse $K$. A semiminor axis of $K$ is either half of the minor axis of $K$ from its midpoint to its endpoint. In the above diagram, $O C_1$ and $O C_2$ are the semiminor axes of $K$.

title: Definition:Ellipse/Vertex
snippet: 500px Let $K$ be an ellipse. A vertex of $K$ is either of the two endpoints of the major axis of $K$. In the above diagram, $V_1$ and $V_2$ are the vertices of $K$.

title: Definition:Ellipsoid
snippet: An ellipsoid is a conicoid whose plane sections are circles or ellipses.

title: Definition:Ellipsoid/Diameter
snippet: A chord of an ellipsoid $\EE$ which passes through the center of $\EE$ is called a diameter of $\EE$.

title: Definition:Ellipsoid/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Ellipsoid == The adjectival form of ellipsoid is ellipsoidal, that is: denoting or concerning an ellipsoid.

title: Definition:Ellipsoid/Major Axis
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an ellipsoid. The major axis of $\EE$ is the chord of $\EE$ which has the greatest length.

title: Definition:Elliptic Curve
snippet: An elliptic curve is a non-singular plane curve $C$ embedded in the Cartesian plane such that: $C$ can be defined by a polynomial equation such that: the coefficients of $C$ are rational the genus of $C$ is $1$ $C$ has at least $1$ rational lattice point.

title: Definition:Elliptic Curve/Also defined as
snippet: == Elliptic Curve: Also defined as == In their definition of elliptic curve, some sources omit to mention explicitly that such a curve must be non-singular. It will be noted, however, that non-singularity is already one of the conditions for a curve to be of genus of $1$, so this condition is technically redundant.

title: Definition:Elliptic Curve/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Elliptic Curve == The study of elliptic curves and their rational lattice points was instrumental in the proof of Fermat's Last Theorem.

title: Definition:Elliptic Curve/Standard Form
snippet: Let $C$ be an elliptic curve embedded in the Cartesian plane. $C$ is expressed in standard form when the equation defining its locus is in the form: $y^2 = x^3 + a x + b$ where: $a$ and $b$ are rational numbers the cubic $x^3 + a x + b$ has distinct zeroes.

title: Definition:Elliptic Function/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\phi: \C \to \C$ be a meromorphic function. Then $\phi$ is an elliptic function it is also doubly periodic. That is, there exist $\omega_1, \omega_2 \in \C$ such that: $(1): \quad \omega_1, \omega_2 \ne 0$ $(2): \quad \dfrac {\omega_1} {\omega_2} \notin \R$ $(3): \quad \forall z \in \C: \map \phi z = \map \phi {z + \omega_1} = \map \phi {z + \omega_2}$ that is: $(3): \quad \forall z \in \C: \forall m, n \in \Z: \map \phi z = \map \phi {z + m \omega_1 + n\omega_2}$

title: Definition:Elliptic Function/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\ds \map y x = \int_0^x \dfrac {\d t} {\sqrt {\map P t} }$ be an elliptic integral, where $\map P t$ is a polynomial of degree $3$ or $4$. Consider the inverse of $\map y x$: $x = \map \phi y$ Then $\phi$ is an elliptic function.

title: Definition:Elliptic Function/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Elliptic Function == Elliptic functions were first explored by in $1827$, after his discovery of them as the inverses of elliptic integrals. then continued the work in . However, it turned out that had actually got there first, but had never got round to publishing his work. noticed a passage in 's (Article $335$) in which it was clear that ' had already arrived at the same results that had done, but some $30$ years before.

snippet: == Source Work == elliptic functions

title: Definition:Elliptic Geometry
snippet: Elliptic geometry is a branch of non-Euclidean geometry in which every straight line that passes through a point meets another straight line.

title: Definition:Elliptic Geometry/Also known as
snippet: == Elliptic Geometry: Also known as == Elliptic geometry is also known as Riemannian geometry, although the latter term properly applies to something far more general.

title: Definition:Elliptic Integral
snippet: == Special Function == An elliptic integral is an integral in the form: $\ds \int_0^x \map R {t, \sqrt {\map P t} } \rd t$ where: $\map P t$ is a polynomial of degree $3$ or $4$ $\map R {t, \sqrt {\map P t} }$ is a rational function of $t$ and $\sqrt {\map P t}$. There exist some special cases:

title: Definition:Elliptic Integral/Also defined as
snippet: == Elliptic Integral: Also defined as == Some sources define an elliptic integral as an integral in the form: $\ds \int_c^x \map R {t, \sqrt {\map P t} } \rd t$ where: $\map P t$ is a polynomial of degree $3$ or $4$ $\map R {t, \sqrt {\map P t} }$ is a rational function of $t$ and $\sqrt {\map P t}$ $c$ is a real constant. Some sources present it in the form: $\ds \int \map R {t, \sqrt {\map P t} } \rd t$ but how useful it is to define it as an indefinite integral is questionable.

title: Definition:Elliptic Integral/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Elliptic Integral == The elliptic integrals were called that because they were first encountered in the problem of determining the length of the perimeter of an ellipse. When the inverse functions of the elliptic integrals were studied, this led to the discovery of elliptic functions.

title: Definition:Elliptic Modulus
snippet: Let $\EE$ be one of Legendre's standard elliptic integrals in the form: $\ds \int \limits_0^x \map F {\sqrt {1 - k^2 v^2} } \rd v$ The coefficient $k$ is known as the (elliptic) modulus of $\EE$.

title: Definition:Elliptic Partial Differential Equation
snippet: Let $\EE$ be the second-order linear partial differential equation: $A \dfrac {\partial^2 f} {\partial x^2} + B \dfrac {\partial^2 f} {\partial x \partial y} + C \dfrac {\partial^2 f} {\partial y^2} + D \dfrac {\partial f} {\partial x} + E \dfrac {\partial f} {\partial y} + F f + G = 0$ where $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, $F$ and $G$ are functions of $x$ and $y$. $\EE$ is an elliptic partial differential equation : $B^2 - 4 A C < 0$

title: Definition:Elliptic Plane
snippet: Let $\SS$ be a sphere. Let antipodal points of $\SS$ be identified with each other. Then what results is called the elliptic plane.

title: Definition:Elliptical Cylinder
snippet: An elliptical cylinder is a cylinder which has a base whose shape is an ellipse.

title: Definition:Elliptical Cylinder/Also defined as
snippet: == Elliptical Cylinder: Also defined as == Some sources define an elliptical cylinder specifying that the bases are to be perpendicular to the generatrices. That is, as refers to as a right elliptical cylinder.

title: Definition:Elliptical Cylinder/Also known as
snippet: == Elliptical Cylinder: Also known as == An elliptical cylinder is also known as an elliptic cylinder.

title: Definition:Elliptical Paraboloid/Also known as
snippet: == Elliptical Paraboloid: Also known as == An elliptical paraboloid is also known as an elliptic paraboloid.

title: Definition:Elliptical Paraboloid/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\PP$ be a paraboloid. Let $P_1$ and $P_2$ be two plane sections of $\PP$ such that both $P_1$ and $P_2$ are parabolas. Let $P_3$ be a plane section of $\PP$ perpendicular to both $P_1$ and $P_2$. Then $\PP$ is an elliptical paraboloid $P_3$ is an ellipse.

title: Definition:Elliptical Paraboloid/Definition 2
snippet: An elliptical paraboloid is a paraboloid which can be embedded in a Cartesian $3$-space and described by the equation: $\dfrac {y^2} {b^2} + \dfrac {z^2} {c^2} = 2 a x$ In this orientation: the plane sections of $\PP$ parallel to the $x$-$y$ plane and the $x$-$z$ plane are parabolas the plane sections of $\PP$ parallel to the $y$-$z$ plane are ellipses.

title: Definition:Elliptical Paraboloid/Definition 2/Also presented as
snippet: == Elliptical Paraboloid: Also presented as == The equation defining an elliptical paraboloid embedded in a Cartesian $3$-space can also be presented in the form: $\dfrac {x^2} {a^2} + \dfrac {y^2} {b^2} = \dfrac z c$ or: $\dfrac {x^2} {a^2} + \dfrac {y^2} {b^2} = \dfrac {2 z} c$

title: Definition:Elongation
snippet: Let $B$ be a solid body under a tensile stress. The elongation of $B$ is the total increase in length of $B$, or the increase in length per unit length of $B$.

title: Definition:Eluding Game
snippet: The eluding game is a two-person game whose mechanics are as follows. The two players are $A$ and $B$. $A$ and $B$ each have three possible moves, the values: $1, 2, 3$ If both choose the same number, $A$ pays to $B$ the amount of the chosen number. Otherwise, $A$ receives the amount of his own number from $B$.
