title: Definition:Equivalent Factorizations
snippet: Let $\struct {D, +, \circ}$ be an integral domain. Let $x$ be a non-zero non-unit element of $D$. Let there be two tidy factorizations of $x$: $x = u_y \circ y_1 \circ y_2 \circ \cdots \circ y_m$ $x = u_z \circ z_1 \circ z_2 \circ \cdots \circ z_n$ These two factorizations are equivalent if one of the following equivalent statements holds: $(1): \quad$ There exists a bijection $\pi: \set {1, \ldots, m} \to \set {1, \ldots, n}$ such that $y_i$ and $z_{\map \pi i}$ are associates of each other for each $i \in \set {1, \ldots, m}$.

title: Definition:Equivalent Linear Representations
snippet: Let $ \struct {G, \cdot}$ be a group. Consider two linear representations $\rho: G \to \GL V$ and $\rho': G \to \GL W$ of $G$. Then $\rho$ and $\rho'$ are called equivalent (linear representations) their correspondent $G$-modules using Correspondence between Linear Group Actions and Linear Representations are isomorphic. Category:Definitions/Representation Theory

title: Definition:Equivalent Metrics
snippet: Let $X$ be a set upon which there are two metrics $d_1$ and $d_2$. That is, $\struct {X, d_1}$ and $\struct {X, d_2}$ are two different metric spaces on the same set $X$. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $X$. Let $n \to \infty$. Suppose that $x_n \to x$ in $\struct {X, d_1}$ $x_n \to x$ in $\struct {X, d_2}$. Then $d_1$ and $d_2$ are equivalent metrics. Category:Definitions/Metric Spaces

title: Definition:Equivalent Subobjects
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $C$ be an object of $\mathbf C$. Let $\map {\mathbf{Sub}_{\mathbf C} } C$ be the category of subobjects of $C$. Two subobjects $m, m'$ of $C$ are said to be equivalent : $m \subseteq m'$ and $m' \subseteq m$ where $\subseteq$ denotes the inclusion relation on subobjects.

title: Definition:Equivalent Systems of Simultaneous Linear Equations
snippet: Let $S_1$ and $S_2$ be two systems of simultaneous linear equations. Then $S_1$ and $S_2$ are equivalent : every solution to $S_1$ is also a solution to $S_2$ and: every solution to $S_2$ is also a solution to $S_1$.

title: Definition:Equivalent Topological Bases
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\mathbb S_1$ and $\mathbb S_2$ be subsets of $\powerset X$, the power set of $X$. Let $\mathbb S_1$ and $\mathbb S_2$ be used as a synthetic basis or synthetic sub-basis to generate topologies for $X$. Let $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$ be the topologies arising from $\mathbb S_1$ and $\mathbb S_2$ respectively. Then $\mathbb S_1$ and $\mathbb S_2$ are equivalent $\tau_1 = \tau_2$.

title: Definition:Equivariant Mapping
snippet: Let $G$ be a group with identity $e$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be sets. Let $\phi_X: G \times X \to X$ and $\phi_Y: G \times Y \to Y$ be group actions: {{eqn | q = \forall \tuple {g, x} \in G \times X | l = g *_X x | o = := | r = \map {\phi_X} {g, x} \in X }} {{eqn | q = \forall \tuple {g, y} \in G \times Y | l = g *_Y y | o = := | r = \map {\phi_Y} {g, y} \in Y }} Let $f: X \to Y$ be a mapping. Then $f$ is an equivariant mapping : $\forall \tuple {g, x} \in G \times X: \map f {g *_X x} = g *_Y \map f x$

title: Definition:Equivariant Mapping/Also known as
snippet: == Equivariant Mapping: Also known as == An equivariant mapping is also known as an equivariant map.

title: Definition:Equivocation
snippet: An equivocation is a shift in meaning of an ambiguous term. If an argument's persuasive force depends on utilizing an equivocation it is fallacious. To make such an argument is to commit the fallacy of equivocation. It can be seen that a fallacy of equivocation is in fact an instance of a fallacy of four terms, two of which are conflated.

title: Definition:Erdős Number
snippet: A person's Erdős number is the minimum number of coauthored publications away from a publication with . The Erdős number of himself is defined as $0$.

title: Definition:Erg/Base Units
snippet: The CGS base units of the erg are: $1 \ \mathrm {erg} = 1 \ \mathrm g \ \mathrm {cm}^2 \ \mathrm s^{-2}$ where: $\mathrm g$ denotes grams $\mathrm {cm}$ denotes centimetres $\mathrm s$ denotes seconds (of time).

title: Definition:Erg/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Erg: Conversion Factors == {{eqn | r = 10^{-7} | c = joules }}

title: Definition:Ergodic Invariant Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \BB}$ be a measurable space. Let $T: X \to X$ be a measurable mapping. Let $\mu$ be a $T$-invariant probability measure on $\struct {X, \BB}$. Then $\mu$ is said to be ergodic : $T$ is an ergodic transformation on $\struct {X, \BB, \mu}$

title: Definition:Ergodic Measure-Preserving Transformation
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \BB, \mu}$ be a probability space. Let $T: X \to X$ be a measure-preserving transformation.

title: Definition:Ergodic Measure-Preserving Transformation/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \BB, \mu}$ be a probability space. Let $T: X \to X$ be a measure-preserving transformation. $T$ is said to be ergodic : for all $A \in \BB$: $T^{-1} \sqbrk A = A \implies \map \mu A \in \set {0, 1}$

title: Definition:Ergodic Measure-Preserving Transformation/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \BB, \mu}$ be a probability space. Let $T: X \to X$ be a measure-preserving transformation. $T$ is said to be ergodic : for all $A \in \BB$: $\map \mu {T^{-1} \sqbrk A \symdif A} = 0 \implies \map \mu A \in \set {0, 1}$ where $\symdif$ denotes the symmetric difference.

title: Definition:Ergodic Measure-Preserving Transformation/Definition 3
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \BB, \mu}$ be a probability space. Let $T: X \to X$ be a measure-preserving transformation. $T$ is said to be ergodic : for all $A \in \BB$: $\ds \map \mu A > 0 \implies \map \mu {\bigcup_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty T^{-n} \sqbrk A} = 1$

title: Definition:Ergodic Measure-Preserving Transformation/Definition 4
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \BB, \mu}$ be a probability space. Let $T: X \to X$ be a measure-preserving transformation. $T$ is said to be ergodic : for all $A, B \in \BB$: $\map \mu A \map \mu B > 0 \implies \exists n \ge 1 : \, \map \mu {T^{-n} \sqbrk A \cap B} > 0$

title: Definition:Ergodic Measure-Preserving Transformation/Definition 5
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \BB, \mu}$ be a probability space. Let $T: X \to X$ be a measure-preserving transformation. $T$ is said to be ergodic : for all measurable $f: X \to \C$: $f \circ T = f$ holds $\mu$-almost everywhere $\implies \exists c \in \C:\, f = c$ holds $\mu$-almost everywhere

title: Definition:Ergodic State
snippet: Let $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \ge 0}$ be a Markov chain on a set $S$. Let $X_i \in S$ be a state of $\sequence {X_n}$. Then $X_i$ is an ergodic state $X_i$: is aperiodic is recurrent has a finite mean recurrence time.

title: Definition:Ergodic Theory
snippet: Ergodic theory is the branch of mathematics which focuses on the long-term behaviour of dynamical systems with an invariant measure.

title: Definition:Ergodicity
snippet: Ergodicity is the property of a time-dependent process such that the limiting distribution of states is independent of the initial state.

title: Definition:Erlang Distribution
snippet: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable on a probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $\Img X = \hointr 0 \infty$. Let $k$ be a strictly positive integer. Let $\lambda$ be a strictly positive real number. $X$ is said to have an Erlang distribution with parameters $k$ and $\lambda$ it has probability density function: $\map {f_X} x = \dfrac {\lambda^k x^{k - 1} e^{- \lambda x} } {\map \Gamma k}$ where $\Gamma$ denotes the gamma function. This is written: $X \sim \map {\operatorname {Erlang} } {k, \lambda}$

title: Definition:Erlangen Program
snippet: The Erlangen program is a method of characterizing systems of geometry based on group theory and projective geometry.

title: Definition:Erlangen Program/Also known as
snippet: == Erlangen Program: Also known as == The Erlangen program is also known as the Erlanger program. In non-American English, program is usually spelt programme. In its original German, the term is Erlangen Programm.

title: Definition:Erlangen Program/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Erlangen Program == The Erlangen program was published by in $1872$ in his . It is named after the , where worked. By $1872$, non-Euclidean geometries had emerged. However, nothing had been done to determine their hierarchy and relationships. 's approach was as follows: Projective geometry was identified as the unifying frame for all other geometries considered by him. Hence the following hierarchy was developed: Affine geometry was more restrictive than projective geometry Euclidean geometry was more restrictive than affine geometry.

title: Definition:Error
snippet: Let $x_0$ be an approximation to a (true) value $x$. The error $\Delta x$ is an indicator of how much difference there is between $x$ and $x_0$.

title: Definition:Error-Correcting Code
snippet: An error-correcting code is a form of encryption that identifies transmission errors, and corrects messages corrupted during transmission. This is usually done by making the transmitted codeword contain extra characters whose purpose is to detect whether the codeword has been corrupted during transmission.

title: Definition:Error-Correcting Code/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Error-Correcting Code == The theory of error-correcting codes was initially developed by and . The method has since been used to correct transmission errors on messages received from outer space on space missions to the planets. As a result, detailed close-up pictures of the planets have been obtained.

title: Definition:Error-Correcting Code/K
snippet: A $k$-error-correcting code is an error-correcting code that can correct up to $k$ transmission errors.

title: Definition:Error-Detecting Code
snippet: An error-detecting code is a form of encryption that identifies transmission errors, but cannot necessarily correct them. This sort of code is convenient when it is easy to resend the message.

title: Definition:Error/Absolute
snippet: Let $x_0$ be an approximation to a (true) value $x$. The absolute error of $x_0$ in $x$ is defined as: $\Delta x := x_0 - x$

title: Definition:Error/Also defined as
snippet: == Error: Also defined as == Let $x_0$ be an approximation to a (true) value $x$. The error $\Delta x$ is an indicator of how much difference there is between $x$ and $x_0$.

title: Definition:Error/Also known as
snippet: == Error: Also known as == An error is also, in some branches of mathematics, known as a residual. Category:Definitions/Errors

title: Definition:Error/Percentage
snippet: Let $x_0$ be an approximation to a (true) value $x$. The percentage error of $x_0$ in $x$ is defined as the relative error expressed as a percentage: $\delta x \, \% := \delta x \times 100$ where $\delta x$ denotes the relative error of $x_0$ in $x$. This, like the relative error, can be defined only when $x \ne 0$.

title: Definition:Error/Relative
snippet: Let $x_0$ be an approximation to a (true) value $x$. The relative error of $x_0$ in $x$ is defined as: $\delta x := \dfrac {\Delta x} x$ where $\Delta x$ denotes the absolute error of $x_0$. This can be defined only when $x \ne 0$.

title: Definition:Error Analysis
snippet: Error analysis is the branch of numerical analysis which considers the propagation of errors within calculations, and the bounds of those errors.

title: Definition:Error Analysis/Motivation
snippet: An algorithm may use many iterations. It is essential to understand how the errors behave from one iteration to the next. If the errors increase in the process, then the final solution may well become meaningless.

title: Definition:Error Mean Square
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of data. The error mean square of $S$ is the error sum of squares of $S$ divided by the degrees of freedom of $S$. Hence the error mean square is an unbiased estimator of variance of error.

title: Definition:Error Sum of Squares
snippet: Error sum of squares is a technique in analysis of variance. It is defined as: the sum of squares of deviations of the individual responses for each experimental unit from the mean response for all units receiving that treatment. It is obtained by dividing the sum of squares by the number of degrees of freedom.

title: Definition:Error Sum of Squares/Also known as
snippet: == Error Sum of Squares: Also known as == Error sum of squares is also known as residual sum of squares.

title: Definition:Error of First or Second Type
Definition:Error of First or Second Type/Also known as
snippet: == Error of First or Second Type: Also known as == An error of the first or second type is also known as an error of the first or second kind.

title: Definition:Escape Speed
snippet: Let a body be propelled vertically upwards from the surface of a planet Let the body keep travelling away from the planet indefinitely. Let resistance from the atmosphere of the planet be considered as negligible. The smallest initial speed at which this is possible is known as the escape speed of the planet.

title: Definition:Escape Speed/Also known as
snippet: == Escape Speed: Also known as == Escape speed is usually (inaccurately) known in common parlance as escape velocity, but the former is more correct.

title: Definition:Essential Image/Measure Space
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $\struct {Y, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\map \BB Y$ be the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $Y$. Let $f : X \to Y$ be $\struct {\Sigma, \map \BB Y}$-measurable. We define the essential range $\map {\operatorname {EssIm} } f$ by: $y \in \map {\operatorname {EssIm} } f$ for each $U \in \tau$ with $y \in U$ we have $\map \mu {f^{-1} \sqbrk U} > 0$.

title: Definition:Essential Image/Resolution of the Identity
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space. Let $\map \BB X$ be the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $X$. Let $\map \BB \C$ be the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\C$. Let $\struct {\HH, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be a Hilbert space over $\C$. Let $\map B {\HH}$ be the space of bounded linear transformations on $\HH$. Let $\EE : \map \BB X \to \map B {\HH}$ be a resolution of the identity. Let $f : X \to \C$ be $\tuple {\map \BB X, \map \BB \C}$-measurable. Let $\sequence {D_i}_{i \mathop \in \N}$ be an analytic basis of $\C$ consisting of open balls.

title: Definition:Essential Mapping
snippet: Let $f: X \to Y$ be a mapping which is not an inessential mapping. Then $f$ is an essential mapping.

title: Definition:Essential Mapping/Also known as
snippet: == Essential Mapping: Also known as == An essential mapping is also known as an essential map.

title: Definition:Essential Singularity
snippet: A (complex) singular point which is neither a removable singularity nor a pole is called an essential singularity.

title: Definition:Essential Singularity/Also defined as
snippet: == Essential Singularity: Also defined as == Some sources impose the condition on an essential singularity that it also be an isolated singularity. Hence an essential singularity would then be defined as an isolated singularity $z_0$ of a complex function $f$ such that a Laurent expansion for $f$ at $z_0$ has a principal part with infinitely many terms. This arises from the result Laurent Expansion of Isolated Essential Singularity.

title: Definition:Essentially Bounded Function
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $f : X \to \R$ be a $\Sigma$-measurable function. We say that $f$ is essentially bounded there exists a real number $c$ such that: $\map \mu {\set {x \in X : \size {\map f x} > c} } = 0$

title: Definition:Essentially Bounded Function/Essential Supremum
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $f : X \to \R$ be an essentially bounded function: $\map \mu {\set {x \in X : \size {\map f x} > c} } = 0$ The essential supremum of $\size {\map f x}$ is the supremum of all possible $c$, and is written $\essup \size {\map f x}$.

title: Definition:Essentially Surjective on Objects Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. Let $F: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be a functor. Then $F$ is said to be essentially surjective on objects : For every object $D$ of $\mathbf D$, there is an object $C$ of $\mathbf C$ such that $F C$ is isomorphic to $D$.

title: Definition:Estimate/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Estimate == The word estimate is the same in its form: to estimate: to make an approximation to a particular estimator. and form. However, they are pronounced slightly differently. The form is pronounced something like es-tim-ut. The form is pronounced something like es-tim-ayt. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Estimation
snippet: Estimation is the use of an estimator to establish an approximate value of a population parameter.

title: Definition:Estimator
snippet: An estimator is a statistic used to establish an approximate value of a population parameter. Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ be random variables. Let the joint distribution of $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ be indexed by a population parameter $\theta$. Let $\delta: \R^n \to \R$ be a real-valued function. The random variable $\hat \theta = \map \delta {X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n}$ is called an estimator of $\theta$.

title: Definition:Estimator/Estimate
snippet: An estimate is a particular realization of an estimator calculated from a particular sample.

title: Definition:Eta Function
snippet: Definition:Dirichlet Eta Function Definition:Dedekind Eta Function

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions
snippet: == Euclid's Definitions == These definitions appear at the beginning of the various Books of .

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book I
snippet: == Euclid's Definitions: Book $\text{I}$ ==

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book I/10 - Right Angle
snippet: When a straight line set up on a straight line makes the adjacent angles equal to one another, each of the equal angles is right, and the straight line standing on the other is called a perpendicular to that on which it stands.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book I/11 - Obtuse Angle
snippet: An obtuse angle is an angle greater than a right angle.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book I/12 - Acute Angle
snippet: An acute angle is an angle less than a right angle.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book I/13 - Boundary
snippet: A boundary is that which is an extremity of anything.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book I/14 - Geometric Figure
snippet: A figure is that which is contained by any boundary or boundaries.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book I/15 - Circle
snippet: A circle is a plane figure contained by one line such that all the straight lines falling upon it from one point among those lying within the figure are equal to one another;

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book I/16 - Center of Circle
snippet: And the point is called the center of the circle.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book I/17 - Diameter of Circle
snippet: A diameter of the circle is any straight line drawn through the center and terminated in both directions by the circumference of the circle, and such a straight line also bisects the center.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book I/18 - Semicircle
snippet: A semicircle is the figure contained by the diameter and the circumference cut off by it. And the center of the semicircle is the same as that of the circle.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book I/19 - Rectilineal Figure
snippet: Rectilineal figures are those which are contained by straight lines, trilateral figures being those contained by three, quadrilateral those contained by four, and multi-lateral those contained by more than four straight lines.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book I/1 - Point
snippet: A point is that which has no part.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book I/20 - Triangles by Sides
snippet: Of trilateral figures, an equilateral triangle is that which has its three sides equal, an isosceles triangle that which has two of its sides alone equal, and a scalene triangle that which has its three sides unequal.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book I/21 - Triangles by Angles
snippet: Further, of trilateral figures, a right-angled triangle is that which has a right angle, an obtuse-angled triangle that which has an obtuse angle, and an acute-angled triangle that which has its three angles acute.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book I/22 - Quadrilaterals
snippet: Of quadrilateral figures, a square is that which is both equilateral and right-angled; an oblong that which is right-angled but not equilateral; a rhombus that which is equilateral but not right-angled; and a rhomboid that which has its opposite sides equal to one another but is neither equilateral nor right-angled. And let quadrilaterals other than these be called trapezia.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book I/23 - Parallel Lines
snippet: Parallel straight lines are straight lines which, being in the same plane and being produced indefinitely in either direction, do not meet one another in either direction.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book I/2 - Line
snippet: A line is breadthless length.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book I/3 - Line Extremities
snippet: The extremities of a line are points.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book I/4 - Straight Line
snippet: A straight line is a line which lies evenly with the points on itself.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book I/5 - Surface
snippet: A surface is that which has length and breadth only.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book I/6 - Surface Extremities
snippet: The extremities of a surface are lines.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book I/7 - Plane Surface
snippet: A plane surface is a surface which lies evenly with the straight lines on itself.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book I/8 - Plane Angle
snippet: A plane angle is the inclination to one another of two lines in a plane which meet one another and do not lie in a straight line.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book I/9 - Rectilineal Angle
snippet: And when the lines containing the angle are straight, the angle is called rectilineal.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book II
snippet: == Euclid's Definitions: Book $\text{II}$ ==

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book II/1 - Containment of Rectangle
snippet: Any rectangular parallelogram is said to be contained by the two straight lines containing the right angle.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book II/2 - Gnomon
snippet: And in any parallelogrammic area let any one whatever of the parallelograms about its diameter with the two complements be called a gnomon.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book III
snippet: == Euclid's Definitions: Book $\text{III}$ ==

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book III/10 - Sector of Circle
snippet: A sector of a circle is the figure which, when an angle is constructed at the center of the circle, is contained by the straight lines containing the angle and the circumference cut off by them.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book III/11 - Similar Segments
snippet: Similar segments of circles are those which admit equal angles, or in which the angles are equal to one another.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book III/1 - Equal Circles
snippet: Equal circles are those the diameters of which are equal, or the radii of which are equal.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book III/2 - Tangent to Circle
snippet: A straight line is said to touch a circle which, meeting the circle and being produced, does not cut the circle.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book III/3 - Tangent Circles
snippet: Circles are said to touch one another which, meeting one another, do not cut one another.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book III/4 - Equally Distant in Circle
snippet: In a circle straight lines are said to be equally distant from the center when the perpendiculars drawn to them from the center are equal.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book III/5 - Greater Distance in Circle
snippet: And that straight line is said to be at a greater distance on which the greater perpendicular falls.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book III/6 - Segment of Circle
snippet: A segment of a circle is the figure contained by a straight line and a circumference of a circle.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book III/7 - Angle of Segment
snippet: An angle of a segment is that contained by a straight line and a circumference of a circle.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book III/8 - Angle in Segment
snippet: An angle in a segment is the angle which, when a point is taken on the circumference of the segment and straight lines are joined from it to the extremities of the straight line which is the base of the segment, is contained by the straight lines so joined.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book III/9 - Stand on Circumference
snippet: And, when the straight lines containing the angle cut off a circumference, the angle is said to stand upon that circumference.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book IV
snippet: == Euclid's Definitions: Book $\text{IV}$ ==

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book IV/1 - Inscribe
snippet: A rectilineal figure is said to be inscribed in a rectilineal figure when the respective angles of the inscribed figure lie on the respective sides of that in which it is inscribed.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book IV/2 - Circumscribe
snippet: Similarly a figure is said to be circumscribed about a figure when the respective sides of the circumscribed figure pass through the respective angles of that about which it is circumscribed.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book IV/3 - Inscribed in Circle
snippet: A rectilineal figure is said to be inscribed in a circle when each angle of the inscribed figure lies on the circumference of the circle.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book IV/4 - Circumscribed about Circle
snippet: A rectilineal figure is said to be circumscribed about a circle, when each side of the circumscribed figure touches the circumference of the circle.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book IV/5 - Circle Inscribed
snippet: Similarly a circle is said to be inscribed in a figure when the circumference of the circle touches each side of the figure in which it is inscribed.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book IV/6 - Circle Circumscribed
snippet: A circle is said to be circumscribed about a figure when the circumference of the circle passes through each angle of the figure about which it is circumscribed.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book IV/7 - Fitted Into Circle
snippet: A straight line is said to be fitted into a circle when its extremities are on the circumference of the circle.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book V
snippet: == Euclid's Definitions: Book $\text{V}$ ==

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book V/10 - Triplicate Ratio
snippet: When four magnitudes are $$ proportional, the first is said to have to the fourth the triplicate ratio of that which it has to the second, and so on continually, whatever be the proportion.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book V/11 - Corresponding Magnitudes
snippet: The term corresponding magnitudes is used of antecedents in relation to antecedents, and of consequents in relation to consequents.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book V/12 - Alternate Ratio
snippet: Alternate ratio means taking the antecedent in relation to the antecedent and the consequent in relation to the consequent.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book V/13 - Inverse Ratio
snippet: Inverse ratio means taking the consequent as antecedent in relation to the antecedent as consequent.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book V/14 - Composition of Ratio
snippet: Composition of a ratio means taking the antecedent together with the consequent as one in relation to the consequent by itself.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book V/15 - Separation of Ratio
snippet: Separation of a ratio means taking the excess by which the antecedent exceeds the consequent in relation to the consequent by itself.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book V/16 - Conversion of Ratio
snippet: Conversion of a ratio means taking the antecedent in relation to the excess by which the antecedent exceeds the consequent.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book V/17 - Ratio Ex Aequali
snippet: A ratio ex aequali arises when, there being several magnitudes and another set equal to them in multitude which makes two and two are in the same proportion, as the first is to the last among the first magnitudes, so is the first to the last among the second magnitudes;Or, in other words, it means taking the extreme terms by virtue of the removal of the intermediate terms.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book V/18 - Perturbed Proportion
snippet: A perturbed proportion arises when, there being three magnitudes and another set equal to them in multitude, as antecedent is to consequent among the first magnitudes, so is antecedent to consequent among the second magnitudes, while, as the consequent is to a third among the first magnitudes, so is a third to the antecedent among the second magnitudes.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book V/1 - Part
snippet: A magnitude is a part of a magnitude, the less of the greater, when it measures the greater.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book V/2 - Multiple
snippet: The greater is a multiple of the less when it is measured by the less.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book V/3 - Ratio
snippet: A ratio is a sort of relation in respect of size between two magnitudes of the same kind.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book V/4 - Existence of Ratio
snippet: Magnitudes are said to have a ratio to one another which are capable, when multiplied, of exceeding one another.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book V/5 - Equality of Ratios
snippet: Magnitudes are said to be in the same ratio, the first to the second and the third to the fourth, when, if any equimultiples whatever be taken of the first and third, and any equimultiples whatever of the second and fourth, the former equimultiples alike exceed, are alike equal to, or alike fall short of, the latter equimultiples respectively taken in corresponding order.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book V/5 - Equality of Ratios/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Equality of Ratios == The definition of equality of ratios was first put together by . Some sources are of the opinion that this definition is "epochal".

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book V/6 - Proportion
snippet: Let magnitudes which have the same ratio be called proportional.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book V/7 - Greater Ratio
snippet: When, of the equimultiples, the multiple of the first magnitude exceeds the multiple of the second, but the multiple of the third does not exceed the multiple of the fourth, then the first is said to have a greater ratio to the second than the third has to the fourth.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book V/8 - Proportion in Three Terms
snippet: A proportion in three terms is the least possible.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book V/9 - Duplicate Ratio
snippet: When three magnitudes are proportional, the first is said to have to the third the duplicate ratio of that which it has to the second.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book VI
snippet: == Euclid's Definitions: Book $\text{VI}$ ==

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book VI/1 - Similar Rectilineal Figures
snippet: Similar rectilineal figures are such as have their angles severally equal and the sides about the equal angles proportional.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book VI/2 - Reciprocally Related Figures
snippet: Two figures are reciprocally related when there are in each of the two figures antecedent and consequent ratios.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book VI/3 - Extreme and Mean Ratio
snippet: A straight line is said to have been cut in extreme and mean ratio when, as the whole line is to the greater segment, so is the greater to the less.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book VI/4 - Height
snippet: The height of any figure is the perpendicular drawn from the vertex to the base.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book VII
snippet: == Euclid's Definitions: Book $\text{VII}$ ==

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book VII/10 - Odd Times Odd
snippet: An odd-times odd number is that which is measured by an odd number according to an odd number.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book VII/11 - Prime Number
snippet: A prime number is that which is measured by an unit alone.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book VII/12 - Relatively Prime
snippet: Numbers prime to one another are those which are measured by an unit alone as a common measure.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book VII/13 - Composite Number
snippet: A composite number is that which is measured by some number.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book VII/14 - Relatively Composite
snippet: Numbers composite to one another are those which are measured by some number as a common measure.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book VII/15 - Multiply
snippet: A number is said to multiply a number when that which is multiplied is added to itself as many times as there are units in the other, and thus some number is produced.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book VII/16 - Plane Number
snippet: And, when two numbers having multiplied one another make some number, the number so produced is called plane, and its sides are the numbers which have multiplied one another.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book VII/17 - Solid Number
snippet: And, when three numbers having multiplied one another make some number, the number so produced is solid, and its sides are the numbers which have multiplied one another.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book VII/18 - Square Number
snippet: A square number is equal multiplied by equal, or a number which is contained by two equal numbers.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book VII/19 - Cube Number
snippet: And a cube is equal multiplied by equal and again by equal, or a number which is contained by three equal numbers.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book VII/1 - Unit
snippet: An unit is that of which each of the things that exist is called one.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book VII/20 - Proportional
snippet: Numbers are proportional when the first is the same multiple, or the same part, or the same parts, of the second that the third is of the fourth.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book VII/21 - Similar Numbers
snippet: Similar plane and solid numbers are those which have their sides proportional.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book VII/22 - Perfect Number
snippet: A perfect number is that which is equal to its own parts.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book VII/2 - Number
snippet: A number is a multitude composed of units.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book VII/3 - Part
snippet: A number is a part of a number, the less of the greater, when it measures the greater;

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book VII/4 - Parts
snippet: but parts when it does not measure it.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book VII/5 - Multiple
snippet: The greater number is a multiple of the less when it is measured by the less.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book VII/6 - Even Number
snippet: An even number is that which is divisible into two equal parts.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book VII/7 - Odd Number
snippet: An odd number is that which is not divisible into two equal parts, or that which differs by an unit from an even number.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book VII/8 - Even Times Even
snippet: An even-times even number is that which is measured by an even number according to an even number.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book VII/9 - Even Times Odd
snippet: An even-times odd number is that which is measured by an even number according to an odd number.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book X
snippet: == Euclid's Definitions: Book $\text{X}$ ==

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book X/1 - Commensurable
snippet: Those magnitudes are said to be commensurable which are measured by the same same measure, and those incommensurable which cannot have any common measure.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book X/2 - Commensurable in Square
snippet: Straight lines are commensurable in square when the squares on them are measured by the same area, and incommensurable in square when the squares on them cannot possibly have any area as a common measure.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book X/3 - Rational Line Segment
snippet: With these hypotheses, it is proved that there exist straight lines infinite in multitude which are commensurable and incommensurable respectively, some in length only, and others in square also, with an assigned straight line. Let then the assigned straight line be called rational, and those straight lines which are commensurable with it, whether in length and in square or square only, rational, but those which are incommensurable with it irrational.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book X/4 - Rational Area
snippet: And let the square on the assigned straight line be called rational and those areas which are commensurable with it rational, but those which are incommensurable with it irrational, and the straight lines which produce them irrational, that is, in case the areas are squares, the sides themselves, but in case they are any other rectilineal figures, the straight lines on which are described squares equal to them.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI
snippet: == Euclid's Definitions: Book $\text{XI}$ ==

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/10 - Similar Equal Solid Figures
snippet: Equal and similar solid figures are those contained by similar planes equal in multitude and in magnitude.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/11 - Solid Angle
snippet: A solid angle is the inclination constituted by more than two lines which meet one another and are not in the same surface, towards all the lines. Otherwise: A solid angle is that which is contained by more than two plane angles which are not in the same plane and are constructed to one point.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/12 - Pyramid
snippet: A pyramid is a solid figure, contained by planes, which is constructed from one plane to one point.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/13 - Prism
snippet: A prism is a solid figure contained by planes of which, namely those which are opposite, are equal, similar and parallel, while the rest are parallelograms.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/14 - Sphere
snippet: When, the diameter of a semicircle remaining fixed, the semicircle is carried round and restored again to the same position from which it began to be moved, the figure so comprehended is a sphere.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/15 - Axis of Sphere
snippet: The axis of the sphere is the straight line which remains fixed about which the semicircle is turned.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/16 - Center of Sphere
snippet: The center of the sphere is the same as that of the semicircle.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/17 - Diameter of Sphere
snippet: A diameter of the sphere is any straight line drawn through the centre and terminated in both directions by the surface of the sphere.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/18 - Cone
snippet: When, one side of those about the right angle in a right-angled triangle remaining fixed, the triangle is carried round and restored again to the same position from which it began to be moved, the figure so comprehended is a cone.And, if the straight line which remains fixed be equal to the remaining side about the right angle which is carried round, the cone will be right-angled; if less, obtuse-angled; and if greater, acute-angled.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/19 - Axis of Cone
snippet: The axis of the cone is the straight line which remains fixed and about which the triangle is turned.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/1 - Solid
snippet: A solid is that which has length, breadth, and depth.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/20 - Base of Cone
snippet: And the base is the circle described by the straight line which is carried round.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/21 - Cylinder
snippet: When, one side of those about the right angle in a rectangular parallelogram remaining fixed, the parallelogram is carried round and restored again to the same position from which it began to be moved, the figure so comprehended is a cylinder.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/22 - Axis of Cylinder
snippet: The axis of the cylinder is the straight line which remains fixed and about which the parallelogram is turned.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/23 - Base of Cylinder
snippet: And the bases are the circles described by the two sides opposite to one another which are carried round.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/24 - Similar Cones and Cylinders
snippet: Similar cones and cylinders are those in which the axes and the diameters of the bases are proportional.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/25 - Cube
snippet: A cube is a solid figure contained by six equal squares.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/26 - Octahedron
snippet: An octahedron is a solid figure contained by eight equal and equilateral triangles.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/27 - Icosahedron
snippet: An icosahedron is a solid figure contained by twenty equal and equilateral triangles.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/28 - Dodecahedron
snippet: A dodecahedron is a solid figure contained by twelve equal, equilateral, and equiangular pentagons.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/2 - Extremity of Solid
snippet: An extremity of a solid is a surface.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/3 - Line at Right Angles to Plane
snippet: A straight line is at right angles to a plane when it makes right angles with all the straight lines which meet it and are in the plane.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/4 - Plane at Right Angles to Plane
snippet: A plane is at right angles to a plane when the straight lines drawn, in one of the planes, at right angles to the common section of the planes are at right angles to the remaining plane.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/5 - Inclination of Straight Line
snippet: The inclination of a straight line to a plane is, assuming a perpendicular drawn from the extremity of the straight line which is elevated above the plane to the plane, and a straight line joined from the point thus arising to the extremity of the straight line which is in the plane, the angle contained by the straight line so drawn and the straight line standing up.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/6 - Inclination of Plane
snippet: The inclination of a plane to a plane is the acute angle contained by the straight lines drawn at right angles to the common section at the same point, one in each of the planes.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/7 - Similarly Inclined
snippet: A plane is said to be similarly inclined to a plane as another is to another when the said angles of the inclinations are equal to one another.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/8 - Parallel Planes
snippet: Parallel planes are those which do not meet.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/9 - Similar Solid Figures
snippet: Similar solid figures are those contained by similar planes equal in multitude.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book X (II)
snippet: == Euclid's Definitions: Book $\text{X (II)}$ ==

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book X (II)/1 - First Binomial
snippet: Given a rational straight line and a binomial, divided into its terms, such that the square on the greater term is greater than the square on the lesser by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with the greater, then, if the greater term be commensurable in length with the rational straight line set out, let the whole be called a first binomial straight line;

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book X (II)/2 - Second Binomial
snippet: but if the lesser term be commensurable in length with the rational straight line set out, let the whole be called a second binomial;

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book X (II)/3 - Third Binomial
snippet: and if neither of the terms be commensurable in length with the rational straight line set out, let the whole be called a third binomial.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book X (II)/4 - Fourth Binomial
snippet: Again, if the square on the greater term be greater than the square on the lesser by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with the greater, then, if the greater term be commensurable in length with the rational straight line set out, let the whole be called a fourth binomial;

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book X (II)/5 - Fifth Binomial
snippet: if the lesser, a fifth binomial;

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book X (II)/6 - Sixth Binomial
snippet: and if neither, a sixth binomial.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book X (III)
snippet: == Euclid's Definitions: Book $\text{X (III)}$ ==

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book X (III)/1 - First Apotome
snippet: Given a rational straight line and an apotome, if the square on the whole be greater than the square on the annex by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with the whole, and the whole be commensurable in length with the rational straight line set out, let the apotome be called a first apotome.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book X (III)/2 - Second Apotome
snippet: But if the annex be commensurable in length with the rational straight line set out, and the square on the whole be greater than that on the annex by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with the whole, let the apotome be called a second apotome.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book X (III)/3 - Third Apotome
snippet: But if neither be commensurable in length with the rational straight line set out, and the square on the whole be greater than the square on the annex by the square on a straight line commensurable with the whole, let the apotome be called a third apotome.

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book X (III)/4 - Fourth Apotome
snippet: Again, if the square on the whole be greater than the square on the annex by the square on a straight line incommensurable with the whole, then, if the whole be commensurable in length with the rational straight line set out, let the apotome be called a fourth apotome;

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book X (III)/5 - Fifth Apotome
snippet: if the annex be so commensurable, a fifth;

title: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book X (III)/6 - Sixth Apotome
snippet: and if neither, a sixth.

title: Definition:Euclid Number
snippet: A Euclid number is a natural number of the form: $E_n := p_n\# + 1$ where $p_n\#$ is the primorial of the $n$th prime number.

title: Definition:Euclid Number/Also defined as
snippet: == Euclid Numbers: Also known as == The term Euclid number is also used by some sources to denote an even perfect number. On , the term Euclidean number is preferred for that concept.

title: Definition:Euclid Number/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Euclid Number == The name Euclid number derives from 's proof of the Infinitude of Prime Numbers. It is often stated (erroneously) that this proof relies on these numbers. However, recall that did not begin by assuming that the set of all primes is finite. His proof, found in as , proceeded as follows: Take any finite set of primes (it could be any set, for example $\set {3, 211, 65537}$). Then it follows that at least one prime exists that is not in that set. However, the numbers themselves are mildly interesting in their own right.

title: Definition:Euclid Number/Sequence
snippet: The sequence of Euclid numbers begins as follows: Category:Definitions/Euclid Numbers

title: Definition:Euclid Prime
snippet: A Euclid prime is a natural number which is both a Euclid number and a prime number.

title: Definition:Euclid Prime/Sequence
snippet: The sequence of Euclid primes begins: $2, 3, 7, 31, 211, 2311, 200 \, 560 \, 490 \, 131, \ldots$ This sequence can be better comprehended as: $\sequence {p_n \# + 1}$ where: $p_n \#$ denotes the primorial of the $n$th prime number $n$ is the sequence: $0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 11, 75, 171, 172, 384, 457, 616, 643, \ldots$

title: Definition:Euclidean
snippet: Geometry: Euclidean Geometry Euclidean Space Topology: Euclidean Topology Euclidean Metric Euclidean Distance Euclidean Norm Abstract Algebra: Euclidean Domain Euclidean Relation All the above are related in some way to, or derived from, the concept of Euclidean geometry. Additional concepts bearing the adjective Euclidean: Number Theory: Euclidean Algorithm

title: Definition:Euclidean Directional Derivative
snippet: Let $\R^n$ be the $n$-dimensional real vector space. Let $p \in \R^n$ be a point. Let $T_p \R^n$ be tha tangent space of $\R^n$ at $p$. Let $v \in T_p \R^n$ be a vector. Let $\map {\mathfrak{X}} {\R^n}$ be the space of smooth vector fields of $\R^n$. Let $Y \in \map {\mathfrak{X}} {\R^n}$ be a vector field.

title: Definition:Euclidean Domain
snippet: Let $\struct {D, +, \circ}$ be an integral domain. Let there exist a Euclidean valuation on $D$. Then $D$ is called a Euclidean domain.

title: Definition:Euclidean Domain/Also known as
snippet: == Euclidean Domain: Also known as == A Euclidean domain is also known as a Euclidean ring.

title: Definition:Euclidean Domain/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Euclidean Domain == A Euclidean domain is so named because, as an algebraic structure, it sustains the concept of the Euclidean Algorithm. himself made no mention of the concept, which is an abstract algebraic concept defined in (mathematically speaking) modern times. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Euclidean Domain/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Euclidean Domain == The term Euclidean domain is introduced with the indefinite article: a Euclidean domain. This is because is pronounced Yoo-klid in English. Category:Linguistic Notes
