title: Definition:Factorable Polynomial
snippet: A factorable polynomial is a polynomial which can be expressed as the product of $2$ or more factors, other than itself and a constant.

title: Definition:Factorial
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be a positive integer.

title: Definition:Factorial/Also known as
snippet: == Factorial: Also known as == While the canonical vocalisation of $n!$ is $n$ factorial, it can often be found referred to as $n$ bang or (usually by schoolchildren) $n$ shriek. Some mathematicians prefer $n$ gosh. Some early sources favour factorial $n$.

title: Definition:Factorial/Definition 1
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be a positive integer. The factorial of $n$ is defined inductively as: $n! = \begin {cases} 1 & : n = 0 \\ n \paren {n - 1}! & : n > 0 \end {cases}$

title: Definition:Factorial/Definition 2
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be a positive integer. The factorial of $n$ is defined as: {{eqn | l = n! | r = \prod_{k \mathop = 1}^n k | c = }} {{eqn | r = 1 \times 2 \times \cdots \times \paren {n - 1} \times n | c = }} where $\ds \prod$ denotes continued product.

title: Definition:Factorial/Historical Note
snippet: The symbol $!$ used on for the factorial, which is now universal, was introduced by in his $1808$ work . Before that, various symbols were used whose existence is now of less importance. Notations for $n!$ in history include the following: $\sqbrk n$ as used by $\mathop{\Pi} n$ as used by $\left\lvert {\kern-1pt \underline n} \right.$ and $\left. {\underline n \kern-1pt} \right\rvert$, once popular in England and Italy. In fact, was using $\left\lvert {\kern-1pt \underline n} \right.$ as recently as the $1920$s. It can sometimes be seen rendered as $\lfloor n$.

title: Definition:Factorial/Multiindices
snippet: Let $\alpha$ be a multiindex, indexed by a set $J$ such that for each $j \in J$, $\alpha_j \ge 0$. Then we define: $\ds \alpha! = \prod_{j \mathop \in J} \alpha_j!$ where the factorial on the right is a factorial of natural numbers. Note that by definition, all but finitely many of the $\alpha_j$ are zero, so the product over $J$ is convergent.

title: Definition:Factorial Experiment
snippet: A factorial experiment is an experiment structured so that several different types of treatment can be compared, at different qualitative or quantitative levels. The design will allow the experimenter to see whether the effects of each factor is additive, or whether they interact. Results are typically analysed by partitioning the between-treatments sum of squares in an ANOVA exercise into: main effects and: interactions. Designs may involve any number of factors and any number of levels of each factor. In a randomized block design, every factor-level combination appears once in each block.

title: Definition:Factorial Experiment/Factor
snippet: One of the different types of treatment being compared in a factorial experiment is known as a factor.

title: Definition:Factorial Experiment/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Factorial Experiments == The technique of factorial experiments was pioneered by in $1934$.

title: Definition:Factorial Experiment/Interaction
snippet: In a factorial experiment, factors are said to interact if their effects are not directly additive.

title: Definition:Factorial Experiment/Main Effect
snippet: In a factorial experiment, the main effects of factors are those which are additive.

title: Definition:Factorial Moment
snippet: Let $X$ be a discrete random variable whose probability generating function is $\map {\Pi_X} s$. The $n$th derivative of $\map {\Pi_X} s$ at $s = 1$: $\dfrac {\d^n} {\d s^n} \map {\Pi_X} 1 = \expect {X \paren {X - 1} \cdots \paren {X - n + 1} }$ is called the $n$th factorial moment of $X$

title: Definition:Factorial Number System
snippet: The factorial number system is a mixed radix positional number system in which the digit in the $i$th column from the right is of base $i$.

title: Definition:Factorial Number System/Also known as
snippet: == Factorial Number System: Also known as == The factorial number system is also known as factoradic. Some sources use the misnomer factorial base, despite the fact that the factorials do not act as a number base. Category:Definitions/Factorial Number System

title: Definition:Factorion
snippet: A factorion (base $b$) is a positive integer which, when expressed in base $b$, equals the sum of the factorials of its digits. When the number base is not given, base $10$ is assumed.

title: Definition:Factorion/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Factorions ==

title: Definition:Factorization/Also known as
snippet: == Factorization: Also known as == Factorization of a polynomial ring is also known as decomposition.

title: Definition:Factorization/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Factorization == The spelling factorization is the US English version. The UK English spelling is factorisation, but the tendency is for the literature to use the factorization form. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Factorization Domain
snippet: A factorization domain is an integral domain in which every element can be written as a finite product of irreducible elements.

title: Definition:Factorization of Matrix
snippet: Factorization of a matrix $\mathbf A$ is the representation of $\mathbf A$ as the product of $2$ or more matrices.

title: Definition:Factorization of Matrix/Also known as
snippet: == Factorization of Matrix: Also known as == A factorization of a matrix is also known as a decomposition.

title: Definition:Fahrenheit
snippet: Fahrenheit is a temperature scale. Its two reference points are: $32 \fahr$, which is set at the melting point of water. $212 \fahr$, which is set at the boiling point of water, as defined at sea level and standard atmospheric pressure. A temperature measured in Fahrenheit is often referred to as so many degrees Fahrenheit.

title: Definition:Fahrenheit/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Fahrenheit: Conversion Factors ==

title: Definition:Fahrenheit/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Fahrenheit == The Fahrenheit scale is based on that proposed in $1724$ by the physicist . He initially defined the lower reference point from the lowest temperature he could achieve, by mixing equal parts of ice and salt and establishing the temperature at which it melted. The upper reference point, $96 \fahr$, was taken to be his best estimate of the temperature of the human body. For scientific purposes it has been all but completely superseded by the Celsius scale.

title: Definition:Fair
snippet: Fair is an meaning without bias.

title: Definition:Fair/Coin
snippet: A fair coin is a coin which has an equal probability of landing heads or tails, that is, $\dfrac 1 2$.

title: Definition:Fair/Die
snippet: A fair die is a die whose physical properties are such that the probabilities of showing each of its faces are equal. That is, for a conventional $6$-sided die, the probabilities are all $\dfrac 1 6$.

title: Definition:Fair Coin/Also known as
snippet: == Fair Coin: Also known as == A fair coin is also known as a normal coin. Category:Definitions/Fair Coins

title: Definition:Fair Game
snippet: A fair game is a game in which the entry cost or stake equals the expected gain.

title: Definition:Faithful
snippet: Faithful Representation Definition:Faithful Linear Representation of Group Faithful Module Faithful Group Action Definition:Faithfully Flat Algebra Definition:Faithful Functor

title: Definition:Faithful Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. Let $F: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be a functor. Then $F$ is faithful for all objects $C_1, C_2$ of $\mathbf C$: $F: \map {\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C} } {C_1, C_2} \to \map {\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf D} } {F C_1, F C_2}, \ f \mapsto F f$ is an injection. Here $\operatorname{Hom}$ signifies a hom class.

title: Definition:Faithful Group Action
snippet: Let $G$ be a group with identity $e$. Let $X$ be a set. Let $\phi: G \times X \to X$ be a group action: $\forall \tuple {g, x} \in G \times X: g * x := \map \phi {g, x} \in X$

title: Definition:Faithful Group Action/Also known as
snippet: == Faithful Group Action: Also known as == A faithful group action is also known as an effective group action.

title: Definition:Faithful Group Action/Definition 1
snippet: Let $G$ be a group with identity $e$. Let $X$ be a set. Let $\phi: G \times X \to X$ be a group action: $\forall \tuple {g, x} \in G \times X: g * x := \map \phi {g, x} \in X$ $\phi$ is faithful $e$ is the only element if $G$ which acts trivially: $\forall g \in G: \paren {\forall x \in X: g * x = x \implies g = e}$

title: Definition:Faithful Group Action/Definition 2
snippet: Let $G$ be a group with identity $e$. Let $X$ be a set. Let $\phi: G \times X \to X$ be a group action. $\phi$ is faithful its permutation representation is injective.

title: Definition:Faithful Group Representation
snippet: A faithful group representation is a group representation which is injective.

title: Definition:Faithful Linear Representation of Group
snippet: Let $ \struct {K, +, \circ}$ be a field. Let $V$ be a vector space over $K$ of finite dimension. Let $\GL V$ be the general linear group of $V$. Let $\struct {G, \cdot}$ be a finite group. Let $\rho : G \to \GL V$ be a linear representation of $G$ on $V$. Then $\rho$ is faithful the kernel of $\rho$ is trivial.

title: Definition:Faithful Module
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $M$ be an $R$-module. Then $M$ is faithful its annihilator is zero.

title: Definition:Faithful Representation
snippet: Definition:Faithful Group Representation Definition:Faithful Linear Representation of Group Definition:Faithful Module Definition:Faithful Group Action

title: Definition:Fallacy
snippet: A (logical) fallacy is a mistake caused by an application of an invalid argument. Logical fallacies abound. Most of the documented fallacies that can be found in the literature arise from linguistic imprecision or deliberately misleading statements, or both. Frequently the commission of fallacies is as deliberate as the telling of lies.

title: Definition:Fallacy/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Fallacy == Fallacies have been the subject of investigation, identification and classification since the time of .

title: Definition:Fallacy of Four Terms
snippet: Consider a categorical syllogism $S$ of the form: {| |- |   Major Premise:   | align="right" | $\map {\mathbf \Phi_1} {A, B}$ |- |   Minor Premise:   | align="right" | $\map {\mathbf \Phi_2} {C, D}$ |- |   Conclusion:   | style="border-style: solid; border-width: 1px 0 0 0" align="right" | $\map {\mathbf \Phi_3} {x, y}$ |} where: $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ are terms of the categorical syllogism each of $\mathbf \Phi_1$, $\mathbf \Phi_2$ and $\mathbf \Phi_3$ is one of the categorical statements $\mathbf A$, $\mathbf E$, $\mathbf I$ or $\mathbf O$ $x$ and $y$ are each…

title: Definition:Falling Factorial
snippet: Let $x$ be a real number (but usually an integer). Let $n$ be a positive integer. Then $x$ to the (power of) $n$ falling is: $\ds x^{\underline n} := \prod_{j \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \paren {x - j} = x \paren {x - 1} \cdots \paren {x - n + 1}$

title: Definition:Falling Factorial/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Falling Factorial == The notation $x^{\underline n}$ for $x$ to the $n$ falling is due to , who used it in $1893$. This is the notation of choice on . A more commonly seen notation (though arguably not as good) is $\paren x_n$. This is known as the Pochhammer function or (together with $x^{\paren n}$ for its rising counterpart) the Pochhammer symbol (after ). See the note on notation in the Rising Factorial entry.

title: Definition:False
snippet: A statement has a truth value of false what it says does not match the way that things are.

title: Definition:False/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on False == The word false is an . Its corresponding is falsehood. The word falsity is sometimes seen, meaning the same thing as falsehood. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:False Balance
snippet: A false balance is a balance which, because of mistakes in its manufacture, cannot be trusted to perform an accurate assessment of weight. There are two ways in which such a balance may be false:

title: Definition:False Balance/Imbalanced Pans
snippet: A false balance with imbalanced pans is a balance whose pans are of different weights.

title: Definition:False Balance/Unequal Arms
snippet: A false balance with unequal arms is a balance whose arms are of different lengths.

title: Definition:Falsidical Paradox
snippet: A falsidical paradox is a result which, as well as being absurd on the surface, is the result of faulty reasoning and so is genuinely false. Such apparent paradoxes can be classified as fallacies.

title: Definition:Falsifiable
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a logical language. Let $\mathscr M$ be a formal semantics for $\LL$.

title: Definition:Falsifiable/Boolean Interpretations
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a WFF of propositional logic. $\mathbf A$ is called falsifiable (for boolean interpretations) : $\map v {\mathbf A} = \F$ for some boolean interpretation $v$ for $\mathbf A$. In terms of validity, this can be rendered: $v \not\models_{\mathrm{BI}} \mathbf A$ that is, $\mathbf A$ is invalid in the boolean interpretation $v$ of $\mathbf A$.

title: Definition:Falsifiable/Formula
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a logical language. Let $\mathscr M$ be a formal semantics for $\LL$. A logical formula $\phi$ of $\LL$ is falsifiable for $\mathscr M$ : $\phi$ is not valid in some structure $\MM$ of $\mathscr M$ That is, there exists some structure $\MM$ of $\mathscr M$ such that: $\MM \not\models_{\mathscr M} \phi$

title: Definition:Falsifiable/Set of Formulas
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a logical language. Let $\mathscr M$ be a formal semantics for $\LL$. A collection $\FF$ of logical formulas of $\LL$ is falsifiable for $\mathscr M$ : Some $\mathscr M$-structure $\MM$ is not a model of $\FF$ That is, there exists some structure $\MM$ of $\mathscr M$ such that: $\MM \not\models_{\mathscr M} \FF$ Category:Definitions/Formal Semantics

title: Definition:Family of Curves
snippet: A family of curves is a set of curves which are described with a common equation, in such a way that all such curves can be generated by varying one or more parameters.

title: Definition:Family of Curves/One-Parameter
snippet: Consider the implicit function $\map f {x, y, c} = 0$ in the cartesian $\tuple {x, y}$-plane where $c$ is a constant. For each value of $c$, we have that $\map f {x, y, z, c} = 0$ defines a relation between $x$ and $y$ which can be graphed in the cartesian plane. Thus, each value of $c$ defines a particular curve. The complete set of all these curve for each value of $c$ is called a one-parameter family of curves.

title: Definition:Family of Curves/One-Parameter/Parameter
snippet: Let $\map f {x, y, c}$ define a one-parameter family of curves $F$. The value $c$ is the parameter of $F$.

title: Definition:Family of Curves/Parameter
snippet: The parameters of a family of curves $\FF$ is a set of real numbers which, when varied, generate all the elements of $\FF$.

title: Definition:Family of Curves/n-Parameter
snippet: An $n$-parameter family of curves is a family of curves which requires $n$ parameters to identify a specific element of that family.

title: Definition:Family of Probability Distributions
snippet: A family of probability distributions is a set of probability distributions with the same general probability density function, differing by one or more parameters.

title: Definition:Family of Probability Distributions/Parameter
snippet: Let $\PP$ be a probability distribution of a particular family. A parameter of $\PP$ is a constant that determines the specific properties of $\PP$.

title: Definition:Family of Surfaces
snippet: A family of surfaces is a set of surfaces which are described with a common equation, in such a way that all such surfaces can be generated by varying one or more parameters.

title: Definition:Family of Surfaces/One-Parameter
snippet: Consider the implicit function $\map f {x, y, z, c} = 0$ in the Cartesian $3$-space where $c$ is a constant. For each value of $c$, we have that $\map f {x, y, z, c} = 0$ defines a relation between $x$, $y$ and $z$ which can be graphed in cartesian $3$-space. Thus, each value of $c$ defines a particular surface. The complete set of all these surfaces for each value of $c$ is called a one-parameter family of surfaces.

title: Definition:Family of Surfaces/One-Parameter/Parameter
snippet: Let $\map f {x, y, z, c}$ define a one-parameter family of surfaces $F$. The value $c$ is the parameter of $F$.

title: Definition:Family of Surfaces/Parameter
snippet: The parameters of a family of surfaces $\FF$ is a set of real numbers which, when varied, generate all the elements of $\FF$.

title: Definition:Fano Plane
snippet: The Fano plane is the finite projective plane of order $2$. It can be denoted: $\operatorname {PG} \left({2, 2}\right)$ where: $\operatorname {PG}$ stands for projective geometry the first parameter $2$ specifies the dimension the second parameter $2$ specifies the order. $\operatorname {PG} \left({2, 2}\right)$ has the following properties: It has $7$ points It has $7$ lines There are $3$ points on each line There are $3$ lines through each point. 400px

title: Definition:Farad
snippet: The farad is the SI unit of capacitance. It is defined as being the amount of capacitance of a capacitor between the plates of which an electric potential of $1$ volt appears when it stores $1$ coulomb of electric charge: $1 \, \mathrm F = 1 \, \mathrm C \, \mathrm V^{-1}$ that is, $1$ coulomb per volt.

title: Definition:Farad/Base Units
snippet: The SI base units of the farad are: $\mathrm F := \mathrm {kg}^{-1} \, \mathrm m^{-2} \, \mathrm s^4 \mathrm A^2$ where: $\mathrm {kg}$ denotes kilograms $\mathrm m$ denotes metres $\mathrm s$ denotes seconds (of time). $\mathrm A$ denotes ampere. This arises from its definition as $\mathrm Q \, \mathrm V^{-1}$, that is: coulombs per volt.

title: Definition:Faraday
snippet: The faraday is defined as the amount of electric charge needed to release one gram-equivalent of a chemical element.

title: Definition:Faraday/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Faraday: Conversion Factors == {{eqn | o = \approx | r = 9 \cdotp 64853 \, 32123 \, 31001 \, 84 \times 10^4 | c = coulombs per mole: $\mathrm {C \, mol^{-1} }$ | cc= }} {{eqn | o = \approx | r = 9 \cdotp 64853 \, 32123 \, 31001 \, 84 \times 10^7 | c = coulombs per kilogram-mole: $\mathrm {C / kg \, mol}$ }} {{eqn | o = \approx | r = 2 \cdotp 89255 \, 33018 \, 664 \times 10^{14} | c = statcoulombs per mole: $\mathrm {statC \, mol^{-1} }$ }}

title: Definition:Faraday/Conversion Factors/Also known as
snippet: == Faraday Conversion Factor: Also known as == The conversion factor $96485 \cdotp 3 \cdots$ is known popularly as the Faraday constant. It is of course the number of coulombs of electric charge contained in $1$ mole of electrons.

title: Definition:Farey Sequence
snippet: A Farey sequence is a chain of subsets of the reduced rational numbers lying in $\Q \cap \closedint 0 1$. For $Q \in \Z_{>0}$, the Farey set $F_Q$ is the set of all reduced rational numbers with denominators not larger than $Q$: $F_Q = \set {\dfrac p q: p = 0, \ldots, Q,\ q = 1, \ldots, Q,\ p \perp q}$ where $p \perp q$ denotes that $p$ and $q$ are coprime.

title: Definition:Farey Sequence/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Farey Sequence == The Farey sequence was first exploited by in $1801$ in creating tables of the decimal expansions for all vulgar fractions whose denominators are less than $100$. In order to make sure he captured them all, he used a technique exploiting the properties of the mediant that originated with . Some $15$ years later, rediscovered this property, and published a paper on the subject. This was subsequently picked up on by , who reproved the results of while crediting with the technique.

title: Definition:Farey Sequence/Historical Note/Mistake
snippet: == Source Work == Farey sequence (of order $n$)

title: Definition:Farey Sequence/Order
snippet: Let $F_Q$ denote the Farey sequence of all reduced rational numbers with denominators not larger than $Q$: $F_Q = \set {\dfrac p q: p = 0, \ldots, Q,\ q = 1, \ldots, Q,\ p \perp q}$ The index $Q$ is called the order of $F_Q$.

title: Definition:Farthest Point
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. Let $H \subseteq A$ be a subset of $A$. Let $p \in A \setminus H$ be a point of $M$ outside $H$ such that: the distance from $p$ to the nearest point in $A$ is greater than for any other point in $A \setminus H$. Then $p$ is the farthest point from $A$.

title: Definition:Fast Fourier Transform
snippet: The fast Fourier transform is a way of evaluating the discrete Fourier transform in a number of operations proportional to $n \ln n$ for a sequence of $n$ points.

title: Definition:Feasible Region
snippet: The feasible region of a linear programming exercise is an area of a graphical presentation in which the points represent solution which fulfil the constraints.

title: Definition:Feasible Solution
snippet: A feasible solution to a linear programming exercise is a point within the feasible region.

title: Definition:Fedorov Group
snippet: A Fedorov group is the symmetry group of a $3$-dimensional configuration in space.

title: Definition:Fedorov Group/Also known as
snippet: == Fedorov Group: Also known as == A Fedorov group can also be defined as a $3$-dimensional space group. Hence some sources refer to a Fedorov group just as a space group. Crystallographers can be seen to refer to these groups as the crystallographic groups, as this is the field in which they originated. Ignorant street-urchins may be found referring to crystallography groups, but they will be sternly corrected and told that a crystallography group is a team of crystallographers, and not a group in the mathematical sense.

title: Definition:Fedorov Group/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Fedorov Group == The Fedorov groups were first enumerated by in $1891$. His original list had $2$ omissions and $1$ duplication. , also in $1891$, independently investigated the same groups, but his list had $4$ omissions and $1$ duplication. In $1892$, and collaborated on the definitive list, via correspondence, establishing that there are $230$ Fedorov groups if chiral copies are taken as distinct, but $219$ if not. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Feigenbaum Constants
snippet: The Feigenbaum constants are a pair of real constants which arise in bifurcation theory.

title: Definition:Feigenbaum Constants/First
snippet: The first Feigenbaum constant is the limiting ratio of each bifurcation interval to the next between every period doubling of a one-parameter mapping: $x_{i + 1} = \map f {x_i}$ where $\map f x$ is a function parameterized by the bifurcation parameter $a$. It is given by the limit: $\ds \delta = \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \dfrac{a_ {n - 1} - a_{n - 2} } {a_n - a_{n - 1} } = 4 \cdotp 66920 \, 16091 \, 02990 \, 67185 \, 32038 \, 20466 \, 20161 \, 72 \ldots$ where $a_n$ are discrete values of $a$ at the $n$th period doubling.

title: Definition:Feigenbaum Constants/Second
snippet: The second Feigenbaum constant $\alpha$ is the ratio between the width of a tine and the width of one of its two subtines (except the tine closest to the fold). A negative sign is applied to $\alpha$ when the ratio between the lower subtine and the width of the tine is measured. Its approximate value is given by: $\alpha \approx 2 \cdotp 50290 \, 78750 \, 95892 \, 82228 \, 39028 \, 73218 \, 21578 \cdots$

title: Definition:Fermat Number
snippet: A Fermat number is a natural number of the form $2^{\paren {2^n} } + 1$, where $n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$. The number $2^{\paren {2^n} } + 1$ is, in this context, often denoted $F_n$.

title: Definition:Fermat Number/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Fermat Number == In $1640$, wrote to that $2^n + 1$ is composite if $n$ is divisible by an odd prime. He also observed that the first $5$ numbers of the form $2^{2^n} + 1$ are all prime. This led him to propose the Fermat Prime Conjecture: that all numbers of this form are prime. On being unable to prove it, he sent the problem to , with the note: I wouldn't ask you to work at it if I had been successful. Pascal unfortunately did not take up the challenge.

title: Definition:Fermat Number/Naming Conventions
snippet: The Fermat number $F_0$ is often referred to as the $1$st Fermat number, so (confusingly) this convention dictates that $F_n$ is the $n + 1$th Fermat number. However, another convention is that $F_0$ can be referred to as the zeroth Fermat number, thus bringing the appellation in line such that $F_n$ is the $n$th Fermat number. Both conventions are in place, sometimes in the same work. For example, , in his of $1997$, refers to $5 = F_1$ in Section $5$ as the $2$nd Fermat number. However, in Section $257$ he defines $F_3 = 2^{2^3} + 1 = 257$ as the $3$rd Fermat number.

title: Definition:Fermat Prime
snippet: A Fermat prime is a Fermat number, that is a number of the form $2^{\paren {2^n} } + 1$, which happens to be prime. In fact, $2^{\paren {2^n} } + 1$ is prime for $n = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$. However, $2^{\paren {2^5} } + 1 = 2^{32} + 1$ is divisible by $641$, as was proved by . No Fermat prime for $n > 4$ has ever been discovered.

title: Definition:Fermat Prime/Sequence
snippet: == Sequence of Fermat Primes == The sequence of Fermat primes begins: {{eqn | l = 2^{\paren {2^0} } + 1 | r = 3 }} {{eqn | l = 2^{\paren {2^1} } + 1 | r = 5 }} {{eqn | l = 2^{\paren {2^2} } + 1 | r = 17 }} {{eqn | l = 2^{\paren {2^3} } + 1 | r = 257 }} {{eqn | l = 2^{\paren {2^4} } + 1 | r = 65 \, 537 }} No other Fermat primes are known.

title: Definition:Fermat Pseudoprime
snippet: Let $q$ be a composite number such that $\exists n \in N: n^q \equiv n \pmod q$. Then $q$ is a Fermat pseudoprime to base $n$.

Hence the full name Fermat pseudoprime is preferred on . Some sources hyphenate the word pseudo-prime. A Fermat pseudoprime is also known as a Fermat liar.

title: Definition:Fermat Pseudoprime/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Fermat Pseudoprime == From as far back as the ancient Chinese, right up until the time of , it was thought that $n$ had to be prime in order for $2^n - 2$ to be divisible by $n$. This used to be used as a test for primality. But it was discovered that $2^{341} \equiv 2 \pmod {341}$, and $341 = 31 \times 11$ and so is composite.

title: Definition:Fermat Quotient
snippet: Let $a$ be a positive integer. Let $p$ be an odd prime. The Fermat quotient of $a$ with respect to $p$ is defined as: $\map {q_p} a = \dfrac {a^{p - 1} - 1} p$

title: Definition:Fermat Set
snippet: The Fermat set is the set of integers: $\left\{ {1, 3, 8, 120}\right\}$ It has the property of being a Diophantine quadruple.

title: Definition:Fermi Coordinates
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be an $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold. Let $P \subseteq M$ an embedded $p$-dimensional submanifold. Let $\pi : NP \to P$ be the normal bundle of $P$ in $M$. Let $V \subseteq NP$ be an open subset. Let $E$ be the normal exponential map. Let $U \subseteq M$ be the normal neighborhood such that $U = \map E V$. Let $\struct {W_0, \psi}$ be a smooth coordinate chart for $P$. Let $\tuple {E_1, \ldots, E_{n - p}}$ be a local orthonormal frame for $NP$. Let $\hat W_0 = \map \psi {W_0} \subseteq \R^p$.

title: Definition:Ferrier's Prime/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Ferrier's Prime == Ferrier's prime was discovered in $1951$ by using a manual desk calculator. It is generally considered to have been the highest known prime at the time, having $44$ digits. However, it was eclipsed by $180 \times \paren {2^{127} - 1} + 1$ ($79$ digits), discovered in the same month by and of Cambridge University. Exactly which was discovered first is debated, but 's is traditionally determined as being earlier. Both were then well and truly superseded in $1952$, when discovered the prime nature of $2^{521} - 1$ and a number of others.

title: Definition:Feuerbach Circle
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle. The Feuerbach circle of $\triangle ABC$ is the circle which passes through each of the $9$ points: the feet of the altitudes of $\triangle ABC$ the midpoints of the sides of $\triangle ABC$ the midpoints of the lines from the vertices of $\triangle ABC$ to the orthocenter of $\triangle ABC$. 500px

title: Definition:Fiber Bundle
snippet: Let $M, E, F$ be topological spaces. Let $\pi: E \to M$ be a continuous surjection. Let $\UU := \set {U_\alpha \subseteq M: \alpha \in I}$ be an open cover of $M$ with index set $I$. Let $\pr_{1, \alpha}: U_\alpha \times F \to U_\alpha$ be the first projection on $U_\alpha \times F$. Let there exist homeomorphisms: $\chi_\alpha: \map {\pi^{-1} } {U_\alpha} \to U_\alpha \times F$ such that for all $\alpha \in I$: $\pi {\restriction}_{U_\alpha} = \pr_{1, \alpha} \circ \chi_\alpha$ where $\pi {\restriction}_{U_\alpha}$ is the restriction of $\pi$ to $U_\alpha \in \UU$.

title: Definition:Fiber Bundle/Also known as
snippet: == Fiber Bundle: Also known as == Some sources refer to a fiber bundle just as a bundle. Some sources use the term twisted product. By an abuse of language, it is common to say that $E$ is a fiber bundle over $M$. One also finds the formulation Let $E \overset \pi \to M$ be a fiber bundle in the literature.

title: Definition:Fiber Bundle/Base Point
snippet: Let $M$ be the base space of a fiber bundle $B = \struct {E, M, \pi, F}$. A point $m \in M$ is called a base point of $B$.

title: Definition:Fiber Bundle/Base Space
snippet: Let $B = \struct {E, M, \pi, F}$ be a fiber bundle. The topological space $M$ is called the base space of $B$.

title: Definition:Fiber Bundle/Bundle Projection
snippet: Let $B = \struct {E, M, \pi, F}$ be a fiber bundle. The continuous surjection $\pi: E \to M$ is called the bundle projection of $B$.

title: Definition:Fiber Bundle/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Fiber Bundle == In British English, the word fibre is used instead of fiber. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Fiber Bundle/Model Fiber
snippet: Let $B = \struct {E, M, \pi, F}$ be a fiber bundle. The topological space $F$ is called the model fiber of $B$.

title: Definition:Fiber Bundle/System of Local Trivializations
snippet: Let $B = \struct {E, M, \pi, F}$ be a fiber bundle. Let $\UU = \set {U_\alpha \subseteq M: \alpha \in I}$ be an open cover of $M$ with index set $I$. Let $\struct {U_\alpha, \chi_\alpha}$ be local trivializations for all $\alpha \in I$. The set $\set {\struct {U_\alpha, \chi_\alpha}: \alpha \in I}$ is called a system of local trivializations of $E$ on $M$.

title: Definition:Fiber Bundle/Total Space
snippet: Let $B = \struct {E, M, \pi, F}$ be a fiber bundle. The topological space $E$ is called the total space of $B$.

title: Definition:Fiber of Truth
snippet: Let $P: X \to \set {\T, \F}$ be a propositional function defined on a domain $X$. The fiber of truth (under $P$) is the preimage, or fiber, of $\T$ under $P$: $\map {P^{-1} } \T := \set {x \in X: \map P x = \T}$ That is, the elements of $X$ whose image under $P$ is $\T$.

title: Definition:Fiber of Truth/Also known as
snippet: == Fiber of Truth: Also known as == The fiber of truth is often referred to also as the solution set for $P$. This is particularly the case in algebraic contexts. Some sources denote the fiber of truth under $P$ as $\sqbrk {\size P}$.

title: Definition:Fiber of Truth/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Fiber of Truth == The phrase fiber of truth (with the same meaning) is occasionally seen in natural language. In particular: ... to extract the fiber of truth from this tissue of lies ... sounds as though it would be used in the context of the courtroom by a lawyer waxing rhetorical. The British English spelling of fiber is fibre. The pronunciation is the same. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Fiber of Truth/Solution
snippet: Let $P: X \to \set {\T, \F}$ be a propositional function defined on a domain $X$. Let $P$ be in the form of an equation in the context of algebra. Let $S = \map {P^{-1} } \T$ be the fiber of truth (under $P$). Then an element of $S$ is known as a solution of $P$.

title: Definition:Fibonacci-Like Sequence
snippet: Let $A = \tuple {a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_{n - 1} }$ be an ordered tuple of numbers. The Fibonacci-like sequence formed from $A$ is defined as: $\map {F_A} k = \begin {cases} \qquad \qquad a_k & : 0 \le k < n \\ & \\ \ds \sum_{k - n \mathop \le j \mathop < k} a_j & : k \ge n \end {cases}$ That is, apart from the first $n$ terms, every term is the sum of the previous $n$ terms. The main term can also be expressed as: $\map {F_A} k = 2 \map {F_A} {k - 1} - \map {F_A} {k - n}$

title: Definition:Fibonacci Nim
snippet: Fibonacci nim is a two-person game whose rules are as follows: $(1): \quad$ The game starts with one pile of $n$ counters. $(2): \quad$ The first player removes a number of counters $c_1$ such that $1 \le c_1 < n$. $(3): \quad$ Each player takes it in turns to remove $c_n$ counters such that $1 \le c_n \le 2 c_{n - 1}$ where $c_{n - 1}$ is the number of counters taken in the other player's prevous move. $(3): \quad$ The person who removes the last counter (or counters) is the winner.

title: Definition:Fibonacci Number
snippet: The Fibonacci numbers are a sequence $\sequence {F_n}$ of integers which is formally defined recursively as: $F_n = \begin {cases} 0 & : n = 0 \\ 1 & : n = 1 \\ F_{n - 1} + F_{n - 2} & : \text {otherwise} \end {cases}$ for all $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$. That is, the next integer in the sequence is found by adding together the two previous ones.

title: Definition:Fibonacci Number/Also known as
snippet: == Fibonacci Numbers: Also known as == According to some sources, the Fibonacci sequence is also known as Lamé's Sequence, after . However, this suggestion is difficult to corroborate. The notation for the $n$th Fibonacci number is not universally standardised. In much professional literature, $u_n$ is used. $F_n$ tends to appear more in amateur publications, but $F_n$ is rapidly taking over as standard. $F_n$ is the notation used in . Category:Definitions/Fibonacci Numbers

title: Definition:Fibonacci Number/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Fibonacci Numbers == famously discussed this sequence in his , in the context of breeding pairs of rabbits. Hence the name Fibonacci numbers, which was given to this sequence by , who studied them in detail. The sequence $\sequence {F_n}$ was known to Indian mathematicians as long ago as the $7$th century C.E. It was also studied by before $1135$, and by in about $1150$. Hence some sources refer to these numbers as the Gopala-Hemachandra numbers. They are also discussed by in his work of $1611$ De Nive Sexangula (On the Six-Cornered Snowflake).

title: Definition:Fibonacci Number/Negative
snippet: The definition of Fibonacci numbers for negative integers is an extension of the definition for positive integers: $F_n = \begin{cases} 0 & : n = 0 \\ 1 & : n = 1 \\ F_{n + 2} - F_{n + 1} & : n for all $n \in \Z$.

title: Definition:Fibonacci String
snippet: Consider the alphabet $\set {\text a, \text b}$. For all $n \in \Z_{>0}$, let $S_n$ be the (finite) string formed as: $S_n = \begin {cases} \text a & : n = 1 \\ \text b & : n = 2 \\ S_{n - 1} S_{n - 2} & : n > 2 \end{cases}$ where $S_{n - 1} S_{n - 2}$ denotes that $S_{n - 1}$ and $S_{n - 2}$ are concatenated. The terms of the sequence $\sequence {S_n}$ are Fibonacci strings.

title: Definition:Fibonomial Coefficient
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ and $k \in \Z$. Then the Fibonomial coefficient $\dbinom n k$ is defined as: $\dbinom n k_\FF = \begin{cases} 0 & : n k \\ 1 & : n \ge 0, k = 0 \\ \dfrac {F_n F_{n - 1} \cdots F_{n - k + 1} } {F_k F_{k - 1} \cdots F_1} = \ds \prod_{j \mathop = 1}^k \dfrac {F_{n - k + j} } {F_j} & : \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$ where $F_n$ denotes the $n$th Fibonacci number.

title: Definition:Field (Abstract Algebra)/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +, \times}$ be an algebraic structure. $\struct {F, +, \times}$ is a field : $(1): \quad$ the algebraic structure $\struct {F, +}$ is an abelian group $(2): \quad$ the algebraic structure $\struct {F^*, \times}$ is an abelian group where $F^* = F \setminus \set {0_F}$ $(3): \quad$ the operation $\times$ distributes over $+$.

title: Definition:Field (Abstract Algebra)/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +, \times}$ be an algebraic structure. Let $\struct {F, +, \times}$ be an integral domain with unity $1_F$ such that every non-zero element $a$ of $F$ has a multiplicative inverse $a^{-1}$ such that: $a \times a^{-1} = 1_F = a^{-1} \times a$ Then $\struct {F, +, \times}$ is a field.

title: Definition:Field (Abstract Algebra)/Definition 3

Let $\struct {F, +, \times}$ be a commutative ring with unity $1_F$ such that every non-zero element $a$ of $F$ has a multiplicative inverse $a^{-1}$ such that: $a \times a^{-1} = 1_F = a^{-1} \times a$ Then $\struct {F, +, \times}$ is a field.

title: Definition:Field (Abstract Algebra)/Definition 4
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +, \times}$ be an algebraic structure. Let $\struct {F, +, \times}$ be a non-trivial division ring whose ring product is commutative. Then $\struct {F, +, \times}$ is a field.

snippet: A field, in the context of physics, is a region of space which is acted on by a point-function. That is, in which a physical quantity is associated with every point of spacetime. The physical quantity in question may be either in vector or scalar form.

title: Definition:Field Automorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +, \circ}$ be a field. Let $\phi: F \to F$ be a (field) isomorphism from $F$ to itself. Then $\phi$ is a field automorphism.

title: Definition:Field Extension
snippet: Let $F$ be a field. A field extension over $F$ is a field $E$ where $F \subseteq E$. That is, such that $F$ is a subfield of $E$. This can be expressed: $E$ is a field extension over a field $F$ or: $E$ over $F$ is a field extension as: $E / F$ is a field extension. $E / F$ can be voiced as $E$ over $F$.

title: Definition:Field Extension/Also known as
snippet: == Field Extension: Also known as == A field extension is also known as an extension field.

title: Definition:Field Extension/Base Field
snippet: Let $E$ be a field extension over a field $F$. Then $F$ is the base field of $E$.

title: Definition:Field Extension/Complex
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +, \times}$ be a subfield of $\struct {\C, +, \times}$, the field of complex numbers. Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ be complex numbers, in or not in $F$. Then $\map F {X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n}$ is the smallest field extension over $F$ containing $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$. Category:Definitions/Field Extensions

title: Definition:Field Extension/Degree
snippet: Let $E / F$ be a field extension of a field $F$. The degree of $E / F$, denoted $\index E F$, is the dimension of $E / F$ when $E$ is viewed as a vector space over $F$.

title: Definition:Field Extension/Degree/Finite
snippet: Let $E / F$ be a field extension of a field $F$. $E / F$ is a finite field extension its degree $\index E F$ is finite.

title: Definition:Field Extension/Degree/Infinite
snippet: Let $E / F$ be a field extension of a field $F$. $E / F$ is an infinite field extension its degree $\index E F$ is not finite.

title: Definition:Field Homomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +, \times}$ and $\struct {K, \oplus, \otimes}$ be fields. Let $\phi: F \to K$ be a mapping such that both $+$ and $\times$ have the morphism property under $\phi$. That is, $\forall a, b \in F$: {{eqn | n = 1 | l = \map \phi {a + b} | r = \map \phi a \oplus \map \phi b }} {{eqn | n = 2 | l = \map \phi {a \times b} | r = \map \phi a \otimes \map \phi b }} Then $\phi: \struct {F, +, \times} \to \struct {K, \oplus, \otimes}$ is a field homomorphism.

title: Definition:Field Monomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +, \circ}$ and $\struct {K, \oplus, *}$ be fields. Let $\phi: F \to K$ be a (field) homomorphism. Then $\phi$ is a field monomorphism $\phi$ is an injection.

title: Definition:Field Negative
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +, \times}$ be a field whose zero is $0_F$. Let $x \in F$. The inverse of $x$ with respect to the addition operation $+$ in the additive group $\struct {F, +}$ of $F$ is referred to as the (field) negative of $x$ and is denoted $-x$. That is, the (field) negative of $x$ is the element $-x$ of $F$ such that: $x + \paren {-x} = 0_F$

title: Definition:Field Norm
snippet: Let $K$ be a field and $L / K$ a finite field extension of $K$. Let $\alpha\in L$.

title: Definition:Field Norm/Definition 1
snippet: Let $K$ be a field and $L / K$ a finite field extension of $K$. Let $\alpha \in L$. By Vector Space on Field Extension is Vector Space, $L$ is naturally a finite dimensional vector space over $K$. Let $\theta_\alpha$ be the linear operator: $\theta_\alpha: L \to L: \beta \mapsto \alpha \beta$ The field norm $\map {N_{L/K} }\alpha$ of $\alpha$ is the determinant of $\theta_\alpha$.

title: Definition:Field Norm/Definition 2
snippet: Let $K$ be a field and $L / K$ a finite field extension of $K$. Let $\alpha \in L$. Let $L / K$ be Galois. By Finite Field Extension has Finite Galois Group, the Galois group $\Gal {L / K}$ is finite. The field norm $\map {N_{L / K}} \alpha$ of $\alpha$ is $\ds \prod_{\sigma \mathop \in \Gal {L / K}} \map \sigma \alpha$.

title: Definition:Field Norm of Complex Number
snippet: Let $z = a + i b$ be a complex number, where $a, b \in \R$. Then the field norm of $z$ is written $\map N z$ and is defined as: $\map N z := \cmod \alpha^2 = a^2 + b^2$ where $\cmod \alpha$ denotes the complex modulus of $\alpha$.

title: Definition:Field Norm of Quaternion
snippet: Let $\mathbf x = a \mathbf 1 + b \mathbf i + c \mathbf j + d \mathbf k$ be a quaternion. Let $\overline {\mathbf x}$ be the conjugate of $\mathbf x$. The (field) norm of $\mathbf x$ is the real number defined as: $\map n {\mathbf x} := \size {\mathbf x \overline {\mathbf x} } = \size {\overline {\mathbf x} \mathbf x} = a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2$

title: Definition:Field Strength
snippet: Let $P$ be a point in a conservative field $V$. The field strength $\map {\mathbf g} {\mathbf r}$ of $V$ at $P$ is given by: {{eqn | l = \map {\mathbf g} {\mathbf r} | o = := | r = \pm \map \nabla \phi | c = $\pm$ according to sign convention adopted }} {{eqn | r = \dfrac {\partial \phi} {\partial x} \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial \phi} {\partial y} \mathbf j + \dfrac {\partial \phi} {\partial z} \mathbf k | c = }} where: $\phi$ denotes the potential at $P$ $\mathbf r$ denotes the position vector of $P$: $\mathbf r = \tuple {x, y, z}$ $\map \nabla \phi$ denotes the gradient of $\phi$ $\tuple…

title: Definition:Field Theory
snippet: Field theory is a branch of abstract algebra which studies fields and other related algebraic structures.

title: Definition:Field Zero
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +, \times}$ be a field. The identity for field addition is called the field zero (of $\struct {F, +, \times}$). It is denoted $0_F$ (or just $0$ if there is no danger of ambiguity).

title: Definition:Field Zero/Also known as
snippet: == Field Zero: Also known as == When it is clear and unambiguous what is being discussed, the field zero is often called just the zero. In the context of number fields, the field zero can also be referred to as the additive identity.

title: Definition:Field of Complex Numbers
snippet: The field of complex numbers $\struct {\C, +, \times}$ is the set of complex numbers under the two operations of addition and multiplication.

title: Definition:Field of Directions
snippet: Consider the following system of differential equations: $(1): \quad \mathbf y' = \map {\mathbf f} {x, \mathbf y, \mathbf y'}$ where $\mathbf y$ is an $n$-dimensional vector. Let the boundary conditions be prescribed $\forall x \in \closedint a b$: $\mathbf y' = \map {\boldsymbol \psi} {x, \mathbf y}$ Let these boundary conditions be consistent for all $x_1, x_2 \in \closedint a b$. Then the family of mutually consistent boundary conditions is called a field of directions for the given system $(1)$. That is, the first-order system is valid in an interval instead of a countable set of points.

title: Definition:Field of Directions/Functional
snippet: Let $\mathbf y$ be an $N$-dimensional vector. Let the functional $J$ be such that: $\ds J \sqbrk {\mathbf y} = \int_a^b \map F {x, \mathbf y, \mathbf y'} \rd x $ Let the following be a family of boundary conditions, presribed $\forall x \in \closedint a b$: $\mathbf y' = \map {\boldsymbol \psi} {x, \mathbf y}$ Let these boundary conditions be self-adjoint and consistent $\forall x_1, x_2 \in \closedint a b$. Then these boundary conditions are called field of directions of the functional $J$.

title: Definition:Field of Formal Laurent Series
snippet: Let $k$ be a field. The ring of formal Laurent series $\map k {\paren X}$ over $k$ in a variable $X$ is also called the field of formal Laurent series.

title: Definition:Field of Integers Modulo Prime
snippet: Let $p \in \Bbb P$ be a prime number. Let $\Z_p$ be the set of integers modulo $p$. Let $+_p$ and $\times_p$ denote addition modulo $p$ and multiplication modulo $p$ respectively. The algebraic structure $\struct {\Z_p, +_p, \times_p}$ is the field of integers modulo $p$.

title: Definition:Field of Integers Modulo Prime/Also denoted as
snippet: == Definiend: Also known as == When the operations are understood to be $+_p$ and $\times_p$, it is usual to use just $\Z_p$ to denote the field of integers modulo $p$. The notation $\Z / p$ and $\Z / p \Z$ are also seen, deriving from Quotient Ring of Integers by Integer Multiples. Some sources use the notation $\map {\mathrm {GF} } p$, in light of the fact that $\struct {\Z_p, +_p, \times_p}$ is a Galois field.

title: Definition:Field of Integration
snippet: A field of integration is a set of values over which a multiple integral is defined.

title: Definition:Field of P-adic Numbers
snippet:
Let $p$ be any prime number. Let $
orm {\,\cdot\,}_p$ be the $p$-adic norm on the rationals $\Q$. Let $\CC$ be the commutative ring of Cauchy sequences over $\struct {\Q, 
orm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$. Let $\NN$ be the set of null sequences in $\struct {\Q, 
orm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$. Let $\Q_p$ denote the quotient ring $\CC \,  ig / \NN$. The field of $p$-adic numbers is the field $\Q_p$. For any Cauchy sequence $\sequence{x_n}$ in $\struct{\Q, 
orm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$, let $\eqclass{x_n}{}$ denote the left coset of $\sequence{x_n}$ in $\Q_p$.

title: Definition:Field of Quotients
snippet: Let $D$ be an integral domain. Let $F$ be a field.

title: Definition:Field of Quotients/Also defined as
snippet: == Field of Quotients: Also defined as == It is common to define a field of quotients simply as a field $F$, instead of a pair $\struct {F, \iota}$. The embedding $\iota$ is then implicit. The field of quotients can also be defined to be the explicit construction from Existence of Field of Quotients.

title: Definition:Field of Quotients/Also known as
snippet: == Field of Quotients: Also known as == Since the construction of the field of quotients $F$ from an integral domain $D$ mirrors the construction of the rationals from $\Z$, $F$ is sometimes called the field of fractions or fraction field of $D$. Some sources prefer the term quotient field, but this can cause confusion with similarly named but unrelated concepts. Common notations include $\map {\operatorname {Frac} } D$, $\map Q D$ and $\map {\operatorname {Quot} } D$.

title: Definition:Field of Quotients/Definition 1
snippet: Let $D$ be an integral domain. A field of quotients of $D$ is a pair $\struct {F, \iota}$ where: $(1): \quad$ $F$ is a field $(2): \quad$ $\iota : D \to F$ is a ring monomorphism $(3): \quad \forall z \in F: \exists x \in D, y \in D_{\ne 0}: z = \dfrac {\map \iota x} {\map \iota y}$

title: Definition:Field of Quotients/Definition 2
snippet: Let $D$ be an integral domain. A field of quotients of $D$ is a pair $\struct {F, \iota}$ such that: $(1): \quad F$ is a field $(2): \quad \iota: D \to F$ is a ring monomorphism $(3): \quad$ If $K$ is a field with $\iota \sqbrk D \subset K \subset F$, then $K = F$. That is, the field of quotients of an integral domain $D$ is the smallest field containing $D$ as a subring.

title: Definition:Field of Quotients/Definition 3
snippet: Let $D$ be an integral domain. A field of quotients of $D$ is a pair $\struct {F, \iota}$ where: $(1): \quad$ $F$ is a field $(2): \quad$ $\iota : D \to F$ is a ring monomorphism $(3): \quad$ it satisfies the following universal property: For every field $E$ and for every ring monomorphism $\varphi: D \to E$, there exists a unique field homomorphism $\bar \varphi: F \to E$ such that $\varphi = \bar \varphi \circ \iota$ That is, the following diagram commutes: $\begin{xy}\xymatrix@+1em@L+2px{D \ar[r]^\iota \ar[dr]_\varphi & F \ar[d]^{\exists_1 \bar \varphi} \\ & E}\end{xy}$

title: Definition:Field of Quotients/Definition 4
snippet: Let $D$ be an integral domain. A field of quotients of $D$ is a pair $\struct {F, \iota}$ which is its total ring of fractions, that is, the localization of $D$ at the nonzero elements $D_{\ne 0}$.

title: Definition:Field of Rational Fractions
snippet: Let $R$ be an integral domain.

title: Definition:Field of Rational Functions
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $K \sqbrk x$ be the integral domain of polynomial forms on $K$. Let $\map K x$ be the set of rational functions on $K$: $\map K x := \set {\dfrac {\map f x} {\map g x}: f \in K \sqbrk x, g \in K \sqbrk x^*}$ where $K \sqbrk x^* = K \sqbrk x \setminus \set {\text {the null polynomial} }$. Then $\map K x$ is the field of rational functions on $K$.

title: Definition:Field of Rational Numbers
snippet: The field of rational numbers $\struct {\Q, + \times, \le}$ is the set of rational numbers under the two operations of addition and multiplication, with an ordering $\le$ compatible with the ring structure of $\Q$. When the ordering $\le$ is subordinate or irrelevant in the context in which it is used, $\struct {\Q, +, \times}$ is usually seen.

title: Definition:Field of Real Numbers
snippet: The field of real numbers $\struct {\R, +, \times, \le}$ is the set of real numbers under the two operations of addition and multiplication, with an ordering $\le$ compatible with the ring structure of $\R$. When the ordering $\le$ is subordinate or irrelevant in the context in which it is used, $\struct {\R, +, \times}$ is usually seen.

title: Definition:Field of Relation
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation. The field of $\RR$ is defined as: $\Field \RR := \set {x \in S: \exists t \in T: \tuple {x, t} \in \RR} \cup \set {x \in T: \exists s \in S: \tuple {s, x} \in \RR}$ That is, it is the union of the domain of $\RR$ with its image.

title: Definition:Field of Relation/Class Theory
snippet: Let $V$ be a basic universe. Let $\RR \subseteq V \times V$ be a relation in $V$. The field of $\RR$ is defined as: $\Field \RR := \set {x \in V: \exists y \in V: \tuple {x, y} \in \RR} \cup \set {y \in V: \exists x \in V: \tuple {x, y} \in \RR}$ That is, it is the union of the domain of $\RR$ with its image.

title: Definition:Fields Medal
snippet: The Fields Medal is the highest award of the , for "oustanding achievement in mathematics". It is a gold medal, awarded once every $4$ years at its , using the funds remaining after the financing of the in in $1924$. It is awarded to no fewer than $2$ and no more than $4$ mathematicians, usually under $40$ years of age. The medals stem from a bequest by , who wanted to provide an award comparable to the in stature. It was his intention to stress the international nature of mathematics, and stated that there should not be attached to the medals: the name of any country, institution or person.

title: Definition:Fifth (Music)
snippet: A fifth is a musical interval whose components have frequencies in the ratio $3 : 2$.

title: Definition:Fifth Power
snippet: A fifth power is an integer which can be expressed as the $5$th power of an integer. The sequence of fifth powers begins: $0, 1, 32, 243, 1024, 3125, 7776, 16807, 32768, 59049, 100000, 161051, \ldots$

title: Definition:Fifth Root/Real
snippet: Let $x \in \R_{\ge 0}$ be a positive real number. The fifth root of $x$ is the real number defined as: $x^{\paren {1 / 5} } := \set {y \in \R: y^5 = x}$ where $x^{\paren {1 / 5} }$ is the $5$th root of $x$. The notation: $y = \sqrt [5] x$ is usually encountered.

title: Definition:Figurate Number
snippet: A figurate number is loosely defined as a (natural) number corresponding to a set of objects which can be arranged in a geometric pattern (in an arbitrary number of dimensions, but usually $2$ or $3$).

title: Definition:Figurate Number/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Figurate Number == Figurate numbers, that is: triangular numbers square numbers pentagonal numbers hexagonal numbers and so on, were classified and investigated by the Pythagorean school in the $6$th century BCE. This was possibly the first time this had ever been done.

title: Definition:Figure (Number)
snippet: A figure is a symbol or combination of symbols representing a number.

title: Definition:Filter
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set. A subset $\FF \subseteq S$ is called a filter of $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ (or a filter on $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$) $\FF$ satisfies the filter axioms:

title: Definition:Filter/Proper Filter
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set. Let $\FF$ be a filter on $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$. Then: $\FF$ is a proper filter on $S$ $\FF \ne S$ That is, $\FF$ is a proper subset of $S$.

title: Definition:Filter Basis
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\powerset S$ denote the power set of $S$.

title: Definition:Filter Basis/Also known as
snippet: == Filter Basis: Also known as == A filter basis is also known as a filter base.

title: Definition:Filter Basis/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\powerset S$ be the power set of $S$. Let $\BB \subset \powerset S$ such that $\O \notin \BB$ and $\BB \ne \O$. Then $\FF := \set {V \subseteq S: \exists U \in \BB: U \subseteq V}$ is a filter on $S$ : $\forall V_1, V_2 \in \BB: \exists U \in \BB: U \subseteq V_1 \cap V_2$ Such a $\BB$ is called a filter basis of $\FF$.

title: Definition:Filter Basis/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\BB$ be a subset of a filter $\FF$ on $S$ such that $\BB \ne \O$. Then $\BB$ is a filter basis of $\FF$ : $\forall U \in \FF: \exists V \in \BB: V \subseteq U$

title: Definition:Filter Basis/Equivalent Filter Bases
snippet: Two filter bases are equivalent they both generate the same filter.

title: Definition:Filter Basis/Generated Filter
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\powerset S$ be the power set of $S$. Let $\BB \subset \powerset S$ be a filter basis of a filter $\FF$ on $S$. $\FF$ is said to be generated by $\BB$.

title: Definition:Filter Generated by Net
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\struct {\Lambda, \preceq}$ be a directed set. Let $\family {x_\lambda}_{\lambda \mathop \in \Lambda}$ be a net. For each $\lambda_0 \in \Lambda$, let $B_{\lambda_0} = \set {x_\lambda : \lambda \succeq \lambda_0}$. Let $\BB = \set {B_{\lambda_0} : \lambda_0 \in \Lambda}$. We define the filter generated by $\family {x_\lambda}_{\lambda \mathop \in \Lambda}$ as the filter generated by $\BB$.

title: Definition:Filter Sub-Basis
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\powerset S$ denote the power set of $S$. Let $\BB \subset \powerset S$ be a set of subsets of $\powerset S$ which satisfies the finite intersection property. That is, the intersection of any finite number of sets in $\BB$ is not empty. Then $\BB$, together with the finite intersections of all its elements, is a basis for a filter $\FF$ on $S$. Thus $\BB$ is known as a sub-basis for $\FF$.

title: Definition:Filter Sub-Basis/Also known as
snippet: == Filter Sub-Basis: Also known as == Some sources do not hyphenate filter sub-basis but instead render it as filter subbasis. Some sources use the term filter sub-base (or filter subbase).

title: Definition:Filter Theory
snippet: Filter theory is a branch of topology which studies filters.

title: Definition:Filter in Ordered Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a preordered set. Let $F$ be a subset of $S$. $F$ is a filter in $\struct {S, \preceq}$ : $F$ is non-empty, filtered and upper.

title: Definition:Filter on Set
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\powerset S$ denote the power set of $S$.

title: Definition:Filter on Set/Also known as
snippet: == Filter on Set: Also known as == A filter on a set is also known as a filter of a set. Category:Definitions/Filters on Sets

title: Definition:Filter on Set/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\powerset S$ denote the power set of $S$. A set $\FF \subset \powerset S$ is a filter on $S$ $\FF$ satisfies the filter on set axioms:

title: Definition:Filter on Set/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\powerset S$ denote the power set of $S$. A set $\FF \subset \powerset S$ is a filter on $S$ $\FF$ satisfies the filter on set axioms:

title: Definition:Filter on Set/Filtered Set
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\FF$ be a filter on $S$. Then $S$ is said to be a set filtered by $\FF$.

title: Definition:Filter on Set/Trivial Filter
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. A filter $\FF$ on $S$ by definition specifically does not include the empty set $\O$. If a filter $\FF$ were to include $\O$, then from Empty Set is Subset of All Sets it would follow that every subset of $S$ would have to be in $\FF$, and so $\FF = \powerset S$. Such a "filter" is called the trivial filter on $S$.

title: Definition:Filtered Algebra
snippet: A filtered algebra is a generalization of the notion of a graded algebra. A filtered algebra over the field $k$ is an algebra $\struct {A_k, \oplus}$ over $k$ which has an increasing sequence $\set 0 \subset F_0 \subset F_1 \subset \cdots \subset F_i \subset \cdots \subset A$ of substructures of $A$ such that: $\ds A = \bigcup_{i \mathop \in \N} F_i$ and that is compatible with the multiplication in the following sense: $\forall m, n \in \N: F_m \cdot F_n \subset F_{n + m}$

title: Definition:Filtered Category
snippet: Let $\mathbf I$ be a category. $\mathbf I$ is filtered, when: $\mathbf I$ is not empty For every two objects $i$ and $i'$ of $\mathbf I$, there exists an object $k$ and morphisms $f: i \to k$ and $f' : i' \to k$ For every two objects $i$ and $j$ of $\mathbf I$ and every two morphisms $u : i \to j$ and $v : i \to j$, there exists an object $k$ a morphism $w : j \to k$, such that $w \circ u = w \circ v$.

title: Definition:Filtered Probability Space/Continuous Time
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\sequence {\mathcal F_t}_{t \ge 0}$ be a continuous-time filtration of $\Sigma$. We say that $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \sequence {\mathcal F_t}_{t \ge 0}, \Pr}$ is a filtered probability space.

title: Definition:Filtered Probability Space/Discrete Time
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\sequence {\mathcal F_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a discrete-time filtration of $\Sigma$. We say that $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \sequence {\mathcal F_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}, \Pr}$ is a filtered probability space.

title: Definition:Filtered Subset
snippet: Let $\left({S, \precsim}\right)$ be a preordered set. Let $H$ be a non-empty subset of $S$. Then $H$ is a filtered subset of $S$ : $\forall x, y \in H: \exists z \in H: z \precsim x$ and $z \precsim y$

title: Definition:Filtration of Sigma-Algebra/Continuous Time
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\sequence {\FF_t}_{t \ge 0}$ be an $\hointr 0 \infty$-indexed family of sub-$\sigma$-algebras of $\Sigma$ such that: $\FF_t \subseteq \FF_s$ whenever $t, s \in \hointr 0 \infty$ are such that $t \le s$. We say that $\sequence {\FF_t}_{t \ge 0}$ is a filtration of $\Sigma$.

title: Definition:Filtration of Sigma-Algebra/Discrete Time
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\sequence {\FF_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be an sequence of sub-$\sigma$-algebras of $\Sigma$. That is: $\FF_i \subseteq \FF_j$ whenever $i \le j$. We say that $\sequence {\FF_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is a filtration of $\Sigma$.

title: Definition:Final Topology
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $I$ be an indexing set. Let $\family {\struct{Y_i, \tau_i}}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an $I$-indexed family of topological spaces. Let $\family {f_i: Y_i \to X}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an $I$-indexed family of mappings.

title: Definition:Final Topology/Definition 1
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $I$ be an indexing set. Let $\family {\struct{Y_i, \tau_i}}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an $I$-indexed family of topological spaces. Let $\family {f_i: Y_i \to X}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an $I$-indexed family of mappings. The final topology on $X$ with respect to $\family {f_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ is defined as: $\tau = \set{U \subseteq X: \forall i \in I: \map {f_i^{-1}} U \in \tau_i} \subseteq \powerset X$

title: Definition:Final Topology/Definition 2
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $I$ be an indexing set. Let $\family {\struct{Y_i, \tau_i}}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an $I$-indexed family of topological spaces. Let $\family {f_i: Y_i \to X}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an $I$-indexed family of mappings. Let $\tau$ be the finest topology on $X$ such that each $f_i: Y_i \to X$ is $\tuple{\tau_i, \tau}$-continuous. Then $\tau$ is known as the final topology on $X$ with respect to $\family{f_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$.

title: Definition:Financial Mathematics
snippet: Financial mathematics is the branch of mathematics which seeks to model financial markets valuing stock derivatives, especially stock options. It mainly uses the methods of stochastic calculus.

title: Definition:Financial Mathematics/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Financial Mathematics == The credibility of the models underlying the discipline of financial mathematics was seriously damaged in $2008$ as a result of the financial crisis. However, criticism of the subject dates back to .

title: Definition:Fine-Structure Constant
snippet: The fine-structure constant is a fundamental physical constant which quantifies the strength of the electromagnetic interaction between elementary charged particles. It is related to the strength of the coupling of an elementary charge $\E$ with the electromagnetic field, by the formula: $\alpha = \dfrac {\E^2} {2 \pi \epsilon_0 h c}$ where: $\E$ is the elementary charge: $1.60217 \, 6634 \times 10^{-19} \, \mathrm C$ $h$ is Planck's constant: $6.62607 \, 015 \times 10^{-34} \, \mathrm J \, \mathrm s$ $c$ is the speed of light: $299 \, 792 \, 458 \, \mathrm m \, \mathrm s^{-1}$ $\epsilon_0$…

title: Definition:Fine-Structure Constant/Also known as
snippet: == Fine-Structure Constant: Also known as == The fine-structure constant is also (rarely) known as the Sommerfeld constant, for . Some sources do not hyphenate: fine structure constant.

title: Definition:Fine-Structure Constant/Dimension
snippet: == Fine-Structure Constant == The fine-structure constant is dimensionless. Category:Definitions/Fine-Structure Constant

title: Definition:Fine-Structure Constant/Value
snippet: == Fine-Structure Constant: Value == {{eqn | l = \alpha | o = \approx | r = 7 \cdotp 29735 \, 25693 \times 10^{-3} | c = }}

title: Definition:Finer Equivalence Relation
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\equiv$ and $\sim$ be equivalence relations on $X$. Then $\equiv$ is finer than $\sim$ : $\forall x, y \in X : x \equiv y \implies x \sim y$

title: Definition:Finer Filter on Set
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\powerset S$ be the power set of $S$. Let $\FF, \FF' \subset \powerset S$ be two filters on $S$. Let $\FF \subseteq \FF'$. Then $\FF'$ is finer than $\FF$.

title: Definition:Finer Filter on Set/Also known as
snippet: == Finer Filter on Set: Also known as == A finer filter than $\FF$ can also be referred to as a superfilter of $\FF$. Category:Definitions/Finer Filters on Sets

title: Definition:Finer Filter on Set/Strictly Finer
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\powerset S$ be the power set of $S$. Let $\FF, \FF' \subset \powerset S$ be two filters on $S$. Let $\FF \subset \FF'$, that is, $\FF \subseteq \FF'$ but $\FF \ne \FF'$. Then $\FF'$ is strictly finer than $\FF$.

title: Definition:Finer Subset (Order Theory)
snippet: Let $L = \struct {S, \preceq}$ be a preordered set. Let $X, Y$ be subsets of $S$. Then $X$ is finer (subset) than $Y$ $\forall x \in X: \exists y \in Y: x \preceq y$

title: Definition:Finer Topology
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$ be topologies on $S$.

title: Definition:Finer Topology/Also known as
snippet: == Finer Topology: Also known as == The terms stronger or larger are often encountered, meaning the same thing as finer. Unfortunately, the term weaker is also sometimes encountered, meaning exactly the same thing. To remove any ambiguity as to which one is meant, it is recommended that finer be used exclusively.

title: Definition:Finer Topology/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$ be topologies on $S$. $\tau_1$ is finer than $\tau_2$ $\tau_1 \supseteq \tau_2$.

title: Definition:Finer Topology/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$ be topologies on $S$. $\tau_1$ is finer than $\tau_2$ the identity mapping $\struct {S, \tau_1} \to \struct {S, \tau_2}$ is continuous.

title: Definition:Finer Topology/Strictly Finer
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$ be topologies on $S$. Let $\tau_1 \supsetneq \tau_2$. $\tau_1$ is said to be strictly finer than $\tau_2$. This can be expressed as: $\tau_1 > \tau_2 := \tau_1 \supsetneq \tau_2$

title: Definition:Finished Branch of Propositional Tableau
snippet: Let $T$ be a propositional tableau. Let $\Gamma$ be a branch of $T$. Then $\Gamma$ is finished : $(1): \quad \Gamma$ is not contradictory $(2): \quad$ Every non-basic WFF on $\Gamma$ is used at some node of $\Gamma$. That is, $\Gamma$ is finished the set $\Delta$ of WFFs of propositional logic which occur along $\Gamma$ is a finished set‎.

title: Definition:Finished Propositional Tableau
snippet: Let $T$ be a propositional tableau. Then $T$ is finished every branch of $T$ is either finished or contradictory.
