title: Definition:Finitary
snippet: Finitary operation: An operation which takes a finite number of operands. Finitary argument: A logical argument which takes a finite number of axioms and can be translated into a finite number of statements.

title: Definition:Finite Algebra over Ring
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $B$ be an $A$-algebra. Then $B$ is finite over $A$ its underlying module is finitely generated.

title: Definition:Finite Algebraic Structure
snippet: A finite algebraic structure is an algebraic structure whose underlying set is finite. Category:Definitions/Abstract Algebra

title: Definition:Finite Cardinal
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$ be a cardinal. Then $\mathbf a$ is described as finite : $\mathbf a < \mathbf a + \mathbf 1$ where $\mathbf 1$ is (cardinal) one. That is, such that $\mathbf a \ne \mathbf a + \mathbf 1$.

title: Definition:Finite Cartesian Product/Also known as
snippet: == Finite Cartesian Product: Also known as == The finite Cartesian product $\ds \prod_{k \mathop = 1}^n S_k$ is also known as the direct product of $\sequence {S_n}$. Some sources refer to it as just the product of $\sequence {S_n}$. Some sources use the notation $\huge {\boldsymbol \times}$ instead of $\ds \prod$.

title: Definition:Finite Category
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Then $\mathbf C$ is said to be a finite category both the collection of its objects $\mathbf C_0$ and the collection of its morphisms $\mathbf C_1$ are finite sets.

title: Definition:Finite Character
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $A$ be a set of subsets of $S$. Then $A$ has finite character for each $x \subseteq S$: $x \in A$ every finite subset of $x$ is in $A$.

title: Definition:Finite Character/Also known as
snippet: == Finite Character: Also known as == To say that: $A$ has finite character is the same as saying that: $A$ is of finite character. Category:Definitions/Finite Character

title: Definition:Finite Character/Also see
snippet: == Finite Character: Also see == Tukey's Lemma, an equivalent of the Axiom of Choice Restricted Tukey's Theorem, an equivalent of the Boolean Prime Ideal Theorem. Category:Definitions/Finite Character

title: Definition:Finite Character/Class Theory
snippet: Let $A$ be a class. Then $A$ has finite character , for all $x$: $x \in A$ every finite subset of $x$ is in $A$.

title: Definition:Finite Character/Mappings
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $\FF$ be a set of mappings from subsets of $S$ to $T$. That is, let $\FF$ be a set of partial mappings from $S$ to $T$. Then $\FF$ has finite character for each partial mapping $f \subseteq S \times T$: $f \in \FF$ for each finite subset $K$ of the domain of $f$, the restriction of $f$ to $K$ is in $\FF$.

title: Definition:Finite Character/Property of Sets
snippet: Let $P$ be a property of sets. Then $P$ has finite character for every set $x$: $x$ has property $P$ every finite subset of $x$ has property $P$.

title: Definition:Finite Class
snippet: Let $A$ be a class. Let there exist a natural number $n$ as defined by the von Neumann construction such that there exists a bijection $\phi$ from $A$ to $n$. Then $A$ is a finite class.

title: Definition:Finite Complement Topology
snippet: Let $S$ be a set whose cardinality is usually specified as being infinite. Let $\tau$ be the set of subsets of $S$ defined as: $H \in \tau \iff \relcomp S H \text { is finite, or } H = \O$ where $\relcomp S H$ denotes the complement of $H$ relative to $S$. Then $\tau$ is the finite complement topology on $S$, and the topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a finite complement space.

title: Definition:Finite Complement Topology/Also known as
snippet: == Finite Complement Topology: Also known as == The finite complement topology is also called the cofinite topology. Some sources are more explicit about the nature of this topology, and call it the topology of finite complements. The finite complement topology can also be referred to as the minimal $T_1$ topology (on a given set). This is justified by Finite Complement Topology is Minimal $T_1$ Topology. This topology is also given by some sources as the Zariski topology, for . However, this is not recommended as there is another so named Zariski topology which is unrelated to this one.

title: Definition:Finite Complement Topology/Countable
snippet: Let $S$ be a countably infinite set. Let $\tau$ be the finite complement topology on $S$. Then $\tau$ is a finite complement topology on a countable space, and $\struct {S, \tau}$ is a countable finite complement space.

title: Definition:Finite Complement Topology/Finite
snippet: It is possible to define the finite complement topology on a finite set $S$, but as every subset of a finite set has a finite complement, it is clear that this is trivially equal to the discrete space. This is why the finite complement topology is usually understood to apply to infinite sets only.

title: Definition:Finite Complement Topology/Uncountable
snippet: Let $S$ be an uncountable set. Let $\tau$ be the finite complement topology on $S$. Then $\tau$ is a finite complement topology on an uncountable space, and $\struct {S, \tau}$ is a uncountable finite complement space.

title: Definition:Finite Continued Fraction/Also known as
snippet: == Finite Continued Fraction: Also known as == A finite continued fraction can be abbreviated FCF, and is also known as: a terminated (continued) fraction a terminating (continued) fraction.

title: Definition:Finite Cyclic Group/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a cyclic group. Then $\struct {G, \circ}$ is a finite cyclic group it is a finite group.

title: Definition:Finite Cyclic Group/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a cyclic group generated by $a \in G$. Then $\struct {G, \circ}$ is a finite cyclic group : $\exists n \in \N: a^n = e$

title: Definition:Finite Difference Operator
snippet: The (finite) difference operator on $f$ comes in a number of forms, as follows.

title: Definition:Finite Difference Operator/Backward Difference/First
snippet: The first backward difference operator on $f$ is defined as: $\nabla \map f {x_r} := \map f {x_r} - \map f {x_{r - 1} }$ for $r = 1, 2, \ldots, n$

title: Definition:Finite Difference Operator/Backward Difference/Second
Definition:Finite Difference Operator/Backward Difference/Unit Step Size
snippet: Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a real function. The backward difference operator on $f$ is defined as: $\map {\nabla f} x := \map f x - \map f {x - 1}$

title: Definition:Finite Difference Operator/Backward Difference/kth
Definition:Finite Difference Operator/Central Difference/First
snippet: The first central difference operator on $f$ is defined as: $\delta_i := \map f {x_{i + 1} } - \map f {x_{i - 1} }$ for $i = 1, 2, \ldots, n - 1$

title: Definition:Finite Difference Operator/Forward Difference/First
snippet: The first forward difference operator on $f$ is defined as: $\Delta \map f {x_i} := \map f {x_{i + 1} } - \map f {x_i}$ for $i = 0, 1, 2, \ldots, n - 1$

title: Definition:Finite Difference Operator/Forward Difference/Second
snippet: The second forward difference operator on $f$ is defined as: {{eqn | l = \map {\Delta^2 f} {x_i} | r = \map \Delta {\map {\Delta f} {x_i} } | c = }} {{eqn | r = \Delta \map f {x_{i + 1} } - \Delta \map f {x_i} | c = }} {{eqn | r = \map f {x_{i + 2} } - 2 \Delta \map f {x_{i + 1} } + \Delta \map f {x_i} | c = }} for $i = 0, 1, 2, \ldots, n - 2$

title: Definition:Finite Difference Operator/Forward Difference/kth
snippet: The $k$th forward difference operator on $f$ is defined as: {{eqn | l = \map {\Delta^k f} {x_i} | r = \map \Delta {\map {\Delta^{k - 1} f} {x_i} } | c = }} {{eqn | r = \Delta^{k - 1} \map f {x_{i + 1} } - \Delta^{k - 1} \map f {x_i} | c = }} {{eqn | r = \sum_{s \mathop = 0}^k \paren {-1}^{k - s} \dbinom k s y_{i + s} | c = }} for $i = 0, 1, 2, \ldots, n - k$

title: Definition:Finite Difference Operator/Preamble
snippet: == Finite Difference Operator: Preamble == 680px Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a real function. Let $y = \map f x$ have known values: $y_k = \map f {x_k}$ for $x_k \in \set {x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_n}$ defined as: $x_k = x_0 + k h$ for some $h \in \R_{>0}$. Category:Definitions/Finite Difference Operators

title: Definition:Finite Difference Operator/Warning
snippet: == Finite Difference Operator: Warning == It should be appreciated that finite difference operators, especially when used in the context of a finite difference table, can be unreliable when $y_0, y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n$ are rounded values. If this is the case, then increasingly serious errors can result in the higher order finite differences.

title: Definition:Finite Difference Table
snippet: A finite difference table is an array which displays sequences of finite differences in an easily comprehended form.

title: Definition:Finite Dimensional Vector Space/Also known as
snippet: == Finite Dimensional Vector Space: Also known as == A finite dimensional vector space is referred to by some sources with a hyphen, thus: finite-dimensional vector space.

title: Definition:Finite Dimensional Vector Space/Notation
snippet: == Finite Dimensional Vector Space: Notation == The dimension of a finite dimensional $K$-vector space $V$ is denoted $\map {\dim_K} V$, or just $\map \dim V$. Some sources use the notation $K^{\dim V}$.

title: Definition:Finite Element Method
snippet: The finite element method is a technique for approximating the solution to a partial differential equation with boundary conditions over a given domain $D$. $D$ is partitioned into elements, typically: triangles for a $2$-dimensional domain tetrahedra for a $3$-dimensional domain. On each element the solution is approximated by an appropriate function, usually a polynomial of small degree. The coefficients that define the polynomials are chosen to satisfy a best approximation criterion.

title: Definition:Finite Enumeration/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Finite Enumeration == A finite enumeration would usually be denoted as: Let $X = \set {x_1, \ldots, x_n}$. Category:Definitions/Enumerations

title: Definition:Finite Extended Real Number
snippet: An extended real number is defined as finite it is a real number. Category:Definitions/Real Numbers

title: Definition:Finite Game
snippet: A finite game is a game in which the set $A_i$ of moves available to player $i$ is finite for each player $i$.

title: Definition:Finite Graph
snippet: A finite graph is a graph with a finite number of edges and a finite number of vertices.

title: Definition:Finite Group
snippet: A finite group is a group of finite order. That is, a group $\struct {G, \circ}$ is a finite group its underlying set $G$ is finite. That is, a finite group is a group with a finite number of elements.

title: Definition:Finite Group/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Finite Group == The theory of finite groups was effectively originated by . Some sources refer to him as the father of finite groups.

title: Definition:Finite Infima Set
snippet: Let $P = \struct{S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $X$ be a subset of $S$. Then finite infima set of $X$, denoted $\map {\operatorname{fininfs}} X$, is defined by $\leftset {\inf A: A \in \map {\mathit{Fin}} X \land A}$ admits an infimum$\rightset{}$ where $\map {\mathit{Fin}} X$ denotes the set of all finite subsets of $X$.

title: Definition:Finite Integral Domain
snippet: A finite integral domain is an integral domain $\left({D, +, \circ}\right)$ such that $D$ is a finite set.

title: Definition:Finite Intersection Axiom
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $T$ be such that: Every set $V_\alpha$ of closed sets of $T$ such that $\ds \bigcap V_\alpha = \O$ contains a finite subset $V_\beta \subseteq V_\alpha$ such that $\ds \bigcap V_\beta = \O$. Then $T$ satisfies the finite intersection axiom.

title: Definition:Finite Intersection Axiom/Also known as
snippet: == Finite Intersection Axiom: Also known as == The finite intersection axiom is also known as the finite intersection property, according to some sources. However, the finite intersection property is generally considered as having a wider context, applying to an arbitrary set of sets.

title: Definition:Finite Intersection Axiom/Also presented as
snippet: == Finite Intersection Axiom: Also presented as == The finite intersection axiom can also be seen presented in the following form: Let $T$ be such that: Every set $V_\alpha$ of closed sets of $T$ for which every finite subset $V_\beta \subseteq V_\alpha$ has the property that $\ds \bigcap V_\beta \ne \O$, then $\ds \bigcap V_\alpha \ne \O$. Then $T$ satisfies the finite intersection axiom.

title: Definition:Finite Intersection Property
snippet: Let $\Bbb S$ be a non-empty set of sets. Let $\Bbb S$ have the property that: the intersection of any finite number of sets in $\Bbb S$ is not empty. Then $\Bbb S$ satisfies the finite intersection property.

title: Definition:Finite Join Preserving Mapping
snippet: Let $L_1 = \struct{S_1, \vee_1, \preceq_1}$ and $L_2 = \struct{S_2, \vee_2, \preceq_2}$ be join semilattices with smallest elements $\bot_1$ and $\bot_2$ respectively. Let $\phi: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping between the underlying sets of $L_1$ and $L_2$. Then: $\phi$ is finite join preserving, denoted $\phi:L_1 \to L_2$ $\forall$ finite $A \subseteq S_1 : \map \phi {\sup A} = \sup \set{\map \phi a : a \in A}$

title: Definition:Finite Join Property
snippet: Let $\struct {B, \vee, \wedge, \neg, \bot, \top}$ be a bounded lattice. Let $F \subseteq B$ be a filter on $B$. Let $J \subseteq B$. Then $J$ has the finite join property with respect to $F$ , for every finite subset $D \subseteq J$: $\forall x_1, x_2, \ldots x_n \in D: x_1 \vee x_2 \vee \dots \vee x_n \notin F$ where $x \vee y$ denotes the join of $x$ and $y$. If $F = \set {\top}$, then $J$ simply has the finite join property. Category:Definitions/Lattice Theory

title: Definition:Finite Measure
snippet: Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. Then $\mu$ is said to be a finite measure : $\map \mu X < \infty$

title: Definition:Finite Measure/Signed Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\mu$ be a signed measure on $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. We say that $\mu$ is a finite signed measure : $\size {\map \mu X} < \infty$

title: Definition:Finite Measure Space
snippet: A measure space $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ is said to be finite $\mu$ is a finite measure.

title: Definition:Finite Meet Preserving Mapping
snippet: Let $L_1 = \struct{S_1, \wedge_1, \preceq_1}$ and $L_2 = \struct{S_2, \wedge_2, \preceq_2}$ be meet semilattices with greatest elements $\top_1$ and $\top_2$ respectively. Let $\phi: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping between the underlying sets of $L_1$ and $L_2$. Then: $\phi$ is finite meet preserving, denoted $\phi:L_1 \to L_2$ $\forall$ finite $A \subseteq S_1 : \map \phi {\inf A} = \inf \set{\map \phi a : a \in A}$

title: Definition:Finite Monoid
snippet: A finite monoid is a monoid whose underlying set is finite. Category:Definitions/Monoids

title: Definition:Finite Order
snippet: Abstract algebra: Finite Order of Algebraic Structure Finite Group: a group of finite order Group theory: Finite Order of Group Element

title: Definition:Finite Ordinal
snippet: Let $\alpha$ be an ordinal. Then $\alpha$ is said to be finite one of the following holds: $\alpha = \O$ $\alpha = \beta^+$ for some finite ordinal $\beta$ where $\O$ denotes the empty set, and $\beta^+$ is the successor ordinal of $\beta$.

title: Definition:Finite Partition (Probability Theory)
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\xi$ be a partition of $\Omega$. Then, $\xi$ said to be a finite partition : $\exists A_1, \ldots, A_n \in \Sigma \setminus \set \O : \xi = \set {A_1, \ldots, A_n}$

title: Definition:Finite Partition Generated by Finite Sub-Sigma-Algebra
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\AA \subseteq \Sigma$ be a finite sub-$\sigma$-algebra. The finite partition generated by $\AA$ is defined as: $\ds \map \xi \AA := \set {\bigcap_{i \mathop = 1}^n B_i : B_i \in \set {A_i, \Omega \setminus A_i} } \setminus \set \O$ where $\AA = \set {A_1, \ldots, A_n}$.

title: Definition:Finite Path
snippet: Let $G$ be a graph. A finite path in $G$ is a path consisting of a finite number of edges.

title: Definition:Finite Population Correction
snippet: Let $P$ be a population of size $N$ from which a sample of size $n$ has been extracted. The finite population correction is the value: $\sqrt {\dfrac {N - n} {N - 1} }$ which is used to adjust the standard error, which becomes: $\sqrt {\dfrac {N - n} {N - 1} } \times \dfrac s {\sqrt n}$ where $\dfrac s {\sqrt n}$ is the standard error.

title: Definition:Finite Population Correction/Motivation
snippet: == Finite Population Correction: Motivation == The standard error of the mean based on a sample of size $n$ assumes that the population is infinite, or at least, so large that the effect of withdrawing items during the sampling process has a negligible effect. If $n$ becomes a significant fraction of the population size, then the finite population correction is needed to adjust the estimate of the standard error. This correction is commonly used when $n$ is larger than $5 \%$ of the population size.

title: Definition:Finite Probability Space
snippet: A finite probability space is a discrete probability space $\left({\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}\right)$ such that the sample space $\Omega$ is finite.

title: Definition:Finite Projective Plane/Order 4
snippet: The finite projective plane of order $4$. It can be denoted: $\operatorname {PG} \left({4, 4}\right)$ where: $\operatorname {PG}$ stands for projective geometry the first parameter $2$ specifies the dimension the second parameter $2$ specifies the order. $\operatorname {PG} \left({4, 4}\right)$ has the following properties: It has $21$ points It has $21$ lines There are $5$ points on each line There are $5$ lines through each point.

title: Definition:Finite Rank Operator
snippet: Let $H, K$ be Hilbert spaces. Let $T: H \to K$ be a linear transformation. Then $T$ is said to be a finite rank operator, or of finite rank, its range, $\Rng T$, is finite dimensional. Note that a finite rank operator is not necessarily bounded.

title: Definition:Finite Real Number
snippet: Let $x$ be a real number. Then $x$ is a finite real number there exists another real number $y$ such that $\size x < \size y$.

title: Definition:Finite Ring
snippet: A finite ring is a ring $\left({R, +, \circ}\right)$ such that $R$ is a finite set. Category:Definitions/Ring Theory

title: Definition:Finite Ring Homomorphism
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be commutative rings with unity. Let $\phi: A \to B$ be a ring homomorphism.

title: Definition:Finite Semigroup
snippet: A finite semigroup is a semigroup of finite order. That is, a semigroup $\struct {S, \circ}$ is a finite semigroup its underlying set $G$ is finite. That is, a finite semigroup is a semigroup with a finite number of elements.

title: Definition:Finite Sequence
snippet: A finite sequence is a sequence with a finite number of terms.

title: Definition:Finite Sequence/Also known as
snippet: == Finite Sequence: Also known as == Some sources use the term word in place of finite sequence. Compare the definition of word in the context of formal systems. Some treatments, in order to stress the difference between a finite sequence and infinite sequence, present this term as finite-sequence.

title: Definition:Finite Set
snippet: A set $S$ is defined as finite : $\exists n \in \N: S \sim \N_{<n}$ where $\sim$ denotes set equivalence. That is, if there exists an element $n$ of the set of natural numbers $\N$ such that the set of all elements of $\N$ less than $n$ is equivalent to $S$. Equivalently, a finite set is a set with a count.

title: Definition:Finite Set/Also known as
snippet: == Finite Set: Also known as == It is a common expression to refer to a finite number when finite set is meant. That is, a finite number of can usually more precisely be worded a finite set of. However, it is often the case that finite number works better, so on both forms will be found. Similarly, the term finitely many can also be seen in a similar context. Category:Definitions/Finite Sets

title: Definition:Finite Set Coding
snippet: Let $A \subset \N$ be a finite subset of the natural numbers. Let $\ds n = \sum_{a \mathop \in A} 2^a$. Then $n$ codes the finite set $A$, or $n$ is the code number for the finite set $A$.

title: Definition:Finite State Machine
snippet: A finite state machine is an ordered tuple: $F = \left({ S, A, I, \Sigma, T }\right)$ where: $S$ is the (finite) set of states $A \subseteq S$ is the set of accepting states $I \in S$ is the initial state $\Sigma$ is the alphabet of symbols that can be fed into the machine $T : \left({ S \times \Sigma }\right) \rightarrow S$ is the transition function. A finite state machine operates as follows: $(1): \quad$ At the beginning, the current state $s$ of the finite state machine is $I$. $(2): \quad$ One by one, the input (a sequence of symbols from $\Sigma$) is fed into the machine.

title: Definition:Finite Sub-Sigma-Algebra
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\AA \subseteq \Sigma$ be a sub-$\sigma$-algebra. Then, $\AA$ is said to be a finite sub-$\sigma$-algebra : $\exists A_1, \ldots, A_n \in \Sigma : \AA = \set {A_1, \ldots, A_n}$

title: Definition:Finite Subset
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $T$ be a subset of $S$ which is a finite set. Then $T$ is a finite subset of $S$. Category:Definitions/Subsets

title: Definition:Finite Suprema Set
snippet: Let $P = \struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $X$ be a subset of $S$. Then the finite suprema set of $X$, denoted $\map {\mathrm {finsups} } X$, is defined as: $\leftset {\sup A: A \in \map {\mathit {Fin} } X \land A}$ admits a supremum$\rightset{}$ where $\map {\mathit {Fin} } X$ denotes the set of all finite subsets of $X$.

title: Definition:Finite Topological Space
snippet: A finite topological space is a topological space whose underlying set is finite.

title: Definition:Finite Topological Space/Also known as
snippet: == Finite Topological Space: Also known as == A finite Topological Space is also known as.

title: Definition:Finite Type
snippet: Definition:Module of Finite Type Definition:Algebra of Finite Type Definition:Morphism of Schemes of Finite Type

title: Definition:Finitely Axiomatizable
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a logical language. Let $\mathscr M$ be a formal semantics for $\LL$. Let $\FF$ be an $\LL$-theory. Then $\FF$ is called finitely axiomatizable there exists a finite axiomatization $\AA$ of $\FF$.

title: Definition:Finitely Branching
snippet: Let $T$ be a tree. Then $T$ is finitely branching $T$ is locally finite.

title: Definition:Finitely Generated
snippet: Definition:Finitely Generated Algebraic Structure Definition:Finitely Generated Monoid Definition:Finitely Generated Group Definition:Finitely Generated Module Definition:Finitely Generated Field Extension Definition:Finitely Generated Algebra

title: Definition:Finitely Generated Algebra
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring. Let $B$ be an $A$-algebra. Then $B$ is finitely generated $B$ has a generator which is finite.

title: Definition:Finitely Generated Algebraic Structure
snippet: Let $\struct {A, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. Let $\struct {A, \circ}$ have a generator which is finite. Then $\struct {A, \circ}$ is finitely generated.

title: Definition:Finitely Generated Field Extension
snippet: Let $E / F$ be a field extension. Then $E$ is said to be finitely generated over $F$ , for some $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n \in E$: $E = F \left({\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n}\right)$ where $F \left({\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n}\right)$ is the field in $E$ generated by $F \cup \left\{{\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n}\right\}$.

title: Definition:Finitely Generated Group
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. $G$ is finitely generated $G$ has a generator which is finite.

title: Definition:Finitely Generated Ideal of Ring
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $I\subseteq R$ be a ideal of $R$. Then $I$ is finitely generated there is a generator for $I$ which is finite.

title: Definition:Finitely Generated Module
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $M$ be a module over $R$. Then $M$ is finitely generated there is a generator for $M$ which is finite.

title: Definition:Finitely Satisfiable
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a logical language. Let $\mathscr M$ be a formal semantics for $\LL$. Let $\FF$ be a collection of logical formulas of $\LL$. Then $\FF$ is finitely satisfiable for $\mathscr M$ : For each finite subset $\FF' \subseteq \FF$, there is some $\mathscr M$-model $\MM$ of $\FF'$ That is, for each such $\FF'$, there exists some structure $\MM$ of $\mathscr M$ such that: $\MM \models_{\mathscr M} \FF'$

title: Definition:Finitism
snippet: Finitism is the philosophical position which accepts the existence only of finite mathematical objects. Hence in the finitist school, the concept of infinity does not exist.

title: Definition:First-Countable Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a first-countable space every point in $S$ has a countable local basis.

title: Definition:First-Countable Space/Also known as
snippet: == First-Countable Space: Also known as == A first-countable space can also be said to satisfy the first axiom of countability Some sources render first-countable space without the hyphen: first countable. aims to be consistent in presentation, and the hyphenated version is preferred.

title: Definition:First-Fit Decreasing Packing Algorithm
snippet: The first-fit decreasing packing algorithm is a refinement of the first-fit packing algorithm for solving the bin packing problem. The algorithm proceeds as follows: $(1): \quad$ Sort the boxes into decreasing height $(2): \quad$ Apply the first-fit packing algorithm. Hence the largest boxes are packed first, and it is more likely to produce an optimal solution than the first-fit packing algorithm.

title: Definition:First-Fit Packing Algorithm
snippet: The first-fit packing algorithm is an algorithm for solving the bin packing problem. The algorithm proceeds as follows: $(1): \quad$ Number the bins into arbitrary order $(2): \quad$ Select the boxes in arbitrary order $(3): \quad$ For each box, place it into the lowest-numbered bin it will fit into.

title: Definition:First-Order Convergence/Also known as
snippet: == First-Order Convergence: Also known as == First-order convergence is also known as linear convergence.

title: Definition:First-Order Property of Sets
snippet: A first-order property of sets is a property defined by a logical formula whose domain is entirely over sets. Thus the quantifiers $\forall x$ and $\exists x$ are valid when $x$ is a set, but $\forall A$ and $\exists A$ are not valid when $A$ is a class. Hence we allow, for example: $\map \phi {A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n, x}$ to be a logical formula whose variables $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n$ represent classes, and are all free, and $x$ is the only free variable representing a set.

title: Definition:First-Order Reaction
snippet: Suppose a body has a tendency to decompose spontaneously into smaller bodies at a rate independent of the presence of other bodies. Then the number of bodies that decompose in a single unit of time is proportional to the total number present. Such a reaction is called a first-order reaction.

title: Definition:First-Order Reaction/Rate Constant
snippet: Let $S$ be a substance which decomposes spontaneously in a first-order reaction. By First-Order Reaction, this is governed by the equation: $x = x_0 e^{-k t}$ where: $x$ is the quantity of $S$ at time $t$ $x_0$ is the quantity of $S$ at time $t = 0$ $k$ is a positive number. The number $k$ is called the rate constant. $k$ is constant for a particular substance, and different substances, in general, have different rate constants.

title: Definition:First Central Difference Operator/Also defined as
snippet: == First Central Difference Operator: Also known as == Some sources define the first central difference operator as: $\delta_{i + 1/2} := \map f {x_i + \dfrac h 2} - \map f {x_i - \dfrac h 2}$ for $i = 1, 2, \ldots, n - 1$ However, the astute reader will immediately notice that, as defined, it is not certain that the function values for $x_i \pm \dfrac h 2$ are not necessarily available, or even defined. Category:Definitions/Central Difference Operator

title: Definition:First Central Difference Operator/Also known as
snippet: == First Central Difference Operator: Also known as == The first central difference operator is also known as the central difference operator, by sources which may not be concerned with higher order finite difference operators.

title: Definition:First Central Difference Operator/Mistake
snippet: == Source Work == finite differences

title: Definition:First Chebyshev Function
snippet: The first Chebyshev function is defined and denoted: $\ds \map \vartheta x := \sum_{p \mathop \le x} \ln p$ where the summation extends over all prime numbers $p$ such that $p \le x$.

title: Definition:First Feigenbaum Constant/Also known as
snippet: == First Feigenbaum Constant: Also known as == The first Feigenbaum constant is also referred to as merely the Feigenbaum constant or Feigenbaum number. As it was the first to be noticed and investigated, it was inevitably named before the second Feigenbaum constant was identified. Some sources give it as the Feigenbaum bifurcation velocity.

title: Definition:First Feigenbaum Constant/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on First Feigenbaum Constant == The first Feigenbaum constant was the result of serendipitous observations by in $1979$. Its precise value may still be a topic of research. Different sources quote it differently. Watch this space.

title: Definition:First Forward Difference Operator/Also known as
snippet: == First Forward Difference Operator: Also known as == The first forward difference operator is also known as just the forward difference operator.

title: Definition:First Fundamental Form
snippet: Let $S$ be a surface of a $3$-dimensional Euclidean space. Let $p$ be a point of $S$. Let $T_pS$ be the tangent space to $S$ at the point $p$. The first fundamental form is the bilinear form: $\operatorname I: T_p S \times T_p S \longrightarrow \R$ induced from the dot product of $\R^3$: $\map {\operatorname I} {x, y} = \innerprod x y$ The first fundamental form is a way to calculate the length of a given line $C \subset S$ or the area of a given bounded region $R \subset S$.

title: Definition:First Integral of System of Differential Equations
snippet: Let $S$ be a system of differential equations. Let $g$ be a function which satisfies $S$. Let $f$ be a function. Let $f$ depend on variables (denoted by ordered tuples here) of $S$ independently as well as through $g$ and its derivatives: $f = \map f {\sequence {x_i} _{1 \mathop \le i \mathop \le n}, \sequence {g^{\paren j} \paren {\sequence {x_i}_{1 \mathop \le i \mathop \le n} }_{0 \mathop \le j \mathop \le k} } }, \quad {n, k} \in \N$ Suppose there exists $g$ such that $f$ is a constant. Then $f$ is the first integral of $S$.

title: Definition:First Kind
snippet: The term first kind is used to distinguish two or more classes of mathematical object of some common overall type.

title: Definition:First Kind/Also known as
snippet: == First Kind: Also known as == Some such objects are referred to as being of the first type rather than the first kind, but the meaning remains the same. Category:Definitions/First Kind

title: Definition:First Order Ordinary Differential Equation
snippet: A first order ordinary differential equation is an ordinary differential equation in which any derivatives with respect to the independent variable have order no greater than $1$. The general first order ODE can be written as: $\map F {x, y, \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} }$ or, using prime notation: $\map F {x, y, y'}$ If it is possible to do so, then it is often convenient to present such an equation in the form: $\dfrac {\d y} {\d x} = \map f {x, y}$ that is: $y' = \map f {x, y}$ It can also be seen presented in the form: $\map \phi {x, y, y'} = 0$

title: Definition:First Order Ordinary Differential Equation/Also known as
snippet: == First Order Ordinary Differential Equation: Also known as == A first order ordinary differential equation is often seen referred to just as a first order differential equation by sources which are not concerned about partial differential equations. Some sources hyphenate: first-order differential equation. The abbreviation ODE is frequently seen, hence first order ODE for first order ordinary differential equation.

title: Definition:First Postulate of Special Theory of Relativity/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on First Postulate of Special Theory of Relativity == The first postulate of the special theory of relativity is an extension and generalization of work done by and .

title: Definition:First Principles
snippet: A proof is constructed from first principles when no reliance is made on other established theorems.

title: Definition:First Quartile/Also known as
snippet: == First Quartile: Also known as == The first quartile is often referred to as the lower quartile.

title: Definition:First Radiation Constant
snippet: The first radiation constant is defined as: $c_1 = 2 h c^2$ where: $h$ denotes Planck's constant $c$ denotes the speed of light.

title: Definition:First Radiation Constant/Also defined as
snippet: The first radiation constant is also seen defined as: $c_1 = 8 \pi h c$ where: $h$ denotes the Planck's constant $c$ denotes the speed of light. This can be obtained from the conventional definition of first radiation constant by multiplying it by $\dfrac {4 \pi} c$.

title: Definition:First Radiation Constant/Also defined as/Dimension
snippet: The first radiation constant when defined as $8 \pi h c$ has the dimension $\mathsf {M L^3 T^{-2} }$. This arises from its definition as Planck's constant multiplied by speed of light: $\mathsf {M L^2 T^{-1} } \times \mathsf {L T^{-1} }$ Category:Definitions/First Radiation Constant Category:Definitions/Dimensions of Measurement

title: Definition:First Radiation Constant/Also defined as/Units
snippet: The SI unit for the first radiation constant when defined as $8 \pi h c$ is given as joule metres: $\mathrm {J \, m}$ The CGS unit for the first radiation constant when defined as $8 \pi h c$ is given as ergs centimetres: $\mathrm {erg \, cm}$ Category:Definitions/First Radiation Constant Category:Definitions/Units of Measurement

title: Definition:First Radiation Constant/Also defined as/Value
snippet: == First Radiation Constant: Value == The value of the first radiation constant when defined as $8 \pi h c$ is: {{eqn | r = 4 \cdotp 99248 \, 2965 \ldots \times 10^{-24} \, \mathrm {J \, m} | c = }} {{eqn | r = 4 \cdotp 99248 \, 2965 \ldots \times 10^{-15} \, \mathrm {erg \, cm} | c = }}

title: Definition:First Radiation Constant/Dimension
snippet: The first radiation constant has the dimension $\mathsf {M L^4 T^{-3} }$. This arises from its definition as Planck's constant multiplied by speed of light squared: $\mathsf {M L^2 T^{-1} } \times \paren {\mathsf {L T^{-1} } }^2$ Category:Definitions/First Radiation Constant Category:Definitions/Dimensions of Measurement

title: Definition:First Radiation Constant/Units
snippet: The SI unit for the first radiation constant is given as watt metres squared per second: $\mathrm {W \, m^2}$ The CGS unit for the first radiation constant is given as ergs centimetre squared per second: $\mathrm {erg \, cm^2 \, s^{-1} }$ Category:Definitions/First Radiation Constant Category:Definitions/Units of Measurement

snippet: == First Radiation Constant: Value == The value of the first radiation constant is: {{eqn | r = 1 \cdotp 19104 \, 2972 \ldots \times 10^{-18} \, \mathrm {W \, m^2} | c = }} {{eqn | r = 1 \cdotp 19104 \, 2972 \ldots \times 10^{-15} \, \mathrm {erg \, cm^2 \, s^{-1} } | c = }} Category:Definitions/First Radiation Constant

title: Definition:Fischer-Griess Monster
snippet: The Fischer-Griess monster $\mathrm M$ is the automorphism group of the Griess algebra.

title: Definition:Fischer-Griess Monster/Also known as
snippet: == Fischer-Griess Monster: Also known as == The Fischer-Griess monster is also known as: the friendly giant the monster sporadic (simple) group or just: the monster (group).

title: Definition:Fischer-Griess Monster/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Fischer-Griess Monster == The existence of the Fischer-Griess Monster was first deduced by in $1973$, but he did not publish this finding. In $1976$, made the same discovery from a different direction. In $1981$, finally managed to construct the actual Fischer-Griess Monster itself.

title: Definition:Fisher's Exact Test
snippet: Fisher's exact test is a test for lack of association in a $2 \times 2$ contingency table. It is based on the hypergeometric distribution. If expected numbers in all cells are not too low (some sources suggest at least $10$), the $\chi^2$ test is a good approximation. It is noted that the quality of approximation does not depend on the characteristics of the sample itself.

title: Definition:Fisher's Exact Test/Also known as
snippet: == Fisher's Exact Test: Also known as == Fisher's exact test is also known as: the Fisher-Irwin test (for and ) the Fisher-Yates test (for and )

title: Definition:Fisher's z-Distribution
snippet: Fisher's $z$-distribution is a probability distribution based on the logarithm of the ratio of two estimators of a common variance.

title: Definition:Fisher's z-Distribution/Also known as
snippet: == Fisher's $z$-Distribution: Also known as == Fisher's $z$-distribution is also known just as the $z$-distribution.

title: Definition:Fisher's z-Distribution/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Fisher's $z$-Distribution == In practice, according to in , Fisher's $z$-distribution is rarely used, and Snedecor's $F$-distribution is used instead.

title: Definition:Fisher's z-Transformation
snippet: Fisher's $z$-transformation is a transformation of the sample estimate $r$ of a bivariate normal correlation coefficient to $z = \arctan r$ so as to give a better approximation to a normal distribution.

title: Definition:Fisher's z-Transformation/Also known as
snippet: == Fisher's $z$-Transformation: Also known as == Fisher's $z$-transformation is also known as just the $z$-transformation.

title: Definition:Fisher-Freeman-Halton Test
snippet: The Fisher-Freeman-Halton test is an extension of Fisher's exact test to the general $r \times c$ contingency table.

title: Definition:Fit
snippet: Consider a mathematical model $\MM$, often in the context of statistics. The fit of $\MM$ is the degree of correspondence between observations in the real world and the behaviour predicted by $\MM$.

title: Definition:Five-Number Summary
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of observations of a quantitative variable. The five-number summary of $S$ consists of:

title: Definition:Five-Number Summary/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Five-Number Summary == The five-number summary was pioneered by in $1977$.

title: Definition:Fixed-Point Representation
snippet: Fixed-point representation is a technique for representing an approximation to a real number $x$ in a given number base $\beta$ by presenting it by means of a fixed number of digits with: a fixed number of digits before the radix point to hold the integer part of $x$ a fixed number of digits after the radix point to hold the fractional part of $x$.

title: Definition:Fixed-Point Representation/Also defined as
snippet: == Fixed-Point Representation: Also defined as == Some sources define fixed-point representation with the default base $10$, without suggesting the possible implementation of other bases.

title: Definition:Fixed-Point Representation/Also known as
snippet: == Fixed-Point Representation: Also known as == Fixed-point representation is also known as fixed-point notation. However, it is the view of that representation is a better descriptive term here than notation.

title: Definition:Fixed Element under Permutation
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\pi: S \to S$ be a permutation on $S$. Let $x \in S$. $x$ is fixed under $\pi$ : $\map \pi x = x$

title: Definition:Fixed Element under Permutation/Moved
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\pi: S \to S$ be a permutation on $S$. Let $x \in S$. $x$ moved by $\pi$ : $\map \pi x \ne x$

title: Definition:Fixed Element under Permutation/Set of Fixed Elements
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\pi: S \to S$ be a permutation on $S$. The set of elements of $S$ which are fixed by $\pi$ can be denoted $\Fix \pi$. Note that: $x \notin S \implies x \in \Fix \pi$

title: Definition:Fixed Field
snippet: Let $F$ be a field. Let $G \le \Aut F$ be a subgroup of the automorphism group of $F$. The fixed field of $G$ is the set: $\Fix G = \set {f \in F : \forall \sigma \in G : \map \sigma f = f}$

title: Definition:Fixed Point
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. Then a fixed point of $S$ under $f$ is an element $x \in S$ such that $\map f x = x$.

title: Definition:Flat (Matroid)

title: Definition:Flat Riemannian Manifold
snippet: Let $M$ be an $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold. $M$ is called the flat Riemannian manifold it is locally isometric to an Euclidean Space. That is, for every point $p \in M$ there is a neighborhood that is isometric to an open set in $\R^n$ with the Euclidean metric.

title: Definition:Floating-Point Operation
snippet: A floating-point operation is an arithmetic operation (addition, subtraction, multiplication or division) performed on floating-point numbers.

title: Definition:Floating-Point Representation
snippet: Floating-point representation is a technique for representing a real number $x$ in a given number base $\beta$ by presenting it uniquely in the form: $x = f \times \beta^e$ where: $f$ is a real number such that $\dfrac 1 \beta \le \size f < 1$, expressed in decimal notation $e$ is an integer.

title: Definition:Floating-Point Representation/Also defined as
snippet: == Floating-Point Representation: Also defined as == Some sources define floating-point representation with the default base $10$, that is: $x = f \times 10^e$ and then allude to the base $2$ implementation as an aside.

title: Definition:Floating-Point Representation/Also known as

title: Definition:Floating-Point Representation/Base
snippet: Let $x$ be a real number expressed in floating-point representation as: $x = f \times \beta^e$ where: $f$ is a real number such that $\dfrac 1 \beta \le \size f < 1$, expressed in decimal notation $e$ is an integer. The number $\beta$ is known as the base of the floating-point representation.

title: Definition:Floating-Point Representation/Computer Implementation
snippet: == Floating-Point Representation: Computer Implementation == Implementation of floating-point representation of a real number: $x = f \times \beta^e$ is subject to the following considerations. Both the mantissa $f$ and the exponent $e$ have a limited range: $f$ is a number with $t$ digits base $\beta$ $e$ lies in an interval $\closedint L U$.

title: Definition:Floating-Point Representation/Exponent
snippet: Let $x$ be a real number expressed in floating-point representation as: $x = f \times \beta^e$ where: $f$ is a real number such that $\dfrac 1 \beta \le \size f < 1$, expressed in decimal notation $e$ is an integer. The integer $e$ is known as the exponent of the floating-point representation.

title: Definition:Floating-Point Representation/Mantissa
snippet: Let $x$ be a real number expressed in floating-point representation as: $x = f \times \beta^e$ where: $f$ is a real number such that $\dfrac 1 \beta \le \size f < 1$, expressed in decimal notation $e$ is an integer. The real number $f$ is known as the mantissa of the floating-point representation.

title: Definition:Floating-Point Representation/Normalized
snippet: Let $x$ be a real number implemented in floating-point representation as: $x = f \times \beta^e$ such that: $x = \pm \sqbrk {0.f_1 f_2 \ldots f_t} \times \beta^e$ This representation is said to be normalized $f_1 \ne 0$.

title: Definition:Floor Function
snippet: right Let $x$ be a real number. Informally, the floor function of $x$ is the greatest integer less than or equal to $x$.

title: Definition:Floor Function/Also known as
snippet: == Floor Function: Also known as == The floor function of a real number $x$ is usually just referred to as the floor of $x$. The floor function is sometimes called the entier function, from the French for integer. The floor of $x$ is also often referred to as the integer part or integral part of $x$, particularly in older treatments of number theory. Some sources give it as the greatest integer function.

title: Definition:Floor Function/Definition 1
snippet: Let $x$ be a real number. The floor function of $x$ is defined as the supremum of the set of integers no greater than $x$: $\floor x := \sup \set {m \in \Z: m \le x}$ where $\le$ is the usual ordering on the real numbers.

title: Definition:Floor Function/Definition 2
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number. The floor function of $x$, denoted $\floor x$, is defined as the greatest element of the set of integers: $\set {m \in \Z: m \le x}$ where $\le$ is the usual ordering on the real numbers.

title: Definition:Floor Function/Definition 3
snippet: Let $x$ be a real number. The floor function of $x$ is the unique integer $\floor x$ such that: $\floor x \le x < \floor x + 1$

title: Definition:Floor Function/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Floor Function == The notation $\floor x$ for the floor function was introduced in the $1960$s by and made popular by .

title: Definition:Floor Function/Notation
snippet: Before around $1970$, the usual symbol for the floor function was $\sqbrk x$. The notation $\floor x$ for the floor function is a relatively recent development. Compare the notation for the corresponding ceiling function, $\ceiling x$, which in the context of discrete mathematics is used almost as much. Some sources use $\map {\mathrm {fl} } x$ for the floor function of $x$. However, this notation is clumsy, and will not be used on .

title: Definition:Flow Chart
snippet: A flow chart is a graphical depiction of an algorithm in which the steps are depicted in the form of boxes connected together by arrows. Let $F$ and $P$ be sets. Let $C = \struct {V, E}$ be a finite digraph. Let $V$ be divided into pairwise disjoint sets $\tuple {V_F, V_P, V_J, V_I, V_O}$. These are assigned specific terms: $V_F$ are the functional boxes $V_P$ are the predicative boxes $V_J$ are the junctions $V_I$ are the entry points $V_O$ are the exit points Let each $b \in V_F$ be assigned a unique $F_b \in F$, and each $b \in V_P$ be assigned a unique $P_b \in P$.

title: Definition:Flow Chart/Also known as
snippet: == Flow Chart: Also known as == A flow chart is also known as a flow diagram.

title: Definition:Flow Chart/Computational History
snippet: Let $C = \struct {V, E}$ be a flow chart. Let $\struct {X, \set {f_g}, \set {f_q}}$ be an interpretation for $C$. Let $\phi = \sequence {\tuple {b_j, x_j}}_j$ be a control path in $\tuple {C, X}$. Let $\phi' = \sequence {\tuple {b_{j_k}, x_{j_k}}}_k$ be the subsequence of $\phi$ containing exactly those $\tuple {b_j, x_j}$ such that: $b_j \in V_F \cup V_P$ For every $b_{j_k}$, let $O_{j_k}$ denote either: $F_{b_{j_k}}$ or: $P_{b_{j_k}}$ depending on whether $b_{j_k} \in V_F$ or $b_{j_k} \in V_P$.

title: Definition:Flow Chart/Control Path
snippet: Let $C = \struct {F, P, V, E}$ be a flow chart. Let $\struct {X, \set {f_g}, \set {p_q}}$ be a interpretation for $C$. Let $\sequence {\tuple {b_j, x_j}}_{1 \mathop \le j \mathop \le N}$ be a finite sequence in $V \times X$. Suppose that, for every $j < N$: $b_j b_{j + 1}$ is an arc in $E$. If $b_j \in V_P$, then: $x_j \in X_{b_j}$. $b_j b_{j + 1}$ is labeled $\top$ $x_j \in p_{b_j}$. Additionally, suppose that, for every $j < N$: If $b_j \in V_F$, then $x_{j + 1} = \map {f_{b_j}} {x_j}$. If $b_j \notin V_F$, then $x_{j + 1} = x_j$.

title: Definition:Flow Chart/Graphical Representation
snippet: == Flow Chart: Graphical Representation == Conventionally, the shape of the box representing a step is dependent upon the type of operation encapsulated within the step: Rectangular for an action, represented by a functional box. A different shape, conventionally a diamond, for a condition, represented by a predicative box. On , the preferred shape for condition boxes is rectangular with rounded corners. This is to maximise ease and neatness of presentation: configuring a description inside a diamond shaped boxes in order for it to be aesthetically pleasing can be challenging and tedious.

title: Definition:Flow Chart/Interpretation
snippet: Let $C = \struct {F, P, V, E}$ be a flow chart. Let $X$ be a set. For each $g \in F$, let $f_g : X \to X$ be a partial mapping on $X$. For each $q \in P$, let $p_q \subseteq X_q \subseteq X$ be a unary relation defined on a subset $X_q$ of $X$. Then, $\struct {X, \set {f_g}, \set {p_q}}$ is an interpretation for $C$.

title: Definition:Flow Chart/Represented Mapping
snippet: Let $C = \struct {V, E}$ be a flow chart. Let $\struct {X, f_g, p_q}$ be an interpretation for $C$. Then, the mapping represented by $C$ is a partial mapping $C_f : V_I \times X \to V_O \times X$ is defined as: For any $\tuple {b, x} \in V_I \times X$: $\tuple {b', x'} = \map {C_f} {b, x}$ is unique such that there is a control path $\sequence {\tuple {b_j, x_j}}_j$ where: $b_1 = b$ and $b_N = b'$ $x_1 = x$ and $x_N = x'$ $b' \in V_O$ If no such control path exists, then $\map {C_f} {b, x}$ is undefined.

title: Definition:Flux
snippet: Let $\mathbf V$ be a vector field which acts on a region of space $R$. Let $S$ be a surface embedded in $R$. The flux through $S$ is the dot product of $\mathbf V$ with the vector area of $S$. Hence flux is a scalar quantity.

title: Definition:Flux/Direction
snippet: While flux is a scalar quantity, it does have a direction. The sign of vector area $\delta S$ through which the flux operates depends upon the right-hand rule according to the direction of rotation around $S$ when describing it. Hence, having decided on the sign of $\delta S$, the flux through $\delta S$ is either: positive, where the angle $\psi$ between the normal to $\delta S$ is acute negative, where the angle $\psi$ between the normal to $\delta S$ is obtuse.

title: Definition:Flux/Illustration
snippet: == Flux: Illustration == 420px $\qquad$ 420px As can be seen, more flux passes through $\delta S$ when it is positioned perpendicular to the direction of $\mathbf v$, as in the diagram on the left, than when not, as in the diagram on the right.

title: Definition:Flux/Informal Definition
snippet: Let $\mathbf V$ be a vector field which acts on a region of space $R$. Let $S$ be a surface embedded in $R$. The concept of flux is most easily pictured in the context of the flow of fluids. Let there be a fluid whose flow is defined by the vector $\mathbf v$. Imagine a small loop of wire enclosing an area element $\delta S$ placed in the fluid, perpendicular to the direction of $\mathbf v$. The flux $F$ of fluid through $\delta S$ is the rate of flow of fluid through the loop.

title: Definition:Flux/Total
snippet: Let $\mathbf V$ be a vector field which acts on a region of space $R$. Let $S$ be a surface embedded in $R$. The total flux through $S$ is the surface integral over $S$ of the dot product of $\mathbf V$ with the vector area of $S$: $F = \ds \int_S \mathbf V \cdot \rd S$ where $\d S$ is an infinitesimal area element of $S$.

title: Definition:Foiaș Constant/Second
snippet: Let $x_1 \in \R_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive real number. Let: $x_{n + 1} = \paren {1 + \dfrac 1 {x_n} }^n$ for $n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$ The second Foiaș constant is defined as the unique real number $\alpha$ such that if $x_1 = \alpha$ then the sequence $\sequence {x_{n + 1} }$ diverges to infinity. No closed-form expression is known.

title: Definition:Force
snippet: A force is an influence which causes a body to undergo a change in velocity. Force is a vector quantity.

title: Definition:Force/Also known as
snippet: == Force: Also known as == Some writers and thinkers subdivide the idea of a force into a push or a pull, but such a dichotomy can serve to confuse the fact that they are in fact both forces. Some treatments of physics and applied mathematics refer to a force as an action, and refer to the opposite force as the reaction to that action.

title: Definition:Force/Dimension
snippet: The dimension of measurement of force is $\mathsf {M L T}^{-2}$. This arises from Newton's Second Law of Motion and its definition as a mass (of dimension $\mathsf M$) multiplied by an acceleration (of dimension $\mathsf {L T}^{-2}$).

title: Definition:Force/Linguistic Note

title: Definition:Force Field
snippet: A force field is a vector field in which the physical quantity associated with every point is a non-contact force which applies to a body placed at that point.

title: Definition:Force Field/Also known as
snippet: == Force Field: Also known as == A force field is often referred to as a field of force. Some writers prefer it, as the term force field is overused in the context of science fiction as a magic McGuffin to achieve a gosh-wow.

title: Definition:Force Polygon
snippet: Let a system of forces $\SS$ act at a point. Let $\SS$ consist of the forces $\mathbf F_1, \mathbf F_2, \ldots, \mathbf F_n$, represented by directed line segments $A_0 A_1, A_1 A_2, \ldots, A_{n - 1} A_n$. The polygon $A_0 A_1 \ldots A_n A_0$ is called the force polygon representing $\SS$. The resultant of $\SS$ is represented by the directed line segment $A_0 A_n$.

title: Definition:Forced Oscillation
snippet: Let an oscillating system $S$ be subjected to an external force $\mathbf F$ which is a periodic function of time. The motion of $S$ that $\mathbf F$ gives rise to is called forced oscillation.

title: Definition:Forced Vibration
snippet: Consider a physical system $S$ whose behaviour can be described with the second order ODE in the form: $(1): \quad \dfrac {\d^2 x} {\d t^2} + 2 b \dfrac {\d x} {\d t} + a^2 x = K \cos \omega x$ for $a, b \in \R_{>0}$. Let $b < a$, so as to make $S$ underdamped. Then the steady-state motion of $S$ is referred to as forced vibration of $S$.

title: Definition:Forced Vibration/Forcing Frequency
snippet: Consider a second order ODE in the form: $\dfrac {\d^2 x} {\d t^2} + 2 b \dfrac {\d x} {\d t} + a^2 x = K \cos \omega x$ for $a, b \in \R_{>0}$. Let $b < a$, so as to make $S$ underdamped. The frequency: $\dfrac \omega {2 \pi}$ is known as the forcing frequency of $S$.

title: Definition:Forecast Function
snippet: Let $T$ be a time series. Let $S$ denote the range of $T$. Let $L$ denote the set of lead times of $T$. Let $t$ denote the origin of $T$. A forecast function $\hat z_t : L \to S$ is a function which provides forecasts of the future values of $T$ at the lead times $L$. The objective is to make the mean squares of the deviations $z_{t + l} - \map {\hat z_t} l$ as small as possible for each lead time $l$. In the above: $\map {\hat z_t} l$ denotes the forecast value of the observation at the timestamp of lead time $l$ $z_{t + l}$ denotes the actual value of the observation at the timestamp of $l$.

title: Definition:Forecasting
snippet: In the context of the discipline of time series analysis, forecasting is the estimation of future observations of a given time series based on knowledge of current and past such observations.
