title: Definition:Function
snippet: The process which is symbolised by an operation is called a function. The operand(s) of the operation can be considered to be the input(s). The output of the function is whatever the operation is defined as doing with the operand(s). A function is in fact another name for a mapping, but while the latter term is used in the general context of set theory and abstract algebra, the term function is generally reserved for mappings between sets of numbers.

title: Definition:Function/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Function == The term function, as used in the modern sense, was first used by in $1694$. The notation $\map f x$ itself appears to have originated with . He used it in two particular contexts: particular conventional examples like trigonometric function and powers and the like $\map y x$ for an arbitrary curve in the plane. Up until the time of , it was accepted that a function was limited to various classes of expression: a polynomial, a finite combination of elementary functions, a power series or a trigonometric series.

title: Definition:Function Space
snippet: A function space is a general concept relating to an abstract space of functions between two sets.

title: Definition:Function Symbol
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a formal language (for example, the language of predicate logic $\LL_1$). A function symbol is a letter of $\LL$ used to describe a function. The name function symbol is a gesture to the reader to make clear what such a symbol should (intuitively) represent in the formal language $\LL$.

title: Definition:Functional
snippet: A functional is a mapping: whose domain is a set of mappings whose codomain is another set of mappings.

title: Definition:Functional/Real
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of mappings. Let $J: S \to \R$ be a mapping from $S$ to the real numbers $\R$: $\forall y \in S: \exists x \in \R: J \sqbrk y = x$ Then $J: S \to \R$ is known as a (real) functional, denoted by $J \sqbrk y$. That is, a (real) functional is a real-valued function whose arguments are themselves mappings.

title: Definition:Functional Analysis
snippet: Functional analysis is a branch of analysis, which studies vector spaces endowed a structure such as inner product, norm or topology. It can be understood as the study of analysis, including calculus, both differential and integral, to Banach spaces.

title: Definition:Functional Equation
snippet: Let $f$ be a real-valued or complex-valued function A functional equation for $f$ is an equation of the form $\map f {x, y, \ldots} = 0$, where the expression for $f$ may contain a finite number of independent variables a finite number of either known or unknown functions for which $f$ is to be solved.

title: Definition:Functional Series
snippet: A functional series is a series of the form: $\ds \sum \map {f_n} x$ such that the terms are functions of an independent variable $x$.

title: Definition:Functional Series/Region of Convergence
snippet: Let $S$ be a functional series of an independent variable $x$. The region of convergence of $S$ is the set of values of $x$ for which $S$ is convergent.

title: Definition:Functionally Complete
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of truth functions. Then $S$ is functionally complete all possible truth functions are definable from $S$.

title: Definition:Functionally Complete/Also known as
snippet: == Functionally Complete: Also known as == A functionally complete set can also be described as expressively adequate. Category:Definitions/Truth Functions

title: Definition:Functor
snippet: Informally, a functor is a morphism of categories. It may be described as what one must define in order to define a natural transformation. This is formalized by defining the category of categories.

title: Definition:Functor/Co- and Contravariance
snippet: == Functor: Co- and Contravariance == Both covariant and contravariant functors are paramount in all of contemporary mathematics. The intention behind defining a functor is to formalise and abstract the intuitive notion of "preserving structure". Functors thus can be understood as a generalisation of the concept of homomorphism in all its instances. This explains why one would be led to contemplate covariant functors. However, certain "natural" operations like transposing a matrix do not preserve the structure as rigidly as a homomorphism (we do have Transpose of Matrix Product, however).

title: Definition:Functor/Covariant
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. A covariant functor $F: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ consists of: An object functor $F_0$ that assigns to each object $X$ of $\mathbf C$ an object $F X$ of $\mathbf D$. An arrow functor $F_1$ that assigns to each arrow $f: X \to Y$ of $\mathbf C$ an arrow $F f : F X \to F Y$ of $\mathbf D$.

title: Definition:Functor Category
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be categories. The functor category $\map {\operatorname{Funct} } {\mathbf C, \mathbf D}$ is the category with:

title: Definition:Functor Creating Colimits
snippet: Let $\mathbf C, \mathbf D$ and $\mathbf J$ be metacategories. Let $F: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be a functor. Then $F$ is said to create colimits of type $\mathbf J$ : For all $\mathbf J$-diagrams $C: \mathbf J \to \mathbf C$ in $\mathbf C$, given a colimit $\paren { {\varinjlim \,}_j \, FC_j, q_j}$ for $FC: \mathbf J \to \mathbf D$ in $\mathbf D$, the colimit: $\paren {{\varinjlim \,}_j \, C_j, p_j}$ exists, and furthermore: $\map F {{\varinjlim \,}_j \, C_j} = {\varinjlim \,}_j \, FC_j$ $F p_j = q_j$ for all objects $j$ of $\mathbf J$.

title: Definition:Functor Creating Limits
snippet: Let $\mathbf C, \mathbf D$ and $\mathbf J$ be metacategories. Let $F: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be a functor. Then $F$ is said to create limits of type $\mathbf J$ : For all $\mathbf J$-diagrams $C: \mathbf J \to \mathbf C$ in $\mathbf C$, given a limit $\paren {{\varprojlim \,}_j \, FC_j, q_j}$ for $FC: \mathbf J \to \mathbf D$ in $\mathbf D$, the limit: $\paren {{\varprojlim \,}_j \, C_j, p_j}$ exists, and furthermore: $\map F {{\varprojlim \,}_j \, C_j} = {\varprojlim \,}_j \, FC_j$ $F p_j = q_j$ for all objects $j$ of $\mathbf J$.

title: Definition:Functor Evaluation Bifunctor
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be categories. Let $\map {\operatorname{Funct}} {\mathbf C, \mathbf D}$ be their covariant functor category. Let $\map {\operatorname{Funct}} {\mathbf C, \mathbf D} \times \mathbf C$ be the product category. The evaluation bifunctor $\operatorname{ev}: \map {\operatorname{Funct}} {\mathbf C, \mathbf D} \times \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ is the covariant functor that sends: {{DefineFunctor |ob = an object $\tuple {F, a}$ to $\map F a$ |mor = a morphism $\tuple {\eta, f}: \tuple {F, a} \to \tuple {G, b}$ to $\map G f \circ \eta_a = \eta_b \circ \map F f$ }}

title: Definition:Functor Preserving Limits
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$, $\mathbf D$ and $\mathbf J$ be metacategories. Let $F: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be a functor. Then $F$ preserves limits of type $\mathbf J$ for all diagrams $D: \mathbf J \to \mathbf C$ with limit ${\varprojlim \,}_j \, D_j$: $\map F {{\varprojlim \,}_j \, D_j} \cong {\varprojlim \,}_j \, F D_j$ where $F D: \mathbf J \to \mathbf D$ is the composition of $F$ with $D$.

title: Definition:Fundamental Circuit (Matroid)
snippet: Let $M = \struct {S, \mathscr I}$ be a matroid. Let $B$ be a base of $M$. Let $x \in S \setminus B$. The fundamental circuit of $x$ in the base $B$, denoted $\map C {x, B}$, is the unique circuit such that: $x \in \map C {x, B} \subseteq B \cup \set x$

title: Definition:Fundamental Dimensions/Also defined as
snippet: == Fundamental Dimensions: Also defined as == For the fundamental dimensions, some sources prefer to use: instead of: Category:Definitions/Fundamental Dimensions

title: Definition:Fundamental Dimensions/Also known as
snippet: == Fundamental Dimensions: Also known as == The fundamental dimensions can also be seen referred to as the basic dimensions.

title: Definition:Fundamental Domain (Lattice)
snippet: Let $L \subset \R^n$ be an integral lattice. Let $B = \tuple {v_1, \ldots, v_n}$ be an ordered basis for $L$. The fundamental domain of $L$ associated to $B$ is the set: $\ds \set {\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \lambda_i v_i: \forall i: 0 \le \lambda_i < 1}$ Category:Definitions/Linear Algebra Category:Definitions/Geometry of Numbers

title: Definition:Fundamental Group/Also known as
snippet: == Fundamental Group: Also known as == The fundamental group of a topological space $T$ is also known more explicitly as the fundamental homotopy group of $T$. The fundamental group of $T$ is also known as the Poincaré group of $T$, for .

title: Definition:Fundamental Group/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {X, x_0}$ be a pointed topological space with base point $x_0$. The fundamental group $\map {\pi_1} {X, x_0}$ of $X$ at the base point $x_0$ is the set of homotopy classes of loops with base point $x_0$ with multiplication of homotopy classes of paths.

title: Definition:Fundamental Group/Definition 2
snippet: Let $* : \map {\pi_n} {X, x_0} \times \map {\pi_n} {X, x_0} \to \map {\pi_n} {X, x_0}$ denote the concatenation of homotopy classes of paths. That is, if $\overline {c_1}, \overline {c_2}$ are two elements of $\map {\pi_n} {X, x_0}$, then: $\overline {c_1} * \overline {c_2} = \overline {c_1 \cdot c_2}$ where $\cdot$ denotes the usual concatenation of paths. Then $\struct {\map {\pi_n} {X, x_0}, *}$ is the $n$th fundamental group of $X$. The first homotopy group is usually called the fundamental group when higher homotopy groups are not in sight.

title: Definition:Fundamental Group/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Fundamental Group == The concept of the fundamental group was defined by in $1895$. The definition was extended to $n > 1$ by in $1932$ and in $1935$.

title: Definition:Fundamental Group Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf{Top}^*$ be the category of pointed topological spaces. Let $\mathbf{Grp}$ be the category of groups. The fundamental group functor is the covariant functor $\pi_1 : \mathbf{Top}^* \to \mathbf{Grp}$ with:

title: Definition:Fundamental Matrix
snippet: Let $\mathbf x' = \map A t \mathbf x$ be a system of $n$ linear first order ODEs. Let $\map \Phi t$ be an $n \times n$ matrix function. Then $\map \Phi t$ is a fundamental matrix of the system $\mathbf x' = \map A t \mathbf x$ : it solves the matrix system $\mathbf X' = \map A t \mathbf X$ $\det \map \Phi t$ is nonvanishing.

title: Definition:Fundamental Solution
snippet: Let $\delta$ be the Dirac delta distribution. Let $D$ be a differential operator with constant coefficients. A fundamental solution is a Schwartz distribution $E \in \map {\DD'} {\R^d}$ such that: $DE = \delta$

title: Definition:Fundamental Truth Table
snippet: The fundamental truth tables are the characteristic truth tables for: Logical Not Conjunction Disjunction Conditional Biconditional as follows:

title: Definition:Fundamental Truth Table/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Fundamental Truth Table == The separate categorization of the characteristic truth tables for these five statement forms appears in . This may be idiosyncratic.

title: Definition:Fundamental Unit
snippet: Fundamental Unit (Number Theory) Fundamental Unit (Physics): One of a set of units for physical quantities from which every other unit can be generated.

title: Definition:Fundamental Unit (Physics)
snippet: A fundamental unit is a unit of measurement for a measurable physical property from which every other unit for that quantity can be derived. The fundamental unit for a particular measurable quantity is chosen by convention. They are the units of the fundamental dimensions of physics.

title: Definition:Fundamental Unit (Physics)/Also known as
snippet: == Fundamental Unit: Also known as == Fundamental units are also known as base units.

title: Definition:Furlong/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Furlong == The word furlong derives from the old English furh lang, meaning furrow long. The terms arise from the days of ploughing in mediaeval times. The furlong was the length of a single furrow, which stretched the whole length of one of the acres into which the land was divided. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Furstenberg Topology
snippet: Let $\Z$ be the set of integers. Let: $\BB := \set {a \Z + b : a,b \in \Z, a \ne 0}$ where: $a \Z + b := \set {a k + b : k \in \Z}$ Let: $\tau := \set {\bigcup \AA : \AA \subseteq \BB}$ Then $\tau$ is called Furstenberg topology on $\Z$.

title: Definition:Future
snippet: The future is the portion of time subsequent to the present. That is, the future is what has not happened yet.

title: Definition:Fuzzy Intersection
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \struct {A, \mu_A}$ and $\mathbf B = \struct {B, \mu_B}$ be fuzzy sets. Then the (fuzzy) intersection of $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ is denoted $\mathbf A \cap \mathbf B$, defined as the fuzzy set such that: The domain of $\mathbf A \cap \mathbf B$ is $A \cap B$ The membership function of $\mathbf A \cap \mathbf B$ is: $\forall x \in A \cap B: \map {\mu_{A \cap B} } x = \map \min {\map {\mu_A} x, \map {\mu_B} x}$ where $\min$ is the min operation.

title: Definition:Fuzzy Logic
snippet: Fuzzy logic is a sub-category of multi-value logic specifically concerned with the study of real-world decision-making.

title: Definition:Fuzzy Logic/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Fuzzy Logic == Fuzzy logic was proposed in $1965$ by . Fuzzy logic has been used, among other things, to control elevators, dishwashers and assembly line strategies in factories.

title: Definition:Fuzzy Logic/Historical Note/Mistake
snippet: == Source Work == fuzzy logic

title: Definition:Fuzzy Set
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\closedint 0 1$ denote the closed unit interval. Let $\mu: S \to \closedint 0 1$ be a mapping. Then $\struct {S, \mu}$ is a fuzzy set.

title: Definition:Fuzzy Set/Domain
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \mu}$ be a fuzzy set. $S$ is the domain of $\struct {S, \mu}$.

title: Definition:Fuzzy Set/Membership Function
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \mu}$ be a fuzzy set. $\mu$ is the membership function of $\struct {S, \mu}$.

title: Definition:Fuzzy Set Theory
snippet: Fuzzy set theory is a version of set theory in which the membership relation is not precisely defined. Hence the membership relation is represented by a real number between $0$ and $1$: $0$ meaning definitely not an element $1$ meaning definitely an element.

title: Definition:G-Delta Set
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. A $G_\delta$ set ($G$-delta set) is a set which can be written as a countable intersection of open sets of $T$.

title: Definition:G-Delta Set/Linguistic Note
snippet: The name $G_\delta$ originates from the German: G for Gebiet, which is German for area or neighborhood (used in the sense open set in this case) $\delta$ (Greek d) for Durchschnitt, which is German for set intersection. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:G-Module Homomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \cdot}$ be a group. Let $\struct {V, \phi}$ and $\struct {W, \mu}$ be $G$-modules. Then a linear transformation $f: V \to W$ is called a $G$-module homomorphism : $\forall g \in G: \forall v \in V: \map f {\map \phi {g, v} } = \map \mu {g, \map f v}$

title: Definition:G-Module Homomorphism/Also known as
snippet: == G-Module Homomorphism: Also known as == Group theorists commonly refer to a $G$-module homomorphism as a $G$-intertwining map or simply an intertwining map. Also the term $G$-equivariant map can be seen.

title: Definition:G-Ordered Class
snippet: Let $A$ be a class. Let $g$ be a progressing mapping. Let $A$ be well-ordered by the subset relation such that: Then $A$ is said to be $g$-ordered.

title: Definition:G-Set
snippet: Let $A$ be a class. Let $g: A \to A$ be a mapping. We say that $x$ is a $g$-set $x$ is an element of every class that is superinductive under $g$.

title: Definition:G-Statistics
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of observations of a quantitative variable. The $g$-statistics on $S$ are the statistical coefficients $g_1$ and $g_2$, defined as: $g_1$ is the skewness $\gamma_1$ of the elements of $S$ $g_2$ is the kurtosis $\gamma_2$ of the elements of $S$.

title: Definition:G-Submodule
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \cdot}$ be a finite group. Let $\struct {V, \phi}$ be a $G$-module. Let $W$ be a vector subspace of $V$. Let $\phi$ be a linear group action when restricted to $G \times W \subseteq G \times V$. Let $\phi_W$ be the restriction of $\phi$ to $G \times W$. Then $\struct {W, \phi_W}$ is called a $G$-submodule of $\struct {V, \phi}$.

title: Definition:G-Tower
snippet: Let $M$ be a class. Let $g: M \to M$ be a progressing mapping on $M$. Let $M$ be minimally superinductive under $g$. Then $M$ is called a $g$-tower.

title: Definition:GCD Domain
snippet: A GCD domain is an integral domain in which any two non-zero elements have a greatest common divisor.

title: Definition:GPS
snippet: GPS, or Global Positioning System, is a technique using signals from satellites to identify the geographical coordinates of an appropriately configured receiver.

title: Definition:Gabriel's Horn
snippet: Gabriel's horn is the name given to the solid of revolution formed by rotating about the $x$-axis the curve: $y = \dfrac 1 x$ 400px

title: Definition:Gabriel's Horn/Also known as
snippet: == Gabriel's Horn: Also known as == Gabriel's horn is also known as Torricelli's trumpet for , who discovered that it paradoxically has a finite volume but infinite surface area. Category:Definitions/Gabriel's Horn

title: Definition:Gal/Also known as
snippet: == Gal: Also known as == The gal is also known as the centimetre per second squared. It is also seen referred to as the centimetre per second per second. This logically arises as its definition as the acceleration that causes a change in velocity of $1$ centimetre per second over the course of $1$ second. Category:Definitions/Gal

title: Definition:Galactic Center
snippet: The galactic center is the point on the galactic equator which is taken to be the center of the (Milky Way) galaxy. It is used as the origin of the galactic coordinate system. Its agreed position in equatorial coordinates is: Right ascension: $17 \, \mathrm h \, 46 \, \mathrm {min}$ Declination: $-28 \degrees \, 56 '$

title: Definition:Galactic Center/Also known as
snippet: == Galactic Center: Also known as == The galactic center is rendered galactic centre in British English.

title: Definition:Galactic Coordinate System
snippet: The galactic coordinate system is an astronomical coordinate system in which measurements are based on the galactic equator. Hence a point on the celestial sphere is located by means of $2$ angular measurements: the galactic longitude $l$, which is the angular distance measured eastwards along the galactic equator from the galactic center the galactic latitude $b$, which is the angular distance measured north or south of the galactic equator.

title: Definition:Galactic Equator
snippet: The galactic equator is the great circle that is the intersection of the plane of the Milky Way with the celestial sphere.

title: Definition:Galactic Equator/Also known as
snippet: == Galactic Equator: Also known as == The galactic equator is also known as the galactic circle.

title: Definition:Galactic Equator/Axis
snippet: The galactic axis is the axis of the great circle that is the galactic equator.

title: Definition:Galactic Equator/Pole
snippet: The galactic poles are the two poles of the great circle that is the galactic equator.

title: Definition:Galaxy
snippet: A galaxy is a system of stars and associated matter bound together by gravitation.

title: Definition:Galaxy/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Galaxy == The word galaxy is derived from the Greek γαλαξίας (galaxias) which means milky. This is a reference to the Milky Way galaxy that contains the Solar System. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Galilean Relativity
snippet: Let $O$ and $O'$ be two observers moving in ordinary $3$-dimensional space. According to Galilean relativity, $O$ and $O'$ will have coordinate systems related by: $\begin {bmatrix} t \\ \mathbf r \end {bmatrix} = \begin {bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ \mathbf v & \mathbf M \end {bmatrix} \begin {bmatrix} t' \\ \mathbf r' \end {bmatrix} + \mathbf c$ where: $t$ and $t'$ are the time coordinates for $O$ and $O'$ respectively $\mathbf r$ and $\mathbf r'$ are the space coordinates for $O$ and $O'$ respectively $\mathbf v$ is the velocity of $O$ $O'$ $\mathbf M$ is a order $3$ square matrix with determinant…

title: Definition:Galilean Transformation
snippet: A Galilean transformation is a transformation between inertial frames of reference which adhere to the postulates of classical mechanics.

title: Definition:Gallon (Imperial)/Also known as
snippet: == Imperial Gallon: Also known as == The imperial gallon is also known as the UK gallon in order specifically to distinguish it from the US gallon. Sources which are of British origin, particularly earlier ones, may refer to this unit merely as the gallon, assuming an understanding by their audience that the gallon is the imperial gallon by default.

title: Definition:Gallon (Imperial)/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Imperial Gallon: Conversion Factors == {{eqn | r = 4 \cdotp 54609 \times 10^{-3} | c = cubic metres }}

title: Definition:Gallon (Imperial)/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Imperial Gallon == Prior to $1824$, there existed a number of different gallons throughout the British Empire. The imperial gallon was defined in $1824$ as a volume close to the ale gallon. Its original definition was the volume of $10$ pounds (approximately $4.5$ kilograms) of distilled water, weighed in air with brass weights with the barometer standing at $30$ inches of mercury ($102$ kilopascals) at a temperature of $62$ degrees Fahrenheit ($17$ degrees Celsius).

title: Definition:Gallon (US)/Also known as
snippet: == US Gallon: Also known as == The US gallon can sometimes be seen rendered as U.S. gallon.

title: Definition:Gallon (US)/Conversion Factors
snippet: == US Gallon: Conversion Factors == {{eqn | r = 3.78541 \, 1784 \times 10^{-3} | c = cubic metres }} Hence $6$ US gallons is approximately $5$ imperial gallons.

title: Definition:Galois Connection
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq_S}$ and $\struct {T, \preceq_T}$ be ordered sets. Let $g: S \to T$ and $d: T \to S$ be mappings. Then $\tuple {g, d}$ is a Galois connection : $g$ and $d$ are increasing mappings $\forall s \in S, t \in T: t \preceq_T \map g s \iff \map d t \preceq_S s$

title: Definition:Galois Connection/Also known as
snippet: In some sources the upper adjoint is called the right adjoint and the lower adjoint is called the left adjoint. The terminology right adjoint and left adjoint is also used to denote the functors of an adjuntion in the context of category theory. So the use of the terms upper adjoint and lower adjoint for a Galois connection serves to differentiate the context of order theory from the context of category theory. The mappings are named for the position that each mapping has with respect to the orderings involved in the defining condition of Galois connection.

title: Definition:Galois Connection/Lower Adjoint
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ and $\struct {T, \precsim}$ be ordered sets. Let $g: S \to T$, $d: T \to S$ be mappings. Let $\tuple {g, d}$ be a Galois connection. Then: $d$ is called the lower adjoint of the Galois connection.

title: Definition:Galois Connection/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Galois Connection == Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ and $\struct {T, \precsim}$ be ordered sets. A Galois connection is often denoted as $f = \struct{\upperadjoint f, \loweradjoint f}$ where $\upperadjoint f : S \to T$ denotes the upper adjoint and $\loweradjoint f : T \to S$ denotes the lower adjoint. When $g : S \to T$ is known to be an upper adjoint of a Galois connection, the lower adjoint can be denoted as $\loweradjoint g : T \to S$.

title: Definition:Galois Connection/Upper Adjoint
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ and $\struct {T, \precsim}$ be ordered sets. Let $g: S \to T$, $d: T \to S$ be mappings. Let $\tuple {g, d}$ be a Galois connection. Then: $g$ is called the upper adjoint of the Galois connection.

title: Definition:Galois Extension
snippet: Let $L / K$ be a finite field extension.

title: Definition:Galois Extension/Arbitrary
snippet: Let $L / K$ be a finite field extension. $L / K$ is a Galois extension it is normal and separable.

title: Definition:Galois Extension/Finite
snippet: Let $L / K$ be a finite field extension.

title: Definition:Galois Extension/Finite/Definition 1
snippet: Let $L / K$ be a finite field extension. $L / K$ is a (finite) Galois extension the fixed field of its automorphism group is $K$: $\map {\operatorname{Fix}_L} {\Gal {L / K} } = K$

title: Definition:Galois Extension/Finite/Definition 2
snippet: Let $L / K$ be a finite field extension. $L / K$ is a (finite) Galois extension it is normal and separable.

title: Definition:Galois Extension/Finite/Definition 3
snippet: Let $L / K$ be a finite field extension $L / K$ is a (finite) Galois extension the order of the automorphism group $\Aut {L / K}$ equals the degree $\index L K$: $\order {\Aut {L / K} } = \index L K$

title: Definition:Galois Field
snippet: A Galois field $\struct {\GF, +, \circ}$ is a field such that $\GF$ is a finite set. The symbol conventionally used to denote a Galois field of $q$ elements is $\map \GF q$.

title: Definition:Galois Field/Also denoted as
snippet: == Galois Field: Also known as == Some sources use the notation $\map {\mathrm {GF} } q$ to denote a Galois field of order $q$. Some sources use $\GF_q$ for $\map \GF q$. Some sources place further emphasis on the formal nature of a Galois field by denoting it $\map {\mathrm {GF} } {p^n}$ or $\map \GF {p^n}$, and so on.

title: Definition:Galois Field/Also known as
snippet: == Galois Field: Also known as == Some sources do not mention , but merely refer to a Galois field as a finite field.

title: Definition:Galois Field/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Galois Field == The study of Galois fields was initiated by in $1830$.

title: Definition:Galois Field/Technical Note
snippet: == Technical Note on Galois Field == Category:Technical Notes

title: Definition:Galois Group of Field Extension
snippet: Let $L / K$ be a field extension. The Galois group of $L / K$ is the subgroup of the automorphism group of $L$ consisting of field automorphisms that fix $K$ point-wise: $\Gal {L / K} = \set {\sigma \in \Aut L: \forall k \in K: \map \sigma k = k}$

title: Definition:Galois Group of Field Extension/Also defined as
snippet: == Galois Group: Also defined as == More generally, we can abandon the condition that $L / K$ be Galois if we choose an algebraic closure $\overline K$ such that $L \subseteq \overline K$ and define: $\Gal {L / K} = \leftset {\sigma: L \to \overline K: \sigma}$ is an embedding of $L$ such that $\sigma$ fixes $K$ point-wise$\rightset {}$ This set will form a group $L / K$ is normal.

title: Definition:Galois Group of Field Extension/Also denoted as
snippet: == Galois Group: Also denoted as == The Galois group of $L / K$ can also be denoted $\map G {L / K}$.

title: Definition:Galois Group of Field Extension/Also known as
snippet: == Galois Group: Also known as == The Galois group of $L / K$ is also known as its automorphism group and denoted $\Aut {L / K}$. Some authors refer to $\Aut {L / K}$ as a Galois group only when $L / K$ is a Galois extension. Some sources use the notation $\map G {L \mid K}$.

title: Definition:Galois Group of Field Extension/Topological Group
snippet: The notation $\Gal {L / K}$ is also a shorthand for the topological group: $\struct {\Gal {L / K}, \tau}$ where $\tau$ is the Krull topology.

title: Definition:Galois Group of Polynomial
snippet: Let $P$ be a polynomial. The Galois group of $P$ is the symmetry group of the roots of $P$.

title: Definition:Galois Theory
snippet: Galois theory is a subfield of abstract algebra which reduces the study of field extensions to the study of the associated Galois groups. Hence it provides a connection between field theory and group theory.

title: Definition:Galois Theory/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Galois Theory == The discipline of Galois theory dates back as far as $1600$ BCE, when the mathematicians of ancient Babylon worked out how to solve the quadratic equation. In the $16$th century, the technique leaked out into the public that the cubic equation was also soluble. Soon after that, extended this method to show how to solve the quartic. The quintic remained unsolved until the early $19$th century, at which point and proved it insoluble.

title: Definition:Gambler's Ruin
snippet: Gambler's ruin is the classic problem to determine the probability that a gambler $G$ with an initial capital of $C$ units becomes bankrupt in a sequence of games in which: $G$ gains $1$ unit of capital with probability $p$ $G$ loses $1$ unit of capital with probability $q = 1 - p$. $G$ is ruined he loses all $C$ units. There is usually a condition that $G$ stops on attaining a total fortune of $N$ units, where $N > C$.

title: Definition:Game
snippet: In the context of game theory, a game is a social situation which involves more than one person. More specifically, a game is a problem of strategy between two or more parties in which all parties involved seek (usually) to maximise their outcome. A game $G$ can be specified by: its players the moves available to each player the preference relation for each player: that is: $G = \stratgame N {A_i} {\succsim_i}$ $G$ can also be specified by: its players the moves available to each player the payoff function for each player: that is: $G = \stratgame N {A_i} {u_i}$

title: Definition:Game/Payoff
snippet: The payoff of a game is the reward or punishment made to a player at the end of the game as a result of combination of the various strategies employed. Let $G$ be a game. Let $N$ be the set of players of $G$. Let $A$ be the set of moves available to player $i \in N$. Let $u_i: A \to \R$ be a the payoff function on $A$. A payoff is the value of $u_i$ for a given $a \in A$.

title: Definition:Game/Player
snippet: Each of the parties involved in a game are called players. In the context of game theory, a player may not necessarily be a person acting alone. A group of people who are collaborating in a game, for example, the members of a football team, can be considered to be a single player.

title: Definition:Game/Rules
snippet: A game is specified completely by its rules. They prescribe for each player a model of rational choice:

title: Definition:Game/Strategy
snippet: A strategy is a complete plan of action that defines what a player will do under all circumstances in a game. In a game with only one move per player, a strategy is identical with a move.

title: Definition:Game Theory
snippet: Game theory is the branch of discrete mathematics which studies mathematical models of conflict and cooperation between intelligent rational decision-makers. Problems in game theory are a special case of those of linear programming.

title: Definition:Game Theory/Also known as
snippet: == Game Theory: Also known as == Game theory can also be seen with the name theory of games. suggests that conflict analysis or interactive decision theory might be better names, but accepts that game theory is what it is called.

title: Definition:Game Theory/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Game Theory == The origins of the mathematical discipline of game theory can be traced to 's . Another early landmark was 's . He also stated, but failed to prove, a special case of the Fundamental Theorem of Games in his paper of . The proof was given in a lecture by , documented as . The field was properly established by and in their of $1944$, as a result of their observation that certain problems in economics were identical with those of games of strategy.

title: Definition:Game of Imperfect Information
snippet: A game of imperfect information is a game in which some information about other players is not known by all the players.

title: Definition:Game of Perfect Information
snippet: A game of perfect information is a game in which all players have complete information on the state of the game.

title: Definition:Gamma Distribution
snippet: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable on a probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $\Img X = \R_{\ge 0}$. $X$ is said to have a gamma distribution if it has probability density function: $\map {f_X} x = \dfrac {\beta^\alpha x^{\alpha - 1} e^{-\beta x} } {\map \Gamma \alpha}$ for $\alpha, \beta > 0$, where $\Gamma$ is the gamma function. This is written: $X \sim \map \Gamma {\alpha, \beta}$ {{questionable|In my Oxford dictionary, the parameters are the other way round.

title: Definition:Gamma Distribution/Also defined as
snippet: == Gamma Distribution: Also defined as == The gamma distribution can also be seen in the form: $\map f x = \dfrac {x^{\alpha - 1} e^{-\alpha / \beta} } {\beta^\alpha \map \Gamma \alpha}$

title: Definition:Gamma Function/Also known as
snippet: == Gamma Function: Also known as == Some authors refer to the gamma function as Euler's gamma function, after . Some French sources call it the Eulerian function.

title: Definition:Gamma Function/Euler Form
snippet: The form of the gamma function is: $\ds \map \Gamma z = \frac 1 z \prod_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \paren {\paren {1 + \frac 1 n}^z \paren {1 + \frac z n}^{-1} } = \lim_{m \mathop \to \infty} \frac {m^z m!} {z \paren {z + 1} \paren {z + 2} \cdots \paren {z + m} }$ which is valid except for $z \in \set {0, -1, -2, \ldots}$.

title: Definition:Gamma Function/Euler Form/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Euler Form of Gamma Function == was the first to find this extension of the factorial to the real numbers. He actually specified it in the form: $\ds n! = \lim_{m \mathop \to \infty} \frac {m^n m!} {\paren{n + 1} \paren{n + 2} \cdots \paren{n + m}}$ He wrote to about it in a letter dated $13$th October $1729$.

title: Definition:Gamma Function/Graph
snippet: The graph of the gamma function is illustrated here for real arguments. The gamma function: $\map \Gamma z$ ( solid line) and $\dfrac 1 {\map \Gamma z}$ ( broken line) The gamma function: $\map \Gamma z$ ( solid line) $\dfrac 1 {\map \Gamma z}$ ( broken line)

title: Definition:Gamma Function/Hankel Form
snippet: The form of the gamma function is: $\ds \frac 1 {\map \Gamma z} = \dfrac 1 {2 \pi i} \oint_\HH \frac {e^t \rd t} {t^z}$ where $\HH$ is the contour starting at $-\infty$, circling the origin in an anticlockwise direction, and returning to $-\infty$. The Hankel form is valid for all $\C$.

title: Definition:Gamma Function/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Gamma Function == The symbol $\map \Gamma z$ for the gamma function was introduced by .

title: Definition:Gamma Function/Integral Form
snippet: The gamma function $\Gamma: \C \setminus \Z_{\le 0} \to \C$ is defined, for the open right half-plane, as: $\ds \map \Gamma z = \map {\MM \set {e^{-t} } } z = \int_0^{\to \infty} t^{z - 1} e^{-t} \rd t$ where $\MM$ is the Mellin transform. For all other values of $z$ except the non-positive integers, $\map \Gamma z$ is defined as: $\map \Gamma {z + 1} = z \map \Gamma z$

title: Definition:Gamma Function/Integral Form/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on the Integral Form of the Gamma Function == The integral form of the gamma function $\Gamma \left({z}\right)$ was discovered by .

title: Definition:Gamma Function/Partial
snippet: Let $m \in \Z_{\ge 0}$. The partial gamma function at $m$ is defined as: $\ds \map {\Gamma_m} z := \frac {m^z m!} {z \paren {z + 1} \paren {z + 2} \cdots \paren {z + m} }$ which is valid except for $z \in \set {0, -1, -2, \ldots, -m}$.

title: Definition:Gamma Function/Partial/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Partial Gamma Function == It is not to be confused with the incomplete gamma function, which is a completely different thing. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Gamma Function/Weierstrass Form
snippet: The form of the gamma function is: $\ds \frac 1 {\map \Gamma z} = z e^{\gamma z} \prod_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \paren {\paren {1 + \frac z n} e^{-z / n} }$ where $\gamma$ is the Euler-Mascheroni constant. The Weierstrass form is valid for all $\C$.

title: Definition:Gantt Chart
snippet: A Gantt chart is a diagram for scheduling problems in operations research where, for example, separate axes for time are allocated to each of $2$ machines. Such a chart is generated following a critical path analysis exercise. Blocks are placed on the time axes, which indicate the time periods when each machine is performing particular jobs.

title: Definition:Gantt Chart/Also known as
snippet: == Gantt Chart: Also known as == A Gantt chart is also known as a cascade chart.

title: Definition:Gantt Chart/Motivation
snippet: A Gantt chart is useful to indicate when machines need to be idle in the case where operations needing more than one machine must be performed in sequence, and later operations which require one machine cannot be started until earlier operations using the other machine are complete, and perhaps also after further additional time delays are needed (for example, for paint to dry or adhesives to set).

title: Definition:Gauge Theory
snippet: A gauge theory is a theory of fields in the context of physics in which the Lagrangian is invariant under local transformations according to Lie groups. The theory is a modern form of 's theory of electromagnetism.

title: Definition:Gauge Theory/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Gauge Theory == The ideas behind gauge theory have been used by to study the geometric and topological properties of $4$-dimensional spaces. He has shown that their properties are fundamentally different from spaces of lower or higher dimension.

title: Definition:Gauge Transformation
snippet: A gauge transformation is a mathematical reformulation of a physical theory that does not change the physical interpretation.

title: Definition:Gauss
snippet: The gauss is the CGS unrationalised electromagnetic unit of magnetic flux density.

title: Definition:Gauss-Jordan Elimination
snippet: Gauss-Jordan elimination is a variant of Gaussian elimination whose effect is to reduce a given matrix $\mathbf A$ to diagonal form.

title: Definition:Gauss-Jordan Elimination/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Gauss-Jordan Elimination == Gauss-Jordan elimination was invented by as a variant of Gaussian elimination. As a means of solving a system of simultaneous equations $\mathbf A \mathbf x = \mathbf b$, Gaussian elimination is preferred, as it requires much less work. When used to calculate the inverse of a square matrix, Gauss-Jordan elimination is sometimes used instead of Gaussian elimination, as they take the same amount of work.

title: Definition:Gauss-Seidel Method
snippet: The Gauss-Seidel method is an iterative method of solving a system of simultaneous equations $\mathbf A \mathbf x = \mathbf b$. For $3$ equations in $3$ unknowns: {{eqn | l = a_{1 1} x_1 + a_{1 2} x_2 + a_{1 3} x_3 | r = b_1 }} {{eqn | l = a_{2 1} x_1 + a_{2 2} x_2 + a_{2 3} x_3 | r = b_2 }} {{eqn | l = a_{3 1} x_1 + a_{3 2} x_2 + a_{3 3} x_3 | r = b_3 }} we may start with arbitrary solutions. In many practical problems, $a_{1 1}$, $a_{2 2}$ and $a_{3 3}$ are large in comparison with $a_{i j}$ for $i \ne j$.

title: Definition:Gauss-Seidel Method/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Gauss-Seidel Method == The Gauss-Seidel method was published by in $1874$, based on earlier work by .

title: Definition:Gauss-Seidel Method/Mistake
snippet: == Source Work == Gauss-Seidel method

title: Definition:Gauss/Also known as
snippet: == Gauss: Also known as == The gauss is also known as the electromagnetic unit of magnetic flux density, abbreviated $\mathrm {e.m.u.}$.

title: Definition:Gauss Error Function
snippet: The Gauss error function is the following improper integral, considered as a real function $\erf : \R \to \R$: $\map {\erf} x = \ds \dfrac 2 {\sqrt \pi} \int_0^x \map \exp {-t^2} \rd t$ where $\exp$ is the real exponential function.

title: Definition:Gauss Error Function/Also known as
snippet: == Gauss Error Function: Also known as == The Gauss error function is also known as just the error function.

title: Definition:Gauss Interpolation Formula
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function. Let $x_0, x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n \in \R$ be equally spaced: $\forall i \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n}: x_i - x_{i - 1} = d$ where $d$ is constant. Let $y_0, y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n$ be values of $x_0, x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ under $f$: $\forall i \in \set {0, 1, 2, \ldots, n}: y_i = \map f {x_i}$ {{stub|Nelson gives that it exists and is useful for interpolation between $x_1$ and $x_{n - 1}$ but does not give details of exactly what it is}}

title: Definition:Gauss Map
snippet: Let $\closedint 0 1$ denote the closed interval from $0$ to $1$. The Gauss map $T : \closedint 0 1 \to \closedint 0 1$ is defined by: $\ds \map T x := \begin{cases} \fractpart {\dfrac 1 x} & : x \in \hointl 0 1 \\ 0 & : x = 0\end{cases}$ where $\fractpart \cdot$ denotes the fractional part.

title: Definition:Gaussian Binomial Coefficient
snippet: Let $q \in \R_{\ne 1}$, $r \in \R$, $m \in \Z_{\ge 0}$. The Gaussian binomial coefficient is an extension of the more conventional binomial coefficient as follows: {{eqn | l = \binom r m_q | o = := | r = \prod_{k \mathop = 0}^{m - 1} \dfrac {1 - q^{r - k} } {1 - q^{k + 1} } | c = }} {{eqn | r = \dfrac {\paren {1 - q^r} \paren {1 - q^{r - 1} } \cdots \paren {1 - q^{r - m + 1} } } {\paren {1 - q^m} \paren {1 - q^{m - 1} } \cdots \paren {1 - q^1} } | c = }} {{eqn | r = \dfrac {\paren {1 - q^r} \paren {1 - q^{r - 1} } \cdots \paren {1 - q^{r - m + 1} } } {\paren {1 - q^m} \paren {1 - q^{m - 1} }…

title: Definition:Gaussian Binomial Coefficient/Also known as
snippet: == Gaussian Binomial Coefficient: Also known as == Some sources refer to this concept as a $q$-nomial coefficient. Some use $q$-binomial coefficient. An early article refers to it as the $q$-generalization of the binomial coefficient. However, 's view is that by referring to a construct by the specific names of the variables in which it is stated limits its flexibility of expression.

title: Definition:Gaussian Curvature
snippet: The Gaussian curvature $\Kappa$ of a surface at a point is the product of the principal curvatures, $\kappa_1$ and $\kappa_2$, at the given point: $\Kappa = \kappa_1 \kappa_2$

title: Definition:Gaussian Curvature/Also known as
snippet: == Gaussian Curvature: Also known as == The Gaussian curvature of a surface at a point is also known as the Gauss curvature. Some sources refer to it as the total curvature. Some sources refer to it as just the curvature of a surface.

title: Definition:Gaussian Curvature/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Gaussian Curvature == The concept of Gaussian curvature was developed by in his $1827$ work .

title: Definition:Gaussian Elimination
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a matrix over a field $K$. Let $\mathbf E$ be a reduced echelon matrix which is row equivalent to $\mathbf A$. The Gaussian elimination method is a technique for converting $\mathbf A$ into $\mathbf E$ by means of a sequence of elementary row operations.

title: Definition:Gaussian Elimination/Also defined as
snippet: == Gaussian Elimination: Also defined as == Some sources do not insist that $\mathbf E$ be a reduced echelon matrix at the end of the Gaussian elimination process, but merely an echelon matrix.

title: Definition:Gaussian Elimination/Also known as
snippet: == Gaussian Elimination: Also known as == Some sources refer to the technique of Gaussian elimination as Gauss elimination. Gaussian elimination is sometimes seen referred to as pivotal condensation.

title: Definition:Gaussian Elimination/Procedure
snippet: == Gaussian Elimination: Procedure == The procedure for Gaussian elimination is as follows: Let $\mathbf A$ be a matrix over a field $F$. Let $\mathbf E$ be a reduced echelon matrix which is row equivalent to $\mathbf A$. Let the first column of $\mathbf A$ containing a non-zero element be column $j$. Let a non-zero element in row $i$ be distinguished. This element $a_{i j} \ne 0$ is called the pivot element. Perform the elementary row operation: $(1): \quad r_1 \leftrightarrow r_i$ This moves the pivot element to $a_{1 j}$.

title: Definition:Gaussian Field
snippet: The Gaussian field is the field of Gaussian rationals under the operations of complex addition and complex multiplication.

title: Definition:Gaussian Hypergeometric Function/Also denoted as
snippet: == Gaussian Hypergeometric Function: Also denoted as == Using the notation of the generalized hypergeometric function, the Gaussian hypergeometric function can be denoted as: $\ds \map { {}_2 F_1} {a, b; c; z}$ or if necessary to draw particular attention to where it came from: $\ds \map { {}_2 F_1} { { {a, b} \atop c} \, \middle \vert \, z}$ Category:Definitions/Gaussian Hypergeometric Function

title: Definition:Gaussian Hypergeometric Function/Also known as
snippet: == Gaussian Hypergeometric Function: Also known as == The Gaussian hypergeometric function is also known as the ordinary hypergeometric function, or just the hypergeometric function Some sources refer to this as Gauss's hypergeometric function or (grammatically inaccurately) Gauss' hypergeometric function.

title: Definition:Gaussian Integer
snippet: A Gaussian integer is a complex number whose real and imaginary parts are both integers. That is, a Gaussian integer is a number in the form: $a + b i: a, b \in \Z$ The set of all Gaussian integers can be denoted $\Z \sqbrk i$, and hence can be defined as: $\Z \sqbrk i = \set {a + b i: a, b \in \Z}$ Some sources use the symbol $J$ for the set $\Z \sqbrk i$.

title: Definition:Gaussian Integer/Also known as
snippet: == Gaussian Integer: Also known as == A Gaussian integer can also be referred to as a complex integer. Some sources render the eponym in lowercase: gaussian integer.

title: Definition:Gaussian Integer/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Gaussian Integer == The concept of a Gaussian integer was introduced by in his papers of $1828$ and $1832$.

title: Definition:Gaussian Integral/One Variable
snippet: The Gaussian Integral (of one variable) is the following improper integral, considered as a real function: $\phi_1: \R \to \R$: $\map {\phi_1} x = \ds \int_{\mathop \to -\infty}^x \frac 1 {\sqrt {2 \pi} } \map \exp {-\frac {t^2} 2 } \rd t$ where $\exp$ is the real exponential function.

title: Definition:Gaussian Integral/Two Variables
snippet: The Gaussian Integral (of two variables) is the following definite integral, considered as a real-valued function: $\phi_2: \set {\tuple {a, b} \in \R^2: a \le b} \to \R$: $\map {\phi_2} {a, b} = \ds \int_a^b \frac 1 {\sqrt {2 \pi} } \map \exp {-\frac {t^2} 2} \rd t$ where $\exp$ is the real exponential function. A common abuse of notation is to denote the improper integrals as: $\ds \map {\phi_2} {a, +\infty} = \lim_{b \mathop \to +\infty} \map {\phi_2} {a, b}$ $\ds \map {\phi_2} {-\infty, b} = \lim_{a \mathop \to -\infty} \map {\phi_2} {a, b}$

title: Definition:Gaussian Integration Rule
snippet: A Gaussian integration rule is a numerical integration rule of the form: $\ds \int_a^b \map w x \map f x \rd x \approx \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n w_i \map f {x_i}$ where $\map w x$ is a non-negative weight function on the interval $\closedint a b$ such that both: the $n$ nodes $x_i$ the weights $w_i$ are chosen to make the approximation exact when $f$ is a polynomial of degree less than or equal to $2 n - 1$. The purpose of the weight function is to build into the rule any special behaviour of the integrand.

title: Definition:Gaussian Integration Rule/Mistake
snippet: == Source Work == Gaussian integration rule

title: Definition:Gaussian Kernel
snippet: The Gaussian kernel of a probability density function is the kernel of the form: $\map k u = \dfrac 1 {\sqrt {2 \pi} } e^{-u^2 / 2}$

title: Definition:Gaussian Kernel/Also known as
snippet: == Gaussian Kernel: Also known as == The Gaussian kernel of a probability density function is also known as the normal kernel.

title: Definition:Gaussian Prime/Definition 1
snippet: Let $x \in \Z \sqbrk i$ be a Gaussian integer. $x$ is a Gaussian prime : it cannot be expressed as the product of two Gaussian integers, neither of which is a unit of $\Z \sqbrk i$ (that is, $\pm 1$ or $\pm i$) it is not itself a unit of $\Z \sqbrk i$.

title: Definition:Gaussian Prime/Definition 2
snippet: A Gaussian prime is a Gaussian integer which has exactly $8$ divisors which are themselves Gaussian integers.

title: Definition:Gaussian Prime/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Gaussian Prime == The concept of a Gaussian prime was introduced by in his papers of $1828$ and $1832$.

title: Definition:Gaussian Process
snippet: Let $S$ be a stochastic process giving rise to a time series $T$. Let the probability distribution of $T$ be a multivariate normal distribution. Then $S$ is called a Gaussian process.

title: Definition:Gaussian Rational/Definition 1
snippet: A Gaussian rational is a complex number whose real and imaginary parts are both rational numbers. That is, a Gaussian rational is a number in the form: $a + b i: a, b \in \Q$

title: Definition:Gaussian Rational/Definition 2
snippet: The field $\struct {\Q \sqbrk i, +, \times}$ of Gaussian rationals is the field of quotients of the integral domain $\struct {\Z \sqbrk i, +, \times}$ of Gaussian integers. This is shown to exist in Existence of Field of Quotients. In view of Field of Quotients is Unique, we construct the field of quotients of $\Z \sqbrk i$, give it a label $\Q \sqbrk i$ and call its elements Gaussian rationals.

title: Definition:Gaussian Rational/Notation
snippet: The set of all Gaussian rationals can be denoted $\Q \sqbrk i$, and hence we have: $\Q \sqbrk i = \set {z \in \C: z = a + b i: a, b \in \Q}$ Category:Definitions/Gaussian Rationals

title: Definition:Gazillion
snippet: Gazillion is a rhetorical flourish to mean a very large number, generally understood to be of the order of an unspecified power of $10$.

title: Definition:Gelfand Transform
snippet: Let $\struct {A, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a commutative Banach algebra over $\C$ such that: the spectrum $\Phi_A$ of $A$ is non-empty. Define $\hat a : \Phi_A \to \C$ by: $\map {\hat a} \phi = \map \phi a$ for each $\phi \in \Phi_A$. We say that $\hat a$ is the Gelfand transform of $a$.

title: Definition:Gelfond's Constant
snippet: Gelfond's constant is the number obtained by raising Euler's number $e$ to the power of $\pi$ (pi): $e^\pi$ Its decimal expansion gives its value to be approximately: $e^\pi \approx 23 \cdotp 14069 \, 26327 \, 79269 \, 00572 \, 90863 \, 67948 \, 54738 \ldots$

title: Definition:Gelfond's Constant/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Gelfond's Constant == Gelfond's constant arises in the context of the $7$th problem of the Hilbert $23$. It was proved to be transcendental in $1929$ by . It was since determined to be a special case of the Gelfond-Schneider Theorem, established .

title: Definition:Gelfond-Schneider Constant
snippet: The Gelfond-Schneider constant is defined as $2$ raised to the power of the square root of $2$: $2^{\sqrt 2}$ Its decimal expansion begins: $2^{\sqrt 2} \approx 2 \cdotp 66514 \, 4$

title: Definition:Gelfond-Schneider Constant/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Gelfond-Schneider Constant == The Gelfond-Schneider constant arises in the context of the $7$th problem of the Hilbert $23$. It had been proved transcendental in $1930$ by . However, as a result of the work done by and in , it could be shown to be a trivial application of the Gelfond-Schneider Theorem. Hence the name of this constant.

title: Definition:General Algebraic Product/Also known as
snippet: == General Algebraic Product: Also known as == The product of $a$ and $b$ is sometimes seen referred to as their sum. This can be confusing and is therefore endorsed on this site only when referring to addition.

title: Definition:General Dirichlet Series
snippet: Let $a_n$ be a sequence in $\C$. Let $\sequence {\lambda_n}$ be a strictly increasing sequence of non-negative real numbers whose limit is infinity. A general Dirichlet series of type $\lambda_n$ is a complex function $f: \C \to \C$ defined by the series: $\ds \map f s = \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n e^{-\lambda_n s}$ which is defined at the points where it converges.

title: Definition:General Dirichlet Series/Also known as
snippet: == General Dirichlet Series: Also known as == Some treatments of the subject of the general Dirichlet series use the possessive style: general Dirichlet's series. However, that makes it sound as though it is named after a high-ranking military officer. Some sources refer to a general Dirichlet series as just a Dirichlet series, but this is also used for the ordinary Dirichlet series. Hence the full form is preferred on .

title: Definition:General Euclidean Metric
snippet: Let $\R^n$ be an $n$-dimensional real vector space. The general Euclidean metrics are defined on $\R^n$ for $p \in \R_{\ge 1}$ as: $\ds \map {d_p} {x, y} := \paren {\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \size {x_i - y_i}^p}^{\frac 1 p}$ where $x = \tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}, y = \tuple {y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n} \in \R^n$. That is, they are the $p$-product metrics on $\R^n$.

title: Definition:General Fibonacci Sequence
snippet: Let $r, s, t, u$ be numbers, usually integers but not necessarily so limited. Let $\sequence {a_n}$ be the sequence defined as: $a_n = \begin{cases} r & : n = 0 \\ s & : n = 1 \\ t a_{n - 2} + u a_{n - 1} & : n > 1 \end{cases}$ Then $\sequence {a_n}$ is a general Fibonacci sequence.

title: Definition:General Fibonacci Sequence/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on General Fibonacci Sequence == The general Fibonacci sequences were first investigated by , who used what are now known Fibonacci numbers and Lucas numbers to investigate the primality of Mersenne numbers.

title: Definition:General Linear Group
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. The set of all nonsingular order-$n$ square matrices over $K$ is a group under (conventional) matrix multiplication. This group is called the general linear group (of degree $n$) and is denoted $\GL {n, K}$, or $\GL n$ if the field is implicit. The field itself is usually $\R$, $\Q$ or $\C$, but can be any field.

title: Definition:General Linear Group/Also denoted as
snippet: == General Linear Group: Also denoted as == Some sources use the notation $\map {\mathrm {GL}_n} K$ for the general linear group instead of $\GL {n, K}$. If $K$ is a Galois field of order $q$, the notations $\map {\mathrm {GL}_n} q$ and $\GL {n, q}$ are also seen. Some sources use $\map {\mathrm {Gl} } {n, r}$ for $\GL {n, \R}$.

title: Definition:General Linear Group/Vector Space
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space. The general linear group over $\GL V$ is the group of all invertible linear transformations of $V$.

title: Definition:General Logarithm/Also known as
snippet: == General Logarithm: Also known as == The logarithm to the base $a$ of $x$ is usually voiced in the abbreviated form: log base $a$ of $x$ or log $a$ of $x$. When $a = 2$, a notation which is starting to take hold for $\log_2 x$ is $\lg x$. This concept is becoming increasingly important in computer science. Category:Definitions/Logarithms

title: Definition:General Logarithm/Binary
snippet: Logarithms base $2$ are becoming increasingly important in computer science. They are often referred to as binary logarithms.

title: Definition:General Logarithm/Binary/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Binary Logarithm == The use of $\lg x$ instead of $\log_2 x$ to denote the binary logarithm was suggested by , and adopted by in his .

title: Definition:General Logarithm/Common
snippet: Logarithms base $10$ are often referred to as common logarithms.

title: Definition:General Logarithm/Common/Characteristic
snippet: Let $n \in \R$ be a positive real number such that $0 < n < 1$. Let $n$ be presented (possibly approximated) in scientific notation as: $a \times 10^d$ where $d \in \Z$ is an integer. Let $\log_{10} n$ be expressed in the form: $\log_{10} n = \begin {cases} c \cdotp m & : d \ge 0 \\ \overline c \cdotp m & : d < 0 \end {cases}$ where: $c = \size d$ is the absolute value of $d$ $m := \log_{10} a$ $c$ is the characteristic of $\log_{10} n$.

title: Definition:General Logarithm/Common/Mantissa
snippet: Let $n \in \R$ be a positive real number such that $0 < n < 1$. Let $n$ be presented (possibly approximated) in scientific notation as: $a \times 10^d$ where $d \in \Z$ is an integer. Let $\log_{10} n$ be expressed in the form: $\log_{10} n = \begin {cases} c \cdotp m & : d \ge 0 \\ \overline c \cdotp m & : d < 0 \end {cases}$ where: $c = \size d$ is the absolute value of $d$ $m := \log_{10} a$ $\log_{10} a$ is the mantissa of $\log_{10} n$.

title: Definition:General Logarithm/Common/Notation for Negative Logarithm
snippet: Let $n \in \R$ be a real number such that $0 0}$ is a (strictly) positive integer. Let $\log_{10} n$ denote the common logarithm of $n$. Then it is the standard convention to express $\log_{10} n$ in the form: $\log_{10} n = \overline d \cdotp m$ where $m := \log_{10} a$ is the mantissa of $\log_{10} n$. The overline notation is commonly read as bar, that is: $\overline 2$ is read as bar two.

title: Definition:General Logarithm/Complex
snippet: Let $z \in \C_{\ne 0}$ be a non-zero complex number. Let $a \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number such that $a \ne 1$. The logarithm to the base $a$ of $z$ is defined as: $\log_a z := \set {y \in \C: a^y = z}$ where $a^y = e^{y \ln a}$ as defined in Powers of Complex Numbers. The act of performing the $\log_a$ function is colloquially known as taking logs.

title: Definition:General Logarithm/Positive Real
snippet: Let $x \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number. Let $a \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number such that $a \ne 1$. The logarithm to the base $a$ of $x$ is defined as: $\log_a x := y \in \R: a^y = x$ where $a^y = e^{y \ln a}$ as defined in Powers of Real Numbers. The act of performing the $\log_a$ function is colloquially known as taking logs.

title: Definition:General Solution
snippet: Let $E$ be an equation in which $x$ is the independent variable. The general solution of $E$ is the set of all $x$ that make $E$ a true statement.

title: Definition:General Solution to Differential Equation/Also known as
snippet: == General Solution to Differential Equation: Also known as == The general solution to a differential equation $\Phi$ can also be referred to as the solution of $\Phi$, but beware of confusing this with the concept of a solution to $\Phi$. The general solution to a differential equation can also be referred to as the general solution of a differential equation. Some sources refer to this general solution as a general integral. Some sources use the terminology complete solution. The term solution set is sometimes encountered.

title: Definition:General Theory of Relativity/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on General Theory of Relativity == The general theory of relativity was published by in $1916$.

title: Definition:Generalized Continued Fraction
snippet: Let $k$ be a field. Informally, a generalized continued fraction in $k$ is an expression of the form: $b_0 + \cfrac {a_1} {b_1 + \cfrac {a_2} {b_2 + \cfrac {a_3} {\ddots \cfrac {} {b_{n - 1} + \cfrac {a_n} {b_n + \cfrac {a_{n + 1} } \ddots } } } } }$ Formally, a generalized continued fraction in $k$ is a pair of sequences $\tuple {\sequence {b_n}_{n \mathop \ge 0}, \sequence {a_n}_{n \mathop \ge 1} }$ in $k$, called the sequence of partial denominators and sequence of partial numerators respectively.

title: Definition:Generalized Continued Fraction/Also known as
snippet: == Generalized Continued Fraction: Also known as == A generalized continued fraction is also known as a general continued fraction. Some sources refer to this merely as a continued fraction, without requiring that the $a_k$ coefficients be $1$.

title: Definition:Generalized Coordinates
snippet: A set of coordinates: $\set {q_1, q_2, \ldots, q_n}$ sufficient to specify the configuration of a mechanical system can be referred to as generalized coordinates.

title: Definition:Generalized Eigenvalue
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ be square matrices of the same order. Let $\lambda$ be a number such that: $\mathbf A \mathbf x = \lambda \mathbf B \mathbf x$ for some non-zero vector $\mathbf x$. Then $\lambda$ is a generalized eigenvalue of $\mathbf A$.

title: Definition:Generalized Eigenvector
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a square matrix of order $n$. Let $\lambda$ be a generalized eigenvalue of $\mathbf A$. Hence: $\mathbf A \mathbf x = \lambda \mathbf B \mathbf x$ for: some non-zero vector $\mathbf x$ some square matrix $\mathbf B$ of order $n$. The vector $\mathbf x$ is known as the generalized eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda$.

title: Definition:Generalized Hilbert Sequence Space
snippet: Let $\alpha$ be an infinite cardinal. Let $I$ be an indexed set of cardinality $\alpha$. Let $A$ be the set of all real-valued functions $x : I \to \R$ such that: $(1)\quad \set{i \in I: x_i \ne 0}$ is countable $(2)\quad$ the generalized sum $\ds \sum_{i \mathop \in I} x_i^2$ is a convergent net. Let $d_2: A \times A \to \R$ be the real-valued function defined as: $\ds \forall x = \family {x_i}, y = \family {y_i} \in A: \map {d_2} {x, y} := \paren {\sum_{i \mathop \in I} \paren {x_i- y_i}^2}^{\frac 1 2}$ The metric space $\struct {A, d_2}$ is the generalized Hilbert sequence space on $\R$ of…

title: Definition:Generalized Inverse Gaussian Distribution
snippet: The generalized inverse Gaussian distribution (GIG) is a three-parameter family of continuous probability distributions with probability density function: $\forall x > 0: \map f x = \dfrac {\paren {a / b}^{p/2} } {2 \map {K_p} {\sqrt{a b} } } x^{\paren {p - 1} } e^{-\paren {a x + b / x} / 2}$ where: $K_p$ is a modified Bessel function of the second kind $a > 0, b > 0, p$ are real.

title: Definition:Generalized Least Squares
snippet: Generalized least squares is a generalization of method of least squares in order to extend its reach to non-linear models.

title: Definition:Generalized Linear Model
snippet: A generalized linear model is a mathematical model in which a function $\map g \mu$ of the expectation $\mu$ of a random variable $Y$ is a linear function of one or more cause variables.

title: Definition:Generalized Linear Model/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Generalized Linear Model == The generalized linear model was conceived and developed by and from $1972$.

title: Definition:Generalized Linear Model/Link Function
snippet: Consider a generalized linear model which is a function $\map g \mu$ of the expectation $\mu$ of a random variable $Y$. The function $\map g \mu$ is known as the link function.

title: Definition:Generalized Linear Model/One Variable
snippet: The generalized linear model for one cause variable $x$ is of the form: $\map g \mu = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$ where $\map g \mu$ is the link function.

title: Definition:Generalized Momentum
snippet: The generalized momentum of analytical (Lagrangian, Hamiltonian) formulations of classical mechanics is defined as the partial derivative of the Lagrangian with regards to the time derivative of generalized coordinates: $p_i = \dfrac {\partial \LL} {\partial \dot q_i}$ where: $p_i$ is the $i$th coordinate of the generalized momenta $\LL$ is the Lagrangian $\dot q_i$ is the time derivative of the generalized coordinates $q_i$.

title: Definition:Generalized Ordered Space
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a totally ordered set. Let $\tau$ be a topology on $S$.

title: Definition:Generalized Ordered Space/Also known as
snippet: == Generalized Ordered Space: Also known as == A generalized ordered space is also known as a suborderable space. It is also often abbreviated as a GO-space.

title: Definition:Generalized Ordered Space/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a totally ordered set. Let $\tau$ be a topology on $S$. $\struct {S, \preceq, \tau}$ is a generalized ordered space : {{item|(1):|$\struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_2$ (Hausdorff) space}} {{item|(2):|there exists a basis for $\struct {S, \tau}$ whose elements are order-convex in $S$}}

title: Definition:Generalized Ordered Space/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a totally ordered set. Let $\tau$ be a topology on $S$. $\struct {S, \preceq, \tau}$ is a generalized ordered space : {{item|(1):|there exists a linearly ordered space $\struct {S', \preceq', \tau'}$}}

title: Definition:Generalized Ordered Space/Definition 3
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a totally ordered set. Let $\tau$ be a topology on $S$. $\struct {S, \preceq, \tau}$ is a generalized ordered space : {{item|(1):|$\struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_2$ (Hausdorff) space}} {{item|(2):|there exists a sub-basis for $\struct {S, \tau}$ each of whose elements is an upper section or lower section in $S$.}}

title: Definition:Generalized Ordered Space/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Generalized Ordered Space == The British English spelling renders as generalised ordered space. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Generalized Pentagonal Number/Definition 1
snippet: Recall the sequence of pentagonal numbers: $0, 1, 5, 12, 22, 35, 51, 70, 92, 117, 145, 176, \ldots$ and the sequence of second pentagonal numbers: $0, 2, 7, 15, 26, 40, 57, 77, 100, 126, 155, 187, \ldots$ The sequence of generalized pentagonal numbers consists of the elements of both of these sequences merged and arranged into ascending order.

title: Definition:Generalized Pentagonal Number/Definition 2
snippet: The generalized pentagonal numbers are the integers obtained from the formula: $GP_n = \begin {cases} \dfrac {m \paren {3 m + 1} } 2 & : n = 2 m \\ \\ \dfrac {m \paren {3 m - 1} } 2 & : n = 2 m - 1 \end {cases}$ for $n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$

title: Definition:Generalized Sum
snippet: Let $\struct {G, +}$ be a commutative topological semigroup. Let $\family {g_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed family of elements of $G$. Consider the set $\FF$ of finite subsets of $I$. Let $\subseteq$ denote the subset relation on $\FF$. By virtue of Finite Subsets form Directed Set, $\struct {\FF, \subseteq}$ is a directed set. Define the net: $\phi: \FF \to G$ by: $\ds \map \phi F = \sum_{i \mathop \in F} g_i$ where $\ds \sum_{i \mathop \in F} g_i$ denotes the summation over $F \in \FF$. Then $\phi$ is denoted: $\ds \sum \set {g_i: i \in I}$ and referred to as a generalized sum.

title: Definition:Generalized Sum/Absolute Net Convergence
snippet: Let $V$ be a Banach space. Let $\family {v_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed family of elements of $V$. Then $\ds \sum \set {v_i: i \in I}$ converges absolutely $\ds \sum \set {\norm {v_i}: i \mathop \in I}$ converges. This nomenclature is appropriate as we have Absolutely Convergent Generalized Sum Converges.

title: Definition:Generalized Sum/Net Convergence
snippet: Let $\struct {G, +}$ be a commutative topological semigroup. Let $\sequence {g_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $G$. The series $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty g_n$ converges as a net or has net convergence the generalized sum $\ds \sum \set {g_n: n \in \N}$ converges.

title: Definition:Generated Algebraic Substructure
snippet: Let $\struct {A, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. Let $G \subseteq A$ be any subset of $A$. The algebraic substructure generated by $G$ is the smallest substructure of $\struct {A, \circ}$ which contains $G$. It is written $\gen G$.

title: Definition:Generated C*-Algebra
snippet: Let $\struct {A, \ast, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a $\text C^\ast$-algebra. Let $S \subseteq A$. Let $B \supseteq S$ be the $\subseteq$-minimal $\text C^\ast$-subalgebra containing $S$. We call $B$ the $\text C^\ast$-algebra generated by $S$ and write: $B = \map {\text C^\ast} S$

title: Definition:Generated Division Subring
snippet: Let $\struct {D, +, \circ}$ be a division ring. Let $S \subseteq D$. The division subring generated by $S$ is the smallest division subring of $D$ containing $S$.

title: Definition:Generated Field Extension
snippet: Let $E / F$ be a field extension. Let $S \subset E$ be a subset of $E$.

title: Definition:Generated Field Extension/Definition 1
snippet: Let $E / F$ be a field extension. Let $S \subset E$ be a subset of $E$. The field extension $F \sqbrk S$ generated by $S$ is the smallest subfield extension of $E$ containing $S$, that is, the intersection of all subfields of $E$ containing $S$ and $F$. Thus $S$ is a generator of $F \sqbrk S$ $F \sqbrk S$ has no proper subfield extension containing $S$.

title: Definition:Generated Field Extension/Definition 2
snippet: Let $E / F$ be a field extension. Let $S \subset E$ be a subset of $E$. Let $F \sqbrk {\set {X_s} }$ be the polynomial ring in $S$ variables $X_s$. Let $\operatorname {ev} : F \sqbrk {\set {X_s} } \to E$ be the evaluation homomorphism associated to the inclusion $S \hookrightarrow E$. The field extension $F \sqbrk S$ generated by $S$ is the set of all elements of $E$ of the form $\map {\operatorname {ev} } f / \map {\operatorname {ev} } g$, where $\map {\operatorname {ev} } g \ne 0$. $S$ is said to be a generator of $F \sqbrk S$.

title: Definition:Generated Ideal of Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring with unity. Let $S \subseteq R$ be a subset of $R$. The ideal generated by $S$ is the smallest ideal of $R$ containing $S$, that is, the intersection of all ideals containing $S$.

title: Definition:Generated Ideal of Ring/Commutative and Unitary
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $S \subseteq R$ be a subset of $R$. The ideal generated by $S$ is the set of all linear combinations of elements of $S$.

title: Definition:Generated Ideal of Ring/Unitary
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring with unity. Let $S \subseteq R$ be a subset of $R$. The ideal generated by $S$ is the set of all two-sided linear combinations of elements of $S$.

title: Definition:Generated Normal Subgroup/Definition 1
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $S \subseteq G$ be a subset. The normal subgroup generated by $S$, denoted $\gen {S^G}$, is the intersection of all normal subgroups of $G$ containing $S$.

title: Definition:Generated Normal Subgroup/Definition 2
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $S \subseteq G$ be a subset. The normal subgroup generated by $S$, denoted $\gen {S^G}$, is the smallest normal subgroup of $G$ containing $S$: $\gen {S^G} = \gen {x S x^{-1}: x \in G}$

title: Definition:Generated Ring Extension
snippet: Let $S$ be a commutative rings with unity. Let $R$ be a subring of $S$ with unity such that the unity of $R$ is the unity of $S$. That is, $S$ is a ring extension of $R$. Let $T \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$.

title: Definition:Generated Ring Extension/Evaluation of Polynomial Ring
snippet: Let $R \sqbrk {\set {X_t} }$ be the polynomial ring in $T$ variables $X_t$. Let $\operatorname {ev} : R \sqbrk {\set {X_t} } \to S$ be the evaluation homomorphism associated with the inclusion $T \hookrightarrow S$. The ring extension $R \sqbrk T$ generated by $T$ is $\Img {\operatorname {ev} }$, the image of $\operatorname {ev}$. $T$ is said to be a generator of $R \sqbrk T$.

title: Definition:Generated Ring Extension/Smallest Subring
snippet: The ring extension $R \sqbrk T$ generated by $T$ is the smallest subring of $S$ containing $T$ and $R$, that is, the intersection of all subrings of $S$ containing $T$ and $R$. Thus $T$ is a generator of $R \sqbrk T$ $R \sqbrk T$ has no proper subring containing $T$ and $R$.

title: Definition:Generated Subgroup/Definition 3

title: Definition:Generated Submodule/Linear Span
snippet: Let $K$ be a division ring or a field. Let $V$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $A \subseteq V$ be a subset of $V$. Then the linear span of $A$, denoted $\span A$ or $\map \span A$, is the set of all linear combinations (of finite length) of vectors in $A$. The linear span of $A$ is formally defined as: $\map \span A = \ds \set {\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \alpha_i v_i: n \in \N_{\ge 1}, \alpha_i \in K, v_i \in A}$

title: Definition:Generated Submodule/Linear Span/Real Vector Space
snippet: Let $n \in \N_{>0}$. Let $\R^n$ be a real vector space. Let $A \subseteq \R^n$ be a subset of $\R^n$. Then the linear span of $A$, denoted $\span A$ or $\map \span A$, is the set of all linear combinations (of finite length) of vectors in $A$. In the case where $A$ is a finite subset of $\R_n$ such that: $A = \set {\mathbf v_1, \mathbf v_2, \dotsc, \mathbf v_k}$ for some $k \in \N_{>0}$, the linear span of $A$ is formally defined as: $\ds \map \span {\mathbf v_1, \mathbf v_2, \dotsc, \mathbf v_k} = \set {\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^k \alpha_i \mathbf v_i: 1 \le i \le k, \alpha_i \in \R, \mathbf v_i…

title: Definition:Generated Submodule/Unitary
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $M$ be a unitary $R$-module. Let $S\subset M$ be a subset. The submodule generated by $S$ is the set of all linear combinations of elements of $S$.

title: Definition:Generated Submonoid
snippet: Let $\struct {M, \circ}$ be a monoid whose identity is $e_M$. Let $S \subseteq M$ Let $H$ be the smallest (with respect to set inclusion) submonoid of $M$ such that $\paren {S \cup \set {e_M} } \subseteq H$. Then $\struct {H, \circ}$ is the submonoid of $\struct {M, \circ}$ generated by $S$. This is written $H = \gen S$. If $S$ is a singleton, for example $S = \set x$, then we can (and usually do) write $H = \gen x$ for $H = \gen {\set x}$.

title: Definition:Generated Submonoid/Generator
snippet: Let $\struct {M, \circ}$ be a monoid Let $S \subseteq M$. Let $\struct {H, \circ}$ be the submonoid of $\struct {M, \circ}$ generated by $S$. Then $S$ is known as a generator of $\struct {H, \circ}$.

title: Definition:Generated Subring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $S \subseteq R$ be a subset. The subring generated by $S$ is the smallest subring of $R$ containing $S$; that is, it is the intersection of all subrings of $R$ containing $S$.

title: Definition:Generated Subspace/Definition 1
snippet: Let $K$ be a division ring. Let $\mathbf V$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $S \subseteq \mathbf V$ be a subset of $\mathbf V$. The subspace generated by $S$ is the intersection of all subspaces of $\mathbf V$ containing $S$.

title: Definition:Generated Subspace/Definition 2

title: Definition:Generating Curve of Surface of Revolution
snippet: Let $H = \set {\tuple {x, y} : y \in \R_{> 0}} \subset \R^2$ be the open upper half-plane. Let $F \subset H$ be a $1$-dimensional embedded submanifold. Let $S_F$ be a surface of revolution. Then $F$ is called the generating curve of $S_F$.

title: Definition:Generating Function
snippet: Let $A = \sequence {a_n}$ be a sequence in $\R$. Then $\ds \map {G_A} z = \sum_{n \mathop \ge 0} a_n z^n$ is called the generating function for the sequence $A$. The mapping $\map {G_A} z$ is defined for all $z$ for which the power series $\ds \sum_{n \mathop \ge 0} a_n z^n$ is convergent. The definition can be modified so that the lower limit of the summation is $b$ where $b > 0$ by assigning $a_k = 0$ where $0 \le k < b$.

title: Definition:Generating Function/Also denoted as
snippet: == Generating Function: Also denoted as == When the sequence is understood, the notation $\map G z$ can be used for its generating function. Different authors may use different symbols for $G_A$, for example: $\map {f_A} z$ $\map U s$ $\map A x$ $\map {\mathrm f} t$

title: Definition:Generating Function/Also known as
snippet: == Generating Function: Also known as == A generating function is also known as an enumerating series, particularly in problems of combinatorics.

title: Definition:Generating Function/Doubly Subscripted Sequence
snippet: Let $A = \sequence {a_{m, n} }$ be a doubly subscripted sequence in $\R$ for $m, n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$. Then $\ds \map {G_A} {w, z} = \sum_{m, \, n \mathop \ge 0} a_{m n} w^m z^n$ is called the generating function for the sequence $A$. The mapping $\map {G_A} {w, z}$ is defined for all $w$ and $z$ for which the power series $\ds \sum_{m, \, n \mathop \ge 0} a_{m n} w^m z^n$ is convergent. The definition can be modified so that the lower limit of the summation is $b$ where $b > 0$ by assigning $a_k = 0$ where $0 \le k < b$.

title: Definition:Generating Function/Extraction of Coefficient
snippet: Let $\map G z$ be the generating function for the sequence $S = \sequence {a_n}$. The coefficient of $z^n$ extracted from $\map G z$ is the $n$th term of $S$, and can be denoted: $\sqbrk {z^n} \map G z := a_n$

title: Definition:Generating Function/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Generating Function == Generating functions were introduced by to solve the general problem of linear recurrences. then extended this theory in his of $1730$, by using differentiation and integration. Then began extending their use to new fields such as combinatorics. took the technique into the field of probability theory in his $1812$ work Many others since have developed the technique further. A generating function is a clothesline on which we hang up a sequence of numbers for display. --

title: Definition:Generating Function/Parameter
snippet: Let $\map {G_A} z$ be a generating function for the sequence $A$. The variable $z$ is a bound variable, known as the parameter of $\map {G_A} z$.

title: Definition:Generating Function/Parameter/Also denoted as
snippet: The symbol used for the parameter varies. $x$ is often used instead. In the field of probability theory $s$ tends to be the symbol of choice. Some authors use $\zeta$, and some use $t$. Category:Definitions/Generating Functions

title: Definition:Generator Set of Filter
snippet: Let $L = \left({S, \wedge, \preceq}\right)$ be a meet semilattice. Let $F$ be a filter on $L$. The generator set $G$ of $F$ is defined as follows: $F = \left({\operatorname{fininfs}\left({G}\right)}\right)^\succeq$ where $\operatorname{fininfs}\left({G}\right)$ denotes the finite infima set of $G$, $G^\succeq$ denotes the upper closure of $G$.

title: Definition:Generator for Primitive Pythagorean Triple
snippet: The generator for a primitive Pythagorean triple is an ordered pair: $G = \left({m, n}\right)$ where $m, n \in \Z$ such that: $m, n \in \Z_{>0}$ are (strictly) positive integers $m \perp n$, that is, $m$ and $n$ are coprime $m$ and $n$ are of opposite parity $m > n$. The primitive Pythagorean triple which has been generated by $G$ is: $\left({2 m n, m^2 - n^2, m^2 + n^2}\right)$

title: Definition:Generator for Pythagorean Triple
snippet: Let $P = \left\{ {a, b, c}\right\}$ be a Pythagorean triple A generator for $P$ is an ordered pair: $G = \left({m, n}\right)$ where $m, n \in \Z$ such that: $a = 2 m n$ $b = m^2 - n^2$ $c = m^2 + n^2$

title: Definition:Generator of Algebra
snippet: Let $\struct {A_R, \oplus}$ be an algebra over a ring $R$. Let $S \subseteq A_R$ be a subset of $A_R$. The subalgebra generated by $S$ is the smallest subalgebra $B_R$ of $A_R$ which contains $S$.

snippet: Let $\struct {A, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. Let $G \subset A$ be a subset.
