title: Definition:Graph Paper
snippet: Graph paper is paper with ruled lines on it corresponding to the coordinate axes of the coordinate system in which one is planning to construct the graph of a mapping, for example.

title: Definition:Graph Parametrization
snippet: Let $U \subseteq \R^n$ be an open subset of $n$-dimensional Euclidean space. Let $f : U \to \R^k$ be a real function. Let $\map \Gamma f$ be the graph of $f$. Let $\gamma_f : U \to \R^n \times \R^k$ be a mapping such that: $\map {\gamma_f} u = \tuple {u, \map f u}$ Then $\gamma_f$ is called the graph parametrization (of $\map \Gamma f$).

title: Definition:Graph Theory
snippet: Graph theory is the branch of mathematics concerned with the structure and properties of graphs. As a (graph-theoretical) graph has the same conceptual definition as a relation, it follows that there is considerable overlap between the fields of graph theory and relation theory.

title: Definition:Graph Theory/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Graph Theory == Graph theory is a relatively new branch of mathematics, most of it having been developed since $1890$.

title: Definition:Graph of Inequality
snippet: A graph of an inequality in $2$ variables can be represented in diagram form as a region of a Cartesian plane.

title: Definition:Graph of Mapping
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. The graph of $f$ is the relation $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ defined as $\RR = \set {\tuple {x, \map f x}: x \in S}$ Alternatively, this can be expressed: $G_f = \set {\tuple {s, t} \in S \times T: \map f s = t}$ where $G_f$ is the graph of $f$. The word is usually used in the context of a diagram: 520px

title: Definition:Graph of Mapping/Also denoted as
snippet: == Graph of Mapping: Also known as == The graph of a mapping $f$ can also be seen denoted: $\map G f$ $\Gamma_f$ $\map \Gamma f$ and so on.

title: Definition:Graph of Real Function
snippet: Let $U \subseteq \R^n$ be an open subset of $n$-dimensional Euclidean space. Let $f : U \to \R^k$ be a real function. The graph $\map \Gamma f$ of the function $f$ is the subset of $\R^n \times \R^k$ such that: $\map \Gamma f = \set {\tuple {x, y} \in \R^n \times \R^k: x \in U \subseteq \R^n : \map f x = y}$ where $\times$ denotes the Cartesian product.

title: Definition:Graph of Relation/Also known as
snippet: == Graph of Relation: Also known as == The graph of a relation is sometimes seen referred to as its truth set. Category:Definitions/Graphs of Relations

title: Definition:Graphical Solution to Simultaneous Equations
snippet: A graphical solution is a method of finding a solution to a pair of simultaneous equations each defining a plane curve. It is performed by plotting the locus of each of the equations and seeing where they intersect. The points of intersection of the curves described by the equations are the solutions.

title: Definition:Graphical Solution to System of Simultaneous Equations
snippet: Consider the following pair of simultaneous equations in $2$ variables: {{eqn | l = \map {f_1} {x, y} | r = 0 }} {{eqn | l = \map {f_2} {x, y} | r = 0 }} The solution to the above simultaneous equations can be found by: plotting the graphs of $f_1$ and $f_2$ on a coordinate plane inspecting the points where these graphs intersect. This is called a graphical solution to the system of simultaneous equations.

title: Definition:Grassmann Coordinates
snippet: Grassmann coordinates are a technique of parameterization of sets of spaces of the same dimension in a Euclidean space.

title: Definition:Grassmann Manifold
snippet: Let $n \in \N_{> 0}$ be a natural number. Let $k \in \N_{> 0}$ be a natural number such that $0 < k < n$. The set $\map {G_k} {\R^n}$ of $k$-dimensional linear subspaces of $\R^n$ is called a Grassmann manifold.

title: Definition:Gravitation
snippet: Gravitation is the tendency of bodies with mass to attract each other. Gravitation is one of the $4$ fundamental forces of nature.

title: Definition:Gravitation/Also known as
snippet: == Gravitation and Gravitational Force: Also known as == Gravitation and gravitational force are also known as gravity. However, this is usually reserved for its common usage as the force of gravity, in particular at the surface of Earth.

title: Definition:Gravitation/Gravitational Force
snippet: The gravitational force on a body $B$ is the force which is exerted on $B$ as a result of the gravitational field whose influence it is under.

title: Definition:Gravitational Field
snippet: Every body which has mass influences every other body which has mass, according to Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation. Thus any body can be considered as being surrounded by a field given rise to by its mass, called a gravitational field. Its value $\mathbf g$ at any point is given by: $\mathbf g = \dfrac {G M} {d^3} \mathbf d$ where: $G$ is the universal gravitational constant $M$ is the mass of the body $\mathbf d$ is the displacement vector from the point to the center of gravity of the body, whose magnitude is $d$.

title: Definition:Gravitational Mass
snippet: Gravitational mass is the property of a body $B$ that determines the gravitational field that $B$ can produce.

title: Definition:Gravitational Mass/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Gravitational Mass == The gravitational mass of a body has been shown to be equivalent to its inertial mass.

title: Definition:Gravity
snippet: Gravity is the tendency for a body to move downwards, as a result of its weight. It is a local manifestation of the phenomenon of gravitation, whether on Earth or some other celestial body

title: Definition:Gravity/Also known as
snippet: == Gravity: Also known as == Gravity is also known as gravitation. However, as it is often referred to in common usage as the force of gravity, in particular at the surface of Earth, it is recommended that the terms are kept separate. Category:Definitions/Gravity

title: Definition:Gravity/Earth
snippet: When used in an unqualified sense, it is usual for the term force of gravity to mean the downward force on a body at the surface of Earth. From Gravity at Earth's Surface, this is approximately $9.8 \ \mathrm N \ \mathrm{kg}^{-1}$ The force of gravity varies across the Earth's surface, and therefore it makes little sense to use it as a standard. However, the adopted a standard value of Acceleration Due to Gravity at Earth's Surface of $9.806 \, 65 \, \mathrm N \, \mathrm{kg}^{-1}$ in $1901$. Category:Definitions/Gravity

title: Definition:Gravity/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Gravity == The word gravity derives from a Latin word meaning weighty.

title: Definition:Gray
snippet: The gray is the SI unit of absorbed dose of ionizing radiation. It is equal to the energy in joules absorbed by $1$ kilogram of matter.

title: Definition:Gray/Symbol
snippet: == Gray: Symbol == The symbol for the gray is $\mathrm {Gy}$.

title: Definition:Gray Code/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Gray Code == The Gray code was invented by in $1947$. A similar code, the Baudot code, had been invented in $1878$ by . The Gray code is widely used in analogue-to-digital conversion, and has very useful error-correcting properties.

title: Definition:Great Circle
snippet: Let $S$ be a sphere. A great circle of $S$ is defined as the intersection of $S$ with a plane passing through the center of $S$. 400px

title: Definition:Great Circle/Axis
snippet: The axis of a great circle $C$ is the straight line that joins the poles of $C$. Category:Definitions/Great Circles

title: Definition:Great Circle/Pole
snippet: This is a special case of the pole of a circle. Let $S$ be a sphere whose center is $O$. Let $C$ be a great circle of $S$. Let $AB$ be the diameter of $S$ situated perpendicular to the plane of $C$. 700px The points $A$ and $B$, where the diameter intersects $S$, are the poles of the great circle $C$.

title: Definition:Great Stellated Dodecahedron
snippet: The great stellated dodecahedron is a Kepler-Poinsot polyhedron composed of $12$ pentagrammic faces with $3$ pentagrams meeting at each vertex.

title: Definition:Great Stellated Dodecahedron/Also known as
snippet: == Great Stellated Dodecahedron: Also known as == Some sources give the great stellated dodecahedron as the greater stellated dodecahedron. Category:Definitions/Great Stellated Dodecahedron

title: Definition:Great Stellated Dodecahedron/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Great Stellated Dodecahedron == The great stellated dodecahedron was discovered by , and later rediscovered by .

title: Definition:Greater Than
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \le}$ be one of the sets of numbers: $\N$, $\Z$, $\Q$, $\R$ under the usual ordering. Let $a, b \in S$ such that $a < b$. Then $b$ is described as being greater than $a$.

title: Definition:Greatest Common Divisor/Also defined as
snippet: == Greatest Common Divisor: Also defined as == Some sources gloss over the fact that at least one of $a$ and $b$ must be non-zero for $\gcd \set{ a, b }$ to be defined. Some sources insist that both $a$ and $b$ be non-zero or strictly positive. Some sources define $\gcd \set {a, b} = 0$ for $a = b = 0$. Category:Definitions/Greatest Common Divisor

title: Definition:Greatest Common Divisor/Also known as
snippet: The greatest common divisor is often seen abbreviated as GCD, gcd or g.c.d. Some sources write $\gcd \set {a, b}$ as $\tuple {a, b}$, but this notation can cause confusion with ordered pairs. The notation $\map \gcd {a, b}$ is frequently seen, but the set notation, although a little more cumbersome, can be argued to be preferable. The greatest common divisor is also known as the highest common factor, or greatest common factor. Highest common factor when it occurs, is usually abbreviated as HCF, hcf or h.c.f. It is written $\hcf \set {a, b}$ or $\map \hcf {a, b}$.

title: Definition:Greatest Common Divisor/Integers
snippet: Let $a, b \in \Z: a \ne 0 \lor b \ne 0$.

title: Definition:Greatest Common Divisor/Integers/Definition 1
snippet: Let $a, b \in \Z: a \ne 0 \lor b \ne 0$. The greatest common divisor of $a$ and $b$ is defined as: the largest $d \in \Z_{>0}$ such that $d \divides a$ and $d \divides b$ where $\divides$ denotes divisibility. This is denoted $\gcd \set {a, b}$. When $a = b = 0$, $\gcd \set {a, b}$ is undefined.

title: Definition:Greatest Common Divisor/Integers/Definition 2
snippet: Let $a, b \in \Z: a \ne 0 \lor b \ne 0$. The greatest common divisor of $a$ and $b$ is defined as the (strictly) positive integer $d \in \Z_{>0}$ such that: $(1): \quad d \divides a \land d \divides b$ $(2): \quad c \divides a \land c \divides b \implies c \divides d$ where $\divides$ denotes divisibility. This is denoted $\gcd \set {a, b}$. When $a = b = 0$, $\gcd \set {a, b}$ is undefined.

title: Definition:Greatest Common Divisor/Integers/General Definition
snippet: Let $S = \set {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n} \subseteq \Z$ such that $\exists x \in S: x \ne 0$ (that is, at least one element of $S$ is non-zero).

title: Definition:Greatest Common Divisor/Integral Domain
snippet: Let $\struct {D, +, \times}$ be an integral domain whose zero is $0$. Let $a, b \in D: a \ne 0 \lor b \ne 0$. Let $d \divides a$ denote that $d$ is a divisor of $a$. Let $d \in D$ have the following properties: $(1): \quad d \divides a \land d \divides b$ $(2): \quad c \divides a \land c \divides b \implies c \divides d$ Then $d$ is called a greatest common divisor of $a$ and $b$ (abbreviated GCD or gcd) and denoted $\gcd \set {a, b}$.

title: Definition:Greatest Common Divisor/Polynomial Ring over Field
snippet: Let $F$ be a field. Let $P, Q, R \in F \sqbrk X$ be polynomials. Then $R$ is the greatest common divisor of $P$ and $Q$ it is a monic greatest common divisor. This is denoted $\gcd \set {P, Q} = R$.

title: Definition:Greatest Common Divisor/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $a, b \in \R$ be commensurable. Then there exists a greatest element $d \in \R_{>0}$ such that: $d \divides a$ $d \divides b$ where $d \divides a$ denotes that $d$ is a divisor of $a$. This is called the greatest common divisor of $a$ and $b$ and denoted $\gcd \set {a, b}$.

title: Definition:Greatest Common Divisor of Set of Integers/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S = \set {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n} \subseteq \Z$ such that $\exists x \in S: x \ne 0$ (that is, at least one element of $S$ is non-zero). The greatest common divisor of $S$: $\map \gcd S = \gcd \set {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n}$ is defined as the largest $d \in \Z_{>0}$ such that: $\forall x \in S: d \divides x$ where $\divides$ denotes divisibility. By convention: $\map \gcd \O = 1$

title: Definition:Greatest Common Divisor of Set of Integers/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S = \set {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n} \subseteq \Z$ such that $\exists x \in S: x \ne 0$ (that is, at least one element of $S$ is non-zero). The greatest common divisor of $S$: $\map \gcd S = \gcd \set {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n}$ is defined as the (strictly) positive integer $d \in \Z_{>0}$ such that: where $\divides$ denotes divisibility. By convention: $\map \gcd \O = 1$

title: Definition:Greatest Element
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. An element $x \in S$ is the greatest element (of $S$) : $\forall y \in S: y \preceq x$ That is, every element of $S$ precedes, or is equal to, $x$. The Greatest Element is Unique, so calling it the greatest element is justified. Thus for an element $x$ to be the greatest element, all $y \in S$ must be comparable to $x$.

title: Definition:Greatest Element/Also known as
snippet: == Greatest Element: Also known as == The greatest element of a collection is also called: The largest element (or biggest element, etc.) The last element The maximum element (but beware confusing with maximal - see above) The unit element (in the context of boolean algebras and boolean rings) Category:Definitions/Greatest Elements

title: Definition:Greatest Element/Class Theory
snippet: Let $V$ be a basic universe. Let $\RR \subseteq V \times V$ be an ordering. Let $A$ be a subclass of the field of $\RR$. An element $x \in A$ is the greatest element of $A$ : $\forall y \in A: y \mathrel \RR x$ Thus for an element $x$ to be the greatest element, all $y \in S$ must be comparable to $x$.

title: Definition:Greatest Element/Subset
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $T \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. An element $x \in T$ is the greatest element of $T$ : $\forall y \in T: y \preceq \restriction_T x$ where $\preceq \restriction_T$ denotes the restriction of $\preceq$ to $T$.

title: Definition:Greatest Set by Set Inclusion
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\powerset S$ be the power set of $S$. Let $\TT \subseteq \powerset S$ be a subset of $\powerset S$. Let $\struct {\TT, \subseteq}$ be the ordered set formed on $\TT$ by the subset relation. Then $T \in \TT$ is the greatest set of $\TT$ $T$ is the greatest element of $\struct {\TT, \subseteq}$. That is: $\forall X \in \TT: X \subseteq T$

title: Definition:Greatest Set by Set Inclusion/Also known as
snippet: == Greatest Set by Set Inclusion: Also known as == The greatest set of a set of sets is also known as a largest set. Category:Definitions/Greatest Set

title: Definition:Greatest Set by Set Inclusion/Class Theory
snippet: Let $A$ be a class. Then a set $M$ is the greatest element of $A$ (with respect to the subset relation) : $(1): \quad M \in A$ $(2): \quad \forall S: \paren {S \in A \implies S \subseteq M}$

title: Definition:Greedy Algorithm
snippet: A greedy algorithm is an algorithm whose decision strategy is such that any choice made at any stage takes no consideration of any future state. The strategy is to make the choice which has the greatest short-term effect towards the long-term goal. In some problems this may not produce the optimum solution.

title: Definition:Greek Numerals/Attic System
snippet: The Greek numerals from the Attic period (c. 500 BCE to c. 300 BCE) are similar to the Roman system: {{eqn | l = \textsf{I}: | o = | r = \)one\( }} $\Pi$ was later written in a different form, with a shorter right leg, and from there it appears to have evolved into $\Gamma$. Numbers were combined in a similar way to Roman numbers, but with additive forms only. For example, $32718$ would have been written $\Mu \Mu \Mu \Xi \Xi \Eta \Eta \Eta \Eta \Eta \Eta \Eta \Delta \Pi \textsf {III}$.

title: Definition:Greek Numerals/Classical Period
snippet: The Greek numerals from the Classical period (c. $600$ BCE to c. $300$ BCE) are as follows: $\begin{array}{ccccccccc} 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 & 7 & 8 & 9 \\ \alpha & \beta & \gamma & \delta & \epsilon & stigma & \zeta & \eta & \theta \\ \hline \\ 10 & 20 & 30 & 40 & 50 & 60 & 70 & 80 & 90 \\ \iota & \kappa & \lambda & \mu & \nu & \xi & \omicron & \pi & koppa \\ \hline \\ 100 & 200 & 300 & 400 & 500 & 600 & 700 & 800 & 900 \\ \rho & \sigma & \tau & \upsilon & \phi & \chi & \psi & \omega & sampi \\ \end{array}$ where $stigma$, $koppa$ and $sampi$ are characters that are not supported by MathJax.

title: Definition:Greenwich Meridian
snippet: The Greenwich meridian is the meridian of Earth which passes through the in , , .

title: Definition:Greenwich Meridian/Also known as
snippet: == Greenwich Meridian: Also known as == The Greenwich meridian has also been known as the following at some stage during the course of its history: the prime meridian the principal meridian the standard meridian and so on. It has since been superseded as the standard meridian.

title: Definition:Greenwich Meridian/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Greenwich Meridian == From $1884$ until $1974$, the Greenwich meridian was used as the prime meridian. That is, the internationally-recognised $0 \degrees$ reference longitude meridian from which all longitude was defined. This has since been superseded by the IERS reference meridian, which is based on a different principle. However, many reference works and textbooks written since $1974$ still refer to the Greenwich meridian as the prime meridian. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Greenwich Meridian/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Greenwich Meridian == The place name Greenwich, in the context of the Greenwich meridian, is pronounced something like Gren-itch or Gren-idge. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Gregory-Newton Backward Difference Formula
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function. Let $x_0, x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n \in \R$ be equally spaced: $\forall i \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n}: x_i - x_{i - 1} = d$ where $d$ is constant. Let $y_0, y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n$ be values of $x_0, x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ under $f$: $\forall i \in \set {0, 1, 2, \ldots, n}: y_i = \map f {x_i}$ Let $x_{n - 1} < x' < x_n$. Let $k = \dfrac {x' - x_{n - 1} } d$.

title: Definition:Gregory-Newton Backward Difference Formula/Also known as
snippet: == Gregory-Newton Backward Difference Formula: Also known as == The Gregory-Newton backward difference formula is also known as: the Newton-Gregory backward difference formula Newton's backward difference formula the backward difference formula and so on.

title: Definition:Gregory-Newton Forward Difference Formula
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function. Let $x_0, x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n \in \R$ be equally spaced: $\forall i \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n}: x_i - x_{i - 1} = d$ where $d$ is constant. Let $y_0, y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n$ be values of $x_0, x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ under $f$: $\forall i \in \set {0, 1, 2, \ldots, n}: y_i = \map f {x_i}$ Let $x_0 < x' < x_1$. Let $k = \dfrac {x' - x_0} d$.

title: Definition:Gregory-Newton Forward Difference Formula/Also known as
snippet: == Gregory-Newton Forward Difference Formula: Also known as == The Gregory-Newton forward difference formula is also known as: the Newton-Gregory forward difference formula Newton's forward difference formula the forward difference formula and so on. Some sources refer to this as Gregory-Newton interpolation, but this is used on to encompass the Gregory-Newton backward difference formula as well.

title: Definition:Gregory-Newton Interpolation
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function. Let $x_0, x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n \in \R$ be equally spaced: $\forall i \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n}: x_i - x_{i - 1} = d$ where $d$ is constant. Let $y_0, y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n$ be values of $x_0, x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ under $f$: $\forall i \in \set {0, 1, 2, \ldots, n}: y_i = \map f {x_i}$

title: Definition:Gregory-Newton Interpolation/Also known as
snippet: == Gregory-Newton Interpolation: Also known as == Gregory-Newton interpolation is also known as Newton-Gregory interpolation.

title: Definition:Gross
snippet: A gross is another name for a set whose cardinality is $12 \times 12$, or $144$.

title: Definition:Gross/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Gross == The word gross, used in its original meaning of a dozen dozen, is falling into disuse. In its place, gross is used as an adjective, mainly in contemporary American slang, to mean distasteful. This arises from the fact that a gross is conventionally viewed as a large number, when applied to a quantity of an everyday commodity. Hence the adverb grossly evolved, which was applied to intensify adjectives, and evolved further to qualify adjectives defining unpleasant qualities.

title: Definition:Gross (Accounting)
snippet: Gross means prior to deductions.

title: Definition:Gross (Accounting)/Profit
snippet: Gross profit is profit before subtracting the operating costs.

title: Definition:Gross (Accounting)/Weight
snippet: The gross weight of an object includes the weight of whatever wrapper, container or shipping means in which the object may be contained.

title: Definition:Grothendieck Universe
snippet: A Grothendieck universe is a set (not a class) which has the properties expected of the universal set $\mathbb U$ of sets in the sense of the Zermelo-Fraenkel axioms with the following properties: $(1): \quad \mathbb U$ is a transitive set: If $u \in \mathbb U$ and $x \in u$ then $x \in \mathbb U$ $(2): \quad$ If $ u, v \in \mathbb U$ then $\set {u, v} \in \mathbb U$ $(3): \quad$ If $u \in \mathbb U$ then the power set $\powerset u \in \mathbb U$ $(4): \quad$ If $A \in \mathbb U$, and $\set {u_\alpha: \alpha \in A}$ is a family of elements $u_\alpha \in \mathbb U$ indexed by $A$, then $\ds…

title: Definition:Group
snippet: A group is a semigroup with an identity (that is, a monoid) in which every element has an inverse.

title: Definition:Group/Also denoted as
snippet: == Group: Also known as == Some sources denote a group using the notation $\gen {G, \circ}$ for $\struct {G, \circ}$.

title: Definition:Group/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Group == The term group was first used by in $1832$, in the context of the solutions of polynomials in radicals. was also involved in this development. The concept of the group as a purely abstract structure was introduced by in his $1854$ paper On the theory of groups. The first one to formulate the set of axioms to define the structure of a group was in $1870$.

title: Definition:Group Action
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group whose identity is $e$.

title: Definition:Group Action/Also defined as
snippet: == Group Action: Also defined as == A (left) group action is sometimes defined as what on is called a permutation representation. As shown in Correspondence Between Group Actions and Permutation Representations, there is a one-to-one correspondence between the two. Category:Definitions/Group Actions

title: Definition:Group Action/Also known as
snippet: == Group Action: Also known as == Some sources refer to a group action as a $G$-action, and refer to the set $X$ upon which it acts as a $G$-set. Some sources use $g \wedge x$ for $g * x$, while some use $g \cdot x$. Some sources introduce the concept with the notation $\map {\phi_g} x$ for $g * x$, before progressing to the latter notation. There is little consistency in the literature; $*$ appears to be popular. $\wedge$ is not generally preferred, because its other uses are somewhat specialized. Category:Definitions/Group Actions

title: Definition:Group Action/Different Approaches
snippet: == Different Approaches to == During the course of an exposition in group theory, it is usual to define a group action as a left group action, without introducing the concept of a right group action. It is apparent during the conventional development of the subject that there is rarely any need to discriminate between the two approaches. Hence, on , we do not in general consider the right group action, and instead present results from the point of view of left group actions alone. Category:Definitions/Group Actions

title: Definition:Group Action/Left Group Action
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group whose identity is $e$. A left group action is an operation $\phi: G \times X \to X$ such that: $\forall \tuple {g, x} \in G \times X: g * x := \map \phi {g, x} \in X$ in such a way that the group action axioms are satisfied:

title: Definition:Group Action/Permutation Representation
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $X$ be a set. Let $\struct {\map \Gamma X, \circ}$ be the symmetric group on $X$. Let $\rho: G \to \struct {\map \Gamma X, \circ}$ be a permutation representation. The group action of $G$ associated to the permutation representation $\rho$ is the group action $\phi: G \times X \to X$ defined by: $\map \phi {g, x} = \map {\rho_g} x$ where $\rho_g : X \to X$ is the permutation representation associated to $\rho$ for $g \in G$ by $\map {\rho_g} x = \map \phi {g, x}$.

title: Definition:Group Action/Right Group Action
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group whose identity is $e$. A right group action is a mapping $\phi: X \times G \to X$ such that: $\forall \tuple {x, g} \in X \times G : x * g := \map \phi {x, g} \in X$ in such a way that the right group action axioms are satisfied:

title: Definition:Group Action/Transformation Group
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group whose identity is $e$. Let $G$ act on $X$. Then $G$ can be referred to as the transformation group of $X$.

title: Definition:Group Action Induced on Stable Subset
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $X$ be a set. Let $\phi : G \times X \to X$ be a group action. Let $S \subset X$ be a stable subset. The group action induced on $S$ is the restriction of $\phi$ to $G \times S$.

title: Definition:Group Action Induced on Subgroup
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $X$ be a set. Let $\phi : G \times X \to X$ be a group action. Let $H \le G$ be a subgroup. The group action induced on $H$ is the restriction of $\phi$ to $H \times X$. Equivalently, the group action induced on $H$ is the group action associated to the permutation representation: $\rho \circ \iota : H \to \struct {\map \Gamma X, \circ}$ where: $\iota : H \to G$ is the inclusion homomorphism $\rho$ is the permutation representation of $\phi$ $\struct {\map \Gamma X, \circ}$ is the symmetric group on $X$.

title: Definition:Group Action by Homeomorphisms
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $X$ be a topological space. Let $\phi: G \times X \to X$ be a group action Then $G$ acts by homeomorphisms for all $g \in G$, the mapping: $\phi_g : X \to X : x \mapsto \phi \left({g, x}\right)$ is a homeomorphism.

title: Definition:Group Action of GL(2,Q) on Irrational Numbers
snippet: Let $\GL {2, \Q}$ be the general linear group on the field of rational numbers. Let $\R \setminus \Q$ be the set of irrational numbers. The standard group action of $\GL {2, \Q}$ on $\R \setminus \Q$ is the group action: $\GL {2, \Q} \times \paren {\R \setminus \Q} \to \R \setminus \Q$: $\paren {\begin {pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end {pmatrix}, x} \mapsto \dfrac {a x + b} {c x + d}$

title: Definition:Group Action on Coset Space
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$. The mapping $*: G \times G / H \to G / H$ by the rule: $\forall g \in G, \forall g' H \in G / H: g * \paren {g' H} := \paren {g g'} H$ is the group action on the (left) coset space $G / H$.

title: Definition:Group Algebra
snippet: Let $\struct {k, + ,\circ}$ be a field. Let $\struct {G, *}$ be a finite group. Then the group algebra $k G$ or $k \sqbrk G$ is the set of all formal sums: $\ds \sum_{g \mathop \in G} \alpha_g g : \alpha_g \in k$ That is, $k \sqbrk G$ is the free vector space over $k$ with basis $G$.

title: Definition:Group Automorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group. Let $\phi: G \to G$ be a (group) isomorphism from $G$ to itself. Then $\phi$ is a group automorphism.

title: Definition:Group Category
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. The group category of $G$ is the monoid category of $G$.

title: Definition:Group Defined by Presentation
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $R$ be a set of group words on $S$. Let $F_S$ be the group of reduced group words on $S$. Let $\map {\mathrm {red} } R$ be the set of reduced forms of elements of $R$. Let $N$ be the normal subgroup generated by $\map {\mathrm {red} } R$ in $F$. The group defined by the presentation $\gen {S \mid R}$ is the quotient group $F_S / N$.

title: Definition:Group Direct Product
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ_1}$ and $\struct {H, \circ_2}$ be groups. Let $G \times H: \set {\tuple {g, h}: g \in G, h \in H}$ be their cartesian product. The (external) direct product of $\struct {G, \circ_1}$ and $\struct {H, \circ_2}$ is the group $\struct {G \times H, \circ}$ where the operation $\circ$ is defined as: $\tuple {g_1, h_1} \circ \tuple {g_2, h_2} = \tuple {g_1 \circ_1 g_2, h_1 \circ_2 h_2}$ This is usually referred to as the group direct product of $G$ and $H$.

title: Definition:Group Direct Product/Also known as
snippet: == Group Direct Product: Also known as == It is commonplace, when the discussion of this topic is restricted to groups, to refer to the group direct product as just the direct product. However, be aware that the latter term encompasses algebraic structures which are not in fact groups. The group direct product is referred to in some sources, when dealing with additive groups, as the (group) direct sum. In such contexts, the symbol $G \times H$ can often be seen as $G \mathop {\dot +} H$. However, there is already a definition of direct sum which does not coincide with this.

title: Definition:Group Direct Product/Finite Product
snippet: Let $\struct {G_1, \circ_1}, \struct {G_2, \circ_2}, \ldots, \struct {G_n, \circ_n}$ be groups. Let $\ds G = \prod_{k \mathop = 1}^n G_k$ be their cartesian product. Let $\circ$ be the operation defined on $G$ as: $\circ := \tuple {g_1, g_2, \ldots, g_n} \circ \tuple {h_1, h_2, \ldots, h_n} = \tuple {g_1 \circ_1 h_1, g_2 \circ_2 h_2, \ldots, g_n \circ_n h_n}$ for all ordered $n$-tuples in $G$. The group $\struct {G, \circ}$ is called the (external) direct product of $\struct {G_1, \circ_1}, \struct {G_2, \circ_2}, \ldots, \struct {G_n, \circ_n}$.

title: Definition:Group Direct Product/General Definition
snippet: Let $\family {\struct {G_i, \circ_i} }_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a family of groups. Let $\ds G = \prod_{i \mathop \in I} G_i$ be their cartesian product. Let $\circ$ be the operation defined on $G$ as: $\circ := \family {g_i}_{i \mathop \in I} \circ \family {h_i}_{i \mathop \in I} = \family {g_i \circ_i h_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ for all sequences in $G$. The group $\struct {G, \circ}$ is called the (external) direct product of $\family {\struct {G_i, \circ_i} }_{i \mathop \in I}$. Category:Definitions/Group Direct Products Category:Definitions/Direct Products

title: Definition:Group Direct Product/Warning
snippet: == Group Direct Product: Warning == Note, in the definition of group direct product that $G$ and $H$, and so on, are not subsets of $G \times H$ and therefore are not subgroups of it either. This is clarified in Factors of Group Direct Product are not Subgroups. However, note that from Subgroups of Group Direct Product Isomorphic with Factors, that there do exist subgroups in $G \times H$ which are isomorphic with $G$ and $H$ of the form: $G \times \set {e_H}$ and $\set {e_G} \times H$ where $e_G$ and $e_H$ are identity elements of $G$ and $H$ respectively.

title: Definition:Group Endomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group. Let $\phi: G \to G$ be a (group) homomorphism from $G$ to itself. Then $\phi$ is a group endomorphism.

title: Definition:Group Epimorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ and $\struct {H, *}$ be groups. Let $\phi: G \to H$ be a (group) homomorphism. Then $\phi$ is a group epimorphism $\phi$ is a surjection.

title: Definition:Group Generated by Reciprocal of z and 1 minus z
snippet: Let: $S = \set {f_1, f_2, f_3, f_4, f_5, f_6}$ where $f_1, f_2, \ldots, f_6$ are complex functions defined for all $z \in \C \setminus \set {0, 1}$ as: {{eqn | l = \map {f_1} z | r = z }} {{eqn | l = \map {f_2} z | r = \dfrac 1 {1 - z} }} {{eqn | l = \map {f_3} z | r = \dfrac {z - 1} z }} {{eqn | l = \map {f_4} z | r = \dfrac 1 z }} {{eqn | l = \map {f_5} z | r = 1 - z }} {{eqn | l = \map {f_6} z | r = \dfrac z {z - 1} }} Let $\circ$ denote composition of functions. Then $\struct {S, \circ}$ is the group generated by $\dfrac 1 z$ and $1 - z$.

title: Definition:Group Homomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ and $\struct {H, *}$ be groups. Let $\phi: G \to H$ be a mapping such that $\circ$ has the morphism property under $\phi$. That is, $\forall a, b \in G$: $\map \phi {a \circ b} = \map \phi a * \map \phi b$ Then $\phi: \struct {G, \circ} \to \struct {H, *}$ is a group homomorphism.

title: Definition:Group Homomorphism/Also defined as
snippet: == Group Homomorphism: Also defined as == In their definition of a group homomorphism, some sources demand further that $\map \phi {e_G} = e_H$, where $e_G$ and $e_H$ are the identity elements of $G$ and $H$, respectively. However, this condition is superfluous, as shown on Group Homomorphism Preserves Identity.

title: Definition:Group Homomorphism/Also known as
snippet: == Group Homomorphism: Also known as == Some sources refer to a group homomorphism as a (group) representation, although the latter term usually has a slightly more specialized definition. Some sources use the term structure-preserving.

title: Definition:Group Monomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ and $\struct {H, *}$ be groups. Let $\phi: G \to H$ be a (group) homomorphism. Then $\phi$ is a group monomorphism $\phi$ is an injection.

title: Definition:Group Presentation
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. A (group) presentation for $G$ is a triple $\tuple {S, R, f}$ where: $S$ is a set $R$ is a set of relations on $S$ $f: \gen {S \mid R} \to G$ is a group isomorphism from the group defined by $\struct {S, R}$.

title: Definition:Group Presentation/Relation
snippet: The standard form of a relation in a group presentation is: $w = e$ where $w$ is a word in the group.

title: Definition:Group Product
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group. The term group product can have two different interpretations:

title: Definition:Group Product/Group Law
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group. The operation $\circ$ can be referred to as the group law.

title: Definition:Group Product/Product Element
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group. Let $a, b \in G$ such that $g = a \circ b$. Then $g$ is known as the product of $a$ and $b$.

title: Definition:Group Relation on Set
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. A group relation on $X$ is a pair $(u, v)$ where $u$ and $v$ are group words on $X$. A group relation $(u, v)$ is also denoted $u=v$.

title: Definition:Group Representation
snippet: Let $G$ be a group whose underlying set consists of abstract symbols. A group representation of $G$ is a homomorphism from $G$ into a group of more familiar objects whose operation is well understood.

title: Definition:Group Representation/Matrix
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a group of matrices. A matrix representation of $G$ is a group homomorphism from $G$ to $H$.

title: Definition:Group Representation/Permutation
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $X$ be a set. Let $\struct {\map \Gamma X, \circ}$ be the symmetric group on $X$. A permutation representation of $G$ is a group homomorphism from $G$ to $\struct {\map \Gamma X, \circ}$.

title: Definition:Group Ring
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $\struct {G, +}$ be a group. The group ring of $G$ over $R$ is the monoid ring of $G$ over $R$.

title: Definition:Group Theory
snippet: Group theory is a branch of abstract algebra which studies groups and other related algebraic structures.

title: Definition:Group Theory/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Group Theory == The field of group theory was initiated by as a consequence of his work on establishing the general solubility criteria of polynomials in radicals. Group theory was originally called the theory of substitutions until 's $1854$ paper On the theory of groups in which he introduced the concept of the abstract group. Nowadays group theory permeates most of modern algebra, and has important applications in such fields as crystallography and quantum mechanics.

title: Definition:Group Type
snippet: An equivalence class under group isomorphism is a (group) type.

title: Definition:Group Word on Set
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. A group word on $S$ is an ordered tuple on the set of literals $S^\pm$ of $S$.

title: Definition:Group of Gaussian Integer Units
snippet: Let $i$ be the imaginary unit: $i = \sqrt {-1}$. Let $U_\C$ be the set of complex numbers defined as: $U_\C = \set {1, i, -1, -i}$ Let $\times$ denote the operation of complex multiplication. The algebraic structure $\struct {U_\C, \times}$ is the group of units of the ring of Gaussian integers.

title: Definition:Group of Outer Automorphisms
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $\Aut G$ be the automorphism group of $G$. Let $\Inn G$ be the inner automorphism group of $G$. Let $\dfrac {\Aut G} {\Inn G}$ be the quotient group of $\Aut G$ by $\Inn G$. Then $\dfrac {\Aut G} {\Inn G}$ is called the group of outer automorphisms of $G$. This group $\dfrac {\Aut G} {\Inn G}$ is often denoted $\Out G$.

title: Definition:Group of Outer Automorphisms/Warning
snippet: == Warning == The name group of outer automorphisms is a misnomer, because: $(1): \quad$ the elements of $\dfrac {\Aut G} {\Inn G}$ are not outer automorphisms of $G$ and $(2): \quad$ the outer automorphisms of $G$ do not themselves form a group.

title: Definition:Group of Permutation Matrices
snippet: The group of permutation matrices of order $n$ is the set of all $n \times n$ permutation matrices with multiplication of matrices.

title: Definition:Group of Rationals Modulo One
snippet: Define a relation $\sim$ on $\Q$ such that: $\forall p, q \in \Q: p \sim q \iff p - q \in \Z$ Then $\left({\Q / \sim, +}\right)$ is a group referred to as the group of rationals modulo one. where: $\sim$ is an equivalence relation as shown in Group of Rationals Modulo One Induces Equivalence Relation $\Q / \sim$ is the quotient set induced by $\sim$ That is, it is the quotient group $\struct{\Q / \Z, \oplus}$, such that: $\forall \eqclass a \sim, \eqclass b \sim \in \Q / \Z: \eqclass a \sim \oplus \eqclass b \sim = \eqclass {a + b} \sim$ where: $\eqclass a \sim$ is the equivalence class on…

title: Definition:Group of Reduced Group Words
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. The group of reduced group words on $S$ is the group $\struct {F_S, \circ}$ such that: $F_S$ is the set of reduced group words on $S$ $\circ$ denotes composition of reduced group words.

title: Definition:Group of Rotation Matrices Order 4
snippet: Consider the algebraic structure $S$ of rotation matrices: $R_4 = \set {\begin {bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end {bmatrix}, \begin {bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end {bmatrix}, \begin {bmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end {bmatrix}, \begin {bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end {bmatrix} }$ under the operation of (conventional) matrix multiplication. $R_4$ is the group of rotation matrices of order $4$.

title: Definition:Group of Units/Monoid
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a monoid. Then the set $U_S$ of invertible elements of $\struct {S, \circ}$ can be referred to as the group of units of $\struct {S, \circ}$. This can be denoted explicitly as $\struct {U_S, \circ}$.

title: Definition:Group of Units/Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring with unity. Then the set $U_R$ of units of $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ is called the group of units of $\struct {R, +, \circ}$. This can be denoted explicitly as $\struct {U_R, \circ}$.

title: Definition:Grouped Data
snippet: Grouped data is an arrangement of observations of continuous data into a subdivision of the range of that data. The lengths of the subintervals of this subdivision are made equal, except for those at either end, which are generally left half-open to accommodate outliers. Hence, with an appropriate choice of subdivision, the grouping gives an immediate intuitive guess for the distribution of the observations.

title: Definition:Grouped Data/Also known as
snippet: == Grouped Data: Also known as == Grouped data is also known as binned data, from the usage of the term bin.

title: Definition:Grouped Data/Bin
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of observations of continuous data. Let the range of $S$ be grouped into a finite subdivision. Each of the subintervals of the subdivision into which the grouped data is assigned is referred to as a bin.

title: Definition:Grouped Data/Mid-Interval Value
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of grouped data. The mid-interval values are the midpoints of the bins into which $S$ has been assigned. For the bins at either end of the subdivision, the midpoints are calculated as though they are the same bin width as the rest of the bins.

title: Definition:Grouping
snippet: A grouping is an arrangement of experimental units into a set of randomized blocks.

title: Definition:Groupoid
snippet: Groupoid (Abstract Algebra): an older term (some suggest obsolete) for what is now called a magma. Groupoid (Category Theory) Category:Definitions/Groupoids Category:Definitions/Abstract Algebra Category:Definitions/Category Theory

title: Definition:Groupoid (Category Theory)/Definition 1
snippet: A groupoid, in the context of category theory, is: a set $G$ a distinguished subset $G^2 \subseteq G \times G$ called the set of composable pairs a product mapping $G^2 \to G \, ,\, \tuple {x, y} \mapsto x y$ an inversion map $G \to G \, ,\, x \mapsto x^{-1}$ such that: {{axiom | n = 1 | q = \forall x \in G | m = \paren {x^{-1} }^{-1} = x }} {{axiom | n = 2 | q = \forall x, y, z \in G | m = \tuple {x, y}, \tuple {y, z} \in G^2 \implies \paren {\tuple {x y, z}, \tuple {x, y z} \in G^2 \land x \paren {y z} = \paren {x y} z} }} {{axiom | n = 3 | q = \forall x \in G | m = \tuple {x, x^{-1} } \in…

title: Definition:Groupoid (Category Theory)/Definition 2
snippet: A groupoid is a category such that every morphism is an isomorphism.

title: Definition:Grötzsch Annulus
snippet: Let $R \in \R_{>1}$. The set: $A := \set {z \in \C: \cmod z > 1 \text{ and } z \notin \hointr R {+\infty} }$ is called a Grötzsch annulus.

title: Definition:Gunter's Chain
snippet: thumb A Gunter's chain is an actual physical chain, measuring $66$ feet in length, designed by for the purposes of surveying. It is made from $100$ links, each measuring $7 \cdot 92$ inches, or one link in length. Category:Definitions/Tools

title: Definition:Gustin's Sequence Space
snippet: Let $X$ be the set: $X = Y \cup \paren {\Z_{>0} \times W}$ where: $Y$ is the set of all finite sequences of (strictly) positive integers with an even number of terms, including the empty sequence denoted $0$ $\Z_{>0}$ is the set of (strictly) positive integers $W$ is the set of all doubleton subsets of $Y$. Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be arbitrary finite sequences. Let: $\alpha \beta$ denote the sequence formed by concatenating $\beta$ to the end of $\alpha$.

title: Definition:Gyromagnetic Ratio
snippet: The gyromagnetic ratio of a particle $P$ is the ratio of its magnetic moment to its angular momentum.

title: Definition:Gyromagnetic Ratio/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Gyromagnetic Ratio: Conversion Factors == Some conversion factors between the various units of gyromagnetic ratio are as follows: Category:Definitions/Gyromagnetic Ratio

title: Definition:Gyromagnetic Ratio/Dimension
snippet: Gyromagnetic ratio has the dimension $\mathsf {I T M^{-1} }$. Category:Definitions/Gyromagnetic Ratio Category:Definitions/Dimensions of Measurement

title: Definition:Gyromagnetic Ratio/Units
snippet: The SI unit for gyromagnetic ratio is radian per second per tesla: $\mathrm {rad \, s^{-1} \, T^{-1} }$ (equivalent to coulomb per kilogram: $\mathrm {C \, kg^{-1} }$). The CGS unit for gyromagnetic ratio is radian per second per gauss: $\mathrm {rad \, s^{-1} \, Gs^{-1} }$. Category:Definitions/Units of Measurement Category:Definitions/Gyromagnetic Ratio

title: Definition:Gyroscope
snippet: A gyroscope is a wheel spinning on a shaft, so mounted so that it can rotate freely in any direction.

title: Definition:Gyroscopic Inertia
snippet: Gyroscopic inertia is the tendency of a spinning wheel to maintain the direction of its axis of rotation in space.

title: Definition:Göbel's Sequence
snippet: Göbel's sequence is the sequence defined recursively as: $x_n = \begin {cases} 1 & : n = 0 \\ \ds \paren {1 + \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} {x_k}^2} / n & : n > 0 \end {cases}$

title: Definition:Göbel's Sequence/General
snippet: Let $m \in \Z_{> 0}$ be a positive integer The $m$-Göbel sequence is the sequence defined recursively as: $x_n = \begin {cases} 1 & : n = 0 \\ \ds \paren {1 + \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} {x_k}^m} / n & : n > 0 \end {cases}$

title: Definition:Göbel's Sequence/Historical Note
snippet: Some sources link Göbel's sequence with the name of , but it appears that the latter has a different sequence named for him. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Gödel's Beta Function
snippet: Gödel's $\beta$ function $\beta: \N^3 \to \N$ is defined as: $\map \beta {x, y, z} = \map {\operatorname{rem} } {x, 1 + \paren {z + 1} \times y}$ where $\operatorname{rem}: \N^2 \to \N$ is defined as: $\map \rem {n, m} = \begin {cases} \text {the remainder when $n$ is divided by $m$} & : m \ne 0 \\ 0 & : m = 0 \end {cases}$

title: Definition:Gödel Number
snippet: A Gödel number is an integer or natural number which is assigned uniquely to an expression in a formal system.

title: Definition:Hadamard's Canonical Factorization
snippet: Let $f: \C \to \C$ be a nonzero entire function of finite rank $p \in \N$. Let $0$ be a zero of $f$ of multiplicity $m\geq0$. Let $\sequence {a_n}$ be the sequence of nonzero zeroes of $f$, repeated according to multiplicity. The canonical representation of $f$ is: $\ds \map f z = z^m e^{\map g z} \prod_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty E_p \paren {\frac z {a_n} }$ where: $g: \C \to \C$ is an entire function $E_p$ denotes the $p$th Weierstrass elementary factor. If $f$ has finitely many zeroes, the product is understood to be finite.

title: Definition:Hadamard Matrix
snippet: A Hadamard matrix $H$ is a square matrix such that:

title: Definition:Hadamard Matrix/Definition 1
snippet: A Hadamard matrix $H$ is a square matrix such that: $(1): \quad$ all the entries of $H$ are either $+1$ or $-1$ $(2): \quad$ all the rows of $H$ are pairwise orthogonal.

title: Definition:Hadamard Matrix/Definition 2
snippet: A Hadamard matrix $H$ is a square matrix such that: $(1): \quad$ all the entries of $H$ are either $+1$ or $-1$ $(2): \quad H H^\intercal = n \mathbf I_n$ where: $H^\intercal$ denotes the transpose of $H$ $\mathbf I_n$ denotes the identity matrix of order $n$ given that the order of $H$ is $n$.

title: Definition:Hadamard Product
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ and $\mathbf B = \sqbrk b_{m n}$ be $m \times n$ matrices over a ring $\struct {R, +, \times}$. The Hadamard product of $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ is written $\mathbf A \circ \mathbf B$ and is defined as follows: $\mathbf A \circ \mathbf B := \mathbf C = \sqbrk c_{m n}$ where: $\forall i \in \closedint 1 m, j \in \closedint 1 n: c_{i j} = a_{i j} \times b_{i j}$

title: Definition:Hadamard Product/Also known as
snippet: == Hadamard Product: Also known as == The Hadamard product is also known as: the (matrix) entrywise product the Schur product, for . Category:Definitions/Hadamard Product

title: Definition:Hadamard Product/Defined Operation
snippet: == Hadamard Product: Defined Operation == It needs to be noted that the operation of Hadamard product is defined only when both matrices have the same number of rows and the same number of columns. Category:Definitions/Hadamard Product

title: Definition:Hahn Decomposition
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\mu$ be a signed measure on $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. We say that $\tuple {P, N}$ is a Hahn decomposition of $\mu$ : $(1): \quad$ $P$ and $N$ are disjoint. $(2): \quad$ $X = P \cup N$ $(3): \quad$ $P$ is $\mu$-positive and $N$ is $\mu$-negative.

title: Definition:Half
snippet: Half is the name given to the rational number $\dfrac 1 2$.

title: Definition:Half-Disc Topology
snippet: Let $P = \set {\tuple {x, y}: x \in \R, y \in \R_{>0} }$ be the open upper half-plane. Let $\struct {P, \tau_d}$ be the open upper half-plane with the Euclidean topology. Let $L$ denote the $x$-axis Let $\BB$ be the set of sets of the form: $\set x \cup \paren {U \cap P}$ where: $x \in L$ $U$ is a Euclidean neighborhood of $x$. Let $\tau^*$ be the topology generated from $\BB$. $\tau^*$ is referred to as the half-disc topology.

title: Definition:Half-Integer
snippet: A half-integer is a number of the form: $n + \dfrac 1 2$ where $n \in \Z$. The set of all half-integers can be defined as: $\left\{{n + \dfrac 1 2: n \in \Z}\right\}$ and can be denoted as $\Z + \dfrac 1 2$.

title: Definition:Half-Open Interval/Also defined as
snippet: == Half-Open Interval: Also defined as == Some sources, when defining a half-open interval, require that $a \preccurlyeq b$. This is to eliminate the degenerate case where the interval is the empty set. Category:Definitions/Intervals

title: Definition:Half-Open Interval/Also known as
snippet: == Half-Open Interval: Also known as == This can often be seen rendered as half open interval. A half-open interval can also be referred to as a half-closed interval. Some sources call it a partly open interval or partly closed interval.

title: Definition:Half-Open Real Interval/Also defined as
snippet: == Half-Open Real Interval: Also defined as == Some sources, when defining a half-open real interval, require that $a < b$. This is to eliminate the degenerate case where the interval is the empty set.

title: Definition:Half-Open Rectangle
snippet: Let $a_1, \ldots, a_n, b_1, \ldots, b_n$ be real numbers. The set: $\ds \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n \hointr {a_i} {b_i} = \hointr {a_1} {b_1} \times \cdots \times \hointr {a_n} {b_n} \subseteq \R^n$ is called a half-open rectangle in $\R^n$ or half-open $n$-rectangle. Here, $\times$ denotes Cartesian product. The collection of all half-open $n$-rectangles is denoted $\JJ_{ho}$, or $\JJ_{ho}^n$ if the dimension $n$ is to be emphasized.

title: Definition:Half-Open Rectangle/Also defined as
snippet: == Half-Open Rectangle: Also known as == Sets of the form: $\horectl {\mathbf a} {\mathbf b} \:= \ds \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n \hointl {a_i} {b_i}$ can equally well be called half-open rectangles as those of the form $\horectr {\mathbf a} {\mathbf b}$. However, these are rarely encountered.

title: Definition:Half-Open Rectangle/Degenerate Case
snippet: In the case where $a_i > b_i$ for some $i$, the half-open rectangle $\ds \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n \hointr {a_i} {b_i}$ degenerates to the empty set $\O$. This is in accordance with the result Cartesian Product is Empty iff Factor is Empty for general Cartesian products. Category:Definitions/Half-Open Rectangles

title: Definition:Half-Open Rectangle/Notation
snippet: == Half-Open Rectangle: Notation == A convenient notation for the half-open rectangle $\ds \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n \hointr {a_i} {b_i}$ is $\horectr {\mathbf a} {\mathbf b}$.

title: Definition:Half-Open Rectangle/Technical Note
snippet: == Technical Note on Half-Open Rectangle == {{LatexFor|for = \horectr {\mathbf a} {\mathbf b} }} This is a custom command designed to implement Wirth interval notation and its derivatives. The name is derived from half-open rectangle on the right. Category:Technical Notes

title: Definition:Half-Plane
snippet: Let $\PP$ denote the plane. Let $\LL$ denote an infinite straight line in $\PP$. Then each of the areas of $\PP$ on either side of $\LL$ is a half-plane.

title: Definition:Half-Plane/Also known as
snippet: == Half-Plane: Also known as == Some sources render half-plane without the hyphen: half plane.

title: Definition:Half-Plane/Closed
snippet: Let $\PP$ denote the plane. Let $\LL$ denote an infinite straight line in $\PP$. Let $\HH$ be a half-plane whose edge is $\LL$. $\HH$ is a closed half-plane $\HH$ includes $\LL$.

title: Definition:Half-Plane/Closed/Left
snippet: Let $\PP$ be a Cartesian plane. Let $\LL$ be the $y$-axis. The closed left half-plane $\HH_{\text {CL} }$ is the area of $\PP$ on the left of and including $\LL$. That is, where $x \le 0$: $\HH_{\text {CL} } := \set {\tuple {x, y}: x \in \R_{\le 0} }$

title: Definition:Half-Plane/Closed/Lower
snippet: Let $\PP$ be a Cartesian plane. Let $\LL$ be the $x$-axis. The closed lower half-plane $\HH_{\text {CL} }$ is the area of $\PP$ below and including $\LL$. That is, where $y \le 0$: $\HH_{\text {CL} } := \set {\tuple {x, y}: y \in \R_{\le 0} }$

title: Definition:Half-Plane/Closed/Right
snippet: Let $\PP$ be a Cartesian plane. Let $\LL$ be the $y$-axis. The closed right half-plane $\HH_{\text {CR} }$ is the area of $\PP$ on the right of and including $\LL$. That is, where $x \ge 0$: $\HH_{\text {CR} } := \set {\tuple {x, y}: x \in \R_{\ge 0} }$

title: Definition:Half-Plane/Closed/Upper
snippet: Let $\PP$ be a Cartesian plane. Let $\LL$ be the $x$-axis. The closed upper half-plane $\HH_{\text {CU} }$ is the area of $\PP$ above and including $\LL$. That is, where $y \ge 0$: $\HH_{\text {CU} } := \set {\tuple {x, y}: y \in \R_{\ge 0} }$

title: Definition:Half-Plane/Edge
snippet: Let $\PP$ denote the plane. Let $\LL$ denote an infinite straight line in $\PP$. Let $\HH$ denote one of the half-planes into which $\LL$ divides $\PP$. Then $\LL$ is called the edge of $\HH$.

title: Definition:Half-Plane/Left
snippet: Let $\PP$ be a Cartesian plane. Let $\LL$ be the $y$-axis.

title: Definition:Half-Plane/Lower
snippet: Let $\PP$ be a Cartesian plane. Let $\LL$ be the $x$-axis.

title: Definition:Half-Plane/Open
snippet: Let $\PP$ denote the plane. Let $\LL$ denote an infinite straight line in $\PP$. Let $\HH$ be a half-plane whose edge is $\LL$. $\HH$ is an open half-plane $\HH$ does not include $\LL$.

title: Definition:Half-Plane/Open/Left
snippet: Let $\PP$ be a Cartesian plane. Let $\LL$ be the $y$-axis. The open left half-plane $\HH_{\text {OL} }$ is the area of $\PP$ on the left of $\LL$. That is, where $x < 0$: $\HH_{\text {OL} } := \set {\tuple {x, y}: x \in \R_{<0} }$

title: Definition:Half-Plane/Open/Lower
snippet: Let $\PP$ be a Cartesian plane. Let $\LL$ be the $x$-axis. The open lower half-plane $\HH_{\text {OL} }$ is the area of $\PP$ below $\LL$. That is, where $y < 0$: $\HH_{\text {OL} } := \set {\tuple {x, y}: y \in \R_{< 0} }$

title: Definition:Half-Plane/Open/Right
snippet: Let $\PP$ be a Cartesian plane. Let $\LL$ be the $y$-axis. The open right half-plane $\HH_{\text {OR} }$ is the area of $\PP$ on the right of $\LL$. That is, where $x > 0$: $\HH_{\text {OR} } := \set {\tuple {x, y}: x \in \R_{>0} }$

title: Definition:Half-Plane/Open/Upper
snippet: Let $\PP$ be a Cartesian plane. Let $\LL$ be the $x$-axis. The open upper half-plane $\HH_{\text {OU} }$ is the area of $\PP$ above $\LL$. That is, where $y > 0$: $\HH_{\text {OU} } := \set {\tuple {x, y}: y \in \R_{> 0} }$

title: Definition:Half-Plane/Right
snippet: Let $\PP$ be a Cartesian plane. Let $\LL$ be the $y$-axis.

title: Definition:Half-Plane/Sign
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a straight line embedded in a cartesian plane $\CC$, given by the equation: $l x + m y + n = 0$ Let $\HH_1$ and $\HH_2$ be the half-planes into which $\LL$ divides $\CC$. Let $u: \CC \to \R$ be the real-valued function on the points in $\CC$ defined as follows: $\forall P = \tuple {x_1, y_1} \in \CC: \map u P = l x_1 + m y_1 + n$ The sign of the half-plane $\HH_j$ is the sign of the value of $\map u Q$ for all $Q \in \HH_j$, for $j \in \set {1, 2}$.

title: Definition:Half-Plane/Upper
snippet: Let $\PP$ be a Cartesian plane. Let $\LL$ be the $x$-axis.

title: Definition:Half-Plane of Convergence
snippet: Let $f \left({s}\right)$ be a (general) Dirichlet series. The half-plane of convergence of $f$ is the set: $\left\{ {s: s \in \C, \operatorname{Re} \left({s}\right) > \sigma_0}\right\}$ where $\sigma_0$ is abscissa of convergence of $f$.

title: Definition:Half-Range Fourier Cosine Series/Also known as
snippet: == Half-Range Fourier Cosine Series: Also known as == Some sources give the half-range Fourier cosine series as just the Fourier cosine series.

title: Definition:Half-Range Fourier Cosine Series/Also see
snippet: == Half-Range Fourier Cosine Series: Also see == Fourier Series for Even Function over Symmetric Range, which justifies the definition Definition:Half-Range Fourier Cosine Series over Range Pi Definition:Half-Range Fourier Sine Series Definition:Half-Range Fourier Series Definition:Half-Range Fourier Series over Range Pi Category:Definitions/Half-Range Fourier Series

title: Definition:Half-Range Fourier Cosine Series/Formulation 1
snippet: Let $\map f x$ be a real function defined on the interval $\openint 0 \lambda$. Then the half-range Fourier cosine series of $\map f x$ over $\openint 0 \lambda$ is the series: $\map f x \sim \dfrac {a_0} 2 + \ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n \cos \frac {n \pi x} \lambda$ where for all $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$: $a_n = \ds \frac 2 \lambda \int_0^\lambda \map f x \cos \frac {n \pi x} \lambda \rd x$

title: Definition:Half-Range Fourier Cosine Series/Formulation 2
snippet: Let $\map f x$ be a real function defined on the interval $\openint a b$. Then the half-range Fourier cosine series of $\map f x$ over $\openint a b$ is the series: $\ds \map f x \sim \frac {A_0} 2 + \sum_{m \mathop = 1}^\infty A_m \cos \frac {m \pi \paren {x - a} } {b - a}$ where for all $m \in \Z_{\ge 0}$: $A_m = \ds \frac 2 {b - a} \int_a^b \map f x \cos \frac {m \pi \paren {x - a} } {b - a} \rd x$

title: Definition:Half-Range Fourier Cosine Series/Range Pi
snippet: Let $\map f x$ be a real function defined on the interval $\openint 0 \pi$. Then the half-range Fourier cosine series of $\map f x$ over $\openint 0 \pi$ is the series: $\map f x \sim \dfrac {a_0} 2 + \ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n \cos n x$ where for all $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$: $a_n = \ds \frac 2 \pi \int_0^\pi \map f x \cos n x \rd x$

title: Definition:Half-Range Fourier Series/Also known as
snippet: == Half-Range Fourier Series: Also known as == Some sources give the half-range Fourier series as: Fourier's half-range series the half-range series.

title: Definition:Half-Range Fourier Sine Series/Also known as
snippet: == Half-Range Fourier Sine Series: Also known as == Some sources give the half-range Fourier sine series as just the Fourier sine series.

title: Definition:Half-Range Fourier Sine Series/Also see
snippet: == Half-Range Fourier Sine Series: Also see == Fourier Series for Odd Function over Symmetric Range, which justifies the definition Definition:Half-Range Fourier Sine Series over Range Pi Definition:Half-Range Fourier Cosine Series Definition:Half-Range Fourier Series Definition:Half-Range Fourier Series over Range Pi Category:Definitions/Half-Range Fourier Series

title: Definition:Half-Range Fourier Sine Series/Formulation 1
snippet: Let $\map f x$ be a real function defined on the interval $\openint 0 \lambda$. Then the half-range Fourier sine series of $\map f x$ over $\openint 0 \lambda$ is the series: $\map f x \sim \ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty b_n \sin \frac {n \pi x} \lambda$ where for all $n \in \Z_{> 0}$: $b_n = \ds \frac 2 \lambda \int_0^\lambda \map f x \sin \frac {n \pi x} \lambda \rd x$

title: Definition:Half-Range Fourier Sine Series/Formulation 2
snippet: Let $\map f x$ be a real function defined on the interval $\openint a b$. Then the half-range Fourier sine series of $\map f x$ over $\openint a b$ is the series: $\ds \map f x \sim \sum_{m \mathop = 1}^\infty B_m \sin \frac {m \pi \paren {x - a} } {b - a}$ where for all $n \in \Z_{> 0}$: $B_m = \ds \frac 2 {b - a} \int_a^b \map f x \sin\frac {m \pi \paren {x - a} } {b - a} \rd x$

title: Definition:Half-Range Fourier Sine Series/Range Pi
snippet: Let $\map f x$ be a real function defined on the interval $\openint 0 \pi$. Then the half-range Fourier sine series of $\map f x$ over $\openint 0 \pi$ is the series: $\map f x \sim \ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty b_n \sin n x$ where for all $n \in \Z_{> 0}$: $b_n = \ds \frac 2 \pi \int_0^\pi \map f x \sin n x \rd x$
