title: Definition:Ideal (Order Theory)
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $I \subseteq S$ be a non-empty subset of $S$. Then $I$ is an ideal of $S$ $I$ satisifies the ideal axioms:

title: Definition:Ideal (Order Theory)/Proper Ideal
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set. Let $\II$ be an ideal on $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$. Then: $\II$ is a proper ideal on $S$ $\II \ne S$ That is, $\II$ is a proper subset of $S$.

title: Definition:Ideal (Physics)
snippet: An ideal (or idealized) object is one in which certain attributes are approximated to zero or infinity.

title: Definition:Ideal Point
snippet: An ideal point is a point at infinity.

title: Definition:Ideal Quotient
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $\mathfrak a, \mathfrak b \subseteq A$ be ideals of $A$. Their ideal quotient is the ideal consisting of elements whose product with $\mathfrak b$ is a subset of $\mathfrak a$: $\ideal {\mathfrak a : \mathfrak b} := \set {x \in A : x \mathfrak b \subseteq \mathfrak a}$

title: Definition:Ideal Quotient of Commutative Ring
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $\mathfrak a, \mathfrak b$ be ideals of $R$. The ideal quotient of $\mathfrak a$ and $\mathfrak b$ is the ideal defined as: $\ds \ideal {\mathfrak a : \mathfrak b} := \set {x \in R : x \mathfrak b \subseteq \mathfrak a}$ where: $x \mathfrak b := \set {x y : y \in \mathfrak b}$

title: Definition:Ideal Theory
snippet: Ideal theory is a branch of abstract algebra which studies ideals of rings.

title: Definition:Ideal in Ordered Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a preordered set. Let $I$ be a subset of $S$. $I$ is ideal in $\struct {S, \preceq}$ : $I$ is non-empty directed and lower.

title: Definition:Ideal of Algebra
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $\struct {A, \ast}$ be an $R$-algebra. Let $\struct {J, \ast}$ be a subalgebra of $\struct {A, \ast}$. We say that $J$ is an ideal of $A$ : for each $a \in A$ and $x \in J$ we have $a \ast x \in J$ and $x \ast a \in J$.

title: Definition:Ideal of Algebra/Left Ideal
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $\struct {A, \ast}$ be an $R$-algebra. Let $\struct {J, \ast}$ be a subalgebra of $\struct {A, \ast}$. We say that $J$ is a left ideal of $A$ : for each $a \in A$ and $x \in J$ we have $a \ast x \in J$.

title: Definition:Ideal of Algebra/Proper Ideal
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $\struct {A, \ast}$ be an $R$-algebra. Let $\struct {J, \ast}$ be a subalgebra of $\struct {A, \ast}$. We say that $J$ is a proper ideal of $A$ : $J \ne A$

title: Definition:Ideal of Algebra/Right Ideal
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $\struct {A, \ast}$ be an $R$-algebra. Let $\struct {J, \ast}$ be a subalgebra of $\struct {A, \ast}$. We say that $J$ is a left ideal of $A$ : for each $a \in A$ and $x \in J$ we have $x \ast a \in J$.

title: Definition:Ideal of Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $\struct {J, +}$ be a subgroup of $\struct {R, +}$. Then $J$ is an ideal of $R$ : $\forall j \in J: \forall r \in R: j \circ r \in J \land r \circ j \in J$ that is, : $\forall r \in R: J \circ r \subseteq J \land r \circ J \subseteq J$ The letter $J$ is frequently used to denote an ideal.

title: Definition:Ideal of Ring/Also known as
snippet: == Ideal of Ring: Also known as == An ideal can also be referred to as a two-sided ideal to distinguish it from a left ideal and a right ideal. Some sources use $I$ to denote an ideal, but on this can be too easily conflated with an identity mapping. Some sources refer to such a two-sided ideal as a normal subring, in apposition with the concept of a normal subgroup.

title: Definition:Ideal of Ring/Left Ideal
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $\struct {J, +}$ be a subgroup of $\struct {R, +}$. $J$ is a left ideal of $R$ : $\forall j \in J: \forall r \in R: r \circ j \in J$ that is, : $\forall r \in R: r \circ J \subseteq J$

title: Definition:Ideal of Ring/Proper Ideal
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. A proper ideal $J$ of $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ is an ideal of $R$ such that $J$ is a proper subset of $R$. That is, such that $J \subseteq R$ and $J \ne R$.

title: Definition:Ideal of Ring/Right Ideal
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $\struct {J, +}$ be a subgroup of $\struct {R, +}$. $J$ is a right ideal of $R$ : $\forall j \in J: \forall r \in R: j \circ r \in J$ that is, : $\forall r \in R: J \circ r \subseteq J$

title: Definition:Idempotence
snippet: Idempotence is a property of an algebraic system, or an element of an algebraic system such that: $E \circledcirc E = E$ for an object $E$ and an operation $\circledcirc$. Let $S$ be a set.

title: Definition:Idempotence/Algebraic Structure
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. Let $\circ$ be an idempotent operation on $S$. Then $\struct {S, \circ}$ is an idempotent algebraic structure.

title: Definition:Idempotence/Also known as
snippet: == Idempotence: Also known as == The concept of idempotence can also be referred to as idempotency.

title: Definition:Idempotence/Element
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\circ: S \times S \to S$ be a binary operation on $S$. Let $x \in S$ have the property that $x \circ x = x$. Then $x \in S$ is described as idempotent under the operation $\circ$.

title: Definition:Idempotence/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Idempotence == The concept of idempotence was introduced in $1870$ by . Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Idempotence/Mapping
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $f: S \to S$ be a mapping. Then $f$ is idempotent : $\forall x \in S: \map f {\map f x} = \map f x$ That is, applying the same mapping a second time to an argument gives the same result as applying it once. And of course, that means the same as applying it as many times as you want. The condition for idempotence can also be written: $f \circ f = f$ where $\circ$ denotes composition of mappings.

title: Definition:Idempotence/Operation
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\circ: S \times S \to S$ be a binary operation on $S$. If all the elements of $S$ are idempotent under $\circ$, then the term can be applied to the operation itself: The binary operation $\circ$ is idempotent : $\forall x \in S: x \circ x = x$

title: Definition:Idempotence/Relation
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation on $S$. Then $\RR$ is idempotent : $\RR \circ \RR = \RR$ where $\circ$ denotes composition of relations.

title: Definition:Idempotent Operator
snippet: Let $\HH$ be a Hilbert space. Let $A \in \map B \HH$ be a bounded linear operator. Then $A$ is said to be (an) idempotent (operator) $A^2 = A$.

title: Definition:Idempotent Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. $R$ is an idempotent ring its ring product $\circ$ is an idempotent operation.

title: Definition:Idempotent Semigroup
snippet: An idempotent semigroup is a semigroup whose operation is idempotent. That is, a semigroup $\struct {S, \circ}$ is idempotent : $\forall x \in S: x \circ x = x$

title: Definition:Idempotent Semigroup/Also known as
snippet: == Idempotent Semigroup: Also known as == There are extensive bodies of research covering idempotent semigroups. In this literature, band is a common synonym for idempotent semigroup. Category:Definitions/Idempotent Semigroups

title: Definition:Identical
snippet: Two objects $A$ and $B$ are identical for every property $P$ that applies to both $A$ and $B$ is such that: $\map P A = \map P B$ That is, if $A$ and $B$ are equal in every way. Category:Definitions/Language Definitions

title: Definition:Identically Zero
snippet: Let $f$ be a mapping whose codomain is a subset of one of the standard number systems $\N$, $\Z$, $\Q$, $\R$ or $\C$. Let $f$ be such that: $\forall x \in \Dom f: \map f x = 0$ That is, $f$ is the constant mapping $f_0$. Then $f$ is described as being identically zero on its domain. Category:Definitions/Analysis

title: Definition:Identification Mapping/Also known as
snippet: == Identification Mapping: Also known as == Some sources refer to the identification mapping as the identification map while others call it the identification function. All roads lead to Rome.

title: Definition:Identification Topology
snippet: Let $\struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ be a topological space. Let $S_2$ be a set. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping. The identification topology on $S_2$ $f$ and $\struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ is defined as: $\tau_2 = \set {V \in \powerset {S_2}: f^{-1} \sqbrk V \in \tau_1}$ That is, it is the set of all subsets of $S_2$ whose preimages under $f$ are elements of $\tau_1$. The identification topology is seen to depend both on $f$ and $\tau_1$.

title: Definition:Identification Topology/Also known as
snippet: == Identification Topology: Also known as == Some sources refer to the identification topology as the quotient topology on $S_2$ $f$ and $\struct {S_1, \tau_1}$. This is reasonable, as we can construct the induced equivalence from an arbitrary mapping $f$ and thence consider the identification topology as the quotient topology. From Identification Topology equals Quotient Topology on Induced Equivalence, it can be seen that they are in fact one and the same thing, but seen from a different point of view.

title: Definition:Identification Topology/Identification Mapping
snippet: Let $\struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ be a topological space. Let $S_2$ be a set. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping. Let $\tau_2$ be the identification topology on $S_2$ with respect to $f$ and $\struct {S_1, \tau_1}$. The mapping $f: S_1 \to S_2$ in this context is called the identification mapping.

title: Definition:Identity
snippet: Equations Identity: an equation which is true for all values of the variables it contains. Abstract algebra: Identity: an element of an algebraic structure with certain properties. Category:Definitions/Identities Category:Definitions/Language Definitions

title: Definition:Identity/Also known as
snippet: == Identity: Also known as == Other terms which are seen that mean the same as identity are: Two-sided identity, to reflect the fact that it is both a left identity and a right identity. Neutral element, which is perfectly okay, but considered slightly old-fashioned. Unit element, but this is not recommended as it is too easy to confuse it with a unit of a ring. Unity, but this is generally reserved for a ring unity or unity of field, and can also mean the number $1$. Zero, but it is best to reserve that term for a zero element. The trivial element, in the context of a group.

title: Definition:Identity (Abstract Algebra)
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure.

title: Definition:Identity (Abstract Algebra)/Left Identity
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. An element $e_L \in S$ is called a left identity (element) : $\forall x \in S: e_L \circ x = x$

title: Definition:Identity (Abstract Algebra)/Right Identity
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. An element $e_R \in S$ is called a right identity (element) : $\forall x \in S: x \circ e_R = x$

title: Definition:Identity (Abstract Algebra)/Two-Sided Identity
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. An element $e \in S$ is called an identity (element) it is both a left identity and a right identity: $\forall x \in S: x \circ e = x = e \circ x$ In Identity is Unique it is established that an identity element, if it exists, is unique within $\struct {S, \circ}$. Thus it is justified to refer to it as the identity (of a given algebraic structure). This identity is often denoted $e_S$, or $e$ if it is clearly understood what structure is being discussed.

title: Definition:Identity (Equation)
snippet: An identity is an equation which is true for all values attained by the variables it contains.

title: Definition:Identity (Equation)/Symbol
snippet: == Identity: Symbol== The symbol $\equiv$ can be used to distinguish an identity from a conditional equation, but frequently (and usually on ) the equals sign $=$ is used instead.

title: Definition:Identity Arithmetic Function
snippet: The identity arithmetic function $\iota: S \to \Z$ is defined for $n \ge 1$ by: $\forall n \in S: \map \iota n = \delta_{n 1}$ where: $S$ is (in theory) any set, but in this context is usually one of the standard number sets $\Z, \Q, \R, \C$ $\delta$ is the Kronecker delta. That is: $\forall n \in S: \map \iota n = \begin {cases} 1 & : n = 1\\ 0 & : n \ne 1 \end {cases}$

title: Definition:Identity Automorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Consider the identity mapping $I_R: R \to R$: $\forall r \in R: \map {I_R} r = r$ Then $I_R$ is the identity automorphism on $R$.

title: Definition:Identity Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. The identity functor on $\mathbf C$ is the functor $\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}: \mathbf C \to \mathbf C$ defined by: {{axiom | lc= For all objects $C$ of $\mathbf C$: | ml = \operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C} C | mo = := | mr = C }} {{axiom | lc= For all morphisms $f: C_1 \to C_2$ of $\mathbf C$: | ml = \operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C} f | mo = := | mr = f }} That $\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}$ constitutes a functor is shown on Identity Functor is Functor.

title: Definition:Identity Mapping
snippet: The identity mapping of a set $S$ is the self-map $I_S: S \to S$ defined as: $I_S = \set {\tuple {x, y} \in S \times S: x = y}$ or alternatively: $I_S = \set {\tuple {x, x}: x \in S}$ That is: $I_S: S \to S: \forall x \in S: \map {I_S} x = x$ That is, it is a mapping in which every element is a fixed element.

title: Definition:Identity Mapping/Also known as
snippet: The identity mapping can also be seen referred to as the identity operator, identity function or identity transformation. Alternative symbols for $I_S$ include $1_S$, $i_S$, $j_S$, $id_S$, $\operatorname {id}_S$, $\operatorname {Id}_S$, $\iota_S$ and $\varepsilon_S$. The subscript is frequently removed if there is no danger of confusion as to the domain under discussion. Some sources use the same symbol for the identity mapping as for the inclusion mapping without confusion, on the grounds that the domain and codomain of the latter are different.

title: Definition:Identity Morphism
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $X$ be an object of $\mathbf C$. The identity morphism of $X$, denoted $\operatorname{id}_X$, is a morphism of $\mathbf C$ subject to: $\operatorname{dom} \operatorname{id}_X = \operatorname{cod} \operatorname{id}_X = X$ $f \circ \operatorname{id}_X = f$ $\operatorname{id}_X \circ g = g$ whenever $X$ is the domain of $f$ or the codomain of $g$, respectively. In most metacategories, the identity morphisms can be viewed as a representation of "doing nothing", in a sense suitable to the metacategory under consideration.

title: Definition:Identity Morphism of Ringed Spaces
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ be a ringed space. The identity morphism (of ringed spaces) of $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ is the pair $\struct {\operatorname{id}_X, \operatorname{id}_{\OO_X}}$. Category:Definitions/Ringed Spaces

title: Definition:Identity Natural Transformation
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be categories. Let $F : \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be a covariant functor. The identity natural transformation $\operatorname{id}_F$ from $F$ to $F$, denoted $\operatorname{id}_F: F \to F$, is defined as: $\forall X \in \mathbf C : \paren{\operatorname{id}_F}_X = \operatorname{id}_{FX}$ where $\operatorname{id}_{FX}$ is the identity morphism of $FX$ in $\mathbf D$.

title: Definition:If
snippet: To say that: a statement $p$ is true if $q$ is true ...is to say that $p$ is a necessary condition for $q$: $p \ \text{if} \ q \dashv \vdash q \implies p$

snippet: The logical connective iff is a convenient shorthand for .

snippet: == Iff: Also known as == Some sources use the term precisely if to mean . Category:Definitions/Iff

title: Definition:Ill-Conditioned Problem
snippet: A problem in numerical analysis is ill-conditioned it is sensitive to small changes in the input data. This sensitivity affects all methods of solution of the problem. Hence such problems are hard to solve accurately.

title: Definition:Ill-Posed Problem
snippet: An ill-posed problem is a problem which may have more than one solution, or in which the solutions depend discontinuously upon the initial data.

title: Definition:Image/Also denoted as
snippet: The notation $\Img f$ to denote the image of a mapping $f$ is specific to . The usual notation is $\map {\mathrm {Im} } f$ or a variant, but this is too easily confused with $\map \Im z$, the imaginary part of a complex number. Hence the non-standard usage $\Img f$. Some sources use $f \sqbrk S$, where $S$ is the domain of $f$. Others just use $\map f S$, but that notation is deprecated on so as not to confuse it with the notation for the image of an element.

title: Definition:Image/Technical Note
snippet: == Technical Note for Image == {{LatexFor|for = \Img {f} }} When the argument is a single character, it is usual to omit the braces: \Img f This command is specific to . Category:Technical Notes

title: Definition:Image (Category Theory)
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a locally small category. Let $f : X \to Y$ be a morphism in $\CC$. An image of $f$ consists of an object $I$ and a monomorphism $m: I \to Y$ such that: $(1): \quad$ There exists a morphism $e : X \to I$ such that $f = m \circ e$. $(2): \quad$ For any object $I'$ with a morphism $e' : X \to I'$ and a monomorphism $m' : I' \to Y$ such that $f = m' \circ e'$, there exists a unique morphism $v : I \to I'$ such that $m = m' \circ v$.

title: Definition:Image (Set Theory)
snippet: The definition of a relation as a subset of the Cartesian product of two sets gives a "static" sort of feel to the concept. However, we can also consider a relation as being an operation, where you feed an element $s \in S$ (or a subset $S_1 \subseteq S$) in at one end, and you get a set of elements $T_s \subseteq T$ out of the other. Thus we arrive at the following definition.

title: Definition:Image (Set Theory)/Mapping
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping.

title: Definition:Image (Set Theory)/Mapping/Element
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. Let $s \in S$. The image of $s$ (under $f$) is defined as: $\Img s = \map f s = \ds \bigcup \set {t \in T: \tuple {s, t} \in f}$ That is, $\map f s$ is the element of the codomain of $f$ related to $s$ by $f$. By the nature of a mapping, $\map f s$ is guaranteed to exist and to be unique for any given $s$ in the domain of $f$.

title: Definition:Image (Set Theory)/Mapping/Mapping
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping.

title: Definition:Image (Set Theory)/Mapping/Mapping/Class Theory
snippet: Let $V$ be a basic universe. Let $A \subseteq V$ and $B \subseteq V$ be classes. Let $f: A \to B$ be a class mapping. The image of $\RR$ is defined and denoted as: $\Img \RR := \set {y \in V: \exists x \in V: \tuple {x, y} \in \RR}$ That is, it is the class of all $y$ such that $\tuple {x, y} \in \RR$ for at least one $x$.

title: Definition:Image (Set Theory)/Mapping/Subclass
snippet: Let $V$ be a basic universe. Let $A \subseteq V$ and $B \subseteq V$ be classes. Let $f: A \to B$ be a class mapping. Let $C \subseteq A$. The image of $C$ under $f$ is defined as: {{eqn | l = f \sqbrk C | r = \set {y \in B: \exists x \in C: \map f x = y} }} {{eqn | r = \set {\map f x: x \in C} }} That is, it is the class of all $y$ such that $\tuple {x, y} \in f$ for at least one $x \in C$.

title: Definition:Image (Set Theory)/Mapping/Subset
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. Let $X \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$.

title: Definition:Image (Set Theory)/Relation
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation.

title: Definition:Image (Set Theory)/Relation/Element
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation. Let $s \in S$. The image of $s$ by (or under) $\RR$ is defined as: $\map \RR s := \set {t \in T: \tuple {s, t} \in \RR}$ That is, $\map \RR s$ is the set of all elements of the codomain of $\RR$ related to $s$ by $\RR$. Thus: $\map \RR s$ is another way to write: $\RR \sqbrk {\set s}$ where $\RR \sqbrk {\set s}$ denotes the image of a subset of $\RR$.

title: Definition:Image (Set Theory)/Relation/Relation
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation. The image of $\RR$ is defined as: $\Img \RR := \RR \sqbrk S = \set {t \in T: \exists s \in S: \tuple {s, t} \in \RR}$

title: Definition:Image (Set Theory)/Relation/Relation/Class Theory
snippet: Let $V$ be a basic universe. Let $\RR \subseteq V \times V$ be a relation in $V$. The image of $\RR$ is defined and denoted as: $\Img \RR := \set {y \in V: \exists x \in V: \tuple {x, y} \in \RR}$ That is, it is the class of all $y$ such that $\tuple {x, y} \in \RR$ for at least one $x$.

title: Definition:Image (Set Theory)/Relation/Relation/General Definition
snippet: Let $\ds \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n S_i$ be the cartesian product of sets $S_1$ to $S_n$. Let $\ds \RR \subseteq \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n S_i$ be an $n$-ary relation on $\ds \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n S_i$. The image of $\RR$ is the set defined as: $\Img \RR := \set {s_n \in S_n: \exists \tuple {s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_{n - 1} } \in \ds \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^{n - 1} S_i: \tuple {s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n} \in \RR}$ The concept is usually encountered when $\RR$ is an endorelation on $S$: $\Img \RR := \set {s_n \in S: \exists \tuple {s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_{n - 1} } \in S^{n - 1}: \tuple {s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n}…

title: Definition:Image (Set Theory)/Relation/Subset
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation. Let $X \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. Then the image set (of $X$ by $\RR$) is defined as: $\RR \sqbrk X := \set {t \in T: \exists s \in X: \tuple {s, t} \in \RR}$

title: Definition:Image Filter
snippet: Let $S_1, S_2$ be sets. Let $\powerset {S_1}$ and $\powerset {S_2}$ be the power sets of $S_1$ and $S_2$ respectively. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ a mapping. Let $\FF \subset \powerset {S_1}$ be a filter on $S_1$. Then $f \sqbrk \FF := \set {U \subseteq S_2: f^{-1} \sqbrk U \in \FF}$ is the image filter of $\FF$ (on $S_2$) with respect to $f$.

title: Definition:Image Set
snippet: Image Set of Mapping, or just Image of Mapping Image Set of Relation, or just Image of Relation

title: Definition:Image of Class under Mapping
snippet: Let $V$ be a basic universe Let $f: V \to V$ be a mapping. Let $A$ be a class. The image of $A$ (under $f$) is defined and denoted as: $f \sqbrk A := \set {y: \exists x \in A: \map f x = y}$ That is, $f \sqbrk A$ is the class of all $\map F x$ where $x \in A$.

title: Definition:Image of Class under Mapping/Warning
snippet: == Image of Class under Mapping: Warning == Let $V$ be a basic universe Let $f: V \to V$ be a mapping. Let $A$ be a class. Let $x \in A$ be a set of sets Then: $f \sqbrk x$ is not necessarily the same as $\map f x$ where: $f \sqbrk x$ denotes the image of $x$ under $f$ where $x$ is treated as a class $\map f x$ denotes the image of $x$ under $f$ where $x$ is treated as an element of the class $A$. Thus: $\map f x$ is what you get by applying $f$ to $x$ $f \sqbrk x$ is what you get by applying $f$ to each of the elements of $x$ (but not $x$ itself) and then gathering the results into a set.

title: Definition:Image of Element under Mapping/Also known as
snippet: The image of an element $s$ under a mapping $f$ is also called the functional value, or value, of $f$ at $s$. The terminology: $f$ maps $s$ to $\map f s$ $f$ assigns the value $\map f s$ to $s$ $f$ carries $s$ into $\map f s$ can be found. The modifier by $f$ can also be used for under $f$. Thus, for example, the image of $s$ by $f$ means the same as the image of $s$ under $f$. In the context of computability theory, the following terms are frequently found: If $\tuple {x, y} \in f$, then $y$ is often called the output of $f$ for input $x$, or simply, the output of $f$ at $x$.

title: Definition:Image of Mapping/Also known as
snippet: == Image of Mapping: Also known as == Some sources refer to this as the direct image of a mapping, in order to differentiate it from an inverse image. Rather than apply a mapping $f$ directly to a subset $A$, those sources often prefer to define the direct image mapping of $f$ as a separate concept in its own right. In the context of set theory, the term image set for $\Img f$ can often be seen. Category:Definitions/Images

title: Definition:Image of Mapping/Also presented as
snippet: == Image of Mapping: Also presented as == The image of a mapping $f: S \to T$ can also be presented in the form: $\Img f = \set {\map f s \in T: s \in S}$

title: Definition:Image of Mapping/Definition 1
snippet: The image of a mapping $f: S \to T$ is the set: $\Img f = \set {t \in T: \exists s \in S: \map f s = t}$ That is, it is the set of values taken by $f$.

title: Definition:Image of Mapping/Definition 2
snippet: The image of a mapping $f: S \to T$ is the set: $\Img f = f \sqbrk S$ where $f \sqbrk S$ is the image of $S$ under $f$.

title: Definition:Image of Relation/Also known as
snippet: The image of a relation $\RR$, when in the context of set theory, is often seen referred to as the image set of $\RR$. Some sources refer to this as the direct image of a relation, in order to differentiate it from an inverse image. Rather than apply a relation $\RR$ directly to a subset $A$, those sources often prefer to define the direct image mapping of $\RR$ as a separate concept in its own right. Other sources call the image of $\RR$ its range, but this convention is discouraged because of potential confusion.

title: Definition:Image of Subset under Mapping/Also known as
snippet: == Image of Subset under Mapping: Also known as == The term image set is often seen for the image of a subset under a mapping. The modifier by $f$ can also be used for under $f$. Thus, for example, the image set of $X$ by $f$ means the same as the image of $X$ under $f$.

title: Definition:Image of Subset under Mapping/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. Let $X \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. The image of $X$ (under $f$) is defined and denoted as: $f \sqbrk X := \set {t \in T: \exists s \in X: \map f s = t}$

title: Definition:Image of Subset under Mapping/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. Let $X \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. The image of $X$ under $f$ is the element of the codomain of the direct image mapping $f^\to: \powerset S \to \powerset T$ of $f$: $\forall X \in \powerset S: \map {f^\to} X := \set {t \in T: \exists s \in X: \map f s = t}$

title: Definition:Image of Subset under Mapping/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Image of Subset under Mapping == In parallel with the notation $f \sqbrk X$ for the direct image mapping of $f$, also employs the notation $\map {f^\to} X$. This latter notation is used in, for example, , and is referred to as the mapping induced by $f$: It should be noted that most mathematicians write $\map f X$ for $\map {f^\to} X$. Now it is quite clear that the mappings $f$ and $f^\to$ are not the same, so we shall retain the notation $f^\to$ to avoid confusion. ...

title: Definition:Image of Topological Space
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ and $Q = \struct {X, \tau'}$ be topological spaces. Let $f: S \to X$ be a mapping. The image (of the topological space $T$) of $f$ is defined as: $\Img f := Q_{f \sqbrk S} = \struct {f \sqbrk S, \tau'_{f \sqbrk S} }$ where $\tau'_{f \sqbrk S}$ denotes the subspace topology on $f \sqbrk S$.

title: Definition:Imaginary Circle
snippet: An imaginary circle is the locus of imaginary points defined by the equation: $\paren {x - a}^2 + \paren {y - b}^2 = -r^2$

title: Definition:Imaginary Number/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Imaginary Number == was one of the first to accept negative numbers, and possibly the first to consider their square roots, which he did in his . When considering the roots of $x^2 + 40 = 10 x$, and determining that they are $5 \pm \sqrt {-15}$, he concluded: These quantities are "truly sophisticated" and that to continue working with them would be "as subtle as it would be useless". As negative numbers were even then considered "false" and "fictitious", no wonder the square roots of negative numbers would be named imaginary.

title: Definition:Imaginary Part/Also denoted as
snippet: == Imaginary Part: Also denoted as == Variants of $\map \Im z$ for the imaginary part of a complex number $z$ are: $\map {\mathrm {Im} } z$ $\mathrm {Im} \set z$ $\map {\mathscr I} z$ $\map {\mathrm {im} } z$ $\map {\mathfrak I} z$ $\map {\mathbf I} z$ or $\mathbf I z$ While the fraktur font is falling out of fashion, because of its cumbersome appearance and difficulty to render in longhand, its use for this application is conveniently unambiguous.

title: Definition:Imaginary Part/Polar Form
snippet: Let $z$ be a complex number expressed in polar form: $z = \polar {r, \theta}$ The imaginary part of $z$ is: $\map \Im z = r \sin \theta$

title: Definition:Imaginary Part (Linear Operator)
snippet: Let $\HH$ be a Hilbert space over $\C$. Let $A \in \map B \HH$ be a bounded linear operator. Then the imaginary part of $A$ is the Hermitian operator: $\Im A := \dfrac 1 {2 i} \paren {A - A^*}$

title: Definition:Imaginary Part of Complex Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\mu$ be a complex measure on $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. From Decomposition of Complex Measure into Finite Signed Measures, there exists unique finite measures $\mu_R$ and $\mu_I$ such that: $\mu = \mu_R + i \mu_I$ We say that $\mu_I$ is the imaginary part of $\mu$.

title: Definition:Imaginary Part of Element of *-Algebra
snippet: Let $\struct {A, \ast}$ be a $\ast$-algebra over $\C$. Let $x \in A$. We define the imafinary part $\map \Im x$ of $x$ by: $\ds \map \Im x = \frac 1 {2 i} \paren {x - x^\ast}$

title: Definition:Imaginary Straight Line
snippet: An imaginary straight line in the Cartesian plane is a straight line whose equation includes the imaginary unit $i$ somewhere in its definition.

title: Definition:Imaginary Unit/Also denoted as
snippet: == Imaginary Unit: Also denoted as == The non-italicized $\mathrm i$ can also be seen. Using the formal definition of complex numbers, the imaginary unit is the ordered pair $\tuple {0, 1}$. When mathematics is applied to engineering, in particular electrical and electronic engineering, the symbol $j$ is usually used This is because $i$ is the standard symbol used to denote the flow of electric current, and to use it also for $\sqrt {-1}$ would cause untold confusion. In some mathematical traditions, the Greek symbol $\iota$ (iota) is used for $i$.

title: Definition:Imaginary Unit/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on the Imaginary Unit == The symbol $i$ that is in widespread use for the imaginary unit was at least partly due to 's influence.

title: Definition:Immediate Predecessor Element
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $a, b \in S$. Then $a$ is an immediate predecessor (element) to $b$ : $(1): \quad a \prec b$ $(2): \quad \neg \exists c \in S: a \prec c \prec b$ That is, there exists no element strictly between $a$ and $b$ in the ordering $\preceq$. That is: $a \prec b$ and $\openint a b = \O$ where $\openint a b$ denotes the open interval from $a$ to $b$. We say that $a$ immediately precedes $b$.

title: Definition:Immediate Predecessor Element/Also defined as
snippet: == Immediate Predecessor Element: Also defined as == Some sources define an immediate predecessor element only in the context of a total ordering. However, the concept remains valid in the context of a general ordering.

title: Definition:Immediate Predecessor Element/Also known as
snippet: == Immediate Predecessor Element: Also known as == Some sources just refer to an immediate predecessor (element) as a predecessor (element). However, compare this with the definition on this site for predecessor element. Category:Definitions/Predecessor Elements

title: Definition:Immediate Predecessor Element/Class Theory
snippet: Let $A$ be an ordered class under an ordering $\preccurlyeq$. Let $a, b \in A$. Then $a$ is an immediate predecessor (element) to $b$ : $(1): \quad a \prec b$ $(2): \quad \neg \exists c \in S: a \prec c \prec b$ We say that $a$ immediately precedes $b$.

title: Definition:Immediate Successor Element
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $a, b \in S$. Then $a$ is an immediate successor (element) to $b$ $b$ is an immediate predecessor (element) to $a$. That is, : $(1): \quad b \prec a$ $(2): \quad \nexists c \in S: b \prec c \prec a$ That is, there exists no element strictly between $b$ and $a$ in the ordering $\preceq$. That is: $a \prec b$ and $\openint a b = \O$ where $\openint a b$ denotes the open interval from $a$ to $b$. We say that $a$ immediately succeeds $b$.

title: Definition:Immediate Successor Element/Also defined as
snippet: == Immediate Successor Element: Also defined as == Some sources define an immediate successor element only in the context of a total ordering. However, the concept remains valid in the context of a general ordering.

title: Definition:Immediate Successor Element/Also known as
snippet: == Immediate Successor Element: Also known as == Some sources just refer to an immediate successor (element) as a successor (element). However, compare this with the definition on this site for successor element. If $a$ immediately succeeds $b$, some sources will say that $a$ covers $b$. Category:Definitions/Successor Elements

title: Definition:Immediate Successor Element/Class Theory
snippet: Let $A$ be an ordered class under an ordering $\preccurlyeq$. Let $a, b \in A$. Then $a$ is an immediate successor (element) to $b$ $b$ is an immediate predecessor (element) to $a$. That is, : $(1): \quad b \prec a$ $(2): \quad \nexists c \in S: b \prec c \prec a$ We say that $a$ immediately succeeds $b$.

title: Definition:Immovable
snippet: An immovable body is one whose position cannot be changed by applying a force to it. It can be considered as having an infinite mass and zero momentum. Category:Definitions/Ideals in Physics

title: Definition:Impedance of Free Space
snippet: Impedance of free space is a physical constant relating the magnitudes of the electric and magnetic fields of electromagnetic radiation travelling through a vacuum. It is defined as: the quotient of the magnitudes of the electric field and magnetic fields of electromagnetic radiation travelling through a vacuum: $\dfrac {\size {\mathbf E} } {\size {\mathbf H} }$ the vacuum permeability multiplied by the speed of light: $\mu_0 c$ the square root of the quotient of the vacuum permeability by the vacuum permittivity: $\sqrt {\dfrac {\mu_0} {\varepsilon_0} }$

title: Definition:Impedance of Free Space/Also known as
snippet: == Impedance of Free Space: Also known as == Impedance of free space is also variously known as: intrinsic impedance of free space wave impedance of free space the vacuum impedance intrinsic impedance of vacuum characteristic impedance of vacuum characteristic impedance of free space wave resistance of free space

title: Definition:Impedance of Free Space/Dimension
snippet: The impedance of free space has the dimension $\mathsf {M L^2 T^{-3} I^{-2} }$. This arises from its definition as: electric field strength per unit magnetic field strength: $\dfrac {\mathsf {M L T^{-3} I^{-1} } } {\mathsf {I L^{-1} } }$ vacuum permeability multiplied by the speed of light: $\mathsf {M L T^{-2} I^{-2} } \times \mathsf {L T^{-1} }$ the square root of the quotient of the vacuum permeability by the vacuum permittivity: $\sqrt {\dfrac {\mathsf {M L T^{-2} I^{-2} } } {\mathsf {M^{-1} L^{-3} T^4 I^2} } } = \sqrt {\mathsf {M^2 L^4 T^{-6} I^{-4} } }$ Category:Definitions/Dimensions…

title: Definition:Impedance of Free Space/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Impedance of Free Space == Prior to the redefinition of the SI units in $2019$, the impedance of free space was defined as $\mu_0 c$, where: $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability, defined as (exactly) $4 \pi \times 10^{-7}$ henries per metre $c$ is the speed of light, defined as (exactly) $299 \, 792 \, 458$ metres per second leading to a value of: $Z_0 := 4 \pi \times 29 \cdotp 97924 \, 58 \, \Omega$ that is: $Z_0 := \pi \times 119 \cdotp 91698 \, 32 \, \Omega$ exactly.

title: Definition:Impedance of Free Space/Units
snippet: The SI unit for the impedance of free space is the ohm: $\Omega$ Category:Definitions/Units of Measurement Category:Definitions/Impedance of Free Space

title: Definition:Impedance of Free Space/Value
snippet: == Impedance of Free Space: Value == The value of the impedance of free space expressed in SI units is: $Z_0 = 376 \cdotp 730313668(57) \, \Omega$ Category:Definitions/Impedance of Free Space

title: Definition:Imperial
snippet: The imperial system is a system of measurement based on traditional established folk measures. Its base units can be understood as being the FPS Base Units

title: Definition:Imperial/Also known as
snippet: == Imperial: Also known as == The imperial or FPS system of measurement is also referred to as the British system.

title: Definition:Imperial/Area
snippet: The imperial units of area are based on a system of units in which each unit is the square of a corresponding imperial length unit. The imperial units of area are as follows:

title: Definition:Imperial/Area/Acre
snippet: The acre is an imperial unit of area. One acre is equal to an oblong measuring $1$ chain by $1$ furlong. That is, measuring $4$ rods, poles or perches by $10$ chains. 810px

title: Definition:Imperial/Area/Acre/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Acre == The acre is a traditional measure of land arising from the days of ploughing in mediaeval times and earlier. It was defined as the area of land that could be ploughed by $1$ ploughman with $1$ ox in $1$ day. It is noted that an acre is not actually defined as a square area, but as an oblong strip $10$ times as long as it is wide. The reason is readily apparent: its length is, as is apparent from its definition, one furlong, that is, furrow-long. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Imperial/Area/Acre/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Acre == The word acre derives from the Old English æcer, meaning open field. It is pronounced ay-ker, and was at one time spelt aker. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Imperial/Area/Rood
snippet: The rood is an imperial unit of area. One rood is equal to an oblong measuring $1$ chain by $2 \frac 1 2$ chains. 400px

title: Definition:Imperial/Area/Square Chain
snippet: The square chain is an imperial unit of area. One square chain is equal to a square of side $1$ chain in length. Category:Definitions/Imperial Category:Definitions/Area

title: Definition:Imperial/Area/Square Foot
snippet: The square foot is an imperial unit of area. One square foot is equal to a square of side $1$ foot in length.

title: Definition:Imperial/Area/Square Inch
snippet: The square inch is an imperial unit of area. One square inch is equal to a square of side $1$ inch in length. The definition is exact.

title: Definition:Imperial/Area/Square Mile
snippet: The square mile is an imperial unit of area. One square mile is equal to a square whose side measures $1$ mile.

title: Definition:Imperial/Area/Square Rod, Pole or Perch
snippet: The square rod, pole or perch is an imperial unit of area. One square rod, pole or perch is equal to a square of side $1$ rod, pole or perch in length. {{eqn | r = 30 \tfrac 1 4 | rr= = \paren {5 \tfrac 1 2}^2 | c = square yards }} {{eqn | r = 272 \tfrac 1 4 | rr= = \paren {16 \tfrac 1 2}^2 | c = square feet }}

title: Definition:Imperial/Area/Square Yard
snippet: The square yard is an imperial unit of area. One square yard is equal to a square of side $1$ yard in length.

title: Definition:Imperial/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Imperial == The imperial system was developed in Britain, and formally defined in $1824$. It was adopted by the British Empire, and widely used in various forms in most English-speaking countries. In the mid-$20$th century, it was officially superseded by the metric system, although is still used for various purposes. For scientific purposes the SI system has replaced it.

title: Definition:Imperial/Length/Rod, Pole or Perch/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Rod, Pole or Perch == The rod, pole and perch are all synonyms for the same (archaic) unit of land measurement. The terms arise from the days of ploughing in mediaeval times. While the ploughman handled the plough, his assistant controlled the oxen, by means of a stick long enough to reach all the oxen from behind the plough. This stick was the original rod, pole or perch, and its standard length (from the back of the plough to the front of the oxen) was a convenient way to measure a field.

title: Definition:Imperial/Volume/Example
snippet: == Examples of Use of Imperial Volume Measure == As the imperial volume measure are related by powers of two, it is possible to use them to express a volume as a binary number of gills. Thus a volume equal to $3815$ gills is: $1$ gill $1$ chopin $1$ pint $0$ quarts $0$ pottles $1$ gallon $0$ pecks $1$ demi-bushel $1$ bushel $1$ kilderkin $0$ barrels $0$ hogsheads $1$ pipe Thus $3815$ gills can be expressed as: $1001110100111$ gills in binary.

title: Definition:Implicit Differentiation
snippet: Implicit differentiation is the differentiation of an implicit function the independent variable.

title: Definition:Implicit Function
snippet: Consider a (real) function of two independent variables $z = \map f {x, y}$. Let a relation between $x$ and $y$ be expressed in the form $\map f {x, y} = 0$ defined on some subset of $\R^2$. If there exists a function: $y = \map g x$ defined on some real interval $\mathbb I$ such that: $\forall x \in \mathbb I: \map f {x, \map g x} = 0$ then the relation $\map f {x, y} = 0$ defines $y$ as an implicit function of $x$.

title: Definition:Implicit Function/General
snippet: Let: $f: \R^{n + 1} \to \R, \tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n, z} \mapsto \map f {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n, z}$ be a real-valued function on $\R^{n + 1}$, where: $\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} \in \R^n, z \in \R$ Let a relation between $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ and $z$ be expressed in the form: $\map f {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n, z} = 0$ defined on some subset $S \subseteq \R^n$.

title: Definition:Impredicative Definition
snippet: An impredicative definition is a definition in which an element of a set is defined by reference to the totality of the elements of the set .

title: Definition:Impredicative Definition/Intuitionist Perspective
snippet: == Impredicative Definition: Intuitionist Perspective == The concept of an impredicative definition is rejected by the intuitionistic school, which rejects the existence of an mathematical object if it cannot exist independently of our ability to prove its existence using a finite number of steps.

Stand-up comedians may wish to take the opportunity to riff on why language hates fractions so much, that they are either improper or merely vulgar. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Improper Integral
snippet: An improper integral is a definite integral over an interval which is not closed, that is, open or half open, and whose limits of integration are the end points of that interval. When the end point is not actually in the interval, the conventional definition of the definite integral is not valid. Therefore we use the technique of limits to specify the integral. Note: In the below, in all cases the necessary limits must exist in order for the definition to hold.

title: Definition:Improper Integral/Also known as
snippet: == Improper Integral: Also known as == An improper integral is also known as an infinite integral.

title: Definition:Improper Integral/Half Open Interval/Open Above
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function which is continuous on the half open interval $\hointr a b$. Then the improper integral of $f$ over $\hointr a b$ is defined as: $\ds \int_a^{\mathop \to b} \map f t \rd t := \lim_{\gamma \mathop \to b^-} \int_a^\gamma \map f t \rd t$

title: Definition:Improper Integral/Half Open Interval/Open Below
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function which is continuous on the half open interval $\hointl a b$. Then the improper integral of $f$ over $\hointl a b$ is defined as: $\ds \int_{\mathop \to a}^b \map f t \rd t := \lim_{\gamma \mathop \to a^+} \int_\gamma^b \map f t \rd t$

title: Definition:Improper Integral/Notation
snippet: == Improper Integral: Notation == < It is common practice to remove the $\to$ sign from the limits of integration, for example: $\ds \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \map f t \rd t$. However, this is not recommended, as confusion can result, in particular when investigating Lebesgue integration. Category:Definitions/Improper Integrals

title: Definition:Improper Integral/Open Interval
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function which is continuous on the open interval $\openint a b$. Then the improper integral of $f$ over $\openint a b$ is defined as: $\ds \int_{\mathop \to a}^{\mathop \to b} \map f t \rd t := \lim_{\gamma \mathop \to a^+} \int_\gamma^c \map f t \rd t + \lim_{\gamma \mathop \to b^-} \int_c^\gamma \map f t \rd t$ for some $c \in \openint a b$.

title: Definition:Improper Integral/Unbounded Closed Interval/Unbounded Above
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function which is continuous on the unbounded closed interval $\hointr a \to$. Then the improper integral of $f$ over $\hointr a \to$ is defined as: $\ds \int_a^{\mathop \to +\infty} \map f t \rd t := \lim_{\gamma \mathop \to +\infty} \int_a^\gamma \map f t \rd t$

title: Definition:Improper Integral/Unbounded Closed Interval/Unbounded Below
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function which is continuous on the unbounded closed interval $\hointl \gets b$. Then the improper integral of $f$ over $\hointl \gets b$ is defined as: $\ds \int_{\mathop \to -\infty}^b \map f t \rd t := \lim_{\gamma \mathop \to -\infty} \int_\gamma^b \map f t \rd t$ Category:Definitions/Improper Integrals

title: Definition:Improper Integral/Unbounded Open Interval/Unbounded Above
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function which is continuous on the unbounded open interval $\openint a \to$. Then the improper integral of $f$ over $\openint a \to$ is defined as: $\ds \int_{\mathop \to a}^{\mathop \to +\infty} \map f t \rd t := \lim_{\gamma \mathop \to a^+} \int_\gamma^c \map f t \rd t + \lim_{\gamma \mathop \to +\infty} \int_c^\gamma \map f t \rd t$ for some $c \in \openint a {+\infty}$. Category:Definitions/Improper Integrals

title: Definition:Improper Integral/Unbounded Open Interval/Unbounded Above and Below
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function which is continuous everywhere. Then the improper integral of $f$ over $\R$ is defined as: $\ds \int_{\mathop \to -\infty}^{\mathop \to +\infty} \map f t \rd t := \lim_{\gamma \mathop \to -\infty} \int_\gamma^c \map f t \rd t + \lim_{\gamma \mathop \to +\infty} \int_c^\gamma \map f t \rd t$ for some $c \in \R$. Usually $c$ is taken to be $0$ as this usually simplifies the evaluation of the expressions.

title: Definition:Improper Integral/Unbounded Open Interval/Unbounded Below
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function which is continuous on the unbounded open interval $\openint \gets b$. Then the improper integral of $f$ over $\openint \gets b$ is defined as: $\ds \int_{\mathop \to -\infty}^{\mathop \to b} \map f t \rd t := \lim_{\gamma \mathop \to -\infty} \int_\gamma^c \map f t \rd t + \lim_{\gamma \mathop \to b^-} \int_c^\gamma \map f t \rd t$ for some $c \in \openint {-\infty} b$. Category:Definitions/Improper Integrals

title: Definition:Improper Integral on Closed Interval Unbounded Above/Also denoted as
snippet: == Improper Integral on Closed Interval Unbounded Above: Also known as == When presenting an improper integral on an unbounded closed interval $\hointr a \to$, it is common to abuse notation and write: $\ds \int_a^\infty \map f t \rd t$ which is understood to mean exactly the same thing as $\ds \int_a^{\mathop \to +\infty} \map f t \rd t$.

title: Definition:Improper Integral on Interval Unbounded Above and Below/Also defined as
snippet: == Improper Integral on Interval Unbounded Above and Below: Also defined as == An improper integral defined over $\R$ can also be seen defined as: $\ds \int_{\mathop \to -\infty}^{\mathop \to +\infty} \map f t \rd t := \lim_{\substack {b \mathop \to \infty \\ a \mathop \to -\infty} } \int_a^b \map f t \rd t$ but this can be argued as being more opaque and hence less intuitively easy to grasp accurately.

title: Definition:Improper Integral on Interval Unbounded Above and Below/Also denoted as
snippet: == Improper Integral on Interval Unbounded Above and Below: Also denoted as == When presenting an improper integral on $\R$, it is common to abuse notation and write: $\ds \int_{-\infty}^\infty \map f t \rd t$ which is understood to mean exactly the same thing as $\ds \int_{\mathop \to -\infty}^{\mathop \to + \infty} \map f t \rd t$.

title: Definition:Improper Integral on Open Above Interval/Also denoted as
snippet: == Improper Integral on Open Above Interval: Also denoted as == When presenting an improper integral on a half open interval $\hointr a b$, it is common to abuse notation and write: $\ds \int_a^b \map f t \rd t$ which is understood to mean exactly the same thing as $\ds \int_a^{\mathop \to b} \map f t \rd t$.

title: Definition:Improper Integral on Open Above Interval/Also presented as
snippet: == Improper Integral on Open Above Interval: Also denoted as == The definition of an improper integral on a half open interval $\hointr a b$ can also be presented as: $\ds \int_a^{\mathop \to b} \map f t \rd t := \lim_{\delta \mathop \to 0^+} \int_a^{b - \delta} \map f t \rd t$

title: Definition:Improper Integral on Open Above Interval/Mistake
snippet: == Source Work == infinite integral (improper integral)

title: Definition:Improper Integral on Open Below Interval/Also denoted as
snippet: == Improper Integral on Open Below Interval: Also denoted as == When presenting an improper integral on a half open interval $\hointl a b$, it is common to abuse notation and write: $\ds \int_a^b \map f t \rd t$ which is understood to mean exactly the same thing as $\ds \int_{\mathop \to a}^b \map f t \rd t$. Category:Definitions/Improper Integrals

title: Definition:Improper Integral on Open Below Interval/Also presented as
snippet: == Improper Integral on Open Below Interval: Also denoted as == The definition of an improper integral on a half open interval $\hointl a b$ can also be presented as: $\ds \int_{\mathop \to a}^b \map f t \rd t := \lim_{\delta \mathop \to 0^+} \int_{a + \delta}^b \map f t \rd t$

title: Definition:Improper Subset/Also defined as
snippet: == Improper Subset: Also defined as == Let us consider treatments of set theory which categorise the empty set $\O$ as a proper subset. Then an improper subset $S$ of a set $T$ is such that: $S = T$ As this is merely a matter of nomenclature, this distinction should not be of great importance. However, it is wise to make sure which usage is intended when it is encountered.

title: Definition:Impulse
snippet: The impulse imparted to a particle $P$ is defined as the integral time of the force acting on $P$ over a finite time: $\mathbf J := \ds \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \mathbf F \rd t$ where: $\mathbf F$ denotes the resultant force applied to $P$ $t_1$ is the instant of time at which $\mathbf F$ starts to be applied $t_2$ is the instant of time at which $\mathbf F$ stops being applied. Impulse is a vector quantity.

title: Definition:Impulsive Force
snippet: An impulsive force is a large force applied for a very short time.

title: Definition:In-Degree
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a digraph. Let $v \in V$ be a vertex of $G$. The in-degree of $v$ in $G$ is the number of arcs which are incident to $v$. It is denoted $\map {\operatorname {indeg}_G} v$, or just $\map {\operatorname {indeg} } v$ if it is clear from the context which digraph is being referred to.

title: Definition:In-Order Traversal of Labeled Tree
snippet: Let $T$ be a binary labeled tree. In-order traversal of $T$ is an algorithm designed to obtain a string representation of $T$. The steps are as follows:

title: Definition:In-Order Traversal of Labeled Tree/Variant 1
snippet: Let $T$ be a binary labeled tree. In-order traversal of $T$ is an algorithm designed to obtain a string representation of $T$. The steps are as follows: $\mathtt{Inorder} (T):$ $n \gets t$, where $t$ is the root node of $T$. If $n$ is a leaf node, output the label of $n$, and stop. Let $T_1$ and $T_2$ be the left and right subtrees of $T$. If $n$ has only one child, skip this step. Output $\mathtt{Inorder} (T_1)$. Output the label of $n$. Output $\mathtt{Inorder} (T_2)$. Stop.

title: Definition:In-Order Traversal of Labeled Tree/Variant 2
snippet: Let $T$ be a binary labeled tree. In-order traversal of $T$ is an algorithm designed to obtain a string representation of $T$. The steps are as follows: $\mathtt{Inorder} (T):$ $n \gets t$, where $t$ is the root node of $T$. If $n$ is a leaf node, output the label of $n$, and stop. Let $T_1$ and $T_2$ be the left and right subtrees of $T$. Output a left bracket $($. If $n$ has only one child, skip this step. Output $\mathtt{Inorder} (T_1)$. Output the label of $n$. Output $\mathtt{Inorder} (T_2)$. Output a right bracket $)$. Stop.

title: Definition:In Phase
snippet: Let $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$ be a harmonic waves expressed in wave number and frequency form as: {{eqn | q = \forall x, t \in \R | l = \map {\phi_1} {x, t} | r = a \map \cos {2 \pi \paren {k x - \nu t} } | c = }} {{eqn | l = \map {\phi_2} {x, t} | r = a \map \cos {2 \pi \paren {k x - \nu t} + \epsilon} | c = }} Let the phase $\epsilon$ be such that $\epsilon \in \set {2 n \pi: n \in \Z}$. Then $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$ are described as being in phase.

title: Definition:Inaccessible by Directed Suprema

title: Definition:Inch/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Inch == The word inch derives ultimately from the same root as ounce, that is, from the Latin word uncia, meaning $\dfrac 1 {12}$ part. In this context, the inch is of course the $\dfrac 1 {12}$ part of a foot. From the same root, the uncial letters of a mediaeval manuscript are letters which are an inch high. Despite the gradual migration to the metric system, the word inch still lives on as a rhetorical flourish for a small distance, for example: Slowly and steadily they inched forward ... Give him an inch and he'll take a mile.

snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a digraph. Let $u, v \in V$ be vertices of $G$. Let $e = \tuple {u, v}$ be an arc that is directed from $u$ to $v$: 320px Then the following definitions are used:

title: Definition:Incident (Graph Theory)/Digraph/Incident From
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a digraph. Let $u, v \in V$ be vertices of $G$. Let $e = \tuple {u, v}$ be an arc that is directed from $u$ to $v$: 320px Then: $e$ is incident from $u$ $v$ is incident from $e$. Category:Definitions/Incidence (Graph Theory) Category:Definitions/Digraphs

title: Definition:Incident (Graph Theory)/Digraph/Incident To

title: Definition:Incident (Graph Theory)/Planar Graph
snippet: 220px Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a planar graph: Then a face of $G$ is incident to an edge $e$ of $G$ if $e$ is one of those which surrounds the face. Similarly, a face of $G$ is incident to a vertex $v$ of $G$ if $v$ is at the end of one of those incident edges. In the above graph, for example, the face $BCEF$ is incident to: the edges $BC, CE, EF, FB$ the vertices $B, C, E, F$.

title: Definition:Incident (Graph Theory)/Undirected Graph
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be an undirected graph. Let $u, v \in V$ be vertices of $G$. Let $e = \set {u, v} \in E$ be an edge of $G$: 320px Then: $u$ and $v$ are each incident with $e$ $e$ is incident with $u$ and incident with $v$.

title: Definition:Inclination between Planes/Definition 1
snippet: The inclination between two intersecting planes is the smaller of the dihedral angles between them.

title: Definition:Inclination between Planes/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\PP_1$ and $\PP_2$ be planes. Let $\mathbf n_1$ and $\mathbf n_2$ be normal vectors to $\PP_1$ and $\PP_2$ respectively, oriented such that the angle $\theta$ between them is such that: $0 \le \theta \le \dfrac \pi 2$ that is: $0 \degrees \le \theta \le 90 \degrees$ The inclination between $\PP_1$ and $\PP_2$ is defined as that $\theta$.

title: Definition:Inclined Plane
snippet: An inclined plane is a plane surface which is neither horizontal nor vertical.

title: Definition:Inclined Plane/Angle of Inclination
snippet: The angle of inclination of an inclined plane $\PP$ is the inclination that a straight line of greatest slope embedded in $\PP$ makes with the horizontal.

title: Definition:Included Set Topology
snippet: Let $S$ be a set which is non-null. Let $H \subseteq S$ be some subset of $S$. We define a subset $\tau_H$ of the power set $\powerset S$ as: $\tau_H = \set {A \subseteq S: H \subseteq A} \cup \set \O$ that is, all the subsets of $S$ which are supersets of $H$, along with the empty set $\O$. Then $\tau_H$ is a topology called the included set topology on $S$ by $H$, or just an included set topology. The topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau_H}$ is called the included set space on $S$ by $H$, or just an included set space.

title: Definition:Inclusion-Preserving Mapping
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be sets. Let $f : A \to B$ be a mapping. Then $f$ is inclusion-preserving for every two sets $a_1, a_2 \in A$: $a_1 \subseteq a_2 \implies f(a_1) \subseteq f(a_2)$

title: Definition:Inclusion-Reversing Mapping
snippet: Let $A, B$ be sets of sets and $\phi: A \to B$ be a mapping. Then $\phi$ is inclusion-reversing : for every pair of sets $a_1, a_2 \in A$ such that $a_1 \subseteq a_2$: $\map \phi {a_2} \subseteq \map \phi {a_1}$

title: Definition:Inclusion Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf D$ be a metacategory, and let $\mathbf C$ be a subcategory of $\mathbf D$. The inclusion functor on $\mathbf C$ is the functor $\Iota_{\mathbf C}: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ defined by: {{DefineFunctor |ob = For all objects $C$ of $\mathbf C$: $\Iota_{\mathbf C} C := C$ |mor = For all morphisms $f: C_1 \to C_2$ of $\mathbf C$: $\Iota_{\mathbf C} f := f$ }}

title: Definition:Inclusion Mapping
snippet: Let $T$ be a set. Let $S\subseteq T$ be a subset. The inclusion mapping $i_S: S \to T$ is the mapping defined as: $i_S: S \to T: \forall x \in S: \map {i_S} x = x$

title: Definition:Inclusion Ordered Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. $\struct {S, \preceq}$ is inclusion ordered set : $\mathord\preceq = \mathord\subseteq \cap \paren {S \times S}$ That means: $\forall x, y \in S: x \preceq y \iff x \subseteq y$

title: Definition:Inclusion Relation on Subobject Classes
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $C$ be an object of $\mathbf C$. The inclusion relation $\subseteq$ on subobject classes of $C$ is defined as follows: $\eqclass m {} \subseteq \eqclass {m'} {}$ there exists a morphism $\eqclass f {}: \eqclass m {} \to \eqclass {m'} {}$

title: Definition:Inclusion Relation on Subobjects
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $C$ be an object of $\mathbf C$. Let $\map {\mathbf{Sub}_{\mathbf C} } C$ be the category of subobjects of $C$. The inclusion relation $\subseteq$ on subobjects of $C$ is defined as follows: $m \subseteq m'$ there exists a morphism $f: m \to m'$

title: Definition:Incomplete Elliptic Integral of the First Kind/Amplitude
snippet: Let $u = \map F {k, \phi}$ denote the incomplete elliptic integral of the first kind. The parameter $\phi$ of $u = \map F {k, \phi}$ is called the amplitude of $u$.

title: Definition:Incomplete Elliptic Integral of the First Kind/Completion
snippet: == Special Function == Let $\map F {k, \dfrac \pi 2}$ denote the incomplete elliptic integral of the first kind. Then: $\map F {k, \dfrac \pi 2} = \map K k$ where $\map K k$ denotes the complete elliptic integral of the first kind.

title: Definition:Incomplete Elliptic Integral of the First Kind/Definition 1
snippet: == Special Function == $\ds \map F {k, \phi} = \int \limits_0^\phi \frac {\d \phi} {\sqrt {1 - k^2 \sin^2 \phi} }$ is the incomplete elliptic integral of the first kind, and is a function of the variables: $k$, defined on the interval $0 < k < 1$ $\phi$, defined on the interval $0 \le \phi \le \pi / 2$.

title: Definition:Incomplete Elliptic Integral of the First Kind/Definition 2
snippet: == Special Function == $\ds \map F {k, \phi} = \int \limits_0^x \frac {\d v} {\sqrt {\paren {1 - v^2} \paren {1 - k^2 v^2} } }$ is the incomplete elliptic integral of the first kind, and is a function of the variables: $k$, defined on the interval $0 < k < 1$ $x = \sin \phi$, where $\phi$ is defined on the interval $0 \le \phi \le \pi / 2$.

title: Definition:Incomplete Elliptic Integral of the Second Kind/Definition 1
snippet: == Special Function == $\ds \map E {k, \phi} = \int \limits_0^\phi \sqrt {1 - k^2 \sin^2 \phi} \rd \phi$ is the incomplete elliptic integral of the second kind, and is a function of the variables: $k$, defined on the interval $0 < k < 1$ $\phi$, defined on the interval $0 \le \phi \le \pi / 2$.

title: Definition:Incomplete Elliptic Integral of the Second Kind/Definition 2
snippet: == Special Function == $\ds \map E {k, \phi} = \int \limits_0^x \dfrac {\sqrt {1 - k^2 v^2} } {\sqrt {1 - v^2}} \rd v$ is the incomplete elliptic integral of the second kind, and is a function of the variables: $k$, defined on the interval $0 < k < 1$ $x = \sin \phi$, where $\phi$ is defined on the interval $0 \le \phi \le \pi / 2$.

title: Definition:Incomplete Elliptic Integral of the Third Kind/Also known as

Then: $\map \Pi {k, n, \dfrac \pi 2} = \map \Pi {k, n}$ where $\map \Pi {k, n}$ denotes the complete elliptic integral of the third kind. Category:Definitions/Incomplete Elliptic Integral of the Third Kind

title: Definition:Incomplete Elliptic Integral of the Third Kind/Definition 1
snippet: == Special Function == $\ds \map \Pi {k, n, \phi} = \int \limits_0^\phi \frac {\d \phi} {\paren {1 + n \sin^2 \phi} \sqrt{1 - k^2 \sin^2 \phi} }$ is the incomplete elliptic integral of the third kind, and is a function of the variables: $k$, defined on the interval $0 < k < 1$ $n \in \Z$ $\phi$, defined on the interval $0 \le \phi \le \pi / 2$.

title: Definition:Incomplete Elliptic Integral of the Third Kind/Definition 2
snippet: == Special Function == $\ds \map \Pi {k, n, \phi} = \int \limits_0^x \frac {\d v} {\paren {1 + n v^2} \sqrt {\paren {1 - v^2} \paren {1 - k^2 v^2} } }$ is the incomplete elliptic integral of the third kind, and is a function of the variables: $k$, defined on the interval $0 < k < 1$ $n \in \Z$ $x = \sin \phi$, where $\phi$ is defined on the interval $0 \le \phi \le \pi / 2$.
