title: Definition:Injection/Definition 1 a
snippet: A mapping $f$ is an injection, or injective : $\forall x_1, x_2 \in \Dom f: x_1 \ne x_2 \implies \map f {x_1} \ne \map f {x_2}$ That is, distinct elements of the domain are mapped to distinct elements of the image.

title: Definition:Injection/Definition 2
snippet: An injection is a relation which is both one-to-one and left-total. Thus, a relation $f$ is an injection : {{eqn | n = 1 | q = \forall x \in \Dom f | l = \tuple {x, y_1} \in f \land \tuple {x, y_2} \in f | o = \implies | r = y_1 = y_2 }} {{eqn | n = 2 | q = y \in \Img f | l = \tuple {x_1, y} \in f \land \tuple {x_2, y} \in f | o = \implies | r = x_1 = x_2 }} {{eqn | n = 3 | q = \forall s \in S: \exists t \in T | l = \tuple {s, t} | o = \in | r = \RR }}

title: Definition:Injection/Definition 3
snippet: Let $f$ be a mapping. Then $f$ is an injection : $f^{-1} {\restriction_{\Img f} }: \Img f \to \Dom f$ is a mapping where $f^{-1} {\restriction_{\Img f} }$ is the restriction of the inverse of $f$ to the image set of $f$.

title: Definition:Injection/Definition 4
snippet: Let $f$ be a mapping. $f$ is an injection : $\forall y \in \Img f: \card {\map {f^{-1} } y} = \card {\set {f^{-1} \sqbrk {\set y} } } = 1$ where: $\Img f$ denotes the image set of $f$ $\card {\, \cdot \,}$ denotes the cardinality of a set $\map {f^{-1} } y$ is the preimage of $y$ $f^{-1} \sqbrk {\set y}$ is the preimage of the subset $\set y \subseteq \Img f$. That is, the preimage of $y$ is a singleton for all $y$ in the image set of $f$.

title: Definition:Injection/Definition 5
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping where $S \ne \O$. Then $f$ is an injection : $\exists g: T \to S: g \circ f = I_S$ where $g$ is a mapping. That is, $f$ has a left inverse.

title: Definition:Injection/Definition 6
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping where $S \ne \O$. Then $f$ is an injection $f$ is left cancellable: $\forall X: \forall g_1, g_2: X \to S: f \circ g_1 = f \circ g_2 \implies g_1 = g_2$ where $g_1$ and $g_2$ are arbitrary mappings from an arbitrary set $X$ to the domain $S$ of $f$.

title: Definition:Injection/Graphical Depiction
snippet: == Diagrammatic Presentation of Injection on Finite Set == The following diagram depicts an injection $f$ from $S$ into $T$: $f: S \to T$ where $S$ and $T$ are the finite sets: {{eqn | l = S | r = \set {a, b, c} }} {{eqn | l = T | r = \set {p, q, r, s} | c = }} and $f$ is defined as: $f = \set {\tuple {a, p}, \tuple {b, s}, \tuple {c, r} }$ Thus the images of each of the elements of $S$ under $f$ are: 320px $S$ is the domain of $f$. $T$ is the codomain of $f$. $\set {p, r, s}$ is the image of $f$.

title: Definition:Injection/Technical Note
snippet: == Technical Note on Injection == Category:Technical Notes

title: Definition:Injective
snippet: Definition:Injection Definition:Injective Object Definition:Injective Module Definition:Injective Morphism

title: Definition:Injective Banach Space
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {Y, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_Y}$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. We say that $Y$ is injective : for each Banach space $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ with closed linear subspace $E$ and bounded linear transformation $T : E \to Y$: there exists a bounded linear transformation $\widetilde T : X \to Y$ extending $T$.

title: Definition:Injective Module
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. A left $R$-module is injective it is an injective object in the category of left $R$-modules.

title: Definition:Injective Object
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $I$ be an object of $\mathbf C$. $I$ is an injective object : for every monomorphism $i: X \to Y$ in $\mathbf C$ and: for every morphism $f : X \to I$ there exists a morphism $g : Y \to I$, such that: $g \circ i = f$

title: Definition:Injective Path
snippet: Let $T$ be a topological space. Let $\mathbb I \subset \R$ be the closed unit interval $\closedint 0 1$. Let $a, b \in T$. An injective path from $a$ to $b$ is a path $f: \mathbb I \to T$ such that $f$ is injective. That is, an injective path from $a$ to $b$ is a continuous injection $f: \mathbb I \to T$ such that $\map f 0 = a$ and $\map f 1 = b$. The mapping $f$ can be described as an injective path (in $T$) joining $a$ and $b$.

title: Definition:Injective Path/Also known as
snippet: == Injective Path: Also known as == An injective path is also referred to by some authors as an arc. However, the latter term is used on for a stronger concept.

title: Definition:Injective Path Component
snippet: Let $T$ be a topological space. Let us define the relation $\sim$ on $T$ as follows: $x \sim y \iff x$ and $y$ are injectively path-connected. We have that $\sim $ is an equivalence relation, so from the Fundamental Theorem on Equivalence Relations, the points in $T$ can be partitioned into equivalence classes. These equivalence classes are called the injective path components of $T$. If $x \in T$, then the injective path component of $T$ containing $x$ (that is, the set of points $y \in T$ with $x \sim y$) can be denoted by $\map {\operatorname {IPC}_x} T$.

title: Definition:Injective Path Component/Also known as
snippet: == Injective Path Component: Also known as == An injective path component is also known as an arc component. However, the latter is used on and elsewhere for a stronger concept.

title: Definition:Injective Resolution
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be an abelian category. Let $X$ be an object in $\mathbf A$. An injective resolution of $X$ is a cochain complex $P := \family {d^i : I^i \to I^{i + 1} }_{i \mathop \in \Z}$ in $\mathbf A$, such that: $(1): \quad \forall i < 0 : I^i = 0$ $(2): \quad I^i$ is injective for all $i \ge 0$ together with a morphism $\varepsilon : X \to I^0$, such that the cochain complex: $\begin{xy} \xymatrix{ \dots \ar[r] & 0 \ar[r] & 0 \ar[r] & X \ar[r]^{\varepsilon} & I^0 \ar[r]^{d^0} & I^1 \ar[r]^{d^1} & I^2 \ar[r]^{d^2} & \dots } \end{xy}$ is exact.

title: Definition:Injective Restriction
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping which is not injective. Then an injective restriction of $f$ is a restriction $g {\restriction_{S'} }: S' \to T$ of $f$ which is an injection.

title: Definition:Injective Space
snippet: Let $Z = \struct {S, \tau_1}$ be a topological space. Then $Z$ is (an) injective (space) for all topological spaces $X = \struct {H, \tau_2}$ and for all continuous mappings $f: H \to S$ and for all topological spaces $Y = \struct {T, \tau_3}$ such that $X$ is topological subspace of $Y$: there exists a continuous mapping $g: T \to S$: $g \restriction H = f$

title: Definition:Injective on Morphisms
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. Let $F: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be a functor. Then $F$ is said to be injective on morphisms for all morphisms $f, g$ of $\mathbf C$: $F f = F g$ implies $f = g$ Note that it is not required that $f$ and $g$ have equal domains or codomains.

title: Definition:Injective on Objects
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. Let $F: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be a functor. Then $F$ is said to be injective on objects for all objects $C_1, C_2$ of $\mathbf C$: $F C_1 = F C_2$ implies $C_1 = C_2$

title: Definition:Injectively Path-Connected
snippet: Injective path-connectedness is a property of a topological space $T$ which relates to the existence of certain continuous injections from a closed real interval (in practice, usually just the closed unit interval) into $T$.

title: Definition:Injectively Path-Connected/Also known as
snippet: == Injectively Path-Connected: Also known as == The term injectively path-connected can also be seen unhyphenated: injectively path connected. Some sources use the term arc connected or arc-connected, but this is usually defined to be a slightly stronger property.

title: Definition:Injectively Path-Connected/Points
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $a, b \in S$ be such that there exists an injective path from $a$ to $b$. That is, there exists a continuous injection $f: \closedint 0 1 \to S$ such that: Then $a$ and $b$ are injectively path-connected in $T$. It is also declared that any point $a$ is injectively path-connected to itself.

title: Definition:Injectively Path-Connected/Subset
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $U \subseteq S$ be a subset of $T$. Let $T' = \struct {U, \tau_U}$ be the subspace of $T$ induced by $U$. Then $T'$ is injectively path-connected in $T$ every two points in $U$ are injectively path-connected in $T'$. That is, $T'$ is injectively path-connected : for every $x, y \in U$, there exists a continuous injection $f: \closedint 0 1 \to S$ such that $\map f 0 = x$ and $\map f 1 = y$.

title: Definition:Injectively Path-Connected/Topological Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is injectively path-connected every two points in $T$ are injectively path-connected in $T$. That is, $T$ is injectively path-connected : $\forall x, y \in S: \exists$ a continuous injection $f: \closedint 0 1 \to S$ such that $\map f 0 = x$ and $\map f 1 = y$.

title: Definition:Injectivity Radius at Point of Riemannian Manifold
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold without boundary. Let $T_ p M$ be the tangent space of $M$ at $p \in M$. Let $\exp_p$ be the restricted exponential map at $p \in M$. Let $\map {B_a} 0 \in T_p M$ be an open ball. Suppose $A_p$ is the set of all $a \in \R_{> 0}$ for which $\exp_p$ is a diffeomorphism from $\map {B_a} 0 \subseteq T_p M$ onto its image. Then the supremum of $A_p$ is called the injectivity radius of $M$ at $p$ and is denoted by $\map {\operatorname{inj} } p$: $\map {\operatorname{inj} } p = \sup {A_p}$

title: Definition:Injectivity Radius of Riemannian Manifold
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold without boundary. Let $\map {\operatorname {inj} } p$ be the injectivity radius at $p \in M$. Suppose $\map {\operatorname {inj} } p = \infty$. Then the infimum of $\map {\operatorname {inj} } p$ over $p \in M$ is called the injectivity radius of $M$ and is denoted by $\map {\operatorname{inj} } M$: $\ds \map {\operatorname{inj} } M = \inf_{p \mathop \in M} {\map {\operatorname {inj} } p}$

title: Definition:Inner Angle of Spherical Triangle
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a spherical triangle on the surface of a sphere whose center is $O$. Let the sides $a, b, c$ of $\triangle ABC$ be measured by the angles subtended at $O$, where $a, b, c$ are opposite $A, B, C$ respectively. Consider the $4$ consecutive parts of $\triangle ABC$: $B, a, C, b$ Then $C$ is known as the inner angle of $B, a, C, b$

title: Definition:Inner Automorphism
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $x \in G$. Let the mapping $\kappa_x: G \to G$ be defined such that: $\forall g \in G: \map {\kappa_x} g = x g x^{-1}$ $\kappa_x$ is called the inner automorphism of $G$ (given) by $x$. The set of inner automorphisms of $G$ is denoted on as $\Inn G$.

title: Definition:Inner Automorphism/Also defined as
snippet: == Inner Automorphism: Also defined as == Some sources define the inner automorphism of $G$ (given) by $x$ as: $\forall g \in G: \map {\kappa_x} g = x^{-1} g x$

title: Definition:Inner Automorphism/Also denoted as
snippet: == Inner Automorphism: Also denoted as == While $\kappa$ is the symbol of choice on to denote an inner automorphism, this is not universal in the literature. Different sources use different symbols, for example: $\pi$, as used by $\varphi$, as used by $K$, as used by $\alpha$, as used by $\phi$, as used by . The set of inner automorphisms of $G$ can be found denoted in a number of ways, for example: $\map {\mathscr I} G$ $\map I G$

title: Definition:Inner Automorphism/Also known as
snippet: == Inner Automorphism: Also known as == An inner automorphism is also known as a conjugation.

title: Definition:Inner Automorphism Group
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. The inner automorphism group of $G$ is the algebraic structure: $\struct {\Inn G, \circ}$ where: $\Inn G$ is the set of inner automorphisms of $G$ $\circ$ denotes composition of mappings.

title: Definition:Inner Jordan Content
snippet: Let $M \subseteq \R^n$ be a bounded subspace of Euclidean $n$-space. Let: $\ds \RR = \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n \closedint {a_i} {b_i}$ be a closed $n$-rectangle that contains $M$. The inner Jordan content of $M$ is defined and denoted as: $\map {m_*} M = \map V \RR - \map {m^*} {\RR \setminus M}$ where: $\map {m^*} {\RR \setminus M}$ denotes the outer Jordan content of $R \setminus M$ That is, the inner Jordan content of $M$ is defined to be the outer Jordan content of the complement of $M$, relative to some fixed $\RR \supseteq M$.

title: Definition:Inner Limit
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a $T_2$ (Hausdorff) topological space. Let $\sequence {C_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence of sets in $X$. The inner limit of $\sequence {C_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is defined as: $\ds \liminf_{n \mathop \to \infty} \ C_n := \set {x \in X: \exists N \text { cofinite set of } \N, \exists x_v \in C_v \paren {v \in N} \text { such that } x_v \to x}$ where $x_v \to x$ denotes convergence in the topology $\tau$.

title: Definition:Inner Model Theory
snippet: Inner model theory is a branch of set theory and model theory which studies certain models of ZFC.

title: Definition:Inner Product/Also defined as
snippet: == Also defined as == Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $\GF$ that is a subfield of $\R$ or $\C$. Let $\innerprod \cdot \cdot: V \times V \to \GF$ be an inner product on $\GF$. Some texts define an inner product only for vector spaces over $\R$ or $\C$. This ensures that for all $v \in V$, the inner product norm: $\norm v = \sqrt {\innerprod v v}$ is a scalar. prefers the more general definition, and lists additional requirement on $\GF$ in theorems where it is needed, such as the Gram-Schmidt Orthogonalization theorem.

title: Definition:Inner Product/Also denoted as
snippet: == Also denoted as == The inner product $\innerprod x y$ can also be denoted as $\left \langle {x; y} \right \rangle$. If there is more than one vector space under consideration, then the notation $\innerprod x y_V$ for a vector space $V$ is commonplace.

title: Definition:Inner Product/Also known as
snippet: == Also known as == Some texts refer to an inner product $\innerprod \cdot \cdot$ as a scalar product As this term is ambiguous, it is not used in this context by . Some texts refer to $\innerprod \cdot \cdot$ as an innerproduct.

title: Definition:Inner Product/Complex Field
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space over a complex subfield $\GF$. A (complex) inner product is a mapping $\innerprod \cdot \cdot: V \times V \to \GF$ that satisfies the complex inner product axioms: That is, a (complex) inner product is a complex semi-inner product with the additional condition $(4)$.

title: Definition:Inner Product/Complex Vector Space
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ be vectors in $\mathbb C^n$. The complex vector inner product of $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ is defined as $\ds \innerprod {\mathbf a} {\mathbf b} = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n a_i \overline b_i$ If $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ are represented as column vectors: $\innerprod {\mathbf a} {\mathbf b} = \mathbf b^\dagger \mathbf a$ where $\mathbf b^\dagger$ is the Hermitian conjugate of $\mathbf b$ and the operation is the matrix product.

title: Definition:Inner Product/Integrable Functions
snippet: Let $f$ and $g$ be real functions that are integrable over the closed real interval $\closedint a b$. The inner product $\innerprod f g$ is defined as: $\innerprod f g = \ds \int_a^b \map f x \map g x \rd x$

title: Definition:Inner Product/Real Field
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space over a real subfield $\GF$. A (real) inner product is a mapping $\innerprod \cdot \cdot: V \times V \to \GF$ that satisfies the real inner product axioms: That is, a (real) inner product is a real semi-inner product with the additional condition $(4)$.

title: Definition:Inner Product Induced by Positive Linear Operator
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {\HH, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be a Hilbert space. Let $\struct {\map D T, T}$ be a positive linear operator on $\HH$. Define a mapping $\innerprod \cdot \cdot_T : \map D T \times \map D T \to \C$ by: $\innerprod \phi \psi_T = \innerprod {\paren {T + I} \phi} \psi$ for each $\tuple {\phi, \psi} \in \map D T \times \map D T$. We say that $\innerprod \cdot \cdot_T$ is the inner product on $\map D T$ induced by $T$.

title: Definition:Inner Product Norm
snippet: Let $\Bbb F$ be a subfield of $\C$. Let $\struct {V, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be an inner product space over $\Bbb F$. Then the inner product norm on $V$ is the mapping $\norm {\, \cdot \,} : V \to \R_{\ge 0}$ given by: $\norm x = \sqrt {\innerprod x x}$ for each $x \in V$.

title: Definition:Inner Product Space
snippet: An inner product space is a vector space together with an associated inner product.

title: Definition:Inner Product Space/Complex Field
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space over a complex subfield $\GF$. Let $\innerprod \cdot \cdot : V \times V \to \GF$ be an complex inner product on $V$. We say that $\struct {V, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ is a (complex) inner product space. That is, a (complex) inner product space is a complex vector space together with an associated complex inner product.

title: Definition:Inner Product Space/Real Field
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space over a real subfield $\GF$. Let $\innerprod \cdot \cdot : V \times V \to \GF$ be an real inner product on $V$. We say that $\struct {V, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ is a (real) inner product space. That is, an (real) inner product space is a real vector space together with an associated real inner product.

title: Definition:Inner Product on Cotangent Space
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $x \in M$ be a base point. Let ${T_x}^* M$ be the cotangent space of $M$ at $x$. Let $\omega, \eta \in {T_x}^* M$ be covector fields. The inner product on the cotangent space is defined by: $\innerprod \omega \eta_g := \innerprod {\omega^\sharp} {\eta^\sharp}_g$ where $\sharp$ denotes the sharp operator. Locally this reads: $\innerprod \omega \eta = g^{ij} \omega_i \eta_j$

title: Definition:Inner Side of Spherical Triangle
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a spherical triangle on the surface of a sphere whose center is $O$. Let the sides $a, b, c$ of $\triangle ABC$ be measured by the angles subtended at $O$, where $a, b, c$ are opposite $A, B, C$ respectively. Consider the $4$ consecutive parts of $\triangle ABC$: $B, a, C, b$ Then $a$ is known as the inner side of $B, a, C, b$

title: Definition:Input Device
snippet: An input device is a device which is used to input information into a computer.

title: Definition:Inradius/Also known as
snippet: == Inradius: Also known as == Some sources hyphenate: in-radius. Category:Definitions/Geometry

title: Definition:Inscribe
snippet: Let a geometric figure $A$ be constructed in the interior of another geometric figure $B$ such that: $(1): \quad$ $A$ and $B$ have points in common $(2): \quad$ No part of $A$ is outside $B$. Then $A$ is inscribed inside $B$.

title: Definition:Inscribe/Circle in Polygon
snippet: A circle is inscribed in a polygon when it is tangent to each of the sides of that polygon: 300px '

title: Definition:Inscribe/Polygon in Circle
snippet: A polygon is inscribed in a circle when each of its vertices lies on the circumference of the circle: 300px That is, the vertices are concyclic. '

title: Definition:Inscribe/Polygon in Polygon
snippet: A polygon is inscribed in another polygon when each of its vertices lies on the corresponding side of the other polygon. '

title: Definition:Inscribe/Polyhedron in Sphere
snippet: A polyhedron is inscribed in a sphere when each of its vertices lies on the surface of the sphere.

title: Definition:Inscribe/Sphere in Polyhedron
snippet: A sphere is inscribed in a polyhedron when it is tangent to each of the faces of that polyhedron.

title: Definition:Inseparable Degree
snippet: Let $E / F$ be a field extension. Let $S \subseteq E$ be the separable closure of $F$ in $E$. The inseparable degree $\index E F_i$ of $E / F$ is the degree $\index E S$.

title: Definition:Inseparable Element of Field Extension
snippet: Let $E/F$ be a field extension. Let $\alpha \in E$ be algebraic over $F$. Then $\alpha$ is inseparable it is not separable.

title: Definition:Inseparable Field Extension
snippet: Let $E/F$ be an algebraic field extension. Then $E/F$ is inseparable it is not separable.

title: Definition:Insertion of Generators
snippet: Let $S$ be a set, and let $S^*$ be its Kleene closure. The insertion of generators (into $S^*$) is the mapping $i: S \to S^*$ defined by: $i \left({s}\right) := \left\langle{s}\right\rangle$ that is, it sends any element $s$ of $S$ to the one-term sequence containing only $s$.

title: Definition:Instance
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a plain WFF in the language of predicate logic. Let $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ be the free variables of $\mathbf C$. Let $\MM$ be a structure for predicate logic of type $\PP$ whose universe set is $M$. Then an instance of $\mathbf C$ in $M$ is the sentence with parameters from $M$ formed by choosing $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n \in M$ and replacing all free occurrences of $x_k$ in $\mathbf C$ by $a_k$ for $k = 1, \ldots, n$.

title: Definition:Instant of Time
snippet: An instant is a specific point in time. Category:Definitions/Time

title: Definition:Instantaneous
snippet: Instantaneous means occurring at, or associated with, a particular time instant.

title: Definition:Instantaneous/Acceleration
snippet: Let $B$ be a body in motion. Let $\Bbb I = \closedint t {t + h}$ be a time interval. Let $\mathbf v_1$ and $\mathbf v_2$ be the velocity of $B$ at $t$ and $t + h$ respectively. Let $\overline {\mathbf a}$ denote the average acceleration of $B$ over $\Bbb I$. The instantaneous acceleration $\mathbf a$ of $B$ at time $t$ is defined as the limit of $\overline {\mathbf a}$ as $h \to 0$: $\mathbf a := \ds \lim_{h \mathop \to 0} \dfrac {\mathbf v_2 - \mathbf v_1} h$

title: Definition:Instantaneous/Center of Rotation
snippet: Let $B$ be a body undergoing rotation. The instantaneous center of rotation of $B$ is the point about which $B$ is rotating at a particular time instant.

title: Definition:Instantaneous/Velocity
snippet: Let $B$ be a body in motion. Let $\Bbb I = \closedint t {t + h}$ be a time interval. Let $\mathbf s_1$ and $\mathbf s_2$ be the displacement of $B$ at $t$ and $t + h$ respectively. Let $\overline {\mathbf v}$ denote the average velocity of $B$ over $\Bbb I$. The instantaneous velocity $\mathbf v$ of $B$ at time $t$ is defined as the limit of $\overline {\mathbf v}$ as $h \to 0$: $\mathbf v := \ds \lim_{h \mathop \to 0} \dfrac {\mathbf s_2 - \mathbf s_1} h$

title: Definition:Instanton
snippet: An instanton is a solution to a certain kind of equation in gauge theories.

title: Definition:Integer
snippet: The numbers $\set {\ldots, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots}$ are called the integers. This set is usually denoted $\Z$. An individual element of $\Z$ is called an integer.

title: Definition:Integer-Valued Function
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a function. Let $S_1 \subseteq S$ such that $f \left({S_1}\right) \subseteq \Z$. Then $f$ is said to be integer-valued on $S_1$. That is, $f$ is defined as integer-valued on $S_1$ the image of $S_1$ under $f$ lies entirely within the set of integers $\Z$. An integer-valued function is a function $f: S \to \Z$ whose codomain is the set of integers $\Z$. That is, $f$ is integer-valued it is integer-valued over its entire domain. Category:Definitions/Integers

title: Definition:Integer/Also known as
snippet: == Integer: Also known as == The integers are also referred to as whole numbers, so as to distinguish them from fractions. However, use of this term is discouraged because it is ambiguous: it can refer to the integers, the positive integers, or the negative integers, depending on the preference of the author. Some sources refer to the integers as rational integers, to clearly distinguish them from the algebraic integers. Some sources use the term directed numbers or signed numbers for integers, so as to distinguish them from the natural numbers which are, by definition defined without a sign.

title: Definition:Integer/Formal Definition
snippet: Let $\struct {\N, +}$ be the commutative semigroup of natural numbers under addition. From Inverse Completion of Natural Numbers, we can create $\struct {\N', +'}$, an inverse completion of $\struct {\N, +}$. From Construction of Inverse Completion, this is done as follows: Let $\boxtimes$ be the cross-relation defined on $\N \times \N$ by: $\tuple {x_1, y_1} \boxtimes \tuple {x_2, y_2} \iff x_1 + y_2 = x_2 + y_1$ From Cross-Relation is Congruence Relation, $\boxtimes$ is a congruence relation.

title: Definition:Integer/Formal Definition/Notation
snippet: Let $\Z$ be the integers defined as a set of ordered pairs of natural numbers. We have that $\eqclass {\tuple {a, b} } \boxminus$ is an equivalence class of ordered pairs of natural numbers under the congruence relation $\boxminus$. As this notation is cumbersome, it is commonplace though technically incorrect to streamline it to $\eqclass {a, b} \boxminus$, or $\eqclass {a, b} {}$. This is generally considered acceptable, as long as it is made explicit as to the precise meaning of $\eqclass {a, b} {}$ at the start of any exposition. Category:Definitions/Integers

title: Definition:Integer/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Integer == The use of $Z$ to denote the set of integers appears to have originated with . Earlier, the symbol $\overline{\mathfrak Z}$ had been used by .

title: Definition:Integer/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Integer == The word integer is pronounced with the stress on the first syllable, and the g is soft (i.e. sounds like j): in-te-jer. This is inconsistent with the pronunciation of its for integral (pertaining to an integer), where the g is hard (as in get): in-te-gral. Also note the use of the word integral as an adjective, which in natural language means necessary or inherent, usually encountered in rhetoric. For further confusion, this is pronounced in-teg-ral, the stress being on the second syllable.

title: Definition:Integer/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Integers == Variants on $\Z$ are often seen, for example $\mathbf Z$, $\ZZ$ and $\mathfrak Z$, or even just $Z$. Some sources use $I$, while others use $\mathbf J$ or a variant.

title: Definition:Integer Coding
snippet: Computability Theory: Code Number for Integer

title: Definition:Integer Combination
snippet: Let $a, b \in \Z$. An integer $n$ of the form: $n = p a + q b: p, q \in \Z$ is an integer combination of $a$ and $b$.

title: Definition:Integer Division
snippet: Let $a, b \in \Z$ be integers such that $b \ne 0$. From the Division Theorem: $\exists_1 q, r \in \Z: a = q b + r, 0 \le r < \size b$ where $q$ is the quotient and $r$ is the remainder. The process of finding $q$ and $r$ is known as (integer) division of $a$ by $b$, and we write: $a \div b = q \rem r$

title: Definition:Integer Division/Exact
snippet: Let $a, b \in \Z$ be integers such that $b \ne 0$. Let: $a \div b = q \rem 0$ where $\div$ denotes integer division. This is an instance of exact division.

title: Definition:Integer Heronian Triangle
snippet: An integer Heronian triangle is a Heronian triangle whose sides are integers.

title: Definition:Integer Interval/Also denoted as
snippet: == Integer Interval: Also known as == Some authorities consider $\closedint m n$ to be an abuse of notation, as there is nothing in it intrinsically to distinguish it from the closed real interval $\set {x \in \R: m \le x \le n}$. Such sources prefer to use the more conventional $\set {m, m + 1, \ldots, n}$, but then again it relies upon the implicit understanding that the domain is the set of integers.

title: Definition:Integer Lattice
snippet: Let $n$ be a positive integer. Let $\R^n$ be the $n$-dimensional real Euclidean space. Let $\CC$ be the Cartesian coordinate system of $n$ dimensions embedded in $\R^n$. The integer lattice in $\R^n$ is the set of points in $\R^n$ which can be defined using coordinates of $\CC$ which are integers. Thus it is the point lattice on $\R^n$ whose basis is the standard ordered basis over $\R^n$: $\BB = \set {\mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_2, \ldots, \mathbf e_n}$ where: $\mathbf e_k := \tuple {\delta_{1 k}, \delta_{2 k}, \ldots, \delta_{n k} }$ $\delta_{j k}$ is the Kronecker delta.

title: Definition:Integer Partition
snippet: A partition of a (strictly) positive integer $n$ is a way of writing $n$ as a sum of (strictly) positive integers.

title: Definition:Integer Partition/Also known as
snippet: == Integer Partition: Also known as == An integer partition can also be referred to as a partition if the context is understood. Some sources may use the word divide to mean to separate into a partition. This usage is generally not recommended, as it may be conflated with division.

title: Definition:Integer Partition/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Integer Partition == Integer partitions were originally studied by . also studied them in some depth, and succeeded in proving a considerable number of their properties.

title: Definition:Integer Partition/Part
snippet: In a partition of a (strictly) positive integer, one of the summands in that partition is referred to as a part. Category:Definitions/Partition Theory

title: Definition:Integer Partition/Partition Function
snippet: The partition function $p: \Z_{>0} \to \Z_{>0}$ is defined as: $\forall n \in \Z_{>0}: \map p n =$ the number of partitions of the (strictly) positive integer $n$.

title: Definition:Integer Reciprocal Space
snippet: Let $\struct {\R, \tau_d}$ be the real number line $\R$ under the usual (Euclidean) topology $\tau_d$. Let $A \subseteq \R$ be the set of all points on $\R$ defined as: $A := \set {\dfrac 1 n : n \in \Z_{>0} }$ That is: $A := \set {1, \dfrac 1 2, \dfrac 1 3, \dfrac 1 4, \ldots}$ Then $\struct {A, \tau_d}$ is the integer reciprocal space.

title: Definition:Integer Sequence
snippet: An integer sequence is a sequence (usually infinite) whose codomain is the set of integers $\Z$.

title: Definition:Integer Square
snippet: An integer square is a square whose sides are integers.

title: Definition:Integer Square/Also known as
snippet: == Integer Square: Also known as == An integer square is also known as an integral square. Category:Definitions/Integer Squares

title: Definition:Integers Modulo m
snippet: Let $m \in \Z$ be an integer. The integers modulo $m$ are the set of least positive residues of the set of residue classes modulo $m$: $\Z_m = \set {0, 1, \ldots, m - 1}$

title: Definition:Integrable Function/Complex
snippet: Let $\mathbb I := \closedint a b$ be a closed real interval. Let $f: \mathbb I \to \C$ be a bounded complex-valued function. Define the real function $x: \mathbb I \to \R$ by: $\forall t \in \mathbb I: \map x t = \map \Re {\map f t}$ Define the real function $y: \mathbb I \to \R$ by: $\forall t \in \mathbb I: \map y t = \map \Im {\map f t}$ where: $\map \Re {\map f t}$ denotes the real part of the complex number $\map f t$ $\map \Im {\map f t}$ denotes the imaginary part of $\map f t$. Suppose that both $x$ and $y$ are Riemann integrable over $\mathbb I$.

title: Definition:Integrable Function/Lebesgue
snippet: Let $\lambda^n$ be a Lebesgue measure on $\R^n$ for some $n > 0$. Let $f: \R^n \to \overline \R$ be an extended real-valued function. Then $f$ is said to be Lebesgue integrable it is $\lambda^n$-integrable. Similarly, for all real numbers $p \ge 1$, $f$ is said to be Lebesgue $p$-integrable it is $p$-integrable under $\lambda^n$.

title: Definition:Integrable Function/Locally Integrable Function
snippet: Let $f : \R^d \to \C$ be a function. Let $K \subseteq \R^d$ be a compact subset. Suppose: $\ds \forall K \subseteq \R^d : \int_K \size {\map f {\mathbf x} } \rd {\mathbf x} < \infty$ where $\mathbf x \in \R^d$ and $\rd {\mathbf x}$ and $\rd {\mathbf x} = \rd x_1 \rd x_2 \ldots \rd x_d$ is the volume element in $\R^d$. {{explain|Clarify the above, the "and $\rd {\mathbf x}$ and $\rd {\mathbf x}$" is confusing and ambiguous}} Then $f$ is called the locally integrable function.

title: Definition:Integrable Function/Measure Space
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $\MM_{\overline \R}$ denote the space of $\Sigma$-measurable, extended real-valued functions . Let $f \in \MM_{\overline \R}, f: X \to \overline \R$ be a measurable function. Then $f$ is said to be $\mu$-integrable : $\ds \int f^+ \rd \mu < +\infty$ and $\ds \int f^- \rd \mu < +\infty$ where $f^+$, $f^-$ are the positive and negative parts of $f$, respectively. The integral signs denote $\mu$-integration of positive measurable functions.

title: Definition:Integrable Function/Measure Space/Complex Function
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $\struct {\C, \map \BB \C}$ be the complex numbers made into a measurable space with its Borel $\sigma$-algebra. Let $f : X \to \C$ be a $\Sigma/\map \BB C$-measurable function. Let $\map \Re f : X \to \R$ and $\map \Im f : X \to \R$ be the real part and imaginary part of $f$ respectively. We say that $f$ is $\mu$-integrable $\map \Re f$ and $\map \Im f$ are (real) $\mu$-integrable.

title: Definition:Integrable Function/Unbounded
snippet: Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a real function. Let $f$ be unbounded on the open interval $\openint a b$. Let: $f^+$ denote the positive part of $f$ $f^-$ denote the negative part of $f$ that is: {{eqn | l = \map {f^+} x | o = := | r = \max \set {0, \map f x} }} {{eqn | l = \map {f^-} x | o = := | r = -\min \set {0, \map f x} }} Let $f^+$ and $f^-$ both be integrable on $\openint a b$. Then $f$ is integrable on $\openint a b$ and its (definite) integral is understood to be: $\ds \int_a^b \map f x \rd x := \int_a^b \map {f^+} x \rd x - \int_a^b \map {f^-} x \rd x$

title: Definition:Integrable Function/Unbounded Above
snippet: Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a positive real function. Let $f$ be unbounded above on the open interval $\openint a b$. Let $f_m$ denote the function $f$ truncated by $m$ for $m \in \Z_{>0}$. Suppose that $f_m$ is Darboux integrable on $\openint a b$ for all $m \in \Z_{>0}$. Suppose also that the following limit exists: $\ds \lim_{m \mathop \to \infty} \int_a^b \map {f_m} x \rd x$ Then $f$ is integrable on $\openint a b$ and can be expressed in the conventional notation of the Darboux integral: $\ds \int_a^b \map f x \rd x$

title: Definition:Integrable Function/p-Integrable
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $f \in \MM_{\overline \R}, f: X \to \overline \R$ be a measurable function. Let $p \ge 1$ be a real number. Then $f$ is said to be $p$-integrable $\mu$ : $\ds \int \size f^p \rd \mu < +\infty$ is $\mu$-integrable.

title: Definition:Integrable Random Variable
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $X$ be a real-valued random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. We say that $X$ is integrable $X$ is $\Pr$-integrable.

title: Definition:Integrable System
snippet: An integrable system is a system of one or more nonlinear partial differential equations whose solutions have special properties.

title: Definition:Integrable System/Also defined as
snippet: == Integrable System: Also known as == An integrable system can also be seen defined as a system of differential equations that can be solved by explicit integration.

title: Definition:Integrable Unbounded Real Function/Also defined as
snippet: Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a real function. Let $f$ be unbounded on the open interval $\openint a b$. Let $f^+$ and $-f^-$ both be integrable on $\openint a b$. Sources which define the negative part of $f$ as negative real function: $\map {f^-} x := \min \set {0, \map f x}$ consequently define the (definite) integral of $f$ as: $\ds \int_a^b \map f x \rd x := \int_a^b \map {f^+} x \rd x - \int_a^b \paren {-\map {f^-} x} \rd x$

title: Definition:Integral
snippet: Commutative algebra: Integral Closure Integrally Closed Integral Element of Ring Extension Integral Ring Extension Ring theory: Integral Domain Integral Polynomial Number theory: Integral Multiple Integral Part Analysis: Integral Calculus Integral: Definite Integral Indefinite Integral Integral: As a synonym for the term solution to a differential equation.

title: Definition:Integral/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Integral == The word integral has the following meanings in mathematics: From the term integral calculus, where it is defined as the subfield of calculus concerned with the rates at which quantities accumulate The form of the word integer, which is in generally deprecated on as much as practical in favour of using the word integer itself as an In abstract algebra, where it arises in the concept of an integral domain. In all of the above, the word is pronounced in-te-gral. In natural language, the integral, meaning necessary or inherent, usually encountered in rhetoric.

title: Definition:Integral Basis
snippet: Let $\struct {G, +}$ be an abelian group. Let $\struct {G, +, \circ}$ be the $\Z$-module associated with $G$. An integral basis for $G$ is a basis of $G$ over $\Z$.

title: Definition:Integral Calculus/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Integral Calculus == The origins of integral calculus can be traced back to the ancient Greek mathematicians' attempts to calculate the area of a circle. may have been the earliest such, with his method of exhaustion, dating from about $360$ BCE. The techniques were used and expanded upon in his work by , to calculate areas and volumes of curvilinear figures. These techniques are often suggested as being the precursors to integral calculus.

title: Definition:Integral Calculus/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Integral Calculus == The term integral calculus is the Anglified version of the neo-Latin phrase calculus integralis, made popular by . At first he suggested calculus summatorius, but in $1696$ he decided with that calculus integralis would be better. Some sources suggest that the name integral, first used by him in $1690$, may well have been coined by .

title: Definition:Integral Closure
snippet: Let $A$ be an extension of a commutative ring with unity $R$. Let $C$ be the set of all elements of $A$ that are integral over $R$. Then $C$ is called the integral closure of $R$ in $A$.

title: Definition:Integral Curvature
snippet: Let $ABC$ be a geodesic triangle on a surface $S$. The integral curvature of $ABC$ is given by: $\ds \int_{ABC} \Kappa \rd a$ where $\Kappa$ is the Gaussian curvature at each point on $ABC$.

title: Definition:Integral Curvature/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Integral Curvature == The concept of integral curvature was developed by in his $1827$ work .

title: Definition:Integral Curve
snippet: Let $\map f {x, y}$ be a continuous real function within a rectangular region $R$ of the Cartesian plane. Consider the first order ODE: $(1): \quad \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} = \map f {x, y}$ 500px Let $P_0 = \tuple {x_0, y_0}$ be a point in $R$. The number: $\paren {\dfrac {\d y} {\d x} }_{P_0} = \map f {x_0, y_0}$ determines the slope of a straight line passing through $P_0$. Let $P_1 = \tuple {x_1, y_1}$ be a point in $R$ close to $P_0$. Then: $\paren {\dfrac {\d y} {\d x} }_{P_1} = \map f {x_1, y_1}$ determines the slope of a straight line passing through $P_1$.

title: Definition:Integral Dependence
snippet: Definition:Integral Element of Ring Extension Definition:Integral Element of Algebra

title: Definition:Integral Domain/Also defined as
snippet: == Integral Domain: Also defined as == Some authors do not specify that an integral domain be commutative. Some sources do not insist that an integral domain needs to be a non-null ring, and hence (either intentionally or by accident) allow a null ring to be classified as an integral domain.

title: Definition:Integral Domain/Also known as
snippet: == Integral Domain: Also known as == Some authors refer to an integral domain as simply a domain. However, this conflicts with the concept of domain in the context of mappings and relations. Therefore, it is always best to refer to an integral domain, as to avoid possible confusion.

title: Definition:Integral Domain/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {D, +, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. $\struct {D, +, \circ}$ is an integral domain it fulfils the conditions of the integral domain axioms, as follows:

title: Definition:Integral Domain/Definition 2
snippet: An integral domain $\struct {D, +, \circ}$ is: a commutative ring with unity in which there are no (proper) zero divisors, that is: $\forall x, y \in D: x \circ y = 0_D \implies x = 0_D \text{ or } y = 0_D$ that is, in which all non-zero elements are cancellable.

title: Definition:Integral Domain/Definition 3
snippet: An integral domain $\struct {D, +, \circ}$ is a commutative ring with unity all of whose non-zero elements are cancellable.

title: Definition:Integral Element of Algebra
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $f : A \to B$ be a commutative $A$-algebra. Let $b \in B$.

title: Definition:Integral Element of Algebra/Definition 1
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $f : A \to B$ be a commutative $A$-algebra. Let $b\in B$. The element $b$ is integral over $A$ it is a root of a monic polynomial in $A \sqbrk x$.

title: Definition:Integral Element of Algebra/Definition 2
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $f : A \to B$ be a commutative $A$-algebra. Let $b\in B$. The element $b$ is integral over $A$ the generated subalgebra $A \sqbrk b$ is a finitely generated module over $A$.

title: Definition:Integral Element of Algebra/Definition 3
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $f : A \to B$ be a commutative $A$-algebra. Let $b \in B$. The element $b$ is integral over $A$ the generated subalgebra $A \sqbrk b$ is contained in a subalgebra $C \le B$ which is a finitely generated module over $A$.

title: Definition:Integral Element of Algebra/Definition 4
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $f : A \to B$ be a commutative $A$-algebra. Let $b\in B$. The element $b$ is integral over $A$ there exists a faithful $A \sqbrk b$-module whose restriction of scalars to $A$ is finitely generated.

title: Definition:Integral Element of Ring Extension
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $R \subseteq A$ be a subring. Then $a \in A$ is said to be integral over $R$ is is a root of a monic nonzero polynomial over $R$.

title: Definition:Integral Equation
snippet: An integral equation is a mathematical equation in which an unknown function appears under an integral sign.

title: Definition:Integral Equation/First Kind
snippet: An integral equation of the first kind is an integral equation of the form: $\map f x = \lambda \ds \int_{\map a x}^{\map b x} \map K {x, y} \map g y \rd x$ where: $\map f x$ and $\map K {x, y}$ are known functions $\map a x$ and $\map b x$ are known functions of $x$, or constant $\map g x$ is an unknown function. Thus an integral equation of the first kind is an example of an integral equation of the third kind: $\map u x \map g x = \map f x + \lambda \ds \int_{\map a x}^{\map b x} \map K {x, y} \map g y \rd x$ where $\map u x \equiv 0$.

title: Definition:Integral Equation/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Integral Equation == The first problem to be solved by an integral equation was the Tautochrone Problem, which solved using what is now known as Abel's Integral Equation in $1823$.

title: Definition:Integral Equation/Kernel
snippet: Consider the integral equation: of the first kind: $\map f x = \lambda \ds \int_{\map a x}^{\map b x} \map K {x, y} \map g y \rd x$ of the second kind: $\map g x = \map f x + \lambda \ds \int_{\map a x}^{\map b x} \map K {x, y} \map g y \rd x$ of the third kind: $\map u x \map g x = \map f x + \lambda \ds \int_{\map a x}^{\map b x} \map K {x, y} \map g y \rd x$ The function $\map K {x, y}$ is known as the kernel of the integral equation.

title: Definition:Integral Equation/Parameter
snippet: Consider the integral equation: of the first kind: $\map f x = \lambda \ds \int_{\map a x}^{\map b x} \map K {x, y} \map g y \rd x$ of the second kind: $\map g x = \map f x + \lambda \ds \int_{\map a x}^{\map b x} \map K {x, y} \map g y \rd x$ of the third kind: $\map u x \map g x = \map f x + \lambda \ds \int_{\map a x}^{\map b x} \map K {x, y} \map g y \rd x$ The number $\lambda$ is known as the parameter of the integral equation.

title: Definition:Integral Equation/Second Kind
snippet: An integral equation of the second kind is an integral equation of the form: $\map g x = \map f x + \lambda \ds \int_{\map a x}^{\map b x} \map K {x, y} \map g y \rd x$ where: $\map f x$ and $\map K {x, y}$ are known functions $\map a x$ and $\map b x$ are known functions of $x$, or constant $\map g x$ is an unknown function. Thus an integral equation of the second kind is an example of an integral equation of the third kind: $\map u x \map g x = \map f x + \lambda \ds \int_{\map a x}^{\map b x} \map K {x, y} \map g y \rd x$ where $\map u x \equiv 1$.

title: Definition:Integral Equation/Third Kind
snippet: An integral equation of the third kind is an integral equation of the form: $\map u x \map g x = \map f x + \lambda \ds \int_{\map a x}^{\map b x} \map K {x, y} \map g y \rd x$ where: $\map u x$, $\map f x$ and $\map K {x, y}$ are known functions $\map a x$ and $\map b x$ are known functions of $x$, or constant $\map g x$ is an unknown function.

title: Definition:Integral Equation of the Second Kind/Homogeneous
snippet: An integral equation of the second kind $\map g x = \map f x + \lambda \ds \int_{\map a x}^{\map b x} \map K {x, y} \map g y \rd x$ is described as homogeneous $\map f x \equiv 0$. That is, if it is of the form: $\map g x = \lambda \ds \int_{\map a x}^{\map b x} \map K {x, y} \map g y \rd x$ where: $\map K {x, y}$ is a known function $\map a x$ and $\map b x$ are known functions of $x$, or constant $\map g x$ is an unknown function.

title: Definition:Integral Ideal
snippet: Let $J \subseteq \Z$ be a non-empty subset of the set of integers. Let $J$ fulfil the following conditions: Then $J$ is an integral ideal.

title: Definition:Integral Lattice
snippet: Let $n$ be a positive integer. An integral lattice in $\R^n$ is a subgroup that is isomorphic to the integer lattice $\Z^n$.

title: Definition:Integral Multiple/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $x, y \in \R$ be real numbers. Then $x$ is an integral multiple of $y$ $x$ is congruent to $0$ modulo $y$: $x \equiv 0 \pmod y$ That is: $\exists k \in \Z: x = 0 + k y$

title: Definition:Integral Multiple/Rings and Fields
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +, \times}$ be a ring or a field whose zero is $0_F$. Let $a \in F$. Let $n \in \Z$ be an integer. Then $n \cdot a$ is an integral multiple of $a$ where $n \cdot a$ is defined as: $n \cdot a := \begin {cases} 0_F & : n = 0 \\ \paren {\paren {n - 1} \cdot a} + a & : n > 1 \\ \size n \cdot \paren {-a} & : n where $\size n$ is the absolute value of $n$. Using sum notation: $\ds n \cdot a := \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n a$

title: Definition:Integral Operator
snippet: Let $X, Y$ be sets of mappings, real or complex numbers. Let $A : X \to Y$ be a mapping such that $A$ is expressible as an integral of elements of $X$ (possibly involving weight functions and kernels). Then $A$ is known as an integral operator. Category:Definitions/Operator Theory

title: Definition:Integral Polynomial
snippet: An integral polynomial is a polynomial over the ring of integers $\Z$.

title: Definition:Integral Ring Extension
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $R\subset A$ be a subring. The ring extension $R \subseteq A$ is said to be integral for all $a \in A$, $a$ is integral over $R$.

title: Definition:Integral Sign
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let: $\ds \int f \rd \mu := \sup \set {\map {I_\mu} g: g \le f, g \in \EE^+}$ denote the $\mu$-integral of the positive measurable function $f$. where: $\MM_{\overline \R}^+$ denotes the space of positive $\Sigma$-measurable functions $\overline \R_{\ge 0}$ denotes the positive extended real numbers $\sup$ is a supremum in the extended real ordering $\map {I_\mu} g$ denotes the $\mu$-integral of the positive simple function $g$ $g \le f$ denotes pointwise inequality $\EE^+$ denotes the space of positive simple functions.

title: Definition:Integral Sign/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Integral Sign == The integral sign $\ds \int \ldots \rd x$ originated with In a manuscript dated $29$th October $1675$ he introduced a long letter $S$ to suggest the first letter of the word summa (Latin for sum). At the time he was using the notation $\operatorname {omn} l$ (that is: omnes lineae, meaning all lines). Then he noted: It will be useful to write $\int$ for $\operatorname {omn}$, thus $\int l$ for $\operatorname {omn} l$, that is, the sum of those $l$'s. At the same time he introduced the differential symbol $\d$.

title: Definition:Integral Transform
snippet: Let $p$ be a variable whose domain is a subset of the set of real numbers $\R$. Let $\closedint a b$ be a closed real interval for some $a, b \in \R: a \le b$. Let $f: \closedint a b \to \R$ be a real function defined on the domain $\closedint a b$. Let $\map K {p, x}$ be a real-valued function defined for all $p$ in its domain and all $x \in \closedint a b$. Let $\map f x \map K {p, x}$ be integrable $x$ for all $p$ in its domain and all $x \in \closedint a b$.

title: Definition:Integral Transform/Image Space
snippet: Let $\map F p$ be an integral transform: $\ds \map F p = \int_a^b \map f x \map K {p, x} \rd x$ Let $T: f \to F$ be the integral operator corresponding to $\map F p$. The domain of $p$ is known as the image space of $T$.

title: Definition:Integral Transform/Kernel
snippet: Let $\map F p$ be an integral transform: $\map F p = \ds \int_a^b \map f x \map K {p, x} \rd x$ The function $\map K {p, x}$ is the kernel of $\map F p$.

title: Definition:Integral Transform/Operator
snippet: Let $\map F p$ be an integral transform: $\map F p = \ds \int_a^b \map f x \map K {p, x} \rd x$ This can be written in the form: $F = \map T f$ where $T$ is interpreted as the (unitary) operator meaning: Multiply this by $\map K {p, x}$ and integrate $x$ between the limits $a$ and $b$. Thus $T$ transforms the function $\map f x$ into its image $\map F p$, which is itself another real function.

title: Definition:Integral of Bounded Measurable Function with respect to Finite Signed Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $f : X \to \R$ be a bounded $\Sigma$-measurable function. Let $\mu$ be a finite signed measure on $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. Let $\tuple {\mu^+, \mu^-}$ be the Jordan decomposition of $\mu$. Then the $\mu$-integral of $f$ is defined by: $\ds \int f \rd \mu = \int f \rd \mu^+ - \int f \rd \mu^-$

title: Definition:Integral of Continuous Function wrt Arc Length
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $\closedint a b$ be a closed real interval. Let $\gamma : \closedint a b \to M$ be a smooth curve segment. Let $f : \closedint a b \to \R$ be a continuous real function. Let $\size {\, \cdot \,}_g$ be the Riemannian inner product norm. Then the integral of $f$ $\gamma$ is defined as: $\ds \int_\gamma f \rd s = \int_a^b \map f t \size {\map {\gamma'} t}_g \rd t$

title: Definition:Integral of Measure-Integrable Function
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $f: X \to \overline \R$, $f \in \map {\LL^1} \mu$ be a $\mu$-integrable function. Then the $\mu$-integral of $f$ is defined by: $\ds \int f \rd \mu := \int f^+ \rd \mu - \int f^- \rd \mu$ where $f^+$ and $f^-$ are the positive and negative parts of $f$, respectively.

title: Definition:Integral of Measure-Integrable Function/Complex Function
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $\struct {\C, \map \BB \C}$ be the complex numbers made into a measurable space with its Borel $\sigma$-algebra. Let $f : X \to \C$ be a $\mu$-integrable function. Let $\map \Re f : X \to \R$ and $\map \Im f : X \to \R$ be the real part and imaginary part of $f$ respectively. We define the integral of $f$ by: $\ds \int f \rd \mu = \int \map \Re f \rd \mu + i \int \map \Im f \rd \mu$

title: Definition:Integral of Measure-Integrable Function over Measurable Set
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space, and let $E \in \Sigma$. Let $f: X \to \overline \R$ be a $\mu$-integrable function. Then the $\mu$-integral of $f$ over $E$ is defined by: $\ds \int_E f \rd \mu := \int \chi_E \cdot f \rd \mu$ where: $\chi_E$ is the characteristic function of $E$ $\chi_E \cdot f$ is the pointwise product of $\chi_E$ and $f$ the integral sign on the denotes $\mu$-integration of the function $\chi_E \cdot f$.

title: Definition:Integral of Positive Measurable Function
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. We define the $\mu$-integral of positive measurable functions, denoted $\ds \int \cdot \rd \mu: \MM_{\overline \R}^+ \to \overline \R_{\ge 0}$, as: $\forall f \in \MM_{\overline \R}^+: \ds \int f \rd \mu := \sup \set {\map {I_\mu} g: g \le f, g \in \EE^+}$ where: $\MM_{\overline \R}^+$ denotes the space of positive $\Sigma$-measurable functions $\overline \R_{\ge 0}$ denotes the positive extended real numbers $\sup$ is a supremum in the extended real ordering $\map {I_\mu} g$ denotes the $\mu$-integral of the positive simple function $g$ $g…

title: Definition:Integral of Positive Measurable Function over Measurable Set
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $A \in \Sigma$. Let $f : X \to \overline \R$ be a positive $\Sigma$-measurable function. Then the $\mu$-integral of $f$ over $A$ is defined by: $\ds \int_A f \rd \mu = \int \paren {\chi_A \cdot f} \rd \mu$ where: $\chi_A$ is the characteristic function of $A$ $\chi_A \cdot f$ is the pointwise product of $\chi_A$ and $f$ the integral sign on the denotes $\mu$-integration of the function $\chi_A \cdot f$.

title: Definition:Integral of Positive Simple Function
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $\EE^+$ denote the space of positive simple functions. Let $f: X \to \R, f \in \EE^+$ be a positive simple function. Suppose that $f$ admits the following standard representation: $\ds f = \sum_{i \mathop = 0}^n a_i \chi_{E_i}$ where $a_0 := 0$, and $\chi$ denotes characteristic function. Then the $\mu$-integral of $f$, denoted $\map {I_\mu} f$, is defined by: $\ds \map {I_\mu} f := \sum_{i \mathop = 0}^n a_i \map \mu {E_i}$

title: Definition:Integral on L-1 Space
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $\map {\mathcal L^1} {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be the Lebesgue $1$-space of $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$. Let $\map {L^1} {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be the $L^1$ space of $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$. We define the integral $I_\mu : \map {L^1} {X, \Sigma, \mu} \to \R$ by: $\ds \map {I_\mu} {\eqclass f \sim} = \int f \rd \mu$ where: $\eqclass f \sim \in \map {L^1} {X, \Sigma, \mu}$, where $\eqclass f \sim$ is the equivalence class of $f \in \map {\LL^1} {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ under the $\mu$-almost everywhere equality relation.

title: Definition:Integrally Closed Integral Domain
snippet: Let $R$ be an integral domain. Then $R$ is integrally closed it is integrally closed in its field of fractions.

title: Definition:Integrally Closed in Ring Extension
snippet: Let $\phi : A \hookrightarrow B$ be a ring extension. Let $C$ be the integral closure of $A$ in $B$. Then $A$ is integrally closed in $B$ $C = \phi(A)$.

title: Definition:Integrand/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Integrand == The term integrand comes from cod-Latin for that which is to be integrated. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Integrating Factor
snippet: Consider the first order ordinary differential equation: $(1): \quad \map M {x, y} + \map N {x, y} \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} = 0$ such that $M$ and $N$ are real functions of two variables which are not homogeneous functions of the same degree. Suppose also that: $\dfrac {\partial M} {\partial y} \ne \dfrac {\partial N} {\partial x}$ Then from Solution to Exact Differential Equation, $(1)$ is not exact, and that method can not be used to solve it.

title: Definition:Integrating Factor/Also known as
snippet: == Integrating Factor: Also known as == An integrating factor is sometimes known as an Euler multiplier, after , who first introduced such a notion.

title: Definition:Integrating Factor/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Integrating Factor == The technique of using an integrating factor to solve a differential equation appears to have been invented by , in $1734$. It was also independently invented by both and . Some sources attribute it to .

title: Definition:Integration/Also known as
snippet: == Integration: Also known as == The process of integration is also known as antidifferentiation.

title: Definition:Integration/Integrand
snippet: In the expression for the definite integral: $\ds \int_a^b \map f x \rd x$ or primitive (that is, indefinite integral: $\ds \int \map f x \rd x$ the function $f$ is called the integrand.

title: Definition:Integration With Respect To
snippet: Let $f$ be a function which is integrable on a domain $D$. Let $F$ be the primitive of $f$: $\ds F = \int \map f x \rd x$ The operation of evaluating the primitive of $f$ is referred to as integration with respect to $x$. Category:Definitions/Integral Calculus

title: Definition:Intelligent Player
snippet: Let $G$ be a game. Let $P$ be a player in $G$. Then $P$ is described as intelligent $P$ knows everything about $G$ that there is to know, and can use that knowledge to make informed decisions about what move to make. In game theory, all players are assumed to be intelligent.

title: Definition:Intensional Logic
snippet: intensional logic is that part of logic which treats inferences involving meanings or identities of meanings.

title: Definition:Intensity of Magnetization
snippet: Intensity of magnetization is a measure of the extent to which a body has been magnetized.

snippet: == Intensity of Magnetization: Conversion Factors == Some conversion factors between the various units of intensity of magnetization are as follows:

title: Definition:Intensity of Magnetization/Dimension
snippet: Intensity of magnetization has the dimension $\mathsf {I L}^{-1}$.

title: Definition:Intensity of Magnetization/Units
snippet: The SI unit for intensity of magnetization is given as amperes per metre: $\mathrm A \, \mathrm m^{-1}$ where: $\mathrm A$ denotes the ampere $\mathrm m$ denotes the metre.

title: Definition:Intensive Definition
snippet: An intensive definition is a definition which defines a term by expressing its meaning.

title: Definition:Intercardinal Directions
snippet: The $4$ intercardinal directions are the directions on (or near) Earth's surface halfway between the cardinal directions:

title: Definition:Intercardinal Directions/Also known as
snippet: == Intercardinal Directions: Also known as == The intercardinal directions are also known as the intercardinal points. This misnomer arises from the concept of the point of the needle of a . Category:Definitions/Intercardinal Directions

title: Definition:Intercept
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a line, a curve or a surface. An intercept of $\CC$ is the intersection of $\CC$ with another line, a curve or a surface. In particular:

title: Definition:Intercept/X-Intercept
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a curve embedded in a cartesian plane. An $x$-intercept of $\CC$ is a point where $\CC$ intersects the $x$-axis. Hence it can also be used for the length of the line segment between that point and the origin.

title: Definition:Intercept/Y-Intercept
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a curve embedded in a cartesian plane. A $y$-intercept of $\CC$ is a point where $\CC$ intersects the $y$-axis. Hence it can also be used for the length of the line segment between that point and the origin.

title: Definition:Interest
snippet: Interest is money paid either: by a borrower or: to an investor for the use of money.

title: Definition:Interest/Compound
snippet: Compound interest is interest which is calculated by: adding the interest which has accrued on the principal calculating the interest on the sum at the end of agreed conversion periods. Such interest is said to be compounded according to that conversion period.

title: Definition:Interest/Simple
snippet: Simple interest is interest which is calculated on the principal only.

title: Definition:Interior
snippet: Topology and metric spaces: The interior of a subset $H$ of a topological space: The largest open set contained in $H$. The interior of a subset $H$ of the complex plane $\C$: The set of all interior points of $H$ The interior of a topological manifold with boundary. Plane Geometry: Interior of a Region Interior of an Angle Interior Angle of a Transversal Interior Angle of a Polygon Complex Analysis: Interior of Jordan Curve

title: Definition:Interior (Complex Analysis)
snippet: Let $H \subseteq \C$ be a subset of the complex plane. The interior of $H$ is the subset of $H$ which consists of the interior points of $H$.

title: Definition:Interior (Topology)
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$.

title: Definition:Interior (Topology)/Definition 1
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. The interior of $H$ is the union of all subsets of $H$ which are open in $T$. That is, the interior of $H$ is defined as: $\ds H^\circ := \bigcup_{K \mathop \in \mathbb K} K$ where $\mathbb K = \set {K \in \tau: K \subseteq H}$.

title: Definition:Interior (Topology)/Definition 2
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. The interior of $H$ is defined as the largest open set of $T$ which is contained in $H$.

title: Definition:Interior (Topology)/Definition 3
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. The interior of $H$ is the set of all interior points of $H$.

title: Definition:Interior (Topology)/Notation
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. The interior of $H$ can be denoted: $\map {\mathrm {Int} } H$ $H^\circ$ The first is regarded by some as cumbersome, but has the advantage of being clear. $H^\circ$ is neat and compact, but has the disadvantage of being less intuitive. On , $H^\circ$ is the notation of choice.

title: Definition:Interior Angle
snippet: Interior Angle of Polygon Interior Angle of Transversal

title: Definition:Interior Ballistics
snippet: Interior ballistics is the sub-branch of ballistics which concerns events up to the instant that a projectile leaves the muzzle of the gun.

title: Definition:Interior Multiplication
snippet: Let $V$ and $V^*$ be a vector space and its algebraic dual. Let $\omega \in \map {\Lambda^k} {V^*}$ be an alternating $k$-tensor. Let $v \in V$ be a vector. Let $v \mathop \lrcorner \omega$ be an alternating $\paren {k - 1}$-tensor such that: $\map {\paren {v \mathop \lrcorner \omega}} {w_1, \ldots, w_{k - 1}} := \map \omega {v, w_1, \ldots, w_{k - 1}}$ Then the mapping $\omega \mapsto v \mathop \lrcorner \omega$ is known as the interior multiplication by $v$. If $\omega$ is a $0$-tensor then: $v \mathop \lrcorner \omega := 0$

title: Definition:Interior Node
snippet: Let $v$ be a node of a tree $T$. Then $v$ is an interior node of a $T$ $v$ not a leaf node.

title: Definition:Interior Point
snippet: Topology and metric spaces: An Interior point of a subset $H$ of a topological space: A point of the interior of $H$. An interior point of a subspace $H$ of a metric space: A point which has an open ball completely contained in $H$. An interior point of a subset $H$ of the complex plane $\C$: A complex number which has a neighborhood completely contained in $H$. Geometry: An interior point of a region is one of the points intuitively understood as being inside the region.

title: Definition:Interior Point (Complex Analysis)
snippet: Let $S \subseteq \C$ be a subset of the complex plane. Let $z \in S$. $z$ is an interior point of $S$ $z$ has an $\epsilon$-neighborhood $\map {N_\epsilon} z$ such that $\map {N_\epsilon} z \subseteq S$.

title: Definition:Interior Point (Topology)
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$.

title: Definition:Interior Point (Topology)/Definition 1
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. Let $h \in H$. Then $h$ is an interior point of $H$ : $h \in H^\circ$ where $H^\circ$ denotes the interior of $H$.

title: Definition:Interior Point (Topology)/Definition 2
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. Let $h \in H$. $h$ is an interior point of $H$ $h$ has an open neighborhood $N_h$ such that $N_h \subseteq H$.

title: Definition:Interior Point (Topology)/Definition 3
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. Let $h \in H$. $h$ is an interior point of $H$ $h$ is an element of an open set of the subspace topology of $H$.

title: Definition:Interior of Circle
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a circle embedded in the plane whose radius is $r$ and whose center is at $O$. The interior of $\CC$ is the set of points in the plane whose distance from $O$ is (strictly) less than $r$.

title: Definition:Interior of Simple Closed Contour
snippet: Let $C$ be a simple closed contour in the complex plane. Let $f : \closedint 0 1 \to \R^2$ be a Jordan curve. Let $\phi : \R^2 \to \C$ be defined by: $\map \phi {x, y} = x + i y$ Let $\Img C = \map \phi {\Img f}$, where $\Img C$ denotes the image of $C$, and $\Img f$ denotes the image of $f$. Then the interior of $C$ is denoted $\Int C$ and defined as: $\Int C = \map \phi {\Int f}$ where $\Int f$ denotes the interior of $f$.

title: Definition:Interlocking Interval Topology
snippet: Let $S = \R_{>0} \setminus \Z_{>0}$ denote the set of (strictly) positive real numbers excluding the positive integers. Let $\BB$ be the family of sets $\family {S_n}_{n \mathop \in \Z_{>0} }$ defined as: $S_n = \set {\openint 0 {\dfrac 1 n} \cup \openint n {n + 1} }$ Then $\BB$ is the basis for a topology $\tau$ on $S$. $\tau$ is referred to as the interlocking interval topology. The topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is referred to as the interlocking interval space.

title: Definition:Intermediate Field
snippet: Let $L / K$ be a field extension. Let $F$ be a field such that: $K \subset F \subset L$ Then $F$ is an intermediate field. Category:Definitions/Field Extensions

title: Definition:Internal Angle/Also known as
snippet: == Internal Angle: Also known as == An internal angle is also known as an interior angle. The vertices and the sizes of the internal angles of those vertices are frequently referred to by the same letter. Thus the angle of vertex $A$ is called angle $A$ and denoted $\angle A$. This is considered by some to be an abuse of notation but its convenience outweighs its disadvantages.

title: Definition:Internal Direct Product
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure with $1$ operation. Let $\struct {A, \circ {\restriction_A} }$ and $\struct {B, \circ {\restriction_B} }$ be closed algebraic substructures of $\struct {S, \circ}$, where $\circ {\restriction_A}$ and $\circ {\restriction_B}$ are the operations induced by the restrictions of $\circ$ to $A$ and $B$ respectively.

title: Definition:Internal Direct Product/Also known as
snippet: == Internal Direct Product: Also known as == Some sources refer to the internal direct product simply as the direct product. Others call it the direct composite. It is also commonplace for sources which evolve their expositions on abstract algebra purely from an arithmetical perspective to refer to the direct sum when the operation is, or derives from, addition.

title: Definition:Internal Direct Product/Decomposition
snippet: Let $\struct {S_1, \circ {\restriction_{S_1} } }, \struct {S_2, \circ {\restriction_{S_2} } }, \ldots, \struct {S_n, \circ {\restriction_{S_n} } }$ be closed algebraic substructures of an algebraic structure $\struct {S, \circ}$ where $\circ {\restriction_{S_1} }, \circ {\restriction_{S_2} }, \ldots, \circ {\restriction_{S_n} }$ are the operations induced by the restrictions of $\circ$ to $S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_n$ respectively. Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be the internal direct product of $S_1$, $S_2, \ldots, S_n$.

title: Definition:Internal Direct Product/General Definition
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure with $1$ operation. Let $\struct {S_1, \circ {\restriction_{S_1} } }, \ldots, \struct {S_n, \circ {\restriction_{S_n} } }$ be closed algebraic substructures of $\struct {S, \circ}$, where $\circ {\restriction_{S_1} }, \ldots, \circ {\restriction_{S_n} }$ are the operations induced by the restrictions of $\circ$ to $S_1, \ldots, S_n$ respectively.

title: Definition:Internal Direct Sum of Modules
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $M$ be an $R$-module. Let $\family {M_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a family of submodules.

title: Definition:Internal Direct Sum of Modules/Definition 1
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $M$ be an $R$-module. Let $\family {M_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a family of submodules. $M$ is the internal direct sum of $\family {M_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ every $m \in M$ can be written uniquely as a summation $\ds \sum m_i$ with each $m_i \in M_i$.

title: Definition:Internal Direct Sum of Modules/Definition 2
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $M$ be an $R$-module. Let $\sequence {M_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a family of submodules. $M$ is the internal direct sum of $\sequence {M_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ : $\ds \bigcup_{i \mathop \in I} M_i$ generates $M$ For all $i \in I$, $M_i \cap \ds \sum_{j \mathop \ne i} M_j = \set 0$

title: Definition:Internal Direct Sum of Modules/Definition 3
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $M$ be an $R$-module. Let $\family {M_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a family of submodules. Let $\ds \bigoplus_{i \mathop \in I} M_i$ be the external direct sum of $\family {M_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$. $M$ is the internal direct sum of $\family {M_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ the mapping given by Universal Property of Direct Sum of Modules is an isomorphism onto $M$.

title: Definition:Internal Direct Sum of Rings
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_n$ be a finite sequence of subrings of $R$. Let $\ds S = \prod_{j \mathop = 1}^n S_j$ be the cartesian product of $S_1$ to $S_n$. Then $S$ is the (ring) direct sum of $S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_n$ the mapping $\phi: S \to R$ defined as: $\map \phi {\left({x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} }\right) = x_1 + x_2 + \cdots x_n$ is an isomorphism from $S$ to $R$.

title: Definition:Internal Direct Sum of Rings/Direct Summand
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_n$ be a sequence of subrings of $R$. Let $\ds S = \prod_{j \mathop = 1}^n S_j$ be the ring direct sum of $S_1$ to $S_n$. In Conditions for Internal Ring Direct Sum it is proved that for this to be the case, then $S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_n$ must be ideals of $R$. Such ideals are known as direct summands of $R$.

title: Definition:Internal Energy at 290 K
snippet: The internal energy at $T = 290 \, \mathrm K$ is $4 \times 10^{-12} \, \mathrm J$.

title: Definition:Internal Force
snippet: Let $B$ be a body. An internal force is a force $\mathbf f$ exerted by one particle $P_1$ of $B$ on another particle $P_2$ of $B$, and to which there exists an equal and opposite reaction exerted by $P_2$ upon $P_1$. Hence internal forces exist in pairs whose individual resultants are zero. Hence the resultant of all the internal forces is also zero.

title: Definition:Internal Group Direct Product
snippet: Let $\struct {H, \circ {\restriction_H} }$ and $\struct {K, \circ {\restriction_K} }$ be subgroups of a group $\struct {G, \circ}$ where $\circ {\restriction_H}$ and $\circ {\restriction_K}$ are the restrictions of $\circ$ to $H, K$ respectively.

title: Definition:Internal Group Direct Product/Also known as
snippet: == Internal Group Direct Product: Also known as == Some authors refer to the internal group direct product $H \times K$ as the normal product of $H$ by $K$. Other sources use the term semidirect product. Some authors call it just the group direct product, but it should not be confused with the external group direct product. Although this is just a more specific example of the internal direct product of general algebraic structures, it is usually defined and treated separately because of its considerable conceptual importance. Category:Definitions/Internal Group Direct Products

title: Definition:Internal Group Direct Product/Definition by Subset Product
snippet: Let $\struct {H, \circ {\restriction_H} }$ and $\struct {K, \circ {\restriction_K} }$ be subgroups of a group $\struct {G, \circ}$ where $\circ {\restriction_H}$ and $\circ {\restriction_K}$ are the restrictions of $\circ$ to $H, K$ respectively. The group $\struct {G, \circ}$ is the internal group direct product of $H$ and $K$ : $(1): \quad \struct {H, \circ {\restriction_H} }$ and $\struct {K, \circ {\restriction_K} }$ are both normal subgroups of $\struct {G, \circ}$ $(2): \quad G$ is the subset product of $H$ and $K$, that is: $G = H \circ K$ $(3): \quad$ $H \cap K = \set e$ where $e$ is…

title: Definition:Internal Group Direct Product/Definition by Unique Expression
snippet: Let $\struct {H, \circ {\restriction_H} }$ and $\struct {K, \circ {\restriction_K} }$ be subgroups of a group $\struct {G, \circ}$ where $\circ {\restriction_H}$ and $\circ {\restriction_K}$ are the restrictions of $\circ$ to $H, K$ respectively. The group $\struct {G, \circ}$ is the internal group direct product of $H$ and $K$ : $(1): \quad \struct {H, \circ {\restriction_H} }$ and $\struct {K, \circ {\restriction_K} }$ are both normal subgroups of $\struct {G, \circ}$ $(2): \quad$ every element of $G$ can be expressed uniquely in the form: $g = h \circ k$ where $h \in H$ and $k \in K$.

title: Definition:Internal Group Direct Product/General Definition
snippet: Let $\sequence {H_n} = \struct {H_1, \circ {\restriction_{H_1} } }, \ldots, \struct {H_n, \circ {\restriction_{H_n} } }$ be a (finite) sequence of subgroups of a group $\struct {G, \circ}$ where $\circ {\restriction_{H_1} }, \ldots, \circ {\restriction_{H_n} }$ are the restrictions of $\circ$ to $H_1, \ldots, H_n$ respectively.

title: Definition:Internal Group Direct Product/General Definition/Definition by Isomorphism
snippet: Let $\sequence {H_n} = \struct {H_1, \circ {\restriction_{H_1} } }, \ldots, \struct {H_n, \circ {\restriction_{H_n} } }$ be a (finite) sequence of subgroups of a group $\struct {G, \circ}$ where $\circ {\restriction_{H_1} }, \ldots, \circ {\restriction_{H_n} }$ are the restrictions of $\circ$ to $H_1, \ldots, H_n$ respectively.

title: Definition:Internal Group Direct Product/General Definition/Definition by Subset Product
snippet: Let $\sequence {H_n} = \struct {H_1, \circ {\restriction_{H_1} } }, \ldots, \struct {H_n, \circ {\restriction_{H_n} } }$ be a (finite) sequence of subgroups of a group $\struct {G, \circ}$ where $\circ {\restriction_{H_1} }, \ldots, \circ {\restriction_{H_n} }$ are the restrictions of $\circ$ to $H_1, \ldots, H_n$ respectively.

snippet: Let $\sequence {H_n} = \struct {H_1, \circ {\restriction_{H_1} } }, \ldots, \struct {H_n, \circ {\restriction_{H_n} } }$ be a (finite) sequence of subgroups of a group $\struct {G, \circ}$ where $\circ {\restriction_{H_1} }, \ldots, \circ {\restriction_{H_n} }$ are the restrictions of $\circ$ to $H_1, \ldots, H_n$ respectively.

title: Definition:Internal Hilbert Space Direct Sum
snippet: Let $\HH$ be a Hilbert space. Let $\family {M_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an $I$-indexed set of pairwise orthogonal subspaces of $\HH$. Then the internal (Hilbert space) direct sum of the $M_i$ is their closed linear span $\vee_i M_i$. It is denoted by $\bigoplus_i M_i$, or $\ds \bigoplus_{i \mathop \in I} M_i$ if the set $I$ is to be stressed. When $I$ is finite, by Closed Linear Subspaces Closed under Setwise Addition, have that: $\ds \bigoplus_{i \mathop \in I} M_i = \sum_{i \mathop \in I} M_i$, where $\ds \sum$ signifies setwise addition.

title: Definition:Internal Orthogonal Sum (Bilinear Space)
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be a field. Let $\left({V, f}\right)$ be a reflexive bilinear space over $\mathbb K$. Let $U, W \subset V$ be subspaces of $V$. Then $V$ is the internal orthogonal (direct) sum of $U$ and $W$ : $V = U \oplus W$, that is, $V$ is the internal direct sum of $U$ and $W$ $U \perp W$, that is, $U$ and $W$ are orthogonal. This is denoted: $V = U\oplus W$.

title: Definition:Internal Point of Subset of Vector Space
snippet: Let $X$ be a vector space over $\R$. Let $B \subseteq X$. Let $x \in B$. We say that $x$ is an internal point of $B$ there exists an absorbing set $A$ such that: $x + A \subseteq B$

title: Definition:Internal Tangent
snippet: Let $C_1$ and $C_2$ be circles embedded in the plane such that: $C_1$ and $C_2$ do not intersect one is not inside the other. Consider the $4$ common tangents to $C_1$ and $C_2$. The internal tangents are the $2$ common tangents which have the circles on opposite sides of the tangent. 400px In the above diagram, the lines are the internal tangents.

title: Definition:Internally Tangent Closed Curves
snippet: Let $\CC_1$ and $\CC_2$ be closed curves which are tangent to each other. $\CC_1$ and $\CC_2$ are internally tangent one of them lies in the interior of the other.

However, there are a number of different definitions for the mile, and they do not all specify the same length. The international mile is sometimes seen referred to as a statute mile, but this is an older term dating back to before the precise $1959$ definition based on the metre.
