title: Definition:International Standard Book Number
snippet: An International Standard Book Number is a codeword made up of digits used to uniquely identify a published . One of the digits represents the language in which the is written. Two of the digits represent the publisher. There is also a check digit to detect transcription errors.

title: Definition:International Standard Book Number/Also known as
snippet: An International Standard Book Number is usually referred to by its abbreviation ISBN.

title: Definition:International Standard Book Number/ISBN-10
snippet: An International Standard Book Number is a codeword used to uniquely identify a published . The ISBN-$10$ format consists of a string of $9$ digits followed by a check digit in the set $\set {0, 1, \ldots, 9, X}$. The check digit $d$ is calculated as follows. Let $c$ be calculated as: $c = \ds \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^9 k d_k \pmod {11}$ where $d_k$ denotes the $k$th digit in the ISBN-$10$. Then the check digit $d$ is defined as: $d = \begin {cases} c & : c \le 9 \\ X &: c = 10 \end {cases}$ Hyphens may be included in the string to separate out the sections for lexicographical convenience.

title: Definition:International Standard Book Number/ISBN-13
snippet: An International Standard Book Number is a codeword used to uniquely identify a published [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book book]. The ISBN-$13$ format consists of a string of $12$ digits followed by a check digit. The check digit $d$ is calculated as: $d = \ds \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^{12} k d_k \pmod {10}$

title: Definition:International Standard Book Number/Linguistic Note
snippet: When referring to an International Standard Book Number by its abbreviation ISBN, beware not to vocalise it as "ISBN number". The word number is already included in the abbreviation ISBN, so does not need to be repeated. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Internet
snippet: The internet is the network interlinking the computers throughout the world to allow communication between them.

title: Definition:Internet/Also known as
snippet: == Internet: Also known as == An old-fashioned and functionally obsolete term for the internet is the World Wide Web. Colloquially it is referred to as the 'net.

title: Definition:Interpolation
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function. Let $y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n$ be known values of $f$ corresponding to $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ respectively. Interpolation is the process of estimating a value $y'$ of $f$ for a value $x$ lying somewhere between $2$ of the values of $x$ whose images are known.

title: Definition:Interpolation/Linear
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function. Let $y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n$ be known values of $f$ corresponding to $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ respectively. Linear interpolation is a form of interpolation in which it is assumed that $\tuple {x_i, y_i}$, $\tuple {x', y'}$ and $\tuple {x_{i + 1}, y_{i + 1} }$ all lie on the same straight line.

title: Definition:Interpretation
snippet: Let $S$ be the codomain of a mapping $f$ whose domain consists of the set of expressions of a formal language $\FF$. Then $S$ together with $f$ are known as an interpretation.

title: Definition:Interpretation/Semantic Rule
snippet: Let $\struct {S, f}$ be an interpretation such that $S$ is the codomain of a mapping $f$ whose domain is a set of expressions of a formal language $\FF$. The mapping $f$ is known as a semantic rule.

title: Definition:Interpretation/Semantic Value
snippet: Let $\struct {S, f}$ be an interpretation such that $S$ is the codomain of a semantic rule $f$ whose domain is a set of expressions $\EE$ of a formal language $\FF$. The image $s \in S$ of an expression $e \in \EE$ under $f$ is known as the semantic value of $e$.

title: Definition:Interquartile Range
snippet: The interquartile range is a measure of dispersion in statistics. Let $Q_1$ and $Q_3$ be first quartile and third quartile respectively. The interquartile range is defined and denoted as: $\operatorname {IQR} := Q_3 - Q_1$

title: Definition:Intersecting Sets
snippet: Two sets $S$ and $T$ intersect : $S \cap T \ne \O$ That is, intersecting sets are such that their intersection is a non-empty set -- they have at least one element in common.

title: Definition:Intersecting Sets/Also known as
snippet: == Intersecting Sets: Also known as == Some sources refer to intersecting sets as non-disjoint sets. Category:Definitions/Intersecting Sets

title: Definition:Intersection
snippet: Set theory: Set intersection: the elements common to two or more sets. Geometry: Geometrical intersection: the points common to two or more geometric figures. Definition:Intersection Product

title: Definition:Intersection (Geometry)
snippet: The intersection of two lines $AB$ and $CD$ is denoted by $AB \cap CD$. The intersection of two geometric figures is the set of points shared by both figures. Note that this use of $\cap$ is consistent with that of its more usual context of set intersection. When two lines intersect, they are said to cut each other.

title: Definition:Intersection Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $F \in \Sigma$. Then the intersection measure (of $\mu$ by $F$) is the mapping $\mu_F: \Sigma \to \overline \R$, defined by: $\map {\mu_F} E = \map \mu {E \cap F}$ for each $E \in \Sigma$.

title: Definition:Intersection Measure/Complex Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\mu$ be a complex measure on $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. Let $F \in \Sigma$. Then the intersection (complex) measure (of $\mu$ by $F$) is the mapping $\mu_F: \Sigma \to \C$, defined by: $\map {\mu_F} E = \map \mu {E \cap F}$ for each $E \in \Sigma$.

title: Definition:Intersection Measure/Signed Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\mu$ be a signed measure on $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. Let $F \in \Sigma$. Then the intersection (signed) measure (of $\mu$ by $F$) is the mapping $\mu_F: \Sigma \to \overline \R$, defined by: $\map {\mu_F} E = \map \mu {E \cap F}$ for each $E \in \Sigma$.

title: Definition:Intersection of Events/Also denoted as
snippet: == Intersection of Events: Also denoted as == Some sources denote the intersection of $A$ and $B$ as $A B$.

title: Definition:Intersection of Family/Also denoted as
snippet: == Intersection of Family: Also denoted as == The set $\ds \bigcap_{i \mathop \in I} S_i$ can also be seen denoted as: $\ds \bigcap_I S_i$ or, if the indexing set is clear from context: $\ds \bigcap_i S_i$ Some sources use the form: $\bigcap \set {S_i: i \in I}$

title: Definition:Intersection of Relations
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $\RR_1$ and $\RR_2$ be relations on $S \times T$. The intersection of $\RR_1$ and $\RR_2$ is the relation $\QQ$ defined by: $\QQ := \RR_1 \cap \RR_2$ where $\cap$ denotes set intersection. Explicitly, for $s \in S$ and $t \in T$, we have: $s \mathrel \QQ t$ both $s \mathrel{\RR_1} t$ and $s \mathrel{\RR_2} t$

title: Definition:Intersection of Relations/General Definition
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $\mathscr R$ be a collection of relations on $S \times T$. The intersection of $\mathscr R$ is the relation $\RR$ defined by: $\ds \RR = \bigcap \mathscr R$ where $\bigcap$ denotes set intersection. Explicitly, for $s \in S$ and $t \in T$: $s \mathrel \RR t$ : $\forall \QQ \in \mathscr R: s \mathrel \QQ t$

title: Definition:Intersection of Set of Sets/Also denoted as
snippet: == Intersection of Set of Sets: Also denoted as == The symbol $\bigcap$ is rendered in display mode as $\ds \bigcap$. Some sources denote $\bigcap \mathbb S$ as $\ds \bigcap_{S \mathop \in \mathbb S} S$.

title: Definition:Intersection of Special Subsets
snippet: Let $g$ be a progressing mapping. Let $x$ be a set. Let $\powerset x$ denote the power set of $x$. Let $A$ be the class of all $x$-special subsets of $\powerset x$ $g$. We denote by $M_x$ the intersection of $A$: $M_x = \bigcap A$

title: Definition:Interval/Closed Interval
snippet: Let $\left({S, \preceq}\right)$ be a totally ordered set. Let $a, b \in S$.

title: Definition:Interval/Half-Open Interval
snippet: Let $\left({S, \preceq}\right)$ be a totally ordered set. Let $a, b \in S$.

snippet: In Wirth interval notation, unbounded intervals of an ordered set $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ are written as follows: {{eqn | l = \hointr a \to | o = := | r = \set {x \in S: a \preccurlyeq x} }} {{eqn | l = \hointl \gets a | o = := | r = \set {x \in S: x \preccurlyeq a} }} {{eqn | l = \openint a \to | o = := | r = \set {x \in S: a \prec x} }} {{eqn | l = \openint \gets a | o = := | r = \set {x \in S: x \prec a} }} {{eqn | l = \openint \gets \to | o = := | r = \set {x \in S} = S }} Category:Definitions/Intervals

title: Definition:Interval/Open Interval
snippet: Let $\left({S, \preceq}\right)$ be a totally ordered set. Let $a, b \in S$.

title: Definition:Interval/Ordered Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set. Let $a, b \in S$. The intervals between $a$ and $b$ are defined as follows:

title: Definition:Interval/Ordered Set/Closed
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set. Let $a, b \in S$. The closed interval between $a$ and $b$ is the set: $\closedint a b := a^\succcurlyeq \cap b^\preccurlyeq = \set {s \in S: \paren {a \preccurlyeq s} \land \paren {s \preccurlyeq b} }$ where: $a^\succcurlyeq$ denotes the upper closure of $a$ $b^\preccurlyeq$ denotes the lower closure of $b$.

title: Definition:Interval/Ordered Set/Endpoint
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set. Let $a, b \in S$. Let: $\closedint a b$ or $\hointr a b$ or $\hointl a b$ or $\openint a b$ be an interval. The elements $a, b \in S$ are known as the endpoints of the interval. $a$ is sometimes called the left hand endpoint and $b$ the right hand end point of the interval.

title: Definition:Interval/Ordered Set/Half-Open
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set. Let $a, b \in S$.

title: Definition:Interval/Ordered Set/Left Half-Open
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set. Let $a, b \in S$. The left half-open interval between $a$ and $b$ is the set: $\hointl a b := a^\succ \cap b^\preccurlyeq = \set {s \in S: \paren {a \prec s} \land \paren {s \preccurlyeq b} }$ where: $a^\succ$ denotes the strict upper closure of $a$ $b^\preccurlyeq$ denotes the lower closure of $b$.

title: Definition:Interval/Ordered Set/Open
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set. Let $a, b \in S$. The open interval between $a$ and $b$ is the set: $\openint a b := a^\succ \cap b^\prec = \set {s \in S: \paren {a \prec s} \land \paren {s \prec b} }$ where: $a^\succ$ denotes the strict upper closure of $a$ $b^\prec$ denotes the strict lower closure of $b$.

title: Definition:Interval/Ordered Set/Right Half-Open
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set. Let $a, b \in S$. The right half-open interval between $a$ and $b$ is the set: $\hointr a b := a^\succcurlyeq \cap b^\prec = \set {s \in S: \paren {a \preccurlyeq s} \land \paren {s \prec b} }$ where: $a^\succcurlyeq$ denotes the upper closure of $a$ $b^\prec$ denotes the strict lower closure of $b$.

title: Definition:Interval Estimate
snippet: An interval estimate is a numerical value of an estimator calculated from a confidence interval.

title: Definition:Interval of Convergence
snippet: Let $\xi \in \R$ be a real number. Let $\ds \map S x = \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty a_n \paren {x - \xi}^n$ be a power series in $x$ about $\xi$. The set of values of $x$ for which $\map S x$ converges is called the interval of convergence of $S$.

title: Definition:Intervention Event
snippet: An intervention event is an event whose occurrence is not characteristic of a particular time series such that it affects the behaviour of that time series. As a result, forecasting future values based upon the past values is likely to be compromised.

title: Definition:Into Linear Isomorphism
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed vector spaces over $\GF$. Let $T : X \to Y$ be a bounded linear transformation. We say that $T$ is an into linear isomorphism $T$ is a linear isomorphism considered as a map $X \to T \sqbrk X$.

title: Definition:Intraclass Correlation
snippet: Intraclass correlation is a concept in analysis of variance.

title: Definition:Intraclass Correlation/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Intraclass Correlation == The concept of intraclass correlation has been superseded by the related idea of variance ratio.

title: Definition:Intransitive Dice
snippet: Intransitive dice are a set of dice with different, non-standard, numbering such that the relation: die $p$ beats die $q$ is a non-transitive relation.

title: Definition:Intransitive Dice/Also known as
snippet: == Intransitive Dice: Also known as == Intransitive dice are also known as non-transitive dice.

title: Definition:Intrinsic Angular Momentum
snippet: == Physical Property == Let $P$ be an elementary particle. The intrinsic angular momentum of $P$ is the angular momentum of $P$ its own axis of rotation.

title: Definition:Intrinsic Angular Momentum/Also known as
snippet: == Intrinsic Angular Momentum: Also known as == Intrinsic angular momentum is also known as spin angular momentum, or just spin.

title: Definition:Intrinsic Equation
snippet: Let $C$ be a curve. An intrinsic equation of $C$ is an equation that defines $C$ using a relation between the intrinsic properties of $C$. Thus an intrinsic equation defines the shape of $C$ without specifying its position relative to an arbitrarily defined coordinate system.

title: Definition:Intrinsic Equation/Also known as
snippet: == Intrinsic Equation: Also known as == Some sources refer to the general intrinsic equation as a natural equation. However, prefers to reserve this term for the specific example where the intrinsic properties used are curvature and torsion.

title: Definition:Intrinsic Equation/Cesàro Equation
snippet: A Cesàro equation is an intrinsic equation for a curve $C$ such that $C$ is expressed in terms of its intrinsic properties in one of either of the following two forms:

title: Definition:Intrinsic Equation/Natural Equation
snippet: A natural equation is an intrinsic equation for a space curve $C$ such that $C$ is expressed in terms of its intrinsic properties: Curvature $\kappa$ Torsion $\tau$

title: Definition:Intrinsic Equation/Whewell Equation
snippet: A Whewell equation is an intrinsic equation for a curve $C$ such that $C$ is expressed in terms of its intrinsic properties: Arc length $s$ Turning angle $\psi$

title: Definition:Intrinsic Property
snippet: Let $C$ be a curve or surface. The intrinsic properties of $C$ are those properties that do not depend on the nature of the embedding of $C$ in a coordinate system.

title: Definition:Intrinsic Property/Examples
snippet: Examples of the intrinsic properties of a curve include: Arc length $s$ Curvature $\kappa$ Turning angle $\psi$ Torsion $\tau$ Radius of curvature $\rho$

title: Definition:Intuitionism
snippet: == Philosophical Position == Intuitionism is the philosophical position that mathematical objects are mental entities that cannot exist independently of our ability to prove their existence using a finite number of steps. Hence a mathematical statement is true only if it can be proved to be so using a finite process. Hence it holds as a basic tenet that the Law of the Excluded Middle is rejected. Intuitionism also rejects the concept of impredicative definitions. Intuitionism is generally considered to be a branch of constructivism.

title: Definition:Intuitionism/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Intuitionism == Intuitionism was originated by . His rejection of the Law of the Excluded Middle caused considerable controversy, especially with and his formalist philosophy.

title: Definition:Intuitionistic Propositional Logic
snippet: The intuitionist school of mathematics is one which adopts the following philosophical position: "Although we may know that it is not the case that a statement $p$ is (provably) false, we don't necessarily know that it is (provably) true either." Thus the intuitionist school rejects the Law of the Excluded Middle. The classical school, by affirming that if a statement is not true it must be false, and if it is not false it must be true, accepts as an axiom that "not not-true" must mean "true".

title: Definition:Intuitionistic Propositional Logic/Also known as
snippet: == Intuitionistic Propositional Logic: Also known as == Some prefer to address this logic by its practitioners, calling it intuitionist (propositional) logic. This field of logic is also (more intuitively) (no pun intended) known as constructive logic or constructivist logic. That is, a mathematical object can not be deduced to exist based on the Law of Excluded Middle -- it specifically needs to be constructed.

title: Definition:Invalid/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Invalid == The word invalid, as used in the logical context, has the stress on the second syllable: in-val-id. Pronounced in-val-id, with the stress on the first syllable, the word means a person who is being treated for an illness. There are plenty of apocryphal tales on the internet where furious users have called the helpdesk to tell the staff that their computer is calling them bad, and an invalid. So let's be careful out there. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Invalid Argument
snippet: An invalid argument is a argument in which the premises do not provide conclusive reasons for the conclusion.

title: Definition:Invalid Argument/Also known as
snippet: == Invalid Argument: Also known as == An invalid argument is also known as a fallacy. Some authors use the term unsound argument to mean invalid argument. However, because of the confusion about the meaning of sound argument, which can be used to mean either valid argument or proof, it is recommended that this term not be used.

title: Definition:Invariance (Statistics)/Property
snippet: An invariance is a property that is unchanged by a transformation.

title: Definition:Invariance (Statistics)/Quantity
snippet: An invariance is a quantity that is unchanged by a transformation.

title: Definition:Invariance (Tensor Theory)
snippet: An invariance in the context of tensor theory is an essential property of tensors under admissible transformations.

title: Definition:Invariant
snippet: An invariant is a property of an object which is retained under an isomorphism of some kind.

title: Definition:Invariant/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Invariant == Invariants were investigated by , who proved important general results about the set of all algebraic invariants of certain groups of transformations. It is noted that the problem of calculation and full description of all possible invariants can be difficult, if not intractable.

title: Definition:Invariant/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Invariant == The property of being invariant is called invariance.

title: Definition:Invariant Functional under Transformation
snippet: Let $y_i$, $F$, $\Phi$, $\Psi$ be real functions. Let $\mathbf y = \sequence {y_i}_{1 \mathop \le i \mathop \le n}$. Let $\ds J \sqbrk {\mathbf y} = \int_{x_0}^{x_1} \map F {x, \mathbf y, \mathbf y'} \rd x$ be a functional. Let: $X = \map \Phi {x, \mathbf y, \mathbf y'}$ $\mathbf Y = \map {\mathbf \Psi} {x, \mathbf y, \mathbf y'}$ Let curve $\gamma$ defined by: $\mathbf y = \map {\mathbf y} x, \quad x_0 \le x \le x_1$ be transformed into a curve $\Gamma$ defined by: $\mathbf Y = \map {\mathbf Y} X, \quad X_0 \le X \le X_1$ Then the functional $J \sqbrk {\mathbf y}$ is invariant under the…

title: Definition:Invariant Mapping Under Equivalence Relation
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $\RR$ be an equivalence relation on $S$. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. Then $f$ is invariant under $\RR$ : $x \mathrel \RR y \implies \map f x = \map f y$

title: Definition:Invariant Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $\theta: X \to X$ be a $\Sigma / \Sigma$-measurable mapping. Then $\mu$ is said to be a $\theta$-invariant measure or to be invariant under $\theta$ : $\forall E \in \Sigma: \map \mu {\theta^{-1} \sqbrk E} = \map \mu E$ where $\theta^{-1} \sqbrk E$ denotes the preimage of $E$ under $\theta$. In terms of a pushforward measure, this can be concisely formulated as: $\theta_* \mu = \mu$

title: Definition:Invariant Metric on Vector Space
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $X$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $d$ be a metric on $X$. We say that $d$ is invariant : $\map d {x, y} = \map d {x + z, y + z}$ for each $x, y, z \in X$.

title: Definition:Invariant Pseudometric on Vector Space
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $X$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $d$ be a pseudometric on $X$. We say that $d$ is invariant : $\map d {x, y} = \map d {x + z, y + z}$ for each $x, y, z \in X$.

title: Definition:Invariant Set
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $f: S \to S$ be a self-map on $S$. Let $T \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. Then $T$ is an invariant set of $f$ : $f \sqbrk Y = Y$

title: Definition:Invariant Set/Also known as
snippet: == Invariant Set: Also known as == An invariant set of a mapping is also known as an invariant subset of a set under a mapping if it is important to attach more emphasis to the set than to the mapping.

title: Definition:Invariant Set/Negatively Invariant
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $f: S \to S$ be a self-map on $S$. Let $T \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$ such that: $f^{-1} \sqbrk T \subseteq T$ Then $T$ is a negatively invariant set of $f$.

title: Definition:Invariant Set/Positively Invariant
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $f: S \to S$ be a self-map on $S$. Let $T \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$ such that: $f \sqbrk T \subseteq T$ Then $T$ is a positively invariant set of $f$.

title: Definition:Invariant Subspace
snippet: Let $H$ be a Hilbert space. Let $A \in \map B H$ be a bounded linear operator. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of $H$. Then $M$ is said to be an invariant subspace for $A$ $h \in M \implies A h \in M$. That is, $AM \subseteq M$.

title: Definition:Invariant Subspace/Normed Vector Space
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ be a normed vector space. Let $Y \subseteq X$ be a subspace of $X$. Let $T : X \to X$ be a linear operator such that $T Y \subseteq Y$. Then $Y$ is called the invariant subspace ( $T$).

title: Definition:Invariant Theory
snippet: Invariant theory is the subfield of abstract algebra which studies the actions of groups on mathematical objects to investigate those aspects which are invariant.

title: Definition:Inverse
snippet: Logic: The inverse of a conditional $p \implies q$ is $\neg p \implies \neg q$ Abstract Algebra: Inverse Element Ring Product Inverse Definition:Inverse Semigroup Definition:Inverse in Inverse Semigroup Linear Algebra Definition:Inverse Linear Transformation Definition:Inverse Linear Operator Relation Theory: Inverse Relation Inverse Image (also known as Preimage) Mapping Theory: Inverse Mapping Inverse of a Mapping Matrix Algebra: Inverse Matrix

title: Definition:Inverse (Abstract Algebra)
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a monoid whose identity is $e_S$.

title: Definition:Inverse (Abstract Algebra)/Inverse
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure with an identity element $e_S$. Let $x, y \in S$ be elements. The element $y$ is an inverse of $x$ : $y \circ x = e_S = x \circ y$ that is, $y$ is both: a left inverse of $x$ and: a right inverse of $x$.

title: Definition:Inverse (Abstract Algebra)/Left Inverse
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a monoid whose identity is $e_S$. An element $x_L \in S$ is called a left inverse of $x$ : $x_L \circ x = e_S$

title: Definition:Inverse (Abstract Algebra)/Right Inverse
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a monoid whose identity is $e_S$. An element $x_R \in S$ is called a right inverse of $x$ : $x \circ x_R = e_S$

title: Definition:Inverse Completion
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a semigroup. Let $\struct {C, \circ} \subseteq \struct {S, \circ}$ be the subsemigroup of cancellable elements of $\struct {S, \circ}$. Let $\struct {T, \circ'}$ be a semigroup defined such that: $(1): \quad \struct {S, \circ}$ is a subsemigroup of $\struct {T, \circ'}$ $(2): \quad$ Every element of $C$ has an inverse in $T$ for $\circ'$ $(3): \quad \gen {S \cup C^{-1} } = \struct {T, \circ'}$ where: $\gen {S \cup C^{-1} }$ denotes the subsemigroup of $\struct {T, \circ'}$ generated by $S \cup C^{-1}$ $C^{-1}$ denotes the inverse of $C$.

title: Definition:Inverse Cosecant/Complex/Arccosecant
snippet: The principal branch of the complex inverse cosecant function is defined as: $\forall z \in \C_{\ne 0}: \map \arccsc z := \dfrac 1 i \, \map \Ln {\dfrac {i + \sqrt {z^2 - 1} } z}$ where: $\Ln$ denotes the principal branch of the complex natural logarithm $\sqrt {z^2 - 1}$ denotes the principal square root of $z^2 - 1$.

title: Definition:Inverse Cosecant/Complex/Definition 1
snippet: Let $z \in \C_{\ne 0}$ be a non-zero complex number. The inverse cosecant of $z$ is the multifunction defined as: $\csc^{-1} \left({z}\right) := \left\{{w \in \C: \csc \left({w}\right) = z}\right\}$ where $\csc \left({w}\right)$ is the cosecant of $w$.

title: Definition:Inverse Cosecant/Complex/Definition 2
snippet: Let $z \in \C_{\ne 0}$ be a non-zero complex number. The inverse cosecant of $z$ is the multifunction defined as: $\csc^{-1} \left({z}\right) := \left\{{\dfrac 1 i \ln \left({\dfrac {i + \sqrt{\left|{z^2 - 1}\right|} e^{\left({i / 2}\right) \arg \left({z^2 - 1}\right)}} z}\right) + 2 k \pi: k \in \Z}\right\}$ where: $\sqrt{\left|{z^2 - 1}\right|}$ denotes the positive square root of the complex modulus of $z^2 - 1$ $\arg \left({z^2 - 1}\right)$ denotes the argument of $z^2 - 1$ $\ln$ denotes the complex natural logarithm considered as a multifunction.

title: Definition:Inverse Cosecant/Real
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number such that $x \le -1$ or $x \ge 1$. The inverse cosecant of $x$ is the multifunction defined as: $\inv \csc x := \set {y \in \R: \map \csc y = x}$ where $\map \csc y$ is the cosecant of $y$.

title: Definition:Inverse Cosecant/Real/Arccosecant
snippet: From Shape of Cosecant Function, we have that $\csc x$ is continuous and strictly decreasing on the intervals $\hointr {-\dfrac \pi 2} 0$ and $\hointl 0 {\dfrac \pi 2}$. From the same source, we also have that: $\csc x \to + \infty$ as $x \to 0^+$ $\csc x \to - \infty$ as $x \to 0^-$ Let $g: \hointr {-\dfrac \pi 2} 0 \to \hointl {-\infty} {-1}$ be the restriction of $\csc x$ to $\hointr {-\dfrac \pi 2} 0$. Let $h: \hointl 0 {\dfrac \pi 2} \to \hointr 1 \infty$ be the restriction of $\csc x$ to $\hointl 0 {\dfrac \pi 2}$.

title: Definition:Inverse Cosecant/Terminology
snippet: == Terminology for Inverse Cosecant == There exists the popular but misleading notation $\csc^{-1} x$, which is supposed to denote the inverse cosecant function. However, note that as $\csc x$ is not an injection, it does not have a well-defined inverse. The $\arccsc$ function as defined here has a well-specified image which (to a certain extent) is arbitrarily chosen for convenience. Therefore it is preferred to the notation $\csc^{-1} x$, which (as pointed out) can be confusing and misleading.

title: Definition:Inverse Cosine/Complex/Arccosine
snippet: The principal branch of the complex inverse cosine function is defined as: $\map \arccos z = \dfrac 1 i \map \Ln {z + \sqrt {z^2 - 1} }$ where: $\Ln$ denotes the principal branch of the complex natural logarithm $\sqrt {z^2 - 1}$ denotes the principal square root of $z^2 - 1$.

title: Definition:Inverse Cosine/Complex/Definition 1
snippet: Let $z \in \C$ be a complex number. The inverse cosine of $z$ is the multifunction defined as: $\cos^{-1} \left({z}\right) := \left\{{w \in \C: \cos \left({w}\right) = z}\right\}$ where $\cos \left({w}\right)$ is the cosine of $w$.

title: Definition:Inverse Cosine/Complex/Definition 2
snippet: Let $z \in \C$ be a complex number. The inverse cosine of $z$ is the multifunction defined as: $\cos^{-1} \left({z}\right) := \left\{{\dfrac 1 i \ln \left({z + \sqrt{\left|{z^2 - 1}\right|} e^{\left({i / 2}\right) \arg \left({z^2 - 1}\right)} }\right) + 2 k \pi: k \in \Z}\right\}$ where: $\sqrt{\left|{z^2 - 1}\right|}$ denotes the positive square root of the complex modulus of $z^2 - 1$ $\arg \left({z^2 - 1}\right)$ denotes the argument of $z^2 - 1$ $\ln$ denotes the complex natural logarithm considered as a multifunction.

title: Definition:Inverse Cosine/Real
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number such that $-1 \le x \le 1$. The inverse cosine of $x$ is the multifunction defined as: $\inv \cos x := \set {y \in \R: \map \cos y = x}$ where $\map \cos y$ is the cosine of $y$.

title: Definition:Inverse Cosine/Real/Arccosine
snippet: From Shape of Cosine Function, we have that $\cos x$ is continuous and strictly decreasing on the interval $\closedint 0 \pi$. From Cosine of Multiple of Pi, $\cos \pi = -1$ and $\cos 0 = 1$. Therefore, let $g: \closedint 0 \pi \to \closedint {-1} 1$ be the restriction of $\cos x$ to $\closedint 0 \pi$. Thus from Inverse of Strictly Monotone Function, $\map g x$ admits an inverse function, which will be continuous and strictly decreasing on $\closedint {-1} 1$. This function is called the arccosine of $x$.

title: Definition:Inverse Cosine/Terminology
snippet: == Terminology for Inverse Cosine == There exists the popular but misleading notation $\cos^{-1} x$, which is supposed to denote the inverse cosine function. The $\arccos$ function as defined here has a well-specified image which (to a certain extent) is arbitrarily chosen for convenience. Therefore it is preferred to the notation $\cos^{-1} x$, which (as pointed out) can be confusing and misleading.

snippet: Let $S$ be the subset of the complex plane: $S = \C \setminus \left\{{0 + i, 0 - i}\right\}$ The inverse cotangent is a multifunction defined on $S$ as: $\forall z \in S: \cot^{-1} \left({z}\right) := \left\{{\dfrac 1 {2 i} \ln \left({\dfrac {z + i} {z - i}}\right) + k \pi: k \in \Z}\right\}$ where $\ln$ denotes the complex natural logarithm as a multifunction.

snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number such that $-1 \le x \le 1$. The inverse cotangent of $x$ is the multifunction defined as: $\inv \cot x := \set {y \in \R: \map \cot y = x}$ where $\map \cot y$ is the cotangent of $y$.

title: Definition:Inverse Cotangent/Real/Arccotangent
snippet: From Shape of Cotangent Function, we have that $\cot x$ is continuous and strictly decreasing on the interval $\openint 0 \pi$. From the same source, we also have that: $\cot x \to + \infty$ as $x \to 0^+$ $\cot x \to - \infty$ as $x \to \pi^-$ Let $g: \openint 0 \pi \to \R$ be the restriction of $\cot x$ to $\openint 0 \pi$. Thus from Inverse of Strictly Monotone Function, $\map g x$ admits an inverse function, which will be continuous and strictly decreasing on $\R$. This function is called the arccotangent of $x$ and is written $\arccot x$.

title: Definition:Inverse Element/Also known as
snippet: == Inverse Element: Also known as == An inverse of $x$ is also known as a two-sided inverse of $x$, symmetric element or negative of $x$. Some sources refer to it as a reciprocal element, which terminology is borrowed from the real numbers under multiplication. The notation used to represent an inverse of an element is often understood to depend on the set and binary operation under consideration. Various symbols are seen for a general inverse, for example $\hat x$, $x'$ and $x^*$. In multiplicative notation: If $s \in S$ has an inverse, it is denoted $s^{-1}$.

title: Definition:Inverse Entourage

title: Definition:Inverse Image Mapping/Mapping/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $\powerset S$ and $\powerset T$ be their power sets. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. The inverse image mapping of $f$ is the mapping $f^\gets: \powerset T \to \powerset S$ that sends a subset $Y \subseteq T$ to its preimage $f^{-1} \sqbrk T$ under $f$: $\forall Y \in \powerset T: \map {f^\gets} Y = \begin {cases} \set {s \in S: \exists t \in Y: \map f s = t} & : \Img f \cap Y \ne \O \\ \O & : \Img f \cap Y = \O \end {cases}$

title: Definition:Inverse Image Mapping/Mapping/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $\powerset S$ and $\powerset T$ be their power sets. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. The inverse image mapping of $f$ is the direct image mapping of the inverse $f^{-1}$ of $f$: $f^\gets = \paren {f^{-1} }^\to: \powerset T \to \powerset S$: That is: $\forall Y \in \powerset T: \map {f^\gets} Y = \set {s \in S: \exists t \in Y: \map f s = t}$

title: Definition:Inverse Image Mapping/Relation
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $\powerset S$ and $\powerset T$ be their power sets. Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation on $S \times T$.

title: Definition:Inverse Image Mapping/Relation/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $\powerset S$ and $\powerset T$ be their power sets. Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation on $S \times T$. The inverse image mapping of $\RR$ is the mapping $\RR^\gets: \powerset T \to \powerset S$ that sends a subset $Y \subseteq T$ to its preimage $\map {\RR^{-1} } Y$ under $\RR$: $\forall Y \in \powerset T: \map {\RR^\gets} Y = \begin {cases} \set {s \in S: \exists t \in Y: \tuple {t, s} \in \RR^{-1} } & : \Img \RR \cap Y \ne \O \\ \O & : \Img \RR \cap Y = \O \end {cases}$

title: Definition:Inverse Image Mapping/Relation/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $\powerset S$ and $\powerset T$ be their power sets. Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation on $S \times T$. The inverse image mapping of $\RR$ is the direct image mapping of the inverse $\RR^{-1}$ of $\RR$: $\RR^\gets = \paren {\RR^{-1} }^\to: \powerset T \to \powerset S$ That is: $\forall Y \in \powerset T: \map {\RR^\gets} Y = \set {s \in S: \exists t \in Y: \tuple {t, s} \in \RR^{-1} }$

title: Definition:Inverse Image Presheaf
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $f: T_1 \to T_2$ be continuous. Let $\mathbf C$ be a category which has all small inductive limits. Let $\FF$ be a $\mathbf C$-valued presheaf on $T_2$. The inverse image presheaf of $\FF$ via $f$ is the presheaf $f^{-1}_{\operatorname {Psh} } \FF$ on $T_1$ with: $\map {\paren {f^{-1}_{\operatorname{Psh} } \FF} } U = \ds \varinjlim_{V \mathop \supseteq \map f U} \map \FF V$ where the inductive limit goes over open $V \subseteq Y$ $\operatorname {res}^U_W$ is the induced map on the inductive limit of…

title: Definition:Inverse Integral Operator
snippet: Let $T: f \to F$ be an integral operator on a function $f$. Let there be a (unitary) operator $T^{-1}: F \to f$ such that for a given $F \left({p}\right)$ there exists a unique $f \left({x}\right)$ such that $f = T \left({f}\right)$. Then $T^{-1}$ is the inverse integral operator of $T$.

title: Definition:Inverse Laplace Transform/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\map f s : S \to \R$ be a function, where $S \subset \R$. Let $F$ be another function such that $F$ is the Laplace transform of $f$. Then, $f$ is the inverse Laplace transform of $F$.

title: Definition:Inverse Laplace Transform/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\map f s: S \to \C$ be a complex function, where $S \subset \C$. The inverse Laplace transform of $f$, denoted $\map F t: \R \to S$, is defined as: {{eqn | l = \map F t | r = \dfrac 1 {2 \pi i} \PV_{c \mathop - i \, \infty}^{c \mathop + i \, \infty} e^{s t} \map f s \rd s | c = }} {{eqn | r = \frac 1 {2 \pi i} \lim_{T \mathop \to \infty} \int_{c \mathop - i \, T}^{c \mathop + i \, T} e^{s t} \map f s \rd s | c = }} where: $\PV$ is the Cauchy principal value of the integral $c$ is any real constant such that all the singular points of $\map f s$ lie to the left of the line $\map \Re s =…

title: Definition:Inverse Limit of Inverse System of Groups
snippet: Let $\sequence {G_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a inverse system of groups with group homomorphisms $\sequence {\theta_n}_{n \mathop \in \N_{>0} }$. The inverse limit of $\sequence {G_n}$ is the group consisting of all coherent sequences of $\sequence {G_n}$. It is written as: $\varprojlim G_n$

title: Definition:Inverse Linear Operator
snippet: Let $X$ be a vector space. Let $A : X \to X$ be an invertible (in the sense of a mapping) linear transformation with inverse mapping $A^{-1} : X \to X$. We say that $A^{-1}$ is the inverse linear operator of $A$.

title: Definition:Inverse Linear Transformation
snippet: Let $V$ and $U$ be vector spaces. Let $A : V \to U$ be an invertible (in the sense of a mapping) linear transformation with inverse mapping $A^{-1} : U \to V$. We say that $A^{-1}$ is the inverse linear transformation of $A$.

title: Definition:Inverse Mapping/Also defined as
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be an injection. Then its inverse mapping is the mapping $g$ such that: $(1): \quad$ its domain $\Dom g$ equals the image $\Img f$ of $f$ $(2): \quad \forall y \in \Img f: \map f {\map g y} = y$ Thus $f$ is seen to be a surjection by tacit use of Restriction of Mapping to Image is Surjection. does not endorse this approach, and considers that its use can cause important insight to be missed.

title: Definition:Inverse Mapping/Also known as
snippet: == Inverse Mapping: Also known as == If $f$ has an inverse mapping, then $f$ is an invertible mapping. Hence, when the inverse (relation) of $f^{-1}$ is a mapping, we say that $f$ has an inverse mapping. Some sources, in distinguishing this from a left inverse and a right inverse, refer to this as the two-sided inverse. Some sources use the term converse mapping for inverse mapping. Category:Definitions/Inverse Mappings

title: Definition:Inverse Mapping/Definition 1
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. Let $f^{-1} \subseteq T \times S$ be the inverse of $f$: $f^{-1} := \set {\tuple {t, s}: \map f s = t}$ Let $f^{-1}$ itself be a mapping: $\forall y \in T: \tuple {y, x_1} \in f^{-1} \land \tuple {y, x_2} \in f^{-1} \implies x_1 = x_2$ and $\forall y \in T: \exists x \in S: \tuple {y, x} \in f$ Then $f^{-1}$ is called the inverse mapping of $f$.

title: Definition:Inverse Mapping/Definition 2
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ and $g: T \to S$ be mappings. Let: $g \circ f = I_S$ $f \circ g = I_T$ where: $g \circ f$ and $f \circ g$ denotes the composition of $f$ with $g$ in either order $I_S$ and $I_T$ denote the identity mappings on $S$ and $T$ respectively. That is, $f$ and $g$ are both left inverse mappings and right inverse mappings of each other. Then: $g$ is the inverse (mapping) of $f$ $f$ is the inverse (mapping) of $g$.

title: Definition:Inverse Mapping/Technical Note
snippet: == Technical Note for Inverse Mapping == {{LatexFor|for = \inv {f} {x} }} When the argument is a single character, it is usual to omit the braces: \inv f x This command is specific to . Category:Technical Notes

title: Definition:Inverse Matrix
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. Let $\mathbf A$ be a square matrix of order $n$. Let there exist a square matrix $\mathbf B$ of order $n$ such that: $\mathbf A \mathbf B = \mathbf I_n = \mathbf B \mathbf A$ where $\mathbf I_n$ denotes the unit matrix of order $n$. Then $\mathbf B$ is called the inverse of $\mathbf A$ and is usually denoted $\mathbf A^{-1}$.

title: Definition:Inverse Matrix/Also known as
snippet: == Inverse Matrix: Also known as == An inverse matrix can also be seen referred to as a reciprocal matrix.

title: Definition:Inverse Matrix/Left
snippet: Let $m, n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ be a matrix of order $m \times n$. Let $\mathbf B = \sqbrk b_{n m}$ be a matrix of order $n \times m$ such that: $\mathbf B \mathbf A = \mathbf I_n$ where $\mathbf I_n$ denotes the unit matrix of order $n$. Then $\mathbf B$ is known as a left inverse (matrix) of $\mathbf A$.

title: Definition:Inverse Matrix/Right
snippet: Let $m, n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ be a matrix of order $m \times n$. Let $\mathbf B = \sqbrk b_{n m}$ be a matrix of order $n \times m$ such that: $\mathbf A \mathbf B = \mathbf I_m$ where $\mathbf I_m$ denotes the unit matrix of order $m$. Then $\mathbf B$ is known as a right inverse (matrix) of $\mathbf A$.

title: Definition:Inverse Morphism
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $f: X \to Y$ be a morphism of $\mathbf C$. A morphism $g: Y \to X$ is said to be an inverse (morphism) for $f$ : $g \circ f = \operatorname{id}_X$ $f \circ g = \operatorname{id}_Y$ where $\operatorname{id}_X$ denotes the identity morphism on $X$. It follows that $f$ is an isomorphism it has an inverse (morphism).

title: Definition:Inverse Point/Also known as
snippet: == Inverse Point: Also known as == An inverse point is also referred to as just an inverse, but this is a word which applies to a number of contexts. Similarly, the images of other geometric objects under an inversive transformation are likewise referred to as just the inverse of those objects.

title: Definition:Inverse Probability
snippet: Inverse probability is a concept used in Bayesian inference for applying an approach to probability theory where reasoning is applied to observations so as to develop hypotheses that may explain them. More generally, the term is used for an attempt to find the probability of an occurrence of a cause event conditional upon a consequential event having occurred.

title: Definition:Inverse Ratio
snippet: Let $R = a : b$ be a ratio. Then the inverse ratio to $R$ is $b : a$.

title: Definition:Inverse Ratio/Also known as
snippet: == Inverse Ratio: Also known as == An inverse ratio is also known as a reciprocal ratio.

title: Definition:Inverse Relation
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation. The inverse relation to (or of) $\RR$ is defined as: $\RR^{-1} := \set {\tuple {t, s}: \tuple {s, t} \in \RR}$ That is, $\RR^{-1} \subseteq T \times S$ is the relation which satisfies: $\forall s \in S: \forall t \in T: \tuple {t, s} \in \RR^{-1} \iff \tuple {s, t} \in \RR$

title: Definition:Inverse Relation/Also known as
snippet: == Inverse Relation: Also known as == An inverse relation is also seen as converse relation. In the context of orderings, the term dual ordering can also be seen. However, do not confuse this with a dual relation. Some sources use the notation $\RR^t$, for example . Others use $\breve \RR$, for example and . Still others use $\RR^\gets$, for example .

title: Definition:Inverse Relation/Class Theory
snippet: Let $V$ be a basic universe. Let $A$ and $B$ be subclasses of $V$. Let $\RR \subseteq A \times B$ be a relation on $A \times B$. The inverse relation to (or of) $\RR$ is defined as the class of all ordered pairs $\tuple {b, a}$ such that $\tuple {a, b} \in \RR$: $\RR^{-1} := \set {\tuple {b, a}: \tuple {a, b} \in \RR}$

title: Definition:Inverse Relation Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf{Rel}$ be the category of relations. The inverse relation (contravariant) functor $C: \mathbf{Rel} \to \mathbf{Rel}$ is the contravariant functor defined by: {{DefineFunctor |ob = $CX := X$ |mor = $C \RR := \RR^{-1}$, the inverse relation to $\RR$ }} That it is in fact a contravariant functor is shown on Inverse Relation Functor is Contravariant Functor.

title: Definition:Inverse Relational Structure
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \RR}$ be a relational structure. Let $\RR^{-1}$ be the inverse of $\RR$. The ordered set $\struct {S, \RR^{-1} }$ is called the inverse relational structure (or just inverse) of $\struct {S, \RR}$.

title: Definition:Inverse Row form of Cayley Table for Group
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a finite group. The Cayley table for $\struct {G, \circ}$ can be presented in a form such that the rows are headed by the inverse elements of the elements which head the corresponding columns. This form is known as the inverse row form of the Cayley table for $\struct {G, \circ}$.

title: Definition:Inverse Secant/Complex/Arcsecant
snippet: The principal branch of the complex inverse secant function is defined as: $\forall z \in \C_{\ne 0}: \map \arcsec z := \dfrac 1 i \, \map \Ln {\dfrac {1 + \sqrt {1 - z^2} } z}$ where: $\Ln$ denotes the principal branch of the complex natural logarithm $\sqrt {1 - z^2}$ denotes the principal square root of $1 - z^2$.

title: Definition:Inverse Secant/Complex/Definition 1
snippet: Let $z \in \C_{\ne 0}$ be a non-zero complex number. The inverse secant of $z$ is the multifunction defined as: $\inv \sec z := \set {w \in \C: \map \sec w = z}$ where $\map \sec w$ is the secant of $w$.

title: Definition:Inverse Secant/Complex/Definition 2
snippet: Let $z \in \C_{\ne 0}$ be a non-zero complex number. The inverse secant of $z$ is the multifunction defined as: $\sec^{-1} z := \set {\dfrac 1 i \map \ln {\dfrac {1 + \sqrt {\size {1 - z^2} } e^{\paren {i / 2} \map \arg {1 - z^2} } } z} + 2 k \pi: k \in \Z}$ where: $\sqrt {\size {1 - z^2} }$ denotes the positive square root of the complex modulus of $1 - z^2$ $\map \arg {1 - z^2}$ denotes the argument of $1 - z^2$ $\ln$ denotes the complex natural logarithm as a multifunction.

title: Definition:Inverse Secant/Real
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number such that $x \le -1$ or $x \ge 1$. The inverse secant of $x$ is the multifunction defined as: $\inv \sec x := \set {y \in \R: \map \sec y = x}$ where $\map \sec y$ is the secant of $y$.

title: Definition:Inverse Secant/Real/Arcsecant
snippet: From Shape of Secant Function, we have that $\sec x$ is continuous and strictly increasing on the intervals $\hointr 0 {\dfrac \pi 2}$ and $\hointl {\dfrac \pi 2} \pi$. From the same source, we also have that: $\sec x \to + \infty$ as $x \to \dfrac \pi 2^-$ $\sec x \to - \infty$ as $x \to \dfrac \pi 2^+$ Let $g: \hointr 0 {\dfrac \pi 2} \to \hointr 1 \to$ be the restriction of $\sec x$ to $\hointr 0 {\dfrac \pi 2}$. Let $h: \hointl {\dfrac \pi 2} \pi \to \hointl \gets {-1}$ be the restriction of $\sec x$ to $\hointl {\dfrac \pi 2} \pi$.

title: Definition:Inverse Secant/Terminology
snippet: == Terminology for Inverse Secant == There exists the popular but misleading notation $\sec^{-1} x$, which is supposed to denote the inverse secant function. However, note that as $\sec x$ is not an injection, it does not have a well-defined inverse. The $\arcsec$ function as defined here has a well-specified image which (to a certain extent) is arbitrarily chosen for convenience. Therefore it is preferred to the notation $\sec^{-1} x$, which (as pointed out) can be confusing and misleading.

title: Definition:Inverse Semigroup
snippet: An inverse semigroup is a semigroup $\struct {S, \circ}$ such that: $\forall a \in S: \exists! b \in S: a = a \circ b \circ a, b = b \circ a \circ b$

title: Definition:Inverse Sine/Complex/Arcsine
snippet: The principal branch of the complex inverse sine function is defined as: $\map \arcsin z = \dfrac 1 i \, \map \Ln {i z + \sqrt {1 - z^2} }$ where: $\Ln$ denotes the principal branch of the complex natural logarithm $\sqrt {1 - z^2}$ denotes the principal square root of $1 - z^2$.

title: Definition:Inverse Sine/Complex/Definition 1
snippet: Let $z \in \C$ be a complex number. The inverse sine of $z$ is the multifunction defined as: $\sin^{-1} \paren z := \set {w \in \C: \sin \paren w = z}$ where $\sin \paren w$ is the sine of $w$.

title: Definition:Inverse Sine/Complex/Definition 2
snippet: Let $z \in \C$ be a complex number. The inverse sine of $z$ is the multifunction defined as: $\sin^{-1} \paren z := \set {\dfrac 1 i \ln \paren {i z + \sqrt {\cmod {1 - z^2} } \exp \paren {\dfrac i 2 \arg \paren {1 - z^2} } } + 2 k \pi: k \in \Z}$ where: $\sqrt {\cmod {1 - z^2} }$ denotes the positive square root of the complex modulus of $1 - z^2$ $\arg \paren {1 - z^2}$ denotes the argument of $1 - z^2$ $\ln$ is the complex natural logarithm considered as a multifunction.

title: Definition:Inverse Sine/Real
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number such that $-1 \le x \le 1$. The inverse sine of $x$ is the multifunction defined as: $\inv \sin x := \set {y \in \R: \map \sin y = x}$ where $\map \sin y$ is the sine of $y$.

title: Definition:Inverse Sine/Real/Arcsine
snippet: From Shape of Sine Function, we have that $\sin x$ is continuous and strictly increasing on the interval $\closedint {-\dfrac \pi 2} {\dfrac \pi 2}$. From Sine of Half-Integer Multiple of Pi: $\map \sin {-\dfrac {\pi} 2} = -1$ and: $\sin \dfrac {\pi} 2 = 1$ Therefore, let $g: \closedint {-\dfrac \pi 2} {\dfrac \pi 2} \to \closedint {-1} 1$ be the restriction of $\sin x$ to $\closedint {-\dfrac \pi 2} {\dfrac \pi 2}$. Thus from Inverse of Strictly Monotone Function, $g \paren x$ admits an inverse function, which will be continuous and strictly increasing on $\closedint {-1} 1$.

title: Definition:Inverse Sine/Terminology
snippet: == Terminology for Inverse Sine == There exists the popular but misleading notation $\sin^{-1} x$, which is supposed to denote the inverse sine function. However, note that as $\sin x$ is not an injection (even though by restriction of the codomain it can be considered surjective), it does not have a well-defined inverse. The $\arcsin$ function as defined here has a well-specified image which (to a certain extent) is arbitrarily chosen for convenience. Therefore it is preferred to the notation $\sin^{-1} x$, which (as pointed out) can be confusing and misleading.

title: Definition:Inverse Square Law
snippet: Two real variables $x$ and $y$ are related by an inverse square law they fulfil the relationship: $\forall x, y \in \R: x \propto \dfrac 1 {y^2} \iff \exists k \in \R, k \ne 0: x y^2 = k$

title: Definition:Inverse Statement
snippet: The inverse of the conditional: $p \implies q$ is the statement: $\neg p \implies \neg q$

title: Definition:Inverse System of Groups
snippet: Let $\sequence {G_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence of groups. For each $n \in \N$, let: $\theta_{n + 1} : G_{n + 1} \to G_n$ be a homomorphism. Then $\sequence {G_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ together with $\sequence {\theta_n}_{n \mathop \in \N_{>0} }$ is called an inverse system (of groups).

title: Definition:Inverse Tangent/Complex
snippet: Let $S$ be the subset of the complex plane: $S = \C \setminus \set {0 + i, 0 - i}$

title: Definition:Inverse Tangent/Complex/Arctangent
snippet: The principal branch of the complex inverse tangent function is defined as: $\map \arctan z := \dfrac 1 {2 i} \, \map \Ln {\dfrac {i - z} {i + z} }$ where $\Ln$ denotes the principal branch of the complex natural logarithm.

title: Definition:Inverse Tangent/Complex/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ be the subset of the complex plane: $S = \C \setminus \set {0 + i, 0 - i}$ The inverse tangent is a multifunction defined on $S$ as: $\forall z \in S: \inv \tan z := \set {w \in \C: \map \tan w = z}$ where $\map \tan w$ is the tangent of $w$.

title: Definition:Inverse Tangent/Complex/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ be the subset of the complex plane: $S = \C \setminus \set {0 + i, 0 - i}$ The inverse tangent is a multifunction defined on $S$ as: $\forall z \in S: \inv \tan z := \set {\dfrac 1 {2 i} \map \ln {\dfrac {i - z} {i + z} } + k \pi: k \in \Z}$ where $\ln$ denotes the complex natural logarithm as a multifunction.

title: Definition:Inverse Tangent/Real
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number. The inverse tangent of $x$ is the multifunction defined as: $\inv \tan x := \set {y \in \R: \map \tan y = x}$ where $\map \tan y$ is the tangent of $y$.

title: Definition:Inverse Tangent/Real/Arctangent
snippet: From Shape of Tangent Function, we have that $\tan x$ is continuous and strictly increasing on the interval $\openint {-\dfrac \pi 2} {\dfrac \pi 2}$. From the same source, we also have that: $\tan x \to + \infty$ as $x \to \dfrac \pi 2 ^-$ $\tan x \to - \infty$ as $x \to -\dfrac \pi 2 ^+$ Let $g: \openint {-\dfrac \pi 2} {\dfrac \pi 2} \to \R$ be the restriction of $\tan x$ to $\openint {-\dfrac \pi 2} {\dfrac \pi 2}$. Thus from Inverse of Strictly Monotone Function, $\map g x$ admits an inverse function, which will be continuous and strictly increasing on $\R$.

title: Definition:Inverse Tangent/Terminology
snippet: == Terminology for Inverse Tangent == There exists the popular but misleading notation $\tan^{-1} x$, which is supposed to denote the inverse tangent function. However, note that as $\tan x$ is not an injection, it does not have a well-defined inverse. The $\arctan$ function as defined here has a well-specified image which (to a certain extent) is arbitrarily chosen for convenience. Therefore it is preferred to the notation $\tan^{-1} x$, which (as pointed out) can be confusing and misleading.

title: Definition:Inverse Trigonometric Function/Also known as
snippet: == Inverse Trigonometric Function: Also known as == An inverse trigonometric function can also be seen as: antitrigonometric function arcus function

title: Definition:Inverse in Inverse Semigroup
snippet: Let $(S, \circ)$ be an inverse semigroup. Let $a\in S$. The inverse of $a$ is the unique element $b\in S$ such that: $a = a \circ b \circ a$ and $b = b \circ a \circ b$ Category:Definitions/Inverse Semigroups

title: Definition:Inverse of Continuous Linear Operator
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be the normed vector space. Let $\map {CL} X := \map {CL} {X, X}$ be a continuous linear transformation space. Let $I \in \map {CL} X$ be the identity element. Suppose $A \in \map {CL} X$ is invertible. Then the unique continuous linear operator denoted $A^{-1} \in \map {CL} X$ is called the inverse of $A$ if $A A^{-1} = A^{-1} A = I$.

title: Definition:Inverse of Elementary Column Operation
snippet: Let $e$ be an elementary column operation which transforms a matrix $\mathbf A$ to another matrix $\mathbf B$. Let $e'$ be an elementary column operation which transforms $\mathbf B$ back to $\mathbf A$. Then $e'$ is the inverse of the elementary column operation $e$.

title: Definition:Inverse of Elementary Row Operation
snippet: Let $e$ be an elementary row operation which transforms a matrix $\mathbf A$ to another matrix $\mathbf B$. Let $e'$ be an elementary row operation which transforms $\mathbf B$ back to $\mathbf A$. Then $e'$ is the inverse of the elementary row operation $e$.

title: Definition:Inverse of Integral Transform
snippet: Let $\map F p$ be an integral transform: $\map F p = \ds \int_a^b \map f x \map K {p, x} \rd x$ The inverse is the integral transform: $\map f x = \ds \int_c^d \map F p \map {K'} {p, x} \rd p$ if there is one.

title: Definition:Inverse of Mapping
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. The inverse of $f$ is its inverse relation, defined as: $f^{-1} := \set {\tuple {t, s}: \map f s = t}$ That is: $f^{-1} := \set {\tuple {t, s}: \tuple {s, t} \in f}$ That is, $f^{-1} \subseteq T \times S$ is the relation which satisfies: $\forall s \in S: \forall t \in T: \tuple {t, s} \in f^{-1} \iff \tuple {s, t} \in f$

title: Definition:Inverse of Mapping/Also denoted as
snippet: == Inverse of Mapping: Also denoted as == For the inverse of a mapping, some sources use the notation $f^\gets$ or $f^{\circ-1}$ instead of $f^{-1}$. Category:Definitions/Inverses of Mappings

title: Definition:Inverse of Mapping/Also known as
snippet: == Inverse of Mapping: Also known as == The inverse of a mapping is also known as its converse. Category:Definitions/Inverses of Mappings

title: Definition:Inverse of Subset/Group
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group. Let $X \subseteq G$. Then the inverse of the subset $X$ is defined as: $X^{-1} = \set {x \in G: x^{-1} \in X}$ or equivalently: $X^{-1} = \set {x^{-1}: x \in X}$

title: Definition:Inverse of Subset/Monoid
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a monoid whose identity is $e_S$. Let $C \subseteq S$ be the set of cancellable elements of $S$. Let $X \subseteq C$. Then the inverse of the subset $X$ is defined as: $X^{-1} = \set {y \in S: \exists x \in X: x \circ y = e_S}$ That is, it is the set of all the inverses of all the elements of $X$.

title: Definition:Inverse of Subset of Topological Group
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \odot, \tau}$ be a topological group. Let $A \subseteq G$. We define the inverse $A^{-1}$ of $A$ by: $A^{-1} = \set {a^{-1} : a \in A}$ where $a^{-1}$ denotes the inverse element of $a \in G$.

title: Definition:Inversion Center/Also known as
snippet: == Inversion Center: Also known as == An inversion center is also known as a center of inversion.

title: Definition:Inversion Mapping
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group. The inversion mapping on $G$ is the mapping $\iota: G \to G$ defined by: $\forall g \in G: \map \iota g = g^{-1}$ That is, $\iota$ assigns to an element of $G$ its inverse.

title: Definition:Inversion Mapping/Topology
snippet: Let $T = \struct {G, \circ, \tau}$ be a topological group. Let $\iota: G \to G$ be the mapping defined as: $\forall x \in G: \map \iota x = x^{-1}$ Then $\iota$ is the inversion mapping of $T$.

title: Definition:Inversion Radius/Also known as
snippet: == Inversion Radius: Also known as == An inversion radius is also known as a radius of inversion.

title: Definition:Inversion Theorem
snippet: Let $\map F p$ be an integral transform: $\map F p = \ds \int_a^b \map f x \map K {p, x} \rd x$ Let $T$ be the integral operator associated with $\map F p$: $F = \map t F$ An inversion theorem is a specification for an inverse integral operator $T^{-1}$ of the form $f = \map {T^{-1} } F$ such that: $\map f x = \ds \int_\alpha^\beta \map F p \map H {x, p} \rd p$ should such an $\map H {x, p}$ exist. It is not necessarily the case that it does exist..

title: Definition:Inversion of Integral Transform
snippet: Let $\map F p$ be an integral transform: $\map F p = \ds \int_a^b \map f x \map K {p, x} \rd x$ The inversion of $F$ is the operation of finding $\map f x$, that is, of solving the integral equation. That is, of finding the inverse of $\map F p$.

title: Definition:Inversive Geometry
snippet: Inversive geometry is the field of geometry concerned with properties which are invariant under inversive transformations.

title: Definition:Inversive Transformation
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a circle in the Euclidean plane $\EE$ whose center is $O$ and whose radius is $r$. For a point $P$ such that $P \ne O$, let be used to construct a ray $\LL$ starting from $O$ and passing through $P$. Let $f: \EE \to \EE$ be the mapping defined as: $\forall P \in \EE: \map f P = P'$ such that: $P'$ is also on $OP$ $OP \times OP' = r^2$ Then $f$ is known as the inversive transformation of $\EE$ $\CC$.

title: Definition:Inversive Transformation/Also known as
snippet: == Inversive Transformation: Also known as == An inversive transformation is also known as: a circular reflection an inversion.

title: Definition:Inversive Transformation/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Inversive Transformation == The study of inversive transformations was first performed systematically by .

title: Definition:Inversive Transformation/Inverse Point
snippet: Let $\EE$ denote the Euclidean plane. Let $f: \EE \to \EE$ be the inversive transformation on $\EE$ with respect to the circle $\CC$ whose center is $O$ and whose radius is $r$. The image $P' := \map f P$ of a point $P$ under the inversive transformation $f$ is referred to as the inverse point of $P$ under $f$. From Inverse Transformation is Involution it also follows that also $P$ is the inverse point of $P'$ under $f$.

title: Definition:Inversive Transformation/Inversion Center
snippet: Let $\EE$ denote the Euclidean plane. Let $f: \EE \to \EE$ be the inversive transformation on $\EE$ with respect to the inversion circle $\CC$ whose center is $O$ and whose radius is $r$. The center $O$ of the inversion circle $\CC$ is known as the inversion center of $f$.

title: Definition:Inversive Transformation/Inversion Circle
snippet: Let $\EE$ denote the Euclidean plane. Let $f: \EE \to \EE$ be the inversive transformation on $\EE$ with respect to the circle $\CC$ whose center is $O$ and whose radius is $r$. The circle $\CC$ is known as the inversion circle of $f$.

title: Definition:Inversive Transformation/Inversion Radius
snippet: Let $\EE$ denote the Euclidean plane. Let $f: \EE \to \EE$ be the inversive transformation on $\EE$ with respect to the inversion circle $\CC$ whose center is $O$ and whose radius is $r$. The radius $r$ of the inversion circle $\CC$ is known as the inversion radius of $f$.

title: Definition:Inversive Transformation/Spherical
snippet: Let $\SS$ be a sphere in the Euclidean space $\EE$ whose center is $O$ and whose radius is $r$. For a point $P$ such that $P \ne O$, let be used to construct a ray $\LL$ starting from $O$ and passing through $P$. Let $f: \EE \to \EE$ be the mapping defined as: $\forall P \in \EE: \map f P = P'$ such that: $P'$ is also on $OP$ $OP \times OP' = r^2$ Then $f$ is known as the (spherical) inversive transformation of $\EE$ $\CC$.

title: Definition:Invertible
snippet: Mapping Theory: Invertible Mapping Abstract Algebra: Invertible Element Invertible Operation Linear Algebra: Invertible Matrix, that is, a Nonsingular Matrix Functional Analysis: Invertible Bounded Linear Operator Invertible Bounded Linear Transformation

title: Definition:Invertible Bounded Linear Operator/Inner Product Space
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be an inner product space. Let $T : X \to X$ be an invertible bounded linear transformation. We say that $A$ is a bounded linear operator.

title: Definition:Invertible Bounded Linear Operator/Normed Vector Space
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \norm \cdot}$ be a normed vector space. Let $T : X \to X$ be an invertible bounded linear transformation. We say that $A$ is a bounded linear operator.

title: Definition:Invertible Bounded Linear Transformation/Inner Product Space
snippet: Let $\struct {V, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ and $\struct {U, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be inner product spaces. Let $A : V \to U$ be a bounded linear transformation. We say that $A$ is invertible as a bounded linear transformation : $A$ has an inverse mapping that is a bounded linear transformation. That is: there exists a bounded linear transformation $B : U \to V$ such that: $A \circ B = I_U$ $B \circ A = I_V$ where $I_U$ and $I_V$ are the identity mappings on $U$ and $V$ respectively. We say that $B$ is the inverse of $A$ and write $B = A^{-1}$.

title: Definition:Invertible Bounded Linear Transformation/Normed Vector Space
snippet: Let $\struct {V, \norm \cdot_V}$ and $\struct {U, \norm \cdot_U}$ be normed vector spaces. Let $A : V \to U$ be a bounded linear transformation. We say that $A$ is invertible as a bounded linear transformation : $A$ has an inverse mapping that is a bounded linear transformation. That is: there exists a bounded linear transformation $B : U \to V$ such that: $A \circ B = I_U$ $B \circ A = I_V$ where $I_U$ and $I_V$ are the identity mappings on $U$ and $V$ respectively. We say that $B$ is the inverse of $A$ and write $B = A^{-1}$. The process of finding an $A^{-1}$ given $A$ is called inverting.

title: Definition:Invertible Continuous Linear Operator
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot\,}_X}$ be a normed vector space. Let $\map {CL} X := \map {CL} {X, X}$ be a continuous linear transformation space. Let $I \in \map {CL} X$ be the identity element. Let $A \in \map {CL} X$. Suppose: $\exists B \in \map {CL} X : A \circ B = B \circ A = I$ where $\circ$ denotes the composition of mappings. Then $A$ is said to be invertible.

title: Definition:Invertible Element
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure which has an identity $e_S$. If $x \in S$ has an inverse, then $x$ is said to be invertible for $\circ$. That is, $x$ is invertible : $\exists y \in S: x \circ y = e_S = y \circ x$

title: Definition:Invertible Fractional Ideal
snippet: Let $R$ be an integral domain with fraction field $K$. Let $I\subseteq K$ be a fractional ideal of $R$. Then $I$ is invertible there exists a fractional ideal $J\subseteq K$ such that their product is the unit ideal of $R$: $I J = \ideal 1$

title: Definition:Invertible Operation
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. The operation $\circ$ is invertible : $\forall a, b \in S: \exists r, s \in S: a \circ r = b = s \circ a$

title: Definition:Involute
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a curve $C$ embedded in a plane.

title: Definition:Involute/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a curve embedded in a plane. Let $\LL$ be the locus of a fixed point on a tangent to $\CC$ as it rolls around $\CC$. The curve $\LL$ is the involute of $\CC$.

title: Definition:Involute/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a curve embedded in a plane. Imagine an ideal (zero thickness) cord $K$ wound round $\CC$. The involute of $\CC$ is the locus of the end of $K$ as it is unwound from $\CC$.

title: Definition:Involute/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Involute == The concept of the involute of a curve in the plane was first introduced by during his analysis of the cycloid in his $1673$ treatise .

title: Definition:Involution
snippet: Real Analysis: Involution: another word for raising a number to a power. Mapping Theory: An involution is a mapping which is its own inverse. Abstract Algebra: Another term for a self-inverse element of a monoid. Involution on Algebra

title: Definition:Involution (Mapping)
snippet: Let $A$ be a set. Let $f: A \to A$ be a mapping on $A$.

title: Definition:Involution (Mapping)/Also known as
snippet: == Involution: Also known as == An involution is also known as an involutive mapping or an involutive function. An involutive mapping can also be found described as self-inverse. Category:Definitions/Involutions

title: Definition:Involution (Mapping)/Definition 1
snippet: Let $A$ be a set. Let $f: A \to A$ be a mapping on $A$. $f$ is an involution : $\forall x \in A: \map f {\map f x} = x$ That is: $f \circ f = I_A$ where $I_A$ denotes the identity mapping on $A$.

title: Definition:Involution (Mapping)/Definition 2
snippet: Let $A$ be a set. Let $f: A \to A$ be a mapping on $A$. $f$ is an involution : $\forall x, y \in A: \map f x = y \implies \map f y = x$

title: Definition:Involution (Mapping)/Definition 3
snippet: Let $A$ be a set. Let $f: A \to A$ be a mapping on $A$. $f$ is an involution $f$ is both a bijection and a symmetric relation. That is, $f$ is a bijection such that: $f = f^{-1}$

title: Definition:Involution on Algebra
snippet: Let $A$ be an algebra over $\C$. Let $\ast : A \to A$ be a mapping satisfying: {{axiom | n = \text C^* 1 | q = \forall x \in A | ml= x^{**} | mo= = | mr= x }} {{axiom | n = \text C^* 2 | q = \forall x \in A | ml= x^* + y^* | mo= = | mr= \paren {x + y}^* }} {{axiom | n = \text C^* 3 | q = \forall x, y \in A | ml= x^* y^* | mo= = | mr= \paren {y x}^* }} {{axiom | n = \text C^* 4 | q = \forall x \in A, c \in \C | ml= \paren {c x}^* | mo= = | mr= \overline c \paren x^* }} We call $\ast$ an involution on $A$.

title: Definition:Involutory Matrix
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a square matrix of order $n$. $\mathbf A$ is an involutory matrix : $\mathbf A^2 = \mathbf I_n$ where $\mathbf I_n$ is the identity matrix of order $n$.

title: Definition:Ion
snippet: An ion is an atom or a fragment of a molecule which has an electric charge on it through having either more or fewer electrons than protons.

title: Definition:Ionization
snippet: Ionization is a process which either removes one or more electrons from, or adds one or more electrons to, an atom.

title: Definition:Iron/54
snippet: == Isotope of Iron == Iron-$54$ is the isotope of iron which has $28$ neutrons in addition to its $26$ protons. Fe-$54$ is one of the $4$ stable isotopes of iron, forming $5.85 \%$ of the naturally occurring iron.

title: Definition:Iron/55
snippet: == Isotope of Iron == Iron-$55$ is the isotope of iron which has $29$ neutrons in addition to its $26$ protons. Fe-$55$ is radioactive, with a half-life of approximately $2.73$ years. Fe-$55$ does not occur naturally.

title: Definition:Iron/56
snippet: == Isotope of Iron == Iron-$56$ is the isotope of iron which has $30$ neutrons in addition to its $26$ protons. Fe-$56$ is the most common of the $4$ stable isotopes of iron, forming $91.8 \%$ of the naturally occurring iron.

title: Definition:Iron/57
snippet: == Isotope of Iron == Iron-$57$ is the isotope of iron which has $31$ neutrons in addition to its $26$ protons. Fe-$57$ is one of the $4$ stable isotopes of iron, forming $2.12 \%$ of the naturally occurring iron.

title: Definition:Iron/58
snippet: == Isotope of Iron == Iron-$58$ is the isotope of iron which has $32$ neutrons in addition to its $26$ protons. Fe-$58$ is one of the $4$ stable isotopes of iron, forming $0.28 \%$ of the naturally occurring iron.

title: Definition:Iron/59
snippet: == Isotope of Iron == Iron-$59$ is the isotope of iron which has $33$ neutrons in addition to its $26$ protons. Fe-$59$ is radioactive, with a half-life of approximately $44.6$ days. Fe-$59$ does not occur naturally.

title: Definition:Iron/60
snippet: == Isotope of Iron == Iron-$60$ is the isotope of iron which has $34$ neutrons in addition to its $26$ protons. Fe-$60$ is radioactive, with a half-life of approximately $2.6 \times 10^6$ years. Fe-$60$ exists on Earth as traces only.

title: Definition:Iron/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Iron == The word iron is pronounced i-on. That is, the r is silent. The symbol Fe used for iron derives from its Latin name ferrum. Category:Linguistic Notes
