title: Definition:Irrational Area
snippet: An irrational area is a geometric figure whose area is an irrational number of units of area. '

title: Definition:Irrational Line Segment
snippet: An irrational line segment is a line segment such that the square of whose length is an irrational number of units of area. '

title: Definition:Irrational Number
snippet: An irrational number is a real number which is not rational. That is, an irrational number is one that can not be expressed in the form $\dfrac p q$ such that $p$ and $q$ are both integers. The set of irrational numbers can therefore be expressed as $\R \setminus \Q$, where: $\R$ is the set of real numbers $\Q$ is the set of rational numbers $\setminus$ denotes set difference.

title: Definition:Irrational Number/Approximation
snippet: From its definition, it is not possible to express an irrational number precisely in terms of a fraction. From Basis Expansion of Irrational Number, it is not possible to express it precisely by a decimal expansion either. However, it is possible to express it to an arbitrary level of precision. Let $x$ be an irrational number whose decimal expansion is $\sqbrk {n.d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots}_{10}$. Then: $\ds n + \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^k \frac {d_j} {10^j} \le x < n + \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^k \frac {d_j} {10^j} + \frac 1 {10^k}$ for all $k \in \Z: k \ge 1$.

title: Definition:Irrational Number/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Irrational Number == It was the ancient Greeks who discovered that the irrational numbers were indispensable in geometry. They were famously discovered by the Pythagoreans. Some sources suggest that this discovery is one of their more important contributions towards civilisation.

title: Definition:Irrational Number/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Irrational Number == The name irrational number is strictly speaking derived from the fact that such a number cannot be defined as the ratio of two integers. It is arguable as to whether the name also has connotations of being nonsensical or beyond reason. The ancient Greeks, whose term for an irrational number was alogon, which evoked a feeling of undesirably chaotic and unstructured, or, perhaps more literally: illogical.

title: Definition:Irrational Number Space
snippet: Let $\mathbb I := \R \setminus \Q$ be the set of irrational numbers. Let $d: \mathbb I \times \mathbb I \to \R$ be the Euclidean metric on $\mathbb I$. Let $\tau_d$ be the topology on $\mathbb I$ induced by $d$. Then $\struct {\mathbb I, \tau_d}$ is the irrational number space.

title: Definition:Irrational Slope Topology
snippet: Let $S = \set {\tuple {x, y}: y \ge 0, x, y \in \Q}$. Let $\theta \in \R \setminus \Q$ be some fixed irrational number. length $\epsilon$]] Let $\BB$ be the set of $\epsilon$-neighborhoods of the form: $\map {N_\epsilon} {x, y} = \set {\tuple {x, y} } \cup \map {B_\epsilon} {x + \dfrac y \theta} \cup \map {B_\epsilon} {x - \dfrac y \theta}$ where: $\map {B_\epsilon} \zeta := \set {r \in \Q: \size {r - \zeta} < \epsilon}$ that is, the open $\epsilon$-ball at $\zeta$ in $\Q^2$.

title: Definition:Irreducible
snippet: Ring Theory: Irreducible Element: An element of an integral domain $D$ is irreducible it has no non-trivial factorization in $D$. Irreducible Polynomial: A polynomial is irreducible over a field it cannot be represented as the product of two or more non-constant polynomials over that field. Topology: Irreducible Space: A topological space is irreducible it cannot be represented as a decomposition of closed sets.

title: Definition:Irreducible (Representation Theory)/G-Module
snippet: A $G$-module is irreducible the corresponding linear representation is irreducible. That is, any proper $G$-submodule is trivial.

title: Definition:Irreducible (Representation Theory)/Linear Representation
snippet: Let $\rho: G \to \GL V$ be a linear representation. Then $\rho$ is irreducible it is not reducible. That is, there exists no non-trivial proper vector subspace $W$ of $V$ such that: $\forall g \in G: \map {\map \rho g} W \subseteq W$

title: Definition:Irreducible Case of Cubic
snippet: Let $P$ be the cubic equation: $a x^3 + b x^2 + c x + d = 0$ such that $a, b, c, d \in \R$ with $a \ne 0$. $P$ is an instance of the irreducible case the discriminant is less than $0$. That is, when $P$ has $3$ real unequal roots.

title: Definition:Irreducible Case of Cubic/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Irreducible Case of Cubic == The irreducible case of the cubic was the one which caused difficulty in Cardano's Formula for its solution. This is because it leads to manipulations that require the cube root of an imaginary number. When this area of algebra was initiated, no such concept was understood.

title: Definition:Irreducible Character
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \cdot}$ be a finite group. Let $V$ be a finite dimensional vector space over a field $F$. Consider a linear representation: $\rho: G \to \GL V$ of $G$ where $\GL V$ denotes the general linear group over $V$. For $g \in G$, let $\map \tr {\map \rho g}$ denote the trace of $\map \rho g$. Let $\chi_\rho: G \to F$ denote the character associated with $\rho$. Then $\chi_\rho$ is irreducible the linear representation $\rho$ is irreducible.

title: Definition:Irreducible Component
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. A subset $Y \subseteq S$ is an irreducible component of $T$ : $Y$ is irreducible $Y$ is not a proper subset of an irreducible subset of $S$. That is, : $Y$ is maximal in the ordered set of irreducible subsets of $S$, ordered by the subset relation.

title: Definition:Irreducible Element of Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {D, +, \circ}$ be an integral domain whose zero is $0_D$. Let $\struct {U_D, \circ}$ be the group of units of $\struct {D, +, \circ}$. Let $x \in D: x \notin U_D, x \ne 0_D$, that is, $x$ is non-zero and not a unit.

title: Definition:Irreducible Element of Ring/Also defined as
snippet: == Irreducible Element of Ring: Also defined as == Some sources define the concept of an irreducible element only on an integral domain $\struct {D, +, \circ}$ which is also Euclidean. Category:Definitions/Irreducible Elements of Rings

title: Definition:Irreducible Element of Ring/Also known as
snippet: == Irreducible Element of Ring: Also known as == An irreducible element of a ring is also known as an atom of a ring, hence described as atomic. Some sources refer to such an element as a prime element of the ring in question.

title: Definition:Irreducible Element of Ring/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {D, +, \circ}$ be an integral domain whose zero is $0_D$. Let $\struct {U_D, \circ}$ be the group of units of $\struct {D, +, \circ}$. Let $x \in D: x \notin U_D, x \ne 0_D$, that is, $x$ is non-zero and not a unit. $x$ is defined as irreducible it has no non-trivial factorization in $D$. That is, $x$ cannot be written as a product of two non-units.

title: Definition:Irreducible Element of Ring/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {D, +, \circ}$ be an integral domain whose zero is $0_D$. Let $\struct {U_D, \circ}$ be the group of units of $\struct {D, +, \circ}$. Let $x \in D: x \notin U_D, x \ne 0_D$, that is, $x$ is non-zero and not a unit. $x$ is defined as irreducible the only divisors of $x$ are its associates and the units of $D$. That is, $x$ has no proper divisors.

title: Definition:Irreducible Equation
snippet: An irreducible equation is an equation of the form: $P = 0$ where $P$ is a irreducible polynomial.

title: Definition:Irreducible Fraction
snippet: A vulgar fraction $q = \dfrac a b$ is irreducible the numerator $a$ and denominator $b$ are coprime.

title: Definition:Irreducible Logical Matrix
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_k$ be a square logical matrix. $\mathbf A$ is irreducible : $\forall i, j \in \closedint 1 k : \exists n \in \Z_{>0}$: element $\tuple {i, j}$ of $\mathbf A^n$ is strictly positive where $\mathbf A^n$ denotes the $n$th power of $\mathbf A$.

title: Definition:Irreducible Markov Chain
snippet: Let $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \ge 0}$ be a Markov chain whose state space is $S$. Let $\sequence {X_n}$ be such that there exists exactly one communicating class over $S$. Then the $\sequence {X_n}$ is known as an irreducible Markov chain.

title: Definition:Irreducible Polynomial
snippet: An irreducible polynomial is a polynomial which is not reducible.

title: Definition:Irreducible Polynomial/Definition 1
snippet: Let $R$ be an integral domain. An irreducible polynomial over $R$ is an irreducible element of the polynomial ring $R \sqbrk X$.

title: Definition:Irreducible Polynomial/Definition 2
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. An irreducible polynomial over $K$ is a nonconstant polynomial over $K$ that is not the product of two polynomials of smaller degree.

title: Definition:Irreducible Polynomial/Definition 3
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. An irreducible polynomial over $K$ is a polynomial over $K$ that is not the product of two nonconstant polynomials.

title: Definition:Irreducible Radical
snippet: An irreducible radical is a radical that cannot be written in a form that does not include a radical.

title: Definition:Irreducible Representation
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $V$ be a $G$-representation. Then $V$ is irreducible the only subrepresentations are $V$ and $0$. Category:Definitions/Representation Theory

title: Definition:Irreducible Scheme
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ be a scheme. Then $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ is irreducible $X$ is an irreducible space.

title: Definition:Irreducible Space/Also known as
snippet: == Irreducible Space: Also known as == An irreducible space is also known as:

title: Definition:Irreducible Space/Definition 1
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is irreducible there exists no cover of $T$ by two proper closed sets of $T$.

title: Definition:Irreducible Space/Definition 2
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is irreducible there is no finite cover of $T$ by proper closed sets of $T$.

title: Definition:Irreducible Space/Definition 3
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is irreducible every two non-empty open sets of $T$ have non-empty intersection: $\forall U, V \in \tau: U, V \ne \O \implies U \cap V \ne \O$

title: Definition:Irreducible Space/Definition 4
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is irreducible every non-empty open set of $T$ is (everywhere) dense in $T$.

title: Definition:Irreducible Space/Definition 5
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is irreducible the interior of every proper closed set of $T$ is empty.

title: Definition:Irreducible Space/Definition 6
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is irreducible the closure of every non-empty open set is the whole space: $\forall U \in \tau: U \ne \O \implies U^- = S$

title: Definition:Irreducible Space/Definition 7
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is irreducible every open set of $T$ is connected.

title: Definition:Irreducible Space/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Irreducible Space == The thinking behind applying the word irreducible to the concept of an irreducible space arises as follows. By definition, we cannot express $X$ as the union of two proper closed sets of $T$. Expressing a space as the union of two smaller closed sets can be considered as reducing it. There are parallels with the concept of an irreducible element of a ring in abstract algebra, which cannot be written as a product of two non-units.

title: Definition:Irreducible Subset
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $A \subseteq S$ be non-empty. Let $\tau_A$ be the subspace topology on $A$ induced by $\tau$. Then $A$ is an irreducible subset (of $S$ in $T$) $\struct {A, \tau_A}$ is an irreducible space.

title: Definition:Irreducible Subset (Topology)
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $A$ be a subset of $S$. Then $A$ is irreducible (subset) $A$ is non-empty and closed and for all closed subsets $B, C$ of $S$: $A = B \cup C \implies A = B$ or $A = C$

title: Definition:Irreflexive Relation/Also defined as
snippet: == Irreflexive Relation: Also defined as == Some sources define an irreflexive relation to be a relation which is not reflexive. Hence, under such a definition, an antireflexive relation would also be classified as an irreflexive relation. Because of such ambiguity of usage, the term irreflexive relation is deprecated on .

title: Definition:Irrotational Motion
snippet: Let $B$ be a body which is in motion. Let the velocities of the individual particles of $B$ be defined by a vector field $\mathbf V$ over $B$. Let the curl of $\mathbf V$ be zero. Then the motion of $B$ is described as being irrotational.

title: Definition:Ishango Bone
snippet: The Ishango bone is a mathematical tool made from a leg bone of a baboon, dating from approximately $25 \ 000$ years ago. It bears a system of markings which may be tally marks, but may in fact be for a more complex purpose. It was found in $1960$ by in the (now the ). It was discovered in the area of near the . One row of marks contains the prime numbers between $10$ and $20$, that is, $11$, $13$, $17$ and $19$, which total $60$. Another row contains $9$, $11$, $19$ and $21$, which also total $60$.

title: Definition:Isobar
snippet: An isobar is a contour line on a weather map indicating points of equal atmospheric pressure.

title: Definition:Isogonal
snippet: Isogonal means having equal angles. However, used as a modifier for polgon and polyhedron, the definition is usually somewhat more subtle, as follows.

title: Definition:Isogonal/Also known as
snippet: == Isogonal: Also known as == The term vertex-transitive has become a popular alternative to isogonal in recent years, in accordance with its definition in the context of graph theory. The word isogonic means the same as isogonal, and sometimes appears.

title: Definition:Isogonal/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Isogonal == The word isogonal derives from the Greek for equal angles. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Isogonal Conjugate
snippet: Let $X$ be a point in the plane containing a triangle $ABC$. 700px Let $A X_A$, $B X_B$ and $C X_C$ be the reflections of the lines $AX$, $BX$, and $CX$ about the angle bisectors at $A$, $B$, and $C$ respectively. The isogonal conjugate of $X$ $\triangle ABC$ is the point $X^{-1}$ at which $A X_A$, $B X_B$ and $C X_C$ concur.

title: Definition:Isogonal Polygon
snippet: Let $P$ be a polygon. Let $P$ be such that it has the property that each vertex can be mapped to every other vertex by means of a symmetry mapping on $P$. Then $P$ is an isogonal polygon.

title: Definition:Isogonal Polygon/Also defined as
snippet: == Isogonal Polygon: Also defined as == Some sources define the term isogonal polygon or isogon to be a synonym for equiangular polygon. However, note that an equiangular polygon is not necessarily isogonal.

title: Definition:Isogonal Polygon/Also known as
snippet: == Isogonal Polygon: Also known as == An isogonal polygon is also known as: an isogon a vertex-transitive polygon.

title: Definition:Isogonal Polyhedron
snippet: Let $P$ be a polyhedron. Let $P$ be such that it has the property that each vertex can be mapped to every other vertex by means of a symmetry mapping on $P$. Then $P$ is an isogonal polyhedron.

title: Definition:Isogonal Polyhedron/Also known as
snippet: == Isogonal Polyhedron: Also known as == The term vertex-transitive polyhedron has become a popular alternative to isogonal polyhedron in recent years, in accordance with its definition in the context of graph theory.

title: Definition:Isohedral Polyhedron
snippet: Let $P$ be a polyhedron. Let $P$ be such that it has the property that each face can be mapped to every other face by means of a symmetry on $P$. Then $P$ is described as an isohedral polyhedron.

title: Definition:Isohedral Polyhedron/Also known as
snippet: == Isohedral Polyhedron: Also known as == The term face-transitive polyhedron has become a popular alternative to isohedral polyhedron in recent years. The term face-regular polyhedron can also be found.

title: Definition:Isohedral Polyhedron/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Isohedral Polyhedron == The word isohedral derives from the Greek for equal faces. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Isolated Point (Complex Analysis)
snippet: Let $S \subseteq \C$ be a subset of the set of real numbers. Let $z \in S$. Then $z$ is an isolated point of $S$ there exists a neighborhood of $z$ in $\C$ which contains no points of $S$ except $z$: $\exists \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \map {N_\epsilon} z \cap S = \set z$ By definition of neighborhood in the context of the complex plane under the usual (Euclidean) metric: $\map {N_\epsilon} z := \set {y \in S: \cmod {z - y} 0}: \set {y \in S: \cmod {z - y} < \epsilon} \cap S = \set z$ Category:Definitions/Complex Analysis

title: Definition:Isolated Point (Metric Space)
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space.

title: Definition:Isolated Point (Metric Space)/Space
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. $a \in A$ is an isolated point of $M$ there exists an open $\epsilon$-ball of $x$ containing no points other than $a$: $\exists \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \map {B_\epsilon} a = \set a$ That is: $\exists \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \set {x \in A: \map d {x, a} < \epsilon} = \set a$

title: Definition:Isolated Point (Metric Space)/Subset
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. Let $S \subseteq A$ be a subset of $A$. $a \in S$ is an isolated point of $S$ there exists an open $\epsilon$-ball of $x$ in $M$ containing no points of $S$ other than $a$: $\exists \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \map {B_\epsilon} a \cap S = \set a$ That is: $\exists \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \set {x \in S: \map d {x, a} < \epsilon} = \set a$

title: Definition:Isolated Point (Real Analysis)
snippet: Let $S \subseteq \R$ be a subset of the set of real numbers. Let $\alpha \in S$. Then $\alpha$ is an isolated point of $S$ there exists an open interval of $\R$ whose midpoint is $\alpha$ which contains no points of $S$ except $\alpha$: $\exists \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \openint {\alpha - \epsilon} {\alpha + \epsilon} \cap S = \set \alpha$ By definition of $\epsilon$-neighborhood in the context of the real number line under the usual (Euclidean) metric: $\map {N_\epsilon} \alpha := \openint {\alpha - \epsilon} {\alpha + \epsilon}$ it can be seen that this definition is compatible with that for a…

title: Definition:Isolated Point (Topology)
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space.

title: Definition:Isolated Point (Topology)/Space
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. $x \in S$ is an isolated point of $T$ : $\exists U \in \tau: U = \set x$ That is, there exists an open set of $T$ containing no points of $S$ other than $x$.

title: Definition:Isolated Point (Topology)/Subset
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$.

title: Definition:Isolated Point of Subset/Definition 1
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. $x \in H$ is an isolated point of $H$ : $\exists U \in \tau: U \cap H = \set x$ That is, there exists an open set of $T$ containing no points of $H$ other than $x$.

title: Definition:Isolated Point of Subset/Definition 2
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. $x \in H$ is an isolated point of $H$ $x$ is not a limit point of $H$. That is, $x$ is not in the derived set of $H$.

title: Definition:Isolated Singularity/Complex Function
snippet: Let $U \subseteq \C$ be an open set. Let $f : U \to \C$ be a holomorphic function. An isolated singularity of $f$ is a point $z_0 \in \C$ for which $U$ is a punctured neighborhood.

title: Definition:Isolated Singularity/Pole
snippet: Let $U$ be an open subset of a Riemann surface. Let $z_0 \in U$. Let $f: U \setminus \set {z_0} \to \C$ be a holomorphic function.

title: Definition:Isolated Singularity/Pole/Definition 1
snippet: Let $U$ be an open subset of a Riemann surface. Let $z_0 \in U$. Let $f: U \setminus \set {z_0} \to \C$ be a holomorphic function. Let $z_0$ be an isolated singularity of $f$. Then $z_0$ is a pole : $\ds \lim_{z \mathop \to z_0} \cmod {\map f z} \to \infty$

title: Definition:Isolated Singularity/Pole/Definition 2
snippet: Let $U$ be an open subset of a Riemann surface. Let $z_0 \in U$. Let $f: U \setminus \set {z_0} \to \C$ be a holomorphic function. Let $z_0$ be an isolated singularity of $f$. Then $z_0$ is a pole $f$ can be written in the form: $\map f z = \dfrac {\map \phi z} {\paren {z - z_0}^k}$ where: $\phi$ is analytic at $z_0$ $\map \phi {z_0} \ne 0$ $k \in \Z$ such that $k \ge 1$.

title: Definition:Isolated Singularity/Riemann Surface
snippet: Let $U$ be an open set of a Riemann surface. Let $z_0 \in U$. Let $f: U \setminus \set {z_0} \to \C$ be a holomorphic function. Then $f$ has an isolated singularity at $z_0$. In most applications, the Riemann surface in question is the complex plane or the Riemann sphere.

title: Definition:Isolated Type
snippet: Let $T$ be an $\LL$-theory. Let $\map \phi {\bar v}$ be an $\LL$-formula in $n$ free variables $\bar v$ such that $T \cup \map \phi {\bar v}$ is satisfiable. Let $p$ be an $n$-type of $T$. We say that $\phi$ isolates $p$ for all $\psi \in p$, we have: $T \models \forall \map {\bar v} {\map \phi {\bar v} \rightarrow \map \psi {\bar v} }$ that is, all $\psi$ are semantic consequences of $\phi$.

title: Definition:Isolated Vertex
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be an undirected graph. Let $v \in V$ be a vertex of $G$. If the degree of $v$ is zero, then $v$ is an isolated vertex.

title: Definition:Isolated Zero
snippet: Let $f: \C \to \C$ be a complex function. Let $\map f {z_0} = 0$ for some $z_0 \in \C$. We say $z_0$ is an isolated zero of $f$ there exists an open ball $B$ containing $z_0$, such that $\map f w \ne 0$ for all $w \in B \setminus \set {z_0}$. Category:Definitions/Complex Analysis

title: Definition:Isolation of Root
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an equation which is dependent upon a real variable $x$. Isolation of a root $x$ of $\EE$ is the process of finding two numbers between which $x$ lies.

title: Definition:Isometric Equivalence of Basic Sequences
snippet:
Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ and $\struct {Y, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_Y}$ be normed vector spaces over $\GF$. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a basic sequence in $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ and $\sequence {y_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a basic sequence in $\struct {Y, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_Y}$. Let $\sqbrk {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ and $\sqbrk {y_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be the closed linear spans of $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ and $\sequence {y_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ respectively.

title: Definition:Isometric Group Action
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $G$ be a group. Suppose $\forall \phi \in G$ the mapping $x \mapsto \phi \cdot x$ is an isometry. Then the group action is said to be an isometric action

title: Definition:Isometric Immersion
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$, $\struct {\tilde M, \tilde g}$ be Riemannian manifolds. Let $F : M \to \tilde M$ be an immersion such that $F^* \tilde g = g$. Then $F$ is called an isometric immersion.

title: Definition:Isometric Isomorphism/Normed Division Ring
snippet:
Let $\struct {R, 
orm {\,\cdot\,}_R}$ and $\struct {S, 
orm {\,\cdot\,}_S}$ be normed division rings. Let $d_R$ and $d_S$ be the metric induced by the norms $
orm {\,\cdot\,}_R$ and $
orm {\,\cdot\,}_S$ respectively. Let $\phi:R 	o S$ be a bijection such that: $(1): \quad \phi: \struct {R, d_R} 	o \struct {S, d_S}$ is an isometry $(2): \quad \phi: R 	o S$ is a ring isomorphism. Then $\phi$ is called an isometric isomorphism. The normed division rings $\struct {R, 
orm {\,\cdot\,}_R}$ and $\struct {S, 
orm {\,\cdot\,}_S}$ are said to be isometrically isomorphic.

title: Definition:Isometric Isomorphism/Normed Vector Space
snippet:
Let $\struct {X, 
orm \cdot_X}$ and $\struct {Y, 
orm \cdot_Y}$ be normed vector spaces. Let $T : X 	o Y$ be a linear isometry. We say that $T$ is an isometric isomorphism $T$ is bijective. If an isometric isomorphism $T : X 	o Y$ exists, we say that $\struct {X, 
orm \cdot_X}$ and $\struct {Y, 
orm \cdot_Y}$ are isometrically isomorphic.

title: Definition:Isometry (*-Algebras)
snippet: Let $\struct {A, \ast}$ be a unital $\ast$-algebra. Let $a \in A$. Let $\mathbf 1_A$ be the identity element of $A$. We say that $a$ is an isometry $a^\ast a = \mathbf 1_A$.

title: Definition:Isometry (Euclidean Geometry)
snippet: Let $\EE$ be a real Euclidean space. Let $\phi: \EE \to \EE$ be a bijection such that: $\forall P, Q \in \EE: PQ = P'Q'$ where: $P$ and $Q$ are arbitrary points in $\EE$ $P'$ and $Q'$ are the images of $P$ and $Q$ respectively $PQ$ and $P'Q'$ denote the lengths of the straight line segments $PQ$ and $P'Q'$ respectively. Then $\phi$ is an isometry. That is, an isometry is a bijection which preserves distance between points.

title: Definition:Isometry (Euclidean Geometry)/Also known as
snippet: == Isometry in the context of Euclidean Geometry: Also known as == An isometry is also known as an isometric mapping, or an isometric map. Texts which approach the subject from the direction of applied mathematics and physics may refer to an isometry as a rigid motion.

title: Definition:Isometry (Euclidean Geometry)/Context
snippet: An isometry is defined usually for either: $n = 2$, representing the plane or: $n = 3$, representing ordinary space.

title: Definition:Isometry (Euclidean Geometry)/Direct
snippet: In the context of Euclidean geometry, a direct isometry is an isometry which preserves orientation. That is, an isometry which is sense-preserving.

title: Definition:Isometry (Euclidean Geometry)/Indirect
snippet: In the context of Euclidean geometry, an indirect isometry is an isometry which reverses orientation. That is, an isometry which is sense-reversing.

title: Definition:Isometry (Hilbert Spaces)
snippet: Let $H$ and $K$ be Hilbert spaces. Let their inner products be $\innerprod \cdot \cdot_H$ and $\innerprod \cdot \cdot_K$ respectively. A linear map $U: H \to K$ is called an isometry : $\forall g,h \in H: \innerprod g h_H = \innerprod {U g} {U h}_K$

title: Definition:Isometry (Inner Product Spaces)
snippet: Let $V$ and $W$ be inner product spaces. Let their inner products be $\innerprod \cdot \cdot_V$ and $\innerprod \cdot \cdot_W$ respectively. Let the mapping $F : V \to W$ be a vector space isomorphism that preserves inner products: $\forall v_1, v_2 \in V : \innerprod {v_1} {v_2}_V = \innerprod {\map F {v_1}} {\map F {v_2}}_W$ Then $F$ is called a (linear) isometry.

title: Definition:Isometry (Metric Spaces)/Also defined as
snippet: == Isometry in the context of Metric Spaces: Also defined as == Some sources do not insist that an isometry be surjective. Make sure to know which prerequisites are used when quoting results about isometries.

title: Definition:Isometry (Metric Spaces)/Also known as
snippet: == Isometry in the context of Metric Spaces: Also known as == An isometry is also known as a metric equivalence. Two isometric spaces can also be referred to as metrically equivalent.

title: Definition:Isometry (Metric Spaces)/Definition 1
snippet: Let $M_1 = \tuple {A_1, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \tuple {A_2, d_2}$ be metric spaces or pseudometric spaces. Let $\phi: A_1 \to A_2$ be a bijection such that: $\forall a, b \in A_1: \map {d_1} {a, b} = \map {d_2} {\map \phi a, \map \phi b}$ Then $\phi$ is called an isometry. That is, an isometry is a distance-preserving bijection.

title: Definition:Isometry (Metric Spaces)/Definition 2
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct {A_1, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct {A_2, d_2}$ be metric spaces or pseudometric spaces. $M_1$ and $M_2$ are isometric there exist inverse mappings $\phi: A_1 \to A_2$ and $\phi^{-1}: A_2 \to A_1$ such that: $\forall a, b \in A_1: \map {d_1} {a, b} = \map {d_2} {\map \phi a, \map \phi b}$ and: $\forall u, v \in A_2: \map {d_2} {u, v} = \map {d_1} {\map {\phi^{-1} } u, \map {\phi^{-1} } v}$

title: Definition:Isometry (Metric Spaces)/Into
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct {A_1, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct {A_2, d_2}$ be metric spaces or pseudometric spaces. Let $\phi: A_1 \to A_2$ be an injection such that: $\forall a, b \in A_1: \map {d_1} {a, b} = \map {d_2} {\map \phi a, \map \phi b}$ Then $\phi$ is called an isometry (from $M_1$) into $M_2$. That is, an isometry (from $M_1$) into $M_2$ is an isometry which is not actually a surjection, but satisfies the other conditions for being an isometry.

title: Definition:Isometry (Riemannian Manifolds)
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ and $\struct {\tilde M, \tilde g}$ be Riemannian manifolds with Riemannian metrics $g$ and $\tilde g$ respectively. Let the mapping $\phi : M \to \tilde M$ be a diffeomorphism such that: $\phi^* \tilde g = g$ Then $\phi$ is called an isometry from $\struct {M, g}$ to $\struct {\tilde M, \tilde g}$.

title: Definition:Isometry Group of Riemannian Manifold
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $\phi : M \to M$ be an isometry of $\struct {M, g}$. The set of all $\phi$ is called the isometry group of $\struct {M, g}$ and is denoted by $\map {\text {Iso}} {M, g}$.

title: Definition:Isometry of Riemannian Manifold
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $\phi : M \to M$ be an isometry such that: $\phi^* g = g$ Then $\phi$ is called the isometry of $\struct {M, g}$.

title: Definition:Isomorphic Objects (Category Theory)
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a category, and let $X, Y$ be objects of $\mathbf C$ $X$ and $Y$ are isomorphic objects there exists an isomorphism $f: X \to Y$.

title: Definition:Isomorphic Structures
snippet: Let $\AA, \BB$ be structures for a signature $\LL$. Then $\AA$ and $\BB$ are said to be isomorphic there exists an isomorphism between $\AA$ and $\BB$.

title: Definition:Isomorphism
snippet: Isomorphism (Abstract Algebra): An isomorphism between two algebraic structures is a bijection which preserves operations. Group isomorphism: an isomorphism between two groups. Ring isomorphism: an isomorphism between two rings. $R$-algebraic structure isomorphism: an isomorphism between two $R$-algebraic structures. Relation Theory: Relation isomorphism: An isomorphism between two relational structures is a bijection which preserves relations. Order Theory: Order isomorphism: A bijection between two ordered sets which is order-preserving in both directions.

title: Definition:Isomorphism/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Isomorphism == The word isomorphism derives from the Greek morphe (μορφή) meaning form or structure, with the prefix iso- meaning equal. Thus isomorphism means equal structure.

title: Definition:Isomorphism (Abstract Algebra)
snippet: An isomorphism is a homomorphism which is a bijection. That is, it is a mapping which is both a monomorphism and an epimorphism. An algebraic structure $\struct {S, \circ}$ is isomorphic to another algebraic structure $\struct {T, *}$ there exists an isomorphism from $\struct {S, \circ}$ to $\struct {T, *}$, and we can write $S \cong T$ (although notation may vary).

title: Definition:Isomorphism (Abstract Algebra)/F-Isomorphism
snippet: Let $R, S$ be rings with unity. Let $F$ be a subfield of both $R$ and $S$. Let $\phi: R \to S$ be an $F$-homomorphism such that $\phi$ is bijective. Then $\phi$ is an $F$-isomorphism. The relationship between $R$ and $S$ is denoted $R \cong_F S$.

title: Definition:Isomorphism (Abstract Algebra)/Field Isomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +, \circ}$ and $\struct {K, \oplus, *}$ be fields. Let $\phi: F \to K$ be a (field) homomorphism. Then $\phi$ is a field isomorphism $\phi$ is a bijection. That is, $\phi$ is a field isomorphism $\phi$ is both a monomorphism and an epimorphism.

title: Definition:Isomorphism (Abstract Algebra)/Group Isomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ and $\struct {H, *}$ be groups. Let $\phi: G \to H$ be a (group) homomorphism. Then $\phi$ is a group isomorphism $\phi$ is a bijection. That is, $\phi$ is a group isomorphism $\phi$ is both a monomorphism and an epimorphism. If $G$ is isomorphic to $H$, then the notation $G \cong H$ can be used (although notation varies).

title: Definition:Isomorphism (Abstract Algebra)/Isomorphic Copy
snippet: Let $\phi: S \to T$ be an isomorphism. Let $x \in S$. Then $\map \phi x \in T$ is known as the isomorphic copy of $x$ (under $\phi$).

title: Definition:Isomorphism (Abstract Algebra)/Monoid Isomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ and $\struct {T, *}$ be monoids. Let $\phi: S \to T$ be a (monoid) homomorphism. Then $\phi$ is a monoid isomorphism $\phi$ is a bijection. That is, $\phi$ is a monoid isomorphism $\phi$ is both a monomorphism and an epimorphism. If $S$ is isomorphic to $T$, then the notation $S \cong T$ can be used (although notation varies).

title: Definition:Isomorphism (Abstract Algebra)/Ordered Structure Isomorphism
snippet: An ordered structure isomorphism from an ordered structure $\struct {S, \circ, \preceq}$ to another $\struct {T, *, \preccurlyeq}$ is a mapping $\phi: S \to T$ that is both: $(1): \quad$ An isomorphism, that is a bijective homomorphism, from the structure $\struct {S, \circ}$ to the structure $\struct {T, *}$ $(2): \quad$ An order isomorphism from the ordered set $\struct {S, \preceq}$ to the ordered set $\struct {T, \preccurlyeq}$.

title: Definition:Isomorphism (Abstract Algebra)/R-Algebraic Structure Isomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n, \ast}_R$ and $\struct {T, \odot_1, \odot_2, \ldots, \odot_n, \otimes}_R$ be $R$-algebraic structures. Let $\phi: S \to T$ be an $R$-algebraic structure homomorphism. Then $\phi$ is an $R$-algebraic structure isomorphism $\phi$ is a bijection.

title: Definition:Isomorphism (Abstract Algebra)/R-Algebraic Structure Isomorphism/Module Isomorphism
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $\struct {G, +_G, \circ}_R$ and $\struct {H, +_H, \circ}_R$ be $R$-modules. Let $\phi: G \to H$ be a module homomorphism. Then $\phi$ is a module isomorphism $\phi$ is a bijection.

title: Definition:Isomorphism (Abstract Algebra)/R-Algebraic Structure Isomorphism/Vector Space Isomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {V, +, \circ}$ and $\struct {W, +', \circ'}$ be $K$-vector spaces. Then $\phi: V \to W$ is a vector space isomorphism : $(1): \quad \phi$ is a bijection $(2): \quad \forall \mathbf x, \mathbf y \in V: \map \phi {\mathbf x + \mathbf y} = \map \phi {\mathbf x} +' \map \phi {\mathbf y}$ $(3): \quad \forall \mathbf x \in V: \forall \lambda \in K: \map \phi {\lambda \mathbf x} = \lambda \map \phi {\mathbf x}$ Category:Definitions/Isomorphisms (Abstract Algebra) Category:Definitions/R-Algebraic Structure Isomorphisms Category:Definitions/Linear Algebra

title: Definition:Isomorphism (Abstract Algebra)/Ring Isomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ and $\struct {S, \oplus, *}$ be rings. Let $\phi: R \to S$ be a (ring) homomorphism. Then $\phi$ is a ring isomorphism $\phi$ is a bijection. That is, $\phi$ is a ring isomorphism $\phi$ is both a monomorphism and an epimorphism.

title: Definition:Isomorphism (Abstract Algebra)/Semigroup Isomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ and $\struct {T, *}$ be semigroups. Let $\phi: S \to T$ be a (semigroup) homomorphism. Then $\phi$ is a semigroup isomorphism $\phi$ is a bijection. That is, $\phi$ is a semigroup isomorphism $\phi$ is both a monomorphism and an epimorphism. If $S$ is isomorphic to $T$, then the notation $S \cong T$ can be used (although notation varies).

title: Definition:Isomorphism (Category Theory)
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a category, and let $X, Y$ be objects of $\mathbf C$. A morphism $f: X \to Y$ is an isomorphism there exists a morphism $g: Y \to X$ such that: $g \circ f = \operatorname{id}_X$ $f \circ g = \operatorname{id}_Y$ where $\operatorname{id}_X$ denotes the identity morphism on $X$. It can be seen that this is equivalent to $g$ being both a retraction and a section of $f$.

title: Definition:Isomorphism (Graph Theory)
snippet: Let $G = \struct {\map V G, \map E G}$ and $H = \struct {\map V H, \map E H}$ be graphs. Let there exist a bijection $F: \map V G \to \map V H$ such that: for each edge $\set {u, v} \in \map E G$, there exists an edge $\set {\map F u, \map F v} \in \map E H$. That is, that: $F: \map V G \to \map V H$ is a homomorphism, and $F^{-1}: \map V H \to \map V G$ is a homomorphism. Then $G$ and $H$ are isomorphic, and this is denoted $G \cong H$. The function $F$ is called an isomorphism from $G$ to $H$.

title: Definition:Isomorphism (Hilbert Spaces)
snippet: Let $H, K$ be Hilbert spaces. Denote by $\innerprod \cdot \cdot_H$ and $\innerprod \cdot \cdot_K$ their respective inner products. An isomorphism between $H$ and $K$ is a map $U: H \to K$, such that: $(1): \quad U$ is a linear map $(2): \quad U$ is surjective $(3): \quad \forall g, h \in H: \innerprod g h_H = \innerprod {U g} {U h}_K$ These three requirements may be summarized by stating that $U$ be a surjective isometry. Furthermore, Surjection that Preserves Inner Product is Linear shows that requirement $(1)$ is superfluous.

title: Definition:Isomorphism (Matroid)
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct{S_1, \mathscr I_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct{S_2, \mathscr I_2}$ be matroids. Let $f : S_1 \to S_2$ be a bijection. Then $f$ is called an isomorphism : $\forall X \subseteq S : X \in \mathscr I_1 \iff \map f X \in \mathscr I_2$ If $f$ is an isomorphism then $M_1$ is said to be isomorphic to $M_2$.

title: Definition:Isomorphism (Root System)
snippet: Let $\struct {E, \Phi}$ and $\struct {E', \Phi'}$ be root systems. Then $\phi: E \to E'$ is an isomorphism of root systems : {{axiom | n = 3 | t = $\forall \alpha, \beta \in \Phi: \innerprod {\map \phi \alpha} {\map \phi \beta} = \innerprod \alpha \beta$}}

title: Definition:Isomorphism Class (Algebraic Structures)
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. Let $\map \II {S, \circ}$ be the class of all algebraic structures which are isomorphic to $S$. Then $\map \II {S, \circ}$ is known as the isomorphism class of $\struct {S, \circ}$.

title: Definition:Isomorphism Class (Ordered Structures)
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered structure. Let $\map \II {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be the class of all ordered structures which are order isomorphic to $S$. Then $\map \II {S, \preccurlyeq}$ is known as the isomorphism class of $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$.

title: Definition:Isomorphism between Structures
snippet: Let $\AA, \BB$ be structures for a signature $\LL$. Then an isomorphism between $\AA$ and $\BB$ is a bijection $\Phi: A \to B$ such that: $A$ and $B$ are the respective underlying sets of $\AA$ and $\BB$ For each function symbol $f$ of arity $n$, we have, for all $a_1, \ldots, a_n \in A$: $\map {f_\BB} { \map \Phi {a_1}, \ldots, \map \Phi {a_n} } = \map \Phi { \map {f_\AA} { a_1, \ldots, a_n } }$ For each predicate symbol $p$ of arity $n$, we have, for all $a_1, \ldots, a_n \in A$: $\map {p_\BB} { \map \Phi {a_1}, \ldots, \map \Phi {a_n} } = \map {p_\AA} { a_1, \ldots, a_n }$ Note that in…

title: Definition:Isomorphism of Categories
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. Let $F: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be a functor. Then $F$ is an isomorphism (of categories) there exists a functor $G: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ such that: $G F: \mathbf C \to \mathbf C$ is the identity functor $I_{\mathbf C}$ $F G: \mathbf D \to \mathbf D$ is the identity functor $I_{\mathbf D}$

title: Definition:Isomorphism of Categories/Inverse
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. Let $F: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ and $G: \mathbf D \to \mathbf C$be functors such that: $G F: \mathbf C \to \mathbf C$ is the identity functor $\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}$ $F G: \mathbf D \to \mathbf D$ is the identity functor $\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf D}$ Then: $G$ is called the (two-sided) inverse (isomorphism) of $F$ $F$ is called the (two-sided) inverse (isomorphism) of $G$

title: Definition:Isomorphism of Categories/Isomorphic Categories
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. Let $F: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be an isomorphism of categories. Then $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ are said to be isomorphic, and we write $\mathbf C \cong \mathbf D$.

title: Definition:Isoperimetric Figures
snippet: Two plane figures are defined as being isoperimetric they have equal perimeters.

title: Definition:Isoperimetrical Problem
snippet: An isoperimetrical problem is a mathematical problem that asks what figure has the greatest area of all those figures which have a perimeter of a given length.

title: Definition:Isosceles/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Isosceles == The word isosceles comes from the Greek: $\iota \sigma \omicron \sigma \kappa \epsilon \lambda \epsilon \varsigma$, that is: from iso meaning equal, and skelos meaning leg. Thus an isosceles triangle is literally an equal-leg triangle. It is pronounced eye-sos-ell-eez, that is, with the emphasis on the second syllable. Note that the c is silent. The word skeleton comes from the same linguistic root. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Isosceles Trapezium
snippet: An isosceles trapezium is a trapezium whose legs are the same length. 300px

title: Definition:Isosceles Triangle/Also defined as
snippet: == Isosceles Triangle: Also defined as == Some sources require that in an isosceles triangle, the third side has to be specifically of a different length than the two defined as being equal. Hence, under such a definition, an equilateral triangle would not be classified as isosceles.

title: Definition:Isothermal Surface
snippet: An isothermal surface is an equal surface $S$ embedded in a body $B$ with respect to a temperature field within $B$. That is, it is a surface $S$ embedded in $B$ on which the temperature is equal throughout $S$.

title: Definition:Isotoxal
snippet: A rectilinear geometric figure $F$ is described as isotoxal for every two edges $e$ and $f$ of $F$ there exists a symmetry mapping which takes $e$ to $f$.

title: Definition:Isotoxal/Also known as
snippet: == Isotoxal: Also known as == An isotoxal geometric figure can also be described as: edge-transitive edge-regular.

title: Definition:Isotoxal Polygon
snippet: Let $P$ be a polygon. Let $P$ be such that it has the property that each side can be mapped to every other side by means of a symmetry mapping on $P$. Then $P$ is an isotoxal polygon.

title: Definition:Isotoxal Polygon/Also known as
snippet: == Isotoxal Polygon: Also known as == An isotoxal polygon is also known as: edge-transitive polygon edge-regular polygon.

title: Definition:Isotoxal Polyhedron
snippet: Let $P$ be a polyhedron. Let $P$ be such that it has the property that each edge can be mapped to every other edge by means of a symmetry mapping on $P$. Then $P$ is an isotoxal polyhedron.

title: Definition:Isotoxal Polyhedron/Also known as
snippet: == Isotoxal Polyhedron: Also known as == An isotoxal polyhedron is also known as: an edge-transitive polyhedron an edge-regular polyhedron.

title: Definition:Isotropic Quadratic Form
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be a field of characteristic $\Char {\mathbb K} \ne 2$. Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb K$. Let $q : V\times V \mapsto \mathbb K$ be a quadratic form. Then $q$ is isotropic it represents $0$. That is: $\map q v = 0$ for some $ v \in V \setminus \set 0$.

title: Definition:Isotropic Riemannian Manifold
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Suppose $M$ is isotropic for all points $p \in M$. Then $M$ is said to be isotropic.

title: Definition:Isotropy
snippet: Physics: Isotropy: the property of there being no preferred direction or position Group Theory: Isotropy Group: also known as a stabilizer Riemannian Geometry: Isotropy Representation a linear representation of an isotropy subgroup.

title: Definition:Isotropy/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Isotropy == The word isotropy derives from Ancient Greek: ἴσος (ísos) meaning equal τρόπος (trópos) meaning turn, way or direction. The adjectival form, which is seen more frequently, is isotropic. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Isotropy (Physics)
snippet: Isotropy is a property of a physical system such that measurements of that system are independent of the direction in which those measurements are taken.

title: Definition:Isotropy Representation
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $\map {\text {Iso}} {M, g}$ be the set of all isometries from $M$ to itself. Let $\map {\text {Iso}_p} {M, g}$ be the isotropy subgroup at $p \in M$. That is, let $\map {\text {Iso}_p} {M, g}$ be the subgroup of $\map {\text {Iso}} {M, g}$ consisting of isometries that fix $p \in M$. Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space of $M$ at $p \in M$. For each $\phi \in \map {\text {Iso}_p} {M, g}$ let $\rd \phi_p$ be a linear mapping such that: $\rd \phi_p : T_p M \to T_p M$ Let $\GL {T_p M}$ be the general linear group over $T_p M$.

title: Definition:Iterated Binary Operation/Also denoted as
snippet: == Iterated Binary Operation: Also denoted as == Depending on the notation that is used for the binary operation, alternative notations for the iterated operation are often seen: $+$ becomes $\sum$ $\cap$ becomes $\bigcap$ $*$ and $\cdot$ may become $\prod$ $\oplus$ becomes $\bigoplus$ and so on. Category:Definitions/Binary Operations

title: Definition:Iterated Binary Operation over Finite Set
snippet: Let $\struct {G, *}$ be a commutative semigroup. Let $S$ be a finite non-empty set. Let $f: S \to G$ be a mapping. Let $n \in \N$ be the cardinality of $S$. Let $g: \N_{<n} \to S$ be a bijection, where $\N_{<n}$ is an initial segment of the natural numbers. The iteration of $*$ of $f$ over $S$, denoted $\displaystyle \prod_{s \mathop \in S} \map f s$, is the indexed iteration of $*$ of the composition $f \circ g$ over $\N_{<n}$: $\displaystyle \prod_{s \mathop \in S} \map f s = \displaystyle \prod_{i \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \map f {\map g i}$

title: Definition:Iterated Binary Operation over Set with Finite Support
snippet: Let $\struct {G, *}$ be a commutative monoid. Let $S$ be a set. Let $f: S \to G$ be a mapping. Let the support $\map \supp f$ be finite. The iteration of $*$ of $f$ over $S$, denoted $\ds \prod_{s \mathop \in S} \map f s$, is the iteration over the finite set $\map \supp f$ of $f$: $\ds \prod_{s \mathop \in S} \map f s = \prod_{s \mathop \in \map \supp f} \map f s$

title: Definition:Iterated Mapping
snippet: Let $f: S \to S$ be a self-map. Let an iteration be associated with $f$ thus: $x_{n + 1} = \map f {x_n}$ for $n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$ Then $f$ is an iterated mapping.

title: Definition:Iterated Mapping/Also known as
snippet: == Iterated Mapping: Also known as == An iterated mapping is also known as an iterated map. Some sources refer to it as an iterative mapping or iterative map

title: Definition:Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma
snippet: The iterated prisoner's dilemma is a game whose mechanics are as follows: Player $A$ and $B$ are to play the prisoner's dilemma game repeatedly. The specifics of the scenario are immaterial; the important point is the payoff table:

title: Definition:Iteration
snippet: Iteration is defined as successive repetitions of a mathematical process, using the output of one stage as the input of the next.

title: Definition:Iterative Modelling
snippet: Let $S$ be a stochastic process based on an equispaced time series. Suppose it has been determined that $S$ should be modelled using a hybrid mechanistic and empirical model. It is supposed that the inputs and outputs of $S$ are available for analysis. If possible, at least $50$ and preferably $100$ observations or more should be used. If there are not available as many as that, it is necessary to use experience and past information to make an informed estimate of a preliminary model. As more data becomes available, the model can be updated.

title: Definition:Iverson's Convention
snippet: Iverson's convention is a notation which allows a compact means of assigning a value of $1$ or $0$ to a proposition $P$, depending on whether $P$ is true or false: $\sqbrk P = \begin {cases} 1 & : \text {$P$ is true} \\ 0 & : \text {$P$ is false} \end {cases}$ It is sometimes seen specified as: $\sqbrk P = \begin {cases} 1 & : \text {$P$ is true} \\ 0 & : \text {$P$ otherwise} \end {cases}$ which can be useful in fields of mathematics where the Law of Excluded Middle does not apply. In each case, $0$ is the very strong zero.

title: Definition:Iverson's Convention/Also known as
snippet: == Iverson's Convention: Also known as == Iverson's convention is also known as the Iverson bracket notation.

title: Definition:Iverson's Convention/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Iverson's Convention == The Iverson's convention was invented by in $1962$. The specific use of square brackets was advocated by to avoid ambiguity in parenthesized logical expressions.

title: Definition:Jack-Knife Resampling
snippet: Jack-knife resampling is a statistical technique mainly used for estimation of bias in a sample estimator of a population parameter. It involves computation of the sample estimator with the omission of one observation at a time over the entire set of observations.

title: Definition:Jack-Knife Resampling/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Jack-Knife Resampling == The technique of jack-knife resampling was pioneered by in $1949$.

title: Definition:Jack-Knife Resampling/Motivation
snippet: == Jack-Knife Resampling: Motivation == Jack-knife resampling is particularly useful when there is no analytic theory to estimate bias. This happens, for example, when the correlation coefficient $r$ of the sample is used as an estimator of the correlation coefficient $\rho$ of the population, for other than a bivariate normal distribution. Computation is at this stage equivalent to that for leave-one-out cross-validation. The computations are computer-intensive, and has largely been superseded by the technique of bootstrapping.

title: Definition:Jacobi's Equation of Functional
snippet: Let: $(1): \quad \ds \int_a^b \map F {x, y, y'} \rd x$ be a functional such that: $\map y a = A$ $\map y b = B$ Let: $(2): \quad \ds \int_a^b \paren {P h'^2 + Q h^2} \rd x$ be a quadratic functional such that: $P = \dfrac 1 2 F_{y'y'}$ $Q = \dfrac 1 2 \paren {F_{yy} - \dfrac \d {\d x} F_{yy'} }$ Then Euler's equation of functional $(2)$: $-\map {\dfrac \d {\d x} } {P h'} + Q h = 0$ is called Jacobi's Equation of functional $(1)$.

title: Definition:Jacobi's Equation of Functional/Dependent on N Functions
snippet: Let: $\ds \int_a^b \map F {x, \mathbf y, \mathbf y'} \rd x$ be a (real) functional, where $\map {\mathbf y} a = A$ and $\map {\mathbf y} b = B$. Let: $\ds \int_a^b \paren {\mathbf h' \mathbf P \mathbf h' + \mathbf h \mathbf Q \mathbf h} \rd x$ be a quadratic functional, where: $P_{ij} = \dfrac 1 2 F_{y_i'y_j'}$ $Q_{ij} = \dfrac 1 2 \paren {F_{y_i y_j} - \dfrac \d {\d x} F_{y_i y_j'} }$ Then the Euler's equation of the latter functional: $-\map {\dfrac \d {\d x} } {\mathbf P \mathbf h'} + \mathbf Q \mathbf h = \mathbf 0$ is called Jacobi's Equation of the former functional.

title: Definition:Jacobi's Iterative Method
snippet: Jacobi's iterative method is an iterative method for solving a system $S$ of simultaneous linear equations. Let $\mathbf A \mathbf x = \mathbf b$ be a system of simultaneous linear equations expressed in matrix form. Let $\mathbf A$ be reduced to the form: $\mathbf A = \mathbf D + \mathbf B$ where $\mathbf D$ denotes the diagonal matrix: $D_{i i} : = A_{i i}$ where: $A_{i i}$ and $D_{i i}$ are the elements at the $i$th row and $i$th column of $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf D$ respectively.

title: Definition:Jacobi's Iterative Method/Also known as
snippet: == Jacobi's Iterative Method: Also known as == Jacobi's iterative method is also known just as the Jacobi method.

title: Definition:Jacobi's Iterative Method/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Jacobi's Iterative Method == published his iterative method in $1845$.

title: Definition:Jacobi's Iterative Method/Motivation
snippet: == Jacobi's Iterative Method: Motivation == Jacobi's iterative method was designed for scenarios in which the diagonal elements of the matrices involved are relatively large. Hence matrices which are diagonally dominant are particularly susceptible to this treatment.

title: Definition:Jacobi Identity
snippet: Let $A$ be an nonassociative algebra, whose bilinear mapping is denoted by $\sqbrk {\, \cdot, \cdot \,}$. Then $A$ satisfies the Jacobi identity : $\forall x, y, z \in A: \sqbrk {x, \sqbrk {y, z} } + \sqbrk {y, \sqbrk {z, x} } + \sqbrk {z, \sqbrk {x, y} } = 0$

title: Definition:Jacobi Symbol
snippet: Let $m \in \Z$ be any integer and $n \in \Z$ be any odd integer such that $n \ge 3$. Let the prime decomposition of $n$ be: $\ds n = \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^r p_i^{k_i}$. Then the Jacobi symbol $\paren {\dfrac m n}$ is defined as: $\ds \paren {\frac m n} = \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^r \paren {\frac m {p_i} }^{k_i}$ where $\paren {\dfrac m {p_i} }$ is defined as the Legendre symbol.

title: Definition:Jacobi Theta Function
snippet: The Jacobi theta functions are defined as follows:

title: Definition:Jacobi Theta Function/First Type
snippet: The Jacobi Theta function of the first type is defined as: $\forall z \in \C: \ds \map {\vartheta_1} {z, q} = 2 \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \paren {-1}^n q^{\paren {n + \frac 1 2}^2} \sin \paren {2 n + 1} z$ where: $q = e^{i \pi \tau}$ $\tau \in \C$ such that $\map \Im \tau > 0$

title: Definition:Jacobi Theta Function/Fourth Type
snippet: The Jacobi Theta function of the fourth type is defined as: $\forall z \in \C: \ds \map {\vartheta_4} {z, q} = 1 + 2 \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \paren {-1}^n q^{n^2} \cos 2 n z$ where: $q = e^{i \pi \tau}$ $\tau \in \C$ such that $\map \Im \tau > 0$

title: Definition:Jacobi Theta Function/Second Type
snippet: The Jacobi Theta function of the second type is defined as: $\forall z \in \C: \ds \map {\vartheta_2} {z, q} = 2 \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty q^{\paren {n + \frac 1 2}^2} \map \cos {2 n + 1} z$ where: $q = e^{i \pi \tau}$ $\tau \in \C$ such that $\map \Im \tau > 0$

title: Definition:Jacobi Theta Function/Third Type
snippet: The Jacobi Theta function of the third type is defined for all complex $z$ by: $\forall z \in \C: \ds \map {\vartheta_3} {z, q} = 1 + 2 \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty q^{n^2} \cos 2 n z$ where: $q = e^{i \pi \tau}$ $\tau \in \C$ such that $\map \Im \tau > 0$

title: Definition:Jacobian
snippet: Let $U$ be an open subset of $\R^n$. Let $\mathbf f = \paren {f_1, f_2, \ldots, f_m}^\intercal: U \to \R^m$ be a vector valued function, differentiable at $\mathbf x = \paren {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}^\intercal \in U$.

title: Definition:Jacobian/Also known as
snippet: == Jacobian: Also known as == Note that both the Jacobian determinant and Jacobian matrix are often called just the Jacobian of $\mathbf f$ at $\mathbf x$. It is advisable to use the full term for whichever is intended unless context makes it obvious which one is meant.

title: Definition:Jacobian/Determinant
snippet: The Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf f$ at $\mathbf x$ is defined to be the determinant of the Jacobian matrix: $\quad \map \det {\mathbf J_{\mathbf f} } := \begin {vmatrix} \map {\dfrac {\partial f_1} {\partial x_1} } {\mathbf x} & \map {\dfrac {\partial f_1} {\partial x_2} } {\mathbf x} & \cdots & \map {\dfrac {\partial f_1} {\partial x_n} } {\mathbf x} \\ \map {\dfrac {\partial f_2} {\partial x_1} } {\mathbf x} & \map {\dfrac {\partial f_2} {\partial x_2} } {\mathbf x} & \cdots & \map {\dfrac {\partial f_2} {\partial x_n} } {\mathbf x} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \map {\dfrac…

title: Definition:Jacobian/Matrix
snippet: The Jacobian matrix of $\mathbf f$ at $\mathbf x$ is defined to be the matrix of partial derivatives: $\quad \mathbf J_{\mathbf f} := \begin{pmatrix} \map {\dfrac {\partial f_1} {\partial x_1} } {\mathbf x} & \cdots & \map {\dfrac {\partial f_1} {\partial x_n} } {\mathbf x} \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \map {\dfrac {\partial f_m} {\partial x_1} } {\mathbf x} & \cdots & \map {\dfrac {\partial f_m} {\partial x_n} } {\mathbf x} \end{pmatrix}$

title: Definition:Jacobian Determinant/Also known as
snippet: == Jacobian Determinant: Also known as == The Jacobian determinant is often called just the Jacobian of $\mathbf f$ at $\mathbf x$. However, this can allow it to be confused with the Jacobian matrix, so it is advised to use the full name unless context establishes which is meant. Some sources present this as $\map \det {J_f}$, but boldface for matrices is usual, and standard on . Other sources present it as either $\mathbf J_{\mathbf f}$ or $J_f$, allowing a further source of confusion between this and the Jacobian matrix.

title: Definition:Jacobian Determinant/Also presented as
snippet: == Jacobian Determinant: Also presented as == A Jacobian determinant can also be written as: $\dfrac {\map \partial {f_1, f_2, \ldots, f_n} } {\map \partial {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} }$ or: $\dfrac {\map \partial {u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_n} } {\map \partial {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} }$ where: $u_j = \map {f_j} {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$

title: Definition:Jacobian Matrix/Also known as
snippet: == Jacobian Matrix: Also known as == The Jacobian matrix is often called just the Jacobian of $\mathbf f$ at $\mathbf x$. However, this can allow it to be confused with the Jacobian determinant, so it is advised to use the full name unless context establishes which is meant. Some sources present this as $J_f$, but boldface for matrices is usual, and standard on . Category:Definitions/Jacobian Matrices

title: Definition:Jacobson Radical
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $\map {\operatorname{maxspec}} R$ be the set of maximal ideals of $R$. Then the Jacobson radical of $R$ is: $\ds \map {\operatorname {Jac} } R = \bigcap_{m \mathop \in \map {\operatorname{maxspec}} R} m$ That is, it is the intersection of all maximal ideals of $R$.

title: Definition:Jacobson Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a commutative ring with unity. Then $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ is a Jacobson ring : every prime ideal of $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ is an intersection of maximal ideals.

title: Definition:Jacobson Ring/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Jacobson Ring == The term Jacobson ring was coined by in honour of 's work on the Jacobson radical. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Jaina Mathematics
snippet: Jainism is a religion and philosophy which was founded in India around the $6$th century BCE. Jaina mathematics is mathematics done by those following Jainism. This has been practised on the Indian subcontinent from the founding of Jainism up to modern times.

title: Definition:James Boundary
snippet:
Let $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ be a Banach space over $\R$. Let $\struct {X^\ast, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_{X^\ast} }$ be the normed dual space of $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$.

title: Definition:James Boundary/Bounded Subset
snippet:
Let $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ be a Banach space over $\R$. Let $\struct {X^\ast, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_{X^\ast} }$ be the normed dual space of $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$. Let $C$ be a bounded subset of $X^\ast$. We say that $B \subseteq C$ is a James boundary for $C$ if for each $x \in X$, there exists $g \in B$ such that: $\ds \map g x = \sup_{f \mathop \in C} \map f x$

title: Definition:James Boundary/Normed Dual Space
snippet:
Let $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ be a Banach space over $\R$. Let $\struct {X^\ast, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_{X^\ast} }$ be the normed dual space of $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$. Let $B_{X^\ast}^-$ be the closed unit ball of $\struct {X^\ast, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_{X^\ast} }$. We say that $B \subseteq B_{X^\ast}^-$ is a James boundary for $X$ if it is a James boundary for $B_{X^\ast}^-$.

title: Definition:Jevons' Number
snippet: Jevons' number is the number $8 \, 616 \, 460 \, 799$. It is $89 \, 681 \times 96 \, 079$.

title: Definition:Jevons' Number/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Jevons' Number == In $1874$, made the assertion: Can the reader say what two numbers multiplied together will produce the number $8616460799$? I think it unlikely that anyone but myself will ever know. History has shown that if an assertion akin to the above has been made, at least one mathematician will attempt to refute it. In this case it was who, in $1903$, presented its factorisation to the American Mathematical Society. A contemporary online integer factorisation tool can do the job in a relative instant.

title: Definition:Joachimsthal's Equation/Circle
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a circle whose radius is $r$ and whose center is at the origin of a Cartesian plane. Let $P = \tuple {x_1, y_1}$ be an arbitrary point in the Cartesian plane. Let $\LL$ be a straight line through $P$ which intersects $\CC$ at points $U$ and $V$. Let $Q = \tuple {x, y}$ be a point on $\LL$. Let $V$ divide $PQ$ in the ratio $k : 1$. Joachimsthal's equation is the quadratic equation describing the coordinates of $U$ and $V$: $k^2 \paren {x^2 + y^2 - r^2} + 2 k \paren {x x_1 + y y_1 - r^2} + \paren { {x_1}^2 + {y_1}^2 - r^2} = 0$

title: Definition:Johansson's Minimal Logic
snippet: Johansson's minimal logic is a subbranch of propositional logic of the intuitionist school. The philosophical position behind it is that it may be the case that the proof rules: The (a statement is either true or false) The (from a contradiction anything can be deduced) do not hold. Thus this philosophical school allows for the foundation of the study of fuzzy logic.

title: Definition:Join
snippet: Group theory: Join of Subgroups: the subgroup formed by the union of two subgroups. Boolean algebras: Join: the operation $\vee$ in a Boolean algebra $\struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \neg}$. Order Theory: Join (Order Theory): the supremum of the set formed by two elements of an ordered set. Graph Theory: Join (Graph Theory): an edge joins two vertices of a graph. Set Theory: A term (rarely used nowadays) for set union.

title: Definition:Join (Boolean Algebra)/Also known as
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \neg}$ be a Boolean algebra. The operation $\vee$ is often called the Boolean sum.

title: Definition:Join (Order Theory)
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $a, b \in S$. Let their supremum $\sup \set {a, b}$ exist in $S$. Then the join of $a$ and $b$ is defined as: $a \vee b = \sup \set {a, b}$ Expanding the definition of supremum, one sees that $c = a \vee b$ : $(1): \quad a \preceq c$ and $b \preceq c$ $(2): \quad \forall s \in S: a \preceq s$ and $b \preceq s \implies c \preceq s$

title: Definition:Join (Topology)
snippet: Let $X, Y$ be topological spaces. Then, the join of $X$ and $Y$ is defined and denoted as: $X \ast Y = \paren {X \times Y \times \closedint 0 1} / \RR$ where: $X \times Y \times \closedint 0 1$ denotes the product space $S / \RR$ denotes the quotient space the equivalence relation $\RR$ is induced by the mapping: $R : X \times Y \times \closedint 0 1 \to X \cup X \times Y \times \openint 0 1 \cup Y$ defined as: $\map R {x, y, t} = \begin{cases} x & : t = 0 \\ \tuple {x, y, t} & : t \in \openint 0 1 \\ y & : t = 1 \end{cases}$

title: Definition:Join Irreducible Element
snippet: Let $\struct{S, \vee, \preceq}$ be a join semilattice. Let $z \in S$. Then $z$ is said to be join irreducible $\forall x, y \in S : x \vee y = z \implies x = z$ or $y = z$

title: Definition:Join Irreducible Element/Also known as
snippet: == Join Irreducible Element: Also known as == The term join irreducible is hyphenated as join-irreducible in some sources. Category:Definitions/Join Irreducible Elements

title: Definition:Join Irreducible Element/Lattice
snippet: Let $L = \struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \preceq}$ be a lattice. Let $z \in S$. Then: $z$ is defined as join irreducible in $L$ $z$ is join irreducible in the join semilattice $\struct {S, \vee, \preceq}$.

title: Definition:Join Irreducible Element of Lattice/Also known as
snippet: == Join Irreducible Element of Lattice: Also known as == The term join irreducible is hyphenated as join-irreducible in some sources.

title: Definition:Join Prime Element
snippet: Let $\struct{S, \vee, \preceq}$ be a join semilattice. Let $z \in S$. Then $z$ is said to be join prime $\forall x, y \in S : z \preceq x \vee y \implies z \preceq x$ or $z \preceq y$

title: Definition:Join Prime Element/Lattice
snippet: Let $L = \struct{S, \vee, \wedge, \preceq}$ be a lattice. Let $z \in S$. Then $z$ is said to be a join prime element in L $z$ is a join prime element in the join semilattice $\struct{S, \vee, \preceq}$

title: Definition:Join Semilattice/Also known as
snippet: == Join Semilattice: Also known as == A join semilattice is also known as an upper semilattice or a $\vee$-semilattice. Some sources hyphenate: join semi-lattice.

title: Definition:Join Semilattice/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Suppose that for all $a, b \in S$: $a \vee b \in S$ where $a \vee b$ is the join of $a$ and $b$ with respect to $\preceq$. Then the ordered structure $\struct {S, \vee, \preceq}$ is called a join semilattice.

title: Definition:Join Semilattice/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \vee}$ be a semilattice. Let $\preceq$ be the ordering on $S$ defined by: $a \preceq b \iff \paren {a \vee b} = b$ Then the ordered structure $\struct {S, \vee, \preceq}$ is called a join semilattice.

title: Definition:Join Semilattice Ideal
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \vee, \preceq}$ be a join semilattice. Let $I \subseteq S$ be a non-empty subset of $S$. Then $I$ is a join semilattice ideal of $S$ $I$ satisifies the join semilattice ideal axioms:

title: Definition:Join of Finite Partitions
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\xi, \eta$ be finite partitions of $\Omega$. The join of $\xi$ and $\eta$ is the finite partition defined as: $\ds \xi \vee \eta := \set {A \cap B : A \in \xi, B \in \eta}$ Similarly, given finite partitions $\xi_1, \ldots, \xi_n$ of $\Omega$: $\ds \bigvee_{k \mathop = 1}^n \xi_k := \set { \bigcap_{k \mathop = 1}^n A_k \; : A_k \in \xi_k \; \text{for}\; \forall k }$

title: Definition:Join of Finite Sub-Sigma-Algebras
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\AA, \BB \subseteq \Sigma$ be finite sub-$\sigma$-algebras. The join of $\AA$ and $\BB$ is the finite sub-$\sigma$-algebra defined as: $\AA \vee \BB := \map \sigma {\AA \cup \BB}$ where $\map \sigma \cdot$ denotes the generated $\sigma$-algebra.

title: Definition:Join of Open Covers
snippet: Let $S$ be a topological space. Let $\alpha, \beta$ be open covers for $S$. The join of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ is the open cover: $\alpha \vee \beta := \set {A \cap B : A \in \alpha, B \in \beta}$ Similarly, given open covers $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n$ for $S$: $\ds \bigvee_{k \mathop = 1}^n \alpha_k := \set {\bigcap_{k \mathop = 1}^n A_k: A_k \in \alpha_k \text { for all $k$} }$

title: Definition:Join of Subgroups
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group. Let $A$ and $B$ be subgroups of $G$. The join of $A$ and $B$ is written and defined as: $A \vee B := \gen {A \cup B}$ where $\gen {A \cup B}$ is the subgroup generated by $A \cup B$. By the definition of subgroup generator, this can alternatively be written: $\ds A \vee B := \bigcap \set {T: T \text { is a subgroup of } G: A \cup B \subseteq T}$

title: Definition:Join of Subgroups/General Definition
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group. Let $H_1, H_2, \ldots, H_n$ be subgroups of $G$. Then the join of $H_1, H_2, \ldots, H_n$ is defined as: $\ds \bigvee_{k \mathop = 1}^n H_k := \gen {\bigcup_{k \mathop = 1}^n H_k}$ or: $\ds \bigvee_{k \mathop = 1}^n H_k := \bigcap \set {T: T \text { is a subgroup of } G: \bigcup_{k \mathop = 1}^n H_k \subseteq T}$

title: Definition:Joint Cumulative Distribution Function
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real-valued random variables on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. The joint cumulative distribution function of $X$ and $Y$ is defined and denoted as: $\forall x, y \in \R: \map {F_{X, Y} } {x, y} := \map \Pr {X \le x, Y \le y}$

title: Definition:Joint Cumulative Distribution Function/Discrete
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $X$ and $Y$ be discrete random variables on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. The joint cumulative distribution function of $X$ and $Y$ is defined and denoted as: $\ds \map {F_{X, Y} } {x, y} := \sum_{x_i \mathop \le x} \sum_{y_j \mathop \le y} \map {p_{i j} } {x, y}$ where $p_{i j}$ denotes the probability density function.

title: Definition:Joint Distribution
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\struct {S, \Sigma'}$ be a measurable space. Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_d$ be random variables on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ taking values in $\struct {S, \Sigma'}$. Define a random vector $X : \Omega \to S^d$ by: $\map X \omega = \tuple {\map {X_1} \omega, \map {X_2} \omega, \ldots, \map {X_d} \omega}$ for each $\omega \in \Omega$. Then the joint distribution of $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_d$ is defined as the probability distribution of $X$.

title: Definition:Joint Distribution/Also known as
snippet: == Joint Distribution: Also known as == A joint distribution is also known as a multivariate distribution. When the number of random variables is $2$, the term bivariate distribution is usually used.

title: Definition:Jointly Scott Continuous
snippet: Let $\struct{S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $f:S \times S \to S$ be a mapping. $f$ is jointly Scott continuous for every relational structure with Scott topology $\struct{S, \preceq, \tau}$ for every topological space $T = \struct{S, \tau}$: $f$ is continuous as a mapping from $T \times T$ into $T$. where $T \times T$ denotes the product space.

title: Definition:Jonckheere-Terpstra Test
snippet: The Jonckheere-Terpstra test is a non-parametric test where: the null hypothesis $H_0$ is that three or more independent samples all come from the same population the alternative hypothesis $H_1$ is that their means $\mu_i$ taken in order show a monotonic trend. That is: $H_0$: that $\mu_1 = \mu_2 = \cdots = \mu_k$ against: $H_1$: that either: $\mu_1 \le \mu_2 \le \cdots \le \mu_k$ or: $\mu_1 \ge \mu_2 \ge \cdots \ge \mu_k$ in which at least one of the inequalities is strict.

title: Definition:Jonckheere-Terpstra Test/Also known as
snippet: == Jonckheere-Terpstra Test: Also known as == The Jonckheere-Terpstra test is also known as the Jonckheere trend test. Category:Definitions/Jonckheere-Terpstra Test

snippet: == Historical Note on Jonckheere-Terpstra Test == The Jonckheere-Terpstra test was devised in $1952$ by , and again independently in $1954$ by .

title: Definition:Jordan Arc
snippet: Let $f: \closedint 0 1 \to \R^2$ be an injective path in the Euclidean plane. Then $f$ is called a Jordan arc.

snippet: == Jordan Arc: Also known as == Some texts refer to a Jordan arc as merely an arc.

title: Definition:Jordan Canonical Form
snippet: Jordan canonical form is a form of block diagonal canonical form to which a square matrix can be reduced by a similarity transformation. Each of the blocks on the diagonal are Jordan matrices, and contain the eigenvalues on the main diagonal.

title: Definition:Jordan Content
snippet: Let $M \subseteq \R^n$ be rectifiable. The Jordan content of $M$ is defined and denoted: $\map m M = \map {m^*} M = \map {m_*} M$ where $m^*$ and $m_*$ denote respectively the outer and inner Jordan content. Those values are equal by definition of a rectifiable set.

title: Definition:Jordan Content/Also known as
snippet: == Jordan Content: Also known as == The Jordan content is often referred to as the Jordan measure, but this is a misnomer as it is does not constitute a measure.

title: Definition:Jordan Curve
snippet: Let $f : \closedint 0 1 \to \R^2$ be a path in the Euclidean plane such that: $\map f {t_1} \ne \map f {t_2}$ for all $t_1 ,t_2 \in \hointr 0 1$ with $t_1 \ne t_2$ $\map f 0 = \map f 1$ Then $f$ is called a Jordan curve.

title: Definition:Jordan Curve/Also defined as
snippet: == Jordan Curve: Also defined as == Some texts change the definition of the codomain of a Jordan curve from $\R^2$ to $X$, where $X$ is alternatively defined as: the complex plane $\C$ a real Euclidean space $\R^n$ a $T_2$ (Hausdorff) topological space $\struct { S, \tau_S }$ This is what defines as an simple loop. Some texts drop the condition that $\map f 0 = \map f 1$ and replace it with the condition: $\map f t \ne \map f 1$ for all $t \in \openint 0 1$ which means they consider a Jordan arc to be a Jordan curve.

title: Definition:Jordan Curve/Also known as
snippet: == Jordan Curve: Also known as == Some texts refer to a Jordan curve as a simple closed curve, or a simple loop.

title: Definition:Jordan Curve/Exterior
snippet: Let $f: \closedint 0 1 \to \R^2$ be a Jordan curve. It follows from the Jordan Curve Theorem that $\R^2 \setminus \Img f$ is a union of two disjoint connected components, one of which is unbounded. This unbounded component is called the exterior of $f$, and is denoted as $\Ext f$.

title: Definition:Jordan Curve/Interior
snippet: Let $f: \closedint 0 1 \to \R^2$ be a Jordan curve. It follows from the Jordan Curve Theorem that $\R^2 \setminus \Img f$ is a union of two disjoint connected components, one of which is bounded. This bounded component is called the interior of $f$, and is denoted as $\Int f$.

title: Definition:Jordan Decomposition
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\mu$ be a signed measure on $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. Let $\tuple {P, N}$ be a Hahn decomposition of $\mu$. Define: $\map {\mu^+} A = \map \mu {A \cap P}$ and: $\map {\mu^-} A = -\map \mu {A \cap N}$ for each $A \in \Sigma$. Then from the Jordan Decomposition Theorem, we have: $\mu = \mu^+ - \mu^-$ and we say that $\tuple {\mu^+, \mu^-}$ is the Jordan decomposition corresponding to $\tuple {P, N}$.

title: Definition:Jordan Decomposition/Also known as
snippet: == Jordan Decomposition: Also known as == A Jordan decomposition is also known as a Hahn-Jordan decomposition (with ). Some sources refer to it as a Hahn decomposition, but recognises the fact that this is a specific refinement of that concept for which it is worth having a separate term.

title: Definition:Jordan Decomposition of Complex Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\mu$ be a complex measure on $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ with real part $\mu_R$ and imaginary part $\mu_I$. Let $\tuple {\mu_1, \mu_2}$ be the Jordan decomposition of $\mu_R$. Let $\tuple {\mu_3, \mu_4}$ be the Jordan decomposition of $\mu_I$. Then: $\mu = \mu_1 - \mu_2 + i \paren {\mu_3 - \mu_4}$ and we say that $\tuple {\mu_1, \mu_2, \mu_3, \mu_4}$ is the Jordan decomposition of $\mu$.

title: Definition:Jordan Matrix
snippet: A Jordan matrix is a square matrix in which: the diagonal elements are all non-zero and equal the elements on the first superdiagonal are all equal to $1$ all other elements are zero.

title: Definition:Josephus Problem
snippet: Consider a collection of $n$ people in a circle. Let them each be eliminated sequentially by counting out every $m$th person (closing the gap after each elimination). For a given a number of people $n$, and a given step size $m$, the problem is to determine the initial position in the circle of the person who remains after all the others have been eliminated.

title: Definition:Josephus Problem/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on the Josephus Problem == The legend describes an incident during the sack of in $\text {67 CE}$ by and his son , both future emperors. The story goes that the Jewish historian , at the time the commander of the Jewish rebels, was holed up in a cave with a bunch of comrades (some sources give the exact number of rebels as $41$), hiding from the Romans. Death was preferable to capture, so they determined a procedure whereby they would all commit ritual suicide. They all stood in a circle, and counted round. Every third person was killed, and the gap was closed.

title: Definition:Joule/Base Units

title: Definition:Juggler Sequence
snippet: Let $m \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be a positive integer. The juggler sequence on $m$ is defined recursively as: $J_m \left({n}\right) = \begin{cases} m & : n = 0 \\ \left\lfloor{\sqrt {J_m \left({n - 1}\right)} }\right\rfloor & : n \text{ even} \\ \left\lfloor{\sqrt {\left({J_m \left({n - 1}\right)}\right)^3} }\right\rfloor & : n \text{ odd} \end{cases}$ where: $\left\lfloor{x}\right\rfloor$ denotes the floor of $x$ $\sqrt x$ denotes the positive square root of $x$.

title: Definition:Julia Set

title: Definition:Julia Set/Definition 1
snippet: Let $f$ be an iterated rational function defined on the extended complex plane $\overline \C$. The Julia set of $f$ is the closed subset of $\overline \C$ which is invariant under $f$.

title: Definition:Julia Set/Definition 2
snippet: Let $f$ be an iterated rational function defined on the extended complex plane $\overline \C$. The Julia set of $f$ is the boundary of the set of those points in $\overline \C$ whose orbits under $f$ are bounded. That is, it is the boundary of the filled Julia set of $f$.

title: Definition:Julia Set/Filled
snippet: Let $f$ be an iterated rational function defined on the extended complex plane $\overline \C$. The filled Julia set of $f$ is the set of those points in $\overline \C$ whose orbits under $f$ are bounded.

title: Definition:K-Algebra
snippet: Let $k$ be a field. A $k$-algebra is a unital associative commutative algebra over $k$.

title: Definition:K-Connected
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a graph. Let $k \in \Z_{>0}$. Then $G$ is $k$-connected : $\card V > k$ $G$ is connected $G$ has no vertex cut $W$ with $\card W < k$. Informally: $G$ is connected and has more than $k$ vertices There is no vertex cut of $G$ containing less than $k$ vertices.

title: Definition:K-Network/CS*-Network
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. A $cs^*$-network $\NN$ on $T$ is a set of subsets of $S$ such that: for every open set $U \subseteq \tau$, for every $x \in U$, for every sequence $\sequence {x_n}$ converging to $x$, there exists some $A \in \NN$ such that: $x_n \in A$ for infinitely many $n$.

title: Definition:K-Network/CS-Network
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. A $cs$-network $\NN$ on $T$ is a set of subsets of $S$ such that: for every open set $U \subseteq \tau$, for every $x \in U$, for every sequence $\sequence {x_n}$ converging to $x$, there exists some $A \in \NN$ such that: $x_n \in A$ for all but finitely many $n$.

title: Definition:K-Network/K-Network
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. A $k$-network $\NN$ on $T$ is a set of subsets of $S$ such that: for every compact set $K$ of $T$ and open set $U \subseteq \tau$ such that $K \subseteq U$, there exists a finite subset $\NN^* \subseteq \NN$ such that: $K \subseteq \bigcup \NN^* \subseteq U$

title: Definition:K-Network/Pseudobase
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. A pseudobase $\NN$ on $T$ is a set of subsets of $S$ such that: for every compact set $K$ of $T$ and open set $U \subseteq \tau$ such that $K \subseteq U$, there exists some $A \in \NN$ such that: $K \subseteq A \subseteq U$
