title: Definition:K2-Hausdorff Space/Definition 1
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a $k_2$-Hausdorff space the diagonal $\Delta$ of $S \times S$ is such that: for every continuous mapping $f: K \to S \times S$ from a compact $T_2$ (Hausdorff) subspace $K$ of $T$, its preimage $f^{-1} \sqbrk \Delta$ is closed in $T$.

title: Definition:K2-Hausdorff Space/Definition 2

title: Definition:Kaprekar's Constant
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a positive integer with $4$ digits, not all of which are equal. Let Kaprekar's process be applied to $n$. The number reached after no more than $8$ iterations is known as Kaprekar's constant, and has the value of $6174$.

title: Definition:Kaprekar's Process
snippet: Kaprekar's process is the repeated application of the Kaprekar mapping to a given positive integer.

title: Definition:Kaprekar Mapping
snippet: The Kaprekar mapping is the arithmetic function $K: \Z_{>0} \to \Z_{>0}$ defined on the positive integers as follows: Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be expressed in some number base $b$ (where $b$ is usually $10$). Let $n'$ be the positive integer created by arranging the digits of $n$ into descending order of size. Let $n' '$ be the positive integer created by arranging the digits of $n$ into ascending order of size. Then: $\map K n = n' - n' '$ making sure to retain any leading zeroes to ensure that $\map K n$ has the same number of digits as $n$.

title: Definition:Kaprekar Number
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. Suppose that $n^2$, when expressed in number base $b$, can be split into two parts that add up to $n$. Then $n$ is a Kaprekar number for base $b$.

title: Definition:Karmarkar's Algorithm
snippet: Karmarkar's algorithm is an algorithm for solving problems in linear programming and certain other more general constrained optimization problems. For large problems it is often faster than the simplex method. While the simplex method searches the boundaries of the feasible region, Karmarkar's algorithm starts its search from an interior point.

title: Definition:Kei Function
snippet: Let $K_n$ denote the modified Bessel function of the second kind. The Kei function is defined as: $\map {\Kei_n} x = \map \Im {\map {K_n} {x \map \exp {\dfrac {\pi i} 4} } }$ where: $\exp$ denotes the exponential function $x$ is real $\map \Im z$ denotes the imaginary part of $z$.

title: Definition:Kei Function/Also known as
snippet: == Kei Function: Also known as == The Kei kunction, along with: its real counterpart the Ker function the Ber function and Bei function are known collectively as the Kelvin functions, for . Some sources report and denote the Kei function uncapitalised: kei function.

title: Definition:Keith Number
snippet: Let $K \in \Z_{>9}$ be an $n$-digit integer, where $n > 1$. Let $A = \left({a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n}\right)$ be the digits of $K$ in order. Let $F_A$ be the Fibonacci-like sequence on $A$. Then $K$ is a Keith number $K$ occurs somewhere in $F_A$.

title: Definition:Keith Number/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Keith Numbers == Keith numbers were first introduced by in . The author coined the name repfigit, but they have since been assigned the name of their creator. They proved a popular topic, and in $1994$, in Volume $26$, Number $3$ of the , several articles on them appeared. The number of known Keith numbers is gradually extended, and as of time of writing ($5$th February $2017$) all Keith numbers have been identified up to $10^{29}$.

title: Definition:Kelvin
snippet: The kelvin is the SI base unit of absolute temperature. Its two reference points are: $0 \ \mathrm K$, which is set at absolute zero, the temperature at which all thermal motion stops $273 \cdotp 16 \ \mathrm K$, which is set at the of water ($0.01 \cels$)

title: Definition:Kelvin-Stokes Theorem/Historical Note

title: Definition:Kelvin Function
snippet: The Kelvin functions are defined as the real parts and imaginary parts of the Bessel functions of the first and modified second kind.

title: Definition:Kendall's Coefficient of Concordance
snippet: Kendall's coefficient of concordance is a test for consistency of more than $2$ sets of rankings. Let $m$ judges independently award ranks $1$ to $n$ to a set of $n$ competitors. Let $s_i$ be the sum of the rankings awarded to competitor $i$. The mean $M$ of the values of $s_i$ is $\dfrac 1 2 m \paren {n + 1}$. The sum of the squares of the deviations from $M$ is given by: $S = \ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \paren {s_i - M}^2$ and Kendall's coefficient of concordance is given by: $W = \dfrac {12 S} {m^2 n \paren {n^2 - 1} }$

title: Definition:Kendall's Coefficient of Concordance/Also known as
snippet: == Kendall's Coefficient of Concordance: Also known as == Some sources report Kendall's coefficient of concordance just as the coefficient of concordance.

title: Definition:Kendall's Coefficient of Concordance/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Kendall's Coefficient of Concordance == Kendall's coefficient of concordance was introduced by in $1939$.

title: Definition:Kendall's Rank Correlation Coefficient
snippet: Kendall's rank correlation coefficient is a test for consistency of $2$ sets of rankings $\sequence a_n$ and $\sequence b_n$ on a set $S$ of $n$ objects. The set $R$ of ordered pairs $\tuple {a_i, b_i}$ is assembled: $R = \set {\tuple {a_i, b_i}: i \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n} }$ and ordered according to $\sequence a$. The number $Q$ of elements of $S$ out of ranking order from $\sequence b$ is counted. Kendall's rank correlation coefficient is then formed: $K = 1 - \dfrac {4 Q} {n \paren {n + 1} }$ which takes values between $-1$ (complete disagreement) and $+1$ (complete agreement).

title: Definition:Kendall's Rank Correlation Coefficient/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Kendall's Rank Correlation Coefficient == Kendall's rank correlation coefficient was devised by in $1938$.

title: Definition:Kepler's Equation
snippet: Consider a system consisting of two bodies $B_1$ and $B_2$ in elliptical orbit around each other. Let $e$ denote the eccentricity of that orbit. Kepler's equation is the equation that describes the relation between the mean anomaly and eccentric anomaly of $B_1$ with respect to $B_2$: $M = E - e \sin E$ where: $M$ is the mean anomaly $E$ is the eccentric anomaly.

title: Definition:Kepler-Poinsot Polyhedron
snippet: A Kepler-Poinsot polyhedron is any of the four regular star polyhedra.

title: Definition:Kepler-Poinsot Polyhedron/Also known as
snippet: == Kepler-Poinsot Polyhedron: Also known as == The Kepler-Poinsot polyhedra (or solids) are sometimes seen referred to as the Kepler-Poinsot stellated polyhedra, but the fact that they are stellated is usually taken for granted. Some sources refer to them as Poinsot solids, preferring to attribute them wholly to . They are also known as the regular star polyhedra.

title: Definition:Kepler-Poinsot Polyhedron/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Kepler-Poinsot Polyhedron == Two of the Kepler-Poinsot polyhedra, the small stellated dodecahedron and the great stellated dodecahedron, were discovered by . They were rediscovered by , who also discovered the other two. In $1812$, demonstrated that there can only be $4$.

title: Definition:Ker Function
snippet: Let $K_n$ denote the modified Bessel function of the second kind. The Ker function is defined as: $\map {\Ker_n} x = \map \Re {\map {K_n} {x \map \exp {\dfrac {\pi i} 4} } }$ where: $\exp$ denotes the exponential function $x$ is real $\map \Re z$ denotes the real part of $z$.

title: Definition:Ker Function/Also known as
snippet: == Ker Function: Also known as == The Ker kunction, along with: its imaginary counterpart the Kei function the Ber function and Bei function are known collectively as the Kelvin functions, for . Some sources report and denote the Ker function uncapitalised: ker function.

title: Definition:Kernel
snippet: Abstract algebra: Kernel of a homomorphism Kernel of a group action Linear algebra: Kernel of Linear Transformation Homological algebra: Kernel of Homomorphism of Differential Complexes Analysis: Kernel of an integral transform Integral equations: Kernel of an integral equation Measure theory: Kernel of a measurable space Kernel Transformation of Measure Kernel Transformation of Positive Measurable Function Category theory: Kernel of a morphism Definition:Kernel in Additive Category

title: Definition:Kernel (Abstract Algebra)/Also denoted as
snippet: == Kernel: Also denoted as == The notation $\map {\mathrm {Ker} } \phi$ can sometimes be seen for the kernel of $\phi$. It can also be presented as $\ker \phi$ or $\operatorname {Ker} \phi$, that is, without the parenthesis indicating a mapping.

title: Definition:Kernel (Category Theory)
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a category. Let $A$ and $B$ be objects of $\mathbf C$. Let $f : A \to B $ be a morphism in $\mathbf C$.

title: Definition:Kernel (Category Theory)/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a category. Let $A$ and $B$ be objects of $\mathbf C$. Let $f : A \to B $ be a morphism in $\mathbf C$. Let $\mathbf C$ have an initial object $0$. A kernel of $f$ is a morphism $\map \ker f \to A$ which is a pullback of the unique morphism $0 \to B$ via $f$ to $A$.

title: Definition:Kernel (Category Theory)/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a category. Let $A$ and $B$ be objects of $\mathbf C$. Let $f: A \to B $ be a morphism in $\mathbf C$. Let $\mathbf C$ have a zero object $0$. A kernel of $f$ is a morphism $\ker(f) \to A$, which is an equalizer of $f$ and the zero morphism $0: A \to B$.

title: Definition:Kernel (Category Theory)/Uniqueness
snippet: == On Uniqueness == Since the kernel is defined by a universal property it is only unique up to unique isomorphism. While for example in group theory the kernel of a group homomorphism $f : G \to H$ is a subset of $G$, not all categorical kernels of $f$ in the category of groups are subsets of $G$.

title: Definition:Kernel (Measure Theory)
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\overline \R_{\ge 0}$ be the set of positive extended real numbers. A kernel is a mapping $N: X \times \Sigma \to \overline{\R}_{\ge0}$ such that: $(1): \quad \forall x \in X: N_x: \Sigma \to \overline \R_{\ge 0}, E \mapsto \map N {x, E}$ is a measure $(2): \quad \forall E \in \Sigma: N_E: X \to \overline \R_{\ge 0}, x \mapsto \map N {x, E}$ is a positive $\Sigma$-measurable function

title: Definition:Kernel Density Estimation
snippet: Kernel density estimation is a nonparametric method for estimating a probability density function of a continuous random variable $X$ based on data forming a (usually large) sample.

title: Definition:Kernel Density Estimation/Bandwidth
snippet: Let there be $n$ data points of a probability density function $f$: $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ For each $x_i$ we can substitute: $u = \dfrac {x - x_i} h$ to make a function of $x$. In this context, $h$ is referred to as the bandwidth of $f$.

title: Definition:Kernel Density Estimation/Kernel
snippet: The kernel of a probability density function of a continuous random variable $X$ is a function $\map k u$ symmetric about $u = 0$. There are several widely used choices used for such a kernel.

title: Definition:Kernel Density Estimation/Usage
snippet: == Kernel Density Estimation: Usage == When using kernel density estimation, the choice of bandwidth has a strong influence on the estimate. Rules exist enabling the user to select a bandwidth which avoids either: overemphasizing local irregularities or: obtaining an oversmoothed estimate. The method is highly computation intensive.

title: Definition:Kernel Transformation of Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $N: X \times \Sigma \to \overline {\R_{\ge 0} }$ be a kernel. The transformation of $\mu$ by $N$ is the mapping $\mu N: \Sigma \to \overline \R$ defined by: $\ds \forall E \in \Sigma: \map {\mu N} E := \int \map {N_E} x \map {\rd \mu} x$ where $\map {N_E} x = \map N {x, E}$.

title: Definition:Kernel Transformation of Positive Measurable Function
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $N: X \times \Sigma \to \overline \R_{\ge 0}$ be a kernel. Let $f: X \to \overline \R$ be a positive measurable function. The transformation of $f$ by $N$ is the mapping $N f: X \to \overline \R$ defined by: $\forall x \in X: N \map f x := \ds \int f \rd N_x$ where $N_x$ is the measure $E \mapsto \map N {x, E}$.

title: Definition:Kernel of Group Action
snippet: Let $G$ be a group with identity $e$. Let $X$ be a set. Let $* : G\times X\to X$ be a group action.

title: Definition:Kernel of Group Action/Definition 1
snippet: Let $G$ be a group with identity $e$. Let $X$ be a set. Let $* : G\times X\to X$ be a group action. The kernel of the group action is the set: $G_0 = \set {g \in G: \forall x \in X: g * x = x}$

title: Definition:Kernel of Group Action/Definition 2
snippet: Let $G$ be a group with identity $e$. Let $X$ be a set. Let $* : G \times X \to X$ be a group action. The kernel of the group action is the kernel of its permutation representation.

title: Definition:Kernel of Group Homomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ and $\struct {H, *}$ be groups. Let $\phi: \struct {G, \circ} \to \struct {H, *}$ be a group homomorphism. The kernel of $\phi$ is the subset of the domain of $\phi$ defined as: $\map \ker \phi := \phi^{-1} \sqbrk {e_H} = \set {x \in G: \map \phi x = e_H}$ where $e_H$ is the identity of $H$. That is, $\map \ker \phi$ is the subset of $G$ that maps to the identity of $H$.

title: Definition:Kernel of Homomorphism of Differential Complexes
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \cdot}$ be a ring. Let: $M: \quad \cdots \longrightarrow M_i \stackrel {d_i} \longrightarrow M_{i + 1} \stackrel {d_{i + 1} } \longrightarrow M_{i + 2} \stackrel {d_{i + 2} } \longrightarrow \cdots$ and $N: \quad \cdots \longrightarrow N_i \stackrel {d'_i} \longrightarrow N_{i + 1} \stackrel {d'_{i + 1} } \longrightarrow N_{i + 2} \stackrel {d'_{i + 2} } \longrightarrow \cdots$ be two differential complexes of $R$-modules. Let $\phi = \set {\phi_i : i \in \Z}$ be a homomorphism $M \to N$. For each $i \in \Z$ let $K_i$ be the kernel of $\phi_i$.

title: Definition:Kernel of Linear Transformation
snippet: Let $\phi: G \to H$ be a linear transformation where $G$ and $H$ are $R$-modules. Let $e_H$ be the identity of $H$. The kernel of $\phi$ is defined as: $\map \ker \phi := \phi^{-1} \sqbrk {\set {e_H} }$ where $\phi^{-1} \sqbrk S$ denotes the preimage of $S$ under $\phi$.

title: Definition:Kernel of Linear Transformation/Vector Space
snippet: Let $\struct {\mathbf V, +, \times}$ be a vector space. Let $\struct {\mathbf V', +, \times}$ be a vector space whose zero vector is $\mathbf 0'$. Let $T: \mathbf V \to \mathbf V'$ be a linear transformation. Then the kernel of $T$ is defined as: $\map \ker T := T^{-1} \sqbrk {\set {\mathbf 0'} } = \set {\mathbf x \in \mathbf V: \map T {\mathbf x} = \mathbf 0'}$

title: Definition:Kernel of Linear Transformation on Vector Space/Also known as
snippet: == Kernel of Linear Transformation on Vector Space: Also known as == The kernel of a linear transformation $T$ on a vector space is also known as the null space on $T$.

title: Definition:Kernel of Magma Homomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a magma. Let $\struct {T, *}$ be an algebraic structure with an identity element $e$. Let $\phi: \struct {S, \circ} \to \struct {T, *}$ be a homomorphism. The kernel of $\phi$ is the subset of the domain of $\phi$ defined as: $\map \ker \phi = \set {x \in S: \map \phi x = e}$ That is, $\map \ker \phi$ is the subset of $S$ that maps to the identity of $T$.

title: Definition:Kernel of Ring Homomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {R_1, +_1, \circ_1}$ and $\struct {R_2, +_2, \circ_2}$ be rings. Let $\phi: \struct {R_1, +_1, \circ_1} \to \struct {R_2, +_2, \circ_2}$ be a ring homomorphism. The kernel of $\phi$ is the subset of the domain of $\phi$ defined as: $\map \ker \phi = \set {x \in R_1: \map \phi x = 0_{R_2} }$ where $0_{R_2}$ is the zero of $R_2$. That is, $\map \ker \phi$ is the subset of $R_1$ that maps to the zero of $R_2$. From Ring Homomorphism Preserves Zero it follows that $0_{R_1} \in \map \ker \phi$ where $0_{R_1}$ is the zero of $R_1$.

title: Definition:Key/Also known as

title: Definition:Killing Equation
snippet:
Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $\map {\mathfrak{X}} M$ be the space of smooth vector fields of $M$. Suppose $Z \in \map {\mathfrak{X}} M$ is a smooth vector field such that: $\ds  orall X, Y \in \map {\mathfrak{X}} M : \map g {
abla_X Z, Y} + \map g {X, 
abla_Y Z} = 0$ where $
abla_X Z$ denotes the covariant derivative of $Z$ along $X$. Then the equation above is the Killing equation for $Z$. Category:Definitions/Differential Equations Category:Definitions/Killing Vector Fields

title: Definition:Killing Tensor
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $K$ be a symmetric tensor field of type $\paren {p, 0}$ with components $K_{\mu_1 \ldots \mu_p}$. Let $\nabla$ be the covariant derivative. Then $K$ is called the Killing tensor (of order $p$) if: $\nabla_{(\alpha} K_{\mu_1 \ldots \mu_p)} = 0$ where $\paren {\ldots}$ denotes the tensor symmetrization. Category:Definitions/Differential Equations Category:Definitions/Killing Tensors

title: Definition:Killing Vector Field
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $\map {\mathfrak X} M$ be the space of smooth vector fields of $M$. Let $X \in \map {\mathfrak X} M$. Let $\LL$ be the Lie derivative. Suppose $\map {\LL_X} g = 0$. Then $X$ is called the Killing vector field.

title: Definition:Kilogram/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Kilogram == 1795: The kilogram was defined as $1000$ times one gram. This itself was defined as the mass of one cubic centimetre of water at the melting point of ice. 1799: The actual reference kilogram was manufactured as a prototype. It had a mass equal to the mass of $1 \, \mathrm {dm}^3$ of water at its maximum density, approximately $4 \cels$. 1875: The was derived from this. This has a mass which is almost exactly equal to the mass of one litre of water.

snippet: == Linguistic Note on Kilogram == The original British English spelling of kilogram was kilogramme. However, this is rarely used nowadays, as the American kilogram is now the international standard.

title: Definition:Kinematic Viscosity
snippet: The kinematic viscosity of a fluid is its dynamic viscosity divided by its density: $\nu = \dfrac \eta \rho$ where: $\eta$ denotes the dynamic viscosity $\rho$ denotes the density.

title: Definition:Kinematic Viscosity/Dimension
snippet: The dimension of measurement of kinematic viscosity is $\mathsf {L^2 T^{-1} }$. Category:Definitions/Dimensions of Measurement Category:Definitions/Kinematic Viscosity

title: Definition:Kinematic Viscosity/Unit
snippet: The SI unit of measurement of kinematic viscosity is the square metre per second. The CGS unit of measurement of kinematic viscosity is the stokes. The FPS unit of measurement of kinematic viscosity is the square foot per second.

title: Definition:Kinematics
snippet: Kinematics is the branch of the mechanics describing the motion of bodies without considering the forces that may affect this motion. Hence it is concerned with such things as the displacements, velocities and accelerations of bodies.

title: Definition:Kinetic Energy
snippet: Let $B$ be a body. The kinetic energy of $B$ is defined as the energy appertaining to $B$ due to its motion. It is a scalar quantity.

title: Definition:Kinetics
snippet: Kinetics is the study of the effects of torques and forces on the motion of physical bodies. It forms one of the two subsections of dynamics, the other subsection being kinematics.

title: Definition:Kinetics/Also defined as
snippet: == Kinetics: Also defined as == The exact nature of the branch of mechanics known as kinetics is not universally well-defined. Some schools of thought consider it as synonymous with dynamics, as the two branches are both concerned with the motion of bodies. Other schools do not use the word kinetics, and instead divide classical mechanics into dynamics, which is specified so as to include statics, and kinematics.

title: Definition:Kleene Closure
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. The Kleene closure of $S$, denoted $S^*$, is the set of all ordered tuples in $S$. The Kleene closure is endowed with the concatenation operation $*$: $\tuple{ S^*, *}$ to form an algebraic structure.

title: Definition:Klein Bottle
snippet: A Klein bottle is a $2$-manifold obtained from the square: $\set {\tuple {x_1, x_2} \in \R^2: \size {x_1}, \size {x_2} \le 1}$ by identifying the edges $x_1 = \pm 1$ and $x_2 = \pm 1$ such that: $\tuple {-1, x_2}$ is identified with $\tuple {1, -x_2}$ for all $x_2$ $\tuple {x_1, -1}$ is identified with $\tuple {x_1, 1}$ for all $x_1$. That is, by identifying both pairs of opposite sides, one with the other, of a square, while twisting the square for one pair: 400px

title: Definition:Klein Four-Group
snippet: == Group Example == The Klein $4$-group, often denoted $K_4$, is a group of $4$ elements, each of which is self-inverse.

title: Definition:Klein Four-Group/Also known as
snippet: == Klein Four-Group: Also known as == The Klein four-group (or Klein's four-group) is also known as the four-group or the Viergruppe. Hence it is often denoted $V$ or $V_4$. The term is not always hyphenated:: Klein four group or Klein's four group four group. Some sources refer to it as the dihedral group of order $4$.

title: Definition:Knight's Tour
snippet: A knight's tour is a puzzle in recreational chess. On a chessboard of arbitrary size, a chess knight is to make a complete tour of the chessboard, visiting each square once and once only and ending up a knight's move from its starting square so that its circuit is continuous.

title: Definition:Knight's Tour/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Knight's Tour == The knight's tour was one of the problems of recreational mathematics considered by .

title: Definition:Knot
snippet: Knot Theory: Knot Unit of Measurement: Knot: $1$ nautical mile per hour Approximation Theory Knot of Spline: one of the points through which a spline is constrained to pass.

title: Definition:Knot (Knot Theory)
snippet: Let $Y$ be a manifold and $X \subset Y$ a submanifold of $Y$. Let $i: X \to Y$ be an inclusion, that is a mapping such that $i \sqbrk X = X$. Then a knotted embedding is an embedding $\phi: X \to Y$ (or the image of such an embedding) such that $\phi \sqbrk X$ is not freely homotopic to $i \sqbrk X$.

title: Definition:Knot (Knot Theory)/Circle Knot
snippet: The description of the sphere is dropped for $\Bbb S^1$ and the term knot is used without qualification for knotted embeddings $\phi: \Bbb S^1 \to \R^3$. Category:Definitions/Knot Theory

title: Definition:Knot (Knot Theory)/Elementary Knot
snippet: Circle knots can often be quite wild and unwieldy - most of modern knot theory concerns itself with a specific kind of knot. These knots are described as a finite set of points in $\R^3$ called $\set {x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n}$, together with line segments from $x_i$ to $x_{i + 1}$ and a line segment from $x_n$ to $x_1$. The union of all these line segments is clearly a circle knot, or an unknot, an embedding of the circle which is homotopic to a circle. Category:Definitions/Knot Theory

title: Definition:Knot (Knot Theory)/Sphere Knot
snippet: A knotted $n$-sphere is a knotted embedding: $\phi: \Bbb S^n \to \R^{n + 2}$ Category:Definitions/Knot Theory

title: Definition:Knot (Unit of Measurement)
snippet: The knot is a unit of speed which is used for air and sea navigation. It is defined as $1$ nautical mile per hour. It is now defined as exactly $1 \, 852$ metres per hour.

title: Definition:Knot (Unit of Measurement)/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Knot: Conversion Factors ==

title: Definition:Knot (Unit of Measurement)/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Knot == The knot is defined in terms of the nautical mile, that is, $1852$ metres or approximately $6076$ feet. However, the admiralty mile, that is, $6080$ feet, has until fairly recently also been used to define the knot. Because of this confusion, it is recommended that the knot is determined to be unsuitable for accurate measurements.

title: Definition:Knot Polynomial
snippet: Context: knot theory. A knot polynomial is a polynomial associated with a knot. Two knots are equivalent their knot polynomials are equal.

title: Definition:Knot Polynomial/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Knot Polynomial == As of time of writing, a common framework within which to understand the knot polynomials has not yet been discovered. A possible strategy has been suggested by , who introduced the concept of the Vassiliev invariant in $1990$, based on his work in singularity theory.

title: Definition:Knot Product
snippet: The product of two knots is informally defined as what you get when you tie those two knots together on the same string.

title: Definition:Knot Theory
snippet: Knot theory is the branch of geometry which studies the embedding of knots in $3$-dimensional space.

title: Definition:Knot Theory/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Knot Theory == Knot theory was first studied by and . Subsequently it was studied in more detail by the physicists , and in the late $19$th century. constructed tables of knots whose planar representations had few crossings, and in particular studied knots which had alternating diagrams. Knot theory has in more recent times been used to study complicated molecules such as DNA.

title: Definition:Knot of Spline/Also known as
snippet: == Knot of Spline: Also known as == The knots of a spline function are also known as nodes. Some sources refer to them as control points.

title: Definition:Knot of Spline/Knot Vector
snippet: Let $\closedint a b$ be a closed real interval. Let $T := \set {a = t_0, t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_{n - 1}, t_n = b}$ form a subdivision of $\closedint a b$. Let $S: \closedint a b \to \R$ be a spline function on $\closedint a b$ on $T$. The ordered $n + 1$-tuple $\mathbf t := \tuple {t_0, t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_{n - 1}, t_n}$ of $S$ is known as the knot vector. Category:Definitions/Knots of Splines

title: Definition:Koch Curve
snippet: The Koch curve is a fractal whose generator is formed by constructing an equilateral triangle one of whose sides occupies the middle third of a straight line segment. The Koch curve is then defined as the limit $\Gamma_\infty$ of the successions of iteratively defined curves, where $\Gamma_{n + 1}$ is constructed from $\Gamma_n$ by replacing each line segment with its generator.

title: Definition:Koch Curve/Also known as
snippet: == Koch Curve: Also known as == The Koch curve is also known as the von Koch curve.

title: Definition:Koch Curve/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Koch Curve == The Koch curve was introduced by in $1904$. By joining the ends of $3$ such Koch curves, he demonstrated the Koch snowflake, an example of a curve of infinite length but enclosing a finite area.

title: Definition:Koch Snowflake
snippet: The Koch snowflake is the fractal generated by taking $3$ Koch curves and joining the endpoints to form a closed curve. This is the $3$rd iteration of the Koch snowflake: 400px

title: Definition:Koch Snowflake/Also known as
snippet: == Koch Snowflake: Also known as == The Koch snowflake is also known as the snowflake curve. Some sources call it the Koch curve, but that name is also applied to the curve which forms one of the $3$ sides of the Koch snowflake.

title: Definition:Koch Snowflake/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Koch Snowflake == The Koch snowflake was introduced by in $1904$. Hence he demonstrated that a curve of infinite length can enclose a finite area.

title: Definition:Koebe Constant
snippet: The Koebe Quarter Theorem states: That constant $\dfrac 1 4$ by which $\size {\map {f'} 0}$ is bounded below can be found referred to as the Koebe constant.

title: Definition:Kolmogorov-Sinai Entropy
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \BB, \mu}$ be a probability space. Let $T: X \to X$ be a $\mu$-preserving transformation. Then the Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy of $T$ is defined as: $\map h T := \sup \set {\map h {T, \AA}: \text {$\AA$ finite sub-$\sigma$-algebra of $\BB$} }$ where: $\map h {T, \AA}$ denotes the entropy of $T$ with respect to $\AA$.

title: Definition:Kolmogorov-Smirnov Test
snippet: A Kolmogorov-Smirnov test is a non-parametric test to determine whether two samples may reasonably be supposed to come from the same probability distribution. The test requires that the cumulative distribution functions are calculated for each of the samples involved.

title: Definition:Kolmogorov-Smirnov Test/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Kolmogorov-Smirnov Test == In $1933$, proposed a non-parametric test to determine whether a sample is consistent with a specified probability distribution. It was extended by in $1939$ to test whether two sample may have come from the same probability distribution.

title: Definition:Koopman Operator on Complex L-2 Space
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \BB, \mu, T}$ be a measure-preserving dynamical system. Let $\map {L^2_\C} \mu$ be the complex-valued $L^2$ space of $\mu$. The Koopman operator $U_T : \map {L^2_\C} \mu \to \map {L^2_\C} \mu$ of $T$ is defined by: $\forall f \in \map {L^2_\C} \mu : \map {U_T} f = f \circ T$ where $f \circ T$ denotes the composition of $T$ and $f$.

title: Definition:Korteweg-de Vries Equation
snippet: The Korteweg-de Vries equation is the partial differential equation: $\dfrac {\partial y} {\partial t} + \dfrac {\partial^3 y} {\partial x^3} + 6 y \dfrac {\partial y} {\partial x} = 0$ where $t$ denotes time and $x$ denotes a space variable. The Korteweg-de Vries equation is classified as an integrable system.

title: Definition:Korteweg-de Vries Equation/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Korteweg-de Vries Equation == The Korteweg-de Vries equation was first introduced by in $1877$. It was later rediscovered by and in $1895$. A solution to this equation is a soliton.

title: Definition:Koszul Connection
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold with or without boundary. Let $E$ be a smooth manifold. Let $\pi : E \to M$ be a smooth vector bundle. Let $\map \Gamma E$ be the space of smooth sections of $E$. Let $\map {\mathfrak{X}} M$ be the space of smooth vector fields on $M$. Let $\map {C^\infty} M$ be the space of smooth real functions on $M$. Let $\nabla : \map {\mathfrak{X}} M \times \map \Gamma E \to \map \Gamma E$ be the map be written $\tuple {X, Y} \mapsto \nabla_X Y$ where $X \in \map {\mathfrak{X}} M$, $Y \in \map \Gamma E$, and $\times$ denotes the cartesian product.

title: Definition:Koti
snippet: Koti is a Jaina word for a hundred-hundred-thousand ($10 \, 000 \, 000$).

title: Definition:Kottman Constant of Banach Space
snippet:
Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X,

orm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$. Let $\KK_X$ be the set of $\sigma > 0$ such that: there exists a sequence $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ in $B_X^-$ such that: $

title: Definition:Kriging
snippet: Kriging is a generalized least-squares technique for interpolation.

title: Definition:Kriging/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Kriging == Kriging was invented by in $1951$. It is widely used in geostatics for problems such as establishing contour lines when given a set of spot values of a relevant random variable.

title: Definition:Kronecker Delta
snippet: Let $\Gamma$ be a set. Let $R$ be a ring with unity whose zero is $0_R$ and whose unity is $1_R$. Then $\delta_{\alpha \beta}: \Gamma \times \Gamma \to R$ is the mapping on the cartesian square of $\Gamma$ defined as: $\quad \forall \tuple {\alpha, \beta} \in \Gamma \times \Gamma: \delta_{\alpha \beta} := \begin{cases} 1_R & : \alpha = \beta \\ 0_R & : \alpha \ne \beta \end{cases}$ This use of $\delta$ is known as the Kronecker delta notation or Kronecker delta convention.

title: Definition:Kronecker Delta/Also denoted as
snippet: == Kronecker Delta: Also denoted as == When used in the context of tensors, the notation can often be seen as ${\delta^i}_j$.

title: Definition:Kronecker Delta/Also presented as
snippet: == Kronecker Delta: Also presented as == The Kronecker delta can be expressed using Iverson bracket notation as: $\delta_{\alpha \beta} := \sqbrk {\alpha = \beta}$

title: Definition:Kronecker Delta/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Kronecker Delta == The Kronecker delta notation was invented by in $1868$.

title: Definition:Kronecker Delta/Number
snippet: Let $\Gamma$ be a set. Then $\delta_{\alpha \beta}: \Gamma \times \Gamma \to \set {0, 1}$ is the mapping on the cartesian square of $\Gamma$ defined as: $\quad \forall \tuple {\alpha, \beta} \in \Gamma \times \Gamma: \delta_{\alpha \beta} := \begin {cases} 1 & : \alpha = \beta \\ 0 & : \alpha \ne \beta \end {cases}$ This use of $\delta$ is known as the Kronecker delta notation or Kronecker delta convention.

title: Definition:Kronecker Product
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ and $\mathbf B = \sqbrk b_{p q}$ be matrices. The Kronecker product of $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ is denoted $\mathbf A \otimes \mathbf B$ and is defined as the block matrix: $\mathbf A \otimes \mathbf B = \begin{bmatrix} a_{11} \mathbf B & a_{12} \mathbf B & \cdots & a_{1n} \mathbf B \\ a_{21} \mathbf B & a_{22} \mathbf B & \cdots & a_{2n} \mathbf B \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ a_{m1} \mathbf B & a_{m2} \mathbf B & \cdots & a_{mn} \mathbf B \end{bmatrix}$ Writing this out in full: $\mathbf A \otimes \mathbf B = \begin{bmatrix} a_{11} b_{11} &…

title: Definition:Kronecker Product/Also known as
snippet: == Kronecker Product: Also known as == The Kronecker product is also known as the matrix direct product.

title: Definition:Kronecker Sum
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_n$ and $\mathbf B = \sqbrk b_m$ be square matrices with orders $n$ and $m$ respectively. The Kronecker sum of $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ is denoted $\mathbf A \oplus \mathbf B$ and is defined as: $\mathbf A \oplus \mathbf B = \paren {\mathbf A \otimes \mathbf I_m} + \paren {\mathbf I_n \otimes \mathbf B}$ where: $\otimes$ denotes the Kronecker product $+$ denotes conventional matrix entrywise addition $\mathbf I_m$ and $\mathbf I_n$ are the unit matrices of order $m$ and $n$ respectively.

title: Definition:Krull Dimension of Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a commutative ring with unity. The Krull dimension of $R$ is the supremum of lengths of chains of prime ideals, ordered by the subset relation: {{eqn | l = \map {\operatorname {dim_{Krull} } } R | r = \sup \set {\map {\mathrm {ht} } {\mathfrak p} : \mathfrak p \in \Spec R} }} {{eqn | r = \sup \set {n \in \N: \exists p_0, \ldots, p_n \in \Spec R: \mathfrak p_0 \subsetneqq \mathfrak p_1 \subsetneqq \cdots \subsetneqq \mathfrak p_n} }} where: $\map {\mathrm {ht} } {\mathfrak p}$ is the height of $\mathfrak p$ $\Spec R$ is the prime spectrum of $R$ In particular,…

title: Definition:Krull Dimension of Scheme
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ be a scheme. Its Krull dimension is the Krull dimension of $X$.

title: Definition:Krull Dimension of Topological Space
snippet: Let $T$ be a topological space. Its Krull dimension $\map {\dim_{\mathrm {Krull} } } T$ is the supremum of lengths of chains of closed irreducible sets of $T$, ordered by the subset relation. Thus, the Krull dimension is $\infty$ if there exist arbitrarily long chains.

title: Definition:Kruskal-Wallis Test
snippet: The Kruskal-Wallis test is an extension of the Wilcoxon rank sum test to test $3$ or more independent samples.

title: Definition:Kruskal-Wallis Test/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Kruskal-Wallis Test == The Kruskal-Wallis test was devised by and in $1952$.

title: Definition:Krypton/82
snippet: == Isotope of Krypton == Krypton-$82$ is the isotope of krypton which has $46$ neutrons in addition to its $36$ protons. Kr-$82$ is the third most common stable isotope of krypton, making up $11.6 \%$ of the krypton found on Earth. Category:Definitions/Krypton Category:Definitions/Examples of Stable Isotopes

title: Definition:Krypton/83
snippet: == Isotope of Krypton == Krypton-$83$ is the isotope of krypton which has $47$ neutrons in addition to its $36$ protons. Kr-$83$ is the least common stable isotope of krypton, making up $11.5 \%$ of the krypton found on Earth. Category:Definitions/Krypton Category:Definitions/Examples of Stable Isotopes

title: Definition:Krypton/84
snippet: == Isotope of Krypton == Krypton-$84$ is the isotope of krypton which has $48$ neutrons in addition to its $36$ protons. Kr-$84$ is the most common stable isotope of krypton, making up $57.0 \%$ of the krypton found on Earth. Category:Definitions/Krypton Category:Definitions/Examples of Stable Isotopes

title: Definition:Krypton/86
snippet: == Isotope of Krypton == Krypton-$86$ is the isotope of krypton which has $50$ neutrons in addition to its $36$ protons. Kr-$86$ is the is the second most common stable isotope of krypton, making up $17.3 \%$ of the krypton found on Earth.

title: Definition:Krypton/86/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Krypton-$86$ == Krypton-$86$ was adopted in $1960$ as the basis of the definition of the metre.

title: Definition:Krypton/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Krypton == The word krypton was taken from the Greek κρυπτός, meaning the hidden one. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Kummer Theory
snippet: Kummer Theory is a branch of abstract algebra and number theory which investigates certain types of field extensions.

title: Definition:Kuratowski Closure Operator/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\cl: \powerset S \to \powerset S$ be a mapping from the power set of $S$ to itself. Then $\cl$ is a Kuratowski closure operator it satisfies the following Kuratowski closure axioms for all $A, B \subseteq S$: {{axiom | n = 2 | m = \map \cl {\map \cl A} = \map \cl A | rc= $\cl$ is idempotent }} {{axiom | n = 3 | m = \map \cl {A \cup B} = \map \cl A \cup \map \cl B | rc= $\cl$ preserves binary unions }} Note that axioms $(3)$ and $(4)$ may be replaced by the single axiom that for any finite subset $\FF$ of $\powerset S$: $\ds \map \cl {\bigcup \FF} = \map {\bigcup_{F…

title: Definition:Kuratowski Closure Operator/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\cl: \powerset S \to \powerset S$ be a mapping from the power set of $S$ to itself. Then $\cl$ is a Kuratowski closure operator it satisfies the following axioms for all $A, B \subseteq X$: {{axiom | n = 2 | t = $\map \cl {A \cup B} = \map \cl A \cup \map \cl B$ | rc= $\cl$ preserves binary unions }} Note that axioms $(2)$ and $(3)$ may be replaced by the single axiom that for any finite subset $\FF$ of $powerset S$: $\ds \map \cl {\bigcup \FF} = \map {\bigcup_{F \mathop \in \FF} } {\map \cl F}$ That is, the axiom that $\cl$ preserves finite unions.

title: Definition:Kuratowski Formalization of Ordered Pair/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Kuratowski Formalization of Ordered Pair == The Kuratowski formalization of the concept of the ordered pair was established in $1914$ in collaboration with .

title: Definition:Kurtosis
snippet: Let $X$ be a random variable with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. The kurtosis of $X$ is a measure of the concentration of $X$ about its expectation.

title: Definition:Kurtosis/Coefficient
snippet: Let $X$ be a random variable with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. The coefficient of kurtosis of $X$ is the coefficient: $\gamma_2 = \dfrac {\mu_4} { {\mu_2}^2} - 3$ where $\mu_i$ denotes the $i$th central moment of $X$.

title: Definition:Kurtosis/Definition 1
snippet: Let $X$ be a random variable with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. The kurtosis of $X$ is a measure of the concentration of $X$ about its expectation. The kurtosis of $X$ is the fourth standardized moment of $X$: $\alpha_4 = \expect {\paren {\dfrac {X - \mu} \sigma}^4}$ where $\expect {\, \cdot \,}$ denotes expectation.

title: Definition:Kurtosis/Definition 2
snippet: Let $X$ be a random variable with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. The kurtosis of $X$ is a measure of the concentration of $X$ about its expectation. The kurtosis of $X$ is defined as: $\alpha_4 = \dfrac {\mu_4} {\paren {\mu_2}^2}$ where $\mu_i$ denotes the $i$th central moment of $X$.

title: Definition:Kurtosis/Incorrect Definition
snippet: The kurtosis of a random variable is often seen described as a measure of how steep the peak is at the mean or the mode. However, this is incorrect. It is more accurate to describe it as a measure of how heavy or fat the tails are.

title: Definition:Kurtosis/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Kurtosis == The word kurtosis derives from the Greek κυρτός (kyrtos or kurtos), meaning curved or arching. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Kurtosis/Notation
snippet: Let $X$ be a random variable with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. The kurtosis of $X$ is usually denoted $\alpha_4$. Some sources denote the kurtosis by the symbol $\Beta_2$ or $\beta_2$.

title: Definition:L-2 Inner Product
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $\map {\LL^2} {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be the Lebesgue $2$-space of $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$. Let $\map {L^2} {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be the $L^2$ space of $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$. We define the $L^2$ inner product $\innerprod \cdot \cdot : \map {L^2} {X, \Sigma, \mu} \times \map {L^2} {X, \Sigma, \mu} \to \R$ by: $\ds \innerprod {\eqclass f \sim} {\eqclass g \sim} = \int \paren {f \cdot g} \rd \mu$ where: $\eqclass f \sim, \eqclass g \sim \in \map {L^2} {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ where $\eqclass f \sim$ and $\eqclass g \sim$ are the equivalence class of…

title: Definition:L1 Metric/Closed Real Interval
snippet: Let $S$ be the set of all real functions which are continuous on the closed interval $\closedint a b$. Let the real-valued function $d: S \times S \to \R$ be defined as: $\ds \forall f, g \in S: \map {d_1} {f, g} := \int_a^b \size {\map f t - \map g t} \rd t$ Then $d_1$ is the $L^1$ metric on $\closedint a b$.

title: Definition:L2 Metric/Closed Real Interval
snippet: Let $S$ be the set of all real functions which are continuous on the closed interval $\closedint a b$. Let the real-valued function $d: S \times S \to \R$ be defined as: $\ds \forall f, g \in S: \map d {f, g} := \paren {\int_a^b \paren {\map f t - \map g t}^2 \rd t}^{\frac 1 2}$ Then $d$ is the $L^2$ metric on $\closedint a b$.

title: Definition:LAST
snippet: LAST stands for LAnguage of Set Theory. It is a formal system designed for the description of sets.

title: Definition:LU Factorization
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a square matrix. An LU factorization of $\mathbf A$ is a factorization of $\mathbf A$ in the form: $\mathbf A = \mathbf {L U}$ where: $\mathbf L$ is a lower triangular matrix $\mathbf U$ is a upper triangular matrix. It is usual to arrange this so that either $\mathbf L$ or $\mathbf U$ has a unit diagonal.

title: Definition:LU Factorization/Also known as
snippet: == LU Factorization: Also known as == An LU factorization is also known as an LU decomposition.

title: Definition:LU Factorization/Backward Substitution
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a square matrix. Let $\mathbf A$ have an LU factorization: $\mathbf A = \mathbf {L U}$ where: $\mathbf L$ is a lower triangular matrix $\mathbf U$ is a upper triangular matrix. Let $\mathbf y$ be the column matrix resulting from the operation of forward substitution: $\mathbf L \mathbf y = \mathbf b$ Then solution of the equation: $\mathbf U \mathbf x = \mathbf y$ now yields the column matrix: $\begin {pmatrix} x_n \\ \vdots \\ x_2 \\ x_1 \end {pmatrix}$ which is the required solution to $\mathbf A \mathbf x = \mathbf b$. This process is known as backward substitution.

title: Definition:LU Factorization/Forward Substitution
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a square matrix. Let $\mathbf A$ have an LU factorization: $\mathbf A = \mathbf {L U}$ where: $\mathbf L$ is a lower triangular matrix $\mathbf U$ is a upper triangular matrix. Solution of the equation: $\mathbf L \mathbf y = \mathbf b$ yields the column matrix: $\begin {pmatrix} y_1 \\ y_2 \\ \vdots \\ y_n \end {pmatrix}$ This process is known as forward substitution.

title: Definition:LU Factorization/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on LU Factorization == An LU factorization is so called from the initial letters of the lower triangular matrix and upper triangular matrix that compose it. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:LU Factorization/Motivation
snippet: == LU Factorization: Motivation == Consider the system of simultaneous equations given in matrix form as: $(1): \quad \mathbf A \mathbf x = \mathbf b$ Given an LU factorization of $\mathbf A$: $\mathbf A = \mathbf L \mathbf U$ $(1)$ can be solved separately as: $\mathbf L \mathbf y = \mathbf b$ and then: $\mathbf U \mathbf x = \mathbf y$ which is more computationally efficient than directly solving $(1)$ by the conventional method.

title: Definition:Labeled Graph
snippet: A labeled graph is a graph whose vertices are each assigned an element from a set of symbols (letters, usually, but this is unimportant). The important thing to note is that the vertices can be distinguished one from another. Note that it is not necessary for all the vertices to be assigned different labels.

title: Definition:Labeled Graph/Also known as
snippet: == Labeled Graph: Also known as == The term labeled graph is rendered in non-American English as labelled graph. Category:Definitions/Labeled Graphs

title: Definition:Labeled Tree
snippet: A labeled tree is a finite tree (which may or may not be rooted) in which each node has attached to it a label. These labels may be any symbol or other object that one can think of, but usually consist of one letter or symbol. The parent function is usually depicted by placing the ancestor above the child and connecting them with a line. The various children of a node may also be considered to be in a particular order. This is usually depicted by placing them in a left-to-right order.

title: Definition:Labeled Tree/Also known as
snippet: == Labeled Tree: Also known as == The term labeled tree is rendered in non-American English as labelled tree.

title: Definition:Labeled Tree for Propositional Logic
snippet: A labeled tree for propositional logic is a system containing: A rooted tree $T$; A countable set $\mathbf H$ of WFFs of propositional logic; A WFF $\map \Phi t$ attached to each non-root node $t$ of $T$. Such a structure can be denoted $\struct {T, \mathbf H, \Phi}$.

title: Definition:Labeled Tree for Propositional Logic/Along a Branch
snippet: Let $\struct {T, \mathbf H, \Phi}$ be a labeled tree for propositional logic. Let $\Gamma$ be a branch of $T$. Let $\mathbf A$ be a WFF that is attached to a node $t \in \Gamma$. Then $\mathbf A$ occurs along $\Gamma$. This includes the case where $\mathbf A \in \mathbf H$, that is, $\mathbf A$ is attached to the root node.

title: Definition:Labeled Tree for Propositional Logic/Ancestor WFF
snippet: Let $\struct {T, \mathbf H, \Phi}$ be a labeled tree for propositional logic. A WFF that is attached to an ancestor node of a node $t$ is called an ancestor WFF of $t$. So a hypothesis WFF is an ancestor WFF of every node of $T$.

title: Definition:Labeled Tree for Propositional Logic/Attached
snippet: Let $\struct {T, \mathbf H, \Phi}$ be a labeled tree for propositional logic. Let $t$ be a non-root node of $T$. Let $\mathbf A$ be a WFF. Then $\mathbf A$ is attached to $t$ $\mathbf A = \map \Phi t$. All the WFFs in the hypothesis set $\mathbf H$ are considered to be attached to the root node.

title: Definition:Labeled Tree for Propositional Logic/Child WFF
snippet: Let $\struct {T, \mathbf H, \Phi}$ be a labeled tree for propositional logic. A WFF that is attached to a child of a node $t$ is called a child WFF of $t$.

title: Definition:Labeled Tree for Propositional Logic/Hypothesis Set
snippet: Let $\struct {T, \mathbf H, \Phi}$ be a labeled tree for propositional logic. The countable set $\mathbf H$ of WFFs of propositional logic is called the hypothesis set. The elements of $\mathbf H$ are known as hypothesis WFFs. The hypothesis set $\mathbf H$ is considered to be attached to the root node of $T$.

title: Definition:Lag
snippet: Let $T$ be a time series. A lag is a constant time interval between two timestamps of $T$. Thus, for every observation $z_t$ of $T$, a pair of observations can be created with a given lag $k$ between them: $\tuple {z_t, z_{t + k} }$

title: Definition:Lagrange's Method of Multipliers
snippet: Lagrange's method of multipliers is a technique for finding maxima or minima of a real-valued function $\map f {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ subject to one or more equality constraints $\map {g_i} {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} = 0$. The solution is found by minimizing: $L = f + \lambda_1 g_1 + \lambda_2 g_2 + \cdots$ the $x_i$ and $\lambda_i$.

title: Definition:Lagrange's Method of Multipliers/Also known as
snippet: == Lagrange's Method of Multipliers: Also known as == Lagrange's method of multipliers is also known as just Lagrange's method. Some sources style it as the Lagrange method of multipliers.

title: Definition:Lagrange's Method of Multipliers/Lagrange Multiplier
snippet: Consider a real-valued function $\map f {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ subject to one or more equality constraints $\map {g_i} {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} = 0$. Let Lagrange's method of multipliers be used to find maxima or minima of $f$ by minimizing: $L = f + \lambda_1 g_1 + \lambda_2 g_2 + \cdots$ the $x_i$ and $\lambda_i$. The coefficients $\lambda_i$ are known as the Lagrange multipliers for this process.

title: Definition:Lagrange Basis Polynomial
snippet: Let $x_0, \ldots, x_n \in \R$ be real numbers. The Lagrange basis polynomials associated to the $x_i$ are the polynomials: $\ds \map {L_j} X := \prod_{\substack {0 \mathop \le i \mathop \le n \\ i \mathop \ne j} } \frac {X - x_i} {x_j - x_i} \in \R \sqbrk X$

title: Definition:Lagrange Multiplier/Also known as
snippet: == Lagrange Multiplier: Also known as == A Lagrange multiplier is also known as an undetermined multiplier.

title: Definition:Lagrange Number
snippet: Let $\xi$ be an irrational number. Consider a real number $L_n$ such that there are infinitely many relatively prime integers $p, q \in \Z$ such that: $\size {\xi - \dfrac p q} < \dfrac 1 {L_n q^2}$ We define the Lagrange number of $\xi$ to be $\map L \xi = \map \sup L$ over all $L$ satisfying the inequality above.

title: Definition:Lagrange multiplier
snippet: The Lagrange multiplier method is used when one needs to find the extreme or stationary points of a function on a set which is a subset of the domain.

title: Definition:Lagrangian
snippet: Let $P$ be a physical system composed of $n \in \N$ particles. Let the real variable $t$ be the time of $P$. For all $i \le n$, let $\map { {\mathbf x}_i} t$ be the position of the $i$th particle. Suppose that the action $S$ of $P$ is of the following form: $\ds S = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} L \rd t$ where $L$ is a mapping of (possibly) $t$, $\map { {\mathbf x}_i} t$ and their derivatives. Then $L$ is the Lagrangian of $P$.

title: Definition:Lagrangian/Also known as
snippet: == Lagrangian: Also known as == A Lagrangian is also known as a Lagrangian function.

title: Definition:Lagrangian Derivative
snippet: Consider a fluid flow $\FF$. The Lagrangian derivative of $\FF$ is the partial derivative $\dfrac \partial {\partial t}$ which measures the rate of change at a fixed point of $\FF$ as different material flows through that point. The rate of change of the quantity $q$ is given by: $\dfrac {\rD q} {\rD t} = \dfrac {\partial q} {\partial t} + \mathbf u \cdot \nabla q$ where $\mathbf u$ is the velocity of $q$.

title: Definition:Lagrangian Derivative/Also known as
snippet: == Lagrangian Derivative: Also known as == A Lagrangian derivative is also known as: a convective derivative a material derivative.

title: Definition:Lagrangian Mechanics
snippet: Lagrangian mechanics is a reformulation of mechanics, where the main object of study is the Lagrangian function.

title: Definition:Laguerre's Differential Equation
snippet: Laguerre's differential equation is the $2$nd order ODE: $x \dfrac {\d^2 y} {\d x^2} + \paren {1 - x} \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} + \alpha y = 0$

title: Definition:Laguerre's Differential Equation/Laguerre Polynomial
snippet: The Laguerre polynomials are the solutions to Laguerre's differential equation: $x \dfrac {\d^2 y} {\d x^2} + \paren {1 - x} \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} + n y = 0$ for $n \in \N$. They are usually denoted $\map {L_n} x$.

title: Definition:Lambert W Function
snippet: Let $e^z: \C \to \C$ be the complex exponential function. Then $\map W z$ is defined to be the multifunction that satisfies: $\map W z e^{\map W z} = z$

title: Definition:Lambert W Function/Lower Branch
snippet: The lower branch of the Lambert W function is the real function $W_{-1}: \hointr {-\dfrac 1 e} 0 \to \hointl \gets {-1}$ such that: $x = \map {W_{-1} } x e^{\map {W_{-1} } x}$

title: Definition:Lambert W Function/Lower Branch/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Lower Branch of Lambert W Function == Though this branch has a generally accepted notation, $W_{-1}$, it does not seem to have a standard name in the literature. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Lambert W Function/Principal Branch/Real Valued
snippet: The principal branch of the Lambert W function is the real function $W_0: \hointr {-\dfrac 1 e} \to \to \hointr {-1} \to$ such that: $x = \map {W_0} x e^{\map {W_0} x}$

title: Definition:Lambert W Function/Real Valued/Graphs
snippet: == Graphs == There are two real-valued branches of the Lambert $W$ Function: The real valued principal branch, $W_0$ The lower branch, $W_{-1}$ 600px Category:Definitions/Lambert W Function

title: Definition:Lamellar Field/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Lamellar Field == The adjective lamellar derives from the Latin noun lamella, which means thin layer. The lamellae to which lamellar field refers are the equal surfaces of the scalar field from which the lamellar vector field is given rise to by way of the gradient operator. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Lamina
snippet: A lamina is an ideal of a (rigid) body embedded in ordinary space such that one of its dimensions is infinitesimal. That is, its thickness can be considered to be uniform and positive, but small enough to be ignored. Such a lamina can be interpreted as a body which is all surface. Thus it has area and (area mass) density but zero thickness.

title: Definition:Lamina/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Lamina == The word lamina derives from the Latin for thin piece of metal, wood, or marble, or plate, leaf, or layer. Hence the plural of lamina is properly laminae, although the form laminas can often be seen. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Lamina/Uniform
snippet: A uniform lamina is a lamina whose (area mass) density is constant.

title: Definition:Lanczos Method
snippet: The Lanczos method is an iterative technique for computing the eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix. It is most often used when the matrix is large and sparse, because each iteration involves a single product between the matrix and a vector.

title: Definition:Language of Arithmetic
snippet: A language of arithmetic is a signature for predicate logic consisting of: the binary operation symbols: $+$ and $\times$ the unary function symbol: $s$ the binary relation symbol: $<$ the constant symbol: $0$

title: Definition:Language of Category Theory

As such, it is considered to have: unary function symbols $\operatorname {Dom}$ and $\operatorname {Cdm}$, called the domain and codomain symbols A ternary relation symbol $R_\circ$, called the composition relation symbol All further descriptions required to determine a formal language are inherited from the definition of the language of predicate logic.

title: Definition:Language of Propositional Logic/Alphabet/Letter
snippet: Part of specifying the language of propositional logic $\LL_0$ is to specify its letters. The letters of $\LL_0$, called propositional symbols, is an arbitrary collection $\PP_0$ of symbols which has no limit on its extent. It is usual to specify them as a limited subset of the English alphabet with appropriate subscripts. A typical set of propositional symbols would be, for example: $\PP_0 = \set {p_1, p_2, p_3, \ldots, p_n, \ldots}$

At we aim to incorporate all these different approaches, and thus we have come to separately define the formal language.

title: Definition:Language of Propositional Logic/Formal Grammar/WFF
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be approved of by the formal grammar of propositional logic. Then $\mathbf A$ is called a well-formed formula of propositional logic. title: Definition:Laplace's Equation
snippet: == Equation == Laplace's equation is a second order PDE of the form: $\dfrac {\partial^2 \psi} {\partial x^2} + \dfrac {\partial^2 \psi} {\partial y^2} + \dfrac {\partial^2 \psi} {\partial z^2} = 0$ or: $\nabla^2 \psi = 0$ where $\nabla^2$ denotes the Laplacian operator.

title: Definition:Laplace's Equation/Also known as
snippet: == Laplace's Equation: Also known as == Laplace's equation is also known as the equation of continuity, but that term usually has a wider definition. Some sources render it as (the) Laplace equation.

title: Definition:Laplace's Equation/Complex Plane
snippet: == Equation == Let $D \subseteq \C$ be an open subset of the set of complex numbers $\C$. Let $f: D \to \C$ be a complex function on $D$. Let $u, v: \set {\tuple {x, y} \in \R^2: x + i y = z \in D} \to \R$ be the two real-valued functions defined as: {{eqn | l = \map u {x, y} | r = \map \Re {\map f z} }} {{eqn | l = \map v {x, y} | r = \map \Im {\map f z} }} where: $\map \Re {\map f z}$ denotes the real part of $\map f z$ $\map \Im {\map f z}$ denotes the imaginary part of $\map f z$.

title: Definition:Laplace's Equation/Complex Plane/Polar Form
snippet: == Equation == Let $D \subseteq \C$ be an open subset of the set of complex numbers $\C$. Let $f: D \to \C$ be a complex function on $D$. Let $u, v: \set {\tuple {x, y} \in \R^2: x + i y = z \in D} \to \R$ be the two real-valued functions defined as: {{eqn | l = \map u {x, y} | r = \map \Re {\map f z} }} {{eqn | l = \map v {x, y} | r = \map \Im {\map f z} }} where: $\map \Re {\map f z}$ denotes the real part of $\map f z$ $\map \Im {\map f z}$ denotes the imaginary part of $\map f z$.

title: Definition:Laplace Distribution
snippet: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable on a probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $\Img X = \R$. Let $\mu$ be a real number. Let $b$ be a strictly positive real number. $X$ is said to have a Laplace distribution with parameters $\mu$ and $b$ it has probability density function: $\map {f_X} x = \dfrac 1 {2 b} \map \exp {- \dfrac {\size {x - \mu} } b}$ This is written: $X \sim \map {\operatorname {Laplace} } {\mu, b}$

title: Definition:Laplace Transform
snippet: Let $f: \R_{\ge 0} \to \mathbb F$ be a function of a real variable $t$, where $\mathbb F \in \set {\R, \C}$. The Laplace transform of $f$, denoted $\laptrans f$ or $F$, is defined as: $\ds \laptrans {\map f t} = \map F s = \int_0^{\to +\infty} e^{-s t} \map f t \rd t$ whenever this improper integral converges. If this improper integral does not converge, then $\laptrans {\map f t}$ does not exist. Here $\laptrans f$ is a complex function of the variable $s$.

title: Definition:Laplace Transform/Also see
snippet: == Laplace Transform: Also see == Definition:Inverse Laplace Transform

title: Definition:Laplace Transform/Applications in Physics
snippet: == Applications of Laplace Transforms in Physics == Signal Processing: The domain of $f$ is the time domain The domain of $\laptrans f$ is the frequency domain.

title: Definition:Laplace Transform/Discontinuity at Zero
snippet: Let $f: \R_{> 0} \to \mathbb F$ be a function of a real variable $t$, where $\mathbb F \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $f$ be discontinuous or not defined at $t = 0$. Then the Laplace transform of $f$ is defined as: $\ds \laptrans {\map f t} = \map F s = \int_{0^+}^{\to +\infty} e^{-s t} \map f t \rd t = \lim_{\epsilon \mathop \to 0^+} \int_\epsilon^{\to +\infty} e^{-s t} \map f t \rd t$ whenever this improper integral converges. If this improper integral does not converge, then $\laptrans {\map f t}$ does not exist.

title: Definition:Laplace Transform/Graphical Interpretation
snippet: Define $\gamma$ as the integrand of $\ds \int_0^{\to +\infty} e^{-s t} \map f t \rd t$ as a function of $\map f t$, $s$, and $t$: $\map \gamma {\map f t, t; s} = \map f t \, e^{-s t}$ For any particular function $f$, holding $s$ fixed, the integrand of the Laplace Transform $\kappa$ can be interpreted as a contour. That is, for a given function $f$ and a particular complex number $s_0$ held constant: $\map \kappa t: \R_{\ge 0} \to \C$ $\map \kappa t = \map \gamma {\map f t, t; s_0}$ is a parameterization of a contour.

title: Definition:Laplace Transform/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Laplace Transform == Despite the fact that the Laplace transform bears the name of , they were first used by to solve differential equations. Also during the course of solutions of differential equations, advanced sophisticated applications of Laplace transforms.

title: Definition:Laplace Transform/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Laplace Transform == The function which serves as the argument of a Laplace transform is usually denoted by means of a lowercase letter, for example $f$, $g$, $y$, and so on. The Laplace transform of this function is then denoted by the corresponding uppercase letter, that is $F$, $G$, $Y$, and so on. Hence we have: $\laptrans {\map f t} = \map F s$ However, note that some sources reverse the cases of the symbols used to denote the functions under discussion: $\laptrans {\map F t} = \map f s$ Notation for the Laplace transform varies throughout the literature.

title: Definition:Laplace Transform/Restriction to Reals
snippet: Although the definition of the Laplace transform has $s$ be a complex variable, sometimes the restriction of $\map {\laptrans f} s$ to wholly real $s$ is sufficient to solve a particular differential equation. Therefore, elementary textbooks introducing the Laplace transform will often write something like the following: ... where we assume at present that the parameter $s$ is real. Later it will be found useful to consider $s$ complex.

title: Definition:Laplacian/Also known as
snippet: == Laplacian: Also known as == The Laplacian is also known as the Laplace operator, Laplace's operator or Laplace-Beltrami operator. The last name is usually used in the context of submanifolds in Euclidean space and on (pseudo-)Riemannian manifolds. Category:Definitions/Laplacian

title: Definition:Laplacian/Riemannian Manifold
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $f \in \map {C^\infty} M : M \to \R$ be a smooth mapping on $M$. Let $\grad$ be the gradient operator. Let $\operatorname {div}$ be the divergence operator. The Laplace-Beltrami operator of $f$ is defined as: $\nabla^2 f := \map {\operatorname {div} } {\grad f}$

title: Definition:Laplacian/Riemannian Manifold/Also denoted as
snippet: == Laplacian: Also denoted as == In the context of Riemannian manifolds, the Laplacian can be seen as $\Delta f$, particularly in older texts. The $\nabla^2$ form is to be used on as it allows less opportunity for ambiguity and misunderstanding. Category:Definitions/Laplacian

title: Definition:Laplacian/Scalar Field
snippet: Let $\R^n$ denote the real Cartesian space of $n$ dimensions. Let $\map U {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ be a scalar field over $\R^n$. Let the partial derivatives of $U$ exist throughout $\R^n$. The Laplacian of $U$ is defined as: $\ds \nabla^2 U := \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n \dfrac {\partial^2 U} {\partial {x_k}^2}$

title: Definition:Laplacian/Scalar Field/Cartesian 3-Space
snippet: Let $R$ be a region of Cartesian $3$-space $\R^3$. Let $\map U {x, y, z}$ be a scalar field acting over $R$. The Laplacian of $U$ is defined as: $\nabla^2 U := \dfrac {\partial^2 U} {\partial x^2} + \dfrac {\partial^2 U} {\partial y^2} + \dfrac {\partial^2 U} {\partial z^2}$ where $\nabla$ denotes the del operator.

title: Definition:Laplacian/Vector Field
snippet: Let $\map {\R^n} {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ denote the real Cartesian space of $n$ dimensions. Let $\tuple {\mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_2, \ldots, \mathbf e_n}$ be the standard ordered basis on $\R^n$. Let $\mathbf V: \R^n \to \R^n$ be a vector field on $\R^n$: $\forall \mathbf x \in \R^n: \map {\mathbf V} {\mathbf x} := \ds \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^n \map {V_k} {\mathbf x} \mathbf e_k$ where each of $V_k: \R^n \to \R$ are real-valued functions on $\R^n$.

title: Definition:Laplacian/Vector Field/Cartesian 3-Space
snippet: Let $R$ be a region of Cartesian $3$-space $\R^3$. Let $\map {\mathbf V} {x, y, z}$ be a vector field acting over $R$.

title: Definition:Laplacian/Vector Field/Cartesian 3-Space/Definition 1
snippet: Let $R$ be a region of Cartesian $3$-space $\R^3$. Let $\map {\mathbf V} {x, y, z}$ be a vector field acting over $R$. The Laplacian on $\mathbf V$ is defined as: $\nabla^2 \mathbf V = \dfrac {\partial^2 \mathbf V} {\partial x^2} + \dfrac {\partial^2 \mathbf V} {\partial y^2} + \dfrac {\partial^2 \mathbf V} {\partial z^2}$

title: Definition:Large Calorie
snippet: The large calorie is a CGS unit of heat energy. It was originally defined as equal to the energy required to raise the temperature of $1$ kilogram of water by $1 \cels$. However, it is noted that this energy depends upon the initial temperature of the water itself. Hence it is now usually defined as $1000$ times the value of the international calorie This unit is generally used in the food industry to provide an estimate of the energy provided by particular foods.

title: Definition:Laspeyres Index
snippet: Let the prices of a set of $k$ commodities in the base year be $p_{0 1}, p_{0 2}, \ldots, p_{0 k}$. Let the quantities sold of each of those $k$ commodities in the base year be $q_{0 1}, q_{0 2}, \ldots, q_{0 k}$. Let the corresponding prices and quantities of those $k$ commodities in the $n$th year after the base year be $p_{n 1}, p_{n 2}, \ldots, p_{n k}$ and $q_{n 1}, q_{n 2}, \ldots, q_{n k}$. The Laspeyres index is the index number calculated as: $L_{0 n} = \dfrac {\ds \sum_j p_{n j} \, q_{0 j} } {\ds \sum_j p_{0 j} \, q_{0 j} }$

title: Definition:Latin Square
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be some given (strictly) positive integer $n$. A Latin square of order $n$ is a square array of size $n \times n$ containing $n$ different symbols, such that every row and column contains exactly one of each symbol. That is, each row and column is a permutation of the same $n$ symbols.

title: Definition:Latin Square/Column
snippet: Let $\mathbf L$ be a Latin square. The columns of $\mathbf L$ are the lines of elements reading down the page.

title: Definition:Latin Square/Element
snippet: Let $\mathbf L$ be a Latin square of order $n$. The individual $n \times n$ symbols that go to form $\mathbf L$ are known as the elements of $\mathbf L$. The element at row $i$ and column $j$ is called element $\left({i, j}\right)$ of $\mathbf L$, and can be written $a_{i j}$, or $a_{i, j}$ if $i$ and $j$ are of more than one character. If the indices are still more complicated coefficients and further clarity is required, then the form $a \left({i, j}\right)$ can be used.

title: Definition:Latin Square/Element/Index
snippet: Let $\mathbf L$ be a Latin square of order $n$. Let $a_{i j}$ be an element of $\mathbf L$. Then the subscripts $i$ and $j$ are referred to as the indices (singular: index) of $a_{i j}$. Category:Definitions/Latin Squares

title: Definition:Latin Square/Experimental Design
snippet: In the context of design theory, a Latin square allows classification by three mutually orthogonal factors which can be denoted by rows, columns and conventional "Latin" letters. Treatments are designated by letters, and allocated to units under restricted randomization, each treatment occurring exactly once in each row and column. Hence the Latin square provides a useful double-blocking system to increase precision, by reducing two potential sources of variation not relating to treatments.

title: Definition:Latitude/Celestial
snippet: Let $P$ be a point on the celestial sphere. The celestial latitude of $P$ is the angle subtended by the the arc of the vertical circle through $P$ between $P$ and the ecliptic. If $P$ is closer to the north ecliptic pole, the celestial latitude is defined as latitude $\beta \degrees$ north, where $\beta \degrees$ denotes $\beta$ degrees (of angle), written $\beta \degrees \, \mathrm N$. If $P$ is closer to the south ecliptic pole, the celestial latitude is defined as latitude $\beta \degrees$ south, written $\beta \degrees \, \mathrm S$.

title: Definition:Latitude/Galactic
snippet: Let $P$ be a point on the celestial sphere. The galactic latitude of $P$ is the angular distance measured north or south of the galactic equator. It ranges from: $0 \degrees$ to $90 \degrees$ north $0 \degrees$ to $90 \degrees$ south where $0 \degrees$ is the galactic latitude of the galactic equator itself. This is denoted $l$.

title: Definition:Latitude/Terrestrial
snippet: Let $J$ be a point on Earth's surface that is not one of the two poles $N$ and $S$. Let $\bigcirc NJS$ be a meridian passing through $J$, whose endpoints are by definition $N$ and $S$. Let $\bigcirc NJS$ pass through the equator at $L$. The (terrestrial) latitude of $J$ is the (spherical) angle $\sphericalangle LOJ$ , where $O$ is the center of Earth. 500px If $J$ is in the northern hemisphere of Earth, the latitude is defined as latitude $n \degrees$ north, where $n \degrees$ denotes $n$ degrees (of angle), written $n \degrees \, \mathrm N$.

title: Definition:Latitude Circle of Surface of Revolution
snippet: Let $S_C$ be a surface of revolution. Let its smooth local parametrization be of the form: $\map X {t, \theta} = \tuple {\map y t \cos \theta, \map y t \sin \theta, \map x t}$ Then the $\theta$-coordinate curves $\theta \mapsto \map X {t_0, \theta}$ are called the latitude circles.
