title: Definition:Liouville's Constant/Also known as
snippet: == Liouville's Constant: Also known as == Some sources refer to Liouville's constant as Liouville's number. However, this leaves it open to being confused with a general Liouville number, of which Liouville's constant is a particular instance.

title: Definition:Liouville's Constant/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Liouville's Constant == Liouville's constant was created by in $1844$ as an example of a real number which is provably transcendental. He constructed several such numbers, of which this is the simplest.

title: Definition:Liouville Function
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$, that is, a strictly positive integer. The Liouville function is the function $\lambda: \Z_{>0} \to \Z_{>0}$ defined as: $\lambda \left({n}\right) = \left({-1}\right)^{\Omega \left({n}\right)}$ where $\Omega \left({n}\right)$ is the number of prime factors of $n$, counted with multiplicity.

title: Definition:Liouville Number
snippet: A real number $x$ is a Liouville number if for all $n \in \N$, there exist $p, q \in \Z$ (which may depend on $n$) with $q > 1$ such that: $0 < \size {x - \dfrac p q} < \dfrac 1 {q^n}$

title: Definition:Lipschitz Continuity
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ and $M' = \struct {A', d'}$ be metric spaces. Let Let $f: A \to A'$ be a mapping. Then $f$ is a Lipschitz continuous mapping there exists a positive real number $K \in \R_{\ge 0}$ such that: $\forall x, y \in A: \map {d'} {\map f x, \map f y} \le K \map d {x, y}$ That is, the distance between the images of two points lies within a fixed multiple of the distance between the points.

title: Definition:Lipschitz Continuity/Lipschitz Constant
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ and $M' = \struct {A', d'}$ be metric spaces. Let $f: A \to A'$ be a (Lipschitz continuous) mapping such that: $\forall x, y \in A: \map {d'} {\map f x, \map f y} \le K \map d {x, y}$ where $K \in \R_{\ge 0}$ is a positive real number. Then $K$ is a Lipschitz constant for $f$.

title: Definition:Lipschitz Continuity/Point
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ and $M' = \struct {A', d'}$ be metric spaces. Let Let $f: A \to A'$ be a mapping. Let $a \in A$. $f$ is a Lipschitz continuous at $a$ there exists a positive real number $K \in \R_{\ge 0}$ such that: $\forall x \in A: \map {d'} {\map f x, \map f a} \le K \map d {x, a}$

title: Definition:Lipschitz Continuity/Real Function
snippet: Let $A \subseteq \R$. Let $f: A \to \R$ be a real function. Let $I \subseteq A$ be a real interval on which: $\exists K \in \R_{\ge 0}: \forall x, y \in I: \size {\map f x - \map f y} \le K \size {x - y}$ Then $f$ is Lipschitz continuous on $I$. The constant $K$ is known as a Lipschitz constant for $f$.

title: Definition:Lipschitz Equivalence/Metric Spaces
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct {A_1, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct {A_2, d_2}$ be metric spaces. Let $f: M_1 \to M_2$ be a mapping such that $\exists h, k \in \R_{>0}$ such that: $\forall x, y \in A: h \map {d_2} {\map f x, \map f y} \le \map {d_1} {x, y} \le k \map {d_2} {\map f x, \map f y}$ Then $f$ is a Lipschitz equivalence, and $M_1$ and $M_2$ are described as Lipschitz equivalent.

title: Definition:Lipschitz Equivalence/Metrics/Definition 1
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct {A, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct {A, d_2}$ be metric spaces on the same underlying set $A$. Let $\exists h, k \in \R_{>0}$ such that: $\forall x, y \in A: h \map {d_2} {x, y} \le \map {d_1} {x, y} \le k \map {d_2} {x, y}$ Then $d_1$ and $d_2$ are described as Lipschitz equivalent.

title: Definition:Lipschitz Equivalence/Metrics/Definition 2
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct {A, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct {A, d_2}$ be metric spaces on the same underlying set $A$. Let $\exists K_1, K_2 \in \R_{>0}$ such that: $(1): \quad \forall x, y \in A: \map {d_2} {x, y} \le K_1 \map {d_1} {x, y}$ $(2): \quad \forall x, y \in A: \map {d_1} {x, y} \le K_2 \map {d_2} {x, y}$ Then $d_1$ and $d_2$ are described as Lipschitz equivalent.

title: Definition:Lipschitz Equivalence/Terminology
snippet: Despite the close connection with the concept of Lipschitz continuity, this concept is rarely seen in mainstream mathematics, and appears not to have a well-established name. The name Lipschitz equivalence appears in : There does not appear to be a standard name for this; the name we use is reasonably appropriate ... Sometimes the name strong equivalence (and strongly equivalent metrics) is used.

title: Definition:Lipschitz Quaternion
snippet: A Lipschitz quaternion is a quaternion whose components are all integers. The set $\Bbb L$ of all Lipschitz quaternions can therefore be defined as: $\Bbb L = \set {a + b \mathbf i + c \mathbf j + d \mathbf k \in \H: a, b, c, d \in \Z}$

title: Definition:Lipschitz Seminorm
snippet: Let $\struct {X_\mathbf A, \sigma_\mathbf A}$ be a shift of finite type. Let $\theta \in \openint 0 1$. Let $\map {F_\theta} {X_\mathbf A}$ be the Lipschitz space on $X_\mathbf A$. The Lipschitz seminorm of $f \in \map {F_\theta} {X_\mathbf A}$ is defined as: $\ds \size f_\theta := \sup_{n \mathop \in \N} \dfrac {\map {\mathrm {var}_n} f} {\theta ^n}$ where $\mathrm {var}_n$ denotes the $n$th variation.

title: Definition:Lipschitz Space
snippet: Let $\struct {X _\mathbf A, \sigma_\mathbf A}$ be a shift of finite type. Let $\theta \in \openint 0 1$. The Lipschitz space on $X _\mathbf A$ with respect to the metric $d_\theta$ is defined as: $\ds \map {F_\theta} {X_\mathbf A} := \set {f \in \map C {X _\mathbf A, \C} : \sup_{n \mathop \in \N} \dfrac {\map {\mathrm {var}_n} f} {\theta^n} < \infty}$ where: $\map C {X _\mathbf A, \C}$ denotes the continuous mapping space $\mathrm {var}_n$ denotes the $n$th variation

title: Definition:Liquid Pouring Problem
snippet: A liquid pouring problem is one where the object is to obtain a measure of $x$ volume units, given: (usually) $2$ vessels (without markings) which can measure $a$ and $b$ volume units each an unlimited reservoir from which one can fill the vessels, and usually empty them back into it.

title: Definition:Lissajous-Bowditch Figure
snippet: A Lissajous-Bowditch figure is a plane curve which is the locus of a point whose coordinates move in simple harmonic motion. The specific shape of a Lissajous-Bowditch figure depends on the relative frequencies and phases of the two motions.

title: Definition:Lissajous-Bowditch Figure/Also known as
snippet: == Lissajous-Bowditch Figure: Also known as == A Lissajous-Bowditch figure is also known as: a Lissajous figure a Bowditch curve.

title: Definition:Literal
snippet: A literal is either: an atom $p$ of propositional logic, that is, a statement, or the negation $\neg p$ of an atom $p$. In the language of propositional logic, these correspond to: a letter $p$ the WFF $\neg p$, where $p$ is a letter.

title: Definition:Literal/Negative
snippet: A negative literal is the negation $\neg p$ of an atom $p$ of propositional logic.

title: Definition:Literal/Positive
snippet: A positive literal is an atom $p$ of propositional logic.

title: Definition:Litre/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Litre: Conversion Factors == {{eqn | r = 10^{-3} | c = cubic metres }}

title: Definition:Litre/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on the Litre == The litre was originally defined as the volume of: $1 \, \mathrm {kg}$ (kilogram) of water at $4 \cels$ (degrees Celsius) at standard atmospheric pressure: $760 \, \mathrm {mm}$ (millimetres) of mercury. Hence, by this definition, the litre was equivalent to $1000 \cdotp 028 \, \mathrm {cm}^3$.

title: Definition:Litre/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Litre == The spelling litre is the one adopted by the International Bureau of Weights and Measures. Liter is the variant used in standard American English. While attempts in general to standardise on American English, the name of this unit is one place where a deliberate decision has been made to use the international spelling, in order to provide consistency with the British spelling of metre.

title: Definition:Little-O Estimate for Real Function at Infinity/Definition 1
snippet: Let $f$ and $g$ be real functions defined on a neighborhood of $+ \infty$ in $\R$. Let $\map g x \ne 0$ for $x$ sufficiently large. $f$ is little-$\oo$ of $g$ as $x \to \infty$ : $\ds \lim_{x \mathop \to \infty} \frac {\map f x} {\map g x} = 0$

title: Definition:Little-O Estimate for Real Function at Infinity/Definition 2
snippet: Let $f$ and $g$ be real functions defined on a neighborhood of $+ \infty$ in $\R$. $f$ is little-$\oo$ of $g$ as $x \to \infty$ : $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{> 0}: \exists x_0 \in \R: \forall x \in \R: x \ge x_0 \implies \cmod {\map f x} \le \epsilon \cdot \cmod {\map g x}$

title: Definition:Little-O Notation
snippet: Little-$\oo$ notation occurs in a variety of contexts.

title: Definition:Little-O Notation/Also known as
snippet: == Also denoted as == The little-$\oo$ notation, along with big-$\OO$ notation, are also referred to as Landau's symbols or the Landau symbols, for . Category:Definitions/Little-O Notation

title: Definition:Little-O Notation/Complex Point
snippet: Let $f$ and $g$ be complex functions. Let $z_0 \in \C$ be such that there exists a punctured neighborhood of $z_0$ on which $f$ and $g$ are defined. We say $f$ is little-$\oo$ of $g$, and denote: $\map f z \in \map \oo {\map g z} \text{ as } z \to z_0$ $\ds \lim_{z \mathop \to z_0} \dfrac {\size {\map f z} } {\size {\map g z} } = 0$ where $\size {\, \cdot \,}$ denotes the complex modulus. Category:Definitions/Little-O Notation

title: Definition:Little-O Notation/General Definition/Point
snippet:
Let $X$ be a topological space. Let $V$ be a normed vector space over $\R$ or $\C$ with norm $
orm {\,\cdot\,}$. Let $f, g: X 	o V$ be functions. Let $x_0 \in X$. The statement $\map f x = \map \oo {\map g x}$ as $x 	o x_0$ is equivalent to the statement: For all $\epsilon > 0$, there exists a neighborhood $U$ of $x_0$ such that $
orm {\map f x} \le \epsilon \cdot 
orm {\map g x}$ for all $x \in U$ Category:Definitions/Little-O Notation

title: Definition:Little-O Notation/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Little-$\oo$ Notation == The expression $\map f n \in \map \oo {\map g n}$ is read as: $\map f n$ is little-$\oo$ of $\map g n$ Similarly, when expressed in the notation of sequences, $a_n \in \map \oo {b_n}$ is read as: $a_n$ is little-$\oo$ of $b_n$ While it is correct and accurate to write: $\map f n \in \map \oo {\map g n}$ or: $a_n \in \map \oo {b_n}$ it is a common abuse of notation to write: $\map f n = \map \oo {\map g n}$ or: $a_n = \map \oo {b_n}$ This notation offers some advantages. Category:Definitions/Little-Omega Notation

title: Definition:Little-O Notation/Real/Infinity
snippet: Let $f$ and $g$ be real functions defined on a neighborhood of $+ \infty$ in $\R$.

title: Definition:Little-O Notation/Sequence/Definition 1
snippet: Let $g: \N \to \R$ be a real sequence, expressed here as a real-valued function on the set of natural numbers $\N$. Then $\map \oo g$ is defined as: $\map \oo g = \set {f: \N \to \R: \forall c \in \R_{>0}: \exists n_0 \in \N: \forall n > n_0: \size {\map f n} \le c \cdot \size {\map g n} }$

title: Definition:Little-O Notation/Sequence/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\sequence {a_n}$ and $\sequence {b_n}$ be sequences of real or complex numbers. Let $b_n \ne 0$ for all $n$. $a_n$ is little-$\oo$ of $b_n$ : $\ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \frac {a_n} {b_n} = 0$

title: Definition:Little-O Notation/Sequence/Informal Definition
snippet: Let $g: \N \to \R$ be a real sequence, expressed here as a real-valued function on the set of natural numbers $\N$. $\oo$-notation is used to define an upper bound for $g$ which is not asymptotically tight. Thus, let $f: \N \to \R$ be another real sequence, expressed here as a real-valued function on the set of natural numbers $\N$. Then: $\map f n = \map \oo {\map g n}$ means that $\map f n$ becomes insignificant relative to $\map g n$ as $n$ approaches (positive) infinity.

title: Definition:Little-Omega Notation/Also known as
snippet: == $\Omega$ Notation: Also known as == Note that in the Greek alphabet, $\omega$ is the minuscule counterpart of the capital letter $\Omega$. Hence the former is called little-omega and the latter big-omega. Some sources, therefore, write $\omega$ notation as little-$\omega$ notation, despite the fact that $\omega$'s "little"-ness is intrinsic. may sometimes adopt this convention if clarity is improved. Category:Definitions/Little-Omega Notation

title: Definition:Little-Omega Notation/Definition 1
snippet: Let $g: \N \to \R$ be a real sequence, expressed here as a real-valued function on the set of natural numbers $\N$. Then $\map \omega g$ is defined as: $\map \omega g = \set {f: \N \to \R: \forall c \in \R_{>0}: \exists n_0 \in \N: \forall n > n_0: 0 \le c \cdot \size {\map g n} < \size {\map f n} }$

title: Definition:Little-Omega Notation/Definition 2
snippet: Let $f: \N \to \R, g: \N \to \R$ be two real sequences, expressed here as real-valued functions on the set of natural numbers $\N$. Let: $\ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} {\frac {\map f n} {\map g n} } = \infty$ Then: $\map f n \in \map \omega {\map g n}$

title: Definition:Little-Omega Notation/Definition 3
snippet: Let $f: \N \to \R, g: \N \to \R$ be two real sequences, expressed here as real-valued functions on the set of natural numbers $\N$. Then: $\map f n \in \map \omega {\map g n}$ $\map g n \in \map \oo {\map f n}$ where $\oo$ denotes little-$\oo$ notation.

title: Definition:Little-Omega Notation/Informal Definition
snippet: Let $g: \N \to \R$ be a real sequence, expressed here as a real-valued function on the set of natural numbers $\N$. $\omega$-notation is used to define a lower bound for $g$ which is not asymptotically tight. Thus, let $f: \N \to \R$ be another real sequence, expressed here as a real-valued function on the set of natural numbers $\N$. Then: $\map f n = \map \omega {\map g n}$ means that $\map f n$ becomes arbitrarily large relative to $\map g n$ as $n$ approaches (positive) infinity.

title: Definition:Little-Omega Notation/Notation
snippet: == Notation for $\omega$ Notation == The expression $\map f n \in \map \omega {\map g n}$ is read as: $\map f n$ is little-omega of $\map g n$ While it is correct and accurate to write: $\map f n \in \map \omega {\map g n}$ it is a common abuse of notation to write: $\map f n = \map \omega {\map g n}$ This notation offers some advantages. Category:Definitions/Little-Omega Notation

title: Definition:Lituus
snippet: The lituus is the locus of the equation expressed in polar coordinates as: $r^2 = \dfrac {a^2} \theta$ 600px

title: Definition:Lituus/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Lituus == The word lituus literally means trumpet in Latin. An ancient Roman-Etruscan trumpet differs in shape from the contemporary instrument. It is also a fancy staff or wand used in certain religious rituals. Its shape echoes that of the lituus. Its plural form is litui.

title: Definition:Ljunggren Equation
snippet: The Ljunggren equation is the indeterminate Diophantine equation: $x^2 + 1 = 2 y^4$

title: Definition:Load
snippet: Let $M$ be a machine. The load on $M$ is an external force applied to a particular part of $M$ which is to be affected by the effort applied to $M$. Hence it can be considered as the (reactive) force exerted by $M$ which is to be overcome by the (active) force exerted on $M$.

title: Definition:Loaded Die
snippet: A loaded die is a die which has been modified so as to increase the probability of one or more faces appearing, at the expense of the other faces.

title: Definition:Loaded Die/Also known as
snippet: == Loaded Die: Also known as == A loaded die is also known as a weighted die.

title: Definition:Local Basis
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $x$ be an element of $S$.

title: Definition:Local Basis/Also defined as
snippet: == Local Basis: Also defined as == Some more modern sources suggest that in order to be a local basis, the neighborhoods of which the set $\BB$ consists do not need to be open. Such a structure is referred to on as a neighborhood basis. Category:Definitions/Local Bases

title: Definition:Local Basis/Also known as
snippet: == Local Basis: Also known as == A local basis is also known as a neighborhood basis, but that term is used on for a weaker notion. Category:Definitions/Local Bases

title: Definition:Local Basis/Local Basis for Open Sets
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $x$ be an element of $S$. A local basis at $x$ is a set $\BB$ of open neighborhoods of $x$ such that: $\forall U \in \tau: x \in U \implies \exists H \in \BB: H \subseteq U$ That is, such that every open neighborhood of $x$ also contains some set in $\BB$.

title: Definition:Local Basis/Neighborhood Basis of Open Sets
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $x$ be an element of $S$. A local basis at $x$ is a set $\BB$ of open neighborhoods of $x$ such that every neighborhood of $x$ contains a set in $\BB$. That is, a local basis at $x$ is a neighborhood basis of $x$ consisting of open sets.

title: Definition:Local Compactness Property
snippet: A local compactness property is a property that specifies a form of (topological) compactness that may apply in a given neighborhood within a given topological space, but not necessarily the topological space as a whole.

title: Definition:Local Compactness Property/Also known as
snippet: == Local Compactness Property: Also known as == A local compactness property is also known as a localized compactness property. The latter term is aesthetically displeasing, so a decision was made to use the former.

title: Definition:Local Coordinate Map
snippet: Let $M$ be a topological manifold. Let $\struct {U, \phi}$ be a chart of $M$. Then $\phi$ is known as the local coordinate map.

title: Definition:Local Coordinates
snippet: Let $M$ be an $n$-dimensional manifold. Let $p \in X$, and let $U \subseteq M$ be a neighbourhood of $p$. Let $\phi$ be the local coordinate map of $M$ such that: $\map \phi p = \tuple {\map {x_1} p, \map {x_2} p, \ldots \map {x_n} p}$ The component mappings $\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots x_n}$ of $\phi$ are known as the local coordinates around $p$.

title: Definition:Local Diffeomorphism
snippet: Let $n$ and $k$ be natural numbers. Let $U \subset \R^n$ be an open subset of $\R^n$. Let $f: U \to \R^n$ be a mapping. Then $f$ is a local $C^k$-diffeomorphism every $a \in U$ has a open neighborhhood such that the restriction of $f$ to it is a $C^k$-diffeomorphism on its image.

title: Definition:Local Diffeomorphism/Smooth Manifold
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be smooth manifolds with or without boundary. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. Then $f$ is a local diffeomorphism every point $p \in S$ has a open neighborhood $U$ such that: $f \sqbrk U$ is open in $T$ $f {\restriction_U}: U \to f \sqbrk U$ is a diffeomorphism. where $f \sqbrk U$ denote the image of $U$ under $f$. $f {\restriction_U}$ denote the restriction of $f$ to $U$.

title: Definition:Local Dimension of Topological Space
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space. Let $x \in X$. The local dimension of $X$ at $x$ is the supremum of lengths of chains of closed irreducible sets of $T$ containing $x$, ordered by the subset relation. Thus, the Krull dimension is $\infty$ there exist arbitrarily long chains containing $x$.

title: Definition:Local Frame
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $U \subseteq M$ be an open set. Let $\sigma = \tuple {\sigma_1, \ldots \sigma_k}$ be an ordered $k$-tuple of local sections over $U$. Suppose at each $p \in U$ the values of $\sigma$ constitute a basis for $M_p$. Then $\sigma$ is known as a local frame for $M$.

title: Definition:Local Gravitational Constant
snippet: The local gravitational constant is the value of the acceleration $g$ caused by the gravitational field given rise to by whatever body or bodies are in a position to exert that gravitational force. In the everyday context, $g$ is the acceleration due to the gravitational field of Earth at whatever point on or near its surface the observer happens to be. Thus in this context it is approximately equal to $9 \cdotp 8 \ \mathrm {m \, s^{-2} }$.

title: Definition:Local Gravitational Constant/Values
snippet: The local gravitational constant at the surface of Earth varies according to location, as can be seen from the following examples: {{eqn | l = g | o = \approx | r = 9 \cdotp 7801 | c = $\mathrm {m \, s^{-2} }$ | cc= at the equator }} {{eqn | l = g | o = \approx | r = 9 \cdotp 8321 | c = $\mathrm {m \, s^{-2} }$ | cc= at the North Pole }} {{eqn | l = g | o = \approx | r = 9 \cdotp 8119 | c = $\mathrm {m \, s^{-2} }$ | cc= at }}

title: Definition:Local Homeomorphism
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be topological spaces. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. Then $f$ is a local homeomorphism every $x \in S$ has a open neighborhhood $U \subseteq S$ such that: $f[U]$ is an open subset of $T$, and $f {\restriction_U}: U \to f[U]$, the restriction of $f$ to $U$, is a homeomorphism.

title: Definition:Local Isometry
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ and $\struct {\tilde M, \tilde g}$ be Riemannian manifolds. Let $p \in M$ be a point. Let $\phi : M \to \tilde M$ be a mapping such that for each $p$ there is a neighborhood $U$ such that $\bigvalueat \phi U$ is an isometry onto an open subset of $\tilde M$. Then $\phi$ is called the local isometry.

title: Definition:Local Krull Dimension of Scheme
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ be a scheme. Let $x \in X$. The local Krull dimension at $x$ is the local dimension of $X$ at $x$.

title: Definition:Local Maximum/Also known as
snippet: == Local Maximum: Also known as == A local maximum is also known as a relative maximum. Collectively, local maxima and local minima can be referred to as turning points.

title: Definition:Local Maximum/Warning
snippet: == Local Maximum: Warning == In the definition of a local maximum, note the requirement for the intervals to be open. A closed interval of course includes the value of $f$ at its end points and so every closed interval attains a maximum. Category:Definitions/Local Maxima

title: Definition:Local Membership Relation
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $C$ be an object of $\mathbf C$. The local membership relation $\in_C$ between variable elements $z: Z \to C$ and subobjects $m: M \to C$ of $C$ is defined by: $z \in_C m$ there exists an $f: Z \to M$: $z = m \circ f$. If $z \in_C m$, one says that $z$ is a local member of $m$.

title: Definition:Local Minimum/Also known as
snippet: == Local Minimum: Also known as == A local minimum is also known as a relative minimum. Collectively, local maxima and local minima can be referred to as turning points.

title: Definition:Local Minimum/Warning
snippet: == Local Minimum: Warning == In the definition of a local minimum, note the requirement for the intervals to be open. A closed interval of course includes the value of $f$ at its end points and so every closed interval attains a minimum. Category:Definitions/Local Minima

title: Definition:Local Minimum in Set of Reals
snippet: Let $X$ be a subset of $\R$, the set of all real numbers. Let $x \in X$. Then $x$ is local minimum in set $X$ : $\exists y \in \R: y < x \land \openint y x \cap X = \O$

title: Definition:Local Ring/Commutative
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity.

title: Definition:Local Ring/Commutative/Definition 1
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. The ring $A$ is local it has a unique maximal ideal.

title: Definition:Local Ring/Commutative/Definition 2
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. The ring $A$ is local it is nontrivial and the sum of any two non-units is a non-unit.

title: Definition:Local Ring/Commutative/Definition 3
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $M \subseteq A$ be the subset of the non-units of $A$. The ring $A$ is local $M$ is a proper ideal of $A$.

title: Definition:Local Ring/Noncommutative
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring with unity.

title: Definition:Local Ring/Noncommutative/Definition 1
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. $R$ is a local ring it has a unique maximal left ideal.

title: Definition:Local Ring/Noncommutative/Definition 2
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. $R$ is a local ring it has a unique maximal right ideal.

title: Definition:Local Ring/Noncommutative/Definition 3
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $\operatorname {rad} R$ be its Jacobson radical. Then $R$ is a local ring the quotient ring $R / \operatorname {rad} R$ is a division ring.

title: Definition:Local Ring/Noncommutative/Definition 4
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. $R$ is a local ring : $R$ is nontrivial the sum of any two non-units of $R$ is a non-unit of $R$.

title: Definition:Local Ring Homomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {A, \mathfrak m}$ and $\struct {B, \mathfrak n}$ be commutative local rings. Let $f : A \to B$ be a unital ring homomorphism.

title: Definition:Local Ring Homomorphism/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {A, \mathfrak m}$ and $\struct {B, \mathfrak n}$ be commutative local rings. Let $f : A \to B$ be a unital ring homomorphism. The homomorphism $f$ is local the image $f(\mathfrak m) \subseteq \mathfrak n$.

title: Definition:Local Ring Homomorphism/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {A, \mathfrak m}$ and $\struct {B, \mathfrak n}$ be commutative local rings. Let $f : A \to B$ be a unital ring homomorphism. The homomorphism $f$ is local the preimage $\map {f^{-1} } {\mathfrak n} \supseteq \mathfrak m$.

title: Definition:Local Ring Homomorphism/Definition 3
snippet: Let $\struct {A, \mathfrak m}$ and $\struct {B, \mathfrak n}$ be commutative local rings. Let $f : A \to B$ be a unital ring homomorphism. The homomorphism $f$ is local the preimage $\map {f^{-1} } {\mathfrak n} = \mathfrak m$.

title: Definition:Local Sub-Basis
snippet: Let $\left({X, \tau}\right)$ be a topological space. Let $x \in X$. Then a local sub-basis of $x$ relative to $\tau$ is a neighborhood sub-basis of $x$ consisting of open sets.

title: Definition:Local Trivialization
snippet: Let $\struct {E, M, \pi, F}$ be a fiber bundle. Let $\pr_1: M \times F \to M$ be the first projection on $M \times F$. By definition of fiber bundle, for every point $m \in M$ there exists an open neighborhood $U$ of $m$ and a homeomorphism: $\chi: \pi^{-1} \sqbrk U \to U \times F$ such that: $\pi {\restriction}_U = \pr_1 \mathop \circ \chi$ where $\pi {\restriction}_U$ is the restriction of $\pi$ to $U$. Then the ordered pair $\struct {U, \chi}$ is called a local trivialization of $E$ over $U$.

title: Definition:Locale (Lattice Theory)
snippet: Let $\mathbf{Loc}$ denote the category of locales. An object of $\mathbf{Loc}$ is called a locale. That is, a locale is a complete lattice $\struct {L, \preceq}$ satisfying the infinite join distributive law:

title: Definition:Locale (Lattice Theory)/Frames vs Locales
snippet: == Frames vs Locales vs Complete Heyting Algebras == If we are only concerned with category theoretic objects, the terms frame and locale and complete Heyting algebra are synonymous. (See Characterization of Locale) It is only when we consider the associated morphisms that they become different: For frames the associated morphisms are frame homomorphisms. (See Definition:Category of Frames). For locales the associated morphisms are continuous maps. (See Definition:Category of Locales).

title: Definition:Locale Isomorphism
snippet: Let $\mathbf{Loc}$ denote the category of locales. Let $L_1 = \struct{S_1, \preceq_1}$ and $L_2 = \struct{S_2, \preceq_2}$ be locales. Let $f: L_1 \to L_2$ be a continuous map between $L_1$ and $L_2$. Then: $f$ is a locale isomorphism there exists a frame isomorphism $\phi : L_2 \to L_1$ such that $f = \phi^{\operatorname{op}}$

title: Definition:Locale of Open Sets Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf{Top}$ denote the category of topological spaces. Let $\mathbf{Loc}$ denote the category of locales. The (locale of) open sets functor, denoted $\Omega : \mathbf{Top} \to \mathbf{Loc}$, is the covariant functor defined by:

title: Definition:Locale of Topological Space
snippet: The locale of topological space $T = \struct{S, \tau}$, denoted $\map \Omega T$, is the ordered set $\struct{\tau, \subseteq}$ where $\subseteq$ denotes the subset relation on $\tau$.

title: Definition:Localic Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf{Top}$ denote the category of topological spaces. Let $\mathbf{Loc_*}$ denote the category of locales with localic mappings. The localic functor, denoted $\operatorname{Lc} : \mathbf{Top} \to \mathbf{Loc_*}$, is the covariant functor defined by: {{DefineFunctor |ob = $\map {\operatorname{Lc} } T := $ the locale of topological space $T$ |mor = $\map {\operatorname{Lc} } f := $ the localic mapping induced by continuous mapping $f$ }}

title: Definition:Localic Mapping Induced by Continuous Mapping
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct{S_1, \tau_1}, T_2 = \struct{S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $f: T_1 \to \T_2$ be a continuous mapping. Let $\map \Omega {T_1}, \map \Omega {T_2}$ be the locales of $T_1$ and $T_2$ respectively. Let $\map \Omega f : \map \Omega {T_2} \to \map \Omega {T_1}$ be the frame homomorphism of $f$ (where $\map \Omega {T_1}, \map \Omega {T_2}$ are considered to be frames). Then the localic mapping $\upperadjoint {\map \Omega f } : \map \Omega {T_1} \to \map \Omega {T_2}$ that is the upper adjoint of $\map \Omega f$ is called the localic mapping induced by $f$.

title: Definition:Localic Spectrum Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf{Loc_*}$ denote the category of frames with localic mappings. Let $\mathbf{Top}$ denote the category of topological spaces. The (localic) spectrum functor, denoted $\operatorname {Sp} : \mathbf{Loc_*} \to \mathbf{Top}$, is the covariant functor defined by: {{DefineFunctor |ob = $\map {\operatorname {Sp} } L := $ the spectrum of locale $L$ |mor = $\map {\operatorname {Sp} } f := $ the continuous mapping induced by $f$ }}

title: Definition:Localization

title: Definition:Localization of Module
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $S \subseteq A$ be a multiplicatively closed subset. Let $A_S$ be the localization of $A$ at $S$. Let $M$ be an $A$-module. A localization of $M$ at $S$ is a pair $\struct {M_S, \iota}$ where: $M_S$ is an $A_S$-module $\iota : M \to M_S$ is the localization map, an $A$-module homomorphism to the restriction of scalars of $M_S$ to $A$ such that: For every $A_S$-module $N$ and $A$-module homomorphism $f: M \to \operatorname{res}_A^{A_S}N$ to the restriction of scalars to $A$, there exists a unique $A_S$-module homomorphism $g : M_S \to N$ such that…

title: Definition:Localization of Ring
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $S \subseteq A$ be a multiplicatively closed subset of $A$. A localization of $A$ at $S$ is a pair $\struct {A_S, \iota}$ where: $A_S$ is a commutative ring with unity, the actual localization $\iota: A \to A_S$ is a ring homomorphism, the localization homomorphism such that: $(1): \quad \map \iota S \subseteq A_S^\times$, where $A_S^\times$ is the group of units of $A_S$ $(2): \quad$ For every pair $\tuple {B, g}$ where: $B$ is any ring with unity $g: A \to B$ is a ring homomorphism such that $\map g S \subseteq B^\times$ there exists a unique…

title: Definition:Localization of Ring/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Localization of Ring == The word localization is spelt localisation in non-US English. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Localization of Ring at Element
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $f \in A$ be an element. The localization of $A$ at $f$ is the localization of $A$ at the set of powers $\set {1, f, f^2, \ldots}$: $A_f = \paren {\set {1, f, f^2, \ldots} }^{-1}A$

title: Definition:Localization of Ring at Prime Ideal
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $\mathfrak p$ be a prime ideal of $A$. The localization of $A$ at $\mathfrak p$ is the localization of $A$ at the complement $A \setminus \mathfrak p$: $A_{\mathfrak p} = \paren {A \setminus \mathfrak p}^{-1}A$

title: Definition:Locally Bounded/Family of Mappings
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. Let $\FF = \family {f_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a family of mappings defined on $M$. Then $\FF$ is said to be locally bounded : for all $x \in A$, there is some neighbourhood $N$ of $x$ such that $\FF$ is uniformly bounded on $N$.

title: Definition:Locally Bounded/Mapping
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. Let $f$ be a mapping defined on $M$. Then $f$ is said to be locally bounded : for all $x \in A$, there is some neighbourhood $N$ of $x$ such that $f \sqbrk N$ is bounded.

title: Definition:Locally Bounded Topological Vector Space
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological vector space. We say that $X$ is locally bounded : there exists a von Neumann-bounded open neighborhood of ${\mathbf 0}_X$.

title: Definition:Locally Compact Hausdorff Space
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a $T_2$ (Hausdorff) space.

title: Definition:Locally Compact Hausdorff Space/Definition 1
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a $T_2$ (Hausdorff) topological space. $T$ is a locally compact Hausdorff space each point of $S$ has a compact neighborhood. That is, $T$ is weakly locally compact.

title: Definition:Locally Compact Hausdorff Space/Definition 2
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a $T_2$ (Hausdorff) space. $T$ is a locally compact Hausdorff space each point has a neighborhood basis consisting of compact sets. That is, $T$ is locally compact (in the general sense).

title: Definition:Locally Compact Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is locally compact : every point of $S$ has a neighborhood basis $\BB$ such that all elements of $\BB$ are compact.

title: Definition:Locally Compact Space/Also defined as
snippet: == Locally Compact Space: Also known as == A locally compact space is sometimes defined as what on is called a weakly locally compact space. There is no clear consensus on the definition of local compactness, although there appears to be a modern trend in favor of the definition used here. A concept that is more often used and about which there is no disagreement, is that of a locally compact Hausdorff space. Category:Definitions/Locally Compact Spaces

title: Definition:Locally Compact Topological Group
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \odot, \tau}$ be a topological group.

title: Definition:Locally Compact Topological Group/Also known as
snippet: == Locally Compact Topological Group: Also known as == A locally compact topological group is also known as a locally compact group.

title: Definition:Locally Compact Topological Group/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \odot, \tau}$ be a topological group. We say that $\struct {G, \odot, \tau}$ is a locally compact topological group $\struct {G, \tau}$ is a locally compact Hausdorff space.

title: Definition:Locally Compact Topological Group/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \odot, \tau}$ be a topological group. Let $e$ be the identity element of $\struct {G, \odot}$. We say that $\struct {G, \odot, \tau}$ is a locally compact topological group $\struct {G, \tau}$ is a $T_2$ space and: there exists an open neighborhood $U$ of $e$ such that the topological closure of $U$ in $\struct {G, \tau}$ is compact.

title: Definition:Locally Compact Topological Vector Space
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological vector space. We say that $X$ is locally compact : there exists a von Neumann-bounded open neighborhood of ${\mathbf 0}_X$ with compact closure.

title: Definition:Locally Connected Space/Definition 1
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct{S, \tau}$ is locally connected each point of $T$ has a local basis consisting entirely of connected sets in $T$.

title: Definition:Locally Connected Space/Definition 2
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is locally connected $T$ is weakly locally connected at each point of $T$. That is, a topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is locally connected each point of $T$ has a neighborhood basis consisting of connected sets of $T$.

title: Definition:Locally Connected Space/Definition 3
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is locally connected it has a basis consisting of connected sets in $T$.

title: Definition:Locally Connected Space/Definition 4
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is locally connected the components of the open sets of $T$ are also open in $T$.

title: Definition:Locally Convex Space
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a vector space over $\GF$. Let $\mathcal P$ be a set of seminorms on $X$. We call the pair $\struct {X, \mathcal P}$ a locally convex space over $\GF$.

title: Definition:Locally Convex Space/Hausdorff
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \PP}$ be a locally convex space. We say that $\struct {X, \PP}$ is Hausdorff $\PP$ is separating.

title: Definition:Locally Convex Space/Standard Topology
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \PP}$ be a locally convex space. For each $p \in \PP$, $\epsilon > 0$ and $y \in X$, define: $\map {B_p} {\epsilon, x} = \set {y \in X : \map p {y - x} 0, \, x \in X}$ Let $\tau$ be the topology generated by $\SS$. We call $\tau$ the standard topology on $\struct {X, \PP}$.

title: Definition:Locally Convex Topological Vector Space
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological vector space over $\GF$. We say that $\struct {X, \tau}$ is a locally convex topological vector space : there exits a local basis $\BB$ for ${\mathbf 0}_X$ in $\struct {X, \tau}$ such that: each $A \in \BB$ is convex.

title: Definition:Locally Convex Topology Consistent with Dual System
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\innerprod E F$ be a dual system. Let $\PP$ be a set of seminorms on $E$. Let $\tau$ be the standard topology on $\struct {E, \PP}$. Let $\struct {E, \tau}^\ast$ be the topological dual space of $\struct {E, \tau}$. We say that $\tau$ is consistent with $\innerprod E F$ if $\struct {E, \tau}^\ast = \set {x \mapsto \innerprod x f : f \in F}$. We may write this as simply $\struct {E, \tau}^\ast = F$, with the identification of $f \in F$ and $x \mapsto \innerprod x f$ understood.

title: Definition:Locally Euclidean Space
snippet: Let $M$ be a topological space. Let $d \in \N$ be a natural number. Then $M$ is a locally Euclidean space of dimension $d$ each point in $M$ has an open neighbourhood which is homeomorphic to an open subset of Euclidean space $\R^d$.

title: Definition:Locally Euclidean Space/Also defined as
snippet: == Locally Euclidean Space: Also known as == Some authorities impose the condition on a locally Euclidean space that it also be a $T_2$ (Hausdorff) space. This is now rare. considers it unhelpful, and perhaps a holdover from early days in the history of development of this still growing field. Hausdorffness is generally taken for granted in the definition of a topological manifold, whose definition now has to specify its Hausdorff nature explicitly, rather than assuming it inherited from its underlying locally Euclidean space. Category:Definitions/Locally Euclidean Spaces

title: Definition:Locally Euclidean Space/Complex
snippet: Let $M$ be a $T_2$ (Hausdorff) topological space. $M$ is a complex locally Euclidean space of dimension $d$ each point in $M$ has an open neighbourhood which is homeomorphic to an open set of the complex Euclidean space $\C^d$. Category:Definitions/Topological Spaces Category:Definitions/Hausdorff Spaces

title: Definition:Locally Finite
snippet: Locally Finite Set of Subsets Locally Finite Cover Locally Finite Graph

title: Definition:Locally Finite Cover
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a cover of a topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$. Then $\CC$ is a locally finite cover of $S$ : each $x \in S$ has a neighborhood $N_x$ which intersects a finite number of sets in $\CC$.

title: Definition:Locally Finite Graph
snippet: A locally finite graph $G$ is an infinite graph where every vertex of $G$ has finite degree.

title: Definition:Locally Finite Set of Subsets
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\FF$ be a set of subsets of $S$. Then $\FF$ is locally finite each element of $S$ has a neighborhood which intersects a finite number of sets in $\FF$.

title: Definition:Locally Hausdorff Space
snippet: A topological space $\struct {S, \tau}$ is a locally Hausdorff space every point of $S$ has a neighborhood which is $T_2$ (Hausdorff).

title: Definition:Locally Injectively Path-Connected Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is locally injectively path-connected it has a basis consisting entirely of injectively path-connected sets.

title: Definition:Locally Injectively Path-Connected Space/Also known as
snippet: == Locally Injectively Path-Connected Space: Also known as == A locally injectively path-connected space is also known as a locally arc-connected space. However, the latter is used on and elsewhere for a stronger concept. Some sources do not hyphenate: locally injectively path connected space.

title: Definition:Locally Integrable Function Space
snippet: Let $f : \R^d \to \C$ be a locally integrable function. The set of all $f$ is called the locally integrable function space and is denoted by $\map {L^1_{loc} } {\R^d}$.

title: Definition:Locally Metrizable Space
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. The space $T$ is locally metrizable : every point of $S$ is contained in an open set that is metrizable in the subspace topology.

title: Definition:Locally Minimizing Admissible Curve
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $I = \closedint c d$ be a closed real interval. Let $\gamma : I \to M$ be an admissible curve. Suppose for all $t_0 \in I$ there exists a neighborhood $I_0 \subseteq I$ such that if $a, b \in I_0$ and $a < b$ then the restriction $\gamma \restriction_{\closedint a b}$ is minimizing. Then $\gamma$ is said to be locally minimizing.

title: Definition:Locally Noetherian Scheme
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ be a scheme. Then $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ is locally noetherian every $x \in X$ is has an affine open neighborhood $U \subseteq X$ such that the ring $\map {\OO_X} U$ is noetherian.

title: Definition:Locally Path-Connected Space/Also known as
snippet: == Locally Path-Connected Space: Also known as == A locally path-connected space is also known as a locally $0$-connected space, which can appear abbreviated as an $LC^0$ space. Some sources do not hyphenate: locally path connected space.

title: Definition:Locally Path-Connected Space/Definition 1
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a locally path-connected space each point of $T$ has a local basis consisting of path-connected sets in $T$.

title: Definition:Locally Path-Connected Space/Definition 2
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a locally path-connected space each point of $T$ has a neighborhood basis consisting of path-connected sets in $T$.

title: Definition:Locally Path-Connected Space/Definition 3
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a locally path-connected space it has a basis consisting of path-connected sets in $T$.

title: Definition:Locally Path-Connected Space/Definition 4
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a locally path-connected space the path components of open sets of $T$ are also open in $T$.

title: Definition:Locally Pseudometrizable Space
snippet: A topological space $\struct {S, \tau}$ is locally pseudometrizable every point of $T$ has a neighborhood which is pseudometrizable.

title: Definition:Locally Ringed Space
snippet: A locally ringed space is a ringed space $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ such that the stalks of the structure sheaf $\OO_X$ are local rings.

title: Definition:Locally Small Category
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Then $\mathbf C$ is said to be locally small all of its hom classes are sets. That is, for all objects $X, Y \in \mathbf C_0$ of $\mathbf C$: $\map {\operatorname {Hom}_{\mathbf C} } {X, Y} = \set {f \in \mathbf C_1: f: X \to Y}$ is a set.

title: Definition:Locally Uniform Absolute Convergence
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space. Let $\struct {V, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a normed vector space. Let $\sequence {f_n}$ be a sequence of mappings $f_n: X \to V$. Then the series $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty f_n$ converges locally uniformly absolutely the series $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \norm {f_n}$ converges locally uniformly.

title: Definition:Locally Uniform Absolute Convergence of Product
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space. Let $\struct {\mathbb K, \norm {\,\cdot\,} }$ be a valued field. Let $\sequence {f_n}$ be a sequence of mappings $f_n: X \to \mathbb K$. Then the infinite product $\ds \prod_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty f_n$ converges locally uniformly absolutely every point of $X$ has a neighborhood on which it converges uniformly absolutely.

title: Definition:Locally Uniform Convergence/Complex Functions
snippet: Let $U \subseteq \C$ be an open set. Let $\sequence {f_n}$ be a be a sequence of functions $f_n : U \to \C$. For $z \in U$, let $\map {D_r} z$ be the open disk of radius $r$ about $z$. Then $f_n$ converges to $f$ locally uniformly : for each $z \in U$, there is an $r \in \R_{>0}$ such that $f_n$ converges uniformly to $f$ on $\map {D_r} z$ and: $\map {D_r} z \subseteq U$

title: Definition:Locally Uniform Convergence/General Definition
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\struct {M, d}$ be a metric space. Let $\sequence {f_n}$ be a sequence of mappings $f_n: X \to M$. Then $f_n$ converges locally uniformly to $f: X \to M$ every point of $X$ has a neighborhood on which $f_n$ converges uniformly to $f$.

title: Definition:Locally Uniform Convergence/Series
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space. Let $V$ be a normed vector space. Let $\sequence {f_n}$ be a sequence of mappings $f_n: X \to V$. Then the series $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty f_n$ converges locally uniformly the sequence of partial sums converges locally uniformly. Category:Definitions/Uniform Convergence

title: Definition:Locally Uniform Convergence of Product
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a weakly locally compact topological space. Let $\struct {\mathbb K, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a valued field. Let $\sequence {f_n}$ be a sequence of locally bounded mappings $f_n: S \to \mathbb K$.

title: Definition:Locally Uniform Convergence of Product/Definition 1
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a weakly locally compact topological space. Let $\struct {\mathbb K, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a valued field. Let $\sequence {f_n}$ be a sequence of locally bounded mappings $f_n: S \to \mathbb K$. The infinite product $\ds \prod_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty f_n$ converges locally uniformly every point of $T$ has a compact neighborhood on which it converges uniformly.

title: Definition:Locally Uniform Convergence of Product/Definition 2
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a weakly locally compact topological space. Let $\struct {\mathbb K, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a valued field. Let $\sequence {f_n}$ be a sequence of locally bounded mappings $f_n: S \to \mathbb K$. The infinite product $\ds \prod_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty f_n$ converges locally uniformly it converges uniformly on every compact subspace of $T$.

title: Definition:Locally Uniform Convergence of Product/Warning
snippet: == Definition:Locally Uniform Convergence of Product: Warning == As with uniform convergence, the notion of locally uniform convergence of a product is delicate. Hence one usually restricts its definition to locally bounded mappings. Category:Definitions/Locally Uniform Convergence of Product

title: Definition:Located Vector
snippet: A located vector is a vector quantity with a specified initial point.

title: Definition:Loculus of Archimedes
snippet: The loculus of Archimedes is a dissection of the square into $14$ pieces: 500px The dissection is constructed as follows: $D$, $E$ and $F$ are on the midpoints of the sides of the square $T$ is the midpoint of $BD$ $C$ is the midpoint of its line $M$ is the midpoint of $AG$ $K$ is on the line $AH$ $O$ is on the line $BC$. The object is to rearrange the pieces to form different geometric figures.

title: Definition:Loculus of Archimedes/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Loculus of Archimedes == The loculus of Archimedes appears in a fragmentary form in an Arabic manuscript The Book of Archimedes on the Division of the Figure Stomaschion. It is also in the which was discovered by in $1906$. Note that the version in the is presented in rectangular form, and has been transformed here into a square, so as to match its usual presentation.

title: Definition:Loculus of Archimedes/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Loculus of Archimedes == The word loculus is Latin for little box. The word Ostomachion derives from the Greek Ὀστομάχιον, which means bone-fight, from ὀστέον (osteon), meaning bone, and μάχη (mache), which means fight, battle, or combat. That is, it is a combat (with the mind), a puzzle, whose tools are pieces manufactured out of bones, or pieces of ivory. The word Stomachion, which appears in some ancient manuscripts, appears to be a corruption of Ostomachion.

title: Definition:Locus
snippet: A locus is a set of points which satisfy a particular condition. Such points usually form a curve or a surface, depending on the context.

title: Definition:Locus/Also known as
snippet: == Locus: Also known as == Some sources refer to a locus merely as a curve.

title: Definition:Locus/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Locus == The plural of locus is loci, pronounced either loak-ee or loak-eye. opines that the word is obsolete.

title: Definition:Loess
snippet: Loess is a modification of the lowess technique for fitting a smooth curve to a large data set that does not involve the separate process for reducing the influence of outliers.

title: Definition:Loess/Also defined as
snippet: == Loess: Also defined as == Some sources use the term loess as a synonym for lowess. However, the two techniques are different: lowess includes a process to reduce the influence of outliers, while loess does not.

title: Definition:Loess/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Loess == The word loess is an acronym for locally estimated scatterplot smoothing. The word is also used in the field of geology for a type of rock formed from windblown sediment. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Log Normal Distribution
snippet: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable on a probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $\Img X = \R_{>0}$. $X$ is said to have a log normal distribution it has probability density function: $\ds \map {f_X} x = \dfrac 1 {\sigma \sqrt {2 \pi} x } \map \exp {-\dfrac {\paren {\map \ln x - \mu}^2} {2 \sigma^2} }$ for $\mu \in \R, \sigma \in \R_{> 0}$.

title: Definition:Log Tables
snippet: Log tables are a set of reference tables for calculation of common logarithms of real numbers. They consist of a set of lookup tables for the mantissa of the common logarithm of the number in question. It is then the task of the user to provide the characteristic by inspection.

title: Definition:Log Tables/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Log Tables == Before the advent of inexpensive electronic calculators, the use of log tables was a standard technique for multiplication of multi-digit numbers. The technique consisted of: $(1): \quad$ Use the log tables to find the logarithms of $x$ and $y$ to obtain $\log_{10} x$ and $\log_{10} y$. $(2): \quad$ Add those logarithms to obtain $\log_{10} x y$. $(3): \quad$ Use the log tables to find the antilogarithm of $\log_{10} x y$. The result is $x y$. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Logarithm
snippet: == Natural Logarithm ==

title: Definition:Logarithm/Base
snippet: Let $\log_a$ denote the logarithm function on whatever domain: $\R$ or $\C$. The constant $a$ is known as the base of the logarithm.

title: Definition:Logarithm/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Logarithm == The initial invention of the logarithm was by , who used a base $\dfrac {9 \, 999 \, 999} {10 \, 000 \, 000}$. , who invented the slide rule, added a table of natural logarithms to his English translation of 's book. In $1685$, established that logarithms can be considered as exponents. In $1694$, made the same discovery. Logarithms in their modern form are as a result of the original work done by . was the first one to create a consistent theory of the logarithm of a negative number and of an imaginary number.

title: Definition:Logarithm/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Logarithm == The word logarithm comes from the Ancient Greek λόγος (lógos), meaning word or reason, and ἀριθμός (arithmós), meaning number. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Logarithmic Coordinate System
snippet: A logarithmic coordinate system is a Cartesian coordinate system in which the axes are marked with logarithmic scales.

title: Definition:Logarithmic Decrement
snippet: Consider a physical system $S$ whose behaviour can be described with the second order ODE in the form: $(1): \quad \dfrac {\d^2 x} {\d t^2} + 2 b \dfrac {\d x} {\d t} + a^2 x = 0$ for $a, b \in \R_{>0}$. Let $b < a$, so as to make $S$ underdamped. 600px Let $T$ be the period of oscillation of $S$. Let $x_1$ and $x_2$ be successive local maxima of $x$. From Ratio of Successive Local Maxima for Underdamped Free Vibration: $\dfrac {x_1} {x_2} = e^{b T}$ The logarithmic decrement of $S$ is defined as: $\map \ln {\dfrac {x_1} {x_2} } = b T$

title: Definition:Logarithmic Differentiation
snippet: Logarithmic differentiation is the technique of obtaining the derivative of an arithmetic expression by obtaining its (natural) logarithm before differentiation.

title: Definition:Logarithmic Distribution
snippet: Let $X$ be a discrete random variable on a probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. $X$ has the logarithmic distribution if it has probability density function: $\map \Pr {X = k} = -\dfrac {\theta^k} {k \ln \paren {1 - \theta} }$ where: $k = 1, 2, \ldots$ $\theta \in \openint 0 1$

title: Definition:Logarithmic Distribution/Also known as
snippet: == Logarithmic Distribution: Also known as == The logarithmic distribution is also known as the log-series distribution.

title: Definition:Logarithmic Distribution/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Logarithmic Distribution == The logarithmic distribution was designed by in $1941$. It is widely used in studies of species diversity.

title: Definition:Logarithmic Graph Paper
snippet: Logarithmic graph paper is graph paper in which both coordinate axes are marked with a logarithmic scale.

title: Definition:Logarithmic Graph Paper/Also known as
snippet: == Logarithmic Graph Paper: Also known as == Logarithmic graph paper is also known as log-log graph paper, reflecting the fact that both coordinate axes use a logarithmic scale. Hence note that logarithmic graph paper would then be used for what on is defined as semilogarithmic graph paper. Category:Definitions/Logarithmic Graph Paper

title: Definition:Logarithmic Integral
snippet: Let $x \in \R_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive real number. The logarithmic integral of $x$ is defined as: $\ds \map \li x = \PV_0^x \frac {\d t} {\ln t}$ where: $\ln$ denotes the natural logarithm function $\PV$ denotes the Cauchy principal value. That is, as $\dfrac 1 {\ln t}$ has discontinuities at $t = 0$ and $t = 1$: $\map \li x = \begin {cases} \ds \lim_{\varepsilon \mathop \to 0^+} \paren {\int_\varepsilon^x \frac {\rd t} {\ln t} } & 0 1 \end {cases}$

title: Definition:Logarithmic Integral/Also defined as
snippet: == Logarithmic Integral: Also defined as == By defining the integrand of the logarithmic integral to be $0$ at $t = 0$, the lower limit can be taken in the first integral to be $0$. Hence: $\map \li x = \begin {cases} \ds \int_0^x \frac {\rd t} {\ln t} & : 0 \le x 1 \end {cases}$

title: Definition:Logarithmic Integral/Also known as
snippet: == Logarithmic Integral: Also known as == The logarithmic integral is also seen referred to as the integral logarithm.

title: Definition:Logarithmic Integral/Eulerian
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number such that $x > 2$. The Eulerian logarithmic integral of $x$ is defined as: $\ds \map \Li x = \int_2^x \frac {\d t} {\ln t}$ where $\ln$ denotes the natural logarithm function.

title: Definition:Logarithmic Integral/Eulerian/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Eulerian Logarithmic Integral == The Eulerian logarithmic integral was conjectured by when he was $14$ or $15$ to be a good approximation for the prime-counting function. Hence the first statement of this particular form of the Prime Number Theorem.

title: Definition:Logarithmic Integral/Warning
snippet: == Logarithmic Integral: Warning == The logarithmic integral and the Eulerian logarithmic integral are not consistently denoted in the literature (some sources use $\map \li x$ to indicate the Eulerian version, for example). It is therefore important to take care which is being referred to at any point.

title: Definition:Logarithmic Mean Value
snippet: Let $f: \N \to \C$ be an arithmetic function. The logarithmic mean value of $f$ is the limit: $\map L f = \ds \lim_{x \mathop \to \infty} \frac 1 {\ln x} \sum_{n \mathop \le x} \frac {\map f n} n$ if it exists.

title: Definition:Logarithmic Spiral
snippet: The logarithmic spiral is the locus of the equation expressed in polar coordinates as: $r = a e^{b \theta}$ 600px

title: Definition:Logarithmic Spiral/Also known as
snippet: == Logarithmic Spiral: Also known as == Other names for the logarithmic spiral include: equiangular spiral exponential spiral logistic spiral.

title: Definition:Logarithmic Spiral/Also presented as
snippet: == Logarithmic Spiral: Also presented as == The logarithmic spiral can also be presented in the forms: {{eqn | l = \map \ln {\dfrac r a} | r = \theta \cot b }} {{eqn | l = r | r = a e^{\theta \cot b} }}

title: Definition:Logarithmic Spiral/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Logarithmic Spiral == The logarithmic spiral was investigated in some depth by . He directed that on his death a logarithmic spiral would be engraved on his tombstone, with the motto Eadem mutata resurgo (Though changed I arise the same).

title: Definition:Logarithmic Transformation
snippet: Let $X$ be a random variable whose values are positive. A logarithmic transformation of $X$ is a mapping of $X$ to $Y = \ln X$.

title: Definition:Logic
snippet: Logic is the study of the structure of statements and their truth values, divorced from their conceptual content. It has frequently been defined as the science of reasoning. According to : Nearly a hundred definitions of it have been given. ... It will, however, generally be conceded that its central problem is the classification of arguments, so that all those that are bad are thrown into one division, and all those which are good into another... The best way to find out what logic is is to do some. Logic ... consists of deduction. ...

title: Definition:Logic/Also known as
snippet: == Logic: Also known as == Some sources introduce the term formal logic, but there is little to justify this as a concept separate from that of just logic.

title: Definition:Logic/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Logic == The study of logic was begun by the ancient Greeks; some sources attribute its invention directly to . Their education system stressed the importance of competence in philosophy and rhetoric. In order to excel in rhetoric, it was necessary to master logic. The stoic school extended 's initial creation, and further developed in more recent times by . However, those later discoveries were not fully appreciated at the time, and when work was done in the early $20$th century to expand our understanding of the subject, their work was in fact duplicated.

title: Definition:Logic Gate
snippet: A logic gate is an idealized representation of a device whose purpose is to implement a logical connective in an electronic circuit.

title: Definition:Logical Argument
snippet: A logical argument (or just argument) is a process of creating a new statement from one or more existing statements. An argument proceeds from a set of premises to a conclusion, by means of logical implication, via a procedure called logical inference. An argument may have more than one premise, but only one conclusion. While statements may be classified as either true or false, an argument may be classified as either valid or invalid.

title: Definition:Logical Argument/Finitary
snippet: A finitary argument is a logical argument which starts with a finite number of axioms, and can be translated into a finite number of statements.

title: Definition:Logical Axiom/Also known as
snippet: == Logical Axiom: Also known as == The name primitive proposition can sometimes be found for logical axiom.

title: Definition:Logical Complement
snippet: The (logical) complement of a propositional formula $\mathbf A$ is the negation of $\mathbf A$, that is, $\neg \mathbf A$. Conversely, the complement of $\neg \mathbf A$ is defined to be $\mathbf A$.

title: Definition:Logical Complement/Complementary Pair
snippet: For any propositional formula $\mathbf A$, the set $\left\{{\mathbf A, \neg \mathbf A}\right\}$ is called a complementary pair of formulas.

title: Definition:Logical Connective
snippet: A logical connective is an object which either modifies a statement, or combines existing statements into a new statement, called a compound statement. It is almost universal to identify a logical connective with the symbol representing it. Thus, logical connective may also, particularly in symbolic logic, be used to refer to that symbol, rather than speaking of a connective symbol separately. In mathematics, logical connectives are considered to be truth-functional.

title: Definition:Logical Connective/Also defined as
snippet: == Logical Connective: Also defined as == Some sources reserve the term logical connective for what on is defined as a binary logical connective, on the grounds that a unary logical connective does not actually "connect" anything. However, this is a trivial distinction which can serve only to confuse.

title: Definition:Logical Connective/Also known as
snippet: == Logical Connective: Also known as == Other terms for logical connective which may be encountered include:

title: Definition:Logical Connective/Binary
snippet: A binary logical connective is a logical connective whose effect on its compound statement is determined by the truth value of two substatements. In the field of symbolic logic, the following four (symbols for) binary logical connectives are commonly used:

title: Definition:Logical Connective/Phrase of Connection
snippet: Let $\circ$ represent a logical connective. The natural language phrase which is represented by $\circ$ is called a phrase of connection. Thus the phrase of connection represented by:

title: Definition:Logical Connective/Unary
snippet: A unary logical connective is a logical connective whose effect on its compound statement is determined by the truth value of one substatement. In standard Aristotelian logic, there are four of these. The only non-trivial one is logical not, as shown on Unary Truth Functions.

title: Definition:Logical Equivalence
snippet: If two statements $p$ and $q$ are such that: $p \vdash q$, that is: $p$ therefore $q$ $q \vdash p$, that is: $q$ therefore $p$ then $p$ and $q$ are said to be (logically) equivalent. That is: $p \dashv \vdash q$ means: $p \vdash q$ and $q \vdash p$ Note that because the conclusion of an argument is a single statement, there can be only one statement on either side of the $\dashv \vdash$ sign. In symbolic logic, the notion of logical equivalence occurs in the form of provable equivalence and semantic equivalence.

title: Definition:Logical Equivalence/Also denoted as
snippet: == Logical Equivalence: Also denoted as == Some sources denote $p \dashv \vdash q$ by $p \leftrightarrow q$. Others use $p \equiv q$. In modal logic, logical equivalence is expressed as: $\Box \paren {p \equiv q}$ On , during the course of development of general proofs of logical equivalence, the notation $p \leadstoandfrom q$ is used as a matter of course. {{LatexFor|for = \Box \paren {p \equiv q} }} Note that in Distinction between Logical Implication and Conditional, the distinction between $\implies$ and $\leadsto$ is explained.

title: Definition:Logical Equivalence/Also known as
snippet: == Logical Equivalence: Also known as == Two logically equivalent statements are also referred to as: interderivable equivalent equipollent equipotent strictly equivalent coimplicant

title: Definition:Logical Form
snippet: Logical form is a term used to mean the logical structure of an argument or statement independent of its content or semantic meaning.

title: Definition:Logical Formula
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a formal language used in the field of symbolic logic. Then the well-formed formulas of $\LL$ are often referred to as logical formulas. They are symbolic representations of statements, and often of compound statements in particular.

title: Definition:Logical Implication
snippet: In a valid argument, the premises logically imply the conclusion. If the truth of one statement $p$ can be shown in an argument directly to cause the meaning of another statement $q$ to be true, then $q$ follows from $p$ by logical implication. We may say: $p$, therefore $q$ and write $p \vdash q$. $q$, because $p$ and write $q \dashv p$.

title: Definition:Logical Implication/Also known as
snippet: == Logical Implication: Also known as == The term logical consequence can often be seen as a synonym for logical implication.

title: Definition:Logical Implication/Distinction with Conditional
snippet: == Distinction between Logical Implication and Conditional == It is important to understand the difference between: $A \implies B$: If we assume the truth of $A$, we can deduce the truth of $B$ and: $A \leadsto B$: $A$ is asserted to be true, therefore it can be deduced that $B$ is true When $A$ is indeed true, the distinction is less important than when the truth of $A$ is in question, but it is a bad idea to ignore it.

title: Definition:Logical Inference
snippet: Logical inference is the process used in natural deduction to deduce the validity of statement forms from other statement forms by use of proof rules. Given a set of logical formulae and the proof rules, we (logically) infer other formulae. Hence, in essence, logical inference is the process of reaching a conclusion from a set of premises.

title: Definition:Logical Inference/Also known as
snippet: == Logical Inference: Also known as == The term logical inference is often used as just inference. This process is sometimes called logical derivation or just derivation. However, beware that derivation has a range of different meanings.

title: Definition:Logical Language
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a formal language used in symbolic logic. Then $\LL$ is called a logical language.

title: Definition:Logical Matrix
snippet: A logical matrix is a matrix whose entries are all either $0$ or $1$.

title: Definition:Logical Matrix/Also known as
snippet: == Logical Matrix: Also known as == A logical matrix is also known as a boolean matrix, for . Some sources use the term $\tuple {0, 1}$-matrix.

title: Definition:Logical NAND
snippet: NAND (that is, not and), is a binary connective, written symbolically as $p \uparrow q$, whose behaviour is as follows: $p \uparrow q$ is defined as: it is not the case that $p$ and $q$ are both true. $p \uparrow q$ is voiced: $p$ nand $q$

title: Definition:Logical NAND/Boolean Interpretation
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ be propositional formulas. Let $\uparrow$ denote the logical NAND operator. The truth value of $\mathbf A \uparrow \mathbf B$ under a boolean interpretation $v$ is given by: $\map v {\mathbf A \uparrow \mathbf B} = \begin {cases} \T & : \map v {\mathbf A} = \F \text { or } \map v {\mathbf B} = \F \\ \F & : \text {otherwise} \end{cases}$ Category:Definitions/Logical NAND

title: Definition:Logical NAND/Notational Variants
snippet: Various symbols are encountered that denote the concept of logical NAND: {| border="1" cellpadding="4" cellspacing="0" style="font-weight:bold; text-align:center; |- ! Symbol ! Origin ! Known as |- | $p \mid q$ | | Sheffer stroke |- | $p \uparrow q$ | | Also sometimes referred to as the Sheffer stroke |- | $p \mathop {\mathsf {NAND} } q$ | | |- | $p \mathop / q$ | | who refer to it as the stroke function |- | $p \mathop {\bar \curlywedge} q$ | | Modified Ampheck |} The all-uppercase rendition NAND originates from the digital electronics industry, where, because NAND is Functionally Complete,…

title: Definition:Logical NAND/Truth Function
snippet: The NAND connective defines the truth function $f^\uparrow$ as follows: {{eqn | l = \map {f^\uparrow} {\F, \F} | r = \T }} {{eqn | l = \map {f^\uparrow} {\F, \T} | r = \T }} {{eqn | l = \map {f^\uparrow} {\T, \F} | r = \T }} {{eqn | l = \map {f^\uparrow} {\T, \T} | r = \F }} Category:Definitions/Logical NAND Category:Definitions/Truth Functions

title: Definition:Logical NAND/Truth Table
snippet: The characteristic truth table of the logical NAND operator $p \uparrow q$ is as follows: $\begin{array}{|cc||c|} \hline p & q & p \uparrow q \\ \hline \F & \F & \T \\ \F & \T & \T \\ \T & \F & \T \\ \T & \T & \F \\ \hline \end{array}$

title: Definition:Logical NAND/Truth Table/Matrix Form
snippet: The characteristic truth table of the logical NAND operator $p \uparrow q$ can be presented in matrix form as follows: $\begin {array} {c|cc} \uparrow & \T & \F \\ \hline \T & \F & \T \\ \F & \T & \T \\ \end {array}$ Category:Definitions/Logical NAND Category:Definitions/Truth Tables

title: Definition:Logical NAND/Truth Table/Number
snippet: The truth table number of the logical NAND operator $p \uparrow q$ is as follows: Ascending order: $1110$ or $\T\T\T\F$ Descending order: $0111$ or $\F\T\T\T$ Category:Definitions/Logical NAND Category:Definitions/Truth Tables

title: Definition:Logical NOR
snippet: NOR (that is, not or), is a binary connective, written symbolically as $p \downarrow q$, whose behaviour is as follows: $p \downarrow q$ is defined as: neither $p$ nor $q$ is true. $p \downarrow q$ is voiced: $p$ nor $q$ The symbol $\downarrow$ is known as the Quine arrow, named after .

title: Definition:Logical NOR/Boolean Interpretation
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ be propositional formulas. Let $\downarrow$ denote the logical NOR operator. The truth value of $\mathbf A \downarrow \mathbf B$ under a boolean interpretation $v$ is given by: $\map v {\mathbf A \downarrow \mathbf B} = \begin {cases} \T & : \map v {\mathbf A} = \map v {\mathbf B} = \F \\ \F & : \text {otherwise} \end {cases}$ Category:Definitions/Logical NOR

title: Definition:Logical NOR/Truth Table
snippet: The characteristic truth table of the logical NOR operator $p \downarrow q$ is as follows: $\begin {array} {|cc||c|} \hline p & q & p \downarrow q \\ \hline \F & \F & \T \\ \F & \T & \F \\ \T & \F & \F \\ \T & \T & \F \\ \hline \end {array}$

title: Definition:Logical NOR/Truth Table/Matrix Form
snippet: The characteristic truth table of the logical NOR operator $p \downarrow q$ can be presented in matrix form as follows: $\begin {array} {c|cc} \downarrow & \T & \F \\ \hline \T & \F & \F \\ \F & \F & \T \\ \end {array}$ Category:Definitions/Logical NOR Category:Definitions/Truth Tables

title: Definition:Logical Not
snippet:
The logical not or (logical) negation operator is a unary connective whose action is to reverse the truth value of the statement on which it operates. $
eg p$ is defined as: It is not the case that $p$ is true The statement $
eg p$ is called the negation of $p$. $
eg p$ is voiced not $p$.

title: Definition:Logical Not/Also known as
snippet: == Logical Not: Also known as == The (logical) negation of a statement is also referred to as the denial of that statement. Treatments which consider logical connectives as functions may refer to this operator as the contradictory function.
