Note that by Image is Subset of Codomain: $\Img f \subseteq \Cdm f$ There are no other such constraints upon the domain, image and codomain.

title: Definition:Mapping/General Definition
snippet: Let $\ds \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n S_i$ be the cartesian product of sets $S_1$ to $S_n$. Let $\ds \RR \subseteq \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n S_i$ be an $n$-ary relation on $\ds \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n S_i$. Then $\RR$ is a mapping : $\ds \forall x := \tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{n - 1} } \in \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^{n - 1} S_i: \forall y_1, y_2 \in S_n: \tuple {x, y_1} \in \RR \land \tuple {x, y_2} \in \RR \implies y_1 = y_2$ and $\ds \forall x := \tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{n - 1} } \in \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^{n - 1} S_i: \exists y \in S_n: \tuple {x, y} \in \RR$ Thus, a mapping is an $n$-ary…

title: Definition:Mapping/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Mapping == Let $f$ be a mapping. This is usually denoted $f: S \to T$, which is interpreted to mean: $f$ is a mapping with domain $S$ and codomain $T$ $f$ is a mapping of (or from) $S$ to (or into) $T$ $f$ maps $S$ to (or into) $T$. The notation $S \stackrel f {\longrightarrow} T$ is also seen. For $x \in S, y \in T$, the usual notation is: $f: S \to T: \map f s = y$ where $\map f s = y$ is interpreted to mean $\tuple {x, y} \in f$. It is read $f$ of $x$ equals $y$. This is the preferred notation on . Sometimes the brackets are omitted: $f x = y$, as seen in , for example.

title: Definition:Mapping/Notation/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Notation for Mapping == The notation $\map f x$ was introduced by .

title: Definition:Mapping/Notation/Warning
snippet: == Notation for Mapping == The notation: Let $\map f x$ be a mapping (or function) ... is an abuse of notation. If $f: S \to T$ is a mapping, then $\map f x \in T$ for all $x \in S$. Thus $\map f x$ is a mapping $\Img f$ is a set of mappings. The point is that, as used here, $\map f x$ is not a mapping, but it is the image of $x$ under $f$. Hence it is preferable not to talk about: the function $\cos x$ but instead should say: the function $\cos$ or: the function $x \mapsto \cos x$ although for the latter it would be better to also specify the domain and codomain.

title: Definition:Mapping/Technical Note
snippet: == Technical Note for Mapping == {{LatexFor|for = \map {f} {x} }} When the argument is a single character, it is usual to omit the braces: \map f x This command is specific to . Category:Technical Notes

title: Definition:Mapping Induced on Powerset
snippet: The mapping induced on a powerset can be either of two concepts:

title: Definition:Mapping Preserves Infimum
snippet: Let $\left({S_1, \preceq_1}\right)$, $\left({S_2, \preceq_2}\right)$ be ordered sets. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping.

title: Definition:Mapping Preserves Infimum/All
snippet: $f$ preserves all infima for every subset $F$ of $S_1$, $f$ preserves the infimum of $F$.

title: Definition:Mapping Preserves Infimum/Filtered
snippet: $f$ preserves filtered infima for every filtered subset $F$ of $S_1$, $f$ preserves the infimum of $F$.

title: Definition:Mapping Preserves Infimum/Finite
snippet: $f$ preserves finite infima for every finite subset $F$ of $S_1$, $f$ preserves the infimum of $F$.

title: Definition:Mapping Preserves Infimum/Meet
snippet: $f$ preserves meet for every pair of elements $x, y$ of $S_1$, $f$ preserves the infimum of $\set {x, y}$.

title: Definition:Mapping Preserves Infimum/Subset
snippet: Let $F$ be a subset of $S_1$. $f$ preserves infimum of $F$ $F$ admits a infimum in $\struct {S_1, \preceq_1}$ implies $\map {f^\to} F$ admits an infimum in $\struct {S_2, \preceq_2}$ and $\map \inf {\map {f^\to} F} = \map f {\inf F}$

title: Definition:Mapping Preserves Supremum
snippet: Let $\left({S_1, \preceq_1}\right)$, $\left({S_2, \preceq_2}\right)$ be ordered sets. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping.

title: Definition:Mapping Preserves Supremum/All
snippet: $f$ preserves all suprema for every subset $F$ of $S_1$, $f$ preserves the supremum of $F$.

title: Definition:Mapping Preserves Supremum/Directed
snippet: $f$ preserves directed suprema for every directed subset $F$ of $S_1$, $f$ preserves the supremum of $F$.

title: Definition:Mapping Preserves Supremum/Finite
snippet: $f$ preserves finite suprema for every finite subset $F$ of $S_1$, $f$ preserves the supremum of $F$.

title: Definition:Mapping Preserves Supremum/Join
snippet: $f$ preserves join for every pair of elements $x, y$ of $S_1$, $f$ preserves the supremum of $\left\{ {x, y}\right\}$.

title: Definition:Mapping Preserves Supremum/Subset
snippet: Let $F$ be a subset of $S_1$. $f$ preserves supremum of $F$ $F$ admits a supremum in $\struct {S_1, \preceq_1}$ implies: $\map {f^\to} F$ admits a supremum in $\struct {S_2, \preceq_2}$ and $\map \sup {\map {f^\to} F} = \map f {\sup F}$

title: Definition:Mapping Reduction
snippet: Let $\Sigma, \Sigma'$ be finite sets. Let: be sets of finite strings over $\Sigma$ and $\Sigma'$ respectively, where: $\Sigma^*$ denotes the set of all finite strings over the alphabet $\Sigma$. Let $f : \Sigma^* \to \Sigma'^*$ be a computable function such that, for all $w \in \Sigma^*$: $w \in L \iff \map f w \in L'$ Then, $f$ is a mapping reduction from $L$ to $L'$. If any such $f$ exists, then $L$ is mapping reducible to $L'$, which is denoted as: $L \le_m L'$

title: Definition:Mapping Reduction/Also known as
snippet: == Mapping Reduction: Also known as == The mapping $f$ is frequently called a many-one reduction. Likewise, $L$ is many-one reducible to $L'$.

title: Definition:Mapping Theory
snippet: Mapping theory is the subfield of set theory concerned with the properties of mappings.

title: Definition:Mappings Separating Points
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space. Let $\family {Y_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed family of topological spaces for some indexing set $I$. Let $\family {f_i : X \to Y_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed family of continuous mappings. The family $\family {f_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ is a family of mappings separating points : $\forall x, y \in X : \paren {x \ne y} \implies \paren {\exists i \in I : \map {f_i} x \ne \map {f_i} y}$ In this case, the family $\family {f_i}$ is said to separate points.

title: Definition:Mappings Separating Points from Closed Sets
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space. Let $\family {Y_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed family of topological spaces for some indexing set $I$. Let $\family {f_i : X \to Y_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed family of continuous mappings. The family $\family {f_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ is a family of mappings separating points from closed sets : $\forall x \in X, F \subseteq X : \leftparen {x \notin F \land F}$ is closed $\rightparen {\implies \exists i \in I : \map {f_i} x \notin f_i \sqbrk F^-}$ where $f_i \sqbrk F^-$ denotes the closure of $f_i \sqbrk F$.

title: Definition:Marginal Distribution
snippet: Consider a bivariate distribution $D$ of two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$. The marginal distribution of $X$ is the probability distribution of $D$ $X$.

title: Definition:Marginal Distribution Function
snippet: Consider a bivariate distribution $D$ of two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$. The marginal distribution function of $X$ is written $\map {F_1} x$, and similarly for $Y$ where it is written $\map {F_2} y$.

title: Definition:Marginal Probability Density Function
snippet: Consider a bivariate distribution $D$ of two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$. The marginal probability density function of $X$ is the probability density function of the marginal distribution of $X$ defined as $\map {f_1} x = \ds \int_{-\infty}^\infty \map f {x, t} \rd t$ Similarly for $Y$, which is denoted $\map {f_2} y$

title: Definition:Marginal Probability Density Function/Also known as
snippet: == Marginal Probability Density Function: Also known as == A marginal probability density function is also known as a marginal frequency function.

title: Definition:Marginal Probability Mass Function
snippet: Let $\left({\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}\right)$ be a probability space. Let $X: \Pr \to \R$ and $Y: \Pr \to \R$ both be discrete random variables on $\left({\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}\right)$. Let $p_{X, Y}$ be the joint probability mass function of $X$ and $Y$. Then the probability mass functions $p_X$ and $p_Y$ are called the marginal (probability) mass functions of $X$ and $Y$ respectively.

title: Definition:Marginal of Measure on Product Space
snippet: Let $\struct {X_1, \Sigma_1}$ and $\struct {X_2, \Sigma_2}$ be measurable spaces. Let $\Sigma_1 \otimes \Sigma_2$ be the product $\sigma$-algebra. Let $\pi$ a measure on $\Sigma_1 \otimes \Sigma_2$. The marginal of $\pi$ on $X_i$ for $i \in \set {1,2}$ is the measure $\mu_i$ on $\Sigma_i$ defined as: $\forall A \in \Sigma_i : \map {\mu_i} A := \map \pi {\set { \struct {x_1, x_2} \in X_1 \times X_2 : x_i \in A } }$

title: Definition:Marked Leaf
snippet: Let $T$ be a semantic tableau. Let $t$ be a leaf of $T$. Then $t$ is marked it has occurred in Step 3 of the Semantic Tableau Algorithm. Otherwise, it is called unmarked.

title: Definition:Marked Leaf/Closed
snippet: Let $T$ be a semantic tableau. A marked leaf $t$ of $T$ is marked closed its label $\map U t$ contains a complementary pair. This can be designated by adding to $t$ a second label $\times$.

title: Definition:Marked Leaf/Open
snippet: Let $T$ be a semantic tableau. A marked leaf $t$ of $T$ is marked open its label $\map U t$ does not contain a complementary pair. This can be designated by adding to $t$ a second label $\odot$.

title: Definition:Markov Chain
snippet: Let $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \ge 0}$ be a stochastic process over a countable set $S$. $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \ge 0}$ is a Markov chain it satisfies the Markov property: $\condprob {X_{n + 1} = i_{n + 1} } {X_0 = i_0, X_1 = i_1, \ldots, X_n = i_n} = \condprob {X_{n + 1} = i_{n + 1} } {X_n = i_n}$ for all $n \ge 0$ and all $i_0, i_1, \ldots, i_{n + 1} \in S$. That is, such that the conditional probability of $X_{i + 1}$ is dependent only upon $X_i$ and upon no earlier values of $\sequence {X_n}$. That is, the state of $\sequence {X_n}$ in the future is unaffected by its history.

title: Definition:Markov Chain/Also defined as
snippet: == Markov Chain: Also defined as == The pure mathematical definition of a Markov chain is as a sequence with probabilistic properties. However, a Markov chain is frequently defined in terms of a time series, where each of the indices directly corresponds to a time instant. Hence one may discuss a Markov chain using the notation $\sequence {X_{t_n} }_{n \mathop \ge 0}$ where $t_0, t_1, \ldots, t_n, \ldots$ are time instants. The usual situation is that the time instants are equally spaced, but that is not strictly necessary.

title: Definition:Markov Chain/Also known as
snippet: == Markov Chain: Also known as == A Markov chain is also known by some sources as a Markov process. However, the latter is properly a stochastic process whose transitions may take place on a continuous timescale, and may also have a continuous domain. Some sources use the spelling Markoff chain.

title: Definition:Markov Chain/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Markov Chain == The concept of the Markov chain was introduced by in $1906$.

title: Definition:Markov Chain/Homogeneous
snippet: Let $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \ge 0}$ be a Markov chain on a countable set $S$. $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \ge 0}$ is homogeneous $\condprob {X_{n + 1} = j} {X_n = i}$ does not depend on the value of $n$ for all $i, j \in S$. That is: the transition probabilities are constant.

title: Definition:Markov Chain/State
snippet: Let $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \ge 0}$ be a Markov chain on a countable set $S$. The state of the Markov chain $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \ge 0}$ for a given $k$ is the value of $X_n$ when $n = k$.

title: Definition:Markov Chain/State Space
snippet: Let $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \ge 0}$ be a Markov chain on a countable set $S$. The set $S$ is called the state space of the Markov chain.

title: Definition:Markov Chain/Transition Matrix
snippet: Let $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \ge 0}$ be a Markov chain on a finite set $S$ of cardinality $n$. The transition probabilities for $\sequence {X_n}$ can be expressed in the form of a square matrix of order $n$ thus: $\begin {pmatrix} p_{00} & p_{01} & p_{02} & \cdots & p_{0n} \\ p_{10} & p_{11} & p_{12} & \cdots & p_{1n} \\ p_{20} & p_{21} & p_{22} & \cdots & p_{2n} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ p_{n0} & p_{n1} & p_{n2} & \cdots & p_{nn} \end {pmatrix}$ such that: $\forall j: \ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n p_{ij} = 1$ This square matrix is known as the transition matrix for…

title: Definition:Markov Chain/Transition Probability
snippet: Let $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \ge 0}$ be a Markov chain on a countable set $S$ satisfying the Markov property: $\condprob {X_{n + 1} = i_{n + 1} } {X_0 = i_0, X_1 = i_1, \ldots, X_n = i_n} = \condprob {X_{n + 1} = i_{n + 1} } {X_n = i_n}$ for all $n \ge 0$ and all $i_0, i_1, \ldots, i_{n + 1} \in S$. Let $p_{r s}$ denote the probability that if $X_n = r$ then $X_{n + 1} = s$. Then $p_{r s}$ is called the transition probability from $r$ to $s$. Hence $p_{r r}$ is the probability that if $X_n = r$, it stays in state $r$.

title: Definition:Markov Chain/Transition Time
snippet: Let $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \ge 0}$ be a Markov chain on a countable set $S$. The transition time of a given term $X_i$ is the instant of time corresponding to the index $i$.

title: Definition:Markov Process
snippet: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable which varies over time. Let $X_t$ denote the value of $X$ at time $t$. Then $X$ is a Markov process the future behaviour of $X$ is dependent only upon the value of $X$ at the present time.

title: Definition:Markov Process/Also known as
snippet: == Markov Process: Also known as == A Markov process is also known as a Markov chain. However, the latter term is usually reserved for a stochastic process whose transition times consist of a countable sequence and whose state space is also countable. Some sources use the spelling Markoff process.

title: Definition:Mars
snippet: Mars is the fourth planet of the solar system from the sun. Its orbit lies between those of Earth and Jupiter.

title: Definition:Mars/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Mars == The orbital period of Mars was measured by the as: $12,59;57,17$ days as represented using the Babylonian number system. This is seen to represent the number in decimal notation as approximately: $779 \cdotp 955$ days The modern figure is $779 \cdotp 936$ days

title: Definition:Martingale/Continuous Time
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \sequence {\FF_t}_{t \ge 0}, \Pr}$ be a filtered probability space. Let $\sequence {X_t}_{t \ge 0}$ be an adapted stochastic process. We say that $\sequence {X_t}_{t \ge 0}$ is a $\sequence {\FF_t}_{t \ge 0}$-martingale : $(1) \quad$ $X_t$ is integrable for each $t \in \hointr 0 \infty$ $(2) \quad \forall s, t \in \hointr 0 \infty, \, 0 \le s < t: \expect {X_t \mid \FF_s} = X_s$ Equation $(2)$ is understood as follows: for any version $\expect {X_t \mid \FF_s}$ of the conditional expectation of $X_t$ given $\FF_s$, we have: $\expect {X_t \mid \FF_s} = X_s$ almost…

title: Definition:Martingale/Discrete Time
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \sequence {\FF_n}_{n \ge 0}, \Pr}$ be a filtered probability space. Let $\sequence {X_n}_{n \ge 0}$ be an adapted stochastic process.

title: Definition:Martingale/Discrete Time/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \sequence {\FF_n}_{n \mathop \ge 0}, \Pr}$ be a filtered probability space. Let $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \ge 0}$ be an adapted stochastic process. We say that $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is a $\sequence {\FF_n}_{n \ge 0}$-martingale : $(1): \quad$ $X_n$ is integrable for each $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ $(2): \quad \forall n \ge 0: \expect {X_{n + 1} \mid \FF_n} = X_n$.

title: Definition:Martingale/Discrete Time/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \sequence {\FF_n}_{n \mathop \ge 0}, \Pr}$ be a filtered probability space. Let $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \ge 0}$ be an adapted stochastic process. We say that $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \ge 0}$ is a $\sequence {\FF_n}_{n \mathop \ge 0}$-martingale : $(1): \quad$ $X_n$ is integrable for each $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ $(2): \quad \forall n \in \Z_{\ge 0}, \, \forall m \ge n: \expect {X_m \mid \FF_n} = X_n$.

title: Definition:Mascheroni Construction
snippet: A Mascheroni construction is a geometric construction whose only tool is the compasses.

title: Definition:Mascheroni Construction/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Mascheroni Construction == The compass-only Euclidean constructions now known as Mascheroni constructions are named for . However, this technique had already been invented by , who published it in his in $1672$. This fact only came to general light in $1928$, when the latter work was rediscovered.

title: Definition:Mass
snippet: The mass of a body is a fundamental physical quantity related to how much matter it contains. Mass is equivalent to inertia. Mass also determines the degree to which a body creates or is affected by a gravitational field. It is a scalar quantity.

title: Definition:Mass/Dimension
snippet: == Dimension of Mass == Mass is one of the fundamental dimensions of physics. In dimensional analysis it is assigned the symbol $\mathsf M$. Category:Definitions/Dimensions of Measurement Category:Definitions/Mass

title: Definition:Mass/Symbol
snippet: == Mass: Symbol == The usual symbol used to denote the mass of a body is $m$.

title: Definition:Mass/Units
snippet: The units of measurement of mass are as follows: The SI unit of mass is the kilogram $\mathrm {kg}$. The CGS unit of mass is the gram $\mathrm g$. The FPS unit of mass is the pound $\mathrm {lb}$. Thus: $1 \ \mathrm {kg} = 10^3 \ \mathrm g$ $1 \ \mathrm {lb} = 0.453 \, 592 \, 37 \ \mathrm{kg}$

title: Definition:Mass Density
snippet: Mass density is a physical quantity. The mass density of a body $\BB$ at a point $P$ of $\BB$ is defined as: $\map \rho P = \ds \lim_{\Delta V \mathop \to 0} \dfrac {\Delta m} {\Delta V}$ where: $\Delta V$ is the volume of a small region of $\BB$ containing $P$ $\Delta m$ is the mass of the part of $\BB$ occupying $\Delta V$. Mass density is a scalar quantity.

title: Definition:Mass Density/Also known as
snippet: == Mass Density: Also known as == Mass density is usually known just as density, but there are multiple usages for that term. If it is necessary to distinguish between mass density, area mass density and linear mass density, the term volumetric mass density can be used. will generally use the unadorned term density in its exposition unless there is cause for confusion.

title: Definition:Mass Density/Area
snippet: The area mass density of a two-dimensional body $\BB$ at a point $P$ of $\BB$ is defined as: $\map \rho P = \ds \lim_{\Delta A \mathop \to 0} \dfrac {\Delta m} {\Delta A}$ where: $\Delta A$ is the area of a small region of $\BB$ containing $P$ $\Delta m$ is the mass of the part of $\BB$ occupying $\Delta A$.

title: Definition:Mass Density/Area/Dimension
snippet: The dimension of area mass density is $\mathsf M \mathsf L^{-2}$: mass per unit area. Category:Definitions/Area Mass Density Category:Definitions/Dimensions of Measurement

title: Definition:Mass Density/Area/Symbol
snippet: The usual symbol used to denote area mass density is $\rho_A$ (Greek letter rho). However, some sources simply use $\rho$ if the context makes it clear that it refers to area mass density rather than volume mass density. Occasionally, $\sigma$ (Greek letter sigma) is also used, but this is more commonly used for surface charge density. Category:Definitions/Area Mass Density

title: Definition:Mass Density/Area/Units
snippet: The SI units of area mass density are $\mathrm {kg} \ \mathrm m^{-2}$ (kilograms per square metre). The CGS units of area mass density are $\mathrm g \ \mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ (grams per square centimetre). Thus: $1 \ \mathrm g \ \mathrm{cm}^{-2} = 10 \ \mathrm{kg} \ \mathrm m^{-2}$ Category:Definitions/Area Mass Density Category:Definitions/Units of Measurement

title: Definition:Mass Density/Dimension
snippet: The dimension of (mass) density is $\mathsf {M L}^{-3}$: mass per unit volume. Category:Definitions/Mass Density Category:Definitions/Dimensions of Measurement

title: Definition:Mass Density/Homogeneous Body
snippet: The mass density of a homogeneous body $\BB$ is found by finding its total mass and dividing it by its total volume: $\rho = \dfrac m V$ where: $m$ is the mass of $\BB$ $V$ is the volume of $\BB$.

title: Definition:Mass Density/Linear
snippet: The linear mass density of a one-dimensional body $\BB$ at a point $P$ of $\BB$ is defined as: $\map \rho P = \ds \lim_{\Delta L \mathop \to 0} \dfrac {\Delta m} {\Delta L}$ where: $\Delta L$ is the length of a small region of $\BB$ containing $P$ $\Delta m$ is the mass of the part of $\BB$ occupying $\Delta L$.

title: Definition:Mass Density/Linear/Dimension
snippet: The dimension of linear mass density is $\mathsf M \mathsf L^{-1}$: mass per unit length. Category:Definitions/Linear Mass Density Category:Definitions/Dimensions of Measurement

title: Definition:Mass Density/Linear/Symbol
snippet: The usual symbol used to denote linear mass density is $\mu$ (Greek letter mu). Sometimes $\lambda$ (Greek letter lambda) is also used. Category:Definitions/Linear Mass Density

title: Definition:Mass Density/Linear/Units
snippet: The SI units of linear mass density are $\mathrm {kg} \ \mathrm m^{-1}$ (kilograms per metre). The CGS units of linear mass density are $\mathrm g \ \mathrm{cm}^{-1}$ (grams per centimetre). Thus: $1 \ \mathrm{kg} \ \mathrm m^{-1} = 10 \ \mathrm g \ \mathrm{cm}^{-1}$ Category:Definitions/Linear Mass Density Category:Definitions/Units of Measurement

title: Definition:Mass Density/Symbol
snippet: == Mass Density: Symbol == The usual symbol used to denote (mass) density of a body is $\rho$ (Greek letter rho). Some sources use $d$, but that has so many other uses that it may become confused with other things.

title: Definition:Mass Density/Units
snippet: The SI units of mass density are $\mathrm {kg} \, \mathrm m^{-3}$ (kilograms per cubic metre). The CGS units of mass density are $\mathrm g \, \mathrm{cm}^{-3}$ or, less formally: $\mathrm g / \mathrm {cc}$ (grams per cubic centimetre). The FPS units of mass density are $\mathrm {lb} \, \mathrm {ft}^{-3}$ (pounds per cubic foot).

title: Definition:Mass Susceptibility
snippet: Mass susceptibility is a measure of how a substance will become magnetized under a magnetic field.

title: Definition:Mass Susceptibility/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Mass Susceptibility: Conversion Factors == Some conversion factors between the various units of mass susceptibility are as follows: {{eqn | r = 4 \pi \times 10^{-3} | c = per kilogram }}

title: Definition:Mass Susceptibility/Dimension
snippet: Mass susceptibility has the dimension $\mathsf M^{-1}$. {{questionable| has units of $\mathrm {kg}^{-1}$ for this quantity, while Wikipedia has units of $\mathsf {L^3 M^{-1} }$, thereby making it a density susceptibility.}} Category:Definitions/Dimensions of Measurement Category:Definitions/Mass Susceptibility

title: Definition:Mass Susceptibility/Units
snippet: Mass susceptibility is reported in SI unit as per kilogram: $\mathrm {kg^{-1} }$. Mass susceptibility is reported in SI unit as e.m.u. per gram: $\mathrm {e.m.u. \, g^{-1} }$. {{questionable| has units of $\mathrm {kg}^{-1}$ for this quantity, while Wikipedia has units of $\mathsf {L^3 M^{-1} }$, thereby making it a density susceptibility.}} Category:Definitions/Units of Measurement Category:Definitions/Mass Susceptibility

title: Definition:Master Code/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Master Code == {{Neologism|master code|as a convenient way to refer to the vector space $\map V {n, p}$.}} Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Matched Pair
snippet: A matched pair is a pair of experimental units in an experiment so that each member of the pair is as similar to the other as possible in the characteristics that may influence the response to a treatment. Then, if two treatments are being compared, one is allocated at random to each member of the pair. The technique can be expanded to form matched groups for comparing more than two treatments.

title: Definition:Matched Pair/Also known as
snippet: == Matched Pair: Also known as == Matched pairs are also known as paired observations.

title: Definition:Matching
snippet: Let $G$ be a graph. A matching of $G$ is a subset of the edge set of $G$ in which no two edges share a common vertex.

title: Definition:Matching/Also defined as
snippet: == Matching: Also known as == Some sources, when defining a matching, specify that the graph upon which it is defined has to be a bipartite graph.

title: Definition:Matching Pennies
snippet: Matching pennies is a two-person game whose mechanics are as follows. There are two players: $A$ and $B$. Each player puts down a coin, traditionally a , either head or tail up, without showing it to the other player. The coins are then uncovered. If they both show the same side, $A$ is deemed to have won, and he takes both coins. If they show different sides, $B$ is deemed to have won, and he takes both coins.

title: Definition:Mathematical Anxiety
snippet: Mathematical anxiety is a debilitating mental condition causing anxiety about one's ability to do mathematics.

title: Definition:Mathematical Biology
snippet: Mathematical biology is the branch of mathematics concerned with biological processes.

title: Definition:Mathematical Induction
snippet: == Proof Technique == Mathematical induction is a proof technique which works in two steps as follows: $(1): \quad$ A statement $Q$ is established as being true for some distinguished element $w_0$ of a well-ordered set $W$. $(2): \quad$ A proof is generated demonstrating that if $Q$ is true for an arbitrary element $w_p$ of $W$, then it is also true for its immediate successor $w_{p^+}$. The conclusion is drawn that $Q$ is true for all elements of $W$ which are successors of $w_0$. It is established in a number of contexts, according to how it is to be used.

title: Definition:Mathematical Induction/Terminology
snippet: == Terminology of Mathematical Induction ==

title: Definition:Mathematical Logic
snippet: Mathematical logic is a sub-branch of symbolic logic in which the foundations of the assumptions upon which rest mathematics itself are investigated and made rigorous.

title: Definition:Mathematical Logic/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Mathematical Logic == The roots of mathematical logic originate with the work of , who first made an attempt to formally define the rules of logic in mathematical terms. Its development as a serious discipline was directly inspired by Hilbert's program, as an attempt to create a consistent and complete set of axioms that would render mathematics completely rigorous. This did not go the way had planned, as Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems proved that there were always going to true statements in mathematics which could never be proved.

title: Definition:Mathematical Model
snippet: A mathematical model is an equation, or a system of equations, whose purpose is to provide an approximation to the behavior of a real-world phenomenon.

title: Definition:Mathematical Model/Constant
snippet: Let $P$ be a stochastic process which is being modelled by means of a model $M$. A constant of $M$ is a number which implements some aspect of $P$ which is not changed during the evolution of $P$.

title: Definition:Mathematical Model/Parameter
snippet: Let $P$ be a stochastic process which is being modelled by means of a model $M$. A parameter of $M$ is a number which implements some aspect of $P$ which is designed so as to be able to be modified during the evolution of $P$ as a result of analysis of the behaviour of $P$ over time.

title: Definition:Mathematical Philosophy
snippet: Mathematical philosophy is the name given to an approach to the investigation of the foundations of mathematics as pioneered by at around the start of the $20$th century. Further developments on this topic are usually considered part of mathematical logic.

title: Definition:Mathematical Physics
snippet: Mathematical physics is the branch of mathematics concerned with the development of mathematical methods for application to problems in physics. The application of mathematics to problems in physics and the development of mathematical methods suitable for such applications and for the formulation of physical theories.Definition from the [http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Mathematical_Physics Journal of Mathematical Physics].

title: Definition:Mathematical Programming
snippet: Mathematical programming is the branch of applied mathematics which applies techniques from computer science to solve problems in economics.

title: Definition:Mathematical Recreations
snippet: Mathematical recreations is the branch of mathematics which exists recreational mathematical topics.

title: Definition:Mathematical System
snippet: A mathematical system is a set $\SS = \struct {E, O, A}$ where: $E$ is a non-empty set of elements $O$ is a set of relations and operations on the elements of $E$ $A$ is a set of axioms concerning the elements of $E$ and $O$.

title: Definition:Mathematical Theory
snippet: A mathematical theory, or just theory, is a concept in mathematical logic. Let $U$ be a set of logical formulas. Let $\map \TT U$ be the set of all logical formulas $P$ such that $P$ is a semantic consequence of $U$. That is, let $\map \TT U = \set {P: U \models P}$. Then $\TT$ is called the (mathematical) theory of $U$. The elements of $\map \TT U$ are called theorems of $U$. The elements of $U$ are called the axioms of $\map \TT U$.

title: Definition:Mathematici
snippet: The Mathematici were a branch of the Pythagorean school. While acknowledging the religious underpinnings of Pythagoreanism, they focused on learning and scientific study. Hence they were considered progressive. The Nathematici were supposedly founded by . Category:Definitions/Schools

title: Definition:Mathematics
snippet: == An attempt at a definition == From : Mathematics is the academic discipline, and its supporting body of knowledge, that involves the study of such concepts as quantity, structure, space and change. Other practitioners of mathematics maintain that mathematics is the science of pattern, and that mathematicians seek out patterns whether found in numbers, space, science, computers, imaginary abstractions, or elsewhere. Mathematicians explore such concepts, aiming to formulate new conjectures and establish their truth by rigorous deduction from appropriately chosen axioms and definitions.

title: Definition:Mathematics/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Mathematics == The intellectual discipline of mathematics goes back at least $5000$ years. Unlike most subjects, the truths discovered way back then are still valid, relevant and applicable now.

title: Definition:Mathieu's Equation
snippet: Mathieu's equation is the second-order ordinary differential equation: $\dfrac {\d^2 y} {\d x^2} + \paren {a + b \cos 2 x} y = 0$ where $a$ and $b$ are real constants.

title: Definition:Matrix
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $m, n \in \Z_{>0}$ be strictly positive integers. An $m \times n$ matrix over $S$ (said $m$ times $n$ or $m$ by $n$) is a mapping from the cartesian product of two integer intervals $\closedint 1 m \times \closedint 1 n$ into $S$. When the set $S$ is understood, or for the purpose of the particular argument irrelevant, we can refer just to an $m \times n$ matrix. The convention is for the variable representing the matrix itself to be represented in $\mathbf {boldface}$.

title: Definition:Matrix/Also known as
snippet: == Matrix: Also known as == A matrix is often considered as an array of two dimensions. However, the usual convention nowadays is to reserve the term array for the written-down denotation of a matrix. The notation $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ is a notation which is not yet seen frequently. $\mathbf A = \paren {a_{i j} }_{m \times n}$ or $\mathbf A = \paren {a_{i j} }$ are more common. However, the notation $\sqbrk a_{m n}$ is gaining in popularity because it better encapsulates the actual order of the matrix itself in the notational form.

title: Definition:Matrix/Column
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be an $m \times n$ matrix. For each $j \in \closedint 1 n$, the columns of $\mathbf A$ are the ordered $m$-tuples: $c_j = \tuple {a_{1 j}, a_{2 j}, \ldots, a_{m j} }$ where $c_j$ is called the $j$th column of $\mathbf A$. A column of an $m \times n$ matrix can also be treated as a $m \times 1$ column matrix in its own right: $c_j = \begin {bmatrix} a_{1 j} \\ a_{2 j} \\ \vdots \\ a_{m j} \end {bmatrix}$ for $j = 1, 2, \ldots, n$.

title: Definition:Matrix/Diagonal
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a matrix. A diagonal of $\mathbf A$ is a diagonal line of elements of $\mathbf A$.

title: Definition:Matrix/Diagonal/Antidiagonal
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ be a matrix. An antidiagonal of $A$ is a diagonal of $\mathbf A$ lying perpendicular to the main diagonal of $\mathbf A$. That is, a set of elements $\map a {r + k, s - k}$.

title: Definition:Matrix/Diagonal/Main
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ be a matrix. The elements $a_{j j}: j \in \closedint 1 {\min \set {m, n} }$ constitute the main diagonal of $\mathbf A$. That is, the main diagonal of $\mathbf A$ is the diagonal of $\mathbf A$ from the top left corner, that is, the element $a_{1 1}$, running towards the lower right corner.

title: Definition:Matrix/Diagonal/Main Antidiagonal
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ be a matrix. The main antidiagonal of $\mathbf A$ is the antidiagonal of $\mathbf A$ from the top right corner, that is, the element $a_{1 n}$, running towards the lower left corner.

title: Definition:Matrix/Diagonal/Subdiagonal
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ be a matrix. The subdiagonals of $A$ are the diagonals of $\mathbf A$ lying parallel to and below the main diagonal of $\mathbf A$. That is, the elements $\map a {r + k, s + k}$ where $s < r$.

title: Definition:Matrix/Diagonal/Superdiagonal
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ be a matrix. The superdiagonals of $A$ are the diagonals of $\mathbf A$ lying parallel to and above the main diagonal of $\mathbf A$. That is, the elements $\map a {r + k, s + k}$ where $s > r$.

title: Definition:Matrix/Element
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be an $m \times n$ matrix over a set $S$. The individual $m \times n$ elements of $S$ that go to form $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ are known as the elements of the matrix. The element at row $i$ and column $j$ is called element $\tuple {i, j}$ of $\mathbf A$, and can be written $a_{i j}$, or $a_{i, j}$ if $i$ and $j$ are of more than one character. If the indices are still more complicated coefficients and further clarity is required, then the form $a \tuple {i, j}$ can be used.

title: Definition:Matrix/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Matrix == The concept of a matrix is generally considered to have originated with . was the first to regard a matrix as an operator on a tuple of variables.

title: Definition:Matrix/Indices
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be an $m \times n$ matrix. Let $a_{i j}$ be the element in row $i$ and column $j$ of $\mathbf A$. Then the subscripts $i$ and $j$ are referred to as the indices (singular: index) of $a_{i j}$.

title: Definition:Matrix/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Matrix == The plural form of matrix is matrices, pronounced may-tri-seez. Compare with index (plural indices), apex (plural apices), and so on.

title: Definition:Matrix/Lower Triangular Elements
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ be a matrix. The elements $a_{i j}: i > j$ are called the lower triangular elements.

title: Definition:Matrix/Order
snippet: Let $\sqbrk a_{m n}$ be an $m \times n$ matrix. Then the parameters $m$ and $n$ are known as the order of the matrix.

title: Definition:Matrix/Order/Column
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be an $n \times 1$ column matrix. Then the order of $\mathbf A$ is defined as being $n$. Category:Definitions/Orders of Matrices Category:Definitions/Column Matrices

title: Definition:Matrix/Order/Row
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a $1 \times n$ row matrix. Then the order of $\mathbf A$ is defined as being $n$. Category:Definitions/Orders of Matrices Category:Definitions/Row Matrices

title: Definition:Matrix/Row
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be an $m \times n$ matrix. For each $i \in \closedint 1 m$, the rows of $\mathbf A$ are the ordered $n$-tuples: $r_i = \tuple {a_{i 1}, a_{i 2}, \ldots, a_{i n} }$ where $r_i$ is called the $i$th row of $\mathbf A$. A row of an $m \times n$ matrix can also be treated as a $1 \times n$ row matrix in its own right: $r_i = \begin {bmatrix} a_{i 1} & a_{i 2} & \cdots & a_{i n} \end {bmatrix}$ for $i = 1, 2, \ldots, m$.

title: Definition:Matrix/Square Matrix
snippet: An $n \times n$ matrix is called a square matrix. That is, a square matrix is a matrix which has the same number of rows as it has columns. A square matrix is usually denoted $\sqbrk a_n$ in preference to $\sqbrk a_{n n}$.

title: Definition:Matrix/Square Matrix/Order
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be an $n \times n$ square matrix. That is, let $\mathbf A$ have $n$ rows (and by definition $n$ columns). Then the order of $\mathbf A$ is defined as being $n$.

title: Definition:Matrix/Underlying Structure
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a matrix over a set $S$. The set $S$ can be referred to as the underlying set of $\mathbf A$. In the context of matrices, however, it is usual for $S$ itself to be the underlying set of an algebraic structure in its own right. If this is the case, then the structure $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n}$ (which may also be an ordered structure) can be referred to as the underlying structure of $\mathbf A$. When the underlying structure is not specified, it is taken for granted that it is one of the standard number systems, usually the real numbers $\R$.

title: Definition:Matrix/Upper Triangular Elements
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ be a matrix. The elements $a_{i j}: i < j$ are called the upper triangular elements.

title: Definition:Matrix/Zero Row or Column
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ be an $m \times n$ matrix whose underlying structure is a ring or field (usually numbers). If a row or column of $\mathbf A$ contains only zeroes, then it is a zero row or a zero column.

title: Definition:Matrix Addition
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \cdot}$ be a ring.

title: Definition:Matrix Algebra
snippet: Matrix algebra is the subfield of algebra whose subjects of manipulation are matrices.

title: Definition:Matrix Congruence
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $n$ be a positive integer. Let $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ be square matrices of order $n$ over $R$. Then: $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ are congruent there exists a nonsingular matrix $\mathbf P \in R^{n \times n}$ such that $\mathbf B = \mathbf P^\intercal \mathbf A \mathbf P$ where $\mathbf P^\intercal$ denotes the transpose of $\mathbf P$.

title: Definition:Matrix Direct Sum
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ and $\mathbf B = \sqbrk b_{p q}$ be matrices. The matrix direct sum of $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ is denoted $\mathbf A \oplus \mathbf B$ and is defined as: $\mathbf A \oplus \mathbf B := \begin {bmatrix} \mathbf A & \mathbf 0 \\ \mathbf 0 & \mathbf B \end {bmatrix}$ where $\mathbf 0$ is a zero matrix, the upper-right $\mathbf 0$ being $m \times q$ and the lower left $\mathbf 0$ being $n \times p$.

title: Definition:Matrix Entrywise Addition
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ be matrices of numbers. Let the orders of $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ both be $m \times n$. Then the matrix entrywise sum of $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ is written $\mathbf A + \mathbf B$, and is defined as follows: Let $\mathbf A + \mathbf B = \mathbf C = \sqbrk c_{m n}$. Then: $\forall i \in \closedint 1 m, j \in \closedint 1 n: c_{i j} = a_{i j} + b_{i j}$ Thus $\mathbf C = \sqbrk c_{m n}$ is the $m \times n$ matrix whose entries are made by performing the adding corresponding entries of $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$.

title: Definition:Matrix Entrywise Addition/Also known as
snippet: == Matrix Entrywise Addition: Also known as == The operation of matrix entrywise addition is usually referred to as just matrix addition. Similarly, the matrix entrywise sum is likewise usually just called the matrix sum. However, it needs to be made clear that there are a number of different operations on matrices which are also referred to as matrix addition, so there are contexts in which it is wise to make clear which is meant. Category:Definitions/Matrix Entrywise Addition

title: Definition:Matrix Entrywise Addition/Defined Operation
snippet: == Matrix Entrywise Addition: Defined Operation == It needs to be noted that the operation of matrix entrywise addition is defined only when both matrices are of the same order. That is, they have the same number of rows and the same number of columns.

title: Definition:Matrix Entrywise Addition/General
snippet: Let $\mathbf A_1, \mathbf A_2, \ldots, \mathbf A_k$ be matrices all of order of $m \times n$. Then the matrix entrywise sum of $\mathbf A_1, \mathbf A_2, \ldots, \mathbf A_k$ is written $\mathbf A_1 + \mathbf A_2 + \ldots + \mathbf A_k$, and is defined as follows: Then: $\forall i \in \closedint 1 m, j \in \closedint 1 n: K_{i j} = \paren {a_1}_{i j} + \paren {a_2}_{i j} + \cdots + \paren {a_k}_{i j}$ where $\paren {a_l}_{i j}$ is the element of $\mathbf A_l$ whose indices are $\tuple {i, j}$.

title: Definition:Matrix Entrywise Addition/Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \cdot}$ be a ring. Let $\map {\MM_R} {m, n}$ be a $m \times n$ matrix space over $R$. Let $\mathbf A, \mathbf B \in \map {\MM_R} {m, n}$. Then the matrix entrywise sum of $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ is written $\mathbf A + \mathbf B$, and is defined as follows. Let $\mathbf A + \mathbf B = \mathbf C = \sqbrk c_{m n}$.

title: Definition:Matrix Equivalence
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $\mathbf A, \mathbf B$ be $m \times n$ matrices over $R$.

title: Definition:Matrix Equivalence/Definition 1
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $\mathbf A, \mathbf B$ be $m \times n$ matrices over $R$. Let there exist: a nonsingular square matrix $\mathbf P$ of order $n$ over $R$ a nonsingular square matrix $\mathbf Q$ of order $m$ over $R$ such that: $\mathbf B = \mathbf Q^{-1} \mathbf A \mathbf P$ Then $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ are equivalent. We write: $\mathbf A \equiv \mathbf B$

title: Definition:Matrix Equivalence/Definition 2
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $\mathbf A, \mathbf B$ be $m \times n$ matrices over $R$. $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ are equivalent they are the relative matrices, to (possibly) different ordered bases, of the same linear transformation. We write: $\mathbf A \equiv \mathbf B$

title: Definition:Matrix Exponential
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a constant square matrix of order $n$. The matrix exponential of $\mathbf A$, denoted $e^{t \mathbf A}$ or $e^{\mathbf A t}$, is defined as the unique solution to the initial value problem: $(1): \quad \map {\dfrac \d {\d t} } X = \mathbf A X$ $(2): \quad \map X {\mathbf 0_n} = \mathbf I_n$ where: $\mathbf I_n$ is the unit matrix of order $n$ $X$ is an order $n$ square matrix which is a function of the real variable $t$ $\mathbf 0_n$ is the zero matrix of order $n$ $\map {\dfrac \d {\d t} } X$ is the derivative of $X$ $t$.

title: Definition:Matrix Notation (Bounded Linear Operator)
snippet: Let $H$ be a Hilbert space. Let $A \in \map B H$ be a bounded linear operator on $H$. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of $H$; denote by $M^\perp$ its orthocomplement. Observe that $M \oplus M^\perp \cong H$ by Direct Sum of Subspace and Orthocomplement. The associated isomorphism $U$ induces a bounded linear operator $A'$ on $M \oplus M^\perp$. $A'$ can be written as the matrix: $\begin{pmatrix} W & X \\ Y & Z \end{pmatrix}$ where $W \in \map B M$, $X \in \map B {M^\perp, M}$, $Y \in \map B {M, M^\perp}$, $Z \in \map B {M^\perp}$.

title: Definition:Matrix Partition
snippet: A partition of a matrix $\mathbf M$ is a separation of all the elements of $\mathbf M$ into a number of matrices of lower order. Those lower order matrices are known as submatrices.

title: Definition:Matrix Product (Conventional)
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ be an $m \times n$ matrix over $R$. Let $\mathbf B = \sqbrk b_{n p}$ be an $n \times p$ matrix over $R$. Then the matrix product of $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ is written $\mathbf A \mathbf B$ and is defined as follows. Let $\mathbf A \mathbf B = \mathbf C = \sqbrk c_{m p}$.

title: Definition:Matrix Product (Conventional)/Also known as
snippet: == Conventional Matrix Product: Also known as == It is believed that some sources refer to the (conventional) matrix product as the Cauchy product after . However, the latter has a different definition on , and is applied to infinite series. Further rumours suggest that may also have lent his name to this concept. However, corroboration has proven difficult to obtain. Category:Definitions/Conventional Matrix Multiplication

title: Definition:Matrix Product (Conventional)/Conformable
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ be matrices. It needs to be emphasised that matrix product can be defined on $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ are conformable. That is, if the number of rows of one is equal to the number of columns of the other.

title: Definition:Matrix Product (Conventional)/Einstein Summation Convention
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ be an $m \times n$ matrix over $R$. Let $\mathbf B = \sqbrk b_{n p}$ be an $n \times p$ matrix over $R$. The matrix product of $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ can be expressed using the Einstein summation convention as: Then: $c_{i j} := a_{i k} \circ b_{k j}$ The index which appears twice in the expressions on the is the entry $k$, which is the one summated over. It can also be presented as: $c_i^j := a^i_k \circ b^k_j$ where the superscripts and subscripts indicate that the matrix in question is a $\tuple {1, 1}$-tensor.

title: Definition:Matrix Product (Conventional)/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on (Conventional) Matrix Product == This mathematical process defined by the (conventional) matrix product was first introduced by . Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Matrix Product (Conventional)/Notation
snippet: == Conventional Matrix Product: Notation == To denote the (conventional) matrix product of $\mathbf A$ with $\mathbf B$, the juxtaposition notation is always used: $\mathbf C = \mathbf A \mathbf B$ We do not use $\mathbf A \times \mathbf B$ or $\mathbf A \cdot \mathbf B$ in this context, because they have specialised meanings. Category:Definitions/Conventional Matrix Multiplication

title: Definition:Matrix Product (Conventional)/Post-Multiplication
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ be an $m \times n$ matrix over $R$. Let $\mathbf B = \sqbrk b_{n p}$ be an $n \times p$ matrix over $R$. Let $\mathbf A \mathbf B$ be the product of $\mathbf A$ with $\mathbf B$. Then $\mathbf A$ is post-multiplied by $\mathbf B$.

title: Definition:Matrix Product (Conventional)/Pre-Multiplication
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ be an $m \times n$ matrix over $R$. Let $\mathbf B = \sqbrk b_{n p}$ be an $n \times p$ matrix over $R$. Let $\mathbf A \mathbf B$ be the product of $\mathbf A$ with $\mathbf B$. Then $\mathbf B$ is pre-multiplied by $\mathbf A$.

title: Definition:Matrix Scalar Product
snippet: Let $\GF$ denote one of the standard number systems. Let $\map \MM {m, n}$ be the $m \times n$ matrix space over $\GF$. Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n} \in \map \MM {m, n}$. Let $\lambda \in \GF$ be any element of $\Bbb F$. The operation of scalar multiplication of $\mathbf A$ by $\lambda$ is defined as follows. Let $\lambda \mathbf A = \mathbf C$. Then: $\forall i \in \closedint 1 m, j \in \closedint 1 n: c_{i j} = \lambda a_{i j}$ $\lambda \mathbf A$ is the scalar product of $\lambda$ and $\mathbf A$.

title: Definition:Matrix Scalar Product/Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ be an $m \times n$ matrix over $\struct {R, +, \circ}$. Let $\lambda \in R$ be any element of $R$. The scalar product of $\lambda$ and $\mathbf A$ is defined as follows. Let $\lambda \circ \mathbf A = \mathbf C$. Then: $\forall i \in \closedint 1 m, j \in \closedint 1 n: c_{i j} = \lambda \circ a_{i j}$ Thus $\sqbrk c_{m n}$ is the $m \times n$ matrix composed of the product of $\lambda$ with the corresponding elements of $\mathbf A$.

title: Definition:Matrix Scalar Product/Scalar
snippet: Let $\map \MM {m, n}$ be a matrix space of order $m \times n$ on which scalar multiplication is defined. Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n} \in \map \MM {m, n}$. Let $\lambda$ be an element of the underlying structure such that: $\mathbf C = \lambda \mathbf A$ where the notation denotes scalar multiplication. The element $\lambda$ of the underlying structure of $\map \MM {m, n}$ is known as a scalar. Category:Definitions/Matrix Scalar Product

title: Definition:Matrix Similarity
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $n \in \N_{>0}$ be a natural number. Let $\mathbf A, \mathbf B$ be square matrices of order $n$ over $R$.

title: Definition:Matrix Similarity/Definition 1
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $n \in \N_{>0}$ be a natural number. Let $\mathbf A, \mathbf B$ be square matrices of order $n$ over $R$. Let there exist a nonsingular square matrix $\mathbf P$ of order $n$ over $R$ such that $\mathbf B = \mathbf P^{-1} \mathbf A \mathbf P$. Then $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ are similar. We write: $\mathbf A \sim \mathbf B$

title: Definition:Matrix Similarity/Definition 2
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $n \in \N_{>0}$ be a natural number. Let $\mathbf A, \mathbf B$ be square matrices of order $n$ over $R$. $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ are similar they are the relative matrices, to (possibly) different ordered bases, of the same linear operator. We write: $\mathbf A \sim \mathbf B$

title: Definition:Matrix Space
snippet: Let $m, n \in \Z_{>0}$ be (strictly) positive integers. Let $S$ be a set. The $m \times n$ matrix space over $S$ is defined as the set of all $m \times n$ matrices over $S$, and is denoted $\map {\MM_S} {m, n}$. Thus, by definition: $\map {\MM_S} {m, n} = S^{\closedint 1 m \times \closedint 1 n}$ If $m = n$ then we can write $\map {\MM_S} {m, n}$ as $\map {\MM_S} n$.

title: Definition:Matrix Space/Complex
snippet: Let $m, n \in \Z_{>0}$ be (strictly) positive integers. Let $\C$ denote the set of complex numbers. The $m \times n$ matrix space over $\C$ is referred to as the complex matrix space, and can be denoted $\map {\MM_\C} {m, n}$. If $m = n$ then we can write $\map {\MM_\C} {m, n}$ as $\map {\MM_\C} n$.

title: Definition:Matrix Space/Real
snippet: Let $m, n \in \Z_{>0}$ be (strictly) positive integers. Let $\R$ denote the set of real numbers. The $m \times n$ matrix space over $\R$ is referred to as the real matrix space, and can be denoted $\map {\MM_\R} {m, n}$. If $m = n$ then we can write $\map {\MM_\R} {m, n}$ as $\map {\MM_\R} n$.

title: Definition:Matrix Theory
snippet: Matrix theory is the field of mathematics which studies matrices.

title: Definition:Matroid/Dependent Set
snippet: Let $M = \struct {S, \mathscr I}$ be a matroid. A subset of $S$ that is not an element of $\mathscr I$ is called a dependent subset of $M$.

title: Definition:Matroid/Examples

title: Definition:Matroid/Independent Set
snippet: Let $M = \struct{S, \mathscr I}$ be a matroid. An element of $\mathscr I$ is called an independent subset of $M$.

title: Definition:Matroid Induced by Affine Independence
snippet: Let $\R^n$ be the $n$-dimensional real Euclidean space. Let $S = \set {x_1, \dots, x_r}$ be a finite subset of $\R^n$. Let $\mathscr I$ be the set of affinely independent subsets of $S$. Then $\struct {S, \mathscr I}$ is called the matroid induced by affine independence on $S$.

title: Definition:Matroid Induced by Algebraic Independence
snippet: Let $L / K$ be a field extension. Let $S \subseteq L$ be a finite subset of $L$. Let $\mathscr I$ be the set of algebraically independent subsets of $S$. Then $\struct {S, \mathscr I}$ is called the matroid induced by algebraic independence over $K$ on $S$.

title: Definition:Matroid Induced by Linear Independence/Abelian Group
snippet: Let $\struct {G, +}$ be a torsion-free Abelian group. Let $\struct {G, +, \times}$ be the $\Z$-module associated with $G$. Let $S$ be a finite subset of $G$. Let $\mathscr I$ be the set of linearly independent subsets of $S$. Then the ordered pair $\struct {S, \mathscr I}$ is called the matroid induced by linear independence in $G$ on $S$.

title: Definition:Matroid Induced by Linear Independence/Vector Space
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space. Let $S$ be a finite subset of $V$. Let $\mathscr I$ be the set of linearly independent subsets of $S$. Then the ordered pair $\struct{S, \mathscr I}$ is called a matroid induced on $S$ by linear independence in $V$.

title: Definition:Matroid Theory
snippet: Matroid Theory is the branch of mathematics which concerns the role which matroids play in disparate branches of combinatorial theory and algebra such as graph theory, lattice theory, combinatorial optimization, and linear algebra.

title: Definition:Matter
snippet: Matter is the stuff of which the physical universe is composed. At a certain level, can be considered as a form of energy. Matter is (to a first degree of approximation) composed of atoms.

title: Definition:Matter/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Matter == The adjectival form of matter is material. However, material is often used in a noun form to mean matter or substance, particularly when it is used to mean .

title: Definition:Max Operation
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a totally ordered set. The max operation is the binary operation on $\struct {S, \preceq}$ defined as: $\forall x, y \in S: \map \max {x, y} = \begin{cases} y & : x \preceq y \\ x & : y \preceq x \end{cases}$

title: Definition:Max Operation/General Definition
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a totally ordered set. Let $S^n$ be the cartesian $n$th power of $S$. The max operation is the $n$-ary operation on $\struct {S, \preceq}$ defined recursively as: $\forall x := \family {x_i}_{1 \mathop \le i \mathop \le n} \in S^n: \map \max x = \begin {cases} x_1 & : n = 1 \\ \map \max {x_1, x_2} & : n = 2 \\ \map \max {\map \max {x_1, \ldots, x_{n - 1} }, x_n} & : n > 2 \\ \end {cases}$ where $\map \max {x, y}$ is the binary max operation on $S^2$.

title: Definition:Max Operation/General Definition/Real Numbers
snippet: The max operation on the real cartesian space $\R^n$ is the real-valued function $\max: \R^n \to \R$ defined recursively as: $\forall x := \family {x_i}_{1 \mathop \le i \mathop \le n} \in \R^n: \map \max x = \begin {cases} x_1 & : n = 1 \\ \map \max {x_1, x_2} & : n = 2 \\ \map \max {\map \max {x_1, \ldots, x_{n - 1} }, x_n} & : n > 2 \\ \end {cases}$ where $\map \max {x, y}$ is the binary max operation on $\R \times \R$.

title: Definition:Maximal/Element
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \RR}$ be a relational structure. Let $T \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$.

title: Definition:Maximal/Set
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\powerset S$ be the power set of $S$. Let $\TT \subseteq \powerset S$ be a subset of $\powerset S$. Let $\struct {\TT, \subseteq}$ be the ordered set formed on $\TT$ by $\subseteq$ considered as an ordering. Then $T \in \TT$ is a maximal set of $\TT$ $T$ is a maximal element of $\struct {\TT, \subseteq}$. That is: $\forall X \in \TT: T \subseteq X \implies T = X$

title: Definition:Maximal Atlas/Also known as
snippet: == Maximal Atlas: Also known as == A maximal atlas is also known as a complete atlas. Some sources call a maximal atlas simply as an atlas, and refer to an atlas as a pre-atlas.

title: Definition:Maximal Chain
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $\struct {T, \preceq} \subseteq \struct {S, \preceq}$ be a chain in $\struct {S, \preceq}$ such that there is no other chain in $\struct {S, \preceq}$ which has $\struct {T, \preceq}$ as a proper subset. Then $\struct {T, \preceq}$ is a maximal chain in $S$. Category:Definitions/Chains (Order Theory)

title: Definition:Maximal Compact Topology
snippet: Let $X = \Z_{>0} \times \Z_{>0}$ be the set of all lattice points $\tuple {i, j}$ of the Cartesian plane where $i$ and $j$ are both (strictly) positive integers. Let $S = X \cup \set {x, y}$ where $x$ and $y$ are two new elements of $X$. Let $\tau$ be the topology defined on $S$ as follows: Each lattice point of $S$ is an open point.

title: Definition:Maximal Condition on Submodules
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $M$ be an $A$-module. Let $\struct {D, \subseteq}$ be the set of submodules of $M$ ordered by the subset relation. Then the hypothesis: Every non-empty subset of $D$ has a maximal element is called the maximal condition on submodules.

title: Definition:Maximal Element/Also defined as
snippet: == Maximal Element: Also defined as == Most treatments of the concept of a maximal element restrict the definition of the relation $\RR$ to the requirement that it be an ordering. However, this is not strictly required, and this more general definition as used on is of far more use.

title: Definition:Maximal Element/Also known as
snippet: == Maximal Element: Also known as == Some sources refer to a maximal element as a coatom or an anti-atom.

title: Definition:Maximal Element/Class Theory
snippet: Let $A$ be a class. An element $x \in A$ is a maximal element of $A$ : $\forall y \in A: x \not \subset y$ That is, $x$ a proper subset of no element of $A$.

title: Definition:Maximal Element/Comparison with Greatest Element
snippet: Compare the definition of a maximal element with that of a greatest element. Consider the ordered set $\struct {S, \preceq}$ such that $T \subseteq S$. An element $x \in T$ is the greatest element of $T$ : $\forall y \in T: y \preceq x$ That is, $x$ is comparable with, and succeeds, or is equal to, every $y \in S$. An element $x \in S$ is a maximal element of $T$ : $x \preceq y \implies x = y$ That is, $x$ succeeds, or is equal to, every $y \in S$ which is comparable with $x$. If all elements are comparable wth $x$, then such a maximal element is indeed the greatest element.

title: Definition:Maximal Element/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \RR}$ be a relational structure. Let $T \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. An element $x \in T$ is a maximal element (under $\RR$) of $T$ : $x \mathrel \RR y \implies x = y$
