title: Definition:Maximal Geodesic
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $I, \tilde I \subseteq \R$ be open real intervals. Let $\gamma : I \to M$ and $\tilde \gamma : \tilde I \to M$ be geodesics. Suppose there is no $\tilde I$ properly containing $I$ over which $\tilde \gamma$ is restricted to $\gamma$: $\neg \exists \tilde I : I \subsetneqq \tilde I : \tilde \gamma \restriction_I = \gamma$ Then $\gamma$ is said to be a maximal geodesic.

title: Definition:Maximal Ideal
snippet: Definition:Maximal Ideal of Ring Definition:Maximal Left Ideal of Ring Definition:Maximal Right Ideal of Ring Definition:Maximal Ideal of Algebra Definition:Maximal Left Ideal of Algebra Definition:Maximal Right Ideal of Algebra

title: Definition:Maximal Ideal of Algebra
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $\struct {A, \ast}$ be an $R$-algebra. Let $\struct {J, \ast}$ be a proper ideal of $\struct {A, \ast}$. We say that $J$ is a maximal ideal of $A$ : there is no ideal $I$ such that $J \subsetneq I$.

title: Definition:Maximal Ideal of Algebra/Left
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $\struct {A, \ast}$ be an $R$-algebra. Let $\struct {J, \ast}$ be a proper left ideal of $\struct {A, \ast}$. We say that $J$ is a maximal left ideal of $A$ : there is no left ideal $I$ such that $J \subsetneq I$.

title: Definition:Maximal Ideal of Algebra/Right
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $\struct {A, \ast}$ be an $R$-algebra. Let $\struct {J, \ast}$ be a proper right ideal of $\struct {A, \ast}$. We say that $J$ is a maximal right ideal of $A$ : there is no right ideal $I$ such that $J \subsetneq I$.

title: Definition:Maximal Ideal of Ring
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. An ideal $J$ of $R$ is maximal : $(1): \quad J \subsetneq R$ $(2): \quad$ There is no ideal $K$ of $R$ such that $J \subsetneq K \subsetneq R$. That is, $J$ is a maximal element of the set of all proper ideals of $R$ ordered by the subset relation.

title: Definition:Maximal Ideal of Ring/Left
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. A left ideal $J$ of $R$ is a maximal left ideal : $(1): \quad J \subsetneq R$ $(2): \quad$ There is no left ideal $K$ of $R$ such that $J \subsetneq K \subsetneq R$. Category:Definitions/Maximal Ideals of Rings

title: Definition:Maximal Ideal of Ring/Right
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. A right ideal $J$ of $R$ is a maximal right ideal : $(1): \quad J \subsetneq R$ $(2): \quad$ There is no right ideal $K$ of $R$ such that $J \subsetneq K \subsetneq R$. Category:Definitions/Maximal Ideals of Rings

title: Definition:Maximal Normal Subgroup
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $N \le G$ be a proper normal subgroup. Then $N$ is a maximal normal subgroup of $G$ : For every normal subgroup $M$ of $G$, $N \subseteq M \subseteq G$ implies $N = M$ or $M = G$. That is, there is no normal subgroup of $G$, except $N$ and $G$ itself, which contains $N$.

title: Definition:Maximal Planar Graph
snippet: A maximal planar graph is a simple planar graph of maximum size, that is, with the maximum number of edges. That is, a maximal planar graph is a simple planar graph to which adding an edge will render it no longer planar.

title: Definition:Maximal Spectrum of Ring
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. The maximal spectrum of $A$ is the set of maximal ideals of $A$: $\operatorname{Max} \: \Spec A = \set {\mathfrak m \lhd A : \mathfrak m \text { is maximal} }$ where $I \lhd A$ indicates that $I$ is an ideal of $A$. The notation $\operatorname {Max} \: \Spec A$ is also a shorthand for the locally ringed space $\struct {\operatorname {Max} \: \Spec A, \tau, \OO_{\map {\operatorname {Max Spec} } A} }$ where: $\tau$ is the Zariski topology on $\map {\operatorname {Max Spec} } A$ $\OO_{\map {\operatorname {Max Spec} } A}$ is the structure sheaf of $\map…

title: Definition:Maximal Subgroup
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $M \le G$ be a proper subgroup of $G$. Then $M$ is a maximal subgroup of $G$ : For every subgroup $H$ of $G$, $M \subseteq H \subseteq G$ means $M = H$ or $H = G$. That is, there is no subgroup of $G$, except $M$ and $G$ itself, which contains $M$.

title: Definition:Maximally Symmetric Densely-Defined Linear Operator
snippet: Let $\struct {\HH, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be a Hilbert space over $\C$. Let $\tuple {\map D T, T}$ be a symmetric densely-defined linear operator. We say that $\tuple {\map D T, T}$ is maximally symmetric : whenever $\tuple {\map D S, S}$ is a symmetric densely-defined linear operator extending $\tuple {\map D T, T}$, we have $\tuple {\map D S, S} = \tuple {\map D T, T}$.

title: Definition:Maximin Strategy/Also known as
snippet: == Maximin Strategy: Also known as == A maximin strategy is also known as a maximin criterion.

title: Definition:Maximising Player
snippet: Let $G$ be a two-person game whose players are identified with the symbols $A$ and $B$. It is the convention that the first of the players listed (in this case $A$) is distinguished from the other and referred to as the maximising player.

title: Definition:Maximizers of Real Function
snippet: Let $f: X \to \R$ be a real-valued function. The set of maximisers of a $f$ are denoted: $\ds \arg \max_{x \mathop \in X} \map f x$

title: Definition:Maximum/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Maximum == The plural form of maximum is maxima.

title: Definition:Maximum Likelihood Estimation
snippet: Maximum likelihood estimation is the procedure to choose the value of an estimator in order to maximize the likelihood.

title: Definition:Maximum Likelihood Estimator
snippet: Let $\FF$ be a one-parameter family of probability distributions whose parameter is $\theta$. Let $X$ be a continuous random variable belonging to a member of $\FF$. Let $\map {\mathrm L} \theta$ be the likelihood function of $\theta$ $X$. A maximum likelihood estimator is an estimator for $\theta$ to maximize $\map {\mathrm L} \theta$.

title: Definition:Maximum Likelihood Estimator/Properties
snippet: Let $\FF$ be a one-parameter family of probability distributions whose parameter is $\theta$. Let $X$ be a continuous random variable belonging to a member of $\FF$. Let $\EE$ be a maximum likelihood estimator for $\theta$ $X$. Then $\EE$ is usually: consistent efficient but not always unbiased.

title: Definition:Maximum Spanning Tree
snippet: Let $G$ be a weighted graph. A maximum spanning tree for $G$ is a spanning tree for $G$ which has a maximum total weight.

title: Definition:Maximum Value of Functional
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of mappings. Let $y, \hat y \in S: \R \to \R$ be real functions. Let $J \sqbrk y: S \to \R $ be a functional. Let $J$ have a (relative) extremum for $y = \hat y$. Suppose, $J \sqbrk y - J \sqbrk {\hat y} \le 0$ in the neighbourhood of $y = \hat y$. Then this extremum is called the maximum of the functional $J$.

title: Definition:Maximum Value of Real Function/Absolute
snippet: Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a real function. Let $f$ be bounded above by a supremum $B$. It may or may not be the case that $\exists x \in \R: \map f x = B$. If such a value exists, it is called the (absolute) maximum of $f$ on $S$, and that this (absolute) maximum is attained at $x$.

title: Definition:Maximum Value of Real Function/Local
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function defined on an open interval $\openint a b$. Let $\xi \in \openint a b$. Then $f$ has a local maximum at $\xi$ : $\exists \openint c d \subseteq \openint a b: \forall x \in \openint c d: \map f x \le \map f \xi$ That is, there is some subinterval on which $f$ attains a maximum within that interval.

title: Definition:Maximum Value of Real Function/Local/Strict
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function defined on an open interval $\openint a b$. Let $\xi \in \openint a b$. $f$ has a strict local maximum at $\xi$ : $\exists \openint c d \subseteq \openint a b: \forall x \in \openint c d: \map f x < \map f \xi$

title: Definition:Maxwell
snippet: The maxwell is the CGS unrationalised electromagnetic unit of magnetic flux.

title: Definition:Maxwell's Equations/Also known as
snippet: == Maxwell's Equations: Also known as == Maxwell's equations are also known as Maxwell's laws. Category:Definitions/Maxwell's Equations

title: Definition:Maxwell/Also known as
snippet: == Maxwell: Also known as == The maxwell is also known as the electromagnetic unit of magnetic flux, abbreviated $\mathrm {e.m.u.}$.

title: Definition:McNemar's Test
snippet: McNemar's test is a non-parametric test which is used to determine differences in proportions of related samples. It is often used to test whether a stimulus has produced a response in a particular direction.

title: Definition:McNemar's Test/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on McNemar's Test == McNemar's test was devised by in $1947$.

title: Definition:Meager Space
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $A \subseteq S$. $A$ is meager in $T$ it is a countable union of subsets of $S$ which are nowhere dense in $T$.

title: Definition:Meager Space/Also known as
snippet: == Meager Space: Also known as == A set which is meager in $T$ is also called of the first category in $T$.

title: Definition:Meager Space/Linguistic Note
snippet: The word meager (British English: meagre) is a somewhat old-fashioned word meaning deficient, lacking, scrawny etc. It originates from the French maigre, meaning thin in the sense of unhealthily skinny.

title: Definition:Meager Space/Non-Meager
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $A \subseteq S$. $A$ is non-meager in $T$ it cannot be constructed as a countable union of subsets of $S$ which are nowhere dense in $T$. That is, $A$ is non-meager in $T$ it is not meager in $T$.

title: Definition:Mean
snippet: Algebra: Arithmetic mean, also known as the common mean Geometric mean Arithmetic-geometric mean Harmonic mean Quadratic mean The following are hybrid concepts: Weighted mean Heronian mean Hölder mean (also known as the power mean or generalized mean) Real Analysis: Mean Value of Function Geometry: Golden mean Mean point: another term for centroid Probability Theory, the term is used for: Expectation Definition:Mean Deviation Definition:Mean Absolute Deviation Definition:Mean Square Deviation Definition:Mean Squared Error Statistics: Sample mean Category:Definitions/Algebra…

title: Definition:Mean Absolute Deviation
snippet: Let $S = \set {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ be a set of observations. Let $\bar x$ denote a measure of central tendency of $S$. The mean absolute deviation $\bar x$ of $S$ is defined as the arithmetic mean of the absolute values of the deviation of the elements of $S$ from $\bar x$ : $\ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \dfrac 1 n \size {x_i - \bar x}$

title: Definition:Mean Absolute Deviation/Continuous Random Variable
snippet: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable. Let $m$ denote the median of $X$. Let the frequency function of $X$ be $f$. The mean absolute deviation of $X$ is defined as: $\ds \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \size {x - m} \map f x \rd x$

title: Definition:Mean Absolute Deviation/Discrete Random Variable
snippet: Let $X$ be a discrete random variable. Let $\bar x$ denote a measure of central tendency of $X$. The mean absolute deviation of $X$ is the first absolute moment of $X$ about $\bar x$.

title: Definition:Mean Axis of Ellipsoid
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an ellipsoid. The mean axis of $\EE$ is the diameter of $\EE$ which is perpendicular to both the major axis of $\EE$ and the minor axis of $\EE$.

title: Definition:Mean Calorie/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Mean Calorie: Conversion Factors == {{eqn | o = \approx | r = 1 \cdotp 164 \times 10^{-6} | c = kilowatt-hours }} {{eqn | o = \approx | r = 2 \cdotp 615 \times 10^{19} | c = electron volts }} Category:Definitions/Calorie

title: Definition:Mean Calorie/Symbol
snippet: == Mean Calorie: Symbol == The symbol used to denote the mean calorie is $\mathrm {cal_{mean} }$. Category:Definitions/Calorie

title: Definition:Mean Curvature
snippet: Let $C$ be a curve defined by a real function which is twice differentiable. Let $\delta \psi$ be the angle of contingence with respect to $2$ points $P$ and $Q$ on $C$. Let $\delta s$ be the arc length of $C$ between $P$ and $Q$. The mean curvature of $C$ between $P$ and $Q$ is defined as $\dfrac {\delta \psi} {\delta s}$.

title: Definition:Mean Deviation
snippet: Let $S = \set {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ be a set of observations. Let $\bar x$ denote a measure of central tendency of $S$. The mean deviation $\bar x$ of $S$ is defined as the arithmetic mean of the deviation of the elements of $S$ from $\bar x$: $\ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \dfrac 1 n \paren {x_i - \bar x}$

title: Definition:Mean Deviation/Also known as
snippet: == Mean Deviation: Also known as == Mean deviation is also known as average deviation.

title: Definition:Mean Deviation/Continuous Random Variable
snippet: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable. Let $m$ denote the median of $X$. Let the frequency function of $X$ be $f$. The mean deviation of $X$ is defined as: $\ds \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \paren {x - m} \map f x \rd x$

title: Definition:Mean Deviation/Discrete Random Variable
snippet: Let $X$ be a discrete random variable. Let $\bar x$ denote a measure of central tendency of $X$. The mean deviation of $X$ is the first moment of $X$ about $\bar x$.

title: Definition:Mean Solar Day/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Mean Solar Day: Conversion Factors ==

title: Definition:Mean Square
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of numbers. The mean square of $S$ is the arithmetic mean of the squares of the elements of $S$: $s^2 = \dfrac 1 n \ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n {x_i}^2$ where $S = \set {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$.

title: Definition:Mean Square Deviation
snippet: Let $S = \set {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ be a set of observations. Let $\bar x$ denote a measure of central tendency of $S$. The mean square deviation $\bar x$ of $S$ is defined as the arithmetic mean of the square of the deviation of the elements of $S$ from $\bar x$: $\ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \dfrac 1 n \paren {x_i - \bar x}^2$

title: Definition:Mean Square Deviation/Continuous Random Variable
snippet: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable. Let $m$ denote the median of $X$. Let the frequency function of $X$ be $f$. The mean square deviation of $X$ is defined as: $\ds \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \paren {x - m}^2 \map f x \rd x$

title: Definition:Mean Square Deviation/Discrete Random Variable
snippet: Let $X$ be a discrete random variable. Let $\bar x$ denote a measure of central tendency of $X$. The mean square deviation of $X$ is the second moment of $X$ about $\bar x$.

title: Definition:Mean Squared Error
snippet: The mean squared error is the expected value of the square of the difference between an estimator $T$ and the true parameter value $\theta$.

title: Definition:Mean Squared Error/Also known as
snippet: == Mean Squared Error: Also known as == The term mean squared error is commonly abbreviated to m.s.e., M.S.E. or MSE.

title: Definition:Mean Squared Error of Estimator
snippet: Let $\theta$ be a population parameter of some population. Let $\mathbf X$ be a random sample from this population. Let $\hat \theta$ be an estimator of $\theta$. The mean squared error of $\hat \theta$ is defined by: $\map {\operatorname {MSE} } {\hat \theta} = \expect {\paren {\map {\hat \theta} {\mathbf X} - \theta}^2} $

title: Definition:Mean Sun
snippet: The mean sun is an imaginary point on the celestial sphere that moves along the celestial equator with a uniform rate of motion equal to the mean rate of motion of the sun along the ecliptic.

title: Definition:Mean Value of Function
snippet: Let $f$ be an integrable function on some closed interval $\closedint a b$. The mean value of $f$ on $\closedint a b$ is defined as: $\ds \frac 1 {b - a} \int_a^b \map f x \rd x$

title: Definition:Mean Value of Function/Also known as
snippet: == Mean Value of Function: Also known as == The mean value of a function is also known as its average value.

title: Definition:Mean Value over Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $f$ be a $\mu$-integrable function on a domain $D$. The mean value of $f$ on $D$ is defined as: $\ds \frac 1 {\map \mu D} \int_D \map f \rd \mu$

title: Definition:Mean of Grouped Data
snippet: Let $\mathsf C_1, \mathsf C_2, \cdots, \mathsf C_n$ be class intervals of data. Let $m_i$ be the class mark of the $i$th class interval. Let $f_i$ be the frequency of the $i$th class interval. The mean of the grouped data for $\mathsf C_1, \mathsf C_2, \cdots, \mathsf C_n$ is defined as: $\ds \bar x_{\mathsf C} := \frac 1 n \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n m_i f_i$

title: Definition:Mean of Stochastic Process
snippet: Let $S$ be a stochastic process giving rise to a time series $T$. The mean of $S$ over an interval $Q$ is the arithmetic mean of the observations of $T$ over all the timestamps within $Q$.

title: Definition:Meaningful Product
snippet: Let $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ be a semigroup. Let $a_1, \ldots, a_n$ be a sequence of elements of $S$. Then we define a meaningful product of $a_1, \ldots, a_n$ inductively as follows: If $n = 1$ then the only meaningful product is $a_1$. If $n > 1$ then a meaningful product is defined to be any product of the form: $\left({a_1 \ldots a_m}\right)\left({a_{m+1} \ldots a_n}\right)$ where $m < n$ and $\left({a_1 \ldots a_m}\right)$ and $\left({a_{m+1} \ldots a_n}\right)$ are meaningful products of $m$ and $n - m$ elements respectively.

title: Definition:Measurable Function/Banach Space Valued Function
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $I$ be a real interval. Let $X$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $f : I \to X$ be a function. We say that $f$ is measurable if there exists a sequence of simple functions $\sequence {f_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ such that: $\ds \map f t = \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \map {f_n} t$ for Lebesgue almost all $t \in I$.

title: Definition:Measurable Function/Extended Real-Valued Function/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $E \in \Sigma$. Then a function $f: E \to \overline \R$ is said to be $\Sigma$-measurable on $E$ : $\forall \alpha \in \R: \set {x \in E: \map f x \le \alpha} \in \Sigma$

title: Definition:Measurable Function/Extended Real-Valued Function/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $E \in \Sigma$. Let $\Sigma_E$ be the trace $\sigma$-algebra of $E$ in $\Sigma$. Let $\map \BB {\overline \R}$ be the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on the extended real number space. Let $f : E \to \overline \R$ be an extended real-valued function. We say that $f$ is ($\Sigma$-)measurable : $f$ is $\Sigma_E \, / \, \map \BB {\overline \R}$-measurable.

title: Definition:Measurable Function/Extended Real-Valued Function/Definition 3
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $E \in \Sigma$. Then a function $f: E \to \overline \R$ is said to be $\Sigma$-measurable on $E$ at least one of the following holds: $(1) \quad$ $\forall \alpha \in \R : \set {x \in E : \map f x \le \alpha} \in \Sigma$ $(2) \quad$ $\forall \alpha \in \R : \set {x \in E : \map f x \alpha} \in \Sigma$

title: Definition:Measurable Function/Positive
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $S \in \set {\R, \overline \R}$. Let $f : X \to S$ be a $\Sigma$-measurable function. We say that $f$ is a positive $\Sigma$-measurable function : $f \ge 0$ where $\ge$ denotes pointwise inequality.

title: Definition:Measurable Function/Real-Valued Function/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $E \in \Sigma$. Then a function $f: E \to \R$ is said to be $\Sigma$-measurable on $E$ : $\forall \alpha \in \R: \set {x \in E: \map f x \le \alpha} \in \Sigma$

title: Definition:Measurable Function/Real-Valued Function/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $E \in \Sigma$. Let $\Sigma_E$ be the trace $\sigma$-algebra of $E$ in $\Sigma$. Let $\map \BB \R$ be the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on $\R$. Let $f : E \to \R$ be a real-valued function. We say that $f$ is ($\Sigma$-)measurable : $f$ is $\Sigma_E \, / \, \map \BB \R$-measurable.

title: Definition:Measurable Function/Real-Valued Function/Definition 3
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $E \in \Sigma$. Then a function $f: E \to \R$ is said to be $\Sigma$-measurable on $E$ at least one of the following holds: $(1): \quad \forall \alpha \in \R : \set {x \in E : \map f x \le \alpha} \in \Sigma$ $(2): \quad \forall \alpha \in \R : \set {x \in E : \map f x \alpha} \in \Sigma$

title: Definition:Measurable Function/Real-Valued Function/Definition 4
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $E \in \Sigma$. Then a function $f: E \to \R$ is said to be $\Sigma$-measurable on $E$ : $\forall a, b \in \R, a < b: \set {x \in E: a < \map f x < b} \in \Sigma$

title: Definition:Measurable Mapping
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ and $\struct {X', \Sigma'}$ be measurable spaces. A mapping $f: X \to X'$ is said to be $\Sigma \, / \, \Sigma'$-measurable : $\forall E' \in \Sigma': f^{-1} \sqbrk {E'} \in \Sigma$ That is, the preimage of every measurable set under $f$ is again measurable.

title: Definition:Measurable Mapping/Also known as
snippet: == Measurable Mappings: Also known as == When no danger of ambiguity arises, a $\Sigma \, / \, \Sigma'$-measurable mapping $f$ may simply be called measurable.

title: Definition:Measurable Property
snippet: A measurable property is a property of a physical system which can be compared against a standard unit of measurement to provide a numerical value defining the quantity of that property.

title: Definition:Measurable Property/Measurement
snippet: Measurement is the process of determining the quantity of a measurable property according to some given scale of measurement. A measurement is reported as a (real) number multiplied by a unit of measurement for that quantity.

title: Definition:Measurable Set
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. A subset $S \subseteq X$ is said to be ($\Sigma$-)measurable $S \in \Sigma$.

title: Definition:Measurable Set/Also presented as
snippet: == Measurable Set: Also presented as == Some sources present the Carathéodory condition as: $\map {\mu^*} A = \map {\mu^*} {A \cap S} + \map {\mu^*} {A \cap \map \complement S}$ rather than using the $A \setminus S$ form. While $A \cap \map \complement S$ is more unwieldy and cumbersome than $A \setminus S$, it does present the Carathéodory condition in a neatly symmetrical form. Category:Definitions/Measurable Sets

title: Definition:Measurable Set/Arbitrary Outer Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\mu^*$ be an outer measure on $X$. A subset $S \subseteq X$ is called $\mu^*$-measurable it satisfies the Carathéodory condition: $\map {\mu^*} A = \map {\mu^*} {A \cap S} + \map {\mu^*} {A \setminus S}$ for every $A \subseteq X$. The set of $\mu^*$-measurable sets is denoted $\map {\mathfrak M} {\mu^*}$ and is a $\sigma$-algebra over $X$.

title: Definition:Measurable Set/Subset of Reals
snippet: A subset $S$ of the real numbers $\R$ is said to be Lebesgue measurable, or frequently just measurable, for every set $A \subseteq \R$: $\map {\lambda^*} A = \map {\lambda^*} {A \cap S} + \map {\lambda^*} {A \setminus S}$ where $\lambda^*$ is the Lebesgue outer measure. The set of all measurable sets of $\R$ is frequently denoted $\mathfrak M_\R$ or just $\mathfrak M$.

title: Definition:Measurable Set/Subsets of Real Space
snippet: A subset $S$ of $\R^n$ is said to be Lebesgue measurable, frequently just measurable, for every set $A \subseteq \R^n$: $m^* A = \map {m^*} {A \cap S} + \map {m^*} {A \setminus S}$ where: $A \setminus S$ denotes the set difference between $A$ and $S$ $m^*$ is defined as: $\ds \map {m^*} S = \inf_{\set {I_k}: S \mathop \subseteq \cup I_k} \sum \map v {I_k}$ where: $\set {I_k}$ are a sequence of sets satisfying: $I_k = \closedint {a_1} {b_1} \times \dots \times \closedint {a_k} {b_k}$ $\map v {I_n}$ is the volume $\ds \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n \size {b_i - a_i}$ the infimum ranges over all such…

title: Definition:Measurable Space
snippet: Let $\Sigma$ be a $\sigma$-algebra on a set $X$. Then the pair $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ is called a measurable space.

title: Definition:Measurable Stochastic Process/Continuous Time
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \sequence {\FF_t}_{t \ge 0}, \Pr}$ be a filtered probability space. Let $\sequence {X_t}_{t \ge 0}$ be a $\hointr 0 \infty$-indexed family of real-valued random variables. Let $\map \BB {\hointr 0 \infty}$ be the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\hointr 0 \infty$. Let $\Sigma \otimes \map \BB {\hointr 0 \infty}$ be the product $\sigma$-algebra of $\Sigma$ and $\map \BB {\hointr 0 \infty}$.

title: Definition:Measure-Preserving Dynamical System
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \BB, \mu}$ be a probability space. Let $T: X \to X$ be a measure-preserving transformation. Then $\struct {X, \BB, \mu, T}$ is called to be a measure-preserving dynamical system.

title: Definition:Measure-Preserving Mapping
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \BB, \mu}$ and $\struct {Y, \CC, \nu}$ be probability spaces. Let $\phi: X \to Y$ be a $\BB / \CC$-measurable mapping. $\phi$ is said to be measure-preserving if: $\forall C \in \CC: \map \mu {\phi^{-1} \sqbrk C} = \map \nu C$

title: Definition:Measure-Preserving Transformation
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \BB, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $T: X \to X$ be a measurable mapping. $T$ is called a measure-preserving transformation $\mu$ is invariant under $T$.

title: Definition:Measure (Geometry)
snippet: A geometric quantity $A$ is said to measure another quantity $B$ when the size of $A$ is a divisor of the size of $B$. Category:Definitions/Geometry

title: Definition:Measure Space
snippet: A measure space is a triple $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ where: $X$ is a set $\Sigma$ is a $\sigma$-algebra on $X$ $\mu$ is a measure on $\Sigma$. Thus it is a measurable space $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ with a measure.

title: Definition:Measure Theory
snippet: Measure theory is the subfield of analysis concerned with the properties of measures, particularly the Lebesgue measure.

title: Definition:Measure of Central Tendency
snippet: A measure of central tendency is a central or typical value for a probability distribution or set of sample data. The most important examples are often introduced at elementary school level conveniently alliterated as mean, mode and median:

title: Definition:Measure of Central Tendency/Also known as
snippet: Some sources refer to central tendency as centrality. The term location can also be seen.

title: Definition:Measure of Dispersion
snippet: A measure of dispersion is a way to determine how spread out or scattered the observations are in a given sample.

title: Definition:Measure of Dispersion/Also known as
snippet: == Measure of Dispersion: Also known as == A measure of dispersion is also known as a measure of spread.

title: Definition:Measure of Finite Stieltjes Function
snippet: Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a finite Stieltjes function. Let $\mu_f$ be the pre-measure of $f$. Let $\mu$ be the unique measure extending $\mu_f$ provided on Pre-Measure of Finite Stieltjes Function Extends to Unique Measure. Then $\mu$ is called the measure of $f$. This definition makes $\mu$ a measure on $\map \BB \R$, the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\R$.

title: Definition:Measure with Density
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $f: X \to \overline \R_{\ge 0}$ be a positive $\mu$-measurable function. Then the measure with density $f$ $\mu$, denoted $f \mu$, is defined by: $\map {f \mu} E := \ds \int_E f \rd \mu$ where $\ds \int_E f \rd \mu$ is the $\mu$-integral of $f$ over $E$.

title: Definition:Measurement/Also known as
snippet: == Measurement: Also known as == A measurement of a quantity can also be referred to as a measure of it, but the term measure has a specialised meaning in the context of measure theory.

title: Definition:Mechanical Advantage
snippet: Let $M$ be a machine. The mechanical advantage of $M$ is defined as the ratio of the load on $M$ to the effort applied to $M$. That is, the mechanical advantage of $M$ is the (reactive) force exerted by $M$ divided by the (active) force exerted on $M$. Thus when $M$ is in equilibrium: $\mathrm {MA} = \dfrac L E$ where: $L$ denotes the load on $M$ $E$ denotes the effort applied to $M$.

title: Definition:Mechanical Curve
snippet: A mechanical curve is a curve which cannot be constructed using a compass and straightedge. Note that while it is not possible to construct such a curve in this manner, it may well be possible to construct as many points on it as required.

title: Definition:Mechanics
snippet: Mechanics is the branch of applied mathematics concerned with the motion of and forces on bodies.

title: Definition:Mechanistic Model
snippet: Let $P$ be a real-world phenomenon whose physical characteristics are completely understood. Then it is possible to construct a mathematical model which completely and exactly describes it. Such a model is referred to as a mechanistic model.

title: Definition:Medial
snippet: A medial is a strictly positive real number which is the mean proportional between two rational line segments which are commensurable in square only. Thus a magnitude $a \in \R_{>0}$ is medial $a$ is of the form: $a = \rho \sqrt [4] k$ where: $\rho$ is a rational number $k$ is a rational number whose square root is irrational.

title: Definition:Medial Area
snippet: A medial area is an area which is equal to the square on a medial straight line. Thus an area $A$ is medial it is of the form: $A = \rho^2 \sqrt k$ where: $\rho$ is a rational number $k$ is a rational number whose square root is irrational.

title: Definition:Medial Triangle
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle. The medial triangle of $\triangle ABC$ is the triangle formed by joining the midpoint of each of the sides of $\triangle ABC$. 600px In the above, the triangle $\triangle DEF$ is the medial triangle of $\triangle ABC$.

title: Definition:Median
snippet: Geometry: Median of Triangle: a cevian which bisects the opposite Median of Trapezium: a straight line which bisects the legs of a trapezium Statistics: Median: The number in the middle, when ordered by size, of a data set: Median of Discrete Random Variable Median of Continuous Random Variable

title: Definition:Median (Statistics)
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of ordinal data. Let $S$ be arranged in order of size. The median is the element of $S$ that is in the middle of that ordered set. Suppose there are an odd number of elements of $S$ such that $S$ has cardinality $2 n - 1$. The median of $S$ in that case is the $n$th element of $S$. Suppose there are an even number of elements of $S$ such that $S$ has cardinality $2 n$. Then the middle of $S$ is not well-defined, and so the median of $S$ in that case is the arithmetic mean of the $n$th and $n + 1$th elements of $S$.

title: Definition:Median Test
snippet: The median test is a distribution-free test to determine whether two populations have the same median. A sample is taken from each population. The median $m$ is calculated of all values in the samples combined. Then a $2 \times 2$ array is formed such that: the rows correspond to each sample the colums correspond to numbers of the sample values above and below $m$. Then Fisher's exact test is performed to test for any difference in proportions above and below $m$. Differing proportions indicate that the samples have different medians.

title: Definition:Median of Continuous Random Variable
snippet: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable on a probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $X$ have probability density function $f_X$. A median of $X$ is defined as a real number $m_X$ such that: $\ds \map \Pr {X < m_X} = \int_{-\infty}^{m_X} \map {f_X} x \rd x = \frac 1 2$ That is, $m_X$ is the first $2$-quantile of $X$. Hence it is also the $50$th percentile of $X$.

title: Definition:Median of Continuous Random Variable/Warning
snippet: == Median of Continuous Random Variable: Warning == Care should be directed towards the uniqueness of medians. For example, if $\map {f_X} x = 0$ on some closed real interval $\closedint a b$ of $x$, we may have $\ds \int_{-\infty}^{m_X} \map {f_X} x \rd x = \frac 1 2$ for all $m_X \in \closedint a b$. Category:Definitions/Medians

title: Definition:Median of Trapezium
snippet: Let $\Box ABCD$ be a trapezium. 300px The median of $\Box ABCD$ is the straight line through the midpoints of the legs of $\Box ABCD$. In the above diagram, $EF$ is the median of the trapezium $\Box ABCD$.

title: Definition:Median of Trapezium/Also known as
snippet: == Median of Trapezium: Also known as == The median of a trapezium is also known as its midline.

title: Definition:Median of Triangle
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle. 400px A median is a cevian which bisects the opposite. In the above diagram, $CD$ is a median.

title: Definition:Median of Triangle/Also known as
snippet: == Median of Triangle: Also known as == Some sources refer to the median of a triangle as a midline, but this term is used on and elsewhere for a different concept.

title: Definition:Mediant
snippet: Let $r, s \in \Q$ be rational numbers. Let $r$ and $s$ be expressed as: $r = \dfrac a b, s = \dfrac c d$ where $a, b, c, d$ are integers such that $b > 0, d > 0$. Then the mediant of $r$ and $s$ is $\dfrac {a + c} {b + d}$.

title: Definition:Medium
snippet: A medium is a fluid $F$ through which a body $B$ can pass.

title: Definition:Meet
snippet: Order Theory Meet (Order Theory): the infimum of the set formed by two elements of an ordered set. Boolean algebras: Meet: the operation $\wedge$ in a Boolean algebra $\struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \neg}$. Set Theory: A term (rarely used nowadays) for set intersection. Set Meeting Set: For a family of sets, having a non-empty intersection.

title: Definition:Meet-Continuous Lattice
snippet: Let $\left({S, \preceq}\right)$ be a meet semilattice. Then $\left({S, \preceq}\right)$ is meet-continuous $\left({S, \preceq}\right)$ is up-complete and (MC): for every an element $x \in S$ and a directed subset $D$ of $S$: $x \wedge \sup D = \sup \left\{ {x \wedge d: d \in D}\right\}$

title: Definition:Meet-Irreducible Open Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $W \in \tau$. Then $W$ is a meet-irreducible open set : $W$ is meet-irreducible in the frame $\struct {\tau, \subseteq}$

title: Definition:Meet (Boolean Algebra)/Also known as
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \neg}$ be a Boolean algebra. The operation $\wedge$ is often called the Boolean product.

title: Definition:Meet (Order Theory)
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $a, b \in S$, and suppose that their infimum $\inf \set {a, b}$ exists in $S$. Then $a \wedge b$, the meet of $a$ and $b$, is defined as: $a \wedge b = \inf \set {a, b}$ Expanding the definition of infimum, one sees that $c = a \wedge b$ : $(1): \quad c \preceq a$ and $c \preceq b$ $(2): \quad \forall s \in S: s \preceq a$ and $s \preceq b \implies s \preceq c$

title: Definition:Meet Closed
snippet: Let $L = \left({S, \wedge, \preceq}\right)$ be a meet semilattice. Let $X$ be a subset of $S$. Then $X$ is meet closed $\forall x, y \in X: x \wedge y \in X$

title: Definition:Meet Irreducible Element
snippet: Let $\left({S, \wedge, \preceq}\right)$ be a meet semilattice. Let $g \in S$. Then $g$ is meet irreducible : $\forall x, y \in S: g = x \wedge y \implies g = x$ or $g = y$

title: Definition:Meet Irreducible Element/Also known as
snippet: == Meet Irreducible Element: Also known as == The term meet irreducible element is hyphenated as meet-irreducible element in some sources.

title: Definition:Meet Irreducible Element/Lattice
snippet: Let $L = \struct{S, \vee, \wedge, \preceq}$ be a lattice. Let $z \in S$. Then: $z$ is defined as meet irreducible in $L$ $z$ is meet irreducible in the meet semilattice $\struct{S, \wedge, \preceq}$.

title: Definition:Meet Irreducible Element of Lattice/Also known as
snippet: == Meet Irreducible Element of Lattice: Also known as == The term meet irreducible is hyphenated as meet-irreducible in some sources.

title: Definition:Meet Semilattice/Also known as
snippet: == Meet Semilattice: Also known as == A meet semilattice is also known as an lower semilattice or a $\wedge$-semilattice. Some sources hyphenate: meet semi-lattice.

title: Definition:Meet Semilattice/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Suppose that for all $a, b \in S$: $a \wedge b \in S$, where $a \wedge b$ is the meet of $a$ and $b$. Then the ordered structure $\struct {S, \wedge, \preceq}$ is called a meet semilattice.

title: Definition:Meet Semilattice/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \wedge}$ be a semilattice. Let $\preceq$ be the ordering on $S$ defined by: $a \preceq b \iff \paren {a \wedge b} = a$ Then the ordered structure $\struct {S, \wedge, \preceq}$ is called a meet semilattice.

snippet: A megaflop is a measure of calculation speed of a computer. $1$ megaflop $= 1$ million floating point operations per second.

snippet: Consider the expression: $\ds M = \map {\lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} } {\sum_{\substack {p \mathop \le n \\ \text {$p$ prime} } } \dfrac 1 p - \ln \ln n}$ Then: $M \approx 0 \cdotp 26149 \, 72128 \, 47642 \, 78375 \, 54268 \, 38608 \, 69585 \, 90516 \ldots$ The constant $M$ is known as the Meissel-Mertens Constant.

title: Definition:Mellin Transform
snippet: Let $\map f t: \R_{\ge 0} \to \C$ be a function of a real variable $t$. The Mellin transform of $f$ is defined and denoted as: $\ds \map {\MM \set {\map f t} } s := \int_0^{\to +\infty} t^{s - 1} \map f t \rd t$ wherever this improper integral exists. Here $\map \MM f$ is a complex function of the variable $s$.

title: Definition:Mellin Transform/Also denoted as
snippet: == Mellin Transform: Also denoted as== The Mellin transform can also be denoted $\phi$, hence: $\map \phi s := \map {\MM \set {\map f t} } s$ Category:Definitions/Mellin Transforms

title: Definition:Membership Relation
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\powerset S$ denote the power set of $S$. Let $\RR \subseteq S \times \powerset S$ be the relation defined as: $\tuple {x, A} \in \RR \iff x \in A$ Thus $\RR$ is the relation between elements of $S$ and subsets of $S$ expressing membership.

title: Definition:Memory Storage Device
snippet: A memory storage device is an item of computer hardware which stores information for later access.

title: Definition:Menger Space
snippet: A Menger space is a topological space that satisfies the selection principle $\map {S_{fin} } {\OO, \OO}$: for every sequence of open covers $\UU_n$ for $n \in \N$, there exist finite subsets $\FF_n \subseteq \UU_n$ such that $\ds \bigcup_{n \mathop \in \N} \FF_n$ is also an open cover.

title: Definition:Mensuration
snippet: Mensuration is the branch of applied mathematics concerned with the measurement of angles, lengths, areas and volumes of geometric figures.

snippet: == Mercator's Constant: Also known as == Mercator's constant is also known as the alternating harmonic series. Some sources refer to it as Gregory's constant, either for , or , both of whom were early pioneers into the result of sums of convergent series.

title: Definition:Mercator's Projection
snippet: Mercator's projection is the geometric projection of a sphere $\SS$ onto the plane. It is obtained by: circumscribing a cylinder $\CC$ about $\SS$ projecting each point $P$ on the surface of $\SS$ onto $\CC$ along the ray from the center of $\SS$ through $P$ unrolling $\CC$ onto the plane.

title: Definition:Mercator's Projection/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Mercator's Projection == Mercator's projection was originally designed by in $1569$, in order to present a map of Earth's surface. In this context, the cylinder circumscribing Earth intersects it along the equator.

snippet: Definition:Mercury (Planet) Definition:Mercury (Chemical Element)

title: Definition:Mercury (Planet)
snippet: Mercury is the innermost planet of the solar system. Its orbit lies within that of Venus. Category:Definitions/Solar System

title: Definition:Meridian/Terrestrial
snippet: A (terrestrial) meridian is a semi-great circle on Earth's surface whose endpoints are Earth's poles. 600px

title: Definition:Meridian/Terrestrial/Prime
snippet: A prime meridian is a terrestrial meridian which is determined by history and circumstance to be the international reference meridian which terrestrial longitude is defined.

title: Definition:Meridian/Terrestrial/Principal
snippet: A principal meridian is an arbitrary reference meridian of Earth which is used in a given context to determine (terrestrial) longitude. Usually this is for land surveying.

title: Definition:Meridian Section
snippet: Let $S$ be a surface of revolution. A meridian section of $S$ is a plane section of $S$ that contains the axis of revolution of $S$.

title: Definition:Meridian of Surface of Revolution
snippet: Let $S_C$ be a surface of revolution. Let its smooth local parametrization be of the form: $\map X {t, \theta} = \tuple {\map y t \cos \theta, \map y t \sin \theta, \map x t}$ Then the $t$-coordinate curves $t \mapsto \map X {t, \theta_0}$ are called the meridians of $S_C$.

title: Definition:Meromorphic Function
snippet: Let $U \subset \C$ be an open subset of the complex plane $\C$.

title: Definition:Meromorphic Function/Definition 1
snippet: Let $U \subset \C$ be an open subset of the complex plane $\C$. A meromorphic function on $U$ is a holomorphic function on all of $U$ except for a set of poles of $f$.

title: Definition:Meromorphic Function/Definition 2
snippet: Let $U \subset \C$ be an open subset of the complex plane $\C$. A meromorphic function on $U$ is a complex function that can be expressed as the ratio of two holomorphic functions. That is: $\map f z = \dfrac {\map g z} {\map h z}$ where: $g: \C \to \C$ and $h: \C \to \C$ are holomorphic $z \in \C$ such that $\map h z \ne 0$

title: Definition:Meromorphic Function/Definition 3
snippet: Let $U \subset \C$ be an open subset of the complex plane $\C$. A meromorphic function on $U$ is a complex function whose only singular points are poles.

title: Definition:Mersenne Number
snippet: A Mersenne number is a natural number of the form $2^p - 1$, where $p$ is prime. The number $2^p - 1$, in this context, can be denoted $M_p$.

title: Definition:Mersenne Number/Also defined as
snippet: == Mersenne Number: Also defined as == A Mersenne number can also be seen defined as a natural number of the form $2^n - 1$, where $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ or $n \in \Z_{> 0}$, but that leads to the singularly boring sequence: $\paren {0,} 1, 3, 7, 15, 31, 63, 127, 255, 511, 1 \, 023, 2 \, 047, 4 \, 095, 8 \, 191, 16 \, 383, 32 \, 767, \ldots$

title: Definition:Mersenne Prime
snippet: A Mersenne prime is a Mersenne number which happens to be prime. That is, it is a prime number of the form $2^p - 1$. The number $2^p - 1$ is, in this context, often denoted $M_p$.

title: Definition:Mersenne Prime/GIMPS
snippet: The Great Internet Mersenne Prime Search, known as G.I.M.P.S. (or just GIMPS), has become a gathering place for Number Theorists interested in the discovery of the Mersenne primes. It was founded by in early $1996$. All the Mersenne primes discovered from November $1996$ onwards have been discovered by this team. In particular August and September of $2008$ alone, both the $45$th and $46$th Mersenne primes were discovered: $M_{43,112,609}$ (a $12,978,189$ digit number) and $M_{37,156,667}$ (an $11,185,272$ digit number) becoming the first Mersenne primes of $10$ million digits to be found.

title: Definition:Mersenne Prime/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Mersenne Primes == Mersenne primes are named for , who published a book in $1644$, in which he claimed that the only primes $p \le 257$ for which $2^p - 1$ is prime are $2, 3, 5, 7, 13, 17, 19, 31, 67, 127$ and $257$. He was not entirely correct, as shall be seen. Previous to that, the special nature of these primes had been noted by , who showed that if $2^n - 1$ is prime, then $2^{n - 1} \paren {2^n - 1}$ is perfect. The first four primes of this form were known to him.

title: Definition:Mersenne Prime/Index
snippet: The index of the Mersenne prime $M_p = 2^p - 1$ is the (prime) number $p$.

title: Definition:Mersenne Prime/Mistake
snippet: == Source Work == Mersenne numbers or Mersenne primes

title: Definition:Mesokurtic
snippet: Let $X$ be a random variable with kurtosis equal to $3$. Then $X$ is described as mesokurtic.

title: Definition:Mesokurtic/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Mesokurtic == The term mesokurtic arises from meso meaning middle, and the Greek κυρτός (kyrtos or kurtos), meaning curved or arching.

title: Definition:Message
snippet: A message is a discrete piece of information which is being transmitted through a channel. Its likelihood of accurate transmission is the subject of the branch of mathematics known as information theory.

title: Definition:Meta-Lindelöf Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a meta-Lindelöf space every open cover of $S$ has a point countable open refinement.

title: Definition:Metacategory
snippet: A metacategory is a metagraph subject to extra restrictions. As such, a metacategory $\mathbf C$ consists of: A collection $\mathbf C_0$ of objects $X, Y, Z, \ldots$ A collection $\mathbf C_1$ of morphisms $f, g, h, \ldots$ between its objects The morphisms of $\mathbf C$ are subjected to: {{axiom | n = \text C 1 | lc= Composition | t = For objects $X, Y, Z$ and morphisms $X \stackrel {f} {\longrightarrow} Y \stackrel {g} {\longrightarrow} Z$ with $\operatorname{cod} f = \operatorname{dom} \, g$, there exists a morphism: $g \circ f : X \to Z$ called the composition of $f$ and $g$.

title: Definition:Metacompact Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a metacompact space every open cover of $S$ has an open refinement which is point finite.

title: Definition:Metacompact Space/Also known as
snippet: == Metacompact Space: Also known as == A metacompact space is also referred to as:

title: Definition:Metagraph
snippet: A metagraph $\GG$ consists of: objects $X, Y, Z, \ldots$ morphisms $f, g, h, \ldots$ between its objects These are subjected to the following two axioms: {{axiom | n = 1 | lc= Domains | t = Every morphism $f$ has associated an object $\operatorname{dom} f$, called the domain of $f$ }} {{axiom | n = 2 | lc= Codomains | t = Every morphism $f$ has associated an object $\operatorname{cod} f$, called the codomain of $f$ }} A metagraph is purely axiomatic, and does not use set theory.

title: Definition:Metal
snippet: A metal is a substance which is characterised by the fact that its atoms have a number of conduction electrons. These are electrons which are able to flow more or less freely through the substance. This gives rise to an electric current. The atoms themselves, positively charged, remain fixed.

title: Definition:Metal/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Metals ==

title: Definition:Metal/Examples/Copper
snippet: == Example of Metal == Copper is an example of a metal.

title: Definition:Metal/Examples/Tungsten
snippet: == Example of Metal == Tungsten is an example of a metal.

title: Definition:Metalanguage
snippet: A metalanguage is a language, either formal or: natural, which is used to make statements about another language.

title: Definition:Metalanguage/Formal Systems
snippet: In the context of formal systems, a metalanguage is a formal language used to specify another formal language.

title: Definition:Metalanguage/Metasymbol
snippet: A metasymbol is a symbol used in a metalanguage to represent an arbitrary collation in the object language. Metasymbols are deliberately taken from a set of symbols that are not in the alphabet of the object language in question. On , metasymbols are usually taken from any of: uppercase letters: $P, Q, R, \ldots$ and subscripted versions: $P_1, P_2, \ldots$ the Greek alphabet: $\phi, \chi, \psi, \ldots$ and their subscripted versions: $\phi_1, \phi_2, \ldots$ uppercase bold: $\mathbf A, \mathbf B, \mathbf C, \ldots$ and their subscripted versions: $\mathbf A_1, \mathbf A_2, \ldots$ Which…

title: Definition:Metalanguage/Metasyntax
snippet: The syntax of a metalanguage is called a metasyntax of the object language of that metalanguage. Note that it is a metasyntax, as a given object language may have multiple metalanguages to define it.

title: Definition:Metalanguage/Object Language
snippet: The object language of a metalanguage is the language described by that metalanguage.

title: Definition:Metamodel
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a formal system with deductive apparatus $\DD$. A metamodel $\MM$ for $\LL$ is an interpretation for $\LL$. Thus, it assigns meanings to all of the undefined terms of $\LL$. Further, it specifies a means for deciding if a sentence of $\LL$ is to be considered true in $\MM$. It is then required that all the sentences derivable by the deductive apparatus $\DD$ are true in $\MM$. From the above specification, it follows that a metamodel $\MM$ is a conceptual device, in that it does not require to be founded on rigorous mathematical foundations.

title: Definition:Metasymbol/Also known as
snippet: == Metasymbol: Also known as == A metasymbol can also be referred to as: a metalogical variable a metalogical symbol a metasyntactic variableAs immortalized by in Men at Arms: the dog Gaspode says, "Clothing has never been what you might call a thingy of dog wossname." Then he adds: "Two metasyntactic variables there. Sorry.". Some sources also use the term propositional variable, but this has subtly different meaning on .

title: Definition:Metasyntax/Also defined as
snippet: == Metasyntax: Also known as == In some contexts, the metalanguage itself is referred to as a metasyntax.

title: Definition:Metatheorem
snippet: A metatheorem of a metalanguage $\LL$ about an object language $\FF$ is a theorem about $\FF$ which is not part of $\FF$. It is usual for $\FF$ to be a formal system or a formal language.

title: Definition:Method of Exhaustion
snippet: The method of exhaustion is a technique for calculating an approximation to the physical extent of a geometric figure whose extremities are curved lines. To measure the area of a circle, for example, this is done by: Circumscribing a polygon around the circle Inscribing a polygon inside the circle Measuring the areas of those polygons Noting that the area of the circle is between those two Increasing the number of sides on those polygons to make them closer and closer to the circle and each other. As the number of sides of the polygons increases, their areas become ever closer to each other.

title: Definition:Method of Exhaustion/Also known as
snippet: == Method of Exhaustion: Also known as == The method of exhaustion is also known as Archimedes' method, for .

title: Definition:Method of Exhaustion/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Method of Exhaustion == The method of exhaustion was invented by in around $370$ BCE. It was later exploited to good effect by , and is used throughout during the course of calculating volumes of solid figures. Some sources credit with invention of the method, but this is incorrect.

title: Definition:Method of Indivisibles
snippet: The method of indivisibles is a technique for calculating the physical extent of a geometric figure whose extremities are curved lines. The technique is to divide the geometric figure up into slices, that is: for an area, to divide a surface into lines placed side by side as a cloth is made of threads for a volume, to divide a solid figure into planes stacked one on top of another like the pages of a book.

title: Definition:Method of Indivisibles/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Method of Indivisibles == The method of indivisibles was presented by in his $1635$ work , as an extension of 's technique for finding volumes of revolution.

title: Definition:Method of Least Squares (Approximation Theory)
snippet: Let there be a set of points $\set {\tuple {x_k, y_k}: k \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n} }$ plotted on a Cartesian $x y$ plane which correspond to measurements of a physical system. Let it be required that a straight line is to be fitted to the points. The method of least squares is a technique of producing a straight line of the form $y = m x + c$ such that: the points $\set {\tuple {x_k', y_k'}: k \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n} }$ are on the line $y = m x + c$ $\forall k \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n}: x_k' = x_k$ $\ds \sum_n \paren {y_k' - y_k}^2$ is minimised. 500px

title: Definition:Method of Least Squares (Approximation Theory)/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Method of Least Squares == The method of least squares was invented by .

title: Definition:Method of Least Squares (Statistics)
snippet: The method of least squares, in the context of statistics, is a method to estimate parameters, particularly in regression models.

title: Definition:Method of Moments
snippet: The method of moments is the process of estimation of parameters of a probability distribution by equating the first $k$ sample moments and solving the resulting equations. There are more efficient techniques for such estimation, but this is relatively simple and intuitive.

snippet: == Metre == The cubic metre is the SI unit of volume.

title: Definition:Metre/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Metre == 1671: measured the length $L$ of a simple pendulum whose period is $1$ second, and proposed a unit of measurement $2 L$, which was to be called the universal toise. 1675: suggested the term metre as the length of this pendulum. It differs from the modern metre by half a centimetre. It was soon established that as Acceleration Due to Gravity varies considerably according to location, this was not a sustainable definition to maintain a standard.

title: Definition:Metre/Historical Note/Mistake

title: Definition:Metre/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Metre == The word metre originated with who pioneered the concept of a universal set of fundamental units. He used the term metro cattolico from the Greek μέτρον καθολικόν (métron katholikón), that is universal measure. This word gave rise to the French word mètre which was introduced into the English language in $1797$. The spelling metre is the one adopted by the International Bureau of Weights and Measures.

title: Definition:Metre/Square Metre
snippet: The square metre is the SI unit of area.

snippet: == Metric: Also defined as == If $\struct {A, d}$ is a pseudometric space or quasimetric space, this definition still applies. We also find that a pseudometric and a quasimetric are also both found to be categorised in the literature as metrics and distance functions.

title: Definition:Metric/Also denoted as
snippet: == Metric: Also denoted as == Some authors use a variant of $d$ for a metric, for example $\eth$. The $d$ is of course for distance function, used at least as often as metric. Others use, for example, $\rho$.

title: Definition:Metric/Also known as
snippet: == Metric: Also known as == The metric $d$ in a metric space $\struct {A, d}$ is frequently referred to as a distance function on $A$. The two terms are used interchangeably on this website, although metric is preferred. Some sources call a metric just a distance, but that is a general term with a number of interpretations.

title: Definition:Metric/Shift of Finite Type
snippet: Let $\struct {X _\mathbf A, \sigma_\mathbf A}$ be a shift of finite type. Let $\theta \in \openint 0 1$. Then the metric $d_\theta$ on $X _\mathbf A$ is defined by: $\forall x, y \in X_\mathbf A : \map {d_\theta} {x, y} = \theta ^N$ where: $ N := \sup \set {n \in \N \cup \set \infty: x_i = y_i \text { for all } i \in \openint {-n} n}$ $\theta ^\infty := 0$ Here we consider the suprema related to the extended natural numbers $\struct {\N \cup \set \infty, \le}$.

title: Definition:Metric (Curvilinear Coordinates)
snippet: Let $S$ be an infinitesimal arc. Let $\d s$ be the length of $S$ Then: {{eqn | r = \sum_{i, j} {h_{i j} }^2 \rd q_i \rd q_j | c = for $i, j \in \set {1, 2, 3}$ }} where: $\d x$, $\d y$ and $\d z$ are the lengths of the projections of $S$ on the $x$-axis, $y$-axis and $z$-axis respectively $\d q_i$ is the projection of $S$ onto the unit normal to the curvilinear coordinate surface determined by $q_i$, for $i \in \set {1, 3}$ the coefficients $h_{i j}$ specify the nature of the curvilinear coordinate system $\QQ$ being utilised.

title: Definition:Metric Compatible Connection

Let $\map {\mathfrak X} M$ be the space of smooth vector fields on $M$. Let $\nabla$ be a connection in $TM$. Let $\innerprod \cdot \cdot$ be the Riemannian or pseudo-Riemannian scalar product.

title: Definition:Metric Induced by Smooth Immersion
snippet: Let $\struct {\tilde M, \tilde g}$, $\struct {M, g}$ be Riemannian manifolds. Let $F : M \to \tilde M$ be a smooth immersion. Suppose, the metric $g$ is such that $g = F^* \tilde g$. Then $g$ is called the metric induced by $F$.

title: Definition:Metric Invariant under Group Action
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $G$ be a group. Suppose $\forall \phi \in G$ the mapping $x \mapsto \phi \cdot x$ is an isometry. Then the metric $g$ is said to be invariant under $G$.

title: Definition:Metric Projection

Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {\HH, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be a Hilbert space over $\GF$. Let $
orm {\, \cdot \,}_\HH$ be the inner product norm. Let $C \subseteq \HH$ be a non-empty closed convex set. For each $x \in \HH$, let $\map {\pi_C} x$ be the unique point in $C$ such that: $\ds 
orm {x - \map {\pi_C} x}_\HH = \inf_{z \mathop \in C}

title: Definition:Metric Space/Notation

title: Definition:Metric Space/Point

title: Definition:Metric Spaces (Mathematical Branch)
snippet: Metric spaces is the branch of mathematics in which the topology on a topological space is derived from a notion of distance or metric. The notion of a metric gives rise to the treatment of convergent sequences and limits, as well as continuity of mappings. It is closely aligned with the branch of analysis.

title: Definition:Metric Subspace
snippet: Let $\struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. Let $H \subseteq A$. Let $d_H: H \times H \to \R$ be the restriction $d \restriction_{H \times H}$ of $d$ to $H$. That is, let $\forall x, y \in H: \map {d_H} {x, y} = \map d {x, y}$. Then $d_H$ is the metric induced on $H$ by $d$ or the subspace metric of $d$ (with respect to $H$). The metric space $\struct {H, d_H}$ is called a metric subspace of $\struct {A, d}$.

title: Definition:Metric System
snippet: The metric system is the colloquial term for the system of measurement based on the metre. Its main characteristic is that its units are constructed on a decimal system.

title: Definition:Metric System/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Metric System == The concept of a metric system was first floated by in $1585$. promoted the idea in the $18$th century. Subsequently, in $1790$, the French government invited a number of scientists to recommend a system of measurement, and also to propose a new unit of length. By $1795$, the idea had taken hold, and the metre, the litre and the gram had been introduced. The metre was defined as being $10^{-7}$ the distance from the North Pole to the equator, based on measurements between and . Subsequently this distance was shown to be inaccurate.

title: Definition:Metric System/Mass/Kilogram
snippet: The kilogram is the SI base unit of mass. It is defined as follows: $1$ kilogram is the quantity of mass that would make the fixed numerical value of the Planck constant $h$ to be $6 \cdotp 62607015 \times 10^{-34}$ when expressed in the unit Joule seconds. The Joule second is equal to $1 \, \mathrm {kg} \, \mathrm m^2 \, \mathrm s^{−1}$, where the metre and the second are defined in terms of: the speed of light $c$ the time of transition between the two hyperfine levels of the ground state of the caesium $133$ atom at rest at $0 \, \mathrm K$.

title: Definition:Metric System/Mass/Milligram
snippet: The milligram is an SI unit of mass. $1$ milligram is defined as $= \dfrac 1 {1 \, 000}$ of a gram.

title: Definition:Metric System/Mass/Tonne
snippet: The tonne is an SI unit of mass. $1$ tonne is defined as $= 1000$ kilograms.

title: Definition:Metric Tensor
snippet: Consider a smooth manifold $\MM$ on the real space $\R^n$. Consider a Riemannian metric $\d s$ on $\MM$ between nearby points $\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ and $\tuple {x_1 + \d x_1, x_2 + \d x_2, \ldots, x_n + \d x_n}$ defined in the form: $\ds \d s^2 = \sum_{i, j \mathop = 1}^n \map {g_{i j} } x \rd x_i \rd x_j$ where each $g_{i j}$ is a suitable real-valued function of $x_1, \ldots, x_n$. The $\map {g_{i j} } x$ are the components of a symmetric covariant tensor field. This symmetric covariant tensor field is known as the metric tensor on $\MM$.

title: Definition:Metrical Geometry
snippet: Metrical geometry is the study of points, lines, surfaces and volumes in real space, and is based on the concepts of distance and angle. It is what is usually understood in the everyday world as geometry proper.

title: Definition:Metrically Complete Connected Riemannian Manifold
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a connected Riemannian manifold. Let $d_g$ be the Riemannian distance. Then $M$ is called the (metrically) complete manifold if every Cauchy sequence in $M$ converges with respect to the distance function $d_g$.

title: Definition:Metrizable Space/Definition 1

title: Definition:Min Operation
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a totally ordered set. The min operation is the binary operation on $\struct {S, \preceq}$ defined as: $\forall x, y \in S: \map \min {x, y} = \begin {cases} x & : x \preceq y \\ y & : y \preceq x \end {cases}$

title: Definition:Min Operation/General Definition
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a totally ordered set. Let $S^n$ be the cartesian $n$th power of $S$. The min operation is the $n$-ary operation on $\struct {S, \preceq}$ defined recursively as: $\forall x := \family {x_i}_{1 \mathop \le i \mathop \le n} \in S^n: \map \min x = \begin{cases} x_1 & : n = 1 \\ \map \min {x_1, x_2} & : n = 2 \\ \map \min {\map \min {x_1, \ldots, x_{n - 1} }, x_n} & : n > 2 \\ \end{cases}$ where $\map \min {x, y}$ is the binary min operation on $S^2$.

title: Definition:Minimal/Set

title: Definition:Minimal (Model Theory)
snippet: Let $\MM$ be an $\LL$-structure. Let $M$ be the universe of $\MM$. Let $A$ be a subset of $M$. Let $D \subseteq M^n$ be an infinite $A$-definable set. Let $\phi \left({\bar x, \bar a}\right)$ be an $\LL$-formula with parameters $\bar a$ from $A\subseteq M$ and free variables $\bar x$ which defines $D$. $D$ is minimal in $\MM$ every definable subset of $D$ is either finite or cofinite. $\phi$ is minimal in $\MM$ if $D$ is minimal in $\MM$. $D$ and $\phi$ are strongly minimal in $\MM$ $\phi$ is minimal in any elementary extension $\NN$ of $\MM$.

title: Definition:Minimal Element/Comparison with Smallest Element
snippet: Compare the definition of a minimal element with that of a smallest element. Consider the ordered set $\struct {S, \preceq}$ such that $T \subseteq S$. An element $x \in T$ is the smallest element of $T$ : $\forall y \in T: x \preceq y$ That is, $x$ is comparable with, and precedes, or is equal to, every $y \in T$. An element $x \in T$ is a minimal element of $T$ : $y \preceq x \implies x = y$ That is, $x$ precedes, or is equal to, every $y \in T$ which is comparable with $x$. If all elements are comparable with $x$, then such a minimal element is indeed the smallest element.

title: Definition:Minimal Length Path
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a simple graph. Let $u, v \in V$ be vertices of $G$. Let $W$ be the set of all open paths between $u$ and $v$. An open path $p \in W$ is a minimal length path from $u$ to $v$ : there exists no path $q$ beginning at $u$ and ending at $v$ such that the length of $q$ is (strictly) less than the length of $p$.

title: Definition:Minimal Polynomial/Also known as

title: Definition:Minimal Polynomial/Definition 1
snippet: Let $L / K$ be a field extension. Let $\alpha \in L$ be algebraic over $K$. The minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ over $K$ is the unique monic polynomial $f \in K \sqbrk x$ of smallest degree such that $\map f \alpha = 0$.

title: Definition:Minimal Polynomial/Definition 2
snippet: Let $L / K$ be a field extension. Let $\alpha \in L$ be algebraic over $K$. The minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ over $K$ is the unique irreducible, monic polynomial $f \in K \sqbrk x$ such that $\map f \alpha = 0$.

title: Definition:Minimal Polynomial/Definition 3
snippet: Let $L / K$ be a field extension. Let $\alpha \in L$ be algebraic over $K$. The minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ over $K$ is the unique monic polynomial $f \in K \sqbrk x$ that generates the kernel of the evaluation homomorphism $K \sqbrk x \to L$ at $\alpha$. That is, such that for all $g \in K \sqbrk x$: $\map g \alpha = 0$ $f$ divides $g$.

title: Definition:Minimal Polynomial of Square Matrix
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a square matrix of order $n$. The minimal polynomial $m$ of $\mathbf A$ is the monic polynomial of smallest degree such that: $\map m {\mathbf A} = \mathbf 0$ where $\mathbf 0$ is the zero matrix of order $n$.

title: Definition:Minimal Prime
snippet: Let $b \in \N_{>1}$ be a natural number. A minimal prime base $b$ is a prime number whose base-$b$ representation has no proper subsequence which is also a prime number. If $b$ is not specified, then decimal notation (that is, base $10$) is assumed.

title: Definition:Minimal Subgroup
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $M \le G$ be a non-trivial subgroup of $G$. Then $M$ is a minimal subgroup of $G$ : For every subgroup $H$ of $G$, $H \subseteq M$ means $H = M$ or $H = \set e$. That is, there is no subgroup of $M$, except $M$ and $\set e$ itself, which is a subset of $M$.

title: Definition:Minimal Surface
snippet: A minimal surface is a surface on which the mean curvature is zero. That is, such that the principal curvatures are equal but in opposite directions.

title: Definition:Minimal Topology
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\powerset S$ be the power set of $S$. Let $\Theta_S$ be the set of all topologies on $S$: $\Theta_S = \leftset {\tau \in \powerset S: \tau}$ is a topology on $\rightset S$ Let $\Phi: \Theta_S \to \set {\T, \F}$ be a propositional function on $\Theta_S$. Let $\vartheta \in \Theta_S$ have the property that $\map \Phi \vartheta$ and: $\forall \tau \in \Theta_S: \map \Phi \tau \implies \vartheta \subseteq \tau$ That is, $\vartheta$ is the coarsest topology on $S$ which satisfies the propositional function $\Phi$. Then $\vartheta$ is the minimal topology satisfying $\Phi$.

Then the minimization operation on $f$ is written as: $\map {\mu y} {\map f {n, y} = 0}$ and is specified as follows: $\map {\mu y} {\map f {n, y} = 0} = \begin{cases} z & : \map f {n, z} = 0 \text { and } \map f {n, y} \text{ defined and } \forall y: 0 \le y The partial function: $\map g n \approx \map {\mu y} {\map f {n, y} = 0}$ obtained in this way (see Partial Function Equality) is said to be obtained from $f$ by minimization.

title: Definition:Minimization/Relation
snippet: Let $\map \RR {n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_k, y} $ be a $k + 1$-ary relation on $\N^{k + 1}$. Let $n = \tuple {n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_k} \in \N^k$ be fixed. Then the minimization operation on $\RR$ is written as: $\mu y \map \RR {n, y}$ and is specified as follows: $\mu y \map \RR {n, y} = \begin{cases} \text{the smallest } y \in \N \text{ for which } \map \RR {n, y} \text{ holds} & : \text{if there exists such a } y \\ \text{undefined} & : \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$ We can consider the definition for a function to be a special case of this.

title: Definition:Minimizing Curve on Riemannian Manifold
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $L_g$ be the Riemannian length. Let $S$ be the set of all admissible curves in $M$ with same endpoints $p_i, p_f \in M$. Let $\gamma_{min} \in S$ be such that: $\forall \tilde \gamma \in S : \map {L_g} {\gamma_{min}} \le \map {L_g} {\tilde \gamma}$. Then $\gamma_{min}$ is called the minimizing curve.

title: Definition:Minimum/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Minimum == The plural form of minimum is minima.

title: Definition:Minimum Degree
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a graph. Then the minimum degree of $G$ is: $\map \delta G = \min \set {\map {\deg_G} v : v \in V}$ That is, it is the minimum degree of all the vertices of $G$.

title: Definition:Minimum Distance of Linear Code
snippet: Let $C$ be a linear code whose master code is $\map V {n, p}$. The minimum distance $d$ of $C$ is defined as: $\map d C := \ds \min_{u, v \mathop \in C: u \mathop \ne v} \set {\map d {u, v} }$ where $\map d {u, v}$ denotes the Hamming distance between $u$ and $v$.

title: Definition:Minimum Spanning Tree
snippet: Let $G$ be a weighted graph. The minimum spanning tree for $G$ is a spanning tree for $G$ which has a minimum total weight.

title: Definition:Minimum Spanning Tree/Also known as
snippet: == Minimum Spanning Tree: Also known as == A minimum spanning tree is also known as an economy tree. A minimum spanning tree can also be called the minimum connector for $G$.

title: Definition:Minimum Value of Functional
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of mappings. Let $y, \hat y \in S: \R \to \R$ be real functions. Let $J \sqbrk y: S \to \R$ be a functional. Let $J$ have a (relative) extremum for $y = \hat y$. Let $J \sqbrk y - J \sqbrk {\hat y} \ge 0$ in the neighbourhood of $y = \hat y$. Then this extremum is called the minimum of the functional $J$.

title: Definition:Minimum Value of Real Function/Absolute
snippet: Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a real function. Let $f$ be bounded below by an infimum $B$. It may or may not be the case that $\exists x \in \R: \map f x = B$. If such a value exists, it is called the (absolute) minimum of $f$ on $S$, and this absolute minimum is attained at $x$.

title: Definition:Minimum Value of Real Function/Local
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function defined on an open interval $\openint a b$. Let $\xi \in \openint a b$. Then $f$ has a local minimum at $\xi$ : $\exists \openint c d \subseteq \openint a b: \forall x \in \openint c d: \map f x \ge \map f \xi$ That is, there is some subinterval on which $f$ attains a minimum within that interval.

title: Definition:Minimum Value of Real Function/Local/Strict
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function defined on an open interval $\openint a b$. Let $\xi \in \openint a b$. $f$ has a strict local minimum at $\xi$ : $\exists \openint c d \subseteq \openint a b: \forall x \in \openint c d: \map f x > \map f \xi$

title: Definition:Minimum Variance Unbiased Estimator
snippet: Let $S$ be a sample of $n$ observations from a probability distribution with frequency function $\map f {x, \theta}$. Let it be assumed that certain regularity conditions apply. Let it also be assumed that the extremes do not depend on $\theta$. Let $T$ be an unbiased estimator such that: $\var T = \dfrac 1 I$ where: $I = -n \map E {\dfrac {\partial^2 \ln f} {\partial \theta^2} }$ Then $\var T$ is called a minimum variance unbiased estimator. Hence, the smaller the variance, the greater its information content.

title: Definition:Minkowski Functional
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a vector space over $\GF$. Let $A \subseteq X$ be a convex absorbing subset of $X$. The Minkowski functional of $A$ is the real-valued function $\mu_A : X \to \closedint 0 \infty$ defined as: $\forall x \in X: \map {\mu_A} x = \inf \set {t > 0 : \dfrac x t \in A}$

title: Definition:Minkowski Functional/Normed Vector Space
snippet: Let $\Bbb F \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm \cdot}$ be a normed vector space over $\Bbb F$. Let $C$ be an open convex subset of $X$ with $0 \in C$. The Minkowski functional of $C$ is the mapping $p_C : X \to \hointr 0 \infty$ defined as: $\forall x \in X: \map {p_C} x = \inf \set {t > 0 : \dfrac x t \in C}$

title: Definition:Minkowski Metric
snippet: Minkowski metric is the pseudo-Euclidean metric $\bar q^{\tuple {r, 1} }$.

title: Definition:Minkowski Spacetime/Also known as
snippet: == Minkowski Spacetime: Also known as == Minkowski spacetime can also be seen rendered hyphenated, that is, as Minkowski space-time. Other terms that can be found for the same concept: Minkowskian space-time Minkowski space Minkowski world Minkowski universe $\paren {r + 1}$-dimensional Minkowski space

title: Definition:Minkowski Spacetime/Definition 1
snippet: Minkowski spacetime is the pseudo-Euclidean space $\R^{r, 1}$.

title: Definition:Minkowski Spacetime/Definition 2
snippet: Minkowski spacetime is a $4$-dimensional model of physical space and time: $3$ of those dimensions correspond to the position of an event in space the remaining dimension represents the time of that event.

title: Definition:Minkowski Spacetime/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Minkowski Spacetime == realised that the two postulates of the Special Theory of Relativity require space and time to be treated not as separate entitiies, but as a unified $4$-dimensional concept, referred to as spacetime. Hence (Minkowski) spacetime became the frame of all later extensions of the theory of relativity.

title: Definition:Minkowski Sum
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space. Let $A, B$ be two subsets of $V$. Then the Minkowski sum of $A$ and $B$, denoted as $A + B$, is defined as: $A + B := \set {a + b: a \in A, b \in B}$ where the operation $+$ is vector addition. The Minkowski sum is therefore a relation in the power set of $V$ in the sense that it is a mapping: $+: \powerset V^2 \to \powerset V$ Category:Definitions/Linear Algebra

title: Definition:Minor
snippet: Euclidean Number Theory: Minor (Euclidean) Geometry: Minor Axis of Ellipse Semiminor Axis of Ellipse Minor Axis of Hyperbola Categorical Syllogisms: Minor Premise of Syllogism Linear Algebra Minor of Determinant

title: Definition:Minor (Euclidean)
snippet: Let $a, b \in \R_{>0}$ in the forms: $a = \dfrac \rho {\sqrt 2} \sqrt {1 + \dfrac k {\sqrt {1 + k^2} } }$ $b = \dfrac \rho {\sqrt 2} \sqrt {1 - \dfrac k {\sqrt {1 + k^2} } }$ where: $\rho$ is a rational number $k$ is a rational number whose square root is irrational. Then $a - b$ is a minor.

title: Definition:Minor (Euclidean)/Annex
snippet: Let $a, b \in \R_{>0}$ be (strictly) positive real numbers such that $a > b$. Let $a - b$ be a minor. The real number $b$ is called the annex of the minor. Category:Definitions/Euclidean Number Theory

title: Definition:Minor (Euclidean)/Terms
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be two positive real numbers. Let $a - b$ be a minor. The terms of $a - b$ are the elements $a$ and $b$.

title: Definition:Minor (Euclidean)/Whole
snippet: Let $a, b \in \R_{>0}$ be (strictly) positive real numbers such that $a > b$. Let $a - b$ be a minor. The real number $a$ is called the whole of the minor. Category:Definitions/Euclidean Number Theory

title: Definition:Minor Arc
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be points on the boundary $\BB$ of a simple closed curve $\CC$ in the plane. Let $a$ and $b$ divide $\BB$ into unequal parts. The shorter of the arcs described by $a$ and $b$ is referred to as the minor arc of $\BB$.

title: Definition:Minor Arc/Also known as
snippet: == Minor Arc: Also known as == The minor arc of a simple closed curve two points is also known as the short arc.

title: Definition:Minor Axis
snippet: The minor axis of a central conic $\KK$ is the straight line: passing through the center of symmetry of $\KK$ perpendicular to the major axis of $\KK$. This may or may not be defined as being terminated at the covertices of $K$ according to variations of definitions. The distinction should be clear according to usage.

title: Definition:Minor Axis of Ellipse/Definition 1
snippet: 500px Consider an ellipse $K$ whose foci are $F_1$ and $F_2$. The minor axis of $K$ is the line segment through the center of $K$ perpendicular to the major axis of $K$ such that its endpoints are the points of intersection with $K$. In the above diagram, $C_1 C_2$ is the minor axis of $K$.

title: Definition:Minor Axis of Ellipse/Definition 2
snippet: 500px Consider an ellipse $K$ whose foci are $F_1$ and $F_2$. The minor axis of $K$ is the diameter of $K$ which has the smallest length. In the above diagram, $C_1 C_2$ is the minor axis of $K$.

title: Definition:Minor Axis of Ellipsoid
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an ellipsoid. The minor axis of $\EE$ is the diameter of $\EE$ which has the smallest length.

title: Definition:Minor of Determinant
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_n$ be a square matrix of order $n$. Consider the order $k$ square submatrix $\mathbf B$ obtained by deleting $n - k$ rows and $n - k$ columns from $\mathbf A$. Let $\map \det {\mathbf B}$ denote the determinant of $\mathbf B$. Then $\map \det {\mathbf B}$ is an order-$k$ minor of $\map \det {\mathbf A}$. Thus a minor is a determinant formed from the elements (in the same relative order) of $k$ specified rows and columns.

title: Definition:Minor of Determinant/Example
snippet: == Example of Minor of Determinant == Let $D$ be the determinant defined as: $D = \begin {vmatrix} a_{1 1} & a_{1 2} & a_{1 3} \\ a_{2 1} & a_{2 2} & a_{2 3} \\ a_{3 1} & a_{3 2} & a_{3 3} \end{vmatrix}$ Then: $\map D {1, 2 \mid 1, 3} = \begin {vmatrix} a_{1 1} & a_{1 3} \\ a_{2 1} & a_{2 3} \end {vmatrix}$ Note that $\map D {1, 2 \mid 1, 3}$ can also be denoted as $D_{3 2}$. Category:Definitions/Determinants

title: Definition:Minor of Determinant/Notation
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_n$ be a square matrix of order $n$. Let $D := \map \det {\mathbf A}$ denote the determinant of $\mathbf A$. Let: $\set {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_k}$ be the indices of the $k$ selected rows of $\mathbf A$ $\set {b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_k}$ be the indices of the $k$ selected columns of $\mathbf A$ where all of $a_1, \ldots, a_k$ and all of $b_1, \ldots, b_k$ are between $1$ and $n$. Let: $\mathbf B := \mathbf A \sqbrk {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_k; b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_k}$ be the submatrix formed from rows $\set {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_k}$ and columns $\set {b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_k}$.

title: Definition:Minor of Determinant/Notation/Order n-1
snippet: The conventional notation for the minor of a determinant is cumbersome for a minor of order $n - 1$. Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_n$ be a square matrix of order $n$. Let $D := \map \det {\mathbf A}$ denote the determinant of $\mathbf A$. Let a submatrix $\mathbf B$ of $\mathbf A$ be of order $n - 1$. Let: $j$ be the row of $\mathbf A$ which is not included in $\mathbf B$ $k$ be the column of $\mathbf A$ which is not included in $\mathbf B$. Thus, let $\mathbf B := \map {\mathbf A} {j; k}$.

title: Definition:Minuend/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Minuend == The word minuend derives from the Latin minuendus, meaning that which is to be diminished (that is, made smaller). Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Minute/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Minute == The word minute, in the context of the measurement both of time and of angle, derives from its initial definition as a minute part of an hour or of a degree of angle. In this context the word minute (meaning: the aggregation of $60$ seconds) is pronounced min-it. The word minute (as used in the phrase minute part) is pronounced my-nyoot and means small. So the fact that the two words are spelt identically is not a coincidence. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Minute/Symbol/Also known as
