snippet: == Symbol for Minute: Also known as == The symbol ${}^\prime$ is sometimes referred to as a minute mark.

title: Definition:Minute of Angle/Also known as
snippet: == Minute of Angle: Also known as == A minute of angle is also known as a minute of arc, or an arc minute. This term has a definition which is subtly different from the concept of a minute of angle, and so its use in this context on is discouraged.

title: Definition:Minute of Angle/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Minute of Angle == The division of the degrees into $60$ subdivisions originates from the , who used a sexagesimal (base $60$) system for the purposes of mathematics and astronomy.

title: Definition:Minute of Arc
snippet: The minute (of arc) is a unit of measurement of the length of an arc of a circle. It is defined as the length of the arc which subtends $1$ minute (of angle) at the center of the circle.

title: Definition:Minute of Time/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Minute of Time == The division of the hour into $60$ subdivisions originated some undecidable time in the , using the same sexagesimal (base $60$) system that was used to subdivide degrees of angle. These systems of division of time and angle are the last system of measurements which have not been decimalised.

title: Definition:Mirror Property of Primes
snippet: Let $p_n$ denote the $n$th prime number. Let $\map {\operatorname {rev} } {p_n}$ denote the reversal of $p_n$. $p_n$ satisfies the mirror property : $(1): \quad \map {\operatorname {rev} } {p_n}$ is also a prime number $(2): \quad$ the product of the digits of the base $10$ representation of $\map {\operatorname {rev} } {p_n}$ equals $\map {\operatorname {rev} } n$.

title: Definition:Miscellanea
snippet: Miscellanea, in the context of , are more or less relevant factoids whose categorization is difficult or irrelevant.

title: Definition:Miscellaneous Volume Measure
snippet: This page gathers together various units of measurement of volume which can be found in the literature.

title: Definition:Miscellaneous Volume Measure/Cord
snippet: The cord is a unit of volume traditionally used for or . Thus a cord is a quantity of wood that can be stacked in a woodpile $4$ feet long, $8$ feet wide, and $4$ feet high. Category:Definitions/Volume

title: Definition:Miscellaneous Volume Measure/Gallon
snippet: The gallon is a unit of volume traditionally used for fluids, in the main liquids. There are a number of different versions of the gallon, all of approximately the same order of magnitude.

title: Definition:Missing-Plot Technique
snippet: A missing-plot technique is a technique for simplifying the analysis of variance of a designed experiment when observations are accidentally lost.

title: Definition:Mistake
snippet: A mistake (as opposed to an error) is an inaccuracy or (deduced) falsehood caused by (ultimately) human fault. Synonyms include such terms as boob, bloomer, blooper, blunder, cock-up, bug (computer science), mess-up, oversight, howler and other less polite words frequently encountered at the backs of schoolrooms worldwide. Please feel free to add your own.

title: Definition:Mistake/Copypasto
snippet: Suppose a writer has copied a section of material and pasted it into another page, but has inadequately replaced the material which is different between the source and target pages. The writer has committed a copypasto. This is an abbreviation for mistake made while performing a copy and paste operation. Such mistakes can be corrected by meticulous proof-reading. Category:Definitions/Mistakes

title: Definition:Mistake/Glitch
snippet: A glitch is a mistake arising from imperfect typesetting software. These can be corrected by assiduous checking by the writer. Category:Definitions/Mistakes

title: Definition:Mistake/Homophone Horror
snippet: A homophone horror is a mistake caused by the use of a word which sounds the same as, but is spelled differently to, the word intended. A proficient proof-reader is needed to reduce instances of this sort of mistake.

title: Definition:Mistake/Linguistic Note
snippet: The word howler as a synonym for mistake derives from the tendency of those encountering it to howl with laughter in ridicule of the person committing it. The word bug originates from the early days of the computer industry, where a malfunction was found to be caused by an insect, or bug in colloquial American, whose intrusion had compromised the workings. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Mistake/Scanno
snippet: A scanno is a mistake arising from inaccurate scanning and subsequent optical character recognition software. These can be corrected by assiduous checking by the writer. Category:Definitions/Mistakes

title: Definition:Mistake/Spello
snippet: A spello (abbreviation for spelling mistake) is a mistake caused by inadequate spelling skills of the writer. These can sometimes be corrected by the writer having the self-doubt necessary to occasion the act of referring to a reliable manual, for example, a dictionary. A competent proof-reader (that is, one whose spelling skills are more comprehensive than the writer) is usually an adequate resource for reducing spelloes. Category:Definitions/Mistakes

title: Definition:Mistake/Thinko
snippet: A thinko is a mistake caused by inadequate or incorrect thinking by the writer. These can usually be corrected only by the writer passing the work along to another person who is adequately skilled in the area of expertise to be able to understand what has been done wrong. Category:Definitions/Mistakes

title: Definition:Mistake/Typo
snippet: A typo (abbreviation for typographical error) is a mistake arising from pressing the wrong button on the machine via which you are transcribing your thoughts onto a storage medium. These can be corrected by assiduous checking by the writer. Category:Definitions/Mistakes

title: Definition:Mistake/Whoosho
snippet: A whoosho is a mistake caused by a complete failure to understand a concept vital to the accurate communication of an idea. It is also used for a failure to understand or recognise a joke. The word comes from the popular meme of how whoosh is supposedly the sound of whatever it is going over the person's head. "That went so far over my head I didn't even hear it go whoosh." Category:Definitions/Mistakes

title: Definition:Mixed Decimal
snippet: A mixed decimal is a number consisting of a non-zero integer together with a decimal fraction.

title: Definition:Mixed Fraction/Also known as
snippet: == Mixed Fraction: Also known as == A mixed fraction is also known as a mixed number. The terms are interchangeable.

title: Definition:Mixed Strategy
snippet: Let $G$ be a game. A mixed strategy for $G$ is a combination of different strategies for subsequent plays of $G$ which are played with particular frequencies.

title: Definition:Mixed Tensor
snippet: Let $V$ and $V^*$ be a vector space and its algebraic dual. Then a (mixed) tensor $F$ of type $\tuple {k, l}$ is a multilinear map such that: $F : \underbrace {V \times \ldots \times V}_{\text {$k$ times} } \times \underbrace { {V^*} \times \ldots \times {V^*} }_{\text {$l$ times} } \to \R$

title: Definition:Mixed Tensor/Also known as
snippet: == Tensor: Also known as == A mixed tensor of type $\tuple {k, l}$ is also known as a $k$-times covariant and $l$-times contravariant tensor. Some sources refer to a mixed tensor as merely a tensor.

title: Definition:Mnemonic
snippet: A mnemonic is a learning technique whose purpose is to make it easier to remember a fact. It works by making an association with an easily-remembered or commonly-known fact, and translating that fact into that which needs to be learned.

title: Definition:Mnemonic/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Mnemonic == The word mnemonic is of Greek origin, and pronounced without the first m, as ne-mon-nic. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Modal Class
snippet: Let $\mathsf C_1, \mathsf C_2, \cdots, \mathsf C_n$ be class intervals of data. Let $N_1, N_2, \ldots, N_n$ denote the frequency of each of $\mathsf C_1, \mathsf C_2, \cdots, \mathsf C_n$ respectively. The modal class is the class interval $\mathsf C_j$ for which $N_j$ is the greatest. The modal class is not necessarily unique for a given set of data.

title: Definition:Modal Logic
snippet: Modal logic is a branch of logic in which truth values are more complex than being merely true or false, and which distinguishes between different "modes" of truth. There are two operators in classical modal logic, defined for some proposition $P$ dependent on some world $w$: $(1): \quad$ Necessity, represented by $\nec$, defined by: $\nec P : \iff \forall w: \map P w$ $(2): \quad$ Possibility, represented by $\pos$, defined by: $\pos P: \iff \exists w: \map P w$ Modal logic may also have other operators, including: Temporal logic, which uses several operators including present and future…

title: Definition:Modal Operator
snippet: The modal operators are the operators in modal logic defined as follows:

title: Definition:Modal Operator/Necessity
snippet: The necessity operator $\nec$ is the unary modal operator defined for some proposition $P$ dependent on some world $w$: $\nec P : \iff \forall w: \map P w$

title: Definition:Modal Operator/Possibility
snippet: The possibility operator $\pos$ is the unary modal operator defined for some proposition $P$ dependent on some world $w$: $\pos P : \iff \exists w: \map P w$

title: Definition:Modal Proposition
snippet: A modal proposition is a statement in modal logic: It is possible that $A$ is true.

title: Definition:Mode
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of quantitative data. The mode of $S$ is the element of $S$ which occurs most often in $S$. If there is more than one such element of $S$ which occurs equally most often, it is then understood that each of these is a mode. If there is no element of $S$ which occurs more often (in the extreme case, all elements are equal) then $S$ has no mode.

title: Definition:Mode of Continuous Random Variable
snippet: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable on a probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $X$ have probability density function $f_X$. We call $M$ a mode of $X$ if $f_X$ attains its (global) maximum at $M$. Category:Definitions/Probability Theory Category:Definitions/Modes

title: Definition:Model
snippet: Logic: Model (Logic) Model (Predicate Logic) Applied Mathematics: Mathematical Model

title: Definition:Model (Boolean Interpretations)
snippet: Let $\LL_0$ be the language of propositional logic. Let $v: \LL_0 \to \set {\T, \F}$ be a boolean interpretation of $\LL_0$. Then $v$ models a WFF $\phi$ : $\map v \phi = \T$ and this relationship is denoted as: $v \models_{\mathrm {BI} } \phi$ When pertaining to a collection of WFFs $\FF$, one says $v$ models $\FF$ : $\forall \phi \in \FF: v \models_{\mathrm {BI} } \phi$ that is, it models all elements of $\FF$. This can be expressed symbolically as: $v \models_{\mathrm {BI}} \FF$

title: Definition:Model (Boolean Interpretations)/Also denoted as
snippet: == Model: Also denoted as == Often, when the formal semantics of a model is clear to be $\mathrm {BI}$, the formal semantics of boolean interpretations, the subscript is omitted, yielding: $v \models \phi$

title: Definition:Model (Logic)
snippet: Let $\mathscr M$ be a formal semantics for a logical language $\LL$. Let $\MM$ be a structure of $\mathscr M$.

title: Definition:Model (Logic)/Also known as
snippet: == Model: Also known as == If $\MM$ is a model of $\phi$, respectively $\FF$, one sometimes says that $\MM$ models $\phi$, respectively $\FF$.

title: Definition:Model (Logic)/Logical Formula
snippet: Let $\mathscr M$ be a formal semantics for a logical language $\LL$. Let $\MM$ be a structure of $\mathscr M$. Let $\phi$ be a logical formula of $\LL$. Then $\MM$ is a model of $\phi$ : $\MM \models_{\mathscr M} \phi$ that is, $\phi$ is valid in $\MM$. Category:Definitions/Model Theory Category:Definitions/Formal Semantics

title: Definition:Model (Logic)/Set of Logical Formulas
snippet: Let $\mathscr M$ be a formal semantics for a logical language $\LL$. Let $\MM$ be a structure of $\mathscr M$. Let $\FF$ be a set of logical formulas of $\LL$. Then $\MM$ is a model of $\FF$ : $\MM \models_{\mathscr M} \phi$ for every $\phi \in \FF$ that is, it is a model of every logical formula $\phi \in \FF$.

title: Definition:Model (Predicate Logic)
snippet: Let $\LL_1$ be the language of predicate logic. Let $\AA$ be a structure for predicate logic. Then $\AA$ models a sentence $\mathbf A$ : $\map {\operatorname{val}_\AA} {\mathbf A} = \T$ where $\map {\operatorname{val}_\AA} {\mathbf A}$ denotes the value of $\mathbf A$ in $\AA$. This relationship is denoted: $\AA \models_{\mathrm{PL} } \mathbf A$ When pertaining to a collection of sentences $\FF$, one says $\AA$ models $\FF$ : $\forall \mathbf A \in \FF: \AA \models_{\mathrm{PL} } \mathbf A$ that is, it models all elements of $\FF$.

title: Definition:Model Theory
snippet: Model theory is a sub-branch of mathematical logic which studies mathematical structures by means of formal semantics for formal languages.

title: Definition:Model Theory/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Model Theory == Historically, the greatest amount of research in model theory has focused on model theory for predicate logic. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Model Theory for Predicate Logic
snippet: Model theory for predicate logic is the sub-branch of model theory that focuses on predicate logic. In particular, the formal semantics of structures for predicate logic is studied.

title: Definition:Model of Class-Set Theory
snippet: Let $V$ be a collection of objects. Then $V$ is a model of class-set theory it satisfies the axioms of Von Neumann-Bernays-Gödel set theory. Thus: The elements of $V$ are then known as sets The subcollections of $V$ are known as classes.

title: Definition:Model of Rational Choice
snippet: A model of rational choice for a player in a game consists of: $(1): \quad$ A set $A$ of moves from which the player may choose $(2): \quad$ A set $C$ of consequences of each of those moves $(3): \quad$ A consequence function $g: A \to C$ which maps a consequence to each action $(4): \quad$ A preference relation $\succsim$, which is a total ordering on $C$.

title: Definition:Modification of Stochastic Process
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\struct {E, \mathcal E}$ be a measurable space. Let $\sequence {X_i}_{i \in I}$ and $\sequence {\widetilde X_i}_{i \in I}$ be $E$-valued stochastic processes. We say that $\sequence {\widetilde X_i}_{i \in I}$ is a modification of $\sequence {X_i}_{i \in I}$ : $\widetilde X_i = X_i$ almost surely for each $i \in I$.

title: Definition:Modified Bessel Function
snippet: The modified Bessel functions are solutions to Bessel's modified equation: $x^2 \dfrac {\d^2 y} {\d x^2} + x \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} - \paren {x^2 + n^2} y = 0$ These solutions have two main classes: the modified Bessel functions of the first kind $I_n$ and: the modified Bessel functions of the second kind $K_n$.

title: Definition:Modified Bessel Function/First Kind
snippet: A modified Bessel function of the first kind of order $n$ is a modified Bessel function which is non-singular at the origin. It is usually denoted $\map {I_n} x$, where $x$ is the dependent variable of the instance of Bessel's modified equation to which $\map {I_n} x$ forms a solution.

title: Definition:Modified Bessel Function/Order
snippet: Consider Bessel's modified equation: $x^2 \dfrac {\d^2 y} {\d x^2} + x \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} - \paren {x^2 + n^2} y = 0$ Let: $\map {I_n} x$ denote the modified Bessel function of the first kind $\map {K_n} x$ denote the modified Bessel function of the second kind be the solutions of Bessel's modified equation as defined. The parameter $n$ is known as the order of the modified Bessel function. Category:Definitions/Modified Bessel Functions

title: Definition:Modified Bessel Function/Second Kind
snippet: A modified Bessel function of the second kind of order $n$ is a modified Bessel function which is singular at the origin. It is usually denoted $\map {K_n} x$, where $x$ is the dependent variable of the instance of Bessel's modified equation to which $\map {K_n} x$ forms a solution.

title: Definition:Modified Fort Space
snippet: Let $N$ be an infinite set. Let $\set a$ and $\set b$ be singleton sets such that $a \ne b$ and $a, b \notin N$. Let $S = N \cup \set a \cup \set b$. Let $\tau_{a, b}$ be the set of subsets of $S$ defined as: $\tau_{a, b} = \set {H \subseteq N} \cup \set {H \subseteq S: \paren {a \in H \lor b \in H} \land N \setminus H \text { is finite} }$ That is, a subset $H$ of $S$ is in $\tau_{a, b}$ either of the following hold: Then $\tau_{a, b}$ is a modified Fort topology on $a$ and $b$, and the topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau_{a, b} }$ is a modified Fort space.

title: Definition:Modified Kaprekar Mapping
snippet: The modified Kaprekar mapping is the arithmetic function $K: \Z_{>0} \to \Z_{>0}$ defined on the positive integers as follows: Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be expressed in some number base $b$ (where $b$ is usually $10$). Let $n'$ be the positive integer created by: arranging the digits of $n$ into descending order of size then: exchanging the last two digits. Let $n$ be the positive integer created by: arranging the digits of $n$ into ascending order of size then: exchanging the first two digits.

title: Definition:Modified Kaprekar Mapping/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Modified Kaprekar Mapping == The modified Kaprekar mapping is reported by in his $1997$ work to appear in volume $22$ on page $34$ in an article authored by , but this has not been corroborated.

title: Definition:Modified Kaprekar Process
snippet: The modified Kaprekar process is the repeated application of the modified Kaprekar mapping to a given positive integer.

title: Definition:Modified Kaprekar Process/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Modified Kaprekar Process == The modified Kaprekar process is reported by in his $1997$ work to appear in volume $22$ on page $34$ in an article authored by , but this has not been corroborated.

title: Definition:Modified Perfect Faro Shuffle
snippet: A modified perfect Faro shuffle is a shuffle performed on a deck of cards $D$ of size $2 n$. Cut $D$ into $2$ piles $D_1$ (the top half) and $D_2$ (the bottom half) of exactly $n$ cards each. The shuffled deck $D'$ is assembled by alternating the cards in $D$: The cards in positions $2, 4, 6, \ldots, 2 n$ of $D'$ are to be occupied by the cards $1, 2, \ldots, n$ of $D_1$ in the same order The cards in positions $1, 3, 5, \ldots, 2 n - 1$ of $D'$ are to be occupied by the cards $1, 2, \ldots, n$ of $D_2$ in the same order.

title: Definition:Modular Ideal of Algebra
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $\struct {A, \ast}$ be an $R$-algebra. Let $\struct {J, \ast}$ be a ideal of $\struct {A, \ast}$. We say that $J$ is a modular ideal of $\struct {A, \ast}$ : there exists $u \in A$ such that: $a - a u \in J$ and $a - u a \in J$ for each $a \in A$.

title: Definition:Module Automorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {G, +_G, \circ}_R$ be an $R$-module. Let $\phi: G \to G$ be a module isomorphism to itself. Then $\phi$ is a module automorphism.

title: Definition:Module Defined by Ring Homomorphism
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be a rings. Let $f: A \to B$ be a ring homomorphism.

title: Definition:Module Direct Product/Finite Case
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $\struct {M_1, +_1, \circ_1}_R, \struct {M_2, +_2, \circ_2}_R, \ldots, \struct {M_n, +_n, \circ_n}_R$ be $R$-modules. Let: $\ds M = \prod_{k \mathop = 1}^n M_k$ be the cartesian product of $M_1$ to $M_n$. Let: $+$ be the operation induced on $M$ by the operations $+_1, +_2, \ldots, +_n$ on $M_1, M_2, \ldots, M_n$ $\circ$ be defined as $\lambda \circ \tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} = \tuple {\lambda \circ_1 x_1, \lambda \circ_2 x_2, \ldots, \lambda \circ_n x_n}$ The module $\struct {M, +, \circ}_R$ is called the (external) direct product of $M_1$ to $M_n$.

title: Definition:Module Direct Product/General Case
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $\family {\struct {M_i, +_i, \circ_i} }_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a family of $R$-modules. Let: $\ds M = \prod_{i \mathop \in I} M_i$ be the cartesian product of these modules. The operation $+$ induced on $M$ by $\family {+_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ is the operation defined by: $\family {a_i}_{i \mathop \in I} + \family {b_i}_{i \mathop \in I} = \family {a_i +_i b_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ That is, the additive group of the module $M$ is the direct product of the groups $\family {\struct {M_i, +_i} }_{i \mathop \in I}$.

title: Definition:Module Endomorphism
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $M$ be an $R$-module. A module endomorphism of $M$ is a module homomorphism from $M$ to itself.

title: Definition:Module Structure of Algebra over Ring
snippet: Definition:Module Defined by Ring Homomorphism Definition:Underlying Module of Algebra

title: Definition:Module Structure of Polynomial Ring
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $R \sqbrk X$ be a polynomial ring in one variable $X$ over $R$. The $R$-module structure on $R \sqbrk X$ is the module structure as an algebra over $R$.

title: Definition:Module Structure of Ring
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Then $R$ as an $R$-module is the $R$-module $R$ with ring action: $R\times R \to R$ equal to the ring product of $R$.

title: Definition:Module Theory
snippet: Module theory is the branch of abstract algebra which studies modules.

title: Definition:Module of All Mappings
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ be a ring. Let $\struct {M, +_M, \ast}_R$ be an $R$-module. Let $S$ be a set. Let $M^S$ be the set of all mappings from $S$ to $M$. Let: $+$ be the operation induced on $M^S$ by $+_M$ $\forall \lambda \in R: \forall f \in M^S: \forall x \in S: \map {\paren {\lambda \ast f} } x = \lambda \ast \paren {\map f x}$ Then $\struct {M^S, +, \ast}_R$ is the module of all mappings from $S$ to $M$.

title: Definition:Module on Cartesian Product
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ be a ring. Let $n \in \N_{>0}$. Let $+: R^n \times R^n \to R^n$ be defined as: $\tuple {\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n} + \tuple {\beta_1, \ldots, \beta_n} = \tuple {\alpha_1 +_R \beta_1, \ldots, \alpha_n +_R \beta_n}$ Let $\times: R \times R^n \to R^n$ be defined as: $\lambda \times \tuple {\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n} = \tuple {\lambda \times_R \alpha_1, \ldots, \lambda \times_R \alpha_n}$ Then $\struct {R^n, +, \times}_R$ is the $R$-module $R^n$.

title: Definition:Module on Cartesian Product/Special Case
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ be a ring. Let $+: R \times R \to R$ be defined as: $\alpha + \beta = \alpha +_R \beta$ Let $\times: R \times R \to R$ be defined as: $\lambda \times \alpha = \lambda \times_R \alpha$ Then $\struct {R, +, \times}_R$ is the $R$-module $R$.

title: Definition:Module over Group
snippet: Let $\struct {V, +, \cdot}$ be a vector space over a field $\struct {F, +_F, \times_F}$. Let $G$ be a group. Let $\phi : G \times V \to V$ be a linear group action of $G$ on $V$, either: a left linear group action: $\phi : G \times V \to V$ or a right linear group action: $\phi : V \times G \to V$ Then $\struct {V, \phi}$ is called a module over $G$, either a left module or a right module respectively.

title: Definition:Module over Group/Also known as
snippet: == Module over Group: Also known as == A module over $G$, where $G$ is a group, is also known as a $G$-module.

title: Definition:Module over Group/Left
snippet: Let $\struct {V, +, \cdot}$ be a vector space over a field $\struct {F, +_F, \times_F}$. Let $G$ be a group. Let $\phi : G \times V \to V$ be a left linear group action of $G$ on $V$. Then $\struct {V, \phi}$ is called a left module over $G$.

title: Definition:Module over Group/Right
snippet: Let $\struct {V, +, \cdot}$ be a vector space over a field $\struct {F, +_F, \times_F}$. Let $G$ be a group. Let $\phi : V \times G \to V$ be a right linear group action of $G$ on $V$. Then $\struct {V, \phi}$ is called a right module over $G$.

title: Definition:Module over Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ be a ring. Let $\struct {G, +_G}$ be an abelian group. A module over $R$ is an $R$-algebraic structure $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_R$ with one operation $\ast$ which is either a left module or a right module, depending upon whether $\ast$ is defined as: $\ast: R \times G \to G$ or: $\ast: G \times R \to G$ respectively. As follows:

title: Definition:Module over Ring/Also defined as
snippet: == Module over Ring: Also defined as == Sources which deal only with rings with unity often define a module as what on is called a unitary module. Sometimes no distinction is made between the module and the associated ring representation. The word module can also be seen in some older works to mean vector magnitude or vector length. Category:Definitions/Modules over Rings

title: Definition:Module over Ring/Also known as
snippet: == Module over Ring: Also known as == A module over a ring $R$ can, and on often will, also be referred to as an $R$-module.

title: Definition:Module over Ring/Left and Right Modules
snippet: == Left Modules and Right Modules == In the case where the scalar ring is a commutative ring, the difference between a left module and a right module is little more than a notational difference. See: Left Module over Commutative Ring induces Right Module Right Module over Commutative Ring induces Left Module. But this is not the case for a scalar ring that is not commutative.

title: Definition:Moduli Space
snippet: A moduli space is a set of all solutions to certain nonlinear differential equations.

title: Definition:Modulo Addition/Also denoted as
snippet: == Modulo Addition: Also denoted as == Although the operation of addition modulo $m$ is denoted by the symbol $+_m$, if there is no danger of confusion, the conventional addition symbol $+$ etc. is often used instead. The notation for addition of two residue classes modulo $m$ is not usually $\eqclass a m +_m \eqclass b m$. What is more normally seen is $a + b \pmod m$. Category:Definitions/Modulo Addition

title: Definition:Modulo Addition/Definition 1
snippet: Let $m \in \Z$ be an integer. Let $\Z_m$ be the set of integers modulo $m$: $\Z_m = \set {\eqclass 0 m, \eqclass 1 m, \ldots, \eqclass {m - 1} m}$ where $\eqclass x m$ is the residue class of $x$ modulo $m$. The operation of addition modulo $m$ is defined on $\Z_m$ as: $\eqclass a m +_m \eqclass b m = \eqclass {a + b} m$

title: Definition:Modulo Addition/Definition 2
snippet: Let $m \in \Z$ be an integer. Let $\Z_m$ be the set of integers modulo $m$: $\Z_m = \set {0, 1, \ldots, m - 1}$ The operation of addition modulo $m$ is defined on $\Z_m$ as: $\forall a, b \in \Z_m: a +_m b$ equals the remainder after $a + b$ has been divided by $m$

title: Definition:Modulo Addition/Definition 3
snippet: Let $m \in \Z$ be an integer. Let $\Z_m$ be the set of integers modulo $m$: $\Z_m = \set {0, 1, \ldots, m - 1}$ The operation of addition modulo $m$ is defined on $\Z_m$ as: $a +_m b := a + b - k m$ where $k$ is the largest integer such that $k m \le a + b$.

title: Definition:Modulo Arithmetic
snippet: Modulo arithmetic is the branch of abstract algebra which studies the residue class of integers under a modulus. As such it can also be considered to be a branch of number theory.

title: Definition:Modulo Arithmetic/Also known as
snippet: == Modulo Arithmetic: Also known as == The field of modulo arithmetic is known more correctly as modular arithmetic, but modulo arithmetic is more commonly seen. When the topic is introduced to young children in elementary school, the topic is often referred to as clock arithmetic.

title: Definition:Modulo Division
snippet: Let $m \in \Z$ be an integer. Let $\Z_m$ be the set of integers modulo $m$: $\Z_m = \set {0, 1, \ldots, m - 1}$ The operation of division modulo $m$ is defined on $\Z_m$ as: $a \div_m b$ equals the integer $q \in \Z_m$ such that $b \times_m q \equiv a \pmod m$ and is possible only if $q$ is unique modulo $m$. This happens $a$ and $m$ are coprime.

title: Definition:Modulo Division/Divisor
snippet: Let $m \in \Z$ be an integer. Let $\Z_m$ be the set of integers modulo $m$: $\Z_m = \set {0, 1, \ldots, m - 1}$ For all $a, b \in \Z_m$, let $a \div_m b$ denote the operation of division modulo $m$: $a \div_m b$ equals the integer $q \in \Z_m$ such that $b \times_m q \equiv a \pmod m$ The integers $b$ and $q$ are divisors of $a$ modulo $m$.

title: Definition:Modulo Division/Polynomials
snippet: Let $\map f x$ and $\map g x$ be integral polynomials. The operation of polynomial division modulo $m$ is defined as: $\map f x \div_m \map g x$ equals the integral polynomial $\map h x$ such that: $\map g x \times_m \map h x \equiv \map f x \pmod m$ where: $m \in \Z$ is an integer $\equiv$ means that the respective coefficients are congruent modulo $m$ provided such a polynomial exists.

title: Definition:Modulo Multiplication/Also denoted as
snippet: == Modulo Multiplication: Also denoted as == Although the operation of multiplication modulo $m$ is denoted by the symbol $\times_m$, if there is no danger of confusion, the conventional multiplication symbols $\times, \cdot$ etc. are often used instead. The notation for multiplication of two integers modulo $m$ is not usually $\eqclass a m \times_m \eqclass b m$. What is more normally seen is $a b \pmod m$. Category:Definitions/Modulo Multiplication

title: Definition:Modulo Multiplication/Definition 1
snippet: Let $m \in \Z$ be an integer. Let $\Z_m$ be the set of integers modulo $m$: $\Z_m = \set {\eqclass 0 m, \eqclass 1 m, \ldots, \eqclass {m - 1} m}$ where $\eqclass x m$ is the residue class of $x$ modulo $m$. The operation of multiplication modulo $m$ is defined on $\Z_m$ as: $\eqclass a m \times_m \eqclass b m = \eqclass {a b} m$

title: Definition:Modulo Multiplication/Definition 2
snippet: Let $m \in \Z$ be an integer. Let $\Z_m$ be the set of integers modulo $m$: $\Z_m = \set {0, 1, \ldots, m - 1}$ The operation of multiplication modulo $m$ is defined on $\Z_m$ as: $a \times_m b$ equals the remainder after $a b$ has been divided by $m$.

title: Definition:Modulo Multiplication/Definition 3
snippet: Let $m \in \Z$ be an integer. Let $\Z_m$ be the set of integers modulo $m$: $\Z_m = \set {0, 1, \ldots, m - 1}$ The operation of multiplication modulo $m$ is defined on $\Z_m$ as: $a \times_m b := a b - k m$ where $k$ is the largest integer such that $k m \le a b$.

title: Definition:Modulo Operation
snippet: Let $x, y \in \R$ be real numbers. Then the modulo operation is defined and denoted as: $x \bmod y := \begin{cases} x - y \floor {\dfrac x y} & : y \ne 0 \\ x & : y = 0 \end{cases}$ where $\floor {\, \cdot \,}$ denotes the floor function.

title: Definition:Modulo Operation/Modulo One
snippet: Let $x, y \in \R$ be real numbers. Let the modulo operation $\bmod$ be defined as: $x \bmod y := \begin{cases} x - y \floor {\dfrac x y} & : y \ne 0 \\ x & : y = 0 \end{cases}$ Then: $x \bmod 1 = x - \floor x$ from which it follows directly that: $x = \floor x + \paren {x \bmod 1}$

title: Definition:Modulo Operation/Modulo Zero
snippet: Let $x, y \in \R$ be real numbers. Let the modulo operation $\bmod$ be defined as: $x \bmod y := \begin {cases} x - y \floor {\dfrac x y} & : y \ne 0 \\ x & : y = 0 \end {cases}$ Then: $\forall x \in \R: x \bmod 0 = x$ This can be considered as a special case of the modulo operation, but it is interesting to note that most of the results concerning the modulo operation still hold.

title: Definition:Modulo Polynomial Division/Divisor
snippet: Let $\map f x$ and $\map g x$ be integral polynomials. Let $\map f x \div_m \map g x$ denote the operation of polynomial division modulo $m$: $\map f x \div_m \map g x$ equals the integral polynomial $\map h x$ such that: $\map g x \times_m \map h x \equiv \map f x \pmod m$ The polynomials $\map g x$ and $\map h x$ are (polynomial) divisors of $\map f x$ modulo $m$.

title: Definition:Modulo Subtraction
snippet: Let $m \in \Z$ be an integer. Let $\Z_m$ be the set of integers modulo $m$: $\Z_m = \set {\eqclass 0 m, \eqclass 1 m, \ldots, \eqclass {m - 1} m}$ where $\eqclass x m$ is the residue class of $x$ modulo $m$. The operation of subtraction modulo $m$ is defined on $\Z_m$ as: $\eqclass a m -_m \eqclass b m = \eqclass {a - b} m$

title: Definition:Modulo Subtraction/Also denoted as
snippet: == Modulo Subtraction: Also denoted as == Although the operation of subtraction modulo $m$ is denoted by the symbol $-_m$, if there is no danger of confusion, the conventional subtraction symbol $-$ is often used instead. The notation for subtraction of two integers modulo $m$ is not usually $\eqclass a m -_m \eqclass b m$. What is more normally seen is $a - b \pmod m$.

title: Definition:Modulus
snippet: Algebra and Real Analysis: The absolute value $\size x$ of a real number $x$. Modulus of a Multiindex: The modulus of a multiindex $k = \sequence {k_j}_{j \mathop \in J}$ is defined as $\ds \size k = \sum_{j \mathop \in J} k_j$ Complex Analysis: Modulus of Complex Number: the length of a complex number when drawn as a vector on the complex plane. Modulus of Complex-Valued Function: The real-valued function $\size f$ obtained by taking the (complex) modulus of all the values of the complex-valued function $f$.

title: Definition:Modulus/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Modulus == The plural of modulus is moduli. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Modulus (Geometric Function Theory)
snippet: In geometric function theory, the term modulus is used to denote certain conformal invariants of configurations or curve families. More precisely, the modulus of a curve family $\Gamma$ is the reciprocal of its extremal length: $\mod \Gamma := \dfrac 1 {\map \lambda \Gamma}$

title: Definition:Modulus of Change of Base of Logarithm
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be strictly positive real numbers such that $a \ne 1 \ne b$. Let $x$ be a strictly positive real number. Let $\log_a x$ denote the logarithm base $a$ of $x$. Consider the operation Change of Base of Logarithm where by $\log_a x$ is converted to $\log_b x$: $\log_a x = \log_a b \log_b x$ The coefficient $\log_a b$ is known as the modulus of the operation.

title: Definition:Modulus of Complex-Valued Function
snippet: Let $f: S \to \C$ be a complex-valued function. Then the (complex) modulus of $f$ is written $\cmod f : S \to \R$ and is the real-valued function defined as: $\forall z \in S: \map {\cmod f} z = \cmod {\map f z}$

title: Definition:Modulus of Element of C*-Algebra
snippet: Let $\struct {A, \ast, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a $\text C^\ast$-algebra. Let $a \in A$. From Product of Element of C*-Algebra with its Star is Positive, $a^\ast a$ is positive. Hence we can consider the square root $\paren {a^\ast a}^{1/2}$. We define the modulus $\cmod a$ of $a$ by: $\cmod a = \paren {a^\ast a}^{1/2}$

title: Definition:Mole
snippet: == Mole == The mole is the SI base unit of amount of substance. It is defined as exactly Avogadro's number of particles, that is, $6 \cdotp 02214 076 \times 10^{23}$. The specific type of particle under discussion must be specified. They are usually the elementary units of a particular substance under discussion. However, as long as the particles are more-or-less identical, there is no specific limitation to what a mole may be applied to. A beloved teacher of chemistry at a certain editor's school, when covering the subject, would habitually spend some time discussing a mole of cricket balls.

title: Definition:Mole/Also known as
snippet: == Mole: Also known as == Terms formerly used for a mole include: gram-molecule (for a substance whose elementary units are molecules) gram-atom (for a substance whose elementary units are atoms)

title: Definition:Mole/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Mole == The definition of the mole was adopted in November $2018$ as one of the seven SI base units. The previous definition was the number of atoms in $12$ grams of carbon-$12$. The original definition was as the mass in grams of a substance equal to its molecular weight, with atoms of hydrogen taken to be $1$. The definition evolved, via a definition based upon oxygen-$16$, to the carbon-$12$ definition, which was the standard until $2018$. At that point, the mole was defined to be exactly Avogadro's number of particles.

title: Definition:Molecular Weight
snippet: Let $S$ be a substance. Let $S$ be homogeneous. The molecular weight of $S$ is defined as: $W_S = m_S \times \dfrac {12} {m_C}$ where: $m_S$ is the (arithmetic) mean mass of one molecule of $S$ $m_C$ is the mass of one molecule of carbon-12. It is understood that the atoms that compose the molecules of $S$ may be of different isotopes according to their relative natural concentrations at the source of wherever $S$ came from. Hence the use of the (arithmetic) mean mass in the definition of $m_S$.

title: Definition:Molecular Weight/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Molecular Weight == The term molecular weight is a misnomer, as what is being defined here is a mass. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Molecule
snippet: A molecule is an arrangement of atoms, possibly of different elements, which are held together in a configuration which requires the application of external energy to break apart. The molecule is the basic unit of a chemical compound.

title: Definition:Moment (Probability Theory)
snippet: Let $X$ be a random variable on some probability space. Let $a$ be a real number. Then the $n$th moment of $X$ about $a$, usually denoted $\map {\mu_n} a$, is defined as: $\map {\mu_n} a = \expect {\paren {X - a}^n}$ where $\expect X$ denotes the expectation of $X$.

title: Definition:Moment (Probability Theory)/Discrete
snippet: Let $X$ be a discrete random variable. Then the $n$th moment of $X$ is denoted $\mu'_n$ and defined as: $\mu'_n = \expect {X^n}$ where $\expect {\, \cdot \,}$ denotes the expectation function. That is: $\mu'_n = \ds \sum_{x \mathop \in \Omega_X} x^n \map {p_X} x$ whenever this sum converges absolutely. It can be seen from its definition that the expectation of a discrete random variable is its first moment. Also see the relation between the variance of a discrete random variable and its second moment.

title: Definition:Moment Generating Function
snippet: Let $X$ be a random variable. Then the moment generating function of $X$ is defined and denoted as: $\map {M_X} t = \expect {e^{t X} }$ for all $t$ such that this expectation exists.

title: Definition:Moment Generating Function/Also known as
snippet: == Moment Generating Function: Also known as == The term moment generating function is commonly abbreviated to MGF or M.G.F. Category:Definitions/Moment Generating Functions

title: Definition:Moment of Couple
snippet: Let $C$ be a couple composed of the forces $\mathbf F_1$ and $\mathbf F_2$. The moment of $C$ is a vector given by: $\mathbf M = \mathbf F_1 \times \mathbf d$ where: $\mathbf F_1$ is one of the forces that compose $C$ $\mathbf d$ is the displacement from $\mathbf F_1$ to $\mathbf F_2$. Hence: the line of action of $\mathbf M$ is perpendicular to the plane containing $\mathbf F_1$ and $\mathbf F_2$ the magnitude of $\mathbf M$ is equal to $F d$, where: $F$ is the magnitude of $\mathbf F_1$ and $\mathbf F_2$ $d$ is the magnitude of $\mathbf d$.

title: Definition:Moment of Inertia
snippet: Let $B$ be a rigid body which is rotating in space about some axis $\LL$. The moment of inertia of $B$ about $\LL$ is defined as follows:

title: Definition:Moment of Inertia/Continuous
snippet: Let $B$ be a rigid body which is rotating in space about some axis $\LL$. Let each point in $B$ have: a position vector $\mathbf r$ a given frame of reference. a density $\map \rho {\mathbf r}$ a perpendicular distance $\map p {\mathbf r}$ from $\LL$ The moment of inertia of $B$ about $\LL$ is given by: $I := \ds \int_B \paren {\map p {\mathbf r} }^2 \map \rho {\mathbf r} \rd V$ where $\d V$ is an infinitesimal volume element of $B$.

title: Definition:Moment of Inertia/Dimension
snippet: The dimension of measurement of moment of inertia is $\mathsf {M L}^2$. Category:Definitions/Moments of Inertia Category:Definitions/Dimensions of Measurement

title: Definition:Moment of Inertia/Discrete
snippet: Let $B$ be a rigid body which is rotating in space about some axis $\LL$. Let $B$ be composed of a countable number of particles $P_1, P_2, \ldots$ such that: each $P_i$ has mass $m_i$ each $P_i$ has perpendicular distance $r_i$ from $\LL$. The moment of inertia of $B$ about $\LL$ is given by: $I := \ds \sum m_i {r_i}^2$

title: Definition:Moment of Mass
snippet: Let $B$ be a particle Let $\PP$ be a point, a straight line or a plane. The moment of mass of $B$ $\PP$ is defined as the mass of $B$ multiplied by the distance from $B$ to $\PP$.

title: Definition:Momentum/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Momentum == The plural of momentum is momenta.

title: Definition:Money
snippet: Money is a measure of purchasing power. Category:Definitions/Money Category:Definitions/Economics

title: Definition:Monic Polynomial
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity whose unity is $1_R$. Let $f \in R \sqbrk x$ be a polynomial in one variable over $R$. Then $f$ is monic $f$ is nonzero and its leading coefficient is $1_R$. Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring with unity whose unity is $1_R$. Let $\struct {S, +, \circ}$ be a subring of $R$. Let $\ds f = \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^n a_k \circ x^k$ be a polynomial in $x$ over $S$. Then $f$ is a monic polynomial its leading coefficient $a_n$ is $1_R$.

title: Definition:Monic Polynomial/Polynomial Form
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity $1_R$. Let $f = a_0 + a_1 X + \cdots + a_{r-1} X^{r-1} + a_r X^r$ be a polynomial from in the single indeterminate $X$ over $R$. Then $f$ is monic if the leading coefficient of $f$ is $1_R$. Category:Definitions/Monic Polynomials

title: Definition:Monic Polynomial/Sequence
snippet: Let $f = \sequence {a_k} = \tuple {a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots}$ be a polynomial over a field $F$. Then $f$ is a monic polynomial its leading coefficient $a_n$ is $1$.

title: Definition:Mono-Alphabetic Substitution Cipher
snippet: A mono-alphabetic substitution cipher is a substitution cipher in which each individual letter is replaced by a letter, or string of letters, from a single alphabet.

title: Definition:Mono-Alphabetic Substitution Cipher/Also known as
snippet: == Mono-Alphabetic Substitution Cipher: Also known as == The term mono-alphabetic substitution cipher can also be presented without the hyphen: monoalphabetic substitution cipher.

title: Definition:Monochromatic Graph
snippet: A monochromatic graph is a colored graph (either vertex-colored or edge-colored, depending on the context) in which each of the vertices or edges is assigned the same color. Category:Definitions/Graph Colorings Category:Definitions/Ramsey Theory

title: Definition:Monoid
snippet: A monoid is a semigroup with an identity element.

title: Definition:Monoid/Also known as
snippet: == Monoid: Also known as == Some treatments of group theory and abstract algebra do not introduce the term monoid, but simply discuss semigroups which happen to have an identity element. Some sources present the monoid as $\struct {S, \circ, e_S}$ in order to place emphasis on the identity element, but this approach is not endorsed on as it complicates notation to little advantage. Category:Definitions/Monoids

title: Definition:Monoid Automorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a monoid. Let $\phi: S \to S$ be a (monoid) isomorphism from $S$ to itself. Then $\phi$ is a monoid automorphism.

title: Definition:Monoid Category
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a monoid with identity $e_S$. One can interpret $\struct {S, \circ}$ as being a category, with: {{DefineCategory | ob = Only one, say $*$ | mor = $a: * \to *$, for all $a \in S$ | comp = $a \circ b: * \to *$ is defined using the operation $\circ$ of the monoid $S$ | id = $\operatorname{id}_* := e_S: * \to *$ }} The category that so arises is called a monoid category.

title: Definition:Monoid Endomorphism
snippet: Let $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ be a monoid. Let $\phi: S \to S$ be a (monoid) homomorphism from $S$ to itself. Then $\phi$ is a monoid endomorphism.

title: Definition:Monoid Epimorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ and $\struct {T, *}$ be monoids. Let $\phi: S \to T$ be a (monoid) homomorphism. Then $\phi$ is a monoid epimorphism $\phi$ is a surjection.

title: Definition:Monoid Homomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ and $\struct {T, *}$ be monoids. Let $\phi: S \to T$ be a mapping such that $\circ$ has the morphism property under $\phi$. That is, $\forall a, b \in S$: $\map \phi {a \circ b} = \map \phi a * \map \phi b$ Suppose further that $\phi$ preserves identities, that is: $\map \phi {e_S} = e_T$ Then $\phi: \struct {S, \circ} \to \struct {T, *}$ is a monoid homomorphism.

title: Definition:Monoid Ring
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $\struct {G, *}$ be a monoid. Let $R^{\paren G}$ be the free $R$-module on $G$. Let $\set {e_g: g \in G}$ be its canonical basis. By Multilinear Mapping from Free Modules is Determined by Bases, there exists a unique bilinear map: $\circ: R^{\paren G} \times R^{\paren G} \to R^{\paren G}$ which satisfies: $e_g \circ e_h = e_{g \mathop * h}$ Then $R \sqbrk G = \struct {R^{\paren G}, +, \circ}$ is called the monoid ring of $G$ over $R$.

title: Definition:Monoid Ring/Canonical Mapping
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $\struct {G, *}$ be a monoid with identity element $1$. Let $R \sqbrk G$ be the monoid ring of $G$ over $R$. Let $e_1$ be the canonical basis element. The canonical mapping to $R \sqbrk G$ is the mapping $R \to R \sqbrk G$ which sends $r$ to $r * e_1$.

title: Definition:Monomial/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Monomial == Because the word monomial derives ultimately from the late Latin word binomium (binomial), by changing the prefix bi (two in Latin), it should theoretically be mononomial. Monomial is a syncope by haplology of mononomial. The word [https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/mononomial mononomial] does exist in English: it means having a single name. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Monomial Matrix
snippet: A monomial matrix (of order $n$) is an $n \times n$ square matrix with: exactly one element in each row and column which is not $0$ $0$ elsewhere.

title: Definition:Monomial of Free Commutative Monoid
snippet: A monomial in the indexed set $\family {X_j: j \in J}$ is a possibly infinite product: $\ds \prod_{j \mathop \in J} X_j^{k_j}$ with integer exponents $k_j \ge 0$ such that $k_j = 0$ for all but finitely many $j$. Let $\mathbf X = \family {X_j}_{j \mathop \in J}$ and for a multiindex $k = \paren {k_j}_{j \mathop \in J}$ over $J$ define: $\ds \mathbf X^k = \prod_{j \mathop \in J} X_j^{k_j}$ Then a monomial is an object of the form $\mathbf X^k$, where $k$ is a multiindex.

title: Definition:Monomial of Free Commutative Monoid/Degree
snippet: The degree of a monomial is defined as: $\ds \sum_{j \mathop \in J} k_j$ that is, the modulus of the corresponding multiindex. Category:Definitions/Monomials

title: Definition:Monomial of Free Commutative Monoid/Multiplication
snippet: The set of monomials over $\family {X_j: j \in J}$ has multiplication $\circ$ defined by: $\ds \paren {\prod_{j \mathop \in J} X_j^{k_j} } \circ \paren {\prod_{j \mathop \in J} X_j^{k_j'} } = \paren {\prod_{j \mathop \in J} X_j^{k_j + k_j'} }$ which using multiindex addition notation reads: $\mathbf X^k \circ \mathbf X^{k'} = \mathbf X^{k + k'}$ Category:Definitions/Monomials

title: Definition:Monomial of Polynomial Ring
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity.

title: Definition:Monomial of Polynomial Ring/Multiple Variables
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $I$ be a set. Let $R \sqbrk {\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I} }$ be a polynomial ring in $I$ variables $\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$. Let $y \in R \sqbrk {\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I} }$. A monomial of $R \sqbrk {\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I} }$ is an element that is a product of variables; specifically:

title: Definition:Monomial of Polynomial Ring/Multiple Variables/Definition 1
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $I$ be a set. Let $R \sqbrk {\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I} }$ be a polynomial ring in $I$ variables $\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$. Let $y \in R \sqbrk {\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I} }$. The element $y$ is a monomial of $R \sqbrk {\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I} }$ there exists a mapping $a: I \to \N$ with finite support such that: $y = \ds \prod_{i \mathop \in I} X_i^{a_i}$ where: $\prod$ denotes the product with finite support over $I$ $X_i^{a_i}$ denotes the $a_i$th power of $X_i$.

title: Definition:Monomial of Polynomial Ring/Multiple Variables/Definition 2
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $I$ be a set. Let $R \sqbrk {\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I} }$ be a polynomial ring in $I$ variables $\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$. Let $y \in R \sqbrk {\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I} }$. The element $y$ is a monomial of $R \sqbrk {\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I} }$ there exists a finite set $S$ and a mapping $f: S \to \set {X_i : i \in I}$ such that it equals $y = \ds \prod_{s \mathop \in S} \map f s$ where $\prod$ denotes the product over the finite set $S$.

title: Definition:Monomial of Polynomial Ring/One Variable
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $R \sqbrk X$ be a polynomial ring over $R$ in one indeterminate $X$. A monomial of $R \sqbrk X$ is an element that is a power of $X$. Category:Definitions/Monomials

title: Definition:Monomino
snippet: A monomino is a $1$-omino: 100px That is, it is a polyomino consisting of exactly $1$ unit square.

title: Definition:Monomino/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Monomino == The word monomino is a back-formation from the word domino. The prefix mono- comes from ancient Greek meaning one, while -omino suffix derives from the term polyomino, which is in turn derived from domino. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Monomorphism
snippet: Monomorphism (Abstract Algebra) Monomorphism (Category Theory) Definition:Order Embedding, also known as an order monomorphism

title: Definition:Monomorphism/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Monomorphism == The word monomorphism comes from the Greek morphe (μορφή) meaning form or structure, with the prefix mono- meaning single. Thus monomorphism means single (similar) structure.

title: Definition:Monomorphism (Abstract Algebra)
snippet: A homomorphism which is an injection is descibed as monic, or called a monomorphism.

title: Definition:Monomorphism (Abstract Algebra)/Also known as
snippet: == Monomorphism: Also known as == A monomorphism may also be referred to as an embedding.

title: Definition:Monomorphism (Category Theory)
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. A monomorphism is a morphism $f \in \mathbf C_1$ such that: $f \circ g = f \circ h \implies g = h$ for all morphisms $g, h \in \mathbf C_1$ for which these compositions are defined. That is, a monomorphism is a morphism which is left cancellable. One writes $f: C \rightarrowtail D$ to denote that $f$ is a monomorphism.

title: Definition:Monotone
snippet: Mappings: Monotone (Order Theory): A mapping from one ordered set to another is monotone it is either increasing or decreasing. Monotone (Measure Theory): A mapping $f: \SS \to \R$ on an algebra of sets $\SS$ is monotone $A \subseteq B \iff \map f A \le \map f B$. Monotone class: A collection of subsets closed under countable intersections and unions. Monotone Galois connection In all cases, the sense is one of changing always in the same direction.

title: Definition:Monotone/Also known as
snippet: == Monotone: Also known as == Monotone is also seen rendered as monotonic.

title: Definition:Monotone (Measure Theory)
snippet: Let $\SS$ be an algebra of sets. Let $f: \SS \to \overline \R$ be an extended real-valued function, where $\overline \R$ denotes the set of extended real numbers. Then $f$ is defined as monotone or monotonic : $\forall A, B \in \SS: A \subseteq B \iff \map f A \le \map f B$ Category:Definitions/Monotone Category:Definitions/Set Systems

title: Definition:Monotone (Order Theory)/Mapping
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq_1}$ and $\struct {T, \preceq_2}$ be ordered sets. Let $\phi: \struct {S, \preceq_1} \to \struct {T, \preceq_2}$ be a mapping. Then $\phi$ is monotone it is either increasing or decreasing. Note that this definition also holds if $S = T$.

title: Definition:Monotone (Order Theory)/Real Function
snippet: This definition continues to hold when $S = T = \R$. Thus, let $f$ be a real function. Then $f$ is monotone it is either increasing or decreasing.

title: Definition:Monotone (Order Theory)/Sequence
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a totally ordered set. A sequence $\sequence {a_k}_{k \mathop \in A}$ of elements of $S$ is monotone it is either increasing or decreasing.

title: Definition:Monotone (Order Theory)/Sequence/Real Sequence
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $\R$. Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is monotone it is either increasing or decreasing.

title: Definition:Monotone Basis
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $\sequence {e_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a Schauder basis for $X$. We say that $\sequence {e_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is a monotone basis its basis constant is $1$.

title: Definition:Monotone Class
snippet: Let $X$ be a set, and let $\powerset X$ be its power set. Let $\MM \subseteq \powerset X$ be a collection of subsets of $X$. Then $\MM$ is said to be a monotone class (on $X$) for every countable, nonempty, index set $I$, it holds that: $\ds \family {A_i}_{i \mathop \in I} \in \MM \implies \bigcup_{i \mathop \in I} A_i \in \MM$ $\ds \family {A_i}_{i \mathop \in I} \in \MM \implies \bigcap_{i \mathop \in I} A_i \in \MM$ that is, $\MM$ is closed under countable unions and countable intersections.

title: Definition:Monotone Class Generated by Collection of Subsets
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\GG \subseteq \powerset X$ be a collection of subsets of $X$. Then the monotone class generated by $\GG$, $\map {\mathfrak m} \GG$, is the smallest monotone class on $X$ that contains $\GG$. That is, $\map {\mathfrak m} \GG$ is subject to: $(1): \quad \GG \subseteq \map {\mathfrak m} \GG$ $(2): \quad \GG \subseteq \MM \implies \map {\mathfrak m} \GG \subseteq \MM$ for any monotone class $\MM$ on $X$

title: Definition:Monotone Real Function/Also known as
snippet: == Monotone Real Function: Also known as == A monotone function can also be referred to as a monotonic function. Monotone is preferred on because it is shorter and has less syllables, and hence is more economical.

title: Definition:Monotone Sequence/Also known as
snippet: == Monotone Sequence: Also known as == A monotone sequence can also be called a monotonic sequence.

title: Definition:Monotone Sequence of Sets
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\SS \subseteq \powerset X$ be a collection of subsets of $X$. A monotone sequence of sets (in $\SS$) is a sequence $\sequence {A_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ in $\SS$, such that either: $\forall n \in \N: A_n \subseteq A_{n + 1}$ or: $\forall n \in \N: A_n \supseteq A_{n + 1}$ That is, such that $\sequence {A_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is either increasing or decreasing

title: Definition:Monotonicity
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq_1}$ and $\struct {T, \preceq_2}$ be ordered sets. Let $\phi: \struct {S, \preceq_1} \to \struct {T, \preceq_2}$ be a monotone mapping. Then whether $\phi$ is increasing or decreasing is known as the monotonicityof $\phi$. That is: if $\phi$ is such that $x \preceq_1 y \implies \map \phi x \preceq_2 \map \phi y$, then the monotonicity of $\phi$ is increasing if $\phi$ is such that $x \prec_1 y \implies \map \phi x \prec_2 \map \phi y$, then the monotonicity of $\phi$ is strictly increasing if $\phi$ is such that $x \preceq_1 y \implies \map \phi y \preceq_2 \map \phi…

title: Definition:Monster Model
snippet: Let $T$ be a complete $\LL$-theory. A monster model of $T$ whose cardinality $\kappa$ is infinite is a model of $T$ which is saturated and homogeneous. Category:Definitions/Model Theory for Predicate Logic

title: Definition:Monte Carlo Method
snippet: A Monte Carlo method is a technique in statistics for investigating mathematical properties by repeated experiments a large number of times. This is useful when an analytic solution is difficult to obtain.

title: Definition:Monte Carlo Method/Repeated Sampling
snippet: A Monte Carlo method is a method used to explore a probability distribution by repeated sampling.

title: Definition:Monte Carlo Method/Sampling Experiments
snippet: A Monte Carlo method is a solution to a problem by setting up an experiment, repeating it many times, and investigating the outcome.

title: Definition:Mood of Categorical Syllogism
snippet: The mood of a categorical syllogism is the sequence of the $3$ categorical statements $\mathbf A$, $\mathbf E$, $\mathbf I$ or $\mathbf O$ of which the categorical syllogism is comprised.

title: Definition:Moon
snippet: The moon is the single natural satellite of Earth.

title: Definition:Moon/Also known as
snippet: == Moon: Also known as == The moon is often called by its Latin name Luna, for various reasons: Poetic, see for example [http://www.azlyrics.com/lyrics/tompettyandtheheartbreakers/luna.html Luna] by In various scientific contexts, to distinguish it from the natural satellites of other planets, which are also referred to as moons. It can also be referred to just as Moon, but again this is rare outside of poetry. Category:Definitions/Moon

title: Definition:Moore-Penrose Conditions
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a matrix of order $m \times n$ over the complex numbers $\C$. The Moore-Penrose conditions are a set of criteria to determine whether a matrix $\mathbf X$ of order $n \times m$ is the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of $\mathbf A$: {{axiom | n = 3 | ml= \mathbf A \mathbf X | mo= = | mr= \paren {\mathbf A \mathbf X}^* }} {{axiom | n = 4 | ml= \mathbf X \mathbf A | mo= = | mr= \paren {\mathbf X \mathbf A}^* }} where $\mathbf A^*$ denotes the Hermitian conjugate of $\mathbf A$.

title: Definition:Moore-Penrose Pseudoinverse
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a matrix of order $m \times n$ over the complex numbers $\C$.

title: Definition:Moore-Penrose Pseudoinverse/Also known as
snippet: == Moore-Penrose Pseudoinverse: Also known as == A Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse can also be seen hyphenated: Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse. Some sources refer to it as a Moore-Penrose inverse. Some sources refer to it as just a pseudoinverse, or again hyphenated: pseudo-inverse

title: Definition:Moore-Penrose Pseudoinverse/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a matrix of order $m \times n$ where $m \ne n$ over the complex numbers $\C$. The Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of $\mathbf A$ is the unique $n \times m$ matrix $\mathbf A^+$ defined as: $\mathbf A^+ = \begin {cases} \paren {\mathbf A^\intercal \mathbf A}^{-1} \mathbf A^\intercal & : m > n \\ \mathbf A^\intercal \paren {\mathbf A \mathbf A^\intercal}^{-1} & : n < m \end {cases}$ where $\mathbf A^\intercal$ denotes the transpose of $\mathbf A$.

title: Definition:Moore-Penrose Pseudoinverse/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a matrix of order $m \times n$ over the complex numbers $\C$. The Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of $\mathbf A$ is the unique $n \times m$ matrix $A^+$ which satisfies the four Moore-Penrose conditions: where $\mathbf A^*$ denotes the Hermitian conjugate of $\mathbf A$.

title: Definition:Moore-Penrose Pseudoinverse/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Moore-Penrose Pseudoinverse == The concept of the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse was defined by in $1920$, and then again by in $1955$.

title: Definition:Moore Method
snippet: The Moore method is a deductive manner of instruction used in some advanced mathematics courses. Instead of using a textbook, the students are given a list of definitions. Based on these, the students are also given a list of theorems to prove and present in class. This leads the students through the subject material. The Moore method typically limits the amount of material that a class is able to cover, but this is countered by the depth of understanding that listening to lectures cannot give. Category:Definitions/Schools

title: Definition:Morphism
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. A morphism of $\mathbf C$ is an object $f$, together with: A domain $\operatorname {dom} f$, which is an object of $\mathbf C$ A codomain $\operatorname {cod} f$, also an object of $\mathbf C$ The collection of all morphisms of $\mathbf C$ is denoted $\mathbf C_1$. If $A$ is the domain of $f$ and $B$ is its codomain, this is mostly represented by writing: $f: A \to B$ or $A \stackrel f \longrightarrow B$

title: Definition:Morphism/Also known as
snippet: == Morphism: Also known as == A morphism is also known as: an arrow an edge. Category:Definitions/Morphisms

title: Definition:Morphism/Motivation
snippet: == Morphism: Motivation == A morphism is one of the two basic concepts of a metacategory, and therefore of category theory. The other one is the notion of an object. Thus in order to discuss a particular metacategory, it is necessary to specify what exactly its morphisms are. Note that a morphism is defined to be an object. This should not be confused with an object of $\mathbf C$. Usually, the morphisms of a metacategory $\mathbf C$ are not also objects of $\mathbf C$. Category:Definitions/Morphisms

title: Definition:Morphism Category
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Its morphism category, denoted $\mathbf C^\to$, is defined as follows: {{DefineCategory |ob = The morphisms $\mathbf C_1$ of $\mathbf C$ |mor = $g: f \to f'$ is a pair $\tuple {g_1, g_2}$ of morphisms of $\mathbf C$ such that $g_2 \circ f = f' \circ g_1$ |comp = $\tuple {h_1, h_2} \circ \tuple {g_1, g_2} := \tuple {h_1 \circ g_1, h_2 \circ g_2}$, whenever this is defined |id = $\operatorname{id}_f := \tuple {\operatorname{id}_C, \operatorname{id}_D}$ for $f: C \to D$ }} The morphisms of $\mathbf C^\to$ can be made more intuitive by the following diagram:…

title: Definition:Morphism Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. A morphism functor $F$ assigns to each morphism $f$ of $\mathbf C$ a morphism $F f$ of $\mathbf D$.

title: Definition:Morphism Functor/Also known as
snippet: == Morphism Functor: Also known as == A morphism functor $F$ is also known as an arrow functor. Category:Definitions/Morphism Functors

title: Definition:Morphism Property
snippet: Let $\phi: \struct {S, \circ} \to \struct {T, *}$ be a mapping from one algebraic structure $\struct {S, \circ}$ to another $\struct {T, *}$. Then $\circ$ has the morphism property under $\phi$ : $\forall x, y \in S: \map \phi {x \circ y} = \map \phi x * \map \phi y$

title: Definition:Morphism Property/Also known as
snippet: == Morphism Property: Also known as == Some sources refer to the morphism property as the homomorphism condition.

title: Definition:Morphism of Chain Complexes
snippet: Let $\AA$ be an abelian category. Let $\family {C_i, d_i}_{i \mathop \in \Z}$ and $\family {C_i', d_i'}_{i \mathop \in \Z}$ be chain complexes in $\AA$. A morphism of chain complexes from $\family {C_i}_{i \mathop \in \Z}$ to $\family {D_i}_{i \mathop \in \Z}$ is a family of morphisms $\family {f_i: C_i \to C_i'}_{i \mathop \in \Z}$, such that: $\forall i \in \Z: f_{i-1} \circ d_i = d_i' \circ f_i$

title: Definition:Morphism of Cocones
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $D: \mathbf J \to \mathbf C$ be a $\mathbf J$-diagram in $\mathbf C$. Let $\struct {C, c_j}$ and $\struct {C', c'_j}$ be cocones from $D$. Let $f: C \to C'$ be a morphism of $\mathbf C$. Then $f$ is a morphism of cones , for all objects $j$ of $\mathbf J$: $\begin{xy}\xymatrix@+0.5em@L+3px{ D_j \ar[d]_*+{c_j} \ar[dr]^*+{c'_j} \\ C \ar[r]_*+{f} & C' }\end{xy}$ is a commutative diagram.

title: Definition:Morphism of Cones
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $D: \mathbf J \to \mathbf C$ be a $\mathbf J$-diagram in $\mathbf C$. Let $\struct {C, c_j}$ and $\struct {C', c'_j}$ be cones to $D$. Let $f: C \to C'$ be a morphism of $\mathbf C$. Then $f$ is a morphism of cones , for all objects $j$ of $\mathbf J$: $\begin{xy}\xymatrix@+0.5em@L+2px{ C \ar[r]^*+{f} \ar[dr]_*+{c_j} & C' \ar[d]^*+{c'_j} \\ & D_j }\end{xy}$ is a commutative diagram.

title: Definition:Morphism of Presheaves on Topological Space
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space. Let $\mathbf C$ be a category. Let $\FF$ and $\GG$ be $\mathbf C$-valued presheaves on $X$.

title: Definition:Morphism of Ringed Spaces
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ and $\struct {Y, \OO_Y}$ be ringed spaces.

title: Definition:Morphism of Ringed Spaces/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ and $\struct {Y, \OO_Y}$ be ringed spaces. A morphism of ringed spaces from $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ to $\struct {Y, \OO_Y}$ is a pair $\struct {f, f^\sharp}$ where: $f: X \to Y$ is continuous $f^\sharp: \OO_Y \to f_* \OO_X$ is a morphism of sheaves to the direct image sheaf of $\OO_X$ via $f$

title: Definition:Morphism of Ringed Spaces/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ and $\struct {Y, \OO_Y}$ be ringed spaces. A morphism of ringed spaces from $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ to $\struct {Y, \OO_Y}$ is a pair $\struct {f, f^\sharp}$ where: $f : X \to Y$ is continuous $f^\sharp: f^{-1} \OO_Y \to \OO_X$ is a morphism of sheaves from the inverse image sheaf of $\OO_Y$ via $f$

title: Definition:Morphism of Schemes
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ and $\struct {Y, \OO_Y}$ be schemes. A morphism of schemes from $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ to $\struct {Y, \OO_Y}$ is a morphism of locally ringed spaces from $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ to $\struct {Y, \OO_Y}$.

title: Definition:Morphism of Schemes Locally of Finite Type
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ and $\struct {Y, \OO_Y}$ be schemes. Let $f : \struct {X, \OO_X} \to \struct {Y, \OO_Y}$ be a morphism of schemes. $f$ is locally of finite type for all affine open subsets $U \subset Y$, there is an open cover $\family {V_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ of $\map {f^{-1} } U$ by affine open subsets $V_i \subset \map {f^{-1} } U$, such that the ring homomorphism $\map {\OO_Y} U \to \map {\OO_X} {V_i}$ makes $\map {\OO_X} {V_i}$ a finitely generated commutative $\map {\OO_Y} U$-algebra.

title: Definition:Morphism of Schemes of Finite Type
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ and $\struct {Y, \OO_Y}$ be schemes. Let $f : \struct {X, \OO_X} \to \struct {Y, \OO_Y}$ be a morphism of schemes. $f$ is of finite type $f$ is locally of finite type and quasi-compact.

title: Definition:Morphism of Sheaves
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space. Let $\mathbf C$ be a category. Let $\FF$ and $\GG$ be $\mathbf C$-valued sheaves on $X$. A sheaf morphism from $\FF$ to $\GG$ is a presheaf morphism $\FF \to \GG$.

title: Definition:Morphisms-Only Metacategory
snippet: A morphisms-only metacategory is a metamodel for the language of category theory subject to the following axioms:

title: Definition:Morse-Kelley Set Theory
snippet: Morse-Kelley set theory is a system of axiomatic set theory. It is a stronger form of Zermelo-Fraenkel-Skolem set theory which allows not only for first order formulas to specify the existence of properties of sets, but also defines properties by quantifying over properties as well as over sets.

title: Definition:Morse-Kelley Set Theory/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Morse-Kelley Set Theory == Morse-Kelley set theory was devised for the purpose of extending Zermelo-Fraenkel-Skolem set theory so as to allow properties themselves to be further specified. While it is no bad idea to allow further formal axioms to extend the range of what can be defined, it is not possible to formally provide for all possible properties by means of an axiom schema. This was proven by Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems.

title: Definition:Morse Theory
snippet: Morse theory is an approach to topology whereby the topological properties of a manifold $M$ can be described in terms of the singularities of a mapping defined on $M$.

title: Definition:Morse Theory/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Morse Theory == Morse theory was first introduced by in the $1920$s.

title: Definition:Most Significant Digit
snippet: Let $b \in \Z: b \ge 2$ be a number base Let $n$ be a number which is reported to $r$ significant figures, to base $b$, that is: $n = d_1 \times b^k + d_2 \times b^{k - 1} + \dotsb + d_{r - 1} \times b^{k - r + 2} + d_r \times b^{k - r + 1}$ where: $d_1, d_2, \dotsc, d_r$ are the significant figures of $n$ $b^k$ is the largest power of $b$ less than or equal to $n$. Then the digit $d_1$ is known as the most significant digit of $n$. Note that the usual situation is when $b = 10$, but in the field of computer science, binary is usual.

title: Definition:Motion
snippet: A particle or a body is defined as being in motion it is not stationary with respect to the given frame of reference. Thus motion is the state of changing position.

title: Definition:Move
snippet: A move is an action by a player in a game made according to the rules.

title: Definition:Move/Also known as
snippet: == Move: Also known as == Some texts refer to a move as an action, but the latter word already has several uses in mathematics.

title: Definition:Moving Average
snippet: A moving average is a technique of smoothing a time series by replacing each observation with the mean of, more usually, weighted mean of the observation and a specified number of the previous observations.

snippet: == Nomenclature for Moving Average Model == The name moving average model is a bit of a misnomer because: $\text{(a)}: \quad$ the weights $1, -\theta_1, -\theta_2, \ldots$ need not all add up to $1$ (and in fact will generally not do so) $\text{(b)}: \quad$ the weights need not in fact all be positive.
