title: Definition:Muggle
snippet: A muggle is a person who is mathematically illiterate. Specifically, it refers to those who do not realise that they are indeed embarrassingly mathematically unsophisticated, and insist on peppering their speech with mathematical-sounding phrases, like Q.E.D (on believing they have won an argument) or I had $n$ pints of beer last night (being under the impression that $n$ means "a big unspecified number").

title: Definition:Muggle/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Muggle == The word muggle comes from the popular series by : a muggle in this context is a human with no magical powers. The word muggle is not exclusive to the field of mathematics; a notable usage of muggle is in to refer to a non-hacker. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Multi-Digit Integer
snippet: Let $b \in \N_{>1}$ be a natural number greater than $1$. An $n$-digit integer base $b$ is an integer which has no more than $n$ digits when expressed in base $b$. That is, it is strictly less than $b^n$.

title: Definition:Multi-Person Game
snippet: A multi-person game is a game which has (strictly) more than two players.

title: Definition:Multi-Person Game/Also known as
snippet: == Multi-Person Game: Also known as == A multi-person game can also be referred to as an $n$-person game if the number $n$ of players is known.

title: Definition:Multi-Value Logic
snippet: Multi-value logic is a branch of logic in which it is admissible for a statements to have a truth value other than just true or false.

title: Definition:Multi-Value Logic/Also known as
snippet: == Multi-Value Logic: Also known as == Multi-value logic is also known as many-valued logic.

title: Definition:Multi-Value Logic/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Multi-Value Logic == The concept of multi-value logic was introduced by in $1921$.

title: Definition:Multibrot Set
snippet: Let $n \in \Z$ be an integer such that $n > 2$ The multibrot $n$ set $M_n$ is the subset of the complex plane defined as follows: Let $c \in \C$ be a complex number. Let $T_c: \C \to \C$ be the complex function defined as: $\forall z \in \C: \map {T_c} z = z^n + c$ Then $c \in M_n$ the sequence: $\tuple {0, \map {T_c} 0, \map { {T_c}^2} 0, \ldots}$ is bounded.

title: Definition:Multifunction/Also known as
snippet: == Multifunction: Also known as == A multifunction is also known as a many-valued function, a multiple-valued function or a multi-valued function. On the terse form multifunction is preferred. When the number of values is known to be $n$, the multifunction can be referred to as an $n$-valued function.

title: Definition:Multifunction/Branch
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be sets. Let $f: A \to B$ be a multifunction on $A$. Let $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a partitioning of the codomain of $f$ such that: $\forall i \in I: f \restriction_{A \times S_i}$ is a mapping. Then each $f \restriction_{A \times S_i}$ is a branch of $f$.

title: Definition:Multifunction/Principal Branch
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be sets. Let $f: A \to B$ be a multifunction on $A$. Let $\sequence {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a partitioning of the codomain of $f$ into branches. It is usual to distinguish one such branch of $f$ from the others, and label it the principal branch of $f$.

title: Definition:Multifunction/Principal Value
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be sets. Let $f: A \to B$ be a multifunction on $A$. Let $x \in A$ be an element of the domain of $f$. The principal value of $x$ is the element $y$ of the principal branch of $f$ such that $\map f x = y$.

title: Definition:Multigraph
snippet: A multigraph is a graph that can have more than one edge between a pair of vertices. That is, $G = \struct {V, E}$ is a multigraph if $V$ is a set and $E$ is a multiset of doubleton subsets of $V$. 400px The graph above is a multigraph because of the double edge between $v_2$ and $v_3$ and the triple edge between $v_5$ and $v_6$.

title: Definition:Multigraph/Also defined as
snippet: == Multigraph: Also defined as == Sources differ on whether a multigraph must or only may contain multiple edges. Similarly, sources differ on whether a multigraph may contain loops, and whether a loop counts as a double edge. If there is any ambiguity, and especially if it matters to the proof, these conditions should be specified.

title: Definition:Multigraph/Multiple Edge
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a multigraph. A multiple edge is an edge of $G$ which has another edge with the same endvertices. That is, where there is more than one edge that joins any pair of vertices, each of those edges is called a multiple edge.

title: Definition:Multigraph/Multiplicity
snippet: The multiplicity of a multigraph is the maximum multiplicity of its (multiple) edges. Category:Definitions/Multigraphs

title: Definition:Multigraph/Simple Edge
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a multigraph. A simple edge is an edge $u v$ of $G$ which is the only edge of $G$ which is incident to both $u$ and $v$. Category:Definitions/Edges of Graphs Category:Definitions/Multigraphs

title: Definition:Multiindex/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Multiindex == The plural of multiindex (or multi-index) is multiindices (or multi-indices). Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Multiindex/Modulus
snippet: Let $k = \sequence {k_j}_{j \mathop \in J}$ be a multiindex. The modulus of such a multiindex $k$ is defined by: $\ds \size k = \sum_{j \mathop \in J} k_j$ Note that, since by definition all but finitely many of the $k_j$ are zero, this summation is convergent.

title: Definition:Multiindex Power Notation
snippet: Let $M$ be a commutative monoid. Let $I$ be a set. Let $\mathbf x = \family {x_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a family of elements of $M$. Let $\mathbf a = \family {a_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a family of natural numbers of finite support. We denote $\ds \mathbf x^{\mathbf a} = \prod_{i \mathop \in I} x_i^{a_i}$ where: $x_i^{a_i}$ is the $a_i$th power of $x_i$ $\prod$ denotes product with finite support Category:Definitions/Polynomial Theory

title: Definition:Multilateral Polygon/Also known as
snippet: == Multilateral Polygon: Also known as == The term multilateral polygon can also be seen hyphenated: multi-lateral polygon. A polygon with $n$ sides is known as an $n$-gon.

title: Definition:Multilinear Mapping
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ be a commutative ring. Let $\struct {A_1, +_1, \circ_1}_R, \struct {A_2, +_2, \circ_2}_R, \ldots, \struct {A_n, +_n, \circ_n}_R, \struct {A_{n + 1}, +_{n + 1}, \circ_{n + 1} }_R$ be $R$-modules. Let $\oplus: A_1 \times A_2 \times \cdots \times A_n \to A_{n+1}$ be a multiary operator with the property that: $\forall \struct {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n} \in A_1 \times A_2 \times \cdots \times A_n$: $a_1 \mapsto a_1 \oplus a_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus a_n$ is a linear transformation from $A_1$ to $A_{n+1}$ $a_2 \mapsto a_1 \oplus a_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus a_n$ is a linear…

title: Definition:Multinomial
snippet: A multinomial is an expression which has $2$ or more terms.

title: Definition:Multinomial Coefficient
snippet: Let $k_1, k_2, \ldots, k_m \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be positive integers. The multinomial coefficient of $k_1, \ldots, k_m$ is defined as: $\dbinom {k_1 + k_2 + \cdots + k_m} {k_1, k_2, \ldots, k_m} := \dfrac {\paren {k_1 + k_2 + \cdots + k_m}!} {k_1! \, k_2! \, \ldots k_m!}$

title: Definition:Multinomial Coefficient/Trinomial
snippet: Let $k_1, k_2, k_3 \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be positive integers. The trinomial coefficient of $k_1, k_2, k_3$ is a particular case of a multinomial coefficient, defined as: $\dbinom {k_1 + k_2 + k_3} {k_1, k_2, k_3} := \dfrac {\paren {k_1 + k_2 + k_3} !} {k_1! \, k_2! \, k_3!}$

title: Definition:Multinomial Distribution
snippet: Let $X$ be a discrete random variable on a probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. At each of $n$ trials, let $X$ have $r$ possible outcomes with probabilities $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n$ such that $\sum p_i = 1$. Then $X$ has the multinomial distribution. The probabilities of the various outcomes are given by the terms of the expansion of: $\paren {p_1 + p_2 + \cdots + p_r}^n$

title: Definition:Multiple/Integer
snippet: Let $\Z$ denote the set of integers. Let $x, y \in \Z$. Let $x$ be a divisor of $y$. Then $y$ is a multiple of $x$.

title: Definition:Multiple/Integral Domain
snippet: Let $\struct {D, +, \circ}$ be an integral domain. Let $x, y \in D$. Let $x$ be a divisor of $y$. Then $y$ is a multiple of $x$.

title: Definition:Multiple Comparisons
snippet: Consider a designed experiment in which a number of non-independent comparisons are made between means for all units receiving the same treatment. Then significance tests and interval estimates based on the $t$-distribution and Snedecor's $F$-distribution are no longer valid. Similar difficulties arise if a large number of comparisons are possible, but attention is confined to the ones that look "interesting" because they seem to indicate large differences. These difficulties are overcome by using multiple-comparison tests.

title: Definition:Multiple Correlation Coefficient
snippet: Context: multiple regression. Let the expectation of a random variable $Y$ be given by: $\expect y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 \cdots$ Let the least-squares regression estimators of $y$ corresponding to the observed $y_i$ be denoted $\hat y_i$. Then the multiple correlation coefficient is the product moment correlation coefficient between the $y_i$ and $\hat y_i$, and is denoted $R$.

title: Definition:Multiple Edge/Also known as
snippet: == Multiple Edge: Also known as == A multiple edge is also known as parallel edges.

title: Definition:Multiple Edge/Multiplicity
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a multigraph. The multiplicity of an edge is the number of edges having the same pair of endvertices. For example, simple edges have multiplicity $1$. Thus, an edge is a multiple edge its multiplicity exceeds $1$. Category:Definitions/Multigraphs

title: Definition:Multiple Integral
snippet: A multiple integral is an integral which involves two or more successive integrations, in which one variable is integrated at a time, while the others remain constant.

title: Definition:Multiple Integral/Also known as
snippet: == Multiple Integral: Also known as == A multiple integral is also known as an iterated integral.

title: Definition:Multiple Integral/Darboux
snippet: Let $n \in \N$ be a natural number. Let $R \subseteq \R^n$ be a closed rectangle in $\R^n$. Let $f : R \to \R$ be a bounded real-valued function on $R$. Suppose that: $\ds \underline {\int_R} \map f x \rd x = \overline {\int_R} \map f x \rd x$ where $\ds \underline {\int_R}$ and $\ds \overline {\int_R}$ denote the lower Darboux integral and upper Darboux integral, respectively.

title: Definition:Multiple Integral/Double
snippet: Let $f: \R^2 \to \R$ be a real-valued function of $2$ independent variables. The double integral of $f$ those independent variables is defined as: $\ds \map \int {\int \map f {x, y} \rd x} \rd y$ where: $\map f {x, y}$ is integrable $\ds \int \map f {x, y} \rd x$ is the integral $x$ of $\map f {x, y}$, keeping $y$ constant and is denoted: $\ds \iint \map f {x, y} \rd x \rd y$

title: Definition:Multiple Integral/Triple
snippet: Let $f: \R^3 \to \R$ be a real-valued function of $3$ independent variables. The triple integral of $f$ those independent variables is defined as: $\ds \map \int {\iint \map f {x, y, z} \rd x \rd y} \rd z$ where: $\map f {x, y, z}$ is integrable $\ds \iint \map f {x, y, z} \rd x \rd y$ is the double integral $\paren {x, y}$ of $\map f {x, y, z}$, keeping $z$ constant and is denoted: $\ds \iiint \map f {x, y, z} \rd x \rd y \rd z$

title: Definition:Multiple Linear Regression/General
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be a random variable. Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_p$ also be random variables for $p \in \N_{>1}$ Let $\mathbb x$ be a vector of $p$ explanatory variables from $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_p$. Let $\bstheta$ be a vector of $q$ unknown parameters Let the regression of $Y$ on $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ be expressible in the form: $\expect {Y \mid \mathbf x} = \map f {\mathbf x, \bstheta}$ Then $\expect {Y \mid \mathbf x}$ is known as general multiple linear regression.

title: Definition:Multiple Point
snippet: Let $C$ be a locus. A singular point $P \in C$ is called a multiple point $C$ intersects itself at $P$ such that there are $2$ or more tangents to $C$ at $P$.

title: Definition:Multiple Point/Also known as
snippet: == Multiple Point: Also known as == A multiple point is also known as a $k$-tuple point, where $k$ is the number of intersecting tangents.

title: Definition:Multiple Pointed Algebra
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $I$ be a set. An $I$-pointed algebra over $R$ is an ordered pair $(A, f)$ where: $A$ is an algebra over $R$ $f : I \to A$ is a mapping

title: Definition:Multiple Pointed Set
snippet: Let $I$ be a set. An $I$-pointed set is an ordered pair $\struct {A, f}$ where: $A$ is a set $f : I \to A$ is a mapping

title: Definition:Multiple Pointed Topology
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $A$ be a finite set whose cardinality is greater than $1$. Let $D = \struct {A, \set {\O, A} }$ be the indiscrete space on $A$. Let $T \times D$ be the product space of $T$ and $D$. Then $T \times D$ is known as the multiple pointed topology on $T$. It is seen that $T \times D$ is conceptually equivalent to taking the space $T$ and replacing each point with a finite set of topologically indistinguishable points.

title: Definition:Multiple Regression
snippet: Multiple regression is an extension of regression in which there are $p$ explanatory variables where $p > 1$: $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_p$

title: Definition:Multiple Regression/Linear
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be a random variable. Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_p$ also be random variables for $p \in \N_{>1}$ Let the regression of $Y$ on $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ be expressible in the form: $\expect {Y \mid x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_p} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_2 + \beta_2 x_2 + \ldots + \beta_n x_n$ Then $\expect {Y \mid x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_p}$ is known as multiple linear regression.

title: Definition:Multiple Root
snippet: A multiple root is a root of an equation which appears more than once.

title: Definition:Multiple Root/Also known as
snippet: == Multiple Root: Also known as == A multiple root of multiplicity $n$ is known as an $n$-tuple root. It is also known as a repeated root.

title: Definition:Multiple Root/Multiplicity
snippet: The multiplicity of a multiple root is the number of times it appears.

title: Definition:Multiple of Codeword in Linear Code
snippet: Let $\map V {n, p}$ denote the linear $\tuple {n, n}$-code modulo $p$. The operation of multiplication on $\map V {n, p}$ is defined as follows. Let $A$ be an elements of $\map V {n, p}$, that is, a sequence of length $n$ of residue classes modulo $p$. Let $a_k$ denote the $k$th term of $A$. Let $c \in \Z_p$ be an element of the set $\Z_p$ of residue classes modulo $p$. Then $c A$ is the sequence of length $n$ of residue classes modulo $p$ whose $k$th term $c_k$ is defined as: $c_k : = c \times_p a_k$ where $\times_p$ denotes the operation of multiplication modulo $p$.

title: Definition:Multiplicand/Also defined as
snippet: == Multiplicand: Also defined as == In the context of continued products, for example $\ds \prod_{i \mathop \in S} a_i$, each of the objects $a_i$ are referred to as the multiplicands of the expression. Category:Definitions/Multiplication

title: Definition:Multiplicand/Also known as
snippet: == Multiplicand: Also known as == In algebraic systems where multiplication is commutative, it is commonplace to treat both the multiplier and multiplicand as the same sort of object, and refer to them both as factors. Category:Definitions/Multiplication

title: Definition:Multiplicand/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Multiplicand == The word multiplicand means that which is to be multiplied. The -and derives from the of Latin verbs, expressing future necessity: that which needs to be done. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Multiplicand of Continued Product/Also known as
snippet: == Multiplicand of Continued Product: Also known as == The multiplicand of a continued product is also known as the set of multiplicands. Category:Definitions/Continued Products

title: Definition:Multiplication
snippet: Multiplication is the basic operation $\times$ everyone is familiar with. For example:

title: Definition:Multiplication/Complex Numbers
snippet: The multiplication operation in the domain of complex numbers $\C$ is written $\times$. Let $z = a + i b, w = c + i d$ where $a, b, c, d \in \R$. Then $z \times w$ is defined as: $\paren {a + i b} \times \paren {c + i d} = \paren {a c - b d} + i \paren {a d + b c}$ This follows by the facts that: Real Numbers form Field and thus real multiplication is distributive over real addition the entity $i$ is such that $i^2 = -1$.

title: Definition:Multiplication/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Multiplication == The symbol $\times$ for multiplication was invented by . However, he was criticized by , as it was in his view too similar to the letter $x$. himself preferred the symbol $\cdot$.

title: Definition:Multiplication/Integers
snippet: The multiplication operation in the domain of integers $\Z$ is written $\times$. Let us define $\eqclass {\tuple {a, b} } \boxtimes$ as in the formal definition of integers. That is, $\eqclass {\tuple {a, b} } \boxtimes$ is an equivalence class of ordered pairs of natural numbers under the congruence relation $\boxtimes$. $\boxtimes$ is the congruence relation defined on $\N \times \N$ by $\tuple {x_1, y_1} \boxtimes \tuple {x_2, y_2} \iff x_1 + y_2 = x_2 + y_1$. In order to streamline the notation, we will use $\eqclass {a, b} {}$ to mean $\eqclass {\tuple {a, b} } \boxtimes$, as suggested.

title: Definition:Multiplication/Mistake
snippet: == Source Work == multiplication

title: Definition:Multiplication/Multiplicand
snippet: Let $a \times b$ denote the operation of multiplication on two objects. The object $b$ is known as the multiplicand of $a$. That is, it is the object which is to be multiplied by the multiplier. Note that the nature of $a$ and $b$ has deliberately been left unspecified. They could be, for example, numbers, matrices or more complex expressions constructed from such elements.

title: Definition:Multiplication/Multiplier
snippet: Let $a \times b$ denote the operation of multiplication on two objects. The object $a$ is known as the multiplier of $b$. That is, it is the object which is to multiply the multiplicand. Note that the nature of $a$ and $b$ has deliberately been left unspecified. They could be, for example, numbers, matrices or more complex expressions constructed from such elements.

title: Definition:Multiplication/Natural Numbers
snippet: Let $\N$ be the natural numbers. Multiplication on $\N$ is the basic operation $\times$ everyone is familiar with. For example: $3 \times 4 = 12$ $13 \times 7 = 91$ Every attempt to describe the natural numbers via suitable axioms should reproduce the intuitive behaviour of $\times$. The same holds for any construction of $\N$ in an ambient theory.

title: Definition:Multiplication/Natural Numbers/Addition
snippet: Let $\N$ be the natural numbers. Let $+$ denote addition. The binary operation $\times$ is recursively defined on $\N$ as follows: $\forall m, n \in \N: \begin {cases} m \times 0 & = 0 \\ m \times \paren {n + 1} & = m \times n + m \end {cases}$ This operation is called multiplication. Equivalently, multiplication can be defined as: $\forall m, n \in \N: m \times n := \mathop {+^n} m$ where $\mathop {+^n} m$ denotes the $n$th power of $m$ under $+$.

title: Definition:Multiplication/Notation
snippet: There are several variants of the notation for multiplication: $n \times m$ This is usually used when numbers are under consideration, for example: $3 \times 5 = 15$. However, it can be used in the context of algebra where extra clarity is needed. $n m$ This is most common in algebra, but not with numbers, as it is difficult to make it obvious where one number ends and the next number begins. $\paren n \paren m$ This form can be used for either symbols denoting variables or numbers, for example: $\paren 3 \paren 4 = 12$. $n \cdot m$ or $n .

title: Definition:Multiplication/Product
snippet: Let $a \times b$ denote the operation of multiplication on two objects $a$ and $b$. Then the result $a \times b$ is referred to as the product of $a$ and $b$. Note that the nature of $a$ and $b$ has deliberately been left unspecified. They could be, for example, numbers, matrices or more complex expressions constructed from such elements.

title: Definition:Multiplication/Rational Numbers
snippet: The multiplication operation in the domain of rational numbers $\Q$ is written $\times$. Let $a = \dfrac p q, b = \dfrac r s$ where $p, q \in \Z, r, s \in \Z \setminus \set 0$. Then $a \times b$ is defined as $\dfrac p q \times \dfrac r s = \dfrac {p \times r} {q \times s}$. This definition follows from the definition of and proof of existence of the field of quotients of any integral domain, of which the set of integers is one.

title: Definition:Multiplication/Real Numbers
snippet: The multiplication operation in the domain of real numbers $\R$ is written $\times$. From the definition, the real numbers are the set of all equivalence classes $\eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {}$ of Cauchy sequences of rational numbers. Let $x = \eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {}, y = \eqclass {\sequence {y_n} } {}$, where $\eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {}$ and $\eqclass {\sequence {y_n} } {}$ are such equivalence classes. Then $x \times y$ is defined as: $\eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {} \times \eqclass {\sequence {y_n} } {} = \eqclass {\sequence {x_n \times y_n} } {}$

title: Definition:Multiplication of Cuts
snippet: Let $0^*$ denote the rational cut associated with the (rational) number $0$. Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be cuts. The operation of multiplication is defined on $\alpha$ and $\beta$ as: $\alpha \beta := \begin {cases} \size \alpha \, \size \beta & : \alpha \ge 0^*, \beta \ge 0^* \\ -\paren {\size \alpha \, \size \beta} & : \alpha where: $\size \alpha$ denotes the absolute value of $\alpha$ $\size \alpha \, \size \beta$ is defined as in Multiplication of Positive Cuts $\ge$ denotes the ordering on cuts. In this context, $\alpha \beta$ is known as the product of $\alpha$ and $\beta$.

title: Definition:Multiplication of Homotopy Classes of Paths
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\alpha, \beta$ be homotopy classes of paths in $T$. Let $f, g: \closedint 0 1 \to S$ be representative paths for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ respectively. Let $\map f 1 = \map g 0$. The product of the homotopy classes $\alpha$ and $\beta$ is the homotopy class of the concatenated path $f * g$.

title: Definition:Multiplication of Order Types
snippet: Let $\struct {S_1, \preccurlyeq_1}$ and $\struct {S_2, \preccurlyeq_2}$ be ordered sets. Let $\alpha := \map \ot {S_1, \preccurlyeq_1}$ and $\beta := \map \ot {S_2, \preccurlyeq_2}$ denote the order types of $\struct {S_1, \preccurlyeq_1}$ and $\struct {S_2, \preccurlyeq_2}$ respectively. Let $\alpha \cdot \beta$ be defined as: $\alpha \cdot \beta:= \map \ot {\struct {S_1, \preccurlyeq_1} \otimes^a \struct {S_2, \preccurlyeq_2} }$ where $\otimes^a$ denotes the antilexicographic product operator. The operation $\cdot$ is known as order type multiplication or multiplication of order types.

title: Definition:Multiplication of Polynomials
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $\struct {S, +, \circ}$ be a subring of $R$. Let $x \in R$. Let: $\ds f = \sum_{j \mathop = 0}^n a_j x^j$ $\ds g = \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^n b_k x^k$ be polynomials in $x$ over $S$ such that $a_n \ne 0$ and $b_m \ne 0$. The product of $f$ and $g$ is defined as: $\ds f g := \sum_{l \mathop = 0}^{m + n} c_l x^l$ where: $\ds \forall l \in \set {0, 1, \ldots, m + n}: c_l = \sum_{\substack {j \mathop + k \mathop = l \\ j, k \mathop \in \Z} } a_j b_k$

title: Definition:Multiplication of Polynomials/Polynomial Forms
snippet: Let $\ds f = \sum_{k \mathop \in Z} a_k \mathbf X^k$ and $\ds g = \sum_{k \mathop \in Z} b_k \mathbf X^k$ be polynomial forms in the indeterminates $\set {X_j: j \in J}$ over $R$. The product of $f$ and $g$ is defined as: $\ds f \circ g := \sum_{k \mathop \in Z} c_k \mathbf X^k$ where: $\ds c_k = \sum_{\substack {p + q \mathop = k \\ p, q \mathop \in Z} } a_p b_q$

title: Definition:Multiplication of Polynomials/Sequence
snippet: Let: $f = \sequence {a_k} = \tuple {a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots}$ and: $g = \sequence {b_k} = \tuple {b_0, b_1, b_2, \ldots}$ be polynomials over a field $F$. Then the operation of (polynomial) multiplication is defined as: $f g := \tuple {c_0, c_1, c_2, \ldots}$ where $\ds c_i = \sum_{j \mathop + k \mathop = i} a_j b_k$

title: Definition:Multiplication of Positive Cuts
snippet: Let $0^*$ denote the rational cut associated with the (rational) number $0$. Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be positive cuts, that is, cuts such that $\alpha \ge 0^*$ and $\beta \ge 0^*$, where $\ge$ denotes the ordering on cuts. Let the operation of multiplication be defined on $\alpha$ and $\beta$ as: $\gamma := \alpha \beta$ where $\gamma$ is the set of all rational numbers $r$ such that either: $r < 0$ or $\exists p \in \alpha, q \in \beta: r = p q$ where $p \ge 0$ and $q \ge 0$. In this context, $\gamma$ is known as the product of $\alpha$ and $\beta$.

title: Definition:Multiplication of Schwartz Distribution by Smooth Function
snippet: Let $d \in \N$ be a natural number. Let $\alpha \in \map {C^\infty} {\R^d}$ be a smooth function. Let $T \in \map {\DD'} {\R^d}$ be a Schwartz distribution. Then the multiplication of a Schwartz distribution by a smooth function $\alpha T$ is defined by: $\alpha \map T \phi := \map T {\alpha \phi}$ where $\phi \in \map \DD {\R^d}$ is a test function.

title: Definition:Multiplicative Arithmetic Function
snippet: Let $f : \N \to \C$ be an arithmetic function. Then $f$ is multiplicative : $m \perp n \implies \map f {m n} = \map f m \map f n$ where $m \perp n$ denotes that $m$ is coprime to $n$. That is, a multiplicative arithmetic function is one where the value of a product of two coprime numbers equals the product of the value of each one individually.

title: Definition:Multiplicative Function
snippet: Number Theory: Definition:Multiplicative Arithmetic Function Definition:Completely Multiplicative Function Ring Theory: Definition:Multiplicative Function on Ring Definition:Multiplicative Function on UFD

title: Definition:Multiplicative Function on Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $f: R \to \R$ be a (real-valued) function on $R$. $f$ is a multiplicative function on $R$ : $\forall x, y \in R: \map f {x \circ y} = \map f x \times \map f y$ That is, a multiplicative function on $R$ is one where the value of the product of two elements of $R$ equals the product of their values.

title: Definition:Multiplicative Function on UFD
snippet: Let $R$ be a unique factorization domain. Let $f : R \to \C$ be a complex-valued function. Then $f$ is multiplicative : For all coprime $x, y\in R$: $f \left({x y}\right) = f \left({x}\right) f \left({y}\right)$

title: Definition:Multiplicative Group
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +, \times}$ be a field. Let $F^* := F \setminus \set 0$ be the set $F$ less its zero. The group $\struct {F^*, \times}$ is known as the multiplicative group of $F$.

title: Definition:Multiplicative Group/Also defined as
snippet: == Multiplicative Group: Also defined as == A multiplicative group is also defined as a group $G$ such that: the elements of $G$ are numbers the operation is multiplication and denoted by concatenation: $a b$ the identity is $1$.

title: Definition:Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers
snippet: The multiplicative group of complex numbers $\struct {\C_{\ne 0}, \times}$ is the set of complex numbers without zero under the operation of multiplication.

title: Definition:Multiplicative Group of Complex Roots of Unity
snippet: Let $n \in \Z$ be an integer such that $n > 0$. Let $U_n := \set {z \in \C: z^n = 1}$ denote the set of complex $n$th roots of unity. Let $\struct {U_n, \times}$ be the algebraic structure formed by $U_n$ under complex multiplication. Then $\struct {U_n, \times}$ is the multiplicative group of complex $n$th roots of unity.

title: Definition:Multiplicative Group of Positive Rational Numbers
snippet: The multiplicative group of positive rational numbers $\struct {\Q_{> 0}, \times}$ is the set of (strictly) positive rational numbers under the operation of multiplication.

title: Definition:Multiplicative Group of Positive Real Numbers
snippet: The multiplicative group of positive real numbers $\left({\R_{> 0}, \times}\right)$ is the set of (strictly) positive real numbers under the operation of multiplication. Thus real multiplication is: Well-defined on $\R_{> 0}$ Closed on $\R_{> 0}$ Associative on $\R_{> 0}$ Commutative on $\R_{> 0}$ The identity of $\left({\R_{> 0}, \times}\right)$ is $1$ Each element of $\left({\R_{> 0}, \times}\right)$ has an inverse.

title: Definition:Multiplicative Group of Rational Numbers
snippet: The multiplicative group of rational numbers $\struct {\Q_{\ne 0}, \times}$ is the set of rational numbers without zero under the operation of multiplication.

title: Definition:Multiplicative Group of Real Numbers
snippet: The multiplicative group of real numbers $\struct {\R_{\ne 0}, \times}$ is the set of real numbers without zero under the operation of multiplication.

title: Definition:Multiplicative Group of Reduced Residues
snippet: Let $m \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. Let $\Z'_m$ denote the reduced residue system modulo $m$. Consider the algebraic structure: $\struct {\Z'_m, \times_m}$ where $\times_m$ denotes multiplication modulo $m$. Then $\struct {\Z'_m, \times_m}$ is referred to as the multiplicative group of reduced residues modulo $m$.

title: Definition:Multiplicative Identity
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +, \times}$ be a field. The identity element of the multiplicative group $\struct {F^*, \times}$ of $F$ is called the multiplicative identity of $F$. It is often denoted $e_F$ or $1_F$, or, if there is no danger of ambiguity, $e$ or $1$.

title: Definition:Multiplicative Identity/Also known as
snippet: == Multiplicative Identity: Also known as == The multiplicative identity of a field $F$ can also be referred to as the unity of $F$. This arises from its roles as the unity of the ring that $\struct {F, +, \times}$ is by definition of a field. The term unit is often used for unity. It is preferred that this is not used on as it can be confused with a unit of a ring, which is a different thing altogether.

title: Definition:Multiplicative Inverse
snippet: Let $\strut {A_F, \oplus}$ be a unitary algebra whose unit is $1$ and whose zero is $0$. Let $a \in A_F$ such that $a \ne 0$. A multiplicative inverse of $a$ is an element $b \in A_F$ such that: $a \oplus b = 1 = b \oplus a$

title: Definition:Multiplicative Inverse/Field
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +, \times}$ be a field whose zero is $0_F$. Let $a \in F$ such that $a \ne 0_F$. Then the inverse element of $a$ with respect to the $\times$ operator is called the multiplicative inverse of $F$. It is usually denoted $a^{-1}$ or $\dfrac 1 a$.

title: Definition:Multiplicative Inverse/Number
snippet: Let $\Bbb F$ be one of the standard number fields: $\Q$, $\R$, $\C$. Let $a \in \Bbb F$ be any arbitrary number. The multiplicative inverse of $a$ is its inverse under multiplication and can be denoted: $a^{-1}$, $\dfrac 1 a$, $1 / a$, and so on. $a \times a^{-1} = 1$

title: Definition:Multiplicative Magic Square
snippet: A multiplicative magic square is an arrangement of $n^2$ distinct numbers into an $n \times n$ square array such that: the product of the elements of each row the product of the elements in each column the product of the elements along each diagonal are the same.

title: Definition:Multiplicative Magic Square/Magic Constant
snippet: The magic constant of a multiplicative magic square is the number that each of the rows and columns multiplies up to.

title: Definition:Multiplicative Magic Square/Order
snippet: An $n \times n$ multiplicative magic square is called an order $n$ multiplicative magic square.

title: Definition:Multiplicative Monoid of Integers Modulo m
snippet: Let $m \in \Z$ such that $m > 1$. The multiplicative monoid of integers modulo $m$ $\struct {\Z_m, \times_m}$ is the set of integers modulo $m$ under the operation of multiplication modulo $m$.

title: Definition:Multiplicative Notation
snippet: Multiplicative notation, also called product notation, is a convention for representing a binary operation of an algebraic structure. Let $S$ be such an algebraic structure, and let $x, y \in S$. $x y$ is used to indicate the result of the operation on $x$ and $y$. There is no symbol used to define the operation itself. $e$ or $1$ is used for the identity element. $x^{-1}$ is used for the inverse element. $x^n$ is used to indicate the $n$th power of $x$. This notation is usual in group theory when discussing the general group.

title: Definition:Multiplicative Order of Integer
snippet: Let $a$ and $n$ be integers. Let there exist a positive integer $c$ such that: $a^c \equiv 1 \pmod n$ Then the least such integer is called the (multiplicative) order of $a$ modulo $n$.

title: Definition:Multiplicative Persistence
snippet: Let $n \in \N$ be a natural number. Let $n$ be expressed in decimal notation. Multiply the digits of $n$ together. Repeat with the answer, and again until a single digit remains. The number of steps it takes to reach $1$ digit is called the multiplicative persistence of $n$.

title: Definition:Multiplicative Persistence/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Multiplicative Persistence ==

title: Definition:Multiplicative Relation
snippet: Let $L = \struct {S, \wedge, \preceq}$ be a meet semilattice. Let $\RR$ be a relation on $S$. Then $\RR$ is multiplicative (relation) $\forall a, x, y \in S: \paren {\tuple {a, x}, \tuple {a, y} \in \RR \implies \tuple {a, x \wedge y} \in \RR}$

title: Definition:Multiplicative Semigroup of Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. The semigroup $\struct {R, \circ}$ is known as the multiplicative semigroup of $R$.

title: Definition:Multiplicatively Closed
snippet: Definition:Multiplicatively Closed Subset of Ring

title: Definition:Multiplicatively Closed Subset of Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {A, +, \circ}$ be a ring with unity $1_A$ and zero $0_A$. Let $S \subseteq A$ be a subset. Then $S$ is multiplicatively closed : $(1): \quad 1_A \in S$ $(2): \quad x, y \in S \implies x \circ y \in S$

title: Definition:Multiplicatively Perfect Number
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a positive integer. $n$ is multiplicatively perfect the product of the divisors of $n$ is equal to $n^2$.

title: Definition:Multiplicity
snippet: Real Analysis: Multiplicity of Root Complex Analysis: Multiplicity of Zero Graph Theory: Edge Multiplicity Graph Multiplicity Number Theory: Multiplicity of Prime Factor Linear Algebra: Algebraic Multiplicity Geometric Multiplicity

title: Definition:Multiplicity (Complex Analysis)
snippet: Let $f: \C \to \C$ be a function. Suppose there is $a \in \C$ such that $\map f a = 0$. Then $a$ is said to be a zero of multiplicity $k$ there exists non-zero $L \in \R$ such that: $\ds \lim_{z \mathop \to a} \dfrac {\cmod {\map f z} } {\cmod {z - a}^k} = L$ Category:Definitions/Complex Analysis

title: Definition:Multiplicity (Polynomial)
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $P \in R \left[{X}\right]$ be a nonzero polynomial. Let $a \in R$ be a root of $P$. The multiplicity of $a$ in $P$ is the largest positive integer $n$ such that $\left({X - a}\right)^n$ divides $P \left({X}\right)$ in $R \left[{X}\right]$. A double root is a root of multiplicity at least $2$. Category:Definitions/Polynomial Theory

title: Definition:Multiplier (Gaussian Elimination)
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a matrix over a field $K$. Let it be required that $\mathbf A$ converted to a reduced echelon matrix $\mathbf E$ by means of Gaussian elimination. Let the leftmost column of $\mathbf A$ containing a non-zero element be column $j$. Let $a_{i j} \ne 0$ be the distinguished element in row $i$ chosen as the pivot element. The numbers $\dfrac {a_{k j} } {a_{i j} }$ for each row $k$ are called the multipliers the pivot element $a_{i j}$.

title: Definition:Multiplier Algebra

Define: {{eqn | l = \tuple {L_1, R_1} +_{\map M A} \tuple {L_2, R_2} | o = := | r = \tuple {L_1 +_{\map B A} L_2, R_1 +_{\map B A} R_2} }} {{eqn | l = \lambda \circ_{\map M A} \tuple {L_1, R_1} | o = := | r = \tuple {\lambda \circ_{\map B A} L_1, \lambda \circ_{\map B A} R_1} }} {{eqn | l = \tuple {L_1, R_1} \times_{\map M A} \tuple {L_2, R_2} | o = := | r = \tuple {L_1 L_2, R_2 R_1} }} where $+_{\map B A}$ and $\circ_{\map B A}$ are the respective operations on…

title: Definition:Multiply Perfect Number
snippet: A multiply perfect number is a positive integer $n$ such that the sum of its divisors is equal to an integer multiple of $n$.

title: Definition:Multiply Perfect Number/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Multiply Perfect Number == was the first to discover the smallest triperfect number $120$. He suggested to that it would be an interesting exercise to hunt down further examples of multiply perfect numbers. They were actively investigated between $1631$ and $1647$ by , , , and . Many new ones have been found since.

title: Definition:Multiply Perfect Number/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Multiply Perfect Number == Note that the word multiply in the term multiply perfect number is an adverb: a word that qualifies an adjective. As such it should be interpreted as multiple-ly, that is, in the form of being a multiple, and is pronounced something like mul-ti-plee. Do not confuse with the verb form of multiply, meaning to perform an act of multiplication, which is pronounced something like mul-ti-pligh. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Multiply Perfect Number/Order
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a multiply perfect number such that the sum of its divisors is equal to $m \times n$. Then $n$ is multiply perfect of order $m$.

title: Definition:Multiresolution Analysis

Let $\sequence {V_j}_{j \in \Z}$ be a sequence of closed linear subspaces of $\map {L^2} \R$. $\sequence {V_j}_{j \in \Z}$ is a multiresolution analysis (MRA) : it satisfies: {{axiom | n = \text{MRA} 1 | mo= \cdots V_2 \subseteq V_1 \subseteq V_0 \subseteq V_{-1} \subseteq V_{-2} \cdots }} {{axiom | n = \text{MRA} 2 | mo= \overline {\bigcup_{j \in \Z} V_j} = \map {L^2} \R }} {{axiom | n = \text{MRA} 3 | mo= \bigcap_{j \in \Z} V_j = \set 0 }} {{axiom | n = \text{MRA} 4 | q = \forall j \in \Z | mo= f \in V_j \iff…

title: Definition:Multiset
snippet: A multiset is a pair $\struct {S, \mu}$ where: $S$ is a set $\mu: S \to \N_{>0}$ is a mapping to the strictly positive natural numbers For $s \in S$ the natural number $\map \mu s$ is called the multiplicity of $s$. Note that the multiplicities of elements is finite: we do not allow infinitely many occurrences of the same element, though the set $S$ itself may be finite, countably infinite or uncountably infinite.

title: Definition:Multiset/Technical Note
snippet: == Technical Note for Multiset == {{LatexFor|for = \multiset {a, b, b, c} }} This command is specific to . The underlying conventional $\LaTeX$ implementation to achieve this is: \left\lbrace \! \left\lbrace {a, b, b, c} \right\rbrace \! \right\rbrace} Category:Technical Notes

title: Definition:Multitape Turing Machine
snippet: A multitape Turing machine is a generalization of the standard Turing machine. Instead manipulating a single tape of symbols, the machine may have any finite number thereof, each with its own read-write head. The machine chooses its moves for each tape based on the symbols read by every tape.

title: Definition:Multitape Turing Machine/Head Displacement
snippet: Let $M = \struct {Q, \Sigma, \Gamma, \delta, q_0, B, F}$ be a $k$-tape Turing machine. Let $A_0 \vdash \dots \vdash A_j \vdash \dots A_n$ be a sequence of moves in $M$. Let $\sequence {d_0, \dots, d_j, \dots, d_{n - 1}}$ be the trajectory of tape $i$ from $A_0$. Then, the displacement of tape $i$ from $A_0$ to $A_n$ is defined as the integer: $C_R - C_L$ where: $C_D$ is the number of $j = 0, \dots, n - 1$ such that $d_j = D$ Category:Definitions/Turing Machines

title: Definition:Multitape Turing Machine/Head Trajectory
snippet: Let $M = \struct {Q, \Sigma, \Gamma, \delta, q_0, B, F}$ be a $k$-tape Turing machine. Let $A_0 \vdash A_1 \vdash \dotsm \vdash A_j \vdash \dotsm$ be a finite or infinite sequence of moves in $M$. For each $j$, write: $A_j = \tuple {X_{1j}^* q_j Y_{1j} Z_{1j}^*, \dots, X_{kj}^* q_j Y_{kj} Z_{kj}^*}$ and: $\map \delta {q_j, Y_{1j}, \dots, Y_{kj}} = \tuple {q_{j + 1}, Y_{1\paren{j + 1}}, \dots, Y_{k\paren{j + 1}}, d_{1j}, \dots, d_{kj}}$ The trajectory of the head on tape $i$ from description $A_0$ is the sequence: $\sequence {d_{i1}, d_{i2}, \dotsc, d_{ij}, \dotsc}$ That is, the sequence of…

title: Definition:Multitape Turing Machine/Monotone-Right Tape
snippet: Let $M = \struct {Q, \Sigma, \Gamma, \delta, q_0, B, F}$ be a $k$-tape Turing machine. Let $i \in \set {1, 2, \dots, k}$ Tape $i$ of $M$ is monotone-right : for any $q \in Q$ and $x_1, \dots, x_k \in \Gamma$ such that $\map \delta {q, x_1, \dots, x_k}$ is defined, if: $\map \delta {q, x_1, \dots, x_k} = \tuple {q', x'_1, \dots, x'_k, d_1, \dots, d_k}$ we have that $d_i \ne L$ That is, tape $i$ never shifts left on any transition. Category:Definitions/Turing Machines

title: Definition:Multitape Turing Machine/Read-Only Tape
snippet: Let $M = \struct {Q, \Sigma, \Gamma, \delta, q_0, B, F}$ be a $k$-tape Turing machine. Let $i \in \set {1, 2, \dots, k}$. Tape $i$ of $M$ is read-only : for any $q \in Q$ and $x_1, \dots, x_k \in \Gamma$ such that $\map \delta {q, x_1, \dots, x_k}$ is defined, if: $\map \delta {q, x_1, \dots, x_k} = \tuple {q', x'_1, \dots, x'_k, d_1, \dots, d_k}$ we have that $x_i = x'_i$ In other words, the symbol written on tape $i$ is always the same as the symbol read, on every possible transition. Category:Definitions/Turing Machines

title: Definition:Multitape Turing Machine/Write-Only Tape
snippet: Let $M = \struct {Q, \Sigma, \Gamma, \delta, q_0, B, F}$ be a $k$-tape Turing machine. Let $i \in \set {1, 2, \dots, k}$. Tape $i$ of $M$ is read-only : for any $q \in Q$, $x_1, \dots, x_k \in \Gamma$, and $y_i \in \Gamma$, if $\map \delta {q, x_1, \dots, x_k}$ is defined, then: $\map \delta {q, x_1, \dots, x_i, \dots, x_k} = \map \delta {q, x_1, \dots, y_i, \dots, x_k}$ where $y_i$ takes the place of $x_i$. In other words, the transition function never depends on the symbol read from tape $i$. Category:Definitions/Turing Machines

title: Definition:Multivariate Data
snippet: Multivariate data consists of ordered tuples of observations of a number of variables for each of a number of units.

title: Definition:Music
snippet: Music is the branch of study which creates aesthetically pleasing combinations of sounds.

title: Definition:Music/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Music == The mathematical basis to the study of music has been investigated since as long ago as the Pythagoreans. It was included in the quadrivium as the study of the relative discrete. In the words of Music is a secret arithmetical exercise and the person who indulges in it does not realize that he is manipulating numbers. This was not completely true, as many classical composers deliberately structured their music with specific mathematical structures in mind.

title: Definition:Musical Interval
snippet: A musical interval is a ratio of frequencies of musical notes which is recognised by convention as being particularly aesthetically pleasing or meaningful.

title: Definition:Musical Interval/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Musical Interval == The Pythagoreans noticed that aesthetically pleasing musical intervals were obtained by sounding notes from strings whose lengths were in ratios of small natural numbers: $1 : 2$, $2 : 3$, $3 : 4$ and so on. This may have been one of the inspirations behind their mystical appreciation of the numerical nature of the Universe.

title: Definition:Musical Isomorphisms
snippet: Let $X$ be a smooth vector field. Let $\omega$ be a smooth covector field. Let $X^\flat$ and $\omega^\sharp$ denote the index lowering and index raising of $X$ and $\omega$ respectively. Then the mappings $\flat$ and $\sharp$ are called the musical isomorphisms.

title: Definition:Must Happen
snippet: Let $A$ be an event in a probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Suppose $\map \Pr A = 1$. Then we say (colloquially) that $A$ must happen.

title: Definition:Mutatis Mutandis
snippet: Mutatis mutandis is Latin for what needs changing having been changed. It can be used in place of words like analogously and similarly, and expresses that an argument can be applied to a new situation in an intuitive fashion. For example the proof of Union is Associative can be made into that for Intersection is Associative by mutatis mutandis. In this case, this comes down to replacing $\cup$ by $\cap$, and $\lor$ by $\land$. In particular, the essential flow of the argument was not changed in adapting the proof.

title: Definition:Mutually Singular Measures
snippet:
Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\mu$ be a measure, signed measure or complex measure on $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. Let $
u$ be a measure, signed measure or complex measure on $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. We say that $\mu$ and $
u$ are mutually singular there exists $E \in \Sigma$ such that: $\mu$ is concentrated on $E$ and $
u$ is concentrated on $E^c$. We write: $\mu \perp

title: Definition:Myriad
snippet: Myriad is an archaic word for the number $10 \ 000$ (ten thousand).

title: Definition:Myriad/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Myriad == The word myriad is of Greek origin, and has connotations of vast horde. As pointed out by in his , what may have been a considerable size for a Greek army is a moderate attendance at a present-day sports event.

title: Definition:Möbius Function
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$, that is, a strictly positive integer. The Möbius function is the arithmetic function $\mu: \Z_{>0} \to \set {-1, 0, 1}$ defined as: $\map \mu n = \begin {cases} 1 & : n = 1 \\ 0 & : \exists p \in \mathbb P: p^2 \divides n \\ \paren {-1}^k & : n = p_1 p_2 \ldots p_k: p_i \in \mathbb P \end {cases}$ where $\mathbb P$ denotes the set of all prime numbers. That is: {{eqn | l = \map \mu n | r = \paren {-1}^k | c = if $n$ has $k$ distinct prime divisors. }}

title: Definition:Möbius Strip
snippet: A Möbius strip is a surface with boundary obtained by twisting a side of a rectangle by $180$ degrees, then joining the twisted side and the opposite side of it together. 300px Thus in the above diagram, $AB$ is identified with $CD$.

title: Definition:Möbius Strip/Also known as
snippet: == Möbius Strip: Also known as == Some sources use the term Möbius band, presumably on the grounds that the word strip may be considered inappropriate language to use in front of children and adolescents. In typographic environments where it is impossible or inconvenient to implement the umlaut, the spelling Moebius strip is often seen.

title: Definition:Möbius Strip/Formal Construction
snippet: Let $T$ be the square embedded in the Cartesian plane defined as: $T = \closedint 0 1 \times \closedint 0 1$ Let $T'$ be the quotient space formed from $T$ using the identification mapping $p: T \to T'$ as follows: $\forall \tuple {x, y} \in T: \map p {x, y} = \begin {cases} \tuple {1, 1 - y} & : x = 0 \\ \paren {x, y} & : x \ne 0 \end {cases}$ Then $T'$ is a Möbius strip.

title: Definition:N-Ary Operation/Also known as
snippet: == $n$-Ary Operation: Also known as == An $n$-ary operation is also sometimes referred to as a finitary operation, although the latter term may also encompass multiary operations as well. Category:Definitions/Operations

title: Definition:N-Ary Operation Induced by Binary Operation
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \oplus}$ be a magma. Let $n \ge 1$ be a natural number. Let $G^n$ be the $n$th cartesian power of $G$. The $n$-ary operation induced by $\oplus$ is the $n$-ary operation $\oplus_n: G^n \to G$ defined as: $\map {\oplus_n} f = \ds \bigoplus_{i \mathop = 1}^n \map f i$ where $\bigoplus$ denotes indexed iteration of $f$ from $1$ to $n$.

title: Definition:N-Cube
snippet: Real Analysis: $n$-Cube (Euclidean Space) Graph Theory: $n$-Cube (Graph Theory)

title: Definition:N-Cube (Euclidean Space)
snippet: Let $R, c \in \R$ be real numbers with $R > 0$. Let $\struct {\R^n, d}$ be a Euclidean $n$-Space equipped with the usual metric $d$. An $n$-cube is a subset of $\struct {\R^n, d}$ defined as the cartesian product of closed real intervals of the form: $\ds \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n \closedint {c - R} {c + R}_i$ where $\closedint {c - R} {c + R}_i$ is an interval in the $i$th factor of $\R^n$. The $n$-cube can be concisely expressed as: $\closedint {c - R} {c + R}^n$ in contexts where the indices of the product are unimportant.

title: Definition:N-Graded Ring
snippet: Let $\N$ be the set of natural numbers. An $\N$-graded ring or positively $\Z$-graded ring is a graded ring of type the additive monoid of natural numbers. That is, it is a pair $\struct {R, f}$ where: $R$ is a ring $f$ is a sequence $\sequence {R_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ of subgroups of the additive group of $R$, of which it is the internal direct sum, and such that: $\forall x \in R_n, y \in R_m: x y \in R_{m + n}$

title: Definition:NP-Complete
snippet: A decision problem $L$ is NP-complete any problem in the NP complexity class can be reduced in polynomial time and space to $L$.

title: Definition:NP-Hard Problem
snippet: Suppose it is the case that $P$ is not equal to $NP$. A decision problem $D$ is then defined as NP-hard $D$ cannot be solved in polynomial time.

title: Definition:NP Complexity Class
snippet: In computability theory, $NP$ is a complexity class in which there exists some nondeterministic Turing machine that will either: halt within $\map p {\size x}$ steps or: run forever where: $p$ is a polynomial $\size x$ is the length of the input to the Machine.

title: Definition:NP Problem
snippet: Let $D$ be a decision problem. Then $D$ is an NP problem it runs in nondeterministic polynomial time.

title: Definition:Nadir
snippet: Consider the celestial sphere $C$ with an observer $O$ at the center. Let $Z$ be the zenith of $C$ Let the straight line $ZO$ be produced from $O$ to meet $C$ at $R$. The point $R$ is known as the nadir of $C$. 480px In the above diagram, the nadir is indicated by $R$.

title: Definition:Nagata Criterion
snippet: Let $A$ be a ring. The Nagata criterion reads as follows: Let $S \subseteq A$ be a multiplicatively closed subset of $A$ generated by prime elements. If the localization $A_S$ is a UFD, then so is $A$. By Localization of UFD is UFD, this is equivalent to: Let $S \subseteq A$ be a multiplicatively closed subset of $A$ generated by prime elements. Then the localization $A_S$ is a UFD $A$ is a UFD. Category:Definitions/Factorization

title: Definition:Naive Set Theory
snippet: Naïve set theory, in contrast with axiomatic set theory, is an approach to set theory which assumes the existence of a universal set, despite the fact that such an assumption leads to paradoxes. A popular alternative (and inaccurate) definition describes this as: a non-formalized definition of set theory which describes sets and the relations between them using natural language. However, the discipline is founded upon quite as rigid a set of axioms, namely, those of propositional and predicate logic.

title: Definition:Naive Set Theory/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Naive Set Theory == The pronunciation of naïve is in two syllables, approximately naa-eeve, and means simple in the sense of unsophisticated. Try not to pronounce it nigh-yeeve. In natural language it is usually used in the sense of lacking worldly wisdom. The correct rendition of the word naïve is with a on the i, that is: ï. This has the effect of indicating that the pair of letters involved need to be pronounced as separate syllables. Spelt naive, the word would be expected to be pronounced something more like nave.

title: Definition:Name
snippet: Proper Name: a symbol used to identify a particular object uniquely (otherwise known as a constant or parameter). Arbitrary Name: a symbol assigned to an arbitrarily selected object from a given universe. The context in which these definitions are understood is predicate logic.

title: Definition:Napier's Bones
snippet: Napier's Rods Napier's bones is a device for performing the operation of multiplication of numbers. The device consists of: a set of rods, one for each digit $0$ to $9$, containing the multiples of that number, again from $0$ to $9$, in a column, written as $2$ digits, divided by a diagonal line. a board upon which the rods can be placed, labeled $1$ to $9$ down a column on the left hand side, each digit corresponding to the numbers on the rods The multiplicand is assembled by placing the rods for each of its digit next to each other on the board.

title: Definition:Napierian Logarithm
snippet: The Napierian logarithms are a system of logarithms where: $\log_{\text {Nap} } 10 \, 000 \, 000 = 0$ $\log_{\text {Nap} } 9 \, 999 \, 999 = 1$ Thus: $\log_{\text {Nap} } 10^7 x y = \log_{\text {Nap} } x + \log_{\text{Nap} } y$

title: Definition:Nash Equilibrium
snippet: Let a strategic game $G$ be modelled by: $G = \stratgame N {A_i} {\succsim_i}$ A Nash equilibrium of $G$ is a profile $a^* \in A$ of moves which has the property that: $\forall i \in N: \forall a_i \in A_i: \tuple {a^*_{-i}, a^*_i} \succsim_i \tuple {a^*_{-i}, a_i}$ Thus, for $a^*$ to be a Nash equilibrium, no player $i$ has a move yielding a preferable outcome to that when $a^*_i$ is chosen, given that every other player $j$ has chosen his own equilibrium move. That is, no player can profitably deviate, if no other player also deviates.

title: Definition:Natural Deduction
snippet: Natural deduction is a technique for deducing valid sequents from other valid sequents by applying precisely defined proof rules, by a technique called logical inference. As such, natural deduction forms a proof system, which is focused on practical applicability.

title: Definition:Natural Deduction/Also known as
snippet: == Natural Deduction: Also known as == Natural deduction is seen under various less precise names, for example decision procedure or decision method. Some sources call it the axiomatic method.

title: Definition:Natural Deduction/Motivation
snippet: == Natural Deduction: Motivation == In its practical applicability, natural deduction differs from most proof systems in literature, which are more pedantic and formalistic, but therefore also more rigorous. One may interpret natural deduction as the full-fledged proof system to actually use, once a formalistic alternative has been proved to satisfy all the rules of inference of natural deduction. In doing so, it no longer matters which exact formalism was employed, and one can focus on the mathematical content itself.

title: Definition:Natural Filtration/Continuous Time
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\sequence {X_t}_{t \ge 0}$ be an $\hointr 0 \infty$-indexed family of real-valued random variables. We define the natural filtration $\sequence {\FF_t^X}_{t \ge 0}$ by: $\FF_t^X = \map \sigma {X_s : s \le t}$ for each $t \in \hointr 0 \infty$, where $\map \sigma {X_s : s \le t}$ is the $\sigma$-algebra generated by the family $\set {X_s : s \le t}$.

title: Definition:Natural Filtration/Discrete Time
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\sequence {X_n}_{n \ge 0}$ be a sequence of real-valued random variables. We define the natural filtration $\sequence {\FF_n^X}_{n \ge 0}$ by: $\FF_n^X = \map \sigma {X_0, X_1, \ldots, X_n}$ for each $n \ge 0$, where $\map \sigma {X_0, X_1, \ldots, X_n}$ is the $\sigma$-algebra generated by $\sequence {X_0, X_1, \ldots, X_n}$.

title: Definition:Natural Frequency
snippet: Consider a physical system $S$ whose behaviour can be described with the second order ODE in the form: $(1): \quad \dfrac {\d^2 x} {\d t^2} + 2 b \dfrac {\d x} {\d t} + a^2 x = 0$ for $a, b \in \R_{>0}$. Let $b < a$, so as to make $S$ underdamped. 600px The natural frequency $\nu$ of $S$ is defined as: $\nu = \dfrac 1 T$ where $T$ is the period of the oscillation of $S$.

title: Definition:Natural Isomorphism
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be categories.

title: Definition:Natural Isomorphism between Covariant Functors
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be categories. Let $F, G : \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be covariant functors.

title: Definition:Natural Isomorphism between Covariant Functors/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be categories. Let $F, G : \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be covariant functors. A natural isomorphism from $F$ to $G$ is a natural transformation $\eta : F \to G$ such that for all $X \in \mathbf C$, $\eta_X : FX \to GX$ is an isomorphism in $\mathbf D$.

title: Definition:Natural Isomorphism between Covariant Functors/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be categories. Let $F, G : \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be covariant functors. A natural isomorphism from $F$ to $G$ is an isomorphism in the functor category $\operatorname{Funct}(\mathbf C, \mathbf D)$. That is, a natural transformation $\eta : F \to G$ for which there exists a natural transformation $\xi : G \to F$ such that the compositions $\xi \circ \eta = \operatorname{id}_F$ and $\eta \circ \xi = \operatorname{id}_G$ are identity natural transformations.

title: Definition:Natural Isomorphism between Covariant Functors/Inverse
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be categories. Let $F, G : \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be covariant functors. Let $\eta : F \to G$ and $\xi : G \to F$ be natural transformations such that the compositions $\xi \circ \eta = \operatorname{id}_F$ and $\eta \circ \xi = \operatorname{id}_G$ are identity natural transformations. Then: $\xi$ is called the inverse (natural isomorphism) of $\eta$ $\eta$ is called the inverse (natural isomorphism) of $\xi$

title: Definition:Natural Language
snippet: A natural language is one of the conventional, everyday languages in which people usually communicate. Although there are many natural languages in the world, we are not generally going to distinguish between them, merely lumping them all into the one concept. When natural language is referred to on , it will usually mean English.

snippet: == Natural Logarithm: Also known as == The natural logarithm is sometimes referred to as the Napierian logarithm for , although this name is rare nowadays. It needs to be noted that the Napierian logarithm proper was in fact a different construction. Some sources call it the hyperbolic logarithm.

title: Definition:Natural Logarithm/Complex/Definition 1
snippet: Let $z = r e^{i \theta}$ be a complex number expressed in exponential form such that $z \ne 0$. The complex natural logarithm of $z \in \C_{\ne 0}$ is the multifunction defined as: $\map \ln z := \set {\map \ln r + i \paren {\theta + 2 k \pi}: k \in \Z}$ where $\map \ln r$ is the natural logarithm of the (strictly) positive real number $r$.

title: Definition:Natural Logarithm/Complex/Definition 2
snippet: Let $z \in \C_{\ne 0}$ be a non-zero complex number. The complex natural logarithm of $z$ is the multifunction defined as: $\map \ln z := \set {w \in \C: \exp w = z}$

title: Definition:Natural Logarithm/Complex/Principal Branch
snippet: The principal branch of the complex natural logarithm is usually defined in one of two ways: {{eqn | l = \map \Ln z | r = \map \ln r + i \theta | c = for $\theta \in \hointr 0 {2 \pi}$ }} {{eqn | l = \map \Ln z | r = \map \ln r + i \theta | c = for $\theta \in \hointl {-\pi} \pi$ }} It is important to specify which is in force during a particular exposition.

title: Definition:Natural Logarithm/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Natural Logarithm == The natural logarithm was discovered by accident by in around $1590$, evolving from his invention of the Napierian logarithm as a tool for multiplication of numbers by addition. He had no concept of the notion of the base of a logarithm and certainly did not use Euler's number $e$.

title: Definition:Natural Logarithm/Notation
snippet: The notation for the natural logarithm function is misleadingly inconsistent throughout the literature. It is written variously as: $\ln z$ $\log z$ $\Log z$ $\log_e z$ The first of these is commonly encountered, and is the preferred form on . However, many who consider themselves serious mathematicians believe this notation to be unsophisticated. The second and third are ambiguous (it doesn't tell you which base it is the logarithm of). While the fourth option is more verbose than the others, there is no confusion about exactly what is meant.

title: Definition:Natural Logarithm/Positive Real/Definition 1
snippet: The (natural) logarithm of $x$ is the real-valued function defined on $\R_{>0}$ as: $\ds \forall x \in \R_{>0}: \ln x := \int_1^x \frac {\d t} t$

title: Definition:Natural Logarithm/Positive Real/Definition 2
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number such that $x > 0$. The (natural) logarithm of $x$ is defined as: $\ln x := y \in \R: e^y = x$ where $e$ is Euler's number. That is: $\ln x = \log_e x$

title: Definition:Natural Logarithm/Positive Real/Definition 3
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number such that $x > 0$. The (natural) logarithm of $x$ is defined as: $\ds \ln x := \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} n \paren {\sqrt [n] x - 1}$

title: Definition:Natural Numbers/Also known as
snippet: == Natural Numbers: Also known as == The natural numbers, particularly the set $\set {1, 2, 3, \ldots}$ of non-zero natural numbers, are also known as counting numbers, especially in elementary school. Some sources refer to them as positive integers, often with the implicit understanding that this means strictly positive integers, without actually being specific. Some sources refer to the natural numbers as whole numbers, but that term is also often given to the integers. The term proper numbers can sometimes be seen in popular literature.

title: Definition:Natural Numbers/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Natural Numbers == The natural numbers were the first numbers to be considered. Their earliest use was in the sense of ordinal numbers, when they were used for counting. The origin of the name natural numbers (considered by some authors to be a misnomer) originates with the Ancient Greeks, for whom the only numbers were the strictly positive integers $1, 2, 3, \ldots$ It is customary at this stage to quote the famous of , translated from the German in various styles, for example: God created the natural numbers, and all the rest is the work of man.

title: Definition:Natural Numbers/Inductive Set Definition
snippet: Let $x$ be a set which is an element of every inductive set. Then $x$ is a natural number.

title: Definition:Natural Numbers/Inductive Sets in Real Numbers
snippet: Let $\R$ be the set of real numbers. Let $\II$ be the set of all inductive sets defined as subsets of $\R$. Then the natural numbers $\N$ are defined as: $\N := \ds \bigcap \II$ where $\ds \bigcap$ denotes intersection. It follows from the definition of inductive set that according to this definition, $0 \notin \N$.

title: Definition:Natural Numbers/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Natural Numbers == The words for the individual natural numbers in ancient languages which have now been supplanted by newer ones have in some cases survived in remote places for special purposes. The traditional system of numbers used for counting sheep in certain locales in the British Isles is one example: Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Natural Numbers/Non-Zero
snippet: The natural numbers are often defined so as to exclude zero: The set $\N \setminus \set 0$ is denoted $\N_{>0}$: $\N_{>0} = \set {1, 2, 3, \ldots}$

title: Definition:Natural Numbers/Notation
snippet: == Informal Definition == The notation for the set of natural numbers varies in the literature. Some sources use a different style of letter from $\N$: you will find $N$, $\mathbf N$, etc. However, $\N$ is commonplace and all but universal. The usual symbol for denoting $\set {1, 2, 3, \ldots}$ is $\N^*$, but the more explicit $\N_{>0}$ is standard on . Some authors refer to $\set {0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots}$ as $\tilde \N$, and refer to $\set {1, 2, 3, \ldots}$ as $\N$. Either is valid, and as long as it is clear which is which, it does not matter which is used.

title: Definition:Natural Numbers/Von Neumann Construction
snippet: Let $\omega$ denote the minimally inductive set. The natural numbers can be defined as the elements of $\omega$. Following Definition 2 of $\omega$, this amounts to defining the natural numbers as the finite ordinals. In terms of the empty set $\O$ and successor sets, we thus define: {{eqn | l = 0 | o = := | r = \O = \set {} | c = }} {{eqn | l = 2 | o = := | r = 1^+ = 1 \cup \set 1 = \set {0, 1} | c = }} {{eqn | l = 3 | o = := | r = 2^+ = 2 \cup \set 2 = \set {0, 1, 2} | c = }} This can be expressed in detail as: {{eqn | l = 0 | o = := | r = \O = \set {} | c = }} {{eqn | l = 2 | o = := | r =…

title: Definition:Natural Numbers/Von Neumann Construction/Successor Mapping
snippet: Let $\omega$ denote the minimally inductive set. Let the natural numbers $\N$ be modelled using the Von Neumann construction as the elements of $\omega$: {{eqn | l = 0 | o = := | r = \O = \set {} | c = }} {{eqn | l = 2 | o = := | r = 1^+ = 1 \cup \set 1 = \set {0, 1} | c = }} {{eqn | l = 3 | o = := | r = 2^+ = 2 \cup \set 2 = \set {0, 1, 2} | c = }} The mapping $s: \N \to \N$ defined thus as: $\forall n \in \N: \map s n = n + 1$ is the successor mapping on $\N$.

title: Definition:Natural Numbers/Zermelo Construction
snippet: The natural numbers $\N = \set {0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots}$ can be defined as a series of subsets: $0 := \O = \set {}$ $1 := \set 0 = \set \O$ $2 := \set 1 = \set {\set \O}$ $3 := \set 2 = \set {\set {\set \O} }$ $\vdots$ Thus the natural number $n$ consists of $\O$ enclosed in $n$ pairs of braces.

title: Definition:Natural Numbers/Zermelo Construction/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Zermelo Construction of Natural Numbers == The Zermelo construction of natural numbers was devised by . While the approach is simple, it does not generalize easily to transfinite ordinals. As a result, it is generally considered inferior to the von Neumann construction, which has considerable advantages over it. Hence this approach is rarely seen, and noted for historical reasons only.

title: Definition:Natural Place
snippet: According to the ancient Greek philosophers, everything had a position in the universe where it was most comfortable. That position was referred to as its natural place. Hence, when displaced from its natural place, it would eagerly try to return to that natural place. Hence: a stone, being made of earth, when released from a hand holding it in midair, will push downwards in order to return as soon as possible to the centre of the universe, that is, Earth.

Some sources lose the hyphen: natural subbasis of product topology.

title: Definition:Natural Transformation/Contravariant Functors
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be categories. Let $F, G: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be contravariant functors. A natural transformation $\eta$ from $F$ to $G$ is a mapping on $\mathbf C$ such that: $(1): \quad$ For all $X \in \mathbf C$, $\eta_X$ is a morphism from $F X$ to $G X$ in $\mathbf D$. $(2): \quad$ For all $X, Y \in \mathbf C$ and morphism $f: X \to Y$, the following diagram commutes: $\quad \quad \xymatrix{ F X \ar[d]^{\eta_X} & F Y \ar[d]^{\eta_Y} \ar[l]^{F f} \\ G X & G Y \ar[l]^{G f} }$

title: Definition:Natural Transformation/Covariant Functors
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be categories. Let $F, G : \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be covariant functors. A natural transformation $\eta$ from $F$ to $G$, denoted $\eta: F \to G$, consists of: {{axiom | lc = $\quad \quad \xymatrix{ F X \ar[d]^{\eta_X} \ar[r]^{F f} & F Y \ar[d]^{\eta_Y} \\ G X \ar[r]^{G f} & G Y}$ }}

title: Definition:Natural Transformation/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Natural Transformation == The concept of a natural transformation was introduced by and . It came about during their investigations into vector spaces and their algebraic duals.

title: Definition:Naturally Ordered Semigroup
snippet: The concept of a naturally ordered semigroup is intended to capture the behaviour of the natural numbers $\N$, addition $+$ and the ordering $\le$ as they pertain to $\N$.

title: Definition:Naturally Totally Ordered Semigroup
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ, \preceq}$ be a right naturally totally ordered semigroup and a left naturally totally ordered semigroup. Then $\struct {S, \circ, \preceq}$ is a naturally totally ordered semigroup.

title: Definition:Nautical Mile
snippet: The nautical mile is a unit of length which is used for air and sea navigation. It was originally defined as the length measured along Earth's surface of one minute of latitude along a meridian. It is now defined as exactly $1852$ metres.

title: Definition:Nautical Mile/Also known as
snippet: == Nautical Mile: Also known as == Some sources refer to the nautical mile as the international nautical mile.

title: Definition:Nautical Mile/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Nautical Mile: Conversion Factors ==

title: Definition:Nautical Mile/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Nautical Mile == The concept of defining base units of measurement based on the dimensions of Earth appears to have been introduced by . In the early $1600$s he proposed the nautical mile as one minute of arc, or $\dfrac 1 {60}$ of a degree of latitude on Earth's surface. However, as Earth is not perfectly spherical, but an oblate spheroid, one minute of latitude is not constant. At the equator it is about $1843$ metres, but at the poles it is about $1861$ metres.

title: Definition:Navier-Stokes Equations
snippet: The Navier-Stokes equations are a set of partial differential equations that model the flow of fluid in space. Let $F$ be an ideal incompressible fluid. Let $\map {\mathbf v} {\mathbf x, t}$ be the velocity of $F$ at point $\mathbf x$ and time $t$. Let $\map p {\mathbf x, t}$ be the pressure of $F$ at point $\mathbf x$ and time $t$.

title: Definition:Navigation
snippet: Navigation is the science of identifying location and optimal direction of travel. That is, working out where you are and where you want to go. The context is usually assumed to be on the sea, although the word can be used either figuratively, or in the context of space travel. Category:Definitions/Navigation Category:Definitions/Geographical Coordinates Category:Definitions/Geography

title: Definition:Near-Repdigit Prime
snippet: A near-repdigit prime is a prime number with at least $3$ digits such that all digits are the same except one.

title: Definition:Nearest-Neighbor Decoding
snippet: Nearest-neighbor decoding is a technique for decoding whereby an inadmissible codeword is replaced by the codeword closest to it measured by Hamming distance.

title: Definition:Nearest-Neighbor Decoding/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Nearest-Neighbor Decoding == Nearest-neighbor decoding is rendered in British English as nearest-neighbour decoding.

title: Definition:Nearest Integer Function
snippet: The nearest integer function is defined as: $\forall x \in \R: \nint x = \begin {cases} \floor {x + \dfrac 1 2} & : x \notin 2 \Z + \dfrac 1 2 \\ x - \dfrac 1 2 & : x \in 2 \Z + \dfrac 1 2 \end{cases}$ where $\floor x$ is the floor function.

snippet: == Necessity Operator: Also denoted as == The necessity operator can also be seen in the form $\map {\mathrm L} P$: $\map {\mathrm L} P : \iff \forall w: \map P w$ for some proposition $P$ dependent on some world $w$.
