snippet: Let $\innerprod E F$ be a dual system over $\R$. Let $B \subseteq F$ be non-empty. We define the one-sided prepolar $B_\odot$ of $B$ by: $B_\odot = \set {x \in E : \innerprod x f \le 1 \text { for all } f \in B}$

title: Definition:One-Sided Shift of Finite Type
snippet: Let $k \in \Z_{\ge 2}$. Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{kk}$ be a logical matrix. Let $\Sigma = \set {1, 2, \ldots, k}$. Let: $X_\mathbf A ^+ = \set {x = \sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N} : x_n \in \Sigma, a_{x_n, x_{n + 1} } = 1}$ Let $\sigma : X_\mathbf A ^+ \to X_\mathbf A ^+$ be the forward shift operator. Then the pair $\struct {X _\mathbf A ^+, \sigma}$ is called a one-sided shift of finite type.

title: Definition:One-Tail Test
snippet: Let $\delta$ be a hypothesis test. Let $H_0$ and $H_1$ be the null hypothesis and alternative hypothesis of $\delta$ respectively. Let $\theta$ be the test statistic which is being used to determine whether $H_0$ or $H_1$ holds. Let $H_1$ be a one-sided alternative. Then $\delta$ is known as a one-tail test.

title: Definition:One-Time Pad
snippet: A one-time pad is a method of encryption which relies on a random key being used for a single message only.

title: Definition:One-Way Classification
snippet: One-way classification is the simplest analysis of variance technique, in which treatments are allocated randomly to experimental units.

title: Definition:One-to-Many Relation
snippet: A relation $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ is one-to-many : $\RR \subseteq S \times T: \forall y \in \Img \RR: \tuple {x_1, y} \in \RR \land \tuple {x_2, y} \in \RR \implies x_1 = x_2$ That is, every element of the image of $\RR$ is related to by exactly one element of its domain. Note that the condition on $t$ concerns the elements in the image, not the codomain. Thus a one-to-many relation may leave some element(s) of the codomain unrelated.

title: Definition:One-to-Many Relation/Also known as
snippet: == One-to-Many Relation: Also known as == A one-to-many relation is also known as: a one-many relation an injective relation a left-unique relation a single-rooted relation a one-many correspondence

title: Definition:One-to-One
snippet: One-to-One Mapping, otherwise known as an injection. One-to-One Relation.

title: Definition:One-to-One Relation
snippet: A relation $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ is one-to-one if it is both many-to-one and one-to-many. That is, every element of the domain of $\RR$ relates to no more than one element of its codomain, and every element of the image is related to by exactly one element of its domain.

title: Definition:One (Cardinal)
snippet: The cardinal associated with the singleton $\set \O$ is called one, and is denoted $1$. More informally, this means that one is defined as being the number of elements in a singleton set.

title: Definition:One (Category)
snippet: The category one $\mathbf 1$, is the category with: {{DefineCategory |ob = One object: $*$ |mor = One morphism: the identity morphism $\operatorname{id}_*$. }}

title: Definition:One (Ordinal)
snippet: The ordinal $1$ is defined as: $1 = 0^+$ where $0^+$ denotes the successor of the ordinal $0$.

title: Definition:One Hundred Fowls Problem
snippet: One Hundred Fowls problems are variants of the classic problem:

title: Definition:One Hundred Fowls Problem/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on One Hundred Fowls Problem == According to , One Hundred Fowls problems originated in Chinese texts sometime around the $5$th century CE. However, note that the from India contains one such; while it is possible that it dates to $3$rd century, this is debated. By the $9$th century this sort of problem was well-known throughout the world. It first appeared in European texts in by , where several such problems were posed.

title: Definition:Ones Matrix
snippet: A ones matrix is a matrix all of whose elements are $1$.

title: Definition:Ones Matrix/Square
snippet: A square ones matrix of order $n$ is a square matrix of order $n$ all of whose elements are $1$. It is often denoted $\mathbf J_n$. Category:Definitions/Examples of Matrices Category:Definitions/Square Matrices

title: Definition:Only If
snippet: To say that: a statement $p$ is true only if $q$ is true is to say that: $p$ is a sufficient condition for $q$: Thus: $p \ \text{only if} \ q \dashv \vdash p \implies q$

title: Definition:Open
snippet: Predicate Logic: an open statement is a statement which contains at least one free occurrence of a variable. Topology: Open set: A set $U$ in a topological space $\left({S, \tau}\right)$ such that $U \in \tau$. Open mapping: A mapping $f: T_1 \to T_2$ from a topological space $T_1$ to another $T_2$ which maps open sets in $T_1$ to open sets in $T_2$. Open cover: A cover consisting of open sets. Open neighborhood: A neighborhood which is an open set.

title: Definition:Open Ball
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space or pseudometric space. Let $a \in A$. Let $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number. The open $\epsilon$-ball of $a$ in $M$ is defined as: $\map {B_\epsilon} a := \set {x \in A: \map d {x, a} < \epsilon}$ where $d$ is the distance function on $M$. If it is necessary to show the distance function itself, then the notation $\map {B_\epsilon} {a; d}$ can be used.

title: Definition:Open Ball/Also known as
snippet: == Terminology for Open Ball == There are various names and notations that can be found in the literature for this concept, for example: Open $\epsilon$-ball neighborhood of $a$ (and in deference to the word neighborhood the notation $\map {N_\epsilon} a$, $\map N {a, \epsilon}$ or $\map N {a; \epsilon}$ are often seen) Spherical neighborhood of $a$ Open sphere at $a$ Open $\epsilon$-ball centered at $a$ $\epsilon$-ball at $a$. Some sources use the \varepsilon symbol $\varepsilon$ instead of the \epsilon which is $\epsilon$.

title: Definition:Open Ball/Center
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space or pseudometric space. Let $a \in A$. Let $\map {B_\epsilon} a$ be the open $\epsilon$-ball of $a$. In $\map {B_\epsilon} a$, the value $a$ is referred to as the center of the open $\epsilon$-ball.

title: Definition:Open Ball/Normed Division Ring
snippet:
Let $\struct{R, 
orm {\,\cdot\,} }$ be a normed division ring. Let $a \in R$. Let $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number. The open $\epsilon$-ball of $a$ in $\struct {R, 
orm {\,\cdot\,} }$ is defined as: $\map {B_\epsilon} a = \set {x \in R: 
orm{x - a} < \epsilon}$ If it is necessary to show the norm itself, then the notation $\map {B_\epsilon} {a; 
orm {\,\cdot\,} }$ can be used.

title: Definition:Open Ball/Normed Division Ring/Center
snippet: Let $\struct {R, \norm {\,\cdot\,} }$ be a normed division ring. Let $a \in R$. Let $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number. Let $\map {B_\epsilon} a$ be the open $\epsilon$-ball of $a$. In $\map {B_\epsilon} a$, the value $a$ is referred to as the center of the open $\epsilon$-ball.

title: Definition:Open Ball/Normed Division Ring/Radius
snippet: Let $\struct {R, \norm{\,\cdot\,} }$ be a normed division ring. Let $a \in R$. Let $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number. Let $\map {B_\epsilon} a$ be the open $\epsilon$-ball of $a$. In $\map {B_\epsilon} a$, the value $\epsilon$ is referred to as the radius of the open $\epsilon$-ball.

title: Definition:Open Ball/Normed Vector Space
snippet:
Let $\struct {X, 
orm {\,\cdot\,} }$ be a normed vector space. Let $x \in X$. Let $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number. The open $\epsilon$-ball of $x$ in $\struct {X, 
orm {\,\cdot\,} }$ is defined as: $\map {B_\epsilon} x = \set {y \in X: 
orm{x - y} < \epsilon}$

title: Definition:Open Ball/P-adic Numbers
snippet:
Let $p$ be a prime number. Let $\struct {\Q_p, 
orm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$ be the $p$-adic numbers. Let $a \in R$. Let $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number. The open $\epsilon$-ball of $a$ in $\struct {\Q_p, 
orm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$ is defined as: $\map {B_\epsilon} a = \set {x \in \Q_p: 
orm{x - a}_p < \epsilon}$

title: Definition:Open Ball/P-adic Numbers/Center
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. Let $\struct {\Q_p, \norm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$ be the $p$-adic numbers. Let $a \in R$. Let $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number. Let $\map {B_\epsilon} a$ be the open $\epsilon$-ball of $a$. In $\map {B_\epsilon} a$, the value $a$ is referred to as the center of the open $\epsilon$-ball.

title: Definition:Open Ball/P-adic Numbers/Radius
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. Let $\struct {\Q_p, \norm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$ be the $p$-adic numbers. Let $a \in R$. Let $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number. Let $\map {B_\epsilon} a$ be the open $\epsilon$-ball of $a$. In $\map {B_\epsilon} a$, the value $\epsilon$ is referred to as the radius of the open $\epsilon$-ball.

title: Definition:Open Ball/Radius
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space or pseudometric space. Let $a \in A$. Let $\map {B_\epsilon} a$ be the open $\epsilon$-ball of $a$. In $\map {B_\epsilon} a$, the value $\epsilon$ is referred to as the radius of the open $\epsilon$-ball.

title: Definition:Open Ball/Real Analysis
snippet: Let $n \ge 1$ be a natural number. Let $\R^n$ denote the real Euclidean space of dimension $n$. Let $\norm {\, \cdot \,}$ denote the Euclidean norm. Let $a \in \R^n$. Let $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number. The open (Euclidean) ball of center $a$ and radius $\epsilon$ is the subset: $\map {B_\epsilon} a = \set {x \in \R^n : \norm {x - a} < \epsilon}$

title: Definition:Open Cover
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\CC$ be a cover for $S$. Then $\CC$ is an open cover (of $T$) : $\CC \subseteq \tau$ That is, all the elements of $\CC$ are open sets.

title: Definition:Open Cover/Also known as
snippet: == Open Cover: Also known as == Some sources refer to an open cover as an open covering.

title: Definition:Open Cover/Subset
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H$ be a subset of $S$. Let $\CC$ be a cover of $H$. Then $\CC$ is an open cover for $H$ : $\CC \subseteq \tau$ That is, all the elements of $\CC$ are open sets.

title: Definition:Open Curve
snippet: An open curve is a curve which has two endpoints.

title: Definition:Open Curve/Also known as
snippet: == Open Curve: Also known as == An open curve is also known as an arc, but that term is also used to mean a specific part of a curve. Hence arc will not be used on in that context.

title: Definition:Open Cylindrical Surface
snippet: An open cylindrical surface is a cylindrical surface whose directrix is an open curve.

title: Definition:Open Discrete Set of Subsets
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\UU$ be a set of subsets of $S$. Then $\UU$ is open discrete : $(1) \quad \UU \subseteq \tau$, that is, for all $U \in \UU: U$ is open in $T$ $(2) \quad \UU$ is discrete

title: Definition:Open Disk/Also known as
snippet: == Open Disk: Also known as == The spelling of open disk in British English is open disc.

title: Definition:Open Extension Topology
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $p$ be a new element which is not in $S$. Let $S^*_p = S \cup \set p$. Let $\tau^*_p$ be the set defined as: $\tau^*_{\bar p} = \set {U: U \in \tau} \cup \set {S^*_p}$ That is, $\tau^*_{\bar p}$ is the set of all sets formed by taking all the open sets of $\tau$ and adding to them the set $S^*_p$. Then: $\tau^*_{\bar p}$ is the open extension topology of $\tau$ and: $T^*_{\bar p} = \struct {S^*_p, \tau^*_{\bar p} }$ is the open extension space of $T = \struct {S, \tau}$.

title: Definition:Open Geodesic Ball in Riemannian Manifold
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space at $p \in M$. Let $\exp_p$ be the restricted exponential map. Let $\map {B_\epsilon} 0 \subseteq T_p M$ be the open ball in $T_p M$ with $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ such that $\exp_p$ is a diffeomorphism from $\map {B_\epsilon} 0$ to its image. Then the image set $\map {\exp_p} {\map {B_\epsilon} 0 }$ is called the open geodesic ball in $M$.

title: Definition:Open Interval/Also defined as
snippet: == Open Interval: Also defined as == Some sources, when defining an open interval, require that $a \preccurlyeq b$ or $a \prec b$. Category:Definitions/Intervals

title: Definition:Open Interval/Technical Note
snippet: == Technical Note on Open Interval == {{LatexFor|for = \openint {a} {b} }} This is a custom command designed to implement Wirth interval notation. Category:Technical Notes

title: Definition:Open Invariant
snippet: Let $P$ be a property whose domain is the set of all topological spaces. Suppose that whenever $\map P T$ holds, then so does $\map P {T'}$, where: $T$ and $T'$ are topological spaces $\phi: T \to T'$ is a mapping from $T$ to $T'$ $\phi \sqbrk T = T'$, where $\phi \sqbrk T$ denotes the image of $\phi$ $T'$ is an open set. Then $P$ is an open invariant. Loosely, an open invariant is a property which is preserved in the open image of a mapping.

title: Definition:Open Locally Finite Set of Subsets
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\UU$ be a set of subsets of $S$. Then $\UU$ is open locally finite :

title: Definition:Open Mapping
snippet: Let $\struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $\struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping. Then $f$ is said to be an open mapping : $\forall U \in \tau_1: f \sqbrk U \in \tau_2$ where $f \sqbrk U$ denotes the image of $U$ under $f$.

title: Definition:Open Neighborhood
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $A \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. Let $N_A$ be a neighborhood of $A$. Let: $N_A \in \tau$ That is, let $N_A$ itself be an open set of $T$. Then $N_A$ is called an open neighborhood of $A$ in $T$.

title: Definition:Open Neighborhood/Point
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $x \in S$ be a point of $S$. Let $N_x$ be a neighborhood of $x$ in $T$. Let: $N_x \in \tau$ That is, let $N_x$ itself be an open set of $T$. Then $N_x$ is called an open neighborhood of $x$ in $T$.

title: Definition:Open Neighborhood/Real Analysis/Real Euclidean Space
snippet: Let $n \ge 1$ be a natural number. Let $x \in \R^n$. Let $I \subseteq \R$ be a subset. Then $I$ is an open neighborhood of $x$ $I$ is open and $I$ is a neighborhood of $x$. Category:Definitions/Open Neighborhoods Category:Definitions/Real Euclidean Spaces

title: Definition:Open Neighborhood/Real Analysis/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number. Let $I \subseteq \R$ be a subset. Then $I$ is an open neighborhood of $x$ $I$ is open and $I$ is a neighborhood of $x$. Category:Definitions/Open Neighborhoods Category:Definitions/Real Numbers

title: Definition:Open Point
snippet: Let $T = \left({S, \tau}\right)$ be a topological space. Let $p \in S$ such that $\left\{{p}\right\} \in \tau$. That is, let $\left\{{p}\right\}$ be an open set of $T$. Then $p$ is an open point of $T$.

title: Definition:Open Rectangle
snippet: Let $n \ge 1$ be a natural number. Let $a_1, \ldots, a_n, b_1, \ldots, b_n$ be real numbers. The Cartesian product: $\ds \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n \openint {a_i} {b_i} = \openint {a_1} {b_1} \times \cdots \times \openint {a_n} {b_n} \subseteq \R^n$ is called an open rectangle in $\R^n$ or open $n$-rectangle. The collection of all open $n$-rectangles is denoted $\JJ_o$, or $\JJ_o^n$ if the dimension $n$ is to be emphasized.

title: Definition:Open Rectangle/Degenerate Case
snippet: In the case where $a_i \ge b_i$ for some $i$, the open rectangle $\ds \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n \openint {a_i} {b_i}$ degenerates to the empty set $\O$. This is in accordance with the result Cartesian Product is Empty iff Factor is Empty for general Cartesian products. Category:Definitions/Open Rectangles

title: Definition:Open Rectangle/Notation
snippet: == Open Rectangle: Notation == A convenient notation for the open rectangle $\ds \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n \openint {a_i} {b_i}$ is $\openrect {\mathbf a} {\mathbf b}$.

title: Definition:Open Rectangle/Technical Note
snippet: == Technical Note on Open Rectangle == {{LatexFor|for = \openrect {\mathbf a} {\mathbf b} }} This is a custom command designed to implement Wirth interval notation and its derivatives. Category:Technical Notes

title: Definition:Open Refinement
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\UU$ and $\VV$ be covers of $S$. Then $\VV$ is an open refinement of $\UU$ : That is:

title: Definition:Open Region/Also known as
snippet: == Open Region: Also known as == An open region is referred to by some sources as a domain. However, this conflicts with the concept of domain in the context of mappings and relations. Therefore, the policy is always to use the term open region for this concept, as to avoid possible confusion.

title: Definition:Open Region/Complex
snippet: Let $D \subseteq \C$ be a subset of the set of complex numbers. $D$ is an open region of $\C$ $D$ is: $(1): \quad$ An open set and $(2): \quad$ connected.

title: Definition:Open Region/Plane
snippet: An open region is a region without its boundary, i.e. the interior of such a region. Category:Definitions/Analytic Geometry

title: Definition:Open Set/Complex Analysis/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S \subseteq \C$ be a subset of the set of complex numbers. Let: $\forall z_0 \in S: \exists \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \map {N_{\epsilon} } {z_0} \subseteq S$ where $\map {N_{\epsilon} } {z_0}$ is the $\epsilon$-neighborhood of $z_0$ for $\epsilon$. Then $S$ is an open set (of $\C$), or open (in $\C$). Note that $\epsilon$ may depend on $z_0$.

title: Definition:Open Set/Complex Analysis/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S \subseteq \C$ be a subset of the set of complex numbers. Then $S$ is an open set (of $\C$), or open (in $\C$) every point of $S$ is an interior point.

title: Definition:Open Set/Metric Space
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. Let $U \subseteq A$. Then $U$ is an open set in $M$ it is a neighborhood of each of its elements. That is: $\forall y \in U: \exists \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \map {B_\epsilon} y \subseteq U$ where $\map {B_\epsilon} y$ is the open $\epsilon$-ball of $y$. That is, for every point $y$ in $U$, we can find an $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$, dependent on that $y$, such that the open $\epsilon$-ball of $y$ lies entirely inside $U$. Another way of saying the same thing is that one can not get out of $U$ by moving an arbitrarily small distance from any point in $U$.

title: Definition:Open Set/Normed Vector Space
snippet: Let $V = \struct {X, \norm {\,\cdot\,} }$ be a normed vector space. Let $U \subseteq X$. Then $U$ is an open set in $V$ : $\forall x \in U: \exists \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \map {B_\epsilon} x \subseteq U$ where $\map {B_\epsilon} x$ is the open $\epsilon$-ball of $x$.

title: Definition:Open Set/Pseudometric Space
snippet: Let $P = \struct {A, d}$ be a pseudometric space. An open set in $P$ is defined in exactly the same way as for a metric space: $U$ is an open set in $P$ : $\forall y \in U: \exists \map \epsilon y > 0: \map {B_\epsilon} y \subseteq U$ where $\map {B_\epsilon} y$ is the open $\epsilon$-ball of $y$.

title: Definition:Open Set/Real Analysis/Real Euclidean Space
snippet: Let $n \ge 1$ be a natural number. Let $U \subseteq \R^n$ be a subset. Then $U$ is open (in $\R^n$) : $\forall x \in U : \exists R \in \R_{>0}: \map B {x, R} \subset U$ where $\map B {x, R}$ denotes the open Euclidean ball of radius $R$ centered at $x$.

title: Definition:Open Set/Real Analysis/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $I \subseteq \R$ be a subset of the set of real numbers. Then $I$ is open (in $\R$) : $\forall x_0 \in I: \exists \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \openint {x_0 - \epsilon} {x_0 + \epsilon} \subseteq I$ where $\openint {x_0 - \epsilon} {x_0 + \epsilon}$ is an open interval. Note that $\epsilon$ may depend on $x_0$.

title: Definition:Open Set/Topology
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Then the elements of $\tau$ are called the open sets of $T$. Thus: $U \in \tau$ and: $U$ is open in $T$ are equivalent statements.

title: Definition:Open Set (Metric Space)/Also known as
snippet: == Open Set (Metric Space): Also known as == An open set in a metric space $M = \struct {A, d}$ can also be referred to as: an open set of $M$ open in $M$ a $d$-open set $d$-open. An open set in $M$ is sometimes seen written as open subset of $A$.

title: Definition:Open Set (Neighborhood Space)
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \NN}$ be a neighborhood space. Let $U \subseteq S$ be a neighborhood of each of its elements. Then $U$ is an open set of $S$.

title: Definition:Open Sigma-Discrete Set of Subsets
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\UU$ be a set of subsets of $S$. Then $\UU$ is open $\sigma$-discrete : $(1) \quad \UU \subseteq \tau$, that is, for all $U \in \UU: U$ is open in $T$ $(2) \quad \UU$ is $\sigma$-discrete.

title: Definition:Open Sigma-Locally Finite Set of Subsets
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\UU$ be a set of subsets of $S$. Then $\UU$ is open sigma-locally finite : $(1) \quad \UU \subseteq \tau$, that is, for all $U \in \UU: U$ is open in $T$ $(2) \quad \UU$ is $\sigma$-locally finite

title: Definition:Open Statement
snippet: Let $P$ be a statement. $P$ is an open statement $P$ contains at least one free occurrence of a variables that appears in it.

title: Definition:Open Statement/Also known as
snippet: == Open Statement: Also known as == An open statement can also be seen referred to as an open sentence. The word formula can also be seen.

title: Definition:Open Subscheme
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ be a scheme. Let $U \subset X$ be an open subset. Then the open subscheme defined by $U$ is the restriction $\struct {U, \OO_X {\restriction_U}}$ of $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ to $U$.

title: Definition:Open Subset in Strong Operator Topology
snippet:
Let $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ and $\struct {Y, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_Y}$ be normed vector spaces. Let $\map {CL} {X, Y}$ be a continuous linear transformation space. Let $	au$ be the strong operator topology on $\map {CL} {X, Y}$. Suppose $U \subseteq \map {CL} {X, Y}$ is an open subset such that: $ orall T \in U : \exists \epsilon \in \R_{>0} : \exists n \in \N :  orall k \in \N : k \le n : \exists x_k \in X : \set {S \in \map {CL} {X, Y} :  orall i \in \N : i \le n : 
orm {S x_i - T x_i}_Y < \epsilon } \subseteq U$ Then $U$ is called an open subset in $	au$.

title: Definition:Open Subset in Uniform Operator Topology
snippet:
Let $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ and $\struct {Y, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_Y}$ be normed vector spaces. Let $\map {CL} {X, Y}$ be a continuous linear transformation space. Let $
orm {\, \cdot \,}$ be the supremum operator norm. Let $	au$ be the uniform operator topology induced by $\struct {\map {CL} {X, Y}, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}}$. Suppose $U \subseteq \map {CL} {X, Y}$ is an open subset such that: $ orall T \in U : \exists \epsilon \in \R_{>0} : \set {S \in \map {CL} {X, Y} : 
orm {S - T} < \epsilon} \subseteq U$ Then $U$ is called an open subset in $	au$.

title: Definition:Open Subset in Weak Operator Topology
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ and $\struct {Y, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_Y}$ be normed vector spaces. Let $\mathbb K = \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\map {CL} {X, Y}$ be a continuous linear transformation space. Let $\tau$ be the weak operator topology on $\map {CL} {X, Y}$. Suppose $U \subseteq \map {CL} {X, Y}$ is an open subset such that: $\forall T \in U : \exists \epsilon \in \R_{>0} : \exists n \in \N : \forall k \in \N : k \le n : \exists x_k \in X : \exists \phi_k \in \map {CL} {Y, \mathbb K} : \set {S \in \map {CL} {X, Y} : \forall i \in \N : i \le n : \size {\phi_i \paren{S x_i - T x_i}…

title: Definition:Opening Angle/Also known as
snippet: == Opening Angle: Also known as == The opening angle of a right circular cone is also known as: its aperture its semi-vertical angle.

title: Definition:Operating Characteristic Curve
snippet: An operating characteristic curve is a graph showing the probability of accepting a batch as a function of the proportion of defectives in that batch.

title: Definition:Operation
snippet: An operation is an object, identified by a symbol, which can be interpreted as a process which, from a number of objects, creates a new object.

title: Definition:Operation/Also known as
snippet: == Operation: Also known as == Some sources use the term algebraic operation.

title: Definition:Operation/Arity
snippet: The arity of an operation is the number of operands it uses. The arity of an operation may be, in general, any number. It may even be infinite.

title: Definition:Operation/Arity/Finitary
snippet: A finitary operation is an operation which takes a finite number of operands. Category:Definitions/Operations

title: Definition:Operation/Arity/Multiary
snippet: Certain types of operation have a variable number of operands. An operation which does not have a fixed arity is called multiary.

title: Definition:Operation/Arity/Ternary
snippet: A ternary operation (or three-place operation) is an operation which takes three operands. That is, its arity is $3$. Category:Definitions/Operations

title: Definition:Operation/Arity/Zero
snippet: It is possible to conceive of an operator which takes no operands. A constant can be considered as an operation which takes no operands. That is, it has an arity of zero. There are circumstances in mathematics and logic in which it is advantageous to do so.

title: Definition:Operation/Binary Operation
snippet: A binary operation is the special case of an operation where the operation has exactly two operands. A binary operation is a mapping $\circ$ from the Cartesian product of two sets $S \times T$ to a universal set $\mathbb U$: $\circ: S \times T \to \mathbb U: \map \circ {s, t} = y \in \mathbb U$ If $S = T$, then $\circ$ can be referred to as a binary operation on $S$.

title: Definition:Operation/Binary Operation/Infix Notation
snippet: == Notation == Let $S, T, U$ be sets. Let $\circ: S \times T \to U$ be a binary operation. When $\map \circ {x, y} = z$, it is common to put the symbol for the operation between the two operands: $z = x \circ y$ This convention is called infix notation.

title: Definition:Operation/Binary Operation/Postfix Notation
snippet: Let $\circ: S \times T \to U$ be a binary operation. The convention that places the symbol for the operation after the two operands: $z = x y \mathop \circ$ is called postfix notation. In infix notation it would be presented as: $z = x \circ y$

title: Definition:Operation/Binary Operation/Prefix Notation
snippet: Let $\circ: S \times T \to U$ be a binary operation. The convention that places the symbol for the operation before the two operands: $z = \circ x y$ is called prefix notation.

title: Definition:Operation/Binary Operation/Product
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. Let $\circ$ be the operation on $\struct {S, \circ}$. Let $z = x \circ y$. Then $z$ is called the product of $x$ and $y$. This is an extension of the normal definition of product that is encountered in conventional arithmetic.

title: Definition:Operation/Binary Operation/Product/Left
snippet: Let $x$ and $y$ be elements which are operated on by a given operation $\circ$. The left-hand product of $x$ by $y$ is the product $y \circ x$.

title: Definition:Operation/Binary Operation/Product/Right
snippet: Let $x$ and $y$ be elements which are operated on by a given operation $\circ$. The right-hand product of $x$ by $y$ is the product $x \circ y$.

title: Definition:Operation/N-Ary Operation
snippet: Let $S_1, S_2, \dots, S_n$ be sets. Let $\circ: S_1 \times S_2 \times \ldots \times S_n \to \mathbb U$ be a mapping from the cartesian product $S_1 \times S_2 \times \ldots \times S_n$ to a universal set $\mathbb U$: That is, suppose that: $\circ: S_1 \times S_2 \times \ldots \times S_n \to \mathbb U: \forall \tuple {s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n} \in S_1 \times S_2 \times \ldots \times S_n: \map \circ {s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n} \in \mathbb U$ Then $\circ$ is an $n$-ary operation. Such an $n$-ary operation needs to be defined for all ordered tuples in $S_1 \times S_2 \times \ldots \times S_n$.

title: Definition:Operation/Operand
snippet: An operand is one of the objects on which an operation generates its new object.

title: Definition:Operation/Operation on Set
snippet: An $n$-ary operation on a set $S$ is an $n$-ary operation where: the domain is the cartesian space $S^n$ the codomain is $S$: $\odot: S^n \to S: \forall \tuple {s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n} \in S^n: \map \odot {s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n} \in S$ That is: an $n$-ary operation on $S$ needs to be defined for all tuples in $S^n$ the image of $\odot$ is itself in $S$.

title: Definition:Operation/Operator
snippet: An operator is a symbol used to identify an operation.

title: Definition:Operation/Unary Operation
snippet: A unary operation is the special case of an operation where the operation has exactly one operand. Thus, a unary operation on a set $S$ is a mapping whose domain and codomain are both $S$.

title: Definition:Operation Compatible with Set Equivalence
snippet: Let $F$ be a (unary) operation which can be applied to sets. Then $F$ is compatible with set equivalence : $F \sqbrk A = F \sqbrk B \iff A \sim B$ where: $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary sets $F \sqbrk A$ denotes the image of $A$ under $F$ $\sim$ denotes set equivalence.

title: Definition:Operation Induced by Direct Product
snippet: Let $\struct {S_1, \circ_1}$ and $\struct {S_2, \circ_2}$ be algebraic structures. Let $S = S_1 \times S_2$ be the cartesian product of $S_1$ and $S_2$. Then the operation induced on $S$ by $\circ_1$ and $\circ_2$ is the operation $\circ$ defined as: $\tuple {s_1, s_2} \circ \tuple {t_1, t_2} := \tuple {s_1 \circ_1 t_1, s_2 \circ_2 t_2}$ for all ordered pairs in $S$.

title: Definition:Operation Induced by Direct Product/General Definition
snippet: Let $\struct {S_1, \circ_1}, \struct {S_2, \circ_2}, \ldots, \struct {S_n, \circ_n}$ be algebraic structures. Let $\ds \SS_n = \prod_{k \mathop = 1}^n S_k$ be the cartesian product of $S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_n$. Then the operation induced on $\SS_n$ by $\circ_1, \ldots, \circ_n$ is the operation $\circledcirc_n$ defined as: $\tuple {s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n} \circledcirc_n \tuple {t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_n} := \begin{cases} s_1 \circ_1 t_1 & : n = 1 \\ \tuple {s_1 \circ_1 t_1, s_2 \circ_2 t_2} & : n = 2 \\ \tuple {\tuple {s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_{n - 1} } \circledcirc_{n - 1} \tuple {t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_{n…

title: Definition:Operation Induced by Injection
snippet: Let $\struct {T, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. Let $f: S \to T$ be an injection. Then the operation induced on $S$ by $f$ and $\circ$ is the binary operation $\circ_f$ on $S$ defined by: $\circ_f: S \times S \to S: x \circ_f y := \map {f^{-1} } {\map f x \circ \map f y}$

title: Definition:Operation Induced by Permutation
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure on a set $S$. Let $\sigma: S \to S$ be a permutation on $S$. Let $\circ_\sigma$ be the operation on $S$ defined as: $\forall x, y \in S: x \circ_\sigma y := \map \sigma {x \circ y}$ Then $\circ_\sigma$ is the operation (on $S$) induced by $\sigma$.

title: Definition:Operation Induced by Restriction
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a magma. Let $\struct {T, \circ} \subseteq \struct {S, \circ}$. That is, let $T$ be a subset of $S$ such that $\circ$ is closed in $T$. Then the restriction of $\circ$ to $T$, namely $\circ {\restriction_T}$, is called the (binary) operation induced on $T$ by $\circ$. Note that this definition applies only if $\struct {T, \circ}$ is closed, by which virtue it is a submagma of $\struct {S, \circ}$.

title: Definition:Operation Induced on Quotient Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. Let $\RR$ be a congruence relation on $\struct {S, \circ}$. Let $S / \RR$ be the quotient set of $S$ by $\RR$. The operation $\circ_\RR$ induced on $S / \RR$ by $\circ$ is defined as: $\eqclass x \RR \circ_\RR \eqclass y \RR = \eqclass {x \circ y} \RR$

title: Definition:Operations Research
snippet: Operations research is the branch of applied mathematics which studies the management of human organizations.

title: Definition:Operations Research/Also known as
snippet: == Operations Research: Also known as == Operations research is also known (usually in the UK) as operational research.

title: Definition:Operations on Polynomial Ring of Sequences
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $P \sqbrk R$ be the set of all sequences in $R$: $P \sqbrk R = \set {\sequence {r_0, r_1, r_2, \ldots} }$ such that each $r_i \in R$, and all but a finite number of terms is zero. The operations ring addition $\oplus$, ring negative, and ring product $\odot$ on $P \sqbrk R$ are defined as follows: {{axiom | n = 1 | lc= Ring Addition: | ml= \sequence {r_0, r_1, r_2, \ldots} \oplus \sequence {s_0, s_1, s_2, \ldots} | mo= = | mr= \sequence {r_0 + s_0, r_1 + s_1, r_2 + s_2, \ldots} | c = }} {{axiom | n = 2 | lc= Ring Negative: | ml= -\sequence {r_0, r_1,…

title: Definition:Operator Domain
snippet: An operator domain is a notational tool for indexing a collection of operations on a set. Formally, an operator domain is a set $\Omega$ together with a mapping $a : \Omega \to \N_0$. We also use the notation, for $n \in \N_0$, $\Omega(n) = \{\omega \in \Omega : a(\omega) = n \}$. The elements of $\Omega$ are operators. If $\omega \in \Omega$, then $a(\omega)$ is the arity of the operator $\omega$. The elements of $\Omega(n)$ are the $n$-ary operators of $\Omega$.

title: Definition:Operator Generated by Ordered Subset
snippet: Let $L = \struct {X, \precsim}$ be an ordered set. Let $S = \struct {T, \preceq}$ be an ordered subset of $L$. The operator generated by ordered set $S$ is defined by $\forall x \in X: \map {\map {\operatorname {operator} } S} x := \map {\inf_L} {x^\succeq \cap T}$ where $x^\succeq$ denotes the upper closure of $x$.

title: Definition:Operator Norm
snippet: Let $\HH$ be a Hilbert space. Let $A: \HH \to \HH$ be a bounded linear operator. Let $\norm A$ be the norm of $A$. Then $\norm A$ is referred to as the operator norm on $A$. Category:Definitions/Hilbert Spaces

title: Definition:Operator Theory
snippet: Operator theory is the study of linear operators on function spaces, beginning with differential operators and integral operators.

title: Definition:Operator of Integrated Weighted Derivatives
snippet: Let $n \in \N$. Let $a_i : \closedint a b \to \R$ be Riemann integrable functions. Let $h \in \CC^n \closedint a b$ be a Riemann integrable real-valued function of differentiability class $n$. Then the operator of integrated weighted derivatives is defined as: $\ds \map L h := \int_a^b \sum_{i \mathop = 0}^n \map {a_i} t \map {h^{\paren i} } t \rd t$ where $\ds \int_a^b \map f t \rd t$ denotes the Riemann integral, and $h^{\paren i}$ is the $i$-th derivative of $h$.

title: Definition:Opposite
snippet: Geometry: Opposite (in a Polygon): The opposite side (or angle) to a given side is that side (or angle) which has the same number of sides between it and the side in question. The opposite side (or angle) to a given angle is that side (or angle) which has the same number of sides between it and the angle in question. Opposite (in a Triangle): The side of a triangle which is not one of the sides adjacent to a particular angle is referred to as its opposite. Thus, each angle has an opposite side, and each side has an opposite angle.

title: Definition:Opposite Direction
snippet: Let $\mathbf v$ and $\mathbf w$ be vectors in space. We say that $\mathbf v$ is in the opposite direction to $\mathbf w$ : the lines of action of $\mathbf v$ and $\mathbf w$ are parallel but at the same time: the lines of action of $\mathbf v$ and $\mathbf w$ are not the same. Category:Definitions/Vectors

title: Definition:Opposite Face of Prism/Also known as
snippet: == Opposite Face of Prism: Also known as == The opposite face of a prism can also be referred to as the opposite plane. Category:Definitions/Bases of Prisms

title: Definition:Opposite Force
snippet: Let $B_1$ and $B_2$ be bodies in space. Let $B_1$ apply a force $\mathbf F$ on $B_2$. The opposite force to $\mathbf F$ is the force which $B_2$ applies to $B_1$, according to Newton's Third Law of Motion.

title: Definition:Opposite Force/Also known as
snippet: == Opposite Force: Also known as == The opposite force to a given force is often referred to as the reaction.

title: Definition:Opposite Group
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group. We define a new operation $*$ on $G$ by: $\forall a, b \in G: a * b = b \circ a$ The algebraic structure $\struct {G, *}$ is called the opposite group to $G$.

title: Definition:Opposite Magma
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ and $\struct {S, *}$ be magmas on $S$. $\struct {S, *}$ is the opposite magma of $\struct {S, \circ}$ : $\forall x_1, x_2, x_3 \in S: x_1 \circ x_2 = x_3 \iff x_2 * x_1 = x_3$ The operation $*$ is sometimes referred to as the opposite law of $\circ$.

title: Definition:Opposite Parity/Also known as
snippet: == Opposite Parity: Also known as == Some sources refer to a pair of integers $\set {z_1, z_2}$ having opposite parity as having odd parity. Note the difference between this and the definition of odd parity as being a property of an individual integer as being odd.

title: Definition:Opposite Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \times}$ be a ring. Let $* : R \times R \to R$ be the binary operation on $S$ defined by: $\forall x, y \in S: x * y = y \times x$ The opposite ring of $R$ is the algebraic structure $\struct {R, +, *}$.

title: Definition:Opposite Sides of Symmetric Figure
snippet: Let $F$ be a geometric figure with a center of symmetry $S$. Two sides of $F$ are opposite they are joined by a straight line through the center of symmetry of $F$.

title: Definition:Opposite Vertices of Symmetric Figure
snippet: Let $F$ be a geometric figure with a center of symmetry $S$. Two sides of $F$ are opposite they are joined by a straight line through the center of symmetry of $F$.

title: Definition:Optics
snippet: Optics is the branch of physics which studies the properties of light.

title: Definition:Optimal Strategy
snippet: Let $G$ be a game. Let $P$ be a player of $G$. An optimal strategy for $P$ is a strategy that contributes towards a solution of $G$.

title: Definition:Optimization Theory
snippet: Optimization theory is a branch of mathematics whose aim is to find the "best" solution to a practical problem, often using techniques of numerical analysis. In this context, best is dependent upon the aim of what the solution of the problem is to achieve. Optimization theory encompasses such topics as: the calculus of variations control theory convex optimization theory decision theory game theory linear programming Markov chains network analysis queueing theory and so on.

title: Definition:Optimum Solution
snippet: The optimum solution of a problem in linear programming or optimization theory is the feasible solution which, according to the definition of the problem, is the most desirable.

title: Definition:Optimum Solution/Also known as
snippet: == Optimum Solution: Also known as == An optimum solution is also known as: an optimal solution an optimization Category:Definitions/Optimum Solutions

title: Definition:Or Gate
snippet: An or gate is a logic gate whose purpose is to implement disjunction in a combinatorial circuit.

title: Definition:Oracle Machine
snippet: An oracle machine is an extension of a Turing machine with an additional capability. In addition to manipulating the symbols on its tape (or tapes, in the case of a multitape Turing machine), it can determine if a value belongs to a given language $T$ in a single step.

title: Definition:Orbit
snippet: Group Theory: The orbits of a group action. Physics (and in particular celestial mechanics): The orbit of a body around another body. Dynamical Systems: Orbit of dynamical system: the set of values taken by a variable under an iterated mapping.

title: Definition:Orbit (Group Theory)
snippet: Let $G$ be a group acting on a set $X$.

title: Definition:Orbit (Group Theory)/Definition 1
snippet: Let $G$ be a group acting on a set $X$. The orbit of an element $x \in X$ is defined as: $\Orb x := \set {y \in X: \exists g \in G: y = g * x}$ where $*$ denotes the group action. That is, $\Orb x = G * x$. Thus the orbit of an element is all its possible destinations under the group action.

title: Definition:Orbit (Group Theory)/Definition 2
snippet: Let $G$ be a group acting on a set $X$. Let $\RR$ be the relation on $X$ defined as: $\forall x, y \in X: x \mathrel \RR y \iff \exists g \in G: y = g * x$ where $*$ denotes the group action. From Group Action Induces Equivalence Relation, $\RR$ is an equivalence relation. The orbit of $x$, denoted $\Orb x$, is the equivalence class of $x$ under $\RR$.

title: Definition:Orbit (Group Theory)/Length
snippet: Let $G$ be a group acting on a set $X$. Let $x \in X$. Let $\Orb x$ be the orbit of $x$. The length of the orbit $\Orb x$ of $x$ is the number of elements of $X$ it contains: $\size {\Orb x}$ Category:Definitions/Group Actions

title: Definition:Orbit (Group Theory)/Set of Orbits
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $X$ be a set Let $*: G \times S \to S$ be a group action. Let $\Orb x$ denote the orbit of $x \in X$. From Group Action Induces Equivalence Relation, the relation $\RR_G$ defined as: $x \mathrel {\RR_G} y \iff y \in \Orb x$ is an equivalence relation. The quotient set $X / \RR_G$ is called the set of orbits of $X$ under the action of $G$.

title: Definition:Orbit (Physics)
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be bodies in space. The orbit of $A$ around $B$ is the path taken by $A$ as it travels around $B$ under the influence of the force acting between $A$ and $B$.

title: Definition:Orbit (Physics)/Period
snippet: Let body $A$ be in orbit around body $B$. The period of the orbit is the length of time it takes for $A$ to travel once around $B$ and return to its original position.

title: Definition:Orbit (Physics)/Radius
snippet: Let body $A$ be in orbit around body $B$. Let $\mathbf r$ be the position vector of the center of mass of $A$ the center of mass of $B$ at a particular point in time. The radius of the orbit of $A$ around $B$ is defined as: the position vector $\mathbf r$ or the length of $\mathbf r$. Context will determine which is meant.

title: Definition:Orbital Angular Momentum
snippet: == Physical Property == Let $B_1$ be an body in orbit around another body $B_2$. The orbital angular momentum of $B_1$ $B_2$ is the angular momentum of $B_1$ the center of mass of $B_2$.

title: Definition:Order
snippet: Set Theory: Order of Set: Another word for the cardinality of a set. Abstract Algebra: Order of an Algebraic Structure Group Theory: Order of an Element in a Group Matrix Theory and Linear Algebra: Order of a Matrix Order of a Square Matrix Order of a Determinant Tensor Theory: Order of a Tensor: another term for the rank of a tensor. Number Theory: Multiplicative Order of an Integer: the least positive integer $c$ such that $a^c \equiv 1 \pmod n$. Order of a Sociable Chain: the number of members of a sociable chain.

title: Definition:Order-Convex Set/Also known as
snippet: == Order-Convex Set: Also known as == An order-convex set is also known as just a convex set. However, the concept of a convex set has other applications, so uses the longer form as standard.

title: Definition:Order-Convex Set/Definition 1
snippet: A subset $A$ of an ordered set $\struct {S, \preceq}$ is convex (in $S$) : $\forall x, y \in A: \forall z \in S: x \preceq z \preceq y \implies z \in A$

title: Definition:Order-Convex Set/Definition 2
snippet: A subset $A$ of an ordered set $\struct {S, \preceq}$ is order-convex (in $S$) : $\forall x, y \in A: \forall z \in S: x \prec z \prec y \implies z \in A$

title: Definition:Order-Convex Subset of Natural Numbers
snippet: Let $A \subseteq \N$ be a subset of the set of natural numbers. $A$ is defined as being order-convex (in $\N$) : $\forall x, y, z \in \N: \paren {x, z \in A \land x \le y \le z} \implies y \in A$

title: Definition:Order-Reflecting Mapping
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq_1}$ and $\struct {T, \preceq_2}$ be ordered sets. Let $\phi: S \to T$ be a mapping. Then $\phi$ is an order-reflecting mapping or reflects order : $\forall x, y \in S: \map \phi x \preceq_2 \map \phi y \implies x \preceq_1 y$

title: Definition:Order Automorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $\phi: S \to S$ be an order isomorphism from $\struct {S, \preceq}$ to $\struct {S, \preceq} $. Then $\phi$ is an (order) automorphism.

title: Definition:Order Category/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. One can interpret $\struct {S, \preceq}$ as being a category, with: More formally, we let the morphisms be the elements of the relation ${\preceq} \subseteq S \times S$. Thus, $a \to b$ in fact denotes the ordered pair $\tuple {a, b}$. The category that so arises is called an order category.

title: Definition:Order Category/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Then $\mathbf C$ is an order category : For all objects $C, C'$ of $\mathbf C$, there is at most one morphism $f: C \to C'$ Whenever $f: C \to C'$ is an isomorphism, $C = C'$ Thus, an order category is a skeletal preorder category.

title: Definition:Order Complete Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set.

title: Definition:Order Complete Set/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. $\struct {S, \preceq}$ is order complete : Each non-empty subset $H \subseteq S$ which has an upper bound admits a supremum.

title: Definition:Order Complete Set/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. $\struct {S, \preceq}$ is order complete : Each non-empty subset $H \subseteq S$ which has a lower bound admits an infimum.

title: Definition:Order Completion
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq_S}$ be an ordered set. An ordered set $\struct {T, \preceq_T}$ is an order completion of $S$ : $(1):\quad S \subseteq T$ $(2):\quad {\preceq_T \restriction_S} = {\preceq_S}$, where $\restriction$ denotes restriction $(3):\quad \struct {T, \preceq_T}$ is a complete ordered set $(4):\quad$ For all ordered sets $\struct {T', \preceq_{T'} }$ satisfying $(1), (2)$ and $(3)$, there is a unique increasing injection $\phi: T' \to T$

title: Definition:Order Embedding
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq_1}$ and $\struct {T, \preceq_2}$ be ordered sets. Let $\phi: S \to T$ be a mapping.

title: Definition:Order Embedding/Also known as
snippet: == Order Embedding: Also known as == An order embedding is also known as an order monomorphism. Some sources call it an order-preserving mapping. However, this term is also used in particular on to be the same thing as an increasing mapping: that is, a mapping which preserves an ordering in perhaps only one direction.

title: Definition:Order Embedding/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq_1}$ and $\struct {T, \preceq_2}$ be ordered sets. Let $\phi: S \to T$ be a mapping. $\phi$ is an order embedding of $S$ into $T$ : $\forall x, y \in S: x \preceq_1 y \iff \map \phi x \preceq_2 \map \phi y$ That is, an order embedding is an order-preserving, order-reflecting mapping.

title: Definition:Order Embedding/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq_1}$ and $\struct {T, \preceq_2}$ be ordered sets. Let $\phi: S \to T$ be a mapping. $\phi$ is an order embedding of $S$ into $T$ both of the following conditions hold: $(1): \quad \phi$ is an injection $(2): \quad \forall x, y \in S: x \preceq_1 y \iff \map \phi x \preceq_2 \map \phi y$

title: Definition:Order Embedding/Definition 3
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq_1}$ and $\struct {T, \preceq_2}$ be ordered sets. Let $\phi: S \to T$ be a mapping. $\phi$ is an order embedding of $S$ into $T$ both of the following conditions hold: $(1): \quad \phi$ is an injection $(2): \quad \forall x, y \in S: x \prec_1 y \iff \map \phi x \prec_2 \map \phi y$

title: Definition:Order Embedding/Definition 4
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq_1}$ and $\struct {T, \preceq_2}$ be ordered sets. Let $\phi: S \to T$ be a mapping. Let $T' = \Img S$ be the image of $S$ under $\phi$. $\phi$ is an order embedding of $S$ into $T$ : the restriction of $\phi$ to $S \times T'$ is an order isomorphism between $\struct {S, \preceq_1}$ and $\struct {T', \preceq_2 \restriction_{T' \times T'} }$.

title: Definition:Order Generating Subset
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a preordered set. Let $X$ be a subset of $S$. Then $X$ is order generating : $\forall x \in S: x^\succeq \cap X$ admits an infimum and $x = \map \inf {x^\succeq \cap X}$

title: Definition:Order Indiscernible
snippet: Let $\MM$ be an $\LL$-structure. Let $\struct {I, \le}$ be an infinite ordered set. Let $X = \set {x_i \in \MM: i \in I}$ be an infinite subset of the universe of $\MM$ indexed by $I$. Let $A$ be a subset of the universe of $\MM$. $X$ is (an) order indiscernible (set) over $A$ in $\MM$ : For every $n \in \N$ and every pair of chains $i_1 < \cdots < i_n$ and $j_1 < \cdots < j_n$ in $I$ each with $n$ distinct elements, we have: $\MM \models \map \phi {x_{i_1}, \ldots, x_{i_n} } \iff \map \phi {x_{j_1}, \ldots, x_{j_n} }$ for all $\LL$-formulas $\phi$ with $n$ free variables and parameters from…

title: Definition:Order Isomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq_1}$ and $\struct {T, \preceq_2}$ be ordered sets.

title: Definition:Order Isomorphism/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq_1}$ and $\struct {T, \preceq_2}$ be ordered sets. Let $\phi: S \to T$ be a bijection such that: $\phi: S \to T$ is order-preserving $\phi^{-1}: T \to S$ is order-preserving. Then $\phi$ is an order isomorphism. That is, $\phi$ is an order isomorphism : $\phi$ is bijective $\forall x, y \in S: x \preceq_1 y \implies \map \phi x \preceq_2 \map \phi y$ $\forall p, q \in T: p \preceq_2 q \implies \map {\phi^{-1} } p \preceq_1 \map {\phi^{-1} } q$ So an order isomorphism can be described as a bijection that preserves ordering in both directions.

title: Definition:Order Isomorphism/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq_1}$ and $\struct {T, \preceq_2}$ be ordered sets. Let $\phi: S \to T$ be a surjective order embedding. Then $\phi$ is an order isomorphism. That is, $\phi$ is an order isomorphism : $(1): \quad \phi$ is surjective $(2): \quad \forall x, y \in S: x \preceq_1 y \iff \map \phi x \preceq_2 \map \phi y$

title: Definition:Order Isomorphism/Definition 3
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq_1}$ and $\struct {T, \preceq_2}$ be ordered sets. Let $\phi: S \to T$ be a bijection such that: $\forall x, y \in S: x \preceq_1 y \iff \map \phi x \preceq_2 \map \phi y$ Then $\phi$ is an order isomorphism.

title: Definition:Order Isomorphism/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Order Isomorphism == The concept of order isomorphism was first introduced by .

title: Definition:Order Isomorphism/Isomorphic Sets
snippet: Two ordered sets $\struct {S, \preceq_1}$ and $\struct {T, \preceq_2}$ are (order) isomorphic there exists such an order isomorphism between them. Hence $\struct {S, \preceq_1}$ is described as (order) isomorphic to (or with) $\struct {T, \preceq_2}$, and vice versa. This may be written $\struct {S, \preceq_1} \cong \struct {T, \preceq_2}$. Where no confusion is likely to arise, it can be abbreviated to $S \cong T$.

title: Definition:Order Isomorphism/Well-Orderings
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq_1}$ and $\struct {T, \preceq_2}$ be well-ordered sets. Let $\phi: S \to T$ be a bijection such that $\phi: S \to T$ is order-preserving: $\forall x, y \in S: x \preceq_1 y \implies \map \phi x \preceq_2 \map \phi y$ Then $\phi$ is an order isomorphism. Two well-ordered sets $\struct {S, \preceq_1}$ and $\struct {T, \preceq_2}$ are (order) isomorphic there exists such an order isomorphism between them. Thus $\struct {S, \preceq_1}$ is described as (order) isomorphic to (or with) $\struct {T, \preceq_2}$, and vice versa.

title: Definition:Order Isomorphism/Well-Orderings/Class Theory
snippet: Let $\struct {A, \preccurlyeq_1}$ and $\struct {B, \preccurlyeq_2}$ be well-ordered classes. Let $\phi: A \to B$ be a bijection such that $\phi: A \to B$ is order-preserving: $\forall x, y \in S: x \preccurlyeq_1 y \implies \map \phi x \preccurlyeq_2 \map \phi y$ Then $\phi$ is an order isomorphism.

title: Definition:Order Notation/Abuse of Notation
snippet: == Order Notation: Abuse of Notation == The concept of order notation is properly defined as sets of real sequences that fulfil certain properties a given real sequence. Some sources state that extending to general real functions is an abuse of notation, although an acceptable one.

title: Definition:Order Property
snippet: An order property is a property of an ordered sets which is invariant under order isomorphism. That is, if $\struct {S_1, \preceq_1}$ and $\struct {S_2, \preceq_2}$ are isomorphic ordered sets, and $P$ is a property, then: $\map P {S_1, \preceq_1} \iff \map P {S_2, \preceq_2}$

title: Definition:Order Statistic
snippet: Let $S$ be a sample of ordinal data (that is, that it can be ordered). Let $S$ be arranged into ascending order. The $i$th element of $S$ under that ordering is referred to as the $i$th order statistic. This is usually written $x_{\paren i}$ to distinguish it from the $i$th observation before ordering.

title: Definition:Order Sum
snippet: Let $\struct {S_1, \preccurlyeq_1}$ and $\struct {S_2, \preccurlyeq_2}$ be ordered sets. The order sum $\struct {S_1, \preccurlyeq_1} \oplus \struct {S_2, \preccurlyeq_2}$ of $\struct {S_1, \preccurlyeq_1}$ and $\struct {S_2, \preccurlyeq_2}$ is the ordered set $\struct {T, \preccurlyeq}$ where: $T := S_1 \sqcup S_2 = \paren {S_1 \times \set 0} \cup \paren {S_2 \times \set 1}$ $\preccurlyeq$ is defined as: $\forall \tuple {a, b}, \tuple {c, d} \in T: \tuple {a, b} \preccurlyeq \tuple {c, d} \iff \begin {cases} b = 0 \text { and } d = 1 \\ b = d = 0 \text { and } a \preccurlyeq_1 c \\ b = d =…

title: Definition:Order Sum/Informal Interpretation
snippet: We can consider the order sum $\struct {S \preccurlyeq} := \struct {S_1 \preccurlyeq_1} \oplus \struct {S_2 \preccurlyeq_2}$ as: First the set $S_1$, ordered by $\preccurlyeq_1$ Then the set $S_2$, ordered by $\preccurlyeq_2$ Note that: $\forall x \in S_1, y \in S_2: \tuple {x, 0} \preccurlyeq \tuple {y, 1}$ That is, every element of $S_1$ is comparable with every element of $S_2$. Category:Definitions/Order Sums

title: Definition:Order Theory
snippet: Order theory is the branch of relation theory which studies orderings.

title: Definition:Order Topology/Also known as
snippet: == Order Topology: Also known as == The order topology is also known as the interval topology.

title: Definition:Order Topology/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a totally ordered set. Let $\XX$ be the set of open rays in $S$. Let $\tau$ be the topology on $S$ generated by $\XX$. Then $\tau$ is called the order topology on $S$.

title: Definition:Order Topology/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a totally ordered set. Define: {{eqn | l = \map {\Uparrow} S | r = \set {s^\succ: s \in S} }} {{eqn | l = \map {\Downarrow} S | r = \set {s^\prec: s \in S} }} where $s^\succ$ and $s^\prec$ denote the strict upper closure and strict lower closure of $s$, respectively. The order topology $\tau$ on $S$ is the topology on $S$ generated by $\map {\Uparrow} S \cup \map {\Downarrow} S$.

title: Definition:Order Type
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq_1}$ and $\struct {T, \preccurlyeq_2}$ be ordered sets. Then $S$ and $T$ have the same (order) type they are order isomorphic. The order type of an ordered set $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ can be denoted $\map \ot {S, \preccurlyeq}$.

title: Definition:Order Type of Natural Numbers
snippet: Consider the ordered set $\struct {\N, \le}$ consisting of the set of natural numbers $\N$ under the usual ordering $\le$. That is, $\N$ arranged in increasing order $0, 1, 2, \ldots$ The order type of $\struct {\N, \le}$ is denoted $\omega$ (omega).

title: Definition:Order Type of Rational Numbers
snippet: Consider the ordered set $\struct {\Q, \le}$ consisting of the set of rational numbers under the usual ordering $\le$. The order type of $\struct {\Q, \le}$ is denoted $\eta$ (eta).

title: Definition:Order Type of Rational Numbers/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Order Type of Rational Numbers == The use of $\eta$ to denote the order type of $\struct {\Q, \le}$ dates back to the writings of and . According to and in their of $1996$, this order type, along with that for $\struct {\R, \le}$, has not been greatly studied in recent years. $\eta$ is in fact far more often used to denote a general ordinal.

title: Definition:Order Type of Real Numbers
snippet: Consider the ordered set $\struct {\R, \le}$ consisting of the set of real numbers under the usual ordering $\le$. The order type of $\struct {\R, \le}$ is denoted $\lambda$ (lambda).

title: Definition:Order Type of Real Numbers/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Order Type of Real Numbers == The use of $\lambda$ to denote the order type of $\struct {\R, \le}$ dates back to the writings of and . According to and in their of $1996$, this order type, along with that for $\struct {\Q, \le}$, has not been greatly studied in recent years. $\lambda$ is in fact far more often used to denote an infinite cardinal.

title: Definition:Order Unit
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \succeq}$ be a preordered vector space over the real numbers $\R$. Let $e \in X$. We call $e$ an order unit for $\struct {X, \succeq}$ : for each $x \in X$ there exists $n \in \N$ such that: $n e \succeq x \succeq -n e$

title: Definition:Order of Bessel Function/Also known as
snippet: == Bessel Function: Also known as == Some sources use $p$ to denote the order of the Bessel function. Category:Definitions/Bessel Functions

title: Definition:Order of Cards
snippet: Let $D$ be a deck of cards. The cards in the deck can be considered to be stacked uniformly, usually all in the same orientation, with a card on the top and a card on the bottom. The order of the cards is the total ordering $\prec$ defined as: $a \prec b$ $a$ is somewhere underneath $b$ Category:Definitions/Cards

title: Definition:Order of Contact
snippet: Let $f: \R \to \R$ and $g: \R \to \R$ be real functions. Then $f$ and $g$ have contact of order $k$ at the point $a \in \R$ : {{eqn | n = 1 | l = \map {f^{\paren i} } a | r = \map {g^{\paren i} } a | c = for $0 \le i \le k$ }} {{eqn | n = 2 | l = \map {f^{\paren {k + 1} } } a | o = \ne | r = \map {g^{\paren {k + 1} } } a }} where $f^{\paren n}$ denotes the $n$th derivative of $f$.

title: Definition:Order of Convergence
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be an infinite sequence of numbers or vectors in a normed vector space. Let $\alpha \in \R$. Let $p \in \R_{\ge 1}$. Then $\sequence {x_n}$ converges to $\alpha$ with order $p$ there exists a sequence $\sequence {\epsilon_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ such that: $(1): \quad \size {x_n - \alpha} \le \epsilon_n$ for every $n \in \N$ $(2): \quad \ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \frac {\epsilon_{n + 1} } { {\epsilon_n}^p} = c$ where $c > 0$ If $p = 1$, the constant $c$ is additionally required to be less than $1$.

title: Definition:Order of Convergence/Also known as
snippet: == Order of Convergence: Also known as == Order of convergence is also known as rate of convergence.

title: Definition:Order of Convergence/First Order
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be an infinite sequence of real numbers. Let $\alpha \in \R$. $\sequence {x_n}$ converges to $\alpha$ with order $1$ there exists a sequence $\sequence {\epsilon_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ such that: $(1): \quad \size {x_n - \alpha} \le \epsilon_n$ for every $n \in \N$ $(2): \quad \ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \frac {\epsilon_{n + 1} } {\epsilon_n} = c$ where $0 < c < 1$.

title: Definition:Order of Convergence/Second Order
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be an infinite sequence of real numbers. Let $\alpha \in \R$. $\sequence {x_n}$ converges to $\alpha$ with order $2$ there exists a sequence $\sequence {\epsilon_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ such that: $\size {x_n - \alpha} \le \epsilon_n$ for every $n \in \N$ $(2): \quad \ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \frac {\epsilon_{n + 1} } { {\epsilon_n}^2} = c$ where $0 < c < 1$.

title: Definition:Order of Differential Equation/Also known as
snippet: == Order of Differential Equation: Also known as == Some sources refer to the order of a differential equation as its dimension. Category:Definitions/Order of Differential Equation

title: Definition:Order of Differential Equation/Warning
snippet: == Warning on Order of Differential Equation == Consider the ordinary differential equation: $y' ' - y' ' + y' - y = 0$ At first glance it looks as though it is of the $2$nd order. But after some (fairly obvious) simplification, it is seen that it can be written: $y' - y = 0$ which is of the $1$st order.

title: Definition:Order of Entire Function
snippet: Let $f: \C \to \C$ be an entire function. Let $\ln$ denote the natural logarithm.

title: Definition:Order of Entire Function/Definition 1
snippet: Let $f: \C \to \C$ be an entire function. The order $\alpha \in \closedint 0 {+\infty}$ of $f$ is the infimum of the $\beta \ge 0$ for which: $\map f z = \map \OO {\map \exp {\size z^\beta} }$ or $\infty$ if no such $\beta$ exists, where $\OO$ denotes big-$\OO$ notation.

title: Definition:Order of Entire Function/Definition 2
snippet: Let $f: \C \to \C$ be an entire function. Let $f$ be not identically zero. The order $\alpha \in \closedint 0 {+\infty}$ of $f$ is the infimum of the $\beta \ge 0$ for which: $\ds \map \ln {\max_{\size z \mathop \le R} \size {\map f z} } = \map \OO {R^\beta}$ or $\infty$ if no such $\beta$ exists, where $\OO$ denotes big-$\OO$ notation The order of $0$ is $0$.

title: Definition:Order of Entire Function/Definition 3
snippet: Let $f: \C \to \C$ be an entire function. Let $f$ be non-constant. The order $\alpha \in \closedint 0 {+\infty}$ of $f$ is the limit superior: $\ds \limsup_{R \mathop \to \infty} \frac {\ds \ln \ln \max_{\cmod z \mathop \le R} \cmod f} {\ln R}$ The order of a constant function is $0$.

title: Definition:Order of Entire Function/Finite Order
snippet: Let $f: \C \to \C$ be an entire function. $f$ has finite order its order is a real number. Category:Definitions/Order of Entire Function

title: Definition:Order of Group Element
snippet: Let $G$ be a group whose identity is $e_G$. Let $x \in G$ be an element of $G$.

title: Definition:Order of Group Element/Also denoted as
snippet: The order of an element $x$ in a group is sometimes seen as $\map o x$. Some sources render it as $\map {\operatorname {Ord} } x$. Category:Definitions/Order of Group Elements

title: Definition:Order of Group Element/Also known as
snippet: Some sources refer to the order of an element of a group as its period.

title: Definition:Order of Group Element/Definition 1
snippet: Let $G$ be a group whose identity is $e_G$. Let $x \in G$ be an element of $G$. The order of $x$ (in $G$), denoted $\order x$, is the smallest $k \in \Z_{> 0}$ such that $x^k = e_G$.

title: Definition:Order of Group Element/Definition 2
snippet: Let $G$ be a group whose identity is $e_G$. Let $x \in G$ be an element of $G$. The order of $x$ (in $G$), denoted $\order x$, is the order of the group generated by $x$: $\order x := \order {\gen x}$

title: Definition:Order of Group Element/Definition 3
snippet: Let $G$ be a group whose identity is $e_G$. Let $x \in G$ be an element of $G$. The order of $x$ (in $G$), denoted $\order x$, is the largest $k \in \Z_{>0}$ such that: $\forall i, j \in \Z: 0 \le i < j < k \implies x^i \ne x^j$

title: Definition:Order of Group Element/Finite
snippet: Let $G$ be a group whose identity is $e_G$. Let $x \in G$ be an element of $G$.

title: Definition:Order of Group Element/Finite/Also known as
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. An element of finite order of $G$ is also known as a torsion element of $G$.

title: Definition:Order of Group Element/Finite/Definition 1
snippet: Let $G$ be a group whose identity is $e_G$. Let $x \in G$ be an element of $G$. $x$ is of finite order, or has finite order there exists $k \in \Z_{> 0}$ such that $x^k = e_G$.

title: Definition:Order of Group Element/Finite/Definition 2
snippet: Let $G$ be a group whose identity is $e_G$. Let $x \in G$ be an element of $G$. $x$ is of finite order, or has finite order there exist $m, n \in \Z_{> 0}$ such that $m \ne n$ but $x^m = x^n$.

title: Definition:Order of Group Element/Infinite
snippet: Let $G$ be a group whose identity is $e_G$. Let $x \in G$ be an element of $G$.

title: Definition:Order of Group Element/Infinite/Definition 1
snippet: Let $G$ be a group whose identity is $e_G$. Let $x \in G$ be an element of $G$. $x$ is of infinite order, or has infinite order, there exists no $k \in \Z_{> 0}$ such that $x^k = e_G$: $\order x = \infty$

title: Definition:Order of Group Element/Infinite/Definition 2
snippet: Let $G$ be a group whose identity is $e_G$. Let $x \in G$ be an element of $G$. $x$ is of infinite order, or has infinite order the powers $x, x^2, x^3, \ldots$ of $x$ are all distinct: $\order x = \infty$

title: Definition:Order of Group Element/Infinite/Definition 3
snippet: Let $G$ be a group whose identity is $e_G$. Let $x \in G$ be an element of $G$. $x$ is of infinite order, or has infinite order the group $\gen x$ generated by $x$ is of infinite order. $\order x = \infty \iff \order {\gen x} = \infty$

title: Definition:Order of Infinitesimals
snippet: Let $x$ and $y$ be real variables which tend to the limit $0$. Then $x$ and $y$ are infinitesimals of the same order : $\dfrac x y$ is finite and non-zero. If $\dfrac x y \to 0$, then $x$ is an infinitesimal of higher order than $y$ If $\dfrac x y \to \infty$ or $\dfrac x y \to -\infty$, then $x$ is an infinitesimal of lower order than $y$. Let $\dfrac x {y^n} \to 0$ is finite and non-zero, and $y$ is taken to be the first order. Then $x$ is of $n$th order.

title: Definition:Order of Matrix/Also known as
snippet: == Order of Matrix: Also known as == The order of a matrix can also be referred to as its dimensions, but the term dimension has a different, deeper meaning in linear algebra and this may be a source of confusion. Some sources refer to the size rather than order, which is acceptable enough. Others use the term type, but this word can have different connotations. Some sources do not bother to give the order an actual name, merely referring to, say, an $n \times m$ matrix.

title: Definition:Order of Numbers of Pascal's Triangle/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Order of Numbers of Pascal's Triangle == The concept of categorising the entries of Pascal's triangle into orders, corresponding to its columns, was introduced by himself, in his $1655$ treatise .

title: Definition:Order of Pole
snippet: Let $f: \C \to \C$ be a complex function.

title: Definition:Order of Pole/Definition 1
snippet: Let $f: \C \to \C$ be a complex function. Let $z_0 \in U \subset \C$ be such that $f$ is holomorphic in $U \setminus \set {z_0}$, with a pole at $z_0$. By Existence of Laurent Series there is a series: $\ds \map f z = \sum_{n \mathop \ge n_0}^\infty a_j \paren {z - z_0}^n$ The order of the pole at $z_0$ is defined to be $\size {n_0} > 0$.

title: Definition:Order of Pole/Definition 2
snippet: Let $f: \C \to \C$ be a complex function. Let $z_0 \in U \subset \C$ be such that $f$ is holomorphic in $U \setminus \set {z_0}$, with a pole at $z_0$: By definition $z_0$ is a pole $f$ can be written in the form: $\map f z = \dfrac {\map \phi z} {\paren {z - z_0}^k}$ where: $\phi$ is analytic at $z_0$ $\map \phi {z_0} \ne 0$ $k \in \Z$ such that $k \ge 1$. The order of the pole at $z_0$ is defined to be $k$.

title: Definition:Order of Pole/Simple Pole
snippet: Let $f: \C \to \C$ be a complex function. Let $z_0 \in U \subset \C$ be such that $f$ is holomorphic in $U \setminus \set {z_0}$, with a pole at $z_0$. Let the order of the pole at $z_0$ be $1$. Then $z_0$ is a simple pole.

title: Definition:Order of Rotational Symmetry/Also known as
snippet: == Order of Rotational Symmetry: Also known as == The order of rotational symmetry of a rotational symmetry $R$ is also known as just the order of symmetry of $R$.

title: Definition:Order of Square Matrix/Also known as
snippet: == Order of Square Matrix: Also known as == The order of a square matrix is also known as its dimension.

title: Definition:Order of Structure
snippet: The order of an algebraic structure $\struct {S, \circ}$ is the cardinality of its underlying set, and is denoted $\order S$. Thus, for a finite set $S$, the order of $\struct {S, \circ}$ is the number of elements in $S$.

title: Definition:Order of Structure/Also defined as
snippet: == Order of Structure: Also defined as == Some sources do not define the order of a structure for an underlying set of infinite cardinality, restricting themselves to the finite case.

title: Definition:Order of Structure/Finite Structure
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. Let the underlying set $S$ of $\struct {S, \circ}$ be finite. Then $\struct {S, \circ}$ a finite structure. That is, $\struct {S, \circ}$ is a finite structure $\struct {S, \circ}$ is not an infinite structure.

title: Definition:Order of Structure/Infinite Structure
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. Let the underlying set $S$ of $\struct {S, \circ}$ be infinite. Then $\struct {S, \circ}$ is an infinite structure. That is, $\struct {S, \circ}$ is an infinite structure $\struct {S, \circ}$ is not a finite structure.

title: Definition:Order of Structure/Notation
snippet: == Order of Structure: Notation == Other notations that can sometimes be seen for the order of an algebraic structure $S$ include: $\map \# S$ $\operatorname {order} S$ Some sources use $\map o S$, but this has problems of ambiguity with other uses of $\map o n$: see little-o notation.

title: Definition:Order of Surface
snippet: Let $\SS$ be a surface embedded in ordinary $3$-space. The order of $\SS$ is the degree of the equation whose locus is $\SS$.

title: Definition:Order of Zero
snippet: Let $f: \C \to \C$ be a complex function. Let $U \subset \C$ be such that $f$ is analytic in $U$. Let $x \in U$ be a zero of $f$. That is, let $x$ be such that $\map f x = 0$. Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be the least positive integer such that: $\map {f^{\paren n} } x \ne 0$ where $f^{\paren n}$ denotes the $n$th derivative of $f$. Then $n$ is the order of the zero at $x$.

title: Definition:Order of Zero/Simple Zero
snippet: Let $f: \C \to \C$ be a complex function. Let $U \subset \C$ be such that $f$ is analytic in $U$. Let $x \in U$ be a zero of $f$. Let the order of the zero $x$ be $1$. Then $x$ is a simple zero. Category:Definitions/Complex Analysis

title: Definition:Ordered Basis
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $G$ be a free $R$-module. An ordered basis of $G$ is a sequence $\sequence {a_k}_{1 \mathop \le k \mathop \le n}$ of elements of $G$ such that $\set {a_1, \ldots, a_n}$ is a basis of $G$.

title: Definition:Ordered Class
snippet: Let $V$ be a basic universe. Let $\RR \subseteq V \times V$ be a relation. Let $A$ be a subclass of the field of $\RR$. Let the restriction of $\RR$ to $A$ be an ordering on $A$. Then $A$ is described as being ordered under $\RR$.

title: Definition:Ordered Commutative Semigroup
snippet: An ordered commutative semigroup is an ordered semigroup $\left({S, \circ, \preceq}\right)$ such that $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ is a commutative semigroup.

title: Definition:Ordered Dual Basis
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $\struct {G, +_G, \circ}_R$ be an $n$-dimensional module over $R$. Let $\sequence {a_n}$ be an ordered basis of $G$. Let $G^*$ be the algebraic dual of $G$. Then there is an ordered basis $\sequence {a'_n}$ of $G^*$ satisfying $\forall i, j \in \closedint 1 n: \map {a'_i} {a_j} = \delta_{i j}$. This ordered basis $\sequence {a'_n}$ of $G^*$ is called the ordered basis of $G^*$ dual to $\sequence {a_n}$, or the ordered dual basis of $G^*$.

title: Definition:Ordered Dual Basis/Also known as
snippet: == Ordered Dual Basis: Also known as == An ordered dual basis is also known as a dual basis.

title: Definition:Ordered Field
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ, \preceq}$ be an ordered ring. Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a field. Then $\struct {R, +, \circ, \preceq}$ is an ordered field.

title: Definition:Ordered Field/Also defined as
snippet: == Ordered Field: Also defined as == The term ordered field is frequently used to refer to what we call a totally ordered field. Sources defining partially ordered field vary in their definitions. Some require only a field which is an ordered ring, while others impose further restrictions.

title: Definition:Ordered Field Isomorphism
Definition:Ordered Geometry
snippet: Ordered geometry is a sub-branch of geometry which features the concept of betweenness but, like projective geometry, omitting the basic notion of distance.

title: Definition:Ordered Group
snippet: An ordered group is an ordered structure $\struct {G, \circ, \preceq}$ such that $\struct {G, \circ}$ is a group.

title: Definition:Ordered Group Automorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ, \preceq}$ be an ordered group. An ordered group automorphism from $\struct {G, \circ, \preceq}$ to itself is a mapping $\phi: G \to G$ that is both: $(1): \quad$ A group automorphism, that is, a group isomorphism from the group $\struct {G, \circ}$ to itself $(2): \quad$ An order isomorphism from the ordered set $\struct {G, \preceq}$ to itself.

title: Definition:Ordered Group Isomorphism
snippet: Let $\left({S, \circ, \preceq}\right)$ and $\left({T, *, \preccurlyeq}\right)$ be ordered groups. An ordered group isomorphism from $\left({S, \circ, \preceq}\right)$ to $\left({T, *, \preccurlyeq}\right)$ is a mapping $\phi: S \to T$ that is both: $(1): \quad$ A group isomorphism from the group $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ to the group $\left({T, *}\right)$ $(2): \quad$ An order isomorphism from the ordered set $\left({S, \preceq}\right)$ to the ordered set $\left({T, \preccurlyeq}\right)$.

title: Definition:Ordered Group Monomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ, \preceq}$ and $\struct {T, *, \preccurlyeq}$ be ordered groups. An ordered group monomorphism from $\struct {S, \circ, \preceq}$ to $\struct {T, *, \preccurlyeq}$ is a mapping $\phi: S \to T$ that is both: $(1): \quad$ A group monomorphism from the group $\struct {S, \circ}$ to the group $\struct {T, *}$ $(2): \quad$ An order embedding from the ordered set $\struct {S, \preceq}$ to the ordered set $\struct {T, \preccurlyeq}$.

title: Definition:Ordered Integral Domain/Definition 1
snippet: An ordered integral domain is an integral domain $\struct {D, +, \times}$ which has a strict positivity property $P$: An ordered integral domain can be denoted: $\struct {D, +, \times \le}$ where $\le$ is the total ordering induced by the strict positivity property.

title: Definition:Ordered Integral Domain/Definition 2
snippet: An ordered integral domain is an ordered ring $\struct {D, +, \times, \le}$ which is also an integral domain. That is, it is an integral domain with an ordering $\le$ compatible with the ring structure of $\struct {D, +, \times}$: {{axiom | n = \text {OID} 1 | lc= $\le$ is compatible with ring addition: | q = \forall a, b, c \in D | ml= a \le b | mo= \implies | mr= \paren {a + c} \le \paren {b + c} }} {{axiom | n = \text {OID} 2 | lc= Strict positivity is closed under ring product: | q = \forall a, b \in D | ml= 0_D \le a, 0_D \le b | mo= \implies | mr= 0_D \le a \times b }} where $0_D$ is…

title: Definition:Ordered Integral Domain/Trichotomy Law
snippet: Let $\struct {D, +, \times, \le}$ be an ordered integral domain. Let $P$ be the strict positivity property on $D$ The property: $\forall a \in D: \map P a \lor \map P {-a} \lor a = 0_D$ is known as the trichotomy law. That is: Every element of $D$ is either strictly positive, or strictly negative, or zero.

title: Definition:Ordered Monoid
snippet: An ordered monoid is an ordered structure $\left({S, \circ, \preceq}\right)$ such that $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ is a monoid.

title: Definition:Ordered Pair
snippet: The definition of a set does not take any account of the order in which the elements are listed. That is, $\set {a, b} = \set {b, a}$, and the elements $a$ and $b$ have the same status - neither is distinguished above the other as being more "important".

title: Definition:Ordered Pair/Also known as
snippet: == Ordered Pair: Also known as == Some sources refer to an ordered pair as just a pair, taking the fact that it is ordered for granted. However, this allows confusion with the concept of a doubleton set, so this usage is not recommended. Some sources use couple, but that has a completely different meaning in the context of mechanics. Some sources use the term ordered double.

title: Definition:Ordered Pair/Empty Set Formalization
snippet: The concept of an ordered pair can be formalized by the definition: $\tuple {a, b} := \set {\set {\O, a}, \set {\set \O, b} }$

title: Definition:Ordered Pair/Informal Definition
snippet: The definition of a set does not take any account of the order in which the elements are listed. That is, $\set {a, b} = \set {b, a}$, and the elements $a$ and $b$ have the same status -- neither is distinguished above the other as being more "important". An ordered pair is a two-element set together with an ordering. In other words, one of the elements is distinguished above the other - it comes first. Such a structure is written: $\tuple {a, b}$ and it means: first $a$, then $b$.

title: Definition:Ordered Pair/Kuratowski Formalization
snippet: The definition of a set does not take any account of the order in which the elements are listed. That is, $\set {a, b} = \set {b, a}$, and the elements $a$ and $b$ have the same status - neither is distinguished above the other as being more "important". The concept of an ordered pair can be formalized by the definition: $\tuple {a, b} := \set {\set a, \set {a, b} }$ This formalization justifies the existence of ordered pairs in Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory.

title: Definition:Ordered Pair/Notation
snippet: In the field of symbolic logic and modern treatments of set theory, the notation $\sequence {a, b}$ is often seen to denote an ordered pair. In sources where the possibility of confusion is only minor, one can encounter $a \times b$ for $\tuple {a, b}$ on an ad hoc basis. These notations are not used on , where $\tuple {a, b}$ is used exclusively.

title: Definition:Ordered Pair/Wiener Formalization
snippet: The concept of an ordered pair can be formalized by the definition: $\tuple {a, b} := \set {\set {\O, \set a}, \set {\set b} }$

title: Definition:Ordered Pair/Wiener Formalization/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Wiener Formalization of Ordered Pair == The Wiener formalization of the ordered pair was devised by in $1914$. According to by and , this was the first such scheme for axiomatising the concept of the ordered pair.

title: Definition:Ordered Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $\preceq$ be an ordering compatible with the ring structure of $\struct {R, +, \circ}$. Then $\struct {R, +, \circ, \preceq}$ is an ordered ring.
