title: Definition:Product Moment
snippet: The product moment is a generalization of the concept of moment in the context of probability theory for a bivariate distribution.

title: Definition:Product Notation
snippet: Algebra: Continued product: for example $\ds \prod_{k \mathop = 1}^n x_k$ meaning $x_1 \times x_2 \times \cdots \times x_n$. Abstract algebra, especially group theory and ring theory: Another term for multiplicative notation.

title: Definition:Product Property of Primes
snippet: Let $p_n$ denote the $n$th prime number. $p_n$ satisfies the product property if the product of the digits of its base $10$ representation equals $n$.

title: Definition:Product Riemannian Metric
snippet: Let $\struct {M_1, g_1}$ and $\struct {M_2, g_2}$ be Riemannian manifolds. Let $p \in M$ be a point in $M$. Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space of $M$ at $p$. Let $v, w \in T_p M$ be tangent vectors. Let $\tuple {v_1, v_2}, \tuple {w_1, w_2} \in T_{p_1} M_1 \oplus T_{p_2} M_2$. Let $M_1 \times M_2$ be the product manifold. Let $\tuple {p_1, p_2} \in M_1 \times M_2$ be a point in $M_1 \times M_2$.

title: Definition:Product Sigma-Algebra/Binary Case
snippet: Let $\struct {X_1, \Sigma_1}$ and $\struct {X_2, \Sigma_2}$ be measurable spaces. The product $\sigma$-algebra of $\Sigma_1$ and $\Sigma_2$ is denoted $\Sigma_1 \otimes \Sigma_2$, and defined as: $\Sigma_1 \otimes \Sigma_2 := \map \sigma {\set {S_1 \times S_2: S_1 \in \Sigma_1 \text { and } S_2 \in \Sigma_2} }$ where: $\sigma$ denotes generated $\sigma$-algebra $\times$ denotes Cartesian product. This is a $\sigma$-algebra on the Cartesian product $X \times Y$.

title: Definition:Product Sigma-Algebra/Countable Case
snippet: Let $\sequence {\struct {X_i, \Sigma_i} }_{i \in \N}$ be a sequence of measurable spaces. Let: $\ds S = \set {\prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n A_i \times \prod_{i \mathop = n + 1}^\infty X_i : n \in \N, \, A_i \in \Sigma_i \text { for each } 1 \le i \le n}$ We define the product $\sigma$-algebra of $\Sigma_1, \Sigma_2, \ldots$, written $\ds \bigotimes_{i \mathop = 1}^\infty \Sigma_i$, by: $\ds \bigotimes_{i \mathop = 1}^\infty \Sigma_i = \map \sigma S$ where $\map \sigma S$ denotes the $\sigma$-algebra generated by $S$.

title: Definition:Product Sigma-Algebra/Finite Case
snippet: Let $n \in \N$. Let $\struct {X_1, \Sigma_1}, \struct {X_2, \Sigma_2}, \ldots, \struct {X_n, \Sigma_n}$ be measurable spaces. Let: $\ds S = \set {\prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n S_i : S_i \in \Sigma_i \text { for each } i \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n} }$ We define the product $\sigma$-algebra of $\Sigma_1, \Sigma_2, \ldots, \Sigma_n$, written $\ds \bigotimes_{i \mathop = 1}^n \Sigma_i$, by: $\ds \bigotimes_{i \mathop = 1}^n \Sigma_i = \map \sigma S$ where $\map \sigma S$ denotes the $\sigma$-algebra generated by $S$.

title: Definition:Product Space
snippet: Topology: Product Space (Topology) Metric Spaces: $p$-Product Metric Linear Algebra: Direct Product of Vector Spaces

title: Definition:Product Space (Topology)
snippet: Let $\family {\struct {S_i, \tau_i} }_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed family of topological spaces where $I$ is an arbitrary index set. Let $S$ be the cartesian product of $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$: $\ds S := \prod_{i \mathop \in I} S_i$ Let $\tau$ be the product topology on $S$. The topological space $\struct {X, \tau}$ is called the product space of $\family {\struct {S_i, \tau_i} }_{i \mathop \in I}$.

title: Definition:Product Space (Topology)/Two Factor Spaces
snippet: Let $\struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $\struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $S_1 \times S_2$ be the cartesian product of $S_1$ and $S_2$. Let $\tau$ be the product topology on $S_1 \times S_2$. The topological space $\struct {S_1 \times S_2, \tau}$ is called the product space of $\struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $\struct {S_2, \tau_2}$.

title: Definition:Product Topology
snippet: Let $\family {\struct {X_i, \tau_i} }_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed family of topological spaces where $I$ is an arbitrary index set. Let $\XX$ be the cartesian product of $\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$: $\ds \XX := \prod_{i \mathop \in I} X_i$ For each $i \in I$, let $\pr_i: \XX \to X_i$ denote the $i$th projection on $\XX$: $\forall \family {x_j}_{j \mathop \in I} \in \XX: \map {\pr_i} {\family {x_j}_{j \mathop \in I} } = x_i$ The product topology on $\XX$ is defined as the initial topology $\tau$ on $\XX$ $\family {\pr_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$.

title: Definition:Product Topology/Also known as
snippet: == Product Topology: Also known as == The product topology is also known as the Tychonoff topology, named for . While both of these terms are commonly used on , the preference is for product topology. Various other terms can be found in the literature for the product space, for example: direct product topological product Tychonoff product but these terms are less precise, and there exists the danger of confusion with other similar uses of these terms in different contexts. Note that the topological space $\struct {\XX, \tau}$ itself is never referred to as a Tychonoff space.

title: Definition:Product Topology/Factor Space
snippet: Let $\family {\struct {X_i, \tau_i} }_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed family of topological spaces where $I$ is an arbitrary index set. Let $\struct {\XX, \tau}$ be the product space of $\family {\struct {x_i, \tau_i} }_{i \mathop \in I}$. Each of the topological spaces $\struct {X_i, \tau_i}$ are called the factors of $\struct {\XX, \tau}$, and can be referred to as factor spaces.

title: Definition:Product Topology/Finite Product
snippet: Let $I$ be a finite indexing set. Let $\family {\struct {X_i, \tau_i} }_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed family of topological spaces indexed by $I$. Let $\XX$ be the cartesian product of $\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$: $\ds \XX := \prod_{i \mathop \in I} X_i$ For each $i \in I$, let $\pr_i: \XX \to X_i$ denote the $i$th projection on $\XX$: $\forall \family {x_j}_{j \mathop \in I} \in \XX: \map {\pr_i} {\family {x_j}_{j \mathop \in I} } = x_i$ The product topology on $\XX$ is defined as the initial topology $\tau$ on $\XX$ $\family {\pr_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$.

title: Definition:Product Topology/Natural Basis
snippet: Let $\family {\struct {X_i, \tau_i} }_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed family of topological spaces where $I$ is an arbitrary index set. Let $\XX$ be the cartesian product of $\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$: $\ds \XX := \prod_{i \mathop \in I} X_i$ For each $i \in I$, let $\pr_i: \XX \to X_i$ denote the $i$th projection on $\XX$: $\forall \family {x_j}_{j \mathop \in I} \in X: \map {\pr_i} {\family {x_j}_{j \mathop \in I} } = x_i$ Let $\tau$ be the product topology on $S$.

title: Definition:Product Topology/Natural Sub-Basis
snippet: Let $\family {\struct {X_i, \tau_i} }_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed family of topological spaces where $I$ is an arbitrary index set. Let $\XX$ be the cartesian product of $\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$: $\ds \XX := \prod_{i \mathop \in I} X_i$ For each $i \in I$, let $\pr_i: X \to X_i$ denote the $i$th projection on $X$: $\forall \family {x_j}_{j \mathop \in I} \in X: \map {\pr_i} {\family {x_j}_{j \mathop \in I} } = x_i$ The natural sub-basis on $\XX$ is defined as: $\SS = \set {\pr_i^{-1} \sqbrk U: i \in I, \, U \in \tau_i}$

title: Definition:Product Topology/Two Factor Spaces
snippet: Let $\struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $\struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $S_1 \times S_2$ be the cartesian product of $S_1$ and $S_2$. The product topology $\tau$ on $S_1 \times S_2$ is the topology generated by the natural basis: $\BB = \set {U_1 \times U_2: U_1 \in \tau_1, U_2 \in \tau_2}$

title: Definition:Product UMP (Category Theory)
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $\CC$ be any collection of objects of $\mathbf C$. Let $\map {\mathbf {Dis} } \CC$ be the discrete category on $\CC$, considered as a subcategory of $\mathbf C$. An object $\ds \prod \CC$ and morphisms $\pr_C: \ds \prod \CC \to C$ for each object $C \in \CC$: $\begin{xy} +{\ds \prod \CC} = "CC", +{\map {\mathbf {Dis} } \CC} = "BLL", +{C} = "BL", +{\ldots} = "BC", +{C'} = "BR", "CC";"BL" **@{-} ?>*@{>} ?<>(.5)*!/^1em/{\pr_C}, "CC";"BR" **@{-} ?>*@{>} ?<>(.5)*!/_1em/{\pr_{C'} }, \end{xy}$ satisfy the (product) universal mapping property or (UMP) :

title: Definition:Product UMP (Category Theory)/Property
snippet: == Property for Product UMP == For any object $A$ together with morphisms $a_C: A \to C$ for each object $C \in \CC$, then there exists a unique morphism $a: A \to \ds \prod \CC$ such that: for each $C \in \CC: a_C = \pr_C \circ a$ That is: $\begin{xy} +{A} = "TC", +{\ds \prod \CC} = "CC", +{\map {\mathbf {Dis} } \CC} = "BLL", +{C} = "BL", +{\ldots} = "BC", +{C'} = "BR", "CC";"BL" **@{-} ?>*@{>} ?<>(.5)*!/_1em/{\pr_C}, "CC";"BR" **@{-} ?>*@{>} ?<>(.5)*!/^1em/{\pr_{C'} }, "TC";"CC" **@{--} ?>*@{>} ?<>(.6)*!/_.5em/{a}, "TC";"BL" **@{-} ?>*@{>} ?<>(.5)*!/^1em/{a_C}, "TC";"BR" **@{-} ?>*@{>}…

title: Definition:Product of Affine Spaces
snippet: Let $\EE, \FF$ be affine spaces with difference spaces $E, F$ respectively. Let $\GG = \EE \times \FF$ be the Cartesian product of the sets $\EE, \FF$. Let $G = E \times F$ be the direct product of the vector spaces $E, F$. Define sum and difference operations $+ : \GG \times G \to \GG$ and $- : \GG \times \GG \to G$ by, for all $p, p' \in \EE$ and $q, q' \in \FF$: $\tuple {p, q} + \tuple {p', q'} := \tuple {p + p', q + q'}$ $\tuple {p, q} - \tuple {p', q'} := \tuple {p - p', q - q'}$ Then the set $\GG$ together with the vector space $G$ and the operations $+, -$ is called the product of the…

title: Definition:Product of Cardinals
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be sets. Let $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ be the cardinals associated respectively with $A$ and $B$. Then the product of $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ is defined as: $\mathbf a \mathbf b := \map \Card {A \times B}$ where: $A \times B$ denotes the Cartesian product of $A$ and $B$ $\map \Card {A \times B}$ denotes the cardinal associated with $A \times B$.

title: Definition:Product of Cosets of Subring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $S$ be a subring of $R$. For $a \in R$, let $\paren {a + S}$ denote the coset of $S$ by $a$. Then we define the operation $\odot$, called product of cosets of $S$, on the coset space of $R$ $S$ as: $\forall x, y \in R: \paren {x + S} \odot \paren {y + S} := \paren {\paren {x \circ y} + S}$

title: Definition:Product of Cosets of Subring/Also denoted as
snippet: == Product of Cosets of Subring: Also denoted as == While has denoted the product of cosets of a subring with the symbol $\odot$, this technique has been employed for clarity of definition only. It is common, and indeed ubiquitous, to use the same symbol as the one for ring product: $\forall x, y \in R: \paren {x + S} \circ \paren {y + S} := \paren {\paren {x \circ y} + S}$

title: Definition:Product of Differences
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{> 0}$ be a strictly positive integer. Let $\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ be an ordered $n$-tuple of real numbers. The product of differences of $\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ is defined and denoted as: $\map {\Delta_n} {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} = \ds \prod_{1 \mathop \le i \mathop < j \mathop \le n} \paren {x_i - x_j}$ When the underlying ordered $n$-tuple is understood, the notation is often abbreviated to $\Delta_n$.

title: Definition:Product of Fractional Ideals
snippet: Let $R$ be an integral domain with fraction field $K$. Let $I, J \subseteq K$ be fractional ideals of $R$. The product of $I$ and $J$ is the set of summations: $\ds \set {\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^r a_i b_i : a_i \in I, b_i \in J, r \in \N}$

title: Definition:Product of Functors
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$, $\mathbf C'$, $\mathbf D$, $\mathbf D'$ be categories. Let $F: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ and $G: \mathbf C' \to \mathbf D'$ be covariant functors. Then: the product of $F$ and $G$, denoted by $F \times G:\mathbf C \times \mathbf C' \to \mathbf D \times \mathbf D'$, is the covariant functor defined by: {{DefineFunctor |ob = for each object $\tuple{C, C'} \in \mathbf C \times \mathbf C' : \paren{F \times G} \tuple{C, C'} := \tuple{F C, G C'}$ |mor = for each morphism $\tuple{f, f'} \in \mathbf C \times \mathbf C' : \paren{F \times G} \tuple{f, f'} := \tuple{F f, G f'}$ }} where…

title: Definition:Product of Ideals of Ring
snippet: Let $\left({R, +, \circ}\right)$ be a commutative ring. Let $I,J$ be ideals of $R$.

title: Definition:Product of Inertia
snippet: Let $B$ be a rigid body which is rotating in space about some axis $\LL$. Let $B$ be embedded in Cartesian $3$-space whose origin lies on $\LL$. Let $B$ be composed of a countable number of particles $P_1, P_2, \ldots$ such that: each $P_i$ has mass $m_i$ each $P_i$ has perpendicular distance $r_i$ from $\LL$. each $P_i$ has coordinates $\tuple {x_i, y_i, z_i}$. Then the products of inertia of $B$ about $\LL$ are defined as: {{eqn | l = I_{yz} | r = \sum m_i y_i z_i | c = }} {{eqn | l = I_{zx} | r = \sum m_i z_i x_i | c = }} {{eqn | l = I_{xy} | r = \sum m_i x_i y_i | c = }}

title: Definition:Product of Measurable Spaces/Binary Case
snippet: Let $\struct {X_1, \Sigma_1}$ and $\struct {X_2, \Sigma_2}$ be measurable spaces. The product of $\struct {X_1, \Sigma_1}$ and $\struct {X_2, \Sigma_2}$ is the measurable space: $\struct {X_1 \times X_2, \Sigma_1 \otimes \Sigma_2}$ where $\Sigma_1 \otimes \Sigma_2$ denotes the product $\sigma$-algebra of $\Sigma_1$ and $\Sigma_2$.

title: Definition:Product of Measurable Spaces/Countable Case
snippet: Let $\sequence {\struct {X_i, \Sigma_i} }_{i \in \N}$ be a sequence of measurable spaces. The product of $\struct {X_1, \Sigma_1}, \struct {X_2, \Sigma_2}, \ldots$ is the measurable space: $\ds \struct {\prod_{i \mathop = 1}^\infty X_i, \bigotimes_{i \mathop = 1}^\infty \Sigma_i}$ where $\ds \bigotimes_{i \mathop = 1}^\infty \Sigma_i$ denotes the product $\sigma$-algebra of $\Sigma_1, \Sigma_2, \ldots$.

title: Definition:Product of Measurable Spaces/Finite Case
snippet: Let $n \in \N$. Let $\struct {X_1, \Sigma_1}, \struct {X_2, \Sigma_2}, \ldots, \struct {X_n, \Sigma_n}$ be measurable spaces. The product of $\struct {X_1, \Sigma_1}, \struct {X_2, \Sigma_2}, \ldots, \struct {X_n, \Sigma_n}$ is the measurable space: $\ds \struct {\prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n X_i, \bigotimes_{i \mathop = 1}^n \Sigma_i}$ where $\ds \bigotimes_{i \mathop = 1}^n \Sigma_i$ denotes the product $\sigma$-algebra of $\Sigma_1, \Sigma_2, \ldots, \Sigma_n$. Category:Definitions/Product of Measurable Spaces

title: Definition:Product of Morphisms
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $A, A'$ and $B, B'$ be pairs of objects admitting binary products: $\begin{xy}\xymatrix@R-1em@C+1em@L+3px{ A & A \times A' \ar[l]_*+{p_1} \ar[r]^*+{p_2} & A' \\ B & B \times B' \ar[l]_*+{q_1} \ar[r]^*+{q_2} & B' }\end{xy}$ Let $f: A \to B$ and $f': A' \to B'$ be morphisms.

title: Definition:Production
snippet: The process of extending a straight line segment is called production. Such a straight line segment is said to be produced. The straight line segment can be extended in either direction, thus producing an infinite half-line, or in both directions, thus producing an infinite straight line.

title: Definition:Profile
snippet: Let $G$ be a game. Let $N$ be the set of players of $G$. Let $V$ be a variable defining some aspect of each of the players. The family of values of $V$ is referred to as a profile, denoted: $\family {x_i}_{i \mathop \in N}$ If the fact that $i \in N$ is understood, then $\family {x_i}$ can be used.

title: Definition:Profile/Less Player
snippet: Let $G$ be a game. Let $N$ be the set of players of $G$. Let $V$ be a variable defining some aspect of each of the players. Let $x = \family {x_i}_{i \mathop \in N}$ be a profile of $V$. Then $x_{-i}$ is used to denote $x$ for all players except for $i$: $x_{-i} := \family {x_j}_{j \mathop \in N \setminus \set i}$ Thus the profile $x = \family {x_i}_{i \mathop \in N}$ can be denoted: $\family {x_{-i}, x_i}$ for some $x_i$ for $i \in N$.

title: Definition:Profile of Preference Relations
snippet: Let $G$ be a game. Let $P$ be a player of $G$. Let $C$ be the set $C$ of consequences of the moves available to $P$. The profile $\sequence {\succsim_i^*}$ of preference relations over $C$ is defined as: $\forall a, b \in A: \paren {a \succsim_i b} \iff \paren {\map g a \succsim_i^* \map g b}$

title: Definition:Profinite Group
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \odot, \tau}$ be a topological group.

title: Definition:Profinite Group/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \odot, \tau}$ be a topological group. $\struct {G, \odot, \tau}$ is profinite it is isomorphic in the category of topological groups to a small inverse limit of finite discrete groups, with the limit topology.

title: Definition:Profinite Group/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \odot, \tau}$ be a topological group. $\struct {G, \odot, \tau}$ is profinite it is a compact, totally disconnected $T_2$ space.

title: Definition:Program
snippet: A program is an algorithm which has been written for a computer to execute.

title: Definition:Program/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Program == The British English spelling programme is still used in Britain and elsewhere in, for example, the context of radio programmes and concert programmes, to mean the order of events. However, in the context of computers, the spelling program is universal. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Program Evaluation and Review Technique
snippet: A program evaluation and review technique is an extension of critical path analysis. Its thesis is to work out how changes in the time taken to complete activities will delay or advance the completion time.

title: Definition:Program Evaluation and Review Technique/Also known as
snippet: == Program Evaluation and Review Technique/Also known as == Program evaluation and review technique is usually known by its abbreviation PERT.

title: Definition:Programming Language
snippet: A programming language is a special purpose language used to implement algorithms for a computer to execute.

title: Definition:Progressing Mapping
snippet: Let $C$ be a class. Let $f: C \to C$ be a mapping from $C$ to $C$. Then $f$ is a progressing mapping : $x \in C \implies x \subseteq \map f x$ That is, for each $x \in C$, $x$ is a subset of $\map f x$.

title: Definition:Progressing Mapping/Also known as
snippet: == Progressing Mapping: Also known as == A progressing mapping is also known as an inflationary mapping, which is the term generally used in the context of an arbitrary ordered structure, notably in the field of measure theory. Some sources use the term progressive mapping. The term extensive mapping can also occasionally be seen, but this is not endorsed on because of its possible confusion with the concept of the . Sources which prefer the term function to mapping will tend to use such here: progressing function, inflationary function, and so on. Category:Definitions/Progressing Mappings

title: Definition:Progression
snippet: The word progression is a term used for either sequence or series in the following specific contexts. Because its usage is in general ambiguous, it is deprecated on .

title: Definition:Progressive Stochastic Process/Continuous Time
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \sequence {\FF_t}_{t \ge 0}, \Pr}$ be a filtered probability space. Let $\sequence {X_t}_{t \ge 0}$ be a $\hointr 0 \infty$-indexed family of real-valued random variables. For each $s \in \hointr 0 \infty$, define the map $X^s : \Omega \times \closedint 0 s$ such that: $\map {X^s} {\omega, t} = \map {X_t} \omega$ for each $\tuple {\omega, t} \in \Omega \times \closedint 0 s$. Let $\map \BB {\closedint 0 s}$ be the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\closedint 0 s$.

title: Definition:Progressive Wave/Also known as
snippet: == Progressive Wave: Also known as == A progressive wave is also known as: a moving wave a travelling wave. Category:Definitions/Progressive Waves

title: Definition:Projectile
snippet: A projectile is a body $B$ to which is imparted an initial velocity through a fluid (usually air). Subsequent motion of $B$ depends only on external forces, such as gravitation and air resistance.

title: Definition:Projectile/Angle of Projection
snippet: The angle of projection of a projectile $\PP$ is the inclination of the direction of the initial velocity of $\PP$ with the horizontal.

title: Definition:Projection
snippet: Mapping Theory: Projection (Mapping Theory) Quotient Mapping, also known as projection or canonical projection Projection of Set Product Category Theory: Projection (Category Theory) Projection Functor Geometry: Projection of Point onto Line Projection of Point onto Plane Projection of Line onto Plane Geometry: Geometric Projection Linear Algebra: Vector Projection Scalar Projection Functional Analysis: Projection (Hilbert Spaces) Orthogonal Projection Idempotent Operator, to which some sources refer as a projection

title: Definition:Projection (*-Algebras)
snippet: Let $\struct {A, \ast}$ be a $\ast$-algebra. Let $p \in A$ be Hermitian. We say that $p$ is a projection $p^2 = p$

title: Definition:Projection (Geometry)
snippet: A projection is a mapping from a geometric figure onto a plane according to certain rules.

title: Definition:Projection (Geometry)/Plane
snippet: Let $M$ and $N$ be distinct lines in the plane. 420px The projection on $M$ along $N$ is the mapping $\pr_{M, N}$ such that: $\forall x \in \R^2: \map {\pr_{M, N} } x =$ the intersection of $M$ with the line through $x$ parallel to $N$.

title: Definition:Projection (Hilbert Spaces)
snippet: Let $H$ be a Hilbert space. Let $P \in \map B H$ be an idempotent operator. Then $P$ is said to be a projection : $\ker P = \paren {\Img P}^\perp$ where: $\ker P$ denotes the kernel of $P$ $\Img P$ denotes the image of $P$ $\perp$ denotes orthocomplementation.

title: Definition:Projection (Mapping Theory)
snippet: Let $S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_j, \ldots, S_n$ be sets. Let $\ds \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n S_i$ be the Cartesian product of $S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_n$. For each $j \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n}$, the $j$th projection on $\ds S = \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n S_i$ is the mapping $\pr_j: S \to S_j$ defined by: $\map {\pr_j} {s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_j, \ldots, s_n} = s_j$ for all $\tuple {s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n} \in S$.

title: Definition:Projection (Mapping Theory)/Family of Sets
snippet: Let $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a family of sets. Let $\ds \prod_{i \mathop \in I} S_i$ be the Cartesian product of $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$. For each $j \in I$, the $j$th projection on $\ds S = \prod_{i \mathop \in I} S_i$ is the mapping $\pr_j: S \to S_j$ defined by: $\map {\pr_j} {\family {s_i}_{i \mathop \in I} } = s_j$ where $\family {s_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ is an arbitrary element of $\ds \prod_{i \mathop \in I} S_i$.

title: Definition:Projection (Mapping Theory)/First Projection
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $S \times T$ be the Cartesian product of $S$ and $T$. The first projection on $S \times T$ is the mapping $\pr_1: S \times T \to S$ defined by: $\forall \tuple {x, y} \in S \times T: \map {\pr_1} {x, y} = x$

title: Definition:Projection (Mapping Theory)/Second Projection
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $S \times T$ be the Cartesian product of $S$ and $T$. The second projection on $S \times T$ is the mapping $\pr_2: S \times T \to T$ defined by: $\forall \tuple {x, y} \in S \times T: \map {\pr_2} {x, y} = y$

title: Definition:Projection (Vector Spaces)
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $X$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $P : X \to X$ be a linear transformation. Let $Y$ be a vector subspace of $X$. We say that: $P$ is a projection onto $Y$ $P^2 = P$ and $P \sqbrk X = Y$.

title: Definition:Projection Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories, and let $\mathbf C \times \mathbf D$ be their product. The first projection functor $\pr_1: \mathbf C \times \mathbf D \to \mathbf C$ is defined by: {{DefineFunctor |ob = $\map {\pr_1} {C, D} := C$ for all objects $\tuple {C, D} \in \map {\operatorname{ob} } {\mathbf C \times \mathbf D}$ |mor = $\map {\pr_1} {f, g} := f$ for all morphisms $\tuple {f, g} \in \map {\operatorname{mor} } {\mathbf C \times \mathbf D}$ }} The second projection functor $\pr_2: \mathbf C \times \mathbf D \to \mathbf D$ is defined by: {{DefineFunctor |ob = $\map…

title: Definition:Projection Operator over 2-Sequence Spaces
snippet: Let $\ell^2$ be the $2$-sequence space. Let $\map {CL} {\ell^2} := \map {CL} {\ell^2, \ell^2}$ be the continuous linear transformation space. Let $\mathbf a \in \ell^2$ be such that: $\mathbf a = \tuple {a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots}$ Then by the projection operator over $\ell^2$ we mean the mapping $P_n \in \map {CL} {\ell^2}$ with $n \in \N$ where: $\tuple {a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots} \stackrel {P_n} \mapsto \tuple{a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n, 0, \ldots}$

title: Definition:Projections Associated with Schauder Basis
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a normed vector space over $\GF$. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a Schauder basis for $X$. Let $\sequence {x_n^\ast}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be the coordinate functionals associated with $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$. We define the projections $\sequence {S_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ associated with $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ by taking: $\ds \map {S_n} x = \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n \map {x_k^\ast} x x_k$ for each $n \in \N$ and $x \in X$.

title: Definition:Projective Algebraic Set
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $n \in \N_{>0}$. Let $\map {\mathbb P^n} K$ be the $n$-projective space over $K$. Let $S = K \sqbrk {X_0, \ldots, X_n}$ be the ring of polynomial functions in $n + 1$ variables over $K$. Then a subset $X \subseteq \map {\mathbb P^n} K$ is a projective algebraic set : there is a subset $T \subseteq S$ of homogeneous elements such that: $\ds X = \bigcap_{f \mathop \in T} \set {\struct {x_0 : \cdots : x_n} \in \map {\mathbb P^n} K : \map f {x_0, \ldots, x_n} = 0}$

title: Definition:Projective Geometry
snippet: Projective geometry is the field of geometry concerned with properties which are invariant under projective transformations.

title: Definition:Projective Geometry/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Projective Geometry == The study of projective geometry was pioneered in $1639$ by , as a result of the work he was doing with conic sections. He was influenced by perspective in art, and particularly interested in how a projection of a conic section is itself a conic section. He made the assumption that parallel lines meet at a point at infinity. Like , he considered the parabola to have a second focus at infinity. He studied properties of conic sections which were unchanged under projections. He also made use of the complete quadrangle because of its harmonic ratios.

title: Definition:Projective Module
snippet: Let $A$ be a ring with unity. Let $M$ be an $A$-module. $M$ is projective there exists an $A$-module $N$ such that the direct sum $M \oplus N$ is a free module.

title: Definition:Projective Object
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $P$ be an object of $\mathbf C$. Then $P$ is projective : For all epimorphisms $e: E \twoheadrightarrow X$ and morphisms $f: P \to X$, there exists a morphism $\bar f: P \to E$ such that: $\begin{xy} +{P} = "P", +{X} = "X", +{E} = "E", "P";"E" **@{-} ?>*@{>} ?*!/_.6em/{\bar f}, "P";"X" **@{-} ?>*@{>} ?*!/^.6em/{f}, "E";"X" **@{-} ?>*@2{>} ?<>(.7)*{\vee} ?*!/_.6em/{e}, \end{xy}$ is a commutative diagram, i.e. such that $f = e \circ \bar f$. In this situation, $f$ is said to lift across $e$.

title: Definition:Projective Plane
snippet: Let $\FF$ be a field whose zero is $0$. The projective plane over $\FF$ is the set of points represented by ordered triples $\tuple {x, y, z}$ such that: $x, y, z$ are not all equal to $0$ $x, y, z \in \FF$ for $\lambda \in \FF$ such that $\lambda \ne 0$, the ordered triples $\tuple {x, y, z}$ and $\tuple {\lambda x, \lambda y, \lambda z}$ represent the same point.

title: Definition:Projective Plane/Complex
snippet: The complex projective plane $\C P^2$ is the projective plane over the field of complex numbers.

title: Definition:Projective Plane/Finite
snippet: Let $\GF$ be a finite field. Let $P$ be the projective plane over $\GF$. Then $P$ is known as a finite projective plane.

title: Definition:Projective Plane/Real
snippet: The real projective plane $\R P^2$ is the projective plane over the field of real numbers. That is, it is the topological subspace of the $3$-dimensional real Euclidean space $\R^3$ obtained by removing the origin $\tuple {0, 0, 0}$ and identifying together $\tuple {x, y, z}$ and $\tuple {r x, r y, r z}$ for all $r \in \R_{\ne 0}$.

title: Definition:Projective Resolution
snippet: Let $\AA$ be an abelian category. Let $X$ be an object in $\AA$. A projective resolution of $X$ is a chain complex $P := \family {d_i : P_i \to P_{i - 1} }_{i \mathop \in \Z}$ in $\AA$, such that: $\forall i < 0 : P_i = 0$ $P_i$ is projective for all $i \geq 0$ together with an augmentation map $\varepsilon : P_0 \to X$, such that the chain complex $\begin{xy} \xymatrix{ \dots \ar[r] & P_2 \ar[r]^{d_2} & P_1 \ar[r]^{d_1} & P_0 \ar[r]^{\varepsilon} & X \ar[r] & 0 \ar[r] & 0 \ar[r] & \dots } \end{xy}$ is exact.

title: Definition:Projective Space/Over a Field
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $K$ of dimension $n + 1 \ge 1$. Let $\sim$ be the equivalence relation defined on the set $V \setminus \set 0$ by: $x, y \in V \setminus \set 0: x \sim y \iff \exists \lambda \in K: x = \lambda y$ The projective space associated to $V$ of dimension $n$ over $K$ is the quotient set $\paren {V \setminus \set 0} / \sim$ and is denoted $\map {\mathbb P} V$. If $V = K^{n + 1}$ for $n \ge 0$ a natural number, projective space is sometimes denoted $\map {\mathbb P} {K^{n + 1} } = \map {\mathbb P^n} K$.

title: Definition:Projective Space/Real Projective Space
snippet: Let $\Bbb S^n \subseteq \R^{n+1}$ be an $n$-sphere. Let $\sim$ be the equivalence relation defined on $\Bbb S^n$ by: $x, y \in \Bbb S^n: x \sim y \iff x = -y$ The real projective space of dimension $n$ is the quotient space $\Bbb S^n / \sim$ and is denoted $\Bbb{RP}^n$.

snippet: == Prolate Spheroid: Also known as == A prolate spheroid is also known as a prolate ellipsoid.

title: Definition:Pronic Number
snippet: A pronic number is a natural number which is the product of two consecutive natural numbers.

title: Definition:Pronic Number/Also known as
snippet: == Pronic Number: Also known as == A pronic number is also known as: an oblong number a rectangular number a heteromecic number.

title: Definition:Pronic Number/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Pronic Number == The word pronic appears to be a misspelling of promic, which derives from the Greek promekes, meaning rectangular, oblate, or oblong. However, no less an authority than himself used the term pronic so it seems we are stuck with it.

title: Definition:Pronormal Subgroup
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$. Then $H$ is a pronormal subgroup in $G$ each of its conjugates in $G$ is conjugate to it already in the subgroup generated by $H$ and its conjugate. That is, $H$ is pronormal in $G$ : $\forall g \in G: \exists k \in \gen {H, H^g}: H^k = H^g$ where: $\gen {H, H^g}$ is the subgroup generated by $H$ and $H^g$ $H^g$ is the conjugate of $H$ by $g$.

title: Definition:Proof
snippet: A proof is a valid argument whose premises are all true. Hence a valid argument that has one or more false premises is not a proof. Suppose $P$ is a proposition whose truth or falsehood is to be determined. Constructing a valid argument upon a set of premises, all of which have previously been established as being true, is called proving $P$.

title: Definition:Proof/Also known as
snippet: == Proof: Also known as == Some authors use the term sound argument as a synonym for what is defined here as a proof. However, as some use sound argument to mean the same thing that is defined here as a valid argument, it is recommended that this term not be used. Some authors refer to a proof as a derivation, but that term already has connotations from calculus, so it is preferred not to be used.

title: Definition:Proof/Historical Note

title: Definition:Proof System
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a formal language. A proof system $\mathscr P$ for $\LL$ comprises: Axioms and/or axiom schemata; Rules of inference for deriving theorems. It is usual that a proof system does this by declaring certain arguments concerning $\LL$ to be valid. Informally, a proof system amounts to a precise account of what constitutes a (formal) proof.

title: Definition:Proof System/Formal Proof
snippet: Let $\mathscr P$ be a proof system for a formal language $\LL$. Let $\phi$ be a WFF of $\LL$. A formal proof of $\phi$ in $\mathscr P$ is a collection of axioms and rules of inference of $\mathscr P$ that leads to the conclusion that $\phi$ is a theorem of $\mathscr P$. The term formal proof is also used to refer to specific presentations of such collections. For example, the term applies to tableau proofs in natural deduction.

title: Definition:Proof Technique
snippet: A proof technique is an argument form which can be used as a template for the purpose of structuring a proof.

title: Definition:Proof Theory
snippet: Proof theory is the subfield of mathematical logic which studies proofs as mathematical objects, thus allowing them to be analysed mathematically.

title: Definition:Proof Theory/Also known as
snippet: == Proof Theory: Also known as == Proof theory is also known as metalogic. Some sources use the term metamathematics, but others consider the scope of the latter to be different. The term logical syntax can occasionally be found.

title: Definition:Proof Theory/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Proof Theory == The mathematical branch known as proof theory was initiated by in his attempt to prove the consistency of mathematics. His approach was later developed by , who developed a complete system for the treatment of the subject.

title: Definition:Proper Coloring
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a simple graph.

title: Definition:Proper Coloring/Edge Coloring
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a simple graph. A proper (edge) $k$-coloring of $G$ is defined as an edge coloring from a set of $k$ colors such that no two adjacent edges share a common color. That is, a proper $k$-coloring of $G$ is a mapping $c: E \to \set {1, 2, \ldots k}$ such that: $\forall v \in V: \forall e = \set {u_k, v} \in E: \map c {\set {u_i, v} } \ne \map c {\set {u_j, v} }$

title: Definition:Proper Coloring/Vertex Coloring
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a simple graph. A proper (vertex) $k$-coloring of $G$ is defined as a vertex coloring from a set of $k$ colors such that no two adjacent vertices share a common color. That is, a proper $k$-coloring of $G$ is a mapping $c: V \to \set {1, 2, \ldots k}$ such that: $\forall e = \set {u, v} \in E: \map c u \ne \map c v$

title: Definition:Proper Convex Real Function
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a vector space over $\GF$. Let $f: X \to \overline \R$ be an convex real function. Let $\Dom f$ be the effective domain of $f$. We say that $f$ is proper if $\Dom f \ne \O$ and $\map f x > -\infty$ for all $x \in X$.

title: Definition:Proper Divisor
snippet: Let $\struct {D, +, \circ}$ be an integral domain whose zero is $0_D$ and whose unity is $1_D$. Let $U$ be the group of units of $D$. Let $x, y \in D$. Then $x$ is a proper divisor of $y$ : $(1): \quad x \divides y$ $(2): \quad y \nmid x$ $(3): \quad x \notin U$ That is: $(1): \quad x$ is a divisor of $y$ $(2): \quad x$ is not an associate of $y$ $(3): \quad x$ is not a unit of $D$

title: Definition:Proper Divisor/Also known as
snippet: == Proper Divisor: Also known as == A proper divisor is also known as a proper factor. An older name for a proper divisor of an integer is aliquot part.

title: Definition:Proper Divisor/Integer
snippet: Let $\struct {\Z, +, \times}$ be the ring of integers. Let $x, y \in \Z$. Let $x$ divides $y$ be defined as: $x \divides y \iff \exists t \in \Z: y = t \times x$ in the conventional way. Then $x$ is a proper divisor of $y$ : $(1): \quad x \divides y$ $(2): \quad \size x \ne \size y$ $(3): \quad x \ne \pm 1$ That is: $(1): \quad x$ is a divisor of $y$ $(2): \quad x$ and $y$ are not equal in absolute value $(3): \quad x$ is not equal to either $1$ or $-1$.

title: Definition:Proper Element of Ring
snippet: A non-zero element of a ring which does not have a product inverse is called a proper element.

title: Definition:Proper Extension of Mapping
snippet: Let $f$ and $g$ be mappings such that: $g$ is an extension of $f$ $f \ne g$ That is: $f \subsetneqq g$ Then $g$ is a proper extension of $f$.

title: Definition:Proper Fraction/Also known as
snippet: == Proper Fraction: Also known as == A proper fraction is often also known as a vulgar fraction, but this is usually reserved for the general fraction representing a rational number expressed as one integer over another. Some sources use the term common fraction or simple fraction, but those are also used as other terms for a vulgar fraction.

title: Definition:Proper G-Submodule
snippet: Let $\left({V, \phi}\right)$ be a $G$-module. A $G$-submodule of $V$ is called proper iff it is a proper vector subspace of $V$.

title: Definition:Proper Group Action
snippet: Let $G$ be a topological group. Let $X$ be a topological space. A group action $\phi: G \times X \to X$ is called proper $\phi$ is a proper mapping. Here $G\times X$ is equipped with the product topology.

title: Definition:Proper Heronian Triangle
snippet: A proper Heronian triangle is a Heronian triangle which is specifically not right-angled.

title: Definition:Proper Lower Section (Class Theory)
snippet: Let $A$ be a class under a total ordering $\preccurlyeq$. Let $L$ be a lower section of $A$ such that: $L \ne \O$ $L \ne A$ Then $L$ is known as a proper lower section of $A$ (by $L$).

title: Definition:Proper Mapping
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be topological spaces. A mapping $f: X \to Y$ is proper for every compact subspace $K \subset Y$, its preimage $f^{-1} \sqbrk K$ is also compact.

title: Definition:Proper Mapping/Also defined as
snippet: == Proper Mapping: Also defined as == A proper mapping is sometimes defined as a closed mapping such that the preimage of every point is compact.

title: Definition:Proper Mapping/Also known as
snippet: == Proper Mapping: Also known as == A proper mapping can also be referred to as a proper map or a proper function. standardises on mapping rather than map, and reserves the term function for numbers.

title: Definition:Proper Morphism of Schemes
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ and $\struct {Y, \OO_Y}$ be schemes. Let $f : \struct {X, \OO_X} \to \struct {Y, \OO_Y}$ be a morphism of schemes. $f$ is proper $f$ is separated, of finite type and universally closed.

title: Definition:Proper Name
snippet: A proper name is a symbol or collection of symbols used to identify a particular object uniquely. In contrast with natural language, a proper name has a wider range than being the particular identifying label attached to a particular single entity (be it a person, or a place, or whatever else). For example: Sloth is a proper name for the concept of being lazy. Rain is a proper name for the meteorological phenomenon of water falling from the sky.

title: Definition:Proper Name/Also known as
snippet: == Proper Name: Also known as== Other terms for proper name that can be found are: name individual constant constant, particularly when applied to a number parameter.

title: Definition:Proper Orthogonal Matrix
snippet: Let $\mathbf Q$ be an orthogonal matrix. Then $\mathbf Q$ is a proper orthogonal matrix : $\map \det {\mathbf Q} = 1$ where $\map \det {\mathbf Q}$ is the determinant of $\mathbf Q$.

title: Definition:Proper Relational Structure
snippet: Let $A$ be a set or class. Let $\RR$ be a relation on $A$. Then $\struct {A, \RR}$ is a proper relational structure : For each $a \in A$, the preimage $\map {\RR^{-1} } a$ of $a$ under $\RR$ is a set (or small class).

title: Definition:Proper Subclass
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be classes. Let $B$ be a subclass of $A$. Then $B$ is a proper subclass of $A$ $B \ne A$.

title: Definition:Proper Subcontinuum/Also known as
snippet: == Proper Subcontinuum: Also known as == The term proper subcontinuum can also be found hyphenated: proper sub-continuum.

title: Definition:Proper Subgroup
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group. Then $\struct {H, \circ}$ is a proper subgroup of $\struct {G, \circ}$ : $(1): \quad \struct {H, \circ}$ is a subgroup of $\struct {G, \circ}$ $(2): \quad H \ne G$, that is, $H \subsetneq G$. The notation $H H$, means: $H$ is a proper subgroup of $G$. If $H$ is a subgroup of $G$, but it is not specified whether $H = G$ or not, then we write $H \le G$, or $G \ge H$.

title: Definition:Proper Subgroup/Non-Trivial
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group. Let $\struct {H, \circ}$ be a subgroup of $\struct {G, \circ}$ such that $\set e \subset H \subset G$, that is: $H \ne \set e$ $H \ne G$ Then $\struct {H, \circ}$ is a non-trivial proper subgroup of $\struct {G, \circ}$.

title: Definition:Proper Subring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. A subring $S$ of $R$ is a proper subring of $R$ $S$ is neither the null ring nor $R$ itself.

title: Definition:Proper Subset
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets such that $S$ is a subset of $T$. Let $S \ne T$. Then $S$ is referred to as a proper subset of $T$, and we write: $S \subsetneq T$ or: $S \subsetneqq T$

title: Definition:Proper Subset/Also defined as
snippet: == Proper Subset: Also defined as == Some authors require that $S \ne \O$ for $S$ to be a proper subset of $T$. Hence, under this convention, $S$ is a proper subset of $T$ $\O \subsetneqq S \subsetneqq T$ It is wise to be aware of which definition is in use.

title: Definition:Proper Subset/Also denoted as
snippet: == Proper Subset: Also denoted as == The symbology used by some authors to denote a proper subset is: $A \subset B$ to mean: $A$ is a proper subset of $B$. While this practice is common, it is not recommended on because it is also used by many other authors to mean subset which may or may not be proper.

title: Definition:Proper Subset/Also known as
snippet: == Proper Subset: Also known as == $S \subsetneqq T$ can also be read as: $S$ is properly included in $T$, or $T$ properly includes $S$ $S$ is strictly included in $T$, or $T$ strictly includes $S$ The following usage can also be seen for $S \subsetneqq T$: $S$ is properly contained in $T$, or $T$ properly contains $S$ $S$ is strictly contained in $T$, or $T$ strictly contains $S$ However, beware of the usage of contains: $S$ contains $T$ can also be interpreted as $S$ is an element of $T$. Hence the use of contains is not supported on .

title: Definition:Proper Subset/Improper
snippet: Let $T$ be a set. The term improper subset is relevant in treatments of set theory which define a proper subset $T$ as a subset $S$ of $T$ such that: $0 \subsetneqq S \subsetneqq T$ Under such a regime, $S$ is an improper subset of $T$ either: $S = T$ or: $S = \O$

title: Definition:Proper Subset/Proper Superset
snippet: If $S$ is a proper subset of $T$, then $T$ is a proper superset of $S$. This can be expressed by the notation $T \supsetneqq S$.

title: Definition:Proper Subtower in Set
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\struct {T, \preccurlyeq}$ be a tower in $X$. Then $\struct {T, \preccurlyeq}$ is a proper subtower in $X$ : $T$ is a proper subset of some set $T' \subseteq X$ and: $\struct {T', \preccurlyeq}$ is a tower in $X$.

title: Definition:Proper Subtower in Set/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Proper Subtower in Set == The name proper subtower in set has been specifically coined for , and may or may not appear in the literature. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Proper Variation Field of Family of Curves
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $\gamma$ be an admissible curve on $M$. Let $I = \closedint a b$ is a closed real interval. Let $J$ is an open real interval. Let $\Gamma : J \times I \to M$ be the variation of $\gamma$, where $\times$ denotes the cartesian product. Let $V$ be the variation field of $\Gamma$. Suppose $\map V a = \map V b = 0$. Then $V$ is said to be the proper variation field of $\Gamma$.

title: Definition:Proper Variation of Admissible Curve
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $I = \closedint a b$ be a closed real interval. Let $\gamma : I\to M$ be an admissible curve. Let $\Gamma : J \times I \to M$ be an variation of admissible curve such that: $\ds \forall s \in J : \forall t \in I : \tuple {s, t} \stackrel \Gamma \mapsto \map {\Gamma_s} t$ Suppose: $\ds \forall s \in I : \paren{\map {\Gamma_s} a = \map \gamma a} \land \paren{\map {\Gamma_s} b = \map \gamma b}$ Then $\Gamma$ is called the proper variation of $\gamma$.

title: Definition:Proper Well-Ordering
snippet: Let $V$ be a basic universe. Let $A$ be a class. Let $\RR$ be a well-ordering on $A$. Then $\RR$ is a proper well-ordering : every proper lower section of $A$ is a set.

title: Definition:Proper Zero Divisor
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. A proper zero divisor of $R$ is an element $x \in R^*$ such that: $\exists y \in R^*: x \circ y = 0_R$ where $R^*$ is defined as $R \setminus \set {0_R}$. That is, it is a zero divisor of $R$ which is specifically not $0_R$. The presence of a proper zero divisor in a ring means that the product of two elements of the ring may be zero even if neither factor is zero. That is, if $R$ has proper zero divisor, then $\struct {R^*, \circ}$ is not closed.

title: Definition:Proper Zero Divisor/Also known as
snippet: == Proper Zero Divisor: Also known as == Some authors exclude $0_R$ as a zero divisor and thus refer to a proper zero divisor simply as zero divisor. Some sources hyphenate: proper zero-divisor. Some sources use the more precise term proper divisor of zero.

title: Definition:Properly Divergent/Sequence
snippet: A divergent sequence which is not an oscillating sequence is known as a properly divergent sequence.

title: Definition:Properly Divergent/Series
snippet: Let $s$ be an infinite series: $s = \ds \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^\infty a_k = a_1 + a_2 + a_3 + \cdots$ Then $s$ is a properly divergent series it is a divergent series such that either: $s_n \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$ or: $s_n \to -\infty$ as $n \to \infty$ where $s_n$ is the $n$th partial sum of $s$: $s_n = \ds \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n a_k$

title: Definition:Property
snippet: A property is a concept that specifies an aspect of an object. In the phrase living thing, living is a property that thing has. It creates a distinction between things that are living and things that are not living.

title: Definition:Property (S)
snippet: Let $L = \struct {S, \preceq}$ be an up-complete ordered set. Let $X$ be a subset of $S$. Then $X$ has property (S) for all directed subsets $D$ of $S$: $\sup D \in X \implies \exists y \in D:\forall x \in D: y \preceq x \implies x \in X$

title: Definition:Property of Morphisms
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a category. A property of morphisms of $\mathbf C$ is a subclass of the class of morphisms of $\mathbf C$.

title: Definition:Property of Morphisms Stable Under Composition
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a category. Let $P$ be a property of morphisms of $\mathbf C$. Then $P$ is stable under composition : for any three objects $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ any two morphisms $f, g \in P$ such that $f: X \to Y$ and $g: Y \to Z$ we have: $g \circ f \mathop \in P$

title: Definition:Property of Morphisms Stable Under Pullback
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a category. Let $P$ be a property of morphisms of $\mathbf C$. Then $P$ is stable under pullback : for all morphisms $f : X \to Y$ with $f \mathop \in P$ for all morphisms $g : Z \to Y$ for which the pullback of $f$ and $g$ $\begin{xy}\xymatrix@L+2mu@+1em{ X \times_Y Z \ar[r] \ar[d]^{f'} & X \ar[d]^f \\ Z \ar[r]^g & Y }\end{xy}$ exists we have that $f' \in P$.

title: Definition:Proportion
snippet: Two real variables $x$ and $y$ are proportional one is a constant multiple of the other: $\forall x, y \in \R: x \propto y \iff \exists k \in \R, k \ne 0: x = k y$

title: Definition:Proportion/Also known as
snippet: == Proportion: Also known as == The term direct proportion can frequently be seen for the concept of proportion, in order to specifically distinguish it from inverse proportion. The terms: direct variation mutual variation direct relation, and directly related can also be seen. The term proportion is often known nowadays by the less elegant and more cumbersome word proportionality.

title: Definition:Proportion/Constant of Proportion
snippet: Let the two real variables $x$ and $y$ be proportional: $\forall x, y \in \R: x \propto y \iff \exists k \in \R, k \ne 0: x = k y$ The constant $k$ is known as the constant of proportion.

title: Definition:Proportion/Continued
snippet: Four magnitudes $a, b, c, d$ are in continued proportion $a : b = b : c = c : d$.

title: Definition:Proportion/Inverse
snippet: Two real variables $x$ and $y$ are inversely proportional their product is a constant: $\forall x, y \in \R: x \propto \dfrac 1 y \iff \exists k \in \R, k \ne 0: x y = k$

title: Definition:Proportion/Joint
snippet: Two real variables $x$ and $y$ are jointly proportional to a third real variable $z$ the product of $x$ and $y$ is a constant multiple of $z$: $\forall x, y \in \R: x y \propto z \iff \exists k \in \R, k \ne 0: x y = k z$

title: Definition:Proportion/Perturbed
snippet: Let $a, b, c$ and $A, B, C$ be magnitudes. $a, b, c$ are in perturbed proportion to $A, B, C$ : $a : b = B : C$ $b : c = A : B$ ' Category:Definitions/Proportion

title: Definition:Proposition
snippet: A proposition is a statement which is offered up for investigation as to its truth or falsehood. Loosely, a proposition is a statement which is about to be proved (or disproved).

title: Definition:Proposition/Also defined as
snippet: == Proposition: Also defined as == Some sources, while appreciating the need under certain circumstances to do so, do not distinguish between the concept of a statement, as defined here on , and a proposition, using the terms interchangeably: There are good reasons, which fortunately we do not need to go into, for avoiding the term 'proposition'. On the other hand, we shall, in the early sections of this book, be working with what is known as the Propositional Calculus. We shall use the terms 'statement' and 'proposition' interchangeably.

title: Definition:Propositional Expansion
snippet: Suppose our universe of discourse consists of the objects $\mathbf X_1, \mathbf X_2, \mathbf X_3, \ldots$ and so on. (There may be an infinite number of objects in this universe.)

title: Definition:Propositional Expansion/Existential Quantifier
snippet: Suppose our universe of discourse consists of the objects $\mathbf X_1, \mathbf X_2, \mathbf X_3, \ldots$ and so on. Let $\exists$ be the existential quantifier. What $\exists x: \map P x$ means is: At least one of $\mathbf X_1, \mathbf X_2, \mathbf X_3, \ldots$ has property $P$. This means: Either $\mathbf X_1$ has property $P$, or $\mathbf X_2$ has property $P$, or $\mathbf X_3$ has property $P$, or ...

title: Definition:Propositional Expansion/Universal Quantifier
snippet: Suppose our universe of discourse consists of the objects $\mathbf X_1, \mathbf X_2, \mathbf X_3, \ldots$ and so on. Let $\forall$ be the universal quantifier. What $\forall x: \map P x$ means is: $\mathbf X_1$ has property $P$, and $\mathbf X_2$ has property $P$, and $\mathbf X_3$ has property $P$, and ... This translates into propositional logic as: $\map P {\mathbf X_1} \land \map P {\mathbf X_2} \land \map P {\mathbf X_3} \land \ldots$ This expression of $\forall x$ as a conjunction is known as the propositional expansion of $\forall x$.

title: Definition:Propositional Function
snippet: A propositional function $\map P {x_1, x_2, \ldots}$ is an operation which acts on the objects denoted by the object variables $x_1, x_2, \ldots$ in a particular universe to return a truth value which depends on: $(1): \quad$ The values of $x_1, x_2, \ldots$ $(2): \quad$ The nature of $P$.

title: Definition:Propositional Function/Also known as
snippet: == Propositional Function: Also known as == In various contexts, the term propositional function may be given as: Boolean-valued function condition sentential function propositional formula formula property; on , property refers to the everyday meaning of this word as a synonym of "feature", as can be seen on Definition:Property. predicate: in this context it is compatible with Definition:Predicate. The notation for indicating that $x$ has the property $P$ varies; the notation $P x$ can often be seen.

title: Definition:Propositional Function/Satisfaction
snippet: Let $\map P {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ be an $n$-ary propositional function. If $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ have values which make $\map P {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ true, then the ordered tuple $\tuple {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n}$ satisfies $\map P {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$.

title: Definition:Propositional Logic
snippet: Propositional logic is a sub-branch of symbolic logic in which the truth values of propositional formulas are investigated and analysed. The atoms of propositional logic are simple statements. There are various systems of propositional logic for determining the truth values of propositional formulas, for example: Natural deduction is a technique for deducing valid sequents from other valid sequents by applying precisely defined proof rules, each of which themselves are either "self-evident" axioms or themselves derived from other valid sequents.

title: Definition:Propositional Logic/Also known as
snippet: == Propositional Logic: Also known as == As propositional logic (as are its synonyms) is such a mouthful and takes so long to write, some authors succumb to the temptation to abbreviate it by referring to it more-or-less consistently as PropLog. Propositional logic is also referred to as: zeroth order logic (where first order logic is predicate logic) propositional calculus sentential calculus (where sentential is the adjectival form of sentence) theory of deduction

snippet: Propositional tableaux are a specific subset of the labeled trees for propositional logic.

title: Definition:Prosthaphaeresis
snippet: Prosthaphaeresis is the process whereby multiplication and division are performed by: $(1): \quad$ converting the numbers into a form where they can be added or subtracted $(2): \quad$ performing the addition or subtraction $(3): \quad$ converting the result back again, using the inverse process to step $(1)$.

title: Definition:Prosthaphaeresis/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Prosthaphaeresis == The word prosthaphaeresis or prosthapheiresis is a [http://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/neologism neologism] coined some time in the $16$th century from the two Greek words: prosthesis, meaning addition aphaeresis or apheiresis, meaning subtraction. With the advent of machines to aid the process of arithmetic, this word now has only historical significance. , in his from $2008$, accurately and somewhat diplomatically describes the word as "ungainly".

title: Definition:Prosthaphaeresis/Logarithms
snippet: The logarithmic technique of prosthaphaeresis is based on the rule of the Sum of Logarithms: $\log_b x y = \log_b x + \log_b y$ Any base $b$ can be used. The original tecnhique used Napierian logarithms where the base was $0.9999999$ In due course the common (base $10$) logarithm was used, as developed by , called Briggsian logarithms.

title: Definition:Prosthaphaeresis/Trigonometry
snippet: The trigonometric technique of prosthaphaeresis is based on the formula: $\dfrac {\sin \alpha + \sin \beta} 2 = \map \sin {\dfrac {\alpha + \beta} 2} \, \map \cos {\dfrac {\alpha - \beta} 2}$

title: Definition:Protasis/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Protasis == The word protasis is from the Ancient Greek πρότασις (prótasis), from προτείνω (proteínō), meaning put forward, tender or propose, from πρό (pró) $+$ τείνω (teínō), meaning stretch. The word has been adopted by the theatre world as a word meaning the introductory part of a play, usually its first act. Really would not expect this word to come up in a serious mathematical exposition, but, you know, some people may come across it at some point. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Proth Number
snippet: A Proth number is a natural number of the form: $N = k \times 2^n + 1$ where: $k$ is an odd integer $n$ is a positive integer $2^n > k$ The condition is included, otherwise every odd integer greater than $1$ would be a Proth number.

title: Definition:Proth Number/Sequence
snippet: == Sequence of Proth Numbers == The sequence of Proth numbers begins: $3, 5, 9, 13, 17, 25, 33, 41, 49, 57, 65, \ldots$

title: Definition:Proth Prime
snippet: A Proth prime is a Proth number which is also a prime.

title: Definition:Proth Prime/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Proth Primes ==

title: Definition:Proth Prime/Sequence
snippet: == Sequence of Proth Primes == The sequence of Proth primes begins: $3, 5, 13, 17, 41, 97, 113, 193, 241, 257, 353, \ldots$

title: Definition:Proton
snippet: == Proton == A proton is an elementary particle which contains a single unit of positive elementary electric charge.

title: Definition:Proton/Charge
snippet: == Electric Charge on Proton == The electric charge on the proton is $1.60217 \, 6634 \times 10^{−19}$ coulombs. That is, a positive charge whose magnitude is the value of the elementary charge.

title: Definition:Proton/Mass
snippet: == Mass of Proton == The mass of the proton is given by: {{eqn | l = m_{\mathrm p} | o = \approx | r = 1 \cdotp 67262 \, 19236 \, 9(51) \times 10^{-27} | c = kilograms | cc= }} {{eqn | o = \approx | r = 1 \cdotp 67262 \, 19236 \, 9(51) \times 10^{-24} | c = grams | cc= }}

title: Definition:Proton/Mass/Also known as
snippet: == Mass of Proton: Also known as == The mass of the proton is also known as the proton rest mass.

title: Definition:Proton/Radius
snippet: == Radius of Proton == The actual size of the proton is still unknown. The radius of the proton is approximately $0.8414(19) \times 10^{-15}$ metres.

title: Definition:Proton Moment
snippet: The proton moment is defined as the magnetic moment of the proton:

title: Definition:Proton Moment/Also known as
snippet: == Proton Moment: Also known as == The proton moment is also known as the proton magnetic moment. Category:Definitions/Proton Moment

title: Definition:Provable Consequence
snippet: Let $\mathscr P$ be a proof system for a formal language $\LL$. Let $\FF$ be a collection of WFFs of $\LL$. Denote with $\map {\mathscr P} \FF$ the proof system obtained from $\mathscr P$ by adding all the WFFs from $\FF$ as axioms. Let $\phi$ be a theorem of $\map {\mathscr P} \FF$. Then $\phi$ is called a provable consequence of $\FF$, and this is denoted as: $\FF \vdash_{\mathscr P} \phi$ Note in particular that for $\FF = \O$, this notation agrees with the notation for a $\mathscr P$-theorem: $\vdash_{\mathscr P} \phi$

title: Definition:Provable Consequence/Also defined as
snippet: == Provable Consequence: Also defined as == While this definition of provable consequence is adequate for most proof systems, it is more natural for some of them to define provable consequence in a different way. For example, the tableau proof system based on propositional tableaux. Category:Definitions/Proof Systems

title: Definition:Provable Consequence/Also known as
snippet: == Provable Consequence: Also known as == One also encounters phrases like: $\FF$ proves $\phi$ $\phi$ is provable from $\FF$ to describe the concept of provable consequence. A provable consequence is also known as: a derivable formula a provable formula a logical consequence, but this is mainly used more generally in the context of logical implication.

title: Definition:Provable Equivalence
snippet: Let $\mathscr P$ be a proof system for a formal language $\LL$. Let $\phi, \psi$ be $\LL$-WFFs. Then $\phi$ and $\psi$ are $\mathscr P$-provably equivalent : $\phi \vdash_{\mathscr P} \psi$ and $\psi \vdash_{\mathscr P} \phi$ that is, they are $\mathscr P$-provable consequences of one another. The provable equivalence of $\phi$ and $\psi$ can be denoted by: $\phi \dashv \vdash_{\mathscr P} \psi$

title: Definition:Prüfer Domain
snippet: Let $A$ be an integral domain. Then $A$ is a Prüfer domain if every finitely generated ideal of $A$ is projective. Category:Definitions/Integral Domains

title: Definition:Prüfer Sequence
snippet: A Prüfer sequence of order $n$ is a (finite) sequence of integers: $\left({\mathbf a_1, \mathbf a_2, \ldots, \mathbf a_{n-2}}\right)$ such that $\forall i: 1 \le i \le n-2: 1 \le \mathbf a_i \le n$. That is, it is a (finite) sequence of $n - 2$ integers between $1$ and $n$.

title: Definition:Pseudo-Euclidean Metric
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a pseudo-Riemannian manifold. Let $\tuple {\xi^1, \dotsc, \xi^r, \tau^1, \dotsc, \tau^s}$ be the standard coordinates of $\R^{r + s}$. The pseudo-Euclidean metric (of signature $\tuple {r, s}$) is the pseudo-Riemannian metric, which in the standard coordinates reads: $g = \paren {\d \xi^1}^2 + \dotsb + \paren {\d \xi^r}^2 - \paren {\d \tau^1}^2 - \dotsb - \paren {\d \tau^s}^2$

title: Definition:Pseudo-Euclidean Space of Signature (r,s)
snippet: Let $r, s \in \N$ be natural numbers. Let $\R^{r + s}$ be an $\paren {r + s}$-dimensional real vector space. Let $\tuple {\xi^1 \ldots \xi^r, \tau^1 \ldots \tau^s}$ be standard coordinates of $\R^{r + s}$. Let $\bar q^{\paren {r, s}}$ be a pseudo-Riemannian metric defined by: $\bar q^{\paren {r, s}} = \paren {\d \xi^1}^2 + \ldots \paren {\d \xi^r}^2 - \paren {\d \tau^1}^2 - \ldots - \paren {\d \tau^s}^2$ Then the manifold $\R^{r + s}$ together with metric $\bar q^{\paren {r, s}}$, i.e.

title: Definition:Pseudo-Random Numbers
snippet: Pseudo-random numbers are a sequence of digits or numbers which have been generated by means of an algorithm by means of (usually) a computer. They are not truly random numbers because the calculation of one such number is based on what the previous one was. Hence it is incorrect to suggest that it is not possible to determine what the next one is going to be, because that is not the case. But if the algorithm used is sufficiently complex or calculation-intensive, it is not a trivial exercise for humans to do in their heads.

title: Definition:Pseudo-Riemannian Manifold
snippet: A pseudo-Riemannian manifold is a smooth manifold on the real space $\R^{r+s}$ upon which a pseudo-Riemannian metric has been imposed.

title: Definition:Pseudo-Riemannian Manifold/Dimension
snippet: Let $M$ be a pseudo-Riemannian manifold on the real space $\R^{r + s}$. The dimension of $M$ is $r + s$.

title: Definition:Pseudo-Riemannian Metric
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $p \in M$ be a point in $M$. Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space of $M$ at $p$ with the scalar product $\innerprod \cdot \cdot_p$. Let $g \in \map {\TT^2} M$ be a smooth symmetric 2-tensor field such that for all $p$ its value at $p$ is equal to $\innerprod \cdot \cdot_p$: $\forall p \in M : g_p = \innerprod \cdot \cdot_p$ Suppose $g$ is nondegenerate. Suppose for all $p \in M$ the signature of $g_p$ is the same. Then $g$ is called the pseudo-Riemannian metric.

title: Definition:Pseudo-Riemannian Submanifold
snippet: Let $\struct {\tilde M, \tilde g}$ be a pseudo-Riemannian manifold. Let $i : \tilde M \to M$ be a smooth submanifold, where $i$ is the inclusion mapping. Suppose $i^* \tilde g$ is nondegenerate with constant signature. Then $\struct {M, i^* \tilde g}$ is called the pseudo-Riemannian submanifold (of $\struct {\tilde M, \tilde g}$).

title: Definition:Pseudobase/Also known as
snippet: == Pseudobase: Also known as == A pseudobase is also known as: .

title: Definition:Pseudocompact Space
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. $T$ is a pseudocompact space every continuous real-valued function on $S$ is bounded.

title: Definition:Pseudocomplement
snippet: Let $\struct {L, \wedge, \vee, \preceq}$ be a lattice with smallest element $\bot$. Let $x, x^* \in L$. Then $x^*$ is the pseudocomplement of $x$ : $x^*$ is the greatest element of $L$ such that $x \wedge x^* = \bot$.

title: Definition:Pseudocomplemented Lattice
snippet: Let $\struct {L, \wedge, \vee, \preceq}$ be a lattice with smallest element $\bot$. Then $\struct {L, \wedge, \vee, \preceq}$ is a pseudocomplemented lattice each element $x$ of $L$ has a pseudocomplement. The pseudocomplement of $x$ is denoted $x^*$.

title: Definition:Pseudograph
snippet: Loop-Graph Loop-Multigraph The literature is inconsistent, and it is arguably preferable to use either of the above terms whenever possible.

title: Definition:Pseudoinverse of Bounded Linear Transformation
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \norm \cdot_X}$ and $\struct {Y, \norm \cdot_Y}$ be normed vector spaces. Let $S: X \to Y$ be a bounded linear transformation. Let $T: Y \to X$ be a bounded linear transformation. $S$ and $T$ are pseudoinverse to each other : $T \circ S - I_X$ is compact and: $S \circ T - I_Y$ is compact where: $\circ$ denotes the composition $I_X$ denotes the identity mapping of $X$ $I_Y$ denotes the identity mapping of $Y$

title: Definition:Pseudoinverse of Linear Transformation
snippet: Let $U, V$ be vector spaces. Let $S: U \to V$ be a linear transformation. Let $T: V \to U$ be a linear transformation. $S$ and $T$ are pseudoinverse to each other : $T \circ S - I_U$ is degenerate and: $S \circ T - I_V$ is degenerate where: $\circ$ denotes the composition $I_U$ denotes the identity mapping of $U$ $I_V$ denotes the identity mapping of $V$

title: Definition:Pseudometric
snippet: Let $A$ be a set. Let $d: A \times A \to \R$ be a real-valued function. The difference between a pseudometric and a metric is that a pseudometric does not insist that the distance function between distinct elements is strictly positive.

title: Definition:Pseudometric/Also known as
snippet: == Pseudometric: Also known as == A pseudometric on a pseudometric space can be referred to as a distance function in the same way as a metric on a metric space. Some sources hyphenate: pseudo-metric.

title: Definition:Pseudometric/Pseudometric Space
snippet: A pseudometric space $M = \struct {A, d}$ is an ordered pair consisting of a set $A \ne \O$ together with a pseudometric $d: A \times A \to \R$ which acts on that set.

title: Definition:Pseudometric Induced by Seminorm
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a vector space over $\GF$. Let $p$ be a seminorm on $X$. Define $d_p : X \times X \to \R$ by: $\map {d_p} {x, y} = \map p {x - y}$ for each $x, y \in X$. We say that $d_p$ is the pseudometric induced by $p$.

title: Definition:Pseudometric Space/Also known as
snippet: == Pseudometric Space: Also known as == Some sources hyphenate pseudometric space as pseudo-metric space.

title: Definition:Pseudometrizable
snippet: Pseudometrizable Topology Pseudometrizable Uniformity The UK English spelling of this is pseudometrisable, but it is rarely found.

title: Definition:Pseudometrizable Topology
snippet: Let $\struct {S, d}$ be a pseudometric space. Let $\struct {S, \tau_d}$ be the topological space induced by $d$. Let $T = \struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological space which is homeomorphic to such a $\struct {S, \tau_d}$. Then: $\tau$ is referred to as a pseudometrizable topology and: $T$ is referred to as a pseudometrizable space.

title: Definition:Pseudometrizable Topology/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Pseudometrizable Topology == The British English spelling of pseudometrizable is pseudometrisable, but it is rarely found. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Pseudometrizable Uniformity
snippet: Let $P = \struct {A, d}$ be a pseudometric space. Let $\UU$ be the uniformity on $A$ defined as: $\UU := \set {u_\epsilon: \epsilon \in \R_{>0} }$ where: $\R_{>0}$ is the set of strictly positive real numbers $u_\epsilon$ is defined as: $u_\epsilon := \set {\tuple {x, y}: \map d {x, y} < \epsilon}$ Then $\UU$ is defined as pseudometrizable.

title: Definition:Pseudometrizable Uniformity/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Pseudometrizable == The British English spelling for pseudometrizable is pseudometrisable, but it is rarely found. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Pseudoprime (Number Theory)
snippet: A pseudoprime is a composite number which exhibit behaviour which in some way is more characteristic of a prime number.

title: Definition:Pseudoprime (Order Theory)
snippet: Let $L = \struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \preceq}$ be an up-complete lattice. Let $p \in S$. Then $p$ is pseudoprime there exists a prime ideal $P$ in $L$: $p = \sup P$

title: Definition:Pseudoscalar
snippet: A pseudoscalar is a quantity that behaves like a scalar, except that it changes sign under a parity inversion.

title: Definition:Pseudosphere
snippet: The pseudosphere is the surface of revolution formed by rotating a tractrix around its asymptote.

title: Definition:Ptolemaic Astronomy
snippet: Ptolemaic astronomy was a model of the solar system in which: $(1): \quad$ Earth is the center of the universe $(2): \quad$ All the other celestial bodies orbit around Earth $(3): \quad$ The orbits of those celestial bodies are epicycles.

title: Definition:Ptolemaic Astronomy/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Ptolemaic Astronomy == proposed this model of the solar system in his . It modelled the actual behaviour of the planets to a high degree of accuracy. However, when the heliocentric model of the solar system was proposed, it was realised that the latter model was considerably simpler. When it was determined that the orbits of the planets were in fact elliptical, the resulting model was so much more simple and accurate, the Ptolemaic model was abandoned.

title: Definition:Public Key Cryptography
snippet: Public key cryptography is a technique of cryptography in which the method of encryption is made public, but the decryption is known only to the intended recipients.

snippet: == Pullback: Also known as == In many areas of mathematics, and consequently in many books, $P$ is written as $A \times_C B$. title: Definition:Pullback Finite Partition
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\xi$ be a partition of $\Omega$. Let $T: X \to X$ be a measurable mapping. Let $n \in \N$. title: Definition:Pullback of Quotient Group Isomorphism
snippet: Let $G, H$ be groups. Let $N \lhd G, K \lhd H$ be normal subgroups of $G$ and $H$ respectively. Let: $G / N \cong H / K$ where: $G / N$ denotes the quotient of $G$ by $N$ $\cong$ denotes group isomorphism. Let $\theta: G / N \to H / K$ be such a group isomorphism. The pullback $G \times^\theta H$ of $G$ and $H$ via $\theta$ is the subset of $G \times H$ of elements of the form $\tuple {g, h}$ where $\map \theta {g N} = h K$.

title: Definition:Pulley
snippet: A pulley is a simple machine consisting of: a wheel with (usually) flanged rims around which a cord can run. When a force is applied to the cord, the direction of the force can be changed. 300px $\qquad$ 300px A number of pulleys can be threaded onto the same axle, using a single cord.

title: Definition:Punctiform Space
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a subset of $T$. Then $H$ is punctiform it contains no nondegenerate continua.

title: Definition:Pure Mathematics
snippet: Pure mathematics is the branch of mathematics which is not concerned with real-world applications.

title: Definition:Pure Set Theory
snippet: Pure set theory is a system of set theory in which all elements of sets are themselves sets. Most systems of axiomatic set theory are designed in this way.

title: Definition:Pure Strategy
snippet: Let $G$ be a game. A pure strategy for $G$ is single strategy for consecutive plays of $G$ which is used exclusively. It can be seen that a pure strategy is a special case of a mixed strategy for which the frequencies of all strategies are zero except for one, which is used every time.

title: Definition:Pure Transcendental Extension
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. A pure transcendental extension is a field extension $L / K$ such that: for some set $\left\{ {X_\alpha: \alpha \in A}\right\}$, $L$ is the field of rational functions in the indeterminates $\left\{ {X_\alpha}\right\}$. Category:Definitions/Field Extensions

title: Definition:Purely Inseparable Field Extension
snippet: Let $E / F$ be an algebraic field extension.

title: Definition:Purely Inseparable Field Extension/Definition 1
snippet: The extension $E/F$ is purely inseparable every element $\alpha \in E \setminus F$ is inseparable.

title: Definition:Purely Inseparable Field Extension/Definition 2
snippet: Let $F$ have positive characteristic $p$. The extension $E/F$ is purely inseparable for each $\alpha \in E$ there exists $n \in \N$ such that $\alpha^{p^n} \in F$.

title: Definition:Purely Inseparable Field Extension/Definition 3
snippet: Let $F$ have positive characteristic $p$. The extension $E/F$ is purely inseparable each element of $E$ has a minimal polynomial of the form $X^{p^n} - a$.

title: Definition:Pursuit Curve
snippet: A pursuit curve is a curve constructed to model pursuers and pursuees. The pursuit curve is the curve traced by the pursuers. The pursuee is always on the pursuer's tangent.

title: Definition:Pushdown Automaton
snippet: A pushdown automaton is a septuple: $M = \struct {Q, \Sigma, \Gamma, \delta, q_0, Z, F}$ where: $Q$ is a finite set of states the input alphabet $\Sigma$ is a finite set the stack alphabet $\Gamma$ is a finite set the transition relation $\delta$ is a finite subset of $Q \times \paren {\Sigma \cup \set {\varepsilon} } \times \Gamma \times Q \times \Gamma^*$ $q_0 \in Q$ is the start state $Z \in \Gamma$ is the initial stack symbol $F \subseteq Q$ is the set of accepting states.

title: Definition:Pushforward Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ and $\struct {X', \Sigma'}$ be measurable spaces. Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. Let $f: X \to X'$ be a $\Sigma \, / \, \Sigma'$-measurable mapping. Then the pushforward of $\mu$ under $f$ is the mapping $f_* \mu: \Sigma' \to \overline \R$ defined by: $\forall E' \in \Sigma': \map {f_* \mu} {E'} := \map \mu {f^{-1} \sqbrk {E'} }$ where $\overline \R$ denotes the extended real numbers.

title: Definition:Pushout
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $f: A \to C$ and $g: B \to C$ be morphisms with common codomain. title: Definition:Pushout/Also known as
snippet: == Pushout: Also known as == In many areas of mathematics, and consequently in many books, $S$ is written as $A \coprod_C B$. It is then sometimes called the fibred sum of $A$ and $B$ over $C$. This convention potentially obfuscates $f$ and $g$, and so is not encouraged. Pushout diagrams are also sometimes called Cocartesian squares. Category:Definitions/Pushouts
