A commutative diagram: $\begin{xy} +{C} = "TL", +{A} = "TR", +{B} = "BL", +{S} = "BR", "TL";"TR" **@{-} ?>*@{>} ?<>(.5)*!/_1em/{f}, "TL";"BL" **@{-} ?>*@{>} ?<>(.5)*!/^1em/{g}, "TR";"BR" **@{-} ?>*@{>} ?<>(.5)*!/_1em/{i_1 }, "BL";"BR" **@{-} ?>*@{>} ?<>(.5)*!/^1em/{i_2 }, \end{xy}$ such that $i_1 \circ f = i_2 \circ g$ is said to satisfy the (pushout) universal mapping property (or UMP) :

title: Definition:Puzzle
snippet: A puzzle is a problem which has been posed for entertainment.

title: Definition:Pyramid
snippet: 400px Let $P$ be a polygon. Let $Q$ be a point not in the plane of $P$. From each vertex of $P$, let lines be drawn to $Q$. The polyhedron which is contained by $P$ and the triangles formed by the sides of $P$ and the lines to $Q$ is a pyramid.

title: Definition:Pyramid/Apex
snippet: 400px The vertex of a pyramid which is the common vertex of its triangular faces is called the apex of the pyramid. In the above diagram, $Q$ is the apex.

title: Definition:Pyramid/Axis
snippet: Let $P$ be a pyramid whose base has a center $C$. The axis of $P$ is the straight line from $C$ through the apex of $P$.

title: Definition:Pyramid/Base
snippet: 400px The polygon of a pyramid to whose vertices the apex is joined is called the base of the pyramid. In the above diagram, $ABCDE$ is the base of the pyramid $ABCDEQ$.

title: Definition:Pyramid/Height
snippet: 400px The height of a pyramid is the length of the perpendicular from the plane of the base to its apex. In the above diagram, $h$ is the height.

title: Definition:Pyramid/Lateral Edge
snippet: 400px The lateral edges of a pyramid are the edges which join the vertices of the lateral faces. In the above diagram, the edges $AQ, BQ, CQ, DQ$ and $EQ$ are the lateral edges of the pyramid.

title: Definition:Pyramid/Lateral Face
snippet: 400px The triangular faces of a pyramid which lead to the apex are called the lateral faces of the pyramid. In the above diagram, $ABQ$ and $DEQ$, for example, form two of the $5$ lateral faces of the pyramid $ABCDEQ$.

title: Definition:Pyramid/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Pyramid == The word pyramid derives directly from the Classical Greek πυραμίς (pyramis) whose derivation is unknown. In common parlance the word usually refers to a square pyramid, and usually calls to mind the . The form of pyramid is pyramidal. This is properly pronounced py-ram-i-dal, that is, with the stress on the second syllable.

title: Definition:Pyramid/Oblique
snippet: An oblique pyramid is a pyramid whose axis is not perpendicular to the base.

title: Definition:Pyramid/Regular
snippet: A regular pyramid is a right pyramid whose base is a regular polygon.

title: Definition:Pyramid/Right
snippet: A right pyramid is a pyramid whose axis is perpendicular to the base.

title: Definition:Pyramidal Number
snippet: The pyramidal numbers are integers defined as sums of sequences of polygonal numbers as follows. Let $\map P {k, n}$ be the $n$th $k$-gonal number. Then the $n$th $k$-gonal-based pyramidal number $\map Y {k, n}$ is defined as: $\ds \map Y {k, n} = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \map P {k, i}$

title: Definition:Pyramidal Surface
snippet: Let $B$ be a broken line. Let $P$ be a point which is not in the same plane as $B$. Let $S$ be the surface generated by all the straight lines passing through $P$ which intersect $B$. Then $S$ is a pyramidal surface.

title: Definition:Pyramidal Surface/Directrix
snippet: Let $S$ be a pyramidal surface. The directrix of $S$ is the broken line $B$ which defines $S$.

title: Definition:Pyramidal Surface/Generator
snippet: Let $S$ be a pyramidal surface. The generators of $S$ are the straight lines passing through the vertex and intersect the directrix.

title: Definition:Pyramidal Surface/Nappe
snippet: Let $S$ be a pyramidal surface. By its construction, each of the generators of $S$ extend infinitely in both directions from the vertex. Each of the halves of $S$ on either side of the vertex is a nappe.

title: Definition:Pyramidal Surface/Vertex
snippet: Let $S$ be a pyramidal surface. The vertex of $S$ is the distinguished point $P$ through which all the straight lines pass which generated $S$.

title: Definition:Pythagoras's Constant
snippet: Pythagoras's constant is sometimes used to mean $\sqrt 2$, the square root of $2$.

title: Definition:Pythagorean Equation
snippet: The Pythagorean equation is the Diophantine equation: $x^2 + y^2 = z^2$ where $x, y, z$ are integers such that $x, y, z > 0$. Solutions of this equation are known as Pythagorean triples.

title: Definition:Pythagorean Mean
snippet: The Pythagorean means are as follows:

title: Definition:Pythagorean Prime
snippet: A Pythagorean prime is a prime number of the form: $p = 4 n + 1$ where $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ is a positive integer.

title: Definition:Pythagorean Quadrilateral
snippet: A Pythagorean quadrilateral is a convex quadrilateral whose diagonals intersect at right angles, and is formed by fitting four right triangles with integer-valued sides. The interest is finding solutions where no two triangles are similar. The smallest Pythagorean quadrilateral is formed by the triangles with side lengths: $\tuple {25, 60, 65}, \tuple {91, 60, 109}, \tuple {91, 312, 325}, \tuple {25, 312, 313}$ The smallest primitive Pythagorean quadrilateral, where each Pythagorean triple is primitive is: $\tuple {28435, 20292, 34933}, \tuple {284795, 20292, 285517}, \tuple {284795, 181908,…

title: Definition:Pythagorean Triangle
snippet: A Pythagorean triangle is a right triangle whose sides all have lengths which are integers.

title: Definition:Pythagorean Triangle/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Pythagorean Triangle == Pythagorean triangles were known to the ancient Babylonians in about $2000$ BCE. The cuneiform tablet list $15$ sets of Pythagorean triples. It is also clear that the author of that tablet was also familiar with the fact, proved in Solutions of Pythagorean Equation, that the numbers $2 p q$, $p^2 - q^2$ and $p^2 + q^2$ always make a Pythagorean triangle. It is likely that the ancient Greeks, and in particular or one of his disciples, obtained this result from the Babylonians.

title: Definition:Pythagorean Triple
snippet: A Pythagorean triple is an ordered triple of positive integers $\tuple {x, y, z}$ such that $x^2 + y^2 = z^2$. That is, a Pythagorean triple is a solution to the Pythagorean equation.

title: Definition:Pythagorean Triple/Also known as
snippet: == Pythagorean Triple: Also known as == A Pythagorean triple is also known as a (set of) Pythagorean numbers.

title: Definition:Pythagorean Triple/Primitive
snippet: Let $\tuple {x, y, z}$ be a Pythagorean triple such that $x \perp y$ (that is, $x$ and $y$ are coprime). Then $\tuple {x, y, z}$ is a primitive Pythagorean triple.

title: Definition:Pythagorean Triple/Primitive/Canonical Form
snippet: Let $\tuple {x, y, z}$ be a primitive Pythagorean triple. The convention for representing $\tuple {x, y, z}$ as a (primitive) Pythagorean triple is that $x$ is the even element, while $y$ and $z$ are both odd. This is the canonical form of a Pythagorean triple.

title: Definition:Pythagoreans
snippet: The Pythagoreans were a semi-mystical cult which dated from around $550$ B.C.E., founded by . Can claim to be the world's first university. It is feasible to suggest that their initial work in the field of geometry may have formed the basis of at least the first two books of . Attendees of the school were divided into two classes: the Probationers (or listeners) the Pythagoreans. A student was a listener for $3$ years, after which he was allowed to be initiated into the class of Pythagoreans, who were allowed to learn what was considered to be the deeper secrets.

title: Definition:Pythagoreans/Quadrivium
snippet: The quadrivium was the medieval name of the required course of study of the Pythagoreans, which had been adopted by the educational establishments in Europe. The required bodies of knowledge were divided into discrete and continuous: Thus: Arithmetic: study of the absolute discrete Music: study of the relative discrete Geometry: study of the stable continuous Astronomy: study of the moving continuous.

title: Definition:Pythagoreans/Quadrivium/Linguistic Note
snippet: The word quadrivium is a Latin word meaning the four ways, or place where four roads meet (that is, literally: crossroads). Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Pythagoreans/Trivium
snippet: The trivium was the medieval name of the supplementary course of study of the Pythagoreans, adopted by the educational establishments in Europe. These supplementary bodies of knowledge were: Grammar Rhetoric Logic.

title: Definition:Pythagoreans/Trivium/Linguistic Note
snippet: The word trivium is a Latin word meaning the three ways, or place where three roads meet. As the trivium was a preliminary course of study to the quadrivium, and thereby simpler, from this root the word trivial evolved, which has a meaning in accordance with insignificant, self-evident and commonplace, and the like. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Pólya's Urn
snippet: Pólya's urn is an implementation of an urn such that, when a ball of a particular colour is taken out and examined, that ball is replaced and another of the same colour is added. Category:Definitions/Urns Category:Definitions/Probability Theory

title: Definition:Q-Pochhammer Symbol
snippet: Let $a, q \in \C$ be complex numbers. Let $\size q $\paren {a; q}_k := \begin{cases} \ds \prod_{j \mathop = 0}^{k - 1} \paren {1 - a q^j} & : k > 0 \\ 1 & : k = 0 \\ \ds \prod_{j \mathop = 1}^{\size k} \paren {1 - a q^{-j} }^{-1} & : k For brevity, $\paren {a; q}_k$ is oftentimes simply written as $\paren a_k$.

title: Definition:QED
snippet: The initials of quod erat demonstrandum, which is for which was to be demonstrated. These initials were traditionally added to the end of a proof, after the last line which is supposed to contain the statement that was to be proved. The usage is considered hopelessly old-fashioned nowadays, and is rarely seen outside nerd sitcoms. The Halmos symbol $\blacksquare$ is usually used instead. universally uses $\blacksquare$ to signify the end of a proof. The symbol $\Box$ is used to signify the end of a stage part way through a proof, where a subsidiary result is proved.

title: Definition:QED/Also known as
snippet: == QED: Also known as == Some sources render QED as Q.E.D. (that is, with dots). Category:Definitions/QED

title: Definition:QED/Technical Note
snippet: == Technical Note on QED == In order to render $\blacksquare$, use the template . In order to render $\Box$, use the template . When is used, it automatically adds the page on which it is implemented to Category:Proven Results. Category:Technical Notes

title: Definition:QEF
snippet: The initials of quod erat faciendum, which is for which was to be done. These initials were traditionally added to the end of a geometric construction. This is practically never seen nowadays outside translations of . If there is a need for such an indication, the Halmos symbol $\blacksquare$ would be used instead. does not bother to distinguish between use of QEF and the better-known QED, and recommends the use of the template exclusively instead.

title: Definition:QEF/Also known as
snippet: == QEF: Also known as == Some sources render QEF as Q.E.F. (that is, with dots). Category:Definitions/QEF

title: Definition:QEI
snippet: The initials of quod erat inveniendum, which is for which was to be found. These initials were traditionally added after the completion of a calculation (either arithmetic or algebraic). This is practically never seen nowadays outside translations of historical texts. If there were ever a need for such an indication, the Halmos symbol $\blacksquare$ would be used instead. does not bother to distinguish between use of QEI and the better-known QED, and recommends the use of the template exclusively instead.

title: Definition:QEI/Also known as
snippet: == QEI: Also known as == Some sources render QEI as Q.E.I. (that is, with dots). Category:Definitions/QEI

title: Definition:QR Factorization
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a matrix of order $m \times n$ such that $m \ge n$. A QR factorization of $\mathbf A$ is a factorization of $\mathbf A$: $\mathbf A = \mathbf Q \mathbf R$ where: $\mathbf Q$ consists of column vectors which are orthonormal $\mathbf R$ is an upper triangular matrix.

title: Definition:QR Factorization:Existance Of QR Factorization For Square Matrices
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a real square matrix. Then $\mathbf A$ has a QR factorization, that is we can write $\mathbf A = \mathbf Q \mathbf R $ where $\mathbf Q$ is orthogonal $\mathbf R$ is upper triangular

title: Definition:Quadrangle
snippet: A quadrangle is a plane figure consisting of $4$ points joined by straight lines. No $3$ points of a quadrangle are collinear.

title: Definition:Quadrangle/Complete
snippet: A complete quadrangle is a quadrangle whose $4$ points are joined by $6$ lines: one connecting each pair of points. It is complete because every pair is connected. 360px

title: Definition:Quadrangle/Simple
snippet: A simple quadrangle is a quadrangle whose $4$ points are joined by $4$ lines, which may or may not intersect.

title: Definition:Quadrant
snippet: A quadrant is a sector of a circle whose angle is a right angle.

title: Definition:Quadrantal Angle
snippet: A quadrantal angle is an angle that is an integer multiple of a right angle. That is: $90 \degrees$, $180 \degrees$, $270 \degrees$, $360 \degrees$, $450 \degrees$, $540 \degrees$, and so on.

title: Definition:Quadrantal Spherical Triangle
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a spherical triangle. Let one of the sides of $\triangle ABC$ be a right angle: $\dfrac \pi 2$. 500px Then $\triangle ABC$ is known as a quadrantal spherical triangle.

title: Definition:Quadrantal Spherical Triangle/Also known as
snippet: == Quadrantal Spherical Triangle: Also known as == A quadrantal spherical triangle is also known as just a quadrantal triangle.

title: Definition:Quadratic
snippet: The word quadratic describes an expression or an equation involving the square of a given quantity.

title: Definition:Quadratic/Also known as
snippet: == Quadratic: Also known as == An older word for quadratic is quadric, but this is rarely seen nowadays.

title: Definition:Quadratic Algebra
snippet: A quadratic algebra $A$ is a filtered algebra whose generator consists of degree $1$ elements, with defining relations of degree $2$. A quadratic algebra $A$ is determined by a vector space of generators $V = A_1$ and a subspace of homogeneous quadratic relations $S \subseteq V \otimes V$. Thus: $A = \map T V / \gen S$ and inherits its grading from the tensor algebra $\map T V$. If the subspace of relations may also contain inhomogeneous degree $2$ elements, $S \subseteq k \oplus V \oplus \paren {V \otimes V}$, this construction results in a filtered quadratic algebra.

title: Definition:Quadratic Congruence
snippet: A quadratic congruence is a congruence of the form: $a x^2 + b x + c \equiv 0 \pmod n$ where: $n \in \N$ is a natural number $a$, $b$, $c$ are given integers $x$ is an unknown integer.

title: Definition:Quadratic Curve
snippet: A quadratic curve is an algebraic curve which has degree $2$.

title: Definition:Quadratic Curve/Also known as
snippet: == Quadratic Curve: Also known as == A quadratic curve is also known as a quadric. That same term is also seen for quadric surface.

title: Definition:Quadratic Equation
snippet: A quadratic equation is a polynomial equation of the form: $a x^2 + b x + c = 0$ such that $a \ne 0$. From Solution to Quadratic Equation, the solutions are: $x = \dfrac {-b \pm \sqrt {b^2 - 4 a c} } {2 a}$

title: Definition:Quadratic Equation/Also defined as
snippet: == Quadratic Equation: Also defined as == Some older treatments of this subject present this as: An algebraic equation of the form $a x^2 + 2 b x + c = 0$ is called a quadratic equation. It has solutions: $x = \dfrac {-b \pm \sqrt {b^2 - a c} } a$ but this approach has fallen out of fashion. Category:Definitions/Quadratic Equations

title: Definition:Quadratic Equation/Also known as
snippet: == Quadratic Equation: Also known as == A quadratic equation is also known as: an equation of the second degree a polynomial of degree $2$ and so on.

title: Definition:Quadratic Equation/Canonical Form
snippet: The canonical form of the quadratic equation is: $a x^2 + b x + c = 0$ where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are constants.

title: Definition:Quadratic Equation/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Quadratic Equation == The ancient Babylonians knew the technique of solving quadratic equations as long ago as $1600$ BCE. The ancient Greeks, a thousand years or so later, solved quadratics by geometric constructions. The general algebraic formulation of its solution did not appear until at least $100$ CE.

title: Definition:Quadratic Equation in Two Variables
snippet: A quadratic equation in $2$ variables is an equation of the form: $a x^2 + b y^2 + 2 h x y + 2 g x + 2 f y + c = 0$ where $x$ and $y$ are independent variables.

title: Definition:Quadratic Form (Linear Algebra)
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be a field of characteristic $\Char {\mathbb K} \ne 2$. Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb K$. A quadratic form on $V$ is a mapping $q : V \mapsto \mathbb K$ such that: {{axiom | q = \forall v \in V: \forall \kappa \in \mathbb K | m = \map q {\kappa v} = \kappa^2 \map q v }} {{axiom | q = b: V \times V \to \mathbb K | m = \tuple {v, w} \mapsto \map q {v + w} - \map q v - \map q w | rc= is a bilinear form }}

title: Definition:Quadratic Form (Polynomial Theory)
snippet: A quadratic form is a form whose variables are of degree $2$.

title: Definition:Quadratic Form Associated to Sesquilinear Form
snippet: Let $\GF$ be a subfield of $\C$. Let $V$ be a vector space over $\GF$. Let $q : V \times V \to \GF$ be a sesquilinear form. Define $Q : V \to \GF$ by: $\map Q x = \map q {x, x}$ for each $x \in V$. We say that $Q$ is the quadratic form associated with $q$.

title: Definition:Quadratic Function
snippet: A quadratic function is an expression of the form: $\map Q x := a_0 + a_1 x + a_2 x^2$ where $a_0, a_1, a_2$ are constants. The domain of $x$ is usually defined as the real numbers $\R$ or the complex numbers $\C$.

title: Definition:Quadratic Functional
snippet: Let $B \sqbrk {x, y}$ be a bilinear functional. Let $x = y$. Then the functional $A \sqbrk x = B \sqbrk {x, x}$ is called a quadratic functional.

title: Definition:Quadratic Gauss Sum
snippet: Let $p$ be an odd prime. Let $a$ be an integer. The quadratic Gauss sum is: $\ds \map g {a, p} = \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^{p - 1} e^{2 \pi i a n^2 / p}$ Category:Definitions/Number Theory

title: Definition:Quadratic Irrational
snippet: A quadratic irrational is an irrational number of the form: $r + s \sqrt n$ where $r, s$ are rational and $n$ is a positive integer which is not a square.

title: Definition:Quadratic Irrational/Also known as
snippet: == Quadratic Irrational: Also known as == A quadratic irrational is also known as a quadratic surd.

title: Definition:Quadratic Irrational/Reduced
snippet: An irrational root $\alpha$ of a quadratic equation with integer coefficients is a reduced quadratic irrational $(1): \quad \alpha > 1$ $(2): \quad$ its conjugate $\tilde \alpha$ satisfies: $-1 0$. It is also possible (though not required) to ensure that $Q$ divides $D - P^2$. This is actually a necessary assumption for some proofs and warrants its own definition.

title: Definition:Quadratic Irrational/Reduced/Associated
snippet: Let $\alpha$ be a reduced quadratic irrational expressed as: $\alpha = \dfrac {P + \sqrt D} Q$ Then $\alpha$ is associated to $D$ $Q$ divides $D - P^2$.

title: Definition:Quadratic Mean
snippet: Let $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n \in \R$ be real numbers. The quadratic mean of $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is defined as: $Q_n := \ds \sqrt {\frac 1 n \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n x_k^2}$

title: Definition:Quadratic Polynomial
snippet: A quadratic polynomial is a polynomial of degree $2$.

title: Definition:Quadratic Real Algebra
snippet: A quadratic real algebra is a quadratic algebra over the field of real numbers.

title: Definition:Quadratic Residue
snippet: Let $p$ be an odd prime. Let $a \in \Z$ be an integer such that $a \not \equiv 0 \pmod p$. Then $a$ is a quadratic residue of $p$ $x^2 \equiv a \pmod p$ has a solution. That is, : $\exists x \in \Z: x^2 \equiv a \pmod p$

title: Definition:Quadratic Residue/Character
snippet: Let $p$ be an odd prime. Let $a \in \Z$ be an integer such that $a \not \equiv 0 \pmod p$. $a$ is either a quadratic residue or a quadratic non-residue of $p$. Whether it is or not is known as the quadratic character of $a$ modulo $p$.

title: Definition:Quadratic Residue/Non-Residue
snippet: Let $p$ be an odd prime. Let $a \in \Z$ be an integer such that $a \not \equiv 0 \pmod p$. If there is no such integer $x$ such that $x^2 \equiv a \pmod p$, then $a$ is a quadratic non-residue of $p$.

title: Definition:Quadratic Residue/Warning
snippet: == Quadratic Residue: Warning == The definition of the quadratic residue must be qualified as follows: The case where $a = 0$ has been excluded from the definition, despite the fact that $0 = 0^2$ and so is definitely a square. The case where $p = 2$ is also excluded, where the only non-zero residue $1$ is also a square. The main reason for this is so that some useful results can be expressed in a convenient form.

title: Definition:Quadratic Space
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be a field. A quadratic space over $\mathbb K$ is a pair $\tuple {V, q}$ where: $V$ is a vector space over $\mathbb K$ of finite dimension $n > 0$ $q$ is a quadratic form on $V$.

title: Definition:Quadratics
snippet: Quadratics is the branch of algebra which studies quadratic equations.

title: Definition:Quadratrix
snippet: A quadratrix is a device (usually a plane curve) used for the quadrature (that is, to determine the area) of a given geometric figure.

title: Definition:Quadratrix/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Quadratrix == The plural of quadratrix is properly quadratrices, but the word is seldom seen. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Quadratrix of Hippias/Also known as
snippet: == Quadratrix of Hippias: Also known as == The quadratrix of Hippias is also known as the trisectrix of Hippias, as it can be used both for quadrature of the circle and trisection of a general angle. It is also known as the quadratrix of Dinostratus. Some sources call it just the quadratrix, but that is a generic term applied to all such devices.

title: Definition:Quadratrix of Hippias/Definition 1
snippet: The quadratrix of Hippias is the plane curve defined in Cartesian coordinates as: $y = x \map \cot {\dfrac {\pi x} {2 a} }$ for some real constant $a \in \R$. 600px The above diagram illustrates the quadratrix of Hippias.

title: Definition:Quadratrix of Hippias/Definition 2
snippet: The quadratrix of Hippias is the plane curve be generated as follows. Let $\Box ABCD$ be a square of side length $a$. Let a quarter circle be inscribed in $\Box ABCD$ with the center at $A$, the arc going from $B$ to $D$. Let $E$ be a point travelling around the arc $BD$ at a constant angular velocity. Let $F$ be a point travelling along the side $DA$ of $\Box ABCD$ at a constant velocity such that $E$ and $F$ take the same time to travel from the top $CD$ to the bottom $AB$ of $\Box ABCD$. Let $S$ be the point at which the line $AE$ intersects the line through $F$ parallel to $AB$.

title: Definition:Quadratrix of Hippias/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Quadratrix of Hippias == The quadratrix of Hippias was invented by for the purpose of solving the problem of Trisecting the Angle. It was subsequently used by for Squaring the Circle. Its use for both trisection and quadrature (that is, finding area) explains the multiple nature of its names.

title: Definition:Quadrature
snippet: Quadrature is an archaic term for the process of finding the area.

title: Definition:Quadrature/Also defined as
snippet: == Quadrature: Also defined as == The term quadrature is also used to mean the repeated application of the process of quadrature (in its original sense) so as to find the area of a plane figure.

title: Definition:Quadrature/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Quadrature == The term quadrature originated as a word meaning: the process of constructing a square with the same area as some given geometric figure but nowadays the term is usually confined to numerical integration.

title: Definition:Quadrature/Numerical
snippet: Numerical quadrature is the process of evaluating the approximate area of a general plane region using numerical methods, usually (and specifically) numerical integration.

title: Definition:Quadric Surface
snippet: A quadric surface is a surface described by a polynomial equation of the $2$nd degree.

title: Definition:Quadrifolium
snippet: == Quadrifolium == The quadrifolium is the instance of the rhodonea curve for $n = 4$:

title: Definition:Quadrifolium/Also known as
snippet: == Quadrifolium: Also known as == The quadrifolium is also seen referred to as a four-leaved rose, or four-petalled rose. Category:Definitions/Quadrifolium Curves

title: Definition:Quadrifolium/Cosine Form
snippet: The quadrifolium can be defined by the polar equation in the form: $r = a \cos 2 \theta$ where: $0 \le \theta \le 2 \pi$ 400px

title: Definition:Quadrifolium/Sine Form
snippet: The quadrifolium can be defined by the polar equation in the form: $r = a \sin 2 \theta$ where: $0 \le \theta \le 2 \pi$ 400px

title: Definition:Quadrilateral
snippet: A quadrilateral is a polygon with exactly four sides. ' Because it is a polygon, it follows that it also has four vertices.

title: Definition:Quadrilateral/Also defined as
snippet: == Quadrilateral: Also known as == In the context of projective geometry, a quadrilateral is defined as: a plane figure formed by $4$ intersecting lines. Hence what is defined on in the context of metrical geometry as a quadrilateral is referred to in that context as a simple quadrilateral.

title: Definition:Quadrilateral/Also known as
snippet: == Quadrilateral: Also known as == A quadrilateral can also (rarely) be found referred to as a tetragon. In the context of projective geometry, such a construct is known as a simple quadrilateral. Compare this with the concept of a complete quadrilateral.

title: Definition:Quadrilateral/Dart
snippet: A dart is an irregular quadrilateral with a reflex angle. 500px

title: Definition:Quadrilateral/Dart/Deltoid
snippet: A deltoid is a dart such that: the $2$ sides which are adjacent to the reflex angle are equal to each other the other $2$ sides are also equal to each other. 500px In the above diagram, the figure on the right is a deltoid.

title: Definition:Quadrilateral/Kite
snippet: A kite is an irregular quadrilateral which has both pairs of adjacent sides equal and which specifically does not have a reflex angle. 300px

title: Definition:Quadrilateral/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Quadrilateral == The word quadrilateral derives from the Latin for four sides. Similarly, the word tetragon derives from the Greek for four sides. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Quadrilateral/Oblong
snippet: An oblong is a quadrilateral whose angles are all right angles, but whose sides are not all the same length: 400px

title: Definition:Quadrilateral/Opposite Sides
snippet: Let $Q$ be a quadrilateral. Two sides of $Q$ are opposite they are adjacent to completely different pairs of vertices of $Q$. 300px Thus in quadrilateral $\Box ABCD$ above, the sides $AB$ and $CD$ are opposite.

title: Definition:Quadrilateral/Opposite Vertices
snippet: Let $Q$ be a quadrilateral. Two vertices of $Q$ are opposite they are adjacent to completely different pairs of sides of $Q$. 300px Thus in quadrilateral $\Box ABCD$ above, the vertices $\angle ABC$ and $\angle CDA$ are opposite.

title: Definition:Quadrilateral/Parallelogram
snippet: A parallelogram is a quadrilateral whose opposite sides are parallel to each other, and whose sides may or may not all be the same length. 450px

title: Definition:Quadrilateral/Rectangle
snippet: A rectangle is a quadrilateral all of whose angles are equal to a right angle, and whose sides may or may not all be the same length. '

title: Definition:Quadrilateral/Rhomboid
snippet: A rhomboid is a parallelogram whose sides are not all the same length. Its angles may or may not all be equal.

title: Definition:Quadrilateral/Rhombus
snippet: A rhombus is a parallelogram whose sides are all the same length. 350px Its angles may or may not all be equal.

title: Definition:Quadrilateral/Square
snippet: A square is a regular quadrilateral. That is, a regular polygon with $4$ sides. That is, a square is a plane figure with four sides all the same length and whose angles are all equal. 200px

title: Definition:Quadrilateral/Trapezium/Base
snippet: 700px The bases of a trapezium are its $2$ parallel sides. In the above diagram, the bases of the given trapezia are $AB$ and $DC$, $EF$ and $HG$, and $IJ$ and $KL$. Category:Definitions/Trapezia

title: Definition:Quadrilateral/Trapezium/Height

title: Definition:Quadrilateral/Trapezium/Leg
snippet: 700px The legs of a trapezium are its $2$ sides adjacent to the bases. In the above diagram, the legs of the given trapezia are $AD$ and $BC$, $EH$ and $FG$, and $IK$ and $JL$. Category:Definitions/Trapezia

title: Definition:Quadrilateral/Trapezoid
snippet: A trapezoid is a quadrilateral with no parallel sides. 300px

title: Definition:Quadrillion/Long Scale
snippet: Quadrillion is a name for $10^{24}$ in the long scale system: One quadrillion $= 10^{6 \times 4}$

title: Definition:Quadrillion/Long Scale/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Quadrillion (Long Scale) == Some authorities insist that the British usage of quadrillion to mean $10^{24}$, that is $1 \, 000 \, 000^4$, is no longer used.

title: Definition:Quadrillion/Short Scale
snippet: Quadrillion is a name for $10^{15}$ in the short scale system: One quadrillion $= 10^{3 \times 4 + 3}$

title: Definition:Quadrillion (Long Scale)/Also defined as
snippet: == Quadrillion: Also defined as == In the short scale system: One quadrillion $= 10^{3 \times 4 + 3} = 10^{15}$

title: Definition:Quadrillion (Short Scale)/Also defined as
snippet: == Quadrillion: Also defined as == In the long scale system: One quadrillion $= 10^{6 \times 4} = 10^{24}$

title: Definition:Quadruply Perfect Number
snippet: A quadruply perfect number is a positive integer $n$ such that the sum of its divisors is equal to $4$ times $n$.

title: Definition:Quadruply Perfect Number/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Quadruply Perfect Numbers ==

title: Definition:Quality Control
snippet: Quality control is the industrial procedure for: making sure that processes undergone, or goods being produced are meeting specifications indicating whether or not corrective action should be taken to correct problems. It uses such techniques as control charts, cusum charts and acceptance sampling.

title: Definition:Quality of Integer Triple
snippet: Let $\tuple {a, b, c}$ be an ordered triple of (strictly) positive integers. The quality of $\tuple {a, b, c}$ is defined and denoted as: $\map q {a, b, c} := \dfrac {\ln c} {\map \ln {\map \Rad {abc} } }$ where $\Rad$ denotes the radical of an integer.

title: Definition:Quantal Response
snippet: A quantal response is a situation in which an individual subject to a stimulus can show only one possible response, if any.

title: Definition:Quantified Statement
snippet: A quantified statement is a simple statement in predicate logic whose subject is qualified by either the universal quantifier or the existential quantifier. That is, it is either a universal statement or an existential statement. Category:Definitions/Predicate Logic

title: Definition:Quantifier
snippet: The universal quantifier $\forall$ and the existential quantifier $\exists$ are referred to collectively as quantifiers.

title: Definition:Quantifier/Also defined as
snippet: == Quantifier: Also defined as == Some sources explicitly categorize the quantifiers as operators.

title: Definition:Quantile/Continuous
snippet: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable on a probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $X$ have probability density function $f_X$. Let $q \in \Z_{\ge 1}$ be a strictly positive integer. Then for $k \in \Z: 0 < k < q$, $x$ is the $k$th $q$-quantile : {{eqn | l = \map \Pr {X < x} | r = \int_{-\infty}^x \map {f_X} t \rd t | c = }}

title: Definition:Quantile/Discrete
snippet: Let $S$ be a finite set of ordinal data. When defining a set of $q$-quantiles on $S$, there may well be no unique class boundary in $S$ which fit the definition of quantile as given here. This difficulty may be overcome by making appropriate modifications.

title: Definition:Quantile/Informal Definition
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of quantitative data. Let $S$ be arranged in order of size. Let $q \in \Z_{\ge 1}$ be a strictly positive integer. Let the range of $S$ be divided into exactly $q$ class intervals such that the probability of an instance of $S$ falling into an arbitrary instance of one of these class intervals is equal to $\dfrac 1 q$. That is, the class intervals are designed so as to have the same number of elements in them. Then the class boundaries are known as the quantiles of $X$.

title: Definition:Quantitative Property
snippet: A quantitative property is a property of a physical system which exists in a range of values corresponding with a number, such that the system can be described as having a particular number of a unit of measurement of that property. Category:Definitions/Physical Quantities Category:Definitions/Physics

title: Definition:Quantum
snippet: A quantum is a fixed value of a quantum phenomenon such that the values allowed to be taken by that quantum phenomenon are (positive) integer multiple of that quantum. A physical quantity that exhibits such a property is referred to as quantized.

title: Definition:Quantum/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Quantum == The plural of quantum is quanta. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Quantum Mechanics
snippet: Quantum mechanics is the branch of physics concerned with the behaviour of matter at the smallest scale accessible to observation. It seeks to explain and model results of experiments by assuming that certain physical quantities can exist only in integer multiples of some fixed quantum.

title: Definition:Quantum Mechanics/Also known as
snippet: == Quantum Mechanics: Also known as == Quantum mechanics is also known as quantum physics. It is not clear whether there is actually a qualitative difference between the two terms.

title: Definition:Quantum Mechanics/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Quantum Mechanics == Quantum mechanics was developed in the early $20$th century.

title: Definition:Quantum Phenomenon
snippet: A quantum phenomenon is a quantitative property which is restricted to a (positive) integer multiple of a quantum. The nature of the quantum is dependent upon the nature of the given property.

title: Definition:Quark
snippet: A quark is a theoretical elementary particle that is postulated to form one of the components of such as the proton and neutron. The electric charge on a quark is an integer multiple of $\dfrac 1 3$ of the elementary charge $\E$.

title: Definition:Quart
snippet: The quart is a unit of volume which can be defined in one of the following ways:

title: Definition:Quarter
snippet: == Rational Number == A quarter is the rational number $\dfrac 1 4$. Category:Definitions/Specific Numbers Category:Definitions/Quarter

title: Definition:Quartic
snippet: The word quartic is used to indicate a mathematical expression of the $4$th degree.

title: Definition:Quartic/Also known as
snippet: == Quartic: Also known as == A quartic is also known as a biquadratic.

title: Definition:Quartic Curve
snippet: A quartic curve is an algebraic curve which has degree $4$.

title: Definition:Quartic Equation
snippet: A quartic equation is a polynomial equation of the form: $a x^4 + b x^3 + c x^2 + d x + e = 0$ such that $a \ne 0$.

title: Definition:Quartic Equation/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Quartic Equation == The solution of the quartic equation followed soon after the solution of the cubic. It was included in 's of $1545$, along with his solution of the cubic, which had been solved some few decades earlier by . It was solved by , who was a student of 's.

title: Definition:Quartic Function
snippet: A quartic function is an expression of the form: $\map Q x := a_0 + a_1 x + a_2 x^2 + a_3 x^3 + a_4 x^4$ where $a_0, a_1, a_2, a_3, a_4$ are constants. The domain of $x$ is usually defined as the real numbers $\R$ or the complex numbers $\C$.

title: Definition:Quartic Polynomial
snippet: A quartic polynomial is a polynomial of degree $4$.

title: Definition:Quartile
snippet: Let $D$ be a finite collection of data regarding some quantitative variable. Let $D$ be divided into precisely $4$ class intervals. A $Q$th quartile is a value in the interval defined by the $Q$th class such that: $\dfrac Q 4$ of the data in $D$ fall at or below the value chosen $1 - \dfrac Q 4$ of the data in $D$ fall at or above the value chosen. Arbitrarily more precise definitions may be contrived as necessary to define a unique quartile for a given study. A common convention is:

title: Definition:Quartile/Also known as
snippet: == Quartile: Also known as == The first quartile is often referred to as the lower quartile. The third quartile is often referred to as the upper quartile. The term second quartile is often not used, and instead the median is referred to exclusively.

title: Definition:Quartile/First
snippet: Let $D$ be a finite collection of data regarding some quantitative variable. The first quartile of $D$ is defined as the median of the data values in $D$ below and not including the second quartile $Q_2$. It is commonly denoted $Q_1$.

title: Definition:Quartile/Second
snippet: Let $D$ be a finite collection of data regarding some quantitative variable. The second quartile of $D$ is defined as the median of $D$. It is commonly denoted $Q_2$.

title: Definition:Quartile/Third
snippet: Let $D$ be a finite collection of data regarding some quantitative variable. The third quartile of $D$ is defined as the median of the data values in $D$ above and not including the second quartile $Q_2$. It is commonly denoted $Q_3$.

title: Definition:Quasi-Affine Variety
snippet: Let $k$ be a field. Let $n \ge 1$ be an Integer. Let $k^n$ be equipped with Zariski topology. Then a subset $Y \subseteq k^n$ is an quasi-affine variety $Y$ is an open set of an affine algebraic variety.

title: Definition:Quasi-Coherent Sheaf of Modules
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ be a ringed space. Let $\FF$ be a sheaf of modules $\FF$ over $\OO_X$. Let $\FF$ be such that: there exists a cover ${\family {U_i} }_{i \mathop \in I}$ of $X$ such that: $\FF {\restriction U}$ is a sheaf of modules over $\OO_X {\restriction U}$ presented by global sections. Then $\FF$ is quasi-coherent.

title: Definition:Quasi-Compact Morphism of Schemes
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ and $\struct {Y, \OO_Y}$ be schemes. Let $f : \struct {X, \OO_X} \to \struct {Y, \OO_Y}$ be a morphism of schemes. $f$ is quasi-compact for all quasi-compact open subsets $U \subset Y$, the set $\map {f^{-1} } U \subset X$ is quasi-compact.

title: Definition:Quasi-Compact Scheme
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ be a scheme. Then $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ is quasi-compact $X$ is compact.

title: Definition:Quasi-Concave Total Preordering
snippet: Let $R^n$ be a real vector space. Let $\precsim$ be a total preordering on $\R^n$. Let $\precsim$ be such that: for all $b \in \R^n$, the set $\set {a \in \R^n: b \precsim a}$ is convex. Then $\precsim$ is quasi-concave.

title: Definition:Quasi-Crystal
snippet: A quasi-crystal is a structure similar to a true crystal.

title: Definition:Quasi-Crystal/Historical Note
snippet: == Quasi-Crystals: Historical Note == Quasi-crystals were discovered in the $1980$s. Unlike true crystals, they can have $5$-fold symmetry.

title: Definition:Quasi-Reflexive Relation
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation in $S$.

title: Definition:Quasi-Reflexive Relation/Class Theory
snippet: Let $V$ be a basic universe Let $\RR \subseteq V \times V$ be a relation. $\RR$ is quasi-reflexive : $\forall x \in \Field \RR: \tuple {x, x} \in \RR$ where $\Field \RR$ denotes the field of $\RR$.

title: Definition:Quasi-Reflexive Relation/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation in $S$. $\RR$ is quasi-reflexive : $\forall x, y \in S: \tuple {x, y} \in \RR \implies \tuple {x, x} \in \RR \land \tuple {y, y} \in \RR$

title: Definition:Quasi-Reflexive Relation/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation in $S$. $\RR$ is quasi-reflexive : $\forall x \in \Field \RR: \tuple {x, x} \in \RR$ where $\Field \RR$ denotes the field of $\RR$.

title: Definition:Quasi-Reflexive Relation/Definition 3
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation in $S$. $\RR$ is quasi-reflexive $\RR$ is both left quasi-reflexive and right quasi-reflexive.

title: Definition:Quasi-Separated Morphism of Schemes
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ and $\struct {Y, \OO_Y}$ be schemes. Let $f : \struct {X, \OO_X} \to \struct {Y, \OO_Y}$ be a morphism of schemes. $f$ is quasi-separated the diagonal morphism $\Delta_f : X \to X \times_Y X$ is quasi-compact.

title: Definition:Quasiamicable Numbers
snippet: Let $m \in \Z_{>0}$ and $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be (strictly) positive integers.

title: Definition:Quasiamicable Numbers/Definition 1
snippet: Let $m \in \Z_{>0}$ and $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be (strictly) positive integers. $m$ and $n$ are quasiamicable numbers : the sum of the proper divisors of $m$ is equal to $n$ and: the sum of the proper divisors of $n$ is equal to $m$.

title: Definition:Quasiamicable Numbers/Definition 2
snippet: Let $m \in \Z_{>0}$ and $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be (strictly) positive integers. $m$ and $n$ are quasiamicable numbers : $\map {\sigma_1} m = \map {\sigma_1} n = m + n + 1$ where $\sigma_1$ denotes the divisor sum function.

title: Definition:Quasicomponent
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let the relation $\sim$ be defined on $T$ as follows: $x \sim y \iff T$ is connected between the two points $x$ and $y$ That is, each separation of $T$ includes a single open set $U \in \tau$ which contains both $x$ and $y$. We have that $\sim$ is an equivalence relation, so from the Fundamental Theorem on Equivalence Relations, the points in $T$ can be partitioned into equivalence classes. These equivalence classes are called the quasicomponents of $T$.

title: Definition:Quasigroup
snippet: A quasigroup is a magma $\struct {S, \circ}$ which has the Latin square property. That is, such that $\forall a \in S$, the left and right regular representations $\lambda_a$ and $\rho_a$ are permutations on $S$. That is:

title: Definition:Quasigroup/Left Quasigroup
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a magma. $\struct {S, \circ}$ is a left quasigroup : for all $a \in S$, the left regular representation $\lambda_a$ is a permutation on $S$. That is: $\forall a, b \in S: \exists ! x \in S: a \circ x = b$

title: Definition:Quasigroup/Right Quasigroup
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a magma. $\struct {S, \circ}$ is a right quasigroup : for all $a \in S$, the right regular representation $\rho_a$ is a permutation on $S$. That is: $\forall a, b \in S: \exists ! x \in S: x \circ a = b$

title: Definition:Quasimetric
snippet: Let $A$ be a set. Let $d: A \times A \to \R$ be a real-valued function. The difference between a quasimetric and a metric is that a quasimetric does not insist that the metric between distinct elements is commutative, that is, that $\map d {x, y} = \map d {y, x}$.

title: Definition:Quasimetric/Also known as
snippet: == Quasimetric: Also known as == A quasimetric on a quasimetric space can be referred to as a distance function in the same way as a metric on a metric space. However, the position of is that this is not recommended, as it can lead to confusion. Category:Definitions/Quasimetrics

title: Definition:Quasimetric/Quasimetric Space
snippet: A quasimetric space $M = \struct {A, d}$ is an ordered pair consisting of a set $A \ne \O$ together with a quasimetric $d: A \times A \to \R$ which acts on $A$.

title: Definition:Quasiperfect Number
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be a positive integer.

title: Definition:Quasiperfect Number/Definition 1
snippet: = Definition == Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be a positive integer. Let $A \left({n}\right)$ denote the abundance of $n$. $n$ is quasiperfect $A \left({n}\right) = 1$.

title: Definition:Quasiperfect Number/Definition 2
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be a positive integer. $n$ is quasiperfect : $\map {\sigma_1} n = 2 n + 1$ where $\map {\sigma_1} n$ denotes the divisor sum function of $n$.

title: Definition:Quasiperfect Number/Definition 3
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be a positive integer. $n$ is quasiperfect it is exactly one less than the sum of its aliquot parts.

title: Definition:Quasiuniform Space
snippet: Let $\UU$ be a quasiuniformity on a set $S$. Let a topology $\tau$ be induced by $\UU$. The resulting topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is called a quasiuniform space. A quasiuniform space $T$ induced by a quasiuniformity $\UU$ can be denoted $\struct {\struct {S, \UU}, \tau}$, or just $\struct {S, \UU}$ if it is understood that $\tau$ is the topology created from $\UU$.

title: Definition:Quasiuniformity
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. A quasiuniformity on $S$ is a set of subsets $\UU$ of the cartesian product $S \times S$ satisfying the following quasiuniformity axioms: That is, a quasiuniformity on $S$ is a filter on the cartesian product $S \times S$ (from $(\text U 1)$ to $(\text U 3)$) which also fulfils the condition: $\forall u \in \UU: \exists v \in \UU$ such that whenever $\tuple {x, y} \in v$ and $\tuple {y, z} \in v$, then $\tuple {x, z} \in u$ which can be seen to be an equivalent statement to $(\text U 4)$. $u \circ v$ in this context can be seen to be equivalent to composition of relations.

title: Definition:Quasiuniformizable Space
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Then $T$ is quasiuniformizable there exists a quasiuniformity $\UU$ on $S$ such that $\struct {\struct {S, \UU}, \tau}$ is a quasiuniform space.

title: Definition:Quasiuniformizable Space/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Quasiuniformizable == The British English spelling for quasiuniformizable is quasiuniformisable. It would be convenient if there could be a simpler term coined which can be used instead. Eight syllables is rather a lot. On the other hand, as every Topological Space is Quasiuniformizable, the concept is probably not that important to need one. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Quaternary Notation
snippet: Quaternary notation is the positional number system whose base is $4$. That is, every number $x \in \R$ is expressed in the form: $\ds x = \sum_{j \mathop \in \Z} r_j 4^j$ where: $\forall j \in \Z: r_j \in \set {0, 1, 2, 3}$ Category:Definitions/Positional Number Systems

title: Definition:Quaternion
snippet: A quaternion is a number in the form: $a \mathbf 1 + b \mathbf i + c \mathbf j + d \mathbf k$ where: $a, b, c, d$ are real numbers $\mathbf 1, \mathbf i, \mathbf j, \mathbf k$ are entities related to each other in the following way: The set of all quaternions is usually denoted $\H$.

title: Definition:Quaternion/Addition
snippet: The sum of two quaternions $\mathbf x_1 = a_1 \mathbf 1 + b_1 \mathbf i + c_1 \mathbf j + d_1 \mathbf k$ and $\mathbf x_2 = a_2 \mathbf 1 + b_2 \mathbf i + c_2 \mathbf j + d_2 \mathbf k$ is defined as: $\mathbf x_1 + \mathbf x_2 := \paren {a_1 + a_2} \mathbf 1 + \paren {b_1 + b_2} \mathbf i + \paren {c_1 + c_2} \mathbf j + \paren {d_1 + d_2} \mathbf k$

title: Definition:Quaternion/Algebra over Field
snippet: An algebra of quaternions can be defined over any field as follows: Let $\mathbb K$ be a field, and $a$, $b \in \mathbb K$. Define the quaternion algebra $\left\langle{ a,b }\right\rangle_\mathbb K$ to be the $\mathbb K$-vector space with basis $\{1, i, j, k\}$ subject to: $i^2 = a$ $j^2 = b$ $ij = k = -ji$ Formally this could be achieved as a multiplicative presentation of a suitable group, or as a linear subspace of a finite extension of $\mathbb K$. Taking $\mathbb K = \R$ and $a = b = -1$ we see that this generalises Hamilton's quaternions. Category:Definitions/Quaternions

title: Definition:Quaternion/Also denoted as
snippet: == Quaternion: Also denoted as == Some sources use $V$ for the set of quaternions $\H$. Some sources develop a more abstract presentation for this structure, and use symbols such as $\lambda_0$, $\lambda_1$, $\lambda_2$ and $\lambda_3$ instead of $\mathbf 1$, $\mathbf i$, $\mathbf j$ and $\mathbf k$.

title: Definition:Quaternion/Construction from Cayley-Dickson Construction
snippet: The set of quaternions $\Bbb H$ can be defined by the Cayley-Dickson construction from the set of complex numbers $\C$. From Complex Numbers form Algebra, $\C$ forms a nicely normed $*$-algebra. Let $a, b \in \C$. Then $\tuple {a, b} \in \Bbb H$, where: $\tuple {a, b} \tuple {c, d} = \tuple {a c - d \overline b, \overline a d + c b}$ $\overline {\tuple {a, b} } = \tuple {\overline a, -b}$ where: $\overline a$ is the complex conjugate of $a$ and $\overline {\tuple {a, b} }$ is the conjugation operation on $\Bbb H$.

title: Definition:Quaternion/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Quaternions == The quaternions were famously conceived by in $1843$, who was so proud of his flash of insight that he carved: $i^2 = j^2 = k^2 = i j k = -1$ into the stone of on $16$th October $1843$. They were introduced as a way of generalizing of the complex numbers in the plane in order to have a tool to model phenomena in $3$ dimensions. However, it is also worth noting that independently came up with the same concept in $1819$.

title: Definition:Quaternion Conjugate/Quaternion Conjugation
snippet: The operation of quaternion conjugation is the mapping: $\overline \cdot: \mathbb H \to \mathbb H: \mathbf x \mapsto \overline{\mathbf x}$. where $\overline{\mathbf x}$ is the quaternion conjugate of $x$. That is, it maps a quaternion to its quaternion conjugate. Category:Definitions/Quaternions

snippet: Let $\mathbf x = a \mathbf 1 + b \mathbf i + c \mathbf j + d \mathbf k$ be a quaternion, where $a, b, c, d \in \R$.

title: Definition:Quaternion Modulus/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\mathbf x = a \mathbf 1 + b \mathbf i + c \mathbf j + d \mathbf k$ be a quaternion, where $a, b, c, d \in \R$. The (quaternion) modulus of $\mathbf x$ is the real-valued function defined and denoted as: $\size {\mathbf x} := \sqrt {a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2}$

title: Definition:Quaternion Modulus/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\mathbf x = a \mathbf 1 + b \mathbf i + c \mathbf j + d \mathbf k$ be a quaternion, where $a, b, c, d \in \R$. Let $\mathbf x$ be expressed in matrix form: $\mathbf x = \begin {bmatrix} a + b i & c + d i \\ -c + d i & a - b i \end {bmatrix}$ The (quaternion) modulus of $\mathbf x$ is the real-valued function defined and denoted as: $\size {\mathbf x} := \sqrt {\map \det {\mathbf x} }$

title: Definition:Queen's Tour
snippet: A queen's tour is a puzzle in recreational chess. On a chessboard of arbitrary size, a chess queen is to make a complete tour: passing over every square at least once returning to its square of origin using as few moves as possible.

title: Definition:Queen's Tour/Re-entrant
snippet: A re-entrant queen's tour is a queen's tour which starts and ends on the same square.

title: Definition:Queuing Theory
snippet: Queuing theory is the branch of mathematics which studies the stochastic processes involving problems relating to customer waiting and service time, where there is a random element in customer arrivals and/or times taken to serve the customers.

title: Definition:Queuing Theory/Also known as
snippet: == Queuing Theory: Also known as == Queuing theory can also be spelled queueing theory. Category:Definitions/Queuing Theory

title: Definition:Quintal Notation
snippet: Quintal notation is the positional number system whose base is $5$. That is, every number $x \in \R$ is expressed in the form: $\ds x = \sum_{j \mathop \in \Z} r_j 5^j$ where: $\forall j \in \Z: r_j \in \set {0, 1, 2, 3, 4}$

title: Definition:Quintal System
snippet: A quintal system is a number system in which the base is $5$.

title: Definition:Quintal System/Also known as
snippet: == Quintal System: Also known as == A quintal system is also known as quinary. Category:Definitions/Quintal Systems

title: Definition:Quintessence/Also known as
snippet: Quintessence was originally known as aether.

title: Definition:Quintessence/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Quintessence == wrote about quintessence, while naming it the aether.

title: Definition:Quintessence/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Quintessence == The word quintessence more or less literarily means fifth spirit, fifth essence. It is the famous fifth element beloved of science fiction and fantasy entertainment. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Quintic
snippet: The word quintic is used to indicate a mathematical expression of the $5$th degree.

title: Definition:Quintic Curve
snippet: A quintic curve is an algebraic curve which has degree $5$.

title: Definition:Quintic Equation
snippet: Let $\map f x = a x^5 + b x^4 + c x^3 + d x^2 + e x + f$ be a polynomial function over a field $\mathbb k$ of degree $5$. Then the equation $\map f x = 0$ is the general quintic equation over $\mathbb k$.

title: Definition:Quintic Equation/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Quintic Equation == published what he thought was a solution to the quintic equation in $1683$, but pointed out that it was fallacious. tried and failed to solve it, but he did develop new methods for solving the quartic, as did . consolidated everything that was known about solutions to equations of degree less than $5$ in his of $1770$. He noted that the usual attempt to find a solution by permutation of roots fails for the quintic. In $1799$ published his $2$-volume in which he tried to prove its insolubility, but he appeared to be unsuccessful.

title: Definition:Quintic Polynomial
snippet: A quintic polynomial is a polynomial of degree $5$.

title: Definition:Quintillion/Long Scale
snippet: Quintillion is a name for $10^{30}$ in the long scale system: One quintillion $= 10^{6 \times 5}$

title: Definition:Quintillion/Short Scale
snippet: Quintillion is a name for $10^{18}$ in the short scale system: One quintillion $= 10^{3 \times 5 + 3}$

title: Definition:Quota Sample
snippet: A quota sample is a sample in which the units are not chosen randomly. Instead, the interview is required to choose a certain number of units in a number of different categories.

title: Definition:Quotient/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Quotient == The word quotient derives from the Latin word meaning how often. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Quotient (Integer Division)
snippet: Let $a, b \in \Z$ be integers such that $b \ne 0$. From the Division Theorem: $\forall a, b \in \Z, b \ne 0: \exists_1 q, r \in \Z: a = q b + r, 0 \le r < \size b$ The value $q$ is defined as the quotient of $a$ on division by $b$, or the quotient of $\dfrac a b$.

title: Definition:Quotient (Integer Division)/Also known as
snippet: == Quotient in context of Integer Division: Also known as == A quotient in this context is also known as a partial quotient.

title: Definition:Quotient (Integer Division)/Real
snippet: Let $x, y \in \R$ be real numbers such that $y \ne 0$. The quotient of $x$ on division by $y$ is defined as the value of $q$ in the expression: $\forall x, y \in \R, y \ne 0: \exists! q \in \Z, r \in \R: x = q y + r, 0 \le r < \size y$ From the definition of the Modulo Operation: $x \bmod y := x - y \floor {\dfrac x y} = r$ it can be seen that the quotient of $x$ on division by $y$ is defined as: $q = \floor {\dfrac x y}$

title: Definition:Quotient (Polynomial Division)
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +, \circ}$ be a field whose zero is $0_F$ and whose unity is $1_F$. Let $X$ be transcendental over $F$. Let $F \sqbrk X$ be the ring of polynomials in $X$ over $F$. Let $\map A x$ and $\map B x$ be polynomials in $F \sqbrk X$ such that the degree of $B$ is non-zero. From the Division Theorem for Polynomial Forms over Field: $\exists \map Q x, \map R x \in F \sqbrk X: \map A x = \map Q x \map B x + \map R x$ such that: $0 \le \map \deg R < \map \deg B$ where $\deg$ denotes the degree of a polynomial.

title: Definition:Quotient Algebra
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $A$ be a $R$-algebra. Let $I$ be an ideal of $A$. Let $A/I$ be the quotient module of $A$ modulo $I$. For $a, b \in A$, define $\ast : \paren {A/I}^2 \to A/I$ by: $\paren {a + I} \ast \paren {b + I} = a b + I$ We say that $\struct {A/I, \ast}$ is the quotient algebra of $A$ modulo $I$.

title: Definition:Quotient Epimorphism
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a congruence relation on an algebraic structure $\struct {S, \circ}$. Let $q_\RR: \struct {S, \circ} \to \struct {S / \RR, \circ_\RR}$ denote the quotient mapping from $\struct {S, \circ}$ to the quotient structure $\struct {S / \RR, \circ_\RR}$: $\forall x \in S: \map {q_\RR} x = \eqclass x \RR$ where $\eqclass x \RR$ denotes the equivalence class of $x$ under $\RR$. Then $q_\RR$ is referred to as the quotient epimorphism from $\struct {S, \circ}$ to $\struct {S / \RR, \circ_\RR}$. This is usually encountered in the context of specific algebraic structures thus:

title: Definition:Quotient Epimorphism/Group
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $N$ be a normal subgroup of $G$. Let $G / N$ be the quotient group of $G$ by $N$. The mapping $q_N: G \to G / N$ defined as: $\forall x \in G: \map {q_N} x = x N$ is known as the quotient (group) epimorphism from $G$ to $G / N$.

title: Definition:Quotient Epimorphism/Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring whose zero is $0_R$ and whose unity is $1_R$. Let $J$ be an ideal of $R$. Let $\struct {R / J, +, \circ}$ be the quotient ring defined by $J$. The mapping $\phi: R \to R / J$ given by: $\forall x \in R: \map \phi x = x + J$ is known as the quotient (ring) epimorphism from $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ (on)to $\struct {R / J, +, \circ}$.

title: Definition:Quotient Group
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $N$ be a normal subgroup of $G$. Then the left coset space $G / N$ is a group, where the group operation is defined as the coset product: $\paren {a N} \paren {b N} = \paren {a b} N$ $G / N$ is called the quotient group of $G$ by $N$.

title: Definition:Quotient Group/Also known as
snippet: == Quotient Group: Also known as == A quotient group is also known as a factor group.

title: Definition:Quotient Group/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Quotient Group == The idea of a quotient group appeared in the work of in the $1860$s. However, the modern formulation using cosets did not appear till the work of in $1889$, fairly late on in the history of group theory.

title: Definition:Quotient Group/Motivation
snippet: == Motivation for == In Kernel is Normal Subgroup of Domain it was shown that the kernel of a group homomorphism is a normal subgroup of its domain. In that result it has been shown that every normal subgroup is a kernel of at least one group homomorphism of the group of which it is the subgroup. We see that when a subgroup is normal, its cosets make a group using the group operation defined as in this result. However, it is not possible to make the left or right cosets of a non-normal subgroup into a group using the same sort of group operation.

title: Definition:Quotient Mapping
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be an equivalence on a set $S$. Let $\eqclass s \RR$ be the $\RR$-equivalence class of $s$. Let $S / \RR$ be the quotient set of $S$ determined by $\RR$. Then $q_\RR: S \to S / \RR$ is the quotient mapping induced by $\RR$, and is defined as: $q_\RR: S \to S / \RR: \map {q_\RR} s = \eqclass s \RR$ for all $s \in S$. Effectively, we are defining a mapping on $S$ by assigning each element $s \in S$ to its equivalence class $\eqclass s \RR$. If the equivalence $\RR$ is understood, $\map {q_\RR} s$ can be written $\map q s$.

title: Definition:Quotient Mapping/Also known as
snippet: == Quotient Mapping: Also known as == The quotient mapping is also known as: the quotient function from $S$ to $S / \RR$ the canonical surjection from $S$ to $S / \RR$ the canonical map, canonical mapping or canonical projection from $S$ onto $S / \RR$ the natural mapping from $S$ to $S / \RR$ the natural surjection from $S$ to $S / \RR$ the classifying map or classifying mapping (as it classifies the elements of $S$ into those various equivalence classes) the projection from $S$ to $S / \RR$ Some sources denote the quotient mapping by $\natural_\RR$. This is logical, as $\natural$ is the .

title: Definition:Quotient Mapping (Topology)
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a surjective continuous mapping. Let $f$ fulfil this condition: For all $U \subseteq S_2$, if $f^{-1} \sqbrk U$ is open in $T_1$, then $U$ is open in $T_2$. Then $f$ is a quotient mapping.

title: Definition:Quotient Metric on Vector Space
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $X$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $d$ be an invariant metric on $X$. Let $N$ be a vector subspace of $X$. Let $X/N$ be the quotient vector space of $X$ modulo $N$. Let $\pi : X \to X/N$ be the quotient mapping. We define the quotient metric on $X/N$ induced by $d$ by: $\ds \map {d_N} {\map \pi x, \map \pi y} = \inf_{z \mathop \in N} \map d {x - y, z}$ for each $\map \pi x, \map \pi y \in X/N$.

title: Definition:Quotient Module
snippet: Let $M$ be an $R$-module whose underlying abelian group is $\struct {M, +}$. Let $N$ be a submodule of $M$ and $\struct {N, +}$ be the underlying abelian group. Let $M / N$ be the quotient group. Define the (left linear) ring action on $M / N$ as: $\forall r \in R, \forall a \in M : r \circ \paren {a + N} := r a + N$ where $a + N$ denotes the coset of $N$ by $a$ in $M / N$. Then $\struct {M / N, +, \circ}$ is the quotient $R$-module of $M$ by $N$. {{improve|As submodule is defined on , $N$ merely has to be a subset of $M$ and not actually a subgroup.

title: Definition:Quotient Norm
snippet:
Let $X$ be a normed vector space. Let $N$ be a closed linear subspace of $X$. Let $X/N$ be the quotient vector space of $X$ modulo $N$. Let $\pi : X 	o X/N$ be the quotient mapping associated with $X/N$. We define the quotient norm $
orm \cdot_{X/N}$ by: $\ds 
orm {\map \pi x}_{X/N} = \inf_{z \in N} 
orm {x - z}$ for each $x \in X$.

title: Definition:Quotient Normed Algebra
snippet:
Let $\struct {R, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_R}$ be a normed division ring. Let $\struct {A, 
orm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a normed algebra. Let $I$ be a closed ideal of $A$. Let $A/I$ be the quotient algebra of $A$ modulo $I$. Let $
orm {\, \cdot \,}_{A/I}$ be the quotient norm. We say that $\struct {A/I, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_{A/I} }$ is the quotient normed algebra of $A$ modulo $I$.

title: Definition:Quotient Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $J$ be an ideal of $R$. Let $R / J$ be the coset space of $R$ $J$. Let the operation $+$ be defined on $R / J$ by addition of cosets of $J$: $\forall x, y: \paren {x + J} + \paren {y + J} := \paren {x + y} + J$ Let us also define the operation $\circ$ on $R / J$ by by product of cosets of $J$: $\forall x, y: \paren {x + J} \circ \paren {y + J} := \paren {x \circ y} + J$ The algebraic structure $\struct {R / J, +, \circ}$ is called the quotient ring of $R$ by $J$.

title: Definition:Quotient Ring/Also denoted as
snippet: == Quotient Ring: Also known as == While the inline form of the fraction notation $R / J$ is usually used for a quotient ring, some presentations use the full $\dfrac R J$ form. It is usual for the latter form to be used only when either of both of the expressions top and bottom are more complex than single symbols. Category:Definitions/Quotient Rings

title: Definition:Quotient Ring/Also known as
snippet: == Quotient Ring: Also known as == A quotient ring is also known as a factor ring. Some sources refer to this as a residue class ring.

title: Definition:Quotient Set
snippet: Let $\RR$ be an equivalence relation on a set $S$. For any $x \in S$, let $\eqclass x \RR$ be the $\RR$-equivalence class of $x$. The quotient set of $S$ induced by $\RR$ is the set $S / \RR$ of $\RR$-classes of $\RR$: $S / \RR := \set {\eqclass x \RR: x \in S}$

title: Definition:Quotient Space/Also known as
snippet: == Quotient Space: Also known as == A quotient space is also known as a factor space.

title: Definition:Quotient Space (Topology)/Also known as
snippet: == Quotient Space in context of Topology: Also known as == A quotient space is also known as an identification space and a factor space. However, note that an identification space is often (and on ) used for a more general concept.

title: Definition:Quotient Space by Group Action
snippet: Let $G$ be a group acting on a topological space $X$. The quotient of $X$ by the action of $G$, denoted $X / G$, is the set of orbits equipped with the quotient topology.

title: Definition:Quotient Structure
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. Let $\RR$ be a congruence relation on $\struct {S, \circ}$. Let $S / \RR$ be the quotient set of $S$ by $\RR$. Let $\circ_\RR$ be the operation induced on $S / \RR$ by $\circ$. The quotient structure defined by $\RR$ is the algebraic structure: $\struct {S / \RR, \circ_\RR}$ If there is no danger of confusion, we can drop the $\RR$ from $\circ_\RR$ and use $\circ$ for both the operation on $S$ and the induced operation on $S / \RR$.

title: Definition:Quotient Topological Vector Space
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological vector space over $\GF$. Let $N$ be a linear subspace of $X$. Let $X/N$ be the quotient vector space of $X$ modulo $N$. Let $\tau_N$ be the quotient topology on $X/N$. We say that $\struct {X/N, \tau_N}$ is the quotient topological vector space of $X$ modulo $N$.

title: Definition:Quotient Topology
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be an equivalence relation on $S$. Let $q_\RR: S \to S / \RR$ be the quotient mapping induced by $\RR$.

title: Definition:Quotient Topology/Definition 1
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be an equivalence relation on $S$. Let $q_\RR: S \to S / \RR$ be the quotient mapping induced by $\RR$. Let $\tau_\RR$ be the identification topology on $S / \RR$ by $q_\RR$: $\tau_\RR := \set {U \subseteq S / \RR: q_\RR^{-1} \sqbrk U \in \tau}$ Then $\tau_\RR$ is the quotient topology on $S / \RR$ by $q_\RR$.

title: Definition:Quotient Topology/Quotient Space
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be an equivalence relation on $S$. Let $q_\RR: S \to S / \RR$ be the quotient mapping induced by $\RR$. Let $\tau_\RR$ be the quotient topology on $S / \RR$ by $q_\RR$: $\tau_\RR := \set {U \subseteq S / \RR: \map {q_\RR^{-1} } U \in \tau}$ The quotient space of $S$ by $\RR$ is the topological space whose points are elements of the quotient set of $\RR$ and whose topology is $\tau_\RR$: $T_\RR := \struct {S / \RR, \tau_\RR}$

title: Definition:Quotient Vector Space
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space. Let $M$ be a vector subspace of $V$. Then the quotient (vector) space of $V$ modulo $M$, denoted $V / M$, is defined as: $\set {x + M : x \in X}$ where $x + M$ is the Minkowski sum of $x$ and $M$. Furthermore, $V / M$ is considered to be endowed with the induced operations: $\paren {x + M} +_{V / M} \paren {y + M} := \paren {x + y} + M$ $\alpha \circ_{V / M} \paren {x + M} := \alpha x + M$ From Quotient Vector Space is Vector Space, it is shown that, $+_{V / M}$ and $\circ_{V / M}$ are well-defined, provided that $M$ is a vector subspace of $V$.

title: Definition:Quotient of Division over Euclidean Domain/Also known as
snippet: == Quotient of Division over Euclidean Domain: Also known as == A quotient in the context of division over a Euclidean domain is also known as a partial quotient when the remainder is not zero. Category:Definitions/Quotients of Division over Euclidean Domain

title: Definition:R-Algebraic Structure
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ be a ring. Let $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n}$ be an algebraic structure with $n$ operations.

title: Definition:R-Algebraic Structure/Also defined as
snippet: == R-Algebraic Structure: Also defined as == Most sources do not present the general $R$-algebraic structure with $n$ operations, but limit themselves to those with either $1$ or $2$ operations: $\struct {S, \circ, \ast}_R$ or $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ast}_R$. (for better or worse) has made the decision to explore the possibility of the general $n$-operation underlying algebraic structure.

title: Definition:R-Algebraic Structure/Also known as
snippet: == R-Algebraic Structure: Also known as == An $R$-algebraic structure is also known as an algebraic structure over (the ring) $R$, but this terminology is not as clear, and so is discouraged on . It should of course be noted that the $R$ in the name $R$-algebraic structure derives directly from the symbol (in this case $R$) used to denote the scalar ring. If your exposition uses a different symbol, then you would amend the name to match the symbol.

title: Definition:R-Algebraic Structure/Examples
snippet: == Examples of $R$-Algebraic Structures ==

title: Definition:R-Algebraic Structure/Examples/1 Operation
snippet: == Example of R-Algebraic Structure == An $R$-algebraic structure with $1$ operation is an $R$-algebraic structure such that the underlying structure is an algebraic structure with $1$ operation: $\struct {S, \circ, \ast}_R$ Thus it is constructed from: a ring $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ an algebraic structure with $1$ operation: $\struct {S, \circ}$ a ring action $\ast$ defined either as: a left ring action $\ast: R \times S \to S$ or: a right ring action $\ast: S \times R \to S$

title: Definition:R-Algebraic Structure/Examples/2 Operations
snippet: == Example of R-Algebraic Structure == An $R$-algebraic structure with $2$ operations is an $R$-algebraic structure such that the underlying structure is an algebraic structure with $2$ operations: $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ast}_R$ Thus it is constructed from: a ring $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ an algebraic structure with $2$ operations: $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2}$ a ring action $\ast$ defined either: $\ast: R \times S \to S$ or: $\ast: S \times R \to S$

title: Definition:R-Algebraic Structure/Left
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ be a ring. Let $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n}$ be an algebraic structure with $n$ operations. Let $\ast: R \times S \to S$ be a binary operation. Then $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n, \ast}_R$ is a left $R$-algebraic structure with $n$ operations. If the number of operations in $S$ is either understood or general, it is just called an left $R$-algebraic structure, and can be denoted $\struct {S, \ast}_R$.

title: Definition:R-Algebraic Structure/Right
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ be a ring. Let $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n}$ be an algebraic structure with $n$ operations. Let $\ast: S \times R \to S$ be a binary operation. Then $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n, \ast}_R$ is a right $R$-algebraic structure with $n$ operations. If the number of operations in $S$ is either understood or general, it is just called an right $R$-algebraic structure, and can be denoted $\struct {S, \ast}_R$.

title: Definition:R-Algebraic Structure/Ring Action
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n, \ast}_R$ be an $R$-algebraic structure with $n$ operations, where: $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ is a ring $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n}$ is an algebraic structure with $n$ operations. The operation $\ast$, whether it be: $\ast: R \times S \to S$ as in a left $R$-algebraic structure or: $\ast: S \times R \to S$ as in a right $R$-algebraic structure is known as the ring action on $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n, \ast}_R$.

title: Definition:R-Algebraic Structure/Underlying Structure
snippet: Let $\SS := \struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n, \ast}_R$ be an $R$-algebraic structure with $n$ operations. The algebraic structure $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n}$ upon which $\SS$ is constructed is known as the underlying structure of $\SS$.

title: Definition:R-Algebraic Structure Automorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n, \ast}_R$ be an $R$-algebraic structure. Let $\phi: S \to S$ be an $R$-algebraic structure isomorphism from $S$ to itself. Then $\phi$ is an $R$-algebraic structure automorphism. This definition continues to apply when $S$ is a module, and also when it is a vector space.

title: Definition:R-Algebraic Structure Endomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n, \ast}_R$ be an $R$-algebraic structure. Let $\phi: S \to S$ be an $R$-algebraic structure homomorphism from $S$ to itself. Then $\phi$ is an $R$-algebraic structure endomorphism. This definition continues to apply when $S$ is a module, and also when it is a vector space.

title: Definition:R-Algebraic Structure Epimorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n, \ast}_R$ and $\struct {T, \odot_1, \odot_2, \ldots, \odot_n, \otimes}_R$ be $R$-algebraic structures. Then $\phi: S \to T$ is an $R$-algebraic structure epimorphism : $(1): \quad \phi$ is a surjection $(2): \quad \forall k: k \in \closedint 1 n: \forall x, y \in S: \map \phi {x \circ_k y} = \map \phi x \odot_k \map \phi y$ $(3): \quad \forall x \in S: \forall \lambda \in R: \map \phi {\lambda \ast x} = \lambda \otimes \map \phi x$ This definition also applies to modules, and also to vector spaces.

title: Definition:R-Algebraic Structure Homomorphism
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n, \ast}_R$ and $\struct {T, \odot_1, \odot_2, \ldots, \odot_n, \otimes}_R$ be $R$-algebraic structures. Let $\phi: S \to T$ be a mapping. Then $\phi$ is an $R$-algebraic structure homomorphism : {{axiom | n = 1 | lc= | q = \forall k \in \closedint 1 n: \forall x, y \in S | ml= \map \phi {x \circ_k y} | mo= = | mr= \map \phi x \odot_k \map \phi y | rc= }} {{axiom | n = 2 | lc= | q = \forall x \in S: \forall \lambda \in R | ml= \map \phi {\lambda \ast x} | mo= = | mr= \lambda \otimes \map \phi x | rc= }} where $\closedint 1 n…

title: Definition:R-Algebraic Structure Isomorphism/Examples
snippet: == Examples of $R$-Algebraic Structure Isomorphisms ==

title: Definition:R-Algebraic Structure Isomorphism/Examples/1 Operation
snippet: == Example of $R$-Algebraic Structure Isomorphism == Let $\struct {S, \circ, \ast}_R$ and $\struct {T, \odot, \otimes}_R$ be $R$-algebraic structures each with $1$ operation. Let $\phi: S \to T$ be a bijection which is a $R$-algebraic structure homomorphism. Then $\phi$ is an $R$-algebraic structure isomorphism.

title: Definition:R-Algebraic Structure Isomorphism/Examples/2 Operations
snippet: == Example of $R$-Algebraic Structure Isomorphism == Let $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ast}_R$ and $\struct {T, \odot_1, \odot_2, \otimes}_R$ be $R$-algebraic structures each with $2$ operations. Let $\phi: S \to T$ be a bijection which is a $R$-algebraic structure homomorphisms. Then $\phi$ is an $R$-algebraic structure isomorphism.

title: Definition:R-Algebraic Structure Monomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n, \ast}_R$ and $\struct {T, \odot_1, \odot_2, \ldots, \odot_n, \otimes}_R$ be $R$-algebraic structures. Then $\phi: S \to T$ is an $R$-algebraic structure monomorphism : $(1): \quad \phi$ is an injection $(2): \quad \forall k: k \in \closedint 1 n: \forall x, y \in S: \map \phi {x \circ_k y} = \map \phi x \odot_k \map \phi y$ $(3): \quad \forall x \in S: \forall \lambda \in R: \map \phi {\lambda \ast x} = \lambda \otimes \map \phi x$. That is, : $(1): \quad \phi$ is an injection $(2): \quad \phi$ is an $R$-algebraic structure homomorphism.

title: Definition:R-Balanced Mapping
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $M$ be a right $R$-module and $N$ be a left $R$-module. Let $M \times N$ be their cartesian product. Let $P$ be an abelian group. An $R$-balanced mapping $f : M \times N \to P$ is a biadditive mapping with: $\forall m \in M: \forall n \in N: \forall r \in R: \map f {m \cdot r, n} = \map f {m, r \cdot n}$
