snippet: A topological space $\struct {S, \tau}$ is an $R_0$ space :

title: Definition:R0 Space/Also known as
snippet: == $R_0$ Space: Also known as == An $R_0$ space is also known as a symmetric space.

title: Definition:R1 Space
snippet: A topological space $\struct {S, \tau}$ is an $R_1$ space : every arbitrary pair of topologically distinguishable elements $x, y \in S$ are separated by neighborhoods. That is: for two arbitrary topologically distinguishable elements $x, y \in S$, $x$ and $y$ both have neighborhoods in $T$ which are disjoint.

title: Definition:R1 Space/Also known as
snippet: == $R_1$ Space: Also known as == An $R_1$ space is also known as a preregular space.

title: Definition:RSA 129/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note RSA $129$ == RSA $129$ is one of a number of large ($100$ digits and over) semiprimes offered up as a factorisation challenge by , and as a demonstration of the effectiveness of their encryption algorithm now known as RSA. In $1993$, a concerted effort was made by over $600$ academics and hobbyists, moderated over the Internet, to crack the code and so decipher the message which was hidden thereby. It took less than a year to reveal the secret message: The magic words are squeamish and ossifrage.

title: Definition:RSA 130/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note RSA $130$ == RSA $130$ is one of a number of large ($100$ digits and over) semiprimes offered up as a factorisation challenge by , and as a demonstration of the effectiveness of their encryption algorithm now known as RSA. On $12$th April $1996$, RSA $130$ was successfully factorised into its $2$ prime factors by a Dutch team.

title: Definition:RSA Algorithm
snippet: The RSA algorithm is a technique of encoding a message such that the method of encoding can be made public without compromising the security. Let Alice be sending a message to Bob. Alice and Bob both agree on two large primes $p$ and $q$, each having at least $100$ digits. Let $M = p q$. $M$ can be made public if they so wish. Let $K = \paren {p - 1} \paren {q - 1}$. $K$ is to be kept secret. Let Alice choose some number $a$ such that $a \perp K$. $a$ is made known to Bob, and may even be made public. Alice represents her message in a series of numbers in the range $0$ to $M$.

title: Definition:RSA Algorithm/Also known as
snippet: == RSA Algorithm: Also known as == The RSA algorithm can also be referred to as the RSA code or the RSA cipher.

title: Definition:RSA Algorithm/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on RSA Algorithm == , and invented the RSA algorithm as an implementation of a trapdoor function. The original $2$ large primes selected by had $63$ digits each. He estimated that a powerful computer to a $1977$ specification would take of the order of $4 \times 10^{16}$ years to factorise their product.

title: Definition:Radial Component
snippet: Consider a vector $\mathbf v$ embedded in a polar plane. Let $\mathbf v$ be applied at a point $p$. Let: $\mathbf v_r$ be the component of $\mathbf v$ in the direction of the radial coordinate of $p$ $\mathbf v_\theta$ be the component of $\mathbf v$ in the direction of the angular coordinate of $p$ The component $\mathbf v_r$ is the radial component of $\mathbf v$.

title: Definition:Radial Distance Function
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be an $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold. Let $U_p$ be the normal neighborhood of $p \in M$. Let $\tuple {x^i}$ be the local coordinates on $U_p$ centered at $p \in M$. Then the mapping $r : U_p \to \R$ defined by $\ds \map r x = \sqrt {\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n x_i^2}$ is called the radial distance function.

title: Definition:Radial Geodesic in Normal Neighborhood
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be an $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold. Let $U_p$ be the normal neighborhood for $p \in M$. Let $\struct {U_p, \tuple {x^i}}$ be a normal coordinate chart. Let $I \subseteq \R$ be a real interval such that $0 \in I$. Let $\map \gamma t : I \to M$ be the geodesic such that: $\map \gamma 0 = p$ Suppose: $\map \gamma I \subseteq U$ Then $\gamma$ is called the radial geodesic.

title: Definition:Radial Interval Topology
snippet: Let $S$ denote the Cartesian coordinate plane. Let $\BB$ be: the set of all open intervals disjoint from the origin which lie on a straight line through the origin together with sets of the form: $\ds \bigcup \set {I_\theta: 0 \le \theta < \pi}$ where each $I_\theta$ is a non-empty open interval whose center is at the origin on the straight line whose slope is $\tan \theta$. Let $\tau$ be the topology whose basis is $\BB$. Then $\tau$ is known as the radial interval topology. The corresponding topological space $\struct {S, \tau}$ is known as the radial interval space.

title: Definition:Radial Vector Field
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be an $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold. Let $U_p$ be the normal neighborhood of $p \in M$. Let $\tuple {x^i}$ be the local coordinates on $U$ centered at $p \in M$. Let $\map r x : U_p \to \R$ be the radial distance function. Then the vector field $\partial_r$ on $U \setminus \set p$, where $\setminus$ denotes the set difference, defined by $\ds \partial_r = \frac {x^i}{\map r x} \frac {\partial}{\partial x^i}$ is called the radial distance function.

title: Definition:Radian/Also known as
snippet: == Radian: Also known as == Radian measure is also known as circular measure.

snippet: == Technical Note for Radian == This command is specific to . Category:Technical Notes

title: Definition:Radical Extension
snippet: Let $L / F$ be a field extension. Then $L$ is a radical extension of $F$ there exist $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_m \in F$ and $n_1, \ldots, n_2 \in \Z_{>0}$ such that: $(1): \quad L = K \sqbrk {\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_m}$ $(2): \quad \alpha_1^{n_1} \in F$ $(3): \quad \forall i \in \N_m: \alpha_i^{n_i} \in F \sqbrk {\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_{i-1} }$ where $K \sqbrk {\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_m}$ and $F \sqbrk {\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_{i-1} }$ are generated field extensions. Category:Definitions/Field Extensions

title: Definition:Radical Ideal of Ring
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $I$ be an ideal of $A$. Then $I$ is a radical ideal it is equal to its radical.

title: Definition:Radical of Ideal of Ring
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $I$ be an ideal of $A$.

title: Definition:Radical of Ideal of Ring/Definition 1
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $I$ be an ideal of $A$. The radical of $I$ is the ideal of elements of which some power is in $I$: $\map \Rad I := \set {a \in A: \exists n \in \N_{>0} : a^n \in I}$

title: Definition:Radical of Ideal of Ring/Definition 2
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $I$ be an ideal of $A$. Let $A / I$ be the quotient ring of $A$ by $I$. Let $\Nil {A / I}$ be its nilradical. Let $\pi: A \to A / I$ be the quotient epimorphism from $A$ onto $A / I$. The radical of $I$ is the preimage of $\Nil {A / I}$ under $\pi$: $\map \Rad I = \pi^{-1} \sqbrk {\Nil {A / I} }$

title: Definition:Radical of Integer
snippet: Let $n \in \Z$ be an integer.

title: Definition:Radical of Integer/Also known as
snippet: == Radical of Integer: Also known as == The radical of an integer $n$ is also known as the square-free kernel of $n$.

title: Definition:Radical of Integer/Definition 1
snippet: Let $n \in \Z$ be an integer. The radical of $n$ is the product of the distinct prime factors of $n$.

title: Definition:Radical of Integer/Definition 2
snippet: Let $n \in \Z$ be an integer. The radical of $n$ is the largest square-free integer which divides $n$.

title: Definition:Radicand
snippet: Let $\sqrt [n] P$ denote the $n$th root of an expression. Then $P$ is the radicand of $\sqrt [n] P$. That is, it is the object whose $n$th root is to be taken.

title: Definition:Radicand/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Radicand == The word radicand comes from: the word radical, itself deriving from the Latin radix meaning root the suffix -and, originating from the Latin form, loosely meaning that which needs to be ... That is, radicand literally means that which needs to have its root extracted. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Radioactive Decay
snippet: Radioactive decay is a first-order reaction in which the atoms of a substance may spontaneously break apart, thereby turning into atoms of a different substance. The probability of an individual atom decaying is an intrinsic property of the given chemical element. Having decayed, that atom is now transformed into an atom of a different type, and so is not subject to any further occurrences of that particular decay process. However, the new atom may have its own particular (different) mode of decay itself.

title: Definition:Radioactive Decay/Half-Life
snippet: The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the time it takes for exactly half of an arbitrary quantity of that isotope to undergo radioactive decay. Thus it is the time it takes for exactly half of an arbitrary quantity of that isotope to remain.

title: Definition:Radioactive Decay/Half-Life/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Half-Lives of Radioactive Elements == This page lists isotopes of some radioactive elements and their half-lives.

title: Definition:Radioactive Decay/Radioactive Element
snippet: A chemical element whose isotopes are all subject to radioactive decay is known as a radioactive element.

title: Definition:Radioactive Decay/Radioactive Isotope
snippet: An isotope of a chemical element which is subject to radioactive decay is known as a radioactive isotope.

title: Definition:Radioactive Decay/Stable
snippet: An isotope of a chemical element which is not subject to radioactive decay is described as stable. It follows that the half-life of such an element is infinite.

title: Definition:Radiocarbon Dating/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Radiocarbon Dating == The technique of radiocarbon dating was devised by . He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in $1960$ for his work in dating archaeological objects. He determined the half-life of carbon-14 to be approximately $5600$ years. Hence he established that the measurable life age span using this test was from $1000$ to $30 \, 000$ years.

title: Definition:Radiometric Dating
snippet: Radiometric dating is a technique whose purpose is to work out the age $T$ of a physical object $B$. The pieces of information are known: $(1): \quad$ The ratio $r_0$ of a radioactive isotope $E_R$ of a chemical element $E$ to its stable isotope $E_S$ in $B$ at the time it came into being $(2): \quad$ The ratio $r$ of $E_R$ to $E_S$ at the time now $(3): \quad$ The half-life of the radioactive isotope $E_R$ It is known from scientific investigation what $r_0$ is when a physical object is created. It is also known from scientific investigation what the rate of radioactive decay of $E_R$ is.

title: Definition:Radiometric Dating/Radiocarbon Dating
snippet: Radiocarbon dating is a specific application of radiometric dating which is used to determine how long a piece of organic matter has been dead. Because of bombardment by cosmic rays, the ratio of (radioactive) carbon-14 to (stable) carbon-12 in the atmosphere of Earth is fairly constant. This ratio is known. The ratio of carbon-14 to carbon-12 in a living organism is the same as it is in Earth's atmosphere, by biological respiration. However, when the organism dies, it no longer respires, and the carbon in its body stays where it was at the time of its death.

title: Definition:Radium/226
snippet: == Isotope of Radium == Radium-$226$ is the isotope of radium which has $138$ neutrons in addition to its $88$ protons. Ra-$226$ is radioactive, with a half-life of approximately $1600$ years. It has the longest half-life of all the isotopes of radium.

title: Definition:Radium/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Radium == The name radium is derived from the modern Latin, meaning to shed rays. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Radius
snippet: Geometry: Radius of a Circle: a straight line segment whose endpoints are the center and the circumference of the circle. Radius of a Sphere: a straight line segment whose endpoints are the center and the surface of the sphere. Radius of Regular Polygon: Long Radius Short Radius Analytic Geometry: The radial coordinate of a point $P$ in a system of polar coordinates is also known as the radius of $P$.

title: Definition:Radius/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Radius == The plural of radius is radii, pronounced ray-dee-eye. This irregular plural form stems from the Latin origin of the word radius, meaning ray. The ugly incorrect form can apparently be found, but rarely in a mathematical context. The form radial usually means directed along a radius.

title: Definition:Radius of Circle/Also defined as
snippet: == Radius of Circle: Also defined as == The radius of a circle can also be used to refer to the length of the line from the center to the circumference.

title: Definition:Radius of Complex Disk
snippet: Let $\map B {a, R}$ be the open (complex) disk $\set {z \in \C: \cmod {z - a} < R}$. Let $\map {\overline B} {a, R}$ be the closed (complex) disk $\set {z \in \C: \cmod {z - a} \le R}$. In either case, the parameter $R$ is referred to as the radius of $\map B {a, R}$ or $\map {\overline B} {a, R}$.

title: Definition:Radius of Convergence/Complex Domain
snippet: Let $\xi \in \C$ be a complex number. For $z \in \C$, let: $\ds \map f z = \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty a_n \paren {z - \xi}^n$ be a power series about $\xi$. The radius of convergence is the extended real number $R \in \overline \R$ defined by: $R = \ds \inf \set {\cmod {z - \xi}: z \in \C, \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty a_n \paren {z - \xi}^n \text{ is divergent} }$ where a divergent series is a series that is not convergent. As usual, $\inf \O = +\infty$.

title: Definition:Radius of Convergence/Real Domain
snippet: Let $\xi \in \R$ be a real number. Let $\ds \map S x = \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty a_n \paren {x - \xi}^n$ be a power series about $\xi$. Let $I$ be the interval of convergence of $\map S x$. Let the endpoints of $I$ be $\xi - R$ and $\xi + R$. (This follows from the fact that $\xi$ is the midpoint of $I$.) Then $R$ is called the radius of convergence of $\map S x$. If $\map S x$ is convergent over the whole of $\R$, then $I = \R$ and thus the radius of convergence is infinite.

title: Definition:Radius of Convergence of Real Power Series/Also known as
snippet: == Radius of Convergence of Real Power Series: Also known as == The radius of convergence of a real power series is also known as the limit of convergence. However, this can cause confusion with other definitions of limit, and so is deprecated on .

title: Definition:Radius of Curvature
snippet: The radius of curvature of a curve $C$ at a point $P$ is defined as the reciprocal of the absolute value of its curvature: $\rho = \dfrac 1 {\size k}$

title: Definition:Radius of Curvature/Cartesian Coordinates
snippet: Let $C$ be a curve defined by a real function which is twice differentiable. Let $C$ be embedded in a cartesian plane. The radius of curvature of $C$ at a point $P$ can be expressed in cartesian coordinates as: $\rho = \size {\dfrac {\paren {1 + y'^2}^{3/2} } {y' '} }$ where: {{eqn | l = y' | o = := | r = \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} }} {{eqn | l = y' ' | o = := | r = \dfrac {\d^2 y} {\d x^2} }}

title: Definition:Radius of Curvature/Parametric Form/Cartesian
snippet: Let $C$ be a curve defined by a real function which is twice differentiable. Let $C$ be embedded in a cartesian plane and defined by the parametric equations: $\begin{cases} x = \map x t \\ y = \map y t \end{cases}$ The radius of curvature $\rho$ of $C$ at a point $P = \tuple {x, y}$ is given by: $\rho = \dfrac {\paren {x'^2 + y'^2}^{3/2} } {\size {x' y' ' - y' x' '} }$ where: $x' = \dfrac {\d x} {\d t}$ is the derivative of $x$ $t$ at $P$ $y' = \dfrac {\d y} {\d t}$ is the derivative of $y$ $t$ at $P$ $x' '$ and $y' '$ are the second derivatives of $x$ and $y$ $t$ at $P$.

title: Definition:Radius of Gyration
snippet: Let $B$ be a rigid body which is rotating in space about some axis $\LL$. Let $P$ be a point on $B$ at which, or from which, a transfer of energy has the maximum effect. The radius of gyration of $B$ is the distance from $P$ to $\LL$.

title: Definition:Radius of Sphere/Also defined as
snippet: == Radius of Sphere: Also defined as == The radius of a sphere can also be used to refer to the length of the line from the center to the surface.

title: Definition:Radix Point/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Radix Point == The earliest known use of the technique of the radix point is the Babylonian number system. This was a sexagesimal system which used a specific symbol to separate the integer part from the fractional part.

title: Definition:Radon-Nikodym Derivative
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\map {\mathcal M^+} {X, \Sigma, \R}$ be the space of positive real-valued measurable functions. Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be $\sigma$-finite measures on $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ such that: $\nu$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$. Let $\sim$ be the $\mu$-almost everywhere equality relation on $\map {\mathcal M} {X, \Sigma, \R}$ restricted to the space of positive real-valued measurable functions $\map {\mathcal M^+} {X, \Sigma, \R}$.

title: Definition:Radon Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a $T_2$ (Hausdorff) space. Let $\map \BB X$ denote the Borel $\sigma$-algebra generated by $\tau$. Let $\MM$ be a $\sigma$-algebra over $X$ such that $\map \BB X \subseteq \MM$. Let $\mu : \MM \to \overline \R$ be a measure on $\MM$, where $\overline \R$ denotes the set of extended real numbers. Then $\mu$ is called a Radon measure, : $(1): \quad \map \mu K < \infty$ for all compact sets $K \subseteq X$ $(2): \quad \map \mu B = \sup \leftset {\map \mu K : K \subseteq B, K}$ is compact for all $\rightset {B \in \MM}$.

title: Definition:Radon Point
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of $n + 2$ points in a real Euclidean space $\R^n$ of $n$ dimensions. Let $S$ be partitioned into $2$ subsets whose convex hulls have at least one point in their intersection. Such a point of intersection is known as a Radon point of $S$.

title: Definition:Radon Transform
snippet: The Radon transform is a transform which reconstructs a function from the values of its integral over a set of lines in the plane. It is used for measuring data from incomplete observations.

title: Definition:Radon Transform/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Radon Transform == The Radon transform was discovered by in $1917$.

title: Definition:Ramanujan-Nagell Equation
snippet: The Ramanujan-Nagell equation is the Diophantine equation: $x^2 + 7 = 2^n$

title: Definition:Ramanujan-Nagell Equation/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Ramanujan-Nagell Equation == conjectured in $1913$ that the equation $x^2 + 7 = 2^n$ had only $5$ integer solutions. The same conjecture was made independently in $1943$ by . The conjecture was proved in $1948$ by Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Ramanujan-Nagell Number
snippet: A Ramanujan-Nagell number is a positive integer of the form $2^m - 1$ which is also triangular.

title: Definition:Ramanujan Phi Function
snippet: The two argument Ramanujan phi function, $\map \phi {a, n}$, is defined for $a \in \Z, a > 1$ as: $\ds \map \phi {a, n} = 1 + 2 \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n \dfrac 1 {\paren {a k }^3 - a k}$

title: Definition:Ramanujan Phi Function/One Argument
snippet: When $n$ is omitted, the one argument Ramanujan phi function, $\map \phi a$, is defined as: {{eqn | l = \map \phi a | r = \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \map \phi {a, n} | c = }} {{eqn | r = 1 + 2 \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^{\infty} \dfrac 1 {\paren {a k }^3 - a k} | c = }}

title: Definition:Ramanujan Sum
snippet: Let $e: \R \to \C$ be the mapping defined as: $\forall \alpha \in \R: \map e \alpha := \map \exp {2 \pi i \alpha}$ For $q \in \N_{>0}$, $n \in \N$, the Ramanujan sum is defined as: $\ds \map {c_q} n = \sum_{\substack {1 \mathop \le a \mathop \le q \\ \gcd \set {a, q} \mathop = 1} } \map e {\frac {a n} q}$

title: Definition:Ramsey Number
snippet: Ramsey's Theorem states that in any coloring of the edges of a sufficiently large complete graph, one will find monochromatic complete subgraphs. More precisely, for any given number of colors $c$, and any given integers $n_1, \ldots, n_c$, there is a number $\map R {n_1, \ldots, n_c}$ such that: if the edges of a complete graph of order $\map R {n_1, \ldots, n_c}$ are colored with $c$ different colors, then for some $i$ between $1$ and $c$, it must contain a complete subgraph of order $n_i$ whose edges are all color $i$.

title: Definition:Ramsey Theory
snippet: Ramsey theory is a branch of combinatorics that studies the conditions under which order must appear.

title: Definition:Random Error
snippet: A random error is the discrepancy between an observation and a value predicted by a particular model. Such an error represents uncontrolled variation. Random errors are usually assumed to be independent with a normal distribution and zero expectation.

title: Definition:Random Node/Also known as
snippet: == Random Node: Also known as == A random node is also known as a chance node or chance vertex.

title: Definition:Random Numbers
snippet: Random numbers are a sequence of digits or numbers, usually in a given range, such that each number has an equal probability of occurring for each term. In the ideal, it is impossible to predict which number will occur next.

title: Definition:Random Numbers/Methods of Generation
snippet: == Methods of Generation of Random Numbers == The traditional method of generation of random numbers is to draw from a container of tokens, identical but for the number written on them. Computers can be used to generate pseudo-random numbers, but these are not technically speaking actual random numbers.

title: Definition:Random Numbers/Motivation
snippet: == Random Numbers: Motivation == A table of random numbers is an effective tool for selecting elements from a population.

title: Definition:Random Sample/Methods of Generation
snippet: == Methods of Generation of Random Samples == Tables of random samples from certain probability distributions are available commercially. However, it is usual nowadays for simulations or Monte Carlo models to use a computer to generate effectively random samples.

title: Definition:Random Sample (Probability Theory)
snippet: Let $X_i$ be a random variable with $\Img {X_i} = \Omega$, for all $1 \le i \le n$. Let $F_i$ be the cumulative distribution function of $X_i$ for all $1 \le i \le n$. We say that $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ form a random sample of size $n$ if: $X_i$ and $X_j$ are independent if $i \ne j$ $\map {F_1} x = \map {F_i} x$ for all $x \in \Omega$ for all $1 \le i, j \le n$.

title: Definition:Random Sample (Probability Theory)/Also known as
snippet: == Random Sample: Also known as == If $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ form a random sample, they are said to be independent and identically distributed, commonly abbreviated i.i.d. Category:Definitions/Random Samples (Probability Theory)

title: Definition:Random Sample (Probability Theory)/Continuous Distribution
snippet: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with a known probability distribution. Let $\map f X$ be the frequency function of $X$. A random sample of values of $X$ is obtained by selecting values $s$ such that: $\map \Pr {s \in \openint x {x + \delta x} } = \map f x \delta x$ That is, the probability that $s$ is in a given interval is proportional to the length of the interval.

title: Definition:Random Sample (Probability Theory)/Discrete Distribution
snippet: Let $X$ be a discrete random variable with a known probability distribution. Let $\map f X$ be the frequency function of $X$. A random sample of values of $X$ is obtained by selecting values $s$ such that: $\map \Pr {s = x_i} = \map f {x_i}$ That is, the probability that $s$ is a given value is determined completely by the frequency function of $X$ at that value.

title: Definition:Random Sample (Statistics)
snippet: Let $P$ be a population. A sample taken from $P$ is a random sample it is chosen in such a way that every possible sample of the same size has an equal probability of being selected.

title: Definition:Random Sample (Statistics)/With Replacement
snippet: Let $S$ be a random sample taken from a population $P$ in such a way that each element $x$ may occur multiple times in $S$. Then the procedure for selecting $x$ is known as sampling with replacement. That is, once $x$ has been chosen from $P$, it is "replaced" back into $P$, with the possibility of it being selected more than once.

title: Definition:Random Sample (Statistics)/Without Replacement
snippet: Let $S$ be a random sample taken from a population $P$ in such a way that each element $x$ may occur once and once only in $S$. Then the procedure for selecting $x$ is known as sampling without replacement. That is, once $x$ has been chosen from $P$, it is not "replaced" back into $P$, and so cannot be selected again.

title: Definition:Random Selection
snippet: A manner of selecting objects from some larger collection of objects is said to be random if the selection is made according to chance. That is, there is no strict rule or procedure that predictably determines the outcome of the selection. See experiment and random variable for a precise mathematical treatment of randomness.

title: Definition:Random Variable
snippet: == Informal Definition == A random variable is a number whose value is determined unambiguously by an experiment.

title: Definition:Random Variable/Also known as
snippet: == Random Variable: Also known as == Other words used to mean the same thing as random variable are: stochastic variable chance variable variate. The image $\Img X$ of $X$ is often denoted $\Omega_X$.

title: Definition:Random Variable/Continuous
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $X$ be a real-valued random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ such that the domain of $X$ is a continuum. We say that $X$ is a continuous random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ : $\ds \lim_{\delta x \mathop \to 0} \map \Pr {X \in \openint x {x + \delta x} } = \map f x \delta x$ where $f$ is the frequency function on $X$.

title: Definition:Random Variable/General Definition
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\struct {S, \Sigma'}$ be a measurable space. A random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$, taking values in $\struct {S, \Sigma'}$, is a $\Sigma \, / \, \Sigma'$-measurable mapping $X : \Omega \to S$.

title: Definition:Random Variable/General Definition/Notation
snippet: == Notation == As an abuse of notation, we may write: $\set {\omega \in \Omega : \map P {\map X \omega} }$ as $\set {\map P X}$ for any propositional function of $\map X \omega$ such that: $\set {\omega \in \Omega : \map P {\map X \omega} }$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. We may therefore write, for example: $\map \Pr {\set {\omega \in \Omega : \map X \omega \in B} }$ for some $B \in \Sigma'$, as: $\map \Pr {\set {X \in B} }$ Usually the curly brackets are dropped and we write: $\map \Pr {\set {\omega \in \Omega : \map X \omega \in B} } = \map \Pr {X \in B}$ Category:Definitions/Random Variables

title: Definition:Random Variable/Real-Valued/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. A real-valued random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ is a $\Sigma$-measurable function $X : \Omega \to \R$. That is, a function $X : \Omega \to \R$ is a real-valued random variable : $X^{-1} \sqbrk {\hointl {-\infty} x} = \set {\omega \in \Omega : \map X \omega \le x} \in \Sigma$ for each $x \in \R$, where: $\hointl {-\infty} x$ denotes the unbounded closed interval $\set {y \in \R: y \le x}$ $X^{-1} \sqbrk {\hointl {-\infty} x}$ denotes the preimage of $\hointl {-\infty} x$ under $X$.

title: Definition:Random Variable/Real-Valued/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\map \BB \R$ be the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on $\R$. Let $X$ be a random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ taking values in $\struct {\R, \map \BB \R}$. Then we say that $X$ is a real-valued random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Category:Definitions/Random Variables

title: Definition:Random Variable/Real-Valued/Notation
snippet: == Notation == As an abuse of notation, we may write: $\set {\omega \in \Omega : \map X \omega \le x}$ as $\set {X \le x}$ $\set {\omega \in \Omega : \map X \omega \ge x}$ as $\set {X \ge x}$ $\set {\omega \in \Omega : \map X \omega x}$ as $\set {X > x}$ $\set {\omega \in \Omega : \map X \omega = x}$ as $\set {X = x}$ $\set {\omega \in \Omega : \map X \omega \in A}$ as $\set {X \in A}$ Generally, we write: $\set {\omega \in \Omega : \map P {\map X \omega} }$ as $\set {\map P X}$ for any propositional function of $\map X \omega$ such that: $\set {\omega \in \Omega : \map P {\map X \omega} }$…

title: Definition:Random Vector
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $n \in \N$. Let $\struct {S_1, \Sigma_1}$, $\struct {S_2, \Sigma_2}$, $\ldots$, $\struct {S_n, \Sigma_n}$ be measurable spaces. Let: $\ds S = \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n S_i$ For each integer $1 \le i \le n$, let $X_i$ be a random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ taking values in $\struct {S_i, \Sigma_i}$. Define a function $\mathbf X : \Omega \to S$ by: $\map {\mathbf X} \omega = \tuple {\map {X_1} \omega, \map {X_2} \omega, \ldots, \map {X_n} \omega}$ for each $\omega \in \Omega$. We call $\mathbf X$ a random vector.

title: Definition:Random Walk/One Dimension
snippet: Let $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \ge 0}$ be a Markov chain whose state space is the set of integers $\Z$. Let $\sequence {X_n}$ be such that $X_{n + 1}$ is an element of the set $\set {X_n + 1, X_n, X_n - 1}$. Then $\sequence {X_n}$ is a one-dimensional random walk.

title: Definition:Randomized Block
snippet: A randomized block is a grouping of experimental units. The number of units in each block must be a multiple of the number of treatments. This of course includes the case where the number of units is equal to the number of treatments. Each treatment is applied to exactly the same number of units in each block, and is allocated to those units within each block at random.

title: Definition:Randomized Block/Also known as
snippet: == Randomized Block: Also known as == A randomized block is also known just as a block.

title: Definition:Randomized Block Design
snippet: A randomized block design is an experimental design in which the experimental units are grouped into randomized blocks so that all units in each block are as similar as possible with regard to a chosen characteristic that might affect observations. Hence all experimental units in a given block are treated as though they are indistinguishable.

title: Definition:Randomized Block Design/Additive Component
snippet: Let an analysis of variance exercise use an instance of a randomized block design. In addition to the between-treatments sum of squares and error sum of squares, there are also additive component sums of squares. These correspond to: treatments (usually expressed by Latin letters) rows columns errors.

title: Definition:Randomized Block Design/Also defined as
snippet: == Randomized Block Design: Also defined as == In more sophisticated treatments of randomized block design, it is not necessary for the number of experimental units in each block to be a multiple of the number of treatments. However, analysis then becomes more complicated.

title: Definition:Randomized Block Design/Also known as
snippet: == Randomized Block Design: Also known as == A randomized block design is also known as just a block design by many sources. However, prefers to reserve the latter term for a more abstract concept.

title: Definition:Range
snippet: Relation Theory Range of Relation Analysis Range of Real Function Statistics Range Applied Mathematics and Mechanics: Range of Projectile

title: Definition:Range (Statistics)
snippet: Range is a measure of dispersion of a set of observations. Let $S$ be a set of observations of a quantitative variable. The range of $S$ is defined as: $\map R S := \map \max S - \map \min S$ where $\map \max S$ and $\map \min S$ are the greatest value of $S$ and the least value of $S$ respectively.

title: Definition:Range (Statistics)/Infinite
snippet: For certain random variables, it is possible that the range may be infinite, in the sense that it is technically unbounded.

title: Definition:Range of Real Function/Also known as
snippet: == Range of Real Function: Also known as == Modern treatments of the subject are usually more precise. In particular, the word range may be taken to mean codomain. Category:Definitions/Ranges of Real Functions

title: Definition:Range of Relation
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation, or (usually) a mapping (which is, of course, itself a relation). The range of $\RR$, denoted is defined as one of two things, depending on the source. On it is denoted $\Rng \RR$, but this may be non-standard.

title: Definition:Range of Relation/Also denoted as
snippet: == Range of Relation: Also denoted as == Some sources use the notation $\map {\mathrm {Ran} } \RR$ for the range of a relation (or the same all in lowercase). Some sources use $\map {\mathsf {Ran} } \RR$. Some use $R_\RR$.

title: Definition:Range of Relation/Codomain
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation, or (usually) a mapping (which is, of course, itself a relation). The range of $\RR$ can be defined as $T$. As such, it is the same thing as the term codomain of $\RR$.

title: Definition:Range of Relation/Image
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation, or (usually) a mapping (which is, of course, itself a relation). The range of $\RR$ can be defined as: $\Rng \RR = \set {t \in T: \exists s \in S: \tuple {s, t} \in \RR}$ Defined like this, it is the same as what is defined as the image of $\RR$.

title: Definition:Range of Relation/Warning
snippet: == Range of Relation: Warning == Because of the ambiguity in definition, it is advised that the term range not be used in this context at all. Instead that the term Codomain or Image be used as appropriate. This is the approach to be taken consistently in . Category:Definitions/Ranges (Relation Theory)

title: Definition:Range of Sequence
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in A}$ be a sequence. The range of $\sequence {x_n}$ is the set: $\set {x_n: n \mathop \in A}$

title: Definition:Range of Sequence/Also known as
snippet: == Range of Sequence: Also known as == Other terms for the range of a sequence include: the associated set of the sequence the image of the sequence. Some treatments do not bother to give it a name at all, merely referring to it as the set of its elements.

title: Definition:Rank/Linear Transformation
snippet: Let $\phi$ be a linear transformation from one vector space to another. Let the image of $\phi$ be finite-dimensional. Then its dimension is called the rank of $\phi$ and is denoted $\map \rho \phi$.

title: Definition:Rank/Matrix
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $\mathbf A$ be an $m \times n$ matrix over $K$.

title: Definition:Rank (Matroid)
snippet: Let $M = \struct{S, \mathscr I}$ be a matroid. Let $\rho : \powerset S \to \Z$ be the rank function of $M$. The rank of $M$, denoted by $\map \rho M$, is the image of $S$ under $\rho$, that is: $\map \rho M = \map \rho S$.

title: Definition:Rank (Set Theory)
snippet: Let $A$ be a set. Let $V$ denote the von Neumann hierarchy. Then the rank of $A$ is the smallest ordinal $x$ such that $A \in \map V {x + 1}$, given that $x$ exists.

title: Definition:Rank (Statistics)
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of sample data which has been assigned a ranking $\RR$. The index of a given $x \in S$ according to $\RR$ is known as its rank.

title: Definition:Rank Correlation Coefficient
snippet: A rank correlation coefficient is a statistical coefficient which measures the degree of agreement of a set of subjective rankings.

title: Definition:Rank Function
snippet: Relation Theory: Rank Function on a relational structure $\struct {S, \RR}$: a mapping $\operatorname {rk}$ from $S$ to a well-ordered set $\struct {T, \prec}$ such that: $\forall x, y \in S: \paren {x \ne y \text { and } \tuple {x, y} \in \RR} \implies \map {\operatorname {rk} } x \prec \map {\operatorname {rk} } y$ Matroid theory: Rank Function of a matroid $M = \struct {S, \mathscr I}$: the mapping from the power set of $S$ into the integers defined by: $\forall A \subseteq S : \map \rho A = \max \set {\size X : X \subseteq A \land X \in \mathscr I}$

title: Definition:Rank Function (Matroid)
snippet: Let $M = \struct {S, \mathscr I}$ be a matroid. The rank function of $M$ is the mapping $\rho : \powerset S \to \Z$ from the power set of $S$ into the integers defined by: $\forall A \subseteq S : \map \rho A = \max \set {\size X : X \subseteq A \land X \in \mathscr I}$ where $\size A$ denotes the cardinality of $A$.

title: Definition:Rank Function for Relation
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \RR}$ be a relational structure. Let $\struct {T, \prec}$ be a strictly well-ordered set. Let $\operatorname {rk}: S \to T$ be a mapping such that: $\forall x, y \in S: \paren {x \ne y \text { and } \tuple {x, y} \in \RR} \implies \map {\operatorname {rk} } x \prec \map {\operatorname {rk} } y$ $\operatorname {rk}$ is known as a rank function for $\RR$.

title: Definition:Rank of Entire Function
snippet: Let $f: \C \to \C$ be an entire function. Let $\sequence {a_n}$ be the sequence of non-zero zeroes of $f$, repeated according to multiplicity. The rank of $f$ is: the smallest positive integer $p \ge 0$ for which the series $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \size {a_n}^{-p - 1}$ converges or: $\infty$ if there is no such integer. If $f$ has finitely many zeroes, its rank is $0$.

title: Definition:Rank of Free Group
snippet: Let $F$ be a free group. The rank of $F$ is the dimension of its abelianization as a module over $\Z$.

title: Definition:Rank of Matrix/Also known as
snippet: == Rank of Matrix: Also known as == The rank of a matrix can also be referred to as: its row rank its column rank. Some sources denote the rank of a matrix $\mathbf A$ as: $\map {\mathrm {rk} } {\mathbf A}$ When defined as the order of the largest non-zero determinant that can be extracted from $\mathbf A$ by selecting rows and columns, it can be seen referred to as the determinantal rank of the matrix.

title: Definition:Rank of Matrix/Definition 1
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $\mathbf A$ be an $m \times n$ matrix over $K$. The rank of $\mathbf A$, denoted $\map \rho {\mathbf A}$, is the dimension of the subspace of $K^m$ generated by the columns of $\mathbf A$. That is, it is the dimension of the column space of $\mathbf A$.

title: Definition:Rank of Matrix/Definition 2
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $\mathbf A$ be an $m \times n$ matrix over $K$. Let $\mathbf A$ be converted to echelon form $\mathbf B$. Let $\mathbf B$ have exactly $k$ non-zero rows. Then the rank of $\mathbf A$, denoted $\map \rho {\mathbf A}$, is $k$.

title: Definition:Rank of Matrix/Definition 3
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $\mathbf A$ be an $m \times n$ matrix over $K$. The rank of $\mathbf A$, denoted $\map \rho {\mathbf A}$, is the largest number of elements in a linearly independent set of rows of $\mathbf A$.

title: Definition:Rank of Matrix/Definition 4
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $\mathbf A$ be an $m \times n$ matrix over $K$. The rank of $\mathbf A$, denoted $\map \rho {\mathbf A}$, is the largest number of elements in a linearly independent set of columns of $\mathbf A$.

title: Definition:Rank of Matrix/Definition 5
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $\mathbf A$ be an $m \times n$ matrix over $K$. The rank of $\mathbf A$, denoted $\map \rho {\mathbf A}$, is the order of the largest non-zero determinant that can be extracted from $\mathbf A$ by selecting rows and columns.

title: Definition:Rankine
snippet: The Rankine is a unit of absolute temperature. Its two reference points are: $0 \rankine$, which is set at absolute zero, the temperature at which all thermal motion stops $491 \cdotp 67 \rankine$, which is set at the of water.

title: Definition:Rankine/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Rankine: Conversion Factors ==

title: Definition:Ranking
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of discrete data which has been linearly ordered by a total ordering $\QQ$. The ranking of $x \in S$ is the index of $x$ in the sequence induced on $S$ by $\QQ$.

title: Definition:Ranking/Also known as
snippet: == Ranking: Also known as == A ranking is often known as a rank, but prefers ranking as the name suggests emphasis on the process of creating the ordering upon which the ranking is assigned. Hence on the term rank in this context refers specifically to the index of a given $x \in S$ under the ranking imposed upon $S$. Ranked data can be referred to as ordinal data, for which it is useful to compare the term ordinal variable.

title: Definition:Ranking/Motivation
snippet: It is often possible to generate a ranking on a set $S$ of observations without assigning precise measurements of the data being ordered. For example, objects can often be ranked by height without actually measuring those heights precisely. Many non-parametric tests are based on rankings, and use these even when precise measurements are indeed available.

title: Definition:Rare Number
snippet: A rare number is a non-palindromic integer $n$ which has the property that $n + r$ and $n - r$ are both square, where $r$ is the reversal of $n$.

snippet: == Examples of Rare Numbers ==

title: Definition:Rate
snippet: The rate of a physical process is its (first) derivative with respect to time. Loosely speaking, it means how fast something progresses, with a wider scope than change in physical displacement.

title: Definition:Rate/Dimension
snippet: A rate has dimension $\mathsf T^{-1}$. Category:Definitions/Rate

title: Definition:Rate Function
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space. Let $\overline \R_\ge$ be the positive extended real number line. Let $I : X \to \overline \R_\ge$ be a function. Then $I$ is a rate function $I$ is lower semicontinuous.

title: Definition:Rate of Change
snippet: The rate of change of a physical quantity is its (first) derivative with respect to an independent variable which is usually, but not exclusively, time. Loosely speaking, it means how fast something changes, with a wider scope than change in physical displacement.

title: Definition:Rate of Change/Decrease
snippet: A rate of decrease is a rate of change measured in a strictly negative direction. Hence a negative rate of decrease is a rate of increase.

title: Definition:Rate of Change/Dimension
snippet: Let a physical quantity $P$ have dimension $\mathsf D$. Then the rate of change of $P$ time has dimension $\mathsf {D T}^{-1}$. Category:Definitions/Dimensions of Measurement

title: Definition:Rate of Change/Increase
snippet: A rate of increase is a rate of change measured in a strictly positive direction.

title: Definition:Rate of Change/Time
snippet: When the independent variable of a rate of change is time, it is commonplace to take that fact for granted, and refer merely to its rate of change.

title: Definition:Ratio
snippet: Let $x$ and $y$ be quantities which have the same dimensions. Let $\dfrac x y = \dfrac a b$ for two numbers $a$ and $b$. Then the ratio of $x$ to $y$ is defined as: $x : y = a : b$ It explicitly specifies how many times the first number contains the second. '

title: Definition:Ratio/3 Terms
snippet: Let $a$, $b$ and $c$ be numbers. The ratio of $3$ terms: $a : b : c$ means: The ratios of $a$ to $b$, of $b$ to $c$ and of $a$ to $c$ are equivalent to $a : b$, $b : c$ and $a : c$ respectively.

title: Definition:Ratio/Antecedent
snippet: Let $x$ and $y$ be quantities which have the same dimensions. Let $x : y$ denote the ratio of $x$ to $y$. Then $x$ is known as the antecedent of $x : y$.

title: Definition:Ratio/Consequent
snippet: Let $x$ and $y$ be quantities which have the same dimensions. Let $x : y$ denote the ratio of $x$ to $y$. Then $y$ is known as the consequent of $x : y$.

title: Definition:Ratio/Equality
snippet: == Equality of Ratios == Let $p, q, r, s$ be quantities. Then $p : q = r : s$ if, for any (strictly) positive integers $m$ and $n$, $n p m q$ according as $n r m s$ respectively. ' Category:Definitions/Ratios

title: Definition:Ratio/Existence
snippet: == Existence of Ratio == A ratio exists between two quantities $x$ and $y$ : $\exists m, n \in \Z: m x > n, n y > m$ This condition is known as the Archimedean property. ' Category:Definitions/Ratios

title: Definition:Ratio/Terms
snippet: The numbers or symbols composing a ratio are known as its terms:
