title: Definition:Reduced Quartic
snippet: A reduced quartic is a quartic equation in the form: $y^4 + p y^2 + q y + r = 0$ That is, such that it is both monic and depressed.

title: Definition:Reduced Residue System
snippet: Let $m \in \Z_{> 0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. The reduced residue system modulo $m$, denoted $\Z'_m$, is the set of all residue classes of $k$ (modulo $m$) which are prime to $m$: $\Z'_m = \set {\eqclass k m \in \Z_m: k \perp m}$ Thus $\Z'_m$ is the set of all coprime residue classes modulo $m$: $\Z'_m = \set {\eqclass {a_1} m, \eqclass {a_2} m, \ldots, \eqclass {a_{\map \phi m} } m}$ where: $\forall k: a_k \perp m$ $\map \phi m$ denotes the Euler phi function of $m$.

title: Definition:Reduced Residue System/Least Positive
snippet: Let $m \in \Z_{> 0}$. The least positive reduced residue system modulo $m$ is the set of integers: $\set {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{\map \phi m} }$ with the following properties: $\map \phi m$ is the Euler $\phi$ function $\forall i: 0 < a_i < m$ each of which is prime to $m$ no two of which are congruent modulo $m$.

title: Definition:Reduced Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Then $R$ is a reduced ring it contains no nilpotent elements except the zero.

title: Definition:Reducible Equation
snippet: A reducible equation is an equation of the form: $P = 0$ where $P$ is a reducible polynomial.

title: Definition:Reducible Fraction
snippet: Let $q = \dfrac a b$ be a vulgar fraction. Then $q$ is defined as being reducible $q$ is not in canonical form. That is, there exists $r \in \Z: r \ne 1$ such that $r$ is a divisor of both $a$ and $b$. Such a fraction can therefore be reduced by dividing both $a$ and $b$ by $r$.

title: Definition:Reducible G-Module
snippet: Let $M$ be a $G$-module. Then $M$ is reducible the corresponding linear representation is reducible.

title: Definition:Reducible Linear Representation
snippet: Let $\rho: G \to \GL V$ be a linear representation. $\rho$ is reducible there exists a non-trivial proper vector subspace $W$ of $V$ such that: $\forall g \in G: \map {\map \rho g} W \subseteq W$ That is, such that $W$ is invariant for every linear operator in the set $\set {\map \rho g: g \in G}$.

title: Definition:Reducible Polynomial/Definition 1
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. A reducible polynomial over $K$ is a nonconstant polynomial over $K$ that can be expressed as the product of two polynomials over $K$ of smaller degree.

title: Definition:Reducible Polynomial/Definition 2
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. A reducible polynomial over $K$ is a polynomial over $K$ that can be expressed as the product of two nonconstant polynomials.

title: Definition:Reducible Polynomial/Mistake
snippet: == Source Work == reducible polynomial

title: Definition:Reducible Radical
snippet: A reducible radical is a radical that can be written in a rationalized form.

title: Definition:Reducing Subspace
snippet: Let $H$ be a Hilbert space. Let $A \in \map B H$ be a bounded linear operator. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of $H$; denote by $M^\perp$ its orthocomplement. Then $M$ is said to be a reducing subspace for $A$ both $M$ and $M^\perp$ are invariant subspaces for $A$. That is, $AM \subseteq M$ and $A M^\perp \subseteq M^\perp$.

title: Definition:Reduct of Structure
snippet: Let $\LL, \LL'$ be signatures of the language of predicate logic. Let $\LL$ be a subsignature of $\LL'$. Let $\AA, \AA'$ be structures for $\LL, \LL'$, respectively. Then $\AA$ is called the reduct of $\AA'$ to $\LL$ : For all function symbols $f$ of $\LL$, one has $f_{\AA'} = f_\AA$ For all predicate symbols $p$ of $\LL$, one has $p_{\AA'} = p_\AA$ where $f_{\AA'}$ is the interpretation of the function symbol $f$ in the structure $\AA'$. Symbolically, one may write $\AA = \AA' {\restriction_\LL}$.

title: Definition:Reduction Formula (Calculus)
snippet: Let $f: \R \times \Z_{\ge 0}: \R$ be a Darboux integrable real-valued function on $\R \times \N$. Let: $\ds I_n = \int \map f {x, n} \rd x$ for some $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$. A reduction formula is a recurrence relation of the form: $\ds I_k = \map g {I_n}$ such that $k < n$. That is, it is a technique to reduce the integer parameter in the integrand in order to allow evaluation of the integral at, usually, $n = 0$ or $n = 1$. This technique relies upon the supposition that $\map f {x, 0}$ or $\map f {x, 1}$ can be integrated directly.

title: Definition:Reduction Formula (Trigonometry)
snippet: A reduction formula in the context of trigonometry is a formula that gives a trigonometric function of an angle plus or minus one or more right angles.

title: Definition:Reduction of Group Word on Set
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $w$ be a group word on $X$. A reduction of $w$ is a finite sequence of group words $\tuple {w^{\paren 0}, \ldots, w^{\paren n} }$ such that: $w^{\paren 0} = w$ $w_{i + 1}$ is an elementary reduction of $w_i$, for all $i \in \set {0, \ldots, n - 1}$ $w^{\paren n}$ is reduced

title: Definition:Reduction to First Figure
snippet: Reduction to the first figure is a method for determining the validity of a categorical syllogism, as follows: There are two forms this procedure takes:

title: Definition:Reduction to First Figure/Direct
snippet: Direct reduction to the first figure is a form of the reduction to the first figure method for determining the validity of a categorical syllogism. This form of the method works forward from the first figure using various rules of categorical statements in order to derive valid patterns of other figures.

title: Definition:Reduction to First Figure/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Reduction to First Figure == This technique for analysis of categorical syllogisms was devised by . Reduction is of great historical interest, as being perhaps the earliest known attempt to derive conclusions systematically from given assumptions. Though 's presentation is crude and informal by modern standards of rigour, it is possible to follow the outlines of his programme and derive the valid syllogisms as conclusions, by purely propositional calculus reasoning, from a very small set of syllogistic assumptions. -- : $\S 4.4$: The Syllogism

title: Definition:Reduction to First Figure/Indirect
snippet: Indirect reduction to the first figure is a form of the reduction to the first figure method for determining the validity of a categorical syllogism. This form of the method works backward by supposing that a pattern is not valid, and then deriving a contradiction against a known valid pattern in the first figure. Hence by Reductio ad Absurdum the pattern is deduced to be valid.

title: Definition:Reed-Solomon Code
snippet: Let $\GF_q$ be the finite field whose underlying set is $\set {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_q}$ such that $a_q = 0$. The $k$th Reed-Solomon code $\GF_q$ is the linear code of length $q - 1$ defined as: the set of all $\paren {q - 1}$-tuples $\tuple {\map f {a_1}, \map f {a_2}, \ldots, \map f {a_1} }$ where $f$ ranges over all polynomials of degree at most $k - 1$ with coefficients in $\GF_q$.

title: Definition:Reed-Solomon Code/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Reed-Solomon Code == The Reed-Solomon codes were invented by and in $1960$. They are now in common use in many data storage and transmission applications, as they have good error-detection and correction properties.

title: Definition:Reference Table
snippet: A reference table is a set of pages, arranged usually in book form, containing arrays of (usually) numbers arranged in rows and columns for ease of look-up. They have been generally superseded by computers now, but facility in their use is generally considered advantageous.

title: Definition:Reference Table/Also known as
snippet: == Reference Table: Also known as == A set of reference tables is often known just as the tables. Category:Definitions/Reference Tables

title: Definition:Refinement
snippet: Topology: A refinement of a cover Group Theory: A refinement of a normal series

title: Definition:Refinement of Cover
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\UU = \set {U_\alpha}$ and $\VV = \set {V_\beta}$ be covers of $S$. Then $\VV$ is a refinement of $\UU$ : $\forall V_\beta \in \VV: \exists U_\alpha \in \UU: V_\beta \subseteq U_\alpha$ That is, every element of $\VV$ is the subset of some element of $\UU$.

title: Definition:Refinement of Cover/Also defined as
snippet: == Refinement of Cover: Also known as == Although specified for the cover of a set, a refinement is usually used in the context of a topological space.

title: Definition:Refinement of Cover/Coarser Cover
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\UU = \set {U_\alpha}$ and $\VV = \set {V_\beta}$ be covers of $S$. Let $\VV$ be a refinement of $\UU$. Then $\UU$ is coarser than $\VV$.

title: Definition:Refinement of Cover/Finer Cover
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\UU = \set {U_\alpha}$ and $\VV = \set {V_\beta}$ be covers of $S$. Let $\VV$ be a refinement of $\UU$. Then $\VV$ is finer than $\UU$.

title: Definition:Refinement of Finite Subdivision
snippet: Let $\closedint a b$ be a closed interval. Let $P, Q$ be finite subdivisions of $\closedint a b$. We say that $Q$ is a refinement of $P$, or that $Q$ is finer than $P$ : $P$ is a subset of $Q$.

title: Definition:Refinement of Normal Series
snippet: Let $G$ be a group whose identity is $e$. Let $\sequence {G_i}_{i \mathop \in \closedint 0 n}$ be a normal series for $G$: $\sequence {G_i}_{i \mathop \in \closedint 0 n} = \tuple {\set e = G_0 \lhd G_1 \lhd \cdots \lhd G_{n - 1} \lhd G_n = G}$ Let $\sequence {H_j}_{j \mathop \in \closedint 0 m}$ be another normal series for $G$: $\sequence {H_j}_{j \mathop \in \closedint 0 m} = \tuple {\set e = H_0 \lhd H_1 \lhd \cdots \lhd H_{m - 1} \lhd H_m = G}$ such that $\sequence {G_i}_{i \mathop \in \closedint 0 n} \subseteq \sequence {H_j}_{j \mathop \in \closedint 0 m}$ Then $\sequence {H_j}_{j…

title: Definition:Refinement of Normal Series/Proper Refinement
snippet: A proper refinement of a normal series is a refinement which is not equal to the original normal series. That is, it contains extra (normal) subgroups which are not present in the original normal series.

title: Definition:Refinement of Partition (Probability Theory)
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\xi, \eta$ be partitions of $\Omega$. Then $\xi$ said to be a refinement of $\eta$ : $\ds \forall A \in \eta : A = \bigcup \set {B \in \xi : B \subseteq A}$ It is written as: $\eta \le \xi$

title: Definition:Reflection/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Reflection == In older texts, you sometimes see the word reflexion, which is merely an archaic spelling of reflection. Contemporary authors in various more-or-less literary genres occasionally affect this outdated spelling, but in mathematics texts written since the middle of the $20$th century, the reflexion spelling is vanishingly rare. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Reflection (Geometry)
snippet: A reflection in the context of Euclidean geometry is an isometry from a Euclidean Space $\R^n$ as follows. A reflection is defined usually for either: $n = 2$, representing the plane or: $n = 3$, representing ordinary space.

title: Definition:Reflection (Geometry)/Plane
snippet: A reflection $\phi_{AB}$ in the plane is an isometry on the Euclidean Space $\Gamma = \R^2$ as follows. Let $AB$ be a distinguished straight line in $\Gamma$, which has the property that: $\forall P \in AB: \map {\phi_{AB} } P = P$ That is, every point on $AB$ maps to itself. Let $P \in \Gamma$ such that $P \notin AB$. Let a straight line be constructed from $P$ to $O$ on $AB$ such that $OP$ is perpendicular to $AB$. Let $PO$ be produced to $P'$ such that $OP = OP'$. 400px Then: $\map {\phi_{AB} } P = P'$ Thus $\phi_{AB}$ is a reflection (in the plane) in (the axis of reflection) $AB$.

title: Definition:Reflection (Geometry)/Plane/Axis
snippet: Let $\phi_{AB}$ be a reflection in the plane in the straight line $AB$. Then $AB$ is known as the axis (of reflection) of $\phi_{AB}$.

title: Definition:Reflection (Geometry)/Point
snippet: A point reflection $\psi_O$ in space is an isometry on the Euclidean Space $\Gamma = \R^3$ as follows. Let $O$ be a distinguished point in $\Gamma$, called the inversion point, which has the property that: $\map {r_\alpha} O = O$ That is, $O$ maps to itself. Let $P \in \Gamma$ such that $P \ne O$. Let $OP$ be joined by a straight line. Let $PO$ be produced to $P'$ such that $OP = OP'$. Then: $\map {\psi_O} P = P'$ Thus $\phi_S$ is a point reflection (in space) in (the inversion point) $O$.

title: Definition:Reflection (Geometry)/Point/Inversion Point
snippet: Let $\psi_O$ be a point reflection in the Euclidean Space $\Gamma = \R^3$. The point $O$ in $\Gamma$ such that: $\map {\psi_O} O = O$ is called the inversion point of $\psi_O$. Category:Definitions/Geometric Reflections

title: Definition:Reflection (Geometry)/Space
snippet: A reflection $\phi_S$ in space is an isometry on the Euclidean Space $\Gamma = \R^3$ as follows. Let $S$ be a distinguished plane in $\Gamma$, which has the property that: $\forall P \in S: \map {\phi_S} P = P$ That is, every point on $S$ maps to itself. Let $P \in \Gamma$ such that $P \notin S$. Let a straight line be constructed from $P$ to $O$ on $S$ such that $OP$ is perpendicular to $S$. Let $PO$ be produced to $P'$ such that $OP = OP'$. 600px In the above diagram, $ABCD$ is in the plane of $S$.

title: Definition:Reflection (Geometry)/Space/Plane
snippet: Let $\phi_S$ be a reflection in space in the plane $S$. Then $S$ is known as the plane of reflection of $\phi_S$.

title: Definition:Reflection Formula
snippet: Let $f$ be a real or complex function. A reflection formula is a functional equation relating $\map f {a - x}$ to $\map f x$ for some $a \in \Dom f$.

title: Definition:Reflection Formula/Also known as
snippet: == Reflection Formula: Also known as == A reflection formula is also known as a reflection relation. It is common in the literature to use the term functional equation when reflection formula is meant. However, as a reflection formula is a specific instance of a functional equation, this is excusable.

title: Definition:Reflection Matrix
snippet: Let $\tuple {\mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_2, \mathbf e_3}$ be the orthonormal basis of a Cartesian coordinate system $C$ on (ordinary) space $S$. Let $O$ be the origin of $C$. Let $\tuple {\mathbf e'_1, \mathbf e'_2, \mathbf e'_3}$ be the orthonormal basis of another Cartesian coordinate system $C'$ on $S$, also with origin $O$ and with the same orientation as $C$. The reflection matrix $R$ from $C$ to $C'$ is the square matrix of order $3$: where $a_{i j}$ is defined as: for $i, j \in \set {1, 2, 3}$.

title: Definition:Reflectional Symmetry
snippet: Let $F$ be a geometric figure. Let there exist a reflection which is also a symmetry of $F$. Then $F$ has a reflectional symmetry. Thus a reflectional symmetry is itself a symmetry which is a reflection.

title: Definition:Reflex Angle
snippet: A reflex angle is an angle which has a measure between that of a straight angle and that of a full angle.

title: Definition:Reflexive Bilinear Form
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be a field. Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb K$. Let $b$ be a bilinear form on $V$. Then $b$ is reflexive : $\forall v, w \in V: \map b {v, w} = 0 \implies \map b {w, v} = 0$

title: Definition:Reflexive Bilinear Space
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be a field. Let $\struct {V, f}$ be a bilinear space over $\mathbb K$. Then $\struct {V, f}$ is reflexive $f$ is a reflexive bilinear form.

title: Definition:Reflexive Closure/Intersection of Reflexive Supersets
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a relation on a set $S$. Let $\QQ$ be the set of all reflexive relations on $S$ that contain $\RR$. The reflexive closure of $\RR$ is denoted $\RR^=$, and is defined as: $\RR^= := \bigcap \QQ$ That is: $\RR^=$ is the intersection of all reflexive relations on $S$ containing $\RR$.

title: Definition:Reflexive Closure/Smallest Reflexive Superset
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a relation on a set $S$. The reflexive closure of $\RR$ is defined as the smallest reflexive relation on $S$ that contains $\RR$ as a subset. The reflexive closure of $\RR$ is denoted $\RR^=$.

title: Definition:Reflexive Closure/Union with Diagonal
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a relation on a set $S$. The reflexive closure of $\RR$ is denoted $\RR^=$, and is defined as: $\RR^= := \RR \cup \set {\tuple {x, x}: x \in S}$ That is: $\RR^= := \RR \cup \Delta_S$ where $\Delta_S$ is the diagonal relation on $S$.

title: Definition:Reflexive Reduction
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a relation on a set $S$. The reflexive reduction of $\RR$ is denoted $\RR^\ne$, and is defined as: $\RR^\ne := \RR \setminus \set {\tuple {x, x}: x \in S}$

title: Definition:Reflexive Relation
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation in $S$.

title: Definition:Reflexive Relation/Class Theory
snippet: Let $V$ be a basic universe. Let $A$ be a class, by definition a subclass of $V$. Let $\RR \subseteq A \times A$ be a relation in $V$. $\RR$ is reflexive on $A$ : $\forall x \in A: \tuple {x, x} \in \RR$

title: Definition:Reflexive Relation/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation in $S$. $\RR$ is reflexive : $\forall x \in S: \tuple {x, x} \in \RR$

title: Definition:Reflexive Relation/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation in $S$. $\RR$ is reflexive it is a superset of the diagonal relation: $\Delta_S \subseteq \RR$

title: Definition:Reflexive Space
snippet:
Let $\struct {X, 
orm \cdot_X}$ be a normed vector space. Let $\struct {X^{\ast \ast}, 
orm \cdot_{X^{\ast \ast} } }$ be the second normed dual of $\struct {X, 
orm \cdot_X}$. Let $J : X 	o X^{\ast \ast}$ be the evaluation linear transformation. We say that $X$ is reflexive : $J$ is an isometric isomorphism.

title: Definition:Reflexive Transitive Closure
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a relation on a set $S$.

title: Definition:Reflexive Transitive Closure/Reflexive Closure of Transitive Closure
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a relation on a set $S$. The reflexive transitive closure of $\RR$ is denoted $\RR^*$, and is defined as the reflexive closure of the transitive closure of $\RR$: $\RR^* = \paren {\RR^+}^=$

title: Definition:Reflexive Transitive Closure/Smallest Reflexive Transitive Superset
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a relation on a set $S$. The reflexive transitive closure of $\RR$ is denoted $\RR^*$, and is defined as the smallest reflexive and transitive relation on $S$ which contains $\RR$.

title: Definition:Reflexive Transitive Closure/Transitive Closure of Reflexive Closure
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a relation on a set $S$. The reflexive transitive closure of $\RR$ is denoted $\RR^*$, and is defined as the transitive closure of the reflexive closure of $\RR$: $\RR^* = \paren {\RR^=}^+$

title: Definition:Reflexivity
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation in $S$.

title: Definition:Region/Also known as
snippet: == Region: Also known as == A region is also known as a domain, but that term already has several wider meanings.

title: Definition:Region/Complex
snippet: Let $D \subseteq \C$ be a subset of the set of complex numbers. $D$ is a region of $\C$ : $(1): \quad$ $D$ is non-empty $(2): \quad$ $D$ is path-connected.

title: Definition:Region/Metric Space
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. A region of $M$ is a subset $U$ of $M$ such that $U$ is: $(1): \quad$ non-empty $(2): \quad$ path-connected.

title: Definition:Region/Plane
snippet: A point set $R$ in the plane is a region : $(1): \quad$ Each point of $R$ is the center of a circle all of whose elements consist of points of $R$ $(2): \quad$ Each point of $R$ can be joined by a curve consisting entirely of points of $R$.

title: Definition:Regression
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables. The regression of $Y$ on $X$ for a given value of $x$ is the mapping defined and denoted as: $\forall x \in X: \map f {Y, x} := \expect {Y \mid x}$ where $\expect {Y \mid x}$ denotes the expectation of $Y$ conditional upon $x$.

title: Definition:Regression/Cause Variable
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables. Let $\map f {Y, x}$ denote the regression of $Y$ on $X$ for a given value of $x$. The variable $x$ is known as the cause variable.

title: Definition:Regression/Effect Variable
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables. Let $\map f {Y, x}$ denote the regression of $Y$ on $X$. The random variable $Y$ is known as the effect variable.

title: Definition:Regression/Informal Definition
snippet: A regression is a model which describes how the expectation of one random variable depends on one or more other random variables.

title: Definition:Regression Analysis
snippet: Regression analysis is the field of study which concerns identifying the values of the regression coefficients of a regression.

title: Definition:Regression Coefficient
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables. Let the regression of $Y$ on $x$, for a given value of $x$, be expressible in the form: $\expect {Y \mid x} = \ds \sum_{i \mathop = 0}^n \beta_i x^i$ The coefficients $\beta_i$ are known as the regression coefficients, and are usually unknown.

title: Definition:Regression Model
snippet: Let $S$ be a stochastic process based on an equispaced time series. Let the values of $S$ at timestamps $t, t - 1, t - 2, \dotsc$ be $z_t, z_{t - 1}, z_{t - 2}, \dotsc$ Let $\tilde z_t, \tilde z_{t - 1}, \tilde z_{t - 2}, \dotsc$ be deviations from a constant mean level $\mu$: $\tilde z_t = z_t - \mu$ Let $M$ be a linear filter model defined as $\tilde z_t = \phi_1 \tilde x_1 + \phi_2 \tilde x_2 + \dotsb + \phi_p \tilde x_p + a$ which relates a dependent variable $z$ to a set of independent variables $x_1, x_2, \dotsc, x_p$ plus an error term $a$. $M$ is known as a regression model.

title: Definition:Regular

title: Definition:Regular/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Regular == The mathematical meaning of regular evolves from its natural language usage to mean obeying rules, uniform, occurring at equal time intervals or according to a common pattern, and therefore predictable. Its linguistic origin is from the Latin rēgulāris, meaning guided by a rule or rules. This ultimately originates from Proto-Indo-European reg-, meaning to move in a straight line. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Regular Cardinal
snippet: Let $\kappa$ be an infinite cardinal. Then $\kappa$ is a regular cardinal : $\map {\mathrm {cf} } \kappa = \kappa$ That is, the cofinality of $\kappa$ is equal to itself.

title: Definition:Regular Closed Set
snippet: Let $T$ be a topological space. Let $A \subseteq T$. Then $A$ is regular closed in $T$ : $A = A^{\circ -}$ That is, $A$ equals the closure of its interior.

title: Definition:Regular Closed Set/Also known as
snippet: == Regular Closed Set: Also known as == Some sources refer to a regular closed set as a regularly closed set, but this is not used on . Category:Definitions/Regular Closed Sets

title: Definition:Regular Continued Fraction
snippet: Definition:Continued Fraction, as opposed to a generalized continued fraction Definition:Simple Continued Fraction Definition:Continued Fraction Expansion of Real Number

title: Definition:Regular Curve
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $I \subseteq \R$ be a real interval. Let $\gamma : I \to M$ be a smooth curve. For all $t \in I$ let $T_{\map \gamma t} M$ be the tangent space of $M$ at the point $\map \gamma t$. Then $\gamma$ is called a regular curve : $\forall t \in I : \map {\gamma'} t \ne 0$

title: Definition:Regular Curve/3-Dimensional Real Vector Space
snippet: Let $\alpha : I \to \R^3$ be a smooth curve. $\alpha$ is said to be regular : $\forall t \in I : \map {\alpha'} t \ne \bszero_{\R^3}$ where: $\alpha'$ denotes the derivative of $\alpha$ $\bszero_{\R^3}$ denotes the zero vector in $\R^3$

title: Definition:Regular Distribution
snippet: Let $f \in \map {L^1_{loc} } {\R^d}$ be a locally integrable function. Let $T_f : \map {\DD} {\R^d} \to \C$ be a Schwartz distribution associated with $f$. Then $T_f$ is called the regular distribution.

title: Definition:Regular Dodecahedron/Also known as
snippet: == Regular Dodecahedron: Also known as == It is commonplace for authors to refer to a regular dodecahedron as just an dodecahedron, glossing over the fact of its regularity.

title: Definition:Regular Dodecahedron/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on the Regular Dodecahedron == In , this object is referred to just as a dodecahedron. According to the Pythagorean tradition, the regular dodecahedron was the symbol associated with the sphere of the fixed stars, and later with the quintessence of the medieval alchemists.

title: Definition:Regular Domain
snippet: Let $M$ be a topological manifold. Let $D \subseteq M$ be a submanifold. Suppose $D$ is a closed, embedded, codimension-$0$ submanifold with a boundary. Then $D$ is called the regular domain.

title: Definition:Regular Element
snippet: Definition:Cancellable Element Definition:Regular Element of Ring

title: Definition:Regular Element of Ring
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $a \in A$. Then $a$ is regular element of $A$ $a$ is not a zero divisor of $A$.

title: Definition:Regular Element of Ring/Also known as
snippet: == Regular Element of Ring: Also known as == A regular element of a ring is also known as a non-zero-divisor. Category:Definitions/Regular Elements of Rings

title: Definition:Regular Expression
snippet: A regular expression is an algebraic structure on an alphabet $\Sigma$ defined as follows: The empty-set regular expression, $\O$, is a regular expression. The empty-word regular expression, $\epsilon$, is a regular expression. Every $\sigma \in \Sigma$ is a regular expression. (These are called literals.) If $R_1$ and $R_2$ are regular expressions, $R_1 R_2$ is a regular expression (concatenation). If $R_1$ and $R_2$ are regular expressions, $R_1 \mid R_2$ is a regular expression (alternation). If $R$ is a regular expression, $R^*$ is a regular expression (Kleene star).

title: Definition:Regular Graph
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be an simple graph whose vertices all have the same degree $r$. Then $G$ is called regular of degree $r$, or $r$-regular.

title: Definition:Regular Greek Cross
snippet: A regular Greek cross is a dodecagon which is formed by placing $5$ squares all of the same size so that $4$ of them abut the central $5$th square: 300px

title: Definition:Regular Greek Cross/Also known as
snippet: == Regular Greek Cross: Also known as == Some sources refer to a regular Greek cross as a symmetrical Greek cross, but this is a bad term, because in a particular sense all Greek crosses are symmetrical.

title: Definition:Regular Group
snippet: Let $S$ be a (finite) set with $n$ elements. Let $G$ be a permutation group on $S$. Then $G$ is a regular group $G$ has order $n$.

title: Definition:Regular Icosahedron/Also known as
snippet: == Regular Icosahedron: Also known as == Occasionally an author may refer to a regular icosahedron as just an icosahedron, glossing over the fact of its regularity. It is wise to make sure of what is meant.

title: Definition:Regular Icosahedron/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on the Regular Icosahedron == In , this object is referred to just as an icosahedron. According to the Pythagorean tradition, the regular icosahedron was the symbol for the element water.

title: Definition:Regular Level Set
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $f \in \map {C^\infty} M : M \to \R$ be a smooth real-valued function. Let $p \in M$ be a base point in $M$. Let $\d f_p$ be the differential of $f$ at $p$. Let $c \in \R$. Let $\inv f c$ be a level set. Suppose every point of $\inv f c$ is a regular point of $f$: $\forall p \in \inv f c : \d f_p \ne 0$ Then $\inv f c$ is called a regular level set.

title: Definition:Regular Locale
snippet: Let $L = \struct {S, \preceq}$ be a locale. Let $\eqslantless$ denote the well inside relation on $L$. Then $L$ is said to be a regular locale : $\forall a \in S : a = \sup \set {b \in S : b \eqslantless a}$

title: Definition:Regular Octahedron/Also known as
snippet: == Regular Octahedron: Also known as == It is commonplace for authors to refer to a regular octahedron as just an octahedron, glossing over the fact of its regularity.

title: Definition:Regular Octahedron/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on the Regular Octahedron == in refers to this object just as an octahedron. According to the Pythagorean tradition, the regular octahedron was the symbol for the element air.

title: Definition:Regular Open Set
snippet: Let $T$ be a topological space. Let $A \subseteq T$. Then $A$ is regular open in $T$ : $A = A^{-\circ}$ That is, $A$ equals the interior of its closure.

title: Definition:Regular Point
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $f \in \map {\CC^\infty} M : M \to \R$ be a smooth real-valued function. Let $p \in M$ be a base point in $M$. Let $\d f_p$ be the differential of $f$ at $p$. Suppose $\d f_p \ne 0$. Then $p$ is called a regular point of $f$.

title: Definition:Regular Polygon/Also known as
snippet: == Regular Polygon: Also known as == In , a regular polygon is referred to as an equilateral and equiangular polygon. Some sources use the word perfect or symmetrical instead of regular. The term regular $n$-gon is usually used nowadays to specify a regular polygon with a specific number, that is $n$, sides. The specific name is usually invoked only in order to draw attention to the fact that such a regular polygon has a particularly interesting set of properties.

title: Definition:Regular Polygon/Apothem
snippet: The apothem of a regular polygon $P$ is defined as the perpendicular distance from the center of $P$ to one of its sides. 300px In the above, the length of $OM$ is the apothem of the regular polygon.

title: Definition:Regular Polygon/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Regular Polygons == Specific instances of regular polygons with specific numbers of sides are as follows: $3$ sides: Equilateral Triangle $4$ sides: Square $5$ sides: Regular Pentagon $6$ sides: Regular Hexagon $7$ sides: Regular Heptagon $8$ sides: Regular Octagon $9$ sides: Regular Nonagon or Regular Enneagon $10$ sides: Regular Decagon $11$ sides: Regular Hendecagon or Regular Undecagon $12$ sides: Regular Dodecagon $17$ sides: Regular Heptadecagon Category:Definitions/Examples of Regular Polygons

title: Definition:Regular Polyhedron
snippet: A regular polyhedron is a polyhedron: $(1): \quad$ whose faces are congruent regular polygons $(2): \quad$ each of whose vertices is the common vertex of the same number of faces.

title: Definition:Regular Prime
snippet: A regular prime is a prime number $p$ that is not a divisor of the class number of the field obtained by adjoining to the rational numbers a primitive $p$th root of unity.

title: Definition:Regular Prime/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Regular Primes == The concept of a regular prime was conceived by in $1850$ in his work on Fermat's Last Theorem. He proved that Fermat's Last Theorem holds for all exponents $p$ such that $p$ is a regular prime.

title: Definition:Regular Prism
snippet: A regular prism is a right prism whose bases are regular polygons.

title: Definition:Regular Prism/Also defined as
snippet: == Regular Prism Also defined as == Some sources define a regular prism such that, in addition, each of the lateral faces are squares. refers to such a regular prism as a uniform prism. Please do not confuse with the concept of square prism, because that is a prism with a square base. Category:Definitions/Regular Prisms

title: Definition:Regular Prism/Also known as
snippet: == Regular Prism: Also known as == A regular prism is also known as a right-regular prism. There appears not to be a standard term for an oblique prism whose bases are regular polygons.

title: Definition:Regular Pyramid/Slant Height
snippet: The slant height of a regular pyramid $P$ is the height of one of the lateral faces of $P$.

title: Definition:Regular Representations
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a magma.

title: Definition:Regular Representations/Also defined as
snippet: Some treatments of abstract algebra and group theory define the regular representations for semigroups. Some define it only for groups. Category:Definitions/Regular Representations

title: Definition:Regular Representations/Left Regular Representation
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a magma. Let $a \in S$ be arbitrary. The mapping $\lambda_a: S \to S$ is defined as: $\forall x \in S: \map {\lambda_a} x = a \circ x$ This is known as the left regular representation of $\struct {S, \circ}$ with respect to $a$.

title: Definition:Regular Representations/Right Regular Representation
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a magma. Let $a \in S$ be arbitrary. The mapping $\rho_a: S \to S$ is defined as: $\forall x \in S: \map {\rho_a} x = x \circ a$ This is known as the right regular representation of $\struct {S, \circ}$ with respect to $a$.

title: Definition:Regular Space/Also known as
snippet: == Regular Space: Also known as == A regular space is also known as a regular Hausdorff space, for .

title: Definition:Regular Star Polygon
snippet: Let $n \in \N$ be a natural number such that $n \ge 3$. Let $m \in \N$ such that $m < n$ and such that $m$ and $n$ are coprime. Let $\CC$ be a circle whose circumference has been divided into $n$ equal arcs by $n$ points equally spaced. A regular star polygon is a plane figure formed by constructing a line segment joining every $m$th point of those $n$ equally spaced points. Such a regular star polygon can be denoted $\set {n / m}$.

title: Definition:Regular Star Polygon/Also known as
snippet: == Regular Star Polygon: Also known as == A regular star polygon is also known as just a star polygon.

title: Definition:Regular Surface
snippet: A subset $S \subseteq \R^3$ is a regular surface for each $p \in S$ there exist: a neighborhood $V \subseteq \R^3$ of $p$ an open set $U \subseteq \R^2$ a surjective mapping $\mathbf x : U \to V \cap S$, written as: $\map {\mathbf x} {u, v} := \struct {\map x {u, v}, \map y {u, v}, \map z {u, v} }$ such that: $(1): \quad \map x {u, v}, \map y {u, v}, \map z {u, v}$ are smooth $(2): \quad \mathbf x: U \to V \cap S$ is a homeomorphism $(3): \quad$ For each $q \in U$, the differential $\d_q \mathbf x: \R^2 \to \R^3$ of $\mathbf x$ at $q$ is one-to-one

title: Definition:Regular Surface/Also known as
snippet: == Regular Surface: Also known as == A regular surface is also known as a surface. It can also be referred to as a $2$-manifold.

title: Definition:Regular Tessellation
snippet: A regular tessellation is a tessellation such that: Its tiles consist of congruent regular polygons No vertex of one tile may lie against the side of another tile.

title: Definition:Regular Tetrahedron/Also known as
snippet: == Regular Tetrahedron: Also known as == It is commonplace for authors to refer to a regular tetrahedron as just a tetrahedron, glossing over the fact of its regularity.

title: Definition:Regular Tetrahedron/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on the Regular Tetrahedron == The concept of a regular tetrahedron is not mentioned explicitly by in . The first reference to it is in : According to the Pythagorean tradition, the regular tetrahedron was the symbol for the element fire.

title: Definition:Regular Value
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be smooth manifolds. Let $f: X \to Y$ be a smooth mapping. Then a point $y \in Y$ is called a regular value of $f$ the pushforward of $f$ at $x$: $f_* \vert_x: T_x X \to T_y Y$ is surjective for every $x \in \map {f^{-1} } y \subseteq X$.

title: Definition:Related Angles
snippet: Related angles are angles which have the same absolute values for their trigonometric functions.

title: Definition:Related Angles/Also known as
snippet: == Related Angles: Also known as == Related angles are also known as reference angles.

title: Definition:Relation
snippet: Let $S \times T$ be the cartesian product of two sets $S$ and $T$. A relation on $S \times T$ is an ordered triple: $\RR = \tuple {S, T, R}$ where $R \subseteq S \times T$ is a subset of the Cartesian product of $S$ and $T$. What this means is that a relation relates (certain) elements of one set or class $S$ with (certain) elements of another, $T$. Not all elements of $S$ need to be related to every (or even any) element of $T$ (but see Trivial Relation).

title: Definition:Relation/Abuse of Notation
snippet: == Abuse of Notation for Relation == By abuse of notation, the usual technique for denoting a relation $\RR$ on $S \times T$ is: $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ thereby endorsing the approach of defining a relation as a subset of a Cartesian product. Similarly, it is equally common to denote the expression $s \mathrel \RR t$ as: $\tuple {s, t} \in \RR$ While this approach conflates the relation with its truth set, it is sufficiently convenient and widespread as to be endorsed by .

title: Definition:Relation/Also known as
snippet: == Relation: Also known as == In this context, technically speaking, what has been defined as a relation can actually be referred to as a binary relation. In the field of predicate logic, a relation can be seen referred to as a relational property. Some sources use the term correspondence for what is defined here as relation, reserving the term relation for what on is defined as endorelation, that is, a relation on $S \times S$ for some set $S$.

title: Definition:Relation/Class Theory
snippet: Let $V$ be a basic universe. Let $A$ and $B$ be subclasses of $V$. A relation $\RR$ is a subclass of the Cartesian product $A \times B$. Note that in this context either or both of $A$ and $B$ can be $V$ itself.

title: Definition:Relation/General Definition
snippet: Let $\ds \Bbb S = \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n S_i = S_1 \times S_2 \times \ldots \times S_n$ be the cartesian product of $n$ sets $S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_n$. An $n$-ary relation on $\Bbb S$ is an ordered $n + 1$-tuple $\RR$ defined as: $\RR := \struct {S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_n, R}$ where $R$ is an arbitrary subset $R \subseteq \Bbb S$. To indicate that $\tuple {s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n} \in R$, we write: $\map \RR {s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n}$

title: Definition:Relation/Graph
snippet: Let $S \times T$ be the cartesian product of two sets $S$ and $T$. Let $\RR$ be a relation on $S \times T$. The graph of $\RR$ is the set of all ordered pairs $\tuple {s, t}$ of $S \times T$ such that $s \mathrel \RR t$: $\map \TT \RR = \set {\tuple {s, t}: s \mathrel \RR t}$

title: Definition:Relation/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Relation == That which is defined in the mathematical context as a relation is usually referred to in natural language, as a relationship. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Relation/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Relation == Let $\RR$ be a relation. If $\tuple {x, y}$ is an ordered pair such that $\tuple {x, y} \in \RR$, we use the notation: $s \mathrel \RR t$ or: $\map \RR {s, t}$ and can say: $s$ bears $\RR$ to $t$ $s$ stands in the relation $\RR$ to $t$ If $\tuple {s, t} \notin \RR$, we can write: $s \not \mathrel \RR t$, that is, by drawing a line through the relation symbol.

title: Definition:Relation/Relation as Mapping
snippet: It is possible to define a relation as a mapping from the cartesian product $S \times T$ to the Boolean domain $\set {\text {true}, \text {false} }$: $\RR: S \times T \to \set {\text {true}, \text {false} }: \forall \tuple {s, t} \in S \times T: \map \RR {s, t} = \begin{cases} \text {true} & : \tuple {s, t} \in \RR \\ \text {false} & : \tuple {s, t} \notin \RR \end{cases}$ This is called the characteristic function of the relation. However, care needs to be taken that a mapping then cannot be defined as a particular instance of a relation, as this would be circular.

title: Definition:Relation/Relation as Ordered Pair
snippet: Some sources define a relation between $S$ and $T$ as an ordered pair: $\struct {S \times T, \map P {s, t} }$ where: $S \times T$ is the Cartesian product of $S$ and $T$ $\map P {s, t}$ is a propositional function on ordered pairs $\tuple {s, t}$ of $S \times T$. Note that this approach leaves the domain and codomain inadequately defined. This situation arises in the case that $S$ or $T$ are empty, whence it follows that $S \times T$ is empty, but $T$ or $S$ are not themselves uniquely determined.

title: Definition:Relation/Relation as Subset of Cartesian Product
snippet: Most treatments of set theory and relation theory define a relation on $S \times T$ to refer to just the truth set itself: $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ where: $S \times T$ is the Cartesian product of $S$ and $T$. Thus under this treatment, $\RR$ is a set of ordered pairs, the first coordinate from $S$ and the second coordinate from $T$. This approach leaves the precise nature of $S$ and $T$ undefined.

title: Definition:Relation/Technical Note
snippet: The expression: $s \mathrel \RR t$ is produced by the following $\LaTeX$ code: s \mathrel \RR t Category:Technical Notes

title: Definition:Relation/Unary Relation
snippet: As a special case of an $n$-ary relation on $S$, note that when $n = 1$ we define a unary relation on $S$ as: $\RR \subseteq S$ That is, a unary relation is a subset of $S$.

title: Definition:Relation Compatible with Operation
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a closed algebraic structure. Let $\RR$ be a relation on $S$. Then $\RR$ is compatible with $\circ$ : $\forall x, y, z \in S: x \mathrel \RR y \implies \paren {x \circ z} \mathrel \RR \paren {y \circ z}$ $\forall x, y, z \in S: x \mathrel \RR y \implies \paren {z \circ x} \mathrel \RR \paren {z \circ y}$

title: Definition:Relation Conversely Compatible with Operation
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a closed algebraic structure. Let $\RR$ be a relation in $S$. Then $\RR$ is conversely compatible with $\circ$ : $\forall x, y, z \in S: \paren {x \circ z} \mathrel \RR \paren {y \circ z} \implies x \mathrel \RR y$ $\forall x, y, z \in S: \paren {z \circ x} \mathrel \RR \paren {z \circ y} \implies x \mathrel \RR y$

title: Definition:Relation Conversely Compatible with Operation/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Relation Conversely Compatible with Operation == Category:Definitions/Compatible Relations

title: Definition:Relation Isomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {S_1, \RR_1}$ and $\struct {S_2, \RR_2}$ be relational structures. Let there exist a bijection $\phi: S_1 \to S_2$ such that: $(1): \quad \forall \tuple {s_1, t_1} \in \RR_1: \tuple {\map \phi {s_1}, \map \phi {t_1} } \in \RR_2$ $(2): \quad \forall \tuple {s_2, t_2} \in \RR_2: \tuple {\map {\phi^{-1} } {s_2}, \map {\phi^{-1} } {t_2} } \in \RR_1$ Then $\struct {S_1, \RR_1}$ and $\struct {S_2, \RR_2}$ are isomorphic, and this is denoted $S_1 \cong S_2$.

title: Definition:Relation Segment
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\RR$ be a relation on $X$. Let $x \in X$. Then the $\RR$-segment of $x$, denoted by $x^\RR$, is defined by: $x^\RR := \set {y \in X: \tuple {y, x} \in \RR}$

title: Definition:Relation Strongly Compatible with Operation
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a closed algebraic structure. Let $\RR$ be a relation in $S$. Then $\RR$ is strongly compatible with $\circ$ : $\forall x, y, z \in S: x \mathrel \RR y \iff \paren {x \circ z} \mathrel \RR \paren {y \circ z}$ $\forall x, y, z \in S: x \mathrel \RR y \iff \paren {z \circ x} \mathrel \RR \paren {z \circ y}$. That is, $\RR$ is compatible with $\circ$ and conversely compatible with $\circ$.

title: Definition:Relation Strongly Compatible with Operation/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Relation Conversely Compatible with Operation == Category:Definitions/Compatible Relations

title: Definition:Relation Theory
snippet: Relation theory is the subfield of set theory concerned with the properties of relations and relational structures. As a relation has the same conceptual definition as a (graph-theoretical) graph, it follows that there is considerable overlap between the fields of relation theory and graph theory.

title: Definition:Relation as Mapping/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Relation as Mapping == The approach to defining a relation as a characteristic function from the cartesian product is taken in . This approach is rarely taken in more modern texts.

title: Definition:Relation of Group Presentation/Also known as
snippet: == Relation of Group Presentation: Also known as == A relation in a group presentation is also known as a defining relation. It is also known as a relator.

title: Definition:Relational Closure
snippet: Let $A$ be a class. Let $\RR \subseteq A \times A$ be a relation. Let $x$ be a small class that is a subset of $A$. The relational closure of $x$ is the smallest small class containing $x$ that is also $\RR$-transitive.

title: Definition:Relational Loop
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a relation on a set $S$. Let $a_1, a_2, \ldots a_n$ be elements of $S$. A relational loop on $S$ takes the form: $\tuple {a_1 \mathrel \RR a_2 \land a_2 \mathrel \RR a_3 \dots \land a_{n - 1} \mathrel \RR a_n \land a_n \mathrel \RR a_1}$ That is, it is a subset of $\RR$ of the form: $\set {\tuple {a_1, a_2}, \tuple {a_2, a_3}, \ldots, \tuple {a_{n - 1}, a_n}, \tuple {a_n, a_1} }$

title: Definition:Relational Structure
snippet: A relational structure is an ordered pair $\struct {S, \RR}$, where: $S$ is a set $\RR$ is an endorelation on $S$.

title: Definition:Relational Structure/Warning
snippet: == Warning concerning Relational Structures == In the context of class theory, it is common to abuse notation by writing $\struct {C, \RR}$ when $C$ is a class and $\RR$ is a relation on $C$, and to call this a relational structure. One must take care, as if $C$ is a proper class then it cannot be a member of any class. By the set-theoretic definitions for ordered pairs, if $\struct {C, \RR}$ is an ordered pair then $C$ is a member of some class, which is a contradiction.

title: Definition:Relational Structure with Topology
snippet: A triple $\left({S, \preceq, \tau}\right)$ is a relational structure with topology where $\preceq$ is a relation on $S$ and $\tau$ is a topology on $S$.

title: Definition:Relative
snippet: Relative is a word meaning: subject to some stated assumption or with respect to some chosen value.

title: Definition:Relative Acceleration
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be bodies in ordinary space. Let $\mathbf a_A$ and $\mathbf a_B$ be the accelerations of $A$ and $B$ in some frame of reference $\RR$. The acceleration $\mathbf a_{AB}$ of $A$ relative to $B$ is defined as: $\mathbf a_{AB} := \mathbf a_A - \mathbf a_B$

title: Definition:Relative Algebraic Closure
snippet: Let $L / K$ be a field extension. The relative algebraic closure of $K$ contained in $L$ is the set of all elements of $L$ that are algebraic over $K$.

title: Definition:Relative Complement
snippet: Let $S$ be a set, and let $T \subseteq S$, that is: let $T$ be a subset of $S$. Then the set difference $S \setminus T$ can be written $\relcomp S T$, and is called the relative complement of $T$ in $S$, or the complement of $T$ relative to $S$. Thus: $\relcomp S T = \set {x \in S : x \notin T}$

title: Definition:Relative Complement/Also known as
snippet: == Relative Complement: Also known as == Some authors refer to the relative complement as just the (set) complement, and use the term relative complement for the set difference $S \setminus T$ when the stipulation $T \subseteq S$ is not required. Others emphasize the connection with set difference by referring to the relative complement as a proper difference. Thus, in this view, the relative complement is a specific case of a set difference.

title: Definition:Relative Complement/Notation
snippet: == Relative Complement: Notation == Different notations for the relative complement $\relcomp S T$ mainly consist of variants of the $\complement$: $\map {\CC_S} T$ $\map {\mathbf C_S} T$ $\map {c_S} T$ $\map {C_S} T$ $\map {\mathrm C_S} T$ or sometimes: $\map {T^c} S$ $\map {T^\complement} S$ and sometimes the brackets are omitted: $C_S T$ If the superset $S$ is implicit, then it can be omitted: $\map \complement T$ etc. See the notation for set complement.

title: Definition:Relative Complement/Technical Note
snippet: == Technical Note on Relative Complement == {{LatexFor|for = \relcomp {S} {T} }} This is a custom construct which has been set up specifically for the convenience of the users of . Note that there are two arguments to this operator: the subscript, and the part between the brackets. If either part is a single symbol, then the braces can be omitted, for example: \relcomp S T Category:Technical Notes
