snippet: == Venn Diagram for Relative Complement == The relative complement $\relcomp S T$ of the set $T$ $S$ is illustrated in the following Venn diagram by the red area: 300px

title: Definition:Relative Density/Also known as
snippet: == Relative Density: Also known as == Relative density is also known as specific gravity.

title: Definition:Relative Density/Gas
snippet: Let $B$ be a body of gas. The relative density of $B$ is the ratio of the mass of $B$ to the mass of an equal volume of air at the same temperature and atmospheric pressure.

title: Definition:Relative Density/Solid or Liquid
snippet: Let $B$ be a body which is either solid or liquid. The relative density of $B$ is the ratio of the mass of $B$ to the mass of an equal volume of water at $4 \cels$.

title: Definition:Relative Density of Gas/Also defined as
snippet: == Relative Density of Gas: Also known as == The relative density of a gas can also be defined hydrogen, again at the same temperature and atmospheric pressure.

title: Definition:Relative Density of Solid or Liquid/Also defined as
snippet: == Relative Density of Solid or Liquid: Also known as == The relative density of a solid or liquid can also be defined water at a different temperature from $4 \cels$. Exactly what temperature needs to be established in such a case.

title: Definition:Relative Efficiency
snippet: Let $T_1$ and $T_2$ be estimators of a parameter $\theta$. Let $n_1$ and $n_2$ respectively be the sample sizes needed to give $T_1$ and $T_2$ the same variance. The relative efficiency of $T_1$ $T_2$ is defined as $\dfrac {n_2} {n_1}$.

title: Definition:Relative Efficiency of Unbiased Estimators
snippet: Let $\theta$ be a population parameter of some statistical model. Let $\delta_1$ and $\delta_2$ be unbiased estimators of $\theta$. The relative efficiency of $\delta_2$ $\delta_1$ is defined as the ratio: $\dfrac {\var {\delta_2} } {\var {\delta_1} }$ where $\var {\delta_1}$ denotes the variance of $\delta_1$.

title: Definition:Relative Error/Also defined as
snippet: Let $x_0$ be an approximation to a (true) value $x$. The relative error of $x_0$ in $x$ can also be defined as: $\delta x \approx \dfrac {\Delta x} {x_0}$ where: $\Delta x$ denotes the absolute error of $x_0$ $\approx$ indicates that the value is but approximate. This can be particularly useful when the true value $x$ can only be speculated.

title: Definition:Relative Frequency
snippet: Let $S$ be a sample or a finite population. Let $\omega$ be a qualitative variable, or a class interval of a quantitative variable. The relative frequency of $\omega$ is defined as: $\map {\operatorname {RF} } \omega := \dfrac {f_\omega} n$ where: $f_\omega$ is the (absolute) frequency of $\omega$ $n$ is the number of individuals in $S$.

title: Definition:Relative Frequency Model
snippet: The relative frequency model is a mathematical model that defines the probability of an event occurring as follows: $\map \Pr {\text {event occurring} } := \dfrac {\paren {\text {observed number of times event has occurred in the past} } } {\paren {\text {observed number of times event has occurred or not occurred} } }$ That is, the probability of an event happening is defined as the relative frequency of a finite number of events of a particular type in some finite reference class of events.

title: Definition:Relative Matrix
snippet: Linear Algebra: Relative Matrix of Linear Transformation

title: Definition:Relative Matrix of Bilinear Form
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $M$ be a free $R$-module of finite dimension $n>0$. Let $\BB = \sequence {b_m}$ be an ordered basis of $M$. Let $f : M \times M \to R$ be a bilinear form. The matrix of $f$ relative to $\BB$ is the $n \times n$ matrix $\mathbf M_{f, \BB}$ where: $\forall \tuple {i, j} \in \closedint 1 n \times \closedint 1 n: \sqbrk {\mathbf M_{f, \BB} }_{i j} = \map f {b_i, b_j}$

title: Definition:Relative Matrix of Linear Transformation
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring with unity. Let $G$ be a free $R$-module of finite dimension $n > 0$ Let $H$ be a free $R$-module of finite dimension $m > 0$ Let $\sequence {a_n}$ be an ordered basis of $G$. Let $\sequence {b_m}$ be an ordered basis of $H$. Let $u : G \to H$ be a linear transformation.

title: Definition:Relative Matrix of Linear Transformation/Warning
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring with unity. Let $G$ be a free $R$-module of finite dimension $n>0$ Let $H$ be a free $R$-module of finite dimension $m>0$ Let $\sequence {a_n}$ be an ordered basis of $G$. Let $\sequence {b_m}$ be an ordered basis of $H$. Let $u : G \to H$ be a linear transformation. Consider the matrix of $u$ relative to $\sequence {a_n}$ and $\sequence {b_m}$: $\sqbrk {u; \sequence {b_m}, \sequence {a_n} }$ Note the order in which the bases are presented in this expression $\sqbrk {u; \sequence {b_m}, \sequence {a_n} }$.

title: Definition:Relative Matrix of Quadratic Form
snippet: Let $K$ be a field of characteristic $\Char K \ne 2$. Let $V$ be a vector space over $K$ of finite dimension $n > 0$. Let $\BB$ be an ordered basis of $V$. Let $q$ be a quadratic form on $V$. Its matrix relative to $\BB$ is the matrix of its associated bilinear form relative to $\BB$, denoted $\mathbf M_{q, \BB}$.

title: Definition:Relative Pseudocomplement
snippet: Let $\struct {L, \wedge, \vee, \preceq}$ be a lattice. Let $x, y \in L$. Then the relative pseudocomplement of $x$ with respect to $y$ is the greatest element $z \in L$ such that $x \wedge z \preceq y$, if such an element exists. The relative pseudocomplement of $x$ with respect to $y$ is denoted $x \to y$.

title: Definition:Relative Risk
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be a events. Let the probability of $A$ occurring be $p_A$ and the probability of $B$ occurring be $p_B$. The relative risk of $A$ to $B$ is defined as $\dfrac {p_A} {p_B}$.

title: Definition:Relative Risk/Also defined as
snippet: == Relative Risk: Also defined as == Relative risk is also defined as being the same as the odds ratio $\theta = \dfrac {\theta_A} {\theta_B}$, where: $\theta_A$ is the odds on $A$: $\theta_A = \dfrac {p_A} {1 - p_A}$ $\theta_B$ is the odds on $B$: $\theta_B = \dfrac {p_B} {1 - p_B}$

title: Definition:Relative Scheme
snippet: Let $S$ be a scheme. A (relative) scheme over $S$ is a morphism of schemes $p : X \to S$ for some scheme $X$.

title: Definition:Relative Semantic Equivalence
snippet: Let $\FF$ be a theory in the language of predicate logic.

title: Definition:Relative Semantic Equivalence/Term
snippet: Let $\FF$ be a theory in the language of predicate logic. Let $\tau_1, \tau_2$ be terms. Then $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$ are semantically equivalent with respect to $\FF$ : $\map {\operatorname{val}_\AA} {\tau_1} \sqbrk \sigma = \map {\operatorname{val}_\AA} {\tau_2} \sqbrk \sigma$ for all models $\AA$ of $\FF$ and assignments $\sigma$ for $\tau_1,\tau_2$ in $\AA$. Here $\map {\operatorname{val}_\AA} {\tau_1} \sqbrk \sigma$ denotes the value of $\tau_1$ under $\sigma$.

title: Definition:Relative Semantic Equivalence/WFF
snippet: Let $\FF$ be a theory in the language of predicate logic. Let $\mathbf A, \mathbf B$ be WFFs. Let $\mathbf C$ be the universal closure of $\mathbf A \iff \mathbf B$. Then $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ are semantically equivalent with respect to $\FF$ : $\FF \models_{\mathrm{PL}} \mathbf C$ That is, $\mathbf C$ is a semantic consequence of $\FF$.

title: Definition:Relative Separable Closure
snippet: Let $E/F$ be a field extension. The (relative) separable closure of $F$ in $E$ is the intermediate field consisting of all separable elements of $E$ over $F$.

title: Definition:Relative Uncertainty
snippet: Relative uncertainty is a measure of the uncertainty of a measurement relative to the measured value itself. Relative uncertainty is typically expressed as a percentage of the measured value.

title: Definition:Relative Velocity
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be bodies in ordinary space.

title: Definition:Relative Velocity/Definition 1
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be bodies in ordinary space. Let the frame of reference $\RR$ be such that $B$ is stationary $\RR$. Let $\mathbf v_{AB}$ be the velocity of $A$ $\RR$. Then $\mathbf v_{AB}$ is the velocity of $A$ relative to $B$.

title: Definition:Relative Velocity/Definition 2
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be bodies in ordinary space. Let $\mathbf v_A$ and $\mathbf v_B$ be the velocities of $A$ and $B$ in some frame of reference $\RR$. The velocity $\mathbf v_{AB}$ of $A$ relative to $B$ is defined as: $\mathbf v_{AB} := \mathbf v_A - \mathbf v_B$

title: Definition:Relatively Closed Set
snippet: Let $T = \left({S, \tau}\right)$ be a topological space. Let $A \subseteq B \subseteq S$.

title: Definition:Relatively Closed Set/Definition 1
snippet: Let $T = \left({S, \tau}\right)$ be a topological space. Let $A \subseteq B \subseteq S$. $A$ is relatively closed in $B$ $A$ is closed in the relative topology of $B$.

title: Definition:Relatively Closed Set/Definition 2
snippet: Let $T = \left({S, \tau}\right)$ be a topological space. Let $A \subseteq B \subseteq S$. $A$ is relatively closed in $B$ there is a closed set $C \subseteq S$ with $C \cap B = A$.

title: Definition:Relatively Compact Subspace
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $T_H = \struct {H, \tau_H}$ be a subspace of $T$. Let $\map \cl H$ be the closure of $H$ in $T$. Then $T_H$ is relatively compact in $T$ $\map \cl H$ is compact.

title: Definition:Relatively Compact Subspace/Also known as
snippet: == Relatively Compact Subspace: Also known as == A relatively compact subspace may be referred to as a precompact subspace. This is not to be confused with a totally bounded metric space, which may also be called precompact.

title: Definition:Relatively Prime Integer Topology
snippet: Let $\Z_{>0}$ denote the set of (strictly) positive integers. Let $\BB$ be the set of sets $\set {\map {U_a} b: a, b \in \Z_{>0} }$ where: $\map {U_a} b = \set {b + n a \in \Z_{>0}: \gcd \set {a, b} = 1}$ where $\gcd \set {a, b}$ denotes the greatest common divisor of $a$ and $b$. Then $\BB$ is the basis for a topology $\tau$ on $\Z_{>0}$. $\tau$ is then referred to as the relatively prime integer topology. The topological space $T = \struct {\Z_{>0}, \tau}$ is referred to as the relatively prime integer space.

title: Definition:Relativisation
snippet: Let $p$ be a well-formed formula of the language of set theory. Let $A$ be a class. The relativisation of $p$ to $A$ shall be denoted $p^A$ and shall be defined recursively on the symbols in $p$: $x \in y ^A \iff x \in y$ $\left({\neg p}\right)^A \iff \neg p^A$ $\left({p \land q}\right)^A \iff \left({p^A \land q^A}\right)$ $\left({\forall x: P \left({x}\right)}\right)^A \iff \forall x: \left({ x \in A \implies P \left({x}\right)^A}\right)$ Thus, the relativisation of $p$ is simply the well-formed formula achieved when replacing all instances of $\forall x$ with $\forall x \in A$.

title: Definition:Relativistic Mass
snippet: Let $B$ be a body in motion in space. The relativistic mass of $B$ is its mass induced by the speed it is moving the speed of light $c$. For speeds which are small relative to $c$, the difference between the mass and the relativistic mass of $B$ is negligible.

title: Definition:Relativistic Mass/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Relativistic Mass == Not only has the concept of relativistic mass been predicted by the special theory of relativity, it has been verified experimentally.

title: Definition:Relativistic Mechanics
snippet: Relativistic mechanics is the study of the physical laws describing the motion of and forces on bodies whose velocities are approaching the speed of light.

title: Definition:Relativity Theory
snippet: Relativity theory is the branch of physics concerned with: the behaviour of matter travelling at speeds that are an appreciable fraction of the speed of light the structure of spacetime the theory of gravitation. The theory was developed in two stages:

title: Definition:Relativity Theory/Also known as
snippet: == Relativity Theory: Also known as == Relativity theory can also be referred to as the theory of relativity. Category:Definitions/Relativity Theory

title: Definition:Relativity Theory/General
snippet: The general theory of relativity extends the special theory of relativity by considering observers in non-inertial frames of reference.

title: Definition:Relativity Theory/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Relativity Theory == Relativity theory was conceived by in the early $20$th century. The two theories that it comprises led to a re-analysis of the concepts of space and time, and of the interrelationship between measurement and observer.

title: Definition:Relativity Theory/Special
snippet: The special theory of relativity is concerned with the phenomena of physics as experience by two observers moving relative to one another at constant velocity. Hence it is restricted to inertial frames of reference.

title: Definition:Reliability
snippet: The reliability of a device $D$ is the probability $\map {\mathrm R} t$ that $D$ will not fail in the time interval $\openint 0 t$.

title: Definition:Remainder
snippet: Let $a, b \in \Z$ be integers such that $b \ne 0$. From the Division Theorem, we have that: $\forall a, b \in \Z, b \ne 0: \exists_1 q, r \in \Z: a = q b + r, 0 \le r < \size b$ The value $r$ is defined as the remainder of $a$ on division by $b$, or the remainder of $\dfrac a b$.

title: Definition:Remainder/Also known as
snippet: == Remainder: Also known as == A remainder as defined here is also known as a principal remainder.

title: Definition:Remainder/Real
snippet: Let $x, y \in \R$ be real numbers such that $y \ne 0$. The remainder of $x$ on division by $y$ is defined as the value of $r$ in the expression: $\forall x, y \in \R, y \ne 0: \exists! q \in \Z, r \in \R: x = q y + r, 0 \le r < \size y$ From the definition of the Modulo Operation: $x \bmod y := x - y \floor {\dfrac x y}$ it can be seen that the remainder of $x$ on division by $y$ is defined as: $r = x \bmod y$

title: Definition:Removable Singularity/Complex Function
snippet: Let $U \subseteq \C$ be an open set. Let $f : U \to \C$ be a complex function. An isolated singularity of $f$ is a removable singularity $f$ can be extended to a holomorphic function $f: U \to \C$.

title: Definition:Renaming Mapping
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. The renaming mapping $r: S / \RR_f \to \Img f$ is defined as: $r: S / \RR_f \to \Img f: \map r {\eqclass x {\RR_f} } = \map f x$ where: $\RR_f$ is the equivalence induced by the mapping $f$ $S / \RR_f$ is the quotient set of $S$ determined by $\RR_f$ $\eqclass x {\RR_f}$ is the equivalence class of $x$ under $\RR_f$.

title: Definition:Reparametrization of Admissible Curve
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $\closedint a b, \closedint c d$ be closed real intervals. Let $\gamma : \closedint a b \to M$ be an admissible curve. Let $\phi : \closedint c d \to \closedint a b$ be a homeomorphism. Let $\tuple {c_0, \ldots, c_k}$ be a finite subdivision of $\closedint c d$. Suppose $\tuple {c_0, \ldots, c_k}$ is such that for all $i \in \N : 1 \le i \le k$ the restriction of $\phi$ to each subinterval $\closedint {c_{i - 1}} {c_i}$ is a diffeomorphism onto its image.

title: Definition:Reparametrization of Curve
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $I, I' \subseteq \R$ be real intervals. Let $\gamma : I \to M$ be a smooth curve. Let $\phi : I' \to I$ be a diffeomorphism. Let $\tilde \gamma$ be a curve defined by: $\tilde \gamma := \gamma \circ \phi : I' \to M$ where $\circ$ denotes the composition of mappings $\gamma$ and $\phi$. Then $\tilde \gamma$ is called the reparametrization of $\gamma$.

title: Definition:Repdigit/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Repdigit Number == The derivation of the term repdigit is clear: it comes from repeated digit. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Repdigit Number
snippet: Let $b \in \Z_{>1}$ be an integer greater than $1$. Let a (positive) integer $n$, greater than $b$, be expressed in base $b$. $n$ is a repdigit base $b$ all of the digits of $n$ are the same digit. For example: $55555$ or: $3333_4$ that second one being in base 4.

title: Definition:Repeated Integration Rule
snippet: A repeated integration rule is a technique whereby the interval of integration is first divided into a subdivisions, each of which then has a numerical integration rule applied.

title: Definition:Repellor
snippet: Let $S$ be a dynamical system in a space $X$. Let $T$ be an iterative mapping in $S$: $x_{n + 1} = \map T {x_n}$ A repellor is an invariant set $A$ in $X$ from which nearby points $x$ diverge.

title: Definition:Replacement Operation
snippet: The replacement operation on two variables $a$ and $b$ is denoted: $a \gets b$ and is interpreted as: the value of variable $a$ is to be replaced by the current value of variable $b$, while leaving the value of variable $b$ the same.

title: Definition:Replacement Operation/Examples
snippet: == Examples of use of Replacement Operation ==

title: Definition:Replication
snippet: In a designed experiment, the replication is the number of experimental units to which each treatment is applied. In many experimental designs, all treatments get equal replication.

title: Definition:Replicative Function
snippet: A replicative function is a real function $f$ such that: $\ds \forall n \in \Z_{\ge 0}: \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \map f {x + \frac k n} = \map f {n x}$ where $\sum$ denotes indexed summation.

title: Definition:Representable Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a locally small category. Let $\mathbf{Set}$ be the category of sets. Let $F: \mathbf C \to \mathbf{Set}$ be a covariant functor. Then $F$ is representable there exists an object $C \in \mathbf C$ such that $F$ is naturally isomorphic to the covariant hom functor $\map {\operatorname{Hom} } {C, \cdot}$. That is, $F$ is representable $F$ has a representation.

title: Definition:Representation
snippet: Definition:Group Representation Definition:Permutation Representation Definition:Matrix Representation Definition:Linear Representation Definition:Ring Representation Definition:Representation of Functor

title: Definition:Representation Theorem
snippet: A representation theorem is a theorem that states that every abstract structure with certain properties is isomorphic to another (abstract or concrete) structure.

title: Definition:Representation Theory
snippet: Representation theory is a branch of abstract algebra which studies algebraic structures (usually finite groups) by representing their elements as linear transformations of vector spaces.

title: Definition:Representation Theory/Also known as
snippet: == Representation Theory: Also known as == Representation theory is also known as character theory.

title: Definition:Representation of C*-Algebra
snippet: Let $\struct {A, \ast, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a $\text C^\ast$-algebra. Let $\struct {\HH, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be a Hilbert space over $\C$. Let $\map B \HH$ be the space of linear operators on $\HH$, considered as a $\text C^\ast$-algebra. Let $\pi : A \to \map B \HH$ be a $\ast$-algebra homomorphism. In the case of $A$ unital with identity element ${\mathbf 1}_A$, take $\map \pi { {\mathbf 1}_A} = I_{\map B \HH}$. We call $\tuple {\pi, \HH}$ a representation of $\struct {A, \ast, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$.

title: Definition:Representation of Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a locally small category. Let $\mathbf{Set}$ be the category of sets. Let $F : \mathbf C \to \mathbf{Set}$ be a covariant functor. A representation of $F$ is a pair $\tuple {C, \eta}$ where: $C$ is an object of $\mathbf C$; $\eta : \map {\operatorname {Hom} } {C, \cdot} \to F$ is a natural isomorphism with the covariant hom functor of $C$.

title: Definition:Representative Sample
snippet: A representative sample is a sample which in certain respects is typical of the population from which it is drawn.

title: Definition:Represented by Quadratic Form
snippet: Let $R$ be an integral domain. Let $M$ be an $R$-module. Let $q : M \to R$ be a quadratic form. Let $a\in R$. Then $q$ represents $a$ (over $R$) there exists $x \in M \setminus \set 0$ with $\map q x = a$.

title: Definition:Repunit
snippet: Let $b \in \Z_{>1}$ be an integer greater than $1$. Let a (positive) integer $n$, greater than $b$ be expressed in base $b$. $n$ is a repunit base $b$ $n$ is a repdigit number base $b$ whose digits are $1$. That is, $n$ is a repunit base $b$ all of the digits of $n$ are $1$. When $b$ is the usual base $10$, $n$ is merely referred to as a repunit.

title: Definition:Repunit/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Repunit == According to , in his of $1986$, the term repunit was coined by .

title: Definition:Repunit/Index
snippet: The index of a repunit is the number of digits it has. Thus a repunit with $n$ digits can be referred to as $R_n$.

title: Definition:Repunit/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Repunit == The derivation of the term repunit is clear: it comes from repeated unit. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Repunit Prime
snippet: Let $b \in \Z_{>1}$ be an integer greater than $1$. A repunit prime base $b$ is a repunit base $b$ which is prime. When $b$ is the usual base $10$, such a prime is merely referred to as a repunit prime.

title: Definition:Repunit Prime/Also known as
snippet: == Repunit Prime: Also known as == Some sources are inevitably going to refer to a repunit prime as a prime repunit. Some sources use the term isoprime.

title: Definition:Repunit Prime/Index
snippet: The index of a repunit prime is the number of digits it has. Thus $R_n$ denotes a repunit prime with $n$ digits.

title: Definition:Residual
snippet: Residuals are the differences $e_i$ between the observed values $y_i$ and values $\hat y_i$ predicted by a model: $e_i = y_i - \hat y_i$

title: Definition:Residual/Also known as
snippet: == Residual: Also known as == A residual is also known as an error.

title: Definition:Residual Spectrum of Densely-Defined Linear Operator
snippet: Let $\struct {\HH, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be a Hilbert space over $\C$. Let $\struct {\map D T, T}$ be a densely-defined linear operator. We define the residual spectrum $\map {\sigma_r} T$ as the set of $\lambda \in \C$ such that: $T - \lambda I$ is injective but $\map {\paren {T - \lambda I} } {\map D T}$ is not everywhere dense in $\HH$.

title: Definition:Residual Variation
snippet: The residual variation is the variation which is not accounted for by a model fitted to data and which is determined by the residuals.

title: Definition:Residue
snippet: Complex Analysis Residue: the coefficient of $\paren {z - z_0}^{-1}$ in the Laurent series of a complex function Number Theory Residue: an integer $a$ is a residue of $m$ of order $n$ $\exists x \in \Z: x^n \equiv a \pmod m$ for $m, n \in \N$ where $a \perp m$. Modulo Arithmetic Residue: an integer congruent to $a$ modulo $m$. Field Theory Residue Field the quotient ring $R / m$ of a commutative local ring $R$ by its maximal ideal $m$.

title: Definition:Residue (Complex Analysis)
snippet: Let $f: \C \to \C$ be a complex function. Let $z_0 \in U \subset \C$ such that $f$ is analytic in $U \setminus \set {z_0}$. Then by Existence of Laurent Series, there is a Laurent series: $\ds \sum_{j \mathop = -\infty}^\infty a_j \paren {z - z_0}^j$ such that the sum converges to $f$ in $U - \set {z_0}$. The residue at a point $z = z_0$ of $f$ is defined as $a_{-1}$ in that Laurent series. It is denoted $\Res f {z_0}$ or just $\map {\mathrm {Res} } {z_0}$ when $f$ is understood.

title: Definition:Residue (Modulo Arithmetic)/Also defined as
snippet: == Residue (Modulo Arithmetic): Also known as == Some sources define the residue to be the smallest (non-negative) integer congruent to $a$ modulo $z$, that is, what on is designated as the least positive residue. Category:Definitions/Residues (Modulo Arithmetic)

title: Definition:Residue (Number Theory)
snippet: Let $m, n \in \N$ be natural numbers. Let $a \in \Z$ be an integer such that $a$ is not divisible by $m$. Then $a$ is a residue of $m$ of order $n$ : $\exists x \in \Z: x^n \equiv a \pmod m$ where $\equiv$ denotes modulo congruence.

title: Definition:Residue (Number Theory)/Nonresidue
snippet: Let $m, n \in \N$ be natural numbers. Let $a \in \Z$ be an integer such that $a$ is not divisible by $m$. $a$ is a nonresidue of $m$ of order $n$ there does not exist $x \in \Z$ such that: $x^n \equiv a \pmod m$ where $\equiv$ denotes modulo congruence.

title: Definition:Residue Class
snippet: Let $m \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. Let $\RR_m$ be the congruence relation modulo $m$ on the set of all $a, b \in \Z$: $\RR_m = \set {\tuple {a, b} \in \Z \times \Z: \exists k \in \Z: a = b + k m}$ We have that congruence modulo $m$ is an equivalence relation. So for any $m \in \Z$, we denote the equivalence class of any $a \in \Z$ by $\eqclass a m$, such that: {{eqn | l = \eqclass a m | r = \set {x \in \Z: a \equiv x \pmod m} | c = }} {{eqn | r = \set {x \in \Z: \exists k \in \Z: x = a + k m} | c = }} {{eqn | r = \set {\ldots, a - 2 m, a - m, a, a + m, a + 2 m, \ldots} | c…

title: Definition:Residue Class/Also defined as
snippet: == Residue Class: Also defined as == In their definition of a residue class, some sources are lax at defining $m$ as a strictly positive integer, and the restriction becomes clear only during further development of the theory. Some sources with particular aims in mind are deliberately explicit about specifying that $m > 1$.

title: Definition:Residue Class/Also known as
snippet: == Residue Class: Also known as == Residue classes are sometimes known as congruence classes (modulo $m$).

title: Definition:Residue Division Ring Induced by Non-Archimedean Norm
snippet:
Let $\struct {R, 
orm {\,\cdot\,}}$ be a non-Archimedean normed division ring. Let $\OO$ be the valuation ring induced by the non-Archimedean norm $
orm {\,\cdot\,}$. Let $\PP$ be the valuation ideal induced by the non-Archimedean norm $
orm {\,\cdot\,}$. The residue division ring induced by the norm $
orm {\,\cdot\,}$ is the quotient ring $\OO / \PP$. If $R$ is a field then the quotient ring $\OO / \PP$ is called the residue field induced by the norm $
orm {\,\cdot\,}$.

title: Definition:Residue Field of Local Ring
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative local ring. Let $m$ be its maximal ideal. The residue field of $R$ is the quotient ring $R / m$.

title: Definition:Resistance
snippet: Resistance is a measure of how difficult it is to pass an electric current through a conductor. It is defined as the electromotive force needed to push a unit current through that conductor. It is conventionally denoted $R$.

title: Definition:Resistance/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Resistance: Conversion Factors == Some conversion factors between the various units of resistance are as follows: {{eqn | l = \text {corresponds to} | o = | r = 10^9 | c = abohm (or e.m.u. of resistance) }} {{eqn | l = \text {corresponds to (approximately)} | o = | r = \dfrac 1 9 \times 10^{-11} | c = statohm (or e.s.u. of resistance) }}

title: Definition:Resistance/Dimension
snippet: The dimension of measurement of resistance is: $\mathsf {M L^2 T^{−3} I^{−2} }$ This derives from its definition as: $R = \dfrac {\text {EMF} } {\text {current} }$

title: Definition:Resistance/Unit
snippet: The SI unit of resistance is the ohm $\Omega$: $1 \, \Omega = 1 \, \mathrm V \, \mathrm A^{-1}$ In the CGS unrationalised electromagnetic system, the base unit of resistance is the abohm $\mathrm {ab\Omega}$. In the CGS unrationalised electrostatic system, the base unit of resistance is the statohm $\mathrm {stat\Omega}$. Category:Definitions/Units of Measurement Category:Definitions/Resistance

title: Definition:Resistor
snippet: A resistor is an electrical component whose purpose is to introduce resistance into an electronic circuit.

title: Definition:Resolution of Vectors
snippet: Let $\mathbf v$ be a vector. The process of determining two or more vectors $\mathbf v_1, \mathbf v_2, \ldots, \mathbf v_n$ that, when added together, have an equivalent effect to $\mathbf v$, is called resolution. The vector $\mathbf v$ is said to be resolved into components $\mathbf v_1, \mathbf v_2, \ldots, \mathbf v_n$.

title: Definition:Resolution of the Identity
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space. Let $\map \BB X$ be the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $X$. Let $\struct {\HH, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be a Hilbert space over $\C$. Let $\map B {\HH}$ be the space of bounded linear transformations on $\HH$. Let $\EE : \map \BB X \to \map B {\HH}$ be a function. For each $x, y \in \HH$, define $\EE_{x, y} : \map \BB X \to \C$ by: $\map {\EE_{x, y} } A = \innerprod {\map \EE A x} y$ for each $A \in \map \BB X$.

title: Definition:Resolvent Set/Bounded Linear Operator
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \norm \cdot}$ be a Banach space over $\C$. Let $A : X \to X$ be a bounded linear operator. Let $I : X \to X$ be the identity mapping on $X$. Let $\map \rho A$ be the set of $\lambda \in \C$ such that $A - \lambda I$ is invertible as a bounded linear transformation We call $\map \rho A$ the resolvent set of $A$.

title: Definition:Resolvent Set/Densely-Defined Linear Operator
snippet: Let $\HH$ be a Hilbert space over $\C$. Let $\struct {\map D T, T}$ be a closed densely-defined linear operator. We define the resolvent set of $T$, $\map \rho T$, as the set of $\lambda \in \C$ for which: $T - \lambda I$ is injective, $\map {\paren {T - \lambda I} } {\map D T}$ is everywhere dense in $\HH$, and $\paren {T - \lambda I}^{-1}$ is bounded. Note that if $\map D T = \HH$ and $T$ is bounded, we realise we may have a conflict with the definition of its resolvent set as a bounded linear operator.

title: Definition:Resolvent Set/Unital Algebra
snippet: Let $A$ be a unital algebra over $\C$. Let $x \in A$. Let $\map G A$ be the group of units of $A$. Let: $\map {\rho_A} x = \set {\lambda \in \C : \lambda {\mathbf 1}_A - x \in \map G A}$ We call $\map {\rho_A} x$ the resolvent set of $x$ in $A$.

title: Definition:Resonance
snippet: Let $S$ be an oscillating system undergoing forced oscillation with frequency $\omega$. Let $\omega$ be such that $S$ responds with maximum amplitude. Then $S$ is said to be in resonance.

title: Definition:Resonance Frequency
snippet: Consider a second order ODE in the form: $\dfrac {\d^2 x} {\d t^2} + 2 b \dfrac {\d x} {\d t} + a^2 x = K \cos \omega x$ for $a, b \in \R_{>0}$. Let $b < a$, so as to make $S$ underdamped. Let the forcing frequency $\omega$ be such that $S$ is in resonance. Then $\omega$ is known as the resonance frequency.

title: Definition:Rest-Mass Energy
snippet: The rest-mass energy of a body is the amount of energy that would be released if the body is turned completely to energy.

title: Definition:Rest Mass
snippet: The rest mass of a body is its mass when it is at rest.

title: Definition:Rest Mass/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Rest Mass == Classical mechanics makes no distinction between the mass of a body and its rest mass. However, when the body moves, its effective mass increases. When the speed of the body becomes an appreciable fraction of the speed of light, this increase becomes significant. This mass caused by the body's motion then referred to as its relativistic mass. The famous Einstein's Mass-Energy Equation $E = m c^2$ connects the two concepts together.

title: Definition:Restitution
snippet: Restitution is the restoration to some original state of a body, in particular following an elastic deformation.

title: Definition:Restricted Dipper Operation
snippet: Let $m, n \in \N_{>0}$ be non-zero natural numbers. Let $\N_{< \paren {m \mathop + n} }$ denote the initial segment of the natural numbers: $\N_{< \paren {m \mathop + n} } := \set {0, 1, \ldots, m + n - 1}$ Let $\N^*_{< \paren {m \mathop + n} }$ denote the set defined as $\N_{< \paren {m \mathop + n} } \setminus \set 0$: $\N^*_{< \paren {m \mathop + n} } := \set {1, 2, \ldots, m + n - 1}$ The restricted dipper operation $+^*_{m, n}$ is the binary operation on $\N^*_{< \paren {m \mathop + n} }$ defined as: $\forall a, b \in \N^*_{< \paren {m \mathop + n} }: a +^*_{m, n} b = \begin{cases} a + b…

title: Definition:Restricted Dipper Operation/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Restricted Dipper Operation == The term dipper was coined by in the context of inductive semigroups. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Restricted Dipper Relation
snippet: Let $m, n \in \N_{>0}$ be non-zero natural numbers. The restricted dipper relation $\RR^*_{m, n}$ is the restriction of the dipper relation $\RR_{m, n}$ on $\N$: $\forall x, y \in \N_{>0}: x \mathrel {\RR^*_{m, n} } y \iff \begin {cases} x = y \\ m \le x < y \text { and } n \divides \paren {y - x} \\ m \le y < x \text { and } n \divides \paren {x - y} \end {cases}$

title: Definition:Restricted Dipper Relation/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Restricted Dipper Relation == The term dipper was coined by in the context of inductive semigroups. While takes pains to define this relation with his usual attention to detail, he does not actually assign it a name. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Restricted Dipper Semigroup
snippet: Let $m, n \in \N_{>0}$ be non-zero natural numbers. Let $\RR^*_{m, n}$ be the restricted dipper relation on $\N$: $\forall x, y \in \N_{>0}: x \mathrel {\RR^*_{m, n} } y \iff \begin {cases} x = y \\ m \le x 0} / \RR^*_{m, n}$ be the quotient set of $\N_{>0}$ induced by $\RR^*_{m, n}$. Let $\oplus^*_{m, n}$ be the operation induced on $\map {D^*} {m, n}$ by addition on $\N_{>0}$. A restricted dipper (semigroup) is a semigroup which is isomorphic to the algebraic structure $\struct {\map {D^*} {m, n}, \oplus^*_{m, n} }$.

title: Definition:Restricted Dipper Semigroup/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Restricted Dipper Relation == The term dipper was coined by in the context of inductive semigroups. 's approach is to bracket both the dipper semigroup and the restricted dipper semigroup into the same conceopt, referring to them both as dippers. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Restricted Existential Quantifier
snippet: Let $A$ be a class in ZF. The restricted existential quantifier is denoted $\exists x \in A$ and is defined as the following definitional abbreviation: $\exists x \in A: \map P x \quad \text{for} \quad \exists x: \paren {x \in A \land \map P x}$ where $\map P x$ is any well-formed formula of the language of set theory. Category:Definitions/Predicate Logic Category:Definitions/Zermelo-Fraenkel Class Theory

title: Definition:Restricted Exponential Map
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g, \nabla}$ be a Riemannian or pseudo-Riemannian manifold without boundary endowed with the Levi-Civita connection. Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space of $M$ at $p \in M$. Let $TM$ be the tangent bundle of $M$. Let $\EE \subseteq TM$ be the domain of the exponential map. Let $\EE_p = \EE \cap T_p M$. Then the restricted exponential map, denoted by $\exp_p$, is the mapping $\exp : \EE_p \to M$.

title: Definition:Restricted P-adic Metric/Definition 2
snippet: Let $p \in \N$ be a prime. Let $d: \Z^2 \to \R_{\ge 0}$ be the mapping defined as: $\forall x, y \in \Z: \map d {x, y} = \begin {cases} 0 & : x = y \\ \dfrac 1 r & : x - y = p^{r - 1} k: r, k \in \Z, p \nmid k \end {cases}$ Then $d$ is known as the restricted $p$-adic metric on $\Z$.

title: Definition:Restricted Universal Quantifier
snippet: Let $A$ be a class in ZF. The restricted universal quantifier is denoted $\forall x \in A$ and is defined as the following definitional abbreviation: $\forall x \in A: \map P x \quad \text{for} \quad \forall x: \paren {x \in A \implies \map P x}$ where $\map P x$ is any well-formed formula of the language of set theory. Category:Definitions/Predicate Logic Category:Definitions/Zermelo-Fraenkel Class Theory

title: Definition:Restriction/Mapping
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. Let $X \subseteq S$. Let $f \sqbrk X \subseteq Y \subseteq T$. The restriction of $f$ to $X \times Y$ is the mapping $f {\restriction_{X \times Y} }: X \to Y$ defined as: $f {\restriction_{X \times Y} } = f \cap \paren {X \times Y}$ If $Y = T$, then we simply call this the restriction of $f$ to $X$, and denote it as $f {\restriction_X}$.

title: Definition:Restriction/Notation
snippet: == Notation == The use of the symbol $\restriction$ is a recent innovation over the more commonly-encountered $\vert$. Thus the notation $\RR \vert_{X \times Y}$ and $\struct {T, \circ \vert_T}$, etc. are currently more likely to be seen than $\RR {\restriction_{X \times Y} }$ and $\struct {T, \circ {\restriction_T} }$. No doubt as the convention becomes more established, $\restriction$ will develop. It is strongly arguable that $\restriction$, affectionately known as the harpoon, is preferable to $\vert$ as the latter is suffering from the potential ambiguity of overuse.

title: Definition:Restriction/Operation
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. Let $A, B \subseteq S$. The restriction of $\circ$ to $A \times B$ is denoted $\circ {\restriction_{A \times B} }$, and is defined as: $\forall a \in A, b \in B: a \mathbin {\circ {\restriction_{A \times B} } } b = a \circ b$ The notation $\circ {\restriction_{A \times B} }$ is generally used only if it is necessary to emphasise that $\circ {\restriction_{A \times B} }$ is strictly different from $\circ$ (through having a different domain). When no confusion is likely to result, $\circ$ is generally used for both.

title: Definition:Restriction/Relation
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a relation on $S \times T$. Let $X \subseteq S$, $Y \subseteq T$. The restriction of $\RR$ to $X \times Y$ is the relation on $X \times Y$ defined as: $\RR {\restriction_{X \times Y} }: = R \cap \paren {X \times Y}$ where $R \subseteq S \times T$ is the subset of the Cartesian product of $S$ and $T$ which defines the relation $\RR$. If $Y = T$, then we simply call this the restriction of $\RR$ to $X$, and denote it as $\RR {\restriction_X}$.

title: Definition:Restriction/Relation/Also known as
snippet: == Restriction of Relation: Also known as == Some sources refer to $\RR {\restriction_X}$ as the relation induced on $X$ by $\RR$. Category:Definitions/Restrictions

title: Definition:Restriction/Relation/Class Theory
snippet: Let $V$ be a basic universe. Let $\RR \subseteq V \times V$ be a relation in $V$. Let $A \subseteq V$ be a class. The restriction of $\RR$ to $A$ is the relation on $A \times A$ defined as: $\RR {\restriction_A}: = \RR \cap \paren {A \times A}$ Note that the parenthesis is not necessary in the above, but it does make the meaning clearer.

title: Definition:Restriction of Measure to Trace Sigma-Algebra of Measurable Set
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. Let $A \in \Sigma$. Let $\Sigma_A$ be the trace $\sigma$-algebra of $A$ in $\Sigma$. We define the restriction of $\mu$ to $\Sigma_A$, written $\mu \restriction_{\Sigma_A}$, as the restriction of $\mu$ to $\Sigma_A$ as a mapping.

title: Definition:Restriction of Ordering
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $T \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. Then the restriction of $\preceq$ to $T$, denoted $\preceq \restriction_T$, is defined as: ${\preceq \restriction_T} := {\preceq} \cap \paren {T \times T}$ viewing ${\preceq} \subseteq S \times S$ as a relation on $S$. Here, $\times$ denotes Cartesian product. Thence the restriction of $\preceq$ to $T$ is an instance of a restriction of a relation.

title: Definition:Restriction of Presheaf to Open Set
snippet: Let $C$ be a category. Let $X$ be a topological space. Let $\FF$ be a $C$-valued presheaf on $X$. Let $U \subset X$ be open. The restriction of $\FF$ to $U$ is the restriction of the contravariant functor $\FF$ to the subcategory $U$.

title: Definition:Restriction of Ringed Space to Open Set
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ be a ringed space. Let $U \subset X$ be an open subset. Let $\OO_X {\restriction_U}$ denote the restriction of $\OO_X$ to $U$. The restriction of $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ to $U$ is the pair $\struct {U, \OO_X {\restriction_U} }$.

title: Definition:Restriction of Scalars of Module
snippet: Let $R$ and $S$ be commutative rings with unity. Let $f : R \to S$ be a ring homomorphism. Let $M$ be an $S$-module with ring representation $\rho$. The restriction of scalars of $M$ to $R$ via $f$ is the $R$-module with ring representation $\rho \circ f$.

title: Definition:Resultant
snippet: Vector Algebra: Resultant: Another name for vector sum. Simultaneous Equations: Resultant: Another name for eliminant. Category:Definitions/Linear Algebra

title: Definition:Retract (Topology)
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ be a topological space. Let $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be a topological subspace of $T_1$. Then $T_2$ is a retract of $T_1$ there exists a continuous retraction $f: S_1 \to S_2$ of $T_1$.

title: Definition:Retract (Topology)/Absolute
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ be a topological space. Let $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be a topological subspace of $T_1$. Let $T_2$ be a retract of $T_1$. $T_2$ is an absolute retract of $T_1$ : for every closed subspace $B$ of a $T_4$ space $T$ such that $B$ is homeomorphic to $A$, then $B$ is a retract of $T$.

title: Definition:Retraction (Category Theory)
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $f: C \to D$ be a morphism of $\mathbf C$. A retraction of $f$ is a morphism $g: D \to C$ such that: $g \circ f = \operatorname{id}_C$ where $\operatorname{id}_C$ denotes the identity morphism on $C$.

title: Definition:Retraction (Category Theory)/Also known as
snippet: == Retraction: Also known as == A retraction is also known as a left inverse.

title: Definition:Retraction (Category Theory)/Retract
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $f: C \to D$ be a morphism. Let $g: D \to C$ be a retraction of $f$. Then $D$ is said to be a retract of $C$.

title: Definition:Retraction (Topology)
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ be a topological space. Let $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be a topological subspace of $T_1$. That is: $S_2 \subseteq S_1$ Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping. Then $f$ is a retraction of $T_1$ : $\forall s \in S_2: \map f s = s$

title: Definition:Retrograde Analysis
snippet: Retrograde analysis is a technique used to determine the sequence of chess moves which were played that led to a given position.

title: Definition:Reversal
snippet: Let $m = \sqbrk {a_n a_{n - 1} a_{n - 2} \ldots a_2 a_1 a_0}$ be an integer expressed in base $10$. That is: $m = \ds \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^n a_k 10^k$ Its reversal $m'$ is the integer created by writing the digits of $m$ in the opposite order: $m' = \sqbrk {a_0 a_1 a_2 \ldots a_{n - 2} a_{n - 1} a_n}$ That is: $m' = \ds \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^n a_{n - k} 10^k$

title: Definition:Reverse-and-Add
snippet: Let $m \in \Z_{>0}$ be a positive integer expressed in decimal notation. Let $r: \Z_{>0} \to \Z_{>0}$ be the mapping defined as: For all $n \in \Z_{>0}$: reverse the digits of $m$ and add the result to $m$. The mapping $r$ is the reverse-and-add operation.

title: Definition:Reverse-and-Add/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Reverse-and-Add == There has been a lot of work in recent years on the results of iterating the reverse-and-add process, in several number bases. The usual aim of the exercise is to determine how long it takes until a palindromic number appears. Most of the research has, as can be expected, been done on numbers expressed in base $10$ notation. Of the $900$ numbers with $3$ digits, $90$ are already palindromic and $735$ require between $1$ and $5$ iterations. The first $10 \, 000$ numbers contain $5996$ which have not yielded a palindrome.

title: Definition:Reversed Contour
snippet: Let $\R^n$ be a real cartesian space of $n$ dimensions. Let $C$ be a contour in $\R^n$. Then $C$ is defined as a concatenation of a finite sequence $C_1, \ldots, C_n$ of directed smooth curves in $\R^n$. The reversed contour of $C$ is denoted $-C$ and is defined as the concatenation of the finite sequence: $-C_n, -C_{n - 1}, \ldots, -C_1$ where $-C_i$ is the reversed directed smooth curve of $C_i$ for all $i \in \set {1, \ldots, n}$.

title: Definition:Reversed Contour/Complex Plane
snippet: Let $C$ be a contour in the complex plane $\C$. Then $C$ is defined as a concatenation of a finite sequence $\sequence {C_1, \ldots, C_n}$ of directed smooth curves in $\C$. The reversed contour of $C$ is denoted $-C$ and is defined as the concatenation of the finite sequence: $-C_n, -C_{n-1}, \ldots, -C_1$ where $-C_k$ is the reversed directed smooth curve of $C_k$ for all $i \in \set {1, \ldots, n}$.

title: Definition:Reversed Directed Smooth Curve
snippet: Let $\R^n$ be a real cartesian space of $n$ dimensions. Let $C$ be a directed smooth curves in $\R^n$. Let $C$ be parameterized by the smooth path $\gamma: \closedint a b \to \R^n$. The reversed directed smooth curve of $C$ is denoted $-C$ and is defined as the directed smooth curve that is parameterized by: $\rho: \closedint a b \to \R^n: \map \rho t = \map \gamma {a + b - t}$

title: Definition:Reversed Directed Smooth Curve/Complex Plane
snippet: Let $C$ be a directed smooth curve in the complex plane $\C$. Let $C$ be parameterized by the smooth path $\gamma: \closedint a b \to \C$. The reversed directed smooth curve of $C$ is denoted $-C$ and is defined as the directed smooth curve that is parameterized by: $\rho: \closedint a b \to \C: \map \rho t = \map \gamma {a + b - t}$ From Reversed Directed Smooth Curve is Directed Smooth Curve, it follows that $-C$ is a directed smooth curve.

title: Definition:Reynolds Number
snippet: Definition Let $B$ be a body $B$ passing through a fluid $F$. The Reynolds number $\mathrm {Re}$ for $B$ is defined as: $\mathrm {Re} = \dfrac {v l} \nu$ where: $v$ is the speed of $B$ through $F$ $l$ is a representative length of $B$ $\nu$ is the kinematic viscosity of $F$.

title: Definition:Rhombohedron
snippet: A rhombohedron is a parallelepiped each of whose faces is a rhombus: 300px Hence it is a parallelepiped whose edges are all the same length.

Thus the criterion for all the edges to be the same length is not required to hold. defines a rhombohedron to be a hexagonal prism, but this is surely a mistake.

title: Definition:Riccati Equation
snippet: The Riccati equation is the first order ordinary differential equation: $y' = p \left({x}\right) + q \left({x}\right) y + r \left({x}\right) y^2$

title: Definition:Ricci Flow
snippet: Ricci flow is a technique that uses properties of solutions to certain partial differential equations.

title: Definition:Richardson Extrapolation
snippet: Let $\map f h$ be an approximation to an unknown quantity $a$ of the form: $\map f h = a + c_1 h^2 + c_2 h^4 + \cdots$ where $h$ is small and $c_1$, $c_2$ and so on are unknown constants. Richardson extrapolation forms the new approximation to $a$: $\hat f = \dfrac 1 3 \paren {\map f h - 4 \map f {\dfrac h 2} }^4$ Hence from: {{eqn | n = 2 | l = \map f {\dfrac h 2} | r = a + c_1 \dfrac {h^2} 4 + c_2 \paren {\dfrac h 2}^4 + \cdots }} it can be seen that the new approximation is obtained by subtracting $4$ times equation $(2)$ from equation $(1)$ to eliminate the $h^2$ terms.

title: Definition:Richardson Extrapolation/Also known as
snippet: == Richardson Extrapolation: Also known as == Richardson extrapolation is also known as deferred correction.

title: Definition:Riemann-Christoffel Tensor
snippet:
A Riemann-Christoffel tensor is a tensor field which expresses the curvature of a Riemannian manifold. The Riemann-Christoffel tensor is given in terms of the Levi-Civita connection $
abla$ by: $\map R {u, v} w = 
abla_u 
abla_v w - 
abla_v 
abla_u w - 
abla_{\sqbrk {u, v} } w$ where $\sqbrk {u, v}$ is the Lie bracket of vector fields. It measures the extent to which the metric tensor is not locally isometric to that of Euclidean space.

title: Definition:Riemann-Christoffel Tensor/Also known as
snippet: == Riemann-Christoffel Tensor: Also known as == The Riemann-Christoffel tensor is also known as the Riemann curvature tensor or the Riemann-Christoffel curvature tensor.

title: Definition:Riemann-Christoffel Tensor/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Riemann-Christoffel Tensor == The concept of a Riemann-Christoffel tensor was originated by in his application of a Riemannian manifold to the question of heat conduction.

title: Definition:Riemann-Stieltjes Integral
snippet: Let $\Bbb I = \closedint a b$ be a closed real interval. Let $f, \alpha : \Bbb I \to \R$ be real functions that are bounded on $\Bbb I$. Then, $f$ is Riemann-Stieltjes integrable with respect to $\alpha$ on $\closedint a b$ : there exists some $A \in \R$ such that, for every $\epsilon > 0$, there is a finite subdivision $P_\epsilon$ of $\Bbb I$ such that: for every Riemann-Stieltjes sum $\map S {P, f, \alpha}$ of $f$ with respect to $\alpha$ for a subdivision $P$, where $P$ is finer than $P_\epsilon$: $\size {\map S {P, f, \alpha} - A} < \epsilon$ The real number $A$ is called the…

title: Definition:Riemann-Stieltjes Integral/General Limits of Integration
snippet: The notation for the Riemann-Stieltjes integral: $\ds A = \int_a^b f \rd \alpha = \int_a^b \map f x \rd \map \alpha x$ is defined for $a b$, then: $\ds \int_a^b f \rd \alpha = \int_a^b \map f x \rd \map \alpha x := - \int_b^a f \rd \alpha$ whenever $f$ is Riemann-Stieltjes integrable with respect to $\alpha$ on $\closedint b a$.

title: Definition:Riemann-Stieltjes Sum
snippet: Let $\Bbb I = \closedint a b$ be a closed real interval. Let $f, \alpha : \Bbb I \to \R$ be a real functions that are bounded on $\Bbb I$. Let $P = \set {x_0, x_1, \dotsc, x_n}$ be a finite subdivision of $\closedint a b$. For each $k \in \set {1, \dotsc, n}$, let $t_k \in \closedint {x_{k - 1} } {x_k}$. Then, the summation: $\ds \map S {P, f, \alpha} = \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n \map f {t_k} \paren {\map \alpha {x_k} - \map \alpha {x_{k - 1} } }$ is a Riemann-Stieltjes sum of $f$ with respect to $\alpha$ for the subdivision $P$.

title: Definition:Riemann Integral/Also denoted as
snippet: == Riemann Integral: Also denoted as == The notation: $\ds \int_a^b f$ can occasionally be seen to denote a Riemann integral, but this is not endorsed by . Category:Definitions/Riemann Integrals

title: Definition:Riemann Integral/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Riemann Integral == Consider the Riemann sum: $\ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \map f {c_i} \Delta x_i$ Historically, the definite integral was an extension of this type of summation such that: The finite difference $\Delta x$ is instead the infinitely small difference $\rd x$ The finite sum $\ds \Sigma$ is instead of the sum of an infinite number of infinitely small quantities: $\ds \int$ Hence the similarity in notation: The notion of "infinitely small" does not exist in the modern formulation of real numbers.

title: Definition:Riemann P-symbol/Also known as
snippet: == Riemann P-symbol: Also known as == The Riemann P-symbol is also known as the Papperitz symbol, for . Category:Definitions/Riemann P-symbol

title: Definition:Riemann Sphere
snippet: Let $f_1: \C \to \R^2$ be defined as: $\forall z \in \C: \map {f_1} z = \tuple {\map \Re z, \map \Im z}$ Let $f_2: \R^2 \to \R^3$ be the inclusion map: $\forall \tuple {a, b} \in \C^2: \map {f_2} {a, b} = \tuple {a, b, 0}$ Let $f = f_2 \circ f_1$. Let $F: \C \to \map \PP {\R^3}$ be defined as the mapping which takes $z$ to the closed line interval from $\tuple {0, 0, 1}$ to $\map f z$ for all $z \in \C$. Let $G = \set {x, y, z: x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1}$.

title: Definition:Riemann Sum
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function defined on the closed interval $\mathbb I = \closedint a b$. Let $\Delta$ be a subdivision of $\mathbb I$. For $1 \le i \le n$: let $\Delta x_i = x_i - x_{i - 1}$ let $c_i \in \closedint {x_{i - 1} } {x_i}$. The summation: $\ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \map f {c_i} \Delta x_i$ is called a Riemann sum of $f$ for the subdivision $\Delta$.

title: Definition:Riemann Surface
snippet: A Riemann surface is a connected complex manifold of dimension $1$.

title: Definition:Riemann Surface/Also defined as
snippet: == Riemann Surface: Also defined as == Some authors do not require a Riemann surface to be connected or second-countable. Note that by Radó's Theorem, a connected Riemann surface is automatically second-countable. Category:Definitions/Riemann Surfaces

title: Definition:Riemann Surface/Elliptic/Definition 1
snippet: A Riemann surface is elliptic its universal cover is the Riemann sphere.

title: Definition:Riemann Surface/Elliptic/Definition 2
snippet: A Riemann surface is elliptic it admits a metric of constant positive curvature.

title: Definition:Riemann Surface/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Riemann Surface == The Riemann surface was invented by as a device for clarifying the nature of multiple-valued functions in the complex plane. This invention led directly to the Riemann Mapping Theorem.

title: Definition:Riemann Surface/Hyperbolic/Definition 1
snippet: A Riemann surface is hyperbolic its universal cover is the unit disk.

title: Definition:Riemann Surface/Hyperbolic/Definition 2
snippet: A Riemann surface is hyperbolic it admits a metric of constant negative curvature.

title: Definition:Riemann Surface/Motivation
snippet: == Riemann Surface: Motivation == A Riemann surface allows a holomorphic function to be defined as a single-valued function without branches.

title: Definition:Riemann Surface/Parabolic/Definition 1
snippet: A Riemann surface is parabolic its universal cover is the complex plane.

title: Definition:Riemann Surface/Parabolic/Definition 2
snippet: A Riemann surface is parabolic it admits a metric of zero curvature.

title: Definition:Riemann Zeta Function
snippet: The Riemann $\zeta$ (zeta) function is the complex function defined on the half-plane $\map \Re s > 1$ as the series: $\ds \map \zeta s = \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \frac 1 {n^s}$

title: Definition:Riemann Zeta Function/Also known as
snippet: == Riemann Zeta Function: Also known as == The Riemann zeta function is also often known as just the zeta function. Some sources use hyphens: Riemann zeta-function or zeta-function Some sources style it as Riemann's zeta function.

title: Definition:Riemann Zeta Function/Critical Line
snippet: Consider the Riemann zeta function $\map \zeta s$. Let $s = \sigma + i t$. The line defined by the equation $\sigma = \dfrac 1 2$ is known as the critical line. Hence the popular form of the statement of the Riemann Hypothesis: All the nontrivial zeroes of the Riemann zeta function lie on the critical line. 520px

title: Definition:Riemann Zeta Function/Critical Strip
snippet: == Riemann Hypothesis == Consider the Riemann zeta function $\map \zeta s$. Let $s = \sigma + i t$. The region defined by the equation $0 < \sigma < 1$ is known as the critical strip. 520px

title: Definition:Riemann Zeta Function/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Riemann Zeta Function == Investigation of what is now known as the Riemann zeta function goes back as far as , who showed in $1744$ that $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \frac 1 {n^s} = \prod_{\text {$p$ prime} } \frac 1 {1 - p^{-s} }$. The Riemann zeta function was discussed by in his $1859$ article . In that paper he made several statements about that function. Studying it led to his proof of the Prime Number Theorem. All of the statements made in that paper have now been proved except for one.

title: Definition:Riemann Zeta Function/Zero
snippet: The zeroes of the Riemann $\zeta$ function are, according to the conventional definition of the zero of a (complex) function, the points $s \in \C$ such that: $\map \zeta s = 0$

title: Definition:Riemann Zeta Function/Zero/Nontrivial
snippet: The nontrivial zeroes of the Riemann $\zeta$ function are the zeroes of $\zeta$ that are not trivial.

title: Definition:Riemann Zeta Function/Zero/Trivial
snippet: The trivial zeroes of the Riemann $\zeta$ function are the strictly negative even integers : $\set {n \in \Z: n = -2 \times k: k \in \N_{\ne 0} } = \set {-2, -4, -6, \ldots}$

title: Definition:Riemannian Arc Length Function of Admissible Curve
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $\closedint a b \subseteq \R$ be a closed real interval. Let $\gamma : \closedint a b \to M$ be an admissible curve. The (Riemannian) arc length function of $\gamma$ is the real function $s : \closedint a b \to \R$ defined by: $\ds \map s t := \map {L_g} {\valueat \gamma {\closedint a t} } = \int_a^t \size {\gamma}_g \rd t$ where $L_g$ is the Riemannian length of $\gamma$, and $\size {\, \cdot \,}_g$ is the Riemannian inner product norm.

title: Definition:Riemannian Covering
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ and $\struct {\tilde M, \tilde g}$ be Riemannian manifolds. Let $\pi : \tilde M \to M$ be a smooth covering map. Suppose $\pi$ is a local isometry. Then $\pi$ is called a Riemannian covering.

title: Definition:Riemannian Curvature
snippet: Let $\MM$ be a smooth manifold on the real space $\R^n$. Let $\d s$ be a Riemannian metric applied to $\MM$. The Riemannian curvature of $\MM$ is defined by an expression using the metric tensor of $\MM$ and the Riemann-Christoffel tensor.

title: Definition:Riemannian Density
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be an $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold. Let $\tuple {E_i}$ be an local orthonormal frame. Let $\mu$ be a positive smooth density such that: $\forall \tuple {E_i} : \map \mu {E_1, \ldots, E_n} = 1$ Then $\mu$ is known as the Riemannian density.

title: Definition:Riemannian Distance
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a connected Riemannian manifold. Let $p,q \in M$ be points. Let $\gamma_{pq} : \closedint 0 1 \to M$ be an admissible curve such that $\map \gamma 0 = p$ and $\map \gamma 1 = q$. Let $\map {L_g} {\gamma_{pq}}$ be the Riemannian length of $\gamma_{pq}$. Then the Riemannian distance between $p$ and $q$, denoted by $\map {d_g} {p, q}$, is the infimum of all such curves $\gamma_{pq}$: $\ds \map {d_g} {p, q} := \inf_{\gamma_{pq} \mathop \in M} \map {L_g} {\gamma_{pq}}$

title: Definition:Riemannian Geometry
snippet: Riemannian geometry is the branch of differential geometry that studies Riemannian manifolds.

title: Definition:Riemannian Geometry/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Riemannian Geometry == The concept of Riemannian geometry originated from in $1854$, in his trial lecture (published as ) to apply for position of Privatdozent (unpaid lecturer) at Göttingen. The contents of this lecture proved to be exactly the correct model for 's General Theory of Relativity: Riemann's geometry of an $n$-dimensional space bears the same relation to Euclidean geometry of an $n$-dimensional space as the general geometry of curved surfaces bears to the geometry of the plane.

title: Definition:Riemannian Inner Product Norm
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $p \in M$ be a point. Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space of $M$ at $p$. Let $v \in T_p M$ be a vector. Then the Riemannian inner product norm of $v$ is: $\ds \size {v}_g := \sqrt {g_p \innerprod v v}$ where $g_p$ is the Riemannian metric at $p$.

title: Definition:Riemannian Length of Admissible Curve
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $\closedint a b$ be a closed real interval. Let $\gamma : \closedint a b \to M$ be an admissible curve. Then the (Riemannian) length of $\gamma$, denoted by $\map {L_g} \gamma$, is defined by: $\ds \map {L_g} \gamma := \int_a^b \size {\map \gamma t}_g \rd t$ where $\size {\map \gamma t}_g$ is the Riemannian inner product norm.

title: Definition:Riemannian Manifold
snippet: A $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold is a pair $\struct {M, g}$ where $M$ is a $n$-dimensional smooth manifold and $g$ is a Riemannian metric on $M$.

title: Definition:Riemannian Manifold/Also known as
snippet: == Riemannian Manifold: Also known as == A Riemannian manifold is also known as a Riemannian space, or Riemann space. Some sources use the term Riemannian geometry, although on the term is used to refer to the mathematical branch that studies Riemannian manifolds.

title: Definition:Riemannian Manifold/Dimension
snippet: Let $M$ be a $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold. The dimension of $M$ is $n$.

title: Definition:Riemannian Manifold/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Riemannian Manifold == The concept of a Riemannian manifold was originated by in his trial lecture (published as Ueber die Hypothesen, welche der Geometrie zu Grande liegen) to apply for position of Privatdozent (unpaid lecturer) at Göttingen.

title: Definition:Riemannian Manifold Isotropic at Point
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $I_p$ be the isotropy representation at $p \in M$. Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space of $M$ at $p \in M$. Let $S_p \subseteq T_p M$ be the set of unit vectors in $T_p M$. Suppose $I_p$ acts transitively on $S_p$. Then $M$ is said to be isotropic at $p$.

title: Definition:Riemannian Manifold with Boundary
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold with a boundary. Let $g$ be a Riemannian metric. Then the pair $\tuple {M, g}$ is called the Riemannian manifold with a boundary.

title: Definition:Riemannian Metric
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $p \in M$ be a point in $M$. Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space of $M$ at $p$ with the inner product $\innerprod \cdot \cdot_p$. Let $g \in \map {\TT^2} M$ be a smooth covariant 2-tensor field such that for all $p$ its value at $p$ is equal to $\innerprod \cdot \cdot_p$: $\forall p \in M : g_p = \innerprod \cdot \cdot_p$ Then $g$ is known as a Riemannian metric on $M$.

title: Definition:Riemannian Metric/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Riemannian Metric == The concept of a Riemannian metric was originated by in his trial lecture (published in $1854$ as ) to apply for position of Privatdozent (unpaid lecturer) at Göttingen.

title: Definition:Riemannian Metric/Interpretation
snippet: == Riemannian Metric: Interpretation == Consider a smooth manifold $\MM$ on the real space $\R^n$. A Riemannian metric on $\MM$ is a metric $\d s$ between nearby points $\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ and $\tuple {x_1 + \d x_1, x_2 + \d x_2, \ldots, x_n + \d x_n}$ by means of the quadratic differential form: $\ds \d s^2 = \sum_{i, j \mathop = 1}^n \map {g_{i j} } x \rd x_i \rd x_j$ where each $g_{i j}$ is a suitable real-valued function of $x_1, \ldots, x_n$. Usually the $g_{i j}$ are taken so as to form a non-zero determinant.

title: Definition:Riemannian Metric Mapping
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $TM$ and $T^*M$ be tangent and cotangent bundles of $M$. Let $p \in M$ be a base point. Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space of $M$ at $p$. Let $v, w \in T_p M$ be tangent vectors. Then the bundle homomorphism is the mapping $\hat g : T M \to T^* M$ such that: $\forall p \in M : \forall v, w \in T_p M : \map {\map {\hat g} v} w = \map {g_p} {v, w}$

title: Definition:Riemannian Submanifold
snippet: Let $M$ be an immersed submanifold with or without a boundary. Let $g$ be a metric induced on $M$. Then $\struct {M, g}$ is called the Riemannian submanifold.

title: Definition:Riemannian Submersion
snippet: Let $\struct {\tilde M, \tilde g}$, $\struct {M, g}$ be Riemannian manifolds. Let $\pi : \tilde M \to M$ be a smooth submersion. Let $x \in \tilde M$, $p \in M$ be points in $\tilde M$ and $M$. Let $H_x$ be a horizontal tangent space at $x$. Let $T_p M$ be a tangent space of $M$ at $p \in M$. Let $g_p$ be a Riemannian metric at $p$.

title: Definition:Riemannian Volume Form/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be an oriented $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold. Let $T^* M$ be the cotangent bundle of $M$. Let $\tuple {\epsilon^1, \ldots, \epsilon^n}$ be a local oriented orthonormal coframe of $T^* M$. The Riemannian volume form, denoted by $\rd V_g$, is an $n$-form such that: $\rd V_g = \epsilon^1 \wedge \ldots \wedge \epsilon^n$

title: Definition:Riemannian Volume Form/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be an oriented $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold. Let $T M$ be the tangent bundle of $M$. Let $\tuple {E_1, \ldots, E_n}$ be a local oriented orthonormal frame of $T M$. The Riemannian volume form, denoted by $\rd V_g$, is an $n$-form such that: $\map {\rd V_g} {E_1, \ldots, E_n} = 1$

title: Definition:Riemannian Volume Form/Definition 3
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be an oriented $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold. Let $\tuple {x_1, \ldots, x_n}$ be a set of local oriented coordinates. Let $g_{i j}$ be a local form of metric $g$. The Riemannian volume form, denoted by $\d V_g$, is an $n$-form such that: $\d V_g = \sqrt {\map \det {g_{i j} } } \rd x^1 \wedge \ldots \wedge \rd x^n$

title: Definition:Riesel Number
snippet: Let $k$ be an odd positive integer. Then $k$ is a Riesel number : For all positive integers $n$, the number $k \, 2^n - 1$ is composite.

title: Definition:Riesel Number/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Riesel Number == In $1956$, proved that there are an infinite number of Riesel numbers. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Riesel Number/Sequence
snippet: == Sequence == The sequence of known Riesel numbers starts: $509 \,203, 762 \,701, 777 \,149, 790 \,841, 992 \,077, 1 \,106 \,681, 1 \,247 \,173, \ldots$ It is conjectured that $509 \,203$ is the smallest Riesel number. However, there are smaller candidates that are still being checked. Category:Definitions/Riesel Numbers

title: Definition:Rig
snippet: A rig is an additive semiring $\struct {S, *, \circ}$ in which $\struct {S, *}$ is a monoid. Alternatively, this is a semiring in which $\struct {S, *}$ is a commutative monoid. That is, $\struct {S, *, \circ}$ is a rig $\struct {S, *, \circ}$ satisfies the rig axioms: Note that the zero element needs to be specified here as an axiom: $\text M 2$. By Ring Product with Zero, in a ring, the property $\text M 2$ of the zero element follows as a consequence of the ring axioms.

title: Definition:Rig/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Rig == The term rig originated as a jocular suggestion: a ring without negative elements. Category:Linguistic Notes

snippet: A right-angled triangle is also often referred to as a right triangle. Category:Definitions/Right Triangles

title: Definition:Right-Continuous Filtration of Sigma-Algebra
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\sequence {\FF_t}_{t \ge 0}$ be a continuous-time filtration of $\Sigma$. We say that $\sequence {\FF_t}_{t \ge 0}$ is right-continuous for each $t \in \hointr 0 \infty$, we have: $\FF_{t^+} = \FF_t$ where $\FF_{t^+}$ is the right-limit of $\sequence {\FF_t}_{t \ge 0}$ at $t$.

title: Definition:Right-Hand Derivative
snippet: Let $B$ be a Banach space over the set of real numbers $\R$. Let $f: \R \to B$ be a mapping from $\R$ to $B$. The right-hand derivative of $f$ is defined as the right-hand limit: $\ds \map {f'_+} x = \lim_{h \mathop \to 0^+} \frac {\map f {x + h} - \map f x} h$ If the right-hand derivative exists, then $f$ is said to be right-hand differentiable at $x$.

title: Definition:Right-Hand Derivative/Real Function
snippet: Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a real function. The right-hand derivative of $f$ is defined as the right-hand limit: $\ds \map {f'_+} x = \lim_{h \mathop \to 0^+} \frac {\map f {x + h} - \map f x} h$ If the right-hand derivative exists, then $f$ is said to be right-hand differentiable at $x$.

title: Definition:Right-Hand Rule/Also known as
snippet: == Right-Hand Rule: Also known as == The right-hand rule can also be seen rendered unhyphenated: right hand rule. Category:Definitions/Right-Hand Rule

title: Definition:Right-Hand Rule/Axial Vector
snippet: Let $\mathbf V$ be an axial vector acting with respect to an axis of rotation $R$. Consider a right hand with its fingers curled round $R$ so that the fingers are pointed in the direction of rotation of $\mathbf V$ around $R$. The right-hand rule is the convention that the direction of $\mathbf V$ is the direction in which the thumb is pointing: 250px

title: Definition:Right-Hand Rule/Cross Product
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ be vector quantities. The right-hand rule for the vector cross product $\mathbf a \times \mathbf b$ is a consequence of the determinant definition: $\mathbf a \times \mathbf b = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k\\ a_i & a_j & a_k \\ b_i & b_j & b_k \\ \end{vmatrix}$ when embedded in the conventional right-hand Cartesian $3$-space: 450px Let a right hand be placed such that: the $3$rd finger is at right-angles to both the thumb and index finger, upwards from the palm the thumb points along the direction of $\mathbf a$ the index finger points…

title: Definition:Right-Hand Rule for Axial Vector/Also known as
snippet: == Right-Hand Rule: Also known as == The right-hand rule for axial vectors is also known as the right-hand screw rule. This is because it defines the direction of motion of a conventional screw: turn it in a clockwise direction and it screws in.

title: Definition:Right-Handed Cartesian 3-Space/Also known as
snippet: == Right-Handed Cartesian 3-Space: Also known as == A right-handed orientation of a Cartesian $3$-Space is also referred to as the positive orientation. Some sources refer to the $3$ coordinate axes in a right-handed Cartesian 3-space as a right-handed triad.

title: Definition:Right-Handed Cartesian Plane/Also known as
snippet: == Right-Handed Cartesian Plane: Also known as == A right-handed orientation of a Cartesian plane is also referred to as: the positive orientation the standard orientation the anticlockwise orientation.

title: Definition:Right-Invariant Riemannian Metric
snippet: Let $G$ be a Lie group. Let $\struct {G, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Suppose $g$ is invariant under all right translations $R_\phi : G \to G$: $\forall \phi \in G : {R_\phi}^* g = g$ where $*$ denotes the pullback of $g$ by $R_\phi$. Then $g$ is said to be right-invariant.

title: Definition:Right-Limit Filtration of Sigma-Algebra
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\sequence {\FF_t}_{t \ge 0}$ be a continuous-time filtration of $\Sigma$. For each $s \in \hointr 0 \infty$, let $\FF_{s+}$ be the right-limit of $\sequence {\FF_t}_{t \ge 0}$ at $t$. We say that $\sequence {\FF_{t+} }_{t \ge 0}$ is the right-limit filtration associated with $\sequence {\FF_t}_{t \ge 0}$.

title: Definition:Right-Limit of Filtration of Sigma-Algebra
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\sequence {\FF_t}_{t \ge 0}$ be a continuous-time filtration of $\Sigma$. For each $t \in \hointr 0 \infty$ we define the right-limit at $t$, $\FF_{t+}$ by: $\ds \FF_{t+} = \bigcap_{s > t} \FF_s$

title: Definition:Right-Regular Antiprism
snippet: A right-regular antiprism is an antiprism such that: its bases are regular polygons its lateral faces are isosceles triangles.

title: Definition:Right-Regular Antiprism/Also defined as
snippet: == Right-Regular Antiprism: Also known as == Some sources define a right-regular antiprism as an antiprism whose bases are regular polygons, making no restriction of the nature of the lateral faces.

title: Definition:Right-Total Relation
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation. Then $\RR$ is right-total : $\forall t \in T: \exists s \in S: \tuple {s, t} \in \RR$ That is, every element of $T$ is related to by some element of $S$. That is, : $\Img \RR = T$ where $\Img \RR$ denotes the image of $\RR$.

title: Definition:Right-Truncatable Prime
snippet: A right-truncatable prime is a prime number which remains prime when any number of digits are removed from the right hand end.

title: Definition:Right Angle
snippet: A right angle is an angle that is equal to one quarter of a full angle. That is, equal to one half of a straight angle.

title: Definition:Right Ascension
snippet: Let $P$ be a point on the celestial sphere. The right ascension of $P$ is the angular distance measured eastwards along the celestial equator from the vernal equinox. This is denoted $\alpha$ or $\mathrm {RA}$. Conventionally, right ascension is measured in units of time rather than angle. Hence $24$ hours corresponds to $360$ degrees.

title: Definition:Right Cancellable Mapping
snippet: A mapping $f: X \to Y$ is right cancellable (or right-cancellable) : $\forall Z: \forall \paren {h_1, h_2: Y \to Z}: h_1 \circ f = h_2 \circ f \implies h_1 = h_2$ That is, for any set $Z$: If $h_1$ and $h_2$ are mappings from $Y$ to $Z$ then $h_1 \circ f = h_2 \circ f$ implies $h_1 = h_2$.

title: Definition:Right Cancellable Operation
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. The operation $\circ$ in $\struct {S, \circ}$ is right cancellable : $\forall a, b, c \in S: a \circ c = b \circ c \implies a = b$ That is, all elements of $\struct {S, \circ}$ are right cancellable.

title: Definition:Right Circular Cone
snippet: A right circular cone is a cone: whose base is a circle in which there is a line perpendicular to the base through its center which passes through the apex of the cone: which is made by having a right-angled triangle turning along one of the sides that form the right angle. 300px '

title: Definition:Right Circular Cone/Acute-Angled
snippet: Let $K$ be a right circular cone. Then $K$ is acute-angled the opening angle of $K$ is an acute angle. ' Category:Definitions/Right Circular Cones

title: Definition:Right Circular Cone/Directrix
snippet: Let $K$ be a right circular cone. Let $B$ be the base of $K$. The circumference of $B$ is the directrix of $K$.

title: Definition:Right Circular Cone/Generating Angle
snippet: 300px Let $K$ be a right circular cone. Let point $A$ be the apex of $K$. Let $O$ be the center of the base of $K$. Let $B$ be the endpoint of a diameter of the base of $K$. Then the angle $\angle OAB$ is the generating angle of $K$.

title: Definition:Right Circular Cone/Generatrix
snippet: 300px Let $K$ be a right circular cone. Let $A$ be the apex of $K$. Let $B$ be the base of $K$. Then a line joining the apex of $K$ to its directrix is a generatrix of $K$.

title: Definition:Right Circular Cone/Height
snippet: Let $K$ be a right circular cone. The height of $K$ is the length of the line segment from the center of the base of $K$ to the apex of $K$.

snippet: Let $K$ be a right circular cone. Then $K$ is obtuse-angled the opening angle of $K$ is an obtuse angle. ' Category:Definitions/Right Circular Cones

title: Definition:Right Circular Cone/Right-Angled
snippet: Let $K$ be a right circular cone. Then $K$ is right-angled the opening angle of $K$ is a right angle. ' Category:Definitions/Right Circular Cones

title: Definition:Right Circular Cone/Similar Cones
snippet: Let $h_1$ and $h_2$ be the lengths of the axes of two right circular cones. Let $d_1$ and $d_2$ be the lengths of the diameters of the bases of the two right circular cones. Then the two right circular cones are similar : $\dfrac {h_1} {h_2} = \dfrac {d_1} {d_2}$ ' Category:Definitions/Right Circular Cones

title: Definition:Right Circular Cone/Slant Height
snippet: Let $K$ be a right circular cone. The slant height of $K$ is the length of a line segment from the directrix to the apex.
