title: Definition:Ring of Square Matrices
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. Let $\map {\MM_R} n$ denote the $n \times n$ matrix space over $R$. Let $+$ denote the operation of matrix entrywise addition. Let $\times$ be (temporarily) used to denote the operation of conventional matrix multiplication. The algebraic structure: $\struct {\map {\MM_R} n, +, \times}$ is known as the ring of square matrices of order $n$ over $R$

title: Definition:Ring of Square Matrices/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Ring of Square Matrices == When referring to the operation of matrix multiplication in the context of the ring of square matrices: $\struct {\map {\MM_R} n, +, \times}$ we must have some symbol to represent it, and $\times$ does as well as any. However, we do not use $\mathbf A \times \mathbf B$ for matrix multiplication $\mathbf A \mathbf B$, as it is understood to mean the vector cross product, which is something completely different. Category:Definitions/Square Matrices

title: Definition:Ring under Ring
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. A ring under $A$ is a pair $(B, f)$ where: $B$ is a commutative ring with unity $f : A \to B$ is a unital ring homomorphism

title: Definition:Ring with Unity
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a non-null ring. Then $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ is a ring with unity the multiplicative semigroup $\struct {R, \circ}$ has an identity element. Such an identity element is known as a unity. It follows that such a $\struct {R, \circ}$ is a monoid.

title: Definition:Ring with Unity/Also known as
snippet: == Ring with Unity: Also known as == Other names for ring with unity include: ring with a one, or ring with $1$ ring with a multiplicative identity or just ring with identity unitary ring unital ring unit ring Some sources simply refer to a ring, taking the presence of the unity for granted. On , the term ring does not presuppose said presence.

title: Definition:Ringed Space
snippet: A ringed space is a pair $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ where: $X$ is a topological space $\OO_X$ is a sheaf of commutative rings with unity on $X$.

title: Definition:Ringed Space/Structure Sheaf
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ be a ringed space. The structure sheaf of $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ is the term $\OO_X$.

title: Definition:Ringoid (Abstract Algebra)
snippet: A ringoid is a triple $\struct {S, *, \circ}$ where: That is: {{eqn | q = \forall a, b, c \in S | l = a \circ \paren {b * c} | r = \paren {a \circ b} * \paren {a \circ c} }} {{eqn | q = \forall a, b, c \in S | l = \paren {a * b} \circ c | r = \paren {a \circ c} * \paren {b \circ c} }}

title: Definition:Rise
snippet: Let $P_1 = \tuple {x_1, y_1}$ and $P_2 = \tuple {x_2, y_2}$ be points in the Cartesian plane. The rise from $P_1$ to $P_2$ is the difference between their ordinates: $y_2 - y_1$

title: Definition:Rise/Also known as
snippet: == Rise: Also known as == The rise between two points is also known as their $y$-step.

title: Definition:Rising Factorial
snippet: Let $x$ be a real number (but usually an integer). Let $n$ be a positive integer. Then the rising factorial with $n$ terms of $x$ is defined as: $\ds x^{\overline n} := \prod_{j \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \paren {x + j} = x \paren {x + 1} \cdots \paren {x + n - 1}$

title: Definition:Rising Factorial/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Rising Factorial == The notation $x^{\overline n}$ for $x$ to the $n$ rising is due to , who used it in $1893$. This is the notation of choice on . A more commonly seen notation (though arguably not as good) is $x^{\paren n}$. This is known as the Pochhammer function or (together with $\paren x_n$ for its falling counterpart) the Pochhammer symbol (after ). However, depending on the context, either $\paren x_n$ or $x^{\paren n}$ can be used to indicate the rising factorial.

title: Definition:Ritz Method
snippet: Let $\MM$ be a normed linear space. Let $J\sqbrk y$ be a functional defined on space $\MM$. Let $\sequence{\phi_n}$ be an infinite sequence of mappings in $\MM$. Let $\MM_n$ be an $n$-dimensional linear subspace of $\MM$, spanned by first $n$ mapping of $\sequence{\phi_n}$. Let $\eta_n = \boldsymbol \alpha \boldsymbol \phi$, where $\boldsymbol \alpha$ is a real $n$-dimensional vector. Minimise $J \sqbrk {\eta_n}$ $\boldsymbol\alpha$. Then $J \sqbrk {\eta_n}$ is an approximate minimum of $J \sqbrk y$, and is denoted by $\mu_n$. This method is known as Ritz method.

title: Definition:Ritz Sequence
snippet: Let $\sequence {\phi_n}$ be an infinite sequence of mappings in a normed linear space, where: $\phi_n: \R \to \R$ Let this sequence be constrained by the requirements defined in the definition of the Ritz method. Then the sequence $\set {\phi_n}$ can be called a Ritz Sequence.

title: Definition:River Crossing Problem
snippet: A river crossing problem concerns a group of people, who may or may not have a collection of objects, which need to cross a river. The constraints of the problem are generally of the form: $(1): \quad$ The boat can carry only a limited cargo, thereby making it impossible for the crossing to be made in one go $(2): \quad$ Certain combinations of people or objects or both may not be left alone or in combination on either bank of the river. In some versions of the problem, there are one or more islands midstream at which people or objects may be left for a while.

title: Definition:River Crossing Problem/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on River Crossing Problem == The earliest known occurrences of river crossing problems appear in by . There appear to be $3$ main types: $(1): \quad$ A number of jealous men and their sisters, or missionaries and cannibals, where there are constraints on who can be left alone with whom $(2): \quad$ A person trying to transport livestock and foodstuffs, where there are constraints on which may be left alone with what $(3): \quad$ A person trying to transport goods or people, where there are constraints on the weight which can be transported at one time.

title: Definition:Rng
snippet: In the context of abstract algebra, a rng is a ring $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ which specifically does not have a unity. That is, such that the semigroup $\struct {R, \circ}$ does not have an identity element.

title: Definition:Rng/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Rng == The name rng arises from its nature as a ring with no identity element. The word rng is a (or possibly ), hence linguistic rules are to a certain extent arbitrary. However, it is generally agreed that the word rng is pronounced rung. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Robbins Constant
snippet: The Robbins constant $R$ is defined as the mean distance $D$ between $2$ points chosen at random from the interior of a unit cube: {{eqn | l = R | r = \frac {4 + 17 \sqrt 2 - 6 \sqrt3 - 7 \pi} {105} + \frac {\map \ln {1 + \sqrt 2 } } 5 + \frac {2 \, \map \ln {2 + \sqrt 3} } 5 }}

title: Definition:Robbins Constant/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Robbins Constant == The Robbins constant arises from a question posed by in $1977$ in the in the context of a general cuboid of arbitrary dimensions. The published solution, submitted by applied the result to a general unit cube and presented the result in a format similar to that given here.

title: Definition:Robust Estimator
snippet: An estimator which: behaves like an optimum estimator when the assumptions for that estimator hold. gives estimates which are almost as efficient when the assumptions break down is called a robust estimator.

title: Definition:Robustness
snippet: The robustness of a hypothesis test or estimation procedure is a measure of how much it is affected by departures from assumptions on which it is based. If such a test or estimation procedure is affected just a little, then it is said to be robust. Robustness to outliers is important in practice.

title: Definition:Rocket
snippet: A rocket is a device whose means of propulsion works by throwing material out of one end at high speed in order to take advantage of the Principle of Conservation of Momentum to move in the opposite direction. Category:Definitions/Rocket Science

title: Definition:Rocket Science
snippet: Rocket science is the branch of physics concerned with the propulsion of rockets.

title: Definition:Rod
snippet: A rod is an idealized straight body which has: length linear mass density but whose width is approximated to zero. A rod can be defined as rigid or flexible, according to the needs of the model to which it may contribute.

title: Definition:Rod/Uniform
snippet: A uniform rod is a rod whose linear mass density is constant throughout.

title: Definition:Roentgen
snippet: The roentgen is a quantity of either x-rays or gamma rays which produces, together with its secondaries, a total of $2 \cdotp 082 \times 10^9$ electron-ion pairs in $0 \cdotp 001293$ gram of air.

title: Definition:Roll
snippet: Let $B$ be a body in motion through a fluid while subject to a gravitational field. In practice, this will be an aircraft, spacecraft or projectile, or a ship on the sea, for example. The roll of the motion of $B$ is the angular motion of $B$ about an axis which coincides with the direction of motion of $B$.

title: Definition:Rolling Friction
snippet: Rolling friction is the friction encountered when a body rolls over a surface without sliding.

title: Definition:Roman Numerals
snippet: The Roman numerals are: To express other numbers than these, symbols are placed next to each other so as to cumulate: for example: $\text {II}$ means $2$ $\text {CCXVI}$ means $216$. For brevity in presentation, the technique is used of placing a smaller denomination in front of a larger one so as to subtract the former from the latter For example: $\text {IV}$ means $4$ $\text {XCIX}$ means $99$ (although $\text {IC}$ could be used, it is not).

title: Definition:Roman Numerals/Also presented as
snippet: == Roman Numerals: Also presented as == It is commonplace to present Roman numerals in lowercase: $\text {i, v, x, l, c, d, m}$ Category:Definitions/Roman Numerals

title: Definition:Roman Numerals/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Roman Numerals == Before the adoption of the Arabic numerals, abacism was the usual technique for doing arithmetic, originating in ancient times. It is still used in rural areas of, for example, the Asian steppes, where writing materials are not to be wasted and electronic aids are un-needed. With the invention of the techniques offered by the so-called Arabic numerals in mediaeval times, an alternative method of doing arithmetic developed, called algorism. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Roman Numerals/Uses
snippet: == Uses of Roman Numerals == The Roman numerals are used today almost solely for enumeration in certain traditional contexts: $(1): \quad$ The presentation of years in dates, especially embedded in the masonry of buildings to indicate its year of construction $(2): \quad$ In the context of the cartesian plane, Roman numerals are traditionally used to enumerate the quadrants $(3): \quad$ Enumerations of lists, particularly when sublists are required which (because of the presentational style selected by the author) need different styles of presentation, for example: "See section $1 \…

title: Definition:Roman Numerals/Warning
snippet: == Roman Numerals: Warning == Because of the similarity in shape between the letter $\text I$ and the number $1$, it is a common mistake to confuse them and use $1$ where $\text I$ should be used. Consequently, hilariously clumsy-looking constructions can be found in published works (usually in [http://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/pretentious pretentious] artwork such as can often be found on the covers of contemporary musical product) such as $\text V 1 1 1$ for $\text {VIII}$. Even more hilarous is hearing muggles vocalise the above as vee wun wun wun. Category:Definitions/Roman Numerals

title: Definition:Roman Weights and Measures
snippet: The Roman system of weights is a system of mass units originating from the time of the Roman empire. This system continued to be used throughout Europe, although it evolved in different directions according to use.

title: Definition:Roman Weights and Measures/Mass
snippet: The Roman units of mass are as follows:

title: Definition:Roman Weights and Measures/Mass/Calcus
snippet: The calcus is the smallest unit of mass in the Roman system of weights. $1$ calcus $= \dfrac 1 8$ scrupulus. Its value in modern units is estimated to be approximately $2.2$ grains, or approximately $0.14$ grams.

title: Definition:Roman Weights and Measures/Mass/Libra
snippet: The libra is a unit of mass that was part of the Roman system of weights. $1$ libra $= 12$ unciae. Its value in modern units is estimated to be approximately $5 \, 076$ grains or $329$ grams.

title: Definition:Roman Weights and Measures/Mass/Libra/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Libra == The libra has continued to be used throughout history, and evolved into the pound. Hence the symbol $\text{lb}$ to indicate pound weight. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Roman Weights and Measures/Mass/Libra/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Libra == The word libra is a Latin word that literally means balance. Its plural is librae. In , it is referred to (in passing) as a unit, but this has not been corroborated. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Roman Weights and Measures/Mass/Scrupulus
snippet: The scrupulus is a unit of mass that was part of the Roman system of weights. $1$ scrupulus $= \dfrac 1 {24}$ uncia $= 8$ calci. Its value in modern units is estimated to be approximately $17.6$ grains, or approximately $0.14$ grams.

title: Definition:Roman Weights and Measures/Mass/Siliqua
snippet: The siliqua is a unit of mass in the Roman system of weights. $1$ siliqua $= \dfrac 1 6$ scrupulus $= \dfrac 1 {144}$ uncia. Its value in modern units is estimated to be approximately $2.9$ grains, or approximately $0.19$ grams. Its modern equivalent is the carat.

title: Definition:Roman Weights and Measures/Mass/Uncia
snippet: The uncia is a unit of mass that was part of the Roman system of weights. $1$ uncia $= \dfrac 1 {12}$ libra $= 24$ scrupuli. Its value in modern units is estimated to be approximately $423$ grains or $27.4$ grams.

title: Definition:Romberg Integration
snippet: Let $\closedint a b$ be a closed real interval. Let $f$ be a function over $\closedint a b$. Let Richardson extrapolation be iteratively applied with repeated trapezium rule approximations having subinterval lengths: $h_k = \dfrac {b - a} {2^{k - 1} }$ for $k = 1, 2, \ldots$ This process is known as Romberg integration.

title: Definition:Romberg Integration/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Romberg Integration == Romberg integration was invented by in $1955$.

title: Definition:Rook Matrix
snippet: An $8 \times 8$ logical matrix in which: at most one element in each row and column is $1$ is known as a rook matrix. Not all rows and columns necessarily have a $1$ in them.

title: Definition:Root
snippet: Inverse ← Division/Biaction Super root/Tetraction → Analysis: Root of a number: If $y^m = x$ then $x = \sqrt [m] y$, and $x$ is the $m$th root of $y$. Root of an equation: The roots of an equation $E$ are the values of the variables for which $E$ is true. Root of a mapping (or function): The roots of a mapping $f$ are the values of $x$ for which $\map f x = 0$. Root of a polynomial: the roots of a polynomial $f$ are the values of $x$ for which $\map f x = 0$.

title: Definition:Root Node/Also known as
snippet: == Root Node: Also known as == The root node of a rooted tree can be referred to as just its root.

title: Definition:Root System
snippet: Let $E$ be a real vector space with inner product $\innerprod \cdot \cdot$. A root system $\Phi \subset E$ is a finite set of nonzero vectors in $E$ (called roots) such that: By Reflection Formula (Geometry), axiom $(3)$ may be rewritten {{axiom | n = 3 | t = $\forall \alpha, \beta \in \Phi: \beta - 2 \dfrac {\innerprod \alpha \beta} {\innerprod \alpha \alpha} \alpha \in \Phi$}} By the vector projection formula, axiom $(4)$ may be written {{axiom | n=4 | t=$\forall \alpha, \beta \in \Phi: 2 \dfrac {\innerprod \alpha \beta} {\innerprod \alpha \alpha} \in \Z$}} The notation $\innerprod \alpha…

title: Definition:Root of Congruence
snippet: Let $f$ be the congruence defined as: $\map f x \equiv 0 \pmod n$ A root of $f$ is an integer $a$ such that: $\map f a \equiv 0 \pmod n$

title: Definition:Root of Equation
snippet: Let $\map E x$ be a mathematical expression representing an equation which is dependent upon a variable $x$. A root of $\map E x$ is a constant which, when substituted for $x$ in $\map E x$, makes $\map E x$ a true statement.

title: Definition:Root of Equation/Extraction
snippet: The process of finding roots of a given equation is referred to as extraction.

title: Definition:Root of Mapping
snippet: Let $f: R \to R$ be a mapping on a ring $R$. Let $x \in R$. Then the values of $x$ for which $\map f x = 0_R$ are known as the roots of the mapping $f$.

title: Definition:Root of Mapping/Also known as
snippet: == Root of Mapping: Also known as == The ring $R$ is often the field of real numbers $\R$ or field of complex numbers $\C$. In this case, for a given function $f$, the roots are usually known as the zeroes of the function $f$.

title: Definition:Root of Number
snippet: Let $x, y \in \R_{\ge 0}$ be positive real numbers. Let $n \in \Z$ be an integer such that $n \ne 0$. Then $y$ is the positive $n$th root of $x$ : $y^n = x$ and we write: $y = \sqrt[n] x$ Using the power notation, this can also be written: $y = x^{1/n}$ When $n = 2$, we write $y = \sqrt x$ and call $y$ the positive square root of $x$. When $n = 3$, we write $y = \sqrt [3] x$ and call $y$ the cube root of $x$. Note the special case where $x = 0 = y$: $0 = \sqrt [n] 0$

title: Definition:Root of Number/Also known as
snippet: == Root of Number: Also known as == A root of a number is also known as: a radical a radix.

title: Definition:Root of Number/Extraction
snippet: The process of evaluating roots of a given real number is referred to as extraction.

title: Definition:Root of Number/Index
snippet: Let $\sqrt [n] x$ denote the $n$th root of $x$. The number $n$ is known as the index of the root. If $n$ is not specified, that is $\sqrt x$ is presented, this means the square root.

title: Definition:Root of Polynomial
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $f \in R \sqbrk x$ be a polynomial over $R$. A root in $R$ of $f$ is an element $x \in R$ for which $\map f x = 0$, where $\map f x$ denotes the image of $f$ under the evaluation homomorphism at $x$.

title: Definition:Root of Polynomial/Also known as
snippet: == Root of Polynomial: Also known as == A root of a polynomial is also known as a zero.

title: Definition:Root of Unity
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{> 0}$ be a strictly positive integer. Let $F$ be a field. The $n$th roots of unity of $F$ are defined as: $U_n = \set {z \in F: z^n = 1}$

title: Definition:Root of Unity/Complex
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. The complex $n$th roots of unity are the elements of the set: $U_n = \set {z \in \C: z^n = 1}$

title: Definition:Root of Unity/Complex/First
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. In Complex Roots of Unity in Exponential Form it is shown that the complex $n$th roots of unity are the elements of the set: $U_n = \set {e^{2 i k \pi / n}: k \in \N_n}$ The root $e^{2 i \pi / n}$ is known as the first (complex) $n$th root of unity.

title: Definition:Root of Unity/Complex/Order
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{> 0}$ be a strictly positive integer. Let $U_n$ denote the complex $n$th roots of unity: $U_n = \set {z \in \C: z^n = 1}$ Let $z \in U_n$. The order of $z$ is the smallest $p \in \Z_{> 0}$ such that: $z^p = 1$ Category:Definitions/Complex Roots of Unity

title: Definition:Root of Unity/Complex/Primitive
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. Let $U_n$ denote the complex $n$th roots of unity: $U_n = \set {z \in \C: z^n = 1}$ A primitive (complex) $n$th root of unity is an element $\alpha \in U_n$ such that: $U_n = \set {1, \alpha, \alpha^2, \ldots, \alpha^{n - 1} }$ Equivalently, an $n$th root of unity is primitive its order is $n$.

title: Definition:Root of Unity/Order
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{> 0}$ be a strictly positive integer. Let $F$ be a field. Let $U_n = \set {z \in F: z^n = 1}$ be the $n$th roots of unity of $F$. Let $z \in U_n$. The order of $z$ is the smallest $p \in \Z_{> 0}$ such that: $z^p = 1$ Category:Definitions/Roots of Unity

title: Definition:Root of Unity/Primitive
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{> 0}$ be a strictly positive integer. Let $F$ be a field. Let $U_n$ denote the set of all $n$th roots of unity.

title: Definition:Root of Unity Modulo m
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a positive integer. Let $m \in \Z_{>1}$ be a positive integer greater than one. Then $a$ is an $n^{th}$ root of unity modulo $m$ : $a^n \equiv 1 \pmod m$ Solving the following equation over the smallest integers modulo $m$: $\ds \paren {a^n - 1} = \paren {a - 1} \paren {\sum_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} a^k} \equiv 0 \pmod m$ will produce the roots. Any root found will also have $a + k m$ as a solution, where $k \in \Z$ is any integer. Euler's Function $\map \phi m$ root of unity modulo $m$ is the set of all positive integers less than $m$.

title: Definition:Rooted Subtree
snippet: Let $\struct {T, r_T}$ be a rooted tree. A rooted subtree of $T$ is a rooted tree $\struct {S, r_S}$ such that: $S$ is a subtree of $T$ $r_S = r_T$ Note that the second condition implies that $r_T \in S$.

title: Definition:Rooted Tree
snippet: A rooted tree is a tree with a countable number of nodes, in which a particular node is distinguished from the others and called the root node: 300px

title: Definition:Rooted Tree/Also known as
snippet: == Rooted Tree: Also known as == In some contexts, in which only a rooted tree would make sense, the term tree is often used.

title: Definition:Rooted Tree/Ancestor Node
snippet: Let $T$ be a rooted tree with root $r_T$. Let $t$ be a node of $T$. An ancestor node of $t$ is a node in the path from $t$ to $r_T$.

title: Definition:Rooted Tree/Ancestor Node/Proper
snippet: Let $T$ be a rooted tree with root $r_T$. Let $t$ be a node of $T$. A proper ancestor node of $t$ is an ancestor node of $t$ that is not $t$ itself.

title: Definition:Rooted Tree/Branch
snippet: Let $T$ be a rooted tree with root node $r_T$. A subset $\Gamma$ of $T$ is a branch all the following conditions hold: $(1): \quad$ The root node $r_T$ belongs to $\Gamma$ $(2): \quad$ The parent of each node in $\Gamma \setminus \set {r_T}$ is in $\Gamma$ $(3): \quad$ Each node in $\Gamma$ either: $\text {(a)}: \quad$ is a leaf node of $T$ or: $\text {(b)}: \quad$ has exactly one child node in $\Gamma$. Informally, a branch of a rooted tree is the path from the root to a leaf.

title: Definition:Rooted Tree/Branch/Finite
snippet: Let $T$ be a rooted tree with root node $r_T$. Let $\Gamma$ be a branch of $T$. Then $\Gamma$ is finite it has exactly one leaf node.

title: Definition:Rooted Tree/Branch/Infinite
snippet: Let $T$ be a rooted tree with root node $r_T$. Let $\Gamma$ be a branch of $T$. Then $\Gamma$ is infinite it has no leaf node at the end.

title: Definition:Rooted Tree/Branch/Length
snippet: Let $T$ be a rooted tree with root node $r_T$. Let $\Gamma$ be a finite branch of $T$. The length of $\Gamma$ is defined as the number of ancestors of the leaf at the end of that branch.

title: Definition:Rooted Tree/Child Node
snippet: Let $T$ be a rooted tree with root $r_T$. Let $t$ be a node of $T$. The child nodes of $t$ are the elements of the set: $\set {s \in T: \map \pi s = t}$ where $\map \pi s$ denotes the parent mapping of $s$. That is, the children of $t$ are all the nodes of $T$ of which $t$ is the parent.

title: Definition:Rooted Tree/Child Node/Grandchild Node
snippet: Let $T$ be a rooted tree with root $r_T$. Let $t$ be a node of $T$. A child of a child node of a node $t$ can be referred to as a grandchild node of $t$. In terms of the parent mapping $\pi$ of $T$, a grandchild node of $t$ is a node $s$ such that: $\map \pi {\map \pi s} = t$ Category:Definitions/Descendant Nodes

title: Definition:Rooted Tree/Descendant
snippet: Let $T$ be a rooted tree with root $r_T$. Let $t$ be a node of $T$. A descendant node $s$ of a $t$ is a node such that $t$ is in the path from $s$ to $r_T$. That is, the descendant nodes of $t$ are all the nodes of $T$ of which $t$ is an ancestor node.

title: Definition:Rooted Tree/Parent Node
snippet: Let $T$ be a rooted tree whose root is $r_T$. Let $t$ be a node of $T$. From Path in Tree is Unique, there is only one path from $t$ to $r_T$. Let $\pi: T \setminus \set {r_T} \to T$ be the mapping defined by: $\map \pi t := \text {the node adjacent to $t$ on the path to $r_T$}$ Then $\map \pi t$ is known as the parent node of $t$. The mapping $\pi$ is called the parent mapping.

title: Definition:Rooted Tree/Proper Descendant
snippet: Let $T$ be a rooted tree with root $r_T$. Let $t$ be a node of $T$. A proper descendant node of $t$ is a descendant of $t$ which is not $t$ itself. Category:Definitions/Descendant Nodes

title: Definition:Rooted Tree/Root Node
snippet: Let $T$ be a rooted tree. The root node of $T$ is the node of $T$ which is distinguished from the others by being the ancestor node of every node of $T$.

title: Definition:Rooted Tree/Sibling
snippet: Let $T$ be a rooted tree with root $r_T$. Two children of the same node of $T$ are called siblings. That is, siblings are nodes which both have the same parent. Category:Definitions/Rooted Trees

title: Definition:Roster Notation
snippet: Roster notation is the technique of specifying the elements in a set by listing them between a pair of braces $\set{}$.

title: Definition:Rotating Frame of Reference
snippet: A rotating frame of reference is a non-inertial frame of reference which is undergoing a rotation in space an inertial frame of reference.

title: Definition:Rotation
snippet: Geometry: Rotation: an isometry on a Euclidean Space which maps a straight line through a distinguished point to another straight line at a given angle to it. Permutation Theory Rotation: A permutation of a string over an alphabet.

title: Definition:Rotation (Geometry)
snippet: A rotation in the context of Euclidean geometry is an isometry on a Euclidean space $\R^n$ as follows. A rotation is defined usually for either: $n = 2$, representing the plane or: $n = 3$, representing ordinary space.

title: Definition:Rotation (Geometry)/Angle
snippet: Let $r_\theta$ be a rotation in the Euclidean Space $\Gamma = \R^n$. Let $\map {r_\theta} P = P'$ about a point $O$ on the axis of rotation of $r_\theta$. The number $\theta$ which defines the angle $POP'$ is called the rotation angle or angle of rotation of $r_\theta$.

title: Definition:Rotation (Geometry)/Axis
snippet: Let $r_\theta$ be a rotation in the Euclidean Space $\Gamma = \R^n$. The set $A$ of points in $\Gamma$ such that: $\forall P \in A: \map {r_\theta} P = P$ is called the axis of rotation of $r_\theta$.

title: Definition:Rotation (Geometry)/Plane
snippet: A rotation $r_\alpha$ in the plane is an isometry on the Euclidean Space $\Gamma = \R^2$ as follows. Let $O$ be a distinguished point in $\Gamma$, which has the property that: $\map {r_\alpha} O = O$ That is, $O$ maps to itself. Let $P \in \Gamma$ such that $P \ne O$. Let $OP$ be joined by a straight line. Let a straight line $OP'$ be constructed such that: $(1): \quad OP' = OP$ $(2): \angle POP' = \alpha$ such that $OP \to OP'$ is in the anticlockwise direction: 300px Then: $\map {r_\alpha} P = P'$ Thus $r_\alpha$ is a rotation (in the plane) of (angle) $\alpha$ about (the axis) $O$.

title: Definition:Rotation (Geometry)/Space
snippet: A rotation $r_\theta$ in space is an isometry on the Euclidean Space $\Gamma = \R^3$ as follows. Let $AB$ be a distinguished straight line in $\Gamma$, which has the property that: $\forall P \in AB: \map {r_\theta} P = P$ That is, all points on $AB$ map to themselves. Let $P \in \Gamma$ such that $P \notin AB$. Let a straight line be constructed from $P$ to $O$ on $AB$ such that $OP$ is perpendicular to $AB$.

title: Definition:Rotation (Geometry)/Space/Vector Form
snippet: A space rotation $r_\theta$ can be expressed as an axial vector $\mathbf r_\theta$ such that: the direction of $\mathbf r_\theta$ is defined to be its axis of rotation the length of $\mathbf r_\theta$ specifies its angle of rotation of $\mathbf r_\theta$ to an appropriate scale. 400px

title: Definition:Rotation (Permutation Theory)
snippet: Let $\tuple {a_1, \ldots, a_n}$ be a string over an alphabet $A$. A rotation is a mapping $r: A^n \to A^n$ given by: $\tuple {a_1, \ldots, a_n} \mapsto \tuple {a_{\map \phi 1}, \cdots, a_{\map \phi n} }$ where $\phi$ is a permutation on $n$ letters. Category:Definitions/Permutations on n Letters

title: Definition:Rotation Angle/Negative
snippet: Let $\theta$ be the rotation angle of a rotation in the Euclidean Space $\Gamma = \R^n$. $\theta$ is defined as being negative the rotation it measures is in the clockwise direction.

title: Definition:Rotation Angle/Positive
snippet: Let $\theta$ be the rotation angle of a rotation in the Euclidean Space $\Gamma = \R^n$. $\theta$ is defined as being positive the rotation it measures is in the anticlockwise direction.

title: Definition:Rotation Matrix
snippet: Let $\tuple {\mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_2, \mathbf e_3}$ be the orthonormal basis of a Cartesian coordinate system $C$ on (ordinary) space $S$. Let $O$ be the origin of $C$. Let $\tuple {\mathbf e'_1, \mathbf e'_2, \mathbf e'_3}$ be the orthonormal basis of another Cartesian coordinate system $C'$ on $S$, also with origin $O$ and with the same orientation as $C$.

title: Definition:Rotation of Axes
snippet: A rotation of axes is a coordinate transformation in which the coordinate axes are rotated through a fixed angle.

title: Definition:Rotational Motion
snippet: Let $B$ be a body which is in motion. Let the velocities of the individual particles of $B$ be defined by a vector field $\mathbf V$ over $B$. Let the curl of $\mathbf V$ be non-zero. Then the motion of $B$ is described as being rotational.

title: Definition:Rotational Symmetry
snippet: Let $F$ be a geometric figure. Let there exist a rotation which is also a symmetry of $F$. Then $F$ has a rotational symmetry. Thus a rotational symmetry is itself a symmetry which is a rotation.

title: Definition:Rotational Symmetry/Axis
snippet: Let $F$ be a geometric figure. Let $\map R F$ be a rotational symmetry around the axis of rotation $AB$. Then $AB$ is referred to as an axis of rotational symmetry of $F$.

title: Definition:Rotational Symmetry/Order
snippet: Let $F$ be a geometric figure. Let $\map R F$ be a rotational symmetry around the axis $AB$. Let the angle of rotation of $R$ be $\dfrac {360 \degrees} n$, that is: $\dfrac {2 \pi} n$ radians. Then $R$ is referred to as a (rotational) symmetry of order $n$.

title: Definition:Rotational Vector Field
snippet: Let $R$ be a region of space. Let $\mathbf V$ be a vector field acting over $R$. Then $\mathbf V$ is a rotational vector field the curl of $\mathbf V$ is not everywhere zero: $\curl \mathbf V \not \equiv \bszero$ That is, $\mathbf V$ is not conservative.

title: Definition:Rothberger Space
snippet: A Rothberger space is a topological space that satisfies the selection principle $\map {S_1} {\OO, \OO}$: for every sequence of open covers $\UU_n$ for $n \in \N$, there exist choices $V_n \in \UU_n$ such that $\set {V_n: n \in \N}$ is also an open cover.

title: Definition:Rothberger Space/Also known as
snippet: == Rothberger Space: Also known as == A Rothberger space is also known as a property $C' '$ space.

title: Definition:Rough Contact
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be bodies in contact. Let the frictional force between $A$ and $B$ be non-zero. Then the contact between $A$ and $B$ is referred to as a rough contact.

title: Definition:Rough Surface
snippet: Let $B$ be a solid body. The surface of $B$ is described as rough friction is generated when another body slides along $B$.

title: Definition:Rough Vector Field on Smooth Manifold
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $TM$ be the tangent bundle of $M$. Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space at $p \in M$. A rough vector field on $M$ is a mapping $X : M \to TM$, not necessarily continuous, such that: $\forall p \in M : X_p \in T_p M$ where $X_p$ denotes the value of $X$ at $p$.

title: Definition:Roulette
snippet: A roulette is the locus of a point on, or associated with, a curve that rolls without sliding an another curve or straight line.

title: Definition:Rounding
snippet: Rounding is the process of approximation of a value of a variable to a multiple of a given power of whatever number base one is working in (usually decimal). Let $n \in \Z$ be an integer. Let $x \in \R$ be a real number. Let $X \in \Q$ such that: $X = 10^n \floor {\dfrac x {10^n} + \dfrac 1 2}$ or: $X = 10^n \ceiling {\dfrac x {10^n} - \dfrac 1 2}$ where $\floor {\, \cdot \,}$ denotes the floor function and $\ceiling {\, \cdot \,}$ denotes the ceiling function. Then $X$ is defined as $x$ rounded to the nearest $n$th power of $10$.

title: Definition:Rounding/Also known as
snippet: == Rounding: Also known as == When $n < 0$, the terminology used tends to be: $x$ rounded to the nearest $m$th decimal place where $m = -n$.

title: Definition:Rounding/Error
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number. Let $n \in \Z$ be an integer. Let $X \in \Q$ be equal to $x$ rounded to the nearest $n$th power of $10$. The rounding error caused by the rounding of $x$ to $X$ is defined as: $e_R = \size {x - X}$

title: Definition:Rounding/Integer
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number. Let $X \in \R$ such that: $X = \floor {x + \dfrac 1 2}$ Then $X$ is defined as $x$ rounded to the nearest integer.

title: Definition:Rounding/Treatment of Half
snippet: Let $n \in \Z$ be an integer. Let $x \in \R$ be a real number. Consider the situation when $\dfrac x {10^n} + \dfrac 1 2$ is an integer. That is, $\dfrac x {10^n}$ is exactly midway between the two integers $\dfrac x {10^n} - \dfrac 1 2$ and $\dfrac x {10^n} + \dfrac 1 2$. Recall that the general philosophy of the process of rounding is to find the closest approximation to $x$ to a given power of $10$. Thus there are two equally valid such approximations: $\dfrac x {10^n} - \dfrac 1 2$ and $\dfrac x {10^n} + \dfrac 1 2$ between which $\dfrac x {10^n}$ is exactly midway.

title: Definition:Rounding/Treatment of Half/Round Down
snippet: Let $n \in \Z$ be an integer. Let $x \in \R$ be a real number. Consider the situation when $\dfrac x {10^n} + \dfrac 1 2$ is an integer. That is, $\dfrac x {10^n}$ is exactly midway between the two integers $\dfrac x {10^n} - \dfrac 1 2$ and $\dfrac x {10^n} + \dfrac 1 2$. The round down convention is that the smaller of those two integers is used: $X = 10^n \ceiling {\dfrac x {10^n} - \dfrac 1 2}$ where $X$ is the rounded value.

title: Definition:Rounding/Treatment of Half/Round Up
snippet: Let $n \in \Z$ be an integer. Let $x \in \R$ be a real number. Consider the situation when $\dfrac x {10^n} + \dfrac 1 2$ is an integer. That is, $\dfrac x {10^n}$ is exactly midway between the two integers $\dfrac x {10^n} - \dfrac 1 2$ and $\dfrac x {10^n} + \dfrac 1 2$. The round up convention is that the larger of those two integers is used: $X = 10^n \floor {\dfrac x {10^n} + \dfrac 1 2}$ where $X$ is the rounded value.

title: Definition:Rounding/Treatment of Half/Round to Even
snippet: Let $n \in \Z$ be an integer. Let $x \in \R$ be a real number. Consider the situation when $\dfrac x {10^n} + \dfrac 1 2$ is an integer. That is, $\dfrac x {10^n}$ is exactly midway between the two integers $\dfrac x {10^n} - \dfrac 1 2$ and $\dfrac x {10^n} + \dfrac 1 2$. The round to even convention is that the nearest even integer to $\dfrac x {10^n}$ is used: $X = \begin {cases} 10^n \floor {\dfrac x {10^n} + \dfrac 1 2} & : \text {$\floor {\dfrac x {10^n} + \dfrac 1 2}$ even} \\ 10^n \ceiling {\dfrac x {10^n} - \dfrac 1 2} & : \text {$\floor {\dfrac x {10^n} + \dfrac 1 2}$ odd} \end…

title: Definition:Rounding Error/Also defined as
snippet: == Rounding Error: Also defined as == Some sources define a rounding error to be $X - x$. Other sources define a rounding error to be $x - X$. Using such conventions, a rounding error can be either positive or negative. Using the convention $\size {x - X}$, a rounding error can only be positive. Category:Definitions/Rounding Errors

title: Definition:Rounding Error/Also known as
snippet: == Rounding Error: Also known as == A rounding error is also known as a roundoff error.

title: Definition:Row
snippet: Logic: Row of a Truth Table Matrix Theory and Linear Algebra: Row of a Matrix Combinatorics Row of a Latin Square

title: Definition:Row Equivalence
snippet: Two matrices $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}, \mathbf B = \sqbrk b_{m n}$ are row equivalent if one can be obtained from the other by a finite sequence of elementary row operations. This relationship can be denoted $\mathbf A \sim \mathbf B$.

title: Definition:Row Matrix
snippet: A row matrix is a $1 \times n$ matrix: $\mathbf R = \begin {bmatrix} r_{1 1} & r_{1 2} & \cdots & r_{1 n} \end {bmatrix}$ That is, it is a matrix with only one row.

title: Definition:Row Matrix/Also known as
snippet: == Row Matrix: Also known as == Some earlier sources can be seen referring to a row matrix as a row vector. However, it is probably better not to use this terminology, as it can cause confusion between a matrix space and a vector space.

title: Definition:Row Operation
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ be an $m \times n$ matrix over a field $K$. A row operation on $\mathbf A$ is a sequence of elementary row operations performed on $\mathbf A$ in turn.

title: Definition:Row Operation/Also defined as
snippet: == Row Operation: Also known as == Some sources define a row operation as defines an elementary row operation.

title: Definition:Row Rank
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a matrix. The row rank of $\mathbf A$ is the dimension of the row space of $\mathbf A$.

title: Definition:Row Space
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $\mathbf A$ be a matrix over $R$.

title: Definition:Row Space/Definition 1
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $\mathbf A$ be a matrix over $R$. Let $\mathbf A^\intercal$ denote the transpose of $\mathbf A$. Let the columns of $\mathbf A^\intercal$ be members of a vector space. The row space of $\mathbf A$ is defined as the column space of $\mathbf A^\intercal$.

title: Definition:Row Space/Definition 2
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $\mathbf A$ be a matrix over $R$. The row space of $\mathbf A$ is defined as the vector space of all linear combinations of the rows of $\mathbf A$.

title: Definition:Row Stochastic Matrix/Also known as
snippet: == Row Stochastic Matrix: Also known as == Some sources refer to row stochastic matrix as just a stochastic matrix.

title: Definition:Row Sum
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a matrix of numbers. Let $r$ be a row of $\mathbf A$. The row sum of $r$ is the sum of all the elements in $r$.

title: Definition:Royal Society
snippet: The Royal Society is the UK's academy of scientists.

title: Definition:Royal Society/Fellow
snippet: A member of the Royal Society is known as a fellow of the Royal Society.

title: Definition:Royal Society/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Royal Society == The Royal Society was founded in $1660$.

title: Definition:Rubidium/87
snippet: == Isotope of Rubidium == Rubidium-$87$ is the isotope of rubidium which has $50$ neutrons in addition to its $37$ protons. Rb-$87$ is radioactive, with a half-life of approximately $48.8 \times 10^9$ years. Category:Definitions/Rubidium Category:Definitions/Examples of Radioactive Isotopes

title: Definition:Rubidium/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Rubidium == The word rubidium derives from the Latin word rubidus, meaning deep red, after the colour of the lines in its emission spectrum. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Rubik's Cube
snippet: Rubik's cube is a toy consisting of a plastic cube divided into $27$ smaller cubes, interlocking at the center cube and allowing each face to rotate independently of the others. Each of the $6$ faces of the main cube is colored with one of six contrasting colors. Rotating the faces of the cube causes these $6$ faces to become mixed up. The object of the exercise is to restore the $6$ faces to their original single colors.

title: Definition:Rubik's Cube/Basic Moves
snippet: The set of basic moves of the Rubik's cube can be denoted: $\set {U, D, L, R, F, B}$ where $U$, $D$, $L$, $R$, $F$, $B$ are in Singmaster notation.

title: Definition:Rubik's Cube/Center Facet
snippet: 600px Of each of the $9$ facets of each face of Rubik's cube, the ones in the centers of the faces are called the center facets. The set of center facets can be denoted $S_Z$. The set of center facets is: $S_Z = \set {F, U, R, L, B, D}$

title: Definition:Rubik's Cube/Center Facet/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Center Facet of Rubik's Cube == In the notation $S_Z$ for the center facets of Rubik's cube, the subscript $Z$ is for zentrum, which is German for center. $C$ cannot be used, because $S_C$ is already in use as the symbol denoting the set of corner facets.

title: Definition:Rubik's Cube/Corner Facet
snippet: 600px Of each of the $9$ facets of each face of Rubik's cube, the $4$ in the corners of the face are called the corner facets. The set of corner facets can be denoted $S_C$. For example: $flu$, $fru$, $frd$, $fld$ are the corner facets of the front face $ulb$, $urb$, $urf$, $ulf$ are the corner facets of the up face and so on.

title: Definition:Rubik's Cube/Edge Facet
snippet: 600px Of each of the $9$ facets of each face of Rubik's cube, the $4$ on the edges of the face are called the edge facets. The set of edge facets can be denoted $S_E$. For example: $fu$, $fr$, $fd$, $fl$ are the edge facets of the front face $ul$, $ub$, $ur$, $uf$ are the edge facets of the up face and so on.

title: Definition:Rubik's Cube/Face
snippet: The faces of a Rubik's cube are simply the $6$ faces of the main cube which constitutes Rubik's cube. Category:Definitions/Rubik's Cube

title: Definition:Rubik's Cube/Facet
snippet: 600px Each of the $9$ small squares into which the faces of Rubik's cube is subdivided is called a facet.

title: Definition:Rubik's Cube/Subcube
snippet: Each of the $26$ small visible cubes into which Rubik's cube is subdivided is called a subcube. The $27$th cube is in the interior of Rubik's cube and therefore has no visible faces. Category:Definitions/Rubik's Cube

title: Definition:Ruelle-Perron-Frobenius Operator/One-Sided Shift Space of Finite Type
snippet: Let $\struct {X_\mathbf A ^+, \sigma}$ be a one-sided shift of finite type. Let $\map C {X _\mathbf A ^+, \C}$ be the continuous mapping space. Let $F_\theta^+$ be the space of Lipschitz functions on $X_\mathbf A ^+$. Let $B$ be either $\map C {X _\mathbf A ^+, \C}$ or $F_\theta^+$. Let $f \in B$. The Ruelle-Perron-Frobenius operator $\LL_f : B \to B$ is defined as: $\ds \forall g \in B : \map {\paren {\LL_f g} } x := \sum_{y \mathop \in \map {\sigma^{-1} } x} e^{\map f y} \map g y$ where $\map {\sigma^{-1} } x$ denotes the preimage of $x$ under $\sigma$: $\map {\sigma^{-1} } x = \set…

title: Definition:Ruffini-Horner Method
snippet: The Ruffini-Horner method is a technique for finding the roots of polynomial equations in $1$ real variable. Let $E_0$ be the polynomial equation in $x$: $\map p x = 0$ Suppose that a root $x_0$ being sought is the positive real number expressed as the decimal expansion: $x_0 = \sqbrk {abc.def}$ The process begins by finding $a$ by inspection. We then form a new equation $E_1$ whose roots are $100 a$ less than those of $E_0$. This will have a root $x_1$ in the form: $x_1 = \sqbrk {bc.def}$ Similarly, $b$ is found by inspection.

title: Definition:Ruffini-Horner Method/Also known as
snippet: == Ruffini-Horner Method: Also known as == The Ruffini-Horner method is also known just as Horner's method. However, that name is also given to Horner's rule, so to avoid ambiguity and misunderstanding it is deprecated on .

title: Definition:Ruffini-Horner Method/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Ruffini-Horner Method == The Ruffini-Horner method was given by in $1804$. It was later given independently in $1819$ by . However, a similar iterative method had previously been devised by in the $13$th century.

title: Definition:Rule of False Position
snippet: The rule of false position is a method of successive approximations to obtain the root of an equation $\map f x = 0$ from an initial estimate or estimates of that root. It is similar to the bisection method, except that the interval in which the root is known to lie does not need to be bisected; any intermediate value may be chosen. This can allow the root to be found more quickly than using the bisection method. There are variants on this method:

title: Definition:Rule of False Position/Also known as
snippet: == Rule of False Position: Also known as == The rule of false position is also known by its Latin name regula falsi. It is also known as the method of false position. Some sources refer to it as trial and improvement.

title: Definition:Rule of False Position/Double Position
snippet: thumb The method of double position is a category of the rule of false position in which two estimates $a_0$ and $b_0$ are made such that $\map f {a_0}$ and $\map f {b_0}$ are both close to zero but of opposite sign. These estimates are then used as starting values in the formula: $a_{n + 1} = a_n - \dfrac {\paren {b_n - a_n} \map f {a_n} } {\map f {b_n} - \map f {a_n} }$ where, for $n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$, $b_{n + 1}$ is chosen from $a_n$ and $b_n$ so that $\map f {b_{n + 1} }$ is of opposite sign to $\map f {a_{n + 1} }$.

title: Definition:Rule of False Position/Simple Position
snippet: The method of simple position is a category of the rule of false position in which a single estimate $a_0$ is made, and an iteration of the form: $a_{n + 1} = \map g {a_n}$ is used, for $n = 1, 2, \ldots$

title: Definition:Rule of Formation
snippet: Let $\FF$ be a formal language whose alphabet is $\AA$. The rules of formation of $\FF$ are the rules which define how to construct collations in $\AA$ which are well-formed. That is, the rules of formation tell you how to build collations featuring symbols from the alphabet $\AA$ which are part of the formal language $\FF$. The rules of formation of a formal language together constitute its formal grammar. There are no strict guidelines on what a rule of formation should look like, since they are employed to produce such strict guidelines.

title: Definition:Rule of Formation/Also known as
snippet: == Rule of Formation: Also known as == Rules of formation are also referred to in some sources as rules of syntax. Some sources prefer the construct formation rules.

title: Definition:Rule of Inference
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a formal language. Part of defining a proof system $\mathscr P$ for $\LL$ is to specify its rules of inference. A rule of inference is a specification of a valid means to conclude new theorems in $\mathscr P$ from given theorems and axioms of $\mathscr P$. Often, the formulation of rules of inference also appeals to the notion of provable consequence to be able to deal with assumptions as part of a proof.

title: Definition:Rule of Inference/Also known as
snippet: == Rule of Inference: Also known as == A rule of inference is also known as: an inference rule a rule of transformation or a transformation rule a rule of derivation a rule of proof a rule of deduction. With all these, literature might have a specific meaning attached, so be careful before treating any of these as synonyms. On , proof rule and rule of inference are the terminology of choice and are used interchangeably.

title: Definition:Rule of Inference/Structure
snippet: In most cases, an application of a proof rule can be given a structure, as follows: Definition: This specifies what the proof rule actually does. Note the careful use of can and may in the definition: Can implies that it is possible to achieve something based on the structure of the system which is being constructed. May implies that this is what this particular proof rule is allowing you to do. Abbreviation: When deriving a sequent, it is convenient to use a precisely defined shorthand to indicate which rule is being applied at a particular point.

title: Definition:Ruled Surface
snippet: A ruled surface is a surface which can be generated by a moving straight line.

title: Definition:Ruler
snippet: A ruler is a straightedge with a scale included on it to to measure or construct straight lines of a given length.

title: Definition:Rules for Abbreviation of WFF of Propositional Logic/Adding Brackets
snippet: == Rules for Abbreviation of WFFs == The standard abbreviation is usually easier to read than the WFF it came from. However, it is sometimes convenient to clarify a particularly complicated WFF by adding brackets. Hence, for example, in order to emphasise that the negation sign has a higher binding priority than a binary connective, we might wish to write: $\paren {\neg \mathbf A} \land \mathbf B$ instead of: $\neg \mathbf A \land \mathbf B$. This would also be termed an abbreviation, even though it is not actually any shorter.

title: Definition:Run (Analytic Geometry)
snippet: Let $P_1 = \tuple {x_1, y_1}$ and $P_2 = \tuple {x_2, y_2}$ be points in the Cartesian plane. The run from $P_1$ to $P_2$ is the difference between their abscissae: $x_2 - x_1$

title: Definition:Run (Analytic Geometry)/Also known as
snippet: == Run: Also known as == The run between two points is also known as their $x$-step.

title: Definition:Run (Statistics)
snippet: A run is a sequence of observations which follows some specified pattern.

title: Definition:Runge-Kutta Method
snippet: A Runge-Kutta method is one of a family of numerical differentiation techniques for solving differential equations of the form: $\dfrac {\d y} {\d x} = \map f {x, y}$ given an initial condition $\map y a = y_a$. Such a method generates a sequence of approximations: $\map y n \approx \map y {x_n}$ in which $y_{n + 1}$ is a linear combination of values of $\map f {x, y}$ evaluated with $x \in \closedint {x_n} {x_{n + 1} }$ and various arguments $y$.

title: Definition:Runge-Kutta Method/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Runge-Kutta Method == The Runge-Kutta methods were devised by in $1895$, and independently by in $1901$.

title: Definition:Russell Class
snippet: The Russell class, denoted $\operatorname{Ru}$, equals the class of all sets $x$ that are not elements of themselves: $\operatorname{Ru} = \set {x: x \notin x}$

title: Definition:Rusty Compass
snippet: A rusty compass is (despite what its name may make it seem) an ideal tool for drawing circles. It differs from a normal compass in that, once it has been opened, it is too stiff and rusty to be changed. Hence it can draw circles with only one radius.

title: Definition:Rusty Compass/Also known as
snippet: == Rusty Compass: Also known as == A rusty compass is also known as a fixed compass. Category:Definitions/Compasses

title: Definition:Rydberg Constant
snippet: == Physical Constant == The Rydberg constant is the physical constant in the Rydberg Formula that relates the wavenumber of a photon released or absorbed by a hydrogen atom to the quantum state transition of its electron. Its value is equal to the minimum wavenumber of a photon that is capable of ejecting a ground-state electron from a hydrogen atom. $R_\infty = \dfrac {m_\E \E^4} {8 \varepsilon_0^2 h^3 c}$ where: $m_\E$ denotes the electron rest mass $\E$ denotes the elementary charge $\varepsilon_0$ denotes the vacuum permittivity $h$ denotes Planck's constant $c$ denotes the speed of light.

title: Definition:Rydberg Constant/Dimension
snippet: The Rydberg constant has the dimension $\mathsf {L^{-1} }$.

title: Definition:Rydberg Constant/Value
snippet: == Rydberg Constant: Value == The value of the Rydberg constant is: {{eqn | l = R_\infty | o = \approx | r = 1 \cdotp 09737 \, 31568 \, 160(21) \times 10^7 | c = $\mathrm {m^{-1} }$ }} {{eqn | o = \approx | r = 1 \cdotp 09737 \, 31568 \, 160(21) \times 10^5 | c = $\mathrm {cm^{-1} }$ }}

title: Definition:Rydberg Energy
snippet: The Rydberg energy is the energy of the photon whose wavenumber is the Rydberg constant.

title: Definition:Rydberg Energy/Also known as
snippet: == Rydberg Energy: Also known as == The Rydberg energy is also known as the Rydberg unit, as it is used as a unit of measurement in certain contexts. Category:Definitions/Rydberg Energy

title: Definition:Rydberg Energy/Value
snippet: == Rydberg Energy: Value == The value of the Rydberg energy is: {{eqn | l = \mathrm {Ry} | o = \approx | r = 13 \cdotp 60569 \, 31229 \, 94(26) | c = electron volts }} {{eqn | o = \approx | r = 2 \cdotp 17987 \, 23611 \, 035(42) \times 10^{-18} | c = joules }}

title: Definition:SI/Energy
snippet: Various SI units of energy which have specific names are as follows:

title: Definition:SI/Energy/Electron Volt
snippet: The electron volt is a SI unit of energy. It is defined as: the amount of kinetic energy gained by a single electron accelerating from rest through an electric potential difference of $1$ volt in a vacuum.

title: Definition:SI/Energy/Joule
snippet: The joule is the SI unit of energy. It is defined as being: the energy transferred to (or work done on) a body when a force of $1$ newton acts on that body in the direction of the force's motion through a distance of $1$ metre the energy dissipated as heat when an electric current of one ampere passes through a resistance of one ohm for one second. Thus: $1 \, \mathrm J = 1 \, \mathrm N \, \mathrm m$

title: Definition:SI/Energy/Kilojoule
snippet: The kilojoule is an SI unit of energy.

title: Definition:SI/Energy/Kilowatt-Hour
snippet: The kilowatt-hour is an SI unit of energy. It is defined as being: the energy expended when a power of $1$ kilowatt is applied for $1$ hour.

title: Definition:SI/Energy/Megajoule
snippet: The megajoule is an SI unit of energy.

title: Definition:SI/Energy/Milliwatt-Hour
snippet: The milliwatt-hour is an SI unit of energy. It is defined as being: the energy expended when a power of $1$ milliwatt is applied for $1$ hour.

title: Definition:SI/Force
snippet: Various SI units of force which have specific names are as follows:

title: Definition:SI/Force/Kilogram Force
snippet: The kilogram force is an SI unit of force. It is defined as being: The gravitational force exerted on a mass of one kilogram on the surface of Earth. In this context, the value of the standard acceleration due to gravity is used, taken to be $9.80665 \, \mathrm m \, \mathrm s^{-2}$.

title: Definition:SI/Force/Newton
snippet: The newton is an SI unit of force. It is defined as being: The amount of force required to accelerate a mass of one kilogram at a rate of one metre per second squared. This arises from Newton's Second Law of Motion, which states that such an acceleration exists under the influence of such a force.

title: Definition:SI/Power
snippet: Various SI units of power which have specific names are as follows:

title: Definition:SI/Power/Kilowatt
snippet: The kilowatt is an SI unit of power.

title: Definition:SI/Power/Watt
snippet: The watt is the SI unit of power. It is defined as being the rate at which $1$ joule of energy is uniformly transformed in $1$ second: $1 \, \mathrm W = 1 \, \mathrm J \, \mathrm s^{-1}$ Hence it can be understood as: the rate at which work is done when the velocity of a body is held constant at $1$ metre per second against a constant opposing force of $1$ newton the rate at which work is performed when an electric current of $1$ ampere flows across an electrical potential difference of $1$ volt.

title: Definition:SI/Pressure
snippet: Various SI units of pressure which have specific names are as follows:

title: Definition:SI/Pressure/Megapascal
snippet: The megapascal is an SI unit of pressure.

title: Definition:SI/Pressure/Pascal
snippet: The pascal is the SI unit of pressure. It is defined as being: The amount of pressure required to apply a force of $1$ newton over an area of $1$ square metre

title: Definition:SI Supplementary Units/Also defined as
snippet: == SI Supplementary Units: Also defined as == Some sources categorize the supplementary units as base units. Some, however, categorize them as derived SI units. The decision to treat them as separate from both, and to use them directly for the construction of further derived SI units, has been generally accepted.

title: Definition:SI Units
snippet: The SI Units are the elements of the .

snippet: The base SI units are as follows: | metre | $\mathrm m$ | $\mathsf L$: Length | $l$ | kilogram | $\mathrm {kg}$ | $\mathsf M$: Mass | $m$ | second | $\mathrm s$ | $\mathsf T$: Time | $t$ | ampere | $\mathrm A$ | $\mathsf I$: Electric Current | $I$ | kelvin | $\mathrm K$ | $\Theta$: Temperature | $T$ | candela | $\mathrm {cd}$ | $\mathsf J$: Luminous Intensity | $I_v$ | mole | $\mathrm {mol}$ | $\mathsf N$: Amount of Substance | $n$
