snippet: The units derived from the SI base units include the following: | Square metre | $\mathrm m^2$ | Area | $\mathsf L^2$ | $\mathrm m^2$ | Cubic metre | $\mathrm m^3$ | Volume | $\mathsf L^3$ | $\mathrm m^3$ | colspan="6" align = "center"| Mechanics | Newton | $\mathrm N$ | Force | $\mathsf M \mathsf L \mathsf T^{-2}$ | $\mathrm {kg} \, \mathrm m \, \mathrm s^{-2}$ | Mass times acceleration | Joule | $\mathrm J$ | Energy and work | $\mathsf M \mathsf L^2 \mathsf T^{-2}$ | $\mathrm {kg} \, \mathrm m^2 \, \mathrm s^{-2}$ | $\mathrm N \, \mathrm m$ | Watt | $\mathrm W$ | Power | $\mathsf M \mathsf…

title: Definition:SI Units/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on SI Units == The SI units originated in the work done by to establish a decimal system for weights and measures.

title: Definition:SI Units/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on SI Units == The abbreviation SI in the term SI units is from the French Le Système International d'Unités (the ).

title: Definition:SI Units/Supplementary Units
snippet: The supplementary SI units are as follows: | radian | $\mathrm {rad}$ | $\text {none}$ | plane angle | $\theta$ | steradian | $\mathrm {sr}$ | $\text {none}$ | solid angle |

title: Definition:Saddle Point (Game Theory)
snippet: Let $G$ be a two-player zero-sum game. Let $G$ be defined by a payoff table $T$. Let $E$ be an entry in $T$ such that: $E$ is the smallest entry in its row $E$ is the largest entry in its column. Then $E$ is a saddle point of $G$.

title: Definition:Saddle Point (Geometry)
snippet: Let $\SS$ be a surface defined by the Cartesian equation $z = \map f {x, y}$. Let $P$ be a point on $\SS$ such that: the partial derivatives $\dfrac {\partial z} {\partial x}$ and $\dfrac {\partial z} {\partial y}$ are both zero but: there is no local maximum or local minimum at $P$. Then $P$ is a saddle point of $\SS$.

title: Definition:Safe Prime
snippet: == Safe Prime == A safe prime is a prime number $p$ of the form: $p = 2 q + 1$ where $q$ is also a prime number. It follows from this definition that $q$ is a Sophie Germain prime.

title: Definition:Salem Constant
snippet: The Salem constant is the greatest real root of Lehmer's polynomial: $x^{10} + x^9 - x^7 - x^6 - x^5 - x^4 - x^3 + x + 1 = 0$ Its value is approximately: $1 \cdotp 17628 \, 08182 \, 599 \ldots$

title: Definition:Salem Constant/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Salem Constant == The Salem constant was discovered by in $1933$. It was conjectured in $1977$ by that it is the smallest of the Salem numbers.

title: Definition:Salem Number
snippet: A Salem number is a real algebraic integer $\alpha$ such that: $\alpha > 1$ its conjugate roots all have absolute value no greater than $1$, at least one of which has absolute value exactly $1$.

title: Definition:Salient Angle
snippet: Let $P$ be a polygon. Let $V$ be a vertex of $P$ whose internal angle $A$ is less than $180 \degrees$. Then $A$ is known as a salient angle.

title: Definition:Salient Point
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a curve. A salient point of $\CC$ is a point on $\CC$ where two branches meet and have different tangents.

title: Definition:Same Parity/Also known as
snippet: == Same Parity: Also known as == Some sources refer to a pair of integers $\set {z_1, z_2}$ having the same parity as having even parity. Note the difference between this and the definition of even parity as being a property of an individual integer as being even.

title: Definition:Sample
snippet: A sample is a non-empty, finite, proper subset of a population.

title: Definition:Sample/Size
snippet: The size of a sample is the number of elements it has. Thus a sample containing $n$ observations is a sample of size $n$.

title: Definition:Sample Correlation Coefficient
snippet: Let $S = \sequence {x_i, y_i}$ be a sequence of paired observations from a population. The sample correlation coefficient of $S$ is given by: $r = \dfrac {s_{x y} } {\sqrt {s_{x x} s_{y y} } }$ where: $s_{x y}$ denotes the sum of the products of deviations of $x_i$ and $y_i$ from their means $s_{x x}$ and $s_{y y}$ are the sums of the squares of the deviations of $x_i$ and $y_i$ from their respective means.

title: Definition:Sample Covariance
snippet: Let $S$ be a sample of $n$ paired observations $\tuple {x_i, y_i}$ for $i \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n}$. The sample covariance of $S$ is: $c_{x y} = \ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \dfrac 1 n \paren {x_i - \hat x} \paren {y_i - \hat y}$ where $\hat x$ and $\hat y$ are the means of $\set {x_i: i \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n} }$ and $\set {y_i: i \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n} }$ respectively.

title: Definition:Sample Distribution Function
snippet: Let $S = \set {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ be a sample of size $n$ of ordinal data. Let $x_{\paren i}$ be the $i$th order statistic in $S$. The sample distribution function $\map {S_n} x$ is defined as the function on $S$ which takes the values: $\map {S_n} x = \begin {cases} 0 & : x \le x_{\paren 1} \\ \\ \dfrac i n & : x_{\paren i} \le x \le x_{\paren {i + 1} } \\ \\ 1 & : x \ge x_{\paren n} \end {cases}$

title: Definition:Sample Distribution Function/Also known as
snippet: == Sample Distribution Function: Also known as == A sample distribution function is also known as an empirical distribution function.

title: Definition:Sample Mean
snippet: Let $S = \set {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ be a random sample from a population. The sample mean of $S$ is defined and denoted as: $\overline x = \ds \sum \dfrac {x_i} n$

title: Definition:Sample Mean of Stochastic Process
snippet: Let $S$ be a stochastic process giving rise to a time series $T$. The sample mean of $S$ over a set of $N$ successive values $\set {z_1, z_2, \dotsb, z_N}$ is defined as: $\overline z := \dfrac 1 N \ds \sum_{t \mathop = 1}^N z_t$

title: Definition:Sample Path of Stochastic Process
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\struct {E, \EE}$ be a measurable space. Let $\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an $E$-valued stochastic process. For each $\omega \in \Omega$, define $p_\omega: I \to E$ by: $\map {p_\omega} i = \map {X_i} \omega$ for each $i \in I$. We call the mappings $p_\omega$ the sample paths of $\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$.

title: Definition:Sample Space
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an experiment. The sample space of $\EE$ is usually denoted $\Omega$ (Greek capital omega), and is defined as the set of all possible outcomes of $\EE$.

title: Definition:Sample Space/Also denoted as
snippet: == Sample Space: Also known as == Some sources denote the sample space of an experiment $\EE$ as $S$.

title: Definition:Sample Space/Discrete
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an experiment. Let $\Omega$ denote the sample space of $\EE$. If $\Omega$ is a countable set, whether finite or infinite, then it is known as a discrete sample space.

title: Definition:Sample Statistic
snippet: A sample statistic is a numerical description of a sample.

title: Definition:Sample Statistic/Also known as
snippet: == Sample Statistic: Also known as == A sample statistic can also be seen referred to as just a statistic when it is not necessary to emphasize the distinction between a sample statistic and a population parameter. Another word for sample statistic is datum. Also note the plural form statistics (as used in this context), also known as data. The word data is more commonly encountered than statistics, as the latter word is also used to mean the mathematical discipline as opposed to these particular elements.

title: Definition:Sample Statistic/Continuous
snippet: Data which can be described with a continuous variable obtained by the process of measurement are known as continuous data.

title: Definition:Sample Statistic/Discrete
snippet: Data which can be described with a discrete variable are known as discrete data.

title: Definition:Sample Statistic/Raw
snippet: Raw data are collected data which have not been organized or analysed in any way.

title: Definition:Sample Survey
snippet: A sample survey is a study to estimate characteristics of a population in which those characteristics are observed for only a portion of that population.

title: Definition:Sample Variance
snippet: Let $S = \set {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ be a sample of size $n$. The sample variance of $S$ is the second central moment of $S$.

title: Definition:Sample Variance/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S = \set {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ be a sample of size $n$. The sample variance (of $S$) is defined and denoted as: ${s_x}^2 := \dfrac 1 n \ds \sum_i \paren {x_i - \overline x}^2$ where $\overline x$ denotes the sample mean of $S$.

title: Definition:Sample Variance/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S = \set {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ be a sample of size $n$. The sample variance (of $S$) is defined and denoted as: ${s_x}^2 := \dfrac 1 n \ds \sum_i {x_i}^2 - \paren {\sum_i x_i}^2$

title: Definition:Sample Variance of Stochastic Process
snippet: Let $S$ be a stochastic process giving rise to a time series $T$. The sample variance of $S$ over a set of $N$ successive values $\set {z_1, z_2, \dotsb, z_N}$ is defined as: $\ds \hat \sigma_z^2 := \frac 1 N \sum_{t \mathop = 1}^N \paren {z_t - \overline z}^2$ where $\overline z$ denotes the sample mean of $S$ over $\set {z_1, z_2, \dotsb, z_N}$.

title: Definition:Sampling Distribution
snippet: A sampling distribution is the probability distribution of a statistic.

title: Definition:Sampling Error
snippet: Let $E$ be an estimate of a population parameter based on a sample. Let $P$ be the true value of the population parameter. The sampling error is the difference between $E$ and $P$.

title: Definition:Sampling Frame
snippet: A sampling frame is a specification of all units in a population in sufficient detail in order that a random sample may be selected.

title: Definition:Sampling Frame/Also known as
snippet: == Sampling Frame: Also known as == A sampling frame is also known just as a frame.

title: Definition:Sampling Function
snippet: The sampling function is the Schwartz distribution $\operatorname {III}_T: \map \DD \R \to \R$ defined as: $\forall x \in \R: \map {\operatorname {III}_T } x := \ds \sum_{n \mathop \in \Z} \map \delta {x - T n}$ where: $T \in \R_{\ne 0}$ is a non-zero real number $\delta$ denotes the Dirac delta distribution. When $T = 1$, it is usually omitted: $\forall x \in \R: \map {\operatorname {III} } x := \ds \sum_{n \mathop \in \Z} \map \delta {x - n}$

title: Definition:Sampling Function/2 Dimensional
snippet: Let $\operatorname {III}: \R \to \R$ denote the sampling function. The $2$-dimensional form of $\operatorname {III}$ is defined and denoted: $\forall x, y \in \R: \map {\operatorname { {}^2 III} } {x, y} := \map {\operatorname {III} } x \map {\operatorname {III} } y$

title: Definition:Sampling Function/Also known as
snippet: == Sampling Function: Also known as == The sampling function $\operatorname {III}$ can also be seen referred to as: the replicating function the Dirac comb. It can be referred to and voiced as shah.

title: Definition:Sampling Function/Graph
snippet: The graph of the sampling function $\operatorname {III}: \map \DD \R \to \R$ is illustrated below: 600px It is to be understood that the blue arrows represent rays from the $x$-axis for constant $n \in \Z$.

title: Definition:Sampling Function/Linguistic Note
snippet: The name shah for the sampling function derives from its similarity in shape and appearance to the Russian Ш, whose name is itself pronounced shah. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Sampling Theory
snippet: Sampling theory is the branch of statistics which studies obtaining samples and making inferences about population parameters using such samples as a basis.

title: Definition:Satisfaction/Tuple
snippet: An ordered $n$-tuple $T$ is said to satisfy an open statement $S$ the predicate of $S$ is true of $T$.

title: Definition:Satisfiable
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a logical language. Let $\mathscr M$ be a formal semantics for $\LL$.

title: Definition:Satisfiable/Boolean Interpretations
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a WFF of propositional logic. $\mathbf A$ is called satisfiable (for boolean interpretations) : $\map v {\mathbf A} = \T$ for some boolean interpretation $v$ for $\mathbf A$. In terms of validity, this can be rendered: $v \models_{\mathrm{BI}} \mathbf A$ that is, $\mathbf A$ is valid in the boolean interpretation $v$ of $\mathbf A$.

title: Definition:Satisfiable/Formula
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a logical language. Let $\mathscr M$ be a formal semantics for $\LL$. A logical formula $\phi$ of $\LL$ is satisfiable for $\mathscr M$ : $\phi$ is valid in some structure $\MM$ of $\mathscr M$ That is, there exists some structure $\MM$ of $\mathscr M$ such that: $\MM \models_{\mathscr M} \phi$

title: Definition:Satisfiable/Set of Formulas
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a logical language. Let $\mathscr M$ be a formal semantics for $\LL$. A collection $\FF$ of logical formulas of $\LL$ is satisfiable for $\mathscr M$ : There is some $\mathscr M$-model $\MM$ of $\FF$ That is, there exists some structure $\MM$ of $\mathscr M$ such that: $\MM \models_{\mathscr M} \FF$

title: Definition:Saturated Model
snippet: Let $T$ be an $\LL$-theory. Let $\kappa$ be an infinite cardinal. A model $\MM$ of $T$ is $\kappa$-saturated for every subset $A$ of the universe of $\MM$ of cardinality strictly less than $\kappa$, and for every $n \in \N$, every complete $n$-type $p$ over $A$ is realized in $\MM$. That is, $\MM$ is $\kappa$-saturated for all $A \subseteq \MM$ with $\card A < \kappa$, and for all $n \in \N$, each $p \in \map {S_n^\MM} A$ is realized in $\MM$. We say $\MM$ is saturated it is $\kappa$-saturated where $\kappa$ is the cardinality of the universe of $\MM$.

title: Definition:Saturated Multiplicatively Closed Subset of Ring
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $S \subseteq A$ be a multiplicatively closed subset. Then $S$ is saturated it equals its saturation, that is: $x, y \in A, xy \in S \implies x,y \in S$

title: Definition:Saturated Set (Equivalence Relation)
snippet: Let $\sim$ be an equivalence relation on a set $S$. Let $T\subset S$ be a subset.

title: Definition:Saturated Set (Equivalence Relation)/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\sim$ be an equivalence relation on a set $S$. Let $T \subset S$ be a subset. $T$ is saturated it equals its saturation: $T = \overline T$ Category:Definitions/Equivalence Relations

title: Definition:Saturated Set (Equivalence Relation)/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\sim$ be an equivalence relation on a set $S$. Let $T\subset S$ be a subset. $T$ is saturated it is a union of equivalence classes: $\ds \exists U \subset S : T = \bigcup_{u \mathop \in U} \eqclass u {}$ Category:Definitions/Equivalence Relations

title: Definition:Saturated Set (Equivalence Relation)/Definition 3
snippet: Let $\sim$ be an equivalence relation on a set $S$. Let $T\subset S$ be a subset. $T$ is saturated it is the preimage of some set under the quotient mapping: $\exists V \subset S / \sim \; : T = q^{-1} \left[{V}\right]$ Category:Definitions/Equivalence Relations

title: Definition:Saturation
snippet: In Abstract Algebra: Definition:Saturation (Group Action) Definition:Saturation of Multiplicatively Closed Subset of Ring In the context of Equivalence Relations: Definition:Saturation (Equivalence Relation) Definition:Saturated Set (Equivalence Relation) In Logic: Definition:Saturated Model

title: Definition:Saturation (Equivalence Relation)
snippet: Let $\sim$ be an equivalence relation on a set $S$. Let $T\subset S$ be a subset.

title: Definition:Saturation (Equivalence Relation)/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\sim$ be an equivalence relation on a set $S$. Let $T\subset S$ be a subset. The saturation of $T$ is the set of all elements that are equivalent to some element in $T$: $\overline T = \{s \in S : \exists t\in T : s\sim t\}$ Category:Definitions/Equivalence Relations

title: Definition:Saturation (Equivalence Relation)/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\sim$ be an equivalence relation on a set $S$. Let $T \subset S$ be a subset. The saturation of $T$ is the union of the equivalence classes of its elements: $\ds \overline T = \bigcup_{t \mathop \in T} \eqclass t \sim$ Category:Definitions/Equivalence Relations

title: Definition:Saturation (Equivalence Relation)/Definition 3
snippet: Let $\sim$ be an equivalence relation on a set $S$. Let $T\subset S$ be a subset. The saturation of $T$ is the preimage of its image under the quotient mapping: $\overline T = q^{-1} \sqbrk {q \sqbrk T}$ Category:Definitions/Equivalence Relations

title: Definition:Saturation (Group Action)
snippet: Let $G$ be a group acting on a set $X$. Let $S\subset X$ be a subset.

title: Definition:Saturation (Group Action)/Definition 1
snippet: Let $G$ be a group acting on a set $X$. Let $S\subset X$ be a subset. The saturation of $S$ is its saturation by the equivalence relation induced by the action. Category:Definitions/Group Actions

title: Definition:Saturation (Group Action)/Definition 2
snippet: Let $G$ be a group acting on a set $X$. Let $S \subset X$ be a subset. The saturation of $S$ is the union of its images under the group action: $\overline S = \ds \bigcup_{g \mathop \in G} g S$ Category:Definitions/Group Actions

title: Definition:Saturation of Ideal by Multiplicatively Closed Subset
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $\mathfrak a \subseteq A$ be an ideal. Let $S \subseteq A$ be a multiplicatively closed subset.

title: Definition:Saturation of Multiplicatively Closed Subset of Ring
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $S \subseteq A$ be a multiplicatively closed subset.

title: Definition:Saturn
snippet: Saturn is the sixth planet of the solar system from the sun. Its orbit lies between those of Jupiter and Uranus. Category:Definitions/Solar System

title: Definition:Sawtooth Wave
snippet: A sawtooth wave is a periodic real function $S: \R \to \R$ defined as follows: $\forall x \in \R: \map S x = \begin {cases} x & : x \in \openint {-\lambda} \lambda \\ \map S {x + 2 \lambda} & : x +\lambda \end {cases}$ where $\lambda$ is a given real constant

title: Definition:Sawtooth Wave/Graph
snippet: Let $S$ be the sawtooth wave defined as: $\forall x \in \R: \map S x = \begin {cases} x & : x \in \openint {-\lambda} \lambda \\ \map S {x + 2 \lambda} & : x +\lambda \end {cases}$ The graph of $S$ is given below: 800px Category:Definitions/Sawtooth Waves

title: Definition:Sawtooth Wave/Inverse
snippet: An inverse sawtooth wave is a periodic real function $S: \R \to \R$ defined as follows: $\forall x \in \R: \map S x = \begin {cases} -x & : x \in \openint {-\lambda} \lambda \\ \map S {x + 2 \lambda} & : x +\lambda \end {cases}$ where $\lambda$ is a given real constant

title: Definition:Sawtooth Wave/Inverse/Graph
snippet: Let $S$ be the inverse sawtooth wave defined as: $\forall x \in \R: \map S x = \begin {cases} -x & : x \in \openint {-\lambda} \lambda \\ \map S {x + 2 \lambda} & : x +\lambda \end {cases}$ The graph of $S$ is given below: 800px Category:Definitions/Sawtooth Waves

title: Definition:Sawtooth Wave/Points of Discontinuity
snippet: Let $S$ be the sawtooth wave or inverse sawtooth wave defined as: $\forall x \in \R: \map S x = \begin {cases} \pm x & : x \in \openint {-\lambda} \lambda \\ \map S {x + 2 \lambda} & : x +\lambda \end {cases}$ The points $\paren {2 r + 1} \lambda$, for $r \in \Z$, are jump discontinuities. The values $\map S {\paren {2 r + 1} \lambda}$ may or may not be explicitly defined. It is a common approach to include one of the endpoints of the interval from $-\lambda$ to $\lambda$, in order to ensure that the domain of $S$ is simply defined.

title: Definition:Scalar/Abstract Algebra
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n, \ast}_R$ be an $R$-algebraic structure with $n$ operations, where: $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n}$ is an algebraic structure with $n$ operations $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ is the scalar ring of $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n, \ast}_R$. The elements of the scalar ring $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ are called scalars. The obvious instantiations are the following:

title: Definition:Scalar/Module
snippet: Let $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_R$ be a module, where: $\struct {G, +_G}$ is an abelian group $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ is the scalar ring of $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_R$. The elements of the scalar ring $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ are called scalars.

title: Definition:Scalar/Vector Space
snippet: Let $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_K$ be a vector space, where: $\struct {G, +_G}$ is an abelian group $\struct {K, +_K, \times_K}$ is the scalar ring of $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_K$. The elements of the scalar ring $\struct {K, +_K, \times_K}$ are called scalars.

title: Definition:Scalar (Matrix Theory)
snippet: Let $\map \MM {m, n}$ be a matrix space of order $m \times n$ over an underlying structure $R$. The elements of $R$ are referred to as scalars.

title: Definition:Scalar (Tensor Theory)
snippet: A scalar is a tensor of order $0$.

title: Definition:Scalar Addition/Module
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ be a ring. Let $\struct {G, +_G}$ be an abelian group. Let $M := \struct {G, +_G, \circ}_R$ be the corresponding module over $R$ (either a left module or a right module). The ring addition operation $+_R$ on $M$ is known as scalar addition on $M$. Category:Definitions/Module Theory Category:Definitions/Scalar Addition

title: Definition:Scalar Addition/Vector Space
snippet: Let $\struct {K, +_K, \times_K}$ be a field. Let $\struct {G, +_G}$ be an abelian group. Let $V := \struct {G, +_G, \circ}_K$ be the corresponding vector space over $K$. The field addition operation $+_K$ on $V$ is known as scalar addition on $V$. Category:Definitions/Vector Spaces Category:Definitions/Scalar Addition

title: Definition:Scalar Algebra
snippet: Scalar algebra is the application of the rules of conventional algebra in order to manipulate scalar quantities.

title: Definition:Scalar Division/Vector Quantity
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$ be a vector quantity. Let $m$ be a scalar quantity. The operation of scalar division by $m$ of $\mathbf a$ is defined as: $\dfrac {\mathbf a} m = \dfrac 1 m \size {\mathbf a}$ that is, scalar multiplication by $\dfrac 1 m$ of $\mathbf a$.

title: Definition:Scalar Field (Physics)
snippet: Let $F$ be a field which acts on a region of space $S$. Let the point-function giving rise to $F$ be a scalar quantity. Then $F$ is a scalar field.

title: Definition:Scalar Matrix
snippet: A scalar matrix is a diagonal matrix all of whose elements are equal.

title: Definition:Scalar Multiplication/Also known as
snippet: == Scalar Multiplication: Also known as == Some sources refer to scalar multiplication as exterior multiplication. In the more general context of an $R$-algebraic structure, it is often referred to as the ring action of $R$ upon $S$.

title: Definition:Scalar Multiplication/Module
snippet: Let $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_R$ be an module (either a left module or a right module or both), where: $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ is a ring $\struct {G, +_G}$ is an abelian group. The operation $\ast: R \times G \to G$ is called scalar multiplication.

title: Definition:Scalar Multiplication/Vector Quantity
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$ be a vector quantity. Let $m$ be a scalar quantity. The operation of scalar multiplication by $m$ of $\mathbf a$ is denoted $m \mathbf a$ and defined such that: the magnitude of $m \mathbf a$ is equal to $m$ times the magnitude of $\mathbf a$: $\size {m \mathbf a} = m \size {\mathbf a}$ the direction of $m \mathbf a$ is the same as the direction of $\mathbf a$.

title: Definition:Scalar Multiplication/Vector Space
snippet: Let $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_K$ be a vector space, where: $\struct {K, +_K, \times_K}$ is a division ring $\struct {G, +_G}$ is an abelian group. The operation $\ast: K \times G \to G$ is called scalar multiplication.

title: Definition:Scalar Multiplication by Negative Scalar
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$ be a vector quantity. Let $-m$ be a negative scalar quantity. The operation of scalar multiplication by $-m$ of $\mathbf a$ is defined as: $-m \mathbf a := \paren {-m} \mathbf a = m \paren {-\mathbf a}$ that is, the negative of the scalar product of $m$ with $\mathbf a$.

title: Definition:Scalar Potential
snippet: Let $R$ be a region of ordinary space. Let $\mathbf V$ be a conservative vector field over $R$. By Vector Field is Expressible as Gradient of Scalar Field iff Conservative, there exists a scalar field $S$ over $R$ such that: $\grad S = \mathbf V$ where $\grad$ denotes the gradient operator. Then $S$ is referred to as the scalar potential of $\mathbf V$.

title: Definition:Scalar Product
snippet: Scalar Multiplication: the operation of multiplying a vector $\mathbf a$ by a scalar $\lambda$ to form a new vector $\lambda \mathbf a$. Matrix Scalar Product: the operation of multiplying a matrix $\mathbf A$ by a scalar $\lambda$ to form a new matrix $\lambda \mathbf A$. Dot Product: the operation $\mathbf a \cdot \mathbf b$ whereby two vector quantities $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ of the same dimension are combined to form a scalar.

title: Definition:Scalar Product Space
snippet: A scalar product space is a finite-dimensional vector space equipped with a scalar product.

title: Definition:Scalar Projection
snippet: Let $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ be vector quantities.

title: Definition:Scalar Projection/Also known as
snippet: == Scalar Projection: Also known as == The scalar projection of $\mathbf u$ onto $\mathbf v$ is also known as: the scalar component the scalar resolution the scalar resolute of $\mathbf u$ in the direction of $\mathbf v$. The notation for $u_{\parallel \mathbf v}$ also varies throughout the literature. The following forms can sometimes be seen: $u_1$ $\norm {\proj_\mathbf v \mathbf u}$ Category:Definitions/Vector Projections

title: Definition:Scalar Projection/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ be vector quantities. The scalar projection of $\mathbf u$ onto $\mathbf v$, denoted $u_{\parallel \mathbf v}$, is the magnitude of the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf u$ onto a straight line which is parallel to $\mathbf v$. Hence $u_{\parallel \mathbf v}$ is the magnitude $\norm {\mathbf u} \cos \theta$, where: $\norm {\mathbf u}$ is the magnitude of $\mathbf u$ $\cos \theta$ is the angle between $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$. 340px

title: Definition:Scalar Projection/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ be vector quantities. The scalar projection of $\mathbf u$ onto $\mathbf v$ is defined and denoted: $u_{\parallel \mathbf v} = \dfrac {\mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v} {\norm {\mathbf v} }$ where: $\cdot$ denotes the dot product $\norm {\mathbf v}$ denotes the magnitude of $\mathbf v$. 340px

title: Definition:Scalar Projection/Definition 3
snippet: Let $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ be vector quantities. The scalar projection of $\mathbf u$ onto $\mathbf v$ is defined and denoted: $u_{\parallel \mathbf v} = \mathbf u \cdot \mathbf {\hat v}$ where: $\cdot$ denotes the dot product $\mathbf {\hat v}$ denotes the unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf v$. 340px

title: Definition:Scalar Quantity
snippet: A scalar quantity is a real-world concept that needs for its model a mathematical object which contains only one (usually numeric) component.

title: Definition:Scalar Quantity/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Scalar Quantities ==

title: Definition:Scalar Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n, \ast}_R$ be an $R$-algebraic structure with $n$ operations, where: $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ is a ring $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n}$ is an algebraic structure with $n$ operations $\ast: R \times S \to S$ is the ring action. Then the ring $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ is called the scalar ring of $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n, \ast}_R$. If the scalar ring is understood, then $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n, \ast}_R$ can be rendered $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n, \ast}$.

title: Definition:Scalar Ring/Module
snippet: Let $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_R$ be a module, where: $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ is a ring $\struct {G, +_G}$ is an abelian group $\ast: R \times G \to G$ is a binary operation. Then the ring $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ is called the scalar ring of $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_R$. If the scalar ring is understood, then $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_R$ can be rendered $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}$.

title: Definition:Scalar Ring/Unitary Module
snippet: Let $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_R$ be a unitary module, where: $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ is a ring with unity $\struct {G, +_G}$ is an abelian group $\ast: R \times G \to G$ is the ring action. Then the ring $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ is called the scalar ring of $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_R$. If the scalar ring is understood, then $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_R$ can be rendered $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}$.

title: Definition:Scalar Ring/Vector Space over Division Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_K$ be a vector space over a division ring, where: $\struct {K, +_K, \times_K}$ is a division ring $\struct {G, +_G}$ is an abelian group $\struct {G, +_G}$ $\ast: K \times G \to G$ is the ring action. Then the division ring $\struct {K, +_K, \times_K}$ is called the scalar division ring of $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_K$, or just scalar ring. If the scalar division ring is understood, then $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_K$ can be rendered $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}$. Category:Definitions/Vector Algebra

title: Definition:Scalar Ring/Zero Scalar
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n, \ast}_R$ be an $R$-algebraic structure with $n$ operations, where: $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ is a ring $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n}$ is an algebraic structure with $n$ operations $\ast: R \times S \to S$ is a binary operation. Let $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ be the scalar ring of $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n, \ast}_R$. The zero of the scalar ring is called the zero scalar.

title: Definition:Scalar Triple Product
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$, $\mathbf b$ and $\mathbf c$ be vectors in a Cartesian $3$-space: where $\tuple {\mathbf i, \mathbf j, \mathbf k}$ is the standard ordered basis of $\mathbf V$.

title: Definition:Scalar Triple Product/Also known as
snippet: == Scalar Triple Product: Also known as == The scalar triple product is also known as the triple scalar product. Some sources denote the scalar triple product as $\sqbrk {\mathbf a \mathbf b \mathbf c}$.

title: Definition:Scalar Triple Product/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$, $\mathbf b$ and $\mathbf c$ be vectors in a Cartesian $3$-space: where $\tuple {\mathbf i, \mathbf j, \mathbf k}$ is the standard ordered basis. The scalar triple product of $\mathbf a$, $\mathbf b$ and $\mathbf c$ is defined and denoted as: $\sqbrk {\mathbf a, \mathbf b, \mathbf c} := \mathbf a \cdot \paren {\mathbf b \times \mathbf c}$ where: $\cdot$ denotes dot product $\times$ denotes vector cross product.

title: Definition:Scalar Triple Product/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$, $\mathbf b$ and $\mathbf c$ be vectors in a Cartesian $3$-space: where $\tuple {\mathbf i, \mathbf j, \mathbf k}$ is the standard ordered basis. The scalar triple product of $\mathbf a$, $\mathbf b$ and $\mathbf c$ is defined and denoted as: $\sqbrk {\mathbf a, \mathbf b, \mathbf c} := \begin {vmatrix} a_i & a_j & a_k \\ b_i & b_j & b_k \\ c_i & c_j & c_k \\ \end {vmatrix}$ where $\begin {vmatrix} \ldots \end {vmatrix}$ is interpreted as a determinant.

title: Definition:Scale
snippet: Scale of Measurement: a tool for providing a measurement of a measurable physical quantity $Q$ by means of an indication at a particular point on that scale. Definition:Scale of Magnitude

title: Definition:Scale of Measurement
snippet: A scale is a tool for providing a measurement of a measurable physical quantity $Q$ by means of an indication at a particular point on that scale.

title: Definition:Scale of Measurement/Linear
snippet: A linear scale is a scale of measurement such that measurements of a quantity satisfy a linear function with respect to the indications on the scale itself. There are two basic types of linear scale:

title: Definition:Scale of Measurement/Linear Interval
snippet: A linear interval scale is a scale of measurement which has an arbitrary zero, but measurements of a quantity such as $x$ and $y$ performed on two such scales satisfy a relationship of the form: $y = m x + c$ Hence, in addition to the relationship of equality and ordering, measurements on a linear interval scale are such that for any two quantities the ratios of the differences for each scale is constant.

title: Definition:Scale of Measurement/Linear Ratio
snippet: A linear ratio scale is a scale of measurement with a fixed zero, such that measurements of a quantity such as $x$ and $y$ performed on two such scales satisfy a relationship of the form: $y = m x$ Hence, in addition to the relationship of equality and ordering, ratios of measurements for each scale is constant.

title: Definition:Scale of Measurement/Logarithmic
snippet: A logarithmic scale is a scale of measurement on which the measurement of a quantity is proportional to the logarithm of that quantity.

title: Definition:Scale of Measurement/Nominal
snippet: A nominal scale is a scale of measurement which merely allocates items into categories. The only meaningful relationship between items so assigned is that of: equality, when items belong to the same category or: non-equality, when items belong to different categories.

title: Definition:Scale of Measurement/Normal Probability
snippet: A normal probability scale is a scale of measurement which enables the plotting of the cumulative distribution function of a normal distribution as a straight line.

title: Definition:Scale of Measurement/Ordinal
snippet: A ordinal scale is a scale of measurement which allocates items into categories which themselves can be ordered. The items themselves may not necessarily be ordered individually. Hence in addition to the relationship of equality, items may also be ranked according to category such that the inequalities $$ may be meaningful.

title: Definition:Scaled Euclidean Metric
snippet: Let $\R_{>0}$ be the set of strictly positive real numbers. Let $\delta: \R_{>0} \times \R_{>0} \to \R$ be the metric on $\R_{>0}$ defined as: $\forall x, y \in \R_{>0}: \map \delta {x, y} = \dfrac {\size {x - y} } {x y}$ Then $\delta$ is the scaled Euclidean metric on $\R_{>0}$.

title: Definition:Scaled Euclidean Metric/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Scaled Euclidean Metric == Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Scatter Diagram
snippet: A scatter diagram is a technique of graphical representation of the distribution of ordered pairs of random variables. The ordered pairs are treated as points in a Cartesian plane: the first coordinate along the $x$-axis and the second coordinate along the $y$-axis.

title: Definition:Scatter Diagram/Also known as
snippet: == Scatter Diagram: Also known as == A scatter diagram is also known as a scattergram or a scatterplot / scatter plot.

title: Definition:Scattered Space/Also defined as
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. According to , a topological space $T$ is defined as scattered: ... if it contains no non-empty dense-in-itself subsets; ... and it is immaterial whether those subsets are closed or not. On the other hand, [https://planetmath.org/scatteredspace PlanetMath's definition] specifically requires that in order for a space to be classified as scattered, only its closed subsets are required to contain one or more isolated points.

title: Definition:Scattered Space/Also known as
snippet: == Scattered Space: Also known as == A scattered space is also known as a dispersed space.

title: Definition:Scattered Space/Definition 1
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is scattered it contains no non-empty subset which is dense-in-itself. That is, $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is scattered every non-empty subset $H$ of $S$ contains at least one point which is isolated in $H$.

title: Definition:Scattered Space/Definition 2
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is scattered it contains no non-empty closed set which is dense-in-itself. That is, $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is scattered every non-empty closed set $H$ of $S$ contains at least one point which is isolated in $H$.

title: Definition:Schauder Basis
snippet: Let $\Bbb F \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm \cdot}$ be a normed vector space over $\Bbb F$. Let $\set {e_n : n \in \N}$ be a countable subset of $X$.

title: Definition:Schauder Basis/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\Bbb F \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm \cdot}$ be a normed vector space over $\Bbb F$. Let $\set {e_n : n \in \N}$ be a countable subset of $X$. We say that $\set {e_n : n \in \N}$ is a Schauder basis for $X$ : for each $x \in X$, there exists a unique sequence $\sequence {\map {\alpha_j} x}_{j \mathop \in \N}$ in $\Bbb F$ such that: $\ds x = \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^\infty \map {\alpha_j} x e_j$ where convergence of the infinite series is understood in $\struct {X, \norm \cdot}$.

title: Definition:Schauder Basis/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\Bbb F \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm \cdot}$ be a normed vector space over $\Bbb F$. Let $\set {e_n : n \in \N}$ be a countable subset of $X$. We say that $\set {e_n : n \in \N}$ is a Schauder basis for $X$ : $(1): \quad$ for each $x \in X$, there exists a sequence $\sequence {\alpha_j}_{j \mathop \in \N}$ in $\Bbb F$ such that: $\ds x = \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^\infty \alpha_j e_j$ $(2): \quad$ whenever $\sequence {\alpha_j}_{j \mathop \in \N}$ is a sequence in $\Bbb F$ such that: $\ds \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^\infty \alpha_j e_j = 0$ we have $\alpha_j = 0$ for each $j \in \N$…

title: Definition:Scheme
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ be a locally ringed space. Let $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ be such that: every point $x \in X$ has an open neighborhood $U_x$ such that: the restriction of $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ to $U_x$ is an affine scheme. Then $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ is called a scheme.

title: Definition:Scheme of Abbreviation
snippet: When translating from a series of sentences in natural language into a collection of propositional formulas in symbolic logic, it is necessary to replace each simple statement with a statement label. As stated in the definition of statement label, it is imperative that each statement be replaced with a different label. A scheme of abbreviation is the list of simple statements, together with their associated statement labels, for reference and unambiguous key in order to translate any conclusion reached back into natural language.

title: Definition:Scheme of Abbreviation/Abbreviation
snippet: An abbreviation is an ordered pair of which: .

title: Definition:School
snippet: A school is a group of thinkers who espouse a particular philosophical position.

title: Definition:Schreier Domain
snippet: A ring $A$ is a Schreier domain it is an integrally closed integral domain in which every non-zero element is primal. Category:Definitions/Ring Theory Category:Definitions/Factorization

title: Definition:Schrödinger's Equation/Also known as
snippet: == Schrödinger's Equation: Also known as == Schrödinger's equation can be seen referred to as Schrödinger's wave equation by some authors.

title: Definition:Schrödinger's Equation/Time Independent
snippet: $-\dfrac {\hbar^2} {2 m} \nabla^2 \psi + V \psi = E \psi$ where: $\psi$ is the wave function whose nature is to be determined $V$ denotes the potential energy (usually positional) $E$ denotes the total energy of the system $m$ denotes the mass of the particle whose motion is described by $\psi$ $\hbar$ is Planck's reduced constant: $\hbar = \dfrac h {2 \pi}$

title: Definition:Schur Decomposition
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a square matrix. A Schur decomposition for $\mathbf A$ is a decomposition of $\mathbf A$ in the form: $\mathbf A = \mathbf Q \mathbf T \mathbf Q^\dagger$ where: $\mathbf T$ is an upper triangular matrix $\mathbf Q$ is a unitary matrix $\mathbf Q^\dagger$ denotes the Hermitian conjugate of $\mathbf Q$.

title: Definition:Schur Decomposition/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Schur Decomposition == The concept of a Schur decomposition was introduced by in $1909$.

title: Definition:Schur Space
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ be a normed vector space over $\GF$. We say that $X$ is a Schur space a sequence $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ in $X$ converges in norm to ${\mathbf 0}_X$ it converges weakly to ${\mathbf 0}_X$.

title: Definition:Schwartz Distribution
snippet: Let $\map \DD {\R^d}$ be a test function space. Let $\phi, \psi \in \map \DD {\R^d}$ be test functions. Let $\alpha \in \C$ be a complex number. Let $\sequence {\phi_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a convergent sequence in $\map \DD {\R^d}$ with the limit $\phi \in \map \DD {\R^d}$. Suppose a mapping $T : \map \DD {\R^d} \to \C$ is linear and continuous: $\forall \psi, \phi \in \map \DD {\R^d} : \map T {\phi + \psi} = \map T \phi + \map T \psi$ $\forall \phi \in \map \DD {\R^d} : \forall \alpha \in \C : \map T {\alpha \cdot \phi} = \alpha \cdot \map T \phi$ $\paren {\phi_n \stackrel \DD…

title: Definition:Schwartz Distribution/Also denoted as
snippet: == Schwartz Distribution: Also denoted as == The mapping $\map T \phi$ corresponding to the Schwartz distribution $T$ is presented by some sources as $\innerprod T \phi$.

title: Definition:Schwartz Distribution/Also known as
snippet: == Schwartz Distribution: Also known as == A Schwartz distribution is also known as a generalized function. Many sources refer to a Schwartz distribution as just a distribution, but that allows confusion with the concept of a probability distribution.

title: Definition:Schwartz Distribution/Notation
snippet: == Schwartz Distribution: Notation == To avoid confusion between a Schwartz distribution and the generating function involved, one can write the function as a subscript. Suppose we have a Schwartz distribution $T_f : \map \DD \R \to \C$ and a test function $\phi \in \map \DD \R$. This would correspond to the following mapping: $\ds \phi \stackrel {T_f} \longrightarrow \int_{-\infty}^\infty \map f x \map \phi x \rd x$

title: Definition:Schwartz Space
snippet: The set of all Schwartz test functions $\phi : \R \to \C$ is called the Schwartz space and is denoted by $\map {\SS} \R$.

title: Definition:Schwartz Test Function
snippet: Let $\phi : \R \to \C$ be a complex-valued function. Let $\phi \in \map {C^\infty} \R$ be smooth. Suppose $\phi$ is bounded in the following way: $\ds \forall m, l \in \N : \sup_{x \mathop \in \R} \size {x^l \map {\phi^{\paren m}} x} < \infty$ where $\phi^{\paren m}$ denotes the $m$-th derivative of $\phi$. Then $\phi$ is known as a Schwartz test function.

title: Definition:Schwartz Test Function/Also known as
snippet: == Schwartz Test Function: Also known as == Schwartz test functions are also called rapidly decreasing functions.

title: Definition:Schwartz Test Function/Multivariable
snippet: Let $\phi \in \map {C^\infty} {\R^n}$ be smooth. Then $\phi$ called a Schwartz test function : $\ds \sup _{\size \alpha \le N} \sup_{x \in \R^n} \paren {1 + \norm x^2}^N \size {\map {\frac {\partial^{\size \alpha} f}{\partial ^{\alpha_1} x_1 \cdots \partial ^{\alpha_N} x_N }} x} < +\infty$ for all natural numbers $N \in \N$, where: $\partial/\partial x_i$ denotes the partial derivative with respect to $x_i$ $\norm \cdot$ denotes the Euclidean norm on $\R^n$ $\size \alpha := \size {\alpha_1} + \cdots + \size {\alpha _N}$ for $\alpha = \tuple {\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_N} \in \N ^N$

title: Definition:Schwarz Function
snippet: Let $f: \R \to \C$ be a function. $f$ is a Schwarz function : $\forall c \in \R, n \in \N_0: \size {\map {f^{\paren n} } x} = \map \oo {\size x^c}$ where: $f^{\paren n}$ denotes the $n$th derivative $\oo$ is the little-$\oo$ notation.

title: Definition:Science
snippet: Science is the systematic discovery and organization of knowledge which is done by making testable explanations and predictions about the universe.

title: Definition:Science/Linguistic Note
snippet: The word science comes from the Latin word scientia, meaning "knowledge. The first c is silent, hence the pronunciation si-ense. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Scientific Notation
snippet: Scientific notation is an implementation of floating-point representation for representing approximations to (usually large) numbers by presenting them in the form: $n \approx m \times 10^e$ where: $m$ is a rational number such that $1 \le m < 10$, expressed in decimal notation $e$ is an integer.

title: Definition:Scientific Notation/Also known as
snippet: == Scientific Notation: Also known as == Scientific notation can also be seen referred to as: exponential notation standard form index notation.

title: Definition:Scientific Notation/Base
snippet: Let $n$ be a number expressed in scientific notation as: $n \approx m \times 10^e$ The number $10$, in this context, is referred to as the base.

title: Definition:Scientific Notation/Exponent
snippet: Let $n$ be a number expressed in scientific notation as: $n \approx m \times 10^e$ The number $e$ is known as the exponent.

title: Definition:Scientific Notation/Mantissa
snippet: Let $n$ be a number expressed in scientific notation as: $n \approx m \times 10^e$ The number $m$ is known as the mantissa.

title: Definition:Scope
snippet: Scope of an Occurrence: The smallest well-formed part containing a given occurrence in a well-formed formula Scope (Logic): The statements that a logical connective connects, whether this be simple or compound. In the case of a unary connective, there will be only one such statement. This subsumes the definitions: Scope of a Connective: The scope of a connective in a well-formed formula of propositional logic is the shortest well-formed part of that well-formed formula containing this connective.

title: Definition:Scope (Logic)
snippet: Let $\LL_0$ be the language of propositional logic. Let $\circ$ be a connective of $\LL_0$. Let $\mathbf W$ be a well-formed formula of $\LL_0$.

title: Definition:Scope (Logic)/Connective
snippet: Let $\LL_0$ be the language of propositional logic. Let $\circ$ be a connective of $\LL_0$. Let $\mathbf W$ be a well-formed formula of $\LL_0$.

title: Definition:Scope (Logic)/Quantifier
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a WFF of the language of predicate logic. Let $Q$ be an occurrence of a quantifier in $\mathbf A$. Let $\mathbf B$ be a well-formed part of $\mathbf A$ such that $\mathbf B$ begins (omitting outer parentheses) with $Q x$. That is, such that $\mathbf B = \paren {Q x: \mathbf C}$ for some WFF $\mathbf C$. $\mathbf B$ is called the scope of the quantifier $Q$.

title: Definition:Scope of Connective/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\LL_0$ be the language of propositional logic. Let $\circ$ be a connective of $\LL_0$. Let $\mathbf W$ be a well-formed formula of $\LL_0$. The scope of an occurrence of $\circ$ in $\mathbf W$ is defined as: the smallest well-formed part of $\mathbf W$ containing this occurrence of $\circ$. where: smallest means the well-formed part of $\mathbf W$ whose length is least containing means such that it is a substring of $\mathbf W$.

title: Definition:Scope of Connective/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\LL_0$ be the language of propositional logic. Let $\circ$ be a connective of $\LL_0$. Let $\mathbf W$ be a well-formed formula of $\LL_0$. The scope of an occurrence of $\circ$ in $\mathbf W$ is defined as: the set of statements that it connects, whether simple or compound. The arity of $\circ$ determines the cardinality of this set. In the case of a unary connective, there will be only one such statement.

title: Definition:Scope of Occurrence
snippet: Let $\FF$ be a formal language with alphabet $\AA$. Let $\mathbf A$ be a well-formed formula of $\FF$. Let $a$ be a fixed occurrence of some element of $\AA$ in $\mathbf A$. Then the scope of $a$ is the smallest well-formed part of $\mathbf A$ that contains $a$.

title: Definition:Score
snippet: A score is another name for a set whose cardinality is $20$.

title: Definition:Score/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Score == Biblical language often uses the word score when discussing ages: The days of our years are three score years and ten; and if by reason of strength they be fourscore years, yet is their strength labor and sorrow; for it is soon cut off, and we fly away. -- Psalm $90$: $10$ The term a score or scores is used in colloquial language to mean a moderately large number.

title: Definition:Scott Sigma
snippet: Let $L = \struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Scott sigma $\map \sigma L$ is a set of subsets of $S$ and equals to $\leftset {U \subseteq S: U}$ is upper and has property (S)$\rightset{}$

title: Definition:Scott Topology
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an up-complete ordered set. Let $T = \struct {S, \preceq, \tau}$ be a relational structure with topology. Then $T$ has the Scott topology : $\tau$ is the set of all upper and inaccessible by directed suprema subsets of $S$.

title: Definition:Screw (Geometry)
snippet: A screw is an isometry on the real Euclidean space $\R^3$ defined as a combination of: a rotation about an axis a translation along that same axis of rotation.

title: Definition:Screw (Machine)
snippet: A screw is a simple machine consisting of: a cylindrical or conical body a helical groove cut into its surface Thus it can be considered as a wedge wound in the form of a helix. When the end of the screw $S$ is placed against a substance, a rotation of $S$ about its axis causes a translation of $S$ along this axis, and into the substance.

title: Definition:Screw (Machine)/Thread
snippet: The helical groove cut into the surface of a screw is called its thread.

title: Definition:Scruple/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Scruple: Conversion Factors ==

title: Definition:Scrupulus/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Scrupulus == The scrupulus continued to be used as a unit of mass in Europe after the fall of Rome, evolving into the apothecaries' scruple. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Scrupulus/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Scrupulus == The word scrupulus is the [https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/diminutive diminutive form] of the Latin word scrupus, meaning sharp stone. Its plural form is scrupuli. The forms scrupulum, scripulum, scriptulum, scriplus and scriptulus can be found. The word scriptulum is also associated with the lines on a draughtboard. Its secondary meaning of anxiety, uneasiness, doubt, and so on, evolved into the present-day scruple, which can be interpreted to mean a concern about personal morality. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Sealed-Bid Auction
snippet: A sealed-bid auction is a game in the following format: An object $F$ is to be assigned to a player in a set $\left\{ {1, 2, \ldots, n}\right\}$ in exchange for a payment. The valuation of $F$ by player $i$ is $v_i$, and: $v_1 > v_2 > \cdots > v_n > 0$ Each player simultaneously submits a non-negative number, called a bid. $F$ is then given to the player with the lowest index among those who submit the highest bid, in exchange for a payment.

title: Definition:Sealed-Bid Auction/First Price
snippet: A first price auction is a sealed-bid auction in which the payment made by the winner is the price which is bid by that player.

title: Definition:Sealed-Bid Auction/Second Price
snippet: A second price auction is a sealed-bid auction in which the payment made by the winner is the highest bid made by the players who did not win. So if only one player submits the highest bid, the price paid is the second highest bid.

title: Definition:Secant/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Secant == The word secant comes from the Latin secantus (that which is cutting), the present participle of secare to cut. This arises from the fact that it is the length of the line from the origin which cuts the tangent line. It is pronounced with the emphasis on the first syllable and a long e: see-kant. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Secant Function/Complex
snippet: Let $z \in \C$ be a complex number. The complex function $\sec z$ is defined as: $\sec z = \dfrac 1 {\cos z}$ where $\cos z$ is the cosine of $z$. The definition is valid for all $z \in \C$ such that $\cos z \ne 0$. Category:Definitions/Secant Function

title: Definition:Secant Function/Definition from Circle/First Quadrant
snippet: Consider a unit circle $C$ whose center is at the origin of a cartesian plane. 500px Let $P$ be the point on $C$ in the first quadrant such that $\theta$ is the angle made by $OP$ with the $x$-axis. Let a tangent line be drawn to touch $C$ at $A = \tuple {1, 0}$. Let $OP$ be produced to meet this tangent line at $B$. Then the secant of $\theta$ is defined as the length of $OB$. Hence in the first quadrant, the secant is positive.

title: Definition:Secant Function/Definition from Circle/Fourth Quadrant
snippet: Consider a unit circle $C$ whose center is at the origin of a cartesian plane. 500px Let $P$ be the point on $C$ in the fourth quadrant such that $\theta$ is the angle made by $OP$ with the $x$-axis. Let a tangent line be drawn to touch $C$ at $A = \tuple {1, 0}$. Let $OP$ be produced to meet this tangent line at $B$. Then the secant of $\theta$ is defined as the length of $OB$. Hence in the fourth quadrant, the secant is positive.

title: Definition:Secant Function/Definition from Circle/Second Quadrant
snippet: Consider a unit circle $C$ whose center is at the origin of a cartesian plane. 500px Let $P$ be the point on $C$ in the second quadrant such that $\theta$ is the angle made by $OP$ with the $x$-axis. Let a tangent line be drawn to touch $C$ at $A = \tuple {1, 0}$. Let $OP$ be produced to meet this tangent line at $B$. Then the secant of $\theta$ is defined as the length of $OB$. As $OP$ needs to be produced in the opposite direction to $P$, the secant is therefore a negative function in the second quadrant.

title: Definition:Secant Function/Definition from Circle/Third Quadrant
snippet: Consider a unit circle $C$ whose center is at the origin of a cartesian plane. 500px Let $P$ be the point on $C$ in the third quadrant such that $\theta$ is the angle made by $OP$ with the $x$-axis. Let a tangent line be drawn to touch $C$ at $A = \tuple {1, 0}$. Let $OP$ be produced to meet this tangent line at $B$. Then the secant of $\theta$ is defined as the length of $OB$. As $OP$ needs to be produced in the opposite direction to $P$, the secant is therefore a negative function in the third quadrant.

title: Definition:Secant Function/Definition from Triangle
snippet: 400px In the above right triangle, we are concerned about the angle $\theta$. The secant of $\angle \theta$ is defined as being $\dfrac{\text{Hypotenuse}} {\text{Adjacent}}$.

title: Definition:Secant Function/Real
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number. The real function $\sec x$ is defined as: $\sec x = \dfrac 1 {\cos x}$ where $\cos x$ is the cosine of $x$. The definition is valid for all $x \in \R$ such that $\cos x \ne 0$. Category:Definitions/Secant Function

title: Definition:Secant Line
snippet: Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a real function. Let the graph of $f$ be depicted on a Cartesian plane. 400px A secant to $f$ is a straight line which intersects the graph of $f$ in (at least) two points. In the above diagram, the secant is the line $AB$ in .

title: Definition:Secant Method
snippet: Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a real function which has a root which is to be found. The secant method is an iterative technique for achieving this, by setting up the following iterative function: $x_{n + 1} = x_n - \dfrac {\map f {x_n} \paren {x_n - x_{n - 1} } } {\map f {x_n} - \map f {x_{n - 1} } }$ for $n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$ where $x_0$ and $x_1$ are first approximations to the root. 600px Convergence is not guaranteed.

title: Definition:Second-Countable Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a second-countable space its topology has a countable basis.

title: Definition:Second-Countable Space/Also known as
snippet: == Second-Countable Space: Also known as == A second-countable space is also known as: Such a space can also be said to satisfy the second axiom of countability. Some sources render the term without the hyphen: second countable. aims to be consistent in presentation, and the hyphenated version is preferred.

title: Definition:Second-Order Convergence/Also known as
snippet: == Second-Order Convergence: Also known as == Second-order convergence is also known as quadratic convergence.

title: Definition:Second-Order Reaction
snippet: Let $\AA$ and $\BB$ be two chemical substances in solution which react together to form a compound $\CC$. Let the reaction occur by means of the molecules of $\AA$ and $\BB$ colliding and interacting as a result. Then the rate of formation of $\CC$ is proportional to the number of collisions in unit time. This in turn is jointly proportional to the quantities of $\AA$ and $\BB$ which have not yet transformed. Such a chemical reaction is called a second-order reaction.

title: Definition:Second/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Second == The word second, in the context of the measurement of time and of angle, derives from the fact that it was originally specified as a second minute part of an hour or of a degree of angle. The minute had already been defined as a minute part of an hour. The use of the word second in English, in this specific context, started near the end of the $16$th century. Category:Linguistic Notes‎

title: Definition:Second Chebyshev Function
snippet: The second Chebyshev Function $\psi: \R \to \R$ is defined as follows:

title: Definition:Second Chebyshev Function/Definition 1
snippet: The second Chebyshev Function $\psi: \R \to \R$ is defined as: $\ds \forall x \in \R: \map \psi x := \sum_{k \mathop \ge 1} \sum_{p^k \mathop \le x} \ln p$ where, for each $k$, the summation extends over all powers of prime numbers $p$ such that $p^k \le x$.

title: Definition:Second Chebyshev Function/Definition 2
snippet: The second Chebyshev Function $\psi: \R \to \R$ is defined as: $\ds \forall x \in \R: \map \psi x := \sum_{1 \mathop \le n \mathop \le x} \map \Lambda n$ where $\Lambda$ is the von Mangoldt function.

title: Definition:Second Chebyshev Function/Definition 3
snippet: The second Chebyshev Function $\psi: \R \to \R$ is defined as: $\ds \forall x \in \R: \map \psi x := \sum_{p \mathop \le x} \floor {\log_p x} \ln p$ where: the summation extends over all prime numbers $p$ such that $p \le x$ $\floor {\, \cdot \,}$ denotes the floor function.

title: Definition:Second Difference Estimate
snippet: Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a real function. Let $y = \map f x$ have known values: $y_k = \map f {x_k}$ for $x_k \in \set {x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_n}$ defined as: $x_k = x_0 + k h$ for some $h \in \R_{>0}$. The second difference estimate on $f$ is defined as: $\map {f' '} x \approx \dfrac {\map f {x + h} - 2 \map f x + \map f {x - h}} {h^2}$

title: Definition:Second Figure of Categorical Syllogism/Also known as
snippet: == Second Figure of Categorical Syllogism: Also known as == The second figure of a categorical syllogism is classically known as the figure of exclusions, from the fact that in order to be valid, its conclusion needs to be negative. Category:Definitions/Second Figure of Categorical Syllogism

title: Definition:Second Kind
snippet: The term second kind is used to distinguish two or more classes of mathematical object of some common overall type.

title: Definition:Second Kind/Also known as
snippet: == Second Kind: Also known as == Some such objects are referred to as being of the second type rather than the second kind, but the meaning remains the same. Category:Definitions/Second Kind

title: Definition:Second Normed Dual
snippet:
Let $\struct {X, 
orm \cdot_X}$ be a normed vector space. Let $\struct {X^\ast, 
orm \cdot_{X^\ast} }$ be the normed dual of $\struct {X, 
orm \cdot_X}$. We define the second normed dual, written $\struct {X^{\ast \ast}, 
orm \cdot_{X^{\ast \ast} } }$ as the normed dual of $\struct {X^\ast, 
orm \cdot_{X^\ast} }$.

title: Definition:Second Order Fibonacci Number
snippet: The second order Fibonacci numbers are a sequence $\sequence {\FF_n}$ of integers which is formally defined recursively for all $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ as: $\FF_n = \begin{cases} 0 & : n = 0 \\ 1 & : n = 1 \\ \FF_{n - 1} + \FF_{n - 2} + F_{n - 2} & : \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$ where $F_{n - 2}$ denotes the $n - 2$th Fibonacci number.

title: Definition:Second Order Ordinary Differential Equation
snippet: A second order ordinary differential equation is an ordinary differential equation in which any derivatives with respect to the independent variable have order no greater than $2$. The general second order ODE can be written as: $\ds \map F {x, y, \frac {\d y} {\d x}, \frac {\d^2 y} {\d x^2} }$ or, using prime notation: $\map F {x, y, y^\prime, y^{\prime \prime} }$

title: Definition:Second Order Ordinary Differential Equation/Also known as
snippet: == Second Order Ordinary Differential Equation: Also known as == A second order ordinary differential equation is often seen referred to just as a second order differential equation by sources which are not concerned about partial differential equations. Some sources hyphenate: second-order differential equation. The abbreviation ODE is frequently seen, hence second order ODE for second order ordinary differential equation.

title: Definition:Second Order Ordinary Differential Equation/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Second Order ODE == Much of the theory of second order ODEs was progressed by .

title: Definition:Second Order Partial Differential Equation
snippet: A second order partial differential equation is a partial differential equation in which any derivatives with respect to the independent variable have order no greater than $2$. Category:Definitions/Differential Equations

title: Definition:Second Pentagonal Number
snippet: The second pentagonal numbers are those denumerating a collection of objects which can be arranged in the form of a regular pentagon. They can be denoted: $\map {P'} 1, \map {P'} 2, \map {P'} 3, \ldots$

title: Definition:Second Pentagonal Number/Definition 1
snippet: The second pentagonal numbers are the integers obtained by applying the Closed Form for Pentagonal Numbers to negative $n$: $\map {P'} n = \dfrac {-n \paren {-3 n - 1} } 2$

title: Definition:Second Pentagonal Number/Definition 2
snippet: The second pentagonal numbers are the integers obtained from formula: $\map {P'} n = \dfrac {n \paren {3 n + 1} } 2$ for $n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$

title: Definition:Second Principle of Finite Induction/Also known as
snippet: == Second Principle of Finite Induction: Also known as == Some sources refer to the Second Principle of Finite Induction as the Second Principle of Mathematical Induction, and gloss over the differences between the two proof techniques if they discuss them both at all. Hence the word finite may well not appear in the various published expositions of this technique. The Second Principle of Finite Induction is also known as: the Principle of Complete (Finite) Induction. the Principle of Complete Induction. Various terms are used on , depending on from where the proof may have been sourced.

title: Definition:Second Principle of Finite Induction/Basis for the Induction
snippet: == Terminology of Second Principle of Finite Induction == Consider a Proof by Complete Finite Induction. The step that shows that the integer $n_0$ is an element of $S$ is called the basis for the induction.

title: Definition:Second Principle of Finite Induction/Induction Hypothesis
snippet: == Terminology of Second Principle of Finite Induction == Consider a Proof by Complete Finite Induction. The assumption that $\forall k: n_0 \le k \le n: k \in S$ for some $n \in \Z$ is the induction hypothesis.

title: Definition:Second Principle of Finite Induction/Induction Step
snippet: == Terminology of Second Principle of Finite Induction == Consider a Proof by Complete Finite Induction. The step which shows that $n + 1 \in S$ follows from the assumption that $k \in S$ for all values of $k$ between $n_0$ and $n$ is called the induction step.

title: Definition:Second Principle of Finite Induction/Terminology
snippet: == Terminology of Second Principle of Finite Induction ==

title: Definition:Second Principle of Mathematical Induction/Also known as
snippet: == Second Principle of Mathematical Induction: Also known as == The Second Principle of Mathematical Induction is also known as the Principle of Complete Induction. Both terms are used on . The abbreviation is also used. Some sources call it the Principle of Strong Induction. Such sources may similarly refer to the (First) Principle of Mathematical Induction as the Principle of Weak Induction. These names are misleading, as both principles are equivalent, and so neither is weaker or stronger than the other.

title: Definition:Second Principle of Mathematical Induction/Basis for the Induction
snippet: == Terminology of Second Principle of Mathematical Induction == Consider a Proof by Complete Induction. The step that shows that the proposition $\map P {n_0}$ is true for the first value $n_0$ is called the basis for the induction.

title: Definition:Second Principle of Mathematical Induction/Induction Hypothesis
snippet: == Terminology of Second Principle of Mathematical Induction == Consider a Proof by Complete Induction. The assumption that $\forall j: n_0 \le j \le k: \map P j$ is true for some $k \in \Z$ is the induction hypothesis.

title: Definition:Second Principle of Mathematical Induction/Induction Step
snippet: == Terminology of Second Principle of Mathematical Induction == Consider a Proof by Complete Induction. The step which shows that the truth of $\map P {k + 1}$ follows from the assumption of truth of $P$ for all values of $j$ between $n_0$ and $k$ is called the induction step.

title: Definition:Second Principle of Mathematical Induction/Terminology
snippet: == Terminology of Second Principle of Mathematical Induction ==

title: Definition:Second Quartile/Also known as
snippet: == Second Quartile: Also known as == The term second quartile is rarely used, and the term median is used instead. Category:Definitions/Quartiles

title: Definition:Second Radiation Constant
snippet: The second radiation constant is defined as: $c_2 = \dfrac {h c} k$ where: $h$ denotes Planck's constant $c$ denotes the speed of light $k$ denotes Boltzmann's constant.

title: Definition:Second Radiation Constant/Dimension
snippet: The second radiation constant has the dimension $\mathsf {L \Theta}$. This arises from its definition as Planck's constant multiplied by the speed of light divided by Boltzmann's constant: $\dfrac {\mathsf {M L^2 T^{-1} } \times \mathsf {L T^{-1} } } {\mathsf {M L^2 T^{-2} \Theta^{-1} } }$ Category:Definitions/Second Radiation Constant Category:Definitions/Dimensions of Measurement

title: Definition:Second Radiation Constant/Units
snippet: The SI unit for the second radiation constant is the metre kelvin: $\mathrm {m \, K}$ The CGS unit for the second radiation constant is the centimetre kelvin: $\mathrm {cm \, K}$ Category:Definitions/Second Radiation Constant Category:Definitions/Units of Measurement

title: Definition:Second Radiation Constant/Value
snippet: == Second Radiation Constant: Value == The value of the second radiation constant is: {{eqn | l = c_2 | r = 1 \cdotp 43877 \, 6877 \ldots \times 10^{-2} \, \mathrm {m \, K} | c = }} {{eqn | r = 1 \cdotp 43877 \, 6877 \ldots \, \mathrm {cm \, K} | c = }}

title: Definition:Second of Angle/Also known as
snippet: == Second of Angle: Also known as == A second of angle is also known as a second of arc, or an arc second. This term has a specific definition which is subtly different from the concept of a second of angle, and so its use in this context on is discouraged.

title: Definition:Second of Angle/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Second of Angle == The division of the degrees into $60$ and $3600$ subdivisions originates from the , who used a sexagesimal (base $60$) system for the purposes of mathematics and astronomy.

title: Definition:Second of Arc
snippet: The second (of arc) is a unit of measurement of the length of an arc of a circle. It is defined as the length of the arc which subtends $1$ second (of angle) at the center of the circle.

title: Definition:Second of Time/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Second of Time == The division of the hour into $60$ minutes, and the minute into $60$ seconds, is a relic of the Babylonian number system, which was a sexagesimal (base $60$) system used mainly for astronomical purposes. Up until $1960$, the second was defined as being $\dfrac 1 {86 \, 400}$, that is $\dfrac 1 {60 \times 60 \times 24}$, the length of a mean solar day. This appears first to have been used by in the year $1000$ CE. It had been noted by astronomical observations that the actual (solar) day is gradually lengthening.

title: Definition:Second of Time/Symbol
snippet: The symbol for the second is $\mathrm s$.

title: Definition:Secondary Data
snippet: Secondary data are data which are calculated from primary data.

title: Definition:Secondary Parts of Triangle
snippet: The secondary parts of a triangle are measurements which are derived from the principal parts in some way, for example: the lengths of the medians the sizes of the $3$ exterior angles and so on.

title: Definition:Secondary Term of Syllogism/Also known as
snippet: == Secondary Term of Syllogism: Also known as == Some sources call the secondary term of a categorical syllogism the minor term, whence the name of the minor premise in which it occurs. Others call it the subject of the syllogism, but this is not recommended as it can be a cause for confusion due to its ambiguity. Some sources denote it with the letter $F$.

title: Definition:Section
snippet: Set Theory Upper Section Lower Section Analysis, geometry, number theory and so on: The Golden Section: $\dfrac {1 + \sqrt 5} 2$ Real Analysis: Dedekind Section or Dedekind Cut Geometry: Section: Line section: the intersection of one line with another. Plane section: the intersection of a 3-dimensional figure $F$ with a plane. Cross-Section: a plane section which is perpendicular to an axis of $F$. Topology: Section (Topology) Definition:Section of Presheaf Definition:Global Section of Presheaf

title: Definition:Section/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Section == The word section is derived from the Latin seco, secare, secui, sectum: meaning cut. In all usages of this term, the concept of cut lies at the base of its linguistic derivation. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Section (Category Theory)
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $f: C \to D$ be a morphism of $\mathbf C$. A section of $f$ is a morphism $g: D \to C$ such that: $f \circ g = \operatorname{id}_D$

title: Definition:Section (Category Theory)/Also known as
snippet: == Section in context of Category Theory: Also known as == A section is also known as: a right inverse. Some authors refer to this as a coretraction. Category:Definitions/Morphisms

title: Definition:Section (Topology)
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be topological spaces.

title: Definition:Section (Topology)/Also known as
snippet: == Section: Also known as == Some authors use the word cross section rather than section.

title: Definition:Section (Topology)/Mapping
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be topological spaces. Let $\phi: S \to T$ be a continuous surjective mapping. Let $I_T: T \to T$ be the identity mapping on $T$. Then a section of the mapping $\phi$ is a mapping $\sigma: T \to S$ which is a continuous right inverse of $\phi$: $\sigma: T \to S \text { such that } \phi \circ \sigma = I_T$

title: Definition:Section (Topology)/Mapping/Local
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be topological spaces. Let $U \subseteq T$ be an open set of $T$. Let $\phi: S \to T$ be a continuous surjective mapping. Let $I_U: U \to U$ be the identity mapping on $U$. Then a local section of the mapping $\phi$ is a mapping $\sigma: U \to S$ which is a continuous right inverse of $\phi$: $\sigma: U \to S \text { such that } \phi \circ \sigma = I_U$

title: Definition:Section of Line by Line
snippet: Let a geometrical line $A$ cross over (or intersect) another line $B$. The point where they cross is called the section of the $B$ by $A$ (or equivalently, of $A$ by $B$). Category:Definitions/Geometry

title: Definition:Section of Étalé Space
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\FF$ be a presheaf of sets on $T$. Let $\struct {\map {\mathrm {\acute Et} } \FF, \pi}$ be its étalé space. Let $U \subseteq S$ be open.

title: Definition:Section of Étalé Space/Definition 1
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\FF$ be a presheaf of sets on $T$. Let $\struct {\map {\mathrm {\acute Et} } \FF, \pi}$ be its étalé space. Let $U \subseteq S$ be open. A section of $\map {\mathrm {\acute Et} } \FF$ on $U$ is a continuous mapping $s: U \to \map {\mathrm {\acute Et} } \FF$ such that: $\pi \circ s = I_U$ where $I_U$ is the identity mapping on $U$.

title: Definition:Section of Étalé Space/Definition 2
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\FF$ be a presheaf of sets on $T$. Let $\struct {\map {\mathrm {\acute Et} } \FF, \pi}$ be its étalé space. Let $U \subseteq S$ be open. A section of $\map {\mathrm {\acute Et} } \FF$ on $U$ is a mapping $s: U \to \map {\mathrm {\acute Et} } \FF$ such that: for all $x \in U$ there exists an open neighborhhood $V$ of $x$ in $U$ such that the restriction of $s$ to $V$ is the section associated to some $t \in \map \FF V$.

title: Definition:Sector of Circle
snippet: A sector of a circle is the region bounded by two radii and an arc. ' In the diagram below, $BAC$ is a sector. 300px In fact there are two sectors, together making up the whole of the circle. When describing a sectors by means of its three defining points (as in $BAC$ above), the convention is to report them in the following order: $(1):\quad$ The point on the circumference at the end of the clockwise radius $(2):\quad$ The point at the center of the circle $(3):\quad$ The point on the circumference at the end of the anticlockwise radius Thus in the sector above, $BAC$ describes the sector…

title: Definition:Sector of Circle/Angle
snippet: 300px The angle of a sector of a circle is the angle between the two radii which delimit the sector. In the above diagram, the angle of the sector $BAC$ is $\theta$. The conjugate angle of $\theta$ also forms a sector, denoted $CAB$ (see above).

title: Definition:Sectoral Harmonic
snippet: A sectoral harmonic is a surface harmonic in the form: $\cos m \phi \, \map { {P_n}^m} {\cos \theta}$ or: $\sin m \phi \, \map { {P_n}^m} {\cos \theta}$ such that $m = n$.

title: Definition:Segment
snippet: Geometry: Segment of Circle: The part of a circle cut off by a straight line that cuts the circle into two parts. Line segment: a straight line whose endpoints are both defined. Order theory: (Initial) segment: A subset of a well-ordered set defined as the set of all elements of a well-ordered set which strictly precede a particular element. Weak initial segment: A subset of a well-ordered set defined as the set of all elements of a well-ordered set which precede a particular element. Linear algebra and matrix theory: Segment of Matrix: Another term for a submatrix.

snippet: 300px The base of a segment of a circle is the straight line forming one of the boundaries of the seqment. In the above diagram, $AB$ is the base of the highlighted segment.

title: Definition:Segment of Circle/Major
snippet: Let $AB$ be a chord of a circle $\CC$ defined by the points $A$ and $B$ on the circumference of $\CC$. The major segment of $\CC$ $AB$ is the segment between $AB$ and the major arc of $\CC$ between $A$ and $B$.

title: Definition:Segment of Circle/Minor
snippet: Let $AB$ be a chord of a circle $\CC$ defined by the points $A$ and $B$ on the circumference of $\CC$. The minor segment of $\CC$ $AB$ is the segment between $AB$ and the minor arc of $\CC$ between $A$ and $B$.

title: Definition:Seifert Matrix
snippet: For a knot $K$ with Seifert surface $S$, the Seifert matrix $V$ of $K$ is defined by its entries as: $v_{ij} = \operatorname{lk} \left({ x_i, x_k^* }\right)$ where: the $x_a$ are the generators of the fundamental group $\pi_1(S)$ $x_a^*$ is the positive push-off of $x_a$ $\operatorname{lk}$ is the linking number of the two loops. Category:Definitions/Knot Theory
