title: Definition:Sievert
snippet: The sievert is the SI unit of ionizing radiation. It is defined as the dose of ionizing radiation delivered by a point source of $1$ milligram of radium, enclosed in a platinum container with walls $0.5$ millimeters thick, to a sample $10$ millimeters away over a period of $1$ hour. It is equivalent to $1$ joule per kilogram of irradiated material.

title: Definition:Sigma-Algebra/Also known as
snippet: == Sigma-Algebra: Also known as == The term sigma-algebra can also be seen without the hyphen: sigma algebra. Some sources refer to a sigma-algebra as a sigma-field.

title: Definition:Sigma-Algebra/Definition 1
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\Sigma$ be a system of subsets of $X$. $\Sigma$ is a $\sigma$-algebra over $X$ $\Sigma$ satisfies the sigma-algebra axioms:

title: Definition:Sigma-Algebra/Definition 2
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\Sigma$ be a system of subsets of $X$. $\Sigma$ is a $\sigma$-algebra over $X$ $\Sigma$ satisfies the sigma-algebra axioms:

title: Definition:Sigma-Algebra/Definition 3
snippet: A $\sigma$-algebra $\Sigma$ is a $\sigma$-ring with a unit.

title: Definition:Sigma-Algebra/Definition 4
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. A $\sigma$-algebra $\Sigma$ over $X$ is an algebra of sets which is closed under countable unions.

title: Definition:Sigma-Algebra/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on $\sigma$-Algebra == The $\sigma$ in $\sigma$-algebra is the Greek letter sigma which equates to the letter s. $\sigma$ stands for for somme, which is French for union, and also summe, which is German for union. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Sigma-Algebra Generated by Collection of Mappings
snippet: Let $I$ be an indexing set. Let $\family {\struct {X_i, \Sigma_i} }_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a family of measurable spaces. Let $X$ be a set. Let $\family {f_i: X \to X_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a family of mappings. Then the $\sigma$-algebra generated by $\family {f_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$, $\map \sigma {f_i: i \in I}$, is the smallest $\sigma$-algebra on $X$ such that every $f_i$ is $\map \sigma {f_i: i \in I} \, / \, \Sigma_i$-measurable.

title: Definition:Sigma-Algebra Generated by Collection of Subsets
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\GG \subseteq \powerset X$ be a collection of subsets of $X$.

title: Definition:Sigma-Algebra Generated by Collection of Subsets/Definition 1
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\GG \subseteq \powerset X$ be a collection of subsets of $X$. The $\sigma$-algebra generated by $\GG$, denoted $\map \sigma \GG$, is the smallest $\sigma$-algebra on $X$ that contains $\GG$. That is, $\map \sigma \GG$ is subject to: $(1): \quad \GG \subseteq \map \sigma \GG$ $(2): \quad$ for all $\sigma$-algebras $\Sigma$ on $X$: $\GG \subseteq \Sigma \implies \map \sigma \GG \subseteq \Sigma$

title: Definition:Sigma-Algebra Generated by Collection of Subsets/Definition 2
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\GG \subseteq \powerset X$ be a collection of subsets of $X$. The $\sigma$-algebra generated by $\GG$, $\map \sigma \GG$, is the intersection of all $\sigma$-algebras on $X$ that contain $\GG$.

title: Definition:Sigma-Algebra Generated by Collection of Subsets/Generator
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\GG \subseteq \powerset X$ be a collection of subsets of $X$. Let $\map \sigma {\GG}$ be the $\sigma$-algebra generated by $\GG$. One says that $\GG$ is a generator for $\map \sigma {\GG}$. Also, elements $G$ of $\GG$ may be called generators.

title: Definition:Sigma-Compact Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a $\sigma$-compact space $S$ is the union of the underlying sets of countably many compact subspaces of $T$. This can be expressed more efficiently as: $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is $\sigma$-compact it is covered by a countable set of compact subspaces.

title: Definition:Sigma-Compact Space/Also known as
snippet: == $\sigma$-Compact Space: Also known as == A $\sigma$-compact space is also known as a space that is countable at infinity. Category:Definitions/Sigma-Compact Spaces

title: Definition:Sigma-Discrete Basis
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. A $\sigma$-discrete basis for $T$ is a basis which is the countable union of discrete sets of open sets.

title: Definition:Sigma-Discrete Set of Subsets
snippet: A $\sigma$-discrete set of subsets of a topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a set of subsets of $S$ which is the countable union of a discrete set of subsets.

title: Definition:Sigma-Finite Measure/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. We say that $\mu$ is a $\sigma$-finite (or sigma-finite) measure there exists an exhausting sequence $\sequence {E_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ in $\Sigma$ such that: $\forall n \in \N: \map \mu {E_n} < \infty$

title: Definition:Sigma-Finite Measure/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. We say that $\mu$ is a $\sigma$-finite (or sigma-finite) measure there exists a cover $\sequence {E_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ of $X$ in $\Sigma$ such that: $\forall n \in \N: \map \mu {E_n} < \infty$

title: Definition:Sigma-Finite Measure/Definition 3
snippet: Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. We say that $\mu$ is a $\sigma$-finite (or sigma-finite) measure there exists a partition $\sequence {E_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ of $X$ in $\Sigma$ such that: $\forall n \in \N: \map \mu {E_n} < \infty$

title: Definition:Sigma-Finite Measure/Definition 4
snippet: Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. We say that $\mu$ is a $\sigma$-finite (or sigma-finite) measure it is the countable union of sets of finite measure.

title: Definition:Sigma-Finite Measure Space
snippet: A measure space $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ is said to be $\sigma$-finite (or sigma-finite) $\mu$ is a $\sigma$-finite measure.

title: Definition:Sigma-Locally Compact Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is $\sigma$-locally compact : That is, $T$ is $\sigma$-locally compact : $T$ is the union of countably many compact subspaces every point of $S$ has a local basis $\BB$ such that all elements of $\BB$ are compact.

title: Definition:Sigma-Locally Compact Space/Also defined as
snippet: == Sigma-Locally Compact Space: Also known as == Some sources define a $\sigma$-locally compact space as defines a weakly $\sigma$-locally compact space: There appears to be no appreciation anywhere on Internet-accessible sources that there are two such differing definitions, or that they define different concepts. The difference arises from the frequent confusion between our definitions of a weakly locally compact space and a locally compact space, the difference between which is again frequently omitted in the literature.

title: Definition:Sigma-Locally Finite Basis
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. A $\sigma$-locally finite basis for $T$ is a basis which is the countable union of locally finite sets of open sets.

title: Definition:Sigma-Locally Finite Basis/Also known as
snippet: == Sigma-Locally Finite Basis: Also known as == A $\sigma$-locally finite basis is also known as a countably locally finite basis. The term $\sigma$-discrete basis can also be found.

title: Definition:Sigma-Locally Finite Set of Subsets
snippet: A $\sigma$-locally finite set of subsets of a topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a set of subsets which is the countable union of a locally finite set of subsets.

title: Definition:Sigma-Locally Finite Set of Subsets/Also known as
snippet: == Sigma-Locally Finite Set of Subsets: Also known as == A $\sigma$-locally finite set of subsets is also known as a countably locally finite set of subsets.

title: Definition:Sigma-Ring/Definition 1
snippet: A $\sigma$-ring is a ring of sets which is closed under countable unions. That is, a ring of sets $\Sigma$ is a $\sigma$-ring : $\ds A_1, A_2, \ldots \in \Sigma \implies \bigcup_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty A_n \in \Sigma$

snippet: Let $\Sigma$ be a system of sets. $\Sigma$ is a $\sigma$-ring $\Sigma$ satisfies the $\sigma$-ring axioms:

title: Definition:Sigma-Ring/Definition 3
snippet: Let $\Sigma$ be a system of sets. $\Sigma$ is a $\sigma$-ring $\Sigma$ satisfies the $\sigma$-ring axioms:

title: Definition:Sigma-Ring/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on $\sigma$-Ring == The $\sigma$ in $\sigma$-ring is the Greek letter sigma which equates to the letter s. $\sigma$ stands for for somme, which is French for union. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Sigmoid Curve
snippet: A sigmoid curve is a plane curve which: is the locus of a (strictly) increasing real function has two horizontal asymptotes has exactly one point of inflection.

title: Definition:Sigmoid Curve/Also known as
snippet: == Sigmoid Curve: Also known as == A sigmoid curve is also known as an S-shaped curve, after the shape of an archaic English $S$, that is: $\int$. It is also known as the logistic curve, which is a specific instance of a sigmoid curve.

title: Definition:Sigmoid Curve/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Sigmoid Curve == The word sigmoid derives from the Greek letter "Sigma", and means S-shaped. This derives from the archaic form of the English letter $S$, still in use as the integral sign $\int$.

title: Definition:Sigmoid Function
snippet: The real sigmoid function is defined as: $\map S x = \dfrac 1 {1 + \map \exp {-x} }$ where $\exp$ is the exponential function. 600px

title: Definition:Sign
snippet: Definition:Symbol Mathematical logic: Definition:Sign of Formal Language Propositional logic: Definition:Sign of Propositional Logic Permutation theory: Definition:Sign of Permutation Arithmetic, algebra, analysis and so on: Definition:Sign (Arithmetic) Definition:Sign of Number

title: Definition:Sign (Arithmetic)
snippet: In the context of arithmetic and algebra, the term sign is used to mean one of the operators: Addition: $+$ Subtraction: $-$ Multiplication: $\times$ Division: $\div$ It can also be used to describe a general operator in the context of abstract algebra: $\circ$ and so on.

title: Definition:Sign Test
snippet: The sign test is a nonparametric test of the hypothesis that a population has a given median $M$. If the hypothesis is true, then: about half the sample observations should have a value greater than $M$ about half the sample observations should have a value less than $M$. Excessive numbers above or below $M$ indicate rejection. The critical region for the sign test is the pair of tails of the binomial distribution $\Binomial n {0.5}$.

title: Definition:Sign of Area of Triangle
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle embedded in the plane.

title: Definition:Sign of Area of Triangle/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle embedded in the plane. Let $\theta$ be the angle between $AB$ and $AC$. If the direction of $\theta$ is anticlockwise, then $\triangle ABC$ is defined as having positive area. If the direction of $\theta$ is clockwise, then $\triangle ABC$ is defined as having negative area. 320px Triangle $\triangle ABC$ with Positive Area 320px Triangle $\triangle ABC$ with Negative Area

title: Definition:Sign of Area of Triangle/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle embedded in the plane. Let the sides of $\triangle ABC$ be traversed in the order of its vertices, that is: $AB \to BC \to CA$ If the area of $\triangle ABC$ is thus described in an anticlockwise direction, then $\triangle ABC$ is defined as having positive area. If the area of $\triangle ABC$ is thus described in a clockwise direction, then $\triangle ABC$ is defined as having negative area.

title: Definition:Sign of Number
snippet: The sign of a number is the symbol indicating whether it is: positive, denoted by the symbol $+$ or: negative, denoted by the symbol $-$. Hence a number's sign has evolved to define the fact of the number being positive or negative independently of the symbol itself. Thus: the sign of $3.14159$ is positive and the sign of $-75$ is negative.

title: Definition:Sign of Ordered Tuple
snippet: Let $n \in \N$ be a natural number such that $n > 1$. Let $\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ be an ordered $n$-tuple of real numbers. Let $\map {\Delta_n} {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ be the product of differences of $\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$: $\ds \map {\Delta_n} {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} = \prod_{1 \mathop \le i \mathop 0} - \sqbrk {x 0}$ etc. is Iverson's convention.

title: Definition:Sign of Permutation
snippet: Let $n \in \N$ be a natural number. Let $\N_n$ denote the set of natural numbers $\set {1, 2, \ldots, n}$. Let $\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ be an ordered $n$-tuple of real numbers. Let $\pi$ be a permutation of $\N_n$. Let $\map {\Delta_n} {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ be the product of differences of $\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$.

title: Definition:Sign of Permutation/Also defined as
snippet: == Sign of Permutation: Also defined as == The sign of a permutation $\map \pi {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ can also be defined as: $\map \sgn \pi = \begin {cases} 1 & : \text {if $\pi$ is an even permutation of $\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$} \\ \\ -1 & : \text {if $\pi$ is an odd permutation of $\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$} \\ \\ 0 & : \text {if any two of $\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ are equal} \end {cases}$ The equivalence of these approaches is demonstrated in Sign of Permutation is Plus or Minus Unity.

title: Definition:Sign of Permutation/Also denoted as
snippet: == Sign of Permutation: Also denoted as == Some sources use $\map \epsilon \pi$ or $\map \varepsilon \pi$ to denote the sign of a permutation $\pi$. In physics and applied mathematics, the symbol $e_{i j k}$ can often be found for this concept. In this case, the permutation in question is specifically of the ordered triple $\tuple {i, j, k}$.

title: Definition:Sign of Permutation/Also known as
snippet: == Sign of Permutation: Also known as== The sign of a permutation is also known as its signature or signum. However, on signum is not recommended, in order to keep this concept separate from the signum function on a set of numbers.

title: Definition:Sign of Permutation on n Letters
snippet: Let $n \in \N$ be a natural number. Let $N^*_{\le n}$ denote the set of natural numbers $\set {1, 2, \ldots, n}$. Let $S_n$ denote the set of permutations on $N^*_{\le n}$. Let $\pi \in S_n$ be a permutation of $N^*_{\le n}$. Let $K$ be the cycle decomposition of $\pi$. Let each cycle of $K$ be factored into transpositions. Let $k$ be the total number of transpositions that compose $K$. The sign of $\pi$ is defined as: $\forall \pi \in S_n: \map \sgn \pi = \begin {cases} 1 & : \text {$k$ even} \\ -1 & : \text {$k$ odd} \\ \end {cases}$

title: Definition:Signature (Logic)
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a formal language. A choice of vocabulary for $\LL$ is called a signature for $\LL$.

title: Definition:Signature (Logic)/Predicate Logic
snippet: Let $\LL_1$ be the language of predicate logic. Then a signature for $\LL_1$ is an explicit choice of the alphabet of $\LL_1$. That is to say, it amounts to choosing, for each $n \in \N$: A collection $\FF_n$ of $n$-ary function symbols A collection $\PP_n$ of $n$-ary relation symbols It is often conceptually enlightening to explicitly address the $0$-ary function symbols separately, as constant symbols.

title: Definition:Signature of Hermitian Matrix
snippet: The signature of a Hermitian matrix $\mathbf H$ is the number of positive eigenvalues of $\mathbf H$ minus the number of negative eigenvalues of $\mathbf H$.

title: Definition:Signature of Quadratic Form
snippet: The signature of a quadratic form $Q$ is the number of positive terms of $Q$ minus the number of negative terms of $Q$.

title: Definition:Signature of Symmetric Bilinear Form
snippet: Let $\struct {V, q}$ be the scalar product space. Let $V^*$ be the algebraic dual of $V$. Suppose there exists a basis $\tuple {\beta^i}$ for $V^*$ such that $q$ is expressible as: $q = \paren {\beta^1}^2 + \ldots + \paren {\beta^r}^2 - \paren {\beta^{r + 1}}^2 - \ldots - \paren {\beta^{r + s}}^2$ where: $r, s \in \N : r + s = n$. Then the ordered pair $\tuple {r, s}$ is known as the signature of $q$.

title: Definition:Signed Area
snippet: Consider the plane region described by a graph in the $xy$-plane. The signed area of the region is the area such that: The area of the graph on or above the $x$-axis is defined as positive The area of the graph below the $x$-axis is defined as negative.

title: Definition:Signed Borel Measure
snippet: Let $d \in \N$. Let $\map \BB {\R^d}$ be the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on $\R^d$. Let $\mu$ be a signed measure on $\struct {\R^d, \map \BB {\R^d} }$. We say that $\mu$ is a signed Borel measure on $\R^d$.

title: Definition:Signed Graph
snippet: A signed graph is an undirected network whose functional values are $\pm 1$. The edges of such a graph are known as positive edges and negative edges. It is usual to indicate the functional values by means of just the $+$ or $-$ sign.

title: Definition:Signed Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\mu : \Sigma \to \overline \R$ be an extended real-valued function such that: if $\map \mu A = +\infty$ for some $A \in \Sigma$, then $\map \mu B > -\infty$ for all $B \in \Sigma$. and: if $\map \mu A = -\infty$ for some $A \in \Sigma$, then $\map \mu B < +\infty$ for all $B \in \Sigma$.

title: Definition:Significance Level
snippet: Let $\delta$ be a hypothesis test. Let $H_0$ and $H_1$ be the null hypothesis and alternative hypothesis of $\delta$ respectively. Let $T$ be the test statistic which is being used to determine whether $H_0$ or $H_1$ holds. Let $C$ be the critical region of $\delta$. Let $\alpha$ be the probability that $T$ takes a value in $C$ when in fact $H_0$ holds. $\alpha$ is known as the significance level of $\delta$.

title: Definition:Significance Level/Motivation
snippet: == Significance Levels: Motivation == Until relatively recently, these significance levels have been the only ones which were used in practice. This is because, prior to the advent of high speed electronic computation devices, the process to calculate the $p$-value was time-consuming and generally unfeasible. Hence critical values corresponding to the above significance levels have been tabulated for many of the commonly used test statistics, such as for the $t$-test, the $F$-test and the $\chi$-squared test.

title: Definition:Significant Figures
snippet: Let $n$ be a number expressed in decimal notation. The number of digits to which $n$ is rounded, apart from any digits needed to locate the decimal point, are referred to as the significant figures of $n$. In general the first non-zero digit, reading from left to right, is the first of the run of significant figures.

title: Definition:Significant Figures/Also known as
snippet: == Significant Figures: Also known as == Significant figures are also known as significant digits.

title: Definition:Significant Figures/Ambiguous Presentation
snippet: == Warning == Consider a number $n$ which is reported to $d$ significant figures, but which is larger than $10^d$. Then there will be one or more zero digits between the and the decimal point. Hence, when $n$ is written out in conventional notation, as a string of digits, it is not possible to determine by inspection exactly how many significant figures $n$ is being reported. In order to avoid such ambiguity, it is recommended that such a number be expressed in scientific notation, as this then becomes clear.

title: Definition:Significant Value
snippet: Let $V \in \R$, $\map {V_i} R: \closedint 0 1 \to \R$ be an evaluation function. Let $\map f B: \R \to \R$ be a bound function. The value $V_i$ is said to be a significant value the residue $R$ and the bound $B$ whenever $V \ge \map {V_i} R \map f B$. Category:Fair Cake-Cutting

title: Definition:Signum Function
snippet: Let $X \subseteq \R$ be a subset of the real numbers. The signum function $\sgn: X \to \set {-1, 0, 1}$ is defined as: $\forall x \in X: \map \sgn x := \sqbrk {x > 0} - \sqbrk {x 0}$ etc. denotes Iverson's convention. That is: $\forall x \in X: \map \sgn x := \begin {cases} -1 & : x 0 \end {cases}$

title: Definition:Signum Function/Also known as
snippet: == Signum Function: Also known as == The signum of a number is known, informally and colloquially, as its sign. Hence it can also be seen denoted as $\map {\mathrm {sign} } x$.

title: Definition:Signum Function/Graph
snippet: The graph of the signum function is illustrated below: 400px

title: Definition:Signum Function/Natural Numbers
snippet: The signum function $\sgn: \N \to \set {0, 1}$ is the restriction of the signum function to the natural numbers, defined as: $\forall n \in \N: \map \sgn n := \begin {cases} 0 & : n = 0 \\ 1 & : n > 0 \end{cases}$

title: Definition:Signum Function/Signum Complement
snippet: Let $\sgn: \N \to \set {0, 1}$ be the signum function on the natural numbers. The signum complement function $\overline \sgn: \N \to \set {0, 1}$ is defined as: $\forall n \in \N: \map {\overline \sgn} n := \begin {cases} 1 & : n = 0 \\ 0 & : n > 0 \end {cases}$

title: Definition:Siliqua/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Siliqua == The word siliqua is a Latin word that means carob seed. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Similar
snippet: Similar geometric figures: Geometric figures which have the same shape but of different sizes: Similar triangles Similar segments of circles The definition also applies to similar solid figures: solid figures which have the same shape but of different sizes: Similar cones Similar cylinders Similar planes The term similar can also be used to apply to the position of a geometric figure: Similar inclination Similar situation 's approach was to treat numbers as geometrical objects, hence the definitions: Similar plane numbers Similar solid numbers As a general term in natural language meaning:…

title: Definition:Similar Figures
snippet: Two rectilineal figures are similar : They have corresponding angles, all of which are equal They have corresponding sides, all of which are proportional.

title: Definition:Similar Figures/Algebraic Definition
snippet: Two geometric figures are similar if one can be transformed into the other by means of a similarity mapping.

title: Definition:Similar Figures/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Similarity == The symbol introduced by to denote geometric similarity was the tilde: $\sim$ This is still in use and can still be seen, but is not universal.

title: Definition:Similar Figures/Informal Definition
snippet: Two geometric figures are similar if they have the same shape but not necessarily the same size. It is intuitively understood what it means for two figures to have the same shape.

title: Definition:Similar Inclination
snippet: Category:Definitions/Angles Category:Definitions/Solid Geometry

title: Definition:Similar Planes
snippet: Similar planes are plane figures which are similar. Category:Definitions/Euclidean Geometry

title: Definition:Similar Situation
snippet: Two similar solid figures are said to be in a similar situation corresponding surfaces are similarly inclined and when corresponding edges are parallel.

title: Definition:Similar Situation/Also known as
snippet: == Similar Situation: Also known as == Similar solid figures in a similar situation can also be described as similarly situated. Category:Definitions/Similar Situation

title: Definition:Similar Triangles
snippet: Similar triangles are triangles whose corresponding angles are the same, but whose corresponding sides may be of different lengths. 360px Thus $\triangle ABC$ is similar to $\triangle DEF$: $\angle ABC = \angle EFD$ $\angle BCA = \angle EDF$ $\angle CAB = \angle DEF$

title: Definition:Similarity
snippet: Linear Algebra: Similarity Mapping Self-Similarity Matrix Similarity Set Theory: Set Similarity

title: Definition:Similarity Dimension/Also known as
snippet: == Similarity Dimension: Also known as == The similarity dimension of an object is also known by some sources as its fractal dimension. However, the similarity dimension is just one of a number of such fractal dimensions, and strives to distinguish between them all.

title: Definition:Similarity Mapping
snippet: Let $G$ be a vector space over a field $K$. Let $\beta \in K$. Let $s_\beta: G \to G$ be the mapping on $G$ defined as: $\forall \mathbf x \in G: \map {s_\beta} {\mathbf x} = \beta \mathbf x$ $s_\beta$ is called a similarity (mapping).

title: Definition:Similarity Mapping/Also known as
snippet: == Similarity Mapping: Also known as == An older term for a similarity mapping is similitude.

title: Definition:Similarity Mapping/Scale Factor
snippet: Let $G$ be a vector space over a field $K$. Let $\beta \in K$. Let $s_\beta: G \to G$ be a similarity mapping on $G$: $\forall \mathbf x \in G: \map {s_\beta} {\mathbf x} = \beta \mathbf x$ The coefficient $\beta$ is called the scale factor of $s_\beta$.

title: Definition:Similarity Transformation
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ be similar matrices. A similarity transformation is an operation of changing $\mathbf B$ to $\mathbf A$ by multiplying $\mathbf B$ by a nonsingular matrix $\mathbf Y$ and its inverse $\mathbf Y^{-1}$ such that: $\mathbf A = \mathbf Y^{-1} \mathbf B \mathbf Y$

title: Definition:Similarity Transformation/Also known as
snippet: == Similarity Transformation: Also known as == A similarity transformation is also known as: a collinearity transformation a collineation.

title: Definition:Simple
snippet: Abstract Algebra: Definition:Simple Group Definition:Simple Module Definition:Simple Lie Algebra Definition:Simple Field Extension Linear Algebra Definition:Simple Eigenvalue Continued Fractions: Definition:Simple Continued Fraction Definition:Simple Finite Continued Fraction Vecor Analysis: Definition:Simple Contour Graph Theory: Definition:Simple Graph Definition:Simple Digraph Definition:Simple Edge Measure Theory: Definition:Simple Function

title: Definition:Simple Algebraic Field Extension
snippet: Let $F$ be a field. Let $z$ be a complex number which is algebraic over $F$. Then the smallest field $\map F z$ containing $F$ and $z$ is known as a simple algebraic (field) extension of $F$.

title: Definition:Simple Continued Fraction
snippet: Let $\R$ be the field of real numbers.

title: Definition:Simple Continued Fraction/Also known as
snippet: == Simple Continued Fraction: Also known as == A simple continued fraction is also known as a regular continued fraction. When the context is such that it is immaterial whether a simple continued fraction is finite or infinite, the abbreviation SCF can be used. Some sources refer to a simple continued fraction as just a continued fraction.

title: Definition:Simple Continued Fraction/Finite
snippet: Let $\R$ be the set of real numbers. Let $n \ge 0$ be a natural number. A simple finite continued fraction of length $n$ is a finite continued fraction in $\R$ of length $n$ whose partial denominators are integers that are strictly positive, except perhaps the first. That is, it is a finite sequence $a: \closedint 0 n \to \Z$ with $a_n > 0$ for $n > 0$.

title: Definition:Simple Continued Fraction/Infinite
snippet: Let $\R$ be the field of real numbers. A simple infinite continued fraction is a infinite continued fraction in $\R$ whose partial denominators are integers that are strictly positive, except perhaps the first. That is, it is a sequence $a: \N_{\ge 0} \to \Z$ with $a_n > 0$ for $n > 0$.

title: Definition:Simple Curve
snippet: A simple curve is a curve which does not intersect itself.

title: Definition:Simple Eigenvalue
snippet: An eigenvalue is called simple if it has an algebraic multiplicity equal to $1$.

title: Definition:Simple Extension
snippet: Definition:Simple Field Extension

title: Definition:Simple Field Extension
snippet: Let $E / F$ be a field extension. Then $E$ is a simple (field) extension over $F$ : $\exists \alpha \in E: E = F \sqbrk \alpha$ where $F \sqbrk \alpha$ is the field extension generated by $\alpha$.

title: Definition:Simple Finite Continued Fraction/Also known as
snippet: == Simple Finite Continued Fraction: Also known as == A simple finite continued fraction can be abbreviated SFCF. It is also known as a regular finite continued fraction. The order of the words can be varied, that is finite simple continued fraction for example, but strives for consistency and does not use that form.

title: Definition:Simple Function
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. A real-valued function $f: X \to \R$ is said to be a simple function it is a finite linear combination of characteristic functions: $\ds f = \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n a_k \chi_{S_k}$ where $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ are real numbers and each of the sets $S_k$ is $\Sigma$-measurable.

title: Definition:Simple Function/Banach Space
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $I$ be a real interval. Let $X$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $f : I \to X$ be a function. We say that $f$ is simple there exists: Lebesgue measurable subsets $\Omega_1, \ldots, \Omega_n$ of $I$ with finite Lebesgue measure $x_1, \ldots, x_n \in X$ such that: $\ds \map f t = \sum_{r \mathop = 1}^n x_r \map {\chi_{\Omega_r} } t$ for each $t \in I$.

title: Definition:Simple Graph
snippet: A simple graph is a graph which is: An undirected graph, that is, the edges are defined as doubleton sets of vertices and not ordered pairs Not a multigraph, that is, there is no more than one edge between each pair of vertices Not a loop-graph, that is, there are no loops, that is, edges which start and end at the same vertex Not a weighted graph, that is, the edges are not mapped to a number.

title: Definition:Simple Graph/Also defined as
snippet: == Simple Graph: Also defined as == Some sources impose the condition that a simple graph must have at least one vertex. Some sources also define a simple graph as one which has a finite number of vertices.

title: Definition:Simple Graph/Also known as
snippet: == Simple Graph: Also known as == Authors whose coverage is less general refer to a simple graph as just a graph.

title: Definition:Simple Graph/Also presented as
snippet: == Simple Graph: Also presented as == It is often more convenient to express the elements of the edge set of a simple graph as doubletons, of the form $\set {v_a, v_b}$. Category:Definitions/Simple Graphs

title: Definition:Simple Graph/Formal Definition
snippet: Let $V$ be a set. Let $\RR$ be an endorelation on $V$ which is antireflexive and symmetric. Let $E$ be the set whose elements of the form: $\set {\tuple {v_a, v_b}, \tuple {v_b, v_a} }$. where $\tuple {v_a, v_b}$ and $\tuple {v_b, v_a}$ are elements of $\RR$ A simple graph is an ordered pair $G = \struct {V, E}$, where $V$ and $E$ are defined as above. $V$ is called the vertex set. $E$ is called the edge set.

title: Definition:Simple Group
snippet: A group $G$ is simple it has only $G$ and the trivial group as normal subgroups. That is, the composition length of $G$ is $1$.

title: Definition:Simple Harmonic Motion
snippet: Consider a physical system $S$ whose motion can be expressed in the form of the following equation: $x = A \map \sin {\omega t + \phi}$ where $A$ and $\phi$ are constants. Then $S$ is in a state of simple harmonic motion.

title: Definition:Simple Harmonic Motion/Also defined as
snippet: == Simple Harmonic Motion: Also defined as == Simple harmonic motion can also be characterised in the form: $x = A \map \cos {\omega t + \phi}$ From Sine of Angle plus Right Angle: $\map \sin {\omega t + \phi + \dfrac \pi 2} = \map \cos {\omega t + \phi}$ the two forms can be seen to be equivalent.

title: Definition:Simple Harmonic Motion/Also known as
snippet: == Simple Harmonic Motion: Also known as == Simple harmonic motion can also be referred to as simple harmonic oscillation or simple harmonic vibration. It is commonly abbreviated it SHM.

title: Definition:Simple Harmonic Motion/Amplitude
snippet: Consider a physical system $S$ in a state of simple harmonic motion: $x = A \map \sin {\omega t + \phi}$ The parameter $A$ is known as the amplitude of the motion.

title: Definition:Simple Harmonic Motion/Frequency
snippet: Consider a physical system $S$ in a state of simple harmonic motion: $x = A \map \sin {\omega t + \phi}$ The frequency $\nu$ of the motion of $S$ is the number of complete cycles per unit time: $\nu = \dfrac 1 T = \dfrac \omega {2 \pi}$

title: Definition:Simple Harmonic Motion/In Phase
snippet: Let $S_1$ and $S_2$ be physical systems in a state of simple harmonic motion described respectively by the equations: {{eqn | l = x_1 | r = a_1 \map \cos {\omega t + \alpha_1} }} {{eqn | l = x_2 | r = a_2 \map \cos {\omega t + \alpha_2} }} $S_1$ and $S_2$ are in phase $\alpha_1 = \alpha_2$.

title: Definition:Simple Harmonic Motion/Initial Phase
snippet: Consider a physical system $S$ in a state of simple harmonic motion: $x = A \map \sin {\omega t + \phi}$ The parameter $\phi$ is known as the initial phase of the motion.

title: Definition:Simple Harmonic Motion/Out of Phase
snippet: Let $S_1$ and $S_2$ be physical systems in a state of simple harmonic motion described respectively by the equations: {{eqn | l = x_1 | r = a_1 \map \cos {\omega t + \alpha_1} }} {{eqn | l = x_2 | r = a_2 \map \cos {\omega t + \alpha_2} }} $S_1$ and $S_2$ are out of phase $\alpha_1 \ne \alpha_2$.

title: Definition:Simple Harmonic Motion/Period
snippet: Consider a physical system $S$ in a state of simple harmonic motion: $x = A \map \sin {\omega t + \phi}$ The period $T$ of the motion of $S$ is the time required for one complete cycle: $T = \dfrac {2 \pi} \omega$

title: Definition:Simple Harmonic Motion/Phase
snippet: Consider a physical system $S$ in a state of simple harmonic motion: $x = A \map \sin {\omega t + \phi}$ The expression $\omega t + \phi$ is known as the phase of the motion.

title: Definition:Simple Hypothesis
snippet: Let $\theta$ be a population parameter of some population. Let the parameter space of $\theta$ be $\Omega$. Let $\Omega_0$ and $\Omega_1$ be disjoint subsets of $\Omega$ such that $\Omega_0 \cup \Omega_1 = \Omega$. Consider the hypotheses: $H_0: \theta \in \Omega_0$ $H_1: \theta \in \Omega_1$ We call $H_i$, for $i \in \set {0, 1}$, a simple hypothesis $\Omega_i$ contains only a single element.

title: Definition:Simple Hypothesis Test
snippet: Let $\delta$ be a hypothesis test. Then $\delta$ is a simple hypothesis test the probability distribution of the population random variable is completely specified.

title: Definition:Simple Infinite Continued Fraction/Also known as
snippet: == Simple Infinite Continued Fraction: Also known as == A simple infinite continued fraction can be abbreviated SICF. It is also known as a regular infinite continued fraction. The order of the words can be varied, that is infinite simple continued fraction for example, but strives for consistency and does not use that form.

title: Definition:Simple Matroid
snippet: Let $M = \struct {S, \mathscr I}$ be a matroid. $M$ is called a simple matroid it has no loops or parallel elements.

title: Definition:Simple Order Product
snippet: Let $\struct {S_1, \preccurlyeq_1}$ and $\struct {S_2, \preccurlyeq_2}$ be ordered sets. The simple (order) product $\struct {S_1, \preccurlyeq_1} \otimes^s \struct {S_2, \preccurlyeq_2}$ of $\struct {S_1, \preccurlyeq_1}$ and $\struct {S_2, \preccurlyeq_2}$ is the ordered set $\struct {T, \preccurlyeq_s}$ where: $T := S_1 \times S_2$, that is, the Cartesian product of $S_1$ and $S_2$ $\preccurlyeq_s$ is defined as: $\forall \tuple {a, b}, \tuple {c, d} \in T: \tuple {a, b} \preccurlyeq_s \tuple {c, d} \iff a \preccurlyeq_1 c \text { and } b \preccurlyeq_2 d$

title: Definition:Simple Order Product/Family
snippet: Let $I$ be an indexing set. For each $i \in I$, let $\struct {S_i, \preccurlyeq_i}$ be an ordered set. Let $\ds D = \prod_{i \mathop \in I} S_i$ be the Cartesian product of the family $\family {\struct {S_i, \preccurlyeq_i} }_{i \mathop \in I}$ indexed by $I$. Then the simple order product on $D$ is defined as: $\ds \struct {D, \preccurlyeq_D} := {\bigotimes_{i \mathop \in I} }^s \struct {S_i, \preccurlyeq_i}$ where $\preccurlyeq_D$ is defined as: $\forall u, v \in D: u \preccurlyeq_D v \iff \forall i \in I: \map u i \preccurlyeq_i \map v i$

title: Definition:Simple Pendulum/Also defined as
snippet: == Simple Pendulum: Also defined as == In their definitions of a simple pendulum, some treatments specify that, instead of a rod, the bob is suspended from the pivot by a cord. The treatment is similar to that of the rod, but the behaviour of the simple pendulum when the bob rises above the pivot is different. In all cases, the statement of the problem should define which arrangement is in effect.

title: Definition:Simple Pendulum/Also known as
snippet: == Simple Pendulum: Also known as == A simple pendulum as defined on is often referred to as just a pendulum.

title: Definition:Simple Pendulum/Bob
snippet: The point mass at the free end of the rod of a simple pendulum is called the (pendulum) bob. Hence the bob is free to swing under the effects of the gravitational field.

title: Definition:Simple Pendulum/Ideals
snippet: The ideals of a simple pendulum are as follows: The rod is of zero thickness, infinite stiffness and zero mass. The pivot is immovable and has zero friction. The bob is of zero volume. The gravitation field is (usually) taken to be constant and uniform. The medium in which the simple pendulum moves offers no resistive force, unless otherwise specifically stated.

title: Definition:Simple Pendulum/Period
snippet: The period of a simple pendulum is the time period through which the bob takes to travel from one end of its path to the other, and back again.

title: Definition:Simple Random Sample
snippet: Let $P$ be a population. Let $S \subsetneq P$ be a sample. Then $S$ is a simple random sample (of size $n$) it fulfils the following criteria: The process used to select the individuals of $S$ from $P$ was random; Every individual in $P$ had an equal chance of being selected to be in $S$; Every $n$-combination of $P$ had an equal chance of being constructed as a potential $S$.

title: Definition:Simple Random Sampling
snippet: Simple random sampling is a process of selection of a random sample from a population such that each element of $P$ has an equal probability of being selected at every stage.

title: Definition:Simple Root/Definition 1
snippet: A number $a$ is a simple root of a polynomial equation $\map f x = 0$ : $a$ is a root of $\map f x = 0$ but: $a$ is not a root of $\dfrac {\map f x} {x - a} = 0$.

title: Definition:Simple Root/Definition 2
snippet: Let $a, b, \ldots$ be the roots of a polynomial equation $\map f x = 0$. Hence let $\map f x$ be expressed in terms of its divisors: $\map f x = \paren {x - a}^k \paren {x - b}^l \cdots$ Then $a$ is a simple root of $\map f x = 0$ $k = 1$.

title: Definition:Simple Statement
snippet: A simple statement is a statement which has one subject and one predicate. For example, the statement: London is the capital of England is a simple statement. London is the subject and is the capital of England is the predicate.

title: Definition:Simplex
snippet: A simplex is an $n$-dimensional generalization of a triangle and tetrahedron, for $n \in \Z_{>0}$. A $k$-simplex is a $k$-dimensional polytope which is the convex hull of its $k + 1$ vertices.

title: Definition:Simplex/Definition 1
snippet: A simplex $S$ in $\R^n$ with vertices $\family {\alpha_i}_{i \mathop = 0}^n$ is a set such that: $S = \set {\ds \sum_{i \mathop = 0}^n \theta_i \alpha_i}$ where: $\sequence {\alpha_i}_{i \mathop = 0}^n$ is a sequence of $n + 1$ affinely independent points in $\R^n$ $\sequence {\theta_i}_{i \mathop = 0}^n$ is a sequence of arbitrary real numbers such that: $\forall i \in \set {0, 1, 2, \ldots, n}: \theta_i \in \hointr 0 \to$ $\ds \sum_{i \mathop = 0}^n \theta_i = 1$

title: Definition:Simplex/Definition 2
snippet: A simplex $S$ in $\R^n$ with vertices $\family {\alpha_i}_{i \mathop = 0}^n$ is a set such that: $S = \set {\ds \sum_{i \mathop = 0}^n \theta_i \alpha_i}$ where: $\sequence {\alpha_i}_{i \mathop = 0}^n$ is a sequence of $n + 1$ affinely independent points in $\R^n$ $\sequence {\theta_i}_{i \mathop = 0}^n$ is a sequence of arbitrary real numbers such that: $\forall i \in \set {0, 1, 2, \ldots, n}: \theta_i \in \closedint 0 1$ $\ds \sum_{i \mathop = 0}^n \theta_i = 1$

title: Definition:Simplex/Dimension
snippet: Let $S$ be a $k$-simplex: $S = \set {\ds \sum_{i \mathop = 0}^k \theta_i \alpha_i}$ The parameter $k$ is called the dimension of $S$.

title: Definition:Simplex/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Simplex == The plural of simplex has one of two possible forms: simplexes, pronounced sim-plex-iz simplices, pronounced sim-pli-seez Either can be found on , depending on where the material was sourced from. Compare the plural forms of vertex: vertices and index: indices.

title: Definition:Simplex Algorithm/Optimality Condition
snippet: Consider a linear programming exercise being solved by means of the simplex method. The aim is to find a simplex tableau which satisfies the optimality condition. The optimality condition is that when the objective row of a simplex tableau shows: $0$ in all columns representing basic variables no negative entries then it represents an optimal solution.

title: Definition:Simplex Method
snippet: The simplex method is a technique for solving problems in linear programming. Additional variables, known as slack variables, are introduced to convert inequalities to equations. The feasible solutions are then obtained by an iterative process. These can be set out in arrays called simplex tableaux. Thus the conversion inequalities to equations enables the boundaries of a simplex or feasible region which satisfies the constraints. The optimum solution then lies at a vertex of this simplex.

title: Definition:Simplex Method/Simplex Algorithm
snippet: The simplex algorithm is the algorithm by which the simplex method obtains the optimality condition of a linear programming exercise. Preliminary Consider an objective function: $P = a_1 x_1 + a_2 x_2 + \cdots + a_m x_m$ for basic variables $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_m$ Introduce slack variables to rewrite each constraint defined as an inequality as an equation.

title: Definition:Simplex Tableau
snippet: A simplex tableau is a technique for presenting information obtained by an iterative process during the course of using the simplex method for solving a problem of linear programming. It shows: the current values for each variable in each constraint the current values for each variable in the objective function, held in the bottom row. The variables in question include the slack variables.

title: Definition:Simplex Tableau/Also known as
snippet: == Simplex Tableau: Also known as == A simplex tableau is also known as a tableau. However, that term has a number of usages, so to avoid ambiguity, the full form is preferred on .

title: Definition:Simplex Tableau/Entering Variable
snippet: The basic variable of a simplex tableau with the largest negative entry in the objective row is known as the entering variable.

title: Definition:Simplex Tableau/Leaving Variable
snippet: The slack variable heading the pivotal row of a simplex tableau is known as the leaving variable.

title: Definition:Simplex Tableau/Mistake
snippet: == Source Work == simplex method

title: Definition:Simplex Tableau/Objective Row
snippet: The bottom row of a simplex tableau, that is, the row containing the objective function, is called the objective row of the simplex tableau.

title: Definition:Simplex Tableau/Pivot
snippet: The entry in a simplex tableau which forms the intersection of the pivotal row and the pivotal column is known as the pivot.

title: Definition:Simplex Tableau/Pivotal Column
snippet: The column of a simplex tableau containing the entering variable is known as the pivotal column.

title: Definition:Simplex Tableau/Pivotal Row
snippet: The row of a simplex tableau headed by a slack variable holding the smallest value in the $\text{value}$ column, after having divided it by the value of the entering variable for that row, is known as the pivotal row.

title: Definition:Simplicial Complex
snippet: Let $m \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. A simplicial complex is a finite set $K$ of simplices in $\R^m$ such that: all faces of the simplices in $K$ are included two simplices meet, if at all, in a common face.

title: Definition:Simplicial Polytopic Number
snippet: The simplicial polytopic numbers are those denumerating a collection of objects which can be arranged in the form of a simplex.

title: Definition:Simplified Arens Square
snippet: Let $A$ be the set of points in the interior of the unit square: $A := \set {\tuple {i, j}: 0 < i < 1, 0 < j < 1, i, j \in \R} = \openint 0 1^2$ Simplified Arens square with example local bases marked Let $S$ be the set defined as: $S = A \cup \set {\tuple {0, 0} } \cup \set {\tuple {1, 0} }$ Let $\BB$ be the basis for a topology generated on $S$ be defined by granting: to each point of $A$ the local basis of open sets inherited by $A$ from the Euclidean topology on the unit square; to the other points of $S$ the following local bases: {{eqn | l = \map {U_n} {0, 0} | o = := | r = \set {\tuple…

title: Definition:Simply Connected
snippet: Let $T = \struct{S, \tau}$ be a path-connected topological space.

title: Definition:Simply Connected/Definition 1
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a path-connected topological space. $T$ is said to be simply connected if the fundamental group $\map {\pi_1} T$ of $T$ is trivial.

title: Definition:Simply Connected/Definition 2
snippet: Let $T = \struct{S, \tau}$ be a path-connected topological space. $T$ is said to be simply connected if all loops in $T$ with identical base points are path-homotopic.

title: Definition:Simply Connected/Definition 3
snippet: Let $T = \struct{S, \tau}$ be a path-connected topological space. $T$ is said to be simply connected if all paths in $T$ with identical initial points and final points are path-homotopic.

title: Definition:Simply Connected/Definition 4
snippet: Let $T = \struct{S, \tau}$ be a path-connected topological space. $T$ is said to be simply connected if all loops in $T$ are path-homotopic with a constant loop.

title: Definition:Simulation
snippet: A simulation is a system of mathematical models designed to study a physical system which has a dynamical or stochastic aspect, and very probably both.

title: Definition:Simultaneous Congruences
snippet: A system of simultaneous congruences is a set of polynomial congruences: $\forall i \in \closedint 1 r: \map {P_i} x \equiv 0 \pmod {n_i}$ That is: {{eqn | l = \map {P_1} x | r = 0 | rr= \pmod {n_1} | c = }} {{eqn | l = \map {P_2} x | r = 0 | rr= \pmod {n_2} | c = }} {{eqn | l = \map {P_r} x | r = 0 | rr= \pmod {n_r} | c = }}

title: Definition:Simultaneous Congruences/Linear
snippet: A system of simultaneous linear congruences is a set of linear congruences: $\forall i \in \closedint 1 r : a_i x \equiv b_i \pmod {n_1}$ That is: {{eqn | l = a_1 x | o = \equiv | r = b_1 | rr= \pmod {n_1} | c = }} {{eqn | l = a_2 x | o = \equiv | r = b_2 | rr= \pmod {n_2} | c = }} {{eqn | l = a_r x | o = \equiv | r = b_r | rr= \pmod {n_r} | c = }}

title: Definition:Simultaneous Congruences/Solution
snippet: A solution of a system of simultaneous congruences is a residue class modulo $\lcm \set {n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_r}$ such that any element of that class satisfies all the congruences.

title: Definition:Simultaneous Equations
snippet: A system of simultaneous equations is a set of equations: $\forall i \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, m} : \map {f_i} {x_1, x_2, \ldots x_n} = \beta_i$ That is: {{eqn | l = \beta_1 | r = \map {f_1} {x_1, x_2, \ldots x_n} }} {{eqn | l = \beta_2 | r = \map {f_2} {x_1, x_2, \ldots x_n} }} {{eqn | l = \beta_m | r = \map {f_m} {x_1, x_2, \ldots x_n} }}

title: Definition:Simultaneous Equations/Consistency
snippet: A system of simultaneous equations: $\forall i \in \set {1, 2, \ldots m} : \map {f_i} {x_1, x_2, \ldots x_n} = \beta_i$ that has at least one solution is consistent. If a system has no solutions, it is inconsistent. Category:Definitions/Simultaneous Equations

title: Definition:Simultaneous Equations/Linear Equations
snippet: A system of simultaneous linear equations is a set of linear equations: $\ds \forall i \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, m} : \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n \alpha_{i j} x_j = \beta_i$ That is: {{eqn | l = \beta_1 | r = \alpha_{1 1} x_1 + \alpha_{1 2} x_2 + \cdots + \alpha_{1 n} x_n }} {{eqn | l = \beta_2 | r = \alpha_{2 1} x_1 + \alpha_{2 2} x_2 + \cdots + \alpha_{2 n} x_n }} {{eqn | l = \beta_m | r = \alpha_{m 1} x_1 + \alpha_{m 2} x_2 + \cdots + \alpha_{m n} x_n }}

title: Definition:Simultaneous Equations/Linear Equations/Solution
snippet: Consider the system of simultaneous linear equations: $\ds \forall i \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, m} : \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n \alpha_{i j} x_j = \beta_i$ That is: {{eqn | l = \beta_1 | r = \alpha_{1 1} x_1 + \alpha_{1 2} x_2 + \cdots + \alpha_{1 n} x_n }} {{eqn | l = \beta_2 | r = \alpha_{2 1} x_1 + \alpha_{2 2} x_2 + \cdots + \alpha_{2 n} x_n }} {{eqn | l = \beta_m | r = \alpha_{m 1} x_1 + \alpha_{m 2} x_2 + \cdots + \alpha_{m n} x_n }} Let $\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ satisfy each of the linear equations in $\ds \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n \alpha_{i j} x_j = \beta_i$.

title: Definition:Simultaneous Equations/Solution
snippet: An ordered $n$-tuple $\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ which satisfies each of the equations in a system of $m$ simultaneous equations in $n$ variables is called a solution to, or of, the system.

title: Definition:Simultaneous Equations/Solution Set
snippet: Consider the system of $m$ simultaneous equations in $n$ variables: $\mathbb S := \forall i \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, m} : \map {f_i} {x_1, x_2, \ldots x_n} = \beta_i$ Let $\mathbb X$ be the set of ordered $n$-tuples: $\set {\sequence {x_j}_{j \mathop \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n} }: \forall i \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, m}: \map {f_i} {\sequence {x_j} } = \beta_i}$ which satisfies each of the equations in $\mathbb S$. Then $\mathbb X$ is called the solution set of $\mathbb S$. Thus to solve a system of simultaneous equations is to find all the elements of $\mathbb X$.

title: Definition:Simultaneous Inequalities
snippet: A system of simultaneous inequalities is a set of two or more inequalities that hold simultaneously.

title: Definition:Simultaneous Inequalities/Solution
snippet: The solution to a system of simultaneous inequalities is the set of values which hold for all inequalities in that system.

title: Definition:Simultaneous Linear Equations/Also presented as
snippet: == Simultaneous Linear Equations: Also presented as == A system of simultaneous linear equations is often presented as an instantiation of a linear transformation from one vector space to another.

title: Definition:Simultaneous Linear Equations/Matrix Representation
snippet: A system of simultaneous linear equations can be (and commonly is) expressed in its matrix representation: $\mathbf A \mathbf x = \mathbf b$ where: $\mathbf A = \begin {bmatrix} \alpha_{1 1} & \alpha_{1 2} & \cdots & \alpha_{1 n} \\ \alpha_{2 1} & \alpha_{2 2} & \cdots & \alpha_{2 n} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \alpha_{m 1} & \alpha_{m 2} & \cdots & \alpha_{m n} \\ \end {bmatrix}$, $\mathbf x = \begin {bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ \vdots \\ x_n \end {bmatrix}$, $\mathbf b = \begin {bmatrix} \beta_1 \\ \beta_2 \\ \vdots \\ \beta_m \end {bmatrix}$ are matrices.

title: Definition:Simultaneous Linear Equations/Matrix Representation/Augmented Matrix
snippet: Consider the system of simultaneous linear equations: $\ds \forall i \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, m} : \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n \alpha_{i j} x_j = \beta_i$ expressed in matrix representation as: $\mathbf A \mathbf x = \mathbf b$ Let $\begin {bmatrix} \mathbf A & \mathbf b \end {bmatrix}$ be the block matrix formed from $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf b$. Then $\begin {bmatrix} \mathbf A & \mathbf b \end {bmatrix}$ is known as the augmented matrix of the system.

title: Definition:Simultaneous Linear Equations/Matrix Representation/Matrix of Coefficients
snippet: Consider the system of simultaneous linear equations can be expressed as: $\ds \forall i \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, m} : \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n \alpha_{i j} x_j = \beta_i$ expressed in matrix representation as: $\mathbf A \mathbf x = \mathbf b$ The matrix $\mathbf A$ is known as the matrix of coefficients of the system.

title: Definition:Simultaneously Diagonalizable Matrices
snippet: Let $A$ be a set of diagonalizable matrices. Then $A$ is simultaneously diagonalizable there exists a nonsingular matrix $\mathbf X$ such that: $\forall \mathbf M \in A : \mathbf X^{-1} \mathbf M \mathbf X$ is diagonal.

title: Definition:Sinc Function
snippet: The sinc function is the real function $\sinc: \R \to \R$ defined as: $\forall x \in \R: \map \sinc x := \dfrac {\sin x} x$ where $\sin$ denotes the (real) sine function.

title: Definition:Sinc Function/Also known as
snippet: == Sinc Function: Also known as == The sinc function is also known as the sine cardinal function. Some sources refer to it as the sampling function, but reserves that term for something else.

title: Definition:Sinc Function/Graph
snippet: The graph of the sinc function is illustrated below: 700px

title: Definition:Sine/Complex Function
snippet: The complex sine function $\sin: \C \to \C$ is defined as: {{eqn | q = \forall z \in \C | l = \sin z | r = \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \paren {-1}^n \frac {z^{2 n + 1 } } {\paren {2 n + 1}!} | c = }} {{eqn | r = z - \frac {z^3} {3!} + \frac {z^5} {5!} - \frac {z^7} {7!} + \cdots + \paren {-1}^n \frac {z^{2 n + 1 } } {\paren {2 n + 1}!} + \cdots | c = }}

title: Definition:Sine/Definition from Circle
snippet: The sine of an angle in a right triangle can be extended to the full circle as follows:

title: Definition:Sine/Definition from Circle/First Quadrant
snippet: Consider a unit circle $C$ whose center is at the origin of a cartesian plane. 500px Let $P = \tuple {x, y}$ be the point on $C$ in the first quadrant such that $\theta$ is the angle made by $OP$ with the $x$-axis. Let $AP$ be the perpendicular from $P$ to the $x$-axis. Then the sine of $\theta$ is defined as the length of $AP$. Hence in the first quadrant, the sine is positive.

title: Definition:Sine/Definition from Circle/Fourth Quadrant
snippet: Consider a unit circle $C$ whose center is at the origin of a cartesian plane. 500px Let $P = \tuple {x, y}$ be the point on $C$ in the fourth quadrant such that $\theta$ is the angle made by $OP$ with the $x$-axis. Let $AP$ be the perpendicular from $P$ to the $x$-axis. Then the sine of $\theta$ is defined as the length of $AP$. Hence in the fourth quadrant, the sine is negative.

title: Definition:Sine/Definition from Circle/Second Quadrant
snippet: Consider a unit circle $C$ whose center is at the origin of a cartesian plane. 500px Let $P = \tuple {x, y}$ be the point on $C$ in the second quadrant such that $\theta$ is the angle made by $OP$ with the $x$-axis. Let $AP$ be the perpendicular from $P$ to the $x$-axis. Then the sine of $\theta$ is defined as the length of $AP$. Hence in the second quadrant, the sine is positive.

title: Definition:Sine/Definition from Circle/Third Quadrant
snippet: Consider a unit circle $C$ whose center is at the origin of a cartesian plane. 500px Let $P = \tuple {x, y}$ be the point on $C$ in the third quadrant such that $\theta$ is the angle made by $OP$ with the $x$-axis. Let $AP$ be the perpendicular from $P$ to the $x$-axis. Then the sine of $\theta$ is defined as the length of $AP$. Thus by definition of third quadrant, the sine is negative.

title: Definition:Sine/Definition from Triangle
snippet: 400px In the above right triangle, we are concerned about the angle $\theta$. The sine of $\angle \theta$ is defined as being $\dfrac {\text {Opposite} } {\text {Hypotenuse} }$.

title: Definition:Sine/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Sine == It was who first compiled tables relating the length of the arc of a circle and the length of the chord which gives rise to it, for various angles subtended by the arc. However, he did not actually define the concept of a sine as such. The sine was first discussed by , under the name ardha-jyā, which means half-chord. The symbol $\sin$ for sine appears to have been invented by in his $1657$ work Trigonometrie, although some authors attribute it to .

title: Definition:Sine/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Sine == The sine was originally written about by , under the name ardha-jyā. The word jyā is a word meaning bow-string, and in the mathematical context means the chord of a circle. Thus the word ardha-jyā literally means half-chord. Later the first part of the word tended to be omitted, thereby leaving the word jyā. When the word jyā was translated into , it was interpreted as jiba. Vowels in Arabic are omitted, leaving the word jb. The word jiba in Arabic is meaningless.

title: Definition:Sine/Real Function
snippet: The real sine function $\sin: \R \to \R$ is defined as: {{eqn | q = \forall x \in \R | l = \sin x | r = \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \paren {-1}^n \frac {x^{2 n + 1} } {\paren {2 n + 1}!} | c = }} {{eqn | r = x - \frac {x^3} {3!} + \frac {x^5} {5!} - \cdots | c = }}

title: Definition:Sine/Real Function/Arch
snippet: Each section of the sine function between adjacent zeroes is called an arch of the sine function

title: Definition:Sine Curve
snippet: A sine curve is the graph of a real function which can be expressed in the form: $\forall x \in \R: \map f x = a \map \sin {m x + \epsilon}$ where $a$, $m$ and $\epsilon$ are arbitrary constants. It is usual to suppose that: $a$ and $m$ are non-zero and either: $0 \le \epsilon \le 2 \pi$ or: $-\pi \le \epsilon \le \pi$

title: Definition:Sine Curve/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Sine Curve == The adjective used to describe a sine curve is sinusoidal.

title: Definition:Sine Integral Function
snippet: The sine integral function is the real function $\Si: \R \to \R$ defined as: $\map \Si x = \ds \int_{t \mathop \to 0}^{t \mathop = x} \frac {\sin t} t \rd t$

title: Definition:Sine Integral Function/Also defined as
snippet: == Sine Integral Function: Also defined as == Some sources consider the value of the sine integral function at $x = 0$ as a special case: $\map \Si x = \begin{cases} \ds \int_{t \mathop \to 0}^{t \mathop = x} \frac {\sin t} t \rd t & : x \ne 0 \\ \vphantom x \\ 0 & : x = 0 \\ \end{cases}$ but as $\map \Si 0 = 0$ as an emergent property of the sine integral function, this is not strictly necessary.

title: Definition:Sine Integral Function/Also denoted as
snippet: == Sine Integral Function: Also denoted as == The sine integral function $\map \Si x$ is also seen denoted $\map {Si} x$.

title: Definition:Single Cusp
snippet: A single cusp is a cusp in which the curve is not continuous through the point. That is, $2$ or more parts of the curve meet at a single point.

title: Definition:Single Cusp/Also known as
snippet: == Single Cusp: Also known as == A single cusp is also known as a simple cusp.

title: Definition:Single Cusp/First Kind
snippet: A single cusp of the first kind is a single cusp in which both parts of the curve lie on opposite sides of the coincident tangents defining that single cusp. 310px

title: Definition:Single Cusp/Second Kind
snippet: A single cusp of the second kind is a single cusp in which both parts of the curve lie on the same side of the coincident tangents defining that single cusp. 300px

title: Definition:Singleton
snippet: A singleton is a set that contains exactly one element. The singleton containing only the element $a$ can be written $\set a$. The set $\set a$ is known as the singleton of $a$.

title: Definition:Singleton/Also known as
snippet: == Singleton: Also known as == Some authors refer to a singleton as a unit set. Some refer to it as a one-element set. Some use the phrase singleton set.

title: Definition:Singleton Class
snippet: Let $a$ be a set. The class $\set a$ is a singleton (class). It can be referred to as singleton $a$.

title: Definition:Singleton Graph
snippet: The singleton graph $N_1$ is the simple graph with one vertex: 60px

title: Definition:Singleton Graph/Also known as
snippet: == Singleton Graph: Also known as == The singleton graph can also be referred to as: The $1$-edgeless graph $N_1$ The $1$-complete graph $K_1$ The $1$-path graph $P_1$

title: Definition:Singleton Relation
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation on $S \times T$. Then $\RR$ is a singleton relation : $\exists_1 \tuple {x, y} \in S \times T: \tuple {x, y} \in \RR$ That is, $\RR$ has exactly one element.

title: Definition:Singmaster Notation
snippet: Singmaster notation is a technique for denoting the moves that can be made on a Rubik's cube. Let the cube be facing the user with the $U$ and $D$ faces horizontal and the $F$ face towards the user. In the following, clockwise denotes rotation of a layer of the cube in the direction of the clock as though that face were towards the user. $U$: turns the up face one quarter turn clockwise. $D$: turns the down face one quarter turn clockwise. $L$: turns the left face one quarter turn clockwise. $R$: turns the right face one quarter turn clockwise.

title: Definition:Singular
snippet: Predicate Logic: Singular Statement: A statement made about an object which is identified by means of a proper name. Matrix Algebra: Singular Matrix: a square matrix without an inverse. Set Theory: Singular Cardinal: one whose cofinality is less than itself. Analysis: Singular Point

title: Definition:Singular Boolean Function
snippet: A singular boolean function $s : \mathbb B^k \to \mathbb B$ is a boolean function whose fiber of truth is a singleton subset of $\mathbb B^k$.

title: Definition:Singular Cardinal
snippet: Let $\kappa$ be an infinite cardinal. Then $\kappa$ is a singular cardinal $\map {\mathrm {cf} } \kappa < \kappa$. That is, the cofinality of $\kappa$ is less than itself.

title: Definition:Singular Conjunction
snippet: Let $\Bbb B = \set {\T, \F}$ be a boolean domain. A singular conjunction in the set of propositions of type $\Bbb B^k \to \Bbb B$ is a conjunction of $k$ literals that includes just one conjunct of each complementary pair: $\set {x_j, \neg x_j}$ for each $j: 1 \le j \le k$. A singular proposition $s : \mathbb B^k \to \mathbb B$ can be expressed as a singular conjunction: $s = e_1 \land e_2 \land \ldots \land e_{k - 1} \land e_k$ where: $\forall j \in \closedint 1 k: e_j \in \set {x_j, \neg x_j}$

title: Definition:Singular Matrix
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring with unity. Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. Let $\mathbf A$ be an element of the ring of square matrices $\struct {\map {\MM_R} n, +, \times}$.

title: Definition:Singular Matrix/Also known as
snippet: == Singular Matrix: Also known as == Some authors refer to a singular matrix as a non-invertible matrix.

title: Definition:Singular Matrix/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring with unity. Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. Let $\mathbf A$ be an element of the ring of square matrices $\struct {\map {\MM_R} n, +, \times}$. Let $\mathbf A$ have no inverse. Then $\mathbf A$ is referred to as singular.

title: Definition:Singular Matrix/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring with unity. Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. Let $\mathbf A$ be an element of the ring of square matrices $\struct {\map {\MM_R} n, +, \times}$. Let the determinant of $\mathbf A$ be equal to $0$. Then $\mathbf A$ is referred to as singular.

title: Definition:Singular Measure
snippet: Let $d \in \N$. Let $\map \BB {\R^d}$ be the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on $\R^d$. Let $\lambda$ be the Lebesgue measure on $\struct {\R^d, \map \BB {\R^d} }$. Let $\mu$ be a measure, signed measure or complex measure on $\struct {\R^d, \map \BB {\R^d} }$. We say that $\mu$ is singular $\mu$ and $\lambda$ are mutually singular measures.

title: Definition:Singular Point/Also known as
snippet: == Singular Point: Also known as == A singular point is also known as a singularity. However, this has other similar yet different uses, so it is deprecated on .

title: Definition:Singular Point/Complex
snippet: Let $U \subseteq \C$ be an open set. Let $f : U \to \C$ be a complex function. A singular point of $f$ is a point at which $f$ is not analytic.

title: Definition:Singular Point/Real
snippet: == Definition == Let $C$ be a locus.

title: Definition:Singular Point/Real/Definition 1
snippet: Let $C$ be a locus. A point $P \in C$ is called a singular point $P$ does not have a unique tangent to $C$ which is itself differentiable.

title: Definition:Singular Random Variable
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $X$ be a continuous random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $\map \BB \R$ be the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on $\R$. Let $\lambda$ be the Lebesgue measure on $\struct {\R, \map \BB \R}$. We say that $X$ is singular : there exists a $\lambda$-null set $B$ such that $\map \Pr {X \in B} = 1$.

title: Definition:Singular Simplex
snippet: Let $T$ be a topological space. Let $\Delta_n$ be the standard $n$-simplex. A singular $n$-simplex in $T$ is a continuous mapping: $\phi : \Delta_n \to T$

title: Definition:Singular Solution to Differential Equation
snippet: A singular solution to a differential equation $E$ is a general solution to $E$ which does not contain an arbitrary constant, and hence forms a particular solution on its own.

title: Definition:Singular Solution to Differential Equation/Also known as
snippet: == Singular Solution to Differential Equation: Also known as == Some sources refer to a singular solution as a singular integral.

title: Definition:Singular Solution to Differential Equation/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Singular Solution to Differential Equation == Singular solutions were noted by in $1694$, and also by in $1715$. However, they are generally associated with , who reported on them in $1734$.

title: Definition:Singular Statement
snippet: A singular statement is a statement whose subject is identified by means of a proper name. More generally, it is a statement which contains no variables, either bound or free.

title: Definition:Singular Statement/Designatory Function
snippet: A designatory function is a propositional function which, on replacement of the operand with a constant, becomes an individuating description.

title: Definition:Singular Statement/Individuating Description
snippet: An individuating description is a predicate whose purpose is to uniquely identify a particular object.

title: Definition:Singular Value Decomposition
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a matrix of order $m \times n$. A singular value decomposition of $\mathbf A$ is a decomposition of $\mathbf A$: $\mathbf A = \mathbf U \mathbf D \mathbf V$ where: $\mathbf U$ is a unitary matrix of order $m \times m$ $\mathbf V$ is a unitary matrix of order $n \times n$ $\mathbf D$ is a matrix of order $m \times n$ such that: the off-diagonal elements of $\mathbf D$ are all zero the diagonal elements of $\mathbf D$, of which there are $\min \set {m, n}$, are non-negative and arranged down the main diagonal in non-increasing order.

title: Definition:Singular Value of Matrix
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a matrix of order $m \times n$. Let $\mathbf A = \mathbf U \mathbf D \mathbf V$ be a singular value decomposition of $\mathbf A$. The diagonal elements of $\mathbf D$ are known as the singular values of $\mathbf A$.

title: Definition:Singularity
snippet: Analysis: Singular Point Real Analysis: Infinite Discontinuity

title: Definition:Singularity Theory
snippet: Singularity theory is a branch of mathematics that describes properties of differential functions in terms of their singular points.

title: Definition:Sink
snippet: Graph Theory: Sink node Vector Analysis Sink (Vector Analysis)

title: Definition:Sink (Vector Analysis)
snippet: Let $\mathbf V$ be a vector field acting over a region of space $R$. A sink is a point $P$ in $R$ at which flux leaves $\mathbf V$.

title: Definition:Sixth Power
snippet: A sixth power is an integer which can be expressed as the $6$th power of an integer. The sequence of sixth powers begins: $1, 64, 729, 4096, 15 \, 625, 46 \, 656, 117 \, 649, 26 \, 2144, 531 \, 441, 1 \, 000 \, 000, \ldots$

title: Definition:Size (Inductive Statistics)
snippet: Let $\theta$ be a population parameter of some population. Let $\Omega$ be the parameter space of $\theta$. Let $\Omega_0$ and $\Omega_1$ be disjoint subsets of $\Omega$ such that $\Omega_0 \cup \Omega_1 = \Omega$. Let $\delta$ be a test procedure of the hypotheses: $H_0: \theta \in \Omega_0$ $H_1: \theta \in \Omega_1$ Let $\pi$ be the power function of $\delta$. The size of $\delta$, usually denoted $\alpha$, is defined as: $\ds \alpha = \sup_{\theta \in \Omega_0} \map \pi \theta$

title: Definition:Skeletal Category
snippet: A category is skeletal isomorphic objects are always identical.

title: Definition:Skeleton Puzzle
snippet: A skeleton puzzle is an arithmetical calculation, presented with the full working by means of the appropriate classical algorithm, in which most or all of the digits have been obscured. It is usual to present such a skeleton puzzle with the obscured digits replaced by asterisks. The object of the puzzle is to work out what the digits were. There may or may not be constraints on the values or configurations of the resulting digits, which will be stated in the rubric of the puzzle.

title: Definition:Skew
snippet: Solid Geometry: Skew lines Abstract Algebra: Skew field Probability and Statistics: Skewness

title: Definition:Skew Curve
snippet: A skew curve is a curve which cannot be embedded in the plane.

title: Definition:Skew Curve/Also known as
snippet: == Skew Curve: Also known as == A skew curve is also known as a twisted curve.

title: Definition:Skew Field
snippet: A skew field is a division ring whose ring product is specifically not commutative.

title: Definition:Skew Field/Also known as
snippet: == Skew Field: Also known as == A skew field is also known as a sfield. Some sources do not bother to give a specific name to this concept, but merely refer to a non-commutative division ring.

title: Definition:Skew Lines
snippet: Let $L_1$ and $L_2$ be two straight lines in $3$-dimensional Euclidean space. $L_1$ and $L_2$ are said to be skew , when produced, they are neither intersecting nor parallel.

title: Definition:Skew Lines/Also known as
snippet: == Skew Lines Also known as == Skew lines are also known as agonic.

title: Definition:Skewes' Number
snippet: Skewes' number is: $10^{10^{10^{34} } }$ In Knuth notation this can be presented as: $10 \uparrow \paren {10 \uparrow \paren {10 \uparrow 34} }$

title: Definition:Skewes' Number/Also known as
snippet: == Skewes' Number: Also known as == The name of Skewes' number can also be seen presented as: Skewes number Skewes's number

title: Definition:Skewes' Number/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Skewes' Number == deduced the number which now bears his name in $1933$. referred to it as: the largest number which has ever served any definite purpose in mathematics. By way of comparison, the number of particles in the universe has been estimated at somewhere between $10^{80}$ and $10^{87}$. However, estimate has been reduced somewhat more recently. For example, has shown that there are many $n$ between $6 \cdotp 62 \times 10^{370}$ and $6 \cdotp 69 \times 10^{370}$ for which $\map \pi n$ is less than $\ds \int_2^n \frac {\d x} {\ln x}$.

title: Definition:Skewness
snippet: Skewness is a measure of the asymmetry of a probability distribution about its mean. Let $X$ be a random variable with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. Then the skewness of $X$, usually denoted $\gamma_1$, is defined as: $\gamma_1 = \expect {\paren {\dfrac {X - \mu} \sigma}^3}$ where $\expect X$ denotes the expectation of $X$.

title: Definition:Skewness/Coefficient
snippet: Let $X$ be a random variable with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. The coefficient of skewness of $X$ is the coefficient: {{eqn | l = \gamma_1 | r = \dfrac {\mu_3} { {\mu_2}^{3/2} } | c = }} {{eqn | r = \expect {\paren {\dfrac {X - \mu} \sigma}^3} | c = }} where: $\mu_i$ denotes the $i$th central moment of $X$ $\mu$ denotes the expectation of $X$, that is, its first central moment $\sigma$ denotes the standard deviation of $X$, that is, the square root of its second central moment.

title: Definition:Skewness/Negative
snippet: Let $D$ be a probability distribution. Let $D$ have a coefficient of skewness $\gamma_1$ such that: $\gamma_1 < 0$ Then $D$ is said to have negative skewness.

title: Definition:Skewness/Positive
snippet: Let $D$ be a probability distribution. Let $D$ have a coefficient of skewness $\gamma_1$ such that: $\gamma_1 > 0$ Then $D$ is said to have positive skewness.

title: Definition:Skolem Sequence
snippet: A Skolem sequence of order $n$ is a (finite) sequence $S = \left\{{s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_{2 n}}\right\}$ of $2 n$ integers for which: $(1): \quad$ For every $k \in \left\{{1, 2, \ldots, n}\right\}$ there exist exactly two elements $s_i, s_j \in S$ so that $s_i = s_j = k$ and: $(2): \quad$ If $s_i = s_j = k$ and $i < j$ then $j - i = k$. Category:Definitions/Number Theory

title: Definition:Slack Variable
snippet: Consider the simplex method for solving problems in linear programming. A slack variable is an additional variable introduced to convert an inequality into an equation.

title: Definition:Slack Variable/Basic Solution
snippet: Consider the simplex method for solving problems in linear programming. Let $\II$ be an inequality arising in a problem in linear programming. Let $S$ be a slack variable converting $\II$ into an equation $\EE$. A basic solution to $\EE$ $S$ is a solution to the equation you get when setting $S$ equal to zero.

title: Definition:Slack Variable/Basic Variable
snippet: Consider the simplex method for solving problems in linear programming. Let $\II$ be an inequality arising in a problem in linear programming. Let $\set S$ be a set of slack variables used in converting $\II$ into an equation $\EE$. Let each of the elements of $S$ be assigned zero when obtaining a basic solution to $\EE$ $S$. Then each of the elements of $S$ is known as a basic variable of $\EE$.

title: Definition:Slant Asymptote
snippet: A slant asymptote to the graph of a real function $f$ is an asymptote to $f$ which is a straight line which is neither a vertical asymptote nor a horizontal asymptote.

title: Definition:Slant Height of Frustum of Right Circular Cone
snippet: Let $\FF$ be a frustum of a right circular cone $\CC$. The slant height of $\FF$ is the length of the part of the generatrix of $\CC$ between the bases of $\FF$. 300px In the above diagram, $l$ is the slant height of the depicted frustum.

title: Definition:Slide Rule
snippet: thumb The slide rule is a mechanical analog computer which is used primarily for multiplication and division, and for functions such as exponents, roots, logarithms, and trigonometry. It is not typically designed for addition or subtraction, which is usually performed using other methods.

title: Definition:Slope/Also defined as/1
snippet: == Slope: Also defined as == Slope can also be seen defined as the angle the line makes with the horizontal.

title: Definition:Slope/Also defined as/2
snippet: == Slope: Also defined as == In the context of geography, the slope of a road is often seen defined as the vertical height travelled the actual distance travelled along the road.

title: Definition:Slope/Also known as
snippet: == Slope: Also known as == The slope of a straight line or curve is also sometimes referred to as its gradient. However, that term has a more generic and abstract meaning than does the concept of slope as given here. The word grade can sometimes be seen, but this is discouraged as it has a number of meanings. Some sources suggest that the slope of a straight line is the same as its direction, but this is true only in the plane.

title: Definition:Slope/Curve
snippet: Let $P$ be a point on a curve $\CC$ embedded in a Cartesian plane. The slope of $\CC$ at $P$ is defined as the slope of the tangent to $\CC$ at $P$.

title: Definition:Slope/Straight Line
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a straight line embedded in a Cartesian plane. The slope of $\LL$ is defined as the tangent of the angle that $\LL$ makes with the $x$-axis.

title: Definition:Slope of Straight Line/Also defined as
snippet: == Slope of Straight Line: Also known as == Some sources define the slope of a straight line $\LL$ as the actual angle that $\LL$ makes with the $x$-axis, rather than its tangent. On we specifically mean the tangent of that angle.

title: Definition:Slope of Straight Line/General Form
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a straight line embedded in a Cartesian plane. Let $\LL$ be given by the equation: $l x + m y + n = 0$ The slope of $\LL$ is defined by means of the ordered pair $\tuple {-l, m}$, where: for $m \ne 0$, $\psi = \map \arctan {-\dfrac l m}$ for $m = 0$, $\psi = \dfrac \pi 2$ where $\psi$ is the angle that $\LL$ makes with the $x$-axis. Thus: when $m = 0$, the slope of $\LL$ is $\tuple {l, 0}$ and $\LL$ is parallel to the $y$-axis when $l = 0$, the slope of $\LL$ is $\tuple {0, m}$ and $\LL$ is parallel to the $x$-axis.

title: Definition:Slow g-Tower
snippet: Let $M$ be a class. Let $M$ be a $g$-tower such that $g: M \to M$ is a slowly progressing mapping. Then $M$ is called a slow $g$-tower.

title: Definition:Slowly Progressing Mapping
snippet: Let $C$ be a class. Let $g: C \to C$ be a progressing mapping from $C$ to $C$. Then $g$ is slowly progressing : $\forall x \in \Dom g: \card {\map g x} - \card x \le 1$ That is, for all $x$ in the domain of $g$, the set $\map g x$ has at most $1$ more element than $x$ does.

title: Definition:Slowly Well-Ordered Class under Subset Relation
snippet: Let $N$ be a class. Let $N$ be well-ordered under the subset relation such that the following $3$ conditions hold: Then $N$ is slowly well-ordered under the subset relation.

snippet: The slug per foot per second is a FPS unit of dynamic viscosity.
