title: Definition:Sterling/Penny/New/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on New Penny == The (new) penny was introduced in $1971$ in the United Kingdom on $15$ February $1971$ when the UK coinage system was decimalized. It was defined as $\dfrac 1 {100}$ of the pound sterling. The penny, along with the shilling, was discontinued at that time. At that point, the replaced penny was referred to as an old penny, while the new penny was gradually and progressively referred to just as a penny, in the natural order of evolution of language. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Sterling/Penny/New/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on New Penny == When the new penny replaced the old penny, a new colloquial language needed to evolve in order to distinguish between old pennies and new pennies. While referring to old pennies, the pronunciation of the plural pence had evolved to sound something like p'nce or b'nce or even mce, depending on context. That is, for example, sixpence would come out sounding like six-bnce. Hence the pronunciation of the plural of new penny would be carefully enunciated as new pence, or just pence.

snippet: The symbol for the new penny is $\mathrm p$. Category:Definitions/Sterling

title: Definition:Sterling/Penny/Old/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Old Penny == The (old) penny descended from the Roman denarius, defined as $\dfrac 1 {12}$ of a shilling. The penny, along with the shilling, was discontinued in $1971$ when the UK coinage system was decimalized. In its place was put the (new) penny, which was a completely new coin, $\dfrac {12} 5$ of the (old) penny: physically smaller, but of a similar material. At that point, a penny was referred to as an old penny, while the new penny was gradually and progressively referred to just as a penny, in the natural order of evolution of language. Category:Historical Notes

snippet: The pound (sterling) is the main unit of the Sterling monetary system.

snippet: == Historical Note on Pound Sterling == The pound sterling originated from the Roman standard as the purchasing power of $1$ troy pound (in weight) of silver. Category:Historical Notes

The shilling was discontinued in $1971$ when the UK coinage system was decimalized. It was replaced by a coin of the same value, size, shape and material, called the $5 \mathrm p$ piece. title: Definition:Stern Number
snippet: A Stern number is an odd number which can not be represented in the form: $2 a^2 + p$ where: $a \in \Z_{>0}$ is a (strictly) positive integer $p$ is a prime number.

title: Definition:Stern Number/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Stern Number == On reading about Goldbach's Lesser Conjecture in $1856$, and his students tested all the primes to $9000$, and found the counterexamples $5777$ and $5993$. He then went on to investigate odd integers that cannot be represented in the form $2 a^2 + p$ where $a > 0$. The odd integers that he and his students found were named Stern numbers by in his $1993$ paper which summarised the findings on this topic.

title: Definition:Stern Number/Sequence
snippet: == Sequence of Stern Numbers == The sequence of Stern numbers begins: $1, 3, 17, 137, 227, 977, 1187, 1493, 5777, 5993$ It is not known whether there are any more. Category:Definitions/Stern Numbers

title: Definition:Stern Prime
snippet: A Stern prime is a prime number which can not be represented in the form: $2 a^2 + p$ where: $a \in \Z_{>0}$ is a (strictly) positive integer $p$ is a prime number.

title: Definition:Stern Prime/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Stern Prime == On reading about Goldbach's Lesser Conjecture in $1856$, and his students tested all the primes to $9000$, and found the counterexamples $5777$ and $5993$. He then went on to investigate odd numbers, and more specifically prime numbers, that cannot be represented in the form $2 a^2 + p$ where $a > 0$, thereby disallowing the trivial $2 \times 0^2 + p = p$. Seeming to forget about $3$, he stated that the smallest such prime number was $17$.

title: Definition:Stern Prime/Sequence
snippet: == Sequence of Stern Primes == The sequence of Stern primes begins: $2, 3, 17, 137, 227, 977, 1187, 1493$ It is not known whether there are any more. Category:Definitions/Stern Primes

title: Definition:Stiefel Manifold
snippet: Let $n \in \N_{> 0}$ be a natural number. Let $k \in \N_{> 0}$ be a natural number such that $0 < k < n$. The set $\map {V_k} {\R^n}$ of all orthonormal $k$-frames of $\R^n$ is called a Stiefel manifold. That is, a Stiefel manifold is the set $\map {V_k} {\R^n}$ of orthonormal ordered $k$-tuples of vectors in $\R^n$.

title: Definition:Stieltjes Function
snippet: Let $f: \R \to \overline \R$ be a real function, where $\overline \R$ denotes the extended real numbers. Then $f$ is said to be a Stieltjes function : $(1): \quad f$ is increasing $(2): \quad f$ is left-continuous.

title: Definition:Stieltjes Function of Measure on Real Numbers
snippet: Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\R$ with the Borel $\sigma$-algebra $\map \BB \R$. The Stieltjes function of $\mu$ is the mapping $F_\mu: \R \to \overline \R$ defined by: $\map {F_\mu} x := \begin{cases} \map \mu {\hointr 0 x} & : x > 0 \\ 0 & : x = 0 \\ - \map \mu {\hointr x 0} & : x where $\overline \R$ denotes the extended real numbers.

title: Definition:Stipulative Definition
snippet: A stipulative definition is a definition which defines how to interpret the meaning of a symbol. It stipulates, or lays down, the meaning of a symbol in terms of previously defined symbols or concepts. The symbol used for a stipulative definition is: $\text {(the symbol being defined)} := \text {(the meaning of that symbol)}$ This can be written the other way round: $\text {(a concept being assigned a symbol)} =: \text {(the symbol for it)}$ when it is necessary to emphasise that the symbol has been crafted to abbreviate the notation for the concept.

title: Definition:Stirling's Constant
snippet: Stirling's constant is a name given to the square root of $2$ times $\pi$ (pi). It is approximated by the decimal expansion: $\sqrt {2 \pi} \approx 2 \cdotp 50662 \, 82746 \, 31000 \, 5 \ldots$

title: Definition:Stirling's Constant/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Stirling's Constant == {{Neologism|Stirling's constant|for the square root of $2 \pi$ from its appearance in Stirling's Formula, where it can be seen to be: $\quad \ds \sqrt {2 \pi} \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \dfrac {n! e^n} {n^n \sqrt n}$}}

title: Definition:Stirling Numbers
snippet: Stirling numbers come in various forms. In the below: $\delta_{n k}$ is the Kronecker delta $n$ and $k$ are non-negative integers.

title: Definition:Stirling Numbers/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Stirling Numbers == This formula for the Stirling numbers of the second kind: $\ds x^n = \sum_k {n \brace k} x^{\underline k}$ was the reason started his studies of the Stirling numbers in the first place. They were studied in detail in his of $1730$.

title: Definition:Stirling Numbers/Karamata Notation
snippet: The notation $\ds {n \brack k}$ and $\ds {n \brace k}$ for Stirling numbers is known as Karamata notation.

title: Definition:Stirling Numbers of the First Kind
snippet: Stirling numbers of the first kind come in two forms. In the below: $\delta_{n k}$ is the Kronecker delta $n$ and $k$ are non-negative integers.

title: Definition:Stirling Numbers of the First Kind/Notation
snippet: The notation $\ds {n \brack k}$ for the unsigned Stirling numbers of the first kind is that proposed by and publicised by . The notation $\map s {n, k}$ for the signed Stirling numbers of the first kind is similar to variants of that sometimes given for the unsigned. Usage is inconsistent in the literature.

title: Definition:Stirling Numbers of the First Kind/Signed
snippet: In the below: $\delta_{n k}$ is the Kronecker delta $n$ and $k$ are non-negative integers.

title: Definition:Stirling Numbers of the First Kind/Signed/Definition 1
snippet: Signed Stirling numbers of the first kind are defined recursively by: $\map s {n, k} := \begin{cases} \delta_{n k} & : k = 0 \text{ or } n = 0 \\ \map s {n - 1, k - 1} - \paren {n - 1} \map s {n - 1, k} & : \text{otherwise} \\ \end{cases}$ where: $\delta_{n k}$ is the Kronecker delta $n$ and $k$ are non-negative integers.

title: Definition:Stirling Numbers of the First Kind/Signed/Definition 2
snippet: Signed Stirling numbers of the first kind are defined as the polynomial coefficients $\map s {n, k}$ which satisfy the equation: $\ds x^{\underline n} = \sum_k \map s {n, k} x^k$ where $x^{\underline n}$ denotes the $n$th falling factorial of $x$.

title: Definition:Stirling Numbers of the First Kind/Unsigned
snippet: In the below: $\delta_{n k}$ is the Kronecker delta $n$ and $k$ are non-negative integers.

title: Definition:Stirling Numbers of the First Kind/Unsigned/Complex Numbers
snippet: , in his of $1997$, suggests an extension of the unsigned Stirling numbers of the first kind $\ds {r \brack r - m}$ to the real and complex numbers. However, beyond stating that such a number is a polynomial in $r$ of degree $2 m$, and providing a few examples, he goes no further than that, and the details of this extension are unclear.

title: Definition:Stirling Numbers of the First Kind/Unsigned/Definition 1
snippet: Unsigned Stirling numbers of the first kind are defined recursively by: $\ds {n \brack k} := \begin{cases} \delta_{n k} & : k = 0 \text { or } n = 0 \\ & \\ \ds {n - 1 \brack k - 1} + \paren {n - 1} {n - 1 \brack k} & : \text{otherwise} \\ \end{cases}$ where: $\delta_{n k}$ is the Kronecker delta $n$ and $k$ are non-negative integers.

title: Definition:Stirling Numbers of the First Kind/Unsigned/Definition 2
snippet: Unsigned Stirling numbers of the first kind are defined as the polynomial coefficients $\ds {n \brack k}$ which satisfy the equation: $\ds x^{\underline n} = \sum_k \paren {-1}^{n - k} {n \brack k} x^k$ where $x^{\underline n}$ denotes the $n$th falling factorial of $x$.

title: Definition:Stirling Numbers of the Second Kind
snippet: Let: $\delta_{n k}$ denote the Kronecker delta $n$ and $k$ be non-negative integers.

title: Definition:Stirling Numbers of the Second Kind/Complex Numbers
snippet: , in his of $1997$, suggests an extension of the Stirling numbers of the second kind $\ds {r \brace r - m}$ to the real and complex numbers. However, beyond stating that such a number is a polynomial in $r$ of degree $2 m$, and providing a few examples, he goes no further than that, and the details of this extension are unclear.

title: Definition:Stirling Numbers of the Second Kind/Definition 1
snippet: Stirling numbers of the second kind are defined recursively by: $\ds {n \brace k} := \begin{cases} \delta_{n k} & : k = 0 \text{ or } n = 0 \\ & \\ \ds {n - 1 \brace k - 1} + k {n - 1 \brace k} & : \text{otherwise} \\ \end{cases}$ where: $\delta_{n k}$ is the Kronecker delta $n$ and $k$ are non-negative integers.

title: Definition:Stirling Numbers of the Second Kind/Definition 2
snippet: Stirling numbers of the second kind are defined as the coefficients $\ds {n \brace k}$ which satisfy the equation: $\ds x^n = \sum_k {n \brace k} x^{\underline k}$ where $x^{\underline k}$ denotes the $k$th falling factorial of $x$.

title: Definition:Stirling Numbers of the Second Kind/Notation
snippet: The notation $\ds {n \brace k}$ for Stirling numbers of the second kind is that proposed by and publicised by . Other notations exist. Usage is inconsistent in the literature.

title: Definition:Stirling Numbers of the Second Kind/Technical Note
snippet: == Technical Note for Stirling Numbers of the Second Kind == {{LatexFor|for = \ds {n \brace k} }} The braces around the n \brace k are important. The \ds is needed to create the symbol in its proper house display style. Note that while it appears that \ds \set {n \atop k} should do the same job, it is rendered with a subtle difference: $\ds \set {n \atop k}$ and so is not recommended on . Category:Definitions/Stirling Numbers

title: Definition:Stochastic
snippet: The word stochastic is an adjective which implies randomness. It is generally used to describe a system which is not deterministic, rather than those system which are deterministic apart from a random error.

title: Definition:Stochastic/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Stochastic == The word stochastic is pronounced something like sto-kas-tic. It derives from the Ancient Greek στοχαστικός (stokhastikós), from στοχάζομαι (stokházomai), which means to aim at a target, or to guess. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Stochastic Analysis
snippet: Stochastic analysis is the branch of mathematics which studies the behaviour of stochastic processes.

title: Definition:Stochastic Calculus
snippet: Stochastic calculus is a generalization of calculus to the subject of stochastic processes.

title: Definition:Stochastic Matrix
snippet: A stochastic matrix is a matrix of the transition probabilities of a Markov chain. Hence a stochastic matrix is either a row stochastic matrix or a column stochastic matrix.

title: Definition:Stochastic Matrix/Also defined as
snippet: == Stochastic Matrix: Also defined as == Some sources define a stochastic matrix as a general matrix whose elements are stochastic.

title: Definition:Stochastic Matrix/Column
snippet: A column stochastic matrix is a square matrix such that: all its elements are non-negative all its column sums are equal to $1$.

title: Definition:Stochastic Matrix/Doubly Stochastic
snippet: A doubly stochastic matrix is a stochastic matrix which is both a row stochastic matrix and a column stochastic matrix

title: Definition:Stochastic Matrix/Row
snippet: A row stochastic matrix is a square matrix such that: all its elements are non-negative all its row sums are equal to $1$.

title: Definition:Stochastic Model
snippet: A stochastic model is a mathematical model which incorporates stochastic (random) processes in its definition.

title: Definition:Stochastic Process/Also known as
snippet: == Stochastic Process: Also known as == A stochastic process is also known as a random process.

title: Definition:Stochastic Process/Formal Definition
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\struct {E, \EE}$ be a measurable space. Let $I$ be a set. Let $\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a $I$-indexed family of $E$-valued random variables. We call $\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ a stochastic process.

title: Definition:Stochastic Process/Informal Definition
snippet: A stochastic process is a sequence of random variables representing the evolution of some real-world physical process over time.

title: Definition:Stochastically Larger
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be probability distributions of a common domain $D$. Let $\map F X$ and $\map G Y$ denote the cumulative distribution functions of $X$ and $Y$ respectively. Let: $\map F u \ge \map G u$ for all $u \in D$, with strict inequality for at least some $u$. Then $\map F X$ is stochastically larger than $\map G Y$.

title: Definition:Stoic School
snippet: The stoic school was a school of Greek philosophy which emphasized the importance of goodness and peace of mind gained from living a life of Virtue in accordance with Nature. The writings of its philosophers reveal the first beginnings of the discipline of propositional logic.

title: Definition:Stokes
snippet: The stokes is the CGS base unit of kinematic viscosity.

title: Definition:Stokes/Also known as
snippet: == Stokes: Also known as == The stokes is also known in its form square centimetre per second.

title: Definition:Stokes/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Stokes: Conversion Factors == {{eqn | r = 10^{-4} | c = square metres per second }} Category:Definitions/Stokes

title: Definition:Stolarsky-Harborth Constant
snippet: The Stolarsky-Harborth constant is the lower bound for the number $\beta$ defined as: $\beta > \dfrac {P_n} {n^{\lg 3} }$ where: $P_n$ is the number of odd elements in the first $n$ rows of Pascal's triangle $\lg 3$ denotes the logarithm base $2$ of $3$. Its value is given by: $\beta \approx 0 \cdotp 81255 \, 65590 \, 160063 \, 8769 \ldots$

title: Definition:Stone Space
snippet: Let $S$ be a topological space. Let $S$ be: compact $T_2$ (Hausdorff) totally disconnected. Then $S$ is a Stone space.

title: Definition:Stone Space/Boolean Lattice
snippet: Let $B$ be a Boolean lattice. The Stone space of $B$ is the topological space: $\map S B = \struct {U, \tau}$ where: $U$ is the set of ultrafilters in $B$. $\tau$ is the topology generated by the basis consisting of all sets of the form: $U_b = \set {x \in U: b \in x}$ for each $b \in S$.

title: Definition:Stopped Process
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \sequence {\FF_n}_{n \ge 0}, \Pr}$ be a filtered probability space. Let $\sequence {X_n}_{n \ge 0}$ be an $\sequence {\FF_n}_{n \ge 0}$-adapted stochastic process. Let $T$ be a stopping time with respect to $\sequence {\FF_n}_{n \ge 0}$. We define the stopped process $\sequence {X_n^T}_{n \ge 0}$ by: $\map {X_n^T} \omega = \map {X_{\map T \omega \wedge n} } \omega$ for each $\omega \in \Omega$, where $\wedge$ is the pointwise minimum. We write: $X_n^T = X_{T \wedge n}$

title: Definition:Stopped Sigma-Algebra
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \sequence {\FF_n}_{n \ge 0}, \Pr}$ be a filtered probability space. Let $T$ be a stopping time with respect to $\sequence {\FF_n}_{n \ge 0}$. Let: $\FF_T = \set {A \in \Sigma : A \cap \set {\omega \in \Omega : \map T \omega \le t} \in \FF_t \text { for all } t \in \Z_{\ge 0} }$ We call $\FF_T$ the stopped $\sigma$-algebra associated with $T$.

title: Definition:Stopping Time/Continuous Time
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \sequence {\FF_t}_{t \ge 0}, \Pr}$ be a continuous-time filtered probability space. Let $T : \Omega \to \closedint 0 \infty$ be a random variable. We say that $T$ is a stopping time with respect to $\sequence {\FF_t}_{t \ge 0}$ : $\set {\omega \in \Omega : \map T \omega \le t} \in \FF_t$ for each $t \in \hointr 0 \infty$.

title: Definition:Stopping Time/Discrete Time
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \sequence {\FF_n}_{n \ge 0}, \Pr}$ be a discrete-time filtered probability space. Let $T : \Omega \to \Z_{\ge 0} \cup \set {\infty}$ be a random variable.

title: Definition:Stopping Time/Discrete Time/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \sequence {\FF_n}_{n \ge 0}, \Pr}$ be a discrete-time filtered probability space. Let $T : \Omega \to \Z_{\ge 0} \cup \set {\infty}$ be a random variable. We say that $T$ is a stopping time with respect to $\sequence {\FF_n}_{n \ge 0}$ : $\set {\omega \in \Omega : \map T \omega \le t} \in \FF_t$ for all $t \in \Z_{\ge 0}$.

title: Definition:Stopping Time/Discrete Time/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \sequence {\FF_n}_{n \ge 0}, \Pr}$ be a discrete-time filtered probability space. Let $T : \Omega \to \Z_{\ge 0} \cup \set {\infty}$ be a random variable. We say that $T$ is a stopping time with respect to $\sequence {\FF_n}_{n \ge 0}$ : $\set {\omega \in \Omega : \map T \omega = t} \in \FF_t$ for all $t \in \Z_{\ge 0}$.

title: Definition:Storage Theory
snippet: Storage theory is the branch of probability theory concerned with practical optimisation of physical storage systems.

title: Definition:Straight-Line Homotopy
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be topological spaces. Let $f: X \to Y$, $g: X \to Y$ be continuous mappings. Let $H: X \times \closedint 0 1 \to Y$ be the homotopy between $f$ and $g$ such that: $\forall x \in X : \forall t \in \closedint 0 1 : \map H {x, t} = \map f x + t \paren {\map g x - \map f x}$ Then $H$ is called the straight-line homotopy (between $f$ and $g$).

title: Definition:Straight Angle
snippet: A straight angle is defined to be the angle equal to one half of a full angle.

title: Definition:Straight Angle/Also known as
snippet: == Straight Angle: Also known as == A straight angle is also known as a flat angle.

title: Definition:Straight Line/Also defined as
snippet: == Straight Line: Also defined as == A definition for straight line which is frequently encountered in the popular literature is: A straight line is the shortest distance between two points. This is all very well but it assumes that the line in question terminates at two particular endpoints. However, this is a perfectly valid definition of the concept of a straight line segment. Category:Definitions/Straight Lines

title: Definition:Straight Line Segment/Also known as
snippet: == Straight Line Segment: Also known as == In their definition of a straight line segment, some sources take straightness for granted, and refer to such as just a line segment. Some sources refer to just a segment, but that term has multiple meanings.

title: Definition:Straightedge
snippet: A straightedge is an ideal tool for constructing straight lines. A straightedge is of unlimited length, but has no markings on it, so it cannot be used for measurement. Hence it can be used either: $(1): \quad$ to construct a line segment between two given points, according to Euclid's first postulate or: $(2): \quad$ to extend a line segment in either direction indefinitely, according to Euclid's second postulate.

title: Definition:Straightedge/Also known as
snippet: == Straightedge: Also known as == The word straightedge can also be rendered as straight edge. Some sources hyphenate: straight-edge. Some sources use the term ruler, but this is inaccurate as a ruler is generally understood to have scale markings on it.

title: Definition:Strain
snippet: Strain is a measure of the deformation of a body as a result of stress set up within that body caused by an external force or forces Strain can be expressed as: Change in length per unit length Change in area per unit area Change in volume per unit volume all of which are dimensionless. Or strain can be a shear strain, which is an angular deformation without change in volume. In this case it is measured in radians.

title: Definition:Strange Attractor
snippet: Let $S$ be a dynamical system in a space $X$. Let $T$ be an iterative mapping in $S$: $x_{n + 1} = \map T {x_n}$ A strange attractor under $T$ is an infinite invariant set $A$ in $X$, usually an attractor, with additional properties: $(1): \quad$ The orbits of $T$ exhibit sensitive dependence on initial conditions $(2): \quad$ There exists an open set of points which are attracted to $A$.

title: Definition:Strange Attractor/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Strange Attractor == The term strange attractor was introduced in $1971$ by and .

title: Definition:Strange Family Problem
snippet: A strange family problem is a puzzle concerning the family relationships between people who have intermarried in unusual ways.

title: Definition:Strange Family Problem/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Strange Family Problem == notes that the earliest known strange family problems appear to originate from and . The term strange family problem was coined by himself.

title: Definition:Strassen Algorithm
snippet: The Strassen algorithm is a method for evaluating the product of two square matrices of order $n$.

title: Definition:Strassen Algorithm/Also known as
snippet: == Strassen Algorithm: Also known as == The Strassen algorithm is also known as Strassen's method.

title: Definition:Strassen Algorithm/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on the Strassen Algorithm == The Strassen algorithm was designed by in $1969$.

title: Definition:Strassen Algorithm/Motivation
snippet: The number of operations required when using the Strassen algorithm is proportional to $n^{\lg 7}$, where $\lg$ denotes the binary logarithm $\log_2$ The conventional technique to calculate the matrix product takes $2 n^3$ operations. As $\lg 7 \approx 2.81$ and $2^3 = 3$, for sufficiently large $n$ the Strassen algorithm has a lower algorithmic complexity.

title: Definition:Strategic Game
snippet: A strategic game is a game in which: $(1): \quad$ Each player chooses a strategy once per play $(2): \quad$ The move(s) of each player operates simultaneously. That is, when choosing a move, each player has any information about the move that another player will make. It consists of: A finite set $N$ of players For each player $i \in N$, a non-empty set $A_i$ of moves available to player $i$ For each player $i \in N$, a preference relation $\succsim_i$ on $A = \ds \prod_{j \mathop \in N} A_j$ of player $i$.

title: Definition:Stratified Sample
snippet: A stratified sample is a sample taken from a population which has been partitioned into strata. This division is made so as to better reflect the uniformity of characteristics that exist within each stratum which may not exist between the strata. Separate random samples are taken from each stratum. With the appropriate analysis, more precise estimation of population characteristics can be made. It is a common practice to take samples such that the sizes of the samples are proportional to the stratum sizes.

title: Definition:Stratified Sample/Also known as
snippet: == Stratified Sample: Also known as == A stratified sample is also known as a stratified random sample. Category:Definitions/Stratified Samples

title: Definition:Stratified Sample/Stratum
snippet: A stratum is a component of a partition of a population from which a stratified sample is to be taken.

title: Definition:Stratum/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Stratum == The plural form of stratum is strata. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Stress
snippet: Stress is a measure of the internal reactions of a body which is under the influence of an external force. It is defined as force per unit area. Stress can be tensile, compressive or shear.

title: Definition:Stress-Strain Diagram

The resulting graph is called a stress-strain diagram. 500px The above diagram shows a typical graph of stress against strain. The segment $OA$ represents the region in which Hooke's Law actually applies. The slope of $OA$ is the modulus of elasticity of the material of which the body is composed.
