title: Definition:Subordinate Matrix Norm/Also known as
snippet: == Subordinate Matrix Norm: Also known as == A subordinate matrix norm is also known as a operator matrix norm.

title: Definition:Subring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure with two operations. A subring of $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ is a subset $S$ of $R$ such that $\struct {S, +_S, \circ_S}$ is a ring.

title: Definition:Subring/Also defined as
snippet: == Subring: Also defined as == Sources which deal only with rings with unity typically demand that the unity is also an element of a subring. Some sources insist that $R$ must itself be a ring for $S$ to be definable as a subring, but this limitation is unnecessarily restricting.

title: Definition:Subring Module
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \times}$ be a ring. Let $\struct {S, +_S, \times_S}$ be a subring of $R$. Let $\struct {G, +_G, \circ}_R$ be an $R$-module. Let $\circ_S$ be the restriction of $\circ$ to $S \times G$. The $S$-module $\struct {G, +_G, \circ_S}_S$ is called the subring module induced by $S$.

title: Definition:Subscript
snippet: A subscript is a number (or other symbol, but usually a number) written below and to the right of a given symbol to identify a specific instance of the object that symbol denotes. This is often to reference a specific term of a sequence.

title: Definition:Subsemigroup
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. Let $T \subseteq S$ such that $\struct {T, \circ {\restriction_T} }$, where $\circ {\restriction_T}$ is the restriction of $\circ$ to $T$, is a semigroup. Then $\struct {T, \circ {\restriction_T} }$ is a subsemigroup of $S$. It is usual, for the sake of simplicity, for the same symbol to be used for both $\circ$ and its restriction. Thus we refer to $\struct {T, \circ}$, and we write: $\struct {T, \circ} \subseteq \struct {S, \circ}$

title: Definition:Subsemilattice
snippet: Let $\struct {R, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure with a binary operation. A subsemilattice of $\struct {R, \circ}$ is a subset $S$ of $R$ such that $\struct {S, \circ_S}$ is a semilattice.

title: Definition:Subsemiring
snippet: Let $\struct {S, *, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure with two operations. A subsemiring of $\struct {S, *, \circ}$ is a subset $T$ of $S$ such that $\struct {T, *_T, \circ_T}$ is a semiring.

title: Definition:Subsequence
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in a set $S$. Let $\sequence {n_r}$ be a strictly increasing sequence in $\N$. Then the composition $\sequence {x_{n_r} }$ is called a subsequence of $\sequence {x_n}$.

title: Definition:Subsequence/Also known as
snippet: == Subsequence: Also known as == The word subsequence can also be found presented hyphenated: sub-sequence.

title: Definition:Subsequence/Proper
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in a set $S$. A proper subsequence $\sequence {x_{n_r} }$ of $\sequence {x_n}$ is a subsequence of $\sequence {x_n}$ which is not equal to $\sequence {x_n}$. That is, in which there exist terms of $\sequence {x_n}$ which do not exist in $\sequence {x_{n_r} }$. That is, in which the terms of $\sequence {n_r}$ form a proper subset of $\N$.

title: Definition:Subsequence/Warning
snippet: In the definition of a subsequence, the constraint that $\sequence {n_r}$ be strictly increasing is important. Thus, for example, $x_3, x_1, x_4, x_2, x_9, x_5 \ldots$ is not a subsequence of $\sequence {x_n}$.

title: Definition:Subsequential Limit
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence. Let $\sequence {x_{n_r} }$ be a subsequence of $\sequence {x_n}$. Suppose that $\sequence {x_{n_r} }$ converges to a limit $x$. Then $x$ is called a subsequential limit of $\sequence {x_n}$.

title: Definition:Subset
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. $S$ is a subset of $T$ all of the elements of $S$ are also elements of $T$. This is denoted: $S \subseteq T$ That is: $S \subseteq T \iff \forall x: \paren {x \in S \implies x \in T}$ If the elements of $S$ are not all also elements of $T$, then $S$ is not a subset of $T$: $S \nsubseteq T$ means $\neg \paren {S \subseteq T}$

title: Definition:Subset/Also known as
snippet: == Subset: Also known as == When the concept of the subset was first raised by , he used the terms part and partial aggregate for this concept. $S \subseteq T$ can also be read as: $S$ is contained in $T$, or $T$ contains $S$ $S$ is included in $T$, or $T$ includes $S$ The term weakly includes or weakly contains can sometimes be seen here, to distinguish it from strict inclusion. Hence $\subseteq$ is also called the inclusion relation, or (more rarely) the containment relation. The term weakly includes or weakly contains can sometimes be seen here, to distinguish it from strict inclusion.

title: Definition:Subset/Class
snippet: A set $S$ is a subset of a class $T$ it is a subclass of $T$. Alternatively, a set $S$ is a subset of a class $T$ every element of $S$ is also an element of $T$.

title: Definition:Subset/Euler Diagram
snippet: == Euler Diagram for Subset == The statement that $T$ is a subset of $S$ can be illustrated in the following Euler diagram. 500px

title: Definition:Subset/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Subset == The concept of the subset, set inclusion, was stated by in his initial conception of symbolic logic.

title: Definition:Subset/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Subset == Notation in the literature for the concept of a subset can be confusing. On , the convention is as follows: The notation $\subset$ is deprecated on , on the grounds that it can mean either.

title: Definition:Subset/Superset
snippet: If $S$ is a subset of $T$, then $T$ is a superset of $S$. This can be expressed by the notation $T \supseteq S$. Thus $S \subseteq T$ and $T \supseteq S$ mean the same thing.

title: Definition:Subset Product
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. We can define an operation on the power set $\powerset S$ as follows: $\forall A, B \in \powerset S: A \circ_\PP B = \set {a \circ b: a \in A, b \in B}$ This is called the operation induced on $\powerset S$ by $\circ$, and $A \circ_\PP B$ is called the subset product of $A$ and $B$. It is usual to write $A \circ B$ for $A \circ_\PP B$.

title: Definition:Subset Product/Singleton
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. Let $A \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. Then: $(1): \quad a \circ S := \set a \circ S$ $(2): \quad S \circ a := S \circ \set a$ where $\set a \circ S$ and $S \circ \set a$ denote the subset product of $\set a$ with $S$. That is: $a \circ S = \set {a \circ s: s \in S}$ $S \circ a = \set {s \circ a: s \in S}$

title: Definition:Subset Product Action
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group. Let $\HH$ be the set of subgroups of $G$.

title: Definition:Subset Product Action/Left
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group. Let $\powerset G$ be the power set of $G$. The (left) subset product action of $G$ is the group action $*: G \times \powerset G \to \powerset G$: $\forall g \in G, S \in \powerset G: g * S = g \circ S$

title: Definition:Subset Product Action/Right
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group. Let $\powerset G$ be the power set of $G$. The (right) subset product action of $G$ is the group action $*: G \times \powerset G \to \powerset G$: $\forall g \in G, S \in \powerset G: g * S = S \circ g$

title: Definition:Subset Relation
snippet: The subset relation, written $\subseteq$, is the class of all ordered pairs $\tuple {x, y}$ such that $x$ is a subset of $y$.

title: Definition:Subset Relation on Mappings
snippet: Let $f$ and $g$ be mappings. $f$ is a subset of $g$, denoted $f \subseteq g$, : $\forall x \in \Dom f: \map f x = \map g x$

title: Definition:Subset of Topological Vector Space Properly Supported by Affine Hyperplane at Point
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological vector space over $\R$. Let $A \subseteq X$ be non-empty. Let $f : X \to \R$ be a continuous linear functional. Let $x \in X$. Let $\alpha \in \R$ be such that: the affine hyperplane $\sqbrk {f = \alpha}$ supports $A$ at $x$. Suppose further that: $A \not \subseteq \sqbrk {f = \alpha}$ We say that $A$ is properly supported at $x$.

title: Definition:Subsignature
snippet: Let $\LL, \LL'$ be signatures for the language of predicate logic. Then $\LL$ is said to be a subsignature of $\LL'$, denoted $\LL \subseteq \LL'$, , for each $n \in \N$: $\map {\FF_n} \LL \subseteq \map {\FF_n} {\LL'}$ $\map {\PP_n} \LL \subseteq \map {\PP_n} {\LL'}$ where $\FF_n$ denotes the collection of $n$-ary function symbols, and $\PP_n$ denotes the collection of $n$-ary predicate symbols.

title: Definition:Subsignature/Supersignature
snippet: Let $\LL, \LL'$ be signatures for the language of predicate logic. Let $\LL$ be a subsignature of $\LL'$. Then $\LL'$ is said to be a supersignature of $\LL$, denoted: $\LL' \supseteq \LL$

title: Definition:Substance
snippet: A substance is a particular kind of matter with properties specific to it.

title: Definition:Substance/Also known as
snippet: == Substance: Also known as == A substance can also be referred to as a chemical substance if it is important to emphasise that its chemical properties are under discussion. The word material can also be used, particularly when the substance in question is solid. Category:Definitions/Substance

snippet: Substatement of Compound Statement Substatement of Statement Form

title: Definition:Substatement of Compound Statement/Also known as
snippet: == Substatement of Compound Statement: Also known as == Some sources give this as a component of a compound statement.

title: Definition:Substitution
snippet: Substitution is a word that denotes the process of replacement of every occurrence of a term in an expression or equation with another. Set Theory: Definition:Substitution (Set Theory) Formal Systems: Definition:Substitution (Formal Systems) Definition:Substitution for Well-Formed Part Definition:Substitution for Letter Definition:Alphabetic Substitution Definition:Substitution of Term Definition:Substitution for Metasymbol Mathematical Logic: Definition:Substitution (Mathematical Logic)

title: Definition:Substitution (Formal Systems)/Letter
snippet: Let $\FF$ be a formal language with alphabet $\AA$. Let $\mathbf B$ be a well-formed formula of $\FF$. Let $p$ be a letter of $\FF$. Let $\mathbf A$ be another well-formed formula. Then the substitution of $\mathbf A$ for $p$ in $\mathbf B$ is the collation resulting from $\mathbf B$ by replacing all occurrences of $p$ in $\mathbf B$ by $\mathbf A$. It is denoted as $\map {\mathbf B} {\mathbf A \mathbin {//} p}$. Note that it is not immediate that $\map {\mathbf B} {\mathbf A \mathbin {//} p}$ is a well-formed formula of $\FF$.

title: Definition:Substitution (Formal Systems)/Metasymbol
snippet: Let $S_1$ be a statement form. Let $p$ be a metasymbol which occurs one or more times in $S_1$. Let $T$ be a statement. Let $S_2$ be the string formed by replacing every occurrence of $p$ in $S_1$ with $T$. Then $S_2$ results from the substitution of $p$ by $T$ in $S_1$. $S_2$ is called a substitution instance of $S_1$.

title: Definition:Substitution (Formal Systems)/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Substitution in the context of Formal Languages == There are many alternative notations for $\map {\mathbf B} {\mathbf A' \mathbin {//} \mathbf A}$. These mainly concern the style of the brackets, and sometimes a different symbol (usually $\gets$ or a single $/$) for the slashes $//$. For example: {{item||$\mathbf B \set {\mathbf A \gets \mathbf A'}$}} {{item||$\mathbf B \sqbrk {\mathbf A' \mathbin {//} \mathbf A}$}} {{item||$\map {\mathbf B} {\mathbf A \leadsto \mathbf A'}$}} {{item||$\map {\mathbf B} {\mathbf A / \mathbf A'}$}} {{item||$\ds \map {\mathbf B} {\mathbf A \over…

title: Definition:Substitution (Formal Systems)/Term/In Term
snippet: Let $\beta, \tau$ be terms of predicate logic. Let $x \in \mathrm{VAR}$ be a variable. Let $\map \beta {x \gets \tau}$ be the term resulting from $\beta$ by replacing all occurrences of $x$ by $\tau$. Then $\map \beta {x \gets \tau}$ is called the substitution instance of $\beta$ substituting $\tau$ for $x$.

title: Definition:Substitution (Formal Systems)/Term/In WFF
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a WFF of predicate logic. Let $\tau$ be a term of predicate logic. Let $x \in \mathrm{VAR}$ be a variable. Let $\map {\mathbf A} {x \gets \tau}$ be the WFF resulting from $\mathbf A$ by replacing all free occurrences of $x$ by $\tau$. Then $\map {\mathbf A} {x \gets \tau}$ is called the substitution instance of $\mathbf A$ substituting $\tau$ for $x$.

title: Definition:Substitution (Formal Systems)/Well-Formed Part
snippet: Let $\FF$ be a formal language with alphabet $\AA$. Let $\mathbf B$ be a well-formed formula of $\FF$. Let $\mathbf A$ be a well-formed part of $\mathbf B$. Let $\mathbf A'$ be another well-formed formula. Then the substitution of $\mathbf A'$ for $\mathbf A$ in $\mathbf B$ is the collation resulting from $\mathbf B$ by replacing all occurrences of $\mathbf A$ in $\mathbf B$ by $\mathbf A'$. It is denoted as $\map {\mathbf B} {\mathbf A' \mathbin {//} \mathbf A}$. Note that it is not immediate that $\map {\mathbf B} {\mathbf A' \mathbin {//} \mathbf A}$ is a well-formed formula of $\FF$.

title: Definition:Substitution (Formal Systems)/Well-Formed Part/Example
Definition:Substitution (Set Theory)
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be non-empty sets such that $T$ is not a subset of $S$. Let: $s \in S$ $t \in T \setminus S$ where $\setminus$ denotes set difference. Let $S'$ be the set defined as: $S' = \paren {S \setminus \set s} \cup \set t$ That is, $S'$ is the set obtained by removing $s$ and replacing it with $t$ which is not in $S$. The operation of replacing $s$ with $t$ is known as substitution. Category:Definitions/Set Theory

title: Definition:Substitution Cipher
snippet: A substitution cipher is a cipher in which each letter is encoded by substituting for it a different letter, or string of letters.

title: Definition:Substring
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a formal language with alphabet $\AA$. Let $S$ be a string in $\AA$. Let $T$ be a string in $\AA$ such that: $S = S_1 T S_2$ where: $S_1$ and $S_2$ are strings in $\AA$ (possibly null) $S_1 T S_2$ is the concatenation of $S_1$, $T$ and $S_2$. Then $T$ is called a substring of $S$.

title: Definition:Substring/Proper
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a formal language with alphabet $\AA$. A proper substring of a string $S$ in $\AA$ is a substring of $S$ which is specifically not equal to $S$. Category:Definitions/Substrings

title: Definition:Substructure
snippet: Let $\AA, \BB$ be structures for a signature $\LL$. Let $A, B$ be their respective underlying sets. Then $\AA$ is a substructure of $\BB$, denoted $\AA \subseteq \BB$, : $A \subseteq B$ For each function symbol $f$ of arity $n$, we have $f_\AA = f_\BB \restriction_{A^n}$, where $\restriction$ denotes restriction For each predicate symbol $p$ of arity $n$, we have $p_\AA = p_\BB \restriction_{A^n}$ Note that in particular, for $n = 0$, this reduces to $f_\AA = f_\BB$ and $p_\AA = p_\BB$

title: Definition:Subtangent
snippet: right Let $\CC$ be a plane curve embedded in a Cartesian plane. Let $P$ be a point on $\CC$. Let $\TT$ be the tangent to $\CC$ at $P$. Let $Q$ be the $x$-intercept of $\TT$. Let $AP$ be the line through $P$ perpendicular to the $x$-axis meeting the $x$-axis at $A$. The subtangent to $\CC$ at $P$ is the straight line segment $AQ$. Thus the subtangent is the projection of the length of the tangent onto the $x$-axis.

title: Definition:Subtraction
snippet: Inverse ← Zeraction/Predecessor Division/Biaction →

title: Definition:Subtraction/Also known as
snippet: == Subtraction: Also known as == The result $a - b$ of a subtraction operation is often called the difference between $a$ and $b$. In this context, whether $a - b$ or $b - a$ is being referred to is often irrelevant, but it pays to be careful. In some historical texts, the term subduction can sometimes be seen. Category:Definitions/Subtraction

title: Definition:Subtraction/Complex Numbers
snippet: Let $\struct {\C, +, \times}$ be the field of complex numbers. The operation of subtraction is defined on $\C$ as: $\forall a, b \in \C: a - b := a + \paren {-b}$ where $-b$ is the negative of $b$ in $\C$.

title: Definition:Subtraction/Difference
snippet: Let $a - b$ denote the operation of subtraction on two objects $a$ and $b$. Then the result $a - b$ is referred to as the difference of $a$ and $b$. Note that the nature of $a$ and $b$ has deliberately been left unspecified. They could be, for example, numbers, matrices or more complex expressions constructed from such elements.

title: Definition:Subtraction/Field
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +, \times}$ be a field. The operation of subtraction $a - b$ on $F$ is defined as: $\forall a, b \in R: a - b := a + \paren {-b}$ where $-b$ is the (field) negative of $b$.

title: Definition:Subtraction/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Subtraction == The symbol $-$ for subtraction originated in commerce, along with the symbol $+$ for addition, where they were used by German merchants to distinguish underweight and overweight items. These symbols first appeared in print in $1481$. However, was the first to use it in its current shape, in an unpublished manuscript from $1456$.

title: Definition:Subtraction/Integers
snippet: The subtraction operation in the domain of integers $\Z$ is written "$-$". As the set of integers is the Inverse Completion of Natural Numbers, it follows that elements of $\Z$ are the isomorphic images of the elements of equivalence classes of $\N \times \N$ where two tuples are equivalent if the difference between the two elements of each tuples is the same. Thus subtraction can be formally defined on $\Z$ as the operation induced on those equivalence classes as specified in the definition of integers.

title: Definition:Subtraction/Minuend
snippet: Let $a - b$ denote the operation of subtraction on two objects. The object $a$ is known as the minuend of $a - b$. Note that the nature of $a$ and $b$ has deliberately been left unspecified. They could be, for example, numbers, matrices or more complex expressions constructed from such elements.

title: Definition:Subtraction/Natural Numbers
snippet: Let $\N$ be the set of natural numbers. Let $m, n \in \N$ such that $m \le n$. Let $p \in \N$ such that $n = m + p$. Then we define the operation subtraction as: $n - m = p$ The natural number $p$ is known as the difference between $m$ and $n$.

title: Definition:Subtraction/Naturally Ordered Semigroup
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ, \preceq}$ be a naturally ordered semigroup. Let $m, n \in S$ such that $m \preceq n$. By , there exists a $p \in S$ such that: $m \circ p = n$ This $p$ is the difference between $m$ and $n$, and denoted $n - m$. The operation $-$, assigning to $m, n \in S$ with $m \preceq n$ their difference $n - m$ is called subtraction.

title: Definition:Subtraction/Rational Numbers
snippet: Let $\struct {\Q, +, \times}$ be the field of rational numbers. The operation of subtraction is defined on $\Q$ as: $\forall a, b \in \Q: a - b := a + \paren {-b}$ where $-b$ is the negative of $b$ in $\Q$. Category:Definitions/Rational Numbers Category:Definitions/Subtraction

title: Definition:Subtraction/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $\struct {\R, +, \times}$ be the field of real numbers. The operation of subtraction is defined on $\R$ as: $\forall a, b \in \R: a - b := a + \paren {-b}$ where $-b$ is the negative of $b$ in $\R$.

title: Definition:Subtraction/Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. The operation of subtraction $a - b$ on $R$ is defined as: $\forall a, b \in R: a - b := a + \paren {-b}$ where $-b$ is the (ring) negative of $b$.

title: Definition:Subtraction/Subtrahend
snippet: Let $a - b$ denote the operation of subtraction on two objects. The object $b$ is known as the subtrahend of $a - b$. Note that the nature of $a$ and $b$ has deliberately been left unspecified. They could be, for example, numbers, matrices or more complex expressions constructed from such elements.

title: Definition:Subtraction of Cuts
snippet: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be cuts. Let $\beta - \alpha$ denote the operation on $\alpha$ and $\beta$ defined as $\beta + \paren {-\alpha}$. Then the operator $-$ is known as subtraction, and $\beta - \alpha$ is itself called the difference between $\beta$ and $\alpha$.

title: Definition:Subtrahend/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Subtrahend == The word subtrahend derives from the Latin subtrahendus numerus, meaning number which is to be subtracted. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Subtree
snippet: Definition:Subtree (Graph Theory) Definition:Rooted Subtree Definition:Subtree (Set Theory)

title: Definition:Subtree (Graph Theory)
snippet: Let $T = \struct {V, E}$ be a tree. A subtree of $T$ is a subgraph of $T$ that is also a tree.

title: Definition:Succeed
snippet: Let $\preceq$ be an ordering. Let $a, b$ be such that $a \preceq b$. Then $b$ succeeds $a$. $a$ is then described as being a successor of $b$.

title: Definition:Succeed/Also known as
snippet: The statement $b$ succeeds $a$ can be expressed as $b$ is a succcessor of $a$. If it is important to make the distinction between a succcessor and a strict successor, the term weak successor can be used for succcessor. When the underlying set $S$ of the ordered set $\struct {S, \leqslant}$ is one of the sets of numbers $\N$, $\Z$, $\Q$, $\R$ or a subset, the term is greater than or equal to is usually used instead of succeeds. Category:Definitions/Successor Elements

title: Definition:Successive Over-Relaxation
snippet: Successive over-relaxation is a class of iterative methods for solving a system of simultaneous equations $\mathbf A \mathbf x = \mathbf b$.

title: Definition:Successive Values of Time Series
snippet: Let $T$ be a time series whose observations are $\map z {\tau_1}, \map z {\tau_2}, \dotsb, \map z {\tau_t}, \dotsb$ at an unbroken sequence of timestamps $\tau_1, \tau_2, \dotsb, \tau_t, \dotsb$. When we have $N$ such successive observations, without a missing value, we write: $z_1, z_2, \dotsb, z_t, \dotsb, z_N$ and it is understood that the subscripts correspond directly to the timestamps.

title: Definition:Successive Values of Time Series/Equispaced
snippet: Let $T$ be a time series whose observations are $\map z {\tau_1}, \map z {\tau_2}, \dotsb, \map z {\tau_t}, \dotsb$ at an unbroken sequence of timestamps $\tau_1, \tau_2, \dotsb, \tau_t, \dotsb$. Let $T$ be equispaced with time interval $h$ between adjacent observations. Then $N$ successive observations, written as: $z_1, z_2, \dotsb, z_t, \dotsb, z_N$ occur at timestamps: $\tau_0 + h, \tau_0 + 2 h, \dotsb, \tau_0 + t h, \dotsb, \tau_0 + N h$ Hence we can refer to the observations at timestamp $\tau_0 + t h$ as $z_t$.

title: Definition:Successor
snippet: Successor element: In an ordered set $\struct {S, \preceq}$, $a$ is a successor element to $b$ $b \prec a$. Immediate successor element: In an ordered set $\struct {S, \preceq}$, $a$ is the immediate successor element to $b$ $b \prec a$ and $\nexists c \in S: b \prec c \prec a$. Successor set: If $S$ is a set, then its successor set $S^+$ is defined as $S^+ := S \cup \set S$. Successor mapping: The mapping at the heart of a Peano structure which encapsulates its ability to sustain the Principle of Mathematical Induction.

title: Definition:Successor Mapping
snippet: Let $V$ be a basic universe. The successor mapping $s$ is the mapping on $V$ defined and denoted: $\forall x \in V: \map s x := x \cup \set x$ where $x$ is a set in $V$.

title: Definition:Successor Mapping/Also known as
snippet: == Successor Mapping: Also known as == The successor mapping can also be seen referred to as the successor function. Some sources call this the Halmos function, for who made extensive use of it in his $1960$ work . Various different notations can be found: $\map s x$ $\map S x$ $x^+$ $x'$ Some sources use $x + 1$ rather than $x^+$, on the grounds that these coincide for the natural numbers (when they are seen as elements of the von Neumann construction of natural numbers). and , in their of $2010$, use a variant of $\sigma$ which looks like $o$ with $^\text {-}$ as a close superscript.

title: Definition:Successor Mapping/Peano Structure
snippet: Let $\struct {P, s, 0}$ be a Peano structure. Then the mapping $s: P \to P$ is called the successor mapping on $P$.

title: Definition:Successor Mapping/Successor Set
snippet: Let $V$ be a basic universe. Let $s: V \to V$ denote the successor mapping on $V$. For $x \in V$, the result of applying the successor mapping on $x$ is denoted $x^+$: $x^+ := \map s x = x \cup \set x$ $x^+$ is referred to as the successor (set) of $x$.

title: Definition:Successor Mapping on Natural Numbers
snippet: Let $\N$ be the set of natural numbers. Let $s: \N \to \N$ be the mapping defined as: $s = \set {\tuple {x, y}: x \in \N, y = x + 1}$ Considering $\N$ defined as a Peano structure, this is seen to be an instance of a successor mapping.

title: Definition:Successor Mapping on Peano Structure/Successor Element
snippet: Let $\struct {P, s, 0}$ be a Peano structure. Let mapping $s: P \to P$ denote the successor mapping on $P$. The image element $\map s x$ of an element $x$ is called the successor element or just successor of $x$.

title: Definition:Successor Ordinal
snippet: A successor ordinal is the successor set of an ordinal: $\alpha^+ := \map s \alpha = \alpha \cup \set \alpha$

title: Definition:Sufficient Statistic/Definition 1
snippet: Let $T$ be a sample statistic such that $T$ contains all the information in a random sample that is relevant to the point estimation of a particular parameter $\theta$. Then $T$ is known as a sufficient statistic for $\theta$.

title: Definition:Sufficient Statistic/Definition 2
snippet: Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ form a random sample from a population whose probability distribution is determined by a parameter $\theta$. Let $T$ be a sample statistic. Let $I = \Img {\map T {X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n} }$. Let $D$ be the conditional joint distribution of $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ given $T = t$ and $\theta$. We call $T$ a sufficient statistic for $\theta$ $D$ is independent of the value of $\theta$ for all $t \in I$.

title: Definition:Sufficient Statistic/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Sufficient Statistic == The concept of a sufficient statistic was introduced by in $1921$.

title: Definition:Sufficiently Large
snippet: Let $P$ be a property of real numbers. Then: $\map P x$ holds for all sufficiently large $x$ $\exists a \in \R: \forall x \in \R: x \ge a: \map P x$ That is: There exists a real number $a$ such that for every (real) number not less than $a$, the property $P$ holds. It is not necessarily the case, for a given property $P$ about which such a statement is made, that the value of $a$ actually needs to be known, merely that such a value can be demonstrated to exist.

title: Definition:Sufficiently Large/Also known as
snippet: == Sufficiently Large: Also known as == The term eventually can also be used instead of sufficiently large, in the sense that: $\map P x$ eventually holds for all $x$ means the same as: $\map P x$ holds for all sufficiently large $x$.

title: Definition:Sufficiently Small
snippet: Let $P$ be a property of real numbers. Then: $\map P x$ holds for all sufficiently small $x$ $\exists \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \forall x \in \R: \size x \le \epsilon: \map P x$ That is, : There exists a real number $\epsilon$ such that for every (real) number not more than $\epsilon$ in absolute value, the property $P$ holds. It is not necessarily the case, for a given property $P$ about which such a statement is made, that the value of $\epsilon$ actually needs to be known, merely that such a value can be demonstrated to exist.

title: Definition:Suffix
snippet: A string $T$ is a suffix of a string $S$ $S$ can be formed by concatenating another string $T'$ with $T$: $S = T'T$

title: Definition:Suffix/Proper
snippet: A proper suffix of a string $S$ is a suffix of $S$ which does not equal the whole of $S$.

title: Definition:Sulphate Ion
snippet: == Example of Ion == A sulphate ion is an ion formed from a molecule of sulphuric acid whose hydrogen atoms have been detached. It retains the electrons that at one point belonged to those hydrogen atoms. It can be expressed using the chemical formula $\mathrm S {\mathrm O_4}^{--}$.

title: Definition:Sulphur/32
snippet: == Isotope of Sulphur == Sulphur-$32$ is the isotope of oxygen which has $16$ neutrons in addition to its $16$ protons. S-$32$ is the most common of the $4$ stable isotopes of sulphur, making up $94.8 \%$ of the sulphur found on Earth.

title: Definition:Sulphur/33
snippet: == Isotope of Sulphur == Sulphur-$33$ is the isotope of sulphur which has $17$ neutrons in addition to its $16$ protons. S-$33$ is one of the $4$ stable isotopes of sulphur, forming $0.760 \%$ of the naturally occurring sulphur.

title: Definition:Sulphur/34
snippet: == Isotope of Sulphur == Sulphur-$34$ is the isotope of sulphur which has $18$ neutrons in addition to its $16$ protons. S-$34$ is one of the $4$ stable isotopes of sulphur, forming $4.37 \%$ of the naturally occurring sulphur.

title: Definition:Sulphur/35
snippet: == Isotope of Sulphur == Sulphur-$35$ is the isotope of sulphur which has $19$ neutrons in addition to its $16$ protons. S-$35$ is radioactive, with a half-life of approximately $87.37$ days. S-$35$ exists on Earth as traces only.

title: Definition:Sulphur/36
snippet: == Isotope of Sulphur == Sulphur-$36$ is the isotope of sulphur which has $20$ neutrons in addition to its $16$ protons. S-$36$ is one of the $4$ stable isotopes of sulphur, forming $0.02 \%$ of the naturally occurring sulphur.

title: Definition:Sulphur/Also known as
snippet: == Sulphur: Also known as == In American English, sulphur is spelt sulfur. Category:Definitions/Sulphur

title: Definition:Sulphuric Acid
snippet: Sulphuric acid is the chemical substance whose molecules are composed of $2$ atoms of hydrogen, one atom of sulphur, and $4$ atom of oxygen. It can be expressed using the chemical formula $\mathrm H_2 \mathrm S \mathrm O_4$.

title: Definition:Sum
snippet: Arithmetic: Under the operation of addition of two numbers $a$ and $b$, the sum is the result of the operation $a + b$. Algebra: A summation is a repeated addition on a sequence (either finite or infinite) of numbers, usually signalled by the summation sign: $\ds \sum$ Abstract Algebra, Group Theory: Definition:Direct Sum

title: Definition:Sum/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Sum == In natural language, the word sum is often used to mean the process of operation of any arithmetical calculation. This probably originates from elementary school, where the first excursions into arithmetic occurs via (natural number) addition. Consequently, at that level, all such arithmetic lessons are often referred to as sums. To those with mathematical anxiety, the very word sums may be distressing, while in the humour of children's comics, a popular punishment for a child would be to be sat down at a desk in front of a book titled hard sums.

title: Definition:Sum Over Divisors
snippet: Let $n$ be a positive integer. Let $f: \Z_{>0} \to \Z_{>0}$ be a mapping on the positive integers. Let $d \divides n$ denote that $d$ is a divisor of $n$. Then the sum of $\map f d$ over all the divisors of $n$ is denoted: $\ds \sum_{d \mathop \divides n} \map f d$ Thus, for example: $\ds \sum_{d \mathop \divides 10} \map f d = \map f 1 + \map f 2 + \map f 5 + \map f {10}$ Category:Definitions/Number Theory

title: Definition:Sum of Cardinals
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be sets. Let $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ be the cardinals associated with $A$ and $B$ respectively. Then the sum of $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ is defined as: $\mathbf a + \mathbf b = \map \Card {A \sqcup B}$ where: $A \sqcup B$ denotes the disjoint union of $A$ and $B$ $\map \Card {A \sqcup B}$ denotes the cardinal associated with $A \sqcup B$.

title: Definition:Sum of Densely-Defined Linear Operators
snippet: Let $\HH$ be a Hilbert space. Let $\struct {\map D S, S}$ and $\struct {\map D T, T}$ be densely-defined linear operators. Let: $\map D {S + T} = \map D S \cap \map D T$ Define $S + T : \map D {S + T} \to \HH$ by: $\map {\paren {S + T} } x = S x + T x$ for each $x \in \map D {S + T}$. We say that $\struct {\map D {S + T}, S + T}$ is the sum of $\struct {\map D S, S}$ and $\struct {\map D T, T}$.

title: Definition:Sum of Finite Set
snippet: Let $\mathbb A$ be one of the standard number systems $\N, \Z, \Q, \R, \C$. Let $S \subset \mathbb A$ be a finite subset. The sum of $S$ is the summation of the identity mapping on $S$ over $S$: $\ds \sum S = \sum_{s \mathop \in S} s$ Category:Definitions/Summations

title: Definition:Summand/Also known as
snippet: == Summand: Also known as == The word addend appears to mean the same thing as summand, such that the two words may be used interchangeably. The word term is frequently seen for summand, but term also has other meanings. If it is important to avoid ambiguity then it is recommended that summand is used. The term augend can sometimes be seen for (specifically) the first of a pair of summands, so in the context of $a + b = c$: $a$ is the augend $b$ is the addend $c$ is the sum. In the context of summations, the summand is also known as the set of summands.

title: Definition:Summand/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Summand == The extensions -and and -end derive from the Latin [http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerundive gerundive] forms which impart the meaning that which must be ... to a word. Thus the word summand, and its synonym addend, literally mean: that which must be summed (or added). In natural language, the word addendum is more common than either, and similarly means something which is to be added (usually, by linguistic coincidence, to the end). The archaic term augend has the same lingustic root as augment, which means to make larger.

title: Definition:Summation
snippet: Let $\struct {S, +}$ be an algebraic structure where the operation $+$ is an operation derived from, or arising from, the addition operation on the natural numbers. Let $\tuple {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n} \in S^n$ be an ordered $n$-tuple in $S$.

title: Definition:Summation/Also known as
snippet: == Summation: Also known as == It is common for the term sum to be used for summation. However, despite the fact that summation is longer, and a less-aesthetic neologism for sum, the term summation is preferred on for immediate clarity. Category:Definitions/Summations

title: Definition:Summation/Finite
snippet: Let $\struct {S, +}$ be an algebraic structure where the operation $+$ is an operation derived from, or arising from, the addition operation on the natural numbers. Let the set of values of $j$ which satisfy the propositional function $\map R j$ be finite. Then the summation $\ds \sum_{\map R j} a_j$ is described as being a finite summation.

title: Definition:Summation/Finite Support
snippet: Let $G$ be an abelian group. Let $S$ be a set. Let $f: S \to G$ be a mapping. Let the support $\map \supp f$ be finite. Let $g$ be the restriction of $f$ to $\map \supp f$. The summation of $f$ over $S$, denoted $\ds \sum_{s \mathop \in S} \map f s$, is the summation over the finite set $\map \supp f$ of $g$: $\ds \sum_{s \mathop \in S} \map f s = \sum_{s \mathop \in \map \supp f} \map g s$ Category:Definitions/Summations

title: Definition:Summation/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Summation == The notation $\sum$ for a summation was famously introduced by in $1820$: Le signe $\ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^{i \mathop = \infty}$ indique que l'on doit donner au nombre entier $i$ toutes les valeurs $1, 2, 3, \ldots$, et prendre la somme des termes. (The sign $\ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^{i \mathop = \infty}$ indicates that one must give to the whole number $i$ all the values $1, 2, 3, \ldots$, and take the sum of the terms.) -- However, some sources suggest that it was in fact first introduced by .

title: Definition:Summation/Index Variable
snippet: Consider the summation, in either of the three forms: $\ds \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n a_j \qquad \sum_{1 \mathop \le j \mathop \le n} a_j \qquad \sum_{\map R j} a_j$ The variable $j$, an example of a bound variable, is known as the index variable of the summation.

title: Definition:Summation/Indexed
snippet: Let $\struct {S, +}$ be an algebraic structure where the operation $+$ is an operation derived from, or arising from, the addition operation on the natural numbers. Let $\tuple {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n} \in S^n$ be an ordered $n$-tuple in $S$. The composite is called the summation of $\tuple {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n}$, and is written: $\ds \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n a_j = \paren {a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_n}$

title: Definition:Summation/Inequality
snippet: Let $\struct {S, +}$ be an algebraic structure where the operation $+$ is an operation derived from, or arising from, the addition operation on the natural numbers. Let $\tuple {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n} \in S^n$ be an ordered $n$-tuple in $S$. The summation of $\tuple {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n}$ can be written: $\ds \sum_{1 \mathop \le j \mathop \le n} a_j = \paren {a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_n}$

title: Definition:Summation/Inequality/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Summation by Inequality ==

title: Definition:Summation/Inequality/Multiple Indices
snippet: Let $\ds \sum_{0 \mathop \le j \mathop \le n} a_j$ denote the summation of $\tuple {a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n}$. Summands with multiple indices can be denoted by propositional functions in several variables, for example: $\ds \sum_{0 \mathop \le i \mathop \le n} \paren {\sum_{0 \mathop \le j \mathop \le n} a_{i j} } = \sum_{0 \mathop \le i, j \mathop \le n} a_{i j}$ $\ds \sum_{0 \mathop \le i \mathop \le n} \paren {\sum_{0 \mathop \le j \mathop \le i} a_{i j} } = \sum_{0 \mathop \le j \mathop \le i \mathop \le n} a_{i j}$

title: Definition:Summation/Inequality/Multiple Indices/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Summation by Inequality over Multiple Indices ==

title: Definition:Summation/Inequality/Multiple Indices/Examples/Sum of Subscripts
snippet: == Example of Summation by Inequality over Multiple Indices == Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. Let $a$ be an $n$-tuply subscripted variable. Consider the expression: $\ds \sum_{\substack {j_1 \mathop + j_2 \mathop + \mathop \cdots \mathop + j_n \mathop = n \\ j_i \mathop \ge j_2 \mathop \ge \mathop \cdots \mathop \ge j_n \mathop \ge 0} } a_{j_1 j_2 \ldots j_n}$ For $n = 5$, this means: $a_{11111} + a_{21110} + a_{22100} + a_{31100} + a_{32000} + a_{41000} + a_{50000}$

title: Definition:Summation/Infinite
snippet: Let $\struct {S, +}$ be an algebraic structure where the operation $+$ is an operation derived from, or arising from, the addition operation on the natural numbers. Let an infinite number of values of $j$ satisfy the propositional function $\map R j$. Then the precise meaning of $\ds \sum_{\map R j} a_j$ is: $\ds \sum_{\map R j} a_j = \paren {\lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \sum_{\substack {\map R j \\ -n \mathop \le j \mathop < 0}} a_j} + \paren {\lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \sum_{\substack {\map R j \\ 0 \mathop \le j \mathop \le n} } a_j}$ provided that both limits exist.

title: Definition:Summation/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Summation == The sign $\sum$ is called the summation sign and sometimes referred to as sigma (as that is its name in Greek).

title: Definition:Summation/Propositional Function
snippet: Let $\struct {S, +}$ be an algebraic structure where the operation $+$ is an operation derived from, or arising from, the addition operation on the natural numbers. Let $\tuple {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n} \in S^n$ be an ordered $n$-tuple in $S$. Let $\map R j$ be a propositional function of $j$. Then we can write the summation as: $\ds \sum_{\map R j} a_j = \text{ The sum of all $a_j$ such that $\map R j$ holds}$. If more than one propositional function is written under the summation sign, they must all hold. Such an operation on an ordered tuple is known as a summation.

title: Definition:Summation/Propositional Function/Iverson's Convention
snippet: Let $\ds \sum_{\map R j} a_j$ be the summation over all $a_j$ such that $j$ satisfies $R$. This can also be expressed: $\ds \sum_{j \mathop \in \Z} a_j \sqbrk {\map R j}$ where $\sqbrk {\map R j}$ is Iverson's convention.

title: Definition:Summation/Summand
snippet: Let $\struct {S, +}$ be an algebraic structure where the operation $+$ is an operation derived from, or arising from, the addition operation on the natural numbers. Let $\set {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n} \subseteq S$ be a set of elements of $S$. Let $\map R j$ be a propositional function of $j$. Let: $\ds \sum_{\map R j} a_j$ be an instance of a summation on $\set {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n}$. The set of elements $\set {a_j \in S: 1 \le j \le n, \map R j}$ is called the summand.

title: Definition:Summation/Summand/Infinite
snippet: Let $\struct {S, +}$ be an algebraic structure where the operation $+$ is an operation derived from, or arising from, the addition operation on the natural numbers. Let $A = \set {a_j: j \in \Z} \subseteq S$ be a set of elements of $S$. Let $\map R j$ be a propositional function of $j$. Let: $\ds \sum_{\map R j} a_j$ be an instance of a summation on $A$. Let an infinite number of values of $j$ satisfy $\map R j = \T$. The set of elements $\set {a_j \in A: \map R j}$ is called an infinite summand.

title: Definition:Summation/Vacuous Summation
snippet: Take the summation: $\ds \sum_{\map \Phi j} a_j$ where $\map \Phi j$ is a propositional function of $j$. Suppose that there are no values of $j$ for which $\map \Phi j$ is true. Then $\ds \sum_{\map \Phi j} a_j$ is defined as being $0$. This summation is called a vacuous summation. This is because: $\forall a: a + 0 = a$ where $a$ is a number. Hence for all $j$ for which $\map \Phi j$ is false, the sum is unaffected. This is most frequently seen in the form: $\ds \sum_{j \mathop = m}^n a_j = 0$ where $m > n$.

title: Definition:Summation Operator
snippet: Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a real function. The summation operator $S$ on $f$ is defined as: $\map S f = \ds \sum_{j \mathop = 0}^\infty \map f {x - j} = \map f x + \map f {x - 1} + \map f {x - 2} + \dotsb$

title: Definition:Summation over Finite Index
snippet: Let $\struct {G, +}$ be a commutative monoid. Let $\family {g_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed subset of $G$ where the indexing set $I$ is finite. Let $\set {e_1, e_2, \ldots, e_n}$ be a finite enumeration of $I$. Let $\tuple {g_{e_1}, g_{e_2}, \ldots, g_{e_n} }$ be the ordered tuple formed from the composite mapping $g \circ e: \closedint 1 n \to G$. The summation over $I$, denoted $\ds \sum_{i \mathop \in I} g_i$, is defined as the summation over $\tuple {g_{e_1}, g_{e_2}, \ldots, g_{e_n} }$: $\ds \sum_{i \mathop \in I} g_i = \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n g_{e_k}$

title: Definition:Summation over Finite Subset
snippet: Let $\struct {G, +}$ be a commutative monoid. Let $F \subseteq G$ be a finite subset of $G$. Let $\set {e_1, e_2, \ldots, e_n}$ be a finite enumeration of $F$. Let $\tuple {e_1, e_2, \ldots, e_n}$ be the ordered tuple formed from the bijection $e: \closedint 1 n \to F$. The summation over $F$, denoted $\ds \sum_{g \mathop \in F} g$, is defined as the summation over $\tuple{e_1, e_2, \ldots, e_n}$: $\ds \sum_{g \mathop \in F} g = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n e_i$

title: Definition:Summatory Function
snippet: Let $a: \N \to \C$ be an arithmetic function. Its summatory function is the mapping: $\map A x = \ds \sum_{n \mathop \le x} \map a n$ defined for $x \in \Z_{\ge 0}$.

title: Definition:Sun
snippet: The Sun is the star around which Earth (and the other planets of the solar system) is in orbit.

title: Definition:Superabundant Number
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a positive integer. Then $n$ is superabundant : $\forall m \in \Z_{>0}, m < n: \dfrac {\map {\sigma_1} m} m < \dfrac {\map {\sigma_1} n} n$ where $\sigma_1$ denotes the divisor sum function. That is, $n$ has a higher abundancy index than any smaller positive integer.

title: Definition:Superabundant Number/Sequence
snippet: == Sequence of Superabundant Numbers == The sequence of superabundant numbers begins: $1, 2, 4, 6, 12, 24, 36, 48, 60, 120, 180, 240, 360, 720, 840, 1260, \ldots$ Category:Definitions/Abundant Numbers

title: Definition:Superadditive Function (Algebra)
snippet: Let $\struct {S, +_S}$ and $\struct {T, +_T, \preccurlyeq}$ be semigroups such that $\struct {T, +_T, \preccurlyeq}$ is ordered. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping from $S$ to $T$ which satisfies the relation: $\forall a, b \in S: \map f a +_T \map f b \preccurlyeq \map f {a +_S b}$ Then $f$ is defined as being superadditive. The usual context in which this is encountered is where $S$ and $T$ are both the set of real numbers $\R$ (or a subset of them).

title: Definition:Supercomplete Class
snippet: Let $A$ denote a class. Then $A$ is a supercomplete class : {{axiom | n = 1 | lc= $A$ is transitive: | q = \forall x: \forall y | m = \paren {x \in y \land y \in A \implies x \in A} }} {{axiom | n = 2 | lc= $A$ is swelled: | q = \forall x: \forall y | m = \paren {x \subseteq y \land y \in A \implies x \in A} }}

title: Definition:Superdifferential
snippet: Let $\innerprod X {X'}$ be a dual system over $\R$. Let $C \subseteq X$ be a convex set. Let $f : C \to \R$ be a convex function. Let $x \in C$. We define the superdifferential of $f$ at $x$ as the (possibly empty) set of supergradients of $f$ at $x$. We denote this by $\partial \map f x$. This notation clashes with that of the subdifferential, care will be taken to distinguish the two when they simultaneously appear.

title: Definition:Superfactorial
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be a positive integer. The superfactorial of $n$ is defined as: $n\$ = \ds \prod_{k \mathop = 1}^n k! = 1! \times 2! \times \cdots \times \left({n - 1}\right)! \times n!$ where $k!$ denotes the factorial of $n$.

title: Definition:Superfactorial/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Superfactorials ==

title: Definition:Superfactorial/Sequence
snippet: == Sequence of Superfactorials == The sequence of superfactorials begins: $1, 2, 12, 288, 34 \, 560, 24 \, 883 \, 200, 125 \, 411 \, 328 \, 000, \ldots$

title: Definition:Superfunction
snippet: Let $C, D \subseteq \C$ with $z \in C \implies z + 1 \in C$. Let $F: C \to D$ and $H: D \to D$ be holomorphic functions. Let $\map H {\map F z} = \map F {z + 1}$ for all $z \in C$. Then $F$ is said to be a superfunction of $H$, and $H$ is called a transfer function of $F$. That is, superfunctions are iterations of transfer functions.

title: Definition:Supergradient
snippet: Let $\innerprod X {X'}$ be a dual system over $\R$. Let $C$ be a convex set. Let $f : C \to \R$ be a convex function. Let $x \in C$. We say that $x' \in X'$ is a supergradient for $f$ at $x$ : $\map f y - \map f x \le \innerprod {y - x} {x'}$ for each $y \in C$. We call this inequality the supergradient inequality.

title: Definition:Superharmonic Function
snippet: Let $D$ be a complex domain. A superharmonic function is a continuous real-valued function $f$ such that for every closed disk $\map {B^-} {a; r} \subseteq D$ with center $a$ and radius $r$: $\ds \map f a \ge \int_0^{2 \pi} \map f {a + r e^{i \theta} } \rd \theta$

title: Definition:Superinductive Class
snippet: Let $A$ be a class. Let $g: A \to A$ be a mapping on $A$. Then $A$ is superinductive under $g$ : $A$ is inductive under $g$ $A$ is closed under chain unions. That is: {{axiom | n = 2 | lc= $A$ is closed under $g$: | q = \forall x | m = \paren {x \in A \implies \map g x \in A} }}

title: Definition:Supermartingale/Continuous Time
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \sequence {\FF_t}_{t \ge 0}, \Pr}$ be a filtered probability space. Let $\sequence {X_t}_{t \ge 0}$ be an adapted stochastic process. We say that $\sequence {X_t}_{t \ge 0}$ is a continuous time $\sequence {\FF_t}_{t \ge 0}$-supermartingale : $(1) \quad$ $X_t$ is integrable for each $t \in \hointr 0 \infty$ $(2) \quad \forall s, t \in \hointr 0 \infty, \, 0 \le s < t: \expect {X_t \mid \FF_s} \le X_s$ Equation $(2)$ is understood as follows: for any version $\expect {X_t \mid \FF_s}$ of the conditional expectation of $X_t$ given $\FF_s$, we have: $\expect {X_t…

title: Definition:Supermartingale/Discrete Time/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \sequence {\FF_n}_{n \ge 0}, \Pr}$ be a filtered probability space. Let $\sequence {X_n}_{n \ge 0}$ be an adapted stochastic process. We say that $\sequence {X_n}_{n \ge 0}$ is a discrete time $\sequence {\FF_n}_{n \ge 0}$-supermartingale : $(1): \quad$ $X_n$ is integrable for each $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ $(2): \quad \forall n \in \Z_{\ge 0}: \expect {X_{n + 1} \mid \FF_n} \le X_n$ Equation $(2)$ is understood as follows: for any version $\expect {X_{n + 1} \mid \FF_n}$ of the conditional expectation of $X_{n + 1}$ given $\FF_n$, we have: $\expect {X_{n + 1} \mid…

title: Definition:Supermartingale/Discrete Time/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \sequence {\FF_n}_{n \ge 0}, \Pr}$ be a filtered probability space. Let $\sequence {X_n}_{n \ge 0}$ be an adapted stochastic process. We say that $\sequence {X_n}_{n \ge 0}$ is a $\sequence {\FF_n}_{n \ge 0}$-supermartingale : $(1): \quad$ $X_n$ is integrable for each $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ $(2): \quad \forall n \in \Z_{\ge 0}, \, \forall m \ge n: \expect {X_m \mid \FF_n} \le X_n$.

title: Definition:Superscript
snippet: A superscript is a symbol (often a number) written above and to the right of a given symbol to identify a specific instance of the object that symbol denotes. This is often to reference an specific exponent. When placed in round brackets, it also indicates the order of a derivative.

title: Definition:Superset/Also known as
snippet: == Superset: Also known as == The term superset is rare in the literature. Instead of $T$ is a superset of $S$, the usual terminology is $T$ contains $S$ or $T$ includes $S$.

title: Definition:Supersonic
snippet: The speed of a body $B$ is defined as supersonic its Mach number is greater than $1$. That is, if $B$ is moving faster than the speed of sound in the fluid in which it is moving.

title: Definition:Supertransitive Class
snippet: Let $A$ be a transitive class. Then $A$ is said to be a supertransitive class : $\forall x \in A: \powerset x \subseteq A$ That is, if $A$ contains the power set of all of its elements.

title: Definition:Supplemental Chords
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a circle. Supplemental chords are a pair of chords of $\CC$ joining a point on the circumference of $\CC$ to the two endpoints of a diameter of $\CC$.

title: Definition:Supplementary Angles
snippet: 500px Let $\angle ACB$ be a straight angle. Let $\angle BCD + \angle DCA = \angle ACB$. That is, $\angle DCA = \angle ACB - \angle BCD$. Then $\angle DCA$ is the supplement of $\angle BCD$. Hence, for any angle $\alpha$ (whether less than a straight angle or not), the supplement of $\alpha$ is $\pi - \alpha$. Measured in degrees, the supplement of $\alpha$ is $180 \degrees - \alpha$. If $\alpha$ is the supplement of $\beta$, then it follows that $\beta$ is the supplement of $\alpha$. Hence we can say that $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are supplementary.

title: Definition:Supplementary Angles/Also known as
snippet: == Supplementary Angles: Also known as == Some sources use the term adjacent angles to mean supplementary angles, but has a different definition for that term.

title: Definition:Support
snippet: In abstract algebra: Support of Mapping to Algebraic Structure Support of Real-Valued Function Support of Module Support of Element of Direct Product In analysis and topology: Support of Continuous Mapping Support of Continuous Real-Valued Function In functional analysis: Support of Schwartz Distribution In mapping theory: Support of Permutation Support of Characteristic Function In probability theory Support of Random Variable

title: Definition:Support Functional
snippet:
Let $\struct {X, 
orm \cdot_X}$ be a normed vector space. Let $\struct {X^\ast, 
orm \cdot_{X^\ast} }$ be the normed dual space of $X$. Let $x \in X$. We say that $f \in X^\ast$ is a support functional at $x$ : $(1): \quad$ $
orm f_{X^\ast} = 1$ $(2): \quad$ $\map f x = 
orm x_X$.

title: Definition:Support Point of Subset of Topological Vector Space
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological vector space over $\R$. Let $A \subseteq X$ be non-empty. Let $x \in X$. We say that $x$ is a support point of $A$ there exists a continuous linear functional $f : X \to \R$ that supports $A$ at $x$.

title: Definition:Support of Continuous Mapping/Real-Valued
snippet: Let $f: \R^n \to \R$ be a continuous real-valued function. The support of $f$ is the closure of the set of elements $x$ of $\R^n$ whose values under $f$ are non-zero. That is: $\map \supp f = \cl \set {x \in \R^n: \map f x \ne 0}$ Category:Definitions/Real Analysis

title: Definition:Support of Element of Direct Product
snippet: Let $\family {\struct {S_i, \circ_i} }_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a family of algebraic structures with identity. Let $\ds S = \prod_{i \mathop \in I} S_i$ be their direct product. Let $e_i$ be an identity of $S_i$ for all $i \in I$. Let $m = \family {m_i}_{i \mathop \in I} \in S$. The support of $m$ is defined as: $\supp \set {i \in I: m_i \ne e_i}$

title: Definition:Support of Mapping to Algebraic Structure
Definition:Support of Mapping to Algebraic Structure/Real-Valued Function
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real-valued function. The support of $f$ is the set of elements $x$ of $S$ whose values under $f$ are non-zero: $\map \supp f := \set {x \in S: \map f x \ne 0}$

title: Definition:Support of Module
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $M$ be a unitary $A$-module. The support $\map \supp M$ of $M$ is the set of prime ideals $P$ of $A$ such that the localization of $M$ at $P$ is nonzero: $\map \supp M = \set {P \in \Spec A : M_P \ne 0}$ where $\Spec A$ is the spectrum of $A$. Category:Definitions/Module Theory

title: Definition:Support of Permutation
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $f$ be a permutation on $S$. The support of $f$ is the subset of moved elements: $\map \supp f = \set {x \in S: \map f x \ne x}$

title: Definition:Support of Real-Valued Function/Also known as
snippet: == Support of Real-Valued Function: Also known as == The support of a real-valued function $f$ is also known as the cozero set $f$, and denoted $\map {\operatorname {coz} } f$.

title: Definition:Support of Schwartz Distribution
snippet: Let $\Omega \subseteq \R^n$ be an open set. Let $\map \DD \Omega$ be the space of continuous functions compactly supported in $\Omega$. Let $\map {\DD'} \Omega$ be the distribution space. Let $T \in \map {\DD'} \Omega$ be a Schwartz distribution. The support $\map {\mathrm {supp} } T \subseteq \Omega$ of $T$ is defined by: $x \notin \map {\mathrm {supp} } T$ : there exists an open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ such that: for all $\phi \in \map \DD \Omega$ such that $\map {\mathrm {supp} } \phi \subseteq U$: $\map T \phi = 0$

title: Definition:Support of Vector with respect to Schauder Basis
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a normed vector space over $\GF$. Let $x \in X$. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a Schauder basis for $X$. Let $\sequence {x_n^\ast}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be the coordinate functionals associated with $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$. We define the support of the vector $x$ $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ as the set of $n \in \N$ such that $\map {x_n^\ast} x \ne 0$, and denote it $\map \supp x$.

title: Definition:Supremum
snippet: Supremum of Ordered Set Supremum of Subset of Real Numbers Supremum of Mapping Supremum of Real-Valued Function Supremum of Sequence Supremum of Real Sequence

title: Definition:Supremum/Also defined as
snippet: Some sources refer to the supremum as being the upper bound. Using this convention, any element greater than this is not considered to be an upper bound.

title: Definition:Supremum/Also known as
snippet: Particularly in the field of analysis, the supremum of a set $T$ is often referred to as the least upper bound of $T$ and denoted $\map {\mathrm {lub} } T$ or $\map {\mathrm {l.u.b.} } T$. Some sources refer to the supremum of a set as the supremum on a set. Some sources refer to the supremum of a set as the join of the set and use the notation $\bigvee T$ or $\ds \bigvee_{y \mathop \in T} y$. Some sources introduce the notation $\ds \sup_{y \mathop \in T} y$, which may improve clarity in some circumstances.

title: Definition:Supremum/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Supremum == The plural of supremum is suprema, although the (incorrect) form supremums can occasionally be found if you look hard enough. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Supremum Metric
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $M = \struct {A', d'}$ be a metric space. Let $A$ be the set of all bounded mappings $f: S \to M$. Let $d: A \times A \to \R$ be the function defined as: $\ds \forall f, g \in A: \map d {f, g} := \sup_{x \mathop \in S} \map {d'} {\map f x, \map g x}$ where $\sup$ denotes the supremum. $d$ is known as the supremum metric on $A$.

title: Definition:Supremum Metric/Bounded Continuous Mappings
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct {A_1, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct {A_2, d_2}$ be metric spaces. Let $A$ be the set of all continuous mappings $f: M_1 \to M_2$ which are also bounded. Let $d: A \times A \to \R$ be the function defined as: $\ds \forall f, g \in A: \map d {f, g} := \sup_{x \mathop \in A_1} \map {d_2} {\map f x, \map g x}$ where $\sup$ denotes the supremum. $d$ is known as the supremum metric on $A$.

title: Definition:Supremum Metric/Bounded Real-Valued Functions
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $A$ be the set of all bounded real-valued functions $f: S \to \R$. Let $d: A \times A \to \R$ be the function defined as: $\ds \forall f, g \in A: \map d {f, g} := \sup_{x \mathop \in S} \size {\map f x - \map g x}$ where $\sup$ denotes the supremum. $d$ is known as the supremum metric on $A$.

title: Definition:Supremum Metric/Bounded Real Functions on Interval
snippet: Let $\closedint a b \subseteq \R$ be a closed real interval. Let $A$ be the set of all bounded real functions $f: \closedint a b \to \R$. Let $d: A \times A \to \R$ be the function defined as: $\ds \forall f, g \in A: \map d {f, g} := \sup_{x \mathop \in \closedint a b} \size {\map f x - \map g x}$ where $\sup$ denotes the supremum. $d$ is known as the supremum metric on $A$.

title: Definition:Supremum Metric/Bounded Real Sequences
snippet: Let $A$ be the set of all bounded real sequences. Let $d: A \times A \to \R$ be the function defined as: $\ds \forall \sequence {x_i}, \sequence {y_i} \in A: \map d {\sequence {x_i}, \sequence {y_i} } := \sup_{n \mathop \in \N} \size {x_n - y_n}$ where $\sup$ denotes the supremum. $d$ is known as the supremum metric on $A$.

title: Definition:Supremum Metric/Continuous Real Functions
snippet: Let $\closedint a b \subseteq \R$ be a closed real interval. Let $A$ be the set of all continuous functions $f: \closedint a b \to \R$. Let $d: A \times A \to \R$ be the function defined as: $\ds \forall f, g \in A: \map d {f, g} := \sup_{x \mathop \in \closedint a b} \size {\map f x - \map g x}$ where $\sup$ denotes the supremum. $d$ is known as the supremum metric on $A$.

title: Definition:Supremum Metric/Differentiability Class
snippet: Let $\closedint a b \subseteq \R$ be a closed real interval. Let $r \in \N$ be a natural number. Let $\mathscr D^r \closedint a b$ be the set of all continuous functions $f: \closedint a b \to \R$ which are of differentiability class $r$. Let $d: \mathscr D^r \closedint a b \times \mathscr D^r \closedint a b \to \R$ be the function defined as: $\ds \forall f, g \in \mathscr D^r \closedint a b: \map d {f, g} := \sup_{\substack {x \mathop \in \closedint a b \\ i \in \set {0, 1, 2, \ldots, r} } } \size {\map {f^{\paren i} } x - \map {g^{\paren i} } x}$ where: $f^{\paren i}$ denotes the $i$th…

title: Definition:Supremum Norm
snippet:
Let $S$ be a set. Let $\struct {X, 
orm {\,\cdot\,} }$ be a normed vector space. Let $\BB$ be the set of bounded mappings $S 	o X$. For $f \in \BB$ the supremum norm of $f$ on $S$ is defined as: $
orm f_\infty = \sup \set {
orm {\map f x}: x \in S}$

title: Definition:Supremum Norm/Continuous on Closed Interval Real-Valued Function
snippet: Let $I = \closedint a b$ be a closed real interval. Let $\map C I$ be the space of real-valued functions continuous on $I$. Let $f \in \map C I$. Let $\size {\, \cdot \,}$ denote the absolute value. Suppose $\sup$ denotes the supremum of real-valued functions. Then the supremum norm over $\map C I$ is defined as $\ds \norm {f}_\infty := \sup_{x \mathop \in I} \size {\map f x}$

title: Definition:Supremum Operator Norm
snippet:
Let $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$, $\struct {Y, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_Y}$ be normed vector spaces. Let $\map C {X, Y}$ be the continuous linear transformation space. Let $
orm {\, \cdot \,} : \map C {X, Y} 	o \R$ be the mapping defined by: $ orall A \in \map C {X, Y} : 
orm A := \map \sup {
orm {Ax}_Y : x \in X, 
orm {x}_X \le 1}$ Then $
orm {\, \cdot \,}$ is called the supremum operator norm.

title: Definition:Supremum Seminorm
snippet:
Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $f: X 	o \R$ be a real-valued function. The supremum seminorm of $f$, commonly denoted as $
orm f_\infty$, is defined as: $\ds 
orm f_\infty = \inf_{\substack {N \mathop \in \Sigma \ \map \mu N \mathop = 0} } \sup \set {\size {\map f x}: x 
otin N}$ Observe that for all $M > 
orm f_\infty$: $\map \mu {\set {x \in X: \size {\map f x} \ge M} } = 0$ and that an essentially bounded function is almost everywhere equal to a bounded function.

title: Definition:Supremum of Mapping
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\struct {T, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping from $S$ to $T$. Let $f \sqbrk S$, the image of $f$, admit a supremum. Then the supremum of $f$ (on $S$) is defined by: $\ds \sup_{x \mathop \in S} \map f x = \sup f \sqbrk S$

title: Definition:Supremum of Mapping/Real-Valued Function
snippet: Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real-valued function. Let $f$ be bounded above on $S$.

title: Definition:Supremum of Mapping/Real-Valued Function/Definition 1
snippet: Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real-valued function. Let $f$ be bounded above on $S$. The supremum of $f$ on $S$ is defined by: $\ds \sup_{x \mathop \in S} \map f x := \sup f \sqbrk S$ where $\sup f \sqbrk S$ is the supremum in $\R$ of the image of $S$ under $f$.

title: Definition:Supremum of Mapping/Real-Valued Function/Definition 2
snippet: Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real-valued function. Let $f$ be bounded above on $S$. The supremum of $f$ on $S$ is defined as $\ds \sup_{x \mathop \in S} \map f x := K \in \R$ such that: $(1): \quad \forall x \in S: \map f x \le K$ $(2): \quad \exists x \in S: \forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \map f x > K - \epsilon$

title: Definition:Supremum of Real Sequence
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a real sequence. Let $\set {x_n: n \in \N}$ admit a supremum. Then the supremum of $\sequence {x_n}$) is defined as: $\ds \map \sup {\sequence {x_n} } = \map \sup {\set {x_n: n \in \N} }$

title: Definition:Supremum of Sequence
snippet: A special case of a supremum of a mapping is a supremum of a sequence, where the domain of the mapping is $\N$. Let $\struct {T, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $T$. Let $\set {x_n: n \in \N}$ admit a supremum. Then the supremum of $\sequence {x_n}$) is defined as: $\ds \map \sup {\sequence {x_n} } = \map \sup {\set {x_n: n \in \N} }$

title: Definition:Supremum of Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set. Let $T \subseteq S$. An element $c \in S$ is the supremum of $T$ in $S$ : $(1): \quad c$ is an upper bound of $T$ in $S$ $(2): \quad c \preccurlyeq d$ for all upper bounds $d$ of $T$ in $S$. If there exists a supremum of $T$ (in $S$), we say that: $T$ admits a supremum (in $S$) or $T$ has a supremum (in $S$).

title: Definition:Supremum of Set/Finite Supremum
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set. Let $T \subseteq S$ admit a supremum $\sup T$. If $T$ is finite, $\sup T$ is called a finite supremum.

title: Definition:Supremum of Set/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $T \subseteq \R$ be a subset of the real numbers. A real number $c \in \R$ is the supremum of $T$ in $\R$ : $(1): \quad c$ is an upper bound of $T$ in $\R$ $(2): \quad c \le d$ for all upper bounds $d$ of $T$ in $\R$. If there exists a supremum of $T$ (in $\R$), we say that: $T$ admits a supremum (in $\R$) or $T$ has a supremum (in $\R$). The supremum of $T$ is denoted $\sup T$ or $\map \sup T$.

title: Definition:Supremum of Set/Real Numbers/Propositional Function
snippet: Let $\family {a_j}_{j \mathop \in I}$ be a family of elements of the real numbers $\R$ indexed by $I$. Let $\map R j$ be a propositional function of $j \in I$. Then we can define the supremum of $\family {a_j}_{j \mathop \in I}$ as: $\ds \sup_{\map R j} a_j := \text { the supremum of all $a_j$ such that $\map R j$ holds}$ If more than one propositional function is written under the supremum sign, they must all hold.

title: Definition:Supremum of Set/Real Numbers/Propositional Function/Finite Range
snippet: Let $\family {a_j}_{j \mathop \in I}$ be a family of elements of the real numbers $\R$ indexed by $I$. Let $\map R j$ be a propositional function of $j \in I$. Let the fiber of truth of $\map R j$ be finite. Then the supremum of $\family {a_j}_{j \mathop \in I}$ can be expressed as: $\ds \max_{\map R j} a_j = \text { the maxmum of all $a_j$ such that $\map R j$ holds}$ and can be referred to as the maximum of $\family {a_j}_{j \mathop \in I}$. If more than one propositional function is written under the supremum sign, they must all hold.

title: Definition:Supremum of Set/Real Numbers/Propositional Function/Vacuous Supremum
snippet: Take the indexed supremum: $\ds \sup _{\map \Phi j} a_j$ where $\map \Phi j$ is a propositional function of $j$. Suppose that there are no values of $j$ for which $\map \Phi j$ is true. Then $\ds \sup_{\map \Phi j} a_j$ is defined as being $-\infty$. This supremum is called a vacuous supremum. This is because: $\forall a \in \R: \sup \set {a, -\infty} = a$ Hence for all $j$ for which $\map \Phi j$ is false, the supremum is unaffected. In this context $-\infty$ is considered as minus infinity, the hypothetical quantity that has the property: $\forall n \in \Z: -\infty < n$

title: Definition:Surd
snippet: A surd is an expression containing irrational roots.

title: Definition:Surd/Mixed
snippet: A mixed surd is a surd containing both irrational and rational terms.

title: Definition:Surd/Pure
snippet: A pure surd is a surd containing irrational terms only.

title: Definition:Surface Area
snippet: Surface area is the measure of the total area of the surface of a body. It has two dimensions and is specified in units of length squared. Hence the term square as a general vague term for a quantity in two dimensions. It is a scalar quantity.

title: Definition:Surface Area/Also known as
snippet: == Surface Area: Also known as == The term superficial area can sometimes be found in older texts to mean surface area. Category:Definitions/Surface Area

title: Definition:Surface Area/Symbol
snippet: == Volume: Symbol == The usual symbols used to denote the surface area of a body are $S$ or $A$. Category:Definitions/Area

title: Definition:Surface Charge
snippet: Let $B$ be a body made out of an electrically conducting substance. A surface charge is an electric charge localised to the first few atoms depth of $B$.

title: Definition:Surface Charge Density
snippet: Let $B$ be a body made out of an electrically conducting substance. Let $B$ be under the influence of an electric field $\mathbf E$ under which a surface charge is induced on $B$. Let $\delta S$ be an area element which is smaller than the scale used for a macroscopic electric field, but still large enough to contain many atoms on the surface of $B$. Let $P$ be a point in the vicinity of $\delta S$ whose position vector is $\mathbf r$. Let $\delta V$ be a volume element just thick enough to enclose the whole of the surface charge $\map \sigma {\mathbf r} \delta S$ associated with $\delta S$.

title: Definition:Surface Charge Density/Dimension
snippet: The dimension of surface charge density is $\mathsf {I T L}^{-2}$: electric charge per unit area.

title: Definition:Surface Charge Density/Symbol
snippet: == Surface Charge Density: Symbol == The usual symbol used to denote surface charge density is $\sigma$ (Greek letter sigma).

title: Definition:Surface Charge Density/Units
snippet: The SI units of surface charge density are $\mathrm C \, \mathrm m^{-2}$ (coulombs per square metre). Category:Definitions/Surface Charge Density Category:Definitions/Units of Measurement

title: Definition:Surface Harmonic
snippet: A surface harmonic is a spherical harmonic: $r^n \paren {a_n \map {P_n} {\cos \theta} + \ds \sum_{m \mathop = 1}^n \paren { {a_n}^m \cos m \phi + {b_n}^m \sin m \phi} \map { {P_n}^m} {\cos \theta} }$ such that $r = 1$. That is: $a_n \map {P_n} {\cos \theta} + \ds \sum_{m \mathop = 1}^n \paren { {a_n}^m \cos m \phi + {b_n}^m \sin m \phi} \map { {P_n}^m} {\cos \theta}$

title: Definition:Surface Integral
snippet: Let $S$ be a surface in a vector field $\mathbf F$. Let $\d S$ be a small element of $S$. Let $\mathbf v$ be the vector induced by $\mathbf F$ at the middle of $\d S$. Let $\mathbf {\hat n}$ denote the positive unit normal to $S$ at $\d S$. Let $\mathbf v$ make an angle $\theta$ with $\mathbf {\hat n}$. 380px Hence: $\mathbf v \cdot \mathbf {\hat n} = v \cos \theta \rd S$ where: $\cdot$ denotes dot product $v$ denotes the magnitude of $\mathbf v$.

title: Definition:Surface Integral/Physical Interpretation
snippet: == Physical Interpretation of Surface Integral == Suppose $\mathbf v$ is interpreted as the velocity of some fluid in motion through a surface $S$. Let $P$ be a point $P$ on $S$ at which a positive unit normal $\mathbf {\hat n}$ is constructed. The expression $\mathbf v \cdot \mathbf {\hat n} \rd S$ denotes the amount of fluid passing through $\d S$ perpendicular to $S$ in unit time. It is sufficient to consider this normal component, as the tangential component contributes nothing to the flow through $\d S$.

title: Definition:Surface of Revolution/Definition 1
snippet: Let $F$ be a plane figure. Let $L$ be a straight line in the same plane as $F$. Let $F$ be rotated one full turn about $L$ in $3$-dimensional space. The surface of revolution generated by $F$ around $L$ is the surface of the solid of revolution generated by $F$ around $L$. The usual scenario is that: $(1): \quad$ one of the sides of $F$ is a straight line coincident with $L$ $(2): \quad$ $L$ itself is aligned with one of the coordinate axes, usually the $x$-axis in a cartesian plane $(3): \quad$ Two other sides of $F$ are also straight lines, perpendicular to $L$ $(4): \quad$ The remaining…

title: Definition:Surface of Revolution/Definition 2
snippet: Let $H = \set {\tuple {x, y} : y \in \R_{> 0}} \subset \R^2$ be the open upper half-plane. Let $F \subset H$ be a $1$-dimensional embedded submanifold. The surface of revolution is the subset $S_F \subseteq \R^3$ such that: $S_F = \set {\tuple {x, y, z} : \tuple {\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}, z} \in F}$ where $F$ is the generating curve of the surface of revolution.

title: Definition:Surgery
snippet: Surgery is a technique for making geometric modifications to a topological manifold in order to produce a cobordant manifold with simpler homotopy groups.

title: Definition:Surgery/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Surgery == The concept of surgery was pioneered by in $1961$. It has since been shown to be a powerful tool in the study of the topology of topological manifolds.

title: Definition:Surjection
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping from $S$ to $T$.

title: Definition:Surjection/Also known as
snippet: The phrase $f$ is surjective is often used for $f$ is a surjection. Authors who prefer to limit the jargon of mathematics tend to use the term an onto mapping for a surjection, and onto for surjective. A mapping which is not surjective is thence described as into. A surjection $f$ from $S$ to $T$ is sometimes denoted: $f: S \twoheadrightarrow T$ to emphasize surjectivity. In the context of class theory, a surjection is often seen referred to as a class surjection.

title: Definition:Surjection/Class Theory
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be classes. Let $f: A \to B$ be a mapping from $A$ to $B$. Then $f$ is a surjection : $\Img f = B$ where $\Img f$ denotes the image of $f$. That is, : $\forall y \in B: \exists x \in A: \map f x = y$

title: Definition:Surjection/Definition 1
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping from $S$ to $T$. $f: S \to T$ is a surjection : $\forall y \in T: \exists x \in \Dom f: \map f x = y$ That is, $f$ is right-total. Thus a surjection is a relation which is: Left-total Many-to-one Right-total.

title: Definition:Surjection/Definition 2
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping from $S$ to $T$. $f: S \to T$ is a surjection : $f \sqbrk S = T$ or, in the language and notation of direct image mappings: $\map {f^\to} S = T$ That is, $f$ is a surjection its image equals its codomain: $\Img f = \Cdm f$

snippet: == Diagrammatic Presentation of Surjection on Finite Set == The following diagram illustrates the mapping: $f: S \to T$ where $S$ and $T$ are the finite sets: {{eqn | l = S | r = \set {a, b, c, i, j, k} }} {{eqn | l = T | r = \set {p, q, r, s} | c = }} and $f$ is defined as: $f = \set {\tuple {a, p}, \tuple {b, p}, \tuple {c, q}, \tuple {i, r}, \tuple {j, s}, \tuple {k, s} }$ Thus the images of each of the elements of $S$ under $f$ are: 320px $S$ is the domain of $f$. $T$ is the codomain of $f$. $\set {p, q, r, s}$ is the image of $f$.

title: Definition:Surjection/Technical Note
snippet: == Technical Note on Surjection == Category:Technical Notes

title: Definition:Surjective Restriction
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping which is not surjective. Then a surjective restriction of $f$ is a restriction $g: S' \to T'$ of $f$ such that $g \restriction_{S'}: S' \to T'$ is a surjection.

title: Definition:Surjective on Morphisms
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. Let $F: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be a functor. Then $F$ is said to be surjective on morphisms : For every morphism $g$ of $\mathbf D$, there is a morphism $f$ of $\mathbf C$ such that $F f = g$

title: Definition:Surjective on Objects
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. Let $F: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be a functor. Then $F$ is said to be surjective on objects : For every object $D$ of $\mathbf D$, there is an object $C$ of $\mathbf C$ such that $F C = D$.

title: Definition:Survival Analysis
snippet: Survival analysis is the analysis of data on times to occurrence of a defined quantal response. Typically, the probability distribution of the time to occurrence has a positive skewness. That is, the response of interest tends to occur over a short or moderate timescale for some units, but scattered over a longer timescale for the rest. Data are not always complete: some observations are lost to the study, while others are censored before the response of interest occurs.

title: Definition:Survival Function
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $f: X \to \overline \R$ be a $\Sigma$-measurable function. The survival function of $f$ is the mapping $F_f: \R \to \overline \R$ defined by: $\forall t \in \R: \map {F_f} t := \map \mu {\set {\size f \ge t} }$ where $\set {\size f \ge t}$ denotes the set $\set {x \in X: \size {\map f x} \ge t}$.

title: Definition:Swelled Class
snippet: Let $A$ denote a class. Then $A$ is a swelled class every subclass of every element of $A$ is also an element of $A$. That is, $A$ is swelled : $\forall x: \forall y: \paren {x \subseteq y \land y \in A \implies x \in A}$

title: Definition:Switching Circuit
snippet: A switching circuit is a mechanical, electronic or electromechanical system for controlling the route of information or resources. The study of switching circuits can be considered a field of applied logic.

title: Definition:Syllogism
snippet: A syllogism is an argument with exactly two premises and one conclusion.

title: Definition:Sylow p-Subgroup
snippet: Let $p$ be prime. Let $G$ be a finite group whose order is denoted by $\left\vert{G}\right\vert$.

title: Definition:Sylow p-Subgroup/Definition 1
snippet: Let $p$ be prime. Let $G$ be a finite group whose order is denoted by $\order G$. Let $\order G = k p^n$ where $p \nmid k$. A Sylow $p$-subgroup is a $p$-subgroup of $G$ which has $p^n$ elements.

title: Definition:Sylow p-Subgroup/Definition 2
snippet: Let $p$ be prime. Let $G$ be a finite group. A Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$ is a maximal $p$-subgroup $P$ of $G$. In this context, maximality means that if $Q$ is a $p$-subgroup of $G$ and $P \le Q$, then $P = Q$.

title: Definition:Sylow p-Subgroup/Definition 3
snippet: Let $p$ be prime. Let $G$ be a finite group whose order is denoted by $\order G$. Let $n$ be the largest integer such that: $p^n \divides \order G$ where $\divides$ denotes divisibility. A Sylow $p$-subgroup is a $p$-subgroup of $G$ which has $p^n$ elements.

title: Definition:Symbol
snippet: In its broadest possible sense: A symbol is an object used to represent another object. In a narrower and more "mathematical" sense, a symbol is a sign of a particular shape to which is assigned a meaning, and is used to represent a concept or identify a particular object. It is generally much more convenient to use a symbol than the plain speaking that it replaces, because it is invariably more compact. One character can replace a large number of words.

title: Definition:Symbol/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Symbol == The use of symbols was one of the characteristics that initially distinguished symbolic logic from classical logic.

title: Definition:Symbolic Logic
snippet: Symbolic logic is the study of logic in which the logical form of statements is analyzed by using symbols as tools. Instead of explicit statements, logical formulas are investigated, which are symbolic representations of statements, and compound statements in particular. In Symbolic logic, the rules of reasoning and logic are investigated by means of formal systems, which form a good foundation for the symbolic manipulations performed in this field.

title: Definition:Symbolic Logic/Also known as
snippet: == Symbolic Logic: Also known as == Some sources refer to symbolic logic as mathematical logic, but it is generally preferred to reserve that term for its more specialised branch. The term logistic can be seen for this branch of logic, but this can be confused with the (mathematical) science of logistics. Some sources do not consider it necessary to separate the various approaches, and refer to logic, symbolic logic and mathematical logic synonymous.
