title: Definition:Tensor Product of Modules as Abelian Group
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $M$ be a unitary right module and $N$ a unitary left module over $R$.

title: Definition:Tensor Rank
snippet: Let $F$ be a tensor of type $\tuple {l, k}$. Then the tensor rank of $F$ is the sum $l + k$. In other words, it is the total number of vectors and covectors it can act upon.

title: Definition:Tensor Rank/Also known as
snippet: == Tensor Rank: Also known as == The tensor rank of a tensor is also known as its order.

title: Definition:Tensor Theory
snippet: Tensor theory is the branch of linear algebra which studies tensors.

title: Definition:Tensor Theory/Also known as
snippet: == Tensor Theory: Also known as == The field of tensor theory can also be referred to as tensor analysis.

title: Definition:Tensor Theory/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Tensor Theory == The field of tensor theory was initially developed by , along with as a generalization of vector analysis. It was used by in his formulation of the general theory of relativity. It is important in differential geometry and physics.

title: Definition:Tenth
snippet: Tenth is the English word for $\dfrac 1 {10}$.

title: Definition:Term
snippet: Predicate Logic: Term Logical Term: the subject and the predicate of a simple statement in predicate logic. Algebra: Term of Expression: one of the elements of an expression: in $a \circ b$ then $a$ and $b$ are the terms. Term of Polynomial: in $x^2 + x y + y^2$, each of $x^2$, $x y$ and $y^2$ are its terms. Term of Fraction: the numerator and the denominator.

title: Definition:Term (Natural Language)
snippet: A term is a noun which is assigned a specified definition within mathematics. In a more specialized context, the word term is used for an element of an expression. Category:Definitions/Language Definitions

title: Definition:Term of Expression
snippet: A term is either a variable or a constant. Let $a \circ b$ be an expression. Then each of $a$ and $b$ are known as the terms of the expression. The word term is usually used when the operation $\circ$ is addition, that is $+$.

title: Definition:Term of Sequence
snippet: The elements of a sequence are known as its terms. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence. Then the $k$th term of $\sequence {x_n}$ is the ordered pair $\tuple {k, x_k}$.

title: Definition:Term of Sequence/Also defined as
snippet: == Term of Sequence: Also defined as == Some sources gloss over the fact that a sequence is a mapping and define the terms to be the elements of the range of the sequence: We call $x_n$ the $n$th term of the sequence. -- : $\S 4.2$ However, this simplistic treatment lacks the precision of the definition provided here, and does not endorse it.

title: Definition:Term of Sequence/Also known as
snippet: == Term of Sequence: Also known as == A term of a sequence is referred to by some sources as an element of the sequence. Some sources refer to the general term of a sequence when expressing it by means of a rule.

title: Definition:Term of Sequence/Index
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence. Let $x_k$ be the $k$th term of $\sequence {x_n}$. Then the integer $k$ is known as the index of $x_k$.

title: Definition:Termial
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{> 0}$ be a positive integer. The termial of $n$ is denoted $n?$ and defined as: $\ds n? = \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n k = 1 + 2 + \cdots + n$

title: Definition:Termial/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Termial == The termial was invented by in his . It was devised as an analogy of the factorial, so as to illustrate the extension of the latter to the real numbers.

title: Definition:Termial/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number. The termial of $x$ is denoted $x?$ and defined as: $x? = \dfrac {x \paren {x + 1} } 2$

title: Definition:Terminal Node of Decision Tree/Also known as
snippet: == Terminal Node of Decision Tree: Also known as == A terminal node of a decision tree is also known as a payoff node.

title: Definition:Terminal Object
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. A terminal object of $\mathbf C$ is an object $1 \in \mathbf C_0$ of $\mathbf C$ such that: For all $C \in \mathbf C_0$, there is a unique morphism $C \to 1$.

title: Definition:Terminal P-adic Expansion
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. A $p$-adic expansion $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = m}^\infty d_n p^n$ is terminal or terminates $\exists N \in \N: \forall n \ge N: d_n = 0$

title: Definition:Terminal Point of Vector
snippet: Let $\mathbf u$ be a vector quantity represented by an arrow $\vec {AB}$ embedded in the plane: 300px The point $B$ is the terminal point of $\mathbf u$.

title: Definition:Terminal Speed
snippet: Let a body travelling under a constant force through a medium which resists its progress. The terminal speed of the body is the limiting speed through that medium for the given force.

title: Definition:Terminal Speed/Also known as
snippet: == Terminal Speed: Also known as == Terminal speed is also (less mathematically accurately) referred to as terminal velocity.

title: Definition:Terminating Decimal
snippet: A terminating decimal is a decimal expansion which has a finite number of decimal places.

title: Definition:Terminating Decimal/Also defined as
snippet: == Terminating Decimal: Also defined as == Some sources define a terminating decimal as a recurring decimal whose recurring part is zero.

title: Definition:Terminating Decimal/Also known as
snippet: == Terminating Decimal: Also known as == A terminating decimal is also known as a finite decimal. However, that latter term is too easily confused with the concept of a finite number, and so is not to be used on . Some sources use the term terminating fraction.

title: Definition:Ternary Notation
snippet: Ternary notation is the technique of expressing numbers in base $3$. That is, every number $x \in \R$ is expressed in the form: $\ds x = \sum_{j \mathop \in \Z} r_j 3^j$ where: $\forall j \in \Z: r_j \in \set {0, 1, 2}$

title: Definition:Ternary Relation
snippet: A ternary relation is a relation which involves $3$ operands, as follows: Let $S_1$, $S_2$ and $S_3$ be sets. A ternary relation $\RR$ on $S_1$, $S_2$ and $S_3$ is defined as: $\RR := \struct {S_1, S_2, S_3, R}$ where $R$ is an arbitrary subset $R \subseteq S_1 \times S_2 \times S_3$.

title: Definition:Terrestrial
snippet: The word terrestrial is an adjective whose meaning is loosely of Earth. It is usually used in the context of astronomy and geodesy to refer to concepts which need to be distinguished from their celestial counterparts.

title: Definition:Terrestrial/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Terrestrial == The adjective terrestrial, in the context of astronomy, is derived from the Latin terrestris, from terra (meaning land, earth, ground). finition:Earth|Earth]]. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Terrestrial Colatitude/Also known as
snippet: == Terrestrial Colatitude: Also known as == Terrestrial colatitude is usually known in common parlance as just colatitude. However, this term also encompasses other measurements of colatitude, for example celestial colatitude. Hence on the full term terrestrial colatitude is preferred, so as to forestall ambiguity, unless the context is clear.

title: Definition:Terrestrial Latitude/Also known as
snippet: == Terrestrial Latitude: Also known as == Terrestrial latitude is usually known in common parlance as just latitude. However, this term also encompasses other measurements of latitude, for example celestial latitude and galactic latitude. Hence on the full term terrestrial latitude is preferred, so as to forestall ambiguity, unless the context is clear.

title: Definition:Terrestrial Longitude/Also defined as
snippet: == Terrestrial Longitude: Also defined as == Many sources define the (terrestrial) longitude as so many degrees east (or west) from (or of) the Greenwich meridian. However, the Greenwich meridian has been superseded as the prime meridian by the IERS reference meridian.

title: Definition:Terrestrial Longitude/Also known as
snippet: == Terrestrial Longitude: Also known as == Terrestrial longitude is usually known in common parlance as just longitude. However, this term also encompasses other measurements of longitude, for example celestial longitude and galactic longitude. Hence on the full term terrestrial longitude is preferred, so as to forestall ambiguity, unless the context is clear.

title: Definition:Terrestrial Meridian/Also defined as
snippet: == Terrestrial Meridian: Also defined as == Some sources define a (terrestrial) meridian as be a complete great circle passing through both of Earth's poles. However, this definition is less convenient, and will not be used on .

title: Definition:Terrestrial Meridian/Also known as
snippet: == Terrestrial Meridian: Also known as == In common parlance, a terrestrial meridian is usually referred to as just a meridian. The terrestrial descriptor is added so as to distinguish it from a celestial meridian.

title: Definition:Tesla
snippet: The tesla is the SI unit of magnetic flux density. It is defined as being: The magnetic flux density that generates a force of $1$ newton on an electrical conductor carrying $1$ ampere of electric current. Thus it is equal to $1$ weber of magnetic flux per square metre.

title: Definition:Tesla/Base Units
snippet: The SI base units of the tesla are: $\mathrm T := \mathrm {kg} \, \mathrm s^{-2} \mathrm A^{-1}$ where: $\mathrm {kg}$ denotes kilogram $\mathrm A$ denotes amperes $\mathrm s$ denotes seconds (of time). Category:Definitions/Tesla

title: Definition:Tessellation
snippet: A tessellation is a division of the plane into plane geometric figures, referred to as tiles. The division is made in such a way that the tiles are fitted together with no gaps and no overlaps.

title: Definition:Tessellation/Also known as
snippet: == Tessellation: Also known as == A tessellation is also known as a tiling. Some sources use the spelling tesselation, but this is technically incorrect.

title: Definition:Tessellation/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Tessellation == The word tessellation derives from the Latin tessella, meaning small square. A tessella was a small cubic piece of material used to make mosaics. The word tessella itself derives from tessera, the Latin word for square. This in turn derives from the Greek word τέσσερα (tessera), one of their words for four. The verb form of tessellation is tessellate. Hence when a tessellation can be formed from congruent copies of a polygon or a set of polygons, the polygon or set of polygons is said to tessellate the plane.

title: Definition:Tesseract
snippet: A tesseract is the $4$-dimensional regular polytope corresponding to the cube: 500px

title: Definition:Tesseral Harmonic
snippet: A tesseral harmonic is a surface harmonic in the form: $\cos m \phi \, \map { {P_n}^m} {\cos \theta}$ or: $\sin m \phi \, \map { {P_n}^m} {\cos \theta}$ such that $m < n$.

title: Definition:Test Charge
snippet: A test charge is an arbitrarily small point charge which can be imagined to be introduced into an electric field or magnetic field for the purpose of investigating the theoretical force on that test charge.

title: Definition:Test Function
snippet: Let $\phi : \R^d \to \C$ be a complex-valued function. Let $K \subseteq \R^d$ be a compact subset. Let $K$ be the support of $\phi$: $\map \supp \phi = K$ Let $\phi$ be a smooth function across $K$ all its variables. Then $\phi$ is known as a test function.

title: Definition:Test Function/Also known as
snippet: == Test Function: Also known as == Test functions are also known as bump functions.

title: Definition:Test Function Space
snippet: Denote with $\map \DD {\R^d}$ the set: $\set { \phi: \R^d \to \C, \text{$\phi$ is a test function} }$ of all test functions $\phi: \R^d \to \C$. Then $\map \DD {\R^d}$ is called the test function space. $\map \DD {\R^d}$ is a vector space over $\C$, i.e.: $\forall \psi, \phi \in \map \DD {\R^d} : \phi + \psi \in \map \DD {\R^d}$ $\forall \phi \in \map \DD {\R^d} : \forall \alpha \in \C : \alpha \cdot \phi \in \map \DD {\R^d}$ $\map \DD {\R^d}$ also has a topology.

title: Definition:Test Function Space/Also known as
snippet: == Test Function Space: Also known as == The test function space is also known as the space of test functions. Category:Definitions/Test Function Space

title: Definition:Test Statistic
snippet: Let $\theta$ be a population parameter of some population $P$. Let $\Omega$ be the parameter space of $\theta$. Let $\mathbf X$ be a random sample from $P$. Let $T = \map f {\mathbf X}$ be a sample statistic. Let $\delta$ be a test procedure of the form: reject $H_0$ if $T \in C$ for some null hypothesis $H_0$ and some $C \subset \Omega$. We refer to $T$ as the test statistic of $\delta$.

title: Definition:Test of Homogeneity
snippet: The tests of homogeneity are a class of statistical tests for equality of means, variances, proportions, and so on, applied to samples from different populations.

title: Definition:Testament Problem
snippet: A testament problem is one which attempts to apportion a will fairly, when the terms of the will do not take into account the specific circumstances under which the conditions of the will are to be executed.

title: Definition:Tetra-/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Use of Tetra- == The prefix tetra- can be found in the following contexts: tetrad: a set or ordered tuple with $4$ elements tetragon: a less-common name than quadrilateral for a polygon with $4$ sides and hence $4$ vertices tetrahedron: a polyhedron with $4$ faces tetravalent predicate: a predicate with a valency of $4$

title: Definition:Tetra-/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Tetra- == The prefix tetra- derives from the Classical Greek τέτταρες (téttares) and τέσσαρες (téssares), meaning four. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Tetractys
snippet: The tetractys is a central concept in the mystical beliefs of the Pythagoreans. It consists of $10$ points arranged in a triangle: 300px based on the notions that: $1$ represents the point $2$ represents the line $3$ represents the surface $4$ represents the solid $1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10$ and therefore: $10$ represents the universe.

title: Definition:Tetrad
snippet: A tetrad is a set or tuple which has exactly $4$ elements.

title: Definition:Tetrad/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Tetrad == The word tetrad derives from the Classical Greek τέτταρες (téttares) and τέσσαρες (téssares), meaning four. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Tetrahedral Angle
snippet: A tetrahedral angle is a polyhedral angle with $4$ faces.

title: Definition:Tetrahedral Number
snippet: Tetrahedral numbers are those denumerating a collection of objects which can be arranged in the form of a regular tetrahedron. The $n$th tetrahedral number $H_n$ is defined as: $\ds H_n = \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n T_k$ where $T_k$ is the $k$th triangular number.

title: Definition:Tetrahedral Number/Sequence
snippet: == Sequence of Tetrahedral Numbers == The sequence of tetrahedral numbers begins as follows: $0, 1, 4, 10, 20, 35, 56, 84, 120, 165, 220, 286, 364, \ldots$

title: Definition:Tetrahedron
snippet: 300px A tetrahedron is a polyhedron which has $4$ (triangular) faces. Thus a tetrahedron is a $3$-simplex.

title: Definition:Tetrahedron/Also known as
snippet: == Tetrahedron: Also known as == A tetrahedron is also known as a triangular pyramid. In , a tetrahedron is referred to as a pyramid (with / which has) a triangular base. The first reference to it is in :

title: Definition:Tetrahedron/Apex
snippet: 300px Once the base of a tetrahedron has been identified, the vertex which does not lie on the base is called the apex of the tetrahedron. In the above diagram, given that the base of the tetrahedron $ABCD$ is the triangle $ABC$, the apex is $D$. As all faces of a tetrahedron are triangular by definition, it follows that each of its vertices is the common point of three triangles. Therefore is qualitatively immaterial which vertex is determined to be the apex. This definition is compatible with the definition of the apex of a general pyramid.

title: Definition:Tetrahedron/Base
snippet: 300px One of the faces of a tetrahedron can be chosen arbitrarily, distinguished from the others and identified as the base of the tetrahedron. In the above diagram, $ABC$ is the base of the tetrahedron $ABCD$. As all faces of a tetrahedron are triangular by definition, it is qualitatively immaterial which face is thus chosen. This definition is compatible with the definition of the base of a general pyramid.

title: Definition:Tetrahedron/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Tetrahedron == The word tetrahedron derives from the Classical Greek τετράεδρόν: tetrás (τετράς), meaning four hedron (a form of ἕδρα), meaning base or seat. The technically correct plural of tetrahedron is tetrahedra, but the word tetrahedrons can often be found.

title: Definition:Tetrahedron/Regular
snippet: A regular tetrahedron is a tetrahedron whose $4$ faces are all congruent equilateral triangles. It has: $4$ vertices $6$ edges $4$ faces The regular tetrahedron is an example of a deltahedron.

title: Definition:Tetration
snippet: $y = \map {\operatorname {tet}_b} x$ versus $x$ for various $b$ $f = \map {\operatorname {tet}_b} x$ in the $x, b$ plane with levels $f = \text{const}$.

title: Definition:Tetromino
snippet: A tetromino is a $4$-omino: 500px That is, it is a polyomino consisting of exactly $4$ unit squares.

title: Definition:Tetromino/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Tetromino == The word tetromino is a back-formation from the word domino. The prefix tetr- comes from ancient Greek meaning $4$, while -omino suffix derives from the term polyomino, which is derived in turn from domino. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Thabit Number
snippet: A Thabit number is an integer in the form: $3 \times 2^n - 1$ where $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ is a non-negative integer.

title: Definition:Thabit Number/Sequence
snippet: The sequence of Thabit numbers begins: $2, 5, 11, 23, 47, 95, 191, 383, 767, 1535, 3071, 6143, 12287, 24575, 49151, 98303, \ldots$ Note that the OEIS prefers to start the sequence with a leading $0$, but this feels counterintuitive.

title: Definition:Thabit Pair
snippet: A Thabit pair is an amicable pair formed by an application of Thabit's Rule: $\tuple {2^n a b, 2^n c}$ where $n$ be a positive integer such that: {{eqn | l = b | r = 3 \times 2^{n - 1} - 1 | c = }} {{eqn | l = c | r = 9 \times 2^{2 n - 1} - 1 | c = }} are all prime.

title: Definition:Thabit Prime
snippet: A Thabit prime is a Thabit number which is prime.

title: Definition:Thabit Prime/Sequence
snippet: The sequence of Thabit primes begins: $2, 5, 11, 23, 47, 191, 383, 6143, 786 \, 431, 51 \, 539 \, 607 \, 551, \ldots$ These correspond to the following values of $n$ in their generating expression $3 \times 2^n - 1$: $0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 11, 18, 34, 38, 43, 55, 64, 76, \ldots$

title: Definition:That which produces Medial Whole with Medial Area
snippet: Let $a, b \in \R_{>0}$ be in the forms: $a = \dfrac {\rho \lambda^{1/4} } {\sqrt 2} \sqrt {1 + \dfrac k {\sqrt {1 + k^2} } }$ $b = \dfrac {\rho \lambda^{1/4} } {\sqrt 2} \sqrt {1 - \dfrac k {\sqrt {1 + k^2} } }$ where: $\rho$ is a rational number $k$ is a rational number whose square root is irrational $\lambda$ is a rational number whose square root is irrational. Then $a - b$ is that which produces a medial whole with a medial area.

title: Definition:That which produces Medial Whole with Medial Area/Annex
snippet: Let $a, b \in \R_{>0}$ be (strictly) positive real numbers such that $a > b$. Let $a - b$ be a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole. The real number $b$ is called the annex of the straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole. Category:Definitions/Euclidean Number Theory

title: Definition:That which produces Medial Whole with Medial Area/Terms
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be two positive real numbers. Let $a - b$ be a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole. The terms of $a - b$ are the elements $a$ and $b$.

title: Definition:That which produces Medial Whole with Medial Area/Whole
snippet: Let $a, b \in \R_{>0}$ be (strictly) positive real numbers such that $a > b$. Let $a - b$ be a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole. The real number $a$ is called the whole of the straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole. Category:Definitions/Euclidean Number Theory

title: Definition:That which produces Medial Whole with Rational Area
snippet: Let $a, b \in \R_{>0}$ be in the forms: $a = \dfrac \rho {\sqrt {2 \left({1 + k^2}\right)} } \sqrt{\sqrt {1 + k^2} + k}$ $b = \dfrac \rho {\sqrt {2 \left({1 + k^2}\right)} } \sqrt{\sqrt {1 + k^2} - k}$ where: $\rho$ is a rational number $k$ is a rational number whose square root is irrational $\lambda$ is a rational number whose square root is irrational. Then $a - b$ is that which produces a medial whole with a rational area.

title: Definition:That which produces Medial Whole with Rational Area/Annex
snippet: Let $a, b \in \R_{>0}$ be (strictly) positive real numbers such that $a > b$. Let $a - b$ be a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole. The real number $b$ is called the annex of the straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole. Category:Definitions/Euclidean Number Theory

title: Definition:That which produces Medial Whole with Rational Area/Terms
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be two positive real numbers. Let $a - b$ be a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole. The terms of $a - b$ are the elements $a$ and $b$.

title: Definition:That which produces Medial Whole with Rational Area/Whole
snippet: Let $a, b \in \R_{>0}$ be (strictly) positive real numbers such that $a > b$. Let $a - b$ be a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole. The real number $a$ is called the whole of the straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole. Category:Definitions/Euclidean Number Theory

title: Definition:The Algebra of Sets
snippet: Let $E$ be a universal set. The power set $\powerset E$, together with: the binary operations union $\cup$ and intersection $\cap$ the unary operation complement $\complement$ is referred to as the algebra of sets on $E$.

title: Definition:The Algebra of Sets/Also defined as
snippet: == The Algebra of Sets: Also defined as == Note that an algebra of sets is a more specific concept that is applied to a subset of $\powerset E$ that is closed under union, intersection and complement, and also has a unit. So while the algebra of sets is an algebra of sets, the reverse is not necessarily true. Category:Definitions/The Algebra of Sets

title: Definition:The Algebra of Sets/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on The Algebra of Sets == The concept of an algebra of sets was invented by , after whom Boolean algebra was named.

title: Definition:Theorem
snippet: In all contexts, the definition of the term theorem is by and large the same. That is, a theorem is a statement which has been proved to be true.

title: Definition:Theorem/Also defined as
snippet: == Theorems: Also defined as == Some sources make more of the term theorem than is perhaps merited. For example, has: Theorems are true implications which are usually of special interest. No distinction is made on between theorems that are or are not of "special interest".

title: Definition:Theorem/Formal System
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a formal language. Let $\mathscr P$ be a proof system for $\LL$. A theorem of $\mathscr P$ is a well-formed formula of $\LL$ which can be deduced from the axioms and axiom schemata of $\mathscr P$ by means of its rules of inference. That a WFF $\phi$ is a theorem of $\mathscr P$ may be denoted as: $\vdash_{\mathscr P} \phi$

title: Definition:Theorem/Logic
snippet: A theorem in logic is a statement which can be shown to be the conclusion of a logical argument which depends on no premises except logical axioms. A sequent which denotes a theorem $\phi$ is written $\vdash \phi$, indicating that there are no premises. In this context, $\vdash$ is read as: It is a theorem that ...

title: Definition:Theorem/Mathematics
snippet: The term theorem is used throughout the whole of mathematics to mean a statement which has been proved to be true from whichever axioms relevant to that particular branch. Note that statements which are taken as axioms in one branch of mathematics may be theorems in others.

title: Definition:Theorem (Formal Systems)/Also known as
snippet: == Theorem: Also known as == A theorem $\phi$ of a proof system $\mathscr P$ is also called provable from $\mathscr P$. Category:Definitions/Theorems

title: Definition:Theoretical Physics
snippet: Theoretical physics is the branch of physics concerned with aspects of the natural universe beyond our ability to test them directly.

title: Definition:Theory
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a logical language. Let $\mathscr M$ be a formal semantics for $\LL$. Let $\FF$ be a set of $\LL$-formulas. Then $\FF$ is an $\LL$-theory , for every $\phi \in \LL$: $\FF \models_{\mathscr M} \phi \implies \phi \in \FF$ where $\models_{\mathscr M}$ denotes $\mathscr M$-semantic consequence.

title: Definition:Theory/Set of Formulas
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a logical language. Let $\mathscr M$ be a formal semantics for $\LL$. Let $\FF$ be a set of $\LL$-formulas. Then the $\LL$-theory of $\FF$, denoted $\map T {\FF}$ is the set: $\set {\phi \in \LL: \FF \models_{\mathscr M} \phi}$ where $\models_{\mathscr M}$ denotes $\mathscr M$-semantic consequence.

title: Definition:Theory of Algorithms
snippet: The field of the theory of algorithms is a subfield of computer science which is primarily concerned with determining the existence or non-existence of effective algorithms for the solution of certain computational problems.

title: Definition:Theory of Equations
snippet: The theory of equations is the study of polynomials and their roots.

title: Definition:Theory of Structure
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a logical language. Let $\MM$ be an $\LL$-structure. The $\LL$-theory of $\MM$ is the $\LL$-theory consisting of those $\LL$-sentences $\phi$ such that: $\MM \models \phi$ where $\models$ denotes that $\MM$ is a model for $\phi$. This theory can be denoted $\map {\operatorname{Th} } \MM$ when the language $\LL$ is understood.

title: Definition:Theory of Types
snippet: The theory of types is a system of axiomatic set theory which is originated by appending a further axiom to the stating: A set cannot be an element of itself.

title: Definition:Theory of Types/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Theory of Types == The theory of types was devised by in $1910$ as an attempt to resolve what is now referred to as Russell's Paradox.

title: Definition:Therefore
snippet: If statement $p$ logically implies statement $q$, then we may say: $p$, therefore $q$ and denote it: $p \vdash q$ Hence the symbology: $p, q \vdash r$ means: Given as premises $p$ and $q$, we may validly conclude $r$ So the symbol $\vdash$ is interpreted to mean therefore. Thus, $p, q \vdash r$ reads as: $p$ and $q$, therefore $r$. A fallacy may be indicated by $p, q \not \vdash r$, which can be interpreted as: Given as premises $p$ and $q$, we may not validly conclude $r$.

title: Definition:Therefore/Also known as
snippet: == Therefore: Also known as == The symbol $\vdash$ for therefore is sometimes called the turnstile symbol (or gatepost, or gate post), and is often (misleadingly) called the assertion sign. This is sometimes hyphenated: assertion-sign. Some older literature uses the symbol $\therefore$ but this is falling out of use. In contrast to the $\vdash$ symbol, which is a formal symbol used in proof writing, the $\therefore$ symbol is generally used as shorthand for therefore, and as such is traditionally classified as a punctuation mark.

title: Definition:Thermal Conductivity
snippet: The thermal conductivity of a substance is a measure of its ability to conduct heat.

title: Definition:Thermal Conductivity/Dimension
snippet: The dimension of measurement of thermal conductivity is $\mathsf {M L T^{-3} \Theta^{-1} }$. Category:Definitions/Dimensions of Measurement Category:Definitions/Thermal Conductivity

title: Definition:Thermal Conductivity/Symbol
snippet: There are a number of symbols used to represent thermal conductivity: $k$ $\lambda$ $\kappa$

title: Definition:Thermal Conductivity/Unit
snippet: The SI unit of measurement of thermal conductivity is the watt per metre-kelvin. The FPS unit of measurement of thermal conductivity is the British thermal unit per hour-foot-fahrenheit.

title: Definition:Thermodynamic Calorie/Also known as
snippet: == Thermodynamic Calorie: Also known as == The thermodynamic calorie is also known as the thermochemical calorie. Category:Definitions/Calorie

title: Definition:Thermodynamic Calorie/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Thermodynamic Calorie: Conversion Factors == {{eqn | o = \approx | r = 1 \cdotp 162 \times 10^{-6} | c = kilowatt-hours }} {{eqn | o = \approx | r = 2 \cdotp 611 \times 10^{19} | c = electron volts }}

title: Definition:Thermodynamic Calorie/Symbol
snippet: == Thermodynamic Calorie: Symbols == The symbols used to denote the thermodynamic calorie are $\mathrm {cal_c}$ or $\mathrm {cal_{th} }$. Category:Definitions/Calorie

title: Definition:Thermodynamics
snippet: Thermodynamics is the branch of physics which studies the behaviour of heat.

title: Definition:Theta-Sequence
snippet: Let $\UU$ be an open cover of a topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$. A $\theta$-sequence (that is, theta-sequence) for $\UU$ is a sequence $\sequence {\VV_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ of open covers of $T$ such that:

title: Definition:Theta Function
snippet: The theta functions are a class of special functions of a complex variable that are more general than the trigonometric functions or elliptic functions.

title: Definition:Theta Notation/Also defined as
snippet: == $\Theta$ Notation: Also defined as == Sources which utilise order notation so as to explore the behaviour of algorithms are concerned only with algorithm run times, necessarily positive. Hence they may define the $\Theta$ notation on positive real sequences only, as follows: Let $g: \N \to \R$ be a real sequence, expressed here as a real-valued function on the set of natural numbers $\N$.

title: Definition:Theta Notation/Also known as
snippet: == $\Theta$ Notation: Also known as == Some sources refer to $\Theta$ notation as big-$\Theta$ notation, in parallel with big-$\OO$ and big-$\Omega$. However, it is worth bearing in mind that: There is no Little-Theta Notation and so there is no need to distinguish between big-$\Theta$ and little-$\theta$. Hence consistently use the term $\Theta$ notation, voicing it as theta notation. Category:Definitions/Theta Notation

title: Definition:Theta Notation/Also presented as
snippet: == $\Theta$ Notation: Also presented as == The definition of $\Theta$ notation can also be presented as: $\map f n \in \map \Theta {\map g n}$ $\paren {\map f n \in \map \OO {\map g n} } \text { and } \paren {\map f n \in \map \Omega {\map g n} }$ Category:Definitions/Theta Notation

title: Definition:Theta Notation/Definition 1
snippet: Let $g: \N \to \R$ be a real sequence, expressed here as a real-valued function on the set of natural numbers $\N$. Then $\map \Theta g$ is defined as: $\map \Theta g = \map \OO g \cap \map \Omega g$ where: $\map \OO g$ is big-$\OO$ notation $\map \Omega g$ is big-$\Omega$ notation. That is: $\map \Theta g = \set {f: \N \to \R: \exists c_1, c_2 \in \R_{>0}: \exists n_0 \in \N: \forall n > n_0: 0 \le c_1 \cdot \size {\map g n} \le \size {\map f n} \le c_2 \cdot \size {\map g n} }$

title: Definition:Theta Notation/Definition 2
snippet: Let $f: \N \to \R, g: \N \to \R$ be two real sequences, expressed here as real-valued functions on the set of natural numbers $\N$. Let there exist $c \in \R_{>0}$ such that: $\ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \frac {\map f n} {\map g n} = c$ Then: $\map f n \in \map \Theta {\map g n}$

title: Definition:Theta Notation/Informal Definition
snippet: Let $f: \N \to \R$ and $g: \N \to \R$ be real sequences, expressed as real-valued functions on the set of natural numbers $\N$. $f$ is $\Theta$ of $g$ there exist positive constants $c_1$ and $c_2$ such that $\map f n$ can be "sandwiched" between $c_1 \map g n$ and $c_2 \map g n$ for sufficiently large $n \ge n_0$. It is not as important to determine the values of $c_1$, $c_2$ as it is to establish that such constants exist.

title: Definition:Theta Notation/Motivation
snippet: == Motivation for $\Theta$ Notation == $\Theta$ notation is a type of order notation for typically comparing run-times or growth rates between two growth functions. $\Theta$ is a stronger statement than big-$\OO$ and big-$\Omega$. Category:Definitions/Theta Notation

title: Definition:Theta Notation/Notation
snippet: == Notation for $\Theta$ Notation == The expression $\map f n \in \map \Theta {\map g n}$ is read as: $\map f n$ is theta of $\map g n$ While it is correct and accurate to write: $\map f n \in \map \Theta {\map g n}$ it is a common abuse of notation to write: $\map f n = \map \Theta {\map g n}$ This notation offers some advantages.

title: Definition:Think of a Number
snippet: A think of a number puzzle is usually in the form of a game between two players. Player A asks player B to: Think of a number perhaps with constraints. Let this number be referred to as $n$. Player A asks player B to perform certain arithmetical manipulations on $n$. As a result, player B is left with another number, which we will refer to as $m$. The game now goes one of $2$ ways: $(1): \quad$ Player A announces: The number you have been left with is $m$. $(2): \quad$ Player A asks what $m$ is, and on learning what it is, instantaneously replies: The number you first thought of was $n$.

title: Definition:Think of a Number/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Think of a Number == The think of a number puzzle goes way back in time. discusses it in his posthumous ($1932$) collection as follows, presented on as a historical note: He explains that: He tells you to think of any whole number between $1$ and $100$, and then divide it successively by $3$, $5$ and $7$, telling him the remainder in each case. On receiving this information he promptly discloses the number you thought of. Note, however, that since wrote the above, the from was found to contain a number of examples of this puzzle.

title: Definition:Third Figure of Categorical Syllogism/Also known as
snippet: == Third Figure of Categorical Syllogism: Also known as == The third figure of a categorical syllogism is classically known as the figure of examples, from the fact that in order to be valid, its conclusion needs to be particular. Category:Definitions/Third Figure of Categorical Syllogism

title: Definition:Third Kind
snippet: The term third kind is used to distinguish three or more classes of mathematical object of some common overall type.

title: Definition:Third Kind/Also known as
snippet: == Third Kind: Also known as == Some such objects are referred to as being of the third type rather than the third kind, but the meaning remains the same. Category:Definitions/Third Kind

title: Definition:Third Quartile/Also known as
snippet: == Third Quartile: Also known as == The third quartile is often referred to as the upper quartile.

title: Definition:Thomae Function
snippet: Thomae Function on $\openint 0 1$ The Thomae function $D_M: \R \to \R$ is the real function defined as: $\forall x \in \R: \map {D_M} x = \begin {cases} 0 & : x = 0 \text { or } x \notin \Q \\ \dfrac 1 q & : x = \dfrac p q : p \perp q, q > 0 \end {cases}$ where: $\Q$ denotes the set of rational numbers $p \perp q$ denotes that $p$ and $q$ are coprime (that is, $x$ is a rational number expressed in canonical form)

title: Definition:Thomas's Corkscrew
snippet: Let copies of Thomas's plank be used to construct a corkscrew in the same manner as the Tychonoff plank is used to construct the Tychonoff corkscrew. Thomas's corkscrew is the topological space that results.

title: Definition:Thomas's Plank/Definition 1
snippet: Let $L_n$ be lines embedded in the Cartesian plane $\R^2$ defined as: $\forall n \in \N: L_n = \begin {cases} \set {\tuple {x, 0}: x \in \openint 0 1} & : n = 0 \\ \set {\tuple {x, \dfrac 1 n}: x \in \hointr 0 1} & : n > 0 \end {cases}$ Let $S = \ds \bigcup {n \mathop \in \N}$. Let a topology $\tau$ be applied to $S$, defined as follows: For $n \ge 1$, each point of $L_n$ except for $\tuple {0, \dfrac 1 n}$ is open. neighborhood bases of $\tuple {0, \dfrac 1 n}$ are subsets of $L_n$ with finite complements.

title: Definition:Thomas's Plank/Definition 2
snippet: Let $L := \openint 0 1$ denote the open unit interval. Let $S_1 := L \cup \set p$ denote the Alexandroff extension of $L$. Let $S_2 := \Z_{>0} \cup \set q$ denote the Alexandroff extension of the (strictly) positive integers $\Z_{>0}$. Let $\struct {S, \tau} := \paren {S_1 \times S_2} \setminus \set {\tuple {p, q} }$ be the subspace of the product space $S_1 \times S_2$ with $\set {\tuple {p, q} }$ removed. Thomas's plank is the topological space $\struct {S, \tau}$.

title: Definition:Thomsen Graph
snippet: The Thomsen graph is the complete bipartite graph $K_{3, 3}$: 200px

title: Definition:Thomsen Graph/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Thomsen Graph == When was trying to determine the structure of , he considered the complete bipartite graph $K_{3, 3}$ as one of the possible options. He was incorrect in this assumption, and he never did manage to work out 's structure, but his name became associated with the graph structure. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Thousand
snippet: A thousand is $1000$: $10$ to the power of $3$: $1000 = 10^3 = 10 \times 10 \times 10$

title: Definition:Thousandth
snippet: Thousandth is the English word for $\dfrac 1 {1000}$.

title: Definition:Three-Body Problem
snippet: The three-body problem arises from this question: Given Newton's Laws of Motion and Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation, is it possible accurately to calculate the future positions and velocities of $n$ bodies in space? When $n = 2$, the problem was solved by . However, when $n = 3$, as for example Sun, Moon and Earth, the problem has still not been solved.

title: Definition:Three-Body Problem/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on the Three-Body Problem == The three-body problem was tackled unsuccessfully over and over again by , and throughout the $18$th century. More recently, had a go at it. A number of limited solutions have been worked out, but currently reliance needs to be made on approximation techniques.

title: Definition:Three-Dimensional Figure/Also known as
snippet: == Three-Dimensional Figure: Also known as == A common term for a three-dimensional figure is solid figure. However, this is misleading, as it is usual to be studying the surfaces of such figures, which themselves are not solid as such. Some sources use term solid to mean a solid figure, but tries to limit that term for that particular physical state of matter.

title: Definition:Three-Point Gauss-Chebyshev Rule
snippet: The three-point Gauss-Chebyshev rule is a Gaussian integration rule of the form: $\ds \int_{-1}^1 \dfrac {\map f x} {\sqrt {1 - x^2} } \rd x \approx \dfrac 1 3 \pi \paren {\map f {-\dfrac {\sqrt 3} 2} + \map f 0 + \map f {\dfrac {\sqrt 3} 2} }$

title: Definition:Three-Valued Logic
snippet: Three-valued logic is a class of systems of logic which a proposition three possible truth values, not only the true and false of conventional $2$-valued Aristotelian logic

title: Definition:Three-Valued Logic/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Three-Valued Logic ==

title: Definition:Three-Valued Logic/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Three-Valued Logic == The concept of three-valued logic was proposed by in $1920$.

title: Definition:Three-Valued Logic/Łukasiewicz System
snippet: == Example of Three-Valued Logic == The Łukasiewicz system of three-valued logic accommodates future contingents. Thus, for example, the proposition: It will rain tomorrow is neither true $\T$ nor false $\F$, but instead it is undetermined: $\U$. Hence the Law of Excluded Middle: $p \lor \neg p$ is no longer a tautology, as it may take the truth value $\U$.

title: Definition:Three (Category)
snippet: The category $\mathbf 3$, three, is the category: $\begin{xy} +{\circledast} = "x", +{\star} = "y", +{\bullet} = "z", "x";"y" **@{-} ?>*@{>}, "y";"z" **@{-} ?>*@{>}, "x";"z" **@{-} ?>*@{>} \end{xy}$ with: Three objects, $\circledast$, $\star$ and $\bullet$; and Six morphisms: The three identity morphisms $\operatorname{id}_\circledast$, $\operatorname{id}_\star$, $\operatorname{id}_\bullet$; One non-identity morphism $\circledast \to \star$; One non-identity morphism $\star \to \bullet$; One non-identity morphism $\circledast \to \bullet$.

title: Definition:Thrust
snippet: The thrust of a rocket is defined as the product of the exhaust velocity and the rate at which its fuel is being consumed: $\mathbf t = \mathbf b \paren {\dfrac {\d m} {\d t} }$ where: $\mathbf b$ is the exhaust velocity $m$ is the mass of the rocket as a function of time $t$.

title: Definition:Tidy Factorization
snippet: Let $\struct {D, +, \circ}$ be an integral domain whose unity is $1_D$. Let $\struct {U_D, \circ}$ be the group of units of $\struct {D, +, \circ}$. Any factorization of $x \in D$ can always be tidied into the form: $x = u \circ y_1 \circ y_2 \circ \cdots \circ y_n$ where $u \in \struct {U_D, \circ}$, and may be $1_D$, and $y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n$ are all non-zero and non-units. This is done by forming the ring product of all units of a factorization into one unit, and rearranging all the remaining factors as necessary. Such a factorization is called tidy.

title: Definition:Tied Ranks
snippet: Let $S$ be a set on whose elements a ranking $\RR$ has been applied. Let $2$ or more elements of $S$ be assessed as having the same rank under $\RR$. Then those elements are said to have tied ranks.

title: Definition:Tile
snippet: A tile is a plane geometric figure which forms part of a tessellation. Category:Definitions/Tessellations

title: Definition:Time
snippet: A true definition of what time actually is has baffled philosophers from the dawn of, er, time. Therefore it will be left as an exercise for the reader. It is usually treated as a scalar quantity.

title: Definition:Time-Constructible Function/Definition 1
snippet: Let $f$ be a function. Let there exist a positive integer $n_0$ and a Turing machine $M$ such that: Given a string $1^n$ consisting of $n$ instances of $1$, $M$ stops after exactly $f \left({n}\right)$ steps for all $n \ge n_0$. Then $f$ is time-constructible.

title: Definition:Time-Constructible Function/Definition 2
snippet: Let $f$ be a function. Let there exist a positive integer $n_0$ and a Turing machine $M$ such that: Given a string $1^n$ consisting of $n$ instances of $1$, $M$ outputs the binary representation of $\map f n$ in $\map \OO {\map f n}$ time. Then $f$ is time-constructible.

title: Definition:Time/Dimension
snippet: Time is one of the fundamental dimensions of physics. In dimensional analysis it is assigned the symbol $T$ or $\mathbf T$. It is a scalar quantity which can be mapped directly to the real number line. Category:Definitions/Dimensions of Measurement Category:Definitions/Time

title: Definition:Time/Fourth Dimension
snippet: In the Theory of Relativity, it is convenient to consider time as another dimension in addition to, and treated similarly to, the $3$ dimensions of ordinary space.

title: Definition:Time/Fourth Dimension/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Time as $4$th Dimension == The treatment of time as the $4$th dimension originates with . While introduced as a mathematical convenience, the concept took hold in popular culture as a pseudo-scientific backing for an entire subgenre of science fiction: the time-travel story.

title: Definition:Time/Length
snippet: A quantity of time is usually referred to in natural language in the same terms as linear measure. Thus it is usual to refer to a length of time of an elapsed quantity of time.

title: Definition:Time/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Time == The adjective meaning pertaining to or concerning time is temporal. Note that in the religious context, temporal is often seen to mean of the here-and-now, as opposed to in the spiritual realm. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Time/Symbol
snippet: The usual symbol used to denote time is $t$.

title: Definition:Time/Unit
snippet: The units of measurement of time are universal in all systems of measurement.

title: Definition:Time/Unit/Century
snippet: The century is a derived unit of time. $1$ century $=100$ years. Category:Definitions/Time

title: Definition:Time/Unit/Day
snippet: The day is a derived unit of time, based on the period of rotation of Earth about its axis. In common parlance, this equates to the mean solar day.

title: Definition:Time/Unit/Decade
snippet: The decade is a derived unit of time. $1$ decade $=10$ years. Category:Definitions/Time

title: Definition:Time/Unit/Fortnight
snippet: The fortnight is a derived unit of time. $1$ fortnight $=2$ weeks $=14$ days.

title: Definition:Time/Unit/Fortnight/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Fortnight == The word fortnight derives from its definition as fourteen nights. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Time/Unit/Great Year of Plato
snippet: The great year of Plato is a derived unit of time.

title: Definition:Time/Unit/Great Year of Plato/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Great Year of Plato == The great year of Plato was never actually mentioned by himself. The concept was raised in the context of the precession of the equinoxes, supposed to have been discovered by . It was who (mistakenly or dishonestly) who determined that the time period was $12 \, 960 \, 000$ days, or $36 \, 000$ years of $360$ days. The actual period is approximately $25 \, 800$ years, referred to as a Platonic year.

title: Definition:Time/Unit/Hour
snippet: The hour is a derived unit of time.

title: Definition:Time/Unit/Lunar Month
snippet: The lunar month is defined as the length of time between $2$ new moons. $1$ lunar month $\approx 29 \cdotp 530588$ days or: $1$ lunar month $\approx 29$ days, $12$ hours, $44$ minutes and $2 \cdotp 8$ seconds.

title: Definition:Time/Unit/Millennium
snippet: The millennium is a derived unit of time. $1$ millennium $=1000$ years. Category:Definitions/Time

title: Definition:Time/Unit/Minute
snippet: The minute is a derived unit of time.

title: Definition:Time/Unit/Minute/Symbol
snippet: The symbol for the minute is $\mathrm {min}$. Category:Definitions/Time

title: Definition:Time/Unit/Month
snippet: The month is a derived unit of time. The month is measured only approximately in duration, and is not used as a scientific measure. $1$ month is between $28$ and $31$ days, depending on which month it is.

title: Definition:Time/Unit/Month/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Month == The word month derives from the word moon, from its definition as the approximate duration of one full cycle of phases from new moon to new moon. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Time/Unit/Quarter-Year
snippet: The quarter-year is a derived unit of time. The quarter-year is defined as: $91$ days or $13$ weeks of $7$ days each. Note that a quarter-year is not actually equal to $\dfrac 1 4$ of a year: $\dfrac {365.2422} 4$ days is $\approx 91.31$ days.

title: Definition:Time/Unit/Season
snippet: The season is a derived unit of time. The season is measured only approximately in duration, and is not used as a scientific measure. $1$ season $= 3$ months, although exactly which months fall into which season depends on the locale and the culture. Category:Definitions/Time

title: Definition:Time/Unit/Second
snippet: The second is the SI base unit of time, and also therefore of the MKS system. It is also the base unit of time for the FPS and CGS systems. The second is defined as: the duration of $9 \ 192 \ 631 \ 770$ periods of the radiation corresponding to the transition between the two hyperfine levels of the ground state of the caesium $133$ atom at rest at $0 \ \mathrm K$.

title: Definition:Time/Unit/Week
snippet: The week is a derived unit of time. $1$ week $=7$ days.

title: Definition:Time/Unit/Week/Symbol
snippet: The symbol for the week is $\mathrm {week}$ or $\mathrm {wk}$. Category:Definitions/Time

title: Definition:Time/Unit/Year
snippet: The year is a derived unit of time. It is based on the orbital period of Earth round the sun.

title: Definition:Time/Unit Time
snippet: The usual units of time are seconds, and compound units consisting of multiples of seconds. However, when discussing a general physical process it is convenient to discuss the general situation, in which case the term unit time is used. Thus the specific units are not mentioned. Category:Definitions/Time

title: Definition:Time Dilation
snippet: Time dilation is one of the effects predicted by the special theory of relativity as follows: When two observers move at constant relative velocity, each will observes that the other's clock will operate more slowly. That is, time is different for two observers moving relative to each other. Hence, if a clock ticks at $n$ times per second, an observer moving at speed $v$, that clock will appear to tick $\dfrac n {\sqrt {1 - \dfrac {v^2} {c^2} } }$ times per second.

title: Definition:Time Period
snippet: The time period of a periodic process is the period of the periodic function which models that process. Category:Definitions/Physics Category:Definitions/Applied Mathematics Category:Definitions/Time

title: Definition:Time Series
snippet: A time series is a sequence of observations of a physical process taken at a sequence of instants of time.

title: Definition:Time Series/Actual Value
snippet: An actual value of a time series $T$ is the result of a measurement of an observation at some time $t$. The term is usually made in reference to a forecast value made after its lead time has elapsed, and its timestamp is now the current time.

title: Definition:Time Series/Adjacent Observations
snippet: Two observations of a time series are adjacent the index of one of them is the immediate predecessor of the other (and the other is the immediate successor of the one).

title: Definition:Time Series/Continuous
snippet: A continuous time series is one in which the set of timestamps of the observations forms a continuous function.

title: Definition:Time Series/Current Value
snippet: The current value of a time series $T$ is an observation $x$ of $T$ whose timestamp is the current time. That is, it is the most recent observation.

title: Definition:Time Series/Dependence of Adjacent Observations
snippet: A defining characteristic of a time series is that every pair of adjacent observations is dependent.

title: Definition:Time Series/Discrete
snippet: A discrete time series is such that the timestamps of the observations occur at well-defined instants, separated one from another by a time interval.

title: Definition:Time Series/Equispaced
snippet: A time series is equispaced the time intervals between the timestamps is equal for all pairs of adjacent observations.

title: Definition:Time Series/Forecast Value
snippet: A forecast value of a time series $T$ is an estimate of a future value at some lead time $t + l$.

title: Definition:Time Series/Future Value
snippet: A future value of a time series $T$ is an observation $x$ of $T$ whose timestamp is for some future instant.

title: Definition:Time Series/Origin
snippet: The origin of a time series is an arbitrary timestamp of an observation which is chosen in order that all other timestamps can be measured from that origin. This timestamp is often denoted $\tau_0$.

title: Definition:Time Series/Past Value
snippet: A past value of a time series $T$ is an observation $x$ of $T$ whose timestamp is for some past instant, previous to the current value.

title: Definition:Time Series/Timestamp
snippet: A timestamp of an observation $x$ of a time series is the instant with which $x$ is associated.

title: Definition:Time Series Analysis
snippet: Time series analysis is the discipline of analyzing time series data in order to extract meaningful statistics and other characteristics of the data. Its main activity is concerned with techniques for determining the nature of the dependence of adjacent observations of such time series.

title: Definition:Time Series Analysis/Also known as
snippet: == Time Series Analysis: Also known as == Some sources refer to time series analysis as time-series analysis. Category:Definitions/Time Series Analysis

title: Definition:Time of Day
snippet: The time of day is a measurement of the length of time passed since the start of the day. Category:Definitions/Day Category:Definitions/Time

title: Definition:Tit-For-Tat Strategy
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be two players in a two-person game $G$. Let $G$ be such that it be repeated an arbitrary number of times. A tit-for-tat strategy is a strategy adopted by player $B$, for example, in which $B$ copies the previous play of player $A$.

title: Definition:Tit-For-Tat Strategy/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Tit-For-Tat Strategy == The expression tit-for-tat is a linguistic evolution from the phrase this for that. That is: If you do that, then I will do this in response. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Titanic Prime
snippet: A titanic prime is a prime number with $1000$ digits or more.

title: Definition:Toeplitz Matrix
snippet: A Toeplitz matrix is a square matrix whose diagonals parallel to and including the main diagonal are constant.

title: Definition:Tool
snippet: A tool is a physical device used as an aid to a process. Category:Definitions/Tools Category:Definitions/Proof Techniques Category:Definitions/Language Definitions

title: Definition:Top
snippet: Definition:Top (Logic) Definition:Top of Lattice Definition:Numerator: the top of a fraction $\dfrac a b$ or a rational function $\dfrac {\map P x} {\map Q x}$, and so on.

title: Definition:Top (Logic)
snippet: Top is a constant of propositional logic interpreted to mean the canonical, undoubted tautology whose truth nobody could possibly ever question. The symbol used is $\top$.

title: Definition:Top (Logic)/Boolean Interpretation
snippet: Let $\top$ denote the top constant in the language of propositional logic. There is only one boolean interpretation for $\top$: $\map v \top = \T$ where $\T$ symbolises true.

title: Definition:Top (Logic)/Truth Table
snippet: The characteristic truth table of the top constant $\top$ of propositional logic is as follows: $\begin{array}{|c|} \hline \top \\ \hline \T \\ \hline \end{array}$

title: Definition:Top of Lattice
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \preceq}$ be a lattice.

title: Definition:Top of Lattice/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \preceq}$ be a lattice. Let $S$ admit a greatest element $\top$. Then $\top$ is called the top of $S$.

title: Definition:Top of Lattice/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \preceq}$ be a lattice. Let $\wedge$ have an identity element $\top$. Then $\top$ is called the top of $S$.

title: Definition:Topological Closed Embedding
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be topological spaces. Let $f : X \to Y$ be a mapping. Then $f$ is a (topological) closed embedding : $f$ is a topological embedding its image $f(X)$ is closed in $Y$

title: Definition:Topological Compactness
snippet: The concept of (topological) compactness is a generalization of finiteness in the context of topology. Compactness limits the number of open sets in a topology by specifying conditions that need to be satisfied by its open covers.

title: Definition:Topological Complement of Closed Vector Subspace of Banach Space
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $Y_1$ be a closed vector subspace of $X$. We say that $Y_2$ is the topological complement of $Y_1$ there exists a closed vector subspace $Y_2 \subseteq X$ such that: $X = Y_1 \oplus Y_2$ where $\oplus$ denotes the internal direct sum.

title: Definition:Topological Connectedness
snippet: Connectedness, in the context of topology, denies the existence of certain subsets of a topological space with the property that: $U \cap V^- = \O$ and: $U^- \cap V = \O$ where $U^-$ and $V^-$ denote the closure of $U$ and $V$ respectively. This can be found in various contexts, as follows:

title: Definition:Topological Covering Mapping
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ and $C = \struct {X, \phi}$ be topological spaces. Let $\pi: C \to T$ be a continuous surjection. $\pi$ is a (topological) covering mapping for $T$ (by $C$) every $s \in S$ has an open neighborhood which is evenly covered by $\pi$.

title: Definition:Topological Covering Mapping/Also known as
snippet: == Topological Covering Mapping: Also known as == A topological covering mapping is also known as a topological covering map. When the context is clear, the terms covering mapping and covering map are usually used, but it is to be noted that these terms have further usages.

title: Definition:Topological Covering Mapping/Covering Space
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ and $C = \struct {X, \phi}$ be topological spaces. Let $\pi: C \to T$ be a (topological) covering mapping for $T$ by $C$. Then $C$ is called a covering space for $T$.

title: Definition:Topological Division Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a division ring with zero $0_R$. Let $\tau$ be a topology on $R$. Let the mapping $\phi: R \setminus \set {0_R} \to R$ be defined as: $\map \phi x = x^{-1}$ for each $x \in R \setminus \set {0_R}$ Then $\struct {R, +, \circ, \tau}$ is a topological division ring : $(1): \quad \struct {R, +, \circ, \tau}$ is a topological ring $(2): \quad \phi$ is a $\tau'$-$\tau$-continuous mapping, where $\tau'$ is the $\tau$-relative subspace topology on $R \setminus \set {0_R}$.

title: Definition:Topological Dual Space
snippet: Let $K$ be a topological field. Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological vector space over $K$. Let $\struct {X, \tau}^\ast$ be the vector space of continuous linear functionals on $\struct {X, \tau}$. We say that $\struct {X, \tau}^\ast$ is the topological dual space of $\struct {X, \tau}$.

title: Definition:Topological Dynamical System
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $f: S \to S$ be a continuous mapping. Then $\struct {S, f}$ is called a topological dynamical system.

title: Definition:Topological Field
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +, \circ}$ be a field with zero $0_F$. Let $\tau$ be a topology on $F$. Let $\struct {F, +, \circ, \tau}$ be a topological division ring. Then $\struct {F, +, \circ, \tau}$ is a topological field. That is, a topological field is a commutative topological division ring.

title: Definition:Topological Group
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \odot}$ be a group. On its underlying set $G$, let $\struct {G, \tau}$ be a topological space.

title: Definition:Topological Group/Also defined as
snippet: == Topological Group: Also defined as == Some sources insist that a topological group has to be a $T_2$ space. Category:Definitions/Topological Groups

title: Definition:Topological Group/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \odot}$ be a group. On its underlying set $G$, let $\struct {G, \tau}$ be a topological space. $\struct {G, \odot, \tau}$ is a topological group the following conditions are fulfilled: {{axiom | n = 1 | lc= Continuous Group Product | t = $\odot: \struct {G, \tau} \times \struct {G, \tau} \to \struct {G, \tau}$ is a continuous mapping }} {{axiom | n = 2 | lc= Continuous Inversion Mapping | t = $\iota: \struct {G, \tau} \to \struct {G, \tau}$ such that $\forall x \in G: \map \iota x = x^{-1}$ is also a continuous mapping }} where $\struct {G, \tau} \times \struct {G, \tau}$ is…

title: Definition:Topological Group/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \odot}$ be a group. On its underlying set $G$, let $\struct {G, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let the mapping $\psi: \struct {G, \tau} \times \struct {G, \tau} \to \struct {G, \tau}$ be defined as: $\map \psi {x, y} = x \odot y^{-1}$ $\struct {G, \odot, \tau}$ is a topological group : $\psi$ is a continuous mapping where $\struct {G, \tau} \times \struct {G, \tau}$ is considered as $G \times G$ with the product topology.

title: Definition:Topological Group Homomorphism
snippet: Let $G$ and $H$ be topological groups. A mapping $\phi:G \to H$ is a homomorphism of topological groups if it is a continuous group homomorphism. Category:Definitions/Topological Groups Category:Definitions/Group Homomorphisms

title: Definition:Topological Isomorphism
snippet: Let $K$ be a topological field. Let $\struct {X, \tau_X}$ and $\struct {Y, \tau_Y}$ be topological vector spaces over $K$. Let $T : X \to Y$ be a linear transformation. We say that $T$ is a topological isomorphism $T$ is a linear isomorphism and a homeomorphism.

title: Definition:Topological Lattice
snippet: A topological lattice is a relational structure with topology $\struct {S, \preceq, \tau}$ where $\struct {S, \preceq}$ is a lattice and $\struct {S, \tau}$ is a topological space.

title: Definition:Topological Manifold
snippet: Let $M$ be a $T_2$ (Hausdorff) second-countable locally Euclidean space of dimension $d$. Then $M$ is a topological manifold of dimension $d$.

title: Definition:Topological Manifold/Also known as
snippet: == Topological Manifold: Also known as == A topological manifold of dimension $d$ is often seen referred to as a $d$-manifold.

title: Definition:Topological Manifold/Complex Manifold
snippet: Let $M$ be a second-countable, complex locally Euclidean space of dimension $d$. Let $\mathscr F$ be a complex analytic differentiable structure on $M$. Then $\struct {M, \mathscr F}$ is called a complex manifold of dimension $d$.

title: Definition:Topological Manifold/Differentiable Manifold
snippet: Let $M$ be a second-countable locally Euclidean space of dimension $d$. Let $\mathscr F$ be a $d$-dimensional differentiable structure on $M$ of class $\CC^k$, where $k \ge 1$. Then $\struct {M, \mathscr F}$ is a differentiable manifold of class $\CC^k$ and dimension $d$.

title: Definition:Topological Manifold/Smooth Manifold
snippet: Let $M$ be a second-countable locally Euclidean space of dimension $d$. Let $\mathscr F$ be a smooth differentiable structure on $M$. Then $\struct {M, \mathscr F}$ is called a smooth manifold of dimension $d$.

title: Definition:Topological Manifold/Smooth Manifold/Definition 2
snippet: == Definition 2 == Let $M$ be a topological manifold. Let $\mathscr A$ be a smooth structure on $M$. Then $\struct {M, \mathscr A}$ is called a smooth manifold of dimension $d$.

title: Definition:Topological Manifold with Boundary
snippet: Let $\R^n$ denote the $n$-dimensional Euclidean space. Let $\H^n$ denote the $n$-dimensional closed upper half-space of $\R^n$. A $d$-dimensional topological manifold with boundary is a second-countable $T_2$ (Hausdorff) space $M$ in which every point has a neighborhood homeomorphic either to: a) an open subset of $\R^n$ or: b) an open subset of $\H^n$.

title: Definition:Topological Manifold with Boundary/Boundary
snippet: Let $M$ be a $n$-dimensional topological manifold with boundary. The boundary of $M$, denoted $\partial M$, is the set of all its boundary points.

title: Definition:Topological Manifold with Boundary/Boundary Point
snippet: Let $M$ be a $n$-dimensional topological manifold with boundary. Let $\partial \H^n$ denote the boundary of the closed upper half-space. A point $p \in M$ is a boundary point of $M$ $p$ is in the domain of some boundary chart of $M$ that send $p$ to $\partial \H^n$.

title: Definition:Topological Manifold with Boundary/Chart
snippet: Let $M$ be a $n$-dimensional topological manifold with boundary. Let $\H^n$ denote the closed upper half-space. A chart of $M$ is an ordered pair $\struct {U, \varphi}$, where: $U$ is an open subset of $M$ $\varphi: U \to D \subseteq \R^n$ is a homeomorphism of $U$ onto an open subset $D$ of $\R^n$ or $\H^n$.

title: Definition:Topological Manifold with Boundary/Chart/Boundary
snippet: Let $M$ be a $n$-dimensional topological manifold with boundary. Let $\struct {U, \varphi}$ be a chart of $M$. Let $\partial \H^n$ denote the boundary of the closed upper half-space. The chart $\struct {U, \varphi}$ is a boundary chart $\map \varphi U$ is an open subset of $\H^n$ such that: $\map \varphi U \cap \partial \H^n \ne \O$

title: Definition:Topological Manifold with Boundary/Chart/Interior
snippet: Let $M$ be a $n$-dimensional topological manifold with boundary. Let $\struct {U, \varphi}$ be a chart of $M$. The chart $\struct {U, \varphi}$ is an interior chart $\map \varphi U$ is an open subset of $\R^n$.

title: Definition:Topological Manifold with Boundary/Coordinate Half-Ball
snippet: Let $M$ be a $n$-dimensional topological manifold with boundary. Let $\partial \H^n$ denote the boundary of the closed upper half-space. Let $\struct {U, \varphi}$ denote a a chart where: $U$ is an open subset of $M$ $\varphi: U \to D \subseteq \R^n$ is a homeomorphism of $U$ onto an open subset $D$ of $\R^n$ or $\H^n$. Let $p \in M$. Let $r \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number. Let $\map {B_r} p$ denote an open ball of radius $r$ centered on $p$.

title: Definition:Topological Manifold with Boundary/Interior
snippet: Let $M$ be a $n$-dimensional topological manifold with boundary. The interior of $M$, denoted $\Int M$, is the set of all its interior points.

title: Definition:Topological Manifold with Boundary/Interior Point
snippet: Let $M$ be a $n$-dimensional topological manifold with boundary. A point $p \in M$ is an interior point of $M$ $p$ is in the domain of some interior chart of $M$.

title: Definition:Topological Open Embedding
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be topological spaces. Let $f : X \to Y$ be a mapping. Then $f$ is a (topological) open embedding : $f$ is a topological embedding its image $f(X)$ is open in $Y$

title: Definition:Topological Order Theory
snippet: Topological order theory is the branch of relation theory and topology which studies orderings and topological spaces.

title: Definition:Topological Property
snippet: Let $P$ be a property whose domain is the set of all topological spaces. Suppose that whenever $\map P T$ holds, then so does $\map P {T'}$, where $T$ and $T'$ are topological spaces which are homeomorphic. Then $P$ is known as a topological property. Loosely, a topological property is one which is preserved under homeomorphism.

title: Definition:Topological Property/Also known as
snippet: == Topological Property: Also known as == A topological property is also known as a topological invariant.

title: Definition:Topological Ring
snippet: Let $\struct{R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $\tau$ be a topology over $R$. Then $\struct {R, +, \circ, \tau}$ is a topological ring : $(1): \quad \struct {R, +, \tau}$ is a topological group $(2): \quad \struct {R, \circ,\tau}$ is a topological semigroup.

title: Definition:Topological Semigroup
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a semigroup. On that same underlying set $S$, let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Then $\struct {S, \circ, \tau}$ is a topological semigroup : $\circ: \struct {S, \tau} \times \struct {S, \tau} \to \struct {S, \tau}$ is a continuous mapping where $\struct {S, \tau} \times \struct {S, \tau}$ is considered as $S \times S$ with the product topology.

title: Definition:Topological Space
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\tau$ be a topology on $S$. That is, let $\tau \subseteq \powerset S$ satisfy the open set axioms: Then the ordered pair $\struct {S, \tau}$ is called a topological space. The elements of $\tau$ are called open sets of $\struct {S, \tau}$. In a topological space $\struct {S, \tau}$, we consider $S$ to be the universal set.

title: Definition:Topological Space/Also denoted as
snippet: == Topological Space: Also denoted as == Some authors denote a topological space using the suboptimal $\set {S, \tau}$, which leaves it conceptually unclear as to which is the set and which the topology. This adds unnecessary complexity to the underlying axiomatic justification for the existence of the very object that is being defined.

title: Definition:Topological Space/Also known as
snippet: == Topological Space: Also known as == The topological space $\struct {S, \tau}$ can be referred to as just a space if the context is clear. $\struct {S, \tau}$ can be referred to as the (topological) space $S$ if it is clear what topology is actually carried on it.

title: Definition:Topological Space Induced by Neighborhood Space
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \NN}$ be a neighborhood space. Let $\tau$ be the set of open sets of $\struct {S, \NN}$. Then $\struct {S, \tau}$ is the topological space induced by $\struct {S, \NN}$.

title: Definition:Topological Space of Real-Valued Continuous Functions on Closed Unit Interval
snippet: Let $C \closedint 0 1$ denote the topological space of real-valued continuous functions on the closed unit interval. This object is referred to on as the topological space of real-valued continuous functions on the closed unit interval.

title: Definition:Topological Subspace
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. Define: $\tau_H := \set {U \cap H: U \in \tau} \subseteq \powerset H$ where $\powerset H$ denotes the power set of $H$. Then the topological space $T_H = \struct {H, \tau_H}$ is called a (topological) subspace of $T$. The set $\tau_H$ is referred to as the subspace topology on $H$ (induced by $\tau$).

title: Definition:Topological Subspace/Also defined as
snippet: == Topological Subspace: Also defined as == takes the philosophical position that a topological space may be allowed to be empty. Some sources do not allow this, and insist that the underlying set of a topological space must be non-empty set. Such sources impose the additional constraint that the underlying set of a topological subspace must likewise be a non-empty set. , however, does allow for a topological subspace to be empty. Category:Definitions/Topological Subspaces

title: Definition:Topological Subspace/Also known as
snippet: == Topological Subspace: Also known as == The subspace topology $\tau_H$ induced by $\tau$ can be referred to as just the induced topology (on $H$) if there is no ambiguity. The term relative topology can also be found. A topological subspace is frequently referred just as a subspace if it has been established what it is a subspace of.

title: Definition:Topological Sum
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \tau_1}$ and $\struct {Y, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. The topological sum $\struct {Z, \tau_3}$ of $X$ and $Y$ is defined as: $Z = X \sqcup Y$ where: $X \sqcup Y$ denotes the disjoint union of $X$ and $Y$ $\tau_3$ is the topology generated by $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$.

title: Definition:Topological Surface
snippet: A surface, in the context of topology, is a smooth topological manifold whose dimension is $2$. More briefly, a surface is a smooth $2$-manifold. Category:Definitions/Topology Category:Definitions/Algebraic Topology

title: Definition:Topological Vector Space
snippet: Let $\struct {K, +_K, \circ_K, \tau_K}$ be a topological field. Let $\struct {X, +_X, \circ_X, \tau_X}$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $\tau_X \times \tau_X$ be the product topology of $\tau_X$ and $\tau_X$. Let $\tau_K \times \tau_X$ be the product topology of $\tau_K$ and $\tau_X$. We say that $\struct {X, \tau_X}$ is called a topological vector space : {{axiom | n = 1 | t = $+_X: \struct {X \times X, \tau_X \times \tau_X} \to \struct {X, \tau_X}$ is continuous }} {{axiom | n = 2 | t = $\circ_X : \struct {K \times X, \tau_K \times \tau_X} \to \struct {X, \tau_X}$ is continuous }}

title: Definition:Topologically Complemented Subspace of Banach Space
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $Y$ be a vector subspace of $X$. We say that $Y$ is topologically complemented in $X$ there exists a bounded projection from $X$ onto $Y$.

title: Definition:Topologically Distinguishable
snippet: topologically distinguishable]] Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $x, y \in S$. Then $x$ and $y$ are topologically distinguishable they do not have exactly the same neighborhoods. That is, either: $\exists U \in \tau: x \in U \subseteq N_x \subseteq S: y \notin N_x$ or: $\exists V \in \tau: y \in V \subseteq N_y \subseteq S: x \notin N_y$ or both. That is, at least one of the elements $x$ and $y$ has a neighborhood that is not a neighborhood of the other.

title: Definition:Topologically Distinguishable/Indistinguishable
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $x, y \in S$. The two points $x$ and $y$ are topologically indistinguishable they are not topologically distinguishable. That is they do not exactly the same neighborhoods: $\forall U \in \tau: x \in U \iff y \in U$

title: Definition:Topologically Equivalent Metrics
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct {A, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct {A, d_2}$ be metric spaces on the same underlying set $A$.

title: Definition:Topologically Equivalent Metrics/Definition 1
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct {A, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct {A, d_2}$ be metric spaces on the same underlying set $A$. $d_1$ and $d_2$ are topologically equivalent : For all metric spaces $\struct {B, d}$ and $\struct {C, d'}$: For all mappings $f: B \to A$ and $g: A \to C$: $(1): \quad f$ is $\tuple {d, d_1}$-continuous $f$ is $\tuple {d, d_2}$-continuous $(2): \quad g$ is $\tuple {d_1, d'}$-continuous $g$ is $\tuple {d_2, d'}$-continuous. Such mappings $f$ and $g$ can be referred to as homeomorphisms.

title: Definition:Topologically Equivalent Metrics/Definition 2
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct {A, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct {A, d_2}$ be metric spaces on the same underlying set $A$. $d_1$ and $d_2$ are topologically equivalent : $U \subseteq A$ is $d_1$-open $U \subseteq A$ is $d_2$-open.

title: Definition:Topologically Nilpotent Ring Element
snippet: Let $A$ be a $T_2$ (Hausdorff) topological ring. Let $a \in A$. $a$ is topologically nilpotent the sequence of powers $a^n$ converges to $0$.

title: Definition:Topologist's Sine Curve
snippet: 420px Let $G = \set {\tuple {x, \sin \dfrac 1 x} : 0 < x \le 1}$, considered as a subset of the real number plane with the usual (Euclidean) topology $\struct {\R^2, \tau_d}$. Then the set $G \cup \set {\tuple {0, 0} }$ is called the topologist's sine curve.

title: Definition:Topology/Also defined as
snippet: == Topology: Also defined as == In their definition of topology, many sources include in the open set axioms the additional stipulation that $\O \in \tau$. As established in Empty Set is Element of Topology, this is redundant, since $(\text O 1)$ and $(\text O 1')$ are read to include the union over the empty set, which is equal to $\O$.

title: Definition:Topology/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. A topology on $S$ is a subset $\tau \subseteq \powerset S$ of the power set of $S$ that satisfies the open set axioms: If $\tau$ is a topology on $S$, then $\struct {S, \tau}$ is called a topological space. The elements of $\tau$ are called the open sets of $\struct {S, \tau}$.

title: Definition:Topology/Definition 2
