title: Definition:Topology/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Topology == The word topology is derived from the Greek words τόπος, meaning place, and λόγος, meaning study. This originates from its origins as the study of situation. The word topology was coined by in a letter of $1836$. The word was first published in the title of 's $1847$ book , but never caught on until the $1920$s.

title: Definition:Topology (Mathematical Branch)
snippet: Topology is a geometry of transformations in which the only invariant is continuity. Some sources suggest that it can indeed be described simply as the study of continuity. As such, it is closely interwoven with the branch of analysis.

title: Definition:Topology (Mathematical Branch)/Also defined as
snippet: == Topology: Also defined as == Some sources define topology as: the study of the properties of shapes and space. However, this is inadequate for , as that could easily be used to define geometry.

title: Definition:Topology (Mathematical Branch)/Also known as
snippet: == Topology: Also known as == The original name of the mathematical branch known as topology was geometria situs, or analysis situs (that is: geometry / analysis of position). It is often referred to as rubber-sheet geometry.

title: Definition:Topology (Mathematical Branch)/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Topology == The mathematical branch known as topology originally arose as a sub-branch of geometry. However, it has since evolved such that it contributes to many other mathematical branches.

title: Definition:Topology Defined by Closed Sets
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $F \subseteq \powerset S$ be a subset of its power set satisfying the closed set axioms: The topology defined by $F$ is the topology whose open sets are the complements of elements of $F$: $\tau = \set {U \subseteq S : S \setminus U \in F}$

title: Definition:Topology Generated by Synthetic Basis
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\BB$ be a synthetic basis of $S$.

title: Definition:Topology Generated by Synthetic Basis/Also known as
snippet: == Topology Generated by Synthetic Basis: Also known as == A topology generated by a synthetic basis is also known as a topology arising from a synthetic basis.

title: Definition:Topology Generated by Synthetic Basis/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\BB$ be a synthetic basis of $S$. The topology on $S$ generated by $\BB$ is defined as: $\tau = \set {\bigcup \AA: \AA \subseteq \BB}$ That is, the set of all unions of sets from $\BB$.

title: Definition:Topology Generated by Synthetic Basis/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\BB$ be a synthetic basis of $S$. The topology on $S$ generated by $\BB$ is defined as: $\tau = \set {U \subseteq S: U = \bigcup \set {B \in \BB: B \subseteq U} }$

title: Definition:Topology Generated by Synthetic Basis/Definition 3
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\BB$ be a synthetic basis of $S$. The topology on $S$ generated by $\BB$ is defined as: $\tau = \set {U \subseteq S: \forall x \in U: \exists B \in \BB: x \in B \subseteq U}$

title: Definition:Topology Generated by Synthetic Sub-Basis
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\SS \subseteq \powerset X$ be a synthetic sub-basis on $S$.

title: Definition:Topology Generated by Synthetic Sub-Basis/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\SS \subseteq \powerset S$ be a synthetic sub-basis on $S$. Define: $\ds \BB = \set {\bigcap \FF: \FF \subseteq \SS, \FF \text{ is finite} } \cup \O \cup S$ That is, $\BB$ is the set of all finite intersections of sets in $\SS$, together with the empty set and $S$ itself. Note that $\FF$ is allowed to be empty in the above definition.

title: Definition:Topology Generated by Synthetic Sub-Basis/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\SS \subseteq \powerset X$ be a synthetic sub-basis on $S$. The topology generated by $\SS$, denoted $\map \tau \SS$, is defined as the unique topology on $S$ that satisfies the following axioms: That is, $\map \tau \SS$ is the coarsest topology on $S$ for which every element of $\SS$ is open.

title: Definition:Topology Induced by Atlas
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $A$ be an atlas on $T$. The topology induced by the atlas is the topology generated by the synthetic sub-basis: $\ds \bigcup_{\tuple {U, \, \phi} \mathop \in A} \set {\map {\phi^{-1} } V : V \text { is open in } U} \subset T$

title: Definition:Topology Induced by Division Ring Norm
snippet:
Let $\struct {R, 
orm {\,\cdot\,} }$ be a normed division ring whose norm is $
orm {\,\cdot\,}$. The topology on $\struct {R, 
orm {\,\cdot\,} }$ induced by $
orm {\,\cdot\,}$ is defined as the topology $	au$ generated by the basis consisting of the set of all open balls of $\struct {R, 
orm {\,\cdot\,} }$. Let $d$ be the metric induced by the norm $
orm {\,\cdot\,}$.

title: Definition:Topology Induced by Metric/Also known as
snippet: == Topology Induced by Metric: Also known as == The topological space which is induced by a metric is also known as the topological space associated with the (given) metric space. When the context is clear, the phrase metric topology for $d$ can be used. The metric space whose metric induces this topology can be said to give rise to the topological space.

title: Definition:Topology Induced by Metric/Definition 1
snippet: The topology on the metric space $M = \struct {A, d}$ induced by (the metric) $d$ is defined as the set $\tau$ of all open sets of $M$.

title: Definition:Topology Induced by Metric/Definition 2
snippet: The topology on the metric space $M = \struct {A, d}$ induced by (the metric) $d$ is defined as the topology $\tau$ generated by the basis consisting of the set of all open $\epsilon$-balls in $M$.

title: Definition:Topology Induced by Pseudometric
snippet: Let $\struct {X, d}$ be a pseudometric space. Let $\tau_d$ be the set of all $X \subseteq S$ which are open in the sense that: $\forall y \in X: \exists \epsilon > 0: \map {B_\epsilon} y \subseteq X$ where $\map {B_\epsilon} y$ is the open $\epsilon$-ball of $y$. We call $\tau_d$ the topology on $X$ induced by $d$.

title: Definition:Topology Induced by Quasiuniformity
snippet: Let $\UU$ be a quasiuniformity on a set $S$. Let $\NN \subseteq \powerset S$ be a subset of the power set of $S$, created from $\UU$ by: $\NN := \set {\map u x: u \in \UU, x \in S}$ where: $\forall x \in S: \map u x = \set {y: \tuple {x, y} \in u}$ That is, where $\map u x$ is the image of $x$ under $u$, where $u$ is considered as a relation on $S$. Let $\NN$ be the neighborhood system for a topology $\tau$ on $S$. Then $\tau$ is the topology induced by $\UU$ on $S$.

title: Definition:Topology Induced by Quasiuniformity/Also known as
snippet: == Topology Induced by Quasiuniformity: Also known as == A topology induced by a quasiuniformity is also known as a topology generated by a quasiuniformity.

title: Definition:Topology on Extended Complex Plane
snippet: Let $\overline \C$ denote the extended complex plane. Let the neighborhood of $\infty$ in $\overline \C$ be defined as the complement in $\overline \C$ of the closed and bounded subsets of $\C$. Then $\overline \C$ is a topological space.

title: Definition:Topology on Extended Real Numbers
snippet: Let $\overline \R$ denote the extended real numbers. The (standard) topology on $\overline \R$ is the order topology $\tau$ associated to the ordering on $\overline \R$.

title: Definition:Topology on Étalé Space of Presheaf
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\FF$ be a presheaf of sets on $T$. Let $\map {\operatorname {\acute Et} } \FF$ be its étalé space. The topology on $\map {\operatorname {\acute Et} } \FF$ is the final topology with respect to the sections associated to elements of $\map \FF U$ with $U \subseteq S$ open.

title: Definition:Toroidal Graph
snippet: A toroidal graph is a graph which can be embedded on the surface of a torus without any of the edges meeting at points other than the vertices.

title: Definition:Torque
snippet: Torque is a measure of strength of a force to effect rotation of a body. Let $\mathbf F$ be a force acting at a point on a body $B$. Let $B$ rotate around a point $O$ as a consequence of the action of $\mathbf F$. Let $\mathbf r$ be the position vector of $P$ $O$, that is: $\mathbf r = \vec {OP}$ The torque about $O$ is defined as the cross product of the vector $\mathbf r$ and $\mathbf F$: $\bstau = \mathbf r \times \mathbf F$ Torque is a vector quantity.

title: Definition:Torque/Also known as
snippet: == Torque: Also known as == Torque is also known as the moment of a force, or just moment.

title: Definition:Torque/Dimension
snippet: The dimension of measurement of torque is $\mathsf {M L}^2 \mathsf T^{-2}$. This derives from its definition as: $\text{Force} \times \text {Displacement}$ Category:Definitions/Dimensions of Measurement Category:Definitions/Torque

title: Definition:Torque/Unit
snippet: The SI unit of measurement of torque is the newton-metre. The CGS unit of measurement of torque is the dyne-centimetre. The FPS unit of measurement of torque is the pound-foot.

title: Definition:Torr
snippet: The torr is an metric unit of pressure. It is defined as being: The amount of pressure equal to exactly $\dfrac 1 {760}$ of a standard atmosphere. that is: $\dfrac {101 \, 325} {760}$ of a pascals.

title: Definition:Torr/Also defined as
snippet: == Torr: Also defined as == The torr can also equivalently be defined as: The amount of pressure equal to exactly $\dfrac {101 \, 325} {760}$ pascals. This can be seen to be equivalent to the definition given, as $1$ standard atmosphere is itself defined as exactly $101 \, 325$ pascals. Older sources may give the definition as $1$ millimetre of mercury, but as the latter is no longer defined in terms of standard atmosphere, and $1$ torr is actually now aproximately equal to $0 \cdotp 99999 \, 98575$ millimetre of mercury.

title: Definition:Torr/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Torr: Conversion Factors ==

title: Definition:Torr/Historical Note
snippet: == Torr: Historical Note== The torr was originally defined to be the same as one millimetre of mercury, but since that time both definitions have been altered slightly. Hence the torr and the millimetre of mercury have diverged ever so slightly so they are now different by about $0 \cdotp 00001 \, 5 \%$.

title: Definition:Torsion
snippet: Differential Geometry: Torsion of Curve Abstract Algebra: Group Theory: Torsion Element of Group Torsion Subgroup Torsion Group Commutative Algebra: Definition:Torsion Element of Module Definition:Torsion Submodule Definition:Torsion Module Algebraic Geometry Torsion Point of Elliptic Curve Torsion Point of Algebraic Group

title: Definition:Torsion-Free Group
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Then $G$ is a torsion-free group the only torsion element of $G$ is the group identity element.

title: Definition:Torsion Element of Module
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $M$ be a unitary module over $R$. Let $m \in M$. Then $m$ is a torsion element of $M$ there exists a regular element $a \in R$ with $a m = 0$.

title: Definition:Torsion Group
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Then $G$ is a torsion group all its elements are torsion elements.

title: Definition:Torsion Module
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $M$ be a unitary module over $R$. Then $M$ is a torsion module every element of $M$ is of torsion, that is, $M$ equals its torsion submodule $\map T M$.

title: Definition:Torsion Subgroup
snippet: Let $G$ be an abelian group. Its torsion subgroup $\map T G$ is the subgroup of all torsion elements.

title: Definition:Torsion Submodule
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $M$ be a unitary module over $R$. The torsion submodule $\map T M$ of $M$ is the submodule of all torsion elements of $M$.

title: Definition:Torsion Tensor
snippet:
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $TM$ be the tangent bundle of $M$. Let $
abla$ be a connection in $TM$. Let $\sqbrk {\cdot, \cdot}$ be the Lie bracket. Let $\map {\mathfrak{X}} M$ be the space of smooth vector fields on $M$. Let $	au : \map {\mathfrak{X}} M 	imes \map {\mathfrak{X}} M 	o \map {\mathfrak{X}} M$ be a tensor field such that: $ orall X, Y \in \map {\mathfrak{X}} M : \map 	au {X, Y} := 
abla_X Y - 
abla_Y X - \sqbrk {X, Y}$ Then $	au$ is called the torsion tensor.

title: Definition:Torsion of Curve Parameterized by Arc Length/3-Dimensional Real Vector Space
snippet: Let $\alpha : I \to \R^3$ be a (smooth) curve parameterized by arc length. Let $s \in I$ be such that the curvature $\map \kappa s \ne 0$. The torsion of $\alpha$ at $s$ is the real number $\map \tau s$ defined by: $\map {b'} s = \map \tau s \map n s$ where: $\map {b'} s$ is the derivative of the binormal vector $\map n s$ is the normal vector

title: Definition:Torus/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Torus == The plural of torus can either be the Classical Latin plural tori, or the more modern toruses. On the preferred plural is tori, but the more modern form may also be seen. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Torus (Geometry)
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a circle. Let $\LL$ be a straight line in the same plane as $\CC$ such that $\LL$ may or may not intersect $\CC$. A torus is the surface of revolution formed by rotating $\CC$ one full turn about $\LL$.

title: Definition:Torus (Geometry)/Also defined as
snippet: == Torus in the context of Geometry: Also defined as == Some sources limit the definition of the torus to restrict the straight line so that it does not intersect the circle rotating around it.

title: Definition:Torus (Geometry)/Also known as
snippet: == Torus in the context of Geometry: Also known as == A torus is also known by its informal name anchor ring.

title: Definition:Torus (Topology)
snippet: A torus is a surface obtained by identifying both pairs of opposite sides, one with the other, of a square, while retaining the orientation: 300px Thus in the above diagram, $AB$ is identified with $DC$ and $CB$ with $DA$.

title: Definition:Torus (Topology)/Formal Construction
snippet: Let $T$ be the square embedded in the Cartesian plane defined as: $T = \closedint {-1} 1 \times \closedint {-1} 1$ Let $T'$ be the quotient space formed from $T$ using the identification mapping $p: T \to T'$ as follows: $\forall \tuple {x, y} \in T: \map p {x, y} = \begin {cases} \paren {x, y} & : -1 < x, y < 1 \\ \\ \tuple {-x, y} & : x = \pm 1 \\ \\ \tuple {x, -y} & : y = \pm 1 \end {cases}$ Then $T'$ is a torus .

title: Definition:Torus (Topology)/General/Definition 1
snippet: The $n$-dimensional torus (or $n$-torus) $\Bbb T^n$ is defined as the $n$-fold product space of the $1$-sphere. That is: $\ds \Bbb T^n = \prod_{i \mathop \in \N_{< n}} \Bbb S^1$ where: $\Bbb S^1$ denotes the $1$-sphere $\N_{< n}$ denotes an initial segment of natural numbers $\ds \prod_{i \mathop \in I}$ denotes the product space

title: Definition:Torus (Topology)/General/Definition 2
snippet: The $n$-dimensional torus (or $n$-torus) $\Bbb T^n$ is defined as the space whose points are those of the Cartesian product of $n$ circles: $\Bbb T^n = \underbrace{\Bbb S^1 \times \Bbb S^1 \times \ldots \times \Bbb S^1}_{n \text{ times}}$ and whose topology $\tau_{\Bbb T^n}$ is generated by the basis: $\BB = \set {U_1 \times U_2 \times \cdots \times U_n : U_1, U_2, \ldots, U_n \in \tau_{\Bbb S^1}}$ where $\tau_{\Bbb S^1}$ is the topology of the $1$-sphere.

title: Definition:Torus Group
snippet: The torus group is the direct product of the circle group $C$ with itself: $T := \struct {K, \times} \times \struct {K, \times}$ where: $K = \set {z \in \C: \cmod z = 1}$

title: Definition:Total Curvature
snippet: Let $C$ be a curve defined by a real function which is twice differentiable. Let $\delta \psi$ be the angle of contingence with respect to $2$ points $P$ and $Q$ on $C$. Then $\delta \psi$ is known as the total curvature of $C$ between $P$ and $Q$.

title: Definition:Total Derivative
snippet: Let $\map f {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ be a continuous real function of multiple variables. Let each of $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ be continuous real functions of a single independent variable $t$. Then the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $t$ is defined as: $\ds \frac {\d f}{\d t} = \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n \frac {\partial f} {\partial x_k} \frac {\d x_k}{\d t} = \frac {\partial f} {\partial x_1} \frac {\d x_1}{\d t} + \frac {\partial f} {\partial x_2} \frac {\d x_2}{\d t} + \cdots + \frac {\partial f} {\partial x_n} \frac {\d x_n}{\d t}$ where $\dfrac {\partial f} {\partial x_k}$ is the…

title: Definition:Total Differential/Vector Function
snippet: Let $\map {\R^3} {x, y, z}$ denote the Cartesian $3$-space. Let $\tuple {\mathbf i, \mathbf j, \mathbf k}$ be the standard ordered basis on $\R^3$. Let $\mathbf V$ be a vector field in $\R^3$. Let $\mathbf v: \R^3 \to \mathbf V$ be a vector-valued function on $\R^3$: $\forall P = \tuple {x, y, z} \in \R^3: \map {\mathbf v} P := \map {v_1} P \mathbf i + \map {v_2} P \mathbf j + \map {v_3} P \mathbf k$ Let $v_1, v_2, v_3$ be differentiable.

title: Definition:Total Energy of Particles
snippet: Let $P$ be a physical system composed of a countable number of particles. Suppose the kinetic and potential energy of $P$ is respectively $T$ and $U$. Denote: $E = T + U$ Then $E$ is known as the total energy of $P$.

title: Definition:Total Function
snippet: Let $f: \N^k \to \N$ be a partial function such that $f$ is defined on $S \subseteq \N^k$. Now let $S = \N^k$. That is, the domain of $f$ is then the whole of $\N^k$. Then $f$ is a total function.

title: Definition:Total Ordering
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation on a set $S$.

title: Definition:Total Ordering/Also known as
snippet: == Total Ordering: Also known as == Some sources refer to a total ordering as a linear ordering, or a simple ordering. If it is necessary to emphasise that a total ordering $\preceq$ is not strict, then the term weak total ordering may be used.

title: Definition:Total Ordering/Class Theory
snippet: Let $V$ be a basic universe. Let $\RR \subseteq V \times V$ be a relation. Let $\RR$ be such that: $(1): \quad \RR$ is an ordering on $\Field \RR$ $(2): \quad \forall x, y \in \Field \RR: x \mathop \RR y \lor y \mathop \RR x$ (that is, $x$ and $y$ are comparable) where $\Field \RR$ denotes the field of $\RR$. Then $\RR$ is a total ordering.

title: Definition:Total Ordering/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation on a set $S$. $\RR$ is a total ordering on $S$ : $(1): \quad \RR$ is an ordering on $S$ $(2): \quad \RR$ is connected That is, $\RR$ is an ordering with no non-comparable pairs: $\forall x, y \in S: x \mathop \RR y \lor y \mathop \RR x$

title: Definition:Total Ordering/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation on a set $S$. $\RR$ is a total ordering on $S$ : {{eqn | n = 2 | l = \RR \cap \RR^{-1} | o = \subseteq | r = \Delta_S }} {{eqn | n = 3 | l = \RR \cup \RR^{-1} | r = S \times S }}

title: Definition:Total Ordering Induced by Strict Positivity Property
snippet: Let $\struct {D, +, \times, \le}$ be an ordered integral domain whose zero is $0_D$ and whose unity is $1_D$. Let $P: D \to \set {\T, \F}$ denote the strict positivity property: Then the total ordering $\le$ compatible with the ring structure of $D$ is called the (total) ordering induced by (the strict positivity property) $P$.

title: Definition:Total Preordering
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\precsim$ be a preordering on $S$. Then $\precsim$ is a total preordering on $S$ $\precsim$ is connected. That is, there is no pair of elements of $S$ which is non-comparable: $\forall x, y \in S: x \precsim y \lor y \precsim x$

title: Definition:Total Recursive Function
snippet: In general, a recursive function is a partial function. A total recursive function is a recursive function which is total. Category:Definitions/Recursion Theory

title: Definition:Total Relation
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation on a set $S$. Then $\RR$ is defined as total : $\forall a, b \in S: \tuple {a, b} \in \RR \lor \tuple {b, a} \in \RR$ That is, every pair of elements is related (either or both ways round).

title: Definition:Total Relation/Also known as
snippet: == Total Relation: Also known as == Other terms that can be found that mean the same thing as total relation are: dichotomous relation strictly connected relation complete relation. Some sources use the term dichotomy, but this word is also used for a concept in statistics, so will not be used in this context on .

title: Definition:Total Ring of Fractions
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. The total ring of fractions of $A$ is the localization of $A$ at the set of its regular elements.

title: Definition:Total Semilattice
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \odot}$ be a semilattice. Let $\struct {S, \odot}$ have the property that every subset of $\struct {S, \odot}$ is a subsemilattice. That is, such that every subset of $\struct {S, \odot}$ is closed under $\odot$. Then $\struct {S, \odot}$ is known as a total semilattice.

title: Definition:Total Semilattice/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Total Semilattice == Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Total Variation/Measure Theory/Complex Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\mu$ be a complex measure on $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. Let $\cmod \mu$ be the variation of $\mu$. We define the total variation $\norm \mu$ of $\mu$ by: $\norm \mu = \map {\cmod \mu} X$

title: Definition:Total Variation/Measure Theory/Signed Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\mu$ be a signed measure on $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. Let $\size \mu$ be the variation of $\mu$. We define the total variation $\norm \mu$ of $\mu$ by: $\norm \mu = \map {\size \mu} X$

title: Definition:Total Variation/Real Function/Closed Bounded Interval/Definition 1
snippet: Let $a, b$ be real numbers with $a < b$. Let $f: \closedint a b \to \R$ be a function of bounded variation. Let $\map X {\closedint a b}$ be the set of finite subdivisions of $\closedint a b$. For each $P \in \map X {\closedint a b}$, write: $P = \set {x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_n}$ with: $a = x_0 < x_1 < x_2 < \cdots < x_{n - 1} < x_n = b$ Also write: $\ds \map {V_f} {P ; \closedint a b} = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \size {\map f {x_i} - \map f {x_{i - 1} } }$ We define the total variation $\map {V_f} {\closedint a b}$ of $f$ on $\closedint a b$ by: $\ds \map {V_f} {\closedint a b} = \map {\sup_{P…

title: Definition:Total Variation/Real Function/Closed Bounded Interval/Definition 2
snippet: Let $a, b$ be real numbers with $a < b$. Let $f : \closedint a b \to \R$ be a real function of bounded variation. Let $\map {\PP_F} {\closedint a b}$ be the set of finite subsets of $\closedint a b$. For each finite non-empty subset $\SS$ of $\closedint a b$, write: $\SS = \set {x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_n}$ with: $a \le x_0 < x_1 < x_2 < \cdots < x_{n - 1} < x_n \le b$ Also write: $\ds \map {V_f^\ast} {\SS; \closedint a b} = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \size {\map f {x_i} - \map f {x_{i - 1} } }$ We define the total variation $\map {V_f} {\closedint a b}$ of $f$ on $\closedint a b$ by: $\ds \map {V_f}…

title: Definition:Total Variation/Real Function/Closed Unbounded Interval
snippet: Let $I$ be an unbounded closed interval or $\R$. Let $f: I \to \R$ be a real function. Let $\map {\PP_F} I$ be the set of finite subsets of $I$. For each finite non-empty subset $\SS$ of $I$, write: $\SS = \set {x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_n}$ with: $x_0 < x_1 < x_2 < \cdots < x_{n - 1} < x_n$ Also write: $\ds \map {V_f^\ast} {\SS; I} = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \size {\map f {x_i} - \map f {x_{i - 1} } }$ We define the total variation $\map {V_f} I$ of $f$ on $I$ by: $\ds \map {V_f} I = \sup_{\SS \mathop \in \map {\PP_F} I} \paren {\map {V_f^\ast} {\SS; I} }$

title: Definition:Totally Bounded Metric Space/Also known as
snippet: == Totally Bounded Metric Space: Also known as == A totally bounded metric space is also known as a precompact space.

title: Definition:Totally Bounded Metric Space/Definition 1
snippet: A metric space $M = \struct {A, d}$ is totally bounded : for every $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ there exists a finite $\epsilon$-net for $M$. That is, $M$ is totally bounded : for every $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ there exists a finite set of points $x_1, \ldots, x_n \in A$ such that: $\ds A = \bigcup_{i \mathop = 1}^n \map {B_\epsilon} {x_i}$ where $\map {B_\epsilon} {x_i}$ denotes the open $\epsilon$-ball of $x_i$. That is: $M$ is totally bounded , given any $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$, one can find a finite number of open $\epsilon$-balls which cover $A$.

title: Definition:Totally Bounded Metric Space/Definition 2
snippet: A metric space $M = \struct {A, d}$ is totally bounded : for every $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ there exist finitely many points $x_0, \dots, x_n \in A$ such that: $\ds \inf_{0 \mathop \le i \mathop \le n} \map d {x_i, x} \le \epsilon$ for all $x \in A$.

title: Definition:Totally Disconnected Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a totally disconnected space all components of $T$ are singletons. That is, $T$ is a totally disconnected space it contains no non-degenerate connected sets.

title: Definition:Totally Disconnected Space/Also defined as
snippet: == Totally Disconnected Space: Also defined as == Because of Totally Disconnected but Connected Set must be Singleton, the definition for totally disconnected space is applied by some authors to a topological space containing at least $2$ elements. Category:Definitions/Totally Disconnected Spaces

title: Definition:Totally Disconnected Space/Also known as
snippet: == Totally Disconnected Space: Also known as == A totally disconnected space is also known as a hereditarily disconnected space.

title: Definition:Totally Ordered Class
snippet: Let $V$ be a basic universe. Let $\RR \subseteq V \times V$ be a relation. Let $A$ be a subclass of the field of $\RR$. Let the restriction of $\RR$ to $A$ be a total ordering on $A$. Then $A$ is described as being totally ordered under $\RR$.

title: Definition:Totally Ordered Commutative Semigroup
snippet: A totally ordered commutative semigroup is a totally ordered structure $\left({S, \circ, \preceq}\right)$ such that $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ is a commutative semigroup.

title: Definition:Totally Ordered Field
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +, \circ, \preceq}$ be an ordered ring. Let $\struct {F, +, \circ}$ be a field. Let the ordering $\preceq$ be a total ordering. Then $\struct {F, +, \circ, \preceq}$ is a totally ordered field.

title: Definition:Totally Ordered Group
snippet: A totally ordered group is a totally ordered structure $\left({G, \circ, \preceq}\right)$ such that $\left({G, \circ}\right)$ is a group.

title: Definition:Totally Ordered Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ, \preceq}$ be an ordered ring. Let the ordering $\preceq$ be a total ordering. Then $\struct {R, +, \circ, \preceq}$ is a totally ordered ring.

title: Definition:Totally Ordered Semigroup
snippet: A totally ordered semigroup is a totally ordered structure $\left({S, \circ, \preceq}\right)$ such that $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ is a semigroup.

title: Definition:Totally Ordered Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a relational structure. Then $\struct {S, \preceq}$ is a totally ordered set $\preceq$ is a total ordering.

title: Definition:Totally Ordered Set/Also known as
snippet: == Totally Ordered Set: Also known as == A totally ordered set is also called a simply ordered set or linearly ordered set. It is also known as a toset. This term may be encountered on . Some sources refer to a totally ordered set as an ordered set, using the term partially ordered set for what goes as an ordered set on . Some sources use the term chain, but this word is generally restricted to mean specifically a totally ordered subset of a given ordered set.

title: Definition:Totally Ordered Structure
snippet: Let $\left({S, \circ, \preceq}\right)$ be an ordered structure. That is: $(1): \quad \left({S, \circ}\right)$ is an algebraic structure $(2): \quad \left({S, \preceq}\right)$ is an ordered set $(3): \quad \preceq$ is compatible with $\circ$. When the ordering $\preceq$ is a total ordering, the structure $\left({S, \circ, \preceq}\right)$ is then a totally ordered structure.

title: Definition:Totally Pathwise Disconnected Space/Also known as
snippet: == Totally Pathwise Disconnected Space: Also known as == A totally pathwise disconnected space is also known as a totally path disconnected space or totally path-disconnected space.

title: Definition:Totally Pathwise Disconnected Space/Definition 1
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is totally pathwise disconnected all path components of $T$ are singletons.

title: Definition:Totally Pathwise Disconnected Space/Definition 2
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is totally pathwise disconnected the only continuous mappings from the closed unit interval $\closedint 0 1$ to $T$ are constant mappings.

title: Definition:Totally Separated Space/Also known as
snippet: == Totally Separated Space: Also known as == Some sources refer to a totally separated space as a totally disconnected space. However, has a different definition for that.

title: Definition:Totally Separated Space/Definition 1
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is totally separated : For every $x, y \in S: x \ne y$ there exists a separation $U \mid V$ of $T$ such that $x \in U, y \in V$.

title: Definition:Totally Separated Space/Definition 2
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is totally separated each of its quasicomponents is a singleton set.

title: Definition:Totally Separated Space/Definition 3
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is totally separated , given two arbitrary distinct points $x, y \in S$, there exists a clopen set $A \subseteq X$ such that $x \in A$ and $y \notin A$.

title: Definition:Totally Skew Symmetric Function
snippet: Let $f: \R^n \to \R$ be a real-valued function. Let $f$ be such that, for every pair $\tuple {x_i, x_j}$ in $\R^2$: $\map f {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_i, \ldots, x_j, \ldots, x_n} = -\map f {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_j, \ldots, x_i, \ldots, x_n}$ Then $f$ is a totally skew symmetric function.

title: Definition:Totally Skew Symmetric Function/Also known as
snippet: == Totally Skew Symmetric Function: Also known as == A totally skew symmetric function can also be referred to as just a skew symmetric function. Hyphenated forms can also be seen: totally skew-symmetric function and skew-symmetric function. Some sources refer to a totally skew symmetric function as an alternating function.

title: Definition:Totient/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Totient == The word totient is pronounced to rhyme with quotient, that is: toe-shyent or toe-shent, according to taste. The same applies to its various relatives: nontotient, cototient, noncototient, and so on. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Totitive
snippet: Let $n$ be a natural number. A natural number $m$ is a totitive of $n$ $m$ is: coprime with $n$ not greater than $n$.

title: Definition:Tower in Set
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $T$ be any non-empty subset of $X$ Let $c$ be a fixed choice function on the non-empty subsets $T$ of $X$. Let $\preccurlyeq$ be a well-ordering on $T$. The well-ordered set $\struct {T, \preccurlyeq}$ is a tower in $X$ , for all $t \in T$: $t = \map c {X \setminus \map {S_t} T}$ where $\map {S_t} T$ is the initial segment of $T$ determined by $t$.

title: Definition:Tower of Fields
snippet: A tower of fields: $F_k / F_{k - 1} / \dotsb / F_2 / F_1$ is a finite sequence of field extensions: $F_{j + 1} / F_j$ where $j = 1, \dotsc, k - 1$.

title: Definition:Trace
snippet: Field Theory: Trace (Field Theory) Linear Algebra: Trace (Linear Algebra) Trace of Matrix Trace of Linear Operator Abstract Algebra: Trace $\sigma$-Algebra Mathematical Logic and Computability Theory: Trace Table Riemannian Geometry: Trace of Tensor Solid Geometry: Trace of Space Curve

title: Definition:Trace (Field Theory)
snippet: Let $K$ be a field and $L / K$ a finite field extension of $K$. Then by Vector Space on Field Extension is Vector Space, $L$ is naturally a vector space over $K$. Let $\alpha \in L$, and $\theta_\alpha$ be the linear operator: $\theta_\alpha: L \to L: \beta \mapsto \alpha\beta$ The trace $\map {\operatorname {Tr}_{L / K} } \alpha$ of $\alpha$ is the trace of this linear operator.

title: Definition:Trace (Linear Algebra)/Linear Operator
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space. Let $A: V \to V$ be a linear operator of $V$. The trace of $A$ is the trace of the matrix of $A$ with respect to some basis.

title: Definition:Trace (Linear Algebra)/Matrix
snippet: Let $A = \sqbrk a_n$ be a square matrix of order $n$. The trace of $A$ is: $\ds \map \tr A = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n a_{ii}$

title: Definition:Trace Sigma-Algebra
snippet: Let $X$ be a set, and let $\Sigma$ be a $\sigma$-algebra on $X$. Let $E \subseteq X$ be a subset of $X$. Then the trace $\sigma$-algebra (of $E$ in $\Sigma$), $\Sigma_E$, is defined as: $\Sigma_E := \set {E \cap S: S \in \Sigma}$ It is a $\sigma$-algebra on $E$, as proved on Trace $\sigma$-Algebra is $\sigma$-Algebra.

title: Definition:Trace Table
snippet: Let $P$ be a URM program. The trace table of $P$ consists of: The stage of computation; The number of the instruction of $P$ that is about to be performed; A list of the contents of all the registers used by $P$ at this point. Thus the trace table is a list of the states of the URM program at each stage.

title: Definition:Trace of Element of Algebra over Ring
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $B$ be an algebra over $A$ such that $B$ is a finite-dimensional free module over $A$. Let $b \in B$. Free The trace $\map {\operatorname {Tr}_{B / A} } b$ of $b$ is the trace of the regular representation $\lambda_b : B \to B$ over $A$.

title: Definition:Trace of Matrix/Also known as
snippet: == Trace of Matrix: Also known as == The trace of a matrix is also known as its spur.

title: Definition:Trace of Matrix/Einstein Summation Convention
snippet: Let $A = \sqbrk {a_{ij} }_{1 \mathop \le i, j \mathop \le n}$ be a matrix. The trace of $A$, using the Einstein summation convention, is: $\map \tr A = a_{ii}$

title: Definition:Trace of Space Curve
snippet: Let $S$ be a space curve. Let $P$ be a coordinate plane. A trace of $S$ $P$ is a point at which $S$ intersects $P$.

title: Definition:Trace of Space Curve/Also known as
snippet: == Trace of Space Curve: Also known as == A trace of a space curve is also known as a piercing point.

title: Definition:Trace of Tensor
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $h$ be a covariant $k$-tensor field with $k \ge 2$. Let $h^\sharp$ be a $\tuple {1, k - 1}$-tensor field obtained from $h$ by raising its index. Then the trace of $h$ $g$ is a covariant $\paren {k - 2}$-tensor field defined as: $\tr_g h := \map \tr {h^\sharp}$ where $\tr$ is the trace over a covariant and a contravariant index.

title: Definition:Tractrix/Also defined as
snippet: == Tractrix: Also known as == The tractrix can also be defined the $y$-axis: The tractrix is the locus of a point such that the length $PT$ of the tangent at $P$ to where it intersects the $y$-axis at $T$ is constant. 300px Category:Definitions/Tractrix

title: Definition:Tractrix/Asymptote
snippet: The asymptote of a tractrix is the straight line along which the end of the line segment is being dragged.

title: Definition:Tractrix/Axis
snippet: The axis of a tractrix is the straight line aligned with the initial position of the line segment being dragged.

title: Definition:Tractrix/Definition 1
snippet: The tractrix is the plane curve which is the involute of the catenary. 800px

title: Definition:Tractrix/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ be a cord situated as a (straight) line segment whose endpoints are $P$ and $T$. Let $T$ be dragged in a direction perpendicular to the straight line in which $S$ is aligned. The curve along which $P$ travels is known as a tractrix. 800px

title: Definition:Tractrix/Definition 3
snippet: The tractrix is the locus of a point such that the length $PT$ of the tangent at $P$ to where it intersects the $x$-axis at $T$ is constant. 800px

title: Definition:Tractrix/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Tractrix == The tractrix was first investigated by in $1670$. It was later studied by in $1676$ and in $1692$. also gave some time to it.

title: Definition:Tractrix/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Tractrix == The word tractrix derives from the Latin traho (trahere, traxi, tractum) meaning to pull or to drag. The plural is tractrices.

title: Definition:Trail
snippet: A trail is a walk in which all edges are distinct. A trail between two vertices $u$ and $v$ is called a $u$-$v$ trail.

title: Definition:Trail/Also known as
snippet: == Trail: Also known as == A trail can also be seen referred to as an Eulerian walk, for .

title: Definition:Trail/Subgraph
snippet: The set of vertices and edges which go to make up a trail in a graph $G$ form a subgraph of $G$. This subgraph itself is also referred to as a trail in $G$.

title: Definition:Trajectory (Mechanics)
snippet: Let $B$ be a body (which could be a particle) in motion. The trajectory of $B$ is its path through the medium in which it is moving.

title: Definition:Trajectory of Dynamical System
snippet: Let $S$ be a dynamical system moving from point $A$ to point $B$. The path taken by $S$ is known as the trajectory of $S$.

title: Definition:Trajectory of Point under Iteration
snippet: Let $f: S \to S$ be an iterated mapping on a set $S$. Let $x \in S$ be a point of $S$. The trajectory of $x$ under $f$ is the ordered subset of $S$ consisting of the points: $\tuple {x, \map f x, \map {f^2} x, \ldots}$ where $\map {f^n} x$ is defined as $\map f {\map {f^{n - 1} } x}$, and so on.

title: Definition:Transcendence Degree
snippet: Let $K$ be a field, and let $L/K$ be a field extension of $K$. The transcendence degree of $L/K$ is the largest cardinality of an algebraically independent subset $A \subseteq L$. Category:Definitions/Field Extensions

title: Definition:Transcendental
snippet: Abstract Algebra: Transcendental: Transcendental Field Extension Transcendental over Integral Domain Analysis: Definition:Transcendental Number Definition:Transcendental Entire Function

title: Definition:Transcendental/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Transcendental == The term transcendental, in the sense of meaning non-algebraic, was introduced by .

title: Definition:Transcendental (Abstract Algebra)/Field Extension
snippet: A field extension $E / F$ is said to be transcendental : $\exists \alpha \in E: \alpha$ is transcendental over $F$ That is, a field extension is transcendental it contains at least one transcendental element.

title: Definition:Transcendental (Abstract Algebra)/Field Extension/Element
snippet: Let $E / F$ be a field extension. Let $\alpha \in E$. Then $\alpha$ is transcendental over $F$ : $\nexists \map f x \in F \sqbrk x \setminus \set 0: \map f \alpha = 0$ where $\map f x$ denotes a polynomial in $x$ over $F$.

title: Definition:Transcendental (Abstract Algebra)/Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a commutative ring with unity whose zero is $0_R$ and whose unity is $1_R$. Let $\struct {D, +, \circ}$ be an integral subdomain of $R$. Let $x \in R$. Then $x$ is transcendental over $D$ : $\ds \forall n \in \Z_{\ge 0}: \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^n a_k \circ x^k = 0_R \implies \forall k: 0 \le k \le n: a_k = 0_R$ That is, $x$ is transcendental over $D$ the only way to express $0_R$ as a polynomial in $x$ over $D$ is by the null polynomial.

title: Definition:Transcendental Curve
snippet: A transcendental curve is a curve which is the locus of a set of transcendental functions.

title: Definition:Transcendental Function
snippet: A transcendental function is an analytic function which is not an algebraic function. That is, it cannot be expressed as a polynomial equation.

title: Definition:Transcendental Function/Also defined as
snippet: Some sources define a transcendental function as a real function or complex function which is not an elementary function. However, the distinction between what is and is not an elementary function is more or less arbitrary, consisting of both algebraic functions and those derived from the exponential function, which itself is not algebraic. The current school of thought appears to be that this definition: "not an elementary function" is actually considered to be erroneous. However, the distinction is not considered particularly important nowadays.

title: Definition:Transcendental Number
snippet: A number (either real or complex) is transcendental it is not algebraic.

title: Definition:Transcendental Number/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Transcendental Number == The first numbers that were demonstrated as being transcendental were presented by in $1851$. He did this with the aid of what is now known as Liouville's theorem.

title: Definition:Transcendental Number over Field
snippet: Let $F$ be a field. Let $z$ be a complex number. $z$ is a transcendental number over $F$ $z$ cannot be expressed as a root of a polynomial with coefficients in $F$.

title: Definition:Transfer Function
snippet: Number Theory: Transfer Function: A function that iterates to form a superfunction. Fourier Analysis: Transfer Function: A representation in terms of frequency of the relation between input and output of a linear time-invariant system. Time Series Analysis: Transfer Function: A mathematical function which theoretically models the future output for each possible input..

title: Definition:Transfer Function (Time Series Analysis)
snippet: A transfer function, in the context of time series analysis, is a function of time which theoretically models the future output for each possible input.

title: Definition:Transfinite Ordinal
snippet: Let $\alpha$ be an ordinal. Then $\alpha$ is said to be transfinite it is an infinite set.

title: Definition:Transfinite Ordinal/Also known as
snippet: == Transfinite Ordinal: Also known as == A transfinite ordinal is also known as an infinite ordinal. The term transfinite number can also sometimes be seen. The very word transfinite is a holdover from the tentative steps made by , seeking a language to communicate in which would minimise the challenge of the preconceived notion of the word infinite. The word infinite number is used sporadically in , which often loosely means a number (of whatever type) which is not finite, and used in a context where the meaning is apparent.

title: Definition:Transfinite Sequence
snippet: Let $\alpha$ be an infinite ordinal. Let $\left({x_\beta}\right)_{\beta \mathop \in \alpha}$ be an $\alpha$-indexed family. Then $\left({x_\beta}\right)_{\beta \mathop \in \alpha}$ is called a transfinite sequence.

title: Definition:Transformation
snippet: Algebra: Transformation of Expression Mapping Theory: A synonym for self-map Linear Algebra: Linear Transformation Module Theory: Evaluation Linear Transformation Complex Analysis: Complex Transformation Group Theory: Transformation Group Effective Transformation Group Natural Transformation: Natural Transformation between Covariant Functors Natural Transformation between Contravariant Functors Special Relativity Lorentz Transformation Statistics: Statistical Transformation

title: Definition:Transformation Group/Also known as
snippet: == Transformation Group: Also known as == The transformation group on $X$ can be referred to as the group of transformations on $X$. Category:Definitions/Group Actions

title: Definition:Transformation Matrix
snippet: A transformation matrix is a matrix defining a coordinate transformation.

title: Definition:Transformation Matrix/Also known as
snippet: == Transformation Matrix: Also known as == A transformation matrix is also known as a change of basis matrix.

title: Definition:Transformation of Axes
snippet: A transformation of axes is a coordinate transformation either: $(1): \quad$ a change from one coordinate system to another, for example Cartesian to polar $(2): \quad$ a change in the position of a given coordinate system to another, for example rotation or translation.

title: Definition:Transformation of Axes/Also known as
snippet: == Transformation of Axes: Also known as == A transformation of axes is also known as a change of coordinates.

title: Definition:Transformation of Axes/Motivation
snippet: A transformation of axes from one coordinate system to another is a useful technique to make the solution of a problem easier.

title: Definition:Transformation of Expression
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an expression. A transformation of $\EE$ is a change in the form of $\EE$ by either of both of: by rearrangement of the terms by substitution by another expression.

title: Definition:Transient
snippet: Consider the Decay Equation: $\dfrac {\d y} {\d x} = k \paren {y_a - y}$ where: $k \in \R: k > 0$ $y = y_0$ at $x = 0$ which has the particular solution: $(1): \quad y = y_a + \paren {y_0 - y_a} e^{-k x}$ The term: $\paren {y_0 - y_a} e^{-k x}$ which tends to zero with increasing $x$, is known as the transient part.

title: Definition:Transient/Electronics
snippet: Consider the electronic circuit $K$ consisting of: a resistance $R$ an inductance $L$ in series with a source of electromotive force $E$ which is a function of time $t$. File:CircuitRLseries.png Let the electric current flowing in $K$ at time $t = 0$ be $I_0$. Let a constant EMF $E_0$ be imposed upon $K$ at time $t = 0$. The electric current $I$ in $K$ is given by the equation: $I = \dfrac {E_0} R + \paren {I_0 - \dfrac {E_0} R} e^{-R t / L}$ The term: $\paren {I_0 - \dfrac {E_0} R} e^{-R t / L}$ which dies away to zero over time, is known as the transient part.

title: Definition:Transition Mapping
snippet: Let $B = \struct {E, M, \pi, F}$ be a fiber bundle. Let $\struct {U, \chi}$, $\struct {V, \xi}$ be two local trivializations with $U \cap V \ne \O$. Then the mapping: $\xi \circ \chi^{-1} : U \cap V \times F \to U \cap V \times F$ is called a transition mapping from $\struct {U, \chi}$ to $\struct {V, \xi}$.

title: Definition:Transition Mapping/Also known as
snippet: == Transition Mappings: Also known as == A transition mapping is also known as a transition map.

title: Definition:Transition Mapping between Charts
snippet: Let $M$ be a topological manifold. Let $d$ be a natural number. Let $\struct {U, \phi}$ and $\struct {V, \psi}$ be $d$-dimensional charts of $M$. Let $U \cap V \ne \O$. The transition map from $\phi$ to $\psi$ is the mapping: $\psi \circ \phi^{-1} : \map \phi {U \cap V} \to \map \psi {U \cap V}$

title: Definition:Transition Mapping between Charts/Also defined as
snippet: == Transition Mapping between Charts: Also defined as == In their definition of transition mapping between charts, some sources do not require $U \cap V$ to be non-empty for the transition mapping to be defined.

title: Definition:Transitive
snippet: Relation Theory: Transitivity (Relation Theory) Transitive Closure and Transitive Reflexive Closure Transitive Reduction Group Theory: Transitive Group Action Transitive Subgroup Set Theory: Transitive Set Transitive Closure Class Theory: Transitive Class

title: Definition:Transitive-Closed Class
snippet: Let $K$ be a class Then $K$ is transitive-closed : every transitive subset of $K$ is an element of $K$.

title: Definition:Transitive-Closed Class/Linguistic Note
snippet: The concept appears to have been coined by and under the name $T$-closed class in their of $2010$ for the purpose of an exercise. It is referred to on as a transitive-closed class in order to improve clarity and transparency.

title: Definition:Transitive Class
snippet: Let $A$ denote a class, which can be either a set or a proper class. Then $A$ is transitive every element of $A$ is also a subclass of $A$. That is, $A$ is transitive : $x \in A \implies x \subseteq A$ or: $\forall x: \forall y: \paren {x \in y \land y \in A \implies x \in A}$

title: Definition:Transitive Class/Also known as
snippet: == Transitive Class: Also known as == A transitive class is also known as a complete class. Thus a class which is not transitive can be considered to be a class with "holes" in it.

title: Definition:Transitive Closure
snippet: Transitive Closure of Relation Transitive Closure of Set

title: Definition:Transitive Closure of Relation/Also known as
snippet: == Transitive Closure of Relation: Also known as == Some authors refer to the transitive closure of $\RR$ as the ancestral of $\RR$. The symbolism varies: some authors use $\RR^t$. The literature is inconsistent, so any notation needs explanation when used on .

title: Definition:Transitive Closure of Relation/Finite Chain
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a relation on a set or class $S$. The transitive closure of $\RR$ is the relation $\RR^+$ defined as follows: For $x, y \in S$, $x \mathrel {\RR^+} y$ for some $n \in \N_{>0}$ there exist $s_0, s_1, \dots, s_n \in S$ such that $s_0 = x$, $s_n = y$, and: {{eqn | l = s_{n - 1} | o = \RR | r = s_n }} That is: $\forall k \in \N_n: s_k \mathrel \RR s_{k + 1}$

title: Definition:Transitive Closure of Relation/Intersection of Transitive Supersets
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a relation on a set $S$. The transitive closure of $\RR$ is defined as the intersection of all transitive relations on $S$ which contain $\RR$. The transitive closure of $\RR$ is denoted $\RR^+$.

title: Definition:Transitive Closure of Relation/Smallest Transitive Superset
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a relation on a set $S$. The transitive closure of $\RR$ is defined as the smallest transitive relation on $S$ which contains $\RR$ as a subset. The transitive closure of $\RR$ is denoted $\RR^+$.

title: Definition:Transitive Closure of Relation/Union of Compositions
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a relation on a set $S$. Let: $\RR^n := \begin {cases} \RR & : n = 1 \\ \RR^{n-1} \circ \RR & : n > 1 \end {cases}$ where $\circ$ denotes composition of relations. Finally, let: $\ds \RR^+ = \bigcup_{i \mathop = 1}^\infty \RR^i$ Then $\RR^+$ is called the transitive closure of $\RR$.

title: Definition:Transitive Closure of Set/Definition 1
snippet: Let $x$ be a set. Then the transitive closure of $x$ is the smallest transitive superset of $x$.

title: Definition:Transitive Closure of Set/Definition 2
snippet: Let $x$ be a set. For each natural number $n \in \N_{\ge 0}$ let: $\bigcup^n x = \underbrace {\bigcup \bigcup \cdots \bigcup}_n x$ Then the transitive closure of $x$ is the union of the sets: $\set x, x, \bigcup x, \bigcup^2 x, \dots, \bigcup^n x, \dots$ More precisely: Let $F$ be the mapping on the universal class defined by letting: $\map F A = \bigcup a$ for each set $a$. Let $G$ be the mapping on the natural numbers defined recursively by letting: $\map G 0 = \set x$ $\map G {n^+} = \map F {\map G n}$ for each natural number $n$.

title: Definition:Transitive Group Action
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $S$ be a set. Let $*: G \times S \to S$ be a group action. The group action is transitive for any $x, y \in S$ there exists $g \in G$ such that $g * x = y$. That is, for all $x \in S$: $\Orb x = S$ where $\Orb x$ denotes the orbit of $x \in S$ under $*$.

title: Definition:Transitive Group Action/n-transitive
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $S$ be a set. Let $*: G \times S \to S$ be a group action. Let $n \in \N_{>0}$ be a non-zero natural number. The group action is $n$-transitive for any two ordered $n$-tuples $\tuple {x_1, \ldots, x_n}$ and $\tuple {y_1, \ldots, y_n}$ of pairwise distinct elements of $S$, there exists $g\in G$ such that: $\forall i \in \set {1, \ldots, n} : g * x_i = y_i$

title: Definition:Transitive Group Action on Fibers
snippet: Let $\tilde M$, $M$ be smooth manifolds. Let $\pi : \tilde M \to M$ be a smooth submersion. Let $p,q \in \tilde M$ be base points such that $\map \pi p = \map \pi q$. Let $G$ be a group. Suppose: $\exists \phi \in G : \phi \cdot p = q$ Then the group action is said to be transitive on fibers.

title: Definition:Transitive Reduction/Graph Theory
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a loop-digraph. Let $G$ be expressed formally as a relational structure $\GG$. A transitive reduction of $G$ is denoted $G^-$, and is defined as a transitive reduction of the relation $\GG$. Hence it is a minimal loop-digraph on $V$ which has the same transitive closure as $\GG$.

title: Definition:Transitive Reduction/Relation Theory
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a relation on a set $S$. A transitive reduction of $\RR$ is denoted $\RR^-$, and is defined as a minimal relation on $S$ which has the same transitive closure as $\RR$.

title: Definition:Transitive Relation
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation in $S$.

title: Definition:Transitive Relation/Class Theory
snippet: Let $V$ be a basic universe. Let $\RR \subseteq V \times V$ be a relation in $V$. $\RR$ is a transitive relation : $\tuple {x, y} \in \RR \land \tuple {y, z} \in \RR \implies \tuple {x, z} \in \RR$ that is: $\set {\tuple {x, y}, \tuple {y, z} } \subseteq \RR \implies \tuple {x, z} \in \RR$

title: Definition:Transitive Relation/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation in $S$. $\RR$ is a transitive relation : $\tuple {x, y} \in \RR \land \tuple {y, z} \in \RR \implies \tuple {x, z} \in \RR$ that is: $\set {\tuple {x, y}, \tuple {y, z} } \subseteq \RR \implies \tuple {x, z} \in \RR$

title: Definition:Transitive Relation/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation in $S$. $\RR$ is a transitive relation : $\RR \circ \RR \subseteq \RR$ where $\circ$ denotes composite relation.

title: Definition:Transitive Subgroup
snippet: Let $S_n$ denote the symmetric group on $n$ letters for $n \in \N$. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $S_n$. Let $H$ be such that: for every pair of elements $i, j \in \N_n$ there exists $\pi \in H$ such that $\map \pi i = j$. Then $H$ is called a transitive subgroup of $S_n$.

title: Definition:Transitive with Respect to a Relation
snippet: Let $A$ be a class. Let $\RR$ be a relation on $A$. Let $S$ be a set. Then $S$ is transitive with respect to $\RR$ : $\forall x \in A: \forall y \in S: \paren {x \mathrel \RR y \implies x \in S}$

title: Definition:Transitivity (Relation Theory)
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation in $S$.

title: Definition:Translate
snippet: Let $T$ be a translation mapping on a domain $D$. Let $X \subset T$ be a configuration in $D$. The image set of $X$ under $T$: $T \sqbrk X$ is known as the translate of $X$.

title: Definition:Translation (Logic)
snippet: Translation is the process of conversion of a WFF of symbolic logic back into natural language. Proceed as follows: {{item|\text {(i)}|If the WFF in question has been abbreviated, replace all parentheses to restore it to a formal WFF.}} {{item|\text {(ii)}|Referring to the scheme of abbreviation, replace each statement label with the corresponding simple statement that it represents.}} {{item|\text {(iii)}|Perform the following replacements: {{item|\paren {\lnot \phi}|with: $\paren {\text {it is not the case that $\phi$} }$}} {{item|\paren {\phi \land \psi}|with: $\paren {\text {$\phi$ and…

title: Definition:Translation (Logic)/Also known as
snippet: == Translation (Logic): Also known as == Some authors make completely explicit what this process of translation is by referring to it as: literal translation into natural language (or more usually English) on the basis of a given scheme of abbreviation. When step $\text {(iv)}$ has been used, the term free translation can be used, to add clarity to the fact that linguistic amendments within the scope of the natural language in question.

title: Definition:Translation (Mechanics)
snippet: A translation is a movement in a straight line.

title: Definition:Translation Invariant Measure
snippet: Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\R^n$ equipped with the Borel $\sigma$-algebra $\map \BB {\R^n}$. Then $\mu$ is said to be translation invariant or invariant under translations : $\forall x \in \R^n, \forall B \in \map \BB {\R^n}: \map \mu {x + B} = \map \mu B$ where $x + B$ is the set $\set {x + b: b \in B}$.

title: Definition:Translation Mapping
snippet: A translation (mapping) is a transformation such that the directed line segments joining points to their images all have the same magnitude and direction.

title: Definition:Translation Mapping/Abelian Group
snippet: Let $\struct {G, +}$ be an abelian group. Let $g \in G$. Then translation by $g$ is the mapping $\tau_g: G \to G$ defined by: $\forall h \in G: \map {\tau_g} h = h + \paren {-g}$ where $-g$ is the inverse of $g$ with respect to $+$ in $G$.

title: Definition:Translation Mapping/Affine Space
snippet: Let $\EE$ and $\FF$ be affine spaces. Let $\TT: \EE \to \FF$ be affine transformations. Then $\TT$ is a translation the tangent map $\vec \TT$ is the identity on the tangent space $\vec \EE$.

title: Definition:Translation Mapping/Caution
snippet: It is easy to confuse the mappings $\tau_{\mathbf x}$ and $\tau_{-\mathbf x}$, and the choice made here is arbitrary. The map $\tau_{\mathbf x}$ can be understood (appealing to our planar $\R^2$ intuition) as translating the coordinate axes by $\mathbf x$. Category:Definitions/Translation Mappings

title: Definition:Translation Mapping/Euclidean Space
snippet: A translation $\tau_\mathbf x$ is an isometry on the real Euclidean space $\Gamma = \R^n$ defined as: $\forall \mathbf y \in \R^n: \map {\tau_\mathbf x} {\mathbf y} = \mathbf y - \mathbf x$ where $\mathbf x$ is a vector in $\R^n$. As $\R^n$ is a vector space, $\struct {\R^n, +}$ is an abelian group. Hence this definition is compatible with that of a translation in an abelian group.

title: Definition:Translation Mapping/Vector Space
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $X$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $x \in X$. The translation mapping $\tau_x : X \to X$ is defined as: $\forall y \in X: \map {\tau_x} y = y - x$ where $y - x$ denotes vector subtraction.

title: Definition:Translation Property
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function. $f$ has the translation property : $\forall x_1, x_2, t \in \R: \map f {x_1 + t} - \map f {x_2 + t} = \map f {x_1} - \map f {x_2}$

title: Definition:Translation of Axes
snippet: A translation of axes is a coordinate transformation in which the coordinate axes are transformed into another set of coordinate axes parallel to the first set.

title: Definition:Translation of Subset of Vector Space
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $X$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $E$ be a subset of $X$. Let $x \in X$. We define the translation of $E$ by $x$ as the set: $E + x = \set {u + x : u \in E}$

title: Definition:Transmission Error
snippet: Let $c$ be a transmitted codeword of a message sent over a transmission line $T$. Let $c'$ be the corresponding word received across $T$. Each term of $c'$ may or may not match the corresponding term of $c$. Each term of $c'$ which does not match the corresponding term of $c$ is referred to as an instance of a transmission error.

title: Definition:Transmitted Codeword
snippet: Let $M$ be a message sent over a transmission line $T$. Let $M$ consist of a number of codewords. Each of the codewords comprising $M$, as it is before it has been transmitted across $T$, is referred to as a transmitted codeword.

title: Definition:Transplant (Abstract Algebra)
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. Let $f: S \to T$ be a bijection. Let $\oplus$ be the one and only one operation such that $f: \struct {S, \circ} \to \struct {T, \oplus}$ is an isomorphism. The operation $\oplus$ is called the transplant of $\circ$ under $f$.

title: Definition:Transportation Problem
snippet: A transportation problem is one of a generic class of problems in operations research with a particular structure which allows straightforward solutions. The basic transportation problem concerns a distributor who has storage depots at $S$ locations and needs to deliver goods to customers at $D$ destinations. Delivery costs depend on such things as: distances times taken to deliver mode of transportation used. These costs are assumed to be known, as are the available stocks in each depot and the amount each customer requires.

title: Definition:Transpose
snippet: Linear Algebra: Transpose of a Linear Transformation Transpose of a Matrix

title: Definition:Transpose of Linear Transformation
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring. Let $G$ and $H$ be $R$-modules. Let $G^*$ and $H^*$ be the algebraic duals of $G$ and $H$ respectively. Let $\map {\LL_R} {G, H}$ be the set of all linear transformations from $G$ to $H$. Let $u \in \map {\LL_R} {G, H}$. The transpose of $u$ is the mapping $u^\intercal: H^* \to G^*$ defined as: $\forall y \in H^*: \map {u^\intercal} y = y \circ u$ where $y \circ u$ is the composition of $y$ and $u$.

title: Definition:Transpose of Matrix
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk \alpha_{m n}$ be an $m \times n$ matrix over a set. Then the transpose of $\mathbf A$ is denoted $\mathbf A^\intercal$ and is defined as: $\mathbf A^\intercal = \sqbrk \beta_{n m}: \forall i \in \closedint 1 n, j \in \closedint 1 m: \beta_{i j} = \alpha_{j i}$

title: Definition:Transpose of Matrix/Also denoted as
snippet: == Transpose of Matrix: Also known as == The transpose of a matrix is often seen indicated by a lowercase or uppercase $\text T$: $\mathbf A^t$ $\mathbf A^T$ or $\mathbf A^{\mathrm T}$ $^t\!\mathbf A$ but these are usually considered suboptimal in the contemporary technological environment.

title: Definition:Transposition
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. A transposition on $S$ is a $2$-cycle. That is, a transposition is a permutation $\rho$ on $S$ which exchanges, or transposes, exactly two elements of $S$. Thus if $\rho$ is a transposition which transposes two elements $r, s \in S$, it follows from the definition of fixed elements that: $\Fix \rho = S \setminus \set {r, s}$

title: Definition:Transposition/Adjacent
snippet: Let $S_n$ denote the symmetric group on $n$ letters. An adjacent transposition is a transposition that exchanges two consecutive integers $j$ and $j + 1$, where $1 \le j < n$. In cycle notation, they are denoted: $\begin {pmatrix} j & j + 1 \end {pmatrix}$

title: Definition:Transposition/Also known as
snippet: == Transposition: Also known as == A transposition is colloquially known as a two-letter swap. Category:Definitions/Transpositions

title: Definition:Transposition Cryptography
snippet: Transposition cryptography is a technique for building ciphertext in which a permutation $\pi$ is applied to the plaintext. $\pi$ is known to the recipient of the ciphertext, who will then apply the inverse of $\pi$ to retrieve the plaintext.

title: Definition:Transversal
snippet: Geometry: Transversal (Geometry) Group Theory: Transversal (Group Theory)

title: Definition:Transversal (Geometry)
snippet: A transversal of two straight lines lying in the same plane is a straight line which intersects them in two different points. The transversal is said to cut the two lines that it crosses. 400px In the above diagram, $EF$ is a transversal of the lines $AB$ and $CD$. It is also apparent that: $AB$ is a transversal of the lines $EF$ and $CD$ $CD$ is a transversal of the lines $EF$ and $AB$ although this is not as obvious.

title: Definition:Transversal (Geometry)/Also known as
snippet: == Transversal in context of Geometry: Also known as == A transversal in the context of geometry is also known as a traverse.

title: Definition:Transversal (Geometry)/Alternate Angles
snippet: 400px Alternate angles are interior angles of a transversal which are on opposite sides and different lines. In the above figure, the pairs of alternate angles the transversal $EF$ are: $\angle AHJ$ and $\angle DJH$ $\angle CJH$ and $\angle BHJ$

title: Definition:Transversal (Geometry)/Corresponding Angles
snippet: 400px Corresponding angles are the angles in equivalent positions on the two lines cut by a transversal with respect to that transversal. In the above figure, the corresponding angles with respect to the transversal $EF$ are: $\angle AHJ$ and $\angle CJF$ $\angle AHE$ and $\angle CJH$ $\angle BHE$ and $\angle DJH$ $\angle BHJ$ and $\angle DJF$

title: Definition:Transversal (Geometry)/Exterior Angle
snippet: 400px An exterior angle of a transversal is an angle which is not between the two lines cut by a transversal. In the above figure, the exterior angles with respect to the transversal $EF$ are: $\angle AHE$ $\angle CJF$ $\angle BHE$ $\angle DJF$

title: Definition:Transversal (Geometry)/Interior Angle
snippet: 400px An interior angle of a transversal is an angle which is between the two lines cut by that transversal. In the above figure, the interior angles with respect to the transversal $EF$ are: $\angle AHJ$ $\angle CJH$ $\angle BHJ$ $\angle DJH$

title: Definition:Transversal (Group Theory)
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$. Let $S \subseteq G$ be a subset of $G$.

title: Definition:Transversal (Group Theory)/Left Transversal
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$. Let $S \subseteq G$ be a subset of $G$. $S$ is a left transversal for $H$ in $G$ every left coset of $H$ contains exactly one element of $S$.

title: Definition:Transversal (Group Theory)/Right Transversal
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$. Let $S \subseteq G$ be a subset of $G$. $S$ is a right transversal for $H$ in $G$ every right coset of $H$ contains exactly one element of $S$.

title: Definition:Transversality Conditions
snippet: Let $\map {\mathbf y} x$ be a differentiable vector-valued function. Let $J \sqbrk {\mathbf y}$ be a functional of the following form: $\ds J \sqbrk {\mathbf y} = \int_{P_1}^{P_2} \map F {x, \mathbf y, \mathbf y', \ldots} \rd x$ where $P_1$, $P_2$ are points on given differentiable manifolds $M_1$ and $M_2$. Suppose we are looking for $\mathbf y$ extremizing $J$. The system of equations to be solved consists of differential Euler equations and algebraic equations at both endpoints. Then the set of all algebraic equations at both endpoints are called transversality conditions.

title: Definition:Transverse Axis of Hyperbola/Also defined as
snippet: == Transverse Axis of Hyperbola: Also defined as == Some sources define the transverse axis to be the (infinite) straight line passing through the vertices and foci of $K$. However, at the policy is to define that as the major axis of $K$.

title: Definition:Transverse Axis of Hyperbola/Also known as
snippet: == Transverse Axis of Hyperbola: Also known as == Some sources refer to the transverse axis as the major axis. However, at the policy is to use the latter term to mean the (infinite) straight line passing through the vertices and foci of $K$. Category:Definitions/Hyperbolas

title: Definition:Transverse Component
snippet: Consider a vector $\mathbf v$ embedded in a polar plane. Let $\mathbf v$ be applied at a point $p$. Let: $\mathbf v_r$ be the component of $\mathbf v$ in the direction of the radial coordinate of $p$ $\mathbf v_\theta$ be the component of $\mathbf v$ in the direction of the angular coordinate of $p$ The component $\mathbf v_\theta$ is the transverse component of $\mathbf v$.

title: Definition:Transverse Curve
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $I, J \subseteq \R$ be real intervals. Let $\Gamma : J \times I \to M$ be a one-parameter family of curves, where $\times$ denotes the cartesian product. Let $t \in I$ be constant. Then for all $s \in J$ the map $\map {\Gamma^{\paren t}} s = \map \Gamma {s, t}$ is called the transverse curve.

title: Definition:Transverse Wave
snippet: A transverse wave is a wave whose energy is propagated by the displacement of the medium occurs in a plane which is perpendicular to the direction of propagation.

title: Definition:Trapdoor Function
snippet: A trapdoor function is a mapping $f$ which is: for a given $x$ in the domain of $f$ is easy to calculate for a given $y$ in the image of $f$ is hard to calculate unless a specific piece of information $t$ is supplied, in which case it is easy. That piece of information is known as the trapdoor.

title: Definition:Trapdoor Function/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Trapdoor Function == The concept of a trapdoor function was invented by and in $1975$.

title: Definition:Trapezium/Definition 1
snippet: A trapezium is a quadrilateral which has exactly one pair of sides that are parallel. 700px

title: Definition:Trapezium/Definition 2
snippet: A trapezium is a quadrilateral which has $2$ parallel sides whose lengths are unequal. 700px

title: Definition:Trapezium/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Trapezium == The plural of trapezium is trapezia. The word comes from Latin, in which language it is a neuter noun of the second declension, hence its plural form.

title: Definition:Trapezium and Trapezoid/Usage Differences
snippet: == Trapezium and Trapezoid: Usage Differences == The North American definitions of trapezium and trapezoid differ from most of the rest of the world as follows: a trapezoid has one pair of sides that are parallel a trapezium does not have a pair of parallel sides. This is the opposite way round from the definitions as used in most of the rest of the world, as used by . In order to reduce confusion, when a trapezoid is intended, it may be better to use the term irregular quadrilateral instead of trapezoid.

title: Definition:Traveling Salesman Problem
snippet: == Problem == The traveling salesman problem is the following problem in network analysis: Given any complete (or near-complete) weighted graph, find a minimum-weight Hamilton cycle.

title: Definition:Traveling Salesman Problem/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Traveling Salesman Problem == The UK English spelling of the traveling salesman problem is travelling salesman problem. The traveling salesman problem gets its name from the practical application of a salesman, traveling to a number of cities, looking for the optimum route that will keep the distance traveled to a minimum. It is understood that the distance between each pair of cities is known (thereby establishing that the game plan is a complete weighted graph).

title: Definition:Travelling With and Against the Flow Puzzle
snippet: A travelling with and against the flow puzzle is a problem of the form: A body travels a certain distance $d$ through a medium in the same direction as the constant flow of that medium in a given time $t_1$. The same body travels the same distance $d$ in the opposite direction, that is against the flow of the medium, in a given time $t_2$.
