snippet: Various symbols are encountered that denote the concept of universal quantifier: {| border="1" cellpadding="4" cellspacing="0" style="font-weight:bold; text-align:center; |- ! Symbol ! Origin |- | $\forall x$ | : Untersuchungen über das logische Schließen (1935) |- | $\paren x$ | |- | $\Pi x$ | Łukasiewicz's Polish notation |- | $\wedge x$ or $\bigwedge x$ | |- | $\ds \operatorname{\Large {\textsf A} } \limits_{x, y, \dotsc}$ | |}

title: Definition:Universal Set
snippet: Sets are considered to be subsets of some large universal set. Exactly what this universal set is will vary depending on the subject and context. When discussing particular sets, it should be made clear just what that universal set is. However, note that from There Exists No Universal Set, this universal set cannot be everything that there is.

title: Definition:Universal Set/Also known as
snippet: == Universal Set: Also known as == Some sources refer to the universal set as the universe of discourse, which name is also used for a similar concept in the field of logic. Some sources just use universe, but this has several meanings, depending on the contaxt. Some sources (particularly in the context of probability theory) refer to it as the space.

title: Definition:Universal Set/Notation
snippet: == Universal Set: Notation == The traditional symbol used to signify the universal set is $\mathfrak A$. However, this is old-fashioned and inconvenient, so some newer texts have taken to using $U$ or a variant: has selected $\mathbb U$ as its standard. With this notation, this definition can be put into symbols as: $\forall S: S \subseteq \mathbb U$ The use of $\mathbb U$ or a variant is not universal (no pun intended). Other symbols that may be encountered for the universal set include: $X$ $E$ or $\EE$, or a variant $S$

title: Definition:Universal Statement
snippet: A universal statement is one which expresses the fact that all objects (in a particular universe of discourse) have a particular property. That is, a statement of the form: $\forall x: \map P x$ where: $\forall$ is the universal quantifier $P$ is a predicate symbol. It means: All $x$ (in some given universe of discourse) have the property $P$. Note that if there exist no $x$ in this particular universe, $\forall x: \map P x$ is always true: see vacuous truth.

title: Definition:Universal Statement/Also known as
snippet: == Universal Statement: Also known as == A universal statement can also be referred to as: a universal sentence, or more wordily, a sentence of a universal character a general sentence a general statement.

title: Definition:Universally Compatible Relation
snippet: A relation $\RR$ is universally compatible on a set $S$ it is compatible with every closed operation that can be defined on $S$. Category:Definitions/Abstract Algebra

title: Definition:Universally Congruent
snippet: A equivalence $\RR$ is universally congruent on a set $S$ it is a congruence for every closed operation that can be defined on $S$. Category:Definitions/Congruence Relations

title: Definition:Universe
snippet: Predicate Logic: Universe of Discourse Set Theory: Universal Set Grothendieck Universe Class Theory: Universal Class Statistics: Universe: another word for population. Physics, etc.: Physical Universe: the actual place where we live.

title: Definition:Universe of Discourse
snippet: The universe of discourse is the term used to mean everything we are talking about. When introducing the symbols: $\forall$ (the universal quantifier) or: $\exists$ (the existential quantifier) it is understood that the objects referred to are those in the specified universe of discourse. It is usual to define that universe.

title: Definition:Universe of Discourse/Also known as
snippet: == Universe of Discourse: Also known as == The universe of discourse is also known as: the universe of interpretation the domain of discourse. Some sources use just universe or domain, but those have wider meanings.

title: Definition:Unknown
snippet: An unknown is an indeterminate variable in a system of equations or inequalities whose value the solver is invited to determine.

title: Definition:Unlike Electric Charges/Also known as
snippet: == Unlike Electric Charges/Also known as == Some sources refer to unlike charges as opposite charges. Category:Definitions/Electric Charge

title: Definition:Unlimited Register Machine
snippet: An unlimited register machine, abbreviated URM, is an abstract machine with the following characteristics:

title: Definition:Unlimited Register Machine/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Unlimited Register Machine == The unlimited register machine is a more versatile and easy to understand alternative to the Turing machine, which has the same capabilities and (to a certain extent) to which it is logically equivalent. It was introduced in a paper by and published in $1963$.

title: Definition:Unlimited Register Machine/Instruction Pointer
snippet: The line number of the instruction which is currently about to be executed is known as the instruction pointer. It can be imagined as a special-purpose register in the URM whose purpose is to hold that line number.

title: Definition:Unlimited Register Machine/Null Program
snippet: The null URM program is a URM program which contains no instructions. That is, a URM program whose length is zero.

title: Definition:Unlimited Register Machine/Operation
snippet: When a URM runs a program, it always starts by executing the first instruction of the program. When it has executed an instruction, it moves to the next instruction and executes that one, unless required otherwise by a Jump instruction.

title: Definition:Unlimited Register Machine/Operation/Execution
snippet: The operation of carrying out a basic URM instruction is referred to as execution.

title: Definition:Unlimited Register Machine/Operation/Stage
snippet: The stage of computation (or just stage) of a URM program is the count of how many instructions have been executed. Thus each stage corresponds to the processing of one instruction.

title: Definition:Unlimited Register Machine/Operation/State
snippet: The state of a URM program at a particular stage is defined as: $(1): \quad$ the value of the instruction pointer $(2): \quad$ the values contained by each of the registers that are used by the URM program.

title: Definition:Unlimited Register Machine/Program
snippet: The numbers held in the registers of a URM are manipulated according to a program. A URM program is a finite sequence of basic instructions.

title: Definition:Unlimited Register Machine/Program/Basic Instruction
snippet: The basic instructions of a URM program form a finite sequence and hence can be considered a set indexed by the (positive) integer $1, 2, 3, \ldots$. The basic instructions are as follows: {| border="1" |- ! align="left" | Name ! align="left" | Notation ! align="left" | Effect ! align="left" | Description |- | Zero | $\map Z n$ | $0 \to R_n$ | Replace the number in $R_n$ by $0$. |- | Successor | $\map S n$ | $r_n + 1 \to R_n$ | Add $1$ to the number in $R_n$. |- | Copy | $\map C {m, n}$ | $r_m \to R_n$ | Replace the number in $R_n$ by the number in $R_m$ (leaving the one in $R_m$ as it was).

title: Definition:Unlimited Register Machine/Program/Highest Register
snippet: Let $\Bbb U$ denote the set of all URM programs. Let $P \in \Bbb U$ be a URM program. By definition, $P$ uses a finite number of registers. We define the function $\rho: \Bbb U \to \N$ as follows: $\forall P \in \Bbb U: \map \rho P =$ the highest register number used by $P$ That is, in any URM program $P$, no instruction refers to any register with index greater than $\map \rho P$.

title: Definition:Unlimited Register Machine/Program/Length
snippet: Let $\Bbb U$ denote the set of all URM programs. Let $P \in \Bbb U$ be a URM program. By definition, $P$ is a finite sequence of basic instructions. We define the function $\lambda: \Bbb U \to \N$ as follows: $\forall P \in \Bbb U: \map \lambda P = $ the number of basic instructions that comprise $P$ Thus $\map \lambda P$ is referred to as the length of $P$.

title: Definition:Unlimited Register Machine/Program/Line
snippet: For historical reasons, the index of an instruction in a given URM program is called its line number. We can refer either to the line of the program or the line in the URM.

title: Definition:Unlimited Register Machine/Program/Set
snippet: It is convenient to use $\Bbb U$ to stand for the set of all URM programs.

title: Definition:Unlimited Register Machine/Program/Termination
snippet: A URM program terminates when there are no more instructions to execute. This can happen in either of two ways: $(1): \quad$ If the program executes the last instruction, and this does not involve a Jump to an earlier instruction, the program will stop. $(2): \quad$ If the program executes a Jump instruction to a non-existent instruction, the program will stop.

title: Definition:Unlimited Register Machine/Register
snippet: A URM has a sequence of registers which can store natural numbers: $\set {0, 1, 2, \ldots}$. Any given URM program may make use of only a finite number of these registers. Registers are usually referred to by the subscripted uppercase letters $R_1, R_2, R_3, \ldots$. The number held at any one time by a register is usually referred to by the corresponding lowercase letter $r_1, r_2, r_3, \ldots$.

title: Definition:Unlimited Register Machine/Register/Index
snippet: The subscript (which is a natural number) appended to a URM register is called the index of that register. Hence, for example, the index of register $R_5$ is $5$.

title: Definition:Unordered Tuple
snippet: An unordered tuple is a small class in Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory that contains a finite number of elements. It is written using roster notation and is denoted: $\set {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n}$ that is: $\set {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n} = \set {x: x = a_1 \lor x = a_2 \lor \dots \lor x = a_n}$

title: Definition:Unsatisfiable
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a logical language. Let $\mathscr M$ be a formal semantics for $\LL$.

title: Definition:Unsatisfiable/Boolean Interpretations
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a WFF of propositional logic. $\mathbf A$ is called unsatisfiable (for boolean interpretations) : $\map v {\mathbf A} = \F$ for every boolean interpretation $v$ for $\mathbf A$. In terms of validity, this can be rendered: $v \not \models_{\mathrm {BI} } \mathbf A$ that is, $\mathbf A$ is invalid in every boolean interpretation of $\mathbf A$.

title: Definition:Unsatisfiable/Formula
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a logical language. Let $\mathscr M$ be a formal semantics for $\LL$. A logical formula $\phi$ of $\LL$ is unsatisfiable for $\mathscr M$ : $\phi$ is valid in none of the structures of $\mathscr M$ That is, for all structures $\MM$ of $\mathscr M$: $\MM \not\models_{\mathscr M} \phi$

title: Definition:Unsatisfiable/Set of Formulas
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a logical language. Let $\mathscr M$ be a formal semantics for $\LL$. A collection $\FF$ of logical formulas of $\LL$ is unsatisfiable for $\mathscr M$ : There is no $\mathscr M$-model $\MM$ for $\FF$ That is, for all structures $\MM$ of $\mathscr M$: $\MM \not \models_{\mathscr M} \FF$

title: Definition:Unsigned Stirling Numbers of the First Kind/Technical Note
snippet: == Technical Note for Unsigned Stirling Numbers of the First Kind == {{LatexFor|for = \ds {n \brack k} }} The braces around the n \brack k are important. The \ds is needed to create the symbol in its proper house display style. Note that while it appears that \ds \sqbrk {n \atop k} should do the same job, it is rendered with a subtle difference: $\ds \sqbrk {n \atop k}$ and so is not to be used on . title: Definition:Unsound Argument
snippet: A logical argument which either: is invalid or: has one or more false premises is described as being unsound.

title: Definition:Untouchable Number
snippet: An untouchable number is a (strictly) positive integer that is not the aliquot sum of any integer.

title: Definition:Untouchable Number/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Untouchable Number == The concept of an untouchable number was invented by .

title: Definition:Untouchable Number/Sequence
snippet: == Sequence of Untouchable Numbers == The sequence of untouchable numbers begins: $2, 5, 52, 88, 96, 120, 124, 146, 162, 188, 206, 210, 216, 238, 246, 248, 262, \ldots$

title: Definition:Up-Complete
snippet: Let $\left({S, \precsim}\right)$ be a preordered set. Then $\left({S, \precsim}\right)$ is up-complete : every directed subset of $S$ admits a supremum in $\left({S, \precsim}\right)$.

title: Definition:Up Run
snippet: An up run is a run such that the sequence is increasing.

title: Definition:Upper Adjoint/Technical Note
snippet: == Technical Note on Upper Adjoint == Category:Technical Notes

title: Definition:Upper Bound
snippet: Upper Bound of Ordered Set Upper Bound of Ordered Subset of Real Numbers Upper Bound of Mapping Upper Bound of Real-Valued Function Upper Bound of Sequence Upper Bound of Real Sequence

title: Definition:Upper Bound of Mapping
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping whose codomain is an ordered set $\struct {T, \preceq}$. Let $f$ be bounded above in $T$ by $H \in T$. Then $H$ is an upper bound of $f$.

title: Definition:Upper Bound of Mapping/Real-Valued
snippet: Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real-valued function. Let $f$ be bounded above in $\R$ by $H \in \R$. Then $H$ is an upper bound of $f$.

title: Definition:Upper Bound of Number
snippet: When considering the upper bound of a set of numbers, it is commonplace to ignore the set and instead refer just to the number itself. Thus the construction: The set of numbers which fulfil the propositional function $\map P n$ is bounded above with the upper bound $N$ would be reported as: The number $n$ such that $\map P n$ has the upper bound $N$. This construct obscures the details of what is actually being stated. Its use on is considered an abuse of notation and so discouraged. This also applies in the case where it is the upper bound of a mapping which is under discussion.

title: Definition:Upper Bound of Sequence
snippet: A special case of an upper bound of a mapping is an upper bound of a sequence, where the domain of the mapping is $\N$. Let $\struct {T, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $T$. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be bounded above in $T$ by $H \in T$. Then $H$ is an upper bound of $\sequence {x_n}$.

title: Definition:Upper Bound of Sequence/Real
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a real sequence. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be bounded above by $H \in \R$. Then $H$ is an upper bound of $\sequence {x_n}$.

title: Definition:Upper Bound of Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $T$ be a subset of $S$. An upper bound for $T$ (in $S$) is an element $M \in S$ such that: $\forall t \in T: t \preceq M$ That is, $M$ succeeds every element of $T$.

title: Definition:Upper Bound of Set/Also defined as
snippet: == Upper Bound of Set: Also known as == Some sources use the terminology the upper bound for the notion of supremum.

title: Definition:Upper Bound of Set/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $\R$ be the set of real numbers. Let $T$ be a subset of $\R$. An upper bound for $T$ (in $\R$) is an element $M \in \R$ such that: $\forall t \in T: t \le M$ That is, $M$ is greater than or equal to every element of $T$.

title: Definition:Upper Closure/Element
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set. Let $a \in S$. The upper closure of $a$ (in $S$) is defined as: $a^\succcurlyeq := \set {b \in S: a \preccurlyeq b}$ That is, $a^\succcurlyeq$ is the set of all elements of $S$ that succeed $a$.

title: Definition:Upper Closure/Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set or preordered set. Let $T \subseteq S$. The upper closure of $T$ (in $S$) is defined as: $T^\succeq := \bigcup \set {t^\succeq: t \in T}$ where $t^\succeq$ denotes the upper closure of $t$ in $S$. That is: $T^\succeq := \set {u \in S: \exists t \in T: t \preceq u}$

title: Definition:Upper Darboux Integral
snippet: Let $\closedint a b$ be a closed real interval. Let $f: \closedint a b \to \R$ be a bounded real function. The upper Darboux integral of $f$ over $\closedint a b$ is defined as: $\ds \overline {\int_a^b} \map f x \rd x = \inf_P \map U P$ where: the infimum is taken over all subdivisions $P$ of $\closedint a b$ $\map U P$ denotes the upper Darboux sum of $f$ on $\closedint a b$ belonging to $P$.

title: Definition:Upper Darboux Integral/Also known as
snippet: == Upper Darboux Integral: Also known as == The upper Darboux integral is also known just as the upper integral. Some sources refer to it as the upper Riemann integral.

title: Definition:Upper Darboux Integral/Rectangle
snippet: Let $R$ be a closed rectangle in $\R^n$. Let $f : R \to \R$ be a bounded real-valued function on $R$. The upper Darboux integral of $f$ over $R$ is defined as: $\ds \overline{\int_R} \map f x \rd x = \inf_P \map U P$ where: $P$ ranges over all finite subdivisions of $R$. $\map U P$ denotes the upper Darboux sum of $f$ on $R$ with respect to $P$.

title: Definition:Upper Darboux Sum
Definition:Upper Darboux Sum/Also known as
snippet: == Upper Darboux Sum: Also known as == The notation $\map U {f, P}$ or $\map U {P, f}$ can be used in place of $\map {U^{\paren f} } P$. The upper Darboux sum is also known as: the upper Riemann sum (for ) the upper sum.

title: Definition:Upper Darboux Sum/Rectangle
snippet: Let $R$ be a closed rectangle in $\R^n$. Let $f : R \to \R$ be a bounded real-valued function. Let $P$ be a finite subdivision of $R$. Let $S$ be the set of subrectangles of $P$. For every: $r = \closedint {a_1} {b_1} \times \dotso \times \closedint {a_n} {b_n} \in S$ define: $\ds M_r^{\paren f} = \sup_{x \mathop \in r} \map f x$ $\ds \map v r = \prod_{1 \mathop \le i \mathop \le n} \paren {b_i - a_i}$ Then: $\ds \map {U^{\paren f}} P = \sum_{r \mathop \in S} M_r^{\paren f} \map v r$ is called the upper Darboux sum of $f$ on $R$ with respect to $P$.

title: Definition:Upper Limit (Topological Space)
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $f : S \to \overline \R$ be an extended real valued function. Let $x_0 \in X$. Let $\map \mho {x_0}$ be the set of open neighborhoods of $x_0$ in $\struct {S, \tau}$. We define the upper limit of $f$ at $x_0$ by: $\ds \limsup_{x \mathop \to x_0} \map f x = \inf_{V \in \map \mho {x_0} } \paren {\sup_{x \mathop \in V} \map f x}$

title: Definition:Upper Section
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $U \subseteq S$.

title: Definition:Upper Section/Also known as
snippet: == Upper Section: Also known as == An upper section is also known as an upper set. Variants of this can also be seen: upper-closed set or upward-closed set. Some sources call it an upset or up-set. Sometimes the word section is understood, and such a collection referred to solely with the adjective upper. Category:Definitions/Upper Sections

title: Definition:Upper Section/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $U \subseteq S$. $U$ is an upper section in $S$ : $\forall u \in U: \forall s \in S: u \preceq s \implies s \in U$

title: Definition:Upper Section/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $U \subseteq S$. $U$ is an upper section in $S$ : $U^\succeq \subseteq U$ where $U^\succeq$ is the upper closure of $U$.

title: Definition:Upper Section/Definition 3
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $U \subseteq S$. $U$ is an upper section in $S$ : $U^\succeq = U$ where $U^\succeq$ is the upper closure of $U$.

title: Definition:Upper Semicontinuous
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $f : S \to \overline \R$ be an extended real valued function. Let $x_0 \in S$. We say that $f$ is upper semicontinuous at $x_0$ : $\ds \limsup_{x \mathop \to x_0} \map f x = \map f {x_0}$ where $\limsup$ denotes the upper limit.

title: Definition:Upper Semicontinuous/Subset
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $f : S \to \overline \R$ be an extended real valued function. Let $A \subseteq S$. We say that $f$ is upper semicontinuous on $A$ it is upper semicontinuous at each $x_0 \in S$.

title: Definition:Upper Triangular Matrix/Also defined as
snippet: == Upper Triangular Matrix: Also defined as == Some sources define an upper triangular matrix only as a square matrix.

title: Definition:Upper Wythoff Sequence/Definition 1
snippet: The upper Wythoff sequence is the complementary Beatty sequence on the golden section $\phi$. It starts: $0, 2, 5, 7, 10, 13, 15, 18, 20, 23, 26, 28, 31, 34, \ldots$

title: Definition:Upper Wythoff Sequence/Definition 2
snippet: The upper Wythoff sequence is the Beatty sequence on the square $\phi^2$ of the golden section $\phi$. It starts: $0, 2, 5, 7, 10, 13, 15, 18, 20, 23, 26, 28, 31, 34, \ldots$

title: Definition:Uranium/238
snippet: == Isotope of Uranium == Uranium-$238$ is the isotope of uranium which has $146$ neutrons in addition to its $92$ protons. U-$238$ is radioactive, with a half-life of approximately $4.5 \times 10^9$ years. Category:Definitions/Uranium Category:Definitions/Examples of Radioactive Isotopes

title: Definition:Uranium/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Uranium == The word uranium derives from the name of the planet Uranus, which had been discovered $8$ years before the element had been believed to have been extracted from its ore. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Uranus
snippet: Uranus is the seventh planet of the solar system from the sun. Its orbit lies between those of Saturn and Neptune. Category:Definitions/Solar System

title: Definition:Urn
snippet: An urn is a hypothetical container from which one may draw one of a number of objects (usually defined to be balls) of assorted colours. The idea is that one cannot see the ball one is withdrawing until it is out of the urn. Therefore it is not possible to know in advance what colour ball one is taking. The probability that a particular ball being withdrawn has a particular colour depends entirely on the distribution within the urn of the various colours of the balls within. This is used as an abstraction of a randomizing device in probability theory.

title: Definition:Urysohn Function
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $A, B \subseteq S$ such that $A \cap B = \O$. Let $f: S \to \closedint 0 1$ be a continuous mapping where $\closedint 0 1$ is the closed unit interval. Then $f$ is an Urysohn function for $A$ and $B$ : $f {\restriction_A} = 0, f {\restriction_B} = 1$ That is:

title: Definition:Urysohn Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is an Urysohn space : For two arbitrary distinct elements $x, y \in S$ (that is, $x \ne y$), there exists an Urysohn function for $\set x$ and $\set y$.

title: Definition:Urysohn Space/Also known as
snippet: == Urysohn Space: Also known as == Hence an Urysohn space is also known as: a functionally Hausdorff space, for . a completely $T_2$ space.

title: Definition:Urysohn Space/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Urysohn Space == The name is pronounced something like oo-ree-son, and not yoo-ree-son. Hence when using the to introduce eponymous objects bearing his name, an should be used, not a. Hence: an Urysohn space not: a Urysohn space. This may seem awkward to Anglophones, so please be aware of this point. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Usual Metric
snippet: Let $X$ be one of the standard number fields $\Q$, $\R$, $\C$. Let $X^n$ be a cartesian space on $X$. The usual metric on $X^n$ is the Euclidean metric on $X^n$:

title: Definition:Usual Ordering
snippet: Let $X$ be one of the sets of numbers: $\N$, $\Z$, $\Q$, $\R$. The usual ordering on $X$ is the conventional counting and measuring order on $X$ that is learned when one is initially introduced to numbers.

title: Definition:Usual Ordering/Also known as
snippet: == Usual Ordering: Also known as == The usual ordering is also known as the natural ordering. Category:Definitions/Usual Ordering

title: Definition:Usual Ordering of Ordinals
snippet: Let $\On$ denote the class of all ordinals. The usual ordering $\le$ on $\On$ is the subset relation: $a \le b \iff a \subseteq b$ and its corresponding strict version: $a < b \iff a \subsetneqq b$

title: Definition:Utilities Problem
snippet: The utilities problem is a problem in graph theory as follows: $3$ households are each to be connected to $3$ civic utilities (the archetypes being water, gas and electricity) in such a way that the conduits do not cross. This is equivalent to investigating whether the Thomsen graph (that is, the complete bipartite graph $K_{3, 3}$) is planar.

title: Definition:Utilities Problem/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Utilities Problem == The utilities problem appears first to have been posed by in $1913$. It has become a popular problem in puzzle collections ever since. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Utility Function
snippet: Let $G$ be a game. Let $P$ be a player of $G$. Let $C$ be the set $C$ of consequences of the moves available to $P$. A utility function on $C$ is a mapping from $C$ to the real numbers $\R$ so as to define a preference relation on $C$: $U: C \to \R$ by the condition: $\forall x, y \in C: x \succsim y \iff \map U x \ge \map U y$

title: Definition:Utility Theory
snippet: Utility theory is a branch of decision theory in which decisions are based on the concept of utility or benefit.

title: Definition:Utility Theory/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Utility Theory == An axiomatic foundation to utility theory was developed by and in $1944$. Interest often focuses on determining policies which maximize expected utility.

title: Definition:V Operator on Hilbert Space
snippet: Let $\struct {\HH, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be a Hilbert space over $\C$. Let $\HH \times \HH$ be the Hilbert space direct sum of $\HH$ with itself. Define $V : \HH \times \HH \to \HH \times \HH$ by: $\map V {x, y} = \tuple {-y, x}$ for each $\tuple {x, y} \in \HH \times \HH$. We call $V$ the $V$ operator for $\HH$.

title: Definition:Vacuous
snippet: Logic: A vacuous truth is a statement about a collection of objects none of which exist. By definition, such a statement is understood to be true. A vacuous term is a term of a categorical syllogism $\map F x$ such that nothing in the universe of discourse has the property of the predicate $F$. Set Theory: The vacuous set is the same thing as the empty set, that is, the set with no elements. This Empty Set is Unique. Algebra: A vacuous summation is a summation over an empty set of summands. Such a sum has a value of zero.

title: Definition:Vacuous/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Vacuous == The word vacuous literally means empty. It derives from the Latin word vacuum, meaning empty space. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Vacuous Term
snippet: Let $\map F x$ be a term of a categorical syllogism. Let $\map F x$ be such that there exists no $x$ in the universe of discourse which has the property of the predicate $F$. Then $\map F x$ is known as a vacuous term.

title: Definition:Vacuous Term/Also known as
snippet: == Vacuous Term: Also known as == A vacuous term is also known as an empty term.

title: Definition:Vacuous Truth
snippet: Let $P \implies Q$ be a conditional statement. Suppose that $P$ is false. Then the statement $P \implies Q$ is a vacuous truth, or is vacuously true. It is frequently encountered in the form: $\forall x: \map P x \implies \map Q x$ when the propositional function $\map P x$ is false for all $x$. Such a statement is also a vacuous truth. For example, the statement: All cats who are expert chess-players are also fluent in ancient Sanskrit is (vacuously) true, because (as far as the author knows) there are no cats who are expert chess-players.

title: Definition:Vacuum
snippet: A vacuum is the physical state of being completely empty of matter. It is a physical ideal, and has never been (and probably can never be) fully realised.

title: Definition:Vacuum/Also known as
snippet: == Vacuum: Also known as == In certain contexts in physics, the term free space is used for a volume of space in which there is a vacuum. Category:Definitions/Vacuum

title: Definition:Vacuum/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Vacuum == The word vacuum is a Latin word meaning empty.

title: Definition:Vacuum Permeability
snippet: == Physical Constant == The vacuum permeability is the physical constant denoted $\mu_0$ defined as: $\mu_0:= \dfrac {2 \alpha h} {e^2 c}$ where: $e$ is the elementary charge $\alpha$ is the fine-structure constant $h$ is Planck's constant $c$ is the speed of light defined in $\mathrm m \, \mathrm s^{-1}$ Of the above, only the fine-structure constant $\alpha$ is a measured value; the others are defined. It can be defined as the capability of a magnetic field to permeate a vacuum.

title: Definition:Vacuum Permeability/Also known as
snippet: == Vacuum Permeability: Also known as== The vacuum permeability is also known by the terms: vacuum magnetic permeability permeability of free space permeability of vacuum magnetic constant. Some sources denote the vacuum permeability with the symbol $\Gamma_m$.

title: Definition:Vacuum Permeability/Dimension
snippet: The vacuum permeability has the dimension $\mathsf {M L T^{-2} I^{-2} }$. This arises from its definition as inductance per unit length: $\dfrac {\mathsf {M L^2 T^{-2} I^{-2} } } {\mathsf L}$ Category:Definitions/Dimensions of Measurement Category:Definitions/Vacuum Permeability

title: Definition:Vacuum Permeability/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Vacuum Permittivity == Before the redefinition of the SI base units on $20$ May $2019$, the vacuum permeability was defined as exactly $4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \, \mathrm H \, \mathrm m^{-1}$ (henries per metre). As a consequence, the vacuum permittivity was defined as $\varepsilon_0 = 8 \cdotp 85418 \, 78176 \, 2039 \times 10^{-12} \, \mathrm F \, \mathrm m^{-1}$ (farads per metre) which was derived from the equation: $\varepsilon_0 := \dfrac 1 {\mu_0 c^2}$ where $c$ is the speed of light defined as exactly $299 \, 792 \, 458 \, \mathrm m \, \mathrm s^{-1}$.

title: Definition:Vacuum Permittivity
snippet: == Physical Constant == The vacuum permittivity is the physical constant denoted $\varepsilon_0$ defined as: $\varepsilon_0 := \dfrac {e^2} {2 \alpha h c}$ where: $e$ is the elementary charge $\alpha$ is the fine-structure constant $h$ is Planck's constant $c$ is the speed of light defined in $\mathrm m \, \mathrm s^{-1}$ Of the above, only the fine-structure constant $\alpha$ is a measured value; the others are defined. It can be defined as the capability of an electric field to permeate a vacuum.

title: Definition:Vacuum Permittivity/Also known as
snippet: == Vacuum Permittivity: Also known as == The vacuum permittivity is also known by the terms: permittivity of free space permittivity of empty space permittivity in (or of) vacuum distributed capacitance of the vacuum The term electric constant has now apparently been accepted by many standards organisations worldwide. However, as from $20$ May $2019$, the definition of $\varepsilon_0$ is no longer as a defined constant, but derived ultimately from the fine-structure constant, which is a measured value. Hence many authorities (including ) prefer not to use electric constant.

title: Definition:Vacuum Permittivity/Dimension
snippet: The vacuum permittivity has the dimension $\mathsf {M^{-1} L^{-3} T^4 I^2}$. This arises from its definition as capacitance per unit length: $\dfrac {\mathsf {M^{-1} L^{-2} T^4 I^2} } {\mathsf L}$ Category:Definitions/Dimensions of Measurement Category:Definitions/Vacuum Permittivity

title: Definition:Vacuum Permittivity/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Vacuum Permittivity == Before the redefinition of the SI base units on $20$ May $2019$, the vacuum permittivity was: $\varepsilon_0 = 8 \cdotp 85418 \, 78176 \, 2039 \times 10^{-12} \, \mathrm F \, \mathrm m^{-1}$ (farads per metre) which was derived from the equation: $\varepsilon_0 := \dfrac 1 {\mu_0 c^2}$ where: $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability defined as exactly $4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \, \mathrm H \, \mathrm m^{-1}$ (henries per metre) $c$ is the speed of light defined as exactly $299 \, 792 \, 458 \, \mathrm m \, \mathrm s^{-1}$ However, since $20$ May $2019$, the…

title: Definition:Vague
snippet: A concept is vague if borderline cases for its application occur. That is, if there are "grey areas" where it is unclear whether or not it can be applied.

title: Definition:Vague Convergence of Borel Measures
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\sequence {\mu_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence of Borel measures on $\struct {X, \tau}$. Let $\mu$ be a Borel measure on $\struct {X, \tau}$. Let $\map {C_c} X$ be the set of continuous functions $f : X \to \C$ such that: the support $\map \supp f$ is compact. We say that $\sequence {\mu_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ converges vaguely to $\mu$ : $\ds \int f \rd \mu_n \to \int f \rd \mu$ for all $f \in \map {C_c} X$.

title: Definition:Valency of Predicate/Also known as
snippet: == Valency of Predicate: Also known as == A predicate with a valency of $n$ is also known as an $n$-place predicate.

title: Definition:Valid
snippet: Logic: Valid Argument Formal Systems: Valid (Formal Systems)

title: Definition:Valid/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Valid == The word valid ultimately derives from the same root as the word value. Thus valid can be taken to mean having value. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Valid Argument
snippet: A valid argument is a logical argument in which the premises provide conclusive reasons for the conclusion. When an argument is valid, we may say one of the following:

title: Definition:Valid Argument/Also known as
snippet: == Valid Argument: Also known as == A valid argument is also known as a truth preserving argument. Likewise, validity is also known as truth preservation. Some authors use the term sound argument to mean the same thing that is defined here as a proof. However, as some use sound argument to mean the same thing as a valid argument, it is recommended that this term not be used.

title: Definition:Valid Argument/Linguistic Warning
snippet: == Linguistic Warning on Valid Argument == In natural language, especially when a person is attempting to sound more learned than they are, it is commonplace to discuss the nature of statements as being valid or invalid. What is really meant, of course, is that a statement is either true or false.

title: Definition:Valid Time Indication
snippet: Consider an analog clock with an hour hand $H$ and a minute hand $M$. A valid time indication is an arrangement of $H$ and $M$ which indicates a specific time of day (either a.m. or p.m.).

title: Definition:Valuation
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \cdot}$ be a ring. A valuation on $R$ is a mapping: $\nu: R \to \Z \cup \left\{{+\infty}\right\}$ which fulfils the valuation axioms:

title: Definition:Valuation/Also defined as
snippet: == Valuation: Also defined as == A valuation is usually defined on a field. However, the valuation axioms are as equally well defined, as here on , on a ring. Category:Definitions/Valuations

title: Definition:Valuation Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {D, +, \circ}$ be an integral domain. Let $K$ be the field of quotients of $D$. Let $K$ be such that: for all $x \in K$, either $x \in D$ or $x^{-1} \in D$. Then $D$ is a valuation ring of $K$.

orm x \le 1}$ That is, the valuation ring induced by the non-Archimedean norm $

title: Definition:Value
snippet: Analysis and Number Theory: Value of Variable Absolute Value Value of Continued Fraction Mapping Theory: Value: a synonym for the image of an element in the domain of a mapping Game Theory: Value of Game Value of Matrix Game Physics: Value: the number of units of a particular physical quantity that go to make up a particular physical constant.

title: Definition:Value (Physics)
snippet: Let $K$ be a physical constant. The value of $K$ is defined as the number of units of the specific physical quantity that go to make up $K$. Category:Definitions/Physics

title: Definition:Value of Continued Fraction
snippet: Let $F$ be a field, such as the field of real numbers $\R$.

title: Definition:Value of Continued Fraction/Finite
snippet: Let $F$ be a field, such as the field of real numbers $\R$. Let $n \ge 0$ be a natural number. Let $\sequence {a_k}_{0 \mathop \le k \mathop \le n}$ be a finite continued fraction in $F$. Let $\overline F = F \cup \set \infty$ be extended by infinity.

title: Definition:Value of Continued Fraction/Infinite
snippet: Let $\struct {F, \norm {\,\cdot\,} }$ be a valued field. Let $C = \sequence {a_n}_{n \mathop \ge 0}$ be a infinite continued fraction in $F$. Let $C$ converge to $x \in F$: Then $x$ is the value of $C$.

Then the value of $\mathbf A$ under $\sigma$, denoted $\map {\operatorname{val}_\AA} {\mathbf A} \sqbrk \sigma$, is defined recursively by: If $\mathbf A = \map p {\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_n}$ with $\tau_i$ terms and $p \in \PP_n$ an $n$-ary predicate symbol: $\map {\operatorname{val}_\AA} {\map p {\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_n} } \sqbrk \sigma := \map {p_\AA} {\map {\operatorname{val}_\AA} {\tau_1} \sqbrk \sigma, \ldots, \map…

title: Definition:Value of Formula under Assignment/Sentence
snippet: Let $\AA$ be a structure for predicate logic. Let $\mathbf A$ be a sentence in the language of predicate logic. The value of $\mathbf A$ in $\AA$, denoted $\map {\operatorname{val}_\AA} {\mathbf A}$, is defined as: $\map {\operatorname{val}_\AA} {\mathbf A} := \map {\operatorname{val}_\AA} {\mathbf A} \sqbrk \O$ where $\O$ is the empty mapping considered as an assignment for $\mathbf A$ and $\map { \operatorname{val}_\AA} {\mathbf A} \sqbrk \O$ is the value of $\mathbf A$ under $\O$.

title: Definition:Value of Game
snippet: Let $G$ be a game. The value of $G$ is the payoff resulting from a solution of $G$.

title: Definition:Value of Infinite Continued Fraction/Also known as
snippet: == Value of Infinite Continued Fraction: Also known as == The value of an infinite continued fraction is also known as its limit. Category:Definitions/Continued Fractions

title: Definition:Value of Term under Assignment
snippet: Let $\tau$ be a term in the language of predicate logic $\LL_1$. Let $\AA$ be an $\LL_1$-structure. Let $\sigma$ be an assignment for $\tau$ in $\AA$. Then the value of $\tau$ under $\sigma$, denoted $\map {\operatorname{val}_\AA} \tau \sqbrk \sigma$, is defined recursively by: If $\tau = x$, with $x \in \Dom \sigma$ a variable in the domain of $\sigma$: $\map {\operatorname{val}_\AA} x \sqbrk \sigma := \map \sigma x$ If $\tau = \map f {\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_n}$ with $\tau_i$ terms and $f \in \FF_n$ an $n$-ary function symbol: $\map {\operatorname{val}_\AA} {\map f {\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_n} }…

title: Definition:Valued Field
snippet: Let $\struct {K, +, \circ}$ be a field. Let $\norm {\,\cdot\,}$ be a norm on $K$. Then $\struct {K, \norm{\,\cdot\,} }$ is a valued field.

title: Definition:Valued Field of P-adic Numbers
snippet: Let $p$ be any prime number. Let $\Q_p$ be the field of $p$-adic numbers. Let $\norm {\,\cdot\,}_p$ be the $p$-adic norm on $\Q_p$. The valued field of p-adic numbers is the valued field $\struct {\Q_p, \norm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$.

title: Definition:Van der Pol's Equation
snippet: Van der Pol's equation is a second order ordinary differential equation of the form of a wave equation with a damping factor $\mu$: $\dfrac {\d^2 x} {\d t^2} - \mu \paren {1 - x^2} \dfrac {\d x} {\d t} + x = 0$

title: Definition:Van der Pol's Equation/Also defined as
snippet: == Van der Pol's Equation: Also defined as == Van der Pol's equation can also be seen in the form: $\dfrac {\d^2 x} {\d t^2} - \alpha \paren {1 - x^2} \dfrac {\d x} {\d t} + \beta x = 0$ that is, with two coefficients that can be varied as required.

title: Definition:Van der Pol's Equation/Also known as
snippet: == Van der Pol's Equation: Also known as == The second order ODE van der Pol's equation can also be rendered as the van der Pol equation.

title: Definition:Van der Pol's Equation/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on van der Pol's Equation == Van der Pol's equation was introduced and investigated by from $1927$ in his investigations into the behavior of electronic circuits in early radios. However, its scope has shown itself to extend to model a number of other phenomena in physics and biology.

title: Definition:Van der Pol's Equation/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on van der Pol's Equation == Because of the idiosyncratic nature of the rendering of Dutch surnames with van der in them, the name van der Pol's equation properly starts with a lowercase letter, unless starting a sentence. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Vandermonde Determinant

title: Definition:Vandermonde Determinant/Formulation 1
snippet: The Vandermonde determinant of order $n$ is the determinant defined as: $V_n = \begin {vmatrix} 1 & x_1 & {x_1}^2 & \cdots & {x_1}^{n - 2} & {x_1}^{n - 1} \\ 1 & x_2 & {x_2}^2 & \cdots & {x_2}^{n - 2} & {x_2}^{n - 1} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots \\ 1 & x_n & {x_n}^2 & \cdots & {x_n}^{n - 2} & {x_n}^{n - 1} \end {vmatrix}$

title: Definition:Vandermonde Determinant/Formulation 1/Also presented as/Ones at Top
snippet: The Vandermonde determinant of order $n$ can be presented in various orientations, for example: $V_n = \begin {vmatrix} 1 & 1 & \cdots & 1 \\ x_1 & x_2 & \cdots & x_n \\ {x_1}^2 & {x_2}^2 & \cdots & {x_n}^2 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ {x_1}^{n - 2} & {x_2}^{n - 2} & \cdots & {x_n}^{n - 2} \\ {x_1}^{n - 1} & {x_2}^{n - 1} & \cdots & {x_n}^{n - 1} \end {vmatrix}$

title: Definition:Vandermonde Determinant/Formulation 2
snippet: The Vandermonde determinant of order $n$ is the determinant defined as: $V_n = \begin {vmatrix} x_1 & {x_1}^2 & \cdots & {x_1}^n \\ x_2 & {x_2}^2 & \cdots & {x_2}^n \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ x_n & {x_n}^2 & \cdots & {x_n}^n \end{vmatrix}$

snippet: == Vandermonde Matrix: Also known as == A Vandermonde matrix is often seen referred to as Vandermonde's matrix. The first form is preferred on because it is slightly less grammatically unwieldy than the possessive style. Category:Definitions/Vandermonde Matrices

title: Definition:Vandermonde Matrix/Formulation 1
snippet: The Vandermonde matrix of order $n$ is a square matrix specified variously as: $\begin {bmatrix} 1 & x_1 & {x_1}^2 & \cdots & {x_1}^{n - 2} & {x_1}^{n - 1} \\ 1 & x_2 & {x_2}^2 & \cdots & {x_2}^{n - 2} & {x_2}^{n - 1} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots \\ 1 & x_n & {x_n}^2 & \cdots & {x_n}^{n - 2} & {x_n}^{n - 1} \end {bmatrix}$ That is, such that: $a_{i j} = {x_i}^{j - 1}$

title: Definition:Vandermonde Matrix/Formulation 2
snippet: The Vandermonde matrix of order $n$ is a square matrix specified variously as: $\begin {bmatrix} x_1 & x_2 & \cdots & x_n \\ x_1^2 & x_2^2 & \cdots & x_n^2 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ x_1^n & x_2^n & \cdots & x_n^n \end {bmatrix}$ That is, such that: $a_{i j} = {x_j}^i$

title: Definition:Vanish
snippet: A variable in an equation is said to vanish when (under appropriate conditions) its value becomes zero.

title: Definition:Vanishing Ideal
snippet: Definition:Vanishing Ideal of Set of Prime Ideals Definition:Vanishing Ideal of Subset of Affine Space

title: Definition:Vanishing Ideal of Set of Prime Ideals
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $V \subseteq \Spec A$ be a set of prime ideals of $A$. Its vanishing ideal is its intersection, the set of elements of $A$ that are in each $\mathfrak p \in V$: $\map I V = \bigcap V$

title: Definition:Vanishing Ideal of Subset of Affine Space
snippet: Let $k$ be a field. Let $n \ge 0$ be a natural number. Let $k \sqbrk {X_1, \ldots, X_n}$ be the polynomial ring in $n$ variables over $k$. Let $S \subseteq \mathbb A^n_k$ be a subset of the standard affine space over $k$. Its vanishing ideal is the ideal: $\map I S = \set {f \in k \sqbrk {X_1, \ldots, X_n} : \forall x \in S : \map f x = 0}$

title: Definition:Vanishing Set of Subset of Ring
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $S \subseteq A$ be a subset. The vanishing set of $S$ is the set of prime ideals of $A$ containing $S$: $\map V S = \set {\mathfrak p \in \Spec A: \mathfrak p \supseteq S}$

title: Definition:Variable
snippet: A variable is a label which is used to refer to an unspecified object. A variable can be identified by means of a symbol, for example: $x, y, z, A, B, C, \phi, \psi, \aleph$ It is often convenient to append a subscript letter or number to distinguish between different objects of a similar type: $a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n; S_\phi, S_{\phi_x}, \ldots$ The type of symbol used to define a variable is purely conventional. Particular types of object, as they are introduced, frequently have a particular range of symbols specified to define them, but there are no strict rules on the subject.

title: Definition:Variable/Also known as
snippet: When it occurs in a mathematical equation, a variable is often referred to as an unknown. In the specific context of elementary algebra, the ugly misnomer pronumeral is frequently found in Australia. This was introduced by extension of the concept of a : a symbol that stands in for a numeral, by which the term number is actually meant. Thankfully the term appears not to have caught on in general. Category:Definitions/Variables

title: Definition:Variable/Complex
snippet: A complex variable is a symbol which can stand for any one of a set of complex numbers. The symbols most often used to denote a complex variable are $w$ and $z$.

title: Definition:Variable/Continuous
snippet: A continuous variable is a variable which can take any value between two given values.

title: Definition:Variable/Descriptive Statistics
snippet: A variable is a characteristic property of all individuals in a population or sample. It is a categorization of the population such that each individual can be unambiguously described with respect to said variable.

title: Definition:Variable/Descriptive Statistics/Qualitative Variable
snippet: A qualitative variable $Q$ is a variable such that: $Q$ is not a quantitative variable $Q$ describes each individual as either having, or not having, some specific property.

title: Definition:Variable/Descriptive Statistics/Quantitative Variable
snippet: A quantitative variable is a variable such that: The variable can be described by numbers The performing of arithmetical operations on the data is meaningful.

title: Definition:Variable/Discrete
snippet: A discrete variable is a variable which is not continuous. That is, its domain is finite or countably infinite.

title: Definition:Variable/Domain
snippet: The collection of all possible objects that a variable may refer to has to be specified. This collection is the domain of the variable.

title: Definition:Variable/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Variable == The term variable, as opposed to a constant, was introduced by . However, the concept had already been established by in his work on logic.

title: Definition:Variable/Predicate Logic
snippet: In the context of predicate logic, a variable is often called an object variable or arbitrary name. As such, it is a symbol which is assigned to an arbitrarily selected object from a given universe of discourse. The understanding is that (during the scope of the argument to which it is relevant) the arbitrary name could apply equally well to any of the objects in that universe.

title: Definition:Variable/Propositional Logic
snippet: A statement variable is a variable which is used to stand for an arbitrary and unspecified statement. For a statement variable, a lowercase letter is usually used, for example: $p, q, r, \ldots{}$, and so on or lowercase Greek letters, for example: $\phi, \psi, \chi$ and so on. The citing of a statement variable can be interpreted as an assertion that the statement represented by that symbol is true. That is: $p$ means $p \text { is true}$

title: Definition:Variable/Real
snippet: A real variable is a symbol which can stand for any one of a set of real numbers. The symbols most often used to denote a real variable are $x$ and $y$.

title: Definition:Variable/Restricted
snippet: A restricted variable is a variable whose values are confined to only some of those of which it is capable.

title: Definition:Variable/Satisfaction
snippet: Let $\map P x$ be a propositional function such that $x$ is a variable with a given domain $S$. Let a specific element $a$ of $S$ be substituted for $x$ in $\map P x$ such that $\map P a$ is true. Then $a$ is said to satisfy the propositional function $P$.

title: Definition:Variable/Unrestricted
snippet: An unrestricted variable is a variable whose values are not confined in any way to some only of those of which it is capable.

title: Definition:Variable/Value
snippet: A variable $x$ may be (temporarily, conceptually) identified with a particular object. If so, then that object is called the value of $x$.

title: Definition:Variable Element
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory, and let $C$ be an object of $\mathbf C$. A variable element of $C$ is a morphism $f: B \to C$ with codomain $C$.

title: Definition:Variance
snippet: Variance is a measure of dispersion of a set of observations. Let $X$ be a random variable. The variance of $X$ is defined as the second central moment of $X$.

title: Definition:Variance/Also denoted as
snippet: == Variance: Also known as == The notation $\operatorname {\mathsf {var} } \sqbrk X$ can also be seen for the variance of $X$.

title: Definition:Variance/Continuous
snippet: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable. Then the variance of $X$, written $\var X$, is a measure of how much the values of $X$ varies from the expectation $\expect X$, and is defined as: $\var X := \expect {\paren {X - \expect X}^2}$ That is, the expectation of the squares of the deviations from the expectation. Letting $\mu = \expect X$, this is often given as: $\var X = \expect {\paren {X - \mu}^2}$

title: Definition:Variance/Discrete
snippet: Let $X$ be a discrete random variable. Then the variance of $X$, written $\var X$, is a measure of how much the values of $X$ varies from the expectation $\expect X$, and is defined as:

title: Definition:Variance/Discrete/Definition 1
snippet: Let $X$ be a discrete random variable. Then the variance of $X$, written $\var X$, is a measure of how much the values of $X$ varies from the expectation $\expect X$, and is defined as: $\var X := \expect {\paren {X - \expect X}^2}$ That is: it is the expectation of the squares of the deviations from the expectation.

title: Definition:Variance/Discrete/Definition 2
snippet: Let $X$ be a discrete random variable. Then the variance of $X$, written $\var X$, is defined as: $\ds \var X := \sum_{x \mathop \in \Omega_X} \paren {x - \mu^2} \map \Pr {X = x}$ where: $\mu := \expect X$ is the expectation of $X$ $\Omega_X$ is the image of $X$ $\map \Pr {X = x}$ is the probability mass function of $X$.

title: Definition:Variance/Discrete/Definition 3
snippet: Let $X$ be a discrete random variable. Let $\expect X$ be the expectation of $X$. Then the variance of $X$, written $\var X$, is defined as: $\var X := \expect {X^2} - \paren {\expect X}^2$

title: Definition:Variance/Technical Note
snippet: == Technical Note for Variance == {{LatexFor|for = \var {X} }} When the argument is a single character, it is usual to omit the braces: \var X This command is specific to . Category:Technical Notes

title: Definition:Variance Ratio
snippet: The variance ratio of an analysis of variance exercise is defined as: the ratio of the between-treatments sum of squares to the error sum of squares.

title: Definition:Variance of Random Vector
snippet: Let $\mathbf X$ be a random vector. The variance of $\mathbf X$ is defined by: $\operatorname{var} \left({\mathbf X}\right) = \operatorname{cov} \left({\mathbf X, \mathbf X}\right)$ where $\operatorname{cov}$ is the cross-covariance matrix. Category:Definitions/Probability Theory

title: Definition:Variance of Stochastic Process
snippet: Let $S$ be a stationary stochastic process giving rise to a time series $T$. The variance of $S$ is calculated as: $\sigma_z^2 = \expect {\paren {z_t - \mu}^2} = \ds \int_{-\infty}^\infty \paren {z - \mu}^2 \map p z \rd z$ where $\map p z$ is the (constant) probability mass function of $S$. It is a measure of the spread about the constant mean level $\mu$.

title: Definition:Variation/Complex Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\mu$ be a complex measure on $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. Let $\map P A$ be the set of finite partitions of $A$ into $\Sigma$-measurable sets. We define the variation $\cmod \mu : \Sigma \to \R$ of $\mu$ by: $\ds \map {\cmod \mu} A = \sup \set {\sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n \cmod {\map \mu {A_j} } : \set {A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n} \in \map P A}$ for each $A \in \Sigma$, where the supremum is taken in the set of extended real numbers $\overline \R$.

title: Definition:Variation/Signed Measure/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\mu$ be a signed measure on $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. Let $\struct {\mu^+, \mu^-}$ be the Jordan decomposition of $\mu$. We define the variation $\size \mu$ of $\mu$ by: $\size \mu = \mu^+ + \mu^-$

title: Definition:Variation/Signed Measure/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\mu$ be a signed measure on $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. Let $\map P A$ be the set of finite partitions of $A$ into $\Sigma$-measurable sets. We define the variation $\cmod \mu : \Sigma \to \overline \R$ of $\mu$ by: $\ds \map {\cmod \mu} A = \sup \set {\sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n \cmod {\map \mu {A_j} } : \set {A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n} \in \map P A}$ for each $A \in \Sigma$, where the supremum is taken in the set of extended real numbers $\overline \R$. Category:Definitions/Variation of Signed Measure

title: Definition:Variation Field of Family of Curves
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $\gamma$ be an admissible curve on $M$. Let $I = \closedint a b$ is a closed real interval. Let $J$ is an open real interval. Let $\Gamma : J \times I \to M$ be the variation of $\gamma$, where $\times$ denotes the cartesian product and: $\ds \forall s \in J : \forall t \in I : \tuple {s, t} \stackrel \Gamma \mapsto \map \Gamma {s, t}$ Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space at $p \in M$.

title: Definition:Variation Function
snippet: Let $F : \R \to \R$ be a function that is of bounded variation. We define the variation function $V_F : \R \to \R$ by: $\map {V_F} x = \map {V_F} {\hointl {-\infty} x}$ for each $x \in \R$, where $\map {V_F} {\hointl {-\infty} x}$ denotes the total variation of $F$ on $\hointl {-\infty} x$.

title: Definition:Variation in Sign of Polynomial
snippet: Let $\map P x$ be a polynomial equation over the real numbers: $\pm a_n x^n \mathop \pm a_{n - 1} x^{n - 1} \mathop \pm \cdots \mathop \pm a_1 x \mathop \pm a_0 = 0$ where: the independent variable $x \in \R$ is real the coefficients $a_j \in \R_{\ge 0}$ are all non-negative constants each of the $\pm$ signs can be either positive or negative. A variation in sign of the coefficients of $\map P x$ is an instance of $j \in \set {0, 1, \ldots, n}$ in which a $\pm$ sign changes from positive to negative, or , as $j$ goes from $n$ to $0$, ignoring zero coefficients.

title: Definition:Variation of Admissible Curve
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $I = \closedint a b$ be a closed real interval. Let $\gamma : I\to M$ be an admissible curve. Let $J \subseteq \R$ be an open real interval containing $0$. Let $\Gamma : J \times I \to M$ be an admissible family of curves such that: $\ds \forall s \in J : \forall t \in I : \tuple {s, t} \stackrel \Gamma \mapsto \map {\Gamma_s} t$ Let $\Gamma$ have the property that: $\map {\Gamma_0} t = \map \gamma t$ Then $\Gamma$ is called the variation of $\gamma$.

title: Definition:Variation of Function/One-Sided Shift of Finite Type
snippet: Let $\struct {X _\mathbf A ^+, \sigma_\mathbf A ^+}$ be a one-sided shift of finite type. Let $f : X_\mathbf A ^+ \to \C$ be a continuous function. Let $n \in \N$. The $n$th variation of $f$ is defined as: $\map {\mathrm{var}_n} f := \sup \set {\size {\map f x - \map f y} : x, y \in X_\mathbf A ^+, \; \forall i \in \hointr 0 n : x_i = y_i}$

title: Definition:Variation of Function/Shift of Finite Type
snippet: Let $\struct {X _\mathbf A, \sigma_\mathbf A}$ be a shift of finite type. Let $f : X_\mathbf A \to \C$ be a continuous function. Let $n \in \N$. The $n$th variation of $f$ is defined as: $\map {\mathrm{var}_n} f := \sup \set {\size {\map f x - \map f y} : x, y \in X_\mathbf A, \; \forall i \in \openint {-n} n : x_i = y_i}$

title: Definition:Variation of Real Function
snippet: Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a real function whose domain is the closed real interval $\closedint a b$. The variation of $f$ is defined as: $\ds \map \sup {\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \size {\map f {x_i} - \map f {x_{i - 1} } } }$ where the supremum is taken over all possible finite subdivisions $a = x_0 < x_1 < x_2 < \cdots < x_n = b$ of $\closedint a b$.

title: Definition:Variational Derivative
snippet: Let $\map y x$ be a real function. Let $J = J \sqbrk y$ be a functional dependent on $y$. Let $\map h x$ be a real function, which differs from zero only in the neighbourhood of $x_0$. Consider an increment of functional $\Delta J \sqbrk {y; h}$. Denote the area between $\map y x + \map h x$ and $\map y x$ (or, equivalently, between $\map h x$ and x-axis) as $\Delta \sigma$. Let $\Delta \sigma \to 0$ in such a way, that $\ds \lim_{\Delta \sigma \mathop \to 0} \map \max {\map h x} = 0$ and the length of interval where $\map h x$ differs from 0 would go to 0.

title: Definition:Variational Equation of Differential Equation
snippet: For $n, i \in \N$, let: $\map F {x, \sequence {\map {y^{\paren i} } x}_{0 \mathop \le i \mathop \le n} } = 0$ where $\sequence {\map {y^{\paren i} } x}_{0 \mathop \le i \mathop \le n}$ is a sequence of derivatives of a function $y$, be a differential equation. Let $\map y x, \map g x$ be real functions which solve the given differential equation, such that $\map g x = \map y x + \map h x$ Then, neglecting $\map \OO {h^2}$, the differential equation satisfied by $h$ is called the variational equation of the differential equation $F = 0$.

title: Definition:Variational Principle
snippet: A variational principle is a statement defining a condition that is required to be fulfilled in order to solve a problem in the calculus of variations.

title: Definition:Vassiliev Invariant
snippet: A Vassiliev invariant is an invariant whose purpose is to classify knots.

title: Definition:Vassiliev Invariant/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Vassiliev Invariant == The concept of the Vassiliev invariant was devised by in $1989$, based on his work in singularity theory.

title: Definition:Vector-Valued Function
snippet: Let $f_1, f_2, \ldots, f_n$ be real functions of $t$. Let $\mathbb T \subseteq \R, \mathbb Y \subseteq \R^n$ (where usually $n \ge 2$). Let $\mathbf r$ be a mapping from $\mathbb T \to \mathbb Y$ that maps each $t \in \mathbb T$ to a vector $\tuple {\map {f_1} t, \map {f_2} t, \ldots, \map {f_n} t} \in \mathbb Y$. Then $\mathbf r$ is said to be a vector-valued function (of the parameter $t$). If $\mathbb T$ is not explicitly defined, it is taken to be the intersection of all the domains of $f_1 ,f_2, \cdots, f_n$.

title: Definition:Vector-Valued Function/Component Function
snippet: Let $f_1, f_2, \ldots, f_n$ be real functions of $t$. Let $\mathbb T \subseteq \R, \mathbb Y \subseteq \R^n$ (where usually $n \ge 2$). Let $\mathbf r$ be a vector-valued function from $\mathbb T \to \mathbb Y$. Each $f_1, f_2, \ldots, f_n$ is a component function of $\mathbf r$.

title: Definition:Vector/Affine Geometry
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an affine space. Let $V$ be the tangent space of $\EE$. An element $v$ of $V$ is called a vector.

title: Definition:Vector/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Vector == The term vector was coined by . The meaning he assigned to the concept corresponds closely to the arrow representation as defined on .

title: Definition:Vector/Linear Algebra
snippet: Let $V = \struct {G, +_G, \ast}_K$ be a vector space over $K$, where: $\struct {G, +_G}$ is an abelian group $\struct {K, +_K, \times_K}$ is the scalar ring of $V$. The elements of the abelian group $\struct {G, +_G}$ are called vectors.

title: Definition:Vector/Module
snippet: Let $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_R$ be a module, where: $\struct {G, +_G}$ is an abelian group $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ is the scalar ring of $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_R$. The elements of the abelian group $\struct {G, +_G}$ are called vectors.

title: Definition:Vector/Real Euclidean Space
snippet: A vector is defined as an element of a vector space. We have that $\R^n$, with the operations of vector addition and scalar multiplication, forms a real Euclidean space. Hence a vector in $\R^n$ is defined as an element of the real Euclidean space $\R^n$.

title: Definition:Vector/Real Euclidean Space/Plane Vector
snippet: Consider the real Euclidean space $\R^2$. A vector in $\R^2$ can be referred to as a plane vector.

title: Definition:Vector/Real Euclidean Space/Space Vector
snippet: Consider the real Euclidean space $\R^3$. A vector in $\R^3$ can be referred to as a space vector.

title: Definition:Vector (Vector Space)/Also defined as
snippet: == Vector: Also defined as == Some sources, in their definition of a vector space, restrict the scalar division ring to a field. That is, they insist that the scalar division ring is a commutative. This may need to be borne in mind.

title: Definition:Vector Addition/Also known as
snippet: == Vector Addition: Also known as == Vector addition is also known as composition.

title: Definition:Vector Addition/Module
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ be a ring. Let $\struct {G, +_G}$ be an abelian group. Let $M := \struct {G, +_G, \circ}_R$ be the corresponding module over $R$ (either a left module or a right module). The group operation $+_G$ on $M$ is known as vector addition on $M$. Category:Definitions/Module Theory Category:Definitions/Vector Addition

title: Definition:Vector Addition/Vector Space
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +_F, \times_F}$ be a field. Let $\struct {G, +_G}$ be an abelian group. Let $V := \struct {G, +_G, \circ}_R$ be the corresponding vector space over $F$. The group operation $+_G$ on $V$ is known as vector addition on $V$.

title: Definition:Vector Algebra
snippet: Vector Algebra is the branch of mathematics which studies the algebra of vector spaces.

title: Definition:Vector Algebraic Dual/Also denoted as
snippet: == Vector Algebraic Dual: Also denoted as == The dual, as defined here, is often known as the algebraic dual so as to distinguish it from the topological dual or normed dual space, which are the sets of all linear functionals that are continuous. To distinguish the algebraic dual from the topological dual, the notation $V^\#$ may be used instead of $V^\ast$. Category:Definitions/Algebraic Duals

title: Definition:Vector Algebraic Dual/Also known as
snippet: == Vector Algebraic Dual: Also known as == A vector algebraic dual is also known as an (algebraic) dual space, or a dual vector space. However, beware of confusing it with the topological dual or normed dual space.

title: Definition:Vector Analysis
snippet: Vector analysis is the branch of linear algebra concerned with differentiation and integration of vector spaces, primarily in Euclidean space of $3$-dimensional space.

title: Definition:Vector Analysis/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Vector Analysis == One of the earliest attempts to develop a calculus for working directly on vectors was made by in $1679$, but this was unsuccessful. 's demonstration in $1806$ of a geometrical representation of the complex plane gave the misleading impression that vectors in the Cartesian plane required them to be represented as complex numbers, which held development back for some time. published his in $1827$, which was the forerunner of the more general analysis of geometric forms developed by .

title: Definition:Vector Area
snippet: Let $S$ be a plane surface embedded in Cartesian $3$-space. The vector area of $S$ is a technique of representing $S$ using a vector quantity $\mathbf S$. 380px The magnitude of the vector is determined by the area of $S$, while its direction is defined as the unit normal $\mathbf {\hat n}$ to the plane of $S$. The sign of $\mathbf S = S \, \mathbf {\hat n}$ is determined by the right-hand rule according to the direction of rotation around $S$ when describing it. The shape of $S$ is arbitrary.

title: Definition:Vector Bundle
snippet: Let $B = \struct {E, M, \pi, F}$ be a fiber bundle. Then $B$ is a vector bundle over $M$ the model fiber $F$ is a topological vector space.

title: Definition:Vector Calculus
snippet: Vector calculus is the branch of linear algebra concerned with the application of the techniques of calculus to vector spaces.

title: Definition:Vector Cross Product
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ be vectors in a vector space $\mathbf V$ of $3$ dimensions: where $\tuple {\mathbf i, \mathbf j, \mathbf k}$ is the standard ordered basis of $\mathbf V$.

title: Definition:Vector Cross Product/Also known as
snippet: == Vector Cross Product: Also known as == The vector cross product is often called just the cross product when there is no chance of confusion with other types of cross product. Some sources hyphenate: cross-product. The term vector product can also sometimes be seen, but again this can be ambiguous, because there are different ways of forming a product with vectors.

title: Definition:Vector Cross Product/Complex
snippet: Let $z_1 := x_1 + i y_1$ and $z_2 := x_2 + i y_2$ be complex numbers.

title: Definition:Vector Cross Product/Complex/Definition 1
snippet: Let $z_1 := x_1 + i y_1$ and $z_2 := x_2 + i y_2$ be complex numbers. The cross product of $z_1$ and $z_2$ is defined as: $z_1 \times z_2 = x_1 y_2 - y_1 x_2$

title: Definition:Vector Cross Product/Complex/Definition 2
snippet: Let $z_1$ and $z_2$ be complex numbers in vector form. The cross product of $z_1$ and $z_2$ is defined as: $z_1 \times z_2 = \cmod {z_1} \, \cmod {z_2} \sin \theta$ where: $\cmod {z_1}$ denotes the complex modulus of $z_1$ $\theta$ denotes the angle from $z_1$ to $z_2$, measured in the positive direction.

title: Definition:Vector Cross Product/Complex/Definition 3
snippet: Let $z_1$ and $z_2$ be complex numbers. The cross product of $z_1$ and $z_2$ is defined as: $z_1 \times z_2 := \map \Im {\overline {z_1} z_2}$ where: $\map \Im z$ denotes the imaginary part of a complex number $z$ $\overline {z_1}$ denotes the complex conjugate of $z_1$ $\overline {z_1} z_2$ denotes complex multiplication.

title: Definition:Vector Cross Product/Complex/Definition 4
snippet: Let $z_1$ and $z_2$ be complex numbers. The cross product of $z_1$ and $z_2$ is defined as: $z_1 \times z_2 := \dfrac {\overline {z_1} z_2 - z_1 \overline {z_2}} {2 i}$ where: $\overline {z_1}$ denotes the complex conjugate of $z_1$ $\overline {z_1} z_2$ denotes complex multiplication.

title: Definition:Vector Cross Product/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ be vectors in a vector space $\mathbf V$ of $3$ dimensions: where $\tuple {\mathbf i, \mathbf j, \mathbf k}$ is the standard ordered basis of $\mathbf V$. The vector cross product, denoted $\mathbf a \times \mathbf b$, is defined as: $\mathbf a \times \mathbf b = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ a_i & a_j & a_k \\ b_i & b_j & b_k \\ \end{vmatrix}$ where $\begin {vmatrix} \ldots \end {vmatrix}$ is interpreted as a determinant.

title: Definition:Vector Cross Product/Definition 2
snippet:
Let $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ be vectors in a vector space $\mathbf V$ of $3$ dimensions. The vector cross product, denoted $\mathbf a 	imes \mathbf b$, is defined as: $\mathbf a 	imes \mathbf b = 
orm {\mathbf a} 
orm {\mathbf b} \sin 	heta \, \mathbf {\hat n}$ where: $
orm {\mathbf a}$ denotes the length of $\mathbf a$ $	heta$ denotes the angle from $\mathbf a$ to $\mathbf b$, measured in the positive direction $\hat {\mathbf n}$ is the unit vector perpendicular to both $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ in the direction according to the right-hand rule.

snippet: == Historical Note on Vector Dyad == During the course of development of vector analysis, various notations for the vector dyad were introduced, as follows: {| border="1" cellpadding="4" cellspacing="0" style="font-weight:bold; text-align:left; |- ! title: Definition:Vector Field
snippet: Let $F$ be a field which acts on a region of space $S$. Let the point-function giving rise to $F$ be a vector quantity. Then $F$ is a vector field.

title: Definition:Vector Field/Classification
snippet: == Classification of Vector Fields == Let $R$ be a region of space. Let $\mathbf V$ be a vector field acting over $R$.

title: Definition:Vector Field/Classification/Illustration
snippet: == Illustration of Classification of Vector Fields == Let $R$ be a region of space. Let $\mathbf V$ be a vector field acting over $R$. The following diagram gives a visual impression of the properties of vector fields with various combinations of properties relating to divergence and curl: 800px

title: Definition:Vector Field/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Vector Fields ==

title: Definition:Vector Field/Examples/Electric Field Strength
snippet: == Example of Vector Field == Let $R$ be a region of space in which there exists an electric field. The electric field strength in $R$ gives rise to a vector field over $R$.

title: Definition:Vector Field/Examples/Magnetic Field Strength
snippet: == Example of Vector Field == Let $R$ be a region of space in which there exists an magnetic field. The magnetic field strength in $R$ gives rise to a vector field over $R$.

title: Definition:Vector Field/Examples/Velocity of Fluid
snippet: == Example of Vector Field == In a moving fluid, the velocity $\mathbf v$ of the fluid is an example of a vector field. That is, the velocity $\mathbf v$ at a point $P$ in the fluid is the velocity of the particle which is situated at $P$ at a given instant.

title: Definition:Vector Field along Smooth Curve
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold with or without boundary. Let $TM$ be the tangent bundle of $M$. Let $I \subseteq \R$ be a real inverval. Let $\gamma : I \to M$ be a smooth curve. Let $V : I \to TM$ be a continuous map such that: $\forall t \in I : \map V t \in T_{\map \gamma t} M$ Then $V$ is called the vector field along (smooth) curve $\gamma$.

title: Definition:Vector Field on Smooth Manifold
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $TM$ be the tangent bundle of $M$. Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space at $p \in M$. Then by a vector field on $M$ we mean a continuous mapping $X : M \to TM$ such that: $\forall p \in M : X_p \in T_p M$ where $X_p$ denotes the value of $X$ at $p$.

title: Definition:Vector Finitely Supported with respect to Schauder Basis
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a normed vector space over $\GF$. Let $x \in X$. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a Schauder basis for $X$. Let $\map \supp x$ be the support of $x$ with respect to $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$. We say that $x$ is finitely supported $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ if $\map \supp x$ is finite.

title: Definition:Vector Length
snippet: The length of a vector $\mathbf v$ in a normed vector space $\struct {V, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ is defined as $\norm {\mathbf v}$, the norm of $\mathbf v$.

title: Definition:Vector Length/Also known as
snippet: == Vector Length: Also known as == The length of a vector is also referred to as its module in some older books.

title: Definition:Vector Length/Arrow Representation
snippet: Let $\mathbf v$ be a vector quantity represented as an arrow in a real vector space $\R^n$. The length of $\mathbf v$ is the length of the line segment representing $\mathbf v$ in $\R^n$.

title: Definition:Vector Length/Complex Plane
snippet: == Example of Vector Length == Let $\mathbf v$ be a vector represented in the complex plane $\C$ by the complex number $z = a + b i$. The length of $\mathbf v$ is defined as: $\norm {\mathbf v} = \cmod z$ where $\cmod z = \sqrt {a^2 + b^2}$ is the modulus of $z$. Category:Definitions/Vector Length Category:Definitions/Complex Analysis

title: Definition:Vector Length/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Vector Length ==

title: Definition:Vector Length/Real Number Line
snippet: == Example of Vector Length == Let $\mathbf v$ be a vector represented by an arrow on the real number line. Let: the initial point of $\mathbf v$ be $a \in \R$ the terminal point of $\mathbf v$ be $b \in \R$ The length of $\mathbf v$ is defined as: $\norm {\mathbf v} = \size {b - a}$ the absolute value of $b - a$. Category:Definitions/Vector Length

title: Definition:Vector Length/Real Vector Space
snippet: == Example of Vector Length == Let $\mathbf v$ be a vector represented in the real $n$-space $\R^n$ by an ordered $n$-tuple of components $\tuple {v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n}$. The length of $\mathbf v$ is defined as: $\norm {\mathbf v} = \ds \sqrt {\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n v_i^2}$

title: Definition:Vector Line
snippet: Let $R$ be a region of space in which there exists a vector field $V$ given rise to by a vector quantity $F$. Let $P$ be an arbitrary point in $V$. Let the following procedure be established: Proceed an infinitesimal distance from $P_0$ to $P_1$ in the direction of $\map F {P_0}$. Proceed an infinitesimal distance from $P_1$ to $P_2$ in the direction of $\map F {P_1}$. Continue in this manner to trace out a curve in space whose tangent at any point $Q$ gives the direction of the vector quantity $\map F Q$ at $Q$. This curve is referred to as a vector line.

title: Definition:Vector Line/Also known as
snippet: == Vector Line: Also known as == A vector line is also known as: a line of flow a flux line a field line. In contexts where the vector field in question is (or gives rise to) a force, then the term line of force can be seen.

title: Definition:Vector Line/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Vector Lines ==

title: Definition:Vector Normal to Pseudo-Riemannian Submanifold
snippet: Let $\struct {\tilde M, \tilde g}$ be a pseudo-Riemannian manifold. Let $M \subseteq \tilde M$ be a smooth submanifold with or without boundary in $M$. Let $p \in M$ be a point. Let $T_p \tilde M$ and $T_p M$ be the tangent spaces of $\tilde M$ and $M$ at $p$ respectively. Let $v \in T_p \tilde M$ and $w \in T_p M$ be vectors. Let $\innerprod \cdot \cdot$ be the scalar product induced by the pseudo-Riemannian metric $\tilde g$. Suppose: $\forall w \in T_p M : \innerprod v w = 0$ Then $v$ is said to be normal to $M$ (at $p$).

title: Definition:Vector Normal to Smooth Submanifold
snippet: Let $\struct {\tilde M, \tilde g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $M \subseteq \tilde M$ be a smooth submanifold with or without boundary in $M$. Let $p \in M$ be a point. Let $T_p \tilde M$ and $T_p M$ be the tangent spaces of $\tilde M$ and $M$ at $p$ respectively. Let $v \in T_p \tilde M$ and $w \in T_p M$ be vectors. Let $\innerprod \cdot \cdot$ be the inner product induced by the Riemannian metric $\tilde g$. Suppose: $\forall w \in T_p M : \innerprod v w = 0$ Then $v$ is said to be normal to $M$ (at $p$).

title: Definition:Vector Notation
snippet: Several conventions are found in the literature for annotating a general vector quantity in a style that distinguishes it from a scalar quantity, as follows. Let $\set {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ be a collection of scalars which form the components of an $n$-dimensional vector. The vector $\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ can be annotated as: {{eqn | l = \bsx | r = \tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} }} {{eqn | l = \vec x | r = \tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} }} {{eqn | l = \hat x | r = \tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} }} {{eqn | l = \underline x | r = \tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} }} {{eqn | l = \tilde…

title: Definition:Vector Notation/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Vector Notation == During the course of development of vector analysis, various notations were introduced, as follows: {| border="1" cellpadding="4" cellspacing="0" style="font-weight:bold; text-align:left; |- ! Symbol ! Used by |- | align="center" | $\mathbf a$ | and and |- | align="center" | $\mathscr A$ | |- | align="center" | $\mathfrak A$ | |- | align="center" | $\mathbf A$ | |}

title: Definition:Vector Potential
snippet: Let $R$ be a region of ordinary space. Let $\mathbf V$ be a vector field over $R$. Let $\mathbf V$ be both rotational and solenoidal. Let $\mathbf A$ be a vector field such that $\mathbf V = \curl \mathbf A$. Then $\mathbf A$ is known as the vector potential of $\mathbf V$.

title: Definition:Vector Projection
snippet: Let $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ be vector quantities.

title: Definition:Vector Projection/Also known as
snippet: == Vector Projection: Also known as == The vector projection of $\mathbf u$ onto $\mathbf v$ is also known as: the vector component the vector resolution the vector resolute of $\mathbf u$ in the direction of $\mathbf v$. The notation for $\proj_\mathbf v \mathbf u$ also varies throughout the literature. The following forms can sometimes be seen: $\mathbf u_{\parallel \mathbf v}$ $\mathbf u_1$ Category:Definitions/Vector Projections

title: Definition:Vector Projection/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ be vector quantities. The (vector) projection of $\mathbf u$ onto $\mathbf v$, denoted $\proj_\mathbf v \mathbf u$, is the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf u$ onto a straight line which is parallel to $\mathbf v$. Hence $\proj_\mathbf v \mathbf u$ is a like vector to $\mathbf v$ whose length is $\norm {\mathbf u} \cos \theta$, where: $\norm {\mathbf u}$ is the magnitude of $\mathbf u$ $\cos \theta$ is the angle between $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$. 300px

title: Definition:Vector Projection/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ be vector quantities. The (vector) projection of $\mathbf u$ onto $\mathbf v$ is defined and denoted: $\proj_\mathbf v \mathbf u = \dfrac {\mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v} {\norm {\mathbf v}^2} \mathbf v$ where: $\cdot$ denotes the dot product $\norm {\mathbf v}$ denotes the magnitude of $\mathbf v$. 300px

title: Definition:Vector Projection/Definition 3
snippet: Let $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ be vector quantities. The (vector) projection of $\mathbf u$ onto $\mathbf v$ is defined and denoted: $\proj_\mathbf v \mathbf u = u_{\parallel \mathbf v} \mathbf {\hat v}$ where: $u_{\parallel \mathbf v}$ denotes the scalar projection of $\mathbf u$ on $\mathbf v$ $\mathbf {\hat v}$ denotes the unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf v$. 300px

title: Definition:Vector Quantity
snippet: A vector quantity is a real-world concept that needs for its model a mathematical object with more than one component to specify it. Formally, a vector quantity is an element of a normed vector space, often the real vector space $\R^3$. The usual intellectual frame of reference is to interpret a vector quantity as having: A magnitude A direction.

title: Definition:Vector Quantity/Also known as
snippet: == Vector Quantity: Also known as == A vector quantity in this context is frequently referred to just as a vector.
