However, the term vector applies to a wider variety of objects than the real-world context of the real vector space $\R^3$ Some sources use the term free vector, so as to distinguish it from what is referred to in as a located vector. Further to the arrow representation of a vector quantity, some sources refer to such quantities as arrows. However, that term is not used in this context on , as there are many different contexts for arrow.

title: Definition:Vector Quantity/Arrow Representation
snippet: A vector quantity $\mathbf v$ is often represented diagramatically in the form of an arrow such that: its length is proportional to the magnitude of $\mathbf v$ its direction corresponds to the direction of $\mathbf v$. The head of the arrow then indicates the positive sense of the direction of $\mathbf v$. It can be rendered on the page like so: 300px It is important to note that a vector quantity, when represented in this form, is not in general fixed in space. All that is being indicated using such a notation is its magnitude and direction, and not, in general, a point at which it acts.

title: Definition:Vector Quantity/Component
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$ be a vector quantity embedded in an $n$-dimensional Cartesian coordinate system $C_n$. Let $\mathbf a$ be represented with its initial point at the origin of $C_n$. Let $\mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_2, \ldots, \mathbf e_n$ be the unit vectors in the positive direction of the coordinate axes of $C_n$.

title: Definition:Vector Quantity/Component/Also known as
snippet: == Component of Vector: Also known as == The components of a vector quantity $\mathbf a$ as defined above can also be referred to as the projections of $\mathbf a$. Some older sources refer to them as resolutes or resolved parts.

title: Definition:Vector Quantity/Component/Cartesian 3-Space
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$ be a vector quantity embedded in Cartesian $3$-space $S$. Let $\mathbf i$, $\mathbf j$ and $\mathbf k$ be the unit vectors in the positive directions of the $x$-axis, $y$-axis and $z$-axis respectively. Then: $\mathbf a = x \mathbf i + y \mathbf j + z \mathbf k$ where: $x \mathbf i$, $y \mathbf j$ and $z \mathbf k$ are the component vectors of $\mathbf a$ in the $\mathbf i, \mathbf j, \mathbf k$ directions $x$, $y$ and $z$ are the components of $\mathbf a$ in the $\mathbf i$, $\mathbf j$ and $\mathbf k$ directions.

title: Definition:Vector Quantity/Component/Cartesian Plane
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$ be a vector quantity embedded in a Cartesian plane $P$. Let $\mathbf a$ be represented with its initial point at the origin of $P$. Let $\mathbf i$ and $\mathbf j$ be the unit vectors in the positive direction of the $x$-axis and $y$-axis. Then: $\mathbf a = x \mathbf i + y \mathbf j$ where: $x \mathbf i$ and $y \mathbf j$ are the component vectors of $\mathbf a$ in the $\mathbf i$ and $\mathbf j$ directions $x$ and $y$ are the components of $\mathbf a$ in the $\mathbf i$ and $\mathbf j$ directions.

title: Definition:Vector Quantity/Component/Einstein Summation Convention
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$ be a vector quantity. $\mathbf a$ can be expressed in component form using the Einstein summation convention as: $\mathbf a = a_i \mathbf e_i$

title: Definition:Vector Quantity/Component/X Component
snippet: Let: $\mathbf a = x \mathbf i + y \mathbf j + z \mathbf k$ be a vector quantity embedded in Cartesian $3$-space $S$ where $\mathbf i$, $\mathbf j$ and $\mathbf k$ be the unit vectors in the positive directions of the $x$-axis, $y$-axis and $z$-axis respectively. The value $x$ is known as the $x$ component of $\mathbf a$.

title: Definition:Vector Quantity/Component/Y Component
snippet: Let: $\mathbf a = x \mathbf i + y \mathbf j + z \mathbf k$ be a vector quantity embedded in Cartesian $3$-space $S$ where $\mathbf i$, $\mathbf j$ and $\mathbf k$ be the unit vectors in the positive directions of the $x$-axis, $y$-axis and $z$-axis respectively. The value $y$ is known as the $y$ component of $\mathbf a$.

title: Definition:Vector Quantity/Component/Z Component
snippet: Let: $\mathbf a = x \mathbf i + y \mathbf j + z \mathbf k$ be a vector quantity embedded in Cartesian $3$-space $S$ where $\mathbf i$, $\mathbf j$ and $\mathbf k$ be the unit vectors in the positive directions of the $x$-axis, $y$-axis and $z$-axis respectively. The value $z$ is known as the $z$ component of $\mathbf a$.

title: Definition:Vector Quantity/Equivalence Class
snippet: A vector quantity is an instance of an equivalence class of directed line segments whose lengths and directions are equal. The canonical instance is the one whose initial point is located at the origin.

title: Definition:Vector Space/Also known as
snippet: == Vector Space: Also known as == A vector space is also sometimes called a linear space, especially when discussing the real vector space $\R^n$. Some go further and refer to a linear vector space The notation $\struct {G, +_G, \circ, K}$ can also be seen for this concept.

title: Definition:Vector Space/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {K, +_K, \times_K}$ be a field. Let $\struct {G, +_G}$ be an abelian group. Let $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_K$ be a unitary $K$-module. Then $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_K$ is a vector space over $K$ or a $K$-vector space. That is, a vector space is a unitary module whose scalar ring is a field.

title: Definition:Vector Space/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {K, +_K, \times_K}$ be a field whose unity is $1_K$. Let $\struct {G, +_G}$ be an abelian group. Let $\struct {\map {\mathrm {End} } G, +, \circ}$ be the endomorphism ring of $\struct {G, +_G}$ such that $I_G$ is the identity mapping. Let $\ast: \struct {K, +_K, \times_K} \to \struct {\map {\mathrm {End} } G, +, \circ}$ be a ring homomorphism from $K$ to $\map {\mathrm {End} } G$ which maps $1_K$ to $I_G$. Then $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_K$ is a vector space over $K$ or a $K$-vector space.

title: Definition:Vector Space/Division Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {K, +_K, \times_K}$ be a division ring. Let $\struct {G, +_G}$ be an abelian group. Let $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_K$ be a unitary $K$-module. Then $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_K$ is a vector space over $K$ or a $K$-vector space. That is, a vector space is a unitary module whose scalar ring is a division ring.

title: Definition:Vector Space/Left and Right Vector Space
snippet: == Left Vector Spaces and Right Vector Spaces == In the case where the scalar division ring is a field, the difference between a left vector space and a right vector space is little more than a notational difference. This is demonstrated in: Left Module over Commutative Ring induces Right Module Right Module over Commutative Ring induces Left Module where the commutative ring in question is the scalar field of the vector space, which is of course a type of module, under discussion. But this is not the case for a scalar division ring that is not commutative.

title: Definition:Vector Space Automorphism
snippet: Let $V$ be a $K$-vector space. Let $\phi: V \to V$ be a vector space isomorphism to itself. Then $\phi$ is a vector space automorphism.

title: Definition:Vector Space Decomposition
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space. A (vector space) decomposition of $V$ is a direct sum of eigenspaces that forms $V$.

title: Definition:Vector Space Monomorphism
snippet: Let $V$ and $W$ be $K$-vector spaces. Then $\phi: V \to W$ is a vector space monomorphism : $(1): \quad \phi$ is an injection $(2): \quad \forall \mathbf x, \mathbf y \in V: \map \phi {\mathbf x + \mathbf y} = \map \phi {\mathbf x} + \map \phi {\mathbf y}$ $(3): \quad \forall \mathbf x \in V: \forall \lambda \in K: \map \phi {\lambda \mathbf x} = \lambda \map \phi {\mathbf x}$

title: Definition:Vector Space of All Mappings
snippet: Let $\struct {K, +, \circ}$ be a division ring. Let $\struct {G, +_G, \circ}_K$ be a $K$-vector space. Let $S$ be a set. Let $G^S$ be the set of all mappings from $S$ to $G$. Then $\struct {G^S, +_G', \circ}_K$ is a $K$-vector space, where: $+_G'$ is the (pointwise) addition induced on $G^S$ by $+_G$ $\forall \lambda \in K: \forall f \in G^S: \forall x \in S: \map {\paren {\lambda \circ f} } x = \lambda \circ \paren {\map f x}$ This is the $K$-vector space $G^S$ of all mappings from $S$ to $G$.

title: Definition:Vector Space of Germs of Smooth Functions
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold with or without boundary. Let $p \in M$. Let $\GG_p$ denote the set $\map {C_p^\infty} M$ of all germs of smooth functions at $p$. Let $\sqbrk f_p \in \GG_p$ denote the germ of $f$ at $p$ where $f$ is a smooth function. Then $\struct {\GG_p, +_p, \cdot_p}_\R$ is a vector space over $\R$, in which the operations: $+_p: \GG_p \times \GG_p \to \GG_p$ $\cdot_p: \R \times \GG_p \to \GG_p$ are defined as: {{axiom | lc = vector addition: | q = \forall \sqbrk f_p, \forall \sqbrk g_p \in \GG_p | ml = \sqbrk f_p +_p \sqbrk g_p | mo = := | mr = \sqbrk {f + g}_p }} {{axiom |…

title: Definition:Vector Space of Matrices
snippet: Let $m, n \in \Z_{>0}$ be (strictly) positive integers. Let $\map {\MM_\GF} {m, n}$ be the $m \times n$ matrix space over a field $\GF$. Let $\struct {\map {\MM_\GF} {m, n}, +}$ denote the abelian group formed from $\map {\MM_\GF} {m, n}$ under matrix entrywise addition. Let $\struct {\map {\MM_\GF} {m, n}, +, \times}_\GF$ denote the vector space over $\map {\MM_\GF} {m, n}$ where $\times$ denotes the matrix scalar product. Then $\struct {\map {\MM_\GF} {m, n}, +, \times}_\GF$ can be referred to as the vector space of $m \times n$ matrices.

title: Definition:Vector Space of Sequences with Finite Support
snippet: Let $\struct {K, +, \circ}$ be a division ring. Let $K^\N$ be the set of sequences $\sequence{ a_n }_{n \in \N}$ in $K$. Regard $K^\N$ as a vector space of all mappings from $\N$ to $K$. The vector space of sequences with finite support is the vector subspace of $K^\N$ of sequences with finite support: $\ds \set{ f \in K^\N: \text{$f$ has finite support} }$ There is no standard symbol for the vector space of sequences with finite support.

title: Definition:Vector Space on Cartesian Product
snippet: Let $\struct {K, +_K, \times_K}$ be a division ring. Let $n \in \N_{>0}$. Let $+: K^n \times K^n \to K^n$ be defined as: $\tuple {\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n} + \tuple {\beta_1, \ldots, \beta_n} = \tuple {\alpha_1 +_K \beta_1, \ldots, \alpha_n +_K \beta_n}$ Let $\times: K \times K^n \to K^n$ be defined as: $\lambda \times \tuple {\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n} = \tuple {\lambda \times_K \alpha_1, \ldots, \lambda \times_K \alpha_n}$ Then $\struct {K^n, +, \times}_K$ is the $K$-vector space $K^n$.

title: Definition:Vector Space on Field Extension
snippet: Let $\struct {K, +, \times}$ be a field. Let $L / K$ be a field extension over $K$. Then $\struct {L, +, \times}_K$ is the vector space on $L$ over $K$.

title: Definition:Vector Space over Division Ring/Left Vector Space
Definition:Vector Space over Division Ring/Right Vector Space
Definition:Vector Space over Division Subring
snippet: Let $\struct {L, +_L, \times_L}$ be a division ring. Let $K$ be a division subring of $\struct {L, +_L, \times_L}$ Let $\circ_K$ denote the restriction of $\circ$ to $S \times R$. Let $\struct {G, +_G, \circ}_L$ be a $L$-vector space. The $K$-vector space $\struct {G, +_G, \circ_K}_K$ is called the $K$-vector space obtained from $\struct {L, +_L, \times_L}$ by restricting scalar multiplication.

title: Definition:Vector Space over Division Subring/Special Case
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring with unity whose unity is $1_R$. Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}_R$ be the $R$-vector space. Let $S$ be a division subring of $R$, such that $1_R \in S$. Let $\circ_S$ denote the restriction of $\circ$ to $S \times R$. Then $\struct {R, +, \circ_S}_S$ is the vector space on $R$ over the division subring $S$.

title: Definition:Vector Space over Subring
snippet: Let $K$ be a division subring of the division ring $\struct {L, +_L, \times_L}$. Let $\struct {G, +_G, \circ}_L$ be a $L$-vector space. Then $\struct {G, +_G, \circ_K}_K$ is a $K$-vector space, where $\circ_K$ is the restriction of $\circ$ to $K \times G$. The $K$-vector space $\struct {G, +_G, \circ_K}_K$ is called the $K$-vector space obtained from $\struct {L, +_L, \times_L}$ by restricting scalar multiplication.

title: Definition:Vector Subspace
snippet: Let $K$ be a division ring. Let $\struct {S, +, \circ}_K$ be a $K$-algebraic structure with one operation. Let $T$ be a closed subset of $S$. Let $\struct {T, +_T, \circ_T}_K$ be a $K$-vector space where: $+_T$ is the restriction of $+$ to $T \times T$ and $\circ_T$ is the restriction of $\circ$ to $K \times T$. Then $\struct {T, +_T, \circ_T}_K$ is a (vector) subspace of $\struct {S, +, \circ}_K$.

title: Definition:Vector Subspace/Also known as
snippet: == Vector Subspace: Also known as == A vector subspace is also known as a linear subspace. A vector subspace is frequently referred just as a subspace if it has been established what it is a subspace of.

title: Definition:Vector Subspace/Hilbert Spaces
snippet: Let $K$ be a division ring. Let $\left({S, +, \circ}\right)_K$ be a $K$-algebraic structure with one operation. Let $T$ be a closed subset of $S$. Let $\left({T, +_T, \circ_T}\right)_K$ be a $K$-vector space where: $+_T$ is the restriction of $+$ to $T \times T$ and $\circ_T$ is the restriction of $\circ$ to $K \times T$. Then $\left({T, +_T, \circ_T}\right)_K$ is a (vector) subspace of $\left({S, +, \circ}\right)_K$. When considering Hilbert spaces, one wants to deal with projections onto subspaces.

title: Definition:Vector Subspace/Proper Subspace
snippet: Let $K$ be a division ring. Let $\struct {S, +, \circ}_K$ be a $K$-algebraic structure with one operation. Let $\struct {T, +_T, \circ_T}_K$ be a vector subspace of $\struct {S, +, \circ}_K$. If $T$ is a proper subset of $S$, then $\struct {T, +_T, \circ_T}_K$ is a proper (vector) subspace of $\struct {S, +, \circ}_K$.

title: Definition:Vector Subtraction
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +_F, \times_F}$ be a field. Let $\struct {G, +_G}$ be an abelian group. Let $V := \struct {G, +_G, \circ}_R$ be the corresponding vector space over $F$. Let $\mathbf x$ and $\mathbf y$ be vectors of $V$. Then the operation of (vector) subtraction on $\mathbf x$ and $\mathbf y$ is defined as: $\mathbf x - \mathbf y := \mathbf x + \paren {-\mathbf y}$ where $-\mathbf y$ is the negative of $\mathbf y$. The $+$ on the is vector addition.

title: Definition:Vector Subtraction/Arrow Representation
snippet: Let $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ be vector quantities of the same physical property. Let $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ be represented by arrows embedded in the plane such that: $\mathbf u$ is represented by $\vec {AB}$ $\mathbf v$ is represented by $\vec {AC}$ that is, so that the initial point of $\mathbf v$ is identified with the initial point of $\mathbf u$. 300px Then their (vector) difference $\mathbf u - \mathbf v$ is represented by the arrow $\vec {CB}$.

title: Definition:Vector Sum
snippet: Let $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ be vector quantities of the same physical property.

title: Definition:Vector Sum/Also known as
snippet: == Vector Sum: Also known as == A vector sum is also frequently seen referred to as a resultant.

title: Definition:Vector Sum/Component Definition
snippet: Let $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ be vector quantities of the same physical property. Let $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ be represented by their components considered to be embedded in a real $n$-space: {{eqn | l = \mathbf u | r = \tuple {u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_n} }} {{eqn | l = \mathbf v | r = \tuple {v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n} }} Then the (vector) sum of $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ is defined as: $\mathbf u + \mathbf v := \tuple {u_1 + v_1, u_2 + v_2, \ldots, u_n + v_n}$ Note that the $+$ on the is conventional addition of numbers, while the $+$ on the takes on a different meaning.

title: Definition:Vector Sum/Triangle Law
snippet: Let $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ be vector quantities of the same physical property. Let $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ be represented by arrows embedded in the plane such that: $\mathbf u$ is represented by $\vec {AB}$ $\mathbf v$ is represented by $\vec {BC}$ that is, so that the initial point of $\mathbf v$ is identified with the terminal point of $\mathbf u$. 400px Then their (vector) sum $\mathbf u + \mathbf v$ is represented by the arrow $\vec {AC}$.

title: Definition:Vector Triple Product
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$, $\mathbf b$ and $\mathbf c$ be vectors in a Cartesian $3$-space: where $\tuple {\mathbf i, \mathbf j, \mathbf k}$ is the standard ordered basis of $\mathbf V$. The vector triple product is defined as: $\mathbf a \times \paren {\mathbf b \times \mathbf c}$ where $\times$ denotes the vector cross product.

title: Definition:Vector Triple Product/Also known as
snippet: The vector triple product is also known as the triple vector product. Some sources use the term repeated cross product.

title: Definition:Vectorial Matroid
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space. Let $S$ be a finite subset of $V$. Let $\struct {S, \mathscr I}$ be the matroid induced by linear independence in $V$ on $S$. Then any matroid isomorphic to $\struct {S, \mathscr I}$ is called a vectorial matroid.

title: Definition:Vectorial Mechanics
snippet: Vectorial mechanics is an approach to problems in mechanics which handles quantities as vector quantities and uses vector algebra and vector calculus for their solution.

title: Definition:Vectorialization of Affine Space
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an affine space over a field $k$ with difference space $E$. Let $\RR = \tuple {p_0, e_1, \ldots, e_n}$ be an affine frame in $\EE$. Define a mapping $\Theta_\RR : k^n \to \EE$ by: $\ds \map {\Theta_\RR} {\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n} = p_0 + \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \lambda_i e_i$. By Affine Coordinates are Well-Defined, $\Theta_\RR$ is a bijection.

title: Definition:Vectorization of Matrix
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $m, n \ge 1$ be natural numbers. Let $A = \sqbrk {a_{i j} }$ be a $m \times n$ matrix over $S$.

title: Definition:Vectorization of Matrix/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $m, n \ge 1$ be natural numbers. Let $A = \sqbrk {a_{i j} }$ be a $m \times n$ matrix over $S$. The vectorization of $A$ is the $m n \times 1$ column matrix: $\map {\operatorname {vec} } A = \sqbrk {a_{1 1}, \ldots, a_{m 1}, a_{1 2}, \ldots, a_{m 2}, \ldots, a_{1 n}, \ldots, a_{m n} }^\intercal$ informally obtained by stacking the columns of $A$. That is: $\map {\operatorname {vec} } A_k = a_{\floor {k / m}, k \bmod m}$ where: $\floor {\, \cdot \,}$ is the floor function $\bmod$ is the modulo operation.

title: Definition:Vectorization of Matrix/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $m, n \ge 1$ be natural numbers. Let $A = \sqbrk {a_{i j} }$ be a $m \times n$ matrix over $S$. Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $A$ be an $m \times n$ matrix over $R$. The vectorization of $A$ is its coordinate vector with respect to the standard matrix basis.

title: Definition:Velocity
snippet: The velocity $\mathbf v$ of a body $M$ is defined as the first derivative of the displacement $\mathbf s$ of $M$ from a given point of reference time $t$: $\mathbf v = \dfrac {\d \mathbf s} {\d t}$ Informally, it is described as the rate of change of position. It is important to note that as displacement is a vector quantity, then it follows by definition of derivative of a vector that so is velocity.

title: Definition:Velocity/Dimension
snippet: The dimension of measurement of velocity is $\mathsf {L T^{-1} }$.

title: Definition:Velocity/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Velocity == The first person to treat the velocity as a vector was .

title: Definition:Velocity/Straight Line
snippet: Let $P$ be a particle in motion along a straight line $\LL$ with velocity $\map {\mathbf v} t$ as a function of time $t$. It is conventional to align $\LL$ along the $x$-axis of a Cartesian coordinate system such that the $\mathbf v$ can be expressed as $v \mathbf i$. Then the unit vector $\mathbf i$ of the component vector $v \mathbf i$ is suppressed, and $\map {\mathbf v} t$ is treated as a scalar quantity $\map v t$.

title: Definition:Velocity/Symbol
snippet: == Velocity: Symbol == The usual symbol used to denote the velocity of a body is $\mathbf v$.

title: Definition:Velocity/Unit
snippet: The SI unit of velocity is the the metre per second: $\mathrm {m \, s^{-1} }$. The CGS unit of velocity is the centimetre per second: $\mathrm {cm \, s^{-1} }$. The FPS unit of velocity is the foot per second $\mathrm {ft \, s^{-1} }$.

title: Definition:Velocity/Unit/Centimetre per Second
snippet: == CGS unit of Velocity == The CGS unit of velocity is the centimetre per second.

title: Definition:Velocity/Unit/Foot per Second
snippet: == FPS unit of velocity == The FPS unit of velocity is the foot per second.

title: Definition:Velocity/Unit/Metre per Second
snippet: == SI unit of Velocity == The SI unit of velocity is the metre per second.

title: Definition:Velocity Ratio
snippet: Let $M$ be a machine. The velocity ratio of $M$ is defined as the ratio of the distance moved by the effort applied to $M$ to the distance moved by the load on $M$.

title: Definition:Velocity of Main Curve
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $I, J \subseteq \R$ be real intervals. Let $\map {\Gamma_s} t : J \times I \to M$ be the main curve, where $\times$ denotes the cartesian product. Let $\map {\Gamma_s} t$ be differentiable on $I$. Then the velocity of the main curve is denoted by: $\partial_t \map {\Gamma} {s, t} = \map {\paren {\Gamma_s}'} t$ where: $\partial_t \map {\Gamma} {s, t} \in T_{\map \Gamma {s, t} } M$ $T_p M$ is the tangent space of $M$ at $p \in M$ $\map \Gamma {s, t}$ is the one-parameter family of curves on $M$.

title: Definition:Velocity of Smooth Curve
snippet: Let $I \subseteq \R$ be an interval. Let $\gamma: \R \to \R^n$ be a smooth curve, written in standard coordinates as: $\map \gamma t = \tuple {\map {\gamma^1} t, \ldots, \map {\gamma^n} t}$. The velocity of $\gamma$ at $t \in I$ is defined as: $\map {\gamma'} t = \valueat{\map {\dot \gamma^1} t \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x^1} } {\map \gamma t} + \ldots + \valueat {\map {\dot \gamma^n} t \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x^n} } {\map \gamma t}$

title: Definition:Velocity of Transverse Curve
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $I, J \subseteq \R$ be real intervals. Let $\map {\Gamma^{\paren t} } s : J \times I \to M$ be the transverse curve, where $\times$ denotes the cartesian product. Let $\map {\Gamma^{\paren t} } s$ be differentiable on $J$. Then the velocity of the transverse curve is denoted by: $\partial_s \map {\Gamma} {s, t} = \map {\paren {\Gamma^{\paren t}}'} s$ where: $\partial_s \map {\Gamma} {s, t} \in T_{\map \Gamma {s, t} } M$ $T_p M$ is the tangent space of $M$ at $p \in M$ $\map \Gamma {s, t}$ is the one-parameter family of curves on $M$.

title: Definition:Venn Diagram
snippet: A Venn diagram is a technique for the graphic depiction of the interrelationship between a small number (usually $3$ or fewer) of sets. The following diagram illustrates the various operations between three sets. 500px The circles represent the sets $S_1$, $S_2$ and $S_3$. The white surrounding box represents the universal set $\mathbb U$. Each of the areas inside the various circle represents an intersection between the various sets and their complements, as follows: The gray area represents $S_1 \cap S_2 \cap S_3$. The purple area represents $S_1 \cap S_2 \cap \overline {S_3}$.

title: Definition:Venn Diagram/Also known as
snippet: == Venn Diagram: Also known as == Some sources spell Venn diagram without the uppercase V: venn diagram. Category:Definitions/Venn Diagrams

title: Definition:Venus
snippet: Venus is the second planet of the solar system from the sun. Its orbit lies between those of Mercury and Earth. Category:Definitions/Solar System

title: Definition:Veridical Paradox
snippet: A veridical paradox is a counter-intuitive result which can be demonstrated to be true.

title: Definition:Vernal Equinox/Also known as
snippet: == Vernal Equinox: Also known as == The vernal equinox is also known as the March equinox or the spring equinox. The term northward equinox can also be seen in contexts requiring hemisphere neutrality. Category:Definitions/Equinoxes

title: Definition:Vernal Equinox/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Vernal Equinox == The term vernal equinox derives from the Latin vēr meaning (the season of) spring and aequinoctium, from aequus meaning equal and nox meaning night. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Versed Sine
snippet: The versed sine of an angle is defined as: $\vers \theta = 1 - \cos \theta$

title: Definition:Versed Sine/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Versed Sine == The term versed sine derives from the Latin sinus versus, which literally means turned sine or flipped sine. This arises from the fact that the versed sine is the horizontal distance from the end of the cosine to the edge of the circle, while the sine itself is the vertical distance. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Vertex
snippet: Graph Theory: Vertex of Graph: The vertices of a graph are the points, which may or may not be joined by edges. Geometry and Solid Geometry: Vertex: A point at which $2$ or more line segments meet on the boundary of a geometric figure: Vertex of Polygon: The corners of a polygon are known as its vertices. Vertex of Polyhedron: The corners of a polyhedron are known as its vertices. Vertex of Angle: The point at which the lines containing an angle meet is known as its vertex.

title: Definition:Vertex/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Vertex == The plural of vertex is vertices. The word vertex is Latin for peak, from which the irregular plural form.

title: Definition:Vertex (Geometry)
snippet: A vertex is a point on the boundary of a geometric figure at which $2$ or more line segments meet.

title: Definition:Vertex Cut
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a graph. A vertex cut of $G$ is a set of vertices $W \subseteq \map V G$ such that the vertex deletion $G \setminus W$ is disconnected.

title: Definition:Vertex Deletion
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be an (undirected) graph. Let $W \subseteq V$ be a set of vertices of $G$. Then the graph obtained by deleting $W$ from $G$, denoted by $G - W$, is the subgraph induced by $V \setminus W$. Alternatively: $G - W = \struct {V \setminus W, \set {e \in E : e \cap W = \O} }$ Informally, $G - W$ is the graph obtained from $G$ by removing all vertices in $W$ and all edges incident to those vertices. If $W$ is a singleton such that $W = \set v$, then $G - W$ may be expressed $G - v$.

title: Definition:Vertex Set
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a graph. The set $V$ of vertices in $G$ is called the vertex set. It is often convenient to refer to the vertex set for a given graph $G$ as $\map V G$, especially if there is at any one time more than one graph under consideration.

title: Definition:Vertex Set/Also defined as
snippet: == Vertex Set: Also known as == Some sources further specify that the vertex set cannot be empty. That is, that a graph must have at least one vertex. Hence such sources do not raise the concept of a null graph.

title: Definition:Vertex of Angle/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Vertex of Angle == While the term is used throughout , the concept of the vertex of an angle is never formally defined there. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Vertex of Ellipse/Also defined as
snippet: == Vertex of Ellipse: Also defined as == Some sources also classify the covertices as vertices. That is, they define the vertices as the endpoints of both the major axis and the minor axis.

title: Definition:Vertex of Graph/Also known as
snippet: == Vertex of Graph: Also known as == A vertex of a graph $G$, particularly when $G$ is a tree, is also known as a node.

title: Definition:Vertex of Polytope
snippet: Let $P$ be a polytope. A vertex of $P$ is one of the points at which two or more line segments meet on the boundary of $P$.

title: Definition:Vertex of Simplex
snippet: Let $S$ be a $k$-simplex for some $k \in \Z_{>0}$: $S = \set {\ds \sum_{i \mathop = 0}^k \theta_i \alpha_i}$ A vertex of $S$ is one of the $k + 1$ points $\alpha_0, \alpha_1 \ldots, \alpha_k$.

title: Definition:Vertex of Solid Angle/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Vertex of Solid Angle == While the term vertex (of a solid angle) is used throughout , the concept is never formally defined there. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Vertex of Spherical Triangle/Also known as
snippet: == Vertex of Spherical Triangle: Also known as == A vertex of a spherical triangle is also known as an angle. However, on we prefer to use the term angle to refer to the spherical angle formed by the sides.

title: Definition:Vertex of Spherical Triangle/Angle
snippet: The angles of a spherical triangle $T$ are the spherical angles at each vertex of $T$. 500px

title: Definition:Vertical/Terminology
snippet: == Note on Terminology == The term the vertical is frequently seen, particularly in the context of specifying the spatial orientation of a given (straight) line: the angle it makes to the vertical. It needs to be borne in mind that the terms vertical and horizontal are meaningful only in the context of an environment with a gravitational field, and therefore one where up and down have a meaning. In the context of the presentation of mathematical graphics on, for example, a piece of paper arranged horizontally, the vertical is that direction towards and away from the reader.

title: Definition:Vertical Affine Hyperplane
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \tau_X}$ be a topological vector space over $\R$. Let $X^\ast$ be the topological dual space of $\struct {X, \tau_X}$. Let $\struct {X \times \R, \tau}$ be the direct product of $X$ and $\R$ equipped with the product topology. Let $\paren {X \times \R}^\ast$ be the topological dual space of $\struct {X \times \R, \tau}$. Let $\innerprod \cdot \cdot$ be the canonical duality on $X \times \R$. Let $f \in X^\ast$. We say that: $\set {\tuple {x, \alpha} : X \times \R : \innerprod {\tuple {x, \alpha} } {\tuple {f, 0} } = c}$ is a vertical affine hyperplane in $X \times \R$.

title: Definition:Vertical Angles
snippet: When two straight lines intersect, the angles opposite each other are called vertical angles: 400px In the above diagram: $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are vertical angles $\gamma$ and $\delta$ are vertical angles.

title: Definition:Vertical Angles/Also known as
snippet: == Vertical Angles: Also known as == Vertical angles are also known as vertically opposite angles, or vertical opposite angles.

title: Definition:Vertical Asymptote
snippet: The vertical line $x = L$ is a vertical asymptote of the graph of a real function $f$ either of the following limits exist: {{eqn | l = \lim_{x \mathop \to L} \map f x | r = \infty }} {{eqn | l = \lim_{x \mathop \to L} \map f x | r = -\infty }}

title: Definition:Vertical Circle
snippet: Let $X$ be the position of a star (or other celestial body) on the celestial sphere. The vertical circle through $X$ is defined as the great circle passing through both $X$ and the zenith $Z$.

title: Definition:Vertical Composition of Natural Transformations
snippet: Let $C$ and $D$ be categories. Let $F, G, H: C \to D$ be covariant functors. Let $\eta: F \to G$ and $\xi: G \to H$ be natural transformations. The vertical composition of $\eta$ and $\xi$ is the natural transformation $\xi \circ \eta : F \Rightarrow H$ with $\paren {\xi \circ \eta}_A = \xi_A \circ \eta_A$ for $A \in C$.

title: Definition:Vertical Group Action
snippet: Let $\tilde M$, $M$ be smooth manifolds. Let $\pi : \tilde M \to M$ be a surjective smooth submersion. Let $G$ be a group acting on $\tilde M$. Suppose each element of $G$ takes each fiber to itself: $\forall \phi \in G : \forall p \in \tilde M : \map \pi {\phi \cdot p} = \map \pi p$ Then the action is called to be vertical.

title: Definition:Vertical Line/Definition 1
snippet: A line is vertical it is aligned perpendicular to the horizon. File:Vertical.png

title: Definition:Vertical Line/Definition 2
snippet: A line is vertical it is parallel to the path taken by a body released from rest in a constant gravitational field. File:Vertical.png

title: Definition:Vertical Plane
snippet: A plane is vertical it contains a vertical line.

title: Definition:Vertical Section of Function
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be sets. Let $f : X \times Y \to \overline \R$ be an extended real-valued function. Let $x \in X$. We define the vertical section $f_x$ of $f$ by: $\map {f_x} y = \map f {x, y}$ for each $y \in Y$.

title: Definition:Vertical Section of Set
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be sets. Let $E \subseteq X \times Y$. Let $x \in X$. We define the $x$-vertical section $E_x$ of $E$ by: $E_x = \set {y \in Y : \tuple {x, y} \in E}$

title: Definition:Vertical Tangent Line
snippet: Let $P = \tuple {c, \map f c}$ be a point on the graph of a real function $f$. The vertical line $x = c$ is a vertical tangent line to the graph of $f$ at $P$ any of the following hold: $(1): \quad f$ is right continuous at $c$ and $\ds \lim_{x \mathop \to c^+} \map {f'} x = +\infty$ $(2): \quad f$ is right continuous at $c$ and $\ds \lim_{x \mathop \to c^+} \map {f'} x = -\infty$ $(3): \quad f$ is left continuous at $c$ and $\ds \lim_{x \mathop \to c^-} \map {f'} x = +\infty$ $(4): \quad f$ is left continuous at $c$ and $\ds \lim_{x \mathop \to c^-} \map {f'} x = -\infty$

title: Definition:Vertical Tangent Space
snippet: Let $M, \tilde M$ be smooth manifolds. Let $\tilde g$ be a Riemannian metric on $\tilde M$. Let $\pi : \tilde M \to M$ be a smooth submersion. Let $x \in \tilde M$ be a point. The vertical tangent space at $x$, denoted by $V_x$, is defined as the tangent space to the fiber containing $x$: $V_x := \ker d \pi_x = \map {T_x} {\tilde M_{\map \pi x}}$

title: Definition:Vertical Vector Field
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $x \in M$ be a base point. Let $V_x$ be the vertical tangent space. Let $Y$ be a vector field on $M$. Suppose for each $x \in M$ the value of $Y$ lies in the vertical space of $x$: $\forall x \in M : \valueat Y x \in V_x$ Then $X$ is called a vertical vector field.

title: Definition:Very Strong Zero
snippet: A very strong zero or very strongly zero is a variation of zero such that multiplication with another expression results in $0$ even if the other expression is undefined, such as for example if it contains division by zero.

title: Definition:Vice Versa
snippet: Vice versa is a phrase which means: and the other way around. That is: in reverse order from the way it has been stated.

title: Definition:Vice Versa/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Vice Versa == The phrase vice versa is from the Latin, meaning with the order reversed. It is usually pronounced as it is spelt. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Vigenère Cipher
snippet: A Vigenère cipher is a polyalphabetic substitution cipher which combines several Caesar ciphers working together. It uses $26$ Caesar ciphers, and includes the use of a keyword in the message telling the recipient in which order those Caesar ciphers are to be used.

title: Definition:Vigenère Cipher/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Vigenère Cipher == The concept of a substitution cipher of the style of the Vigenère cipher dates back to Italian cryptographers of the $15$th century. They were developed because a simple monoalphabetic cipher is susceptible to attack by frequency analysis.

title: Definition:Vigenère Cipher/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Vigenère Cipher == The name in the term Vigenère cipher is pronounced something like Vi-zhe-nair. That is, the g is soft, in the French style. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Vigesimal System
snippet: A vigesimal system is a number system in which the base is $20$. In conventional base $20$ notation, every number $x \in \R$ is expressed in the form: $\ds x = \sum_{j \mathop \in \Z} r_j 20^j$ where: $\forall j \in \Z: r_j \in \set {0, 1, \ldots, 19}$

title: Definition:Vigesimal System/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Vigesimal System == The vigesimal system was used by the of until the $18$th century. The system used a zero and was a fully positional system.

title: Definition:Vigesimal System/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Vigesimal System == The word vigesimal derives from the Latin vīgintī, meaning twenty, and vicesimus, meaning twentieth. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Vigintillion/Also known as
snippet: Some sources use the word vigillion for vigintillion.

title: Definition:Vigintillion/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Vigintillion == The word vigintillion is created from the Latin-derived prefix viginti-, meaning twentyfold, together with -illion, a back-formation from the word million.

title: Definition:Vigintillion/Long Scale
snippet: Vigintillion is a name for $10^{120}$ in the long scale system: One vigintillion $= 10^{6 \times 20}$

title: Definition:Vigintillion/Short Scale
snippet: Vigintillion is a name for $10^{63}$ in the short scale system: One vigintillion $= 10^{3 \times 20 + 3}$

title: Definition:Vigintillion/Short Scale/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Vigintillion == One vigintillion ($10^{63}$) is, according to by , the number of grains of sand that it would take to fill the Universe (according to the size that it was believed to be at the time).

title: Definition:Virtual Circle
snippet: A virtual circle is the locus in the Cartesian plane of an equation of the form: $(1): \quad \paren {x - a}^2 + \paren {y - b}^2 + r^2 = 0$ where $a$, $b$ and $r$ are real constants. There are no solutions to $(1)$ in real numbers, and so the locus of $(1)$ consists entirely of imaginary points.

title: Definition:Viscosity
snippet: The viscosity of a fluid is a measure of how large a damping force it exerts upon a body moving through it.

title: Definition:Visible Hemisphere
snippet: The visible hemisphere is the hemisphere of the celestial sphere between the celestial horizon and the zenith. That is, it is the half of the sky that can be seen from Earth at an arbitrary time. The other hemisphere of the celestial sphere is hidden from an observer by Earth itself. 480px

title: Definition:Vitali Set
snippet: A Vitali set is a subset of the real numbers which has no Lebesgue measure.

title: Definition:Volt
snippet: The volt is the SI unit of electromotive force and electric potential. It is defined as being the difference in electric potential between two points of an electrical conductor: when an electric current of $1$ ampere dissipates $1$ watt of power between those points that will impart $1$ joule of energy per coulomb of electric charge that passes through it.

title: Definition:Volt/Base Units
snippet: The SI base units of the volt are: $\mathrm V := \mathrm {kg} \, \mathrm m^2 \mathrm s^{-3} \mathrm A^{-1}$ where: $\mathrm {kg}$ denotes kilograms $\mathrm m$ denotes metres $\mathrm s$ denotes seconds (of time). $\mathrm A$ denotes ampere. This arises from its definition as: $\mathrm J \, \mathrm C^{-1}$, that is: joules per coulomb which is also presentable as: $\mathrm W \, \mathrm A^{-1}$, that is: watts per ampere.

title: Definition:Volterra Integral Equation
snippet: The Volterra integral equations are integral equations of the first and second kind such that the limits of integration are between a constant $a$ and the variable $x$:

title: Definition:Volterra Integral Equation/Also known as
snippet: == Volterra Integral Equations: Also known as == The Volterra integral equations can also be seen in the form Volterra's integral equations.

title: Definition:Volterra Integral Equation of the First Kind
snippet: A Volterra integral equation of the first kind is an integral equation of the form: $\ds \map f x = \lambda \int_a^x \map K {x, y} \map g y \rd y$ where $g$ is an unknown real function.

title: Definition:Volterra Integral Equation of the Second Kind
snippet: A Volterra integral equation of the second kind is an integral equation of the form: $\ds \map g x = \map f x + \lambda \int_a^x \map K {x, y} \map g y \rd y$ where $g$ is an unknown real function.

title: Definition:Volume
snippet: Volume is the measure of the extent of a body. It has three dimensions and is specified in units of length cubed. Hence the term cube as a general vague term for a quantity in three dimensions. It is a scalar quantity.

title: Definition:Volume/Also known as
snippet: == Volume: Also known as == The term capacity can sometimes be seen in texts whose emphasis is on physics and applied mathematics. In non-mathematical literature and popular puzzle pages, less precise terms can be seen, for example cubical contents.

title: Definition:Volume/Dimension
snippet: Volume is a dimension of measurement of physics. The dimension of measurement of volume is: $L^3$ length cubed. Category:Definitions/Dimensions of Measurement Category:Definitions/Volume

title: Definition:Volume/Symbol
snippet: == Volume: Symbol == The usual symbol used to denote the volume of a body is $V$.

title: Definition:Volume/Unit
snippet: The SI unit of volume is the cubic metre: $\mathrm m^3$ The CGS unit of volume is the cubic centimetre: $\mathrm {cm}^3$ or, less formally: $\mathrm {cc}$ Thus: $1 \ \mathrm m^3 = 10^6 \ \mathrm {cm}^3 = 1 \,000 \,000 \ \mathrm {cc}$ Category:Definitions/Units of Measurement Category:Definitions/Volume

title: Definition:Volume Element
snippet: A volume element $\delta V$ is a (usually) infinitesimal volume of space (usually) containing a particular point $P$. In the cartesian $3$-space such a volume element is modelled as a cuboid whose edges are parallel to the coordinate axes and assigned lengths $\delta x$, $\delta y$ and $\delta z$ respectively: 300px

title: Definition:Volume of Compact Riemannian Manifold
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $\rd V_g$ be the Riemannian volume form. Let $M$ be compact. Then the volume of the compact Riemannian manifold $M$, denoted by $\map {\text{Vol}} M$, is defined as: $\ds \map {\text{Vol}} M = \int_M \rd V_g$

title: Definition:Von Mangoldt Function
snippet: The von Mangoldt function $\Lambda: \N \to \R$ is defined as: $\map \Lambda n = \begin {cases} \map \ln p & : \exists m \in \N, p \in \mathbb P: n = p^m \\ 0 & : \text {otherwise} \end {cases}$ where $\mathbb P$ is the set of all prime numbers.

title: Definition:Von Mangoldt Function/Also known as
snippet: == Von Mangoldt Function: Also known as == Some sources dispose of the von, and instead refer to the von Mangoldt function as just the Mangoldt function. Category:Definitions/Von Mangoldt Function

title: Definition:Von Neumann-Bernays-Gödel Set Theory
snippet: Von Neumann-Bernays-Gödel set theory is a system of axiomatic set theory. Its main feature is that it classifies collections of objects into: sets, whose construction is strictly controlled and: classes, which have fewer restrictions on how they may be generated. All sets are classes, but not all classes are sets.

title: Definition:Von Neumann-Bernays-Gödel Set Theory/Also known as
snippet: == Von Neumann-Bernays-Gödel Set Theory: Also known as == Von Neumann-Bernays-Gödel set theory is also known just as von Neumann set theory. It is usually seen abbreviated either as NBG or VNB.

title: Definition:Von Neumann-Bernays-Gödel Set Theory/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Von Neumann-Bernays-Gödel Set Theory == Von Neumann-Bernays-Gödel set theory was proposed by in $1925$ as an alternative to Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory. It was later revised by , and .

title: Definition:Von Neumann-Bounded Subset of Topological Vector Space
snippet: Let $\Bbb F \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological vector space over $\Bbb F$. Let $E \subseteq X$. We say that $E$ is von Neumann-bounded : for each open neighbourhood $V$ of ${\mathbf 0}_X$, there exists $s > 0$ such that $E \subseteq t V$ for each $t > s$ where $t V$ is the dilation of $V$ by $t$.

title: Definition:Von Neumann Hierarchy
snippet: Let $U$ denote the universal class. The von Neumann hierarchy is a mapping $V: \On \to U$ on the ordinals, defined via the Second Principle of Transfinite Recursion: $\map V x = \begin {cases} \O & : x = 0 \\ & \\ \powerset {\map V n} & : x = n^+ \\ & \\ \ds \bigcup_{y \mathop \in x} \map V y & : x \in \operatorname {Lim} \\ \end {cases}$ where: $\powerset x$ denotes the power set of $x$ $\operatorname {Lim}$ denotes the set of limit ordinals.

title: Definition:Vulgar Fraction/Also known as
snippet: == Vulgar Fraction: Also known as == A vulgar fraction is also known as a common fraction a simple fraction.

title: Definition:Vulgar Fraction/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Vulgar Fraction == The original everyday meaning of the word vulgar was at one point common, in the sense usual or everyday. It derives from the Latin [https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/vulgus vulgus], meaning the common people in the sense of the public. Through the process of the [http://www.odlt.org/ballast/euphemism_treadmill.html euphemism treadmill], the word in natural language has since gained the meaning rude or impolite. Incidentally, it is also worth noting that the word common has gone the same way. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:WFF of Propositional Logic/Also known as
snippet: == WFF of Propositional Logic: Also known as == There are many ways the concept of a WFF of propositional logic is addressed in the literature, for instance: However, on , logical formula is a term used to refer to any kind of expression used in symbolic logic, whereas statement form is used in this way in some sources. Hence on WFF of propositional logic and propositional formula are the terms of choice for this concept. Some sources, in their quest to limit the amount of technical terms, use verbosities like sentence in the official sense, but again, this is discouraged by .

title: Definition:WLOG
snippet: Suppose there are several cases which need to be investigated. If the same argument can be used to dispose of two or more of these cases, then it is acceptable in a proof to pick just one of these cases, and announce this fact with the words: Without loss of generality, ..., or just WLOG. When communicating mathematics verbally, it is becoming commonplace to use the vocalisation wullog rather than the timewastingly multisyllabic without loss of generality. Category:Definitions/Language Definitions

title: Definition:Waiting Time
snippet: Let $\sequence X$ be a sequence of events such that the intervals between occurrences obey a stochastic process. The waiting time of $\sequence X$ is defined as the interval between successive events.

title: Definition:Wald's Maximin Model
snippet: Wald's maximin model is the rule based on the general observation that one minimizes the maximum risk when making a wrong decision.

title: Definition:Wald's Maximin Model/Also known as
snippet: == Wald's Maximin Model: Also known as == A Wald's maximin model is also known as: Sometimes minimax is used instead of maximin. Some sources leave off the name, and refer to it as, for example, the minimax principle.

title: Definition:Wald's Maximin Model/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Wald's Maximin Model == Wald's maximin model was formulated by in $1939$. The general consensus is that it is unduly pessimistic.

title: Definition:Walk
snippet: Graph theory: Walk: an alternating series of vertices and edges beginning and ending with a vertex in which each edge is incident with the vertex immediately preceding it and the vertex immediately following it. Closed walk: a walk where the start and end vertices are the same Open walk: a walk where the start and end vertices are not the same Directed walk: a finite or infinite sequence $\sequence {x_k}$ of vertices such that $\forall k \in \N: k + 1 \in \Dom {\sequence {x_k} }: \tuple {x_k, x_{k + 1} } \in A$ Probability theory Random walk

title: Definition:Walk (Graph Theory)
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a graph. A walk $W$ on $G$ is: an alternating sequence of vertices $v_1, v_2, \ldots$ and edges $e_1, e_2, \ldots$ of $G$ beginning and ending with a vertex in which edge $e_j$ of $W$ is incident with the vertex $v_j$ and the vertex $v_{j + 1}$. A walk between two vertices $u$ and $v$ is called a $u$-$v$ walk. To describe a walk on a simple graph it is sufficient to list just the vertices in order, as the edges (being unique between vertices) are unambiguous.

title: Definition:Walk (Graph Theory)/Also known as
snippet: == Walk: Also known as == Some sources refer to a walk as a path, and use the term simple path to define what we have here as a path.

title: Definition:Walk (Graph Theory)/Closed
snippet: A closed walk is a walk whose first vertex is the same as the last. That is, it is a walk which ends where it starts.

title: Definition:Walk (Graph Theory)/Length
snippet: The length of a walk (or a path, or a trail) is the number of edges it has, counting repeated edges as many times as they appear. A walk is said to be of infinite length it has infinitely many edges.

title: Definition:Walk (Graph Theory)/Open
snippet: An open walk is a walk whose first vertex and last vertex are distinct. That is, it is a walk which ends on a different vertex from the one where it starts.

title: Definition:Wall
snippet: A wall is an immovable vertical plane in space to which other physical objects may be attached.

title: Definition:Wall-Sun-Sun Prime
snippet: A Wall-Sun-Sun prime is a prime number $p$ such that: $p^2 \divides F_{p - \paren {p \vert 5} }$ where: $\divides$ denotes divisibility $\paren {p \vert 5}$ denotes the Legendre symbol.

title: Definition:Wallace-Simson Line
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle. Let $P$ be a point on the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$. Construct perpendiculars from $P$ to each of the sides of $\triangle ABC$. Let $D$, $E$ and $F$ be the feet of those perpendiculars. 300px The line $DEF$ called the Wallace-Simson line of the point $P$ $\triangle ABC$.

title: Definition:Wallace-Simson Line/Also known as
snippet: == Wallace-Simson Line: Also known as == The Wallace-Simson line is also known just as the Simson line, or Simson's line. Some sources indicate that it can also be called just the simson.

title: Definition:Wallace-Simson Line/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Wallace-Simson Line == While it is often named just for , it does not appear in his work, and the Simson line was in fact first discovered by in $1797$. He published it in a paper of $1799$. Hence it is often referred to as the Wallace-Simson line instead.

title: Definition:Wallis's Number
snippet: Wallis's number is the real root of the cubic: $x^3 - 2 x - 5 = 0$ Its approximate value is: $2 \cdotp 09455 \, 1 \ldots$

title: Definition:Wallis's Number/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Wallis's Number == The cubic $x^3 - 2 x - 5 = 0$ was used by as a example to demonstrate how Newton's Method could be used to solve certain equations numerically. The real root of this equation has since become known as Wallis's number. It has subsequently been used as a test for a number of different methods of approximation. It is known to over $4000$ digits.

title: Definition:Wallpaper Group
snippet: A wallpaper group is the symmetry group of a $2$-dimensional configuration in the plane.

title: Definition:Wallpaper Group/Also known as
snippet: == Wallpaper Group: Also known as == A wallpaper group is also known as a planar crystallographic group.

title: Definition:Wallpaper Group/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Wallpaper Group == It was long known that there are 17 Wallpaper Groups but this was not proven till $1891$. Category:Historical Notes

title: Definition:Wallpaper Pattern
snippet: A wallpaper pattern is a plane geometrical figure which has translational symmetry in two non-parallel lines.

title: Definition:Warped Product Manifold
snippet: Let $\struct {M_1, g_1}$, $\struct {M_2, g_2}$ be Riemannian manifolds. Let $f : M_1 \to \R_{\mathop > 0}$ be a strictly positive smooth function. Let $p \in M$ be a point. Let $T_p M$ be a tangent space of $M$ at $p$. Let $v \in T_p M$ be a tangent vector. Let $g_p$ be a Riemannian metric of $M$ at $p$.

title: Definition:Water
snippet: Water is the common term for the chemical substance whose molecules are composed of $2$ atoms of hydrogen and $1$ atom of oxygen. It can be expressed using the chemical formula $\mathrm H_2 \mathrm O$.

title: Definition:Watt-Hour
snippet: The watt-hour is an SI unit of energy. It is defined as being: the energy expended when a power of $1$ watt is applied for $1$ hour.

title: Definition:Watt-Hour/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Watt-Hour: Conversion Factors == Category:Definitions/Watt-Hour

title: Definition:Watt/Base Units
snippet: The SI base units of the watt are: $\mathrm W := \mathrm {kg} \, \mathrm m^2 \mathrm s^{-3}$ where: $\mathrm {kg}$ denotes kilograms $\mathrm m$ denotes metres $\mathrm s$ denotes seconds (of time). This arises from the definition of the watt as $\mathrm J \, \mathrm s^{-1}$, that is, joules per second.

title: Definition:Watt/Conversion Factors
snippet: == Watt: Conversion Factors ==

title: Definition:Watt per Metre-Kelvin
snippet: The watt per metre-kelvin is the SI unit of thermal conductivity.

title: Definition:Watt per Metre-Kelvin/Also known as
snippet: == Watt per Metre-Kelvin: Also known as == The watt per metre-kelvin is also presented in some sources as the joule per metre-second-kelvin.

title: Definition:Wave
snippet: A wave is a disturbance in a medium which propagates through that medium with the following properties: $(1): \quad$ energy is propagated between two points in space through that medium $(2): \quad$ the disturbance travels through the medium without causing the medium itself to undergo any permanent displacement.

title: Definition:Wave-Particle Duality
snippet: Wave-particle duality is a phenomenon of quantum mechanics in which a particle can act as a wave, and a wave can act like a particle.

title: Definition:Wave/Direction of Propagation
snippet: The direction in which a wave travels is known as its direction of propagation.

title: Definition:Wave/Disturbance
snippet: The disturbance of a wave at a given point and time is defined as the quantity that the medium is different from its equilibrium.

title: Definition:Wave/Progressive
snippet: A wave whose wave profile actually moves in space over time is called a progressive wave.

title: Definition:Wave Equation
snippet: == Equation == The wave equation is a second order PDE of the form: {{eqn | l = \dfrac 1 {c^2} \dfrac {\partial^2 \phi} {\partial t^2} | r = \dfrac {\partial^2 \phi} {\partial x^2} + \dfrac {\partial^2 \phi} {\partial y^2} + \dfrac {\partial^2 \phi} {\partial z^2} | c = }}

title: Definition:Wave Equation/Also known as
snippet: == Wave Equation: Also known as == The wave equation is referred to as the equation of wave motion by some authors, ostensibly so as not to confuse it with certain entities in the field of quantum physics. However, this confusion may not in fact be actual.

title: Definition:Wave Equation/Also presented as
snippet: == Wave Equation: Also presented as == The wave equation is also seen presented in the form: {{eqn | l = \dfrac {\partial^2 \phi} {\partial t^2} | r = c^2 \paren {\dfrac {\partial^2 \phi} {\partial x^2} + \dfrac {\partial^2 \phi} {\partial y^2} + \dfrac {\partial^2 \phi} {\partial z^2} } | c = }}

title: Definition:Wave Mechanics
snippet: Wave mechanics is the branch of physics concerned with the physical behaviour of waves. As such it provides the mathematical underpinning to the wave mechanical model of quantum mechanics.

title: Definition:Wave Mechanics/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Wave Mechanics == Wave mechanics was developed as a form of quantum mechanics by , based on his solution of wave equations of systems of particles.

title: Definition:Wave Number/Also known as
snippet: == Wave Number: Also known as == The term wave number can also be seen as wavenumber.

title: Definition:Wave Profile
snippet: Let $\phi$ be a wave which is propagated along the $x$-axis with velocity $c$. At $t = 0$, let $\phi = \map f x$. Then $\map f x$ is the wave profile of $\phi$. This can be expressed as: $\paren {\map \phi x}_{t \mathop = 0} = \map f x$

title: Definition:Wavelength
snippet: Wave Mechanics: Wavelength of Periodic Wave Physics: Wavelength

title: Definition:Wavelength/Symbol
snippet: == Wavelength: Symbol == The usual symbol used to denote the wavelength of a wave is $\lambda$.

title: Definition:Wavelength (Physics)
snippet: The wavelength of a wave is the distance travelled in the direction of propagation between two points at the same phase of disturbance in consecutive cycles. That is, it is the distance over which the wave's shape repeats.

title: Definition:Wavelet
snippet: A wavelet is a special function the use of which other functions can be expressed, allowing greater flexibility than Fourier series.

title: Definition:Wavelet/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Wavelet == The concept of the wavelet was introduced in the $1980$s as a concept in pure mathematics. It has since been used a great deal in many applied mathematical contexts.

title: Definition:Way Above Closure
snippet: Let $\left({S, \preceq}\right)$ be an ordered set. Let $x \in S$. The way above closure of $x$, denoted by $x^\gg$, is defined by: $x^\gg := \left\{ {y \in S: x \ll y}\right\}$ where $\ll$ denotes the way below relation.

title: Definition:Way Below Closure
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $x \in S$. The way below closure of $x$, denoted by $x^\ll$, is defined by $x^\ll := \set {y \in S: y \ll x}$ where $y \ll x$ denotes that $y$ is way below $x$.

title: Definition:Way Below Open
snippet: Let $\left({S, \preceq}\right)$ a preordered set. Let $X$ be a subset of $S$. Then $X$ is way below open : $\forall x \in X: \exists y \in X: y \ll x$ where $\ll$ denotes the way below relation.

title: Definition:Weak
snippet: Definition:Weaker Statement Definition:Weak Convergence Definition:Weak Topology Definition:Weakly Locally Compact Space

title: Definition:Weak-* Convergence (Normed Vector Space)
snippet: Let $\Bbb F \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm \cdot}$ be a normed vector space over $\Bbb F$. Let $\sequence {f_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence of bounded linear functionals on $X$. Let $f : X \to \Bbb F$ be a bounded linear functional. Then we say that $\sequence {f_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ converges weakly-$\ast$ (read as "weakly-star") : $\map {f_n} x \to \map f x$ for each $x \in X$. We say that $f$ is a weak-$\ast$ limit of $\sequence {f_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$. We denote this: $f_n \weakstarconv f$

title: Definition:Weak-* Topology
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a topological vector space over $\GF$. Let $X^\ast$ be the topological dual space of $X$. For each $x \in X$, define $x^\wedge : X^\ast \to \GF$ by: $\map {x^\wedge} f = \map f x$ Let: $\sigma = \set {x^\wedge : x \in X}$ Let $w^\ast$ be the initial topology on $X^\ast$ with respect to $\sigma$. We say that $w^\ast$ is the weak-$\ast$ topology of $X^\ast$.

title: Definition:Weak-* Topology Induced by Dual System
snippet: Let $K$ be a topological field. Let $\innerprod X {X'}$ be a dual system over $K$. For each $x \in X$, define $\pi_x : X' \to K$ by: $\map {\pi_x} {x'} = \innerprod x {x'}$ for each $x \in X$. Let: $F = \set {\pi_x : x \in X}$ We define the weak-$\ast$ topology on $X'$ induced by $\innerprod X {X'}$ as the initial topology induced on $X'$ by $F$. This is usually denoted: $\map \sigma {X', X}$

title: Definition:Weak Cauchy Sequence
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological vector space over $\GF$. Let $X^\ast$ be the topological dual of $\struct {X, \tau}$. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $X$. We say that $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is a weak Cauchy sequence : $\sequence {\map f {x_n} }_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is Cauchy in $\GF$ for each $f \in X^\ast$.

title: Definition:Weak Closure
snippet: Let $K$ be a topological field. Let $X$ be a topological vector space with weak topology $w$. Let $H \subseteq X$. We define the weak closure $\map {\cl_w} H$ as the topological closure of $H$ in $\struct {X, w}$. That is: $\ds \map {\cl_w} H = \bigcap \leftset {C \supseteq H: C}$ is weakly closed in $\rightset X$

title: Definition:Weak Convergence
snippet: Functional Analysis: Weak Convergence (Normed Vector Space) Probability Theory: Weak Convergence (Random Variable) Measure Theory: Weak Convergence (Measure)

title: Definition:Weak Convergence (Normed Vector Space)
snippet:
Let $\struct {X, 
orm \cdot}$ be a normed vector space. Let $\struct {X^\ast, 
orm \cdot_{X^\ast} }$ be the normed dual space of $\struct {X, 
orm \cdot}$. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $X$. Let $x \in X$. We say that $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ converges weakly to $x$ : $\map f {x_n} 	o \map f x$ for each $f \in X^\ast$. We say that $x$ is a weak limit of $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$. We denote this: $x_n \weakconv x$

title: Definition:Weak Convergence (Topological Vector Space)
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a topological vector space over $\GF$. Let $X^\ast$ be the topological dual space of $X$. Suppose that: for each $x, y \in X$ with $x \ne y$, there exists $f \in X^\ast$ such that $\map f x \ne \map f y$. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $X$. Let $x \in X$.

title: Definition:Weak Convergence (Topological Vector Space)/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a topological vector space over $\GF$. Let $X^\ast$ be the topological dual space of $X$. Suppose that: for each $x, y \in X$ with $x \ne y$, there exists $f \in X^\ast$ such that $\map f x \ne \map f y$. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $X$. Let $x \in X$. Let $w$ be the weak topology on $X$. We say that $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ converges weakly it converges in $\struct {X, w}$. We write: $x_n \weakconv x$ Category:Definitions/Weak Convergence (Topological Vector Spaces)

title: Definition:Weak Convergence (Topological Vector Space)/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a topological vector space over $\GF$. Let $X^\ast$ be the topological dual space of $X$. Suppose that: for each $x, y \in X$ with $x \ne y$, there exists $f \in X^\ast$ such that $\map f x \ne \map f y$. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $X$. Let $x \in X$. We say that $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ converges weakly to $x$ : for each $f \in X^\ast$ we have $\map f {x_n} \to \map f x$ in $\GF$. Category:Definitions/Weak Convergence (Topological Vector Spaces)

title: Definition:Weak Extremum
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of mappings. Let $y, \hat y \in S: \R \to \R$ be real functions. Let $J \sqbrk y: S \to \R$ be a functional. Suppose there exists $\epsilon \in \R_{> 0}$ such that for $\norm {y - \hat y}_1 < \epsilon$ the expression $J \sqbrk y - J \sqbrk {\hat y}$ has the same sign for all $y$. Here $\norm{\, \cdot \,}_1$ denotes the norm of in the space $C^1$. Then $y = \hat y$ is a weak extremum of the functional $J \sqbrk y$.

title: Definition:Weak Half-Space Generated by Linear Functional
snippet: Let $X$ be a vector space over $\R$. Let $f : X \to \R$ be a linear functional. Let $\alpha \in \R$. Define: $\sqbrk {f \ge \alpha} = \set {x \in X : \map f x \ge \alpha}$ and: $\sqbrk {f \le \alpha} = \set {X \in X : \map f x \le \alpha}$ We say that $\sqbrk {f \ge \alpha}$ and $\sqbrk {f \le \alpha}$ are the weak half-spaces generated by $f$.

title: Definition:Weak Hausdorff Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a weak Hausdorff space : the image $f \sqbrk K$ is closed in $T$.

title: Definition:Weak Hausdorff Space/Also known as
snippet: == Weak Hausdorff Space: Also known as == A weak Hausdorff space is also known as a weakly Hausdorff space.

title: Definition:Weak Open Neighborhood
snippet: Let $K$ be a topological field. Let $X$ be a topological vector space. Let $x \in X$. Let $U \subseteq X$. We say that $U$ is a weak open neighborhood (or weak neighborhood) of $x$ $U$ is weakly open and $x \in U$. Category:Definitions/Weak Topologies on Topological Vector Spaces

title: Definition:Weak Operator Topology
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ and $\struct {Y, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_Y}$ be normed vector spaces. Let $\mathbb K = \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\map {CL} {X, Y}$ be a continuous linear transformation space. Let $F = \set {S \stackrel {p_{x,\phi} } \mapsto \size {\phi \paren{Sx - Tx} } : \map {CL} {X, Y} \to \R : x \in X : \phi \in \map {CL} {Y, \mathbb K} : T \in \map {CL} {X, Y}}$ be a set of maps. Let $\tau$ be the weakest topology on $\map {CL} {X, Y}$ such that every $y \in F$ is continuous. Then $\tau$ is called the weak operator topology on $\map {CL} {X, Y}$.

title: Definition:Weak Retract (Topology)
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Then $T_1$ is a weak retract of $T_2$ there exists a continuous mapping $f: S_2 \to S_2$ such that: $f \circ f = f$ and: $\Img f$ and $T_1$ are homeomorphic.

title: Definition:Weak Topology Induced by Dual System
snippet: Let $K$ be a topological field. Let $\innerprod X {X'}$ be a dual system over $K$. For each $x' \in X'$, define $f_{x'} : X \to K$ by: $\map {f_{x'} } x = \innerprod x {x'}$ for each $x \in X$. Let: $F = \set {f_{x'} : x' \in X'}$ We define the weak topology on $X$ induced by $\innerprod X {X'}$ as the initial topology induced on $X$ by $F$. This is usually denoted: $\map \sigma {X, X'}$

title: Definition:Weak Topology on Topological Vector Space
snippet: Let $K$ be a topological field. Let $X$ be a topological vector space over $K$. Let $X^\ast$ be the topological dual space of $X$. Let $w$ be the initial topology on $X$ with respect to $X^\ast$. We say that $w$ is the weak topology on $X$ : for each $x \in X \setminus \set {\mathbf 0_X}$ there exists $f \in X^\ast$ such that $\map f x \ne 0$. That is, $w$ separates the points of $X$.

title: Definition:Weakly Abnormal Subgroup
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$.

title: Definition:Weakly Abnormal Subgroup/Definition 1
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$. $H$ is weakly abnormal in $G$ : $\forall g \in G: g \in H^{\gen g}$ where $H^{\gen g}$ denotes the smallest subgroup of $G$ containing $H$, generated by the conjugacy action by the cyclic subgroup of $G$ generated by $g$.

title: Definition:Weakly Abnormal Subgroup/Definition 2
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$. $H$ is weakly abnormal in $G$ : if $H \le K \le G$, then $K$ is a self-normalizing subgroup of $G$ where $H \le K$ denotes that $H$ is a subgroup of $K$.

title: Definition:Weakly Abnormal Subgroup/Definition 3
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$. $H$ is weakly abnormal in $G$ : if $H \le K \le G$, then $K$ is a contranormal subgroup of $G$ where $H \le K$ denotes that $H$ is a subgroup of $K$.

title: Definition:Weakly Analytic Function
snippet:
Let $U$ be an open subset of $\C$. Let $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a Banach space over $\C$. Let $\struct {X^\ast, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_{X^\ast} }$ be the normed dual space of $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,} }$. Let $f : U 	o X$ be a mapping. We say that $f$ is weakly analytic : for each $\phi \in X^\ast$, $\phi \circ f : U 	o \C$ is analytic.

title: Definition:Weakly Closed Set
snippet: Let $K$ be a topological field. Let $X$ be a topological vector space with weak topology $w$. Let $C \subseteq X$. We say that $C$ is weakly closed (or $w$-closed) in $X$ $C$ is closed in $\struct {X, w}$. That is, $U = X \setminus C$ is weakly open.

title: Definition:Weakly Compact Linear Transformation/Definition 1
snippet:
Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ and $\struct {Y, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_Y}$ be Banach spaces over $\GF$. Let $T : X 	o Y$ be bounded linear transformation. Let $\cl$ be the closure taken in $\struct {Y, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_Y}$. Let $B_X^-$ be the closed unit ball in $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$. We say that $T$ is weakly compact $\map \cl {T \sqbrk {B_X^-} }$ is weakly compact.

title: Definition:Weakly Compact Linear Transformation/Definition 2
snippet:
Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ and $\struct {Y, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_Y}$ be Banach spaces over $\GF$. Let $T : X 	o Y$ be bounded linear transformation. Let $\cl$ be the closure taken in $\struct {Y, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_Y}$. Let $B_X^-$ be the closed unit ball in $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$. Let $w$ be the weak topology on $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$. Let $\cl_w$ be the closure taken in $\struct {X, w}$. We say that $T$ is weakly compact $\map {\cl_w} {T \sqbrk {B_X^-} }$ is weakly compact.

title: Definition:Weakly Compact Set
snippet: Let $K$ be a topological field. Let $X$ be a topological vector space with weak topology $w$. Let $C \subseteq X$. We say that $C$ is weakly compact (or $w$-compact) in $X$ $C$ is a compact in $\struct {X, w}$. That is, for every collection of weakly open sets $\SS$ such that: $\ds C \subseteq \bigcup_{S \in \SS} S$ there exists a finite subset $\set {S_1, \ldots, S_n} \subseteq \SS$ such that: $\ds C \subseteq \bigcup_{k \mathop = 1}^n S_k$ Category:Definitions/Weak Topologies on Topological Vector Spaces

title: Definition:Weakly Countably Compact Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is weakly countably compact : every infinite subset of $S$ has a limit point in $S$.

title: Definition:Weakly Countably Compact Space/Also known as
snippet: == Weakly Countably Compact Space: Also known as == A space which is weakly countably compact can also be described as limit point compact.

title: Definition:Weakly Dominant Move
snippet: Let $G$ be a game. Let $a$ be a move available to player $P$. Then $a$ is weakly dominant for any move of an opposing player, the payoff of $a$ is not less than the payoff of any other move available to $P$.

title: Definition:Weakly Hereditary Property
snippet: Let $\xi$ be a property whose domain is the set of all topological spaces. Then $\xi$ is a weakly hereditary property : $\map \xi X \implies \map \xi Y$ where $Y$ is any closed set of $X$ when considered as a subspace. That is, whenever a topological space has $\xi$, then so does any closed subspace.

title: Definition:Weakly Inaccessible Cardinal
snippet: An infinite cardinal $\aleph_\kappa$ is weakly inaccessible : $(1): \quad \kappa$ is a limit ordinal. $(2): \quad \aleph_\kappa$ is a regular cardinal.

title: Definition:Weakly Lindelöf Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a weakly Lindelöf space every open cover of $S$ has a countable subset whose union is dense in $T$.

title: Definition:Weakly Locally Compact Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is weakly locally compact every point of $S$ has a compact neighborhood.

title: Definition:Weakly Locally Compact Space/Also known as
snippet: == Weakly Locally Compact Space: Also known as == Some sources refer to a weakly locally compact space as locally compact, but modern developments have introduced a slightly stronger concept for which that term is usually used. Some sources introduce the abbreviation WLC.

title: Definition:Weakly Locally Connected at Point
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $x \in S$.

title: Definition:Weakly Locally Connected at Point/Also known as
snippet: == Weakly Locally Connected at Point: Also known as == If $T$ is weakly locally connected at $x$, it is also said to be connected im kleinen at $x$. Some sources refer to a space which is weakly locally connected at $x$ as locally connected at $x$.

title: Definition:Weakly Locally Connected at Point/Definition 1
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $x \in S$. The space $T$ is weakly locally connected at $x$ $x$ has a neighborhood basis consisting of connected sets.

title: Definition:Weakly Locally Connected at Point/Definition 2
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $x \in S$. The space $T$ is weakly locally connected at $x$ every open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ contains an open neighborhood $V$ of $x$ such that every two points of $V$ lie in some connected subset of $U$.

title: Definition:Weakly Locally Connected at Point/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Connected im Kleinen == The phrase im kleinen is German and means on a small scale.

title: Definition:Weakly Measurable Function
snippet:
Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $\struct {X^\ast, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_{X^\ast} }$ be the normed dual space of $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$. Let $I$ be a real interval. Let $f : I 	o X$ be a function. We say that $f$ is weakly measurable : for each $\phi \in X^\ast$, $\phi \circ f : I 	o \C$ is Lebesgue measurable.

title: Definition:Weakly Mixing Measure-Preserving Transformation
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \BB, \mu}$ be a probability space. Let $T: X \to X$ be a measure-preserving transformation.

title: Definition:Weakly Mixing Measure-Preserving Transformation/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \BB, \mu}$ be a probability space. Let $T: X \to X$ be a measure-preserving transformation. $T$ is said to be weakly mixing : $\ds \forall A, B \in \BB : \lim_{N \mathop\to \infty} \frac 1 N \sum _{n \mathop = 0}^{N-1} \size {\map \mu {A \cap T^{-n} \sqbrk B} - \map \mu A \map \mu B} = 0$ where $T^{-n} \sqbrk B$ denotes the preimage of $B$ under the power $T^n$.

title: Definition:Weakly Mixing Measure-Preserving Transformation/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \BB, \mu}$ be a probability space. Let $T: X \to X$ be a measure-preserving transformation. $T$ is said to be weakly mixing : $T \times T$ is ergodic with respect to $\mu \times \mu$ where $\mu \times \mu$ denotes the product measure on $\struct {X \times X, \BB \otimes \BB}$.

title: Definition:Weakly Mixing Measure-Preserving Transformation/Definition 3
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \BB, \mu}$ be a probability space. Let $T: X \to X$ be a measure-preserving transformation. $T$ is said to be weakly mixing : $T \times T$ is weakly mixing in the sense of Definition 1 $\mu \times \mu$ where $\mu \times \mu$ denotes the product measure on $\struct {X \times X, \BB \otimes \BB}$.

title: Definition:Weakly Mixing Measure-Preserving Transformation/Definition 4
snippet:
Let $\struct {X, \BB, \mu}$ be a probability space. Let $T: X 	o X$ be a measure-preserving transformation. $T$ is said to be weakly mixing : for every ergodic measure-preserving system $\struct {Y, \BB_Y, 
u, S}$, the system: $\struct {X 	imes Y, \BB \otimes \BB_Y, \mu 	imes 
u, T 	imes S}$ is ergodic where $\mu 	imes 
u$ denotes the product measure on $\struct {X 	imes Y, \BB \otimes \BB_Y}$

title: Definition:Weakly Open Set
snippet: Let $K$ be a topological field. Let $X$ be a topological vector space with weak topology $w$. Let $U \subseteq X$. We say that $U$ is weakly open (or $w$-open) in $X$ $U$ is open in $\struct {X, w}$.

title: Definition:Weakly Open Set/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Weakly Open Set == By analogy, an open set of $X$ might be called "strongly open" Indeed this is common if $X$ is say, a Fréchet space. However, in general locally convex spaces, "strong topology" has a more specific meaning, so its use may cause confusion. It is therefore preferable to call the topology on $X$ the original topology, and open sets of $X$ originally open.

title: Definition:Weakly Pronormal Subgroup
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$.

title: Definition:Weakly Pronormal Subgroup/Definition 1
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$. $H$ is weakly pronormal in $G$ : $\forall g \in G: \exists x \in H^{\gen g}: H^x = H^g$ where: $H^{\gen g}$ denotes the smallest subgroup of $G$ containing $H$, generated by the conjugacy action by the cyclic subgroup of $G$ generated by $g$ $H^x$ denotes the conjugate of $H$ by $x$.

title: Definition:Weakly Pronormal Subgroup/Definition 2
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$. $H$ is weakly pronormal in $G$ : if $H \le K \le L \le G$ are such that $K$ is a normal subgroup of $L$, then $K N_L \left({H}\right) = L$ where: $H \le K$ denotes that $H$ is a subgroup of $K$ $N_L \left({H}\right)$ denotes the normalizer of $H$ in $L$.

title: Definition:Weakly Sequentially Complete Topological Vector Space
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological vector space over $\GF$. We say that $\struct {X, \tau}$ is weakly sequentially complete every weak Cauchy sequence in $\struct {X, \tau}$ converges weakly.

title: Definition:Weakly Sigma-Locally Compact Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is weakly $\sigma$-locally compact : That is, $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is weakly $\sigma$-locally compact :

title: Definition:Weakly Sigma-Locally Compact Space/Also known as
snippet: == Weakly $\sigma$-Locally Compact Space: Also known as == A weakly $\sigma$-locally compact space can also be described as exhaustible by compacts. Some sources, when defining a weakly $\sigma$-locally compact space, refer to it as a $\sigma$-locally compact space. However, it is more usual to find a $\sigma$-locally compact space defined as: There appears to be no appreciation anywhere on Internet-accessible sources that there are two such differing definitions, or that they define different concepts.

title: Definition:Weakly Stationary Stochastic Process
snippet: Let $S$ be a stochastic process giving rise to a time series $T$. $S$ is weakly stationary of order $f$ its moments up to some order $f$ depend only on time differences. Such a condition is known as weak stationarity of order $f$.

title: Definition:Weakly Unconditionally Cauchy Series
snippet:
Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $\struct {X^\ast, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_{X^\ast} }$ be the normed dual space of $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $X$. Then $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty x_n$ is weakly unconditionally Cauchy : $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \cmod {\map f {x_n} } < \infty$ for each $f \in X^\ast$.

title: Definition:Weber
snippet: The weber is the SI unit of magnetic flux. It is defined as the total magnetic flux density through a $1 \ \mathrm m^2$ area of space. That is, it is equal to the magnetic flux that, when linking a current loop, produces an electromotive force of $1$ volt as it is reduced to zero at a uniform rate in $1$ second.

title: Definition:Weber/Base Units
snippet: The SI base units of the weber are: $\mathrm {Wb} := \mathrm {kg} \, \mathrm m^2 \, \mathrm s^{-2} \mathrm A^{-1}$ where: $\mathrm {kg}$ denotes kilogram $\mathrm m$ denotes metre $\mathrm s$ denotes seconds (of time) $\mathrm A$ denotes amperes. This arises from its derivation as the $\mathrm T \, \mathrm m^2$: tesla-square metre.

title: Definition:Wedge Product
snippet: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be two differential forms. Let $\alpha$ be an $x$-form. Let $\beta$ be a $y$-form.
