The wedge product $\alpha \wedge \beta$ is defined as the linear antisymmetric map from $F^x \times F^y \to F^{x + y}$, where $F^a$ is the set of $a$-forms in some manifold. Let $x_0$ be a specific point in a manifold $X$. Let $\alpha$ be an $x$-form. Let $\phi$ be a $1$-form. Let there be a set of vectors $\mathbf u_1, \mathbf u_2, \dotsc, \mathbf u_x, \mathbf v \in \map {T_{x_0} } X$.

title: Definition:Wedge Product/Also known as
snippet: == Wedge Product: Also known as == A wedge product is also known as an exterior product.

title: Definition:Weibull Distribution
snippet: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable on a probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $\Img X = \R_{\ge 0}$. $X$ is said to have a Weibull distribution it has probability density function: $\map {f_X} x = \alpha \beta^{-\alpha} x^{\alpha - 1} e^{-\paren {\frac x \beta}^\alpha}$ for $\alpha, \beta \in \R_{> 0}$.

title: Definition:Weibull Distribution/Also defined as
snippet: == Weibull Distribution: Also defined as == Some sources give the probability density function of the Weibull distribution as: $\map {f_X} x = \dfrac k \lambda \paren {\dfrac x \lambda}^{k - 1} \map \exp {-\paren {\dfrac x k} }^k$

title: Definition:Weibull Distribution/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Weibull Distribution == The Weibull distribution was introduced by in $1939$. It is used in reliability studies, and also in meteorology. It is one of the most commonly used extreme value distributions.

title: Definition:Weierstrass's Elliptic Function
snippet: Weierstrass's Elliptic Function is an elliptic function, given for all complex $z$ (except for $z \in \set {2 m \omega_1 + 2 n \omega_2: \tuple {n, m} \in \Z^2}$ where the function has double poles, by Poles of Weierstrass's Elliptic Function) by: $\ds \map \wp {z; \omega_1, \omega_2} = \frac 1 {z^2} + {\sum_{\tuple {n, m} \mathop \in \Z^2 \setminus \tuple {0, 0} } } \paren {\frac 1 {\paren {z - 2 m \omega_1 - 2 n \omega_2}^2} - \frac 1 {\paren {2 m \omega_1 + 2 n \omega_2}^2} }$ where $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ are non-zero complex constants with $\dfrac {\omega_1} {\omega_2}$ having a…

title: Definition:Weierstrass E-Function
snippet: Let $\mathbf y, \mathbf z, \mathbf w : \R \to \R^n$ be $n$-dimensional vector-valued functions. Let $\mathbf y$ be such that $\map {\mathbf y} a = A$ and $\map {\mathbf y} b = B$. Let $F: \R^{2 n + 1} \to \R$ be twice differentiable its (independent) variables. Let $J$ be a functional such that: $\ds J \sqbrk{\mathbf y} = \int_a^b \map F {x, \mathbf y, \mathbf y'} \rd x$ where: $\mathbf y' := \dfrac {\d \mathbf y} {\d x}$ is the derivative of a vector-valued function.

title: Definition:Weierstrass E-Function/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\mathbf y, \mathbf z, \mathbf w$ be $n$-dimensional vectors. Let $\mathbf y$ be such that $\map {\mathbf y} a = A$ and $\map {\mathbf y} b = B$. Let $J$ be a functional such that: $\ds J \sqbrk {\mathbf y} = \int_a^b \map F {x, \mathbf y, \mathbf y'} \rd x$ The following mapping is known as the Weierstrass E-Function of $J \sqbrk {\mathbf y}$: $\map E {x, \mathbf y, \mathbf z, \mathbf w} = \map F {x, \mathbf y, \mathbf w} - \map F {x, \mathbf y, \mathbf z} + \paren {\mathbf w - \mathbf z} F_{\mathbf y'} \paren {x, \mathbf y, \mathbf z}$

title: Definition:Weierstrass E-Function/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\mathbf y, \mathbf z, \mathbf w$ be $n$-dimensional vectors. Let $\mathbf y$ be such that $\map {\mathbf y} a = A$ and $\map {\mathbf y} b = B$. Let $J$ be a functional such that: $\ds J \sqbrk {\mathbf y} = \int_a^b \map F {x, \mathbf y, \mathbf y'} \rd x$ Let $\theta \in \R: 0 < \theta < 1$. The following mapping is known as the Weierstrass E-Function of $J \sqbrk {\mathbf y}$: $\ds \map E {x, \mathbf y, \mathbf z, \mathbf w} = \frac 1 2 \sum_{i, k \mathop = 1}^n \paren {w_i - z_i} \paren {w_k - z_k} F_{y_i' y_k'} \paren {x, \mathbf y, \mathbf z + \theta \paren {\mathbf w - \mathbf z}…

title: Definition:Weierstrass Elementary Factor
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be a positive integer. The $n$th (Weierstrass) elementary factor is the function $E_n: \C \to \C$ defined as: $\map {E_n} z = \begin {cases} 1 - z & : n = 0 \\ \paren {1 - z} \map \exp {z + \dfrac {z^2} 2 + \cdots + \dfrac{z^n} n} & : \text{otherwise} \end {cases}$

title: Definition:Weierstrass Function
snippet: Let $a \in \openint 0 1$. Let $b$ be a strictly positive odd integer such that: $a b > 1 + \dfrac 3 2 \pi$ Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a real function defined by: $\ds \map f x = \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty a^n \map \cos {b^n \pi x}$ for each $x \in \R$. We call $f$ a Weierstrass function.

title: Definition:Weierstrass Function/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Weierstrass Function == first discussed a real function which was continuous everywhere but differentiable nowhere in his lectures in $1861$. The explicit construction given here did not appear in print until one of his students published it (with 's permission) in $1874$.

title: Definition:Weight
snippet: Physics: The weight of a body is the force exerted on it by a gravitational field. Network theory: The weight of an edge or arc of a network is the functional value assigned to that edge or arc by the weight function of that network. Statistics, etc.: A weight function on a set $S$ is a mapping from $S$ to the (usually positive) real numbers. Information theory: The weight of a codeword is the number of its non-zero terms.

title: Definition:Weight (Network Theory)/Also known as
snippet: == Weight: Also known as == In the context of network analysis, the weight of an edge of a network is often referred to as a penalty. Some applications, in which a network is used to model transportation or flow between vertices, interpret the weight of an edge as a capacity. In applications in which a network models steps in a process, the weight of an edge is used to model the time that needs to elapse between activities that are modelled by the vertices.

title: Definition:Weight (Network Theory)/Edge
snippet: Let $N = \struct {V, E, w}$ be a network with weight function $w: E \to \R$. Let $e \in E$. The image of $e$ under $w$ is known as the weight of $e$.

title: Definition:Weight (Network Theory)/Walk
snippet: Let $N = \struct {V, E, w}$ be a network with weight function $w: E \to \R$. Let $PQ = v_1 e_1 v_2 e_2 \ldots e_{n - 1} V_n$ be a walk in $N$. The weight of $PQ$ is defined as the sum of the weights of the edges that constitute $PQ$: $\map w {PQ} := \ds \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^{n - 1} \map w {e_k}$ This definition can also be applied to paths, trails, circuits and cycles.

title: Definition:Weight (Physics)
snippet: The weight of a body is the magnitude of the force exerted on it by the influence of a gravitational field. The context is that the gravitational field in question is usually that of the Earth.

title: Definition:Weight (Physics)/Dimension
snippet: The dimension of weight is $\mathsf {M L T}^{-2}$: mass times acceleration, that is, a force.

title: Definition:Weight (Physics)/Symbol
snippet: == Weight: Symbol == The usual symbol used to denote the weight of a body is $W$.

title: Definition:Weight (Physics)/Units
snippet: The SI unit of weight is $\mathrm N$ (newton). The CGS unit of weight is $\mathrm {dyn}$ (dyne).

title: Definition:Weight (Physics)/Warning
snippet: There is a certain amount of confusion in the common mind between weight and mass. The latter is usually determined by measuring its weight. But while the mass of a body is (under normal circumstances) constant, its weight varies according to its position relative to the gravitational field it is in, and so is not a constant property of that body. However, under usual terrestrial conditions the gravitational field is more or less constant (any differences being detectable only by instruments). This means that the weight and mass of a body are commonly considered "the same".

title: Definition:Weight (Physics)/Weigh
snippet: To weigh a body is to determine its weight, and thence its mass. Similarly we can say that: body $B$ weighs $x$ to mean: the weight of the body $B$ is $x$ and both mean the same thing.

title: Definition:Weight Function
snippet: A weight function on a set $S$ is a mapping from $S$ to the real numbers: $w: S \to \R$ It is common for the requirements of a specific application under discussion for the codomain of $w$ to be restricted to the positive reals: $w: S \to \R_{\ge 0}$ The thing that determines whether a given mapping is a weight function depends more on how it is used.

title: Definition:Weight of Linear Codeword
snippet: Let $C$ be a codeword of a linear code. The weight of $C$ is the number of non-zero terms of $C$.

title: Definition:Weight of Topological Space
snippet: Let $T$ be a topological space. Let $\mathbb B$ be the set of all bases of $T$.

title: Definition:Weight of Topological Space/Definition 1
snippet: Let $T$ be a topological space. Let $\mathbb B$ be the set of all bases of $T$. The weight of $T$ is defined as: $\ds \map w T := \bigcap_{\BB \mathop \in \mathbb B} \card \BB$ where $\card \BB$ denotes the cardinality of $\BB$.

title: Definition:Weight of Topological Space/Definition 2
snippet: Let $T$ be a topological space. Let $\mathbb B$ be the set of all bases of $T$. The weight of $T$ is the smallest cardinality of the elements of $\mathbb B$: $\map w T := \min \set {\card \BB: \BB \in \mathbb B}$

title: Definition:Weighted Least Squares
snippet: Weighted least squares is a generalization of method of least squares applied to a time series $S = \sequence {x_i}$. A weight function is imposed upon the terms of $S$ so as to reduce the influence of observations the further they are away from the current value.

title: Definition:Weighted Least Squares/Bandwidth
snippet: Let $S = \sequence {x_i}$ be a time series upon which a weighted least squares process is imposed. Let $x_c$ denote the current value of $S$. Let $b \in \N$ be such that values $i$ of $S$ further away from $x_C$ than $x_{C - b}$, $x_i$ has no influence over the smoothed value of $S$. Then $b$ is called the bandwidth of the weighted least squares process.

title: Definition:Weighted Mean
snippet: Let $S = \sequence {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ be a sequence of real numbers. Let $W$ be a weight function to be applied to the terms of $S$. The weighted mean of $S$ $W$ is defined as: $\bar x := \dfrac {\ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \map W {x_i} x_i} {\ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \map W {x_i} }$ This means that elements of $S$ with a larger weight contribute more to the weighted mean than those with a smaller weight.

title: Definition:Weighted Mean/Normalized
snippet: Let $S = \sequence {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ be a sequence of real numbers. Let $\map W x$ be a weight function to be applied to the terms of $S$. Let the weights be normalized. Then the weighted mean of $S$ $W$ can be expressed in the form: $\ds \bar x := \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \map W {x_i} x_i$ as by definition of normalized weight function all the weights add up to $1$. This weighted mean is known as a normalized weighted mean.

title: Definition:Weighted Sum
snippet: Let $S = \sequence {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ be a sequence of real numbers. Let $\map W x$ be a weight function to be applied to the terms of $S$. The weighted sum of $S$ is defined as: $\bar x := \ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \map W {x_i} x_i$ This means that elements of $S$ with a larger weight contribute more to the weighted sum than those with a smaller weight.

title: Definition:Weights
snippet: A set of weights consists of a number of solid pieces of matter whose mass is measured and known. They are used as reference masses for the purpose of determining to a certain limit of accuracy the weight of a body whose mass is unknown.

title: Definition:Weird Number
snippet: A weird number is an abundant number which is not at the same time semiperfect.

title: Definition:Weird Number/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Weird Numbers ==

title: Definition:Weird Number/Sequence
snippet: The sequence of weird numbers begins: $70, 836, 4030, 5830, 7192, 7912, 9272, \ldots$

title: Definition:Well-Defined/Also known as
snippet: Some sources use the term consistent for well-defined. Some sources do not hyphenate: well defined.

title: Definition:Well-Defined/Mapping
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. Let $\RR$ be an equivalence relation on $S$. Let $S / \RR$ be the quotient set determined by $\RR$. Let $\phi: S / \RR \to T$ be a mapping such that: $\map \phi {\eqclass x \RR} = \map f x$ Then $\phi: S / \RR \to T$ is well-defined : $\forall \tuple {x, y} \in \RR: \map f x = \map f y$

title: Definition:Well-Defined/Operation
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. Let $\RR$ be a congruence for $\circ$. Let $\circ_\RR$ be the operation induced on $S / \RR$ by $\circ$. Let $\struct {S / \RR, \circ_\RR}$ be the quotient structure defined by $\RR$, where $\circ_\RR$ is defined as: $\eqclass x \RR \circ_\RR \eqclass y \RR = \eqclass {x \circ y} \RR$ Then $\circ_\RR$ is well-defined (on $S / \RR$) : $x, x' \in \eqclass x \RR, y, y' \in \eqclass y \RR \implies \eqclass {x \circ y} \RR = \eqclass {x' \circ y'} \RR$

title: Definition:Well-Defined/Relation
snippet: Let $\RR$ be an equivalence relation on $S$. For $x \in S$, let $\eqclass x \RR$ denote the equivalence class of $x$ under $\RR$. Let $S / \RR$ be the quotient set of $S$ determined by $\RR$. Let $\QQ$ be a relation on $S / \RR$. Then $\QQ$ is well-defined : for arbitrary $x, y, x', y' \in S$ such that: $x \mathrel \RR x'$ $y \mathrel \RR y'$ we have that: $\tuple {\eqclass x \RR, \eqclass y \RR} \in \QQ \iff \tuple {\eqclass {x'} \RR, \eqclass {y'} \RR} \in \QQ$

title: Definition:Well-Formed Formula
snippet: Let $\FF$ be a formal language whose alphabet is $\AA$. A well-formed formula is a collation in $\AA$ which can be built by using the rules of formation of the formal grammar of $\FF$. That is, a collation in $\AA$ is a well-formed formula in $\FF$ it has a parsing sequence in $\FF$.

title: Definition:Well-Formed Formula/Also known as
snippet: == Well-Formed Formula: Also known as == The term well-formed formula is often encountered in its abbreviated form WFF or wff, pronounced something like woof or oof, depending on personal preference. Other names include well-formed word or simply formula. Some less formal approaches use the term statement form or symbolic sentence. (Well-formed) expression is also seen.

title: Definition:Well-Formed Part
snippet: Let $\FF$ be a formal language with alphabet $\AA$. Let $\mathbf A$ be a well-formed formula of $\FF$. Let $\mathbf B$ be a subcollation of $\mathbf A$. Then $\mathbf B$ is a well-formed part of $\mathbf A$ $\mathbf B$ is a well-formed formula of $\FF$.

title: Definition:Well-Formed Part/Proper Well-Formed Part
snippet: Let $\FF$ be a formal language with alphabet $\AA$. Let $\mathbf A$ be a well-formed formula of $\FF$. Let $\mathbf B$ be a well-formed part of $\mathbf A$. Then $\mathbf B$ is a proper well-formed part of $\mathbf A$ $\mathbf B$ is not equal to $\mathbf A$.

title: Definition:Well-Founded Class
snippet: Let $A$ be a class. Then $A$ is well-founded for every non-empty subclass $B \subseteq A$: $\exists x \in B: x \cap B = \O$ Category:Definitions/Class Theory

title: Definition:Well-Founded Ordered Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Then $\struct {S, \preceq}$ is well-founded it satisfies the minimal condition: Every non-empty subset of $S$ has a minimal element. That is, if the ordering $\preceq$ is a well-founded relation.

title: Definition:Well-Founded Relation
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \RR}$ be a relational structure.

title: Definition:Well-Founded Relation/Also known as
snippet: == Well-Founded Relation: Also known as == The term well-founded relation is often used the literature for what on we call a strictly well-founded relation. In order to emphasise the differences between the two, at some point a editor coined the term strongly well-founded relation. However, prefers the less unwieldy term well-founded relation in preference to others. Some sources do not hyphenate, and present the name as wellfounded relation.

title: Definition:Well-Founded Relation/Class Theory
snippet: Let $A$ be a class. Let $\RR$ be a relation on $A$. $\RR$ is a well-founded relation on $A$ : every non-empty subclass $A$ has an initial element.

title: Definition:Well-Founded Relation/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \RR}$ be a relational structure. $\RR$ is a well-founded relation on $S$ : $\forall T \subseteq S: T \ne \O: \exists z \in T: \forall y \in T \setminus \set z: \tuple {y, z} \notin \RR$ where $\O$ is the empty set. That is, $\RR$ is a strictly well-founded relation on $S$ : for every non-empty subset $T$ of $S$, there exists an element $z$ in $T$ such that for all $y \in T \setminus \set z$, it is not the case that $y \mathrel \RR z$.

title: Definition:Well-Founded Relation/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \RR}$ be a relational structure. $\RR$ is a well-founded relation on $S$ : for every non-empty subset $T$ of $S$, $T$ has a minimal element.

title: Definition:Well-Founded Relation/Warning
snippet: == Well-Founded Relation: Warning == According to Strictly Well-Founded Relation is Well-Founded, the Axiom of Foundation implies that every strictly well-founded relation is well-founded. As the definition quantifies over general subclasses, well-foundedness is not a first-order property. Thus it cannot be used in a formula of a theory, like NBG class-set theory, that only allow quantification over sets. For example it cannot be used with the axiom schema of specification in NBG set theory, and statements using it must generally be framed as schemas.

title: Definition:Well-Founded Set
snippet: Let $S$ be a small class. Let $\map V x$ denote the von Neumann hierarchy. Then $S$ is a well-founded set there is some ordinal $x$ such that $S \in \map V x$.

title: Definition:Well-Orderable Set
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. If it is possible to construct an ordering $\preccurlyeq$ on $S$ such that $\preccurlyeq$ is a well-ordering, then $S$ is defined as being well-orderable.

title: Definition:Well-Orderable Set/Class Theory
snippet: Let $A$ be a class. If it is possible to construct an ordering $\preceq$ on $A$ such that $\preceq$ is a well-ordering, then $A$ is defined as being well-orderable.

title: Definition:Well-Ordered Class
snippet: Let $V$ be a basic universe. Let $\RR \subseteq V \times V$ be a relation. Let $A$ be a subclass of the field of $\RR$. Let the restriction of $\RR$ to $A$ be a well-ordering on $A$. Then $A$ is described as being well-ordered under $\RR$.

title: Definition:Well-Ordered Class under Subset Relation
snippet: Let $A$ be a class which is also a nest. Let $A$ have the property that every non-empty subclass of $A$ has a smallest element under the subset relation. Then $A$ is said to be well-ordered under the subset relation.

title: Definition:Well-Ordered Integral Domain
snippet: Let $\struct {D, +, \times \le}$ be an ordered integral domain whose zero is $0_D$.

title: Definition:Well-Ordered Integral Domain/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {D, +, \times \le}$ be an ordered integral domain whose zero is $0_D$. $\struct {D, +, \times \le}$ is a well-ordered integral domain the ordering $\le$ is a well-ordering on the set $P$ of (strictly) positive elements of $D$.

title: Definition:Well-Ordered Integral Domain/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {D, +, \times \le}$ be an ordered integral domain whose zero is $0_D$. $\struct {D, +, \times \le}$ is a well-ordered integral domain every subset $S$ of the set $P$ of (strictly) positive elements of $D$ has a minimal element: $\forall S \subseteq D_{\ge 0_D}: \exists x \in S: \forall a \in S: x \le a$ where $D_{\ge 0_D}$ denotes all the elements $d \in D$ such that $\map P d$.

title: Definition:Well-Ordered Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Then $\struct {S, \preceq}$ is a well-ordered set the ordering $\preceq$ is a well-ordering. That is, every non-empty subset of $S$ has a smallest element: $\forall T \in \powerset S: \exists a \in T: \forall x \in T: a \preceq x$ where $\powerset S$ denotes the power set of $S$. That is, such that $\preceq$ is a well-founded total ordering.

title: Definition:Well-Ordered Set/Also known as
snippet: == Well-Ordered Set: Also known as == The term well-ordered set is sometimes abbreviated as woset. The term is also found unhyphenated: well ordered or wellordered.

title: Definition:Well-Ordering
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set.

title: Definition:Well-Ordering/Also defined as
snippet: == Well-Ordering: Also defined as == uses the term well-ordering to mean what calls a strict strong well-ordering. uses the term well-ordering to mean what calls a strict well-ordering. Category:Definitions/Well-Orderings

title: Definition:Well-Ordering/Class Theory
snippet: Let $V$ be a basic universe. Let $\RR \subseteq V \times V$ be a total ordering. Then $\RR$ is a well-ordering : every non-empty subclass of $\Field \RR$ has a smallest element under $\RR$ where $\Field \RR$ denotes the field of $\RR$.

title: Definition:Well-Ordering/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. The ordering $\preceq$ is a well-ordering on $S$ every non-empty subset of $S$ has a smallest element under $\preceq$: $\forall T \subseteq S, T \ne \O: \exists a \in T: \forall x \in T: a \preceq x$

title: Definition:Well-Ordering/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a ordered set. The ordering $\preceq$ is a well-ordering on $S$ $\preceq$ is a well-founded total ordering.

title: Definition:Well-Tempered Scale
snippet: A well-tempered scale is an octave which has been divided into $12$ equal intervals called semitones.

title: Definition:Well Inside Relation
snippet: Let $L = \struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \preceq}$ be a distributive lattice with greatest element $\top$ and smallest element $\bot$. Let $a, b \in S : a \preceq b$. Then $a$ is said to be well inside $b$, denoted $a \eqslantless b$, : $\exists c \in S : a \wedge c = \bot$ and $b \vee c = \top$

title: Definition:West (Celestial)
snippet: West is the direction along the celestial sphere in the direction of the west point of the horizon.

title: Definition:West (Terrestrial)
snippet: West is the direction on (or near) Earth's surface along the small circle in the opposite direction from Earth's rotation in space about its axis. 600px

title: Definition:West Point of Horizon
snippet: Let an observer $O$ be facing the north point of the horizon $N$, facing directly away from the south point of the horizon $S$. Let the celestial equator meet the celestial horizon at the points $E$ and $W$. Let $W$ be the point on the left of $O$. This is called the west point of the horizon. 480px In the above diagram, the west point of the horizon is indicated by $W$.

title: Definition:West Point of Horizon/Also known as
snippet: == West Point of Horizon: Also known as == The west point of the horizon is also known as the west point.

title: Definition:Western Celestial Hemisphere
snippet: Consider the celestial sphere $C$ with observer $O$. Let $W$ be the west point of the horizon. The western celestial hemisphere is the hemisphere of $C$ defined by the principal vertical circle which contains $W$. 480px

title: Definition:Western Hemisphere
snippet: The western hemisphere of Earth is the hemisphere immediately to the west of the prime meridian. Points in the western hemisphere have longitude between $0 \degrees \, \mathrm W$ (the prime meridian itself) and $180 \degrees \, \mathrm W$.

title: Definition:Weyl Group
snippet: Let $\struct {E, \Phi}$ be a root system. The Weyl group $\mathscr W$ of $\struct {E, \Phi}$ is the subgroup of the general linear group $\map {GL} E$ generated by reflections through the hyperplanes orthogonal to each $\alpha \in \Phi$.

title: Definition:Whiskered Composite of Natural Transformation/Also Known As
snippet: == Whiskered Composite: Also known as == Whiskered composition, left whiskered composition, right whiskered composition and double-sided whiskered composition are also known as whiskering, left whiskering, right whiskering and double-sided whiskering respectively. Some sources refer to left whiskered composition as prewhiskering and right whiskered composition as postwhiskering.

snippet: Let $\mathbf C$, $\mathbf D$, $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf B$ be categories. Let $F, G : \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be covariant functors. Let $\eta: F \to G$ be a natural transformation. Let $H : \mathbf B \to \mathbf C$ and $K : \mathbf D \to \mathbf E$ be covariant functors. Then: the double-sided whiskered composite of $\eta$ by $K$ and $H$, denoted by $K \eta H: K \circ F \circ H \to K \circ G \circ H$, is the natural transformation defined by: for each object $B \in \mathbf B: \paren{K \eta H}_B = K \eta_{_{HB} }$ described diagramatically by: $\xymatrix{ \mathbf B \ar[rr]^H && \mathbf C…

title: Definition:Whiskered Composite of Natural Transformation/Left Whiskered
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$, $\mathbf D$ and $\mathbf B$ be categories. Let $F, G : \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be covariant functors. Let $\eta: F \to G$ be a natural transformation. Let $H : \mathbf B \to \mathbf C$ be a covariant functor. Then: the left whiskered composite of $\eta$ by $H$, denoted by $\eta H: F \circ H \to G \circ H$, is the natural transformation defined by: for each object $B \in \mathbf B: \paren{\eta H}_B = \eta_{_{HB} }$ described diagrammatically by: $\xymatrix{ \mathbf B \ar[rr]^H && \mathbf C \ar@/^4ex/[rr]^F_{}="f" \ar@/_4ex/[rr]_G^{}="g" && \mathbf D \ar@2^\eta "f"; "g" }$

title: Definition:Whiskered Composite of Natural Transformation/Naming Convention
snippet: == Whiskered Composite: Naming Convention == The naming of left whiskered composite and right whiskered composite is based upon the diagrams used to describe the whiskered composite rather than the notation used to represent them. Category:Definitions/Whiskered Composites

title: Definition:Whiskered Composite of Natural Transformation/Right Whiskered
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$, $\mathbf D$ and $\mathbf E$ be categories. Let $F, G : \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be covariant functors. Let $\eta: F \to G$ be a natural transformation. Let $K : \mathbf D \to \mathbf E$ be a covariant functor. Then: the right whiskered composite of $\eta$ by $K$, denoted by $K \eta: K \circ F \to K \circ G$, is the natural transformation defined by: for each object $C \in \mathbf C: \paren{K \eta}_C = K \eta_{_C}$ described diagramatically by: $\xymatrix{ \mathbf C \ar@/^4ex/[rr]^F_{}="f" \ar@/_4ex/[rr]_G^{}="g" && \mathbf D \ar@2^\eta "f"; "g" \ar[rr]^K && \mathbf E }$

title: Definition:White Noise Process
snippet: Let $S$ be a stochastic process consisting of a time series $\map {z_r} t$ such that: the terms of the sequence $\sequence {z_r}$ are independent random variables the terms of $\sequence {z_r}$ are governed by a normal distribution with zero expectation and a given variance $\sigma^2$. Then $S$ is known as a white noise process.

title: Definition:Whole Number
snippet: The phrase whole number is an ambiguous term which could mean either: an integer a natural number a strictly positive integer. Hence it is recommended that a specific instance of the above is used instead.

title: Definition:Wholly Imaginary/Also known as
snippet: == Wholly Imaginary: Also known as == Variants on wholly imaginary are: completely imaginary entirely imaginary purely imaginary a pure imaginary number and so on.

title: Definition:Wholly Real/Abbreviated Notation
snippet: Let $z = a + i b$ be a complex number such that $b = 0$. That is, let $z$ be wholly real: $z = a + 0 i$, or $\tuple {a, 0}$ Despite the fact that $z$ is still a complex number, it is commonplace to use the same notation as if it were a real number, and hence say $z = a$. While it is in theory important to distinguish between a real number and its corresponding wholly real complex number, in practice it makes little difference.

title: Definition:Wholly Real/Also known as
snippet: == Wholly Real: Also known as == Variants on wholly real are: completely real entirely real and so on. Some sources gloss over the distinction between a real number and a wholly real complex number and merely refer to a number of the form $z = a + 0 i$ as a real number.

title: Definition:Wieferich Prime
snippet: A Wieferich prime is a prime number $p$ such that: $p^2 \divides 2^{p − 1} − 1$ where $\divides$ denotes divisibility.

title: Definition:Wieferich Prime/Sequence
snippet: The sequence of Wieferich primes begins: $1093, 3511 \ldots$ No other Wieferich primes exist below $4 \cdotp 968543 \times 10^{17}$.

title: Definition:Wiener Process
snippet: The Wiener process is a stochastic process $W_t$ for time $t \ge 0$ whose purpose is to model the movement of a particle under Brownian motion. Let $P$ be a particle located at the origin at $t = 0$. $W_t$ is characterised by: {{item|(2):|$W_{t + u} - W_t$ where $u \ge 0$ is independent of $W_s$ where $s \le t$}} {{item|(3):|$W_{t + u} - W_t \sim \Gaussian 0 u$ where $u \ge 0$ and $\Gaussian 0 u$ denotes the normal distribution}}

title: Definition:Wilbraham-Gibbs Constant
snippet: The Wilbraham-Gibbs constant is the real number defined as: {{eqn | l = G' | r = \int_0^\pi \dfrac {\sin u} u \rd u | c = }}

title: Definition:Wilcoxon Rank Sum Test
snippet: The Wilcoxon rank sum test is a distribution-free test of the hypothesis that two independent samples come from the same population. The alternative hypothesis may specify: a difference in median only one population distribution is stochastically larger than the other. The observations in the combined samples are arranged in ascending order and replaced by their ranks. Then the test statistic is calculated as the sum of the ranks of the observations in one of the samples. Then either $p$-values can be calculated, or critical values for given sample sizes looked up in published tables.

title: Definition:Wilcoxon Rank Sum Test/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Wilcoxon Rank Sum Test == The Wilcoxon rank sum test was devised by in $1945$.

title: Definition:Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test
snippet: The Wilcoxon signed rank test is a distribution-free test for hypotheses about the mean or median of a symmetric distribution. Deviations of sample values from the hypothesized mean or median $M$ are ranked in order of magnitude. Those deviations are replaced by their rankings, together with a sign to indicate whether that deviation is positive or negative. The test statistic is usually taken to be the sum of the positive rankings. Critical values are tabulated for various sample sizes.

title: Definition:Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test/Also known as
snippet: == Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test: Also known as == The Wilcoxon signed rank test is also known as just the signed rank test.

title: Definition:Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test == The Wilcoxon signed rank test was devised by in $1945$.

title: Definition:Wilson Prime
snippet: A Wilson prime is a prime number $p$ such that: $p^2 \divides \paren {p - 1}! + 1$ where: $\divides$ signifies divisibility $!$ is the factorial operator.

title: Definition:Wilson Prime/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Wilson Prime == The third Wilson prime was discovered by in $1953$, as a result of a computer search in which all numbers up to $10 \, 000$ were tested. This was one of the first examples of a problem in number theory being attacked by a computer. Subsequent searches have reached $2 \times 10^{13}$ without finding a $4$th such prime.

title: Definition:Wilson Prime/Sequence
snippet: The sequence of Wilson primes begins: $5, 13, 563$ The next term in the sequence, if there is one, is greater than $2 \times 10^{13}$.

title: Definition:Winding Number
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a closed plane curve. Let $P$ be a point in the same plane as $\CC$. The winding number of $\CC$ $P$ is the number of times $\CC$ goes around $P$ in an anticlockwise direction.

title: Definition:Winsorization
snippet: Winsorization is a method of estimation along the same lines as forming a trimmed mean, except that instead of throwing the trimmed values away, they are replaced by the closest non-trimmed value.

title: Definition:Winsorization/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Winsorization == The term winsorization was proposed by in $1960$ to commemorate who used it suggested it first.

title: Definition:Wire
snippet: A wire is a rigid body modelled by a specific curve whose width is approximated to zero. It may also be the case that the mass of the wire is also approximated to zero.

title: Definition:Wire (Electricity)
snippet: In the context of electricity, a wire is an ideal electrical conductor: whose length and thickness are arbitrary whose resistance is negligible.

title: Definition:Wirth Interval Notation/Historical Note

It can be considered as either an incomplete ellipsis: "$\ldots$" or as a colon "$:$" lying on its side: $.\,.$ In of $1994$ by , and , it is stated that this notation was: suggested by and but little corroboration can be found on the Internet to support this. had in fact adopted the ellipsis notation: $\paren {a \ldots b}$ in a $1972$ article: ...

title: Definition:Witch of Agnesi
snippet: 620px Let $OAM$ be a circle of radius $a$ whose center is at $\tuple {0, a}$. Let $M$ be the point such that $OM$ is a diameter of $OAM$. Let $OA$ be extended to cut the tangent to the circle through $M$ at $N$. Generate $NP$ perpendicular to $MN$ and $AP$ parallel to $MN$. As $A$ moves around the circle $OAM$, the point $P$ traces the curve known as the witch of Agnesi.

title: Definition:Witch of Agnesi/Also known as
snippet: == Witch of Agnesi: Also known as == The witch of Agnesi is also known as the versiera.

title: Definition:Witch of Agnesi/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Witch of Agnesi == The witch of Agnesi was studied in detail by in the $18$th century, but does not actually originate from her. It had previously been written about by others, for example .

title: Definition:Witch of Agnesi/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Witch of Agnesi == The witch of Agnesi was originally named the versorio by , from the Italian vertere (to turn: the term comes from the rope used to turn a sail). confused the word with versiera, from avversiera, which means witch or she-devil (from the same root as the word adversary, an archaic soubriquet for Satan). It has been suggested that the initial misnaming may have been mischievous. When referred to in other languages, the term witch is not seen, and the less colorful term curve of Agnesi is usually used instead.

title: Definition:Witness Property
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a language of predicate logic. Let $\mathscr M$ be a formal semantics for $\LL$. Let $\FF$ be a set of $\LL$-WFFs. Suppose that, for every $\LL$-WFF of $1$ free variable $\map \phi x$, if: $\FF \models_{\mathscr M} \exists x : \map \phi x$ then there exists some term $t$ containing no variables such that: $\FF \models_{\mathscr M} \map \phi {x := t}$ Then, $\FF$ satisfies the witness property.

title: Definition:Wolf Bone
snippet: The (Czechoslovakian) wolf bone is a wolf bone dating from approximately $30 \ 000$ years ago, bearing $57$ marks which appear to have been made deliberately. It was discovered in $1937$ in at in , by a team led by . The markings are believed to be tally marks, and are arranged in $11$ groups of $5$, with $2$ left over. The untestable hypothesis has been made that the number corresponds to a double lunar period.

title: Definition:Wolstenholme Prime
snippet: A Wolstenholme prime is a prime number $p$ such that $p > 7$ which satisfies the congruence: $\dbinom {2 p - 1} {p - 1} \equiv 1 \pmod {p^4}$ where $\dbinom {2 p - 1} {p - 1}$ denotes a binomial coefficient.

title: Definition:Wonderful Demlo Number
snippet: The Wonderful Demlo numbers are the positive integers defined as the coefficients of the powers of $x$ in the expansion of: $\dfrac {1 + 10 x} {\left({1 - x}\right) \left({1 - 10 x}\right) \left({1 - 100 x}\right)}$

title: Definition:Wonderful Demlo Number/Linguistic Note
snippet: If anybody has the slightest clue as to the origin of the term Wonderful Demlo numbers they are encouraged to share it here. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Wonderful Demlo Number/Sequence
snippet: The sequence of Wonderful Demlo numbers begins: $1, 121, 12 \, 321, 1 \, 234 \, 321, 123 \, 454 \, 321, \ldots$

title: Definition:Woodall Number
snippet: A Woodall number is a positive integer of the form: $n \times 2^n - 1$

title: Definition:Woodall Number/Sequence
snippet: == Sequence == The sequence of Woodall numbers begins: $1, 7, 23, 63, 159, 383, 895, 2047, 4607, 10239, 22527, 49151, 106495, 229375, \ldots$ corresponding to $n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$

title: Definition:Woodall Prime
snippet: A Woodall prime is a Woodall number: $n \times 2^n - 1$ which is also prime.

title: Definition:Woodall Prime/Sequence
snippet: == Sequence == The sequence $\sequence n$ for which $n \times 2^n - 1$ is a prime number begins: $2, 3, 6, 30, 75, 81, 115, 123, 249, 362, 384, 462, 512, 751, \ldots$ The first few of these correspond with the sequence $\sequence n$ of the actual Woodall primes themselves, which begins: $7, 23, 383, 32212254719, 2833419889721787128217599, 195845982777569926302400511, \ldots$

title: Definition:Word
snippet: Abstract algebra: Word: the product of a finite number of elements of a given subset of an algebraic structure. Group Theory: Word: the product of a finite number of elements of a subset $S$ of a given group $G$. Set Theory: Associative Word on Set: an alternative name for an ordered tuple on a set Group Word on Set Formal Systems: Word (Formal Systems): a juxtaposition of symbols from a given alphabet. Natural Language: Word: a collation of letters

title: Definition:Word (Abstract Algebra)
snippet: Let $\struct {M, \circ}$ be a magma. Let $S \subseteq M$ be a subset. A word in $S$ is the product of a finite number of elements of $S$. The set of words in $S$ is denoted $\map W S$: $\map W S := \set {s_1 \circ s_2 \circ \cdots \circ s_n: n \in \N_{>0}: s_i \in S, 1 \le i \le n}$ Note that there is nothing in this definition preventing any of the elements of $S$ being repeated, neither is anything said about the order of these elements.

title: Definition:Word (Abstract Algebra)/Also denoted as
snippet: == Word (Abstract Algebra): Also denoted as == Some sources use $\operatorname {gp} S$ for $\map W S$.

title: Definition:Word (Abstract Algebra)/Context
snippet: == Context of Word == It is usual for the algebraic structure of the concept of a word to be a group, a monoid or a semigroup. However, if the operation $\circ$ is not associative then this definition still holds. Category:Definitions/Words (Abstract Algebra)

title: Definition:Word (Abstract Algebra)/Monoid
snippet: Let $\struct {M, \circ}$ be a monoid whose identity element is $e$. Let $S \subseteq M$ be a subset of $M$. The set of words in $S$ is denoted and defined: $\map W S := \set {\ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^r n_i \cdot s_i : r \in \N, n_i \in \N, s_i \in S}$ where: $n_i \cdot s_i$ denotes the power of $s_i$: $n \cdot a = \begin {cases} e & : n = 0 \\ \paren {\paren {n - 1} \cdot a} \circ a & : n > 0 \end {cases}$ $\ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^r n_i \cdot s_i := \paren {n_1 \cdot s_1} \circ \paren {n_2 \cdot s_2} \circ \cdots \circ \paren {n_r \cdot s_r}$

title: Definition:Word (Formal Systems)
snippet: Let $\AA$ be an alphabet. A word in $\AA$ is a juxtaposition of finitely many (primitive) symbols of $\AA$. Words are the most ubiquitous of collations used for formal languages.

title: Definition:Word (Formal Systems)/Also known as
snippet: == Word in context of Formal Systems: Also known as == Different treatments of formal languages use different terms for word. Examples include formula, sentence and string. However, these alternatives conflict with the concepts logical formula, sentence and string, respectively, in the scope of this site; therefore, their use is discouraged. It is useful to note that in this context word is a synonym for finite string.

title: Definition:Word (Natural Language)
snippet: A word in natural language is intuitively understood as a sequence of sounds which expresses a concept. When written down, it appears as a sequence of letters, each one of which either is, or contributes to, a [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoneme phoneme].

title: Definition:Word Metric
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group. Let $S$ be a generating set for $G$ which is closed under inverses (that is, $x^{-1} \in S \iff x \in S$). The word metric on $G$ with respect to $S$ is the metric $d_S$ defined as follows: For any $g, h \in G$, let $\map {d_S} {g, h}$ be the minimum length among the finite sequences $\tuple {x_1, \dots, x_n}$ with each $x_i \in S$ such that $g \circ x_1 \circ \cdots \circ x_n = h$. Informally, $\map {d_S} {g, h}$ is the smallest number of elements from $S$ that one needs to multiply by to get from $g$ to $h$.

title: Definition:Work
snippet: Let $P$ be a particle whose position vector at time $t$ is $\mathbf r$. Let a force applied to $P$ be represented by the vector $\mathbf F$. Suppose that, during the time interval $\delta t$, $P$ moves from $\mathbf r$ to $\mathbf r + \delta \mathbf r$. The work done by $\mathbf F$ during $\delta t$ is defined to be: $\delta W = \mathbf F \cdot \delta \mathbf r$ where $\cdot$ denotes the dot product. Work is a scalar quantity.

title: Definition:Work/Symbol
snippet: == Work: Symbol == The usual symbols used to denote work are $w$ or $W$.

title: Definition:Work/Unit
snippet: The SI unit of measurement of work is the joule.

title: Definition:Wrapped Cauchy Distribution
snippet: The wrapped Cauchy distribution is a probability distribution used to model directional data which may be clustered in an incomplete arc on the circle.

title: Definition:Wrench
snippet: A wrench is a force combined with a couple whose plane is perpendicular to the line of action of the force.

title: Definition:Wrench/Axis
snippet: In a wrench, the line of action of the force is called the axis of the wrench.

title: Definition:Wronskian
snippet: Let $\map f x$ and $\map g x$ be real functions defined on a closed interval $\closedint a b$. Let $f$ and $g$ be differentiable on $\closedint a b$. The Wronskian of $f$ and $g$ is defined as: $\map W {f, g} = \begin {vmatrix} \map f x & \map g x \\ \map {f'} x & \map {g'} x \\ \end {vmatrix} = \map f x \, \map {g'} x - \map g x \, \map {f'} x$

title: Definition:Wronskian/Also known as
snippet: == Wronskian: Also known as == Some sources preserve the diacritic on the n, that is: Wrońskian, but many consider such refinements to be visual clutter and prefer to discard them. Category:Definitions/Wronskians

Let $f_1, f_2, \ldots, f_n$ be $n - 1$ times differentiable on $\closedint a b$. title: Definition:Wythoff's Game
snippet: Wythoff's game is a two-person game whose rules are as follows: $(1): \quad$ The game starts with two piles of counters. $(2): \quad$ Each player takes it in turns to remove either: A number of counters from one pile A number of counters from both pile such that the number of counters removed from each pile must be equal. $(3): \quad$ The person who removes the last counter (or counters) is the winner.

title: Definition:Wythoff Pair
snippet: A Wythoff pair is an ordered pair of integers of the form: $\tuple {\floor {k \phi}, \floor {k \phi^2} }$ where: $\phi$ denotes the golden section: $\phi = 1 \cdotp 618 \ldots$ $\floor x$ denotes the floor of $x$ $k$ signifies a positive integer: $k \in \Z_{\ge 0}$. Thus the coordinates of a Wythoff pair are corresponding terms of the lower and upper Wythoff sequences.

title: Definition:Wythoff Sequence/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Wythoff Sequence == The upper Wythoff sequence and lower Wythoff sequence were introduced in $1926$ by in a much-cited puzzle page: . Their names originate from the fact that, in the form of Wythoff pairs, they form the winning combinations of Wythoff's game.

title: Definition:X-Axis/Also denoted as
snippet: == $x$-Axis: Also denoted as == Some sources use an abbreviated form to denote the $x$-axis, for example: $\textsf O x$, or $X'OX$.

snippet: $x$-$y$ plane, $y$-$z$ plane and $x$-$z$ plane in Cartesian $3$-space ]] The $x$-$y$ plane is the Cartesian plane embedded in Cartesian $3$-space which contains the $x$-axis and the $y$-axis. It consists of all the points in $S$ such that $z = 0$.

title: Definition:X-Z Plane

snippet: == $y$-Axis: Also denoted as == Some sources use an abbreviated form to denote the $y$-axis, for example: $\textsf O y$, or $Y'OY$.

title: Definition:Y-Z Plane
snippet: $x$-$y$ plane, $y$-$z$ plane and $x$-$z$ plane in Cartesian $3$-space ]] The $y$-$z$ plane is the Cartesian plane embedded in Cartesian $3$-space which contains the $y$-axis and the $z$-axis. It consists of all the points in $S$ such that $x = 0$.

title: Definition:Y Coordinate/Also known as
snippet: == $y$ Coordinate: Also known as == An archaic term for the $y$ coordinate which is sometimes seen is ordinate. Some sources hyphenate: $y$-coordinate.

title: Definition:Yang-Mills Theory
snippet: Yang-Mills theory is a gauge theory based on a special unitary group $\map {SU} N$, or more generally any compact, reductive Lie algebra. Yang–Mills theory seeks to describe the behavior of elementary particles using these non-abelian Lie groups, and is at the core of the unification of the electromagnetic force and weak forces, that is $\map U 1 \times \map {SU} 2$, as well as quantum chromodynamics, the theory of the strong force (based on $\map {SU} 3$). Thus it forms the basis of our understanding of the Standard Model of particle physics. Category:Definitions/Physics

title: Definition:Yard/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Yard == The yard was originally defined in terms of a bronze standard. It was redefined in $1963$ in the UK Weights and Measures Act as exactly $0 \cdotp 9144$ metres.

title: Definition:Yates's Correction
snippet: Let $C$ be a contingency table with $2$ rows and $2$ columns. Let a $\chi$-squared test for lack of association be applied to $C$. Yates's correction is the operation of subtracting $0 \cdotp 5$ from the absolute value of each difference $\size {O_i - E_i}$ before squaring. Hence this $\chi$-squared test is an approximation to Fisher's exact test.

title: Definition:Yates's Correction/Also known as
snippet: == Yates's Correction: Also known as == Yates's correction can also be rendered as Yates' correction.

title: Definition:Yates's Correction/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Yates's Correction == Yates's correction was introduced by in $1934$.

title: Definition:Yaw
snippet: Let $B$ be a body in motion through a fluid while subject to a gravitational field. In practice, this will be an aircraft, spacecraft or projectile, or a ship on the sea, for example. The yaw of the motion of $B$ is the angular motion of $B$ about its vertical axis.

title: Definition:Year/Calendar
snippet: A calendar year is the number of days between dates with the same designation in adjacent years. As a year is not an integral number of days, it is necessarily an approximation to the actual year. {{eqn | r = 365 \text{ or } 366 | c = days, usually, but it depends on the calendar used }}

title: Definition:Year/Mistake

title: Definition:Year/Symbol
snippet: The symbol for the year is $\mathrm {yr}$ or $\mathrm y$. In some scientific contexts $\mathrm a$ (for annus, Latin for year) is used. Category:Definitions/Year

title: Definition:Yield
snippet: Yield is the interest paid on an investment.

title: Definition:Yield Stress
snippet: Let a body $\BB$ be deformed under stress. The yield stress of $\BB$ is the stress above which $\BB$ is no longer elastic, and does not return to the same shape when the stress is removed. If $\BB$ is brittle, it may tend to fracture before reaching the point of deformation.

title: Definition:Yoneda Functor
snippet: Let $C$ be a locally small category. Let $C^{\operatorname{op}}$ be its opposite category. Let $\mathbf{Set}$ be the category of sets. Let $\sqbrk {C^{\operatorname{op} }, \mathbf {Set} }$ be the functor category between them.

title: Definition:Yoneda Functor/Contravariant
snippet: Let $C$ be a locally small category. Let $\mathbf{Set}$ be the category of sets. Let $\sqbrk {C, \mathbf {Set} }$ be the functor category between them. The contravariant Yoneda functor of $C$ is the contravariant functor $h^- : C \to \sqbrk {C, \mathbf {Set} }$ which sends: {{DefineFunctor |ob = an object $X \in C$ to the covariant hom-functor $h^X = \map {\operatorname {Hom} } {X, -}$ |mor = a morphism $f : X \to Y$ to the precomposition natural transformation $h^f : \map {\operatorname {Hom} } {Y, -} \to \map {\operatorname {Hom} } {X, -} : g \mapsto g \circ f$ }}

title: Definition:Youden Square
snippet: A Youden square is an experimental design of the form of an incomplete Latin square. The rows can be viewed as randomized blocks, and the columns can be viewed as balanced incomplete blocks. Hence the Youden square has the feature that unwanted variability is eliminated in more than one direction without being restricted to having both the number of rows and the number of columns equal to the number of treatments.

title: Definition:Youden Square/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Youden Square == The Youden square was originated by in $1936$. picked up on this technique, and discussed it in his of $1938$, co-authored with . himself wrote a paper on the technique in $1937$, and went on to introduce further designs in a paper of $1940$.

title: Definition:Young's Modulus
snippet: Young's modulus is a modulus of elasticity used when an elastic body $B$ is under tension or compression. It is defined as the ratio of applied pressure to the resulting increase or decrease in length per unit length of $B$. That is, it is the ratio of tensile or compressive stress to the associated strain.

title: Definition:Young's Modulus/Symbol
snippet: == Young's Modulus: Symbol == The usual symbol used to denote the Young's modulus of a body is $E$.

title: Definition:Z-Graded Ring
snippet: Let $\Z$ be the set of integers. A $\Z$-graded ring is a graded ring of type the additive group of integers. That is, it is a pair $\struct {R, f}$ where: $R$ is a ring $f$ is a family $\family {R_n}_{n \mathop \in \Z}$ of subgroups of the additive group of $R$, of which it is the internal direct sum, and such that: $\forall x \in R_n, y \in R_m: x y \in R_{m + n}$

title: Definition:Z-Module Associated with Abelian Group
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be an abelian group with identity $e$. Let $\struct {\Z, +, \times}$ be the ring of integers.

title: Definition:Z-Module Associated with Abelian Group/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be an abelian group with identity $e$. Let $\struct {\Z, +, \times}$ be the ring of integers. The $\Z$-module associated with $G$ is the $\Z$-module $\struct {G, \circ, \ast}$ with ring action: $\ast: \Z \times G \to G$: $\tuple {n, x} \mapsto \circ^n x$ where $\circ^n x$ is the $n$th power of $x$.

title: Definition:Z-Module Associated with Abelian Group/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be an abelian group with identity $e$. Let $\struct {\Z, +, \times}$ be the ring of integers. The $\Z$-module associated with $G$ is the $\Z$-module on $G$ with ring representation $\Z \to \map {\operatorname {End} } G$ equal to the initial homomorphism. {{explain|$\map {\operatorname {End} } G$}}

title: Definition:Z-Score/Also defined as
snippet: == $Z$-Score: Also known as == A $Z$-score is also defined as a value of a random variable which has been standardized using: $Z = \dfrac {X - \overline x} s$ where: $\overline x$ denotes the sample mean of $X$ $s$ denotes the sample standard deviation of $X$.

title: Definition:Z^Z Space
snippet: Let $Z = \struct {\Z_{\ge 0}, \tau_d}$ denote the positive integers with the discrete topology. Let $X = \ds \struct {\prod_{i \mathop \in \Z_{\ge 0} } Z, \tau}$ be the space formed on the countable Cartesian product of instances of $Z$ such that $\tau$ is the Tychonoff product topology. Then $X$ is known as the $Z^Z$ (topological) space. Thus $\tau$ can be referred to as the $Z^Z$ topology.

title: Definition:Z Coordinate/Also known as
snippet: == $z$ Coordinate: Also known as== Some sources hyphenate: $z$-coordinate.

title: Definition:Zariski Topology/Affine Space
snippet: Let $k$ be a field. Let $\map {\mathbb A^n} k = k^n$ denote the standard affine space of dimension $n$ over $k$. The Zariski topology on $\map {\mathbb A^n} k$ is the topology on the direct product $k^n$ whose closed sets are the affine algebraic sets in $\map {\mathbb A^n} k$.

title: Definition:Zariski Topology/Prime Spectrum of Ring
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $\Spec A$ be the prime spectrum of $A$. The Zariski topology on $\Spec A$ is the topology with closed sets the vanishing sets $\map V S$ for $S \subseteq A$.

title: Definition:Zariski Topology on Maximal Spectrum of Ring
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $\map {\operatorname {MaxSpec} } A$ be its maximal spectrum.

title: Definition:Zariski Topology on Maximal Spectrum of Ring/Definition 1
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $\map {\operatorname {MaxSpec} } A$ be its maximal spectrum. The Zariski topology on $\map {\operatorname {MaxSpec} } A$ is the topology with as closed sets the maximal zero loci.

title: Definition:Zariski Topology on Maximal Spectrum of Ring/Definition 2
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $\map {\operatorname {MaxSpec} } A$ be its maximal spectrum. The Zariski topology on $\map {\operatorname{MaxSpec} } A$ is the subspace topology induced by the Zariski topology on the prime spectrum $\Spec A$.

title: Definition:Zeckendorf Representation
snippet: Zeckendorf representation is a system for representing a positive integer $n$ by a sequence of digits which are the indices of a sequence of $r$ Fibonacci numbers.

title: Definition:Zeckendorf Representation/Also known as
snippet: == Zeckendorf Representation: Also known as == Some sources refer to Zeckendorf representation as the Fibonacci number system.

title: Definition:Zeckendorf Representation/Definition 1
snippet: Zeckendorf representation is a system for representing a positive integer $n$ by a sequence of digits which are the indices of a sequence of $r$ Fibonacci numbers: $n := \sqbrk {k_1 k_2 k_3 \ldots k_r}_F$ where: $n = F_{k_1} + F_{k_2} + F_{k_3} + \cdots + F_{k_r}$ $k_1 \gg k_2 \gg k_3 \gg \cdots \gg k_r \gg 0$ where $n \gg k$ denotes that $n \ge k + 2$.

title: Definition:Zeckendorf Representation/Definition 2
snippet: Zeckendorf representation is a system for representing a positive integer $n$ by a sequence of digits which are the indices of a sequence of $r$ Fibonacci numbers: $n := \sqbrk {k_1 k_2 k_3 \ldots k_r}_F = \ds \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^r k_i F_i$ where: each $k_i$ equals $0$ or $1$ each pair of adjacent $\tuple {k_i, k_{i + 1} }$ satisfies $k_i k_{i + 1} = 0$ $k_1 = k+0 = 0$

title: Definition:Zenith
snippet: Let an observer $O$ on the surface of Earth be assumed to be the center of the celestial sphere $C$. The zenith $Z$ is the point on $C$ which is vertically overhead. This can be determined by use of a plumb line. 480px In the above diagram, the zenith is indicated by $Z$.

title: Definition:Zenith/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Zenith == The word zenith derives from Medieval Latin cenit, a transliteration of the Arabic سَمْت‎ (samt), meaning direction or path) which is itself anabbreviation of سَمْت اَلرَّأْس‎ (samt ar-raʾs), meaning direction of the head). The US English pronunciation of zenith is zee-nith, while British and other English pronunciation is zen-nith. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Zenith Distance
snippet: Let $X$ be the position of a star (or other celestial body) on the celestial sphere. The zenith distance $\zeta$ of $X$ is defined as the angle subtended by the the arc of the vertical circle through $X$ between $X$ and the zenith.

title: Definition:Zenith Distance/Also known as
snippet: == Zenith Distance: Also known as == The zenith distance is also known as the coaltitude.

title: Definition:Zenzizenzizenzic
snippet: The zenzizenzizenzic of a number is its eighth power.

title: Definition:Zenzizenzizenzic/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Zenzizenzizenzic == The word zenzizenzizenzic derives from square of a squared square; the word zenzic is (or was) German for square. The word is particularly linguistically notable for being the only word in the English language with six Zs in it. Category:Linguistic Notes

title: Definition:Zermelo-Fraenkel-Skolem Set Theory
snippet: Zermelo-Fraenkel-Skolem set theory is a system of axiomatic set theory. It consists of Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory with the inclusion of a system of first order formulas to specify the existence of properties of sets.

snippet: == Historical Note on Zermelo-Fraenkel-Skolem Set Theory == It was who proposed the amendment to Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory to sharpen the specification of the axiom of replacement. He considered it necessary to express the axiom of specification as an infinite number of axioms: one for every first order formula. disagreed forcefully against 's approach, preferring the philosophical position that a property should be allowed to be considered as all possible meaningful conditions, not just propositions in first order logic.

snippet: == Historical Note on Zermelo-Fraenkel Set Theory == first proposed this supposedly rigorous system of axiomatic set theory in $1900$, in order to confront the paradoxes which the axiom of comprehension lead to. It was modified by in $1922$. The system of Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory has formed the basis of most of the formulations of axiomatic set theory which have been created since.

We are far from claiming superiority of ZFC over alternative foundations of mathematics. For whatever reason, it won the competition. It does a decent job; so let us stick to it. It should be pointed out though that, to the best of our knowledge, none of the competitors to ZFC resolves the question of truth or falsity of CH, SH, MA, $\diamondsuit$, or of any other statement whose independence of ZFC has been established by the method of forcing. -- : Introduction

title: Definition:Zero
snippet: Set Theory and Order Theory: The zero ordinal. The zero cardinal. Algebra: The zero of the numbers: The zero of the natural numbers, a concept which follows from, and can be defined from, the definition of the natural numbers as the isomorphism class of a naturally ordered semigroup. From this definition follow: The zero of the integers. The zero of the rational numbers. The zero of the real numbers. The zero of the complex numbers. The zero digit of the number base representation. Abstract Algebra: The zero of the naturally ordered semigroup.

title: Definition:Zero-Limit Sequence in Schwartz Space
snippet: Let $\map \SS \R$ be the Schwartz space. Let $\sequence {\phi_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $\map \SS \R$. Let $\phi \in \map \SS \R$ be a Schwartz test function. Suppose: $\ds \forall l, m \in \N : \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \sup_{x \mathop \in \R} \size {x^l \map {\phi_n^{\paren m} } x} = 0$ where: $\phi^{\paren m}$ denotes the $m$th derivative of $\phi$ $\sup$ denotes the supremum. Then the sequence $\sequence {\phi_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ converges to $\mathbf 0$ in $\map \SS \R$. This can be denoted: $\phi_n \stackrel \SS {\longrightarrow} \mathbf 0$

title: Definition:Zero-Sum Game
snippet: A zero-sum game is a game in which the total of the payoffs to all players is zero.

title: Definition:Zero-Sum Game/Also known as
snippet: == Zero-Sum Game: Also known as == A zero-sum game is also known as a constant sum game.

title: Definition:Zero-Sum Game/Non-Zero
snippet: A non-zero-sum game is a game in which the total of the payoffs to all players is dependent upon the moves made to reach those payoffs.

title: Definition:Zero/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Zero == The Babylonians from the $2$nd century BCE used a number base system of arithmetic, with a placeholder to indicate that a particular place within a number was empty, but its use was inconsistent. However, they had no actual recognition of zero as a mathematical concept in its own right. The Ancient Greeks had no conception of zero as a number. The concept of zero was invented by the mathematicians of India. The from the $3$rd century CE contains the first reference to it.

title: Definition:Zero/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Zero == The Sanskrit word used by the early Indian mathematicians for zero was sunya, which means empty, or blank. In Arabic this was translated as sifr. This was translated via the Latin zephirum into various European languages as zero, cifre, cifra, and into English as zero and cipher. Note that the plural of zero is either zeros or zeroes. On , zeroes is preferred. The word zero can also be used as a , meaning to set (a value) to zero in the context of algorithms and computer science The word zeroize can also be seen in this context.

title: Definition:Zero (Cardinal)
snippet: The cardinal associated with the empty set $\O$ is called zero, and is denoted $0$. More informally, this means that zero is defined as being the number of elements in the empty set.

title: Definition:Zero (Category)
snippet: The category $\mathbf 0$, zero, is the empty category: $\qquad$ with: no objects and consequently: no morphisms.

title: Definition:Zero (Number)
snippet: The number zero is defined as being the cardinal of the empty set.

title: Definition:Zero (Number)/Also known as
snippet: The somewhat outdated term cipher or cypher can on occasion be seen for the number zero, especially when used in the context of a zero digit in a basis representation. In particular, the ciphers of a number are those zero digits which are not themselves significant digits, but which are for indicating place value. The words nought, or its somewhat old-fashioned form naught, can also be seen. Younger children often use the word nothing.

title: Definition:Zero (Number)/Complex
snippet: Let $\C$ denote the set of complex numbers. The zero of $\C$ is the complex number: $0 + 0 i$

title: Definition:Zero (Number)/Naturally Ordered Semigroup
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ, \preceq}$ be a naturally ordered semigroup. Then from , $\struct {S, \circ, \preceq}$ has a smallest element. This smallest element of $\struct {S, \circ, \preceq}$ is called zero and has the symbol $0$. That is: $\forall n \in S: 0 \preceq n$

title: Definition:Zero (Ordinal)
snippet: The zero ordinal, denoted $0$, is the empty set $\O$.

title: Definition:Zero Angle
snippet: The zero angle is an angle the measure of which is $0$ regardless of the unit of measurement.

title: Definition:Zero Angle/Also known as
snippet: == Zero Angle: Also known as == The zero angle is also known as the null angle.

title: Definition:Zero Codeword
snippet: A zero codeword is a codeword whose terms are all zero. Category:Definitions/Information Theory

title: Definition:Zero Complement
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ, \preceq}$ be a naturally ordered semigroup. Let $0$ be the zero of $S$. Let $S^* := \relcomp S {\set 0} = S \setminus \set 0$ be the complement of $\set 0$ in $S$. Then $S^*$ is called the zero complement of $S$.

title: Definition:Zero Digit
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a number. Let $b \in \Z$ such that $b > 1$ be a number base in which $x$ is represented. By the Basis Representation Theorem, $x$ can be expressed uniquely in the form: $\ds x = \sum_{j \mathop \in \Z}^m r_j b^j$ Any instance of $r_j$ being equal to $0$ is known as a zero (digit) of $n$.

title: Definition:Zero Digit/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Zero Digit == The earliest use of a special symbol to be used as a placeholder for a missing denomination in a number expressed in a positional number system was in the Babylonian number system, at around . However, the technique was not transmitted to other cultures. The concept was reinvented by the mathematicians of the Hindu culture in the first few centuries CE. The (dated from between and ) uses it, as a heavy dot. It is also used in the of $458$, but not as a symbol as such. used a positional number system around $500$, but it did not have a zero digit.

title: Definition:Zero Dimensional Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is zero dimensional $T$ has a basis whose sets are all both closed and open.

title: Definition:Zero Dimensional Space/Also known as
snippet: == Zero Dimensional Space: Also known as == Some sources hyphenate: zero-dimensional.

title: Definition:Zero Dimensional Space/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Zero Dimensional Space == The thinking behind applying the term zero dimensional to the concept of a zero dimensional space arises from the idea of the small inductive dimension in the context of the topological space. The small inductive dimension of a topological space is defined to be $1$ greater than the small inductive dimension of its boundary. By Set is Clopen iff Boundary is Empty, a topological space with a basis whose sets are all clopen has no boundary. Thus it follows that such a topological space is considered to be zero dimensional.

title: Definition:Zero Divisor/Algebra
snippet: Let $\struct {A_R, \oplus}$ be an algebra over a ring $\struct {R, +, \cdot}$. Let the zero vector of $A_R$ be $\mathbf 0_R$. Let $a, b \in A_R$ such that $b \ne \mathbf 0_R$. Then $a$ is a zero divisor of $A_R$ : $a \oplus b = \mathbf 0_R$

title: Definition:Zero Divisor/Also defined as
Definition:Zero Divisor/Also known as
snippet: == Zero Divisor: Also known as== Some sources hyphenate, as: zero-divisor. Some sources run the words together: zerodivisor. Some use the more explicit and pedantic divisor of zero.

title: Definition:Zero Divisor/Commutative Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a commutative ring. A zero divisor (in $R$) is an element $x \in R$ such that: $\exists y \in R^*: x \circ y = 0_R$ where $R^*$ is defined as $R \setminus \set {0_R}$. The expression: $x$ is a zero divisor can be written: $x \divides 0_R$

title: Definition:Zero Divisor/Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. A zero divisor (in $R$) is an element $x \in R$ such that either: $\exists y \in R^*: x \circ y = 0_R$ or: $\exists y \in R^*: y \circ x = 0_R$ where $R^*$ is defined as $R \setminus \set {0_R}$. That is, such that $x$ is either a left zero divisor or a right zero divisor. The expression: $x$ is a zero divisor can be written: $x \divides 0_R$

title: Definition:Zero Divisor/Warning
snippet: == Zero Divisor: Warning== Beware the terminology divisor of zero. It is easy to confuse this with the fact that, for every element $a$ of a ring $R$, from Ring Product with Zero we have that $a \circ 0_R = 0_R$. Hence one may say that every such element is a divisor of zero. However, the concept of a zero divisor specifically requires that the $b$ in $a \circ b = 0_R$ is not zero. Category:Definitions/Zero Divisors

title: Definition:Zero Element
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure.

title: Definition:Zero Element/Also defined as
snippet: == Zero Element: Also defined as == Beware of the usage of the term zero element to mean the identity element under the operation of addition: $a + 0 = a = 0 + a$ While zero is indeed a zero element under the operation of multiplication: $a \times 0 = 0 = 0 \times a$ it is not, strictly speaking, a zero element of addition.

title: Definition:Zero Element/Also known as
snippet: == Zero Element: Also known as == A zero element is also sometimes called an annihilator, but this term has a more specific definition in the context of linear algebra. Some sources use the term absorbing element. When discussing an algebraic structure $S$ which has a zero element, then this zero is often denoted $z_S$, $n_S$ or $0_S$. If it is clearly understood what structure is being discussed, then $z$, $n$ or $0$ are usually used.

title: Definition:Zero Homomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {R_1, +_1, \circ_1}$ and $\struct {R_2, +_2, \circ_2}$ be rings with zeroes $0_1$ and $0_2$ respectively. Consider the mapping $\zeta: R_1 \to R_2$ defined as: $\forall r \in R_1: \map \zeta r = 0_2$ Then $\zeta$ is the zero homomorphism from $R_1$ to $R_2$.

title: Definition:Zero Locus

title: Definition:Zero Locus of Set of Polynomials
snippet: Let $k$ be a field. Let $n \ge 1$ be a natural number. Let $A = k \sqbrk {X_1, \ldots, X_n}$ be the polynomial ring in $n$ variables over $k$. Let $I \subseteq A$ be a set. Then the zero locus of $I$ is the set: $\map V I = \set {x \in k^n : \forall f \in I: \map f x = 0}$

title: Definition:Zero Mapping
snippet: Let $\mathbb A$ be one of the standard number systems $\N,\Z,\Q,\R,\C$. Let $S$ be a set. Let $f_0: S \to \mathbb A$ denote the constant mapping: $\forall x \in S: \map {f_0} x = 0$ Then $f_0$ is referred to as the zero mapping.

title: Definition:Zero Mapping/Schwartz Distribution
snippet: Let $\map \DD \R$ be the test function space. Let $\mathbf 0 \in \map {\DD'} \R$ be a Schwartz distribution. Suppose: $\forall \phi \in \map \DD \R : \map {\mathbf 0} \phi = 0$ Then $\mathbf 0$ is referred to as the zero distribution. Category:Definitions/Examples of Schwartz Distributions

title: Definition:Zero Mapping/Vector Space
snippet: Let $Y$ be a vector space. Let $S$ be a set. Let $\mathbf 0_Y$ be the identity element of $Y$. Suppose $\mathbf 0 : S \to Y$ is a mapping such that: $\forall x \in S: \map {\mathbf 0} x = \mathbf 0_Y$ Then $\mathbf 0$ is referred to as the zero mapping.

title: Definition:Zero Matrix
snippet: Let $\Bbb F$ be one of the standard number system $\N$, $\Z$, $\Q$, $\R$ and $\C$. Let $\map \MM {m, n}$ be an $m \times n$ matrix space over $\Bbb F$. The zero matrix of $\map \MM {m, n}$, denoted $\mathbf 0$, is the $m \times n$ matrix whose elements are all zero, and can be written $\sqbrk 0_{m n}$.

title: Definition:Zero Matrix/Also denoted as
snippet: == Zero Matrix: Also known as == Some sources present the zero matrix as $\mathbf O$, that is, using the letter $\text O$, rather than the number $\mathbf 0$, that is, the zero digit.

title: Definition:Zero Matrix/Also known as
snippet: == Zero Matrix: Also known as == Some sources refer to the zero matrix as the null matrix.

title: Definition:Zero Matrix/General Monoid
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a monoid whose identity is $e$. Let $\map {\MM_S} {m, n}$ be an $m \times n$ matrix space over $S$. The zero matrix of $\map {\MM_S} {m, n}$, denoted $\mathbf e$, is the $m \times n$ matrix whose elements are all $e$, and can be written $\sqbrk e_{m n}$.

title: Definition:Zero Matrix/Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring whose zero is $0_R$. Let $\map {\MM_R} {m, n}$ be an $m \times n$ matrix space over $R$. The zero matrix of $\map {\MM_R} {m, n}$, denoted $\mathbf 0_R$, is the $m \times n$ matrix whose elements are all $0_R$, and can be written $\sqbrk {0_R}_{m n}$.

title: Definition:Zero Morphism in Preadditive Category
snippet: Let $A$ be a preadditive category. Let $a, b$ be objects of $A$. The zero morphism $0 : a \to b$ is the identity element of their hom set $\map {\operatorname {Hom} } {a, b}$.

title: Definition:Zero Morphism via Zero Object
snippet: Let $C$ be a category which has a zero object $0$. Let $a, b \in C$ be objects. The zero morphism $0$ from $a$ to $b$ is the composition of the unique morphism $a \to 0$ and the unique morphism $0 \to b$: $0: a \to 0 \to b$

title: Definition:Zero Object
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a category. A zero object of $\mathbf C$ is an object which is initial and terminal.

title: Definition:Zero Operator
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space. Let $A : V \to V$ be a linear operator such that: $\forall v \in H: A v = 0_V$ where $0_V$ is the zero vector of $V$. Then $A$ is called the zero operator, and is denoted as $\mathbf 0$. Category:Definitions/Vector Spaces

title: Definition:Zero Residue Class
snippet: Let $m \in \Z$. Let $\RR_m$ be the congruence relation modulo $m$ on the set of all $a, b \in \Z$: $\RR_m = \set {\tuple {a, b} \in \Z \times \Z: \exists k \in \Z: a = b + k m}$ Let $\eqclass 0 m$ be the residue class of $0$ (modulo $m$): $\eqclass 0 m = \set {x \in \Z: \exists k \in \Z: x = k m}$ Then $\eqclass 0 m$ is known as the zero residue class (modulo $m$).

title: Definition:Zero Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. We say that $H$ is a zero set if there exists a continuous mapping $f: S \to \closedint 0 1$ such that: $H = f^{-1} \sqbrk {\set 0}$

title: Definition:Zero Set/Also defined as
snippet: == Zero Set: Also defined as == In their definition of zero set, some sources suggest that the codomain of the continuous mapping $f$ can be $\R$, and not necessarily be restricted to $\closedint 0 1$.

title: Definition:Zero Set/Also known as
snippet: == Zero Set: Also known as == The term zero set can also be found hyphenated: zero-set.

title: Definition:Zero Subspace
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space with zero vector $\mathbf 0$. Then the set $\paren {\mathbf 0} := \set {\mathbf 0}$ is called the zero subspace of $V$. This name is appropriate as $\paren {\mathbf 0}$ is in fact a subspace of $V$, as proved in Zero Subspace is Subspace.

title: Definition:Zero Vector
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ be a ring. Let $\struct {G, +_G}$ be an abelian group. Let $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_R$ be an $R$-module. The identity of $\struct {G, +_G}$ is usually denoted $\bszero$, or some variant of this, and called the zero vector: $\forall \mathbf a \in \struct {G, +_G, \ast}_R: \bszero +_G \mathbf a = \mathbf a = \mathbf a +_G \bszero$ Note that on occasion it is advantageous to denote the zero vector differently, for example by $e$, or $\bszero_V$ or $\bszero_G$, in order to highlight the fact that the zero vector is not the same object as the zero scalar.

title: Definition:Zero Vector/Also known as
snippet: == Zero Vector: Also known as == A zero vector is also seen referred to as: the null vector, although that term has a more specialised meaning in Riemannian geometry the trivial vector the neutral element, but that term is also used for the more general concept of an identity element. The term origin is sometimes seen, but this has a more precise definition in the context of analytic geometry. Care may therefore need to be taken not to confuse these concepts.

title: Definition:Zero Vector/Euclidean Space
snippet: Let $\struct {\R^n, +, \times}_\R$ be a real vector space. The zero vector in $\struct {\R^n, +, \times}_\R$ is: $\mathbf 0_{n \times 1} := \begin {bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ \vdots \\ 0 \end {bmatrix}$ where $0 \in \R$.

title: Definition:Zero Vector/Vector Quantity
snippet: A vector quantity whose magnitude is zero is referred to as a zero vector.

title: Definition:Zeroth
snippet: Zeroth is the adjectival form of the ordinal number zero.

title: Definition:Zillion
snippet: Zillion is a rhetorical flourish to mean a very large number, generally understood to be of the order of an unspecified power of $10$.

title: Definition:Zonal Harmonic
snippet: Let $H$ be a spherical harmonic in the form: $r^n \paren {a_n \map {P_n} {\cos \theta} + \ds \sum_{m \mathop = 1}^n \paren { {a_n}^m \cos m \phi + {b_n}^m \sin m \phi} \map { {P_n}^m} {\cos \theta} }$ The function $\map {P_n} {\cos \theta}$ is known as a zonal harmonic.

title: Definition:Zone of One Base/Also known as
snippet: == Zone of One Base: Also known as == A zone of one base is also known as a spherical cap.

title: Definition:Zone of Sphere
snippet: A zone of a sphere $\SS$ is a surface formed from the part of the surface of $\SS$ by two parallel planes intersecting $\SS$.

title: Definition:Zone of Sphere/Base
snippet: Each of the two parallel planes defining a zone of a sphere $\SS$ is called a base of the zone.

title: Definition:Zone of Sphere/Height
snippet: The height of a zone of a sphere $\SS$ is defined as the distance between the bases of the zone.

title: Definition:Zone of Sphere/One Base
snippet: A zone of one base is a zone of a sphere $\SS$ in which exactly one of the bases is tangent to $\SS$.

title: Definition:Zone of Sphere/Two Bases
snippet: A zone of two bases is a zone of a sphere $\SS$ in which neither of the bases are tangent to $\SS$.

title: Definition:Zu Chongzhi Fraction
snippet: The Zu Chongzhi fraction is an exceptionally accurate approximation to $\pi$ (pi): $\pi \approx \dfrac {355} {113}$ whose decimal expansion is: $\pi \approx 3 \cdotp 14159 \, 292$

title: Definition:Zu Chongzhi Fraction/Also known as
snippet: == Zu Chongzhi Fraction: Also known as == The Zu Chongzhi fraction is rendered variously according to the transliteration of his name into Latin characters: Tsu Ch'ung-Chi's fraction is an example. The fraction $\dfrac {355} {113}$ is also called Metius' number, for , who discovered it independently in around the $16$th century.

title: Definition:Zu Chongzhi Fraction/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Zu Chongzhi Fraction == The Zu Chongzhi fraction $\dfrac {355} {113}$ as an approximation for $\pi$ (pi) was derived by and his son . fortuitously rediscovered it independently around the $16$th century. He did this by taking the mediant of two limits $\dfrac {377} {120}$ and $\dfrac {333} {106}$ calculated by his father. This is guaranteed to generate a number between those limits, but the usefulness of the approximation was lucky.

title: Definition:Zuckerman Number
snippet: A Zuckerman number is a positive integer which is divisible by the product of its digits.

title: Definition:Étalé Space of Presheaf
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space. Let $\mathbf C$ be a category. Let $\FF$ be a $\mathbf C$-valued presheaf on $X$. The étalé space of $\FF$ is the pair $\struct {\map {\operatorname {\acute Et} } \FF, \pi}$ where: $\map {\operatorname {\acute Et} } \FF$ is the disjoint union $\ds \bigsqcup_{x \mathop \in X} \FF_x$ of stalks of $\FF$ $\pi: \map {\operatorname {\acute Et} } \FF \to X$ is the canonical projection.
